file: $550 MILLION CHINA LOAN IS APPROVED BY I.M.F.txt
text:
ï»¿
The International Monetary Fund today approved a $550 million loan to China, marking that country's largest borrowing from any financial institution.
The Washington-based I.M.F., which makes funds available to countries in balance-of-payments difficulties, said it had approved a so-called standby borrowing arrangement under which China would draw down 450 million special drawing rights (an internationally created reserve asset), equal to $550 million, over the next 12 months.
The fund said that China would also borrow an undisclosed amount from the institution's trust fund, a pool of money raised from the sale of gold. 
It is used to help countries particularly strapped financially. 
The advent of China as a significant borrower at a time when other poor countries are having increasing economic trouble because of higher oil prices could have major financial implications.
China gets $550 million loan approval from International Monetary Fund
Analysts noted that China's demands could reduce funds available for other prospective borrowers. 
China joined the monetary fund and World Bank last year as part of its efforts to draw closer into the world financial and trading network.
The World Bank, the official name of which is the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, chiefly makes development loans to build up the economies of poorer countries. 
It has not announced any loans to China, but a mission from the bank recently returned from a project study, and a lending program could be announced later this year.
In approving China's request for the $550 million, the monetary fund noted that China had started a necessary stabilization program to reduce inflationary pressures and whittle down a deficit in trade and services.
The fund makes loans conditioned upon a country's adoption of economic measures to strengthen its international accounts. 
An analysis by the fund of China's latest measures concluded that the Chinese authorities had embarked on the proper course.
Â 
Reluctant to Borrow Heavily
Although China's foreign exchange position is believed to be relatively healthy, the Chinese have so far been reluctant to borrow heavily in Western capital markets, especially while interest rates remain high.
Analysts noted, however, that China had already been borrowing more heavily in short-term financial markets, especially in Europe and Japan. 
Proceeds have been used mainly to finance energy developments.
The Chinese authorities began a program of rapid economic expansion four years ago. 
But when the steel mills and other heavy manufacturing operations began costing more than the planners contemplated, the program was sharply scaled back.
Â 
Main Objectives Listed
''The main objectives of the Government's economic program for this year,'' the fund said, ''are the elimination of inflationary pressures, the readjustment of the investment pattern to foster resumption of rapid economic growth and to maintain the current account (trade and services) deficit at a sustainable level.''
The fund noted that priority was now being given to investment in light industry, agriculture and energy. 
Last Saturday China's chief economic planner, Deputy Prime Minister Yao Yilin, announced a program of sharp spending cuts and said the Government intended to monitor supply more closely to improve the economic performance.

Amid reports of the worst unrest in Tibet in three decades, officials from the region and its capital city have been on a two- week tour of the United States.
The 13-member delegation arrived in the United States on Oct. 
7.
The delegation, which includes Luo Gar, the Mayor of Lhasa, and Thang Zhengqi, deputy secretary of the Tibetan Autonomous Region, left Boulder today for San Francisco, their final stop.
Boulder was on the group's itinerary because it established a Sister City program with Lhasa two years ago at the behest of local Buddhists. 
But some Buddhists here have denounced the visitors because they are officials of China, which annexed Tibet in 1950.
On Oct. 
1, when 14 people were reported killed in the worst clashes, the Mayor and other members of the delegation were in Chengdu, 750 miles from Lhasa, en route to the United States.
The Mayor played down the anti-Chinese unrest. 
''If it had been really violent,'' he said through an interpreter here, ''we would never have been able to leave the country.''
He said his group had not been in direct contact with colleagues in Lhasa since leaving Shanghai on Oct. 
3.

file: 160 U.S. SCHOLARS IN APPEAL TO CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
In an unusual move, a group of 160 senior American scholars have appealed to the Chinese Government to stop its crackdown on liberal intellectuals.
The scholars, in a letter sent today to the Chinese Ambassador in Washington, Han Xu, said they were ''deeply concerned by the punitive measures adopted against some of China's leading intellectuals in the sciences, social sciences and humanities.''
The authors of the letter, experts on China from 40 American colleges and universities, said they feared the campaign ''will adversely effect China's intellectual vitality'' and might ultimately ''undermine China's effort toward modernization.''
The letter marks the first time American scholars have spoken out as a group about domestic politics in China. 
By contrast with American experts on the Soviet Union, who have often been critical of Moscow for human-rights abuses, China specialists have remained silent and sought to maintain good relations with Beijing.
'We Tried to Be Neutral'
''In the past we tried to be neutral, objective scholars not passing judgment, even during the Cultural Revolution,'' said Merle Goldman, a professor of Chinese history at Boston University who was one of the two organizers of the petition.
''But that was like the Holocaust,'' she said. 
''We can't remain silent again.''
In the Cultural Revolution, from 1966 to roughly 1976, millions of Chinese, especially writers, artists and scholars, were attacked, beaten, shipped off to exile in the countryside or killed.
Mrs. Goldman said the signers of the letter might risk angering the Chinese Government and lose their chance to do research in China, a highly coveted privilege after years in which China was closed to the outside world.
Among the prominent American scholars signing the letter was John K. Fairbank, professor emeritus of history at Harvard University, who is widely regarded as the father of modern Chinese studies in the United States. 
Others included Frederic Wakeman, professor of history at the University of California at Berkeley; Lucian Pye, professor of political science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and Wm. 
Theodore DeBary, professor of East Asian civilization at Columbia University.
The letter was also signed by Chinese-American scholars, including Tu Wei-ming, a professor of history at Harvard; Victor Nee, a sociologist at Cornell University, and Leo Lee, a professor of Chinese language and East Asian civilization at the University of Chicago. 
Professor Lee was the other organizer of the petition.
Â 
University of Michigan Statement
In a separate effort, 21 China specialists at the University of Michigan, which has one of the largest China studies centers in the country, signed a statement that was read in Congressional testimony earlier this month expressing ''concern'' about the campaign in China.
Another open letter to Mr. Deng, expressing shock at ''the severe criticism and punishment'' of intellectuals, has been signed by mostly ethnic Chinese authors and scholars in the United States and Hong Kong, including Chen Ruoxi, who is perhaps the most important Chinese writer outside China.
The statement from Michigan, read by Kenneth Lieberthal, a professor of political science, said events since the ouster in January of Hu Yaobang, the General Secretary of the Communist Party, were ''sadly reminiscent'' of the beginning of the anti-rightist campaign of 1957 and the Cultural Revolution in 1966.
Mr. Lieberthal testified before the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on Asian and Pacific Affairs.
In a telephone interview, Mr. Lieberthal said, ''People here felt it was not productive for American scholars to write directly to China telling them what policies to have.''
But at the same time, he said, the scholars at Michigan, who have been heavily involved in intellectual exchanges with China, felt ''it was not too early to voice our anxieties.''
Â 
Opinions Vary on Crackdown
Among those who signed the Michigan statement was Michel Oksenberg, a professor of political science who was the China specialist on the National Security Council under President Carter and helped work out the normalization of relations between Washington and Beijing in 1978.
Mr. Lieberthal and Mrs. Goldman differed in their interpretation of how serious the current crackdown is. 
The campaign, which began after a series of student demonstrations calling for greater democracy, has led to the ouster from the party of several promiment writers and scientists and widespread attacks in the Chinese press on ''bourgeois liberalism.''
Mr. Lieberthal acknowledged that ''serious damage'' had been done to the efforts by Deng Xiaoping, China's paramount leader, to arrange an orderly succession and build confidence among the country's intellectuals who are needed for its modernization drive. 
But he added, ''the events have not been as negative as one could have feared'' and fewer people have been purged than some experts expected.
On the other hand, Mrs. Goldman said she believed that ''the campaign seems to be intensifying, with the conservatives having the edge.''
Visiting Chinese have told her in the last few days that a famous writer, Liu Xinwu, has been removed as editor of the magazine People's Literature and that another writer, Wang Meng, may have been ousted as Culture Minister.

file: 2 American Tourists Are Still in Chinese Custody.txt
text:
ï»¿
Two Americans detained by the Chinese in Tibet during violent demonstrations a week ago remain in custody, a State Department spokesman said yesterday.
Officials of the Chinese Foreign Ministry in Chengdu told American officials that the two men - John Ackerly, 31 years old, of Cambridge, Mass., and Dr. Blake Kerr, 29, of East Hampton, L.I. 
- were still being held by the Chinese authorities, according to Nancy Beck, the department spokesman in Washington.
The Chinese did not disclose where the Americans were being held or whether they faced criminal charges.
News organizations had reported that the two Americans, who were described as tourists, were detained by the authorities in Lhasa, the Tibetan capital, during nationalist demonstrations last Sunday. 
But until yesterday, it was not known whether they remained in custody.
Â 
Mother 'Desperate to Know'
''We are very glad it has been confirmed that they are detained, that they are alive,'' said Margaret Kerr Richenburg, the mother of Dr. Kerr, who was traveling with his friend from college after graduating from medical school this year. 
''I am really desperate to know they are all right.''
Mr. Ackerly, a lawyer, and Dr. Kerr were in the middle of a three- to four-month tour of Asia and had been in Lhasa for five to six weeks before they were taken into custody, according to Dr. William C. Ackerly, Mr. Ackerly's father, who was interviewed at his home in Cambridge yesterday.
The two men had been friends since they were both undergraduates at Dartmouth College. 
Mr. Ackerly attended law school at American University in Washington, D.C., and Dr. Kerr attended medical school at the State Univesity of New York at Buffalo.
Dr. Ackerly, who last heard from his son by telephone two weeks ago, said: ''John never mentioned a word about politics to us; when he called, he said he was going to visit monasteries.''
''They had been having a wonderful time,'' the father said. 
''We thought they would be in Katmandu by now. 
They are experienced outdoorsmen.''
Climbed Mountains in Peru Dr. Ackerly, who described both men as tall and in good health, said that they had climbed mountains in Peru together and that they liked roughing it and meeting natives in foreign cultures.
The last postcard the family received, on Aug. 
23, seemed untroubled and did not mention political unrest, Dr. Ackerly said.
''This place is like Peru, no showers, no fresh food,'' the postcard from Tibet said. 
''The restaurant serves three things: beer, tea and yak dumplings.''
Telephone calls yesterday from the State Department to the families of the two men in Massachusetts and New York provided their parents with the first official information after 24 hours of anxious waiting. 
They were first told of their sons' plight on Friday in calls from news organizations, and they had been trying to learn more by telephoning China and State Department officials in Washington through the night.
According to Ms. Beck of the State Department, an American consular official from Chengdu will be sent to Lhasa to learn more about the situation.

file: 2 ARRESTED IN SILICON VALLEY THEFT CASE.txt
text:
ï»¿
In the latest of several arrests aimed at curbing the theft of sophisticated technology from companies in California's Silicon Valley, the Federal Bureau of Investigation said yesterday that it had arrested two men on charges of attempting to sell stolen electronics hardware to an agent posing as a representative of the Chinese Government.
In an affidavit filed in New York, the agency said the electronics components involved in the case had been stolen from a division of the General Electric Company in San Jose. 
The parts, worth about $200,000, included integrated circuits, diodes and other components used in the control systems of nuclear plants.
In the latest of several arrests aimed at curbing the theft of sophisticated technology from companies in California's Silicon Valley, the Federal Bureau of Investigation said yesterday that it had arrested two men on charges of attempting to sell stolen electronics hardware to an agent posing as a representative of the Chinese Government.
The affidavit also charged that one of the defendants, John Henry Jackson, had told the F.B.I undercover agent that he would be able to obtain and sell about $20 million worth of hardware used in military radar systems. 
Mr. Jackson, 44 years old, also faces criminal charges that he led a crime ring that stole and remarketed more than 100,000 semiconductors in recent years. 
He is awaiting trial on those charges.
Â 
Inquiry Began Last September
The F.B.I. said the other defendant in the case, Gary Wayne Dotson, 33, was a stockroom employee at General Electric's San Jose facility for three years until he resigned in December. 
The agency declined to provide information on Mr. Jackson's occupation.
An F.B.I. spokesman in San Francisco, Larry Holmquist, said the arrests of the two men, both San Jose residents, followed an undercover investigation that began last September. 
The undercover identity of the agent on the case - a representative of the Chinese Government - ''was pulled out of the air'' and was not selected because of any suspicion that China is involved in the illegal acquisition of proprietary technology, he said.
A spokesman for General Electric's San Jose operation, Bob Bell, said yesterday that the case involving Mr. Jackson and Mr. Dotson was the most serious breach of his company's security that he could remember and that the company's attempts to prevent theft of its products were being intensified.
Nonetheless, Mr. Bell added that the parts involved in the case did not reveal any highly advanced or proprietary technology. 
''You could buy that stuff at any Radio Shack store,'' he said.
Â 
Growing Concern About Losses
The arrests of the two men came a month after the F.B.I. charged 18 Japanese businessmen, many of them employees of Hitachi Ltd. and the Mitsubishi Electric Corporation, with conspiring to steal confidential computer information from the International Business Machines Corporation. 
In that case, the F.B.I. used undercover agents who had established a small electronics company in Silicon Valley as a front for their investigation.
The agency's undercover work has been increased in response to growing concern about the loss of trade and military secrets at electronics companies where employees are sometimes able to conceal tiny, but sophisticated semiconductors in their pockets or clothing as they leave.
In its complaint, the F.B.I. said that in meetings between the two defendants and the F.B.I.'s undercover agent, who is of Chinese descent, an agreement was reached in which the agent would pay $200,000 for the the nuclear plant components. 
Although no money changed hands, the F.B.I. said the parts were shipped by the two defendants to Newark and seized by Federal agents there.
The complaint also said that Mr. Jackson, in conversations with the undercover agent, had said he needed to sell the nuclear plant parts to raise money so he could buy the military radar components. 
The agency did not say where Mr. Jackson had intended to obtain the military hardware.

file: 2 CLING TO CHINA, EVEN AFTER 21 YEARS OF NO CHOICE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Against the scale of suffering that was commonplace here in the first 30 years of Communist rule, the two women were minor casualties, incidental figures in a huge tableau of repression.
But they were Americans, and the punishment they endured seems to have been senseless even by the obscure standards of the time. 
Seraphine and Marjorie Fuller, a devoutly Christian mother and daughter living quietly by themselves in Shanghai, answered a knock on the door one day in 1959 to find agents of the feared Public Security Bureau waiting to take them to a labor camp.
They remained there, somewhere outside Shanghai, for 21 years, sleeping on bedrolls on concrete floors, often desperately hungry, always fearful of marauders among the other foreigners incarcerated with them. 
In the last nine of those years an American President, Richard M. Nixon, visited Shanghai, as did hundreds of other prominent Americans. 
But for all the good it did the Fullers the visitors might as well have never come.
Interview with two women--81-year-old Seraphine Fuller and 62-year-old daughter Marjorie--who from 1959 to 1980 were inmates in Chinese labor camp for foreigners; women, who now live at home for elderly foreigners in Harbin, have declined offer of opportunity to renew their American citizenship, which they renounced after Seraphine's husband abandoned them in 1930; photo; map (M)
To the Chinese the two women were technically stateless, although to guards and fellow inmates at the camp they were never anything but the ''meiguo nuren,'' or American women. 
Three decades before the knock on the door, in bitterness at a husband and father who abandoned them for another woman, they renounced their American papers and vowed to remain together in China.
Â 
Human Tourist Attraction
Five years after they got out of the labor camp, with no more notice or explanation than was vouchsafed when they were seized, they are still the ''American women,'' offered like a tourist attraction to American reporters reaching Harbin. 
In this northeastern China city, 1,000 miles from Shanghai, they live out their lives in a second-floor room of a home for elderly foreigners, the only one in China, resolved to neither regret nor reverse their decision to forsake the United States.
''We're not regretting anything,'' said Seraphine Fuller, 81 years old, sitting at a table on the second-floor landing with her daughter, Marjorie, 62. 
''There is just nothing to regret.''
It was one of the few times that the older woman spoke during a 45-minute conversation that Miss Fuller said was one of the longest she or her mother had had with anyone in years.
The serene look on Mrs. Fuller's face and the way she folded her hands calmly across her lap conveyed the impression of a proud woman at peace with her fate, content to allow her daughter to do the talking. 
From time to time, especially when the talk turned to religion, she smiled or nodded.
To an outsider, their story sounded like a tale of innocent lives wasted. 
But at the table in a ramshackle suburb of Harbin, amid a vista of muddy roads and redbrick factories, there was scarcely a trace of bitterness or even chagrin, save for a moment when a visitor suggested that in renouncing the United States the two women had struck out at the man who abandoned them in the only way they could.
Â 
An Evangelical Conviction
''I suppose in a way we were,'' Miss Fuller said.
The conversation was laced with the younger woman's quick wit and evangelical conviction. 
Her starting point was that they had brought their fate upon themselves by remaining in Shanghai in 1949 when thousands of other foreigners were fleeing before the advancing Communists.
''We elected to stay, so we can't complain,'' she said. 
''We thought they were going to be democratic.''
She laughed, and added, ''You know what the Italians say: Every liberation begins with the hope of freedom and ends in tyranny.''
Seraphine Fuller was born in Harbin at a time when the city was one of the liveliest in the Far East. 
Her father was a Russian who had come to build the railroads that ran east to Vladivostok and south to Port Arthur, now Dalian; her mother was a Polish woman born in the Ukraine.
Â 
European Flavor Once Strong
Though the city was in China the Russian concession at its heart gave it a strongly European flavor, enhanced after 1917 when thousands of White Russians poured across the border to escape the pursuing Red Army.
''Oh my, Harbin. 
It was a beautiful city,'' she said in one of her rare conversational sallies. 
''They called it the Paris of the Orient.''
In the 1920's she was drawn to Shanghai, an even greater center of European settlement. 
There she met and married her husband, a freewheeling merchant who was the son of an American and the child-bride whom he had married in the Chinese community in San Francisco.
Seraphine Fuller's brief marriage ended in 1930, and her husband left for San Francisco. 
Mrs. Fuller and her daughter were left in Shanghai, American citizens who had never been to the United States.
Marjorie Fuller saw her father again in 1939, when he visited the two women in Shanghai and brought his daughter a gift from Japan, an antique ivory carving of a geisha. 
It was one of a pair, and Miss Fuller's last memory of her father is him telling her that one day they would be reunited in America, where they would place the two geishas side by side on the mantelpiece.
Â 
Prized Possession Remains
Nearly half a century later the geisha is Miss Fuller's prized possession, next to her Bible, in the room she shares with her mother. 
In 1962 her father wrote to the two women in labor camp, suggesting that they resume their old lives. 
His daughter said they never replied. 
He would be 89 if he is still alive, but the two women said they had no idea what had become of him.
''It's too late for anything like that now,'' Miss Fuller said, in a phrase that recurs often as she talks of the perspectives that govern their lives. 
''Much too late.''
Although the Chinese provide three meals a day in a dining room at the home, and take residents on trips to the movies and parks, the Fullers keep their distance.
They eat in their room, and have asked to be excused from birthday celebrations. 
They spend much of their time reading the Bible and literature sent to them by an evangelical organization in the United States.
''Everything is dust compared with the word of God,'' Miss Fuller said. 
''Beside that, nothing matters at all.''
Confrontation Over Bible The women said that in the labor camp faith sustained them - but, they said, it also nearly cost them their lives. 
The Cultural Revolution that swept across China in 1966 penetrated even the labor camp, and militants who had set a fire seized their Bible along with other ''bourgeois'' possessions. 
The women clung to the Bible, telling their tormentors that if they wanted it, they would have to throw the women on the fire, too. 
The Bible survived.
In 1980, mother and daughter were summoned by camp guards, told to pack, and driven to the railway station in Shanghai, where they boarded a train for Harbin.
Miss Fuller says the greatest relief was not in leaving the camp but their fellow prisoners.
''There were decent people,'' she said, ''but there were also horrible ones, some of them were murderers, plain and simple. 
If anybody complained the guards would only say, 'You're all foreigners, you sort it out among yourselves.'
''
Since coming to Harbin they have been visited by the United States consul in Shenyang, an industrial city 300 miles south of here, and offered an opportunity to renew their American citizenship. 
Miss Fuller said they had refused because there is nothing for them in the United States that they cannot find here.
''We crossed the Rubicon on that one many, many years ago,'' she said, ''and there's no point in changing things now.''

file: 2 LEADERS FOLLOWED PARALLEL CAREERS WITH CONTRASTING STYLES.txt
text:
ï»¿
Though they have markedly different political styles and personal backgrounds, Zhao Ziyang and the man he replaced yesterday, Hu Yaobang, both owe their rise through the Chinese hierarchy to the same factor: the sponsorship of the country's paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping.
Until Mr. Hu's dismissal, the two men largely had parallel careers, and were often variously regarded as Mr. Deng's successors. 
Their fortunes climbed with Mr. Deng, and they fell into disgrace with him during the Cultural Revolution, only to be appointed to the most senior posts in the party and Government after Mr. Deng rose again and consolidated his power in the early 1980's.
Over the last six years, the two worked closely together but maintained a fairly clear division of labor. 
As Prime Minister, Mr. Zhao presided over the economic changes that are the centerpiece of China's modernization program and traveled widely overseas, including a visit to the United States in 1984, while Mr. Hu concentrated on party policy and internal discipline.
To many in Beijing, both foreigners and Chinese, the two men seemed ideally suited by personality to the roles in which Mr. Deng had cast them. 
Zhao Ziyang (pronounced JOW dzeh-YANG), son of a landlord family, emerged as a polished, articulate and well-dressed statesman, while the diminutive and fiery Hu Yaobang (prounced WHO yow-BANG), born to a poor peasant family, came to be known for his bluntness, earthy wit and impulsiveness.
Â 
'Good Cop' and 'Tough Cop'
As some foreign diplomats saw it, Mr. Zhao often played the role of the ''good cop'' to Mr. Hu's ''tough cop,'' and reaped the benefits that went with that role. 
But in replacing Mr. Hu as General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party, Mr. Zhao now also assumes responsibility for supervising the party's 44 million members, a task expected to test all of his considerable finesse and managerial skills.
Early in his career, in the years immediately following the Chinese Revolution in 1949, Mr. Zhao, now 67, supervised purges of ''class enemies'' in the southern Chinese province of Guangdong, where he was later to serve as party secretary. 
But he is best known within China for the sweeping economic experiments he introduced after he was appointed party secretary and Governor of Sichuan, China's largest province and Mr. Deng's home ground, in 1975.
By dismantling the commune system in the countryside and introducing material incentives, Mr. Zhao freed the pent-up energies of Sichuan's 100 million people and was able to turn the province into the breadbasket of China. 
That success, which led to the liberalization of agricultural policies across China, was particularly appreciated by the country's 800 million peasants, who quickly coined a rhyming couplet, ''for grain (liang), look to Zhao Ziyang,'' in his praise.
''The defect of management in China is that state control is too tight,'' Mr. Zhao said not long after his elevation to Prime Minister in 1980, explaining the decision to extend the Sichuan reforms. 
''It does not provide for enthusiasm for the enterprises.''
Â 
An Earlier Denunciation
Though seen as an innovator in the field of economics, in politics Mr. Zhao has demonstrated the ability to adapt himself to shifts in the party line. 
When the leftist ''Gang of Four'' led by the wife of Mao Zedong purged Mr. Deng toward the end of the Cultural Revolution, Mr. Zhao joined in the denunciation of his patron.
Earlier, at the height of the Cultural Revolution, Mr. Zhao had himself been purged as one of the ''capitalist roaders'' associated with Mr. Deng. In a humiliating public ceremony, Mr. Zhao was paraded through the streets of Canton, capital of the province in which he served, with a dunce cap on his head.
The ''consummate bureaucrat,'' in the words of one Western diplomat, Mr. Zhao has served as a member of the standing committee of the Politburo of the Chinese Communist Party while Prime Minister and has a strong following among younger, modernization-minded party members. 
His major weakness, according to diplomatic and academic analysts, is his lack of military experience or personal ties to leaders of the People's Liberation Army, an institution said to contain large numbers of hard-liners opposed to Mr. Deng's modernization program.
Mr. Hu, 71, is also said to have suffered from a limited military background, though as a teen-ager he accompanied many of the senior party and army leaders on the ''Long March'' through the Chinese countryside. 
Born in Hunan, Chairman Mao's home province, Mr. Hu, who measures less than 5 feet tall, first came into the party as a ''Little Red Devil,'' the Communist youth group.
Â 
Party Boss in Sichuan
Following the Communist victory in 1949, Mr. Hu became the party boss in northern Sichuan, where his performance attracted the attention of Mr. Deng. In 1952 he was transferred to Peking, where he became the head of the Communist Youth League and built up a strong network of relationships with young hopefuls who subsequently emerged, with his help, as party leaders.
Like Mr. Zhao, Mr. Hu was also purged during the Cultural Revolution as a ''revisionist'' and ''counterrevolutionary'' because of his associations with Mr. Deng, with whom he shares a passion for bridge and has often played as partners. 
He is said to have been ''sent down to the countryside'' for menial labor for three years and to have spent an additional five years under house arrest.

file: 2 PAPERS QUOTE JAPANESE LEADER ON ABILITIES OF MINORITIES IN U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
Two Japanese newspapers quoted Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone on Tuesday as having said that because of the presence of ethnic minorities in the United States, that country's ''level is lower'' than Japan's.
The newspapers asserted that Mr. Nakasone was referring to the intellectual level. 
But a spokesman for his party said the Prime Minister had meant the literacy level.
The newspapers, Yomiuri Shimbun and Tokyo Shimbun, reported that on Monday, Mr. Nakasone told a party gathering:
''In a highly developed information society and a highly educated society such as Japan, the people require politics that bravely faces problems. 
In the United States, because there are a considerable number of blacks, Puerto Ricans and Mexicans, the (intellectual) level is lower.''
Word in Parentheses
The two newspapers placed the word meaning ''intelligence'' or ''intellectual'' in parentheses, implying that the reporter had supplemented a direct quote. 
This is common procedure in Japan because Japanese often leave out parts of sentences expecting that their listeners will know what they mean.
Fumikazu Okada, an official of Mr. Nakasone's Liberal Democratic Party, said Mr. Nakasone was referring not to intellectual levels but to literacy rates and had commented that there were many blacks, Puerto Ricans and Mexicans who could not write English.
In a statement issued this afternoon, the Prime Minister said:
''What I was saying there was that the United States made great achievements in the Apollo program and in S.D.I., but there are things Americans have not been able to reach because of multiple nationalities. 
On the contrary, things are easier in Japan because we are a homogeneous society.''
He added, ''I had no intention of committing any racial discrimination or of slandering other countries.''
S.D.I. stands for the Strategic Defense Initiative, the missile defense program also known as ''Star Wars.''
Mr. Nakasone's remarks came just two weeks after he dismissed his Education Minister for comments that offended South Korea and China and just a few days after he returned from Seoul, where he apologized to South Korea's President.
Masayuki Fujio, the former Education Minister, had angered South Koreans by suggesting that they had agreed to Japan's annexation of their nation in the early part of this century - an annexation that Koreans still consider humiliating. 
He also offended Chinese by virtually dismissing Japanese atrocities in China in 1937.
Â 
Views of Nakasone
Early in his political career, Mr. Nakasone gained a reputation as an outspoken nationalist. 
His associates say he has modified these views.
In speeches and campaign slogans, he often refers to ''postwar settlement of accounts,'' a term widely interpreted to mean that Japan should begin a new era unfettered by the concerns and problems of the postwar period.
Mr. Nakasone repeated his call to move to a new political era at the Liberal Democratic Party meeting at which he is reported to have made the remarks about blacks, Puerto Ricans and Mexicans.
Regardless of Mr. Nakasone's intent, minority groups in the United States are not always portrayed positively in Japan.

file: 20 YEARS LATER, INDONESIA MOVES TO MAKE PEACE WITH ITS PAST.txt
text:
ï»¿
Indonesia took two significant steps this week toward narrowing 20-year-old rifts that have separated the nation under President Suharto from the stormy Sukarno era.
On Friday, President Suharto opened Jakarta's new international airport and named it the Sukarno-Hatta Airport. 
President Sukarno and Mohammed Hatta, his Vice President until the two split over President Sukarno's concept of ''guided democracy,'' proclaimed Indonesian independence from the Dutch in 1945.
Indonesian Government, in effort to narrow 20-year-old rifts separating country under Pres Suharto and former Pres Sukarno, opens Jakarta's new international airport and names it Sukarno-Hatta Airport; Indonesian and Chinese trade officials sign agreement to re-establish direct commerce for first time in 18 years (M)
Also on Friday, in Singapore, Indonesian and Chinese trade officials signed an agreement to re-establish direct commerce between the two countries for the first time in 18 years.
The era of President Sukarno -Indonesia's leading political figure for almost half a century, beginning in the 1920's when he emerged as a nationalist fighter against colonial rule - ended after an attempted coup in 1965. 
The planners and motives of the foiled coup have never been definitively determined.
The Government under General Suharto, who gradually eased President Sukarno out of office after the crisis and took full power in 1967, has held China responsible for backing the Indonesian Communist Party, which is believed to have been involved in the unsuccessful coup.
Â 
Thousands Were Killed
The present Indonesian leadership has also suggested that President Sukarno, who had been moving closer to the Communists in his last years in power, may have been a party to the intended military takeover.
After the attempted coup was put down by General Suharto and others loyal to him, thousands of Communist suspects were sought out and killed around the country. 
Many people with Communist links are still imprisoned or denied political rights. 
One such person was recently executed after exhausting all appeals. 
Several others are still under death sentences.
For nearly two decades, publications in Chinese have been banned from Indonesia, with the exception of a small local newspaper. 
All Chinese characters are inked out of foreign publications circulating in the country.
Although there have been no official attempts in Indonesia to obliterate the memory of President Sukarno, whom most Indonesians consider the nation's founder, his place in history has not been embellished in the last two decades. 
Indonesia has been strongly anti-Communist and anti-Chinese under President Suharto. 
Many people who challenged President Sukarno, including some who were arrested as a result, are now in positions of influence.
Â 
More Confidence
But, diplomats say, with the country politically stable and making progress in economic development, President Suharto, who has a reputation as a strong believer in consensus and nonconfrontation, may feel more confident about restoring to President Sukarno a larger place in national history.
At the ceremonies on Friday, President Suharto said the naming of the new airport for the two independence leaders was ''a token of our people's gratefulness for their tireless struggle and their extraordinary services to our nation.''
The achievements of President Sukarno were also publicly praised in April, when Indonesia commemorated the 30th anniversary of the Asia-Africa Conference held in Bandung in 1955. 
The conference, which led later to the founding of the nonaligned movement, was intended to give both President Sukarno and Indonesia, the largest nation in Southeast Asia, a bigger world role.
It was also at Bandung this year that the first public step was taken toward a better relationship with China, with which Jakarta broke all diplomatic and trade links in 1967.
Peking, which has been working to improve its relations with all of the Southeast Asian nations, sent its Foreign Minister, Wu Xueqian, to the Bandung commemoration, where he chatted amiably if briefly with President Suharto. 
For Indonesians, the moment marked a turning point.

file: 22 RARE DEER ARE RETURNED TO NATIVE GROUND IN CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
More than 120 years after an intrepid French missionary peered into an imperial hunting park here and discovered a breed of deer unknown in the West, a joint enterprise by a British aristocrat and American benefactors has brought the animal back to China.
The Pere David deer - named after Father Armand David, a Lazarist missionary and naturalist who toured China in the 19th century - has been extinct in China since at least 1900. 
But an Air France plane that arrived here Saturday from Paris brought 22 of the animals back to their native habitat.
The animals were immediately driven to the location 15 miles southwest of Peking where Father David first saw them in 1865. 
It was then the imperial hunting park of the Manchu emperors, and any unauthorized person killing one of the animals was subject to execution. 
Now it is farmland worked by peasants, part of it recently enclosed to provide a breeding ground for the deer.
British Lord Andrew Howland, great-great-grandson of Duke of Bedford, who acquired Pere David deer from Manchu emperors in 1894, formally hands over 22 deer from species, extinct in China since at least 1900, to Chinese officials at former imperial hunting park at Nanhaizi; photo (M)Called a Precious Gift
As the two crates containing the deer were being taken from the aircraft, Lord Andrew Howland, great-great-grandson of the Duke of Bedford, who acquired examples of the deer from the Manchu court in 1894, formally handed over the animals. 
They were selected from a herd of more than 400 that roam the parkland at Woburn Abbey, the ducal home 45 miles northwest of London.
''This is indeed a precious gift to the Chinese people,'' said Jin Jianming, of the Chinese Government's environmental protection office. 
''The return of these animals has a great historical significance, not only for the preservation of a rare species but for the pleasure of future generations of the Chinese people.''
The deer originally were found in China's northeast provinces but are thought to have been extinct in the wild for hundreds of years. 
They were installed in Nanhaizi, the imperial hunting park, after the Manchu invaders established their dynasty in Peking in 1644. 
In 1894, shortly after the Duke of Bedford acquired the animals that started his herd, a flood breached the wall of the hunting park and the imperial animals escaped.
Contemporary accounts said most of the deer were captured and eaten by local peasants, but some evidently were still living in the Chinese capital at the time of the Boxer Rebellion in 1900. 
Contemporary accounts say the foreign forces, including American marines, who entered Peking to relieve the siege of the diplomatic legations killed and ate the last of the deer.
Â 
Largest Herd at Abbey
Since then, the largest collection of the deer anywhere has been at Woburn Abbey, helping make the abbey one of Britain's largest tourist draws. 
The idea of bringing the deer back to China originated with the owner of the abbey, the Marquess of Tavistock, and with a Czechoslovak-born researcher in animal behavior, Maya Boyd, who works at Oxford University.
Miss Boyd made several journeys to Peking over 18 months to arrange the return of the deer. 
The Chinese authorities spent about $590,000 to acquire the land at Nanhaizi from a local agricultural commune, to enclose it with a 2.4-mile brick wall and to drain and refill the lake that was the centerpiece of the imperial park. 
Grass and trees have also been planted.
The costs of transporting the animals were shared by the Marquess of Tavistock and by several amateur naturalists, among them Lars-Erik Lindblad of Westport, Conn., who owns a travel company that brings American tourists to China.
The return of the deer has created something of a stir among the Chinese, who call the species Sibuxiang, meaning ''the four unlikes.''
According to folk tradition, the reddish-gray animal acquired the name because it was not like the horse, not like the ox, not like the goat and not like the deer traditional in other parts of northern China when the Manchus moved south.

file: 30 YEARS OF SPYING FOR CHINA IS CHARGED.txt
text:
ï»¿
A Federal law-enforcement official said today that a former analyst for the Central Intelligence Agency had admitted that he provided the Chinese Government with extensive intelligence information for 30 years.
The analyst, Larry Wu-Tai Chin, was indicted today by a Federal grand jury on a single count of conspiracy to commit espionage. 
According to the law-enforcement official, the account of Mr. Chin's activities was based largely on his his statements to the authorities. 
The account included the names of the Chinese Communist officials who recruited him and Mr. Chin's rank within the Chinese intelligence service, the official said, Mr. Chin, who the authorities said had been under investigation since December 1983, was arrested early Saturday. 
He has not yet entered a plea but his lawyer, Peter Meyers, said in court last Saturday that Mr. Chin would plead not guilty.
The eight-page indictment said that Mr. Chin had access to classified material ''at all levels, including secret and above,'' in his job as an analyst at the Foreign Broadcast Information Service, an arm of the C.I.A.
Mr. Chin was able to see ''virtually all levels of classified information dealing with China and other aspects of American Far Eastern intelligence,'' another Federal law-enforcement official said.
An Administration official said the security breach caused by Mr. Chin was a serious one and that he ''could have done a lot of damage.''
According to the indictment, the broadcast information service monitors foreign broadcasts and does translation work for other components of the intelligence agency. 
Its analysts would use classified intelligence reports to help assess the foreign broadcasts recorded by the American authorities. 
Additionally, other officials said Mr. Chin's language skills could have involved him in translating documents for a variety of sensitive C.I.A. operations in other segments of the agency.
Â 
A 'Deputy Bureau Chief'
These officials noted that at some points in Mr. Chin's career, he might have been called on by the espionage branch of the agency, which deals with covert agents in the field, as a translator.
The indictment disclosed new details about Mr. Chin's frequent travels to China. 
It said he was promoted to ''deputy bureau chief'' in the People's Republic of China intelligence service in a 1982 trip to Peking.
Prosecutors revealed for the first time that Mr. Chin continued working for the intelligence agency as a contract employee after his retirement in 1981. 
The indictment said that from 1981 to 1985, he worked with the United States Joint Publications Research Service, a division of the agency that does translation for broadcast information service.
The indictment did not specify the type of information Mr. Chin dealt with in his four years with that division. 
But in a criminal complaint filed over the weekend, the Government charged that Chinese intelligence paid Mr. Chin $50,000 in 1982, about a year after he had become a contract employee for the Central Intelligence Agency. 
The indictment charged that Mr. Chin was paid more than $140,000 for all of his activities.
Â 
Kept in Touch at Agency
According to the indictment, Mr. Chin kept in contact with his friends and associates at the agency after his retirement. 
At one point, he told Chinese intelligence about a C.I.A. employee he believed was ''susceptible to recruitment.''
The picture of Mr. Chin that emerged from those who know his family was of an immigrant who had succeeded in the United States and was proud of the accomplishments of his three children.
A family acquaintance described Mr. Chin today as a ''sweet, kind good humored'' family man who had a close relationship with his two sons and daughter. 
One of his sons attended Dartmouth College and is an a doctoral program at Stanford University.

file: 5 NEW WORKS JOIN COOKING BOOKSHELF.txt
text:
ï»¿
AN ECLECTIC quintet of recent cookbooks might be just what is needed for that last-minute Christmas gift. 
In addition, they contain ideas for food gifts to make and for elegant holiday-entertaining dishes.
All the books are by New Jersey authors. 
Three are from the kitchens of popular cooking teachers; the two others are compilations of recipes from a mixed bag of contributors, and the proceeds from their sale will benefit the Paper Mill Playhouse in Millburn and the Newark Museum.
Subjects range from festive Chinese banquets to homey Italian casseroles and from sophisticated international dishes to favorite recipes of actors.
In ''Cooking at Cooktique'' by Silvia Lehrer (Doubleday & Co. 
Inc., $19.95), ''The Chinese Banquet Cookbook'' by Eileen Yin-Fei Lo (Crown Publishers Inc., $17.95) and Anne Casale's ''Italian Family Cooking'' (Ballantine Books, $9.95), the recipes, with their clear, step-by-step instructions, reflect these authors' many years of teaching the culinary ropes in their kitchen-classrooms. 
Questions that might be posed by inexperienced cooks are often anticipated and procedures are well spelled out.
Mrs. Lehrer, whose Tenafly cooking school, Cooktique, often is host to well-known guest chef-instructors, has compiled more than 200 recipes, several of them classics with a contemporary twist. 
Any do-ahead steps are pointed out and, in the lead to each chapter, Mrs. Lehrer provides tips on the best ingredients and techniques.
Herbed squash bisque, a salad of goat cheese, green beans and pine nuts, grilled chicken with two mustards, steamed red snapper with ginger Hollandaise and chocolate-coated pears in raspberry sauce are a few of the cosmopolitan offerings.
One cavil, however, is with the skewered sesame shrimp, which should be marinated for a shorter time in light, rather than dark, soy sauce so as not to be puckeringly salty.
In ''The Chinese Banquet Cookbook,'' Miss Lo has compiled 10 complete banquets from China's regions and more than 100 recipes, many preceded by personal anecdotes about the author's childhood in Canton.
Besides banquets from Canton, Peking, Shanghai, Szechuan and Hunan (including a delicious version of orange beef), there are also dishes from the nomads called the Hakka, as well as vegetarian and traditional New Year celebration recipes.
A teacher at the China Institute in Manhattan and at her Montclair home, Miss Lo's instructions are straightforward. 
Techniques are illustrated with dozens of line drawings.
The subtitle of ''Italian Family Cooking'' is ''Like Mama Used to Make,'' and for Mrs. Casale, a resident of Watchung, it could also read ''Like Father and Father-in-Law Used to Make.''
Both men were professional cooks whose influence on Mrs. Casale was strong.
Proprietor of Annie's Kitchen Cooking School in North Plainfield for several years, Mrs. Casale manages to convey in her writing the cozy enthusiasm and wealth of helpful hints that she has brought to her students.
A fan of the food processor, the author has adapted many of her 250-odd recipes from Northern and Southern Italy, as well as Italian America, to take advantage of shortcuts. 
For example, the pasta chapter gives detailed instructions for both machine and hand methods of preparation.
Desserts are particularly appealing, from the glazed orange cake and the ricotta mousse with raspberry sauce to the espresso cream pie.
The glossy cover of ''The Newark Museum Cookbook'' displays an elegantly set table (actually the opulent Victorian dining room of the museum's Ballantine House).
The comb-bound cookbook - it was edited by a museum trustee, Mrs. Theron L. Marsh of Bernardsville -is a collection of more than 300 recipes contributed by curators, trustees, members and staff of the museum. 
Appropriately, the book is liberally illustrated with black and white pictures of many of the museum's food-related art and objects.
As one would expect from such a communal effort, the originality of the recipes is as diverse as the contributors. 
But with some careful perusing, a number of choice dishes turn up, from Swiss onion soup and honey-curried bay scallops to Greek ragout of lamb and cheesecake with fresh lemon glaze.
The book is available at the museum for $10.95 ($9.95 for members) or by mail from the Publications Department, Newark Museum, 49 Washington Street, P.O. 
Box 540, Newark, N.J. 
07101. Add $2 for postage, handling and, if requested, gift wrapping.
The newest and also most lighthearted of the cookbooks is the comb-bound paperback called ''Cookbook of the Stars,'' a collection of about 116 recipes, some tongue-in-cheek but most serious, contributed by actors and actresses who have appeared at the Paper Mill Playhouse over the years. 
Photographs from the plays are scattered through the book.
Phyllis Diller sent Red and Yellow Catch-a-Fellow squash, Julie Harris contributed lettuce bread (which tastes much like it sounds), Eva Gabor sent a cookie recipe called Kisses of the Officer and there is a marinara sauce from Dom DeLuise. 
(President Reagan's macaroni and cheese recipe shows up in both this and the Newark Museum cookbook.) King's Supermarkets Inc. supplied a grant for the cookbook, and some of the most sophisticated recipes are those in a special section contributed by Joanna Pruess, director of the store's cooking school.
Available at the Paper Mill Playhouse gift shop before performances and at King's Supermarkets, ''Cookbook of the Stars'' is $10.

file: 60 Shout Out Dalai Lama_s Name And Are Seized in Protest in Tibet.txt
text:
ï»¿
About 60 people shouting the name of the Dalai Lama, Tibet's former civil and religious leader, marched today to a Government office, where armed Chinese security forces quickly arrested them.
The marchers, believed to be Buddhist monks in street clothes, did not resist arrest. 
About 2,000 bystanders made no attempt to help them or four monks who were arrested at about the same time in the Jokhang Temple square, where pro-independence protests last week left several people dead.
The Chinese Government has reportedly sent 1,000 armed policemen to Lhasa, the Tibetan capital. 
The troops are to guard against further unrest on Wednesday, the 37th anniversary of the day China occupied Tibet.
Â 
Quiet Day Expected
Tibetans and Chinese questioned on the street said they expected the anniversary to be quiet because of fears that the police would fire on protesters.
Western witnesses said the police fired last Thursday on demonstrators who burned a police station and vehicles in the temple square.
Western doctors in Lhasa said eight Tibetans were shot to death and one unidentified Chinese was stoned to death. 
The authorities said six Chinese policemen were killed. 
It was not known if the Chinese was one of the six.
There was a smaller, less violent protest on Sept. 
27 that resulted in about two dozen arrests. 
The march today was the first significant public protest since Thursday.
Â 
Dalai Lama's Name Chanted
About 100 marchers raised their fists and chanted the name of the Dalai Lama, who fled to exile in India after an uprising against Chinese rule in 1959. 
China annexed Tibet in 1950.
The marchers did not wear the saffron robes usually worn by monks, but they came from the direction of the Drepung monastery, one of three leading monasteries whose members led the independence demonstrations last week. 
The monastery is about five miles west of Lhasa.
Western witnesses said a few were arrested quietly on the way and that others left the march. 
About 60 marchers continued to the gate of the Tibetan regional government office. 
About 100 members of the security forces carrying submachine guns and automatic pistols immediately herded them onto trucks.
Â 
'Very Thoroughly Searched'
''I don't think they were resisting,'' said Derek Olson of Oak Park, Ill. 
''They were very thoroughly searched before being put in the truck.''
Another American witness, Cliff Toliver of Cincinnati, said some bystanders surged forward and shouted when policemen and soldiers struck a marcher. 
No clash ensued.
Mr. Olson said the crowd started to scatter twice, apparently in response to threatening moves from the security people. 
''It was definitely a very panicky situation,'' he said.
Amber Kvanli, like Mr. Olson a student from St. Olaf College in Minnesota, said Tibetans fled in panic from the busy market next to the temple when about 30 armed policemen marched up to four monks who were sitting on the ground chanting.
Â 
Children Gathered Up
''Suddenly people started yelling, moms started gathering their kids, and one young Tibetan came up to me and put me in a doorway,'' she said. 
''The monks stopped chanting, got up and went with the police. 
They left behind their song books and the blankets they were sitting on.''
It was not known what happened to those arrested. 
Monks at the Sera and Drepung monasteries said previously that police came and arrested 47 members and that others were missing after the demonstration Thursday.

She played her first match of the 1982 Federation Cup tournament on a July evening in Santa Clara, Calif., and wasn't seen again in public for eight months. 
Hu Na hid in the homes of sympathetic Chinese families on the West Coast during that time, hoping one day to be granted asylum in the United States. 
Her second wish was to pursue a professional tennis career.
Miss Hu's defection caused an international incident and her whereabouts had all the intrigue of a spy novel. 
The Chinese Government suspended several cultural exchanges with the United States, which eventually granted Miss Hu asylum on April 4, 1983, in Washington. 
She played her first professional match two months later.
Hu Na, who defected to United States from China in 1982, defeats Annabel Croft of Britain in first-round match at Wimbledon; photo (M)
But Miss Hu was not to become another Martina Navratilova, who defected to the United States from Czechoslovakia when she was already one of the highly ranked players in the world. 
Miss Hu was a champion in China but only a qualifier on the women's tour.
''It was very hard because the players were so good,'' she said. 
''I got discouraged because every time my game went up, I'd get injuries.''
Miss Hu is ranked 150th in the Women's Tennis Association rankings but has made the biggest tournament in the world the site of her professional breakthrough. 
She qualified for Wimbledon by winning three difficult matches last week and today became the first Chinese-born player to win a match in the main draw, defeating Annabel Croft of Britain, 6-3, 7-5, in a first-round match.
Â 
'Cracks Under Pressure'
Although Miss Croft may not be well known herself, she is ranked 40th and was the favorite of the hometown crowd. 
It earned her a place on Court One, which is adjacent to Centre Court and usually draws the second- biggest crowd. 
''I was nervous,'' Miss Hu said. 
''There were so many people who came out to see us.''
Miss Hu is 22 years old but her game is just developing. 
The lack of top quality competition in China is one reason, and the customary slow progress made by serve-and-volley players is another. 
At times, it seems as if she has disappeared once again. 
''I think she's improved a lot,'' Miss Croft said. 
''I've been told by other players that she cracks under pressure.''
Any pressure she may face on the tennis court, however, would not begin to compare to what she encountered when she defected. 
She received letters that were reportedly written by her parents, pleading for her return to China. 
She was homesick and did not speak English.
''My English wasn't very good,'' Miss Hu said. 
''I watched 'Three's Company' and 'The Love Boat.'
Jack Tripper was my first teacher.''
Â 
Potential in Question
Jack Tripper is the character played by John Ritter in the television show ''Three's Company.''
Miss Hu has since had other instructors. 
She is attending the United States International College in San Diego, where she lives in a Chinese community with several families, spending a few months with each. 
She speaks English well enough to face her interviews without the aid of an interpreter.
She said she never questioned her decision to leave China. 
Newspaper accounts at the time said that Miss Hu was reluctant to join the Communist Party, as her coach in China requested. 
She said she preferred not to talk about those things today.
Her potential as a player remains in question. 
She has been tutored by such notable coaches as Vic Braden, Harry Hopman and Nick Bollettieri, but has advanced as far as the quarterfinals only three times in 23 tournaments, and those were on the satellite tour. 
She has earned $7,000.
At this point, however, she appreciates some things that most players take for granted. 
It was a thrill for her, she said, to be able to play a match without braiding her hair.

text:

Thirty million Chinese with nothing to do at work are threatened by a bankruptcy law going into effect Tuesday.
Diplomats are divided about whether the law, adopted after years of debate, will force any of China's 400,000 money-losing factories to close.
Some officials have warned of possible unrest if people are thrown out of work in a country with no social security system.
Â 
Yuan Mu, spokesman of the
State Council, said at a news conference on Friday: ''After the bankruptcy law is implemented, some backward firms will go bankrupt and the number of unemployed, currently 2 percent, will rise. 
But the numbers will be small.''
China is allocating 41 million yuan ($11 billion) this year, 15 percent of its total budget, to subsidize state concerns that are losing money. 
The Government hopes to reduce this sum.

text:
ï»¿
''IVE never tried Chinese food,'' confessed Freda Gibson, poking at a mysterious- looking plate of meat-filled dumplings. 
''It has always seemed so, well, foreign.''
For Mrs. Gibson, a native New Zealander, and more than a dozen other older people, it was a night of many firsts.
Elderly New Yorkers representing a variety of the city's ethnic groups were invited to the Flower Drum Restaurant at Second Avenue and 46th Street Tuesday night for a ceremony ushering in the Chinese New Year, which begins today. 
Attending the traditional event honoring the elderly were blacks and people of Italian, Scottish, Irish, German Jewish, Polish, Puerto Rican and Chinese extraction.
Bryan Miller article on party at Flower Drum Restaurant, New York City, honoring elderly and ushering in Chinese New Year 4682, Year of the Rat; photos (M)
''I've been thinking about doing this for two or three years,'' said Pao Peter Lee, owner of the Flower Drum and the organizer of the event. 
''These people symbolically represent the various communities who live in New York. 
In China, older generations are honored this time of year. 
I hope this causes that tradition to spread in this country.''
Mr. Lee and his family celebrate a traditional Chinese New Year annually at the restaurant. 
However, this was the first time so many outsiders had been invited. 
The evening began with firecrackers popping in front of the restaurant and wishes for the best fortune in 4682, the Year of the Rat.
The guests, chosen from three centers for the aging with the cooperation of the New York City Department for the Aging, dined on a multicourse Chinese feast while watching an hourlong ceremony that began with the Dance of the Mouse. 
Two young girls, one wearing a mouse costume, lilted and swirled around the dining room accompanied, the narrator said, by ''elegant and ethereal music'' that transformed the mouse into a ''graceful, sensitive being.''
Sidney Kilpatrick, a wiry man of Scottish-Irish descent, said this was the first time he had been to Manhattan's East Side in at least seven years, even though he lives on West 10th Street near Fifth Avenue. 
Mr. Kilpatrick has been homebound for years because of poor eyesight and a muscle disorder. 
''This place is most marvelous,'' he said, gazing around the ornately decorated dining room.
After the mouse dance Mr. Lee and his family presented strings of longevity pearls, symbolizing prosperity and harmony, to the artist Dong Kingman, who is of Chinese descent. 
Family members then participated in a ceremony signifying respect for elders in Chinese culture: Three generations kowtowed before their elders.
Later the elderly guests were presented with ''scrolls of wisdom,'' signifying the knowledge and judgment that come with age. 
A special citation was presented to Janet Sainer, Commissioner of the Department for the Aging, who was called a ''compassionate and caring pioneer'' in social services for the elderly.
''I think the Chinese have a good tradition dealing with the elderly,'' Commissioner Sainer said. 
''Respect for the family is frequently lost in our society. 
I hope this event can help bring some of it back.''
For Fred Robinson, a 74-year-old great-grandfather, the party evoked his boyhood in Georgia, where he had playmates who were Chinese. 
Mr. Robinson and the other guests said they admired the cohesiveness and love demonstrated by the Lee family. 
''There is nothing better than a family that can stay together these days, nothing better,'' he said.
Mr. Lee's strong sense of family and reverence for tradition are partly rooted in his escape from China after the Communist revolution. 
It took nearly a decade for him arrange for his wife, Tsen Yee Lee, to leave her homeland and come to America. 
Out of gratitude for his good fortune in the United States, Mr. Lee founded the Chee Yue Community Association, which helps Chinese immigrants learn English and find jobs. 
The association's headquarters are around the corner from his restaurant.
The festivities concluded with a chef demonstrating how to make silk- hair-fine ''longevity noodles'' by hand. 
They were served as part of a ginseng firepot soup.
Mrs. Gibson, still rather new to Chinese cuisine, finished her last dumpling, placed the chopsticks beside her plate and remarked: ''It really is very tasty I think, more so than New Zealand food. 
But it is a bit on the greasy side, don't you think?''

text:
ï»¿
Farmers outside Peking are being asked to return any pieces of the Great Wall that they carried off to build houses and pigpens.
The request is part of a campaign begun this month to restore the section of the ancient wall that runs through the mountainous northern rim of the municipality of Peking.
The drive, organized by four Peking- based newspapers, is concentrating initially on Badaling, a section 50 miles north of Peking frequented by tourists. 
But the organizers hope that enough money will be raised to extend the restoration to other parts of the world's most prominent landmark.
Wall Was Built in Sections
Construction of the Great Wall started about 2,500 years ago. 
It was intended to keep out the marauding northern nomads who lived in the regions that are now Mongolia and Manchuria. 
The wall was built across China in sections using slave labor and was finally linked in 214 B.C.
The Great Wall snakes more than 1,500 miles from Shanhaiguan on the Gulf of Bohai westward to Jiayuguan in the desert of Gansu Province. 
The Chinese called it the ''10,000 li wall,'' partly because it so twisted and turned that no one was quite sure of its length. 
Three Chinese li equal an English mile.
American astronauts said the Great Wall was the only man-made feature on Earth visible from the Moon. 
But extensive portions have crumbled away over the centuries. 
Some sections were damaged in a dozen years of war that began with Japan's invasion of China in 1937 and ended with the Communist defeat of the Nationalists in 1949. 
Other parts eroded through neglect.
Since 1950, the Government has allocated more than a million dollars to repair the wall, notably at Badaling, which was made a historical site in 1961. 
Beyond this showcase, whose visitors included President Reagan last April, the once formidable wall has been allowed to deteriorate.
Â 
'Only Dikes of Earth'
The current campaign was galvanized by a recent aerial survey that found only a sixth of the Great Wall north of Peking still intact; two-thirds was in virtual ruins. 
''In some areas, the damage is relatively great,'' said Peking Evening News last month. 
In one 12-mile section, it said, ''there are only dikes of earth amidst the wild grass.''
The survey did not include the remainder of the Great Wall.
Peking Evening News teamed up early this month with Peking Daily, Workers' Daily and Economic Daily to kick off the drive to renovate the Great Wall as a national heritage.
''The Great Wall is the symbol of the Chinese nation,'' said Zhang Zhihua, a Peking Evening News correspondent who is helping to run the campaign. 
''Loving and repairing the Great Wall will reflect the patriotic feelings of the Chinese people.''
Peking Evening News announced that about $240,000 was sent in by donors up to last Saturday. 
Mr. Zhang said that 80 percent of this came from organizations and 20 percent from individuals.
When China launched another fund- raising campaign earlier this year to save the endangered panda, Chinese companies using the panda as their brand name were urged to contribute. 
No such pressure has been put on companies using the Great Wall brand, which is almost as common in China.
But the Great Wall Hotel, a Chinese- American joint venture in Peking, and a factory manufacturing Great Wall raincoats have each sent in $4,350. 
Other contributors have included the state Cultural Relics Bureau, the Ministry of Nuclear Energy, the China Travel Service and the state-run airline C.A.A.C. 
Mr. Zhang said a few foreign donations had come in, but so far ''not very much.''
The vandalism of the Great Wall north of Peking occurred during the 1966-1976 Cultural Revolution, when the anarchy created by leftist policies ''made people have no sense of discipline,'' Mr. Zhang said.
Â 
Offer of Substitute Materials
''For example, some peasants dismantled sections of the Great Wall to repair their houses,'' Mr. Zhang said. 
''One of the points of the present drive is to tell the residents living around the Great Wall to bring back the bricks they took away.''
The authorities in Huairou County, northeast of Peking, have pledged to get the local farmers to turn in the chunks of wall by offering to supply substitute building material to thosewho cannot afford to buy their own.
The drive to restore the Great Wall has focused around Peking, but Su Weiyang, another Peking Daily journalist, said donations and letters had come in from all over China. 
After the Badaling section has been renovated, the work will continue at Mutianyu, another section northeast of Peking that is scheduled to open in late autumn to alleviate the tourist congestion at Badaling.
No other cities in northern China have announced similar drives in their areas. 
The problem has been handled so far by putting the worst parts of the Great Wall off limits to foreign tourists so the extent of damage will not become known.

text:
ï»¿
At the China Central Television station in Peking, a purple creature with a big pink nose appears on television monitors and says: ''Hello there boys and girls. 
This is your cute furry little pal Grover, and today I am going to demonstrate the difference between up and down.''
Television workers here are busily preparing Grover, Kermit the Frog, Cookie Monster, Big Bird and all the other Muppets of the Children's Television Workshop program ''Sesame Street'' for June debuts on Chinese television.
Children's television program "Sesame Street" is being prepared to be shown on Chinese television
The program has not yet been publicized, but translators have been dubbing ''Sesame Street'' into Chinese for several weeks, and workers at the station say there are plans to broadcast the program as many as four days a week in Chinese as a children's learning tool and in English for adult language training.
Given the popularity of studying English and of two American television series broadcast here, both Chinese and foreigners who have seen ''Sesame Street'' believe it may quickly become China's favorite program.
Â 
One Show Is Canceled
China introduced American programming two years ago with the series ''Man From Atlantis.''
Although the series was considered something of a dud in the United States, it became enormously popular in China, partly because Chinese programs have until recently been comparatively dull.
Another American series, a World War II commando saga called ''Garrison's Guerrillas,'' was suddenly taken off the air last week. 
The program was so popular that some Chinese believed street crime dropped every Saturday night when it was shown because all the hoodlums were watching it. 
Others, however, think it led local youth to imitate the violence on the screen.
At a recent national conference on broadcasting, a senior official said that the task of television in China was to ''integrate the universal truth of Marxism-Leninism-Mao Zedong thought with the accomplishment of the four modernizations, correctly publicize the party's line, principles and policies, carry out ideological and political education, popularize cultural and scientific knowledge, enrich people's cultural life, enhance socialist awareness and improve the cultural and scientific standards of the whole nation.''
Where Cookie Monster fits into this was not made clear.

file: A FAIR FOR CHINA BIBLOIPHILES.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's first international book fair opened today in Peking, offering something for bookworms of all tastes - if they could get in.
Browsers who managed to obtain passes could skim 50,000 titles ranging from the Encyclopedia Britannica in Chinese - 10 volumes at $4 apiece - to such children's books as ''Little Panda Loses His Way.''
No books are for sale, but officials said Chinese buyers could place orders for their organizations through the national book importer.
The officials did not say how passes were distributed. 
But for those who obtained one, the weeklong fair was a bibliophile's dream since foreign books are rarely available and extremely expensive in China.
Most of the books are in English, although some of the cramped publishers' stalls at the Peking Exhibition Hall featured titles in French, Russian and other languages.
''I'm actually a fan of English literature,'' said a man leafing through Louis L'Amour's western novel ''Ride the River,'' ''but this is great stuff, too.''
''This place is amazing,'' said a woman whose taste ran to spy novels as she peered down aisles laden with copies of ''Wild California,'' a nature book; ''The Fannie Farmer Cookbook,'' and Edgar Snow's ''Red Star Over China.''
Chinese officials said they planned to hold similar fairs every two years to promote global friendship and the exchange of information. 
They said this was the first such fair in China since the 1949 Communist revolution.
At a news conference last week, the officials said they would screen all the books - 70 percent of them on technical topics - before the fair opened to make sure none contained material insulting to other countries; they did not elaborate.
A total of 1,055 publishing houses from 35 countries were taking part in the fair, with most coming from the United States, the officials said.

The proprietor, Stanley Levy, has a wide acquaintance with food and food techniques and calls this the ''oldest continuing professional cooking school in Fairfield County.''

Joanne Hush's Kitchen, The Greens Farm Store, 1254 East Post Road. 
227-4151.
Â 
Courses: Chinese, Japanese, Dim Sum, Food Processor, Hors D'oeuvres, French, Bread Baking, Children's Courses.
Â 
Classes begin: Sept. 
20. Time: Morning and evening. 
Instructors: Joanne Hush, staff members, Perla Meyers and other guest instructors.
Â 
Maximum in class: 12 in participation courses, 24 in demonstration courses.
Â 
Costs: $30 and up, depending on number of sessions.
An adequate-size kitchen (in the rear of a book and gourmet-supply store), equipped with overhead mirrors and a good range of supplies and tools, is the setting for lessons by Mrs. Hush in her Chinese specialties, and guest demonstration in a variety of food preparation. 
She stocks a variety of oriental foods in her store, as well as numerous gourmet takeout items.
Â 
WILTON
The Culinary Arts, Gateway Shopping Center. 
762-7575.
Â 
Courses: Simply Sensational, French, Italian, Croissants, Food Processor Hors D'oeuvres, Food Processor Breads, Food Processor Desserts, A Holiday Feast, Gifts from the Kitchen, Great Wine Seminar.

Classes begin: Sept. 
23. Time: 10 A.M. to 1 P.M.; 7 to 10 P.M. Instructors: Cecile Rivel, Albert Joarant, Melissa Sere.

Maximum in class: 12 for Simply Senational (full participation class), up to 24 for demonstrationparticipation classes.
Â 
Cost: $30 to $135, depending on the course and the number of sessions.
The proprietor, Cecile Rivel, has been combining her culinarysupply shop with cooking classes for 12 years. 
A large and superbly equipped kitchen in the rear of the store provides extensive viewing space (with the help of wide overhead mirrors) and counter space for observation and participation for considerable numbers. 
There are 12 different courses scheduled, including one called Simply Sensational, which is geared to first timers in the kitchen.

Wilton Adult Education, Box 277. 
762-9046 or 762-2008.
Â 
Courses: Mondays - Food Processor, The Economy of Elegant Dining, Garnishes Galore, Uncanny Canned Cooking; Tuesdays - Microwave Cooking, Mexican, Cake Decorating for Beginners and Advanced; Wednesday - Perfect Pasta, Italian Cuisine; Thursdays - Hors D'oeuvres, Party Planning.

Classes begin: Sept. 
27.Time: 7:30 to 9:30 P.M. Instructors: Numerous.
