text:
ï»¿
FOR the rest of New York, winter, with snowy white trimmings, is still the order of the day, but in Chinatown, resplendent in rich reds and golds, it is the first weekend of the Spring Festival. 
Yesterday, the festival - which is the name for this celebratory season of the Chinese New Year - reached a climax with the customary frenzied Chinatown greeting of the first day of the year, but that is not the end of this joyous event.
Chinatown will continue to be a festival enclave for the remaining two weeks in which this most impressive of the 30 holidays on the Chinese calendar is observed. 
The welcome to the Year of the Rabbit still colors the streets of this ever-expanding and booming Lower East Side area of Chinese settlement. 
A walk along the crowded sidewalks, through Canal Street, down Mott Street, up the Bowery and East Broadway, brings to the discerning eye symbols of the celebration. 
In the buildings along the way, in those that house Chinatown institutions, there are music and dance programs this weekend that will make the assiduous stroller witness to even more of the New Year spirit.
Chinatown, holiday or not, is always an exciting walk-through, and it is even more so during these several weeks. 
As with most Where to eat in Chinatown, page C17. named areas in New York, Chinatown represents not so much geography as a texture of neighborhood, and nowadays East Side Chinatown extends north from Worth Street to Grand Street. 
One may approach Chinatown from any direction and become enmeshed in the spirit of the season, although it may be difficult at times to say whether the involvement is with the festival or the normally frantic swirl of everyday Chinatown. 
Chinese New Year is a time for home celebration, feasting and visiting, but the tradition of public performance has the holiday spilling over into streets and stores.
Canal Street, at the longitude of Centre Street, is a titillating point from which to start a walk eastward. 
The sidewalks are brimming with goods for sale, on building-side and on curbside. 
Live fish are a sidewalk-stall staple at all times, more so at New Year's. 
The Chinese word for fish, yu, is punningly akin to the word for abundance, and it is therefore lucky to have on the table when a year's outlook is in the programming stage; those without money to buy a real fish often have a symbolic wooden one at their hope-laden tables. 
Oranges are in profusion, a golden-hued fruit that hints of golden good fortune. 
Peanuts, pyramided in pretty gift-wrap packages, are the symbol of fertility. 
Dates and lotus seeds and special cakes are in demand, each of them sought for reasons of happy happenstance in nomenclature rather than for nutritional attraction. 
As the chef Kin Jing Mark, who teaches cuisine at the uptown China Institute in America, puts it: ''At New Year's, you don't eat the taste, you eat the meaning.''
Not everything on Canal Street is for the holiday. 
Much that meets the eye on these days meets the eye every day, from the splash of oddly shaped vegetables to the sidewalk Senegalese who was selling knives in what appeared to be a hopeless confusion of French and Cantonese. 
But at the southeast corner of Canal and Mulberry Streets, the florid front of a small store presents a vivid tableau to the passer-by. 
The wares on display are almost entirely for the New Year trade. 
Gold-colored objects, birds, pagodas and such are suspended from small red streamers, embodying two primary holiday colors. 
Some are little bells, others are merely eye-catchers, designed to do so from a friendly wall.
In an earthern dish, there are what appear to be bulbs, of the tulip type familiar to most of us. 
A knowledgeable onlooker allowed that they were sui xien, roots popular to take home at New Year's because they symbolize growth and ultimately sprout into angel-like yellow flowers. 
As with any folklore, interpretations are infinite, and one may make a choice of what is pure fact or charming fiction.
Â 
Joining in the Customs
A right turn onto Mott Street leads into what is Chinatown's main stem. 
Perhaps the bitter battlefield aroma of yesterday's firecracker orgy, which accompanied the fabled lion dance, still hovers over the pavement. 
The Year of the Rabbit is very much in evidence on this narrow, singularly Chinese New York thoroughfare that caters to visitor and inhabitant alike. 
At No. 74A Mott, the window of the Good Field Trading Company is ablaze with red-decor felicitations. 
Two of them, in Chinese, wish prosperity in business - whether on the four seas or, alternatively, on the three rivers. 
Chinese is a culture that bunches things, whether vices or virtues, advantages or disadvantages, in numbered slogans.
Inside, customers are buying hung bao, the little red envelopes, sold in packets, into which gift money, or perhaps certificates, are inserted before being passed on to children. 
There are hundreds of Chinese New Year's cards on sale and, if you want to take up the custom next year, this might be a choice time for a good buy. 
The man behind the counter said that New Year's greetings and general customs remain the same, although there are more regional variations noted these days with the influx of other Chinese into the basically Cantonese ingredient of Chinatown, whose largest element hails from the Taishan district.
Several doors south, at 62 Mott Street, is the home of the Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association, Chinatown's most venerable community institution and operator of a school that trains American-born generations in the ways of the forefathers.
''Every year the celebration is about the same,'' observed Joseph P. C. Mei, president of the association, which sponsors some of the holiday's most public events. 
''This is a time, a cultural thing, for the benefit of all Chinese people, no matter what religion - I'm Christian, myself -they all come to celebrate.''
This weekend, the association's premises will be working overtime on celebrating with a schedule of events free and open to the public, almost all in the auditorium. 
The programs should more than slake a thirst for the music, song and dance of Old China. 
Today at 2:30 P.M., the New York Chinese School is to perform Chinese folk dance and modern songs and offer other entertainment. 
At 7 P.M., Project Open Door of the Chinatown Planning Council and the Chinese Music Club fill the house with Chinese melody.
Tomorrow at 2:30 P.M., that very specialized form of music, Chinese opera, is to take the platform under the ministrations of the Chinese Cultural and Recreation Association of New York. 
From 7 to 9 P.M., the Hsing Yin Chorus of New York raises its voice in song for the season. 
On Sunday at noon, the New York Chinese School's drum and bugle corps is parade on Mott, to be followed at 2 P.M. by the New York Institute of Cantonese program of Chinese music, southern style - southern Chinese, that is. 
At 7 P.M., the Kou-Lien Musical Association tops off the weekend with a final round of Chinese music.
Â 
The Felicitous Homonym
The eye of the visitor threading his way through Chinatown's network of restaurants, groceries, bakeries and gift shops, on Mott Street or any other, may spot pastries of various composition, such as the niangao, a rice cake whose name could also be confused with a phrase meaning ''exalted year.''
For sale, and going like hot cakes, are dumplings that also are filled with felicitous homonym significance.
Continuing on Mott Street, one can make a left U-turn onto the Bowery, where it widens into Chatham Square, with its statue of Confucius and monument to Chinatown's veterans of American wars. 
At 26 Bowery, in an undistinguished walk-up building opposite the southern end of the Confucius Plaza complex, is the Asian Arts Institute and the home of the Asian-American Dance Theater. 
Its quarters, up two steep flights, are dedicated to promoting dance and visual arts, contemporary often linked to traditional.
Tomorrow at 8 P.M. and again on Sunday at 3 P.M., the dance group enters the third season of a series that bears the distinctly un-Chinese double-entendre title of ''D'Asia Vu.''
The program of New Year's celebration will fill the small hall with a sword dance and a contemporary work performed by Kuang-yu Fong, schooled in Peking Opera. 
There is also to be Bell Yung playing Chinese classical music on the gugin, a seven-stringed zither, and the Chinese Music and Arts Hai Yuen Choir performing folk songs. 
All this against a backdrop of an art installation by an artist named Kwok. 
Admission: $7. 
Reservations: 233-2154, 233-8660.
Â 
Where Cultures Meet
If legs and spirit are willing, the pedestrian can cross Chatham Square and continue north along East Broadway, past the Chinatown branch of the New York Public Library, which is just beyond Catherine Street, and under the Manhattan Bridge, which hovers over the venerable Sin Sun movie house. 
East Broadway leads to Seward Park, where the old Jewish influence is still evident even as the tide of Chinatown flows around it. 
East of the park is the old Jewish Daily Forward building, now home to a Chinese organization. 
At Grand Street, turn left, for a walk of several blocks to the Henry Street Settlement Arts for Living Center, at 466 Grand, near Clinton Street, an institution that encapsulates the many cultures, including Hispanic, black, Chinese and Jewish, that flourish in these parts. 
Sunday afternoon belongs, appropriately, to the Chinese. 
At 1 and 3:30 P.M., two groups, Music from China and the Young People's Chinese Cultural Center, join in concert, traditional style.
In the center's modern hall, Music From China's 10 musicians are to join the other organization's 30 dancers, featuring community artists and visiting professionals from China representing regional companies and academies in Beijing, Shanghai and Tianjin. 
Among the highlights: excerpts from the modern Chinese ballet of the classic tale ''Dream of the Red Chamber'' and an eight-woman saber-sword dance choreographed by Pei-pei Gu of the Shanghai Dance Drama Company, as well as pipa solos by Tang Liang-xing, a virtuoso of this Chinese lute.
Admission at the door: $7; in advance, $5; over-65's and students, $3. 
Information: 962-5698.
Â 
An Island of Quiet
To complete the grand tour in an ambiance of quiet contemplation that contrasts with all of the celebratory turmoil, one might look in at one of Chinatown's traditional Buddhist sanctuaries. 
It is customary for Chinese who grew up in the Buddhist tradition to pray at temples during this holiday. 
Chinatown has several temple-like institutions, some geared for visits by other than believers, such as the one on Mott Street north of the Community Center and others squirreled away on side-street second floors. 
There is a particular sense of peace that pervades the ground-floor American Society of Buddhist Studies at 214 Centre Street, two blocks north of Canal Street, which can be reached from the northern boundary of Grand by walking west, past the Bowery, through Little Italy, and then turning south at Centre.
This is not a temple, a full temple, a shaven-headed monk explained through a translator, but for the visitor it might well be. 
It is a high-ceilinged spacious room dominated by a large golden Buddha. 
Worshipers, who come and go during the day, kneel on cushions in a milieu of red hangings, of walls lined with religious statues, of flowers, of incense and, above all, of a profound hush that contrasts with the pushy world at the door.
''It is not a religious day,'' the monk said, ''but people come to pray, for good luck and for peace. 
Some people don't eat meat for the whole month of the New Year celebration, some eat vegetables only maybe for a day or two. 
If you eat vegetables, it means that you didn't kill life, and that is good.''
Â 
An Uptown Briefing
Actually, the ideal briefing to brace oneself for the sights and sounds of Chinese New Year is to be found far uptown from Chinatown in an exhibition in the tasteful and small gallery of the China Institute in America, in a town house at 125 East 65th Street (744-8181). 
The show, sponsored by the institute's Women's Association, takes note of the usual effigy of the kitchen god who has watched the family's conduct all year and will have its godly lips smeared with honey before being sent off in a blaze of fire to the Jade Emperor. 
Hours are 10 A.M. to 5 P.M. Mondays to Fridays; 11 A.M. to 5 P.M. Saturdays and 2 to 5 P.M. Sundays; admission is $1. 
The exhibition runs through Feb. 
15.
There are carvings of food and feasting, examples of red gift envelopes (with Hong Kong coins), sets of games and informative displays, among them one that describes each of the 12 animals of the lunar calendar. 
Those born in the Year of the Rabbit are considered singularly lucky in money matters, are said to make good companions and are caring and sensitive and most compatible with people who entered the world in the Years of the Snake, the Monkey and the Horse. 
Year of the Rabbit people include Confucius, Martin Luther, Albert Einstein, Queen Victoria and Bob Hope. 
Rabbit people are also lively, full of movement and keep escape routes open, according to one Chinese lawyer who cited an old Chinese saying, ''Every rabbit has three dens.''
As you can see, there is more to a Chinese New Year than meets the eye or the mouth.

GRIEVER
An American Monkey King in China. 
By Gerald Vizenor. 
238 pp. 
Normal: Illinois State University/ Fiction Collective/Sun & Moon Press. 
Cloth, $15.95. 
Paper, $8.95.
IMAGINATION is the real world,'' claims the mournful clown Griever de Hocus, ''all the rest is bad television.''
Griever, hero of Gerald Vizenor's second novel, is a Native American of mixed blood who abruptly appears as one of an ill-assorted group of American teachers at a Chinese university in Tianjin. 
Here his trickster heritage of tribal folklore and myth, not to mention his readiness to dream, helps him to cope with a socialist cadre and the closed society it monitors. 
For despite the repudiation of the Cultural Revolution, China remains suspicious of foreign devils. 
At the same time, it struggles with population control and welcomes modernization in the form of plastics, dermabrasion and Western venture capitalism.
Griever screams his rage at these responses into what he calls ''panic holes'' or turns it into playful wisdom in the manner of the monkey kings that populate China's myths of the poor and oppressed. 
Like the monkey kings, other animals - bears, bats, spiders, even mosquitoes - are also seen by Griever to help shape human conduct. 
And so, with a pet rooster for a companion, he follows their lead, playing basketball with hogs and liberating both chickens and political prisoners. 
Later, he disrupts the opening of an extravagant French restaurant and begins a brief affair with a local translator, a dalliance that leads to tragic consequences when it is discovered by her sinister father, a chain-smoking bureaucrat who conceals his contempt for Westerners behind a snakelike smile. 
Among the other figures Griever encounters are an enigmatic Russian painter who protects his hands with white mittens while serving a prison sentence hauling coal and an actor-sage who preserves Griever's history on a picture scroll that introduces his adventures with a cloudy but comic shrewdness that sets the tone for much of the novel.
Like his hero, Mr. Vizenor attempts to overcome the stale political realities of a Communist state through the renewal of language. 
For the characters as well as the reader, his world is laid out like brush strokes in an ink painting.
It is technology, however, rather than metaphor that finally determines the outcome of the novel. 
And after a climactic carnival, the story's magical disregard for time and space collapses under the weight of a high-tech escape from the mainland. 
Griever's often burlesque encounters, like his visionary impulses, reflect his desire to escape rather than confront China's dusty streets and oppressive social conditions. 
Thus his opposition to injustice eventually dissolves into a mere expression of personal vexation. 
The real arena for Griever's wild history is poetic dreamscape.
Though grounded in the author's experience as a teacher in China and in extensive historical references that are scrupulously identified in an epilogue, the novel gains its strength more from associations of color and from the play of words than from bare facts. 
Beyond our need for them, words, as Griever realizes, need us to hold down a sense of place. 
They also need to take off on their own. 
When they do, this modestly experimental, often luminous novel, which won the 1986 Illinois State University/Fiction Collective Award, evokes a world that does not mirror but parallels our own.

Chi Zhongguo, the manager of the Yaxin Silk Weaving Factory, proudly showed off a copy of ''a very famous oil painting'' that his plant had started mass-producing for the American market.
There, in luminous hues more vivid than Leonardo da Vinci's original, was ''The Last Supper,'' being recreated on mechanized looms on 100,000 synthetic velveteen tapestries in a choice of large or small sizes.
The order, from an American importer, is a different one for the Yaxin factory: Eighty percent of its production consists of disposable artificial silk prayer rugs for Moslems, mostly in the Middle East. 
The plant turns out 3 million prayer rugs a year now, Mr. Chi said, virtually all for export.
Profile of Yaxin Silk Weaving Factory in China, which is currently producing tapestry of Leonardo da Vinci's "The Last Supper" for US marketFormer Elegance
When the factory opened as a workshop in 1954, it specialized in elegant yun jin, or cloud-fabric silk brocade, of a quality for which this eastern Chinese city was long renowned. 
It still makes a bit of the gold-threaded fabric for ethnic markets in Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang.
But in a kind of Gresham's Law of weaving, synthetic, machine-woven fabrics have been replacing the silk brocades that were painstakingly hand-loomed. 
As Mr. Chi explained, ''All the old-fashioned looms are now in the countryside because they are not used for production anymore.''
Certainly, no one who has seen the graceful ceramics and delicately patterned material of traditional Chinese design could accuse the Chinese of a lack of taste. 
Even Chinese toys can be found in stores today of a sturdy tin construction that went out in the West with World War II.
Â 
Competing With Hong Kong
But as Chinese industry develops export markets, it finds that its low labor costs let it compete in areas that Hong Kong and Taiwan have dominated with cheaply produced goods.
For example, having found that Westerners find pandas cuddly, Chinese manufacturers have been using the furry black-and-white animal as bait for everything from bamboo screens and bathroom rugs to Christmas tree lights. 
On a more traditional note, a procession of jolly plastic Santa Clauses has been making its way out of the industrial depths of China in time for the Christmas season, which the Chinese do not celebrate.
The Yaxin factory, having moved almost entirely to synthetics, still makes traditional Chinese tapestry scenes such as the pine trees and cranes that symbolize longevity. 
These go mostly to the Japanese market, but in modest quantity.
Â 
Shift to Prayer Rugs
The plant, which exports almost everything it makes, got into the prayer rug business in 1966. 
As output increased, the labor force grew to 1,700, compared with only 60 when it was making brocade in 1954.
By working around the clock on three shifts, the plant now nets 4 million yuan, or nearly $2.4 million, in annual profits, which is impressive by Chinese standards. 
The prayer rugs earned an award as an outstanding product from the Chinese Ministry of Light Industry two years ago.
Mr. Chi said that no Moslems advised the factory on the rugs, which were copied from a pattern supplied by a customer. 
Nor do any appear to go to the estimated 10 million Moslems that live in China; they are only for export.
Â 
Market of 400 Million
''We don't have a clear idea of the population of Moslems,'' Mr. Chi said of his export market. 
''Some say about 400 million. 
But there is a big demand for rugs like this. 
All Moslem people over 16 should have at least one of these.''
Other estimates put the number of Moslems worldwide somewhat higher. 
As part of the Five Pillars of Islam, devout Moslems are enjoined to pray five times a day.
Mr. Chi is a good enough businessman to recognize a market when he sees one. 
''When the rugs get dirty, they throw it away and get another one, like Chinese used to do with towels,'' he explained.
Though China competes with a dozen or so other countries, some Moslem, in making prayer rugs, Mr. Chi insisted that his were better because they had a high-quality cotton backing and an attractive glossy, silk-like pile.
The factory would manufacture more but the chemical fiber thread must be imported, generally from Japan. 
''We're facing a shortage of artificial silk because some people abroad say its production causes pollution,'' Mr. Chi said.
Â 
Exports Through Government
The products themselves are actually ordered and sold through China's foreign trade corporations. 
The prayer rugs, Mr. Chi said, cost about $4.20 apiece to make and are sold to the Government for about $5.40. 
The Government sells them to the importer at a higher wholesale price.
While ''The Last Supper'' is more expensive because of its size and many colors - the large model costs about $15 to make - Mr. Chi said that he would welcome more such Western orders.
''The prayer rug sells only in Moslem areas,'' Mr. Chi said. 
But there is a wider market in the United States and Canada and European countries for other designs, since everyone enjoys a piece of art.''

PAUL TIPPETT was holding forth on the newly scrutable East, talking about the deal that American Motors has made to produce as many as 40,000 Jeeps a year in Peking. 
''This thing took four years to put together,'' he said, ''and it was interesting to see the changes in China during that time. 
They are really serious about coming into the 20th century. 
They say it won't go as fast as we would like, maybe, but they are very serious about doing it.''
Mr. Tippett, who signed the agreement in May as chairman and chief executive officer of A.M.C., said one of the changes he has noted is China's new interest in making things work.
''For instance,'' he said, ''it used to be that the water in the hotels didn't work most of the time. 
The first thing you'd do when you checked in was to put the stopper in the tub and turn on the tap. 
That way, if the water went on in the middle of the night, you'd get some.''
Now, he said, there is a tremendous amount of new construction, and the Chinese are openly critical of their own shortcomings. 
''One time, I was having dinner with the Mayor of Peking,'' he said, ''and I complimented him on the city's new airport. 
It is beautiful, and he thanked me. 
Then he shook his head and said, 'But it's not good enough. 
They are always losing luggage.'
I assured him the problem was not uniquely Chinese.''
Because of the complexity - and not least because of cultural differences - there was concern about the solidity of the Chinese commitment to American Motors right up to the last moment, Mr. Tippett said.
''But,'' he added, ''there's one nice thing about doing business in their system, where one guy makes the decision. 
He'll say, 'This is what we're going to do,' and that's what gets done. 
We asked about prices and profits and whether they had factored in inflation, and that puzzled them a lot. 
Inflation?
They don't have inflation.''
The joint venture with Peking Auto Works is just one of the moves being made to strengthen A.M.C., which, along with its French partner, Renault, has thus far posted sales figures for 1983 that are more than double those of last year.
Much of the success is founded on the Alliance, A.M.C.'s domestically built version of the Renault 9 sedan, and the line has been expanded for 1984 with a hatchback version called the Encore. 
The company's new line was, in fact, what brought Mr. Tippett to New York, and he pointed out that it represents the largest single-year investment in A.M.C.'s history.
''We invested more than a quarter-billion dollars on Cherokee and Wagoneer alone,'' Mr. Tippett said - and the new, little Jeeps are indeed A.M.C.'s biggest news.
Jeep, as everyone concedes, wrote the book on four-wheel drive. 
But the last major revision came 20 years ago, and an edited- down version was needed to face off against Chevrolet's mini- Blazer and Ford's Bronco II in the hotly contested market for sport/ utility compacts.
As a result, the new Cherokees and Wagoneers are 21 inches shorter than their predecessors. 
They are six inches narrower, four inches lower, and they weigh nearly 1,000 pounds less. 
The amazing thing is that interior space remains almost the same.
For those who need or want the big Wagoneer, A.M.C. has retained one full-dress version, which, with its leather upholstery now is called the Gran Wagoneer. 
But the big Cherokee is gone, as are six other models. 
The Spirit has been dropped, along with the Concord, Le Car, Eagle SX-4, Jeep CJ-5 and Renault 18i sedan.
Two engines are available in the down-sized Jeeps. 
There is a new 2.5-liter 4-cylinder and a 2.8- liter V-6, supplied to A.M.C. by General Motors and used head-to- head in the small Blazer. 
Three transmissions also are offered, with four- and five-speed manuals and a three-speed automatic. 
The standard all-wheel drivetrain is called Command-Trac, and it can be shifted from two- to four-wheel drive as the vehicle is moving. 
Selec-Trac, Jeep's fulltime system, is optional.
With a weight of only 2,900 pounds - about 250 pounds less than the offerings from Ford and Chevrolet - the Cherokee feels fairly snappy, even though its acceleration would be less than satisfactory in most other sorts of vehicles.
Inside, there is a nicely done-up dash and low-back bucket seats. 
Instrumentation is relatively complete, although a standard tachometer is missing, a surprising lack in a vehicle that often will be used for trailer towing and low- gear/high-rev off-roading.
The body is more rounded than in the past, with the sheet metal helping aerodynamics and lending its support to a fuel-economy estimate of 24, city, and 33, highway. 
Jeep's rugged good looks have been preserved, though, and the new baby is going to be a strong contender in a segment that is expected to claim a quarter of the four-wheel-drive market by 1985.

text:

Periodically one has to answer a summons from Hwa-Min Hsu, whose good offices are in Canal Street. 
Mr. Hsu knows practically all there is worth knowing about Chinatown, and so any day he is prepared to hold an inspection is a day of enlightenment, a gift. 
This one turned out to be the afternoon of the Chinese massage.
But first, some lunch and a ruminative discussion of various affairs. 
Mr. Hsu is building a hotel in Chatham Square, the first hotel in Chinatown - but it is too early to go into that, he said. 
Some tea and noodles showed up on the table, then some steamed asparagus, followed by a duck.
The Chinese movie theaters are slowly going under as a result of the popularity of video cassettes - but that is a subject for another time. 
Mr. Hsu slept only three hours the night before, a frequent occurrence for a businessman who deals by telephone with Asia. 
This produces stress and tension, and what reduces stress and tension?
Massage. We have arrived!
Mr. Hsu said that a few years back, change visited the barbershops of his native soil, Taiwan, as well as the mainland. 
Women infiltrated. 
What was more, the women offered massages. 
A man - or a woman, for that matter -could be shorn and kneaded into a stress-free puddle all in one stop. 
''We're not talking about porno massage parlors,'' Mr. Hsu cautioned. 
''No sex. 
This is for pressure, for tension. 
That's the job of the barbershop in China.''
One of these emporiums opened in Chinatown two years ago, and another came along soon after. 
Mr. Hsu is but one of many who are nuts about them. 
Even at $25 an hour, he said, it is a great service for the restaurant workers who stand all day, as well as the garment workers who sew for hours, getting themselves down in the back. 
He himself visits twice a week, sometimes forgetting he ought to get a haircut, too. 
As for the old style, all-male, lightless, basement barbershop-mah-jongg parlor of Chinatown days gone by, well, there are still a dozen around, Mr. Hsu pointed out on his after-lunch walk to modernity but they are mostly frequented by older men.
Up one flight of stairs, practically at the foot of the Brooklyn Bridge, Mr. Hsu entered the Ming Kai Barbershop, all chrome and high tech. 
''The male barbershop looks very sloppy,'' he pointed out. 
''This is decorated.''
He was greeted by several women who seemed to know him well. 
There was piped-in music and for a moment it sounded as if Patti Page had lost her mind, but soon it became clear it was the work of a Shanghai stylist.
''Women are better with massage,'' Mr. Hsu continued. 
''The female always does better than the male, always.''
Mr. Hsu then motioned to a darkened room off the well-lighted barbering room. 
In here were six well-padded reclining chairs and five of them were occupied by Chinese men who lay on their stomachs smoking cigarettes while five women in blue skirts and white blouses walked on their backs in their stocking feet, the women keeping their balance by holding on to chrome bars tracked across the ceiling.
It was just past noon, and Mr. Hsu was going to sit for a shampoo, haircut and a little massage tinkering about the head and shoulders. 
''You go in there,'' he said, insisting that ''you'' have the full treatment, soup to nuts, stem to stern. 
In a bit, a woman who would later become known as No. Seven came over and removed jacket, sweater and shoes and loosened the collar wide enough to let in a Shriner. 
Then she went to work.
This was Chinese acupressure, the fingers working down defined highways on the body. 
The trick is to release chi, or trapped energy. 
They begin at the head and don't miss a spot, down to the toe and fingertips.
Some time later, Mr. Hsu stuck his head in the door and said: ''I have to go. 
You stay. 
It's all taken care of. 
Just tip the girl.''
A good while later, from deep in slumber, there came the sound of unenthusiastic applause, thin clapping, that grew in stages so loud that it took ''you's'' breath away, until he put his hand to his lungs and realized someone was trying to beat the daylights out of his chest. 
A voice, ''Uh, the manager, she want to know how long you want the girl to massage?''
The next image that hove into view would have killed a heart patient. 
The vista was a dozen Chinese women, all leaning in close, only one of whom spoke English. 
No. 7 was wringing her sore hands. 
''You'' got up and scattered every greenback he possessed, like birdseed, gave effusive thanks and wobbled down the stairs to greet the night, shirttails flapping, a necktie so curlicued ''you'' could use it to uncork a new Beaujolais. 
''You'' was embarrassed but incredibly relaxed.

text:
ï»¿
It's been quite a season at the Bronx Zoo. 
New York City's two most distinguished - and cuddly - visitors downed 6,800 pounds of bamboo, 736 eggs and 2,208 apples and carrots.
Ling Ling, the male panda, celebrated his second birthday with a dash of whipped cream on his panda bread, which is a soggy soybean and cornmeal mixture. 
More important, the youngster learned to eat bamboo here.
Yong Yong, the female, tore down a mulberry tree or two, fought off an illness last summer and ended up gaining 20 pounds -bringing the 7-year-old's weight to a zaftig 207.
Along the way, the two pandas watched more than 1 million visitors file past, exhibiting themselves in the sort of funny hats, Bermuda shorts and skimpy halter tops you don't get to see a lot of in the mist-shrouded mountains of southwest China.
Â 
But Sunday was the last day of the pandas' six-month visit and the ''pandamonium'' was supposed to be over. 
Over the weekend, people crowded in for one last look. 
Newspapers printed farewell photos. 
Television announcers said goodbye.
The last $83.95 stuffed panda had days earlier been grabbed up. 
So had the hats with the panda faces, the panda salt and pepper shakers and the $5.95 (but not the $9) panda earrings.
All that remained was for Busch Gardens in Tampa, Fla., the next stop for the pandas, to pick up the animals. 
But for reasons unknown to Bronx Zoo officials, that did not happen.
Their current expectation is that the pandas will be claimed tomorrow or Friday. 
But the delightful upshot of the confusion has been to give this week's zoo-goers a nice surprise - pandas without crowding or consternation.
''We're so, so lucky,'' said Lisa Dautrich, who Monday journeyed from Oneonta in upstate New York on the off chance she might have one last chance to pursue her passion for pandas.
A typical day, she happily confided, might find her clad in panda sweater, panda slippers and a panda hat. 
Her house is crammed with stuffed pandas, panda cookie jars and panda pictures. 
She and her husband, Ken, have seen pandas several times at the Washington zoo.
''We have a whole room decorated panda,'' Ken said grimly. 
But not everything about the pandas is warm and cozy. 
For one thing. they don't like each other, and the zoo has chosen to display them in shifts.
Another characteristic of pandas was abundantly clear yesterday morning: They sleep almost incessantly. 
Yong Yong - the only one on display - was cuddled in a ball on top of a pile of branches. 
Each time she scratched, the crowd applauded wildly.
''They remind me of me,'' Ray Mejias, a ticket taker, said. 
''All they do is sleep and eat.''
Â 
Giant pandas have fascinated Americans at least since Theodore Jr. and Kermit, sons of Teddy Roosevelt, became the first Westerners to shoot and kill one in 1929.
Less than a decade later, live pandas had become a national fascination, as Chicago's Brookfield Zoo, and then the Bronx Zoo acquired specimens. 
Panda bathing suits, panda nursery furniture and even a panda cocktail (equal parts plum brandy, apple brandy, gin and orange juice) swept the nation.
But China turned Communist in 1949, and imperialist running dogs saw their panda supply halted. 
Pan-dah, the Bronx Zoo's last panda, died in 1951, and there seemed no hope for a replacement.
Then, in the early 1970's, China began giving pairs of pandas to such foreign capitals as Washington and London - but still none to New York. 
In recent years, an alarmingly shrinking panda population has spurred the Chinese Government to limit panda exports to visits of just a few months.
But even a few months seemed worth the effort to Mayor Koch, who so bedeviled authorities in Beijing, a sister city of New York, that he has said he became known as ''the guy who wants the pandas.''
The pandas arrived in April to be exhibited in the same spot as Pan-dah. 
''The night they arrived was like all Christmases, birthdays and holidays rolled into one,'' James G. Doherty, the zoo's curator, said.
Now, they are leaving what Mr. Doherty calls a void - the same feeling zoo officials in Los Angeles, San Francisco and Toronto had after their panda visits ended.
''It's the kind of feeling you get when a good friend comes to visit and then leaves,'' said an official of the San Francisco Zoo. 
''Very sad,'' said the Los Angeles man. 
Dr. Edgar E. Coons, a behavioral neuroscientist at New York University who has studied humans' affection for pandas, likened their departure to the ''empty feeling you get when the young ones leave the nest.''
Nobody seems to feel emptier than Pam Manning, the pandas' No. 3 keeper. 
''I'm upset,'' she said, holding one of the last pans of apples, carrots and panda bread that she may ever prepare. 
''Ling Ling is really just starting to learn to eat bamboo.''

Official accounts today of the visit to China by a senior Soviet official offered new indications of the limited expectations both Governments appear to have for the occasion.
The official, Ivan V. Arkhipov, a First Deputy Prime Minister, is the most senior Soviet official to come here in 15 years. 
His visit is being closely watched for signs of any thaw in the chilly political relations that have prevailed for nearly a quarter of a century between Moscow and Peking.
Official accounts of visit to China by Ivan V Arkhipov, Soviet First Deputy Prime Minister, offer new indications of limited expectations both Governments appear to have for occasion; Arkhipov is most senior Soviet official to come to country in 15 years (S)
But so far, after two days, both sides have taken care to emphasize the differences that have prevented an improvement in their relations. 
At the same time, they have stressed their readiness to expand trade, economic and scientific exchanges, and to continue their search for better overall ties.
For both sides, the most important fact about the the visit is probably that it is taking place at all, after a last- minute postponement in May when Moscow evidently wished to show its displeasure over Chinese troop clashes with Vietnam and over the warmth displayed when President Reagan came to Peking in April.
Â 
Won't Return for Funeral
The symbolic importance of the Arkhipov visit was underscored today when the Russian remained here rather than return to Moscow for the funeral of Defense Minister Dmitri F. Ustinov, as unofficial reports from the Soviet capital Friday had suggested he might.
The Chinese wariness toward the visit was suggested by the coverage given in today's editions of People's Daily, the Communist Party paper, which put accounts of Mr. Arkhipov's arrival here and the banquet given for him Friday night on the bottom of its back page. 
Important official visitors from friendly countries are generally accorded front-page display.
At the banquet, Mr. Arkhipov and his host, Deputy Prime Minister Yao Yilin, struck a cordial personal note in their speeches that reflected an acquaintance dating back to the Russian's years here heading the Soviet aid program in the 1950's.
The two officials also spoke of their nations' common interest in better ties, Mr. Yao saying China ''sincerely hoped'' for improved relations and Mr. Arkhipov responding that it was in the fundamental interests of both nations ''to put these relations into the orbit of friendship and good-neighborliness.''

file: ADVANTAGES SHIFT SUBTLY IN A DELICATE THREE-HANDED GAME.txt
text:
ï»¿
The United States, China and the Soviet Union last week seemed to be playing another round in an international strategy game, with each side trying to avoid being isolated by the others. 
The stakes were high - if any two joined forces, they might endanger the country left out. 
Playing the game vigorously in Peking, Defense Secretary Caspar W. Weinberger met with Chinese leaders and announced that Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang would come to Washington in January and that President Reagan would be going to Peking in April.
Mr. Reagan's advisers saw the planned trip as a chance to play up his role as a world leader, an obvious asset if he seeks re-election seven months later. 
(The China visit may also provide a convenient reason for rearranging his Asian itinerary, delaying a visit next month to the Philippines, where anti-regime turmoil threatens security and political hazards.)
Subtle shifts in triangular relationships between US, USSR and China in recent years reviewed, with China now perceived as leading in obtaining US concessions without much concrete commitment; Sec Caspar Weinberger and Zhang Aiping illustrated (S)
After Washington reclassified China as a ''friendly power'' and thus eligible for more high technology exports, and the United States agreed to import $800 million of Chinese textiles, Peking seemed ready to reciprocate, at least on the protocol level. 
Washington had urged Mr. Zhao to come so Mr. Reagan could return the visit.
In China, Mr. Weinberger talked up the Soviet threat and the value of closer strategic ties between Washington and Peking. 
He dangled a list of possible ''defensive'' arms China could buy, notably antiaircraft weapons and antitank guns. 
But the Chinese seemed uninterested in pursuing an open military alliance (which could also be difficult for Mr. Reagan, after his repeated pledges of support for Taiwan). 
As a reminder that they were not tying themselves to Washington, the Chinese announced talks on normalizing relations with the Russians would resume on Thursday. 
As to Soviet-American relations, they remained in a frozen state. 
Mr. Reagan last week took a different tack with a ''high road'' speech at the United Nations, stressing the need for arms control accords. 
But he also continued his verbal assault on Moscow for shooting down the South Korean airliner and he accused the Russians of violating previous accords. 
Yuri V. Andropov, the Soviet leader, obviously concerned about the propaganda effects of the plane incident and angered by Mr. Reagan's insults, condemned the Administration on all fronts.
As a result of the poor state of relations with the Russians, Washington's ability to reap benefits from the triangular game is no longer what it was in the early 1970's when the Nixon-Kissinger Administration finessed both Communist countries while avoiding the appearance of ganging up against either. 
This was easier when the Soviet Union and China were in a state of mutual military alert. 
The ability to play the Chinese against the Russians ended in 1980, after the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan. 
President Jimmy Carter cut back relations with Moscow and put off seeking Senate ratification of a strategic arms limitation treaty.
Mr. Carter also sought a strategic relationship with China against the Russians. 
But although Peking had once sought better relations, Washington found it unreceptive when the Carter Administration got around to talking of a virtual alliance. 
The Chinese seemed to decide to stand aloof, although they, even more than Americans, had reason to be concerned about Soviet military actions in Afghanistan and Southeast Asia.
Testing the Waters
China's doubts about cooperating with the United States were fortified when Mr. Reagan, a long-time supporter of Taiwan, became President. 
Prolonged debate ensued about Taiwan and issues such as textile limits, handling of defectors, and whether Pan American World Airways should be allowed to fly to Taipeh.
By last year, the Kremlin sensed it could break out of its isolation in the triangle and try to turn the tables on Washington. 
The Russians began to court the new Chinese leadership, while Peking, seeking to depict itself as a leader of the nonaligned bloc - where being seen as an American ally is a liability - seemed more than willing to test the waters with Moscow. 
In so doing, China put pressure on Washington to yield on Taiwan.
Peking, which has extracted economic and technological assistance in return for normalization with Washington, now is insisting on security concessions from Moscow. 
China wants the Soviet Union to reduce its heavy troop concentration along the Chinese border, pull its forces out of Afghanistan and end its backing for the Vietnamese occupation of Cambodia.
If the United States was the major beneficiary from the triangular relationships of the 1970's, the Chinese seem to have learned the lesson well and emerged as the leading player now. 
Foreign Minister Wu Xueqian, in New York for the United Nations General Assembly, made that clear in a speech to the National Committee on United States-Chinese Relations. 
''China,'' he said, ''always adheres to an independent foreign policy, never attaches itself to any big power or group of powers and never yields to pressure from any big power. 
China has always adhered to principles, neither playing the Soviet card to put pressure on the United States, nor playing the American card to put pressure on the Soviet Union.''
Despite Mr. Wu's protestations, however, American officials were watching to see if Mr. Andropov, having virtually frozen relations with Washington, would now meet Chinese demands at least halfway. 
He could do so by agreeing to reduce Soviet troops in Afghanistan or to a troop pullback from the Chinese border area. 
With Mr. Reagan due to visit China in seven months, there is time for Moscow to act to stay in the game.

file: AFRICAN SCENES_ _GHOSTLY_ RAIDS TO CHINESE AID.txt
text:
ï»¿
A dozen Angolan soldiers, AK-47 assault rifles at the ready, dogged every step taken last week by a group of reporters looking at a refugee camp in Angola's east central province of Moxico. 
The soldiers' presence belied an official myth.
According to Angola's Marxist regime, there is no organized internal opposition. 
Jonas Savimbi and his National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, known as Unita, are ''phantoms.''
Bernard Nossiter discusses present conditions in Angola and Sudan
The only real threats come from South African troops or ''reactionaries,'' an official from the Ministry of Culture explained at great and vehement length recently when this reporter stopped in Angola during a swing through Africa.
In fact Moxico and neighboring provinces are frequently raided by Savimbi guerrillas. 
The military escort joined the group in case the Savimbi ''phantoms'' decided to stage a demonstration for the correspondents. 
They did not, but the gap between the official line and prudent practice was evident.
The Sudan's conservative Moslem society has been strained by female refugees from Ethiopia. 
Fleeing the wars of secession there, the women continue to cling to their form-fitting dresses and their relaxed and easy manner with men. 
They contrast strikingly with the Sudanese women, swathed in concealing robes and rarely present in mixed company.
The Sudan's Commissioner for Refugees, Abdul Rahman el-Beshir, acknowledges as much with a bureaucratic gloss. 
''We welcome strangers in this country,'' he said, ''but there are cultural problems of incompatibility. 
Moslems resent the liberal ways the Ethiopian females are having.''
On city streets, the Ethiopian women are often subjected to obscene taunts and gestures. 
Respectable Sudanese families avoid cafes that the refugee women frequent. 
Some of the Ethiopians are forced or induced into concubinage or prostitution. 
Mr. Rahman speaks with sympathy of ''these wretched people, compelled to leave their country.''
At the airport in Addis Ababa, about 60 Chinese men and one woman sit patiently, most of them dressed in neat Western suits. 
This is no package tour but a purposeful exhibition of Peking's attempt to win friends and influence distant people.
One member of the group looks up from Le Monde to explain that they are doctors, agronomists, engineers, and road and dam builders. 
They are fanning out to Tanzania, Mozambique, Mauritania and the Sudan to show Africans how things are done in China. 
Peking cannot afford much foreign aid in cash but it is rich in technical assistance, an effective way of making its weight felt.
Commissar Marques Wassowowa occupies the palace in Luena from which the Portuguese once governed the Angolan province of Moxico. 
The palace is still splendid with its flagstone courtyard, tiled roof, sweeping paneled dining room facing a curved marble veranda, plush chairs, delicate tiled bath and hospitable jug of Scotch for guests.
But the splendor is fading. 
The carpets are torn, the woodwork cracked. 
The window panes are broken and the plaster molding is chipped. 
The commissar evidently has other priorities.
Whether he should is a question raised by some students of Africa. 
A leading expert, Jean-Claude Concollato, on leave from the Sorbonne to work in the Sudan for the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, contends that much of Africa's instability flows from the lack of strong central government. 
Too many states, he says, are marked by a plethora of regulations whose writ does not run much beyond the ministries.
Even a revolutionary Government like Angola's might find some use in tangible symbols of authority, in keeping up Luena's palace. 
At the very least it would serve as a reminder that scarce capital equipment requires careful maintenance.
The 125-mile road from Khartoum, the Sudan's capital, southward to Wad Medani, runs through a bleak parched landscape almost denuded of trees, peppered with dusty shrubs. 
Walled villages of mud brick bake in the strong sun. 
Scrawny herds of goats and cattle search for fodder. 
The occasional incongruous textile or cement factory breaks the empty horizon.
The Blue Nile runs invitingly alongside, but there is neither capital nor manpower to tap its life-giving waters and irrigate the semi-desert.
When the road bends east to Gedaref, the scene suddenly changes. 
Gum arabic trees, green and promising, fill the skyline. 
Patches of soft green cotton emerge. 
The ground is covered with brown stalks from the sorghum crop. 
Conical thatched-roof houses show that nature is more abundant here.
This region gets three times the rain, and for twice as long, as the country below Khartoum. 
Gedaref is a rich town whose farmers and merchants hire Ethiopian refugees as laborers and servants. 
Failure and success in the Sudan depends not on man but on nature, on the presence or absence of rain.

file: AFTER A 37-YEAR ABSENCE, U.S. VESSELS VISIT CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
As brass bands played, three United States Navy warships, each flying China's flag, tied up here today and became the first American vessels to visit China since the Communists took power.
A gray early-morning haze shrouded the harbor as guns from the arriving American ships fired a 21-gun salute in honor of the Chinese Navy. 
Then, nudged gently by large white tugboats, the guided-missile frigate Rentz loomed through the mist with sailors in blue pea jackets and white caps standing at attention along her entire length.
Three elderly Chinese ships, a destroyer, a frigate and a submarine, were moored nearby with dozens of colorful signal flags flapping from their rigging. 
Chinese sailors stood at attention on deck while a United States Navy band aboard the guided-missile cruiser Reeves struck up ''Happy Days Are Here Again.''
Joining the Reeves and the Rentz on the seven-day port call is the American destroyer Oldendorf.
The visit, announced by Defense Secretary Caspar W. Weinberger last month on a trip to China, is being portrayed by American military and diplomatic officials as a major step in the increasingly close military ties between the two countries.
The visit also comes as details of a $550 million sale of equipment to the Chinese Air Force, announced in April, are being made public.
The commander of the United States Pacific Fleet, Adm. James A. Lyons Jr., was aboard the Reeves and spoke of the importance of the visit to the strategic interests of both countries.
''We recognize this as a historic port visit, a further step in developing and enhancing the relationship between our two countries,'' Admiral Lyons told American and Chinese journalists. 
''A key element in furthering stabilityI in this region is fostering the U.S.-China relationship. 
We also share a common concern that no one country should dominate Asia or the world.''
Â 
Some Advice for Newcomers
Despite the assertions of American officials that the 1,000 sailors had been given no special instructions on how to behave while in China, many of the sailors could be seen clutching a 32-page pamphlet titled ''A Sailor's Liberty Guide to China,'' a document filled with admonitions on proper behavior.
''China does not have bar girls,'' read one warning. 
''Drink in moderation,'' cautioned another passage, while the fiery Chinese liquor mao-tai was introduced with a blunt, ''Watch out.''
The first glitch of the visit did not involve onshore comportment, but naval etiquette. 
Although the Chinese ships across the pier were flying signal flags from their rigging in what the Navy calls ''full dress,'' the American vessels were not similarly bedecked.
Several Navy officers said the Chinese had protested the failure of the American ships to go to ''full dress'' and refused to proceed with the welcoming ceremony until a precise and formal equality had been established.
Hastily, sailors aboard the three American ships began clambering up masts. 
Piles of bright signal flags were produced from lockers, and after nearly two hours they were in place on the American ships.
Adm. Ma Xinchun, the commander of China's northern fleet, which is based here, then strode to the gangplank of the Reeves to officially welcome Admiral Lyons to China.
The last American naval visit to these waters ended on May 24, 1949, as Communist armies pressed south and east. 
The U.S.S. 
Dixie, a repair ship built to service destroyers, took aboard the last Americans in Qingdao and steamed toward Hong Kong.
Qingdao owes its genesis as a major city to 19th-century German colonial designs. 
The Germans held Qingdao for 16 years before losing it in World War I, and the broad avenues carved by German planners are still lined with heavy stone and brick villas.
While it has been more than 37 years since American sailors trudged up Jungshan Road, the main commercial street here, the memory of the Americans has lingered.
''The Jungshan was the world of the Americans,'' said a 79-year-old man who gave his name only as Lao Liang, or ''old Liang.''
''That's where all the action was,'' he said. 
''They paid with American dollars and we took in American dollars.''
Â 
'A Great Event'
Even younger Chinese possess a sort of collective memory of the Americans, a recollection that is usually less than kind. 
''The Americans, they grabbed women and didn't follow traffic signs,'' said Tang Tingxing, a 39-year-old shipyard worker.
Still, as he stood at the gate to the navy yard waiting for a glimpse of the American sailors, Mr. Tang said he was excited about the visit. 
''I think this is a great event,'' he said.
Along Jungshan Road today, the Americans soon found the tall, green bottles of Tsingtao beer that have made this city famous.
At a park dedicated to the 20th-century writer Lu Xun, Patrick M. Stevens, 22, lowered his camera for a moment. 
''I think this is great,'' said the sailor from Amityville, L.I. 
''This is the first ship here in 37 years. 
This is history. 
We're little ambassadors.''

A senior Vietnamese official interviewed in a Polish newspaper has depicted his country with unusual candor as one troubled by grave military, economic and political problems.

Ethnic Chinese Attacked
He added that many of the former entrepreneurs were members of the ethnic Chinese minority and charged that they were linked to a global ''network'' that was conducting economic war against Vietnam. 
He referred to alleged smuggling of goods into Vietnam from Bangkok, Hong Kong and Singapore.
Foreign residents and visitors tend to believe that the goods sent into Vietnam from abroad and traded largely on the black market have provided the people of Vietnam's cities with the margin of survival while the official, Government-run sector is unable to meet basic needs.
Mr. Tung accused China and other enemies of Vietnam of conducting what he characterized as ''small war'' against his country. 
He described this as consisting of ''continuous tension'' created by Chinese military strength on Vietnam's northern border and the fomenting of partisan movements in Cambodia and Laos.

Economically, the Vietnamese official said, ''small war'' consists of the creating of ''economic confusion and disorganization'' of the Vietnamese market by the overseas Chinese.
Â 
'Economic Blockade' Charged
Furthermore, Mr. Tung charged, an ''economic blockade'' is being carried out against Vietnam. 
Presumably, he meant the suspension of various Western and Japanese economic aid programs in retaliation for Vietnam's invasion of Cambodia in 1979 and its continuing occupation of that country.
The Vietnamese official said the three principal tasks facing the Hanoi Government were defense, feeding the population and laying the foundations of a socialist system. 
While southern Vietnam has been Communist for only seven years, the northern half of the country has been Communist since 1954 and governed by a socialist system that even Eastern European Communists consider of excessively doctrinaire rigor.
Referring to Vietnam's serious food shortages, Mr. Tung said that balancing defense requirements against food needs ''has influenced the standard of living.''
But he added, ''When even the United States has the dilemma of cannons versus butter, why shouldn't we have a dilemma, arms versus rice?''
Acknowledging ''serious difficulties in everyday life,'' Mr. Tung asserted that the Vietnamese were not meat eaters and accepted an annual consumption level of 22 pounds a person. 
The assertion, which is not supported by knowledge of Vietnamese eating habits, caused a Pole to remark that the only purpose of publishing the interview was to persuade Poles that some countries were even worse off than Poland.

file: AIDS RESEARCH RIVALS SHARE A MAJOR AWARD.txt
text:
ï»¿
TWO scientific rivals, each playing a central role in finding the virus that causes AIDS and then becoming involved in an international legal dispute over the research, were among those named yesterday as winners of the Albert Lasker Medical Research Awards, an honor that has often gone to people who later won the Nobel Prize.
The two are Dr. Robert C. Gallo of the National Cancer Institute and Dr. Luc Montagnier of the Pasteur Institute in Paris. 
Their research teams each discovered a virus that is now known to cause the deadly acquired immune deficiency syndrome. 
Research at many centers has demonstrated that the two viruses are the same.
In addition to Dr. Gallo and Dr. Montagnier, there were four other awards. 
The winners were Dr. Myron Essex, chairman of the department of cancer biology at the Harvard School of Public Health, who has also made important contributions to AIDS virus research; Dr. Rita Levi-Montalcini, of the Institute of Cell Biology in Rome, and Dr. Stanley Cohen, of Vanderbilt University, experts on cellular growth factors; and Dr. Ma Haide, senior adviser to the Ministry of Health of the People's Republic of China. 
Dr. Ma, an American doctor whose original name was George Hatem, was a physician to Mao ZeDong and made important contributions to public health in China over many years.
The Albert and Mary Lasker Foundation has been making its annual awards for important contributions to medical research and public health since 1944. 
Over the years, 42 Lasker Award winners have later been awarded the Nobel Prize, the most prestigious of all honors for research in medicine, physiology and chemistry.
Three of the six Lasker winners this year are among the world's leaders in AIDS research. 
The disease is caused by a retrovirus that attacks certain vital white blood cells called T lymphocytes and cripples the immune defense system. 
Retroviruses were first linked to human cancer by Dr. Gallo's group in the 1970's with the discovery of a virus that is believed to cause some cases of leukemia. 
This group of retroviruses is now called ''human T-cell lymphotrophic viruses'' because they attack T-cells.
Retroviruses are named for the fact that they reverse the normal genetic message sequence of DNA to RNA for manufacture of protein. 
They have special enzymes, reverse transcriptases, that force an infected cell to translate the genetic message encoded in the virus's RNA into the form of DNA so that the cell is forced to reproduce the virus.
In 1983, Dr. Montagnier reported discovery, in an AIDS patient, of a retrovirus that attacked T-cells. 
His team also developed an antibody test to detect the virus infection in humans. 
The following year, Dr. Gallo published studies of an AIDS-related retrovirus and an antibody test to detect evidence of the virus infection. 
Although their status was unclear at first, the viruses are now generally accepted as being the same and being the cause of AIDS.
In May 1985, a patent was awarded to the United States Government for the antibody test developed by Dr. Gallo's group. 
An earlier application for an American patent by the Pasteur Institute is still to be acted upon. 
Last December, the Pasteur Institute sued the United States Government, contending that Dr. Montagnier's group was the first to isolate the virus and to ''recognize the significance thereof in the development of methods of detection of AIDS and pre-AIDS conditions.''
In July a Federal judge dismissed the suit. 
The Pasteur Institute is appealing the dismissal, and the related dispute over patent rights concerning the antibody tests is still unresolved.
In announcing the 1986 winners yesterday, the foundation made no mention of the dispute. 
Nevertheless, the announcement was revised repeatedly to avoid becoming, itself, a factor in the controversy. 
In the award citations both scientists were credited with ''unique contributions to understanding the cause of AIDS.''
Dr. Montagnier was cited for ''discovery of the retrovirus later shown to be responsible for this major new threat to world health.''
Dr. Gallo's citation honored him for ''his brilliant investigations of human T-cell lymphotrophic viruses, and for his intellectual and scientific leadership in AIDS research.''
Dr. Gallo was also awarded a Lasker prize in 1982 for his research on retroviruses. 
Multiple awards from the foundation have been extremely rare.
In telephone interviews both scientists expressed pleasure over the awards.
Dr. Essex was cited for studies of the effect of retroviral infections in the human immune system and for contributions to the understanding of AIDS as a disease. 
Since the 1970's he has been a frequent collaborator with Dr. Gallo's group at the cancer institute.
Dr. Levi-Montalcini discovered the first known substance that regulates the growth of cells. 
Today it is known as the nerve growth factor. 
The foundation cited her for ''her profoundly original concept that the growth of specific cells is regulated by soluble substances, and for her discovery of Nerve Growth Factor.''
Today several such growth factors are known although their natural roles in living tissues are not altogether clear.
Dr. Cohen, who collaborated with Dr. Montalcini for several years, discovered another of the growth factors, epidermal growth factor, and an enzyme called tyrosine kinase, which today is known to be vital to the metabolism of cells. 
Study of such growth factors is considered important to understanding how humans and animals develop from single fertilized eggs to complete individuals comprising many billions of cells. 
Study of aberrent functioning of such growth factors or their receptors is also a big issue in contemporary cancer research.
In Chinese, Dr. Ma Haide's name means ''virtue from overseas.''
He was born in Buffalo in 1910 and went to China as a young physician in 1933 to study tropical medicine. 
From 1936 to 1949 he served under Mao ZeDong as medical adviser to the Chinese Red Army and thereafter has served the Chinese Government in major public health campaigns against venereal disease and leprosy. 
The citation for his Lasker Award said he made ''legendary contributions to the conquest of venereal disease and the eradication of leprosy in China'' and said his accomplishments ''made medical history and improved the health and well-being of 800 million people.''
The award winners will deliver lectures on their work at a symposium Nov. 
19 at the Rockefeller University. 
Each winner will receive $15,000 and a statuette of the Winged Victory of Samothrace, symbolizing victory over disease, at presentation ceremonies on Nov. 
21.

file: AMERICAN DREAM OF CHINESE FAMILY TURNS BITTERSWEET.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Tsoung Shing Coffee Shop - a little bit of China in the center of Queens - is a place of many beginnings. 
It officially opened three years ago, but its roots date back far longer - to the streets of Hong Kong and a man named Ming You, who left his home and pregnant wife to make a fortune in New York.
Mr. You never did make that fortune. 
In fact, it took 19 years before he earned enough money to send for his wife and the daughter he had never seen.
But it is that daughter, 35-year-old Tina Wong, who stands behind the counter these days at the Tsoung Shing - a combination coffee shop and Chinese restaurant where the cornflakes sit alongside the ginger hot sauce and scrambled eggs share plates with the pork fried rice. 
It is the kind of place that will never make a fortune for anyone, but that an entire family calls home.
Article in occasional series "A New Melting Pot" discusses experience of Chinese family in New YorkMore Work, Less Money
Family-run ethnic restaurants like the Tsoung Shing dot the streets of Elmhurst, a section of Queens that is among the city's newest ethnic outposts and where, according to immigration officials, 20,000 immigrants from 110 countries live. 
The restaurant is the kind of establishment where immigrants have struggled for generations.
''Work, work and more work,'' said Tina Wong, who begins her day at 8 A.M. and stays at the shop until well past midnight. 
''Less and less money.''
There are five tables and a counter in the Tsoung Shing Coffee Shop. 
There is never a line. 
But every morning Tina Wong is there, scrubbing the floor, polishing the counter, mixing the tea. 
Jimmy Wong, her 39-year-old husband, is there, too, washing the tables, chopping the onions, dicing the carrots. 
So is Linda Yim, 33, who also does many of these tasks and whose husband has known Mr. Wong since they were children.
Altogether, two sets of grandparents, two daughters, two husbands, one sister, one brother and one 10-year-old grandaughter work, eat and spend most of their time in this small restaurant with its white plastic counter tops and overhanging prints of Shanghai. 
It is an arduous existence that neither Mr. You nor anyone else in this extended family ever thought they would lead in America, a place where they expected life to be easy and wealth to abound.
''I thought America would be a good country, maybe it would be easy to make a living here,'' said Jimmy Wong, who now spends 12 hours a day over three smoldering woks. 
''But it's not so easy. 
Nobody gives you something.''
But so it is. 
The Tsoung Shing is neither gold mine nor stepping stone for this extended family. 
It is nothing more than a means to pay the rent, clothe the children, run the car. 
Although they live four blocks away, their homes are only places to sleep. 
The families eat all their meals at the restaurant. 
The grandchildren play there. 
The parents balance their checkbooks there. 
They have even conducted Thanksgiving Day dinners there under the smiling faces of the painted porcelain Buddhas.
Â 
Try at Free Enterprise
The beginning of the Tsoung Shing in some ways was the day Mr. Wong strung up the red, white and blue flags on the restaurant's outside facade -May 23, 1979 - a day that marked the family's first stab at free enterprise in this country. 
Since that time no one has taken a vacation. 
Those flags, now slightly frayed, still hang.
''We knew we could make it work,'' says Mr. Wong. ''And it has.''
Spend the day at the Tsoung Shing, which loosely translated means fortune and happiness, and the life of the extended immigrant family comes alive: Their responsibilities are shared, but their roles are sharply defined.
First there is Tina Wong, who limits her cooking to cheese omelets and sandwiches. 
All day she stands at the grill behind the counter, ladling the tea, filling the cooler with soda, trying to decipher the English that some other members of the family do not comprehend.
''Is there any salt in here?'' a customer asked the other day, digging into a plate of chop suey. 
''Yes,'' Mrs. Wong replied. 
''Lots of sauce. 
Lots.''
''I didn't want any salt. 
''Next time order the chow mein,'' she said pleasantly. 
''Not so much sauce.''
Linda Yim and Jimmy Wong are the cooks at the Tsoung Shing. 
Their days are spent in the hot, cramped kitchen where Shanghai specialties like orange-flavor beef, crispy fried bass and cold noodles are turned out with remarkable speed. 
She does all the chopping, mixing, dicing, stuffing, blending and scrambling, and he does the frying, basting, steaming, stirring and roasting. 
Mr. Wong also washes the pots.
Mrs. Yim and Mr. Wong are the owners of the Tsoung Shing, and because of this they are the only ones who are paid and allowed to give orders. 
Mrs. Wong, for example, is rarely welcome in the kitchen. 
It is already crowded - something that patrons can see for themselves since it contains the restaurant's only bathroom. 
But, she concedes, she is also not welcome in the kitchen because she does not know how to cook.
The other day, Mrs. Wong walked into the kitchen to help her husband at the height of lunch hour. 
Even when business is slow, things are hectic in this tiny kitchen. 
But when tables are filled, the scene could be plucked from a Charlie Chaplin movie.
This was one of those days. 
Mr. Wong was busy whipping up a portion of hot and sour soup in one wok, steamed dumplings in another and sweet and sour bean curd in a third. 
A plate of cold sesame noodles waited on the counter. 
There were several back orders for eggplant in garlic sauce, shrimp in chili sauce, Shanghai won-ton soup.
Mrs. Wong rushed in and announced that she was going to prepare an order of fried dumplings to go. 
She threw eight dumplings into a skillet and turned up the flames, but before she realized that she had not used enough oil, the dumplings burned. 
Mrs. Wong spent the rest of the afternoon out front, peeling potatoes at one of the restaurant's rear tables.
''I'm tired,'' she said, jumping up to serve tea to a customer.
Â 
Differing Recollections
How Tina Wong met her husband, Jimmy, is another of the Tsoung Shing's many beginnings. 
She says she met him years ago while he was a sailor on a cargo ship in Hong Kong. 
He says he first saw her on a street corner in Brooklyn.
Be that as it may, they were married 11 years ago and now have two children. 
After school, their oldest child, Jeannie, 10, washes dishes, peels the onions, fries the bacon and fills patrons' cups with tea. 
William, 5, stays at home with Mrs. Wong's parents, except when activity at the restaurant becomes so hectic that they are all called in to help.
''I hope business is slow,'' said Jeannie, who was born in the United States and is sometimes taunted by her friends because she cannot stay home to watch television.
When Mrs. Wong is not at the restaurant, she can probably be found somewhere in Chinatown shopping for food, scouring for bargains. 
She makes the trip there from Elmhurst, she says, because the prices are lower.
The other day, Mrs. Wong went to a fish store on Canal Street in Chinatown, where she walked past a tank of live turtles and picked out a collection of live crabs. 
One crab escaped and Mrs. Wong had to chase it across the store. 
She did all this quickly, confidently and with good humor, stopping to haggle over the price of shrimp, then racing three blocks away to pick up 10 pounds of pork.
Over the years Tina Wong has perfected her shopping. 
She knows where to buy the freshest noodles, how to squeeze the tripe, where to get the meatiest, least expensive spareribs. 
But what might particularly inspire awe among even the most exacting bargain hunter is that, when it comes to cucumbers, she makes a special trip to Essex Street on the Lower East Side and Gus's pickles.
''It's cheaper,'' she explains with authority. 
How Linda Yim decided to go into business with Jimmy Wong is yet another of the Tsoung Shing's many beginnings. 
Mr. Wong's godmother is Mrs. Yim's mother-in-law, a complicated connection that began in Shanghai, continued years ago in Hong Kong and ultimately resulted in their cooking together four years ago in a Chinatown restaurant. 
Neither really knew how to cook before that.
Mr. Wong and Mrs. Yim worked in the Chinatown restaurant for about a year. 
One day, Mrs. Yim's husband, David, who works in another restaurant in Queens, spotted an empty storefront at 86-32 Broadway in Elmhurst with all the fixtures needed for a coffee shop. 
The rent was $800 a month and it was near the subway. 
Several weeks later they moved in, leaving virtually everything intact, not even replacing the white plastic chicken that still sits incongruously in the front window.
If the Tsoung Shing were in Chinatown or SoHo, it might become chic. 
The service is friendly and attentive, the food inspired and prices unbelievably low. 
But in Elmhurst - a place that is often a contradictory fusion between a small town and an international metropolis - the Tsoung Ching Coffee Shop gets lost.
Those in the neighborhood who want a real coffee shop usually head to the Greek diner around the corner. 
Those who crave Chinese cuisine prefer places with dragon wallpaper and duck sauce.
No matter. 
The family works hard just the same - the kind of routine that Mr. You established years before when he got his first job as a short-order cook in Brooklyn. 
But unlike Linda Yim and Jimmy Wong, he never needed to master the art or the tedious preparation of Chinese cooking.
''His specialty was steak and hamburgers,'' Mrs. Wong explained. 
''That's better,'' said Jeannie, who prefers everything that is American. 
She said she would take a steak over orange-flavor beef any day.

text:
