From the number of working elevators to the kinds of movies being sold, the sixth annual American Film Market has an air of quality that it lacked during its first five years.
This yearly bazaar in which distributors of independently made American films peddle their movies to buyers from such places as Japan and Italy, Argentina and Guatemala is, according to Roger Corman, a longtime independent producer, for us ''the most important market in the world.''
Mr. Corman, who has pointed six of his movies, including ''Killbots'' and ''Cocaine Wars,'' to the market being held in Los Angeles this week, added, ''The margin by which the American Film Market exceeds Cannes will increase this year.''
Because 2,500 members of the world press descend on Cannes each May for the film festival, the adjoining market is still the place to introduce a movie. 
However, the 82 members of the American Film Marketing Association report they make more sales at the American market, which is being held this week at the Beverly Hills Hilton in a move from a considerably less elegant hotel in West Hollywood.
Working Elevators
More than 250 movies will be screened, and the weakness of the dollar means that the buyers will have more money with which to purchase theatrical and video rights to the films than they had in 1984 and 1985. 
The strong dollar made those rough years for many of the smaller companies.
Nevertheless, the first thing most sellers mention is the fact that the elevators work.
''And they've set up room service on every floor,'' said Paul Baccus of Filmation. 
''When you're stuck in a hotel room for nine days waiting for people to come by, little things make a difference.''
Actually, the American Film Market approached the Hilton twice before, but the hotel was definitely not interested, according to Tim Kittleson, director of the market. 
Nor were the major studios. 
This year several major studios are selling their smaller, less mainstream movies through the market. 
Norman Katz, chairman of the marketing association, is handling ''Joshua Then and Now'' and ''Key Exchange'' for 20th Century-Fox.
Mr. Katz said the increased status of the market, exemplified by the move to Beverly Hills, ''has attracted groups of people we haven't had here before.''
They include Hollywood producers curious enough to roam the halls, video divisions of the major studios looking to buy cassette rights and representatives of half a dozen banks, including Bankers Trust, Credit Lyonnais and Chemical Bank. 
There are also such new affiliates as Eastman Kodak, every major film laboratory, Bavaria Studios in Munich and three completion bond companies.
''I've attended all the markets to meet people, but we decided to join this year because the market is expanding,'' said Michelle Marshall, president of International Film Completion Company.
In addition, several film organizations have scheduled their seminars and international marketing meetings to coincide with the market. 
They include the Walt Disney Company, Unifrance and the Motion Picture Export Association, the foreign sales trade organization for the major studios.
Â 
Video Rights a Hot Item
The number of buyers interested in video rights continues to rise, with 22 percent exclusively interested in video and another 40 percent buying video and other rights. 
As to the movies for sale, ''There's less poke-in-the-eye horror,'' said Mr. Kittleson.
The market is not devoid of such staples as ''Nightmare on Elm Street 2,'' ''Hollywood Vice Squad'' and ''I Eat Cannibals.''
But also being sold are ''The Trip to Bountiful,'' ''Twice in a Lifetime,'' the new Federico Fellini movie ''Ginger and Fred,'' Roman Polanski's ''Pirates,'' ''Smooth Talk'' and Woody Allen's ''Hannah and Her Sisters.''
For the first time, the Russians have come to observe. 
Two representatives of Sovexportfilm wandered wraithlike through the halls for a few days. 
They left with a pile of forms and said they would return next year as sellers, according to market officials.
Chinafilm, the import-export movie agency in China, came last year as a buyer and is back again this year. 
In January, Chinafilm was transferred out of the Ministry of Culture and into a newly named Ministry of Radio, Film and Television.
Garrie Roman, an American who lives in Hong Kong and has joint ventures in China, including a videocassette duplicating plant, said it appeared to him that to increase movie and television trade with the West, China had decided to get its film and video industry under control and to enforce copyrights. 
Mr. Roman was shepherding an official from the Ministry of Radio, Film and Television at this year's market. 
The official, who asked not be quoted by name, verified that China is working on a copyright law. 
And a document promising a crackdown on video piracy inside China was leaked to market executives.
The official also agreed with Mr. Roman's assertion that China was using videocassettes to bring information about the West to people in the Chinese interior. 
The official said that programming that told how to do things would be particularly welcome, and the only unwanted programs would be those that were pornographic, overly violent, negative about China or those the audience didn't like because the cultural background was too different.
''There are people in the interior who have never seen a foreigner before, and the Government wants to expose them to foreign cultures,'' said Mr. Roman. But with certain reservations. 
Mr. Roman said EMI's ''The Awakening'' passed the censor but, nevertheless, will not be shown. 
''The Awakening,'' which stars Charlton Heston, is a horror movie about an evil Egyptian goddess brought back to life.
''For the last 40 years movies have been a propaganda tool and the only movies released were based on truth,'' Mr. Roman said. 
''They told me 'The Awakening' had to be deferred because the new policy is to eradicate superstition and the people in the country would believe the movie was true.''

file: AMERICAN PERFORMERS LEARN CHINA_S STYLIZED AND INTRICATE TECHNIQUES.txt
text:
ï»¿
SU ZHI and Qu Yongchun usually spend their days teaching advanced classes at the Academy of Chinese Opera in Peking, the central training school in China for performers of the Peking Opera. 
But for the last six weeks, their students have been Americans, in classes and lecture demonstrations held at the Eugene O'Neill Theater Center in Waterford, Conn., and throughout the area.
The two are in the United States in an arrangement worked out by George C. White, president of the O'Neill Center, with the Chinese Theater Association during his trip to Peking last year to direct a Chinese-language production of O'Neill's ''Anna Christie.''
If the notion of a Chinese ''Anna Christie'' is a novel one - and Mr. White may return to Peking next year to direct a Broadway musical in Chinese - the idea of imparting an ancient and complex Eastern theater technique to young Western actors is almost as unusual.
But Miss Su and Mr. Qu are more than master teachers with long experience as Peking Opera acrobats. 
It quickly became apparent in a recent conversation that they were possessed of a vivid sense of humor, practicality and warmth likely to bridge the largest of cultural differences.
Â 
Lecture at Brooklyn Theater
Speaking through an interpreter, Miss Su and Mr. Qu talked last week of their work and their impressions of their American students. 
They were preparing for a lecture-demonstration at the New Theater of Brooklyn, a center for new American theater founded in 1982 and directed by Deborah J. Pope and her associate, Stephen Stettler, who also teaches acting at the O'Neill Center's National Theater Institute.
''The American students have been very clever and very adorable,'' Mr. Qu said. 
''They make us feel very young.''
Miss Su nodded. 
''Perhaps we will cry when we leave,'' she added.
Like Mr. Qu, Miss Su began training in the Peking Opera technique at the age of 10. 
Now 46, she retired from performing in 1964 to begin a career as a teacher of stage-fighting at the Academy. 
Mr. Qu, 52, left the stage last year. 
''I have a 91-year-old mother and there was no one to take care of her,'' he said. 
His wife is an actress who is often on tour. 
''This way, I can go home at lunchtime,'' Mr. Qu explained. 
He grinned. 
''Frankly speaking, I would prefer to be acting. 
But China is still a filial country.''
Â 
Performers Must Specialize
Training for the Peking Opera is rigorous, for in addition to mastering a highly developed, stylized and intricate technique, the performer must specialize in one of many types of characters. 
And within the Peking Opera's specific acting styles there are differences, for example, in the way characters hold out their hands, depending on what age they are.
''The manner of speaking and tone of voice change depending on who the character is and who is addressed,'' Mr. Qu said. 
He imitated a child greeting a father, a father greeting a child, and that same father greeting ''someone he must respect.''
From the young applicants for the first level of training, about 40 or 50 students are chosen annually out of 1,000, a ratio that hasn't changed since Mr. Qu began his studies. 
''It is very competitive,'' he said. 
''You are tested on physique, facial characteristics, voice and acting ability. 
You must study for six years before graduating, and then prepare with advanced training for three years. 
After that, you may call yourself a performer. 
It's difficult. 
George White said that to study Peking Opera requires strength of steel.''
Â 
System of Selection
''It is different from the American system,'' Mr. Qu continued. 
''In China, the student wants to have to do it, but the teachers have to select the students. 
If you are too tall, too thin, too short, too fat, you're out. 
Here, the discipline seems to depend on the student's desire to study.''
To indicate the kind of talent the Academy seeks, Mr. Qu described several final exercises given the youngest applicants. 
''We give them something to act,'' he said. 
He mimed children pretending to grasp a cup of tea. 
The first takes hold of it carefully, the second grabs it clumsily. 
The first child, told to swat an imaginary fly, searches for the insect and hits at it. 
The second lunges immediately. 
''Then if that is O.K., the teacher will do gestures and see how well they follow,'' he said. 
He moved his arms in windmill turns, then imitated arms being thrown stiffly into space. 
The examination concludes with a crucial test on academic subjects.
Applicants for the second, or oldest, level of training must act a scene from the Peking Opera repertory. 
They also are tested on academics and ''politics,'' which Mr. Qu described as ''general social structure and social knowledge.''
The advanced-level exams are as competitive. 
''There are no back doors into the Peking Opera,'' Mr. Qu said.
Â 
'Character Teachers'
Teachers specialize in acrobatics, basic movements such as kicking and bending, floor work, the use of knives and swords, full body movement and ''character teaching,'' which is the most important. 
''It is like a bicycle,'' Mr. Qu said, adding that he and Miss Su are character teachers. 
''Some people make the wheels, some the bars, some the handles. 
But there must be someone to put the whole together.''
Given this high degree of specialization, what were the two able to teach to American acting students with no experience in the Peking Opera style?
''We taught the basic skills,'' Mr. Qu said. 
Method was stressed over theory. 
''Because it was the first time Chinese had come to teach, arrangements were very tight and the students were physically tired,'' Miss Su said.
''In the beginning,'' Mr. Qu said, ''there were some students at the O'Neill Center who thought studying Eastern art didn't make sense in the context of Western theater.''
To make those connections clearer, he said, he would tell his Brooklyn listeners a story. 
''George White took us to Washington, where we met Senator Dodd,'' he said, referring to Christopher J. Dodd, the Connecticut Democrat. 
'' 'Why is your performing different from a movie?'
Senator Dodd asked us. 
'Both are art,' we said. 
'But the techniques are different. 
Movies are closer to daily life. 
The Peking Opera shows ancient life in China. 
It is best compared with Western ballet. 
Does anyone walk on point, spinning around rapidly, in real life?
This is art. 
But film is also real life with art added.'
'' Mr. Qu said that Senator Dodd agreed, and even extended the analogy to politics. 
''His manner of speaking was very artistic,'' Mr. Qu observed. 
''He can also perform.''
And so Mr. Qu and Miss Su taught their American students, whom they will leave early next month, ways to open a door and call someone, to use swords and daggers, and to ride a horse. 
''Now, when they perform things from the past,'' Mr. Qu said, ''they can also use the Peking Opera style.''

file: AMERICAN TRIAL PUTS CHINESE JUSTICE TO THE TEST.txt
text:
ï»¿
When Richard S. Ondrik flew from Peking to this city on April 18, he was as prepared as an American can be for the trade opportunities unfolding in China.
Fifteen hours later, choking on acrid smoke, the Indiana-born energy expert was trapped in a nightmare. 
A fire had broken out in Harbin's Swan Hotel. 
On the 11th floor, an American working with Mr. Ondrik on an oil equipment deal, Alan Eng, was dead. 
The bodies of nine other men who had chosen to jump rather than endure the intense smoke and flame lay on the ground. 
Seven others were seriously injured. 
Chinese investigators quickly zeroed in on Mr. Ondrik as the cause of the fire, accusing him of having fallen asleep with a lighted cigarette. 
After days and nights of interrogation without a lawyer, and a 10-week delay while the matter was bounced around the bureaucracy in Peking, Mr. Ondrik was formally arrested and taken to a detention center where a naked light bulb burned throughout the night. 
After a few days he was formally charged with the ''unintentional crime'' of setting fire to the hotel.
Article on trial of Indiana businessman Richard S Ondrik, who had been accused by Chinese authorities of 'unintentional crime' of causing fire in Harbin's Swan Hotel by falling asleep with lighted cigarette; trial ended in July and verdict is expected by August 15; photos (M)Verdict Expected by Aug. 
15
The ensuing trial ended in July after four days of hearings, and a verdict is expected by Aug. 
15. At the worst, Mr. Ondrik could end up with a seven-year jail term and a bill for compensation to the hotel of $87,600.
Even if the court is lenient, as the chief judge suggested in his closing remarks, the American could spend years paying off damages for which he is uninsured. 
Worse, he may never again be able to function effectively as a businessman in China, a career for which he studied Mandarin and otherwise prepared himself for 10 years.
In some ways he is caught in a web of circumstances that are peculiar to China. 
Long after the case is closed what happened will stand as a warning to Westerners.
Unlike United States courts, Chinese ones do not require a plea of guilty or not guilty, and Mr. Ondrik has staked out a position somewhere in between. 
His account to the investigators, repeated in court, was that he had no recollection of lying down on his bed with a cigarette, but that after the shock of the fire he could not be sure.
Â 
An American Attorney
In affidavits presented to the court by his attorney, Richard C. Goodwin Jr. of Washington, five former roommates attested that they had never seen the American smoking on a bed.
In the end Mr. Ondrik's case rests less on whether he was responsible for the fire than on the more basic question of whether he should be on trial at all. 
Although the article of the Chinese criminal code under which the charge was laid bears some similarity to the United States crimes of criminal negligence and involuntary manslaughter, Mr. Goodwin, for one, says that he knows of no case in which those charges have been laid in an American court against somebody accidentally setting a fire with a cigarette. 
Was the Hotel Safe?
Mr. Ondrik's dinner was sponsored by the Harbin Oil Refinery, to whom the American's Hong Kong-based company, Energy Projects Southeast Asia Ltd., was hoping to sell a compressor. 
At the end of a day that saw the American fly 750 miles and conduct hours of talks, he consumed, by his own testimony, eight to 10 glasses of maotai, four glasses of wine and several beers.
Everything seems to have conspired against the victims. 
Prosecution evidence showed that rooms in the 16-month-old hotel had been designed for smoke and fire detectors, and were wired for them, but the devices themselves remained in storage. 
Plastic wallpaper and hollow plywood doors speeded the fire and there were no emergency exit signs. 
The only fire extinguisher did not work, and there was no alarm. 
The floor attendant, on a 24-hour shift, was off taking a bath and a meal on the eighth floor. 
Some of the testimony implied that the fire exit was locked.
Worse yet, the fire department was not answering its telephone. 
Later, taxi drivers at the hotel said that when the the firetrucks finally arrived, 37 minutes late, they had been fetched by a hotel car.
Â 
North Koreans Died in Fire
After Mr. Ondik's arrest on June 26, Mr. Goodwin had argued at the Foreign Ministry and elsewhere that a trial would be harmful to trade and other ties with the United States. 
But the Chinese were confronted with a more compelling diplomatic consideration, the fact that five of those who died and four of the injured were members of a North Korean Government delegation. 
In the lawyer's view, that ultimately made a trial inevitable.
Barely a week separated Mr. Ondrik's indictment from the opening of the trial, and by the time Mr. Goodwin reached Harbin there were only four days left. 
As a foreigner he was barred from appearing in court or seeing his client in detention, and had to work instead through a Chinese attorney he had engaged in Peking.
The careful collection of physical evidence and statements supporting the state's case marked an improvement on the past, when criminal trials, when they were held at all, were arbitrary in the extreme. 
But once Mr. Ondrik reached court it seemed clear that one fundamental, the assumption of guilt, had changed hardly at all.
By the end of the trial Mr. Goodwin had concluded that challenging the state case in a criminal prosecution here is largely fruitless, ''because the Government cannot be seen to lose.''
Rather than deciding innocence or guilt, he said, the court's function appeared to be ''assessing degrees of responsibility,'' a task it addressed at length in the Ondrik case by reviewing the deficiencies in the hotel's fire equipment and the bungling that ensued once the blaze broke out. 
Two Chinese, the hotel supervisor and the absentee floor attendant, face trials of their own for ''dereliction of duty.''
For his part, Mr. Ondrik seems to have resigned himself to a conviction. 
''It is difficult for me to accept that I am a criminal,'' he told the judges in his final plea. 
''This is partly because the law in my country and in China toward accidents is different. 
However, I am a friend of China and a guest in your country, and if this court decides that vengeance and punishment are necessary according to your laws, then I will accept that.''

file: Amid Turmoil, Journalists Leave Tibet.txt
text:
ï»¿
Fourteen foreign journalists from six countries left Tibet today after being ordered out of the region by the Chinese authorities.
The expulsions came after 20 days of protests, led by monks and other Tibetans, against Chinese rule. 
Another journalist covered by the expulsion order left Lhasa, the capital, on Thursday.
A Chinese official declared that the journalists, including this correspondent, were in Tibet illegally and that any effort to report anti-Chinese protests was prohibited.
Lhasa and at least one other Tibetan city have been the sites of marches led by monks to demand that the Chinese leave Tibet, which was invaded by Chinese troops and finally annexed in 1951. 
In one demonstration on Oct. 
1, it now appears that at least 9 Tibetans and 4 policemen were killed.
Â 
Reporting Severely Limited
After permitting sporadic reports of the protests from Tibet for several days, the Chinese authorities here severed contact with Lhasa, preventing foreign journalists there from reporting directly on events. 
Some accounts were carried to Chengdu, a city 750 miles east of Lhasa, but most reporting has been severely limited.
According to a foreign manager of Lhasa's main tourist hotel, Chinese officials have ordered all foreigners to leave Tibet unless they are on official business or on official tours. 
The Chinese have denied issuing such an order.
On Tuesday, an anti-Chinese march by as many as 100 monks from Drepung Monastery, just outside Lhasa, turned violent when heavily armed Chinese policemen attacked the protesters, beating them with clubs, rifle butts and belts. 
Ninety monks were arrested as they tried to march on the provincial government offices.
Since Tuesday, Lhasa has been very tense. 
Although most shops and market stalls had reopened by Thursday, they closed much earlier than usual, and streets were empty by early evening.
A Chinese restaurant owner in Lhasa said many of the Chinese who had been sent there as government officials had gone home early because they feared being attacked by Tibetans.
Â 
Monasteries Sealed Off
On Wednesday, all of Lhasa's monasteries, the religious heart of Tibetan Buddhism, were sealed off by blockades of policemen brandishing automatic weapons and pistols. 
All local cars and trucks were stopped and their drivers questioned.
The Chinese police have plastered the walls of monasteries with posters denouncing the Dalai Lama, the leader of Tibetan Buddhism, whom they accused of encouraging separatist activity from his exile in Dharmsala, India.
Other Chinese officials have been seen lecturing young monks on China's version of Tibetan history and have interrogated all senior abbots at the monasteries. 
At the Jokhang Cathedral, the most sacred of Buddhism's shrines in Tibet, the Chinese police have occupied the upper floors, using the temple as an observation post.
At least 600 heavily armed policemen arrived in Lhasa during the week. 
On Wednesday, the 37th anniversary of China's invasion, they staged a major show of force by driving a convoy of 20 trucks, including 13 packed with policemen armed with AK-47 assault rifles, through the old Tibetan quarter.
The police have patrolled rooftops of the Tibetan quarter and have set up roadblocks in various parts of Lhasa.
Â 
A Meeting in Lhasa
Efforts by journalists in Tibet to send out reports on the events of the last few days proved almost impossible and were in fact ruled illegal at a meeting in Lhasa shortly after midnight Thursday between a senior Chinese official and 15 foreign reporters.
Yu Wuzhen, the director of Tibet's foreign affairs office, read a statement ordering the 15 foreign reporters out of Tibet. 
Mr. Yu charged the journalists with failing to provide the provincial authorities with what he said was a required 10-day advance notification of their intention to work in Tibet.
The meeting was also attended by two American diplomats who were in Lhasa, Raymond F. Burghardt, the political counselor at the United States Embassy in Beijing, and Scott D. Bellard, a consular officer from Chengdu.

text:

There, on page 3 of People's Daily, organ of the Communist Party, was a postcard-sized photograph of three men in China's Parliament sitting with their hands in their laps while around them hands fluttered aloft. 
It was an extraordinary display of official discord.
The occasion was a vote during the current session of the Parliament in a country where the appearance of public unanimity by Government is hallowed ground.
A good deal of sacred turf has been trampled this week as more than 2,900 delegates to the National People's Congress gather in annual session to hear reports on the Government's performance and to ratify new laws and constitutional amendments. 
But the lockstep behavior of past congresses has dissolved in instances of genuine debate, negative votes and - even more remarkably - substantial coverage of events by China's press.
China's news organization have been awash with reports on the congress, interviewing delegates, publishing accounts of debates in working sessions and explaining contentious issues, like the intransigent and politically volatile problem of inflation. 
Even foreign reporters were invited for the first time to sit in on delegate discussions.
As soon as the congress opened it was clear that this year was going to be different. 
Liu Yiu-chu, a Hong Kong lawyer and delegate from Guangdong Province, abstained on a vote for the members of various committees.
A gasp went through the auditorium. 
The chamber exploded in the flashes of photographers' strobe lights. 
And then she did it again. 
Delegates joined in.
''I do not know how the lists of candidates were formulated, nor do I know the criteria for choosing them,'' Miss Liu told reporters afterward. 
''As a deputy I think I should have such information and clearly know what the procedure is.''
Miss Liu's behavior proved contagious, and at one point 69 delegates voted against the composition of a congress working committee.
Huang Shunxing, who once served in Taiwan's legislature but who now works in China as a scientist and is a delegate to the congress, urged the defeat of 89-year-old Zhou Gucheng as chairman of a committee.
Â 
Some Blunt Language
''He is too old and should be given more time for a rest,'' Mr. Huang said, in the bluntest language heard in public so far. 
After a moment's hesitation, applause surged across the auditorium in the Great Hall of the People.
For the first time in the People's Republic, not a single committee of the congress was elected unanimously.
Not all the delegates were impressed by the collapse of orchestrated tradition, however.
''If we all cast dissenting votes or abstained from voting for our own personal reasons, wouldn't this be extremely disruptive?'' the influential Economic Daily, an economic newspaper, quoted an unnamed delegate as saying.
But another saw that China was looking at something new and more recognizably democratic. 
''Those delegates who abstained or who voted negatively have brought up a new problem in how to conduct elections properly in the future,'' the delegate said. 
''Much attention should be paid to this.''

file: AN OASIS OF PRIVILIGE IN CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
ORVILLE SCHELL is the author of ''Watch Out for the Foreign Guests!''
(Pantheon).
Each evening a middle-aged woman in a simple print dress sits down at a large grand piano set to one side of the hotel lobby and begins to play Mozart, Beethoven and Chopin from sheet music that is so aged that small pieces of yellowed paper break from the edges and drift down onto the keyboard every time she turns a page.
Hotel guests sit at surrounding tables, the murmur of their voices mixing with the sound of music and ice cubes clinking in glasses.
As dusk begins to fall, the chandeliers come on, and some of the guests begin to move toward the hotel's main restaurant, where they sit down at tables set with crisply ironed cloths and choose between such delicacies as salade de magret de canard au vinaigre framboise ($7), cr eme d'artichauts au caviar et filaments de betterave ($2.50), paillard de veau aux chanterelles ($19.50), paupiettes de sole Montrose sauce Nantua ($15), and a list of wines from Italy and Germany as well as France.
Out in front, where chauffeured limousines await their charges just beyond a large fountain, stands a silent phalanx of common people, staring transfixed through the plate- glass windows at the activity inside the brightly lit hotel lobby.
Orville Schell article on opulent Jianguo Hotel, Peking, China; photos (M)
''At night . . . where in hidden springs of electricity flooded the great dining room with light, it became as it were an immense and wonderful aquarium against whose wall of glass the working population of Balbec, the fishermen and also the tradesmen's families, clustering invisibly in the outer darkness, pressed their faces to watch, gently floating upon the golden eddies within, the luxurious life of its occupants, a thing as extraordinary to the poor as the life to strange fishes and mollusks,'' so wrote Marcel Proust at the turn of the century of the Grand Hotel in Normandy, where he used to summer on the coast with his grandmother.
But the scene unfolding around me here is not Balbec or even France before the Great War. 
It is Peking, the Peoples' Republic of China in 1983, a curious place to find the ghost of Marcel Proust, or even a mutation thereof. 
The hotel is the Jianguo (Build the Nation), the first Western-run inn to open in China in 35 years.
Instead of vacationing French aristocrats taking the sea air, the Jianguo is filled with businessmen, tourists and diplomats. 
And instead of Norman ''fishermen'' and ''tradesmen's families,'' it is Chinese workers and peasants who stare into the Jianguo's aquarium-like interior from outside.
The building itself, a sprawling four-story cream-colored structure, is actually an architectural replica of the Palo Alto Holiday Inn in California. 
It is situated on Jianguo- menwai Boulevard outside what used to be the old city wall before the Communists tore it down to build a highway. 
Its neon signs, eternally energetic fountains, extravagant lighting and California styling make it as noticeable among the frieze of gloomy buildings which flank it as one gleaming gold tooth in a mouth of otherwise neglected dentures.
Standing as it does in front of row upon row of dormitory-like housing for the families of Chinese Foreign Ministry employees (where there are usually not even any operable lights in the hallways), the Jianguo fairly sparkles with seductiveness. 
It is a living advertisement for the outside capitalist world with which the denizens of Peking have just begun to become reacquainted after three decades of socialist isolation.
Compared to the crowded, inefficient and noisy world of urban China, where there is literally no place for family members, lovers or friends to sit in quiet comfort and share a meal or conversation, life in the Jianguo Hotel appears like a fantasy incarnate. 
When one steps through these doors, China ends and another world begins. 
The rooms have wall-to-wall carpeting. 
The matching drapes and bedspreads are made of bright floral print fabric that seems as remote to China as tropical foliage in Greenland. 
The private bathrooms are finished with black and white Chinese marble, one of the few interior effects of local origin. 
The king-size beds are all imported from the United States. 
Every room has a color television set, its own air conditioner, a push-button phone and an American-style lamp hanging down from the ceiling on the end of a gold chain. 
Sliding doors open out onto little balconies which overlook an interior court where more fountains bubble away in reflecting pools.
Downstairs, one can dine on quite good Continental cuisine in a candle-lit restaurant staffed with a headwaiter in a dinner jacket, swim in an indoor pool, dance until 2 A.M. in a fully outfitted disco, imbibe a drink at a Western-style bar, knowing that a German and five Swiss hotel managers from the Peninsula Group (of the Peninsula Hotel fame in Hong Kong, which has contracted to run the Jianguo for 10 ears) hold a steady helm. 
No wonder the occupancy rate of the hotel has recently been 99 to 100 percent. 
Even though rooms cost two and three times more ($60 to $70) than Chinese-run hotels, and must be paid for with hard currency, foreign visitors are more than glad to incur the cost.
How did such an aberration ever come into being in a country once so dedicated to eradicating class distinctions and foreign privilege?
It is the brainchild of the Shanghai-born architect and hotel owner Clement Chen Jr., whose offices are in San Francisco, and who owns the Buffalo Hilton Hotel and Holiday Inns in San Francisco and Palo Alto.
Wanting to do something for his native land, and aware of Chinese interest in earning foreign exchange through an expanded tourist industry, he proposed constructing a first-class inn under foreign management in Peking. 
The Chinese, having embarked on their new ''open door policy'' to the West, accepted his plans to build a 480-room hotel, costing $22.6 million, which would be jointly owned, 51 percent by the China International Travel Service and 40 percent by Mr. Chen himself. 
After 20 months of construction, involving the shipment of 200 containers of building supplies from the United States, this curious hostel, which seems to defy the momentum of the whole Chinese Revolution, opened in 1982.
''Let's face it, we live in the 20th century,'' Mr. Chen told me when I called him at his San Francisco office to ask about his conception of the Jianguo. 
''People may enjoy visiting a country with an unfamiliar culture like China, but when they get back to their hotel from a tour in the afternoon, basically they want to be able to relax in a first-class place. 
What I mean to say is, that after the Peking duck, they may still feel a need for some bacon and eggs, a club sandwich or maybe a steak. 
I purposely designed my hotel with these needs in mind, so that once a guest gets inside, he will be able to forget where he is and feel as if he were back home.''
One obvious hurdle to Mr. Chen's notion of opening a hotel in China in which Westerners can ''forget'' where they are, is the ubiquity of the Chinese people themselves. 
No foreign guest would ever be able to imagine that he or she was ''back home'' if the hotel in Peking was open to the Chinese masses as well as foreign guests.
''This was a real problem,'' Mr. Chen acknowledged. 
''But let me tell you a little story. 
One time while we were building the hotel, I decided to go out to a public restaurant here in Peking to eat some jiaozi (steamed dumplings). 
Well, when I got to the restaurant, the first thing I discovered was that I had to get in line with everyone pushing and shoving. 
When I finally worked up to the head of the line, I found that everything was not just noisy and dirty, but that the restaurant didn't even provide bowls or chopsticks for their customers. 
I ended up eating my jiaozi on a piece of newspaper. 
Can you imagine that?
''So, I started thinking,'' Mr. Chen continued. 
''I asked myself whether I wanted to have the restaurants in my hotel look like this. 
And I decided that I didn't, that if I let all these people come in, I would have thousands of them arriving for a cup of tea, and then spending the rest of the day sitting around enjoying the air-conditioning. 
I knew that it would be impossible to run a first class hotel that way.''
As a result, all local Chinese, except the staff of 655, Chinese accompanied by foreigners or high ranking cadres attending official functions are excluded from the Jianguo. 
Security guards hover around the lobby and elevator just to make sure that no trespassers get through.
A hotel like the Jianguo serves its purpose well by providing the foreign community in Peking with an oasis of service and efficiency where there previously was none - the hotel will, for instance, take phone messages for guests, provides stenographic services, and will even accept reservations from independent travelers made abroad through the Peninsula Group (call 213-670-9450 or 312-263- 6069), unlike any other Chinese-run hotel. 
But its presence raises a number of questions about how official Chinese attitudes toward foreigners are evolving.
While understanding China's urgent need to earn foreign exchange and to open up to the outside in order to develop technologically, one still cannot help but wonder what has happened to that extreme sensitivity to flagrant displays of wealth and foreign privilege that so animated China only a few years ago.
Have Chinese Communism and the Chinese people now reconciled themselves to such social contradictions?
Or as more such hotels as the Jianguo open, will they evoke, at least for older people, an earlier and humiliating time when another generation of foreigners lived inside China, but protected by privilege in enclaves of splendid isolation?
Party officials, still sensitive to this humiliating past, are quick to point out the differences. 
The Chinese Government owns a controlling share of the hotel and will fully acquire it for one dollar in 1992. 
Foreigners no longer enjoy such privileges as extra- territoriality, which once made them inviolable to Chinese law, nor are they now allowed to indulge in the kinds of essentially unregulated commercial and evangelical activity which they once were. 
And it is also true, these officials point out, that most other developing countries provide luxury hotels as well as other facilities for those foreign visitors who can afford them.
While it is true that China has changed much over the past few years, and now even espouses such amazing slogans as ''To Get Rich is Glorious,'' somehow the Jianguo still occurs as an anomaly in downtown Peking. 
China is searching for a new identity. 
Just what that new identity will be, and how foreign-run luxury hotels for foreigners will fit into it, is not certain.

file: ANDOVER_S OPENING TO CHINA STUDIES.txt
text:
ï»¿
TO a casual observer the three students sitting around a table in government class at Phillips Academy, a private secondary school in Andover, Mass., look like typical Asian-American teen-agers. 
Wearing jeans and jogging shoes, their books stowed in backpacks on the floor, they listen as Ronald Speirs, the teacher, discusses the checks-and- balances system of the United States Constitution.
But all three of the students are Chinese, who arrived only six weeks previously from the Harbin Institute of Technology in Manchuria. 
They are the fifth group of three students each from the People's Republic of China that have enrolled in the last five years in senior classes at Andover.
Three students from Harbin Institute of Technology study at Phillips Academy in Andover, Mass, in exchange program started in 1980; school is committed to developing intensive four-year Chinese studies program and is one of 36 public and private US high schools to receive Dodge Foundation funding for language and other courses (Education: Winter Survey) (S)
Like their predecessors, who are already enrolled in American colleges and universities, the three Chinese students - Jia Yantao, a man, and Ma Tianyi and Chu Xiaoming, all 19 years old - are spending this year at Andover polishing their spoken English. 
In Harbin foreigners are a curiosity, and they find everything, not only the language, confusing. 
At Andover, however, the three will make new friends and will gradually need each other less and less. 
Surrogate families in the community have already welcomed them into their homes during school holidays.
''It's a tradition at Andover to recruit students from China,'' said Joshua L. Miner, dean of admissions. 
''And it's consistent with the diversity we seek in the student body - we have students from 19 foreign countries this year. 
But having representatives from the world's most populous nation wasn't enough. 
We had to develop a full curriculum for non-Asian students that would include a four-year Chinese language program as well as the courses we already offered in East Asian history, religions and art.''
Established in 1980 through private contacts, the exchange quickly gained approval from the Ministry of Education in Peking. 
There are still problems, however; five years after the first Harbin students arrived on the Andover campus, and three years after instruction in Chinese was first offered, ''The Chinese studies program has not yet begun to grow,'' according to Hale Sturges, chairman of the foreign language department.
Last year at Andover only nine students signed up for beginning Chinese, and this year there are 14. 
The immediate goal is to add a more advanced level of instruction each year, so that taking Chinese will eventually satisfy a student's language requirement. 
Other long-term goals include increasing the number of students of Chinese to 50. 
Many of these advanced students could then continue their studies in Harbin, making the program a real exchange.
This year, for the first time, Harbin sent a visiting scholar, Ni Xiaomin, to perfect her English and to help with Chinese instruction. 
Each Harbin student tutors a few first-year Chinese students. 
Last summer, for the first time, five Andover students visited China for six weeks.
Expenses for the three Harbin students - room, board, tuition, travel and vacations - run about $50,000 a year. 
But Andover's commitment to developing a four-year Chinese studies program is estimated at an additional $100,000 a year. 
These costs are now covered by initial funding from the Geraldine R. Dodge Foundation's $1.3 million China Initiative program, Andover's Kemper Fund for foreign students, general scholarship funds and individual contributors. 
But in the future, according to Dean Miner, Andover must begin a large fund-raising effort to endow the program.
SCHOOLS like Andover face a number of obstacles in setting up strong Chinese programs. 
As of 1980, the year of the most recent study, there were only 1,980 high school students nationwide taking Chinese. 
Geography, inertia, parental bias toward the traditional Romance languages and obsolete teaching materials work against a curriculum balanced between Western and non-Western languages. 
This year, for example, 43 percent of all Andover students take French, 24 percent Spanish, 16 percent Latin, 8 percent Russian, and only 1 percent Chinese.
According to Mr. Sturges, Chinese pedagogy is far behind America's. 
The five available texts, with no graphics, he described as boring. 
''We make do,'' he says, but new texts, correctly paced, with audio-visual aids are needed for students of the 1980's.
Things are improving, however. 
This year Andover was one of 36 public and private high schools, 22 more than in 1983, to receive Dodge Foundation funding. 
Schools willing to make a long-term commitment to teach Chinese language can participate in annual forums such as one held at Ohio State University last summer, in which teachers of Chinese met to share their concerns and explore new ways to help students.
And at the college level, the 13,178 enrollment in Chinese language classes in 1983-84 represents a 16 percent increase over 1980. 
''It's important to get a head start on Chinese,'' said Richard Brod, director of foreign language programs at the Modern Language Association. 
''Unlike the Western languages, without the base of pre-collegiate Chinese, it's not easy to gain functional proficiency in Chinese at the college level.''
The three students at Andover are the youngest of the 10,000 mainland Chinese now studying in the United States, which is only about 3 percent of all foreign students in the country. 
Of the total number of Chinese here, China pays for 5,400. 
The balance are sponsored either by relatives and friends in the United States or through private scholarships. 
Except for a student exchange in the planning stage between the Sidwell Friends School in Washington, D.C., and Peking Middle School No. 2, there is nothing comparable to the Andover-Harbin program at the high school level in the United States; the Chinese students at Andover are the only ones from that country attending American secondary-level schools.
China's population is four times that of the United States but its 800 colleges and universities are barely a quarter of this country's. 
China sends less than 1 percent of its college students here, most at graduate and postgraduate levels in subjects like engineering, computer science or management, which Chinese universities cannot yet offer. 
Most are also trained as teachers.
Those who do come are a highly select group, and the three now at Andover are no exception. 
To gain entrance to Harbin Institute, one of 14 institutions in China that are considered to have special status, they received the highest scores on college-entrance examinations given to 50,000 qualified high school seniors. 
This year at Andover they are taking advanced physics and math, economics, and English and American history for foreign students. 
Eventually, after five or more years of study in America, they will return to the Harbin Institute to teach.
Terry Hoyt is a freelance writer based in New York City.
