A Tang Dynasty court lady, a richly glazed pottery study of a serene aristocrat seated on a bamboo stool, may rewrite the $660,000 record at auction for Tang art when it comes up for sale next week at Sotheby's. 
The gracefully modeled eighth-century tomb figure, owned in recent years by three major collectors of Chinese art, is one of several major Oriental works to be offered at Sotheby's and Christie's next week. 
The presale exhibitions this weekend were timed by the two houses to coincide with the long-awaited opening tomorrow of the Charlotte C. and John C. Weber Galleries of ancient Chinese art at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
The sale at Sotheby's at 2 P.M. Wednesday is to present the Tang court lady for the second time in six years at a Sotheby's auction. 
The sculpture was acquired in the mid-1940's in China by Capt. Sergius N. Ferris Luboshez, a retired United States Navy officer who was sent to the Far East by the State Department at the close of World War II to serve as general counsel to the Foreign Liquidation Commission; the work remained in his collection until it was auctioned for $198,000 at Sotheby's in 1982. 
The buyer, Giuseppe Eskenazi, a London dealer, sold it to C. C. Wang, a Chinese artist living in the United States. 
Last year the court lady changed hands again when Earl Morse, a retired food executive and a major collector of tomb sculpture, acquired it as a present to himself for his 80th birthday. 
The work is being sold from Mr. Morse's estate; he died in February.
''The market is very strong and for something of this rarity, prices are very high,'' said Carol Conover, Sotheby's specialist in Chinese art. 
She said the figure may even exceed her estimate of $450,000 to $650,000, despite repairs to the neck and coiffure, and a replacement of a piece of the blossoming plant stalk in the figure's right hand. 
Ms. Conover said she was optimistic because the prices paid for several major Chinese ceramics at Sotheby's in Hong Kong last week were double the house estimates and most pieces sold for more than Sotheby's expected.
An uncommon 19th-century set of 12 Japanese lacquered zodiac carrying cases, called inro, is one of the highlights of Sotheby's auction of Japanese art at 2 P.M. Wednesday and 10:15 A.M. and 2 P.M. Thursday. Happy Rockefeller is the consignor of these three and four-section small gilded and lacquered silver boxes, the Japanese solution to no pockets in a man's robe.
The set comes in a handsome black lacquer box that has silver mounts, gilded edges, an illustration on the front and four drawers inside for storing the inro, each of which is decorated with one of the 12 signs of the Oriental zodiac - the rat, ox, tiger, hare, dragon, snake, horse, goat, monkey, rooster, dog and boar. 
Although each case is signed by Koma Kansai 2d, a major Edo artist who retired in 1824, its black lacquer box is not signed. 
Peter J. Bufton, Sotheby's specialist in Japanese works of art, said only four zodiac inro have been offered at auction in the West in the last decade. 
The zodiac inro, auctioned in 1965 at Sotheby's in London for $8,400, is estimated to bring $40,000 to $60,000.
Christie's will auction a wide ranging selection of Chinese ceramics and works of art from various owners and from a private collector who acquired his Tang holdings in China in the 1940's, in a sale to be held next Friday at 10 A.M. and 2 P.M.
The most important work in Christie's auction is a rare Tang tomb figure of a lion, the largest of about 10 known to have been auctioned in recent years. 
The lion, shown seated on its haunches with one paw just about to scratch its face, is a lively study depicting the beast as a mythical winged lion as cuddly as a Peking dog.
''In tomb works, you get horses, camels, grooms and court ladies -rarely lions,'' Theow-Huang Tow, one of Christie's Chinese art specialists, said, adding that he knew of fewer than 10. 
He said that lions, which are not indigenous to China, were sometimes sent as gifts to Chinese rulers, which explained, he said, the naturalistic modeling on this work, which is more than 11 inches tall. 
''This lion is particularly interesting because it happens to be larger than most others I have found,'' he said. 
The presale estimate is $300,000 to $400,000.
A private collection of 53 pieces of Chinese ceramic sculpture - acquired by Aurelius Parenti between 1946 and 1948 in China - is to be sold in Christie's afternoon session. 
Mr. Parenti recalled this week that he was working after World War II as a displaced-persons officer with the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Agency in China. 
''A great deal of digging had been going on after the war and most of these things were discovered in that period,'' he said. 
His collection, a well-kept secret until now, contains Han, Wei, Sui and Tang works, of which 25 are horses or horses and riders.
These early works which are offered in a separate catalogue, include ceramics ranging from a Han pottery figure that is expected to sell for $200 to $300, to a Tang horse more than 20 inches tall, that is estimated to bring $40,000 to $50,000.
Â 
Jadeite Vessels
Eighteenth-century Chinese ceramics and jadeite vessels brought astounding prices on May 18 at William Doyle Galleries. 
A pair of K'ang Hsi 18th-century white waterpots, patterned with red flowers and green leaves, estimated to sell for, at most, $16,000, brought $104,500. 
A plain white K'ang Hsi waterpot brought more than 10 times the presale estimate and was sold for $82,500. 
The bidding on a tall white Yung Cheng vase, embellished with red and blue geometric motifs, soared past its top estimate of $5,000 and was sold for $85,250. 
A Chien Lung jadeite vessel that was expected to sell for up to $6,000 brought $55,000. 
The buyers were a New York dealer and a London dealer who were not identified.
''These works were fresh on the market and scarce,'' William Doyle said this week. 
''Works of this quality are not often seen on the market these days - and these were in a collection for decades.''
Â

text:
ï»¿
Commerce Secretary Malcolm Baldrige said today that China and America ''have great potential together'' and promised to help accelerate Western screening procedures for United States high-technology equipment destined for China.
He made the pledge in a toast at a welcoming banquet given by Zheng Tuobin, minister of foreign economic relations and trade.
The two men will be co-chairmen of the third conference of the China-United States Joint Commission on Commerce and Trade that will be held Monday and Tuesday. 
The Chinese are expected to complain about high-technology barriers.
United States Commerce Secretary Malcolm Baldrige, in China as co-chairman of third conference of China-United States Joint Commission on Commerce and Trade, says China and United States have great potential together; promises to help accelerate Western screening procedures for United States high-technology equipment destined for China (M)
Mr. Baldrige, who arrived Saturday, noted that at the first commission meeting in Peking two years ago China's main concern was United States red tape blocking exports of computers and other sophisticated equipment.
''We said then that we had decided to speed it up - it would be good for both of us - and I think the results have shown very clearly in the last two years that we've been able to make tremendous progress on that score,'' he said.
''Now those problems on technology transfer center more outside the United States than they do inside.
''But I will promise you that we will devote the same effort to solving those problems and getting them behind us as we did to the problems we had originally, and I think we will succeed just as well on that score also.''
The problems Mr. Baldrige acknowledged now come from Cocom, which stands for Coordinating Committee, a Paris-based body run by 15 Western allies that screens high-technology exports to Communist countries to protect military security.
Some orders are delayed for months while Cocom member governments review each application.
China, which seeks most-favored-nation treatment from the United States, is expected to request exemption from Cocom procedures. 
On his May 1983 visit, Mr. Baldrige lifted export restrictions against China on ''dual-use'' technology with military potential.
Mr. Zheng said China's economic development would continue to give impetus to United States trade, which reached a high of $6.07 billion last year.

file: BANGLADESH MILITARY LEADER SAYS HE FEARS SOVIET.txt
text:
ï»¿
Lieut. Gen. Hussain Mohammed Ershad, this nation's new military ruler, said in an interview today that he believed the Soviet Union was ''very dangerous.''
He also said that Bangladesh felt nothing but friendship toward the United States and that he thought President Reagan was a strong leader.
General Ershad also confirmed reports that two Soviet Embassy attaches were arrested a week ago while trying, for thus far unexplained reasons, to set fire to nearly 600 reels of movie film.
Â 
Firm on Rooting Out Corruption
In the 75-minute interview, the soft-spoken general, who on March 24 suspended constitutional government, also made the following points:
- Not even family ties with army officers will save the lives of former Cabinet ministers if they are found guilty by military tribunals of corruption. 
''We can hang them,'' General Ershad said.
Lieut Gen Hussain Mohammed Erhsad, new military ruler of Bangladesh, asserts Soviet Union is "very dangerous"
- Democracy will be restored ''without a doubt'' within two years, and unspecified rights of expression and political activity may be restored sooner.
- Western and Chinese diplomats were sounded out for their possible reaction in advance of the coup. 
These diplomats have since said that the aid on which Bangladesh depends will continue. 
All the major nations except the Soviet Union were informed the evening before the coup happened, and India was told some days earlier.
- The Bangladeshi Army includes some ''hot heads,'' in General Ershad's words, who may press for moredrastic changes than the current arrest of half a dozen ministers on charges of corruption and the promise to feed the poor, develop the economy and improve government administration.
Â 
Visited in Unpretentious Office
As General Ershad spoke in fluent English about these points and also handed over written answers to questions submitted in advance, he sat in his comfortable but unpretentious office in Dacca's military cantonment.
The general wore neat camouflage fatigues and black combat boots. 
He smiled easily, sat with practiced composure, and did not smoke. 
He conceded that his offer to accept the surrender of illegal weapons before their possession becomes a capital crime had not been ''a big success.''
The general said he intended to revitalize industry, dismiss unproductive bureaucrats, improve the performance of governmentowned enterprises, ''go all out'' for agriculture, encourage free enterprise, continue the program of the late President Ziaur Rahman of voluntary public works, and improve birth control, saying the country's recent record was so bad that he was ''ashamed'' to talk about it.
General Ershad said that his Government planned some form of land redistribution, but he did not elaborate. 
More than three-quarters of the rural work force is now landless, compared with 50 percent a dozen years ago.
Â 
Details on the Soviet Incident
The Soviet attaches who were arrested March 31 about 20 miles northwest of here while trying to burn the films were charged, an official said in a separate interview, with ''vicious movements,'' endangering the forest and creating a health hazard.
After being held overnight in jail, they were released into the custody of the Soviet Embassy pending an investigation of the 588 reels of movie film that the Government seized.
General Ershad said, ''We're just waiting to find out'' what the films contain and why the two men were trying to burn them. 
The incident is at least the second confrontation with the Soviet Embassy in the past year. 
In June, the embassy attempted to import what appeared to be electronic monitoring equipment. 
It was barred from doing so.
In other remarks on the Soviet Union, General Ershad said: ''We cannot trust them so much. 
They are very crude. 
They have such a mighty military machine.''
Â 
U.S. Responses Called Inadequate
''And it is your fault,'' he added politely, referring to what he called inadequate American responses to past Soviet moves. 
''We are really scared about what they may do next,'' he said about the Russians.
Bangladesh, the former East Pakistan, which became independent in 1971 with India's help, was once considered to lean moderately in the direction of the Soviet Union, which had supported India's policy in the struggle for the independence of Bangladesh while the United States quietly favored Pakistan.
Soviet prestige in Bangladesh gradually declined. 
It fell rapidly after the 1975 assassination of President Sheik Mujibur Rahman, the first Bangladesh leader, who was strongly pro-Indian.
Some diplomats believe that the accession of General Ershad to power reflects a gradual shift in Bangladesh toward China, the Western nations and the Arab oil producers of the Persian Gulf. 
The influence of the Persian Gulf states in this Moslem nation is said to have grown in recent years.
Â 
On Good Terms With Chinese
Concerning China, General Ershad said: ''Peking I can go to any time. 
I have a standing invitation. 
We are on very good military terms.''
Bangladeshi politics have been decidedly secular. 
When asked what world leaders he had admired, General Ershad mentioned only Kemal Ataturk, who transformed the Moslem Turks' Ottoman Empire into a secular democracy after World War I.However, General Ershad said he believed in ''the perfect socialism of Islam.''
In outlining his economic and administrative plans, he said he hoped to foster prosperity by attacking corruption and rationalizing operations.
He complained several times of the nation's inefficiency. 
As he spoke, the lights and air-conditioner in his office went off for several minutes. 
Dacca has several power failures every day.
Â 
Businessmen Assailed on Loans
He attacked businessmen who had taken government loans and never repaid them. 
''You cannot get the money back,'' he said. 
''Some of these people have become very rich. 
Some of them have $10 million out of the country.''
As for industry, he said, ''We have all assembly plants'' - using foreign parts - ''not real industry.''
He lamented the need for importing fuel, food, machinery and consumer goods. 
''In all these,'' he said, ''middlemen take a cut.''
Bangladeshi exports, consisting mainly of jute in addition to hides, skins, leather and tea, are less than half of the value of imports.
Concerning civil service workers, the general said ''decentralization'' would become the basic policy. 
''They have created so many boards, so many offices,'' he said, ''and most of them have no work to do.''
This complaint is shared by foreign agricultural experts, who say that the typically mixed subsistence farms of Bangladesh have been served, if at all, by dozens of competing ministries and agencies.
Â 
Son of a Provincial Lawyer
General Ershad, who is the son of a provincial lawyer and briefly studied law himself before turning to outdoor sports and the army, said he sympathized with the poor.
''They are really suffering,'' he said. 
''They need so little.''
He added. that he would consider it a victory ''if we can create a system where these people can get justice, can get two square meals a day, can have some clothing, can sleep free of lawlessness and threats.'
The general said the number of landless had increased in recent years because some peasants had lost land to unscrupulous neighbors. 
But he added, drawing his eyebrows together in a worried frown, ''We have to motivate the people.''
''Justice and fair play will be made to reign supreme,'' he said in one of the written answers. 
''We will set examples of discipline, austerity and accountability in all walks of life.''
The written responses also mentioned ''a dynamic New Economic Order.''
Â 
'Doesn't Know Where to Begin'
General Ershad sounded some notes of doubt. 
On the great economic problems of this nation of 90 million people, one of the world's poorest, with a gross national product of $100 per capita, he said: ''One does not actually know where to begin. 
But we are trying to tackle them one by one.''
Similarly, when questioned about potential disruption within the army, he replied, ''If some young adventurers take over the country, the consequences will be terrible. 
So we cannot fail.''
Reminded that both of Bangladesh's two most notable rulers were assassinated, he said his ''life style'' had not changed. 
''I cannot sit in a room all the time,'' he said. 
''I have to go out and be among the people. 
Life and death are controlled by God. 
We actually believe this.''

text:
ï»¿
GOOD MASSAGE is a potent tonic for mind and body. 
It can help relieve tension, stress and strain; temporarily aid blood circulation; make joints more supple, and act as a natural tranquilizer to induce pleasurable sedation. 
Medically, when performed by a physician or physical therapist, it can ease the pain of backaches, arthritis, bursitis, whiplash, sciatica and migraines. 
Massage, as a passive form of exercise, is also a valuable substitute for those who are incapable of activity.
Yet massage does not build muscle strength, burn up calories or break up fat cells. 
Unlike physical exercise, the effects are shortlived. 
And some people should not be massaged: those with infections, malignancies, blood clots, redness or contusions, impaired sensation, phlebitis or skin disease. 
In addition, skin that is thin due to injury or burn should not be massaged.
GOOD MASSAGE is a potent tonic for mind and body.
But if one can afford a massage -an hour usually ranges in price from $25 to $50 and up - it can play a useful role in a health program. 
Aside from the heightened sense of well-being it arouses, it relaxes muscles in preparation for physical activity - the reason massage is often used by athletes. 
After a vigorous workout, it may also help relieve muscle tightness and, with the temporary increase in blood circulation, aid the body in removing wastes - such as lactic acid - generated by physical exercise.
In general, the success of any type of massage therapy is linked to the skill of the therapist. 
''Massage has lost a lot of its potential value because it's being done by everyone and everybody,'' says Jack Hofkosh, director of the department of physical therapy at New York University's Institute of Rehabilitation Medicine. 
''There is no reason why somebody who needs a relaxation massage can't go and have a masseur work with him as long as it's understood that it's only going to have a relaxation effect. 
But if it's massage that has to be medically prescribed for a particular condition, you need a physician who is trained to prescribe it properly.''
In New York State, massage therapists must be licensed. 
To be eligible for the examination, an applicant must have graduated from an approved school and have completed 500 hours of rigorous study. 
Fewer than half the states now have licensing requirements, however.
Massage methodology is usually categorized as Eastern (from Japan and China) or Western (from Sweden). 
Offshoots of these range from medical massages to intensive body-working techniques.
The principles of Swedish massage were organized in the early 1800's by Pehr Henrik Ling, a Swedish fencing master and gymnastics instructor who used massage and exercise to treat his own rheumatism.
The French brought massage to the West, and French terminology is often still used. 
The basic movements of Swedish massage are effleurage or gliding strokes; petrissage or kneading;tapotement or stimulating strokes; friction or movements that compress the skin, and vibrating or shaking movements. 
All are done on bare skin that has been lubricated with cream, oil or powder to reduce friction.
Shiatsu massage from Japan (shi meaning finger; atsu, pressure) is sometimes called acupressure, which it resembles and which originated in China nearly 5,000 years ago.
''The ancient Chinese became aware of an increased sensitivity of certain skin areas (called points) when a body organ or function was impaired,'' writes Frances M. Tappan in ''Healing Massage Techniques'' (Reston Publishing Company, Reston, Va., 1978). 
''Consequently some of the relationships between various internal organs and their functions were established.''
In the shiatsu system, pressure can be from hand, elbow or knee and is used upon strategic points - known as tsubos - located along pathways called meridians. 
Improving ''energy flow'' along these paths is said to benefit the health of the internal organs. 
One caution: Having someone walk on your back and apply pressure with the toes is not part of traditional shiatsu; the heavy and inexacting pressure may cause back injury.
Shiatsu usually lasts from 30 minutes to an hour. 
Clothing is worn and no lubricants are used. 
The treatment may be uncomfortable, but should not be painful - it has been referred to as ''hurting good.''
In the area of medical massage, connective tissue and friction massage are both used on specific areas of the body. 
Connective-tissue massage helps to loosen fibrous tissue around muscles and to ease various disorders. 
Friction massage involves intermittent pressure on the body's soft tissues and is often used in treating tendon injuries.
Reflexology is based on the ancient Chinese method of using thumb pressure on specific areas of the feet that correspond to different body organs in an effort to improve their functioning.
In some cases, notably Rolfing and the polarity method, the therapy may be as uncomfortable as the disorder. 
Both systems use heavy and painful pressure purportedly to bring the body into vertical alignment; practitioners claim that normal posture may have become distorted due to stress, injury, illness or even the force of gravity. 
Polarity therapy works on reflex points, like those along the meridians, attempting to free ''energy flow.''
Rolfing manipulates the fasciae, or membranes supporting and sheathing the muscles. 
The premises and outcomes of both types of treatment are in dispute by experts.
Massage is generally thought of as an art form, and massage therapists all have their own styles of operating. 
For instance, at the Helena Rubinstein Beaute salon in Manhattan, Evelina Cardenas, a registered therapist with 35 years of experience, borrows from various disciplines. 
She also uses magnets to ''energize the body,'' tiger balm for sore muscles, a suction machine to ''help cellulite'' and a Chinese technique that gently hammers the soles of the feet ''for alignment.''
The massage therapist William Weslow, with a client list that reads like a Who's Who in dance and theater, is a former soloist with the New York City Ballet and a practitioner of massage for 25 years. 
He has developed a technique that combines strong relaxing strokes, deep muscular pressure and some needed probing - occasionally painful - of tight troubled areas. 
A high point of his treatment is an invigorating scalp massage, which one famed client has described as ''a mild earthquake.''
Between treatments, he advises clients who have upper back and neck problems to take hot baths, use heating pads, rub light balms on the affected areas and sleep with a warm covering to keep the body temperature up at night, which also keeps muscles relaxed.
The aim of his therapy is to increase circulation and bring about relaxation. 
''The biggest compliment someone can give me is falling asleep,'' says Weslow. 
''I know they're totally relaxed.''

file: Beijing Faults U.S. High-Tech Curbs.txt
text:
ï»¿
China today criticized an American decision to curb the export of some high-technology products to China, saying the move was ''not reasonable.''
On Thursday, the State Department announced that it was suspending consideration of whether further high technology could be transferred to China because of what it has said is China's continued sale of Silkworm anti-ship missiles to Iran.
Iranian Silkworm missiles have been blamed for three attacks on targets in Kuwaiti waters in the last nine days, including a strike that damaged an oil-loading terminal on Thursday.
Iran has not confirmed that it was responsible for the attacks, and although it acknowledges having Silkworm missiles, it says it captured them in battle with Iraq.
A Souring in Relations
Iran's Ambassador to China repeated that assertion today and said that his country possessed far more missiles of another variety - the American-made, surface-to-air Stinger - than had been reported.
Referring to reports that Iran may have obtained as many as 16 of the shoulder-fired Stinger missiles from the arsenal of anti-Soviet guerrillas in Afghanistan, Ambassador Alaeddin Boroujerdi, said, ''the number of Stinger missiles we have is much bigger than that.''
The decision by the United States signaled a souring in relations between the two countries, some senior Western diplomats here said. 
Already, China has reacted heatedly to a recent Senate resolution criticizing Beijing's policies towards Tibet and the country's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, has personally accused several Congressmen of ''ignorance and arrogance'' for their views on Tibet.
Nonetheless, the United States Embassy here has made a great effort to portray the high-technology decision as a relatively minor issue and to suggest that relations continue normally.
Â 
China Issues Dispatch
China's reaction to the State Department action was contained in a four-paragraph dispatch issued by the Government-controlled New China News Agency here in Beijing.
''It is not reasonable at all for the United States to halt the review of relaxing controls of high-tech exports to China under the pretext of mounting tension in the gulf,'' the agency said. 
''The current strain in the gulf area is caused by the sustaining and escalating Iran-Iraq war, and further intensified by the military involvement of the big powers there.
''The liberalization of high-tech export controls on China has nothing to do with the situation in the gulf,'' it said.
China has encouraged the United States to expand the range of sophisticated technology that can be imported here, both because it believes the technology will help rejuvenate its industry and because much of its weaponry is outdated.
Â 
China Denies Sales to Iran
The United States has been reviewing requests by China to expand the kinds of products that it can import.
For months, the United States has protested to Beijing about the sale of Silkworm missiles to Iran. 
But China consistently denies that it has sold the missiles or any military equipment, to Iran.
The Silkworm, which is usually guided by radar, is not considered accurate enough to select a particular ship from among several in a small area. 
But when fired into a general area, it is likely to find one of the targets.
As recently as Wednesday, a spokesman for the Foreign Ministry here reiterated his Government's position. 
''We have stated on many occasions that China does not sell arms or missiles to Iran,'' he said.
But The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that the Reagan Administration has shown Chinese officials photographs of Chinese weapons being loaded in China and unloaded in Iran.
The Iranian Ambassador told foreign reporters here that the Silkworm missiles his country had were not Chinese.
American Embassy officials refused to say today whether the Chinese have officially protested the curb on high-technology exports.

file: BEIJING IS BACKED BY ADMINISTRATION ON UNREST IN TIBET.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Reagan Administration voiced support today for China's position in the unrest in Tibet, while the Senate voted without dissent to condemn China for its recent crackdown there.
Anti-Chinese demonstrations in Tibet have turned violent in recent days, with more than 14 people reported killed in one clash on Thursday. 
The protests were renewed today as about 60 people marched to a Government office in Lhasa, the Tibetan capital, where armed Chinese security forces quickly arrested them. 
[Page A8.] The divergent positions taken by the Administration and Congress on the events in Tibet reflect contrasting interests. 
The Administration is reluctant to take positions that might damage Chinese-American relations. 
But the 98-to-0 vote by the Senate today highlights Congressional concern over reports of human rights violations in Tibet, which China took over in 1950.
State Department Assails Vote
The vote is certain to be protested by China as an example of American interference.
State Department officials today voiced strong opposition to the Senate action. 
The measure, an amendment to the State Department authorization bill, also urged President Reagan to meet with the Dalai Lama, Tibet's exiled Buddhist leader.
In addition, it would require Mr. Reagan to certify that China is making progress on resolving human rights issues in Tibet before the United Stats proceeds with any new sales of arms or weapons technology to China.
The amendment does not call for economic sanctions against China, and a provision that would have required the United States to ''reassess and review'' arms sales because of China's actions in Tibet was deleted.
Â 
'Almost Certain Damage' to Ties
One State Department official said that any possible benefits of the Senate action for the Tibetan people were ''insufficient to outweigh the almost certain damage to the U.S.-China bilateral relationship.''
The United States has supported China's stated efforts in recent years to make amends in Tibet after two decades of repression. 
In recent days, the State Department has reaffirmed the American position that Tibet is part of China and that the Dalai Lama is a religious leader, not the head of a government in exile.
The United States has recognized China's sovereignty over Tibet since the 1940's, and has held since 1978 that Tibet is a part of China.
The Dalai Lama, who is both the spiritual and temporal leader of Tibetan Buddhists, fled Tibet in 1959 after Chinese troops crushed an uprising. 
He is now based in Dharmsala, India, although he periodically visits other countries.
His visit to the United States late last month and his testimony before Congressional panels was cited by Beijing as an interference in Chinese affairs.
Although the United States has often protested human rights abuses since the United States and China formally established embassies in each other's capitals in 1979, it has taken great care not to offend Chinese sensibilities.
Â 
Upbeat State Department Report
In a 24-page report to Congress Oct. 
1 on the treatment of minorities in China, written before the recent outbreak of violence, the State Department took a generally upbeat tone on Tibet. 
The report said that, since 1980, the Chinese Government had made a conscious effort to ease tensions and begin economic and other changes.
''Beijing has stressed its commitment to preserve Tibet's unique cultural, linguistic and religious traditions,'' the report concluded, in an effort to ''strengthen social stabilityI.''
Today's Senate action challenges that assertion and calls for the State Department to present an updated human rights report in 60 days.
The amendment accuses Chinese authorities of executing two Tibetans after the Dalai Lama testified before Congress last month. 
It also blames the Chinese police for violent clashes with demonstrators on Sept. 
27 and for killing at least six Tibetans and wounding many others when they opened fire on unarmed demonstrators Thursday.
Â 
Population Transfer Charged
The Senate also charged that China has moved to transfer millions of Chinese into Tibet in an effort to ''make the Tibetan people a minority in their own homeland.''
One State Department official characterized the Senate portrayal of developments in Tibet as ''inaccurate, incomplete and misleading.''
Reiterating a position first articulated after a similar amendment was passed by the House last June, the official faulted the Senate for failing to acknowledge ''significant changes'' in China's policies that, he said, have led to an improvement of human rights conditions in Tibet.
The Senate amendment is expected to be considered by the House after the Senate passes the State Department authorization bill, which then goes to the President for his signature.
Â 
Dalai Lama Peace Plan
The State Department also takes issue with assertions of large Chinese population transfers into Tibet, accepting the Chinese claim that the number of Chinese civilians there has actually declined since 1980.
The Reagan Administration is also unhappy with support on Capitol Hill for a five-point ''peace zone'' proposal made by the Dalai Lama to Congressional leaders during his little-publicized visit to Washington last month. 
The proposal calls for the withdrawal of Chinese troops from Tibet, an end to China's population-transfer policy and negotiations on the future of Tibet.
In a Sept. 
22 letter to Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang of China, Senator Claiborne Pell, Democrat of Rhode Island, Senator Jesse Helms, Republican of North Carolina, and House Democratic and Republican leaders endorsed the proposal of the Dalai Lama as a ''historic step towards resolving the important question of Tibet and alleviating the suffering of the Tibetan people.''
Mr. Pell is chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
Although the Reagan Administration did not comment on the proposal at the time, one State Department official today characterized it as ''a veiled independence plan.''
He added, ''At this particular time, Congressional support for Tibetan independence sends the wrong signal to more-violent elements and could lead to more bloodshed.''
Â 
Plan Linked to Unrest
News of the Dalai Lama's proposal was widely disseminated in Tibet and is believed to have contributed to the atmosphere of unrest. 
So sensitive was his visit to the United States that Chinese authorities protested to the State Department and the American Embassy in Beijing even before his arrival and again after he announced his proposal.
Although the Dalai Lama did not request a meeting with President Reagan during his visit, State Department officials said that any request for a meeting with officials of the executive branch would have been denied because it might have given China the impression that the United States supported his political claims.

file: BEIJING JOURNAL_From Mao to Zhao, He Has Stitched for the Mighty.txt
text:
ï»¿
Mao was a customer. 
So was Zhou Enlai. 
Deng Xiaoping is one now, as are the Communist Party chief, Zhao Ziyang, and the rest of China's inner circle of leaders.
Tian Atong, tailor to the mighty, slipped from an envelope a glossy color photograph - a formal portrait of the five-member Standing Committee of the Communist Party's Politburo. 
He trailed a finger across the print.
''I did these,'' he said. 
''I did each of these suits.''
In the middle of the group, a trim Mr. Zhao was the clear fashion plate in a subtle two-button double-breasted blue pin stripe.
''Not bad, eh?''
Mr. Tian said, his gaze lingering. 
''It's not so wide like the British. 
The waist is narrower, so it looks sleeker.''
Â 
A Cut Above the Rest
Mr. Tian pirouetted into the public eye last month when Mr. Zhao, in a display of nationalist pride, flashed the red and white label of the Hongdu Fashion Corporation inside his suit coat to foreign reporters skeptical of its local origins.
''I hope you will send out a dispatch saying all my suits are made in China and look very smart,'' the new party chief said.
Mr. Tian, it was learned, was the architect of this smartness.
Here in the Chinese capital, where the sartorial skirmishes of Seventh Avenue or the Rue du Faubourg-St.-Honore seem like tepid tea, the political cut of a man is usually, though not always, apparent from the cut of his clothes. 
And it is Mr. Tian, owlish behind his horn-rimmed glasses, who has been called on, time and time again, to cut the fabric.
Â 
'That's My Work'
The most prominent monument to his work is the pale gray, high-collared suit worn by Mao in the 30-foot portrait hanging over the gate to the Forbidden City. 
''That's my work,'' said Mr. Tian, now 63 years old.
In 1937, when he was 13, he left his home in Changshu and followed his brother's footsteps into a Shanghai tailor's shop. 
''I wanted to learn how to be a tailor,'' Mr. Tian said. 
''My brother was a tailor, so he introduced me to a shop where I studied as an apprentice for four years.''
''I worked at a British clothing shop on Nanjing Road until the Japanese came,'' he said. 
''The British people in the shop were interned and I was the only tailor left. 
After the war, the British came back and picked up running the shop.''
After the People's Republic was founded in 1949, Mr. Tian moved to a state-owned garment factory on the other end of Nanjing Road. 
A faint echo of the swagger that put Shanghai onto the fashion map of world travelers in the 1930's and 40's remained for a while, Mr. Tian said, but it dissipated in the march of Communism.
Â 
The Making of the Mao Suit
Still, Mr. Tian retained a mastery of cloth that set him apart from other Shanghai tailors and that brought him to Beijing to make Mao suits for the country's leaders. 
''The first Mao suit I ever made was in 1956, when I came to Beijing,'' Mr. Tian said.
Though it was known formally as a Zhongshan suit, after a style popularized by Sun Yat-sen (or in the Chinese dialect of the north, Sun Zhongshan), the dress adopted by Mao and his colleagues was subtly different.
''We took the pleats out of the pockets,'' he said, transforming the garment of Chinese republicanism into the dress of Communism.
In those days, Mr. Tian said, everything was secret. 
''I never went to measure Mao personally,'' he said. 
''I didn't know him myself. 
His secretaries would come and tell me what he wanted.''
Although nearly every official wore a Mao suit, Mr. Tian said, he made Western-style suits once in a while. 
''In 1960, the Foreign Minister was going abroad and I had to make a Western suit for him,'' Mr. Tian said.
But with the onslaught of the Cultural Revolution and the denunciation of everything Western, particularly in the arts and fashion, Mr. Tian was once again reduced to making Mao suits in dark or light gray - a regimen that he endured until 1980.
Â 
Lapels a Bit Too Narrow
''That year, Zhao Ziyang became Prime Minister,'' Mr. Tian said. 
''He was the first to get a Western suit. 
That first suit, well, the lapels were a bit narrow and the shoulders a little flat. 
Hu Yaobang was also one of the first.''
Mr. Hu, who was the party leader until forced from the post after last winter's student demonstrations, had a proclivity for Western styles, even going to the point of encouraging the Chinese to forsake chopsticks in favor of Western cutlery.
Mr. Tian, who wore a charcoal pin-stripe vest with lapels over a beige wool sweater, wandered into the workshop where he trained young tailors. 
He ran his palm down the front of a chestnut-colored suit coat, still sleeveless, hanging on a plastic mannequin. 
''This is new,'' he said. 
''See, one button. 
Very smart.''
Around him, dozens of tailors worked in rows under flourescent lights. 
Swaths of wool and silk were piled about.
Much of Mr. Tian's time is spent supervising his workshop, which churns out clothing for the leadership. 
His hand becomes more evident, however, when the suit is for Mr. Zhao or other very senior leaders.
''Zhao Ziyang's suits are a little smaller now,'' he confided, snatching a ruler from a sewing table. 
He moved his finger toward the three. 
''He's been doing a lot of exercise these days so he's thinner. 
About three centimeters in the waist.''
Mr. Zhao invited Mr. Tian over this year for a chat about the rag trade. 
''I talked about how difficult it is for Chinese to have new clothes,'' Mr. Tian recalled. 
''He suggested that we set up more clothing shops.''
Â 
A Few Fashion Hard-Liners
Not all the top Chinese want Western creations. 
''Some leaders still want Mao suits,'' he said. 
''They won't wear anything else, Li Xiannian, Peng Zhen, Deng Xiaoping.''
Both Mr. Li, China's President, and Mr. Peng, the chairman of the National People's Congress, are regarded as hard-line Marxists often uncomfortable with what they see as the creeping influence of Western ideas in China. 
Mr. Deng, on the other hand, has been the prime mover behind China's effort to cast off the shackles of traditional Communism.
Mr. Tian earns the same as other senior tailors at Hongdu, about 200 yuan a month, or $54, a salary that perhaps explains the low price of his creations: a vested suit costs just 66 yuan, slightly less than $18.
Mr. Tian turned toward his visitor, sizing up the Paul Stuart suit with the eye of a turkey carver. 
He fondled the gray wool lapel with a thumb and forefinger and muttered, ''A bit old-fashioned, wouldn't you say?''

file: BEIJING JOURNAL_MANICURES_ WHAT WOULD MAO SAY_.txt
text:
ï»¿
As China's campaign against ''bourgeois liberalization'' captures the headlines, Zhen Wen gets her facials.
''We all like to be beautiful,'' said Miss Zhen, a 32-year-old machinery designer, whose blue jeans and feathered hair would blend into any New York crowd.
She waved her arm at the dozens of people around her in a Beijing beauty parlor, luxuriating in their new hairdos, manicures and facial treatments, and added: ''This concerns how people live. 
Bourgeois liberalization concerns ideology, student demonstrations and that kind of thing.''
That sentiment suffuses and consoles Beijing. 
While tempests rage in Communist Party circles, and the Great Hall of the People is filled with calls to exorcise ''bourgeois liberalization,'' most people quietly enjoy their new-found bourgeois pleasures.
Â 
'People Like to Be Beautiful'
''We fight against bourgeois liberalization,'' said Sun Fenghua, a 30-year-old cashier, as a hairdresser expertly shampooed and molded her hair. 
''But Chinese people like to be beautiful, just like other people.''
Some of China's aging leaders, who regularly hail the virtue of ''plain living,'' may take a harder line on preening oneself than does Miss Sun.
But comments like those from Miss Zhen and Miss Sun underscore two facts of life here: how far China has come in the last few years, and the resistance to any broadening of the anti-liberalization campaign that in the last few months has constricted intellectual life and economic experimentation.
In just a few years ,the Chinese people have radically changed their appearance. 
Ethnic Chinese visitors from Hong Kong or Singapore used to be instantly recognizable by their colorful clothes and fashionable haircuts.
Local residents, although they had often graduated from the blue Mao suits that they wore during the Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976, wore dour, drab clothing and plain, unisex haircuts.
Â 
A Rainbow of Colors
Now a visitor to Beijing needs color film. 
Old people still usually wear Mao jackets or other somber colors, but the young wear red, pink, green, blue and other colors that until recently were only seen here in rainbows.
Even the bicycles that jam the capital's streets, although still mostly black and white, are sometimes painted green or blue. 
Young women commonly curl their hair or have it styled in other ways. 
Some wear earrings in newly pierced ears.
''This is civilization,'' Liu Yufen, a 24-year-old kindergarten teacher, said as she displayed the loop earrings running through her lobes.
An unanswered question is whether the leaders of the anti-liberalization campaign, which showed its strength after student demonstrations late last year, frown on such sartorial pleasures. 
Equally uncertain is whether the population would accept a broadening of the campaign to clamp down on the small liberties of fashion that to most people matter more than speeches about remote topics like bourgeois liberalization.
Â 
No Turning Back Seen
''The campaign against bourgeois liberalization is falling on stone-deaf ears,'' said an American businessman living here. 
''And people simply won't allow the Government to push them backward in their daily lives to the way they used to live.''
A Chinese official who runs a company in Washington State that supplies timber to China, Yao Wei, said economic changes would continue, partly because ''it is not possible to stop them - people wouldn't allow it.''
On the other hand, analysts who are more pessimistic say that the Chinese people may not be consulted and that turmoil in the past was not always predictable. 
In the Cultural Revolution, for example, many of the same people who now buy lacy underwear or bright blue bicycles did all they could to undermine their beauty and sex appeal.
For all the uncertainties, there are signs that in its effect on daily life the campaign against liberalization is primarily a retrenchment or a pause instead of a sharp retreat, as some have feared.
Â 
Bikinis in Beijing
Later this month, for example, women body builders wearing bikinis will take part in China's first national body-building and aerobic exercise tournament. 
Chen Haosu, the Deputy Mayor of Beijing, where the tournament will be held, asked people not to overreact to the bikinis, adding, ''Don't classify bikinis in the scope of bourgeois liberalization.''
The Government, however, recently has cracked down on restaurants in southern Guandong Province that use bikini-clad waitresses to entice customers.
This month, the Chinese Army announced that it would go ahead with the reintroduction of military ranks, which were abolished as a mark of class consciousness in 1965.
An exchange for trading bonds opened this month in Tianjin, adding to stock and bond markets already set up within the last year in Beijing, Shanghai, Wuhan and Shenyang.
Â 
Reappearance of the Maid
Other daily pleasures that might strike even an American as bourgeois scarcely raise an eyebrow here. 
Cosmetic surgeons in Beijing and other cities are performing record numbers of breast augmentations, nose corrections and operations to make Chinese eyes look more Caucasian.
Maids, who largely disappeared during the Cultural Revolution, are reappearing with a vengeance. 
There are about 30,000 maids in Beijing alone, almost all of whom started work in the last few years. 
They serve wealthier families for $10 a month, plus room and board. 
Five state-run companies place maids, and five more such companies are being formed.
These days the maids are called by a new name - service attendants -to reduce bourgeois associations, but their work is the same. 
And they apparently have support at high levels.
The general manager of the biggest of the state-run maid-supply companies, Li Ruiqin, said one of her customers was Li Peng, a Soviet-trained Deputy Prime Minister who is widely mentioned as a candidate for the Prime Minister's job.
Li Peng himself apparently sees no contradiction between maintaining the campaign against bourgeois liberalization and retaining his maid, a young woman from Hunan Province.
Miss Li, the company manager, said, ''Our information is that he is very satisfied with her.''

file: Beijing Journal_Out She Goes, Again, Miss Ideological Impurity.txt
text:
ï»¿
In 1947, Daisy Wang walked away with Shanghai's last beauty crown.
Then came Communism, proletarian morality and the conviction that in the workers' and peasants' paradise, beauty was bourgeois. 
Mao suits, in a choice of blue or gray, became the fashion. 
For women, lipstick and nail polish were decadent extravagances.
Perfume, makeup and coiffures have been back for a while, and this year, it appeared, so were beauty pageants. 
But the beast ideological purity, that treacherous ground of uncertainty in Chinese life, has resurfaced and beauty is on the run.
Last month, a local television station announced a contest to crown a Shanghai Maiden. 
A Beijing television station followed suit, declaring a Girls of Youth and Elegance pageant.
Now, the Shanghai event has been canceled while the Beijing affair has retreated from public view. 
Political puritanism, it seems, is back.
Â 
Picking a Beijing Flower
Three weeks ago, wobbling uncertainly on new high heels, 800 young women crowded into the Chongwenmen Cultural Palace to compete for the title of Beijing Flower in the capital's first beauty pageant in more than four decades.
''This is the first such contest in the capital similar to beauty contests in other countries,'' said Long Xinmin, the head of the Beijing television studio. 
''But ours puts as much emphasis on the participants' knowledge, performing technique and moral character as on their appearance and dress.''
Pageant officials printed up score sheets to evaluate the contestants, with categories ranging from ''teeth'' to ''length of legs,'' from ''color of skin'' to ''demeanor,'' from ''makeup'' to ''sense of humor.''
''Such contests are necessary to raise Chinese girls' awareness of grooming and deportment as a whole,'' Lan Guang, one of the eight judges, told the China Daily. 
''Esthetic education and training are also urgently needed in this country. 
The level of the contestant's grooming as a whole is rather low. 
A large number of them don't know what beauty is or how to use makeup or clothes to show off their natural beauty.''
Â 
Now a Closed Affair
Nervous young women were required to show off their talents by singing, dancing, reading aloud and expounding on their knowledge of Chinese culture. 
The finals of the Beijing Flower pageant, an extravaganza of music, color and fashion, was to have been broadcast by Beijing television, with the top 30 women offered modeling jobs.
In any case, those were the plans. 
Now, the Shanghai contest has been scuttled and the Beijing pageant has been reduced to a secret affair in a room somewhere in the city, closed to Chinese and foreign reporters alike and banned from television.
Â 
'Conditions Are Not Yet Ripe'
Shanghai's Communist Party chief, Jiang Zemin, was quoted by the official press agency as saying ''conditions are not yet ripe'' for a beauty pageant. 
An unnamed official was also quoted as saying that the city's economic problems require ''leaders and the 12 million city residents to be of one heart and one mind and to quietly immerse themselves in hard work.''
''It is premature to spend 450,000 yuan'' - about $126,000 - ''on a beauty pageant,'' the official said.
In Beijing, there was more mystery about what had happened, more rumors.
One story has it that the propaganda department of the Communist Party Central Committee frowned on the notion of picking a Beijing Flower and decreed that the show would not go on. 
Another rumor was that Hu Qili, a member of the Standing Committee of the Politburo, the most powerful body in the country, ordered the pageant scrapped.
Â 
'Not Good for the Girls'
Zhu Hansheng, a pageant organizer and a man of irrepressible good humor, deflected suggestions that politics had torpedoed his project. 
But he admitted that the grandiose schemes of last month had evaporated.
''Our way of doing things now is not quite the same as we originally planned,'' Mr. Zhu said, spreading his hands as if dropping a watermelon.
''We don't need to broadcast it on television,'' said Mr. Zhu, a director of the China Television Artists Association. 
''It's not good for the girls.''
No, Mr. Zhu insisted, there had not been any explicit instruction to tone things down.
''If Hu Qili had said stop, we would have had to stop immediately and I wouldn't have agreed to see you,'' he said. 
''China's not too rich. 
Some people don't eat. 
Some people say how can you hold a beauty contest if some people can't eat or dress properly?''
A collaborator in the pageant's organization, Zhang Andong, interrupted, ''We haven't received any directives directly from the authorities, but we can feel the atmosphere.''
''Feeling the atmosphere'' is a talent most Chinese have cultivated with care, for a loss of touch usually means trouble from above.
Mr. Zhu said the Beijing pageant would now be a private affair between the judges and the contestants. 
Previously announced prizes, including a piano, have been withdrawn. 
Instead, he said, the winners will receive ''Olympic-style medals.''
Across the Formosa Strait, Taiwan, which banned such beauty contests until last year, reveled in the attention it attracted by staging the Miss Universe Pageant, which ended today. 
''This kind of publicity is something our Government cannot possibly buy,'' Yao Ying-chi, an official of the ruling Nationalist Party, told The Associated Press in Taipei.
But Mr. Zhu, foreshadowing a sobering of Communist attitudes toward parading female pulchritude, said, ''If the whole country started to do this, it wouldn't be good.''

Â 
Sex-Education Courses
Any discussion of sex has, until very recently, been discouraged, or indeed prohibited, by the moral puritanism brought to China by Communism. 
Those strictures have eased somewhat in the last year with high schools and universities publicizing sex-education courses.
But these classes, eagerly attended according to official reports, are purely pedagogical exercises in mechanics, designed to dispel ignorance and encourage healthy marital lives.
Indeed, eroticism itself is taboo, a pronounced departure from a cultural tradition that for millenia celebrated sexual dalliance. 
During the Ming Dynasty, which endured for nearly three centuries until Manchu invaders claimed the throne in 1644, a vast corpus of erotic literature, so-called ''wind and wave novels,'' appeared in a vernacular prose accessible to any literate person.
Some of these novels, ''Jinpingmei,'' or ''The Golden Lotus,'' and ''Roubutuan,'' or ''The Prayer Mat of Flesh,'' were widely read, never for reasons of prurience, but as social criticisms of public morality and political decadance as well as for their depiction of amorous pursuits.
Wrote the author of ''The Golden Lotus'':
Â 
However minute his precautions,
door bolted, and early home,
between him and her love
towers a wall of precipitous rock.
One spark of youthful desire
and the threads of marriage are snarled.
Though he set her about with bars,
one day he finds the cage empty.
For their part, China's cultural watchdogs have been riveted only by the explicit eroticism in such novels, labeling them ''obscene'' and promptly banning their publication.
Â 
Western Literature Suppressed
Even more, Western literature that explores the erotic has also been long suppressed. 
Last month, however, an obscure publishing house in Hunan announced that it would publish D. H. Lawrence's banned ''Lady Chatterley's Lover,'' a work attacked as pornography by hard-line party elders during a wave of intellectual repression last year.
But Suo Tianzhang, a professor of English who provided an introduction for a new six-volume collection of the Victorian author's works, wrote: ''Lawrence is not a frivolous writer, and his 'Lady Chatterley's Lover' is no pornography. 
What should be admired in him is the all-embracing humanity which pervades his work.''
China's authorities routinely insist that ''obscene publications,'' a loosely defined term, provoke criminality. 
A recent survey of young hooligans, reported by the official Chinese press agency, found that most had been exposed to obscene works.
In from the margins of Chinese life, in the vast arena of average existence, it remains difficult to detect the depth of sexual unease. 
The letters in Liberation Daily begin to provide that insight. 
Of course, in China's male-dominated society, the urge to infidelity not unsurprisingly appears from the pen of unhappy husbands, not disgruntled wives.
It would be unthinkable for a woman to confide her views about sex, inside marriage or outside it, to acquaintances, much less strangers.
Â 
A Beijing Poll, of Sorts
An obscure poll of married workers in Beijing cited in a recent book, ''New Trends in China: Marriage and the Family,'' found that only 35 percent of the couples are ''on good terms'' with their spouses with 2 percent ''in some kind of family crisis.''
The remaining 63 percent, the survey found, fell somewhere between these poles.
More startling, given the climate of strict social conformity, was the finding that 9 percent of couples were ''not opposed to the idea of extramarital sex,'' and that another 4 percent said it was all right to ''take a romantic interest in another person.''
But the three letters emblazoned across page 4 of Liberation Daily suggest that marital discontent is a subject for public discussion and having affairs is no longer unthinkable.
Â 
Competition and Marriage
Li Siyuan, who gave his address as Xinshi South Road in Shanghai, appropriated a formula from the country's process of economic restructuring to buttress his argument for having a mistress.
''The introduction of the mechanism of competition into the economy has drastically transferred our society in a few short years,'' he wrote. 
''People don't deny the usefulness of competition simply because a few factories have gone under. 
Similarly, we should also be advocating competition in marriage and the 'third person' would provide just such a competitive force. 
If society allowed this sort of competition to exist, the two parties to a marriage are bound to feel that with constant hard work the threat of the 'third person' always lurks nearby.''
While there are no explicit laws against infidelity, neighborhood watch committees and the acute shortage of living space conspire against enduring extramarital affairs. 
Even more, the prevailing ethics of Chinese socialism attach an unsavory ideological stigma to individual desires, impulses that imply a rejection of collective order.
But Deng Pengfei, a worker at the Dazhong Rubber Factory, thinks a ''third person'' ultimately will keep families together and offered a brutal Darwinian argument to support his view.
''I heard that in a National park in Alaska,'' Mr. Deng wrote, ''large numbers of deer in the reserve were becoming weak and sick. 
Alarmed, the Government poured funds in to save them, but to no avail. 
Finally, a bright employee introduced a few fierce wolves into the reserve and the sick and the weak were promptly eaten. 
This measure put a stop to the spread of disease and the deer also improved in health since they now had to run to escape from the wolves. 
I don't wish to compare the 'third person' to a wolf, but objectively that person's presence has the same kind of effect on a married couple's life.''

text:

In the two months since student protests led to the dismissal of Hu Yaobang as the party leader, a series of Central Committee documents have attacked the protesters, criticized Mr. Hu and outlined the limits of the campaign against Western ideas.
One of the documents, all of which have been read to party members, said that Mr. Hu had encouraged ''bourgeois liberalization.''
Others contained an denunciation of student protesters by Deng Xiaoping, the paramount leader; an outline of agricultural policy, and instructions on the dissemination of an essay on legal education.
The documents, in the form of party directives, appeared designed to affirm both ideological orthodoxy and the policy of economic change.
Although Mr. Deng, who emerged as an ideological watchdog, was given prominence in the documents, foreign diplomats and some Chinese wonder whether he remains fully in charge or has been weakened by those who oppose economic change.
Â 
Six Documents Circulated
So far, according to Hong Kong press accounts, six documents have been circulated to party units. 
The texts of some of them have been published in Hong Kong.
Last week, a party member read several documents to reporters for The Washington Post, the Kyodo news agency and Agence France-Presse. 
This unusual revelation of party documents prompted speculation over the motivation in releasing the information.
The first document, distributed Jan. 
2, contained remarks by Mr. Deng attacking student protesters and saying that the demonstrations should be suppressed.
''When necessary, we must deal severely with those who defy orders,'' Mr. Deng was quoted as having said in a Politburo meeting Dec. 
30. ''We can afford to shed some blood. 
Just try as much as possible not to kill anyone.''
Referring to Wei Jingshen, a dissident serving a prison term for ''counterrevolutionary propaganda,'' Mr. Deng said:
''The opposition to bourgeois liberalization must be pursued for 20 years. 
We have arrested Wei Jingshen and we will not release him. 
We do not need to pay attention to the faces of foreigners in doing this. 
By doing this we will not tarnish our image abroad.''
Â 
Deng Demanded Purge of 3
In the Politburo meeting, Mr. Deng also called for the purging of Fang Lizhi, an educator; Liu Binyan, a journalist, and Wang Ruowang, a writer, all three of whom were in fact later expelled from the party.
The second document, according to the Hong Kong press, was the text of a speech made by Mr. Deng at a party conference in September, in which he said there were proponents of ''bourgeois liberalization'' within the party.
The third document, issued Jan. 
17, contained a critique of Mr. Hu during his tenure as the party's General Secretary of the party. 
This document, according to the Hong Kong press, was based on a report compiled by Bo Yibo, a deputy chairman of the Central Advisory Commission, a body of elder statesmen.
The document said Mr. Hu's ''attitude toward opposing bourgeois liberalization was not resolute.''
It took issue with a comment said to have been made by Mr. Hu at a gathering of writers that the 1983 campaign against ''spiritual pollution,'' a movement against Western ideas, would not be revived.
''The Central Committee believes that spiritual pollution and bourgeois liberalization are one and the same thing,'' the document said.
It further charged that Mr. Hu did not correctly promote ''ideological rectification'' to insure that party members complied with the current line.
''He said that party rectification was aimed at promoting the economy, that the main criterion of party rectification should be economic results,'' the document said.
Â 
Hu Accused of Adventurism
Mr. Hu was also accused of seeking to stimulate economic development by encouraging greater consumer spending.
''Thus he again committed the mistake of economic adventurism by raising expectations beyond China's reality,'' the document said. 
''In meetings with foreign visitors, he said things that he should not have said about our country's crackdown on economic crimes.''
This point is believed to refer to an 1986 interview given to a Hong Kong publication in which he said that children of senior party leaders had been accused of economic crimes such as fraud and embezzlement and would be dealt with severely.
Among the accused was Hu Shiying, the son of Hu Qiaomu, a Politburo member. 
The son had been accused of embezzling more than 1 million yuan ($270,000).
Hu Yaobang, the party leader, according to the document, made unauthorized speeches.
''He broke party discipline and gave speeches all over the country on many occasions without the authorization of the Central Committee,'' the document said. 
''The result was that a lot of his formulations were not in accord with the Central Committee's.''
Â 
Limits on Anti-Western Drive
The fourth document sets forth rules governing the campaign against bourgeois liberalization. 
In a speech to the nation for the Chinese New Year. 
Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang outlined some of these rules, limiting the purge campaign to among party members.
''The press,'' the document said, ''should unconditionally propagate the party line and policy and should perform the role of the party's mouthpiece. 
It should strengthen the system of censorship.''
Those publications that have committed political mistakes and those of low quality should be closed.''
The fifth document, described as 10,000 words long, has not been published in the Hong Kong press, which says that it deals with agricultural marketing, rural industry and the responsibility system, whereby farmers contract to grow a certain amount for the Government and can sell the rest on the free market.
The sixth document called on party members to publicize a lengthy document on legal education approved Jan. 
22 by the National People's Congress, the nominal legislature.

text:
ï»¿
In a dramatic change in the way local elections are held in Beijing, the city government announced today that there would be more than one candidate for each seat in municipal elections.
It did not explain, however, how candidates would be nominated or how any election campaign would be conducted.
''In order to promote democracy and in order to give the people the opportunity to select the candidates that they will be satisfied with, this time the election will have more candidates than slots available,'' She Diqing, a deputy chairman of the standing committee of the Municipal People's Congress, said in a speech to the committee.
Â 
Student Protests Banned
The announcement, which appeared in Beijing Daily, follows an official crackdown on the wave of student demonstrations that have swept across China demanding wider democracy. 
On Friday, the standing committee issued a set of rules that in effect banned any public protest by students in the capital.
Although some Chinese villages and townships have offered two candidates for a seat in the local legislature, the larger cities operate on a system of a single candidate selected by the local Communist Party, with the voters given no say on who the candidate is.
Â 
Elections in Six Months
Beijing Daily hailed the new policy of having more than one candidate for each race in the capital as promoting greater democracy. 
The elections are to be held within six months. 
[Beijing students erected two anti-Government posters, United Press International reported. 
One said the Communist Government is ''in every respect identical'' to ''the most tyrannical feudal despotisms we've had.''
The other quoted Deputy Prime Minister Wan Li as saying, ''Democracy can only be something which we can bestow on someone as a favor.''] The large cities' system of handpicking party candidates has been the root of at least one outburst of student protest. 
In Hefei, the capital of Anhui Province, students marched early this month to demand that they be allowed to choose candidates for the provincial People's Congress.
Apparently stung by charges of undemocratic behavior, the local government there postponed the election, rescheduling it for Sunday, to give the students time to field their own candidates. 
On Tuesday evening, several thousand students from Qinghua University in Beijing spilled from the campus demanding democracy and freedom of the press. 
The protestors did not, however, appear to specifically challenge local election procedures.
The student demonstrations over the last three weeks have clearly shaken the authorities, who were slow to formulate a response. 
This week, after huge demonstrations in Shanghai that brought out as many as 50,000 people, the local authorities finally struck back by issuing orders virtually banning public protest.
Â 
Havoc From Protests Stressed
At the same time, the local press in Shanghai and Beijing, as well as the national press, have been filled with articles discrediting the motives of the students, emphasizing the upheaval caused by the protests and stressing the primacy of the Communist Party in guiding the program of economic and political changes.
The coverage has focused on the way in which the student demonstrations violated what the papers said were the democratic and constitutional rights of the average citizen, a tactic clearly intended to isolate the students.
Many accounts in recent days have dwelt in detail on the disruption to daily life and production. 
Guangming Daily quoted traffic and factory workers in Shanghai today as saying the students' actions had caused havoc.
''The demonstration blocked traffic and forced several hundred travelers to go on foot,'' the paper said. 
''A lot of workers were late because of the demonstration. 
Some old and weak people, as well as some ill people, were waiting in the cold wind for several hours. 
The demonstrations made more than 3,000 people miss their trains.''
''Speeding economic development and increasing people's living standard require a stable social environment,'' the paper added.
Â 
Likened to Red Guards
Worker's Daily, a paper that supposedly reflects the views of union members, today also used an increasingly heard tactic of identifying the student protesters with the violent and riotous behavior of the Red Guards in the Cultural Revolution, the 10 years of political upheaval triggered by Mao in an effort to destroy what he saw as an archaic and stolid party bureaucracy.
In no case have any students been given access to the press to give their account of the demonstrations or discuss the issues that precipitated them.
Yet even as the press continued to lacerate the students, the action by the Beijing People's Congress in revamping the election process appeared to speak directly to the protesters' call for greater democracy.
In its account of the meeting of the standing committee, Beijing Daily said the changes had been ''vigorously discussed.''
''The delegates said the coming election of a new people's congress constitutes a major development in the city's political life,'' it said.
''With the more intense effort to propagate the law,'' the paper concluded, ''people's political awareness and democratic consciousness is growing stronger and stronger.''
----#5,000 in Nanjing Debates NANJING, China, Dec. 
27 (AP) -About 5,000 students, workers and other residents of Nanjing jammed a traffic circle for the sixth straight night tonight to discuss freedom, economics and the future of China.
Open-air debates and arguments swirled around the foot of Drum Tower, a landmark in this eastern Chinese city of 3 million people.
Unlike pro-democracy street demonstrations in at least eight other Chinese cities this month, there has been no marching nor any confrontations with the authorities in Nanjing. 
There were few uniformed policemen in evidence today, although students said there were many undercover agents.
They said the authorities had made no effort to stop the discussions, which began Monday 22 and attracted crowds of up to 10,000 Wednesday night.
''It's not just the students who want democracy,'' said one worker. 
''Workers and peasants want it too, but we have families to support, and it would be difficult if we lose our jobs.''
The discussion went on for three hours before the crowds began to thin.
At one point, five policemen wandered into the crowd. 
There was a great roar and movement toward the officers, who quickly left.

text:

National Zoo officials celebrated a long-awaited event today when Ling-Ling, the giant panda, gave birth to a squealing, apparently healthy 4-ounce cub.
But while the cub appeared to be doing well, officials were cautious about predicting its chances of survival. 
Ling-Ling has given birth to two other cubs, but neither they nor any other giant panda born in the country survived, said Robert Hoage, the zoo's public affairs director. 
The only other pandas now in the United States are a pair on loan from China to the Bronx Zoo in New York.
Lisa Stevens, the zoo's manager of collection, witnessed the birth at 3:33 A.M. over closed-circuit television.
''I was thrilled, I wanted to jump up and down and go to the phone and call everybody but I couldn't move from the monitor,'' she said.
Ms. Stevens said the cub looked ''very much like a rat'' and had been squealing. 
''The baby appears to be healthy, it has a healthy set of lungs,'' she said. 
If it survives, the cub could grow as large as 6 feet tall and 300 pounds.
Zoo officials were optimistic about the mother's ability to care for her offspring. 
''Ling-Ling is showing totally appropriate behavior,'' cuddling and licking the newborn, Ms. Stevens said.
Officials monitoring the pandas by television said they would not know the sex of the cub until they could get close to it.
Ling-Ling mated with the zoo's male giant panda, Hsing-Hsing, several times in March, a zoo spokesman said.
A cub born to Ling-Ling in 1983 died of a prenatal bronchial infection three hours after birth and another cub was stillborn in 1984.The mother, about 18 years old, is the oldest giant panda in captivity, With the birth, the Panda House is expected to be closed for several months. 
But the public can view Ling-Ling and the cub on closed-circuit television in the Zoo's education building.
Hsing-Hsing and Ling-Ling are usually kept apart, and the father will not be allowed near the cub.
Ling-Ling and Hsing-Hsing were gifts from China in 1972. 
The Chinese Embassy will be given the first opportunity to name the cub.
There are six other surviving pandas bred in captivity outside of China, in Mexico City, Tokyo and Madrid.
It is estimated that fewer than 1,000 giant pandas survive in the wild, and they are listed as an endangered species.

file: Black Africa Leaves China In Quandary.txt
text:
ï»¿
Crowds chanting ''Down with blacks!'' in the eastern city of Nanjing this week have laid bare the gap in China between the official warmth extended to African countries and the suspicion that many Chinese seem to harbor toward African people.
Since 1949 China has cultivated special relations with black Africa. 
The ties have been founded in the spirit of third world camaraderie and in the hope that Mao's brand of agrarian Communism might influence Africa.
China has denounced apartheid in South Africa, and has devoted some of its scarce resources to aid for black Africa. 
It also offers scholarships to Africans, and 1,500 Africans now are studying across China.
But today more than 130 of those African students remained confined to a Government guest house in Yangzhou, 50 miles northeast of Nanjing, to protect them from angry crowds that earlier in the week screamed for the ''black devils'' to face punishment. 
With them were a handful of dark-complexioned Nepalese and Pakistani students who also were threatened by Chinese who in some cases had only a hazy idea of what an African looked like.
Â 
How Recent Unrest Began
The disturbances in Nanjing began after a brawl Saturday night between African students and Chinese students and university employees. 
For seven hours a few thousand Chinese besieged the Africans' dormitory and hurled rocks and bottles while chanting slurs.
Rumors spread that the Africans had beaten up, and perhaps killed, many Chinese. 
Another crowd, outraged that they should go unpunished, gathered on Sunday morning to attack the dormitory and demolish the possessions of the Africans. 
The Africans fled to the train station.
Several hundred students marched through Nanjing this evening, but the streets were generally quiet, Americans there said by telephone.
The Chinese students have said they will demonstrate each evening until the authorities punish the African students who they say are responsible for the initial brawl, which left 11 Chinese students and university employees injured. 
The African students say the Chinese started the fight.
Â 
Beijing Denies Racism Charge
In Beijing, a Foreign Ministry spokesman, Li Zhaoxing, said the authorities were investigating the disturbances and would deal with them in accordance with the law. 
Mr. Li also said the disturbances were not a sign of racism in Chinese society. 
''The incident that has occurred in Nanjing is an isolated one, having nothing to do with racial discrimination,'' he said.
Nonetheless, it is common here to hear racial stereotypes that would make most Americans cringe.
''Chinese students do not like most African students,'' a young Chinese man, an electronics student at Beijing University, said with typical bluntness. 
''The Africans usually are not high quality people. 
They have a bad attitude, and they do bad things.''
Pressed for specifics, the Chinese student said the Africans do not obey university rules, are not punctual and try to lure Chinese women into relationships by lavishing money on them.
Yet if racial stereotypes seem widespread, there also seem to be exceptions. 
Asked about racism, a black American business executive who travels widely in China recalled not a single unpleasant incident. 
While racism exists, the executive said, it usually disappears when the Chinese see a black person who speaks Chinese and is perceived as non-threatening.
Perhaps what is surprising about Chinese racism, the executive mused, is that it is so openly expressed.
Â 
Insults on the Streets
''The racism here is very striking,'' said Boubacar Traore, a philosophy student from the West African country of Mali who has lived in China for 10 years. 
''When we walk on the street, people insult us. 
They call us black devils, and so on. 
Even if we're alone, they insult us. 
And if we're with a girl, they say she's a hooker and is doing it for the money.''
To be sure, Mr. Traore and other Africans say many Chinese are friendly and helpful. 
Yet there is little doubt about the underlying tensions between African and Chinese students. 
Most of the Africans receive Chinese Government scholarships that are several times larger than the stipends the Chinese receive. 
The living conditions are also better: at Hehai University, where the disturbances in Nanjing began, each African has a single room, while Chinese are housed eight to a room.
''They don't like to see a black person living better than they do, while it's more acceptable to see whites getting preferential treatment,'' said Cynthia A. Griffin, a 25-year-old black American studying in Nanjing. 
Some Chinese students apparently feel that Africans should not get special treatment because conditions in their home countries are no better than those in China.
Â 
A Preference for Light Skin
Among themselves, the Chinese tend to regard a light complexion as beautiful. 
Chinese women generally have better marriage prospects if their skin is light, and Chinese poetry exalts light skin as the standard of beauty.
In addition to resentment of the benefits that African students enjoy, and the hostility that is sometimes aroused when they date Chinese women, a common source of conflict has been Chinese complaints that African students hold parties that are too loud. 
Major brawls were reported between Chinese and Africans in Shanghai in 1980 and in Tianjin in 1986, while African students in Beijing demonstrated in January 1987 after an anonymous letter slurring blacks was circulated at several universities in the capital.
Why do the African students come if they believe they face racism?
Some seem to accept it as the price of a better education than they can get at home. 
And some apparently do not know what they will face.
''Many of them had no idea what this country was like until they came,'' said the ambassador of an African country. 
''They have no problems in the classroom, but they regret very much coming here because of experiences outside the classroom.''

file: Blunt Chinese Comentary Says Gorbachev Is Meeting Resistance.txt
text:
