text:
ï»¿
As recently as eight years ago, the Bank of China here was a stodgy outpost of the Beijing Government that barely mattered on the local banking scene.
Since China's opening to the West in the 1970's, however, the bank's growth has been extraordinary. 
Since 1979, deposits have increased 5.8 times, loans have gone up 8.5 times and revenue has increased twelvefold. 
The Bank of China group has taken to capitalist-style competition so swimmingly, in fact, that it has become the second-biggest bank in the colony.
The bank seems to think this is just the beginning. 
It is building a 70-story headquarters that will be Hong Kong's tallest building, with executive offices that offer a view down on the headquarters of the giant Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, the only bank in Hong Kong that is larger.
''It's extremely competitive, both in terms of service and in terms of interest rates,'' said David K. P. Li, chief executive of the Bank of East Asia, another Hong Kong bank that has been expanding. 
''It's very dynamic.''
For some Hong Kong businessmen, deeply apprehensive about what will happen after the colony reverts to Chinese control in 1997, having the Bank of China as a competitor may be strangely reassuring. 
It provides evidence of the Beijing Government's willingness to tolerate capitalistic practices and of its expanding financial stake in the well-being of Hong Kong. 
In the process, China has been gaining financial experience and raising funds for investment on the mainland.
This growing presence in Hong Kong has not been painless, however. 
The Bank of China group seems to be sacrificing profits to gain market share, and diplomats and other bankers have doubts about the quality of its loan portfolio. 
It is also taking some significant risks as it develops its expensive new headquarters in the face of an extremely uncertain property market, and as it makes very long mortgage loans that lead to a mismatch between short-term deposits and long-term loans. 
There are also signs that the Bank of China group will face increasing competition, in Hong Kong as well as China, from other Government-owned financial institutions.
The Bank of China remains secretive, and it refused to make its two top executives in Hong Kong available for interviews. 
One other senior executive did grant an interview, after three months of prodding, but his information was limited. 
He could not say, for example, when the chief executive in Hong Kong, Huang Diyan, assumed office; how old Mr. Huang is; where he lives, or whether he has a car at his disposal. 
Other information was gathered from interviews with competitors, financial analysts and diplomats and from analysis of the limited financial records the bank provides.
Â 
Group of 12 Banks
The Bank of China, which is based in Beijing, heads a group of 12 other Chinese banks and one finance company operating in Hong Kong and the nearby Portuguese enclave of Macao. 
These sister banks operate exclusively in Hong Kong, although eight of them are technically registered in Beijing. 
They remain under the control of the Bank of China, although they have separate boards of directors and distinct specialties.
This Bank of China group missed the profits made by Hong Kong banks in the late 1970's, when the economy was booming and land prices were soaring. 
So the sister banks tried to catch up after China's dramatic policy shift of 1979. 
They hurried into property lending without waiting to develop their skills in credit analysis. 
It was an inauspicious start. 
The property market collapsed in 1982, along with much of Hong Kong's economy, and there are indications that many members of the banking group lost substantial sums of money.
Court records show that several of the banks had lent heavily to the Carrian Group, a Hong Kong investment firm that failed in 1983. 
Apparently, the individual banks did not know that other members of the group had also lent to Carrian. 
To avoid such credit risks, the Bank of China formed a Hong Kong and Macao regional office, which oversees the sister banks and approves large loans. 
The sisters are also linked by computer, and they clear checks among themselves.
Huang Diyan, the chief executive of the regional office, assumed the leadership in late 1985, and shortly thereafter began to shuffle people into retirement. 
Mr. Huang, who previously headed the Bank of China's international division in Beijing, appears to be highly regarded in the Communist hierarchy. 
He is still in his mid-50's -young for a position of authority in China - and last year was named vice chairman of the overall Bank of China. 
Because Mr. Huang is often traveling, the daily management rests with Zhang Xueyao, a pipe-smoking, English-speaking former diplomat who previously headed the Bank of China operation in New York. 
Mr. Zhang, and to a lesser extent Mr. Huang, are playing a more active role in the banking cocktail circuit than their predecessors. 
Neither man, however, speaks Cantonese, the Chinese dialect spoken in Hong Kong.
This has been no obstacle to growth, however, particularly among working-class and middle-class families, who are attracted by a good branch network and excellent mortgage terms. 
Since 1983, the Bank of China has advertised widely.
Â 
Politics Brings New Business
The Bank of China group has also picked up a great deal of commercial business, but it is not clear how much of this is based on merit. 
Many of the group's business clients are the 3,000 companies from China that have opened offices in Hong Kong in the last half-dozen years. 
And many others appear to be corporations, mostly based in Hong Kong, that think it is good politics to maintain at least one account at the Bank of China.
The bank group's staff has doubled since 1979, to 11,000, but reportedly there have been tensions between the recent university graduates and the less-educated middle managers they work under. 
Although some young managers have been promoted very rapidly, many have quit out of frustration, banking rivals say.
''There is a gap between the abilities of the employees and the demands of the job,'' conceded Chen Wen-jing, a senior executive of the Bank of China's regional office. 
As a result, he said, the bank has set up training programs that have been attended by thousands of employees.
Nevertheless, there are strong indications that bad loans are substantial and that profitability is low. 
The problem in making such assessments, however, is that the group's financial reports are sketchy and (with the exception of the four sister banks registered in Hong Kong) are unaudited by outside accounting firms.
Even by their official earnings statements, the profits of many of the banks in the group have fallen in the last few years, after adjusting for a devalued Chinese currency. 
One fairly typical member of the group, for example, the Bank of Communications, reported a $25.3 million profit in 1983, but just $14.9 million in 1985, the most recent year for which figures are available.
The 1985 profit amounted to just a 6.9 percent return on capital, compared with 17.8 percent at the Bank of East Asia, an independent Hong Kong bank.
Some rival bankers complain privately that the cut-rate mortgages and long repayment periods offered by the Bank of China have aggravated an already very competitive banking environment.
''Foreign banks can't match them,'' complained the head of one foreign bank operating in Hong Kong. 
In the last few years, several local banks have failed, and several foreign banks - including the Bank of America and Barclays Bank of Britain - have cut back their presence. 
One reason for these moves may have been the declining profitability of retail banking because of the Bank of China's policies, bankers say.
''They are taking business away,'' said Teresa Ma, an analyst in Hong Kong for Jardine Fleming Securities, ''not from the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, but from the medium-sized Chinese banks.''
Although the Bank of China is often cast as a warrior in a titanic battle with the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, most bankers and analysts see it differently. 
In 1985, the last year for which figures were reported, the Hongkong and Shanghai bank gained market share, analysts said. 
And the two giants tend to pursue somewhat different markets: The Bank of China is after the smaller depositor and borrower, and the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation seeks larger customers, both individual and corporate.
''We are two big players in a very competitive banking scene, but there are a great many others,'' said Michael Broadbent, a spokesman for the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation. 
''We're pretty confident that we can retain our market share.''

Specifically, he thanked Mr. Reagan for a personal letter of friendliness delivered by Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. in June.

Despite efforts at reassurance by the Reagan White House, the Peking leadership remains wary that Mr. Reagan may still decide to authorize the sale of advanced jet fighter planes to Taiwan - a move that Peking has said would be a severe blow to Chinese-American relations. 
Mr. Reagan has shelved the issue so far, but Peking fears that if it accepts offers for military aid from the United States, it might be eventually forced to accept American arms sales to Taiwan.
The former President arrived in Peking last night on a private 10-day visit. 
It was not Mr. Carter's first visit to China, however, as Prime Minister Zhao learned to his surprise at a reception before the banquet. 
When Mr. Zhao asked the standard warm-up question of whether this was a first visit, Mr. Carter replied, '' No.''
Mr. Carter said that as a young submarine officer, he visited Shanghai and Qingdao in 1949. 
In the latter city, he said, he could see the campfires of the surrounding ''Mao forces,'' which had Qingdao surrounded and were preparing for conquest.

'Outstanding Contributions'
This trip was Mr. Carter's first major sojourn abroad since he left the White House, and the Chinese treated him, as the President who formally recognized China, with great respect. 
Prime Minister Zhao, at the beginning of a meeting this morning that lasted 1 hour 45 minutes, said he had made an ''outstanding contribution'' to Chinese-American relations. 
''We will never forget it,'' he said.
According to Jody Powell, the former White House press secretary who accompanied Mr. Carter, Mr. Zhao revealed that he, like Mr. Carter, was a jogger and suggested that they run together in the future.

Strong Ties Emphasized
Like other members of his Administration who have preceded him to China, Mr. Carter emphasized the theme that Chinese-American relations were too valuable and too strategic to trifle with over the unmentioned issue of Taiwan.
''There is no doubt that the cause of world peace has been advanced by this Sino-American friendship,'' Mr. Carter said in his toast tonight.

text:

TO THE STORM The Odyssey of a Revolutionary Chinese Woman. 
By Yue Daiyun and Carolyn Wakeman. 
Illustrated. 405 pp. 
Berkeley: University of California Press. 
$17.95.
WITH their belief in the individual and progress, intellectuals in the 19th century never conceived of 20th-century totalitarian terror. 
Yue Daiyun, the narrator of ''To the Storm,'' had 19th-century views.
A third-generation intellectual who has triumphantly survived waves of political purges, she was born in 1931 in Guizhou province in southern China. 
She was an active member of the flourishing student Communist underground, one of 20 at Peking University admitted to the party in 1949. 
In 1952, when she graduated, there was much revolutionary optimism among her peers.
Miss Yue was elected valedictorian of her class, secured a faculty position and was about to make a brilliant marriage to Tang Yijie, a philosophy professor and the son of the president of the university. 
She had also received early acclaim as a poet -though in 1966, out of fear that her work would be seized and used as incriminating evidence, she burned it all, including the prescient poem ''To the Storm,'' from which the title of this unusual and intimate memoir of a revolution is taken. 
For instead of taking an assured place as part of China's intellectual elite, the couple spent most of the next 30 years in a state of terror of political reprisals.
Like so many bourgeois Communists, Miss Yue was more bourgeois than Communist. 
Her cultural referents included ''Gone With the Wind'' and ''Jean Cristophe''; her father translated Somerset Maugham into Chinese, and her brother liked to sing ''My Old Kentucky Home.''
Her notion of being a good Communist was to to shun a fancy wedding while voicing what she took to be Russian Marxism.
Her idealism too was 19th-century; she was filial and wifely, and she wanted her children to carry on the family's academic tradition. 
She failed to perceive the contradictions in her position: as a student member of the Party, she helped to purge individuals she considered rightist, yet she gloried in her in-laws' social status.
Mao Zedong, whose own origins had been bitterly humble, never trusted intellectuals like her. 
He recognized that they ''tend to be subjective and individualistic, impractical in their thinking and irresolute in action.''
More important, their education and skills in a country where more than 80 percent of the population is rural peasantry gave them oligarchic power to rule and to transfer their power to their children.
When the government moved to smash such intellectuals, one obvious place to attack was the universities. 
Miss Yue was a member of a prominent family and a campus personality as a result of her poetry and academic standing. 
I N 1958 her ordeal began. 
She was declared a rightist enemy of the people by the party and abruptly removed from her nursing infant son and sent to the countryside. 
In Zhaitang she tended pigs and took orders from peasants on a collective farm. 
She endured hard labor, near starvation, isolation and constant physical degradation.
Miss Yue was caught in a familiar trap: to preserve some sense of her own identity while living in demoralizing conditions, she needed to cling to her faith in the revolution she had helped create and believe in the correctness of the party. 
But when she returned to her family in Peking in 1960, infested with lice, her small children were suspicious of her, and her friends avoided contact.
Then, after a brief respite, the Cultural Revolution of the mid-1960's resumed and intensified the purge of intellectuals. 
Miss Yue, Mr. Tang and most of their friends were hunted down and abused; many members of the professional class were killed.
During this anarchic period, many academics were forced to work in what amounted to chain gangs; they had to confess their crimes by singing ditties to jeering children. 
The scholars had to wear dunce caps; their children were deprived of an education and sent to the countryside to become peasants. 
Mr. Tang was branded a member of the ''black gang'' - an academic warlord opposed to Mao - and suffered permanent physical injury.
The chaos finally evolved into rival Red Guard groups. 
The intense Red Guard warfare took a little heat off the academics. 
Ironically, during the next round of political developments, the new Clean the Class Ranks Movement had to sort through so many purged teachers it was difficult for them to know whom to elevate to positions of responsibility. 
Clearly, the soldiers and workers in charge of restructuring the universities had no idea who was who.
Reading between the lines of this detailed and unremorseful account, one senses that the desperate need for well-trained intellectuals that began to be recognized at this point was the reason Miss Yue and Mr. Tang survived and rose again. 
If you are a member of a small, highly trained elite and manage not to be killed, then you might always have a chance for political resurrection when a new group needs you. 
T HE last section of the book gives an interesting account of the machinations of those close to Mao. 
In 1970, as the terror of the previous years subsided, Miss Yue was appointed a ''five same-thing teacher'' - she ate, lived, labored, studied and reformed her thoughts with her students.
During this period Mr. Tang managed to regain some political standing. 
The Clean the Class Ranks Movement, begun in 1968 with the support of Mao's wife, Jiang Qing, needed intelligent leaders like him. 
Miss Yue is a loyal wife in her description of the ensuing events, so a reader can't tell from this distance whether Mr. Tang had a real alternative to becoming a leading member of Liang Xiao, the group of scholars that prepared criticism of Lin Biao. 
Miss Yue says he did not. 
After Mao's death, Mr. Tang was found guilty of leftism in a national trial, and the family was again disgraced.
But by 1977 the terror had waned. 
The couple were rehabilitated and their children allowed to continue their education. 
In a postscript, Miss Yue says her daughter, now married, works in computer science and lives in New York City and her son, a physicist, also lives in America. 
She and her husband have top university jobs in China, and she has been able to visit the United States.
It is an amazing sign of the changes in China that she feels free to publish her story. 
At the end, she reaffirms her faith in the revolution and says she has rejoined the Communist Party -one can't tell whether from continued idealism or expediency.
The book is the result of an unusual collaboration. 
Yue Daiyun and Carolyn Wakeman became friends while Miss Wakeman was teaching English in 1981 in Peking, and Miss Wakeman has shaped Miss Yue's extensive conversations and notes into a first-person memoir. 
It is a valuable report on a world from which we have had little news, by an intelligent woman survivor who was at the center of the turbulence.

It was the practice of the very earliest Chinese emperors, such as those of the Shang Dynasty from around 1,500 to 1,000 B.C., to have a group of slaves slaughtered at the time of their own deaths, so that the souls of the slaves could continue to serve the emperor's soul in the afterlife.
Around 200 B.C., however, these killings gave way to a more civilized practice that eventually developed into one of China's oldest and most refined artistic traditions: ceramic funerary art. 
Under this practice, life-size ceramic sculptures of slaves would be interred with the royal figure.
An exhibit now at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, which continues through May 24, provides the first major museum survey of the tradition of Chinese ceramic funerary art. 
With its 157 sculptures, the exhibition demonstrates that not only human figures, but ceramic sculptures representing the full range of Chinese life, were also made for burial.
In this show are sculptures of cows and cats, of horses and houses, of musicians and dancers, of soldiers and stable boys. 
Many funerary sculptures were made not for emperors but for wealthy landowners, who re-created their entire estates in miniature ceramic form for burial, complete with small models of granaries, rice hulling machinery and irrigation systems of which they were especially proud.
Â 
Four Terra Cotta Sculptures
The centerpiece of the exhibition is a group of four of the famous life-size terra cotta sculptures - a horse and three soldiers - made for the first emperor of the Qin Dynasty, whose tomb in Shaanxi Province has been excavated in recent years and found to hold some 7,000 such sculptures.
''For the imperial tombs, there was a vast bureacracy just getting ready for the burial of the next emperor,'' said Felice Fischer, a curator of Far Eastern art at the Philadelphia Museum who installed the present exhibition. 
''There were workshops and bureaucrats in charge of making sculpture, and they put out edicts regularly on the proper number and size of ceramic figures to be made for persons of given rank.''
The present exhibition is organized chronologically, beginning with funerary sculpture taken from Neolithic burial mounds dating from between 8,000 B.C. and 2,000 B.C. There are a handful of small pieces from the slave-based Shang and Zhou Dynasties, leading up to the life-size Qin sculptures.
It is during the Han Dynasty - a period of national unification, internal peace and economic development that lasted about 400 years around the time of Christ - that Chinese ceramic funerary art flowered. 
Some of the best examples are represented in this show.
Â 
Scenes of Farm and Home Life
In the Han period, work made for wealthy landowners appears, and figures depart from the strict military style of the Qin period into agricultural and domestic tableaux, as well as scenes of music, dance and entertainment.
From the Han Dynasty onward, further technical innovations - such as the use of glazes and paints - appear in the work, which reached its height in the famous three-color glazes of the Tang Dynasty, whose ''tomb guardian'' figures are among this show's most elaborate and impressive pieces.
Among the exhibition's most recent pieces are Ming funerary figures from between A.D. 1368 and 1644, made of the distinctive colorful glazed porcelain that is best-known from the vases of the same period.
Important trends in the cultural history of China can be read in the stylistic evolution of the sculptures in this show. 
In works from the Wei Period, for instance, between A.D. 386 and 556, the soldiers, servants and other figures depicted increasingly come to resemble the staid, impassive image of Buddha, reflecting the increasing contact and trade between China and India at that time.
Â 
Sculpted Camels Also Appear
Later, brilliantly glazed Tang-period sculptures of dromedaries -some with bolts of silk lashed to elaborate saddles - depict the animals used by traders plying the silk route between China and the West. 
The fierce faces and the often stylized, dancing poses of the tomb guardian spirits of the Tang period also reflect an influence from Hindu sculptures depicting that religion's variously warlike and ecstatic deities.
The present exhibition, organized by George Kuwayama, senior curator of Far Eastern Art at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, opened to the public at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and not in Los Angeles, because the Los Angeles museum's exhibition schedule did not permit.
The show will travel to the Museum of Fine Arts in Houston from June 28 to Sept. 
6; to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art from Oct. 
15 to Jan. 
3, 1988, and to the Cleveland Museum of Art from Feb. 
7 to April 10, 1988.

text:

THE China Institute of America, long the territory of those who supported Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek and the Kuomintang Party that ruled Nationalist China before Mao Zedong's Communist takeover, finally opened its arms to the People's Republic, and its diplomats were on hand the other night at a black-tie dinner honoring C. Douglas Dillon.
The gathering at the Helmsley Palace began with drinks, during which 400 guests stood nibbling hors d'oeuvres and studying one another. 
Some Caucasians were either born in China or had ties going back before World War II, and several women wore Chinese attire. 
But it was the Chinese- American women in their embroidered silks and impressive jewels who stole the show, gathering around Grace Chu, whom Millie Chan, a teacher of Chinese cooking who knows not a word of Chinese, introduced as ''the Julia Child of Chinese cuisine.''
Charlotte Curtis article on dinner honoring C Douglas Dillon at Helmsley Palace (M)
Across the room, Liang Yufan, China's chief delegate to the United Nations, was deep in conversation with Morley Cho, the shipping executive. 
The representative, true to People's Republic protocol, wore his immaculately tailored if austere gray uniform with its Mandarin collar. 
He said he was having a nice time.
Several years ago, this political mixture would not have been possible. 
When Chiang and his followers fled to Taiwan, the cultural institute's affection and sympathy went with him. 
Thus was born a segment of the so-called China lobby, which opposed American recognition of Mao's regime. 
But times do change.
In 1979, in step with President Jimmy Carter's normalization agreement, members began to include the occasional Chinese mainlander. 
And last fall, 10 years after President Richard M. Nixon's celebrated rapprochement, the institute officially invited Beijing's diplomats and trade executives.
''This is one of the few organizations I'm for,'' said Shanghai-born Richard King, an associate of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, the accounting concern. 
''It's apolitical.''
''The old wounds are healing,'' said Mrs. Wan-go H.C. 
Weng, the American-born daughter of a leading Kuomintang official. 
''Whether you love Taiwan or the mainland, there's only one China. 
The sooner we all realize that, the better off we'll be.''
Mrs. Weng was in midsentence when Kitty Carlisle Hart, chairman of the State Council of the Arts, arrived clutching the script for her part of the program and practicing her 12 words of Mandarin. 
''She's very good,'' Mrs. Weng said, adding that Bi Jilong, the Under Secretary of the United Nations, was expected.
At that point, Nathan Pusey, former president of Harvard and the dinner chairman, borrowed a taxi whistle from Robert L. Houguet, the banker, and blew a shrill blast. 
''That ought to get them moving,'' Dr. Pusey said, though it did not. 
So he blew it again, and the guests gradually trooped off to dinner. 
They had reached dessert when Dr. Pusey announced that he'd never before been what he called the lead-off man. 
''I gather I'm supposed to calm you down and say a word of welcome,'' he said. 
And when guests went right on talking, he said there was no point in his being there. 
That quieted everyone.
Dr. Pusey said the assembly marked ''our shared love of things Chinese and beyond that our love for Doug,'' a reference to Mr. Dillon. He said, too, that he detected ''a kind of crimson atmosphere,'' a reference not to communism but the dozens, including Mr. Dillon, who went to Harvard. 
He introduced the diplomats. 
He discussed Mr. Dillon's affection for things French, including art, wine and middle-size poodles, and handed the podium on to Mr. Weng, the institute president, who introduced Thomas Lawton of the Freer Gallery of Art, who spoke on the study of Chinese art.
Then came Mrs. Hart, describing eight Chinese paintings Mr. Dillon had given the Metropolitan Museum. 
Finally, Mr. Hoguet, the institute chairman, extolled Mr. Dillon's accomplishments as longtime chairman of the Metropolitan and presented him with a calligraphy scroll. 
Mr. Dillon appeared genuinely touched.
He said he became interested in Chinese, Japanese and East Asian art 15 years ago when he discovered that the museum's holdings ''were so lamentably weak.''
He said, ''The only way we could acquire what we needed was to get it in very large gobs,'' which he did. 
His first gift was 25 major paintings.
''When I began to see these treasures,'' he said, ''it changed my life. 
I fell in love. 
There is no other way to describe it. 
Other people contributed. 
We were then able to acquire other things that interested the museum. 
We're coming along. 
Now, we have 250 paintings.''
The Dillon Galleries also contain porcelains and bronzes from the 11th to the 18th centuries, thereby explaining the choice of words on the honoree's new scroll. 
Translated, it says: ''Looking at the ancient to develop the present.''
What it means, of course, is that you can't understand the present without knowing what went before.
Correction
The Charlotte Curtis column yesterday, on a dinner in honor of C. Douglas Dillon, misidentified the firm of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. 
It is an investment banking house.

FROM THE WINDOW OF HIS SKYSCRAPER office, Hughlyn F. Fierce looks out over Hong Kong harbor, jammed with sampans and junks bound for the South China Sea. 
A senior vice president and Chase Manhattan's man in charge of the Asia-Pacific area, Fierce commands an empire that encompasses 11 nations, 1,500 employees and $5 billion in assets. 
A husky 52-year-old, he wears an amiable expression that belies the large demands he makes on himself - and his staff.
This day, Fierce is talking in his customary, understated manner about his 25-year rise through the ranks of the Chase Manhattan Bank. 
His voice picks up intensity as he reaches the year 1974, when a call for help came from the Freedom National Bank of New York, a Harlem institution in deep trouble. 
Would Fierce, then a vice president in Chase's corporate lending office in Manhattan, take a leave of absence to become president and chief executive officer of the ailing bank?
He had just about decided to refuse the offer, he recalls, because he was concerned that it might hinder his upward mobility at Chase. 
Then his mother, Helen Wilson Fierce, weighed in, urging him to pursue ''a more noble ambition.''
Fierce took the job, and when he returned to Chase three years later, Freedom National was back on its feet.
As it turned out, Fierce's stint at the Harlem bank proved invaluable to his career with Chase. 
It established his credentials as a leader and as an inventor of ingenious solutions for intractable problems. 
And it brought him for the first time into close contact with investment bankers. 
Says Fierce, ''It was John Whitehead who first enlightened me about the business.''
Whitehead, then a senior partner at Goldman, Sachs & Company, is now Deputy Secretary of State.
Those lessons are paying off in Hong Kong. 
In company with other leading American commercial banks scrambling to move beyond their traditional lending activities, Chase has plunged its overseas branches into more lucrative, fee-generating activities - underwriting securities and arranging currency and interest-rate swaps. 
But Chase has come late to the party, where American and foreign banks are locked in frenzied competition on the Asian frontier, and Fierce is struggling to catch up. 
He must inculcate his staff with the ''aggressiveness and tenacity'' required for them to do battle in investment banking. 
''You really have to change their way of business behavior,'' he says.
Last year, Fierce's group, which does not include Japan, earned the lion's share of the $33 million profit Chase reaped on its Pacific Rim operations. 
For a bank with 1987 losses of $895 million on total revenues of almost $11 billion, that represented something of an island in a sea of red ink.
WHEN FIERCE ARRIVED in Hong Kong, in August 1986, he was immediately faced with a crisis: a $30 million loan default by the Wah Kwong Shipping Group, Hong Kong's third-largest shipowner. 
Fierce says, ''You know how when a rookie joins the National Football League and someone comes up and hits him as hard as he can, saying, in effect, 'Welcome to the N.F.L.'?
That's what Wah Kwong was like.''
The shipowner owed $850 million to dozens of creditors. 
A broad restructuring plan had been developed to save the company, victim of a worldwide slump in the shipping market, but it required the approval of all the major players. 
Chase balked - and seized the three ships on which it held mortgages.
Day after day, articles appeared in the local press suggesting that Chase was hindering Wah Kwong's survival. 
The South China Morning Post, the main English-language newspaper, warned in an editorial: ''Think about the reaction of the community at large to the decision by a commercial bank that might ultimately be responsible for the collapse of the entire restructuring scheme.''
It was not until November that calm was restored, with Chase acquiescing to a modified restructuring plan. 
A year later, Wah Kwong was reporting a six-month profit of $12.5 million. 
Meanwhile, Chase sold the three ships for a reported 40 percent of the mortgage value. 
It might have recouped more by waiting for the shipping market to recover, but, Fierce says, ''If we had kept them, there would have been carrying costs. 
There would have been hassles that would have diverted us from the business of making money.''
EIGHT MEMBERS OF THE Asia-Pacific Area Risk Council are sitting around a conference table in Hugh Fierce's Hong Kong office. 
They are there to discuss credit risks of clients and potential clients in their bailiwick, which ranges over a broad arc from South Korea to Pakistan and includes Australia. 
Fierce is seated in front of a huge yellow and blue silk panel adorned with frolicking dragons. 
In a corner of the office a Reuters monitor flashes the latest financial news.
He calls the risk council to order. 
In one of the area countries, he says, ''There is a group that has been assassinating locals. 
We do not know at this time of any assassinations of Westerners, but it is entirely possible that they may identify Western diplomats as targets. 
American bankers could be targets too.''
Fierce suggests that bank records in the country be duplicated, and copies sent elsewhere. 
And he urges his aides to exercise care should they travel to the country. 
Then he moves the meeting along to more typical banking risks - those involving money, not human life.
As the meeting progresses, Fierce pushes and probes. 
A subordinate makes a statement, and Fierce asks, ''Are you comfortable with that?''
The man explains his point at greater length, and Fierce repeats: ''Are you confortable with that?''
The subordinate finally figures out what the boss expects to hear and answers with an unambiguous ''Yes.''
In Asia, where people avoid confrontation or giving offense, where issues are sidestepped rather than tackled head on, Fierce is direct. 
While he thinks of himself as being ''friendly and relaxed,'' he admits that his staff tends to view him as ''intense, striving and unreasonable in my expectations.''
Dennis M. Goggin, the Hong Kong country manager for Chase, once told him, ''You're the kind of person who feels that if Sisyphus had used a little more effort, he would have gotten that rock over the hill.''
Fierce is on the road as much as 50 percent of the time, visiting the bank's offices around the region (''Pushing the troops,'' he calls it) and the headquarters office in Manhattan. 
His schedule also includes encounters with the elite of the business and political worlds, from Y. K. Pao, the Hong Kong shipping and real estate magnate, to Henry Kissinger, a longtime acquaintance. 
One recent visiting fireman was former Vice President Walter F. Mondale; Fierce briefed him on local political and economic issues.
As the new head of the Asia-Pacific group, Fierce was expected to meet what he calls ''some rather challenging goals'' laid down by headquarters - including a 15 percent return on equity. 
He demanded that the various offices in the region raise their income 30 percent to 80 percent. 
At the same time, he cut expenses and staff by 10 percent to 25 percent. 
Last year eight of the countries in the region met their goals.
''In 1987, Hugh set budget standards that nobody, including me, thought were achievable,'' says Arjun K. Mathrani, a senior vice president and country manager for Korea. 
''They were actually exceeded.''
Donald L. Boudreau, Chase's executive vice president for international banking, based in New York, says that ''Asia exceeded its income goals in 1987 -and took many real positioning steps - mostly due to Hugh Fierce's leadership.''
HUGH FIERCE WAS reared in the Bedford-Stuyvesant section of Brooklyn. 
(''We didn't find out it was a ghetto until somebody told us it was a ghetto,'' he says.) His younger brother, Milfred, earned a Ph.D. from Columbia University and is now chairman of Africana Studies at Brooklyn College. 
''What drove my brother and me was my mother and my father,'' Fierce says. 
His father, Millus, worked as a receiving clerk in the textile business, his mother in real estate sales. 
''Daddy was steady and sturdy. 
He made the sun come up each day. 
It was Mama who said, 'The sun is going to be golden.'
''
After graduating from Boy's High School in 1953, Fierce enlisted in the Army and served in France, his introduction to the world beyond Bedford-Stuyvesant. 
Back in the United States, he enrolled at Morgan State University, a black institution in Baltimore. 
It was there he met his future wife, Jewel Marie Crews.
In 1961, with his bachelor's degree in economics in his pocket, Fierce sought work at several banks in New York. 
''It was suggested to me that I might want to select another career,'' he recalls. 
He had no such intention, and he managed to find a trainee position with the Citizens Trust Bank in Atlanta, Ga.
Fierce again made the rounds of New York banks in 1963. 
Now, he recalls, the times were changing: ''The buildup of civil rights activities began to question the conscience of America, particularly of American business.''
He received expressions of interest from several banks, but an interview with Chase's personnel director made his decision easy. 
''You have to understand that my wife and I were living at my mother's house in Brooklyn,'' he says. 
''I went to the Chase Manhattan Bank building and it was 60 stories high, a mass of glass and steel. 
I was tense, nervous, but when I went in to see the personnel director, he put his feet up on his desk. 
He said, 'Relax, don't get serious.'
Then he spilled his coffee and cussed. 
I thought it was great. 
I thought, 'This is the place for me.'
''
Fierce was enrolled in a training program for assistant managers. 
Over a two-year period, he was assigned to several branches. 
In 1967, at the Times Square branch, he was asked to run a risk assessment on a major dress manufacturer. 
''I felt the company had done something with the balance sheet that made them look more positive than they actually were,'' he recalls. 
His analysis impressed the branch manager, and soon Fierce was a loan officer on Times Square. 
He was named a second vice president in 1969 and a vice president three years later.
Then Freedom National Bank called. 
At the time, Freedom had not paid a dividend in nearly three years. 
The average deposit was about $100. 
The Comptroller of the Currency had threatened to close the bank.
Fierce immediately wrote off $2 million in bad loans and put a moratorium on mortgages. 
''When I said stop to the mortgages,'' he says, ''it was to understand what we were doing wrong. 
We had to cut out the cancer. 
We went back into mortgages a year later, with new policies that would keep us from repeating our mistakes.''
In order to make Freedom a viable operation, however, Fierce needed to draw deposits from companies outside Harlem, and he had an idea. 
Major corporations deposit their Government income tax and withholding tax payments in their banks, and there is usually a 10- to 20-day float period before the Government collects its money. 
Fierce called on such companies as A.T.& T., New York Telephone, Heublein, the American Can Company and Philip Morris and convinced them to pass their tax payments through his bank. 
''For 10 days,'' he recalls, ''Freedom would have the use of $20 million. 
It wasn't very much to a large bank, but it meant a lot to Freedom.''
Fierce also arranged a refinancing package for the bank - $3.7 million in preferred stock and a capital note -with the help of Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley & Company, who provided their services gratis. 
''For three years I lived with investment bankers,'' he says. 
Running Freedom, he adds, ''gave me support for the idea that I could handle a much larger opportunity.''
On his return to Chase in 1977, Fierce was appointed a senior credit-policy planner with responsibility for the bank's global loan portfolio. 
But he was based in New York, and he felt he needed overseas experience. 
So he obtained an advanced professional certificate in international finance at New York University's Graduate School of Business Administration, where he had earned his M.B.A. a decade earlier.
Fierce's new academic credentials and his stint at Freedom - a combination he refers to as ''scholarship and scar tissue'' - led to his appointment as general manager of the Chase Manhattan Bank in Singapore in 1979. 
He and his family - the Fierces have three daughters -transferred back to New York in 1981, and he was put in charge of the bank's operations in French-speaking Africa, then all of Africa, then Africa and the Middle East.
Langdon Palmer, now chairman and C.E.O. of the Horizon Bank in Morristown, N.J., preceded Fierce as head of Chase's African operations. 
In March 1982, the two accompanied David Rockefeller, who had stepped down as chairman of Chase a year earlier, on a trip to Cameroon, the Ivory Coast, Nigeria, Senegal, Zimbabwe, Guinea, Zambia and Angola. 
''It was the first time I had ever made a transcontinental flight in the Chase jet,'' says Fierce. 
The trip exemplified the powers and perks of high-level international banking.
In Guinea, the late President Ahmed Sekou Toure proclaimed a national holiday and called for a parade in honor of the visiting bankers. 
In the Ivory Coast, Fierce and Palmer were quartered in a guesthouse alongside the presidential palace. 
While the two men lounged in the swimming pool, liveried houseboys served them champagne in crystal goblets carried on silver trays. 
The bankers ate off solid-gold plates and, as Palmer recalls, told each other, ''This ain't bad.''
IN 1970, THE THREE LARGEST banks in the world, ranked by assets, were American: Bank of America, First National City (which became Citibank) and Chase. 
Eighteen years later, 9 of the top 10 banks in the world are Japanese. 
The leading American bank, Citibank, comes in 22d, and Chase, just ahead of Bank of America, is in 48th place. 
''You can't look to U.S. banks as being as big a factor as we have been in the past,'' Fierce allows. 
''However, I remember the time when the Middle East banks had the money, and I've got this feeling that everything that comes around, goes around.''
Within the United States, commercial banks have been prohibited by the Glass-Steagall Act from owning brokerage firms or engaging in the underwriting of securities. 
Those barriers have been eroding of late -most recently, with last June's Supreme Court decision allowing Chase Manhattan Capital Markets Corporation, an affiliate of the Chase Manhattan Corporation, to underwrite and sell commercial paper domestically.
Outside of the United States, most international banks have been moving aggressively into investment banking, a field already crowded with experienced American players such as Shearson Lehman Hutton and Merrill Lynch, and with British merchant banks that have special claims on the Asian turf they dominated in colonial days.
International banks, especially those in Asia, have downplayed their commercial banking because the Pacific Rim countries are awash in liquidity. 
Japan's Nomura Securities reports that borrowing by East Asian and Southeast Asian countries dropped 24 percent in 1986 and 65 percent in the first quarter of 1987. 
Another major spur to the expansion into activities other than lending has been the banks' woeful track record in Latin America, where they have been forced to write off billions of dollars in loans. 
''As a result of that experience, banks have turned more and more to nontraditional banking enterprises that do not put the bank's assets at risk,'' says Robert F. Grealy, Chase's Asia-Pacific director of international relations. 
''So we're talking about service, currency trading, merger and acquisition arrangements, where the bank performs a service and there's no risk. 
That's what banks would rather be doing.''
The investment banking arm of the Asia-Pacific group, Chase Manhattan Asia Ltd., had, until the late 70's, restricted itself primarily to syndicated lending. 
It then slowly expanded into selling securities and offering fixed-income investments. 
An executive who works at an investment bank in Hong Kong says, ''Bankers Trust took concrete steps toward becoming a merchant bank five to six years ago. 
Chase, in comparison, is viewed as one that is lagging behind in terms of strategy and in terms of implementation.''
''Maybe we missed it by two to three years,'' Fierce acknowledges. 
But he says that Asia-Pacific's achievements last year reflected a concerted effort to catch up. 
''We pushed corporate finance business, which is basically our financial advisory and our merger and aquisition business. 
We started to have special types of corporate finance products - leveraged leasing, for instance. 
It all kind of came together in 1987.''
In a leveraged leasing deal, the bank finds a company with taxable profits to buy equipment - a jet plane, for example. 
The company then leases the jet to an airline. 
Since the purchasing company is able to offset its tax liability with depreciation charges on the equipment, it can afford to offer the airline favorable terms on leasing fees. 
Everyone benefits: the aircraft manufacturer, the purchaser, the airline - and the bank.
Early in 1987, the region's investment banking arm was involved in two leveraged leasing deals, one with CAAC, China's national airline, for $100 million, the other with Cathay Pacific Airways for $91 million. 
At that point, the investment banking group reported directly to Chase headquarters in New York. 
Then, in the space of a few months, Oliver Greeves, head of the group, and two of its top executives left Chase, and Fierce was temporarily put in charge. 
At year's end, the added assignment became permanent.
During the first quarter of 1988, the investment banking group handled eight mergers and acquisitions. 
Among other projects, it underwrote, with two other banks, a $14.1 million equity issue on behalf of an agro-industrial company in Thailand, and it is helping put together a $52 million convertible bond issue for a company in Taiwan.
Several of Chase's competitors in the Hong Kong investment banking community remain unimpressed. 
Says one banker: ''They really have not done much in the way of classical investment banking, merger and acquisition deals, or corporate finance work or even capital markets.''
Another, a Chase alumnus, attributes the bank's record in Asia to its ''formidable name and long-standing relationships in almost every region'' and to the fact that Chase is ''trying hard.''
Still, it remains to be seen whether Chase can maintain its position of influence in Asia in the face of the powerful Japanese and Hong Kong banks, and with increasing competition from American investment banks.
MANY MORNINGS, FIERCE arrives at the bank before 7 o'clock and must awaken the guard before he can get to his office, whip off his suit jacket and set to work. 
He does pause to eat lunch at his desk - a box lunch of cha gai fan, rice with pork and chicken, is a favorite. 
And he may stay late so that he can telephone New York, which is 12 hours behind Hong Kong time.
The Fierces and their teenage daughters, Heather and Brooke, live in an exclusive neighborhood on Barker Road, near Victoria Peak. 
The girls attend the Hong Kong International School, and an older daughter, Holly, lives in Boston. 
The family entertains at the Hong Kong Country Club or the American Club, which, Fierce says, is ''more California than New York.''
Fierce keeps abreast of political developments in such tinderbox areas as Tibet and South Korea, and he closely follows the news from China, which will take control of Hong Kong in 1997.
Already, Fierce says, ''China is a major investor in Hong Kong, if not the major investor.''
From his apartment, he can see the most dramatic evidence of China's increasing presence, the 70-story headquarters of the Bank of China, designed by I. M. Pei. 
Though not due to open until next year, it already dominates the Hong Kong skyline.
Opinions are by no means unanimous about the future of the crown colony. 
On the whole, Fierce says, he is ''a little more positive on China than some people. 
They have been absolutely impeccable in reacting to us and attempting to understand Chase's position.''
But Fierce will probably not be in Hong Kong when it reverts to China. 
Chase tends to rotate its executives' foreign assignments every five years. 
At the end of the fifth year, Fierce plans to come back to New York. 
''Maybe, if someone twisted my arm, I would go to London,'' he says.
No matter where he is assigned, however, Fierce intends to stay with Chase. 
''I grew up in the bank,'' he says. 
''I have a great emotional and professional attachment to it. 
There are days when I think the sun shines on the bank and days when I think the bank is difficult - just like one feels about one's wife or one's kids - but I think that Chase is a very good place to be.''

file: Chasing the Heroin From Plush Hotel to Mean Streets.txt
text:

Group 41 of the Federal Drug Enforcement Administration has been assigned to break up the Chinese Drug rings that transport heroin along ''the China White Trail,'' from the mountains of Thailand to the secret criminal societies of Hong Kong to the quiet Chinese neighborhoods in Queens.
What follows is a firsthand description of undercover drug buys in New York City, of surveillances and arrests.
The account is a kind of diary of impressions and observations of the people and events in the life of Group 41 as it seeks to fulfill its mission in the summer of 1987. 
Plaza Hotel, Wednesday, Time: 5 P.M. Inside the drug world, nothing is quite what it appears. 
Faces are often mirrors. 
Answers are mostly lies. 
Cases have beginnings, but never really end.
So here at the center of an international drug enforcement operation - two rooms under chandeliers and molded ceilings -the drug agents of Group 41 react with a start in their suite at the Plaza Hotel each time the phone rings. 
They know anything can go wrong.
Three agents, ties askew, lean over a coffee table scattered with slices of cold pizza and cans of Diet Coke. 
Another agent, in T-shirt, jeans and sneakers, munches on a tuna sandwich from a delicatessen down the block.
Although renting the Plaza suite may be necessary for an undercover operation involving lavish drug traffickers, the agents are not willing to pay the price of room service. 
''Jeez, $12.50 for a bottle of nuts,'' said one of the agents, looking down the price list of snacks in the room's refrigerator. 
''Can you believe that. 
Who can pay $12.50 for nuts?''
Today's operation involves an undercover American drug agent who has posed as a courier and brought heroin with a street value of $46 million from Bangkok.
If all goes according to plan, representatives of the people who bought the drugs, major Chinese heroin dealers in New York, will pick up the shipment in the lobby of the Plaza.
The agents do not expect to make arrests at the hotel. 
Instead they will follow the drugs, hoping the trail will lead to the major buyers.
At that point the drug agents, in coordination with the Thai and Hong Kong police, will arrest the buyers and sellers on both sides of the Pacific.
''It's a tricky operation,'' said Richard, the 39-year-old special agent who heads the group. 
''But it could pay double dividends.''
For 19 months the 10 agents of Group 41 have performed such operations in an attempt to penetrate the hidden world of Chinese heroin traffickers, As a result of intelligence gathered by the group of white, black and Chinese-American agents, law-enforcement officials recently were able to sketch a striking new picture of the New York heroin industry, a multibillion-dollar business that is now dominated, they say, by Chinese drug traffickers.
In the lives of drug agents each arrest is really just a beginning that leads to new information, new cases and new arrests. 
Each face, each license plate, each address and each criminal relationship is a small piece in the puzzle of the China White Trail. 
The phone rings. 
An agent listens for a moment and hangs up. 
He smiles and says: ''It's show time.''
Plaza Lobby, An Hour Later No one in the milling crowds would notice the middle-aged man in a tan suit, sitting with a green cloth suitcase by his side. 
He is, in fact, an undercover agent playing the part of a corrupt diplomat who has smuggled the heroin on a flight from Bangkok.
Eight feet away, Richard is slouched by a doorway, appearing weary but relaxed. 
His gaze drifts slowly around the lobby but never falls directly on the undercover agent. 
A two-way radio is hidden in his folded newspaper.
Richard is regarded as one of the few experts on international Chinese drug traffickers by United States and European law enforcement officials. 
He is fluent in French, Thai and the Chinese dialects of Mandarin and Cantonese.
Suddenly, a round Chinese man pops through the grand revolving door at the hotel entrance. 
He beams a smile to the undercover courier. 
The courier rises and disappears through the door and down the hotel's front steps.
''We have movement,'' Richard whispers through his radio to a platoon of agents hidden on corners, on benches and in cars. 
Their best protection is the camouflage of New York street life.
Just beyond the hotel awning the Chinese man and the courier lift the suitcase into the trunk of a blue Buick with the New York license plate ZMC 223. 
The car, with two other Asian men in the front seat, pulls out into traffic.
Â 
'Who Is On the Blue Buick?'
In an instant, the undercover agent portraying the diplomat has slipped back into the hotel and Richard is alone on the street, watching the Buick fade away. 
His face freezes. 
Something is definitely not working.
''Who is on the blue Buick, New York plates, Zebra - Michael - Charlie 223?''
Richard says into the radio. 
There is no response. 
''Who is on the blue Buick?''
Richard repeats.
No response. 
Richard mutters a curse.
Somehow, even with seven cars on surveillance and more than a dozen agents in the area, everyone but Richard missed the deal. 
He has one minute, possibly two, to save the New York end of the operation by finding the Buick. 
Richard jumps into a Group 41 car parked nearby. 
#58th Street Chase ''Let's move,'' he says.
The agent behind the wheel, a former surveillance specialist with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, puts his foot on the gas and his car swings down 58th Street after the blue Buick, now the only link that connects the sellers in Hong Kong to the buyers in New York. 
Thanks to several traffic lights, the two agents spot the Buick at the entry ramp to the Queensboro Bridge.
The driver of the Buick, as he careers between lanes and cuts off other cars, may now have noticed a car 50 feet behind, mimicking his every move. 
The agent driving says he has no choice. 
His is the only car trailing the Buick.
Back at the hotel an agent had substituted imitation blocks of heroin for the real drug. 
74th Street In Queens, Time: 1 A.M. A day at the Plaza has turned into dark night in a parked car in Jackson Heights.
The night has brought a pounding summer rainstorm, followed by a cool breeze. 
In the darkness, the smell of fresh-cut lawns and wet sidewalk wafts through the car window as Richard and another agent listen to the sputtering voices of other agents on the radio.
They are parked in a driveway around the corner from the blue Buick. 
The car, with the suitcase still inside its trunk, has sat five hours, ever since the driver parked and entered a brick three-story house on 74th Street in Jackson Heights. 
Four other drug agency cars are parked nearby.
Six times a white Oldsmobile with a bashed fender has circled the block, stopping twice by the side of the Buick. 
The driver, a slender Chinese man with a beeper on his belt, has even stepped out and walked the street. 
Yet he has not opened the trunk.
Â 
Questions on Both Sides
The slender man knows something may be wrong, Richard explains. 
So now he must confront the classic quandary of a drug dealer: Is this really worth the risk?
Am I just being paranoid?
And Richard is facing the classic questions of a drug agent: If he picks it up, should I arrest him here ?
If I follow him, will he lead me to his compatriots?
Such ruminations are interrupted by a distant scream.
''He's gonna kill me!'' yells a voice with a Hispanic accent. 
''He's crazy!''
The two agents jump out of their car and see a small man running down the middle of the street, through the pools of light cast by street lamps.
''He's gonna kill me!'' the man says again, running past.
The agents stare at each other in confusion. 
A gypsy cab is abandoned in mid-road a block away. 
Another man, barrel-chested, with biceps like ham hocks, is running towards them. 
The agents block his path.
Â 
'Please, Let Me Kill Him'
''Please, don't stop me,'' says the pursuer, panting. 
''He tried to sell crack to my 14-year-old sister. 
That's how they sell it, these Colombians, from gypsy cabs. 
Please, let me kill him!''
Richard slaps a palm onto his forehead.
''Oh, just what we need,'' he says. 
''A homicide over crack.''
When there are no police officers around, Federal drug agents must intervene to stop a violent crime. 
Agents on the street sometimes have been drawn out of undercover roles to prevent bank robberies, assaults, even murders. 
But agents are reluctant to jeopardize major drug cases.
Suddenly, a red gypsy cab screeches to a halt at the intersection. 
Seconds later six more cabs from the same company come piling into the area to help their comrade.
A taxi drives onto the sidewalk, a driver jumps out of his cab with a knife in hand. 
An agent leaps on him, thrashing his body up against the car. 
The knife drops inside the car.
By the time the agent looks up again, a row of gypsy cab drivers is out in the street. 
Nine drug agents have come out of hiding and stare back like a line of well-disciplined troops. 
A crowd of onlookers gathers.
''Move on, now,'' Richard yells, flashing his badge. 
''We're taking care of this.''
A precinct patrol car appears and two uniformed officers issue warnings. 
The taxis, the enraged pursuer and the crowd disperse into the night. 
No one is arrested.
The confrontation came and went like the summer thunderclap: sudden, frightening and apparently meaningless. 
Yet it may have had a lasting impact. 
The driver of the white Oldsmobile does not reappear. 
74th Street, Time: 8:30 A.M. The agents of Group 41 stand in the sunlight beside the blue Buick. 
The suitcase is still inside the trunk. 
The agents's eyes are red and some stomachs are raw from too much bad coffee.
The agents hold in their frustration as they question a teen-age Chinese boy who lives in the house on 74th Street where the driver parked the Buick. 
The boy says the driver's name is ''Sammy.''
He entered the house and left through a rear door. 
The boy says he does not know where Sammy is or how to find him. 
The boy's father interrupts. 
''I am so worried about this kid,'' says the father, who was visibly shaken by the arrival of Federal drug agents at his door this morning. 
''I am trying to save money and give him a good home. 
I am going to buy a house in Jersey. 
But he gets involved with gangs.''
Â 
'We'll Try to Do Better'
''It is a very serious business,'' an agent warns.
'' I know, I know,'' says the father. 
''We'll try to do better with him.''
Drug agents in Manhattan have arrested a man they believe was a look-out at the Plaza Hotel. 
The police in Hong Kong are about to arrest four men, one of whom is believed to be associated with 14K, a powerful criminal secret society based in the Crown Colony.
And agents plan to check the home addresses of people who rented the cars seen in yesterday's surveillances. 
The agents will record the names and addresses. 
They will remember the faces.
The operation in New York has ended in disappointment. 
Yet a few new pieces have been fit into the puzzle. 
D.E.A. Office, Tuesday, Time: 10 A.M. ''Sometimes I wish I hadn't chosen this profession,'' Richard says. 
''It is so all consuming, it is impossible to get away. 
It is impossible to have another life.''
A soft-spoken man with a near-academic manner, Richard's eyes dart around an office adorned with the souveneirs of a 16-year career: a plaque from the police in Malaysia and Hong Kong, a bulletproof vest, a poster of the Galerie Roussard in Paris and a poster that says, ''A cleaner Chinatown is up to you.''
Officials say it is from Richard's work in the last year and a half that they learned the size and importance of the China White Trail in the New York region.
Raised in an Italian-American family in Pittsburgh, Richard had no interest in the Chinese until he joined the agency's New York office in 1971 and fell into a group that happened to be handling numerous Southeast Asian heroin cases. 
Soon Richard developed a passion for things Asian, a passion his parents in Pittsburgh would never really understand.
Â 
Advised French Police
In the years that followed he worked in Thailand, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Paris. 
While serving as a special adviser to the French police, he met and married a woman from Korea.
In January 1986, Richard was brought back to New York to form a new group of agents targeting solely Chinese traffickers. 
It was an imposing task, for practically no one in New York had informants inside Chinese drug organizations and no one in law enforcement knew the scope of their activities.
In the first months, the agents of Group 41 walked the streets of Chinatown and cultivated the friendship of agents overseas, hoping that eventually they would get a tip on a heroin shipment coming in.
On Sept. 
10, Group 41 got its first major break. 
They seized 33 pounds of heroin hidden inside Thai furniture and made one arrest. 
A string of other arrests and seizures followed. 
Some defendants agreed to cooperate, introducing the agents to their contacts, suppliers and other organizations.
Â 
'No Letup'
What emerged was a subculture of drug traffickers in New York, with links that extended throughout the overseas Chinese communities of Asia, Europe and South America. 
In some cases the trafficking groups were loose confederations of businessmen and smugglers who associated for a single deal. 
In other cases, they involved complex organizations of dozens of people in Asia, Europe, South America and the United States.
''There's really been no letup since,'' Richard said. 
Shortly after their arrival in New York, Richard's wife began to notice that he was never home. 
Almost everyday she would signal him on his beeper. 
He would call back and say he had no idea what time or even what day he would return.
One evening at their house, she showed him a newspaper advertisement for Jacoby & Meyers, the law firm, and pointed to the firm's telephone number. 
She said with a smile that someday his beeper will tell him to call that number back. 
It will be her new lawyer asking for a divorce.
Â 
Strained Family Relations
Now, whenever Richard's beeper goes off, another agent is likely to crack, ''Uh oh. 
Jacoby & Meyers.''
The joke has a sharp edge to it. 
Many drug agents experience one or more divorces in their careers. 
Few family members can tolerate the tortuous schedules year after year, the exhaustion, the irritation and worst of all, the agents's inability to explain what they are doing with their days and nights.
Despite the hours, the isolation and the anonymity, however, many agents seem almost obsessed with their profession.
Most admit that it is not a crusader's zeal that keeps them on the job - some agents believe they are helping to stop the spread of drugs, others do not. 
Rather, veteran agents say they are people who cannot part with the unspeakable thrill of a chase and the mystery of entering hidden worlds. 
More important, perhaps, they realize that only agents and their informers truly understand what life is like inside a case. 
Once they have left this quiet fraternity, they know, in some strange way, they will always be alone.
''A lot of the time it seems we are tilting at windmills,'' Richard said. 
''I don't know. 
But maybe, when you retire somebody will say 'He was a good manager. 
He made some good cases.'
That is all I ask for.''
Tuesday, Time: 11 A.M. Two agents are loading the last thick wads of $100 bills into the green suitcase that carried the courier's heroin a week ago. 
Every bill has been counted and every serial number has been recorded. 
The suitcase is filled with $850,000.
A Chinese-American agent of Group 41, playing the undercover role, will show the money to two heroin sellers as they sit inside a stretch limousine on the Upper West Side.
He is wearing a gold Rolex watch and a crisp khaki suit. 
His hair is slicked back to suggest he was a tough street youth in Chinatown not long ago. 
Another agent will play the part of his chauffeur, a muscular man clad in a cream-colored jacket, chomping a thick cigar.
This case, one of dozens of cases the group is working on these days, began recently when the undercover agent was introduced to a Chinese couple from Queens who said they could provide large shipments of China White on a regular basis. 
Richard says he believes the couple works for a group of smugglers active in the Bangkok-New York trade.
Â 
An $86,000 Deal
On June 30, the Chinese-American agent met the couple on the corner of Third Avenue and 63d Street. 
The couple and two other men gave the agent a brown paper bag containing a pound and a half of China White. 
Mr. Wong paid them $86,000 in cash.
Group 41 followed the four suspects to Chinatown where, they say, the money was handed off to a fifth person, a short, young Chinese man with a thick mustache. 
They followed the man with the thick mustache to a string of massage and gambling parlors.
The first deal was designed to gain the couple's trust and identify their associates. 
Today the group plans to make arrests. 
The West Side, Tuesday, Time: 5 P.M. Following the flash of the cash as the limousine sat parked on West 66th Street, Group 41 has trailed the couple through Manhattan for hours. 
Now the agents and their quarry have converged on this block across the street from Lincoln Center waiting for the heroin to arrive.
The undercover agent stands with the couple in front of a Coward shoe store. 
A white Camaro pulls up to the curb. 
The undercover agent gives a signal.
''Bingo,'' says another agent who has spent the day as the driver of a yellow taxi.
Â 
Guns at Lunchtime
Suddenly, diners lunching at outdoor tables of the Saloon restaurant see a cab driver jump from his car armed with a revolver. 
Two young, well-dressed women jump from a sports car, also carrying guns. 
Even some diners jump up from their tables, and they, too, are brandishing pistols.
In a moment, a semicircle of agents have surrounded the couple and placed them under arrest.
The couple will later be identfied as 28-year-old Dong Hsiang Chen and Yin Yuen Wong, 29, both of 4045 Ithaca Street in Jackson Heights, Queens, and charged with conspiracy and the sale of narcotics.
Other agents grab the driver of the white Camaro, Lee Hong of 3 Doyers Street in Chinatown. 
From inside his car, they say, they have recovered $7.5 million worth of heroin and a .38-caliber revolver.
''Who are you guys?'' yells a uniformed police officer with his hand on his pistol. 
He confronts what looks like a crowd of Manhattanites suddenly bristling with guns.
Often drug arrests take place before the officers of the local precinct can be warned. 
At such times, the agents can only hope the patrolman on the beat has cool nerves.
''D.E.A.,'' says Richard, flashing his identification.
''Oh,'' says the officer, putting his hand to his chest. 
''That's a relief.''
These arrests again are just a few more pieces falling into place. 
Since last September, Group 41 has seized 155 pounds of heroin and arrested 39 more people - an impressive record by the standards of law enforcement. 
And yet as long as Group 41 is among the few law- enforcement groups in the nation pursuing the mysteries of Chinese organized crime, officials acknowledge that most of the players and their activities will probably never be apprehended or known.
Today's work will continue into the night and into tomorrow morning. 
The prisoners must be read their rights and asked other names, faces and deals. 
The agents must search three houses with warrants. 
And they must pay a visit to a gambling parlor where someone last saw the man with the thick mustache.
And Richard must remember to call his wife. 
No, he will tell her, he cannot say when he will be home.

file: CHEMISTS VISITING CHINA FIND INFORMATION FLOWS ONE WAY.txt
text:
ï»¿
Since establishing diplomatic relations 14 years ago, China and the United States have developed a scientific partnership that has become an important conduit of advanced Western technology to the most populous land on earth. 
But although many fields of Chinese research are now progressing rapidly on their own, growing numbers of American scientists say the flow of scientific information from China to the United States remains a mere trickle.
The lopsided character of American-Chinese exchanges of scientific information was brought home to 14 American chemists who concluded an exchange visit to China this month. 
Dazzled by China's scenic wonders and sumptuous cuisine, the Americans were nevertheless left wondering if they had learned anything of substance in exchange for the professional insights they had offered to their Chinese hosts.
In their two-week visit, delegates from the American Institute of Chemists presented talks and research material based on their specialties, some of which were linked to industrial and military technologies vital to Chinese interests. 
The men and women in the group also brought money for a fund that subsidizes some of the 30,000 Chinese scientists and students China has sent abroad to learn from the West.
At the conclusion of their trip, the Americans professed themselves amply rewarded by the chance to tour China, but most also lamented the fact that the scientific exchange had been essentially a one-way transaction. 
Their experience appears to have been shared by many of the American scientific missions that have visited China in recent years.
Â 
Shortcomings in Technology
Dr. Philip H. Abelson, an organizer of the first delegation sent to China by the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 1978, believes that one reason for the inaccessibility of such information is the relative backwardness of Chinese technology.
''The Chinese don't have all that much to show, and they are naturally reticent about exposing their shortcomings,'' he said. 
''Ideological resistance to disclosing privileged information appears to be declining, but it's still a factor. 
On top of all that, China has always had a negative attitude toward foreigners, and attitudes cannot be changed as easily as switching off a light.''
Dr. Abelson added, ''I would consider making another trip to China myself only if really substantive information were to become available from the Chinese.''
A contrasting explanation for Chinese reticence was offered by William W. Havens, executive secretary of the American Physical Society.
''One-on-one relationships between American and Chinese physicists are generally very productive of results in the pure sciences, especially solid-state and high-energy physics,'' Dr. Havens said in an interview. 
''However, some of our applied-science people have been frustrated in their desire to get a glimpse of Chinese industrial processes - those involving advanced lasers, for example - but the Chinese don't structure exchanges in such a way as to allow such glimpses. 
In fairness, of course, it's hard to imagine an American company like I.B.M. allowing outsiders to see its proprietary processes.''
Â 
Contrast in Approaches
Still, American openness contrasts sharply with Chinese secrecy in many aspects of the scientific relations between the two countries. 
Space technology is typical. 
Although Chinese officials and experts have been given significant access to the technology underlying American space programs, the gesture does not appear to have been reciprocal. 
A large delegation of Chinese space officials invited to Cape Canaveral, Fla., witnessed the destruction of the space shuttle Challenger last Jan. 
28, but to date, no American observers have been permitted to watch a launching from the new rocket pad in western China.
As guests of the China Association for Science and Technology (CAST), the American chemists who visited China this month were treated to some of the most spectacular sights in China - the Great Wall, the picturesque sugarloaf mountains of Guilin, the archeological wonders of Xian, and ancient parks, pagodas and palaces of Peking, Canton and Shanghai. 
They visited a collective farm and exchanged innumerable toasts with Chinese officials at a series of banquets. 
The chemists also saw some tantalizing intimations of advanced Chinese technology.
One of the American delegates was Dr. Abraham L. Landis, a senior scientist at the Hughes Aircraft Company in El Segundo, Calif., who had needed special permission from his employer, a military contractor, to discuss technology with Chinese counterparts. 
Dr. Landis's specialty is a class of plastics called called polyimides, which remain extremely strong even at high temperatures, and therefore have important applications in space and advanced electronics.
Speaking before an audience of about 20 Chinese chemists at the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Peking, he briefly summarized the chemistry and applications of polyimides in the United States, and then listened to a presentation by Prof. Lu Feng-Cai, a scientist whose son is a graduate student in the United States. 
After describing some of the quantum-mechanical calculations that the Chinese team had used in developing advanced polymers, Dr. Lu showed Dr. Landis a perfectly formed polyimide ring with characteristics that might have suited it for use as a bearing or machine part of some kind.
Â 
American Is Surprised
''I had expected the Chinese to have read up the chemical literature on polyimides,'' Dr. Landis said, ''but I was unprepared for that sample of molded polyimide, which graphically demonstrated to me the extent to which Chinese technology has advanced. 
And as for Dr. Lu, I can only say that if I had been in China as a student it would have been a privilege to have had her as a teacher.''
But the Americans were accorded little more than glimpses. 
Dr. Rodney Lu-dai Sung of Fishkill, N.Y., a Chinese-born gasoline chemist at Texaco Inc., spent an entire day briefing Chinese petroleum experts on gasoline additives designed to prevent corrosion, improve combustion, reduce exhaust pollutants and keep engines clean.
''They seemed insatiable for knowledge,'' he said, ''and it became clear to me that although China is a major gasoline producer, the Chinese know next to nothing about chemical additives.''
But Dr. Sung, who holds scores of patents for various gasoline additives, got little in return; his requests to visit a refinery or petroleum laboratory were ignored.
In Peking and Canton, John D. Galligan, a vice president for research and development at the Gillette Company in Boston, described advanced processes for depositing ultra-hard ceramic coatings on the edges of razor blades and on the ball tips of ballpoint pens. 
The processes have important potential applications in metallurgy, including the weapons production.
But although Mr. Galligan's slides and diagrams had been prepared with Chinese titles, his audiences neither commented upon nor questioned his presentation, and it was impossible to discern how much had been absorbed.
''One of the frustrating things,'' said another of the scientists, ''was the almost total lack of feedback from the Chinese.''
Said another: ''Going to China for a scientific exchange was a great experience for all of us. 
But it's one I'm not personally anxious to repeat.''

text:
