It took a Chinese-language petition signed by 3,000 immigrant seamstresses to get it started, and today it will be opened formally: the Garment Industry Day Care Center of Chinatown.
The dedication of the little red- brick schoolhouse in the heart of Chinatown culminates a cooperative effort by government and private business that the city would like to see duplicated, officials said.
Mayor Koch and Matilda Cuomo, the Governor's wife, will be at the opening, and the children, most of whom speak only Chinese, plan to serenade them with their favorite song in English: ''Jingle Bells.''
The cost of the center is being borne, in small part, by the parents of the children themselves. 
The idea for the center, however, came totally from the people involved, immigrant women who labor long hours as they struggle to make their way in their new country.
Garment Industry Day Care Center to open in Chinatown, NYC, after much petitioning by local residents who work small garment shops; children illustrated; Mayor Edward Koch and Mrs Matilda Cuomo to visit; NYC, factory owners' group and parents to share costs (S)Day Care Common in China
''In China, any unit that you belong to has a day-care center as a matter of course,'' said Katie Kwan, a union activist who helped lead a campaign to open the center.
She said the immigrant mothers ''can't believe it when they get here and there's nobody to take care of their kids.''
Because most of the husbands work in restaurants while their wives sew piecework, she said, the children were often taken along to work or left in groups with untrained babysitters for lack of an alternative.
Mrs. Kwan and other members of Local 23-25 of the International Ladies Garment Workers Union drew up a petition and spent their lunch hours carrying it up and down the narrow stairs of many of Chinatown's 500 small garment factories to gather the signatures. 
There were delays, she said, but in the end the union championed their cause.
Â 
Costs Are Subsidized
The center, at 115 Chrystie Street, opened its first classes last Nov. 
28. It now cares for 70 pre-kindergarten children of union members.
The Agency for Child Development of the city's Human Services Administration will be paying about half the operating costs, with funds from the Federal Emergency Jobs Act.
Private assistance comes from the Greater Blouse, Skirt and Undergarment Association Inc., which is made up of owners of the small factories for whom the immigrant seamstresses work. 
The association will pay $32 of the weekly cost of $82 per child.
To cover the rest of the cost, parents will be assessed by the city on a sliding scale pegged to income. 
The cost will range from $2 to $8 a week for each child.
''We would like to be able to market similar services to other employers,'' said Irene Greim, a spokesman for the Agency for Child Development. 
The city benefits by sharing day-care costs, and employers benefit by having the city handle administration, she said.
Â 
Rosh ha-Shanah Observed
The center also provides a service in helping the children adapt to the language and culture of their new home. 
Each of its four classes has at least one teacher who speaks Chinese, said the director, Mee Ling Chin. 
But after the first month or so, once the children get used to school, English will be the order of the day.
There are few signs of China in the decor or curriculum. 
The older children are already beginning to study the alphabet in English, not Chinese characters.
In Alice Leong's classroom, 3- and 4-year-olds are preparing a cardboard dragon for Chinese New Year Feb. 
2. But at Christmas, she said, they learned about Santa Claus, and they will also observe Rosh ha- Shanah, the Jewish New Year.
''We'll celebrate all the holidays,'' she said.

file: China Acts on Joint Ventures.txt
text:
ï»¿
China issued new economic regulations today aimed at attracting greater foreign investment by giving more preferential treatment to joint ventures.
Several Western business sources here thought that the new regulations, which were made public by the State Council, contained little that was new because many of the announced changes had already been quietly put into effect.
But the announcement promised to reduce the confusion that has persisted among Western investors about their rights and obligations in joint ventures with Chinese companies controlled by the state.
China issues new economic regulations aimed at attracting greater foreign investment by giving preferential treatment to joint ventures; new rules are aimed at reducing confusion that has persisted among foreign investors about their rights and obligations in joint ventures with Chinese companies controlled by state (M)
''It's comforting that we have it spelled out,'' a United States representative said.
The new regulations, which supplement China's first joint venture law promulgated in July 1979, apply generally to enterprises that combine Western capital and technology with Chinese factories and labor.
Â 
Exemption for Some Imports
Among other changes, the latest regulations exempt certain imported materials from customs duties and industrial and commercial taxes. 
Previously, Western investors were technically liable for duties on what they imported to make a product in China. 
The products made for export are also now formally exempted from the nation's consolidated industrial and commercial tax.
The purpose of the joint ventures has been to generate foreign currency for China by producing quality goods for export, and investors have been prohibited or strongly discouraged from marketing them inside the country. 
Now joint venture products that China urgently needs or would otherwise import can be mainly sold in the domestic market.
The new legislation now authorizes the department responsible for the joint venture to resolve any foreign- exchange imbalance caused by domestic sales, though it does not specify how. 
The new legislation also stipulates that disputes between the foreign and Chinese partners can be arbitrated in the country where the sued party is situated or in a third country if both sides agree. 
While the Chinese may still insist that disagreements be arbitrated in China, this gives an appearance of greater leeway for the foreign investor.
Â 
Directors' Status Recognized
The board of directors of a joint venture is now regarded as its highest authority and is empowered to make all major decisions under the latest regulations. 
Government departments in charge may offer guidance, assistance and supervision but not actual leadership.
''This provision reflects respect for the right of a joint venture to do business independently,'' Yuan Mu, a State Council spokesman, was quoted as saying at a news conference.
A report on the new regulations on joint ventures circulated today by the official New China News Agency did not clarify some problems that have perplexed Western businessmen.
For example, there was no mention of a requirement that Chinese management be paid on a par with Western executives in the joint venture. 
The Government has the habit of siphoning away most of this Western salary, leaving the Chinese manager with little more than the local prevailing salary.
Some Western businessmen said they were waiting to see to what extent the new rules would make it easier to do business in China. 
''The big question still is: How will it work in practice?'' one American said.

text:

For the second time in two days, China has deleted portions of remarks made by President Reagan on prime time Chinese television.
A significant part was deleted from an interview that Mr. Reagan gave Saturday with the Chinese television network. 
In it, he asserted that ''Americans are people of peace'' who did not threaten China or any other nation and had ''no troops massed on your border.''
This latter part alluded to the heavy concentration of Soviet troops and missiles on China's northern frontiers.
China, for second time in two days, has deleted portions of remarks made by Pres Reagan on prime time Chinese TV; significant part is deleted from interview in which Reagan said that Americans are people of peace who do not threaten China or any other nation and have 'no troops massed on your border;' latter part alludes to heavy concentration of Soviet troops and missiles on China's northern frontiers; photo (M)
On Friday, Chinese television omitted passages of a speech that Mr. Reagan gave to a select Chinese audience in the Great Hall of the People that were even more explicitly critical of the Soviet Union.
Â 
Allusion to Airliner's Downing
In that speech, Mr. Reagan also said that ''American troops are not massed on China's borders'' and occupied no lands. 
''Nor do we commit wanton acts such as shooting 269 innocent people out of the sky for the so-called cause of sacred airspace,'' Mr. Reagan said, alluding to the shooting down of a South Korean airliner by a Soviet jet fighter last September. 
Both cases of deletion reflected Chinese sensitivity over criticism that Mr. Reagan has leveled against the Soviet Union during his visit here. 
Peking has entered into talks with Moscow aimed at normalizing relations, though Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang told Mr. Reagan that there had been no substantive progress. 
It has also invited a Soviet First Deputy Prime Minister, Ivan V. Arkhipov, to visit China in mid-May.
While Chinese-Soviet relations are still cool, China evidently does not want to appear to be returning to the doctrine of strategic cooperation with the United States, which it shelved two and a half years ago in favor of greater identification with the third world.
On Saturday, the Presidential party brushed off the significance of the earlier deletion of Mr. Reagan's remarks.
Â 
President Is Queried
When the President stopped before television cameras during his sightseeing at the Great Wall Saturday afternoon, one television reporter asked him, ''What did you think about your speech being censored?''
Mr. Reagan said he was not upset. 
''You fellas do it all the time,'' he said.
''We don't cut out all the best parts,'' another television reporter said. 
''Yes, you do,'' Mr. Reagan replied,
The Chinese Foreign Ministry's information director, Qi Huaiyuan, when asked about the editing of the videotape of Mr. Reagan's speech Friday, indicated that his Government did not want to let the leader of one country publicly attack another country while in China.
''I have no more comment than that it is inappropriate for the Chinese media to publicize the comments by President Reagan on a third country,'' Mr. Qi told reporters at a news briefing. 
Larry Speakes, the White House spokesman, gave reporters a statement Saturday expressing ''regret'' that the statements in Mr. Reagan's Friday speech that ''would have given the Chinese people a better understanding of our country and its people'' had been cut out of the later rebroadcast.

U.S. Said to Have Been Told
But Mr. Qi said he had informed the White House office of the deletions before Friday's broadcast. 
''I said some paragraphs that concern a third country, and so forth, will be left out,' the official said.

Late last month, a Polish trade delegation concluded an agreement here with the Chinese providing for a 25 percent rise in trade between the countries in 1982.

But the trade agreement seems to have little bearing on the policy of the Chinese, who have been careful to remain aloof from the events taking place in Poland.
There are two interrelated reasons why the Chinese have chosen not to get involved in the political turmoil over Poland, in the view of Western, Communist and third-world diplomats here.
Poland concludes trade agreement with China providing for 25 percent rise in trade between the countries in 1982
The first is that unless the Soviet Union decides to intervene militarily in Poland, the Peking leadership sees no advantage in siding with the United States in what has developed into another superpower confrontation. 
Several diplomats here expressed surprise that the Reagan Administration thought that the Chinese could summon up common cause on the issue.
Â 
Influenced by Internal Factors
''The United States seems to forget that China still considers itself a Communist country,'' a third-world diplomat said. 
The second and possibly more cogent reason is that the rise of an independent trade union in Poland and the consequent liberalization represents an ominous tendency that the Peking leadership does not want to see imitated here, particularly when China is undergoing a delicate transition after the demythification of Mao Zedong.
An East European diplomat agreed that China's view of the Polish situation was influenced ''not only by international factors but also by internal factors.''
The Chinese have stuck to the cautious position spelled out just after martial law was declared in Poland last Dec. 
13. A Foreign Ministry spokesman told reporters on Dec. 
14 that China ''consistently maintained that Polish affairs should be settled by the Polish people themselves.''
Since then, the leadership has reiterated its objection to any outside interference. 
Li Xiannian, a Deputy Chairman of the Chinese Communist Party, told the Italian Communist Party newspaper L'Unita last month that in addition to the Sov iet Uni on, ''the United States also practices hegemonism'' - China's code wo rd f or expans ionist aims.
Â 
Irritated by Deal With Taiwan
When John H. Holdridge, the United States Assistant Secretary of State for Far Eastern and Pacific Affairs, visited Peking last month, the Chinese rejected a request to cooperate in assailing the Soviet Union on Poland. 
The Chinese appeared irritated by the Reagan Administration's bid partly because Peking contends that the continuing sale of American arms to Taiwan is interference in China's internal affairs.
The new trade agreement just concluded between China and Poland is a barter deal valued at 255 million Swiss francs, or about $135.4 million. 
The trade surplus runs in China's favor, with 154 million francs, or about $81 million, worth of Chinese exports and 101 million francs, or about $53 million, worth of Polish exports. 
The two-way trade reportedly involves mostly consumer goods.
East European sources say this is 25 percent higher than the level of Chinese-Polish trade last year. 
But they acknowledge that this rise follows a sharp drop last year, when China cut back on its expenditures in the drive to modernize the country, and trade suffered with Japan as well as Eastern Europe.
The 1982 level is still only 70 percent of the 1980 peak, when Chinese-Polish trade exceeded 400 million Swiss francs, or about $210.6 million, in value.
Even so, said an East European diplomat, ''the Chinese were rather cooperative.''
A Western diplomat said that if the Chinese had postponed the agreement, it might have been interpreted as a political gesture of disapproval at events in Poland.
Â 
Selling Pork to Poland
In a separate deal, China has also agreed to sell Poland 50,000 tons of pork, with payment deferred for 10 years. 
However, this contract was signed last October.
The Chinese press has continued to criticize the Soviet Union on other issues and has given particular prominence to the latest rift between the Soviet and Italian Communist parties.

Events in Poland are usually reported here by quoting the official Polish press agency, but without the additional editorializing that the Chinese press often tucks into its foreign news reports.
After its ideological break with the Soviet Union, China no longer has party-to-party relations with most countries in the Soviet bloc, including Poland, though they maintain diplomatic ties and large embassies.

file: CHINA AND SOVIET PLEASED BY MOOD OF PEKING TALKS.txt
text:
ï»¿
As the most important Soviet visitor in 15 years left for home today, officials on both sides asserted that an important watershed had been passed in the long struggle to re-establish good relations between the two Communist powers. 
Attention among Soviet and Chinese officials here focused less on the economic and technical agreements reached during the nine-day visit of First Deputy Prime Minister Ivan V. Arkhipov than on the warm atmosphere that prevailed throughout his stay.
One Soviet official recalled the situation after President Nixon visited here in 1972, a trip that he said was important more for the fact that it occurred, and for its friendly atmosphere, than for any notable political breakthroughs.
Â 
'Atmosphere Has Been Changed'
''Now,'' the official said, ''our side has come, and although we haven't overcome the big problems, the atmosphere has been changed.''
Chinese Foreign Ministry officials who discussed the trip privately made a similar assessment. 
Peking stuck to its demands that disagreements over Afghanistan and Cambodia and tensions along the Chinese-Soviet border be tackled before normal political ties are resumed, but the officials said there was ''no doubt'' that Mr. Arkhipov's visit had changed matters considerably for the better.
(In Washington, a Reagan Administration official said that the talks represented ''a significant new development'' in relations between the two nations, but added that it was ''not unexpected.'')
For the moment, there is no talk in Peking of a reconciliation as far-reaching as that achieved between China and the United States, and realists on both sides say that factors such as geographical proximity, rivalry within the Communist world and differing domestic policies probably rule out anything like that between Peking and Moscow for many years.
Nonetheless, the new beginning that was referred to frequently by Mr. Ark hipov and the Chinese Politburo members who met him here has many aspects, by no means all of them limited to the basic issues of a five-year trade pact and Soviet technological assistance to outdated Chinese industry that dominated the talks. 
Just as much else in Peking has changed drastically over the last decade, so has the prevailing attitude toward the Russians.
For several years after the border clashes of 1969, antipathy toward the Soviet Union was encouraged. 
The Soviet aid program that had helped China onto its feet after 1949 was derided, with special visits provided for Westerners to Yellow River dam projects and other undertakings that the Russians were said to have botched. 
Children's books depicted Soviet border troops as menacing, and nearly everything the Soviet ''social imperialists'' did at home and abroad was held in contempt. 
Much of this receded with the other excesses of the Cultural Revolution, the leftist-inspired turmoil that gripped China for a decade beginning in 1966. 
But it is only in relatively recent times, since the resumption of six-monthly talks at the Foreign Ministry level in 1982, that a much more tolerant attitude toward the Russians has emerged. 
Though only limited momentum has gathered so far, the manifestations are striking.
Â 
Intererst in Russia Voiced
No longer can Westerners hope to gain points here by adopting a supercilious attitude toward the Soviet Union. 
Inquiries about life in Russia put to Americans who have lived there are sympathetically phrased. 
And not only among the high officials who met Mr. Arkhipov is there a new appreciation of the money and effort expended by the Kremlin on its aid program here during the 1950's.
To a far greater degree than has been the case for 20 years, ordinary Chinese can now learn something about Russians and their culture. 
On the anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution last month Chinese television showed its first contemporary Soviet film in two decades, and the one it picked, ''Moscow Doesn't Believe in Tears,'' a moving depiction of a young woman of rural background struggling to make her way in the capital, won widespread popular acclaim.
About 30 other exchanges have taken place this year. 
China has been host to an exhibition of 20th century Soviet painting, a Soviet writers' group has visited for lectures and discussions and a Russian tenor, Yuri Marusin, won a standing ovation for a concert in which he sang Russian folk songs and selections from Tchaikovsky and Verdi. 
A photo exhibition on Soviet life that was held at the National Gallery during the Nov. 
7 anniversary drew large crowds.
At the Waiwen Bookshop on Wang Fu Jing Street, Peking's principal source of foreign books, an effort has been made to upgrade the selection of Soviet publications. 
Several new Chinese- Russian dictionaries have been printed, there are coffee-table books about the beauties of the Soviet Union and Soviet children's albums offering a glossy view of Russian life are on sale.
However, as in the broader relations between the two countries, reservations remain. 
While the English-language selection at the bookstore includes P. G. Wodehouse, Anthony Burgess and Henry James, among others, the Russian fiction available is mostly 19th or early 20th century classics by Pushkin, Lermontov and Chekhov. 
The only recognized writers of the Soviet period are early ones like Vladimir Mayakovsky, and there is nothing by any Soviet leader, even Stalin.
The choice of Mr. Arkhipov to be the first senior Soviet official to come here since Prime Minister Aleksei N. Kosygin's brief airport stop in 1969 was well taken, since he had headed the Soviet aid program here and evidently made strong friendships with several of the men now in power. 
Insistent gratitude was shown by Politburo members like Chen Yun, who spoke of having got along ''swimmingly'' with the Soviet official in the 1950's.
Mr. Arkhipov responded with some ingratiating remarks of his own about ''the great changes'' now taking place in China under the regime of Deng Xiaoping, which have had a chilly reception from the official Soviet press.
The official New China News Agency even quoted Mr. Arkhipov as having said that the changes constituted ''a magnificent plan for the future.''

''The United States and the Soviet Union belong to the same category,'' said the commentary, which was attributed to the New China News Agency's Washington correspondent, Peng Di.

Such a portrayal was familiar under the late Mao Zedong. 
But with the establishment of diplomatic relations between Washington and Peking and the development of commercial ties, the leadership of Deng Xiaoping muted the references to the United States as a superpower and focused its charge of hegemonism on the Soviet Union.

Possible Reasons for Move
Some Peking-based Western and third world diplomats who noticed the revival of the previous ideological formula have suggested at least two reasons for it.

file: CHINA BELIEVED TO HAVE UNDERSTATED SCALE OF DROUGHT AND FLOOD DISASTERS.txt
text:
ï»¿
Chinese leaders apparently decided late last fall to deliberately understate the dimensions of China's drought and flood calamities in making their first appeal for international relief aid in more than 30 years. 
They are reported to have acted out of fear of alarming donor nations, antagonizing other third world disaster victims and damaging domestic political stabilityI.
According to Chinese officials, Western diplomats and relief workers here, the Peking leadership decided after ''sensitive'' debates to limit their aid appeal to apply only to hard-hit provinces containing about 21 million seriously affected victims of drought and flood because the dimensions of the overall problems were ''too big.''
International relief officials and some Western diplomats estimate that more than 130 million people are facing varying degrees of food shortages in at least nine provinces. 
But they are quick to stress that people are not starving and that the Government's own relief effort is well under way and seems fairly well organized.
Chinese leaders make first appeal for international relief aid in 30 years following country's severe drought and flood disastersNot Like Africans' Plight
''While we are talking about enormous areas and enormous numbers of affected people, China's problems should in no way be compared to the death and starvation among refugees in Africa,'' said a relief worker with experience in both places. 
''There is malnutrition, and some of it is serious and getting more serious. 
There are diseases growing out of it. 
But there is food to guarantee survival, and the Chinese are handling the bulk of the problems themselves with varying degrees of effectiveness.''
Perhaps to underscore the contrast with Africa, earlier this month at a Geneva conference China pledged $1 million to the relief effort for African refugees. 
The pledge was made despite an estimate by a United Nations survey team in March that China would need $700 million in food and other aid for disaster victims in Hebei and Hubei Provinces alone.
Hebei Province encircles Peking and is centered in the north China plain, which Chinese officials have said is into its second year with little or no rain. 
They said the drought is the region's worst in 38 years. 
Parts of at least seven provinces are affected: Liaoning, Hebei, Shanxi, Shaanxi, Ningxia, Gansu and Inner Mongolia.
The meterological bureau reported that between .12 and .8 of an inch of rain fell on parts of this region on April l3 and 14, helping the winter wheat crop planted last fall, but not by much.
Hubei Province in central China was the most seriously hit by torrential rains and subsequent flooding of the Yangtze River last summer. 
The Yangtze crested at its highest level in 26 years. 
To protect cities along the river, including Wuhan, Nanjing and Shanghai, workers hastily broke dozens of embankments along feeder rivers. 
Other burst themselves, inundating rural but heavily populated areas in Hubei and Anhui Provinces.
Chinese officials told the United Nations survey team that 550 people had died in the flooding and that about 41,000 had been injured. 
Whole villages were swept away, as were grain and vegetable crops and farm animals. 
Much land is too waterlogged to grow anything this year, they said.
Â 
Grain Stockpiles Dwindling
Relief officials said the drought in the north was most worrisome because no end to it is in sight and communal and district stockpiles of grain and other food harvested in previous years are rapidly dwindling. 
Reservoirs and rivers have dried up, and the water table in some areas has dropped to the point where villagers cannot dig emergency wells without modern deep-drilling equipment, which is in short supply.
Emergency rations of coarse grains, mainly ground corn, are being distributed, along with some dried cabbage and radishes. 
These provide between 1,200 and l,500 calories per day per person, several hundred calories short of minimum daily requirements of sustenance and child growth. 
Relatives living outside affected regions have been sending or bringing food in as well.
Before quietly approaching the United Nations last November, Chinese officials carefully weighed both the international and domestic political consequences of seeking foreign relief aid. 
Their decision to go ahead involved reversing to some extent a policy of self-reliance that has been a source of propaganda and pride since 1949.
Â 
Self-Reliance Still Stressed
When the United Nations disaster relief co-ordinator announced on March 12 that his organization would open an international appeal on behalf of China, he noted Peking's declaration that self-reliance continues to be a ''basic principle.''
At a news conference on March 31, Du Runsheng, deputy minister in the State Agricultural Commission, said that ''China has always undertaken our obligations'' financially to international organizations such as the United Nations but that in the past China had ''waived its right to benefit.''
He said China viewed its participation as a ''two-way street'' and ''strictly a question of mutual help.''
Mr. Du said the international aid China was seeking was small compared with the country's needs and that the domestic relief effort ''far exceeds'' whatever outside donors will contribute.
Â 
Possibilities for Aid Limited
Some Western diplomats interpreted China's limited request for aid as an effort not to scare away donor nations that might view the dimensions of China's needs as overwhelming. 
They also say that China does not want to antagonize its political friends in the third world that are suffering from their own disasters and are highly conscious that the amount of international relief aid is limited.
While the numbers of people affected seem enormous and while there are ample cases of serious malnutrition and disease, relief officials point out that all numbers in China seem enormous and that distinguishing victims of natural disaster from people affected by the poverty stemming from what the Chinese call man-made disasters is often difficult.
Relief workers believe that one reason the Chinese Government limited their inspections to two provinces is that the officials are loath to allow foreigners to document the effect of the admittedly disastrous consequences of China's agricultural policies over the last quarter-century.
Heavy commune building, central planning that ignored local conditions, tree-cutting and subsequent erosion, misguided irrigation projects causing saline buildup in soil and other policies that are now discredited left hundreds of millions of Chinese peasants with nothing to show for 25 years of toil.
Statistics compiled in the February issue of the magazine Economic Management imply that there were millions of unaccounted-for deaths between 1957, the beginning of the Great Leap Forward, and 1960, which began a period of famine.
Â 
Millions Lack Enough to Eat
At a Communist Party work conference in April 1979, Deputy Chairman Li Xiannian was reliably reported to have said that about 100 million people in China did not have enough to eat. 
That was before the current droughts and last year's floods.
Foreign pledges of aid for China have been trickling in. 
Emergency United Nations shipments of vitamins have arrived and are being distributed to supplement emergency grain rations. 
The European Common Market pledged $6.2 million worth of powdered milk and rapeseed oil along with other food supplies. 
Japan has pledged powdered milk as well.
The Peking leadership, meanwhile, faces a double-edged domestic sword as a consequence of its appeal for outside aid. 
Diplomats say if China discloses the full extent of its needs, it faces domestic criticism for failing at self-reliance. 
If it does not, foreign responses might be embarrassingly small and Mr. Deng's critics could use that as another example of the failure of his cooperation with non-Communist countries.

''The consultations proceeded in a frank, calm and earnest atmosphere,'' the statement said.

31 said 10,000 Soviet visitors came to China in the first nine months of this year, compared with 8,000 in 1983.

file: CHINA CAUTIONS STANFORD ABOUT EXPELLING STUDENT.txt
text:

China has cautioned Stanford University that future cultural exchanges with the United States may be impaired if the university reverses the expulsion of a graduate student who angered Peking while doing research in China.
A lawyer for Stanford, Iris Brest, said the school would not be influenced by the warning, conveyed in a letter from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.
Steven W. Mosher, the student who was dismissed in February 1983, has appealed to the university president, Donald Kennedy, to reinstate him.

China cautions Stanford University that future cultural exchanges with United States may be impaired if university reverses expulsion of graduate student Steven W Mosher; Mosher was dismissed after allegations of 'illegal and seriously unethical conduct' while in China in 1979 and 1980; portrait of Mosher (M)
Mr. Mosher, following the steps prescribed in university regulations, had appealed to three other Stanford officials, who upheld the original decision. 
The appeal to Mr. Kennedy is the final one provided by university rules. 
Mr. Mosher has threatened to sue Stanford if he is not readmitted as a doctoral candidate.
Â 
Student Dismissed in '83
Stanford's anthropology department dismissed Mr. Mosher by a unanimous vote, charging that he was guilty of a pattern of ''illegal and seriously unethical conduct'' while in China in 1979 and 1980.
The school's action touched off a major dispute about academic freedom, with some supporters of Mr. Mosher accusing Stanford of bowing to pressure from China, with whom it has a sizable exchange program. 
China banned further field research by American scholars after Mr. Mosher's departure from the country.
When an anthropology department committee in 1982 was investigating Mr. Mosher's activity in China a senior official of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences wrote to Stanford expressing the hope that the university would deal with him ''severely'' and asking to be informed of the school's decision.
Although neither Stanford nor Mr. Mosher has released a 95-page report prepared by the investigating committee, some members of the anthropology department have said privately that the charges against Mr. Mosher involved bribing local Chinese officials to get government documents, smuggling and making a trip into a province closed to foreigners.

Letter Released by Mosher
The latest Chinese letter to Stanford was made public by Mr. Mosher, who now lives in Fresno, Calif.

''For the future normal and beneficial exchange between our two countries,'' Mr. Wang wrote, ''I trust that you will make a correct judgment based on the facts and properly handle this matter.''
Mr. Mosher, who last year published a book based on his research in rural China, ''Broken Earth,'' a critical account of the conditions of peasant life under Communist rule, has just finished a second book, this one about his trip by van into the restricted province, Guizhou.

file: CHINA CAUTIONS U.S. ON ARMS FOR TAIWAN.txt
text:
ï»¿
China has hardened its public opposition to United States arms sales to Taiwan, warning before the arrival tomorrow of Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. that the development of strategic relations between Washington and Peking could not progress if the sales continued.
A strongly worded commentary, issued by the official New China News Agency and published yesterday by China's Government-controlled newspapers, said that Reagan Administration attempts to ''sell arms to China in exchange for China's consent to U.S. arms sales to Taiwan'' were ''doomed to failure.''
Written by an unnamed senior Chinese official under the pseudonym Hua Xiu, the commentary was the strongest denunciation of arms aid to Taiwan since China and the United States normalized diplomatic relations two-and-a-half years ago. 
It implied a new inflexibility on the Taiwan arms sale issue that some foreign analysts said might divert the emphasis of Mr. Haig's mission from global cooperation against Soviet expansionism to the Taiwan issue.
China denounces US proposal for arms sales to TaiwanThe Chinese Invoke Linkage
The commentary's hard line contrasted sharply with conciliatory statements made in recent weeks by some Foreign Ministry officials and it linked, for the first time, Chinese-American progress in other fields with the Taiwan arms dispute. 
With Mr. Haig clearly in mind, it said:
''Of late, some high-ranking U.S. 
Government officials have repeatedly called attention to China's strategic position and role, and hope to further strategic relations with it through the opening up of certain areas where the two countries are yet to establish links, and other steps. 
Public opinion in China has given enough attention to this and expressed appreciation of this good intention.''
But it then added: ''Hovever, the crux to further strategic relations between the two countries remains that the United States stop developing all contacts with Taiwan that go beyond nongovernmental relations in keeping with the principles laid down in the China-U.S. joint communique on the establishment of diplomatic relations. 
For the moment, the outstanding issue is about the U.S. arms sales to Taiwan.''
Â 
China Willing to Forego Contracts
The Foreign Ministry issued a statement Wednesday saying that China would rather forgo receiving United States arms than accept ''continued U.S. interference in our internal affairs,'' involving arms sales to Taiwan. 
The statement was in response to reports from Washington on the eve of Mr. Haig's departure that the United States wanted to facilitate the sale of military technology to China while continuing to provide defensive military hardware to Taiwan.
The linking of these two aims in press reports, according to Western diplomats, appears to have touched a raw nerve in Peking, whose leaders only a few weeks ago seemed to be willing to go along with the quiet replenishment of military stocks to Taiwan if the United States would postpone a decision on selling an advanced jet fighter known as the FX to that island's military.
The commentary published yesterday said: ''China has made it explicitly clear that it would rather refuse U.S. arms than consent to U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, an interference in China's internal affairs, and that any arms sales to Taiwan by any country will certainly draw strong reactions from China, because this is a principled issue and China will not barter away principles.''
Â 
Issue Arose During U.S. 
Campaign
The Taiwan Relations Act, passed by Congress in March 1979 as a vehicle for maintaining unofficial links with Taiwan, has never been accepted by Peking. 
However, China's leaders did not make a major issue of it beyond official protests until Ronald Reagan, as the Republican Presidential candidate last year, called it ''the law of the land'' and argued that American relations with Taiwan be made ''official.''
The Chinese press accused him then of having ''insulted 1 billion Chinese people,'' and China's leadership has since reacted quickly and negatively to all Reagan Administration statements favoring Taiwan as if they were a betrayal of American commitments under the Shanghai Communique, signed by President Nixon in 1972, and the normalization agreements approved by President Carter in December 1979.
Western diplomats are debating whether Peking's statements before Mr. Haig's arrival reflect genuine anger with Washington or whether leaders were attempting to create a position from which they could claim victory if the United States conceded that sales of advanced fighters or other military equipment to Taiwan was not necessary.
In any case, China's huge but antiquated peasant army is in no position to absorb sophisticated American weapons. 
It cannot afford more than a few bits of military know-how. 
And it is in no position to threaten Taiwan.
Â 
No Dependence on Foreign Arms
''As a country with a population of 1 billion, China has never thought of depending on foreign arms for military buildup,'' the commentary yesterday said. 
''It only tried to import some foreign military know-how to help build up a modern defense system.''
China is now portraying the Taiwan Relations Act as an American effort to create instability in Asia. 
Referring to proposals for arms sales on both sides of the Formosa Strait, the commentary said it was ''nothing but superpower logic to split China.''
China's newspaper for intellectuals, Guangming Daily, published a long denunciation of the Taiwan Relations Act two weeks ago in which it asked:
''Is it possible for some foreign legislation to provide what kind of economic system Hawaii should adopt and what relations it should have with the mainland of the United States?''

file: CHINA CAUTIOUSLY INCREASING ITS WORLDWIDE INVESTMENTS.txt
text:
ï»¿
China, on the eve of Premier Zhao Ziyang's first visit to the United States, is testing the waters of international capitalism.
The experiment, which began on a significant scale only last spring, is being conducted worldwide. 
In the United States, for example, the Chinese province of Guangdong has invested in a meatpacking plant in Clive, Iowa. 
The China International Trust and Investment Corporation has taken a 19 percent interest in Santec, a personal computer company based in Amherst, N.H. 
And the China National Metals and Minerals Import and Export Corporation has joined the Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel Corporation in an international joint venture to trade metals and minerals.
Outside the United States, China is negotiating investments in potash mining in Saskatchewan and wood pulp manufacturing in British Columbia; has bought into a forestry project on the Solomon Islands and has invested in fisheries in Sri Lanka.
According to a State Department estimate, the overall value of such investment abroad by Peking may be as high as $1 billion when Hong Kong real estate is included. 
But analysts say the figure is certain to rise as China becomes more comfortable with the hurly-burly ways of capitalist markets.
Â 
Display of 'Unusual' Confidence
''It shows a confidence by Peking in the international economic system that is certainly unusual for a Communist government,'' said one Administration foreign trade official who asked not to be identified. 
''It also shows a confidence in their own abilities to get out and play with the big boys.''
The issues of bilateral trade and investment are expected to be major topics during the Chinese Prime Minister's visit to the United States and Canada. 
Mr. Zhao, who will be the highest ranking Chinese official to visit Washington since China's leader, Deng Xiaoping, came here in 1979, is expected to sign an agreement on industrial cooperation while in Washington. 
Mr. Zhao left Honolulu today after a day of sightseeing there, and was scheduled to arrive in Williamsburg, Va., early Monday to continue his North American tour. 
He is scheduled to meet with President Reagan on Tuesday.
According to one American official, a nuclear-technology exchange agreement could also be reached during the Chinese Prime Minister's three-day visit to Washington. 
Such a treaty would permit American companies to sell nuclear power reactors to China, which has an ambitious program on the drawing boards to increase electric power generation for several of its major cities.
American analysts say the Chinese have several specific objectives for their investment and trading program: to improve their technical and management skills; raise foreign exchange earnings; get around protectionist barriers that are rising in many of their markets, and secure a stable source of supply of raw materials.
This investment abroad coincides with a rising interest by American companies in joint ventures in China and a new concentration by both Governments on concluding a treaty defining rights and obligations of investors in both countries.
American industrialists see important markets developing in China as it continues with ambitious expansion programs aimed at quadrupling output by the year 2000.
Last year, 20 American companies - including Squibb, Occidental Petroleum, American Motors and Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing - announced expansion moves in China. 
According to the National Council for United States-China Trade, a body with a membership of 500 American companies that facilitates trade with China, the overall stake of the 20 companies is about $100 million.
Along with two-way investment, two-way trade is also picking up. 
According to the council, trade between the two nations could reach a record $5.5 billion to $6 billion this year compared with $4.4 billion last year. 
The rise will be led by growing sales of American capital goods and wheat, the council says.
To date, American companies have been faring well in the China market, Over stiff European, Canadian and even Russian competition, for example, General Electric recently won a contract to provide 200 diesel electric locomotives for Chinese railroads, which will add more than $200 million to the export total this year.
Â 
Big Honeywell Order
And under recently relaxed Washington guidelines for the sale of American high technology goods to China, Honeywell recently won clearance to sell $23 million worth of personal computers.
According to figures filed with the International Monetary Fund, which it joined in 1980, China has accumulated some $20 billion in foreign exchange and gold reserves in recent years. 
But many analysts expect that the reserves may quickly decline as China gets deeper into its domestic industrial expansion programs. 
According to its own estimates, China may be spending as much as $50 billion by the end of the century to expand coal production and $20 billion on offshore oil development.
Some of the expected slack is likely to be taken up through development loans, however. 
With strong American backing after the restoration of full diplomatic ties in December 1978, China became a member of both the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank in 1980 - accepting their disclosure requirements.
Â 
$1 Billion World Bank Loan
China has already received about $1 billion in loans from the World Bank. 
Senior bank officials, such as David W. Berk, acting division chief for China programs, and Edwin R. Lim, senior economist for East Asia and the Pacific region, project that China's borrowing could rise to $2 billion a year in the second half of the 1980's.
Meanwhile, Peking has been putting its huge currency reserves to work in both direct foreign investment and the capital markets.
The China International Trust and Investment Corporation, the vehicle for much of the foreign investment, recently drew $100 million from Tokyo capital markets. 
The Development Corporation of Fujian Province, just across the Formosa Straits from Taiwan, also borrowed around $20 million in Tokyo recently.

file: CHINA CLOSING IN ON MAOIST REMMNANTS.txt
text:

China's Communist Party is about to mount an extensive drive to examine the loyalty of its 40 million members and discipline or expel those who oppose the policies of Deng Xiaoping.
An unannounced work committee has begun mapping details of the campaign for discussion and endorsement shortly by a plenary session of the party's Central Committee, according to Chinese and foreign diplomatic sources.
The campaign, known as a ''rectification of party style,'' could result in the expulsion of a million or more party members who are found to be corrupt, incompetent or too radical for the leadership headed by Mr. Deng.

The correct new party line follows the political pragmatism set out by Mr. Deng in speeches and writings that were published here to great fanfare as his ''Selected Works'' last July. 
A 4,000- character commentary on the front page of People's Daily today pointedly called Mr. Deng's works ''an important ideological preparation for the overall rectification campaign'' that will get under way throughout China this autumn and winter. 
The Communist Party newspaper, implicitly answering doubts by some party hard-liners that Mr. Deng's policies were consistent with orthodox Marxism, said today that ''the handling of both historical and current issues and the principles adopted in the economic, political and cultural fields have demonstrated the high Marxist level of our party and Comrade Deng Xiaoping.''

Many of his innovations have been at variance with the dogma of Mao Zedong.
Â 
Maoists Are a Major Target
A primary target of the new rectification drive will be Maoists who have been obstructing change. 
Many got their government and party sinecures during the Cultural Revolution. 
But the party leadership has also said it wants to clear out those guilty of corruption and other abuses of authority who have damaged the party's prestige among ordinary Chinese.
The campaign was originally announced by the party's General Secretary, Hu Yaobang, at the 12th party congress in September 1982. 
Mr. Hu admitted then that ''it is true that impurities in ideology, style and organization still exist within the party and no fundamental turn for the better has as yet been made in our party style.''
To correct the situation, Mr. Hu said, ''the Central Committee has decided on an overall rectification of party style and consolidation of party organizations, which will proceed by stages and by groups over a period of three years beginning from the latter half of 1983.''
Since then, pilot projects to swing the party rank and file into line have been instituted throughout the nation. 
People's Daily complained last June that ''some problems still remain unsolved.''
It said some party committees were afraid to confront ''the malpractices of some leading cadres.''
Â 
Resistance in the Army
The objections to a rectification drive are believed strongest in the army, but there are also reports of Maoist resistance to Mr. Deng's policies in provinces like Hunan and Guangxi in southern China.
Mr. Deng has already shuffled some key jobs in the provinces and military regions. 
Today's commentary in People's Daily hinted that the new drive would scrutinize the loyalties of party members in the middle echelons.
''All party members, those holding positions at and above county level in particular, must acquire a clear understanding of the stand, point of view and methods Comrade Deng Xiaoping used in dealing with all kinds of problems,'' it said.
The official press has insisted that the campaign will not turn into the kind of witchhunt that the Maoists mounted during the Cultural Revolution. 
''With regard to criticism launched by comrades, we must adopt a comradely approach, stress reasoning and seek truth from facts,'' said Lu Dingyi, a Central Committee member, in a speech People's Daily published in late August. 
''We must oppose the trumping up of charges and exaggeration. 
We must allow comrades to reply to charges.''
The drive is being modeled, at least ostensibly, on the first party rectification campaign that Chairman Mao held at the guerrilla base area of Yanan in 1942 to neutralize the pro-Moscow faction of the party led by Wang Ming.
Â 
'Handful Will Be Expelled'
Mr. Hu said at the party congress 13 months ago that following political study and self-criticism, all party members would have to register anew. 
''Those who still fail to meet the requirements for membership after education shall be expelled from the party or asked to withdraw from it,'' Mr. Hu said. 
However, in recent months there has been virtually no stress on re-registration.
Diplomatic estimates of the number of Chinese who could be stripped of party membership has run from one to three million. 
The leadership has avoided mentioning any percentage, possibly for fear of suggesting a quota of miscreants that zealous subordinates would try to fill.
An Zhiguo, political editor of Beijing Review, wrote in its current issue that ''only a small handful will be expelled from the party.''
''This has once again proved,'' he added, ''that rumors abroad that the party consolidation will be a 'great purge' are groundless.''

UN Security Council fails to choose new Secretary General as China continues to veto Kurt Waldheim's candidacy for third five-year term
China's intentions remain the central question. 
It vetoed Mr. Waldheim twice in 1971 to demonstrate its insistence that the United Nations should be run by someone from Asia, Africa or Latin America. 
Later China relented, abstaining on the third round.
This time there have been six inconclusive rounds of voting thus far. 
Whoever is nominated by the Security Council must still be approved by the 156-nation General Assembly, where election is by a simple majority.
Council members believe that China is waiting for the Latin Americans to put forward a candidate in the expectation that the Soviet Union will then cast a veto and share with the United States the onus of thwarting third-world aspirations.
The Waldheim backers hope that China will then lift its veto, satisfied that it has done its best for a third world whose Council members have been unable to vote together as a solid bloc.
The Soviet Union would not like saying ''no'' to a third-world figure. 
But the Soviet delegate, Oleg A. Troyanovsky, has made it clear that Mr. Waldheim is as much the choice of the Soviet Union as he is of the Western nations.
Through the first six ballots, Mr. Troyanovsky has been telling reporters that he has not cast a single negative vote and he has appeared to enjoy what he views as United States discomfort over rejecting Mr. Salim.
There is no assurance that the Soviet Union would veto every Latin American. 
Ten years ago, it blocked Carlos Ortiz de Rozas of Argentina. 
But since then, Argentina has shipped much needed wheat to the Soviet Union. 
Mr. Ortiz de Rozas is again a potential candidate.
The first Latin candidate to appear openly may be Javier Perez de Cuellar of Peru, until recently a United Nations Under Secretary General. 
Peru has said that it would nominate him if the Council decided that it was deadlocked.
Jeane J. Kirkpatrick of the United States told reporters that there was a long discussion today in the Council chamber to determine when an impasse constituted a deadlock. 
The Council may continue this discussion when it meets again on Friday.
Mr. Waldheim's second term runs out at the end of the year. 
If he survives this election, he will be the first Secretary General to gain three terms.
Those present at today's voting behind closed doors said 11 nations had voted for Mr. Waldheim on each round and four against, including the critical Chinese ballot. 
Mr. Salim received eight votes each time with one ''no'' on the first round and two on the second. 
Six nations abstained in the first round and five in the second round.
All five of the Council's permanent members - the United States, Soviet Union, Britain, France and China -have veto power. 
The three African members, which are thought to have voted steadily for Mr. Salim, are Tunisia, Uganda and Niger. 
The other third-world members, some of which have apparently failed to vote consistently for Mr. Salim, are the Philippines, Mexico and Panama. 
The other members are Japan, Spain, Ireland and East Germany.

file: CHINA COUNTS ITS QUARTER OF THE WORLD_S NOSES.txt
text:
ï»¿
China has begun the largest census in history in a meticulous effort to discover just how many people it has. 
The Peking Government claims about a billion citizens out of a total world population of 4.5 billion, though officials concede that no one knows the exact number of Chinese.
The census drive, which started Thursday and was preceded by a publicity campaign with banners, colorful posters and loudspeakers urging cooperation, is ostensibly a response to a 1974 United Nations call for all countries to undertake a new census before 1985.
But with a baby born in China every 2 seconds, articles and speeches here have stressed that the census is crucial to Peking's task of feeding and clothing its population while trying to catch up industrially with the West.
In addition to providing raw statistics needed for a centrally planned economy, the census is expected to indicate how successful China has been in its stringent birth control policies, which are aimed at holding the population down to 1.2 billion by the year 2000.
PEKING, July 5 - China has begun the largest census in history in a meticulous effort to discover just how many people it has.
When Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang went to register his family Thursday, he told the New China News Agency that the census was of great importance for China's modernization program. 
In a televised talk last month, Deputy Prime Minister Yao Yilin described the census as ''a large-scale investigation of national conditions,'' a phrase that has been echoed since by other Chinese officials.
The Communist Government has counted its citizens twice since taking power in 1949. 
Its first census in 1953 revealed 601 million Chinese. 
In the second census in 1964, the population exceeded 723 million.
Both of these figures were tabulated using the abacus, a manual calculator that has been in wide use in China since the Ming Dynasty six centuries ago.
This time, 29 computers are being used to collate the information. 
The computers will be used for final tallies in every province but Tibet. 
The local tabulations will still be done by abacus.
Taiwan is being included in the census, using the Nationalist Government's figure of 18 million inhabitants, in keeping with Peking's claim that the island is its unrecovered province.
Â 
Five Million Census-Takers
On the mainland, the Government has recruited over five million census-takers and supervisors, a contingent larger than the Chinese armed forces. 
Most started today with bundles of questionnaires, traveling by bicycle or foot in the dense eastern cities. 
Other workers set out several weeks ago in sparsely populated regions like the highlands of Tibet and the prairies of Inner Mongolia.
The census-takers and supervisors are instructed to complete their enumerating and checking by mid-July. 
Then over 100,000 data coders and technicians will work for several months feeding the information through the computers.
The preliminary results are to be released next October, with full census data available by the end of 1984. 
China is officially spending $200 million on its census, but that figure must be multiplied several times to give a true picture of the cost.
Â 
21 I.B.M. 
Computers Used
The United Nations fund for population activities also donated $15.6 million for the Chinese to purchase and install 21 new I.B.M. 
4300 computers. 
China is also using eight other Western computers that it purchased earlier.
The computer network will give China the ability to process other economic data that will be needed in its drive for modernization. 
The new census form, which is printed in green ink on paper half as large as a newspaper page, contains 19 questions, as compared with nine questions in the 1964 census. 
In addition to the old categories of name, age, sex, nationality and occupation, the new questionnaire asks women of childbearing age about children they had last year or expect soon. 
Such questions are meant to help evaluate China's birth control program.
Attempts to count the Chinese are hardly new. 
Population surveys have been carried out for thousands of years through successive dynasties. 
By the end of 1981, the State Statistical Bureau reported that China's population reached 996,220,000, an estimate arrived at through the nationwide household registrations checked twice a year.
Â 
Signs of Official Concern
But the Chinese have long been suspicious of the census and once hid for fear that they might be taxed or drafted into the army. 
Last month, Deputy Prime Minister Yao promised that the new census enumeration ''will in no way affect the citizens' rights and interests and obligations.''
Nonetheless, there have been signs of official concern about potential evasiveness, particularly in the countryside where 800 million peasants live. 
Families sometimes do not report a recent death in order to use the extra ration card to get grain or cotton cloth. 
Couples may conceal the fact that they have several children.
In the cities, thousands of Chinese are thought to have drifted back illegally from the countryside, where many were sent during the Cultural Revolution. 
Even some officials may underreport the local population growth rate to meet family planning targets.
People's Daily warned last spring that ''conditions must be reported exactly as they are at the time. 
No hiding the truth or false reporting will be allowed.''
Recently, a Shanghai peddler was fined $6 amid great publicity for having lied about the registration of his children in a trial census last year.
Â 
37,000 Census-Takers in Peking
One census station in the Tianqiao district of southern Peking today offered a glimpse into how the time-consuming enumeration process works. 
Feng Guilan, one of 37,000 census-takers in Peking, sat at a small table checking off responses from Chen @Zhiqing. 
She recorded that Mr. Chen was 52 years old, repaired trucks for a living, had a son and two daughters and that his 46-year-old wife was not pregnant in 1981.
Miss Feng, who is on a two-month leave from her job as a tea salesclerk, filled out the form, read back the responses and then had Mr. Chen sign the form to acknowledge that it was accurate. 
The procedure took about 15 minutes.
The station supervisor, He Qing, acknowledged that the enumeration was starting slowly. 
''We are not so experienced so we are taking only eight households in these first two hours,'' said Miss He, ''but we'll take up to 20 households tomorrow.''
Shen Yiying, a 23-year-old factory worker, came in to register the family for her mother, who she said was illiterate. 
Ma Zhanyu, a 63-year-old retired worker, brought along a paper written by his son to supplement the information in his maroon-bound household registration document.
Mr. Ma, who lives with his grandchildren, said afterward that he had no misgivings about answering so many questions. 
''Our country will have a clearer idea of its population, how many men there are and how many women,'' Mr. Ma said.
Â 
Small Floating Population
Xie Ruibin, who heads the census group of the local Tianqiao street committee, said that his 223 census workers filled out each household's questionnaire themselves to avoid errors and would later take turns checking each other's findings.
He was asked what happened if a census-taker found someone living in Peking without a legal registration or committing some other violation. 
''The main aim of the census is to get a clearer idea of the population, but if irregularities are found out, they will be dealt with by the departments concerned,'' Mr. Xie said.
While the task is likely to be harder in the countryside, Li Chengrui, the director of the census office, said in a recent article that China had one of the world's smallest floating populations, which would facilitate the work.
The Chinese Government seems confident that the careful census procedure and the use of computers will leave negligible room for error. 
A pilot census undertaken two years ago in Wuxi, a small city northwest of Shanghai, produced a discrepancy of only 17 onethousandths of 1 percent from previous estimates, while another study in a remote area of Inner Mongolia found a discrepancy of nine-tenths of 1 percent.

text:

With a major Communist Party congress scheduled for autumn, the Chinese leadership has been swinging the country back toward its old orthodoxy, with new constraints on foreign contacts and study abroad and a revival of ideological attacks on Western values.
The sour mood developing over the last few months evokes the xenophobia that existed in China before Peking opened its doors to Western influences in the mid-1970's. 
Some diplomats are finding unofficial access to the Chinese people increasingly difficult. 
One European journalist with several tours in China calls the climate the tightest he has seen since before the death of Mao Zedong in 1976.
PEKING, July 30 - With a major Communist Party congress scheduled for autumn, the Chinese leadership has been swinging the country back toward its old orthodoxy, with new constraints on foreign contacts and study abroad and a revival of ideological attacks on Western values.
This all seems to be linked to the 12th Party Congress, at which Deng Xiaoping, China's foremost leader, is expected to try to purge the policy-making bodies of Maoists and supporters of Hua Guofeng, whom he ousted as party chairman last summer. 
Chinese sources expect the congress to begin sometime in September.
Â 
A Protective Maneuver?
Consequently, some Western diplomats speculate that Mr. Deng is using the crackdown to protect his agricultural and economic programs from criticism, since ideological hard-liners fear that his open-door policy of trade with the West is letting in bourgeois ideas that will corrupt the Chinese people.
''The influence of decadent capitalist ideology on certain people, the ideological poisoning it causes and the pollution it produces in the social mood are now much greater and more serious than in any previous period,'' the Weekly Digest said last month.
Such statements in the official press, which inveighs against what the ideological journal Red Flag called ''the corrosive influence of capitalist ideas,'' suggests that positions are already being staked out before the congress.
One Western European diplomat also views such ideological attacks as a ramification of an anticorruption campaign that was begun earlier this year and now appears to have bogged down.
Â 
Foreigners as Scapegoat
The campaign against economic crime never reached the higher echelons of the party and the Government, despite public expectations, and the diplomat said he believed foreigners were now being made a scapegoat because of internal resistance.
''The argument is that corruption isn't basically Chinese and wouldn't exist but for foreign influence,'' the diplomat said. 
''They don't admit that it takes two to make a bribe.''
The most visible sign of the times here has been what another Western diplomat called ''a fairly extensive clampdown'' on unauthorized contacts between Chinese and foreigners. 
Circulars have gone out warning Chinese not to mix socially with foreigners. 
Some Chinese who have Western friends have been summoned for police interrogation, according to the friends.
Foreigners teaching English at some institutes in Peking have been shifted out of communal dormitories into segregated quarters where their students need written permission to visit them.
Â 
Warnings to Schoolchildren
The warnings against foreigners have extended to schoolchildren. 
Ideological guidelines recently promulgated for primary schools by the Ministry of Education instruct third-graders to be wary of foreigners and not to follow them about or accept presents readily.
The case of Lisa Wichser, an American teacher detained and expelled early last month for allegedly stealing state secrets, has been introduced in political study sessions, according to a Chinese student, with an implication that all foreign teachers are possible spies.
Miss Wichser's ''state secrets'' were unpublished economic and agricultural statistics that she had collected for a doctoral thesis. 
Her friend, Yi Xigong, is now in jail here.
Since April 1, the children of high-level Government and party officials have been effectively barred from going abroad to study. 
The unpublished directive, which is understood to apply generally to the children of officials with the rank of deputy minister and above, has reportedly engendered resentment because Mr. Deng and other leaders sent their children abroad before it went into effect. 
Mr. Deng's son is studying at the University of Rochester.
Other Chinese graduates wishing to study abroad must now work for a year before applying, when they will presumably be more ideologically mature. 
In another indication of concern about Western influence, some returning students are being sent through ''reorientation'' courses lasting up to eight weeks, according to a Peking source.
Â 
No Effect on Delegations
The latest prohibitions on foreign travel do not seem to affect official delegations visiting the West. 
A United States Embassy spokesman said the number of Chinese going to the United States on official business rose 54 percent in the first six months of this year over the same period last year.
But delegations are evidently being told to stick together to avoid bourgeois contamination. 
The Workers Daily earlier this month severely criticized several members of a Chinese delegation who split off to enjoy the seamier sights of Hong Kong.
A renewed obsession about state secrets, which in China means whatever the Government chooses not to publish, was evident in an interview with Deng Yingchao, the widow of Prime Minister Zhou Enlai, which Peking newspapers published on July 1, the 61st anniversary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Miss Deng was quoted as saying that she and her husband never discussed classified information with each other and that Mr. Zhou never let relatives and friends into his private office. 
One Western diplomat inferred from this that some other officials probably do, to show off their status.
Â 
'The Sacred Duty'
''Keeping party and state secrets is the sacred duty of every Communist Party member, especially of middle-level and senior officials,'' Miss Deng was quoted as saying.
There has also been a campaign against so-called Western ''pornography,'' which includes rock music tapes as well as racier videotapes and books. 
According to news reports, some young people in Peking and Shanghai were punished for dancing at ''obscene'' private disco parties earlier this year. 
And Canton residents last month were ordered to pull down thousands of ''fishtail'' antennas, which let them watch Hong Kong television.
Such bans reflect a fear within the Chinese leadership that exposure to the West will undercut the appeal of the Communist Party, which already suffers from credibility problems with youth.
The Weekly Digest, a sister publication of The People's Daily, warned in an article last month that ''external reactionary forces'' were waging a campaign of ''peaceful evolution'' to blur the distinctions between capitalism and Marxism and that Chinese students abroad were a main target.
The article went on to label as ''sinister'' such Western ploys as academic and scientific exchanges, foreign radio broadcasts and publications aimed at ''shaking the faith of our younger generation in the party's leadership and the socialist system.''
It remains unclear how long the crackdown will prevail. 
''I don't think it will last beyond the party congress,'' a Western diplomat said. 
But another took the crackdown as proof that the headier days of post-Mao liberalization were over.
The crackdown seems bound to discourage news leaks at the congress, which should be preceded by a closed meeting of the Central Committee. 
Earlier this year, a Chinese editor, Li Guanyi, was sent to prison for five years for divulging details of last summer's session to a foreign journalist.

file: CHINA CRITICIZES JAPAN ON VISIT TO WAR SHRINE.txt
text:
ï»¿
China has issued unusually sharp criticism of Japan, saying through its official press agency that Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone's official visit last week to a shrine for Japanese war dead ''pandered'' to those who wanted to expunge Japan's war guilt.
The statement, published Thursday by the New China News Agency, came a week after Mr. Nakasone and most members of his Cabinet made the first official visit by Japanese Government leaders to the Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo. 
The visit coincided with the 40th anniversary of Japan's surrender in World War II, a war in which China has put its dead at more than 20 million.
The visit had been criticized in much milder terms by a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman on the day before it occurred. 
There was speculation here that the Peking authorities had held off for a week with the stronger criticism so as not to obtrude on the grief in Japan last week over the crash of a Japan Air Lines airliner. 
But the delay appeared to have done little to blunt Chinese feelings.
China's official press agency says Prime Min Yasuhiro Nakasone's official visit to shrine for Japanese war dead 'pandered' to those who want to expunge Japan's war guilt; says Japanese official statements on visit sought to 'obscure' war that was 'unleashed by the Japanese militarists' (M)
''The Chinese people and Government have cherished the hope that the Japanese Government will bow to the historical facts and take an unequivocal stand on that appalling war of aggression and on where the guilt and responsibility lie,'' the press agency said. 
''To their deepest disappointment and regret, the Japanese Government decided, for the first time since the end of the war, to pay an official visit to the shrine.''
Â 
'Mockery' of Asian Sentiments
The commentary said Japanese official statements on the visit ''impress one with the intention to obscure more or less the wicked nature of the war of aggression unleashed by the Japanese militarists - an intention that makes a mockery of the sentiments and aspirations of the Chinese and other Asian peoples.''
It added, ''In making the decision, the Japanese Government has pandered to and has actually emboldened those in Japan who have always wanted to deny the aggressive nature of the war and to reverse the verdict on Japanese militarism long condemned to the dustbin of history.''
Although commentaries by the New China News Agency lack the authority of an official Government statement, the wording left no doubt that the agency spoke for the leadership, whose principal members, including Deng Xiaoping, the paramount leader, fought as guerrillas against the Japanese occupation forces in China. 
The Chinese leaders are planning their commemoration of the war's end at a mass rally in Peking on Sept. 
3.
To some, the criticism of Japan Thursday was reminiscent of a dispute three years ago when China angrily objected to what it called distortions and euphemisms in new Japanese textbooks about the wartime occupation of China. 
Japan promised that changes would be made in the new books.
Before the visit last week to the shrine, official commentaries on the war anniversary here had angled toward China's concern for a friendly relationship with contemporary Japan.
Â 
Tojo and Nanking Massacre
That the visit had touched a raw nerve was still more evident in a commentary published Thursday in the official English-language newspaper, China Daily. 
A regular contributor to the paper, who uses the pseudonym Tong Gang, took a strongly emotional line, saying the visit outraged people of his parents' generation, who still ''curse the war, the Japanese invaders and their leaders, such as Hideki Tojo.''
In the Foreign Ministry statement last week, and again in the New China News Agency article Thursday, the Chinese said General Tojo was among those whom Mr. Nakasone was honoring by visiting the shrine. 
General Tojo, who was Prime Minister at the time of the Pearl Harbor attack, resigned in 1944, was later tried as a war criminal by the Allies and was executed in 1948. 
China Daily linked him to the ''Nanjing massacre'' of December 1937, in which China says the Japanese killed 300,000 people.

text:

Consumers in China, a land where refrigerator doors fall off, the frames of bicycles crack as they are wheeled from the store and the hands of doughnut-sized watches ignore conventional notions of time, are up in arms. 
Or so the country's newspapers say.
In a rare, concerted attack on a Government ministry, newspapers have denounced a decision to cancel the country's first exhibition of the shoddiest consumer goods.
''It is a farce and deception,'' wrote Wu Jincai, a reporter for the official New China News Agency.
The Economic Daily lashed out at the ministry's decision as ''a humiliating disgrace'' for China's consumers.
In August, confronted with a nationwide growl of unhappy consumers, the Ministry of Light Industry declared that it would display the country's worst products - batteries that leak, washing machines that masticate clothes and color televisions that aren't in color.
Â 
Whistle-Blower Hunted
But in a covert collaboration between manufacturers and the ministry, the exhibition was canceled and then an investigation was begun to find the ministry worker who exposed how the decision was made, according to a barrage of articles in the nation's papers that provided a glimpse into decision-making here.
China's ambitious effort to reorder its economic system along more Western lines has borne fruit in the form of a range of consumer goods inconceivable only a decade ago. 
But this new cornucopia has come packed with a great many products that break or do not work.
As industries churned out more radios, tape recorders and washing machines, concern for quality gave way to demands for volume, according to many of China's newspapers. 
As a result, the Ministry of Light Industry, which oversees the production of a vast array of home appliances, bicycles and personal items, decided to exhibit the worst of the consumer goods in an attempt to shame manufacturers into producing better products.
But a few days ago, the ministry announced that the exhibition of shoddy goods ''has triumphantly finished its task.''
The assertion was greeted with astonishment in the normally compliant press.
''The organizers of the exhibition have obviously succumbed to pressure against exposing the inferior quality of some products, which had intensified as the opening date drew near,'' wrote Mr. Wu of the New China News Agency. 
#4,400 Complaints Received The Guangming Daily said that after the ministry announced its intention to stage the exhibition, it received more than 4,400 letters from across China from people complaining about products and urging that they be included in the show.
In the months that followed, the ministry assembled filled a warehouse with poor quality products. 
But, according to The Guangming Daily, the contents of the warehouse were closely guarded and the consumers' letters themselves were deemed secret.
''But someone in the househould appliances bureau under the ministry alerted a television station, which filmed the products and showed them on TV,'' the English-language China Daily wrote.
''A department of the ministry even tried to ferret out the 'informer','' Mr. Wu reported.
Zeng Xialin, the Minister of Light Industry, ''admitted that some people at his ministry were resentful of the exhibition,'' Mr. Wu wrote. 
He quoted the minister as saying, ''To protect their favorite factories, they deleted letters of complaints about their products from the computer.''
Worse, Mr. Wu maintained, ''factories brought pressure to bear upon the ministry.''
''For example, some factory managers threatened to stop supplying Beijing with their goods,'' he said. 
''The abortion of this well-intended event was just what some people expected from the beginning.''
Â 
Looking for Silver Lining
A reporter from Liberation Daily tried to find the silver lining of what was being widely portrayed as a national embarrassment.
''More than 800 repairmen from over 70 factories came to Beijing to repair or replace their low-quality products,'' the reporter, Si Maxin, wrote. 
''We can say that from this the aborted exhibition still contains a glimmer of success.''
But the next day, Mr. Wu pursued his theme by bemoaning the plight of China's consumers.
''Why can't consumers stand up for their rights,'' he asked on the front page of The Economic Daily. 
''In theory, one billion consumers occupy a position of dominance, but every letter of complaint is invariably the voice of only one individual. 
These voices never seem to be able to come together to become loud enough to command attention.''
''Now,'' he concluded, ''everything depends on the consumer. 
China's consumers must be modern consumers. 
They must have a new image, they must have the freedom to be choosy and the right to choose.''

Chinese officials sign contract with Hofstra University that calls on Hofstra to form corporation to seek companies that want to market products or enter joint ventures in China; Hofstra officials say university will receive commission for each agreement it negotiates between China and a United States business (M)
''I admit that it sounds like an unusual role for a university,'' said James M. Shuart, president of the university, in Hempstead, L.I.

Aid to Other Nation Unusual
