file: CHINA ISSUES DRAFT OF HONG KONG LAW.txt
text:
ï»¿
China today issued a draft of a constitution for Hong Kong that would grant considerable autonomy in economic, trade, cultural and political affairs for 50 years after British rule ends in 1997.
''The region shall not practice the socialist system and policies, and will maintain the current capitalist system and life style for 50 years,'' the official New China News Agency said of the provisions of the draft law.
But critics of the draft said it would give China veto power over laws passed by the Hong Kong legislative body. 
They also said the draft could effectively outlaw some forms of political dissent.
The draft is the product of a three-year effort by a committee selected by China's legislators.
Despite China's assurances of autonomy, however, there is tremendous uncertainty among Hong Kong residents about China's intentions toward the regions. 
Already, thousands of middle- and upper-class Hong Kong residents have applied for immigration visas to Canada and Australia.
Â 
Growing Exodus of Residents
Many banks and businesses in Hong Kong are reporting difficulty in finding qualified employees to fill jobs because of the growing exodus of talented and educated young Hong Kong citizens.
The draft, officially called the Basic Law, was drawn up by a 58-member committee, including 23 representatives from Hong Kong. 
Even though all 23 Hong Kong members were selected by China, there is vociferous opposition to the current draft from some Hong Kong representatives.
Chief among the dissenters is Martin Lee, a member of Hong Kong's Legislative Council, the colony's lawmaking body.
''It's supposed to be a mini-constitution for the new administrative district of Hong Kong,'' Mr. Lee said. 
''I'm not happy with it at the moment. 
A great majority of the articles are all right, but about 10 percent are not all right.''
Â 
Wording of Draft Assailed
''But you're not marking an examination paper, so that 90 percent means high marks,'' he said. 
''If you're doing a constitution, if you get one thing wrong you can make the whole thing unworkable.''
Mr. Lee lashed out at provisions of the draft law that would give China the right to revise and interpret the basic law and to change or revoke laws passed by the Hong Kong legislative body. 
In addition, Mr. Lee said the wording of the current draft could effectively outlaw some forms of political dissent against Chinese policy.
''In the years to come it is possible that the central Government may push some unpopular laws into Hong Kong which should really have no place in Hong Kong,'' Mr. Lee said.
China's press agency made no reference to the views of dissenters from the draft. 
Rather, it emphasized the freedoms being granted Hong Kong in the post-colonial era. 
Chinese officials here in Beijing refused to provide a copy of the law to foreign journalists today.
Â 
Dealings With Other Nations
One provision of the draft that would set Hong Kong apart from the rest of China is a guarantee that Hong Kong will exist as an independent financial region.
Hong Kong is also to be allowed to set its own policies on international trade and commerce and aviation and to enter into agreements with other countries in matters of finance, shipping, communications, tourism and sports. 
The former colony will be allowed to display its own flag and seal for these purposes.
In domestic affairs, Hong Kong is to set its own educational, cultural and labor policies without interference from China.
But Mr. Lee pointed to what he said was the relatively weak set of powers to be accorded the post-colonial legislative body in Hong Kong. 
''We pass laws, but don't control polices,'' Mr. Lee said. 
''The result is that such a legislature will be unable to exercise sufficient checks and balances.''
Â 
A Distrust of China
Mr. Lee said the recent surge of emigrating Hong Kong residents reflected distrust of how China would treat the colony after it assumes sovereignty.
''I'm afraid this will add to the sense of unease,'' he said. 
''People go away because they don't see any possible future in Hong Kong.
''Under the formula advocated by the People's Republic itself, it is one country two systems. 
That means Hong Kong people ruling Hong Kong. 
Beijing should not send its people down to rule because they don't know anything about Hong Kong.''

file: CHINA JAILS A HONG KONG EDITOR AS A SPY FOR U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
China disclosed today that it had jailed a Hong Hong newspaper editor for 10 years on charges of spying for the United States.
The announcement, which came amid increasing strains in Chinese-American relations, marked the first time since diplomatic relations were established at the beginning of 1979 that China has implicitly accused the United States of spying.
The editor, Lo Chengxun, who was in charge of a pro-Communist daily in Hong Kong, The New Evening Post, was arrested after being summoned back to Peking a year ago. 
Mr. Lo, who was commonly known in Hong Kong as Lo Fu, had edited the newspaper since 1951. 
He is a Chinese citizen and reportedly a Communist Party member.
PEKING, May 15 - China disclosed today that it had jailed a Hong Hong newspaper editor for 10 years on charges of spying for the United States.Said to Refuse to Appeal
The official New China News Agency, in announcing his prison sentence today, said Mr. Lo ''was arrested on charges of spying for U.S. intelligence'' and had pleaded guilty and declined to appeal the court verdict.
''The judgment handed down by the court,'' the agency went on, ''says Mr. Lo became a spy several years ago for an American intelligence agency, for which he provided important secret information about China's political, diplomatic and military affairs and from which he received regular subsidies.''
The press agency did not specify what information the 62-year-old editor had purportedly passed on to the United States. 
In China, all information is regarded as secret until the party and the Government leadership authorizes its disclosure. 
Many secrets in China would be unclassified in Western countries.
Late last May Lisa Wichser, an American graduate student and teacher, was accused of stealing state secrets and was detained for nearly a week after unreleased agricultural information for her doctoral thesis was found in her room in Peking. 
Miss Wichser was deported, but the Chinese Government never actually accused her of acting on behalf of the United States.
Chinese citizens were often charged with spying for the United States during the rule of Mao Zedong. 
But those more recently arrested as spies are usually accused of working for the Nationalist Government in Taiwan, as happened during a roundup in the industrial city of Tianjin earlier this spring.
Last year Wang Renzhong, then chief of the Communist Party's propaganda department, warned Chinese in the ideological journal Red Flag that some foreigners in China were undoubtedly spies and might try to recruit them, but he named no nationalities.
Consequently, the announcement that Mr. Lo had been found guilty of spying for American intelligence was interpreted by diplomats in China as a measure of Peking's low opinion of its current relations with Washington. 
Those relations, already affected by United States arms sales to Taiwan, hit their lowest point last month after Washington granted political asylum to a Chinese tennis player, Hu Na.
Mr. Lo's detention became common knowledge in Hong Kong last summer. 
There was speculation he had become a victim of a power struggle within the Chinese Government, though no evidence has surfaced to support this.
Chinese have been increasingly warned against fraternizing with foreigners, both at home and abroad, and Mr. Lo's arrest may also have been a warning to Chinese not to have unauthorized contacts with Westerners.
Mr. Lo's newspaper was affiliated with Ta Kung Pao, a Hong Kong daily that reflects the Chinese party line. 
Its publisher, Fei Yiming, has been a delegate to the National People's Congress, China's nominal Parliament. 
Mr. Lo reportedly also held an editorial post on Ta Kung Pao.
Mr. Lo, however, was regarded as somewhat more liberal in his daily column than Mr. Fei. Mr. Lo wrote his column under the pen name of Yang Zhu. 
He was well known in Hong Kong and his commentaries, including those on Chinese-American relations, were read locally for nuances that might suggest a change in Peking's attitudes.
The press agency did not explain how Mr. Lo had supposedly been recruited by United States intelligence agents. 
He was known to have had contacts in Hong Kong with American officials, something that would not have been unusual in that cosmopolitan city.
Washington had invited Mr. Lo to travel to the United States under an international visitors program, but he never took up the invitation.
While his recall indicates the extent to which China retains a hold over the pro-Communist press in Hong Kong, it was not clear why Mr. Lo would have agreed to return to Peking if he were spying for the Untied States.
As a result, his subsequent detention was seen by some in Hong Kong as an example of ''killing the chicken to frighten the monkey,'' as a popular Chinese proverb puts it, or using his case as a warning about the poor state of Chinese-American relations.
The New China News Agency reported today that the Peking Intermediate People's Court had found Mr. Lo guilty of spying on April 29 under Article 97 of the Chinese Criminal Code. 
This suggested that Mr. Lo had been under house arrest and pretrial detention for nearly a year.
The press agency said the written verdict was delivered to him on May 4 and that Mr. Lo had declined to appeal to a higher court, which Chinese law allows in theory. 
His 10-year prison term is to be followed by deprivation of political rights for another three years.
Â 
----
Â 
State Dept. 
Following Case
Â 
Special to the New York Times
WASHINGTON, May 15 - State Department officials had no immediate comment on the report from Peking. 
They said that they had been following Mr. Lo's case, but that, as a matter of policy, they generally did not comment on allegations of spying.

file: CHINA LAGS ON BUYING U.S. GRAIN.txt
text:
ï»¿
China appears likely to default for a second year running on its commitment to buy at least six million tons of American grain under a 1980 agreement, according to Western diplomats here.
As it did last year, China is blaming United States textile policies that it contends are discriminatory, though the 1980 treaty contains no linkage between grain and other products.
This time, the Chinese Government is angry about new United States regulations that textile imports must come under the quota of the country where they originate and not an intermediate country where the imports are processed. 
It has demanded compensation for losses incurred by not being able to have Chinese-made apparel finished in Hong Kong.
The United States Government has agreed to consult with China on its complaint after the November elections, according to the Western diplomats, who declined to be further identified. 
The new rules, which were sought by United States manufacturers, have drawn protests from other exporters besides China, as well as American retailers.
(In Washington, an Administration trade official confirmed that discussions with the Chinese were planned.)
Â 
No Sanctions in Treaty
So far this year, China has bought only half as much United States grain as it promised to purchase and has shipped even less. 
The Chinese-American agreement, which was signed in October 1980, commits the United States to sell, and China to buy, six to eight million tons of wheat and corn annually through 1984. 
It does not, however, provide for sanctions in case of violations.
China bought only 3.8 million tons of grain last year, but promised to make up the shortfall this year. 
This adds up to an obligation to buy and ship more than eight million tons of grain in 1984.
According to United States Department of Agriculture statistics, China had bought 4,196,700 tons of wheat as of Sept. 
20 and shipped only 3.16 million tons. 
To meet its pledge, the Chinese Government would have to ship nearly five million tons more within the next three months.
It has shown no sign of doing so and economic analysts here believe such a task would now be impossible.
Â 
Different Motives Seen
Some diplomats in Peking are skeptical about China's declarations that its purchases of United States grain are being reduced to retaliate against the textile import policies.
They believe that China has cut down its purchases at least in part because recent bumper harvests, caused by rural reforms that reward peasant productivity, are meeting more of its domestic needs.
''It has nothing to do with textiles,'' one Western diplomat insisted. 
''The Chinese don't shoot themselves in the foot if they can help it.''
A front page article in the People's Daily newspaper today reported that the harvest of summer grain, mainly wheat, would rise by four million tons in 1984 because of good conditions.
This tallies with Western estimates that China's wheat production would increase from 81.4 million tons last year to about 85 million this year.
China has also diversified its imports by buying cheaper grain from Australia, Argentina and Canada. 
Western diplomats say that the Chinese have ignored a provision of the Chinese-American grain treaty obligating them to scale down purchases proportionately from other countries if they buy less American grain.
A Host of ComplaintsChina has regularly faulted United States trade restrictions for its failure to buy all the grain that it promised. 
Last year, it held back until the two had reached a new treaty on textile quotas more favorable to Peking.
Earlier this year, Chinese officials attributed the slow rate of grain purchases to the lack of a new maritime agreement giving Chinese ships greater access to American ports. 
In fact, vessels under third-country flags have carried much of the grain.
The Chinese also complained about reports that United States grain was tainted with harmful pesticides. 
American officials visited Peking to assure the Government that none of the grain being sent was infected.
Most recently, China protested about the country-of-origin regulations, which went into effect earlier this month. 
They would prevent Chinese factories from sending half-finished apparel to Hong Kong for completion so that it could enter the United States under Hong Kong's textile quotas.
Â 
No New Negotiations
The United States is not in a position to retaliate against the Chinese shortfall in purchases because the grain agreement contains no sanctions to punish violations by either side. 
Nor can Washington threaten to hold back future deliveries, because there is a glut of grain on the world market.
(Grain trade analysts in Washington said that the drop in China's purchases of American grain would probably be offset somewhat by an increase in grain sales to the Soviet Union, which has maintained an unusually strong buying pace in the last three months. 
But with large supplies of wheat already in storage in this country and another large corn crop expected, any decline in foreign purchases will be felt in this country's grain markets, they said.)
The Western diplomats said that no efforts had been made to negotiate another Chinese-American grain pact after the current one expires at the end of December.
China has canceled orders for 675,000 tons of United States grain in the last four months, according to the Agriculture Department figures. 
It has further canceled orders for 150,000 tons of American grain to be shipped in 1985, after the current four-year treaty expires.
Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang told American correspondents here before he visited the United States last January that China was willing to buy six million tons of grain this year if no other problems arose in the future. 
Chen Muhua, China's Minister for Foreign Trade and Economic Relations, reportedly gave similar assurances when she went to Washington in May.
As a result of China's failure to buy American grain, estimates of the trade turnover this year between the two nations may be revised downward from $5.5 billion to $5 billion. 
In 1983, such trade amounted to $4.4 billion.
U.S. Agrees to Talks
WASHINGTON, Sept. 
28 - The Reagan Administration has agreed to sit down with the Chinese and listen to their complaints about American restrictions on imports of textiles sometime after the elections, a trade official said today.

text:

The Foreign Minster, Wu Xueqian, also said he was planning to meet in New York with Foreign Minister Andrei A. Gromyko of the Soviet Union during the session of the United Nations General Assembly.

Chinese Foreign Min Wu Xueqian, commenting after week of talks with USSR Min Mikhail S Kapitsa, reports major disagreement persists concerning USSR forces along Chinese frontier; also notes issues of USSR intervention in Afghanistan and support for Vietnamese intervention in Cambodia; sees some improvement in US relations but warns US must cut Taiwan arms sales (S)
Mr. Wu spoke at a news conference for American and Canadian reporters the day after the departure of a Soviet Deputy Foreign Minister, Mikhail S. Kapitsa.
The talks Mr. Kapitsa had with Mr. Wu and with Deputy Foreign Minister Qian Qichen were seen by foreign diplomats as evidence of China's interest, despite its distrust of Soviet military strategy, in seeker better relations.
The Foreign Minister responded to one of several written questions at the news conference by saying that he saw ''signs of some improvement'' in relations with the United States. 
But he added that all the hopeful communiques would ''amount only to scraps of paper'' if the United States did not act on its stated intention of reducing arms sales to Taiwan.
The Chinese Foreign Minister said one sign of better relations with the United States was that Washington had been willing to improve the terms of trade between the two countries.
Mr. Wu sidestepped questions on what China expected to result from the visit here next week of Defense Secretary Caspar W. Weinberger. He said the question of arms purchases from the United States was for China's Defense Minister to comment on.
Foreign diplomats said the talks with Mr. Kapitsa, who is one of the Soviet Union's specialists on Chinese affairs, had focused on what China considered to be ''obstacles'' to a normalization of relations.
People's Daily, the principal Chinese newspaper, said in an editorial that Soviet SS-20 nuclear missiles stationed along China's northern border were among the unacceptable threats that the Soviet Union still posed to China's security.
The paper urged the Soviet Union to ''considerably reduce its missiles deployed in Asia.''

Mr. Wu identified the three obstacles as the Soviet military presence along China's northern frontier, the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan and Soviet support for Vietnam's intervention in Cambodia.
Mr. Wu also mentioned the SS-20 missiles. 
Without linking their reduction specifically to an improvement in relations, he said the numbers of these missiles should be ''drastically'' reduced or ''destroyed on site.''
A senior Chinese journalist, Wang Fei, said, ''The Soviet Union is still considered the first threat to the security of China.''
Mr. Wang said there seemed to be some difference of opinion within the Soviet leadership about the importance of maintaining large forces along China's northern border while at the same time supporting Vietnam in its intervention in Cambodia.
In China's view, Mr. Wang said, the Soviet military supports such deployment, while Yuri V. Andropov, the Soviet leader, has yet to make up his mind.

file: China Makes Call to U.S.txt
text:

The Communist Party Chairman, Hu Yaobang, has emphasized China's concern that the United States abide strictly by the provisions of a communique issued last month in which the Reagan Administration pledged to gradually reduce American arms sales to Taiwan.
China has interpreted the document as a pledge by Washington to phase out military sales to Taiwan. 
Mr. Hu specifically mentioned the communique, made public Aug. 
17, in the course of a lengthy report to the opening session of the 12th Chinese party congress on Wednesday.

PEKING, Sept. 
4 - The Communist Party Chairman, Hu Yaobang, has emphasized China's concern that the United States abide strictly by the provisions of a communique issued last month in which the Reagan Administration pledged to gradually reduce American arms sales to Taiwan.Expand Third World Cooperation
Mr. Hu also promised in his report that China would expand its cooperation with other third-world countries and insisted that China would never align itself to any large power or group of powers, a reference to the Soviet Union and the United States and their military allies.
The party Chairman also said that a normalization of relations with the Soviet Union would be possible if Moscow took ''practical steps'' to lift its threat to China's security, but he reiterated that Peking attached importance to Moscow's deeds and not its words.

Step-by-Step Solution

file: CHINA MOVES TO RESURRECT A CREDIBLE LEGAL SYSTEM.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a courtroom in northeastern Shanghai, the defendant stood accused of embezzling three tons of steel plate from his factory by diverting it to a commune's agricultural machinery plant under a false bill of lading.
The defendant, Luo Yuansheng, had confessed during the meticulous police investigation preceding the trial. 
Even before his arrest, he had turned in a television set and $375 given to him by his accomplice at the commune in his home province of Jiangsu.
But Judge Xing Wenhua, flanked on the bench by two people's assessors, or jurors, sternly led him through a recitation of his crime.
Â 
Suspended One-Year Sentence
Mr. Luo, head lowered, told how he had sent the steel to the commune because his daughter worked there and he hoped "the leaders would look after my daughter better."
China moves to resurrect a credible legal system
Judge Xing pronounced the sentence: one year's imprisonment, suspended on condition of good behavior, while Mr. Luo worked at his factory. 
Mr. Luo thanked the court for showing him the error of his ways and was led away.
The trial would have seemed odd in an American courtroom, witht the judge more outspoken than the prosecutor and the defense counsel stressing the defendant's guilt. 
Yet it is part of a major effort since 1979 to resurrect the rule of law in China after its virtual extinction during the Cultural Revolution, when Maoist radicals imposed their own arbitrary notions of right and wrong.
Â 
A Stress on Rights and Duties
The Peking leadership conceded the need for a credible legal system when it promulgated a new state constitution with greater stress on the basic rights and duties of Chinese citizens. 
(Parliament ratified the constitution Saturday. 
Page 22.)
"No citizen is allowed to enjoy privileges that transcend the Constitution and the law," Peng Zhen, a senior official who helped draft the document, told the congress.
The revival of legal justice represents more than an attempt to prevent a recurrence of the anarchy now blamed on Chairman Mao Zedong's widow, Jiang Qing, and the other radicals lumped together as the Gang of Four.
Â 
'A Lot Has Happened'
As China opens to foreign trade and investment, it must provide civil and commercial codes for Western oil companies and other business concerns. 
News laws have already been promulgated on joint ventures and taxation, among other legislation.
"You can alway sget the perspective that not much progress is being made, but in a larger perspective, a lot has happened," said Jerome Alan Cohen, an American lawyer who is a leading authority on Chinese law.
The legal system introduced after the Communist takeover in 1949 borrowed heavily from the Soviet model. 
Work on an indegenous criminal and civil code continued until 1957, when Chairman Mao's "antirightist" campaign circumvented the system to persecute critics and law became increasingly irrelevant. 
The Ministry of Justice closed down in 1959, not to reopen for two decades. 
The Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976 trampled what law still survived.
Â 
'We Were Forced Out'
"The whole legal system was completely damaged," Dai Hanming, a Shanghai attorney, recalled in an interview. 
"There was no question of lawyers' organizations during the Cultural Revolution. 
Even a defendant had no right to get someone to defend him."
Mr. Dai's colleague, Fu Xuanjie, said that "under the Gang of Four, people like us had nothing to do. 
We were forced out into other jobs, to enterprises, factories, the countryside and other parts of the country."
Mr. Dai and Mr. Fu now practice in a Government-run legal advisory office. 
They are among 200 full-time lawyers working with 40 part-time lawyers in Shanghai, a metropolis of 11.8 million people.
Last January it was disclosed that China had 5,500 full-time lawyers and 1,300 part-time ones in a nation of 1 billion people. 
By comparison, the United States, with 231 million people, has 565,000 lawyers, with 42,000 in New York City alone.
Â 
A Target of 2 Million
"We are still understaffed," Mr. Dai said. 
"The demand from the masses is more than we can meet."
The Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping once set a target of 2 million legal workers by the end of the century. 
The Deputy Minister of Justice, Wang Yeuchen, has since announced a more modest goal of one lawyer for every 10,000 urban inhabitants or every 50,000 rural dwellers.
Last month the Ministry of Justice reported that 10,000 students were enrolled in regular law courses at 22 universities and institutes around China and the 4,000 legal workers were studying law at institutes in their spare time. 
The People's Daily newspaper reported last autumn that demobilized army offcers were getting a six-month course in law before being assigned legal duties, which might include judgeships.
Lawyers in China earn $30 to $40 a month, Mr. Dai said, though the most experienced might earn up to $90 a month. 
Legal fees average from 25 cents to $2 per consultation. 
Lawyers in Shanghai spend increasing time on more profitable cases, advising local industries and banks on foreign trade negotiations and contracts.
Â 
Rights of the State
People's Daily reported early this year that many people still confuse Chinese lawyers with those of the capitalist West. 
In China, it said, lawyers are "an important force for upholding the legal system of the state."
Mr. Dai said adversary tactics were alien to China, explaining, "The lawyer's regulations stipulate that our task is first to protect the rights of the state, the collective and the individual and to safeguard the implementation of laws."
While a defendant is entitled to a defense counsel, there is no legal presumption of innocene until proved guilty. 
Trials almost never take place until the defendant has confessed under pretrial interrogation.
Huang Huoqing, China's chief procurator, a position equivalent to that of the United States Attorney General, told the National People's Congress last December that 99.97 percent of the criminals prosecuted during the first nine months of 1981 were found guilty.
A defense lawyer's task is not to suggest that his client is innocent but to protect his legal rights and look for extenuating circumstances that might merit a lighter sentence. 
To visit his client, he needs the Government's permission.
Â 
'There Was No Need to Talk'
Mr. Ni, the lawyer for Mr. Luo, said that he had talked to his client three times before the trial. 
Ma Rongjie, the lawyer assigned to defend the Gang of Four at their trial two years ago, said later that he never met them because "there was no need to talk to them."
Defendants may appeal their conviction to a higher court, but only once. 
"If we followed the system of the court of thrid instance as the final instance and set no deadline, as is done in Japan and many European and American countries, many cases may drag on for years," explained Chen Yison, a prominent jurist.
In addition, a Chinese lawyer is not permitted to seek extensions for his client.
While Mr. Dai estimated that a major trial might last up to two and a half months, the wheels of justice can move at dizzying speeds. 
Five young men who tried to hijack an airliner to Taiwan last July were caught in Shanghai, interrogated, tried, convicted and shot in less than four weeks.
Â 
Sentencing to Cheers of a Crowd
Trials are sometimes made public to show that justice is being served and to warn against lawless behavior.

''If they do not do it, they will fail.''
Compared with exiles who crusade against the Soviet Union's treatment of dissidents and attempts to crush intellectual debate, Dr. Wang and the others working in the Flushing office have labored in relative anonymity.

Denounced by Deng

Mrs. Goldman said that by publishing translations of the speeches of Fang Lizhi, a Chinese astrophysicist recently expelled from the Communist Party for advocating sweeping political changes, China Spring had helped focus attention on issues that were previously unknown or ignored.

About 25,000 copies of the Chinese version of China Spring are circulated outside China, according to Dr. Wang, with 1,000 more smuggled into the People's Republic. 
He counts among his writers and supporters a network of scholars, students and children of officials who supply information ''faster than you can get it from Beijing.''
He reported receiving a tape recording of a speech by Mr. Fang a week after students in Shanghai heard it.

Called Sensational by Some
Dr. Wang's harsh criticism of China's leaders and his publication of articles with titles like ''Massacre of the Innocents,'' referring to birth control in China, have earned the magazine some detractors outside Beijing.
Some Chinese opposed to the Communist Party have split with Dr. Wang, arguing it is better to maintain some ties to Beijing. 
And some experts have criticized the magazine's political analysis as sensational compared with older Hong Kong-based journals.

Although the directive credited Communist rule since 1949 with ''unprecedented achievements,'' it also veered further away from the ideological and egalitarian system that was developed under Mao toward an approach that has been influenced by Western precepts.
Deng Xiaoping, the country's leader, has repeatedly said that improvements in education, particularly in technical and scientific education, are indispensable if China is to achieve his goal of catching up with the economic standards of the West by the middle of the 21st century.
The party directive said the educational changes were intended to train millions of ''independent thinkers and bold trailblazers'' to push the modernization program.

The pragmatic tone of the directive was evident in the approach to secondary education. 
Although 95 percent of the children now attend six-year primary schools, only two-thirds go on to the additional three years of secondary education. 
The total nine years of schooling is now to be made universal in large cities and in coastal areas by 1990, and elsewhere in China proper by 1995. 
Officials at a news conference said remote areas in the west would have to work toward that goal in accordance with ''their own conditions.''
These phases conform to the policy of giving priority to economic growth in coastal areas and other parts of China proper rather than to the undeveloped western regions. 
They also depart from the Maoist principle of giving at least equal treatment to rural areas. 
The pattern of allowing some elements of society to advance more rapidly than others has been a common thread in Mr. Deng's stewardship since 1978.
Another Deng theme, the need to ease the bureaucracy's grip on Chinese life, found its echo in the educational package. 
The document said that ''over-strict control has stunted the vigor'' of education, particularly at the college level.

Another break with Maoist policies was that all but a few exempt categories of students will have to pay for tuition.

Exceptions will be made for those in teacher training, those volunteering for hardship posts in remote areas after graduation and those from exceptionally poor families.
At the secondary level, the biggest change is to come in the shift toward more vocational and technical training.

A senior Chinese economic official said here today that Peking intended to sign contracts this year to import $1 billion worth of advanced Western technology and equipment.
The official, Yuan Baohua, deputy chairman of the State Economic Commission and president of the China Enterprise Management Association, said that 1,000 contracts were involved.

''The imports of foreign capital and foreign technology are now major policies for China's economic construction,'' Mr. Yuan said, speaking through an interpreter.

Part of Modernization Effort
He said the plan was part of China's effort to modernize its economy.
Mr. Yuan said that to finance these imports of Western technology and machinery, China would increase its foreign borrowing this year, seeking loans both from the World Bank and from private Western bankers. 
But he declined to disclose the amount of money Peking plans to raise.
The Chinese official also said his Government intended to introduce new administrative procedures, including tax cuts and reduction of bureaucratic delays, to encourage foreign companies to do business with China and to invest there, either in partnership with Chinese companies or on their own.

And he predicted that in 1985 China would sign even more for up-to-date technology and equipment. 
Peking's aim, he said, is to sign a total of 3,000 with foreign companies from 1983 through 1985.
Pan Chenglie, deputy general sec retary of the Chinese Enterprise Management Association, said here that the priority areas in which China was seeking the help of Western businessmen to develop its economy included farming, energy and transportation, communications, textiles, pharmaceuticals and the manufacture of construction machinery.
Diplomats at the meeting here said China's growing demands for modern Western technology raised strategic problems for the Western countries.
At talks now going on in Paris, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization countries are trying to update the list of militarily useful technology whose export to the Soviet Union, its East European allies or China is banned. 
For several years now, however, the NATO allies have treated China more leniently than the Soviet Union and the East European bloc, believing that by helping build up the Chinese economy they are also strengthening a major rival of the Soviet Union.
European diplomats say the United States has now proposed still more lenient treatment for China, apparently in the belief that American companies stand to profit from China's plans to increase substantially its imports of advanced technology.
France and West Germany, in particular, are reluctant to approve new rules favoring China, especially at a time when the Reagan Administration is seeking much tighter curbs on sales of Western technology to the Eastern bloc countries, which the French and West Germans do not consider fully justified.
The Reagan Administration has sought to promote closer commercial ties with China by easing its ban on high technology exports and negotiating agreements on industrial cooperation, investment rights and nuclear power generation.
Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang and President Reagan signed an industrial cooperation agreement during the Chinese leader's visit to Washington three weeks ago. 
American and Chinese officials expressed the hope that both the nuclear and investment accords could be signed in April when President Reagan goes to Peking. 
Progress was made on both agreements during Mr. Zhao's visit to Washington, according to American officials.
The Commerce Department last year shifted China into the ''friendly but nonaligned'' category in export controls, giving China access to more American high technology. 
Under the relaxed restraints General Electric recently won a contract to provide diesel locomotives and Honeywell has sold the Chinese personal computers.
Mr. Yuan, discussing the administrative changes planned by his Government, said that in the future foreign companies would be encouraged to set up fully owned plants in China if they wished instead of being asked to go into partnership with Chinese companies. 
A new packaging plant opened two months ago in Shanghai by the Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Company represents a precedent for 100 percent foreign- owned companies, Mr. Yuan said.
Foreign companies investing in China will also be allowed to sell more to local Chinese consumers in the future, instead of often being forced to buy much of their plants' output for sale abroad.

In addition, he said the Chinese Government had decided ''to ease tax policy.''

file: CHINA POLICY SHIFT ON STUDY OVERSEAS.txt
text:
ï»¿
Chinese students in the United States have obtained a copy of a Chinese Government document confirming that Beijing has set new limits on the number of years students will be allowed to attend college abroad and has also established central control over who will be allowed to apply for foreign study.
Nine days ago, when asked to respond to reports that China plans a drastic reduction in the number of its students abroad - especially in the United States - a spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington said Beijing's policy of allowing thousands of students to study overseas ''is not changed.''
Officials said yesterday that no one would be available for further comment until Monday.
American experts on China say they have received independent indications of the change in policy. 
They say the change comes at a time of growing concern in Beijing that too many young scholars are staying overseas or are becoming too Westernized. 
The new policy is a sharp departure from the program of letting students go abroad, begun in 1979 as part of modernization efforts by Deng Xiaoping, China's paramount leader.
Obtained From Chinese School
A leader of an ad hoc Chinese student group in the United States, who did not want to be identified, said the document ''was mailed to us by an American who came from China and is a friend of ours.''
The student said: ''It is obtained from a president's office of a major Chinese university. 
Every university president got one, because they need the cooperation of the university to withhold students' transcripts and letters of recommendation. 
We received it Friday.''
The students had previously said they knew of a separate secret directive that called for shifting the flow of Chinese students abroad away from the United States. 
That policy, they said, would limit the proportion of students in the United States to 20 percent of the total sent overseas, compared with the current 68 percent. 
Such a shift would mean a maximum of 600 new Chinese students arriving in this country each year, instead of the approximately 8,000 who have come in each of the past two years.
Asked about the new policy, Merle Goldman, a professor of Chinese history at Boston University, said, ''The Chinese Government is exercised by the brain drain.''
Of the 40,000 students now abroad, she said, between 27,000 and 28,000 are in the United States.
''They are telling more students to come home earlier,'' she said. 
''I know of one student in the humanities who has been here only a short time, but has to return in order to allow someone to come in his place to study the sciences, because only 20 percent of the students going abroad from his university can go to the United States.''
Â 
How Long Students Can Stay
The document obtained Friday by the students is titled ''Document from the State Education Commission (87) Standardized Serial No. 679 - Directive on Issuing Several Specific Regulations on Controlling and Managing Personnel Studying Abroad.''
It says a student who wants to go to the United States to earn a master's degree is limited to 1 and 2 years; a student with a bachelor's degree seeking a doctorate is limited to 5 years, and a student with a master's degree seeking a doctorate is limited to 4 years. 
Similar limits are set for study in other countries, with no student allowed to stay abroad for more than 5 years.
For Chinese, many of whom have only a rudimentary command of English when they arrive, finishing a Ph.D. program in four or five years would be very difficult, the students said.

file: CHINA PREMIER BIDS U.S. KEEP PLEDGE ON TAIWAN.txt
text:

Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang said today that when he visits the White House next week he will not press President Reagan to halt ''immediately or completely'' the sale of United States military hardware to Taiwan.
But he said he expected the United States to abide by the pledge it gave in a joint communique in 1982 to start phasing out such arms deliveries.
Mr. Zhao made the comments in an interview with American and Canadian correspondents based in Peking, whom he agreed to receive before his trip to North America. 
The meeting underscored the importance that Peking appears to attach to the visit, the first official trip by a Chinese Prime Minister to North America.

Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang says when he visits White House next week he will not press Pres Reagan for immediate halt to sale of US military hardware to Taiwan, but he does expect US to abide by pledge it gave in joint communique in 1982 to start phasing out such arms deliveries; says he seeks to develop Chinese-US relations; Zhao's trip will be first official trip by Chinese Prime Minister to North America; photo (M)
The trip by Mr. Zhao, as head of government, opens an exchange of visits with President Reagan, who is scheduled to come here in April.
Â 
Tone Is Conciliatory
Mr. Zhao broke little new ground in a question-and-answer session that lasted an hour and a quarter at the Great Hall of the People. 
But his remarks were clearly conciliatory as he sketched out prospects for cooperation and played down difficulties that have marked the relationship over the last few years.
Although ''great progress'' has been made, Mr. Zhao said, ''the level of Chinese-American relations is far from what should be desired.''
''China attaches importance to the development of Chinese-U.S. relations,'' he declared. 
''We hope that through joint efforts of our two sides we will be able to remove obstacles, so that relations between our two countries can develop on a stable and durable basis.''
The 64-year-old Prime Minister talked animatedly in the pronounced drawl of his native Henan Province, stopping sometimes to sip from a glass of orangeade. 
In contrast to the officials around him, including Foreign Minister Wu Xueqian, Mr. Zhao wore a well-tailored brown Western business suit with a pale yellow shirt and coordinated polka-dot tie.
Â 
Visit Begins in Hawaii
The Prime Minister said he would fly across the United States three times during his trip, which will take him first to Hawaii next weekend. 
He will visit Washington, New York and San Francisco between Jan. 
10 and 16, before going on to Ottawa for the Canadian part of his trip from Jan. 
17 to 23.
Mr. Zhao made clear that the political climate would continue to affect China's economic dealings with the United States.
''The United States is the biggest developed country in the world,'' he told the reporters. 
''It has capital and technology. 
While China is the biggest developing country in the world. 
It has untapped resources and markets. 
So there is much that our two sides can do in developing economic cooperation and trade between our two countries.''
''Of course,'' he continued, ''economic matters are different from political matters, but in the final analysis they are not absolutely separate. 
If the potential in economic cooperation and trade and technological cooperation are to be fully kept, there must be a good political relationship.''
Â 
Taiwan the Main Problem
Turning to the major difficulty, Mr. Zhao reiterated China's position that United States backing for the Nationalist regime on Taiwan constitutes interference in China's internal affairs. 
The Peking Government treats Taiwan as a breakaway province that must be reu nited with the mainland. 
Because the Chinese have struggled for centuries to reunify their country, Mr. Zhao said, ''there is no room for China to make any concessions on the question of Taiwan.''
Mr. Zhao conceded that President Reagan's feeling of friendship toward Taiwan was understandable. 
''China is not against the United States' maintaining unofficial economic, trade and cultural relations with the people in Taiwan,'' he said. 
''Actually, there are relevant provisions for it in the communique establishing diplomatic relations between China and the United States.''
But he insisted that Washington must not regard Taiwan as a separate political entity.
Three joint communiques now govern relations between the two countries, the Prime Minister observed, and China makes no demands beyond them. 
Mr. Zhao alluded to the 1972 Shanghai communique that opened the way to normalization, the document that established formal diplomatic relations on Jan. 
1, 1979 and the communique of Aug. 
17, 1982 that tried to bridge the differences over the Taiwan issue.
Â 
'A Legacy From History'
All these documents accepted the premise that there was only one China, with Peking as its capital, and that Taiwan was an inalienable part.
''The question of U.S. relations with Taiwan is a legacy from history,'' Mr. Zhao said. 
''That was why we did not put it forward as a precondition for the establishment of diplomatic relations between our two countries. 
We left it aside at the time of the establishment of diplomatic relations and were prepared to try to solve this afterward. 
And we waited four years before the Aug. 
17 communique was reached.''
Mr. Zhao observed twice that the 1982 communique stated that American military sales to Taiwan would not exceed in quantity or quality the levels of deliveries in recent years and that the United States intended gradually to reduce the arms sales, leading over a period of time to a final resolution of the problem.
Â 
No 'Drastic Approach' Taken
After more than a year, Mr. Zhao said, the arms sales have not declined in quantity and have improved in quality. 
''The Chinese people are most unhappy about it, but we have not adopted any drastic approach because of this,'' he said.
Mr. Zhao added: ''In my visit to the United States, I'm not going to ask President Reagan or the United States Government to stop the United States arms sales to Taiwan immediately or completely. 
This is how the Chinese side is going to strictly implement the principles embodied in the joint communique.''
In response to another question, Mr. Zhao implicitly denied that China regarded the United States and the Soviet Union as superpowers equally bent on expansionism, as the Chinese press routinely implies.
Â 
Soviet Troop Buildup Noted
''Any big power, if it pursues a hegemonistic policy, is hegemonistic and China cannot but oppose it,'' he said.
Referring to the Soviet buildup of troops along China's northern borders, Mr. Zhao declared: ''I believe that we know better than the Americans where our threat comes from. 
In this regard, we do not equate the United States and Soviet Union either.''
A new Chinese-American cultural agreement is due to be signed. 
Mr. Zhao said that ''many very important'' documents were being discussed but he declined to say if they would be ready in time for his visit. 
''I'm not a fortune teller so I can't tell you,'' he said.

file: CHINA PRESENTS A PLAY ABOUT ITS VIETNAM WAR.txt
text:
ï»¿
A mother asks an old family friend to help get her soldier son transferred from the battlefront. 
''I only have one son,'' she pleads over the telephone. 
''We have done enough for the revolution.''
But she is unable to stop him from being sent off to war, where over half of his company gets wiped out. 
China's enemy this time is Vietnam, and the place is their short but bloody border war in early 1979.
China presents a play about its Vietnam war
A popular new play, ''Wreaths at the Foot of the Mountain,'' has become the ideological highlight of Peking's current theater season. 
It was so well received when first performed in the Manchurian province of Liaoning that the Liaoning People's Art Theater brought it to China's capital in March.
Â 
Party Supports the Play
The Communist Party has given the play its blessing by sending some of its leading comrades to see it.A second drama troupe in Peking is simultaneously performing the play, which is also being shown on television. 
A feature film version is being shot less than a mile from China's tense frontier with Vietnam.
The play has been adopted from a short novel by Li Cunbao, 37 years old, a writer serving in the army. 
The novel was acclaimed when it appeared earlier this year in the literary magazine New China Digest. 
Mr. Li said the novel was based on his interviews with soldiers when he spent four months on the Yunnan front at the time of the border war.
The popularity of the play coincides with the latest round of border clashes, leaving little doubt that Vietnam has been made an authorized artistic target. 
An audience one recent night responded enthusiastically to allusions about Hanoi's ingratitude for help that Peking rendered during Vietnam's war with the United States.
Â 
The Broader Message
Yet the broader message of ''Wreaths at the Foot of the Mountain'' is that China still needs martyrs. 
In an essay in Xinwen Zhaibao, Li Cunbao explained that he was upset to see the army ''disrespected and insulted in public places'' and that he wanted to extol its continuing sacrifices.
The hero of the play, Zhao Mengshen, is a self-indulgent young man assigned to an infantry unit as a political instructor. 
He chafes at the Spartan barracks life, wants to get transferred to a comfortable urban billet and displays character flaws such as dancing to disco music.
His sympathetic mother is a prominent health official whose revolutionary background has given her lots of good connections. 
She agrees to help get him out of the infantry.
But the crusty old division commander rebuffs her. 
The political instructor, Zhao, apologizes to his men for trying to shirk his duty and accompanies them into Vietnam.
The company storms the Vietnamese fortifications, and the selfless company commander is killed by shrapnel when he tosses back a hand grenade hurled by a Vietnamese in hiding. 
Other casualties in the battle include a cheerful new recruit known to his comrades only by the nickname ''Peking.''
Chastened by his baptism of fire, Zhao, the political instructor, resists his mother's entreaties to quit the army. 
When the platoon leader, Jin, is denied a posthumous medal because he violated army discipline by going off to steal sugar cane for his beleaguered troops, Zhao hands the grieving widow his own medal.
The audience seemed moved by the sharp exchanges between Zhao's mother and the blunt old general. 
''It's only natural for me to show concern for my son,'' she argues. 
''My son was on the battlefield. 
Where was your son during the war?''
''Let's go down to the cemetery,'' the general suggests sadly, and there he shows her the unmarked grave of his son, who concealed his family connections by using the nickname of ''Peking.''
The play ends tidily in the tradition of socialist realism. 
The political instructor, Zhao, discovers that his company commander's mother was the wet nurse who raised him from infancy. 
His own mother corrects her selfish maternal attitude.

file: China Rejects Gorbachev Summit Offer.txt
text:
ï»¿
China today rejected a proposal by Mikhail S. Gorbachev, the Soviet leader, to hold a summit meeting with Chinese leaders.
The dismissal of the Soviet leader's overture came in a statement, issued by the Foreign Ministry this morning, that said: ''Chairman Deng Xiaoping has made quite clear the condition for a high-level meeting between China and the Soviet Union. 
At present it is the strong aspiration of the internatonal community that Vietnam should withdraw its troops from Cambodia promptly.''
Mr. Deng is China's senior leader, although he holds only one formal post, that of chairman of the Central Military Commission.
The rejection had been widely anticipated among Western diplomats here.
''Up to now, things will not change unless Vietnam pulls out of Cambodia,'' a Western diplomat said Monday. 
''The Chinese are not prepared to talk to the Soviets at the senior Government or party level until there is progress on this issue.''
Mr. Gorbachev's offer was made in an interview with the Chinese weekly magazine Liaowang that was made available in Moscow Sunday by the official Soviet press agency Tass.
The offer was part of a broad interview with Mr. Gorbachev, the first by a Soviet leader with a Chinese periodical in nearly three decades, that ranged over topics including Soviet-American relations and efforts to restructure the Soviet economy.
Â 
No Menion of Summit Proposal
Although China's newspapers and official press agency reported Mr. Gorbachev's comments on an array of subjects, these publications omitted any mention of his proposal for a summit meeting.
It was not the first time Mr. Gorbachev has suggested conferring with China's leaders. 
In December, he raised the possibility of meeting with Mr. Deng.
That offer was rejected, both by Mr. Deng and by a Foreign Ministry spokesman. 
China has maintained that three conditions must be met before any discussions at the leadership level can occur: the Soviet Union must withdraw from Afghanistan, it must reduce dramatically its armed forces along the Soviet-Chinese border, and Vietnam, which is supported by Moscow, must pull its troops out of Cambodia.
At the time, Mr. Deng told a Japanese visitor, ''Mr. 
Gorbachev has opposed any preconditions although he has said that he is willing to have a meeting with me and even said he would like to come to China. 
My proposal does contain a precondition, that is, the Soviet Union must urge Vietnam to pull out its troops from Cambodia.''
Â 
Major Change Thought Unlikely
Several Western diplomats said Monday that it was unlikely that there would be any substantial change in relations between the two countries.
''I don't expect any dramatic breakthrough in Sino-Soviet relations,'' a Western diplomat said.
As 1987 drew to a close, there was a flurry of discussions between Soviet and Chinese officials as well as several agreements signed between the two countries, including an annual trade protocol, a cultural exchange agreement and an accord calling for the exchange of athletes.
Still, Western diplomats and other analysts here attribute these agreements to a continuing relaxation in relations between Moscow and Beijing. 
They point, for example, to the visit of a Soviet Deputy Foreign Minister, Igor A. Rogachev, to Beijing in late December to brief Chinese officials on the Reagan-Gorbachev summit meeting. 
It was the first time a senior Soviet official has given such a briefing to the Chinese. 
The United States has regularly briefed the Chinese on Soviet-American exchanges.
Nonetheless, publicly the Chinese maintain that relations with Moscow are not likely to warm rapidly. 
Just last week a Foreign Ministry spokesman, Ma Yuzhen, reiterated his Government's expectations.
''Over the past year,'' he said, ''exchanges between China and the Soviet Union have increased to some extent in specific fields. 
As the three major obstacles have not been removed, no progress has been made in Chinese-Soviet political relations. 
China is willing to improve its relations with the Soviet Union and hopes that the Soviet Union will take practical action as soon as possible to remove such obstacles, particularly to urge Vietnam to withdraw its troops from Cambodia.''
Â 
A Growing Flexibility
Despite such seemingly obdurate remarks, some diplomats suggest that there is, at least among a segment of China's foreign policy establishment, a more flexible attitude toward Moscow.
''There hasn't been a dramatic shift in Chinese policy,'' a diplomat said, ''but there has been a shift in attitude by analysts on the Chinese side who see the Soviet overtures not just as a tactical exercise but as a strategic shift in policy, a pulling back somewhat from outside obligations.''
Â 
Comment by Shultz
OTTAWA, Jan. 
11 - Secretary of State George P. Shultz said today that Mr. Gorbachev's offer for a summit meeting with Chinese leaders would not affect American relations with either Moscow or Beijing.
Questioned by a reporter during his visit to Canada, Mr. Shultz said: ''It's not as though this is a new thing. 
And the Chinese have responded before, negatively. 
But I'm not predicting anything.''

file: CHINA RELEASES A CATHOLIC BISHOP WHO WAS JAILED NEARLY 30 YEARS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The 83-year-old Chinese prelate recognized by the Vatican as Bishop of Shanghai, the Rev. Ignatius Kung, was released from prison on parole today after spending nearly 30 years in jail, the New China News Agency announced.
Bishop Kung, whose Chinese name is Gong Pinmei, is the best-known of the hundreds of Chinese clerics who were persecuted by the Communists in the 1950's for their refusal to bow to a movement that severed ties between the Roman Catholic Church in China and the Vatican.
The movement, in effect, placed the church under Communist control. 
Despite the recent liberalizing of many aspects of Chinese life, that control is still in effect.
Rev Ignatius Kung, 83-year-old Chinese prelate recognized by Vatican as Bishop of Shanghai, is released from prison on parole after spending nearly 30 years in jail; Bishop Kung is best-known of hundreds of Chinese clerics who were persecuted by Communists in 1950's for their refusal to bow to movement that severed ties between Roman Catholic Church in China and Vatican (M)Life Term for Treason
The press agency said the Shanghai Higher People's Court made the decision to release the Bishop at a session today. 
It said that in setting aside the life term imposed on him in 1960 for treason, the court found that he had ''admitted his crime and showed repentance during the time he was serving his sentence.''
The agency added that the bishop ''said at the court that he would abide by the law and pledged allegiance to the country.''
The wording seemed to have been carefully chosen to imply that to gain his freedom Bishop Kung had foresworn the authority of the Pope and recognized the legitimacy of the ''self-governing'' Chinese Church, something he had repeatedly refused to do. 
But the ambiguous wording and the absence from the agency's account of any direct statement to that effect by the Bishop suggested that the authorities, not the Bishop, might have relented.
Â 
Diplomats Assess Release
The Bishop's continuing imprisonment has been a standing reminder of the realities of religion in China at a time when the Government here has fostered the notion that all faiths have been released from Communist Party control. 
Western diplomats said the leaders in Peking might have decided that keeping the Bishop in jail was too damaging to their credibility.
Although the official rejection of the Pope's authority over Catholics in China has not changed, recent years have seen a new recognition by senior Chinese officials of the diplomatic power of the Vatican and of the affront that Chinese attitudes have given to Catholics in other countries. 
There have been a number of indirect moves toward improving matters, including the invitation earlier this year to Mother Teresa, the nun who won the Nobel Peace Prize for her work in the Calcutta slums.
Mother Teresa met with high-ranking Vatican officials before coming to China, and while here spent time with Deng Pufang, head of the Chinese Handicapped Association, who is the handicapped son of Deng Xiaoping, China's pre-eminent leader.
Under the revival of the ''indigenous'' Catholic Church in recent years, several hundred churches that had been closed have been reopened, some of them by priests who spent long terms in jail. 
But all are under tight control by the Catholic Patriotic Association, the organization created by the party in 1957 to supplant the Vatican as the church's controlling body.
The Patriotic Association declared some years ago that the position of Bishop of Shanghai was vacant, and it appointed its own man to the post.
Â 
No Reversal of Verdict
Although Mr. Deng has acted to clear the names of party figures who were purged under Mao Zedong, it was evident from the wording of the news article on Bishop Kung that there is to be no reversal of verdict for him. 
The report carefully restated the reasons for his imprisonment, saying ''he was sentenced by the Shanghai Intermediate People's Court as a traitor who used religion as a cloak.''
According to records compiled by Amnesty International and other organizations monitoring human rights in China, as many as 10 other priests are still in jail here, including some who were released and rearrested after Mr. Deng took power in 1978. 
Several of those imprisoned in the 1950's, including at least one bishop, died in prison or labor camp.
Mr. Deng's attitude toward religion is a matter of debate. 
While some diplomats have suggested he might be edging toward an accommodation with the Vatican, others consider it highly improbable that he would tolerate any alternative focus of loyalty to the party.
Although he has instituted sweeping relaxation in many spheres, he has been quick to crack down on any challenge to the party's power.
Â 
Bishop Seized in 1955
It is estimated that two million Catholics live in China, and thousands of them have long regarded the Bishop as a martyr. 
Appointed Bishop of the Shanghai diocese in 1950, he remained staunchly loyal to the Vatican at a time when many Chinese priests were being arrested - and some executed - for doing the same. 
In September 1955, he was seized during a nationwide campaign against ''counter-revolutionaries.''
Five years later, without being released, he was tried along with 13 other priests, who received terms ranging from 5 to 20 years.
Another cleric who suffered a similar fate, Bishop Dominic Tang of Canton, fell sick and was released in 1980 after serving 22 years in prison. 
He was allowed to go to Hong Kong. 
At about the same time, reports from prisoners who had met Bishop Kung in a labor camp and at the central prison in Shanghai, where he has been held in recent years, said he had continued to reject release in return for abjuring the Vatican.
One account was relayed by Yi Lifa, an Iowa University professor who spent 16 years as a prisoner here for purported spying.

file: CHINA REPLACES ITS TOP POLICE MINISTER.txt
text:
ï»¿
In the highest-level shake-up since the resignation of the Communist Party leader three months ago, China today announced the replacement of its Public Security Minister, who directed the country's main police force during student demonstrations last year.
The announcement, the latest of several personnel changes since the demonstrations prompted a backlash against social and economic changes, was approved amid the pageantry of the close of the annual National People's Congress in the Great Hall of the People.
The Communist Party leader who resigned, Hu Yaobang, attended the opening session on March 25 but his seat on the stage was vacant today. 
There have been suggestions that the Minister of Public Security, Ruan Chongwu, was close to Mr. Hu.
In addition to Mr. Hu, prominent casualties of the current campaign against ''bourgeois liberalization'' have included Liu Binyan, a maverick journalist for People's Daily; Zhu Houze, the propaganda chief of the Communist Party, and Fang Lizhi, vice president of the University of Science and Technology in Hefei.
Â 
Sign of Token Opposition
The new minister named today is Wang Fang, the Communist Party Secretary for the last four years in eastern Zhejiang Province.
In a sign of token opposition, two of the 2,674 delegates to the People's Congress raised their hands to vote against Mr. Wang's appointment. 
A handful of delegates also prevented unanimity on other matters, provoking a stir in the cavernous hall and reflecting the growing assertiveness of delegates to the meeting.
The assembly also approved new ministers of Public Health and Light Industry, as well as a new head of the Commission for Economic Restructuring. 
The commission had been headed by the Prime Minister, Zhao Ziyang, who now also serves as party leader. 
It was not clear whether these changes were politically significant. 
The official New China News Agency said all the changes were made at Mr. Zhao's suggestion.
As Police Minister, Mr. Ruan tried to improve the agency's public image by cracking down on police officers who mistreated people they arrested. 
His relative restraint in handling the student demonstrations may have been his downfall, some analysts say.
His successor, Mr. Wang, directed the police in the city of Hangzhou and in Zhejiang Province before becoming vice governor of the province and then the provincial party secretary. 
Mr. Wang, who was purged in 1967 during the Cultural Revolution, is also a member of the Central Committee of the Communist Party.
Â 
Zhao Address Is Endorsed
The People's Congress, which has gained considerably in influence recently, endorsed an address by Mr. Zhao. In it, he warned of the dangers of ''bourgeois liberalization'' but also stressed the need to continue economic advances.
The session also passed a resolution calling on the Government to ''resolutely correct unhealthy tendencies, oppose extravagance and waste, overcome bureaucracy and uphold the principles of hard struggle, self-reliance and building up the country and doing things thriftily.''
The prescriptions seemed to reflect the views of Peng Zhen, 85 years old, the chairman of the National People's Congress Standing Committee.

file: CHINA REPORTS GAIN IN SUPERCONDUCTIVE ALLOYS.txt
text:
ï»¿
Scientists in Beijing have reported producing an alloy that becomes superconducting, losing all resistance to electricity, at a temperature so high it would revolutionize the electrical industry. 
If confirmed, it would be the second major superconductivity advance in a week.
If the Beijing results can be duplicated, Dr. Robert J. Cava of A.T.&T. 
Bell Laboratories said yesterday, ''the world is not going to be the same.''
However, he added that it was not yet clear whether the Chinese had demonstrated total loss of electrical resistance.
On Dec. 
31 his group and one from the University of Houston both reported producing alloys that almost doubled the extremely low temperatures at which some materials become superconducting. 
The Chinese claim would raise the temperature far higher, close to the level where liquid nitrogen could be used to achieve the effect.
This would bring superconductivity within reach of numerous processes involving the transmission of electricity and the generation of strong magnetic fields. 
Normally, substantial energy is lost as electricity passes through a wire or other conductor. 
Such losses limit the intensity of magnetic fields that can be generated and increase energy costs. 
Superconducting materials are already widely used in computers, in efforts to harness the fusion reactions of the sun, and in many other applications.
Â 
Vital Import for Chinese
However, they require far more costly refrigeration systems than those that would be made possible if the Chinese report proves valid. 
If it does, it could rank as modern China's first major achievement in experimental physics.
Superconductivity occurs when one among a variety of materials is cooled almost to absolute zero: the total absence of heat at minus 460 degrees Fahrenheit, or minus 273 degrees Celsius. 
Electrical resistance occurs at all but very low temperatures because atoms in the conducting materials oscillate over wider and wider distances, thus interfering with the flow of an electrical current. 
Extremely low temperatures are normally expressed in degrees Kelvin, with zero degrees equal to absolute zero.
Degree increments in the Kelvin scale are the same as in the Celsius scale. 
In the latter, however, the zero point is the freezing temperature of water; thus, 10 degrees Kelvin is minus 263 degrees Celsius.
Last April the I.B.M. 
Zurich Research Laboratory in Switzerland reported achieving superconductivity at 30 degrees Kelvin in a mixture of barium, lanthanum copper and oxygen. 
It was the first substantial advance in more than a dozen years of worldwide research.
Â 
Other Developments
Since then the University of Tokyo, using the same combination of elements, has confirmed the I.B.M. finding. 
Last week Bell Laboratories in New Jersey and the University of Houston, following up on this new line of attack, reported superconductivity at temperatures of 36 and 40 degrees Kelvin, respectively.
The official New China News Agency has now reported that at the Institute of Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing researchers have produced superconductivity at 70 degrees Kelvin (minus 203 degrees Celsius or minus 333 degrees Fahrenheit).
As in the I.B.M. and Houston experiments, the material was a mixture of barium, lanthanum, copper and oxygen. 
While Bell Labs has been following the same line of research, it has not provided details of its approach. 
Its material became superconducting at normal atmospheric pressure whereas in Houston pressures of several hundred thousand pounds per square inch were required.
China has produced a number of outstanding theoretical physicists, including two Nobel laureates, but has been handicapped in the experimental area. 
Yesterday, Dr. Chien-Shiung Wu, professor of physics at Columbia University, who is former president of the American Physical Society, said that if the Beijing finding was confirmed, it could be China's first historic experimental achievement.
She noted that China had extremely rich resources of rare earth elements, such as lanthanum, upon which fabrication of superconductors depends.
Â 
Progress by Houston Group
Yesterday in Houston, Ru-Ling Meng, a researcher working with the group there led by Dr. Paul C.W. 
Chu, said they had produced fleeting elements of superconductivity at temperatures approaching 70 degrees but that the material proved unstable.
Ms. Meng said she had formerly worked with those conducting the research in Beijing. 
She has been trying to reach her former colleagues by telephone to learn details of their experiments. 
Laboratories throughout the world are believed to be following up on the Chinese experiments and those that presumably inspired them at the I.B.M. laboratory in Switzerland.
According to both the Bell Labs and Houston groups, the Chinese do not yet appear to have applied all the tests of superconductivity to their sample. 
The transition to superconductivity, as temperature is lowered, can be gradual. 
A variety of criteria are use to demonstrate the full transition.
The one reportedly used by the Chinese depends on a sudden drop in electrical resistivity. 
As pointed out yesterday by Dr. Cava, the results of such a test can be misleading. 
Residual resistance being observed may be attributed to impurities in the sample, rather than an absence of true superconductivity.
A more reliable test, he and Ms. Meng said, would be failure of a magnetic field to penetrate the sample in the manner typical of superconductivity.
Dr. Cava noted that while no details of the experiments were yet available, confirmation of the report would be ''very exciting.''
Referring to Chinese use of the I.B.M. mixture, he said, ''We are trying to find out what the Chinese did to it.''
The answer could become available within days.

file: CHINA REPORTS OPIUM IS BEING SMUGGLED TO HONG KONG AND TAIWAN (Reuters) -.txt
text:

Raw opium grown for medical purposes in China is being stolen and smuggled out of the country to dealers in Hong Kong and Taiwan, according to a senior Chinese judicial official.
Xin Deli, deputy head of the judicial office of the Shanghai municipality, said the traffic had been discovered after the capture of some Hong Kong smugglers in possession of the drug, which is the base for morphine and heroin.
''They confessed the raw opium came from China,'' he said. 
Mr. Xin said the opium poppy was planted in some parts of China for medical use. 
''Some people get it and sell it to people from Zhejiang and Guangdong for high prices and then it is resold outside China,'' Mr. Xin said.
Chinese official reports opium grown in China is being smuggled to Hong Kong and Taiwan'Limited Quantities' of Opium
He added that ''limited quantities'' appeared to be involved and that the stolen opium was believed to come from the southern province of Yunnan, a traditional opium-growing area bordering Vietnam, Laos and Burma that has illegally exported it in past years.
Zhejiang lies just south of Shanghai and is reported to have a flourishing smuggling trade with Taiwan, while Guangdong borders the British colony of Hong Kong.
Hong Kong's Narcotics Commissioner, Peter Lee, recently expressed fear that a bumper opium harvest in the area where Burma, Laos and Thailand meet, known as the Golden Triangle, would result in more drugs in the colony.

Â 
No Reports in Press
The Shanghai official said there was no drug problem in his city, China's largest, although some unofficial sources have spoken of drug use by young people in some urban areas.
The unofficial sources added that there were heavy penalties for drug use. 
The fact that there have been no reports of a drug problem in the Chinese press, which usually publicizes antisocial activites as a warning, indicates that there is not a serious problem.
Mr. Xin said the main smuggling trade along the South China coast was in commodities such as tape recorders, watches and other consumer goods that are scarce on the mainland.
The Chinese usually exchange gold and precious objects for the goods, with fishermen from Taiwan and the mainland the main intermediaries along the coast.

17 (AP) - China said today that the agreement with the United States on limiting arms sales to Taiwan was only the first step toward solving the dispute over the island.

Â 
'Served to Break the Stalemate'
''Should the policy makers in Washington insist on handling the relations between the two countries according to this internal law, Chinese-United States relations, instead of being further developed, will certainly face yet another grave crisis,'' the paper said in an editorial to appear in Wednesday's issue.

Mr. Deng led efforts to establish full diplomatic relations with the United States in 1979.

China's state-run domestic news programs dwelled on the Taiwan issue tonight, carrying reports on the communique, the Chinese Foreign Ministry statement and the People's Daily editorial.
Â 
Taiwan Relations Act Denounced
In a statement issued in Washington, President Reagan said the accord was ''fully consistent with the Taiwan Relations Act.''
But the Chinese Foreign Ministry said it ''has nothing to do with the 'Taiwan Relations Act' formulated unilaterally by the United States.''
