file: CHINA SEES NO ADDED GRAIN NEED.txt
text:
ï»¿
With a good harvest in sight, China does not expect to buy any more American grain this year beyond the six million to nine million metric tons already agreed upon for the year, Agriculture Secretary John R. Block said today.
Encouraging the Chinese to purchase more of this year's American crop had been one of the aims of Mr. Block when he arrived Friday for a visit that included talks with China's Agricultural Minister, Lin Hujia, and the Minister of Light Industry, Song Jiwen.
Speaking with reporters before his departure today, Mr. Block said that, ''at each of the meetings with each of the officials that we talked to, I did bring up that we have a large crop in the United States of very high quality at very attractive prices and would encourage the Chinese to look toward additional purchases if they have any needs.''
But he added that the Chinese had said that there was no indication that they would need more than the agreed-upon amount.
Agriculture Secretary John Block reports China is unlikely to make additional grain purchases from US in 1981Four-Year Pact Signed in 1980
China signed a four-year agreement with the United States in 1980 in which it agreed to buy a minimum of six million to eight million metric tons of wheat and corn annually through 1984. 
A metric ton is about 2,205 pounds and is equal to 36.7 bushels of wheat or 39.4 bushels of corn.
With the improvement in relations between the two countries, China has already become the fourth-largest foreign market for American agricultural products, and the largest purchaser of American wheat and cotton. 
American farm sales to China grew fourfold, to $2.2 billion last year from $573 million in 1978, according to Department of Agriculture figures.
To insure satisfactory grain quality, Mr. Block said, the Federal Grain Inspection Service will send a team here to investigate complaints that some grain deliveries have had insects and other foreign matter. 
The Secretary insisted that the problem was not serious. 
''It's just that this is such an important market to us that we're going to service it, as we would with any other important market,'' Mr. Block said.
Â 
Private Groups Plan Offices
To further develop the Chinese market, negotiations are under way for private organizations representing American growers of wheat, soybeans and feed grains to open their own offices in Peking.
The United States Feed Grains Council expects to have an office open here next January. 
United States Wheat Associates, the foreignmarket promotion arm of the American wheat industry, and the American Soybean Association also want to open China offices next year.
Robert M. Book of the United States Food Grain Council, who was traveling with Mr. Block's party, said that ''we would probably like to co-locate with agricultural trade offices; this is what we have done in other places.''
Â 
New $1.5 Million Bakery
This morning in Peking, Secretary Block visited a new $1.5 million bakery that has been built to use United States mechanized bakery equipment and American flour. 
Because Chinese traditionally have eaten rice rather than bread, it is one of the few major bakeries in China.
After it opens later this year, the bakery will be used to train Chinese bakers and as a model for baking technology. 
Its production capacity of 1,500 pounds of bread an hour will be sufficient to provide bread for a population of 50,000.
United States Wheat Associates bought the machinery for the bakery and is also working to help set up a similar model 150-ton flour mill in Peking and a plant making instant noodles in Shanghai.
''China already is our biggest wheat customer in the world so I think they will be using a lot of our wheat,'' Mr. Block said.
Â 
Scientific and Technical Program
The Secretary added that he had also encountered strong interest among the Chinese in more scientific and technical exchanges. 
Under the scientific and technical program begun in 1979, he said, 53 teams will have been exchanged by the end of 1981 and another 75 or 80 are planned.
Mr. Block said that the Chinese had also shown an interest in buying American forestry products and would be discussing this later. 
During the current visit, it was agreed to have teams examine quarantine policies so that some American swine could be sent to China for breeding purposes.
The Secretary had initially planned to stay in China until Wednesday, but dropped the Shanghai part of his visit and left today to assist with the Reagan Administration's new farm bill, which is now being considered by Congress. 
The other members of the trade mission are continuing to Hong Kong, Indonesia, Singapore and India.

file: CHINA SEES SUMMIT WITH SOVIETS IN _89.txt
text:
ï»¿
Deng Xiaoping, China's foremost leader, said today that China and the Soviet Union are likely to hold a summit meeting next year, diplomats reported. 
It would be the first such meeting in 30 years.
Mr. Deng, in a meeting with President Mauno Koivisto of Finland, also expressed confidence that long-strained relations between China and the Soviet Union will improve, members of the Finnish delegation said.
Foreign Minister Qian Qichen is to travel to Moscow later this year, and he is expected to discuss plans for a summit meeting between Mikhail S. Gorbachev, the Soviet leader, and Chinese leaders. 
It is generally believed here that Mr. Gorbachev will visit Beijing next year.
Mr. Deng's statement was the first by a Chinese to predict that the summit meeting, the first since Nikita S. Khrushchev came to China in 1959, would probably take place next year.
Â 
No Place or Time Set
A Foreign Ministry spokeswoman, Li Jinhua, said at a briefing today that it was still too early to name a time or place for the summit meeting.
''The timing for the meeting between the top leaders of the two countries depends on whether the conditions are ripe or not,'' she said. 
''Now is the time for the creation of the conditions.''
Members of the Finnish delegation said Mr. Deng also brought up the three obstacles China has cited as holding up the improvement of Chinese-Soviet relations: Vietnam's occupation of Cambodia, the Soviet military presence in Afghanistan and the Soviet troop concentration on the Chinese border.
A report by the official New China News Agency on the meeting today made no mention of a summit meeting. 
It only quoted Mr. Deng as saying political and economic relations between China and the Soviet Union will never be the same as those of the 1950's, when Moscow dominated Beijing.
Â 
Deng No Longer Travels Abroad
Any summit meeting is likely to take place in Beijing because Mr. Deng, 84 years old, no longer travels abroad. 
Mr. Gorbachev would probably hold talks with Prime Minister Li Peng and the Communist Party General Secretary, Zhao Ziyang, the two men responsible for the day-to-day running of the Government and the ruling party.
As Mr. Deng met with the Finnish delegation today, Prime Minister Li was quoted as denying that a recently announced program to cool off the overheated Chinese economy was a setback for market-oriented innovations.
Mr. Li's comments were made Tuesday and carried by the New China News Agency today.
He said ''some domestic figures and members of the foreign press'' had suggested that China's decision to ''improve the economic environment and rectify the economic order'' over the next two years means a halt in the reforms.
''All these doubts or hesitations show that such people have not yet arrived at a full understanding of the relationship between the key tasks of creating economic stabilityI and bolstering reform,'' he said.
Last month the Communist Party Central Committee outlined a two-year period of belt-tightening to bring under control an economy hit by overspending, serious shortages of raw materials and consumer goods, and an inflation rate of at least 20 percent.

file: CHINA SHARPLY WARNS U.S. ON TEXTILE CURBS.txt
text:

China today made its strongest threat yet of retaliation against American farmers if the United States imposes new restrictions on textile imports announced on Aug. 
3.
''Americans will be forced to swallow their own bitter pill,'' said the authoritative Chinese-language People's Daily in a commentary in today's issue.

A senior trade official said the situation was ''disturbingly reminiscent of what happened last year when we froze imports of Chinese textiles,'' adding, ''U.S. trade to China fell by $1 billion.''
Both the American officials spoke on condition they not be identified.
Â 
Could Embarrass Reagan
A new suspension of wheat purchases could embarrass President Reagan in the farm belt, where he has been attacking former Vice President Walter F. Mondale, the Democratic contender, for supporting the curtailment of grain shipments to the Soviet Union in 1980 after the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan.
The Peking newspaper charged that the United States ''doesn't care about violating bilateral agreements with other countries,'' and said that many legislators, retailers, importers and farmers are concerned about the consequences of the new regulations for United States trade.
These concerns are well founded, the commentary said, because ''there is no reason to believe that only the U.S. can take unilateral action to violate international agreements and to restrict and harm others, and that others will not adopt corresponding measures.''
''Any attempt to impose one's own will on others can only harm trade between countries,'' it warned.
The executive order tightening so- called rules of origin governing imports of apparel goes into effect today for goods ordered after Aug. 
3, the date the order was published in the Federal Register. 
For goods ordered before that date, the old rules apply for shipments through Oct. 
31, That exemption, affecting about $500 million of merchandise that had been ordered for store shelves this Christmas, came in response to protests from retailers, farmers, third world countries and others.
The new rules are intended to prevent what Customs officials say is widespread ''circumvention'' of American textile import quotas. 
This occurs when goods are cut in one country and sewn in another, then enter the United States under the second country's usually more liberal quota.
Industry sources in Hong Kong have estimated that more than $100 million in semifinished Chinese textile products are shipped to Hong Kong alone each year for finishing and re-export to the United States.

Outlook for Wheat Purchases

text:

Deng Xiaoping's campaign to rejuvenate China's sluggish bureaucracy has been stepped up with the naming of a new Shanghai party chief and the promotion of three 42-year-old officers to top military posts.
Earlier this week, the Government announced the appointment of nine new officials to head ministries that play a crucial role in Mr. Deng's modernization drive. 
At the same time, he has been pressing ahead with a shakeout of regional military commanders and top Communist Party and Government officials in the provinces.
Deng Xiaoping's campaign to rejuvenate China's sluggish bureaucracy is stepped up with naming of new Shanghai party chief and promotion of three relatively young officers to top military posts (M)
The latest changes are part of a process that began at least three years ago at lower levels of the bureaucracy. 
Mr. Deng, himself 80 years old, insisted that the retention of power at all levels by aging, poorly educated officials who began their careers in the the revolutionary period was a major obstacle to economic and social change.
He started a drive to ease these officials aside, some of them into retirement and others into advisory positions. 
By the end of last year, about 900,000 party and Government officials had been sent into compulsory retirement, and a process to weed out the armed forces' officer corps had begun.
As well as promoting younger, college-educated men, Mr. Deng has been using the changes to unseat officials with questionable loyalty to his policies. 
An example this month was the removal of Li Desheng, commander of the strategic Shenyang Military Region in the northeast, who was once an ally of Mao Zedong's widow, Jiang Qing. 
Several other elderly commanders in the 11 regions were also sent into retirement, and the number of regions was reduced to seven.
The change in Shanghai, the country's largest city and its industry and commerce hub, appeared to stem partly from dissatisfaction in Peking with the pace at which the city has put into effect the market-oriented policies at the heart of Mr. Deng's program.
The new party secretary in the city, Rui Xingwen, was previously Minister of Urban and Rural Construction and Environmental Protection, which has played a major role in the large building program that has accompanied the economic growth of recent years. 
He replaces Chen Guodong.
The new deputy party secretary, Jiang Zemin, was until this week Minister of the Electronics Industry, another sector that has expanded rapidly under Mr. Deng. Mr. Jiang will also serve as Mayor, or head of the city Government, replacing Wang Daohan.
Other reports confirmed the appointment of a new party secretary, Chen Huiguang, a 46-year-old engineer, in the Guangxi-Zhuang Autonomous Region bordering Vietnam. 
Changes in top posts had previously been announced for the provinces of Sichuan, Shandong, Jilin, Guizhou, Hebei, Jiangxi and Tibet. 
Most of the new appointees are in their 40's and 50's.
The new military appointments involve top positions on the general staff in Peking.

file: CHINA TELLS U.S. ARMS TO TAIWAN ARE CRUCIAL TEST.txt
text:

China publicly warned the United States today not to sell more arms to Taiwan. 
It called the issue a ''severe test'' of whether Washington valued its relations with Peking.
In a tough but carefully worded commentary, the People's Daily said the United States had ''failed to honor its commitment'' to respect China's sovereignty and had ''resorted to various prevarications'' in the three years since full diplomatic relations were established.
The newspaper speaks for the ruling Communist Party, and its commentary amounted to a statement by the Peking leadership. 
It did not elaborate on the accusations and did not mention the State Department's confirmation earlier this week that the United States intended to sell a multimillion dollar package of military spare parts to the Chinese Nationalists in Taiwan.
China publicly warns US not to sell more arms to TaiwanDemands 'Genuine Respect'
''We must state explicitly,'' the commentary said, ''that, if the United States desires to preserve and develop its relations with China, it must seek, on the basis of genuine respect for China's sovereignty, a solution to the issue of selling arms to Taiwan. 
There is no other way.''
Â 
(The United States has not made public the size of the sale to Taiwan, but an American official in Washingto n said it would involve about $97 million in spare parts.)
The commentary comes at a time when the Chinese press has adopted a tougher line toward the United States, linking it with the Soviet Union as the superpowers and criticizing American actions like reconnaissance flights over North Korea. 
Chinese sources have confirmed that the tougher line in the press reflects dissatisfaction over the issue of arms sales to Taiwan.
Peking has viewed such American proposals as selling updated versions of the F-5E jet fighter, which Taiwan already has, as a subterfuge for mollifying China's objections to the sale of new arms. 
A Foreign Ministry spokesman said two days ago that China was asking the United States to clarify its reported decision to sell spare parts.
The Chinese leadership has avoiding saying what it would do if arms sales went through anyway. 
Some officials have said that China would have no option but to retaliate, and one official said this could involve downgrading relations with the United States.
When the Netherlands sold two submarines to Taiwan last summer, China reduced its relations to the level of a liaison office without a resident ambassador. 
Some diplomats have questioned whether China would go so far with the United States.
Some diplomats detected in today's press commentary a note of conciliation in the suggestion that Peking and Washington might discuss differences over the issue of arms sales to Taiwan, which Peking considers part of China.
The People's Daily said that, once the United States recognized that it should stop interfering in China's internal affairs by selling arms to Taiwan, ''the two sides may negotiate ways and means of settling this issue.''
Â 
Encroachment on Sovereignty Seen
One proposal previously rumored to have been made by Peking is that the United States might agree to phase out its arms deliveries over a period of perhaps five years while reiterating its acceptance of the view that there is only one China and that Taiwan is an integral part. 
There is no indication whether such a formula has ever been discussed.
Â 
The People' s Daily said China opposed the sale of arms to Taiwan byall countries , particularly those that had diplomatic relations with Peking.
''Those who insist on selling arms to Taiwan encroach on China's sovereignty and interfere in its internal affairs,'' the commentary said. 
''And the United States is no exception in this matter.''
The paper said a nine-point proposal for peaceful reunification with Taiwan, made in September, had ''created conditions most favorable for ending United States arms sales to Taiwan and United States involvement in internal affairs.''
The proposal offered to give the Chinese Nationalist leaders of Taiwan high positions on the mainland and to let Taiwan retain its own armed forces and economic system.

The commentary today reiterated promises to ''make every effort to resolve the Taiwan question by peaceful means.''
It said that the Chinese people were ''watching whether the United States Government chooses to settle the issue of arms sales to Taiwan properly.''
''This is a severe test for the United States Government that will show whether it truly values its relations with China and whether it has the global strategic pattern in mind,'' the People's Daily said, alluding to what it sees as a need for concerted United States-Chinese policies against the Soviet Union around the world.

file: CHINA TIMES CEASES U.S. PUBLICATIONS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The China Times, considered the most influential Chinese-language newspaper in the United States, has ceased publication.
The paper's publisher, Yu Chi Chung, who also publishes The China Times in Taiwan, abruptly announced earlier this month that he would shut down the American paper because of ''business difficulties.''
Some experts on Chinese politics say, however, that the liberal China Times was the victim of Taiwan politics.
Prof. Andrew Nathan of Columbia University's East Asian Institute, said the events leading up to the demise of The China Times provided ''a window on Taiwanese politics'' as well as evidence of ''the long arm of the K.M.T. into the American press.''
He was referring to Taiwan's ruling party, the Kuomingtang.
The China Times, published in New York City's Chinatown and considered most influential Chinese-language newspaper in United States, ceases publication; paper's publisher, Yu Chi Chung, who also publishes paper in Taiwan, cites 'business difficulties,' but others say liberal publication was victim of Taiwan politics; photo (M)
Professor Nathan added that the events had also shown the tough response by the Taiwan leadership to any suggestion of a reconciliation with Peking, particularly after the recent agreement by Britain to turn over control of Hong Kong to China in 1997.
Â 
Belief in Democracy
''Most Chinese-American intellectuals are very sad because these events are not a good sign for the future of Chinese democracy and a free Chinese press,'' said Lu Keng, the publisher of the independent Chinese-American Sino Daily Express in New York. 
''The conservatives, afraid of any change, remain the dominant faction in the Nationalist Party leadership while the liberals like The China Times believe Taiwan must go the democratic way to compete with mainland China.''
In Washington, a representative of Taiwan's unofficial mission, the Coordinating Council for North American Affairs, referred to a statement by a Government spokesman in Taipei on Nov. 
19.
The spokesman, Dr. Chang King-yuh was quoted as having said that The China Times of America was closed because of ''financial difficulties and personnel problems.''
He said rumors that the Nationalist Government had used pressure to cause the closing were ''groundless.''
Â 
Two American Editions
In Taiwan, The China Times is the largest newspaper, with a circulation of more than one million. 
The American newspaper was separately written and edited, with a more liberal editorial view than its Taiwan counterpart, former employees said. 
Publication began Sept. 
1, 1982, in two locations: New York and Los Angeles. 
The New York edition grew to a circulation of more than 20,000, and the Los Angeles edition had a circulation of 10,000. 
The newspaper, which was published daily and Sundays, employed a total of 200 people.
The newspaper's former chief editorial writer, Yu Kuo Chi, said he believed that the publisher could have overcome his financial difficulties and that the newspaper was closed ''mainly for political reasons - just too liberal for the leaders in Taiwan.''
The paper's problems reportedly erupted last summer over coverage of the Olympic Games in Los Angeles. 
The team from China, participating for the first time, won 15 gold medals. 
While most Taiwan news organizations downplayed the event, The China Times of America gave the Chinese triumph front-page coverage.
This coverage, according to news reports from Taipei, was discussed at a meeting of the Standing Committee of the Central Committee of the Nationalist Party on Sept. 
5. The publisher, a member of the Standing Committee, was accused of ''making propaganda for the Communist bandits.''
The publisher was reported to have responded that his paper had always been attacked by the Communists and that, as for the Olympic Games, the paper was merely reporting the facts.
Then, on Sept. 
12, The China Times of America published an editorial with the headline: ''There Is No Conflict Between Politics and Religion, Only a Reagan Problem.''
Criticism of the Reagan Administration is unusual in Taiwan-American news organizations.
''Reagan and his fundamentalist comrades were the commanders of the Dallas convention,'' the editorial said. 
''They cooperated to produce the most reactionary platform of the Republican Party in several decades.''
In Taiwan, President Chiang Ching- kuo accused the newspaper of ''hurting Sino-American relations.''
Â 
Writers Were Dismissed
Mr. Yu, the publisher, flew to New York on Sept. 
28 and dismissed both the chief editorial writer and the subordinate who wrote the Reagan editorial.
This apparently did not satisfy the Taipei leadership, and the publisher was told that in the future, the ruling party in Taiwan would appoint the general editor, the chief of editorials and the general manager of the American newspaper.
It was reported that until Mr. Yu bowed to these demands, he would not be able to export capital from Taiwan to help finance his American venture.
On Nov. 
11, Mr. Yu announced that the publication would cease.
The closing occurred at a time when the Chinese-American community was nervous over the killing of a Chinese writer, Henry Liu, the author of a biography critical of President Chiang of Taiwan.
''It's unfortunate that pressure from the K.M.T. forced the closure of The China Times,'' said John Wang, a Chinese journalist.''Although it was pro- Taiwan, The China Times reporting on China was balanced and it raised the standard of Chinese journalism in this country. 
It could have been a useful forum to encourage further liberalization in mainland China and strenghten Taiwan's credibility as it moves towards democracy.''
Andrew Kwan, chief editor of another Chinese language newspaper in America, the pro-Peking China Daily News, insisted that financial problems were not the major factor behind the closing, but rather ''pressure from Taiwan.''

file: CHINA TO GET AID OF GEORGIA TECH.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Georgia Institute of Technology will become the first American university to enter into joint ventures to help develop industries in China for the manufacture of advanced-technology products.
The agreement was signed in Peking last weekend by officials of Georgia Tech and the China Association for Science and Technology, an umbrella organization representing hundreds of Chinese professional scientific and engineering groups. 
It will cover products ranging from ultralight aircraft to optical fibers.
According to the terms of the agreement, Georgia Tech will enter into collaborative efforts with the Chinese in the development of small to medium- size technology-based industries in Shenzhen City, near Hong Kong; Tianjin, which is about 70 miles southeast of Peking, and Nantong, about 65 miles northwest of Shanghai.
Georgia Institute of Technology and China Association for Science and Technology sign agreement under which Georgia Tech will help develop small to medium-size technology-based industries in Shenzhen City, Tianjin and Nantong; Chinese are initially expected to put up $500,000 in seed money toward agreement; Reagan Administration backs agreement (M)
As part of the agreement, Georgia Tech is studying the possibility of opening an office in China to coordinate its work. 
In addition, representatives of Chinese industries may be based in Atlanta at the university's Advanced Technology Development Center, a nonprofit organization set up by state and university officials to assist in the development of high technology industries.
Â 
$500,000 From China
A spokesman for Georgia Tech said the Chinese were expected to initially put up about $500,000 in seed money toward the agreement.
By participating in joint venture contracts that could eventually lead to the development, licensing and exporting of specific industrial applications, Georgia Tech has gone well beyond previous arrangements that American universities have had in China.
For the most part, these have been confined to scholarly exchanges that involve representatives of Chinese scientific or academic institutions.
Officials at Georgia Tech said their agreement had the backing of the Reagan Administration, which has relaxed trade restrictions with China. 
Among the members of the Georgia delegation who went to China to sign the agreement was George Busbee, a former Governor of Georgia who is a member of President Reagan's Export Council.
The products identified by the Chinese that could be covered by specific contracts include a variety of technical and consumer items, such as solar energy cells, hearing aids, air-conditioners, high speed elevators, radiophones, electrical circuit boards, woven fabrics, polyester filament and telephone equipment.
Â 
Potential Military Uses
According to the Commerce Department, most of the products on the Chinese list include components or technology that are subject to Government export controls because they have potential military applications. 
As a result, an export license will be required before the products or particular technology can be transferred overseas.
Henry Bourne, vice president for academic affairs at Georgia Tech, said the agreement marked part of what he called a larger trend, in which Chinese scientists will continue to reach out to research laboratories at American universities for help in developing science and engineering technology.
''I don't think we'll occupy a unique position for very long,'' said Dr. Bourne, adding that Georgia Tech ''has very little to lose and a lot to gain for the country as a whole by building these kinds of bridges with the China.''
But a variety of experts on trade and technology with China said they could not say for certain that this agreement would lead to similar relationships with research facilities at other American universities.
''I would be surprised to see a large number of such agreements,'' said Pierre Perrolle, an official with the National Science Foundation in Washington. 
He said what was significant about the agreement was that it reflected ''the loosening that has been going on in the Chinese system that allows a section of industry or a group of academics to experiment with such an approach.''
Â 
Accord With Japanese
The agreement not only reflects the growing Chinese appetite for American technology, but increasing aggressiveness on the part of American universities in seeking research support abroad. 
Last year, for example, Georgia Tech entered into an agreement with Nissho Iwai, a Japanese trading company, to market its technology and inventions in Japan.
In the last five years, financing of university research in this country by Japanese industry has increased dramatically.
Over all, Georgia Tech ranks third in the nation in the amount of public and private support it receives for engineering research and development.
According to A. Ray Moore, a spokesman for Georgia Tech, a representative of the Chinese Association for Science and Technology visited several research sites earlier this year, including the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the Research Triangle complex in North Carolina.
He said the Chinese settled on Georgia Tech, in part, because of the university's new Advanced Technology Development Center. 
The Chinese have since established their own New Technology Development Center, using Georgia Tech as its model.

file: CHINA TRIES TO SHUT THE DOOR ON THE RED GUARDS_ LEGACY.txt
text:
ï»¿
After being piled in warehouses around the capital for nearly two decades, many of the looted antiques lining the tables and walls are dusty and scuffed, and some are badly damaged and have hardly any value at all.
Yet each day they come, men in fraying wool overcoats and ladies in jackets of padded cotton, searching the chilly classrooms of the Guangming Primary School for heirlooms they had assumed to be permanently lost.
Now and then somebody finds a cherished inkstand or a scroll, and others cluster around to share their moment of pleasure.
At the outset of the Cultural Revolution in 1966, Mao Zedong unleashed the youthful fanatics known as Red Guards on a house-to-house rampage against ''feudal dregs'' from China's past, and anybody with antiques or valuables was deemed fair game.
'Reclaiming exhibition' is being held at Guangming Primary School in Peking's Chongwen district; consists of more than 30,000 objects, including scroll paintings, calligraphy, cloisonne, lacquerware and books that were confiscated from homes in 1966 under Cultural Revolution of Mao Zedong; although Revolution ended in 1976, it is only now that Communist Party's decrees on returning confiscated property are beginning to take hold (M)
Now, the looting and the smashing are officially condemned, and a vast haul of property has been put on display.
The ''reclaiming exhibition'' in Peking's Chongwen district consists of more than 30,000 objects, including scroll paintings, calligraphy, cloisonne, lacquerware and books.
Some scrolls date to the Song Dynasty, more than 700 years ago, and would fetch handsome prices at auctions in the West. 
Other items include vanity boxes, bird cages, bamboo bracelets, water pipes and incense burners of the kind that accumulated in even modest Chinese homes.
Â 
'Calamity' Ended in 1976
Although the Cultural Revolution officially ended in 1976 and has been officially proclaimed a ''calamity,'' it is only now that the Communist Party's decrees on returning confiscated property are beginning to take hold. 
The exhibition at the school is the first of its scale to be held in the capital since a detailed Government directive on the matter was issued last year.
Since the early 1980's, families have been able to visit old temples and other places used as warehouses to inquire after lost belongings. 
But because the Red Guards destroyed much of what they took and kept scant records, recoveries were few.
Last spring, officials in Peking, Hangzhou, Tianjin and other major cities began inventorying millions of items for public showings.
At the Guangming school, room after room has been draped with a forest of scrolls. 
Some have been slashed, others torn or crumpled. 
But even for some of these there have been claimants.
''This is definitely mine!'' one man wrote on a ticket attached to a calligraphy scroll that looked as though it had been driven over by a muddy car tire.
One of the most beautiful scrolls could stand as a memorial to the terror of the Red Guards. 
At least two centuries old, it is a delicate silk embroidery in blues and browns showing the last of the Ming emperors about to hang himself from a locust tree overlooking the Forbidden City as peasant rebels overran the imperial stronghold in 1644.
Across the top half of the scroll, the owner scrawled a legend in thick black ink, ''I'm waiting to surrender this work for smashing by the respected Red Guard comrades, because it is nothing but a poisonous weed.''
By defacing the scroll, he apparently hoped to avoid the beating that the Red Guards frequently meted out to the ''bourgeois remnants'' made targets by Mao.
The tactic rarely worked. 
A visitor to the exhibition today, Fu Zhibin, 75 years old, who bicycled miles across the city to look for furniture looted from his home, recalled how he sent a message to the Red Guards inviting them to his 12-room house at 34 Donghuashi Street. 
By showing good will, he said, he thought he could curb their more destructive passions.
Â 
'They Beat Me Anyway'
''It didn't work,'' he said, with a wistful chuckle. 
''They beat me anyway, ransacked my belongings and threw me and my family out of my home.''
Last year, under another aspect of the restitution policies, Mr. Fu received a certificate formally restoring the title to his house. 
He has collected small amounts of rent, but he and his wife must remain in their two-room flat across town until new accommodations are found for the six families who supplanted them in their home. 
Today, the old man had another disappointment when officials at the exhibition told him they had no record of his missing tables and chairs.
The political message of the antiques display is spelled out in a red banner atop the school entrance. 
''Thoroughly negate the Cultural Revolution!'' it says.
Inside, Gao Yushan, the official in charge, invites claimants to read a notice describing the exhibition as a product of the party's policy of ''thoroughly removing the vicious influence of the Cultural Revolution, protecting citizens' property rights and as far as possible solving the problems left over by history.''
The display represents the part of the warehouse haul that officials thought likely to have come from the Chongwen district, a sprawling section to the south of the Forbidden City that has a population of about a million people. 
Chongwen was home to thousands of old bourgeois families, members of the old merchant class and descendants of the imperial mandarinate, many with large collections of antiques.
Claimants must first fill out a form detailing the circumstances of their loss. 
Once Mr. Gao and his assistants are satisfied that they have come in good faith, they are escorted through the exhibits.
If they spot something they believe is theirs, details are written on a white ticket and attached to the item. 
Minor pieces can be picked up after a few days, and more valuable ones must await possible counterclaims.
With only two days of the two-week exhibition to run, 8,000 items have been claimed. 
Among the more valuable scrolls double claims are common, and some articles have attracted three white tickets.

file: CHINA WATCHERS SAY TURMOIL CUT DENG_S POWER.txt
text:
ï»¿
Some China watchers based in Hong Kong have concluded that Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, has been severely weakened in the recent political turmoil in Beijing and may no longer exercise real power.
Mr. Deng, who twice rose from political oblivion in the 1970's, has been the principal force behind the economic restructuring that China has undergone since 1979.
The sweeping changes were introduced to free the country's lethargic economy from strong central control, with innovative management in some areas, a reliance on market forces for some products, and private control of most farm production.
The opinion of the China watchers aside, diplomatic analysts in Beijing and Washington say they generally believe that despite the political and ideological upheaval, Mr. Deng remains firmly in charge.
Innovators Seen as Isolated
The analysts interviewed here, some of whom began watching China when it was closed to Western journalists, navigate partly by a careful scrutiny of the Chinese press, examining nuances and reading between the lines as the mainland Chinese do. 
They are not diplomats and sometimes take issue with diplomats posted in Beijing, but they have proven astute on past factional struggles inside China.
The Chinese and Western analysts interviewed in Hong Kong said Mr. Deng and the innovators he brought to power in the last decade had been isolated and forced from the center of power.
''I think he is now a lame duck,'' said a Hong Kong Chinese who has followed the situation on the mainland for several decades. 
''Deng rested on two legs, Hu Yaobang and Zhao Ziyang. 
One of those legs has been cut from under him.''
On Jan. 
16, Mr. Hu was stripped of his title as General Secretary of the Communist Party, which has 44 million members, after a month of student demonstrations calling for democracy. 
Mr. Zhao, who is Prime Minister, was named Acting General Secretary.
Another analyst here who has studied China since the Communists took over in 1949 took an equally negative view of Mr. Deng's situation.
''Some observers still imagine that he is in the saddle, as the most devastating articles written against 'bourgeois liberalism' cite his words,'' the analyst said. 
''They really make fun of him, quoting his words pronounced at moments when he temporarily adopted words of his enemies.''
Â 
Criticism From the Press
Since the student protests ended early this year, the Chinese press has railed against what it calls ''bourgeois liberalization.''
The phrase is meant to encompass all views that advocate the introduction of Western ideas and values into China.
One analyst pointed to the abrupt manner in which Mr. Hu was removed as evidence of both Mr. Deng's weakened position and the declining power of the Politburo, which is in theory the most powerful body in China.
''They held an enlarged meeting of the Politburo to get rid of Hu,'' the analyst said. 
''The majority at the meeting was non-Politburo members. 
Why did they do this?
The answer is the Politburo is not strong; the power was elsewhere.''
China watchers in Hong Kong cited these developments, among others, to support their view that Mr. Deng was under attack:
* The call last summer for political change, which was identified with Mr. Deng and Mr. Hu, was discussed in September at a preparatory meeting before a plenary session of the Central Committee, but no action was taken.
* China's newspapers carried a previously unpublished speech last week that Mr. Deng delivered in 1962 at a conference to criticize the policies of the Great Leap Forward in 1958 and 1959. 
Mr. Deng attacked the misguided economic policies of Mao Zedong and called for collective leadership in the party. 
''They are using his words against him,'' a Chinese analyst said. 
''By choosing this speech to publish, they are attacking his economic policies the way he attacked Mao's policies.''
* The official Chinese press has sounded a clarion call for China to produce more grain. 
Analysts in Hong Kong saw this as an implicit attack on Mr. Deng's rural policies because it would mean a strengthening of central planning in state agriculture. 
''Grain, grain, grain. 
That means an attack on the peasants in the countryside who are growing other things so they make more money,'' one analyst said.
* Despite the assurance from Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang, the acting party leader, that the campaign against ''bourgeois liberalization'' would be confined to the party, the Chinese military declared that the campaign would permeate the armed forces, the analysts said. 
Publishers, theaters, film studios and artists have also been admonished to watch the political soundness of their work.
One Hong Kong analyst traced the rise of hard-liners - defined by their insistence on party supremacy and a strong distaste for Western ideas in politics, art and literature - to 1984, when Peng Zhen transformed the National People's Congress.
Â 
Congress Makes Real Decisions
Under Mr. Peng's direction, the analysts said, the congress, which had been a powerless quasi legislature that approved decisions by the party's Central Committee, began to make real decisions. 
Mr. Peng and the standing committee have sent delegations abroad; have publicly called for the rule of law, which some observers here view as an attack on party privilege; and have passed major legislation, apparently independent of the party, the most recent example being a bankruptcy law for companies.
An analyst described Mr. Peng as the ''leading voice'' of the hard-liners and the man directing Chinese policy at the moment. 
The People's Congress, led by Mr. Peng, is scheduled to meet in late March, and analysts here believe that a new prime minister will be chosen then. 
Many of the analysts say they expect Li Peng, a Soviet-trained engineer, to be the choice.
The China watchers said the way that the hard-liners marshaled their power remained obscure. 
''We still do not know what really happened,'' one analyst said. 
''But it is clear that a new period has started.''

file: CHINA, CASTING OFF CARE, HAILS THE YEAR OF THE OX.txt
text:
ï»¿
When even the banana sellers take a break the fever of the Lunar New Year has indubitably gripped Peking.
As the festivities celebrated by Chinese throughout the world began here Tuesday amid a blowing snowstorm, young merchants with bicycles were missing from their usual stations outside foreigners' compounds and hotels. 
The bananas are a cover for black- market currency dealings, which have boomed along with the rest of the economy here in recent years.
The closing of the ''banana bank'' was one measure of how the Lunar New Year has changed. 
A decade ago it was deemed reactionary to call it by its traditional name, so it was called the Spring Festival. 
Workers got three days off, as now, but they were well advised to keep their revelries away from neighbors' prying eyes.
Lunar New Year festivities celebrated by Chinese throughout world begin in Peking; workers get three days off to hail year of the ox (M)
Now, Maoist austerity is treated as a bad memory, and the traditional festivities are back in vogue. 
For weeks people have been hanging silk lanterns and laying in food, firecrackers and gifts. 
By 3 P.M. Tuesday, nine hours before the Year of the Rat gave way to the Year of the Ox, everybody who could was slipping out of the plant or office and pointing his bicycle toward home.
Â 
Snow Slows the Traffic
It was a murky day, made duller by an unusually heavy snowstorm. 
By afternoon the sun was a limpid orange ball amid the smog, and the Forbidden City's fluted roofs hung mysteriously in the gloom. 
Everywhere bicyclists were skidding on the snow, and motorized traffic slowed to a crawl. 
Yet through it all there was a zest unmatched here at this season in years.
While Mao Zedong was alive the new year stole in silently, but at midnight all Peking and the region beyond, home to nine million people, erupted in a joyous cacophony. 
As the year 4683 on the old Chinese calendar began, spectators in a high-rise building looking toward the imperial palaces were treated to half an hour of booming firecrackers that lit up the maze of hutungs, or alleyways, that make up much of the city.
The official New China News Agency called it ''the most prosperous New Year ever.''
Along the city's main shopping street of Wangfujing, always crowded, sidewalks were thicker still with urban couples and peasants in from the country struggling out of stores with ''the four new big things'' - color television sets, washing machines, refrigerators and stereos.
Years ago, it was the ''eight treasures,'' less expensive things such as sewing machines and radios, that were most eagerly sought. 
But incomes have risen sharply under market-oriented economic changes, and the problem for many is not cash but supply.
At the One Hundred Varieties Big Building, Peking's principal department store, the newly appointed manager said recently that he could sell 10 times his quota of Japanese television sets, at $650 each, 18 months' income for a factory worker.
Â 
Leader Shuns the Limelight
On the whole the man behind the changes, Deng Xiaoping, has inverted the old personality cult, preferring to shun the limelight. 
But as the holiday began the association between Mr. Deng and the new prosperity showed through in some official quarters. 
A typical New China News Agency dispatch quoted a peasant woman aboard a train outside Peking as having credited Mr. Deng's ''flexible economic policy'' for her holiday well-being.
The woman was one of 600 million travelers expected to take advantage of the break, more than half the population. 
At Peking station, where officials were reprimanded for unannounced train cancellations that stranded 10,000 passengers overnight on Jan. 
1, workers were bracing for a surge of six million holidaymakers. 
Many of these will be peasants heading into town for festivities that have been revived for the first time in several decades.
Officials are expecting 800,000 people at an open-air ''temple fair'' at Ditan Park, site of the Ming dynasty's Temple of the Earth. 
The centerpiece of the Lunar New Year for centuries, temple fairs were proscribed in the 1950's.

There are consultants to advise on medical problems, traffic regulations and family planning, and magicians, comedians, wrestlers and bare-chested men competing in a nearly forgotten sport that involves tossing and catching a 30-foot bamboo pole topped with lanterns and bells.

As always in China, food is at the heart of the celebrations.

file: CHINA, TO RELIEVE UNEMPLOYMENT, GIVES PRIVATE SECTOR MORE LEEWAY.txt
text:

China today moved closer to becoming a mixed economy by formally acknowledging a need for more private enterprise to alleviate its chronic unemployment problem.
The country's two top policy-making bodies, the Communist Party Central Committee and the Government, proposed in a joint decision that new jobs be created increasingly by private businesses as well as by collective, or cooperative, enterprises.
The decision, reached Oct. 
17 but made public only today, signaled a change in the Communist Chinese position of the last three decades that the state owes every able-bodied adult a job.
''Under the state's overall planning and guidance,'' the joint decision said, ''people get jobs arranged by labor departments or get organized on a voluntary basis or find jobs themselves.''
China's Communist Party Central Committee and Government acknowledges need for more private enterprise to relieve nation's unemployment problemsDetails of New Program
In the decision, China's leadership asserted that the state-run and cooperative sectors would still constitute the basic form of economic activity in the nation but said they needed to be supplemented by self-employment ''within a certain limit.''
To encourage private enterprise, every self-employed person in China will now be permitted to have two helpers and five apprentices, according to today's announcement.
Originally, upon the Communists' takeover of China in 1949, private enterprise was permitted on a very small scale. 
An entrepreneur was allowed to employ only members of his family. 
About a year and a half ago, an entrepreneur was permitted to add two apprentices and later five apprentices in certain trades. 
The new decision, by allowing a total of seven employees, will help Chinese to set up larger retail businesses.
''Private business has resumed and expanded, but it still does not meet the needs of the country's national economy,'' said the decision, which was circulated today by The People's Daily and the New China News Agency.
Â 
Extent of Unemployment
Although the precise extent of urban unemployment is unclear, previous articles in the ideological journal Red Flag and elsewhere have suggested that about 10 million Chinese were unemployed at the end of last year, out of an urban work force of approximately 115 million.
The Chinese authorities had hoped to find 10 million new jobs this year, which would still leave about 4 million unemployed because that many people are expected to finish school and seek jobs. 
But indications are that there will be no more than 7 million new jobs.
Only 10 of China's 29 provinces, municipalities and autonomous regions have managed to find jobs for all those who left high school before 1979. 
Of the remaining 19, there are 14 that hope to reach that target by the end of the year, according to a report last month.
Facing a wait of several years for jobs, some young people have started devising their own work, initially by repairing bicycles, tailoring, taking photographs and other relatively simple neighborhood trades.
Â 
Preference for State Jobs
At the end of last March, more than 1.26 million Chinese had registered as self-employed, according to the General Administration for Industry and Commerce. 
Just over half of these were in the major cities. 
Canton, for example, has reported having 14,000 self-employed persons, 48 percent of them youths.
But more young Chinese seem to prefer jobs in the state sector, where they are guaranteed a job for life without having to work very hard. 
Recognizing this preference for what is nicknamed the ''iron rice bowl,'' the decision that was announced today urged that the new approval of private enterprise be widely publicized ''to allay people's misgivings.''
Private businesses have proved useful for China's leaders because they not only reduce the pool of unemployed but also provide services that state-owned businesses have been too inept or unwilling to provide.
The new decision also envisions a ''significant expansion'' in the number of cooperatives, in which workers form an enterprise and split the profits. 
These function much like cooperatives in freeenterprise countries. 
But young Chinese have sometimes been wary of joining cooperatives because their job tenure and pension benefits are not assured.
Â 
Helping People Find Work
According to the State Bureau of Labor, there are now 2,300 labor service companies helping young people in China to find temporary jobs in state factories or to set up their own cooperative enterprises. 
The new decision today proposes that more of these offices be encouraged.
A Chinese labor specialist, Kang Yonghe, reported last month that the labor service companies had found jobs for 2.35 million Chinese in more than 32,000 cooperatives.
In the joint decision, the Government and Communist Party leadership said that restrictions on private and cooperative enterprise should be changed and that self-employed people should be treated with as much political respect as workers in state enterprises.
But the decision added that self-employed and cooperative workers should accept state supervision and abide by the state's policies and laws. 
There was no mention of whether such workers would be included in the social welfare benefits that state-employed workers enjoy.
Â 
Peasants' Separate Status
The announcement does not appear to affect China's 800 million peasants, who live on communes and state farms, although Peking has also encouraged them to take more responsibility in the last few years.
China's leadership has attributed the unemployment problem to the radical leftist rule of the Cultural Revolution. 
During this period, from 1966 to 1976, schools were closed and millions of young people were sent off to work in rural areas. 
This created a tremendous labor surplus when they later returned home to the cities, and some have been sent back to the countryside.
In the last three years, Peking says it has found jobs for 20 million people.

file: China-South Korea Trade_ Boom, Yes, but a Quiet One.txt
text:
ï»¿
Chinese maps still show a single Korea, with its capital in the north. 
But these days map-makers and nearly everyone else in China are very conscious of Seoul and the rest of South Korea.
China and South Korea do not have diplomatic relations, but their informal relations are growing rapidly, even though such ties are largely unacknowledged. 
Trade is booming, and investment is beginning to rise sharply. 
Ships are moving cargoes between the two countries, and business executives and economists are exchanging visits.
Trade between China and South Korea will total $3 billion to $4 billion this year, about double last year's level and far more than the $513 million in 1987 trade between China and North Korea, economists have estimated.
Â 
Some Goods Move Directly
Most of the trade between China and South Korea is indirect, through Hong Kong and Japan, but Korean and Chinese sources say some South Korean ships flying Panamanian or Liberian flags go directly from the Korean ports of Pusan or Inchon to the Chinese ports of Tianjin, Lianyungang or Dalian.
Yet the relationships remain notably unofficial.
Behind an unmarked door in Beijing's Jianguo Hotel, for example, South Korea's Daewoo Group has been operating an unofficial office since July. 
It was set up as a vanguard for an operation that could include substantial investments in Chinese industry.
This summer Daewoo opened a factory in Fujian Province that is turning out 100,000 refrigerators a year, with output scheduled to double next year.
Â 
More Factories Proposed
Daewoo also is considering another refrigerator factory of the same size in Shandong Province, as well as two large factories that would make refrigerator compressors.
Daewoo would also like to invest at least $1 billion in a plant that would produce more than 300,000 automobiles a year, said Willie K. Park, who runs the Daewoo office here. 
Among the other projects Daewoo is considering, he said, are a giant petrochemical plant and a personal computer factory. 
The company is also studying the use of Chinese labor for construction projects abroad.
''We Koreans understand China,'' Mr. Park said. 
''You Americans come here, and you don't understand this stage of China's development, because it occurred a long time ago in your history. 
But when I was in high school in Korea, the situation then was like China is today.''
Two miles away, at the Beijing Hotel, a South Korean rival, the Samsung Group, has opened its unofficial outpost. 
Both companies' offices are staffed by Korean-Americans who use United States passports and nominally represent Hong Kong companies - actually subsidiaries of Daewoo or Samsung. 
Investments are also made in the name of Hong Kong or American subsidiaries.
More companies could follow. 
A survey by the Federation of Korean Industries suggests that 75 percent of South Korea's large companies might like to invest in China.
Â 
Embarrassment for Beijing
The blossoming relationships are something of an embarrassment for the Chinese Government, which refuses to recognize South Korea and speaks glowingly of its friendship with Communist North Korea. 
But North Korea has been closer to the Soviet Union than to China, and in the last decade China has appeared exasperated by North Korea's reluctance to liberalize its economic system as well as its foreign relations.
In April, on the birthday of the North Korean leader, Kim Il Sung, the Soviet Union gave him a new limousine. 
China was more frugal: its Communist Party leader, Zhao Ziyang, is said to have sent flowers.
Nevertheless, China is clearly trying to play down its economic dealings with South Korea and to keep them on an unofficial basis.
Ambivalence was shown when China allowed South Korean airliners to fly over China during the Olympics, extended the privilege to Oct. 
31 and ended it in November.
''The Chinese-South Korean relationship is developing very rapidly, especially in trade and maybe in sports and academic exchanges,'' said a Japanese diplomat in Beijing. 
''But in politics I think China will continue to pursue this very prudently.''
Although China has refused to let South Korea open a trade office in Beijing, it has proposed that South Korea and the nearby Chinese province of Shandong open reciprocal trade offices. 
The Koreans have not yet formally accepted this idea.
Â 
Provinces Pursuing Action
So far China has designated only Shandong Province to do business with South Korea, but Chinese and Korean sources say northeastern Liaoning Province may also have been quietly allowed to do so.
Other provinces are going ahead without Beijing's formal approval.
In addition to the refrigerator factory in Fujian Province, a South Korean-financed $10 million pharmaceutical plant is being built near Beijing. 
A delegation from Hubei Province visited South Korea this month to consider opening a trade office, and a delegation from the Chinese coastal city of Lianyungang is now in Korea for the same reason.
A Chinese official said some provinces had not been authorized to open trade offices and would be reprimanded if they did. 
The central Government has been trying to regain authority from local and regional authorities, which might make it harder for some of the provinces to advance their projects with South Korea.
But Shandong and Liaoning Provinces are likely to open offices in Seoul within a year, the official said.
China and South Korea ''would make a good fit,'' said Christine Wong, an economist at the University of California at Santa Cruz who specializes in China. 
As wages rise in Korea, she said, companies there are considering shifting some processing to lower-wage countries, including China. 
Also South Korean prices are lower than those in Japan or the United States, she noted, and the Koreans have international connections and marketing experience that the Chinese could find useful.
Â 
A Big Market but Difficult
South Korean business executives seem torn between awe at the magnitude of the potential Chinese market and apprehension about the difficulties of doing business in China.
''I was very happy as a tourist, but as a business investor I would be very cautious,'' said Kim Hiyong, the president of Tong-Yang Mool-San Inc., a Korean company that produces metal products from cutlery to farm machinery. 
Mr. Kim spent 25 days in China last month as part of a delegation looking for business opportunities. 
Chinese workers are not well motivated, he said, and there is a shortage of skilled labor.
Many South Koreans seem to hope for political as well as economic advantages from relations with China.
''In general, it is not wise to be hasty,'' Kim Young Sam, a Korean opposition leader, said in a telephone interview. 
''But improving relations with China and also the U.S.S.R. would simultaneously improve relations and dialogue with North Korea.''
Moscow is also establishing trade relations with South Korea.
Growing links between South Korea and China could also encourage further study of Seoul's economic strategy, which has some appeal in Beijing because of its mix of central planning and market incentives. 
Many Chinese officials and academics have visited South Korea recently. 
One of China's most influential economists, Wu Jinglian, was there.
One economist recently wrote in a South Korean magazine, ''This was my first trip to South Korea, and it impressed me in ways that will live with me for a long time.''

Alternatively, did Mr. Deng decide that Mr. Hu was not good enough to succeed him and return to a more active role?
Mao did this several times, removing his choices as successor and throwing China into turmoil.

''According to the experts, it was no problem for Chinese engineers to design the propulsion systems and aeromechanics of a rocket like the U.S. 
Honest John. 
The problem lay in the complicated electronics, precision instruments and sensitive meters.''
China responded to the Soviet rebuff by launching its own program. 
But Marshal Nie said the Russian attitude began to change after October 1956. 
Although he did not mention it, this was the time of the 20th Congress of the Soviet Communist Party at which Khrushchev denounced Stalin and began putting policies of his own into effect. 
The result was a 1957 meeting in Moscow at which Marshal Nie secured a Soviet agreement to assist in developing Chinese nuclear missiles.
Â 
Limited Aid From Russians
The Marshal said that the Russians were poor partners from the start, limiting their assistance to ''a few outdated missiles'' and other equipment that helped China but fell far short of a whole-hearted effort to pull Peking into the nuclear club. 
Moreover, the Marshal said, ''even this help didn't last long,'' and collapsed completely when the broader relationship between the two nations foundered amid ideological hostility in 1960.
''The Soviets wanted to leave China at a stage where we could only replicate what they made, keeping us dependent and several steps behind their own development,'' the Marshal said.
In the wake of the Soviet pullout and the food shortages of 1960, the Marshal said, the Politburo decided to cut back on other research programs and on conventional weapons spending to push the nuclear program.
The Marshal makes much of the speed with which Chinese scientists developed and tested the first atomic bomb, only eight years after first envisioning a nuclear program and four years after embarking on a all-out effort of their own. 
The explosion of a hydrogen bomb on June 14, 1967, meant that China had moved to the more powerful type of weapon in only three years, compared to the 10 years taken by the United States and the Soviet Union, he said.

file: CHINA_S BIRTH GOALS MEET REGIONAL RESISTANCE.txt
text:
ï»¿
A Communist Party official in Guangdong Province was dismissed from his job at a petroleum plant and expelled from the party recently for ''feudal thinking'' after he and his wife - they already had six daughters -tried once more to produce a son.
Elsewhere in this coastal province, two women were locked up for 15 days as ''sorceresses'' for inciting pregnant women at their farm commune to flee from family-planning workers. 
All but 9 of the 325 women with unauthorized pregnancies were later given abortions and intrauterine devices.
Those incidents, reported by the Canton radio, are but two skirmishes in a desperate battle that the provincial authorities have been waging over birth control. 
Harsher reports reaching Hong Kong last summer charged that thousands of pregnant women in eastern Guangdong were rounded up and forced to have abortions.
China's birth control goals are meeting stubborn regional resistance
Family planning officials deny that such Draconian tactics are being used. 
But they acknowledge that there is stubborn resistance among Guangdong's 58.8 million inhabitants to the national goal of a one-child family.
An expanding population is the biggest obstacle that China confronts in its push to modernize itself. 
With close to one billion people, China accounts for 23 percent of the world's population but has only 7 percent of its arable land. 
It is estimated that 30 percent of China's national income has been spent raising those born since the Communist takeover in 1949. 
China has adopted a stringent birth control policy. 
Yet a baby is born in China every two seconds.
With half of the population still under 21 years old, a worrisome new baby boom looms as more Chinese approach marriageable age. 
China hopes to hold its population to 1.2 billion by the year 2000, but national family planning officials like Chen Muhua have expressed apprehension over whether this target can be met.
Graced with a lush terrain and warm climate, Guangdong Province is one of China's three most densely populated provinces. 
Its population exceeds that of France, though it is little more than a third as large.
After Mao Zedong's assurance that a large population was ''a good thing,'' Guangdong reached a staggering 4.4 percent annual growth in 1962. 
This has since been brought down, but it still failed to hold to last year's goal of 1.3 percent, instead exceeding 1.5 percent.
Compared with a growth of 1.4 percent in all of China last year, the population of the United States rose by less than 1 percent and that of the Soviet Union by eight-tenths of 1 percent. 
The populations of all three countries have roughly doubled over the last 60 years, but only in China, because of the large number of people involved, has birth control been adopted as an official policy.
The population of China grew from an estimated 476 million in 1920 to 971 million in 1980, in an area of 3.8 million square miles. 
In comparison, the United States, with an area of 3.02 million square miles, had a population of 227 million in 1980. 
The Soviet Union, with an area of 8.6 million square miles, had a population of 265 million that year.
Â 
Incentives and Penalties
Discussing the continuing increase in population in China, Li Hanbo, the deputy director of Guangdong's family planning program, said:
''One of the reasons for a high growth rate is that we have too many families having three or more children.''
Last year, he said, only 27 percent of families took the pledge to have just one child, while 24 percent already had three children or more.
Local legislation augmenting the national family planning directives has given Guangdong some of the strongest incentives and penalties in China. 
Late marriages are encouraged, for example, and students who marry face expulsion from school.
Counties and municipalities set annual quotas for the number of babies who may be born. 
A couple wanting a child must apply for an allotment, with women who marry late getting first priority.
Couples taking the pledge to have just one child are issued pocket-size plastic-bound certificates entitling them to priority for housing and medical care and their child to free kindergarten, schooling and health care. 
If they have a second child, they must reimburse the Government for all the benefits and bonuses.
The system works best in the overcrowded city of Canton, where, Mr. Li said, ''90 percent of families have just one child and very few have three children.''
Â 
Mobilizing the Whole Family
In Canton's downtown district of Yuexiu, Huang Pei, the local family planning director, said that nearly 94 percent of the women of childbearing age were limiting themselves to one child. 
Consulting her small blue notebook, she noted that her district recorded 951 abortions last year, of which at least 80 were beyond the fourth month of pregnancy. 
Asked whether abortions were allowed even in the final month of pregnancy, she said, ''It happens.''
Miss Huang said her teams ''conduct painstaking and careful ideological work 10 or even 20 times on a person'' to dissuade a mother from having another child. 
''We mobilize everyone in the family, not just mothers and fathers but also brothers, sisters and so forth,'' the district director said.
Zhang Zhi, director of the Wuyang Electric Fan Factory, said his 263 employees of childbearing age had been allocated the right to have 18 babies this year. 
''We've had two so far, and five more women are pregnant,'' Mr. Zhang said. 
Among its other incentives, he said, the factory rewarded single children of employees with cash presents on holidays.
''In the countryside, the situation is just the other way around,'' sighed Mr. Li. Peasants have clung to a tradition of having large families to help them in the fields and to support them in old age. 
''The biggest problem is the old habits and customs of 7,000 years,'' explained Miss Huang. 
''They put too much emphasis on having sons.''
Â 
Undercut by Recent Policies
Mr. Li conceded that family planning had been undercut by recent changes in agricultural policy that paid farmers more if they produced more. 
In Guangdong, as elsewhere in China, this has made having children profitable again. 
Without the former policy of work points, Mr. Li said, ''production brigades and teams have no way to punish them if they have more children.''
He added, ''Farmers feel that the land belongs to them and children belong to them too, so they can have as many as they want.''
Peasants are tacitly allowed to have two children but not three. 
''Many families in the countryside want a second child if the first is a girl,'' Mr. Li explained. 
''Our provincial office shows great sympathy because they do have a practical problem. 
It is difficult for the family to manage if there is only one girl. 
We have not proclaimed this as a policy, but if it happens in the grass roots, we would not object. 
But if the second child is also a girl, they have to accept it.''
Mr. Li said family planning workers commonly spent three or four months persuading a couple not to have more children. 
''On the average, each person takes 10 times to be persuaded,'' Mr. Li said. 
''The most difficult person can take up to 100 times.''
On their visits, he said, some workers were cursed or even beaten up by peasants.
The authorities have been accused of playing rough in return. 
Last July, Zhengming, a Hong Kong publication sympathetic to the Peking Government, gave what it said were details of a ''ruthless struggle'' under way in Guangdong's Huiyang prefecture to cut the number of expected babies by 47,000.
Â 
Zeal of Local Officials
A reporter from Zhengming who visited eastern Guangdong reported how vigilantes abducted pregnant women on the streets and hauled them off, sometimes handcuffed or trussed, to abortion clinics. 
Other women, he said, were locked in detention cells or hauled before mass rallies and harangued into consenting to abortions. 
The reporter referred to ''aborted babies which were actually crying when they were born.''
Zhengming attributed such coercion to the zeal of local officials pushing to meet their quotas rather than to explicit directives from above. 
It noted that the ''desired results'' of achieving 47,000 fewer births went conspicuously unreported by Southern Daily, Canton's party newspaper.
Mr. Li said enemies of family planning had exaggerated or distorted the facts. 
He cited a case in Enping county in which two policemen hitched a ride with a truck carrying women off to a clinic to get contraceptives and this was ''misunderstood'' by spectators. 
In Dongguan county, he said, a young man, seeing pregnant women going off for abortions, had tugged at the arm of a plump friend, though she wasn't pregnant, and this joke started ''rumors.''
''There is no question of forcing pregnant women to have an abortion,'' Mr. Li said. 
''We first persuade them to take contraceptive measures so they will not produce more children. 
If they have just one child after marriage, it's reasonable. 
We deal mostly with couples having two children. 
After three children, we demand that they take sterilization measures. 
If they refuse, we must devote more time and more people to come to them.''
Â 
'A Few Stubborn People'
Mr. Li referred to ''a few stubborn people refusing to do what should be done, adding, ''If we don't take harsh measures, the majority would not be happy about it.''
Those with one or two children can have their wages cut 10 percent or more if they keep having children. 
There have been reports of recalcitrant couples having their electricity and water cut off. 
The authorities are even empowered to seize the family television set, bicycle or sewing machine.
''We set a time limit,'' Mr. Li said. 
''If they fail, the punishment will be upgraded. 
If some families can't afford cash, we will take away their property, because if we are not severe on these people, the majority will not be satisfied.''
Even so, he said, some peasants feel that the potential earning power of sons could offset any financial penalties.
Of some 7 million women of childbearing age in Guangdong, 600,000 had reported abortions last year. 
Unofficial estimates indicate that abortions exceeded the number of live births. 
A Canton physician told a foreigner of abortions being performed on the delivery table.
But a single or double intrauterine coil of stainless steel wire is the most prevalent birth control device. 
After being fitted at local clinics, some women have tried to take the coils out. 
In Longchuan county, Mr. Li said, one woman's husband tried to remove the device, and she began hemorrhaging so badly that she had to be rushed to the hospital. 
''We deliberately publicized the incident to warn other people,'' he said.
Â 
Sterilization Is Promoted
Attempts to promote sterilization have been more successful with women than with men. 
At the Daxin Handicrafts Factory in Canton, Zhang Yunfang, head of the local women's organization, said the factory director and the party secretary, both women, ''set a very fine example'' for the employees by undergoing sterilization. 
They were followed by 29 other women and one man.
''In the feudal system of imperial China, they had eunuchs in the courts,'' Mr. Li said. 
''So some men feel that sterilization will affect their sex life. 
The women also worry that their man's physical health will be affected.''
This year, the growth target for Guangdong is again 1.3 percent, slightly higher than the 1.2 percent national rate, and officials will feel even more pressure to meet it by whatever means. 
The alternative, officials like Li Hanbo point out, is a runaway population subsisting on resources insufficient to maintain, let alone improve, the living standard.
Mr. Li observed that it cost more to prevent a birth in Guangdong than to raise a rural child to the age of 15, an expense reckoned at about $865. 
The hope in the countryside, he said, is to get half of the families to have only one child and the rest not to have three or more.
''Though that's the case, the ideological work is still hard,'' Mr. Li said. 
''There are still cases of some families having four, five, six children and even more.''
Some party workers, he reported, ''say that we have had many difficult things since liberation, but this is the most difficult.''
