file: CHINA_S CAREER LADDERS ARE CROWDED BY GERONTOCRACY.txt
text:
ï»¿
Hao Jianxiu is a success story by any criterion. 
As a teen-aged textile worker in Qindao, she devised a spinning method that bears her name. 
Eleven years later, she graduated as a textile engineer and swiftly became deputy director of a factory. 
She also rose to prominence in the trade union apparatus, the Women's Federation and the Communist Party. 
Yet what surprises Chinese is not these accomplishments in themselves, nor even her positions as minister of China's textile industry and new alternate member of the Communist Party secretariat. 
It is that Hao Jianxiu has come so far so young. 
She is 47 years old. 
At such an age, many American executives and officials approach the top of the ladder, but not in China.
Some shifts have been detected in the makeup of China's new Central Committee but average age of members of ruling political bureau still remains above 70
The 12th party congress last month endorsed the need for younger and more vigorous talent, but the followup was less than sweeping. 
Ye Jianying, the chairman of China's nominal parliament, quoted Tang poetry in praise of youth. 
Then he hung on to his party posts, a doddering 85-year-old soldier who did not fade away. 
And the average age of members of the new ruling political bureau still is above 70. 
Normally, Mr. Ye, as de facto head of state, would play host to West Germany's President, Karl Carstens, who was scheduled to arrive in Peking today on an official visit. 
But because Mr. Ye is too frail for even this ceremonial role, the duties are being taken by his deputy Peng Zhen, who is only 80 years old.
China's gerontocracy has presented its pragmatic new leaders with a problem not so much of age as of outlook. 
The upper ranks of party and government remain clogged with old revolutionary veterans, intolerant of change and suspicious of technical advances. 
A plan to limit the tenure of ''leading party comrades'' was scrapped at the congress. 
Hu Qiaomu, a party theoretician, reported that after ''repeated deliberation'' it was decided not to set any strict age limit, ostensibly to ensure a stable transition to younger leaders.
Those who can offer most in China's industrialization drive, usually called intellectuals because they went beyond high school, have yet to recover fully from the persecution of the Cultural Revolution, when higher education was proof that the offender had cut himself off from the masses. 
The Guangming Daily recently revealed that less than 16 percent of the party's nearly 40 million members had more than secondary schooling. 
Discrimination against such people, it added, remained so strong that some intellectuals had waited up to 20 years for membership and it was not unusual for people to be admitted only after they were dead.
New Central Committee Members
Yet some shifts have been detected in the makeup of the new Central Committee, which functions as a sort of parliament. 
Well over half of its 210 full members, and 80 percent of its 138 alternate members, are newcomers. 
Professional expertise and relative youth are most apparent among the alternates. 
Li Bing is a top cancer researcher. 
Another woman, Ding Fengying, who is 39 years old, is a Deputy Governor of Hubei province in central China. 
Qian Xuesen is a specialist in rockets. 
Han Xu is a new Deputy Foreign Minister who negotiated the recent communique on Taiwan with the United States. 
Jiang Xinxiong is a 51-year-old expert in nuclear fuel and Deputy Minister of Nuclear Industry. 
Wang Meng, a respected writer, is hardly young but he has courted controversy with his literary outspokenness. 
Their prominence symbolizes a shift in priorities, but it does not necessarily follow that they will move up later. 
Only 15 of the new full members had been alternates.
Among full members, who wield more political weight, change is less apparent. 
At least 40 still came in uniform from the armed forces, while 35 others came from the policymaking state council. 
Of 29 provincial party secretaries, 21 are on the Central Committee. 
Nonetheless, the Minister of Culture, Zhu Muzhi, called the new Central Committee ''more revolutionary, younger, better educated and more professional.''
Two-thirds were under 60 years old, and only 16 were over 70, he said.
Predicting China's future leadership is risky, not only because of the system's secretiveness but also because the Cultural Revolution shattered so many rising careers. 
When Mao Zedong died six years ago, Deng Xiaoping was still in disgrace for having advocated the kind of pragmatism that is dominant now. 
Still, some new faces in the party's upper ranks are being taken seriously. 
One is Hu Quli, 53, who earned a reputation for vigor as the mayor of the industrial city of Tianjin. 
Mr. Hu now directs the Central Committee's general office, the party's administrative arm.
Another recent arrival, Qiao Shi, 58, held prominent jobs in the state-run iron and steel industry and is now director of the Central Committee's liaison department,
dealing with foreign Communist parties. 
Both came up through the Communist Youth League once headed by Hu Yaobang, the party general secretary.
But China has a long way to go in promoting its best and brightest into positions of influence. 
Chen Yun, a Politburo economic planner, warned the congress that unless the age gap was narrowed, ''the cause of communism may suffer a setback in China.''
But after urging promotion of more young and middle-aged functionaries, the 77-yearold Mr. Chen added a significant caveat. 
If it came to a choice between political reliability and professional competence, he said, ''we should pay more attention to the former.''

file: CHINA_S CATHOLICS RESTORE A CHURCH IN PEKING.txt
text:
ï»¿
The independent Chinese Catholic Church has restored a large 19th-century church in Peking, in time for use before Christmas, an Italian religious news agency said today.
An Vatican radio expert on Catholiism in China said the church would probably be used by the Patriotic Catholic Association, the group that was created by the Chinese authorities in 1957 to supplant the Vatican as the controlling body.
The religious news agency, Agenzia di Informazioni Missionarie, which is operated by missionary orders, identified the Peking church as the Church of the Savior, a large building built in 1887, and said that Catholics had collected money to install an organ.
The agency said it would be the third church to reopen in Peking in recent months as part of a more relaxed Government attitude toward Catholics.
The Church of the Savior was closed in the 1950's, and Maoist Red Guards used it as a warehouse during the Cultural Revolution, the agency said.
Â 
Gesture Toward Catholics
The Vatican radio expert said of the reopening, ''It could be a genuine gesture or it could be political, in the sense that the Government wants to demonstrate that there is religious freedom in China, or simply that it seeks the support of Chinese Catholics.''
The Vatican seemed at pains to portray the decision as a Government gesture toward Catholics, who have been treated more liberally of late, after repression during the Cultural Revolution. 
The Vatican radio said recently that 51 Catholic churches were reopened by the Chinese authorities last month in Fujian Province alone.
The Chinese Catholic Church broke with the Vatican in 1957 under Government pressure and now ordains its own bishops and priests. 
Rejecting the innovations of the Second Vatican Council (1962-65), the Chinese church still celebrates mass in Latin.
The Chinese Government's Religious Affairs Bureau, which supervises religious faiths in China, estimates that there are as many as three million Catholics in the country.
Pope John Paul II has rejected the contention of the Chinese church that it is Catholic, but he has said that he favors a warming of ties with China. 
He repeated that appeal in a special message to the Chinese people in July.
Â 
Taiwan Ties a Stumbling Block
Similarly, the Vatican has played down its links with Taiwan, presumably in the hope of eventually establishing ties with Peking. 
The Vatican's diplomatic relations with Taiwan have been a stumbling block to normalization of relations with Peking.
China has continued to crack down on priests and faithful suspected of maintaining ties with the Vatican. 
But recent developments have rekindled Vatican hopes for improvement.
There have been visits by Roman Catholic prelates to China, including discussions with leaders of the Chinese church. 
Last January, the Rev. Aloysius Jin Luxian, who long supported ties with Rome, was appointed Auxiliary Bishop of Shanghai.
In July, a Shanghai court released the Rev. Ignatius Kung, 84 years old, who was appointed Bishop of Shanghai by the Vatican in 1950 and spent more than 30 years in forced-labor camps after having been accused of anti-Government activity.
The Vatican's astronomical observatory recently signed an agreement of cooperation with China, including the transfer to a Chinese university of a telescope from the observatory at Castel Gandolfo.

file: CHINA_S CATHOLICS SEE LIFE THROUGH TINTED PLASTIC.txt
text:
ï»¿
A few colored windows cast glowing rainbows across the bare stone floor of the Xujiahui Catholic Cathedral in southwestern Shanghai. 
The windows look like traditional stained glass, but their panes have been fashioned from plastic by Catholic priests who made plastic umbrella handles during the grim years of the Cultural Revolution.
Militant Red Guards smashed the original windows. 
They pulled down the twin spires, too, destroyed the bells, burned the wooden altar and turned the Gothic-style cathedral into a food warehouse.
SHANGHAI - A few colored windows cast glowing rainbows across the bare stone floor of the Xujiahui Catholic Cathedral in southwestern Shanghai.
After official tolerance for religion was revived, repairs got under way in 1980 and services resumed. 
This Christmas bells chimed out from the restored 170-foot towers for the first time in 16 years as worshipers packed into the cathedral for mass.
Â 
Chinese Tradition Put First
The plastic windows, rebuilt from the materials at hand to evoke a more eternal beauty, are symbolic of the Catholic Church that has survived in China today.
''China's Catholic Church is working according to Chinese tradition first, then according to Catholic doctrine and to the Scripture,'' said the Rev. Shen Baozhi, a 57-year-old priest at the cathedral who also serves as secretary to Shanghai's 90-year-old bishop, Louis Zhang Jiasu.
To survive under Communism, the Chinese church broke with the Vatican in 1957 and since then has rebuffed overtures for a reconciliation. 
It functions under state auspices as the Patriotic Catholic Association, having consecrated over 60 of its own bishops without Rome's permission.
The State Council's Administration of Religious Affairs, which watches religion for the Peking Government, estimated that there were as many as three million Catholics and 700,000 Protestants in China, as many as when the Communists took over in 1949. 
This would still amount to little more than a third of 1 percent of the population.
Â 
Support for the Communists
Michael Fu @Tieshan, who was consecrated as Bishop of Peking three years ago, described his church's position of accommodation with the state in a recent interview.
''We believe in God but at the same time we are citizens of the republic,'' Bishop Fu said. 
''We support the Communist Party but of course we don't believe in atheism. 
We love the socialist motherland and our faithful contribute to the socialist construction of the country.''
In return for such loyalty, the regime of Deng Xiaoping has permitted 11 Catholic churches to open in the Shanghai area alone, where Father Shen says there are 100,000 practicing Catholics and 45 working priests. 
Two Catholic cathedrals draw worshipers in Peking. 
A 92-year-old cathedral in Canton that was also severely damaged by militants has just reopened.
In October the first Catholic seminary was set up at @Sheshan, outside Shanghai, with 36 young seminarians who needed parental permission to enroll. 
At a suburban commune near Peking six other student priests have been taking courses that include the Bible, Latin, English language, basic theology, liturgy - and politics.
Â 
Some Sympathy From West
Such freedom has been earned by rejecting allegiance to Rome. 
A new Constitution adopted by China's nominal Parliament this month reasserted the right of Chinese to ''enjoy freedom of religious belief'' but forbade its use for ''counterrevolutionary activities'' and, with the Vatican in mind, declared that ''no religious affairs may be dominated by any foreign country.''
Similar independence by China's Protestants has met some sympathy from Western Protestant churchmen like the Archbishop of Canterbury, who visited a Protestant seminary in Nanjing last January. 
But the schism between the Chinese Catholic Church and the Vatican seems, if anything, to have widened.
In June 1981, when Pope John Paul II appointed the Rev. Dominic Tang, a Jesuit who spent 22 years in Chinese jails, to the vacant post of Archbishop of Canton, the Catholic Patriotic Association rejected the move as interference in China's internal affairs. 
Last March it denounced the Pope for comparing the lot of Chinese Catholics with the persecution of the early Christians, with Bishop Michael Yang @Gaojin accusing the Pope personally of ''vicious slanders.''
An appeal by the Pope last month for a resumption of contacts between the Holy See and the Chinese church went ignored, as was a similar appeal last February.
Â 
Political Differences With Rome
Father Shen, talking in his cathedral study, mentioned the political differences with the Vatican. 
He noted that the Vatican still had diplomatic links with the Nationalist regime on Taiwan, though these are reduced to the level of charge d'affaires.
''After liberation,'' he contended, ''the Vatican ordered our Chinese Catholic Church not to love our country. 
According to the conscience of Chinese Catholicism and the spirit of God we cannot submit to the control of the Vatican.''
Chinese Catholic officials play down reports of an underground church maintaining allegiance to Rome. 
In an interview last year Bishop Ye @Yinyou of Canton conceded that one existed but that it was unimportant. 
Bishop Fu told a visitor this month that ''of course, there are a few people who are not clear about the relationship between the Vatican and themselves.''
But a middle-aged worker encountered near Shanghai suggested that a shadow church did exist. 
He was educated in a Catholic mission school, he said, and would not attend the Shanghai cathedral ''because it is against the Pope.''
Instead, he said, he and his Catholic friends held their own services at home. 
As for the religious climate, the man said: ''It is better now, but not entirely. 
I hope some day the church will be as free as in the United States.''
Father Shen, who was ordained in 1953, recalled what he and his colleagues endured in the Cultural Revolution. 
''Apart from our own suffering, the church was also damaged and the glass windows were broken,'' he said. 
''The Bibles and missals were taken out and burned.''
Â 
Priests Restored After '79
''With the beginning of the Cultural Revolution we were forced to stop holding services,'' Father Shen said. 
''Five of us priests got together and ran a small factory, producing Plexiglas umbrella handles to support ourselves. 
After 1979 we priests were restored to our original positions. 
So now we feel very happy and so do the other Catholics.''
Father Shen felt that it would be insulting to seek help from abroad, now that the Chinese church had severed its links with the Vatican.
''Catholicism came to China through the spirit of God,'' Father Shen said. 
''We don't agree with the idea that Christianity was brought in by foreign countries. 
It came not by the grace of foreigners, but by the grace of God.''

file: CHINA_S CATHOLICS_ A NATION UNTO ITSELF MOVES TO MEET THE VATICAN.txt
text:
ï»¿
Pope John Paul II, who has based his globe-trotting pontificate on finely tuned diplomatic acumen and pastoral compassion, is going to face a severe test of those skills as he pursues his ''heartfelt longing'' for closer relations with Catholics in China.
Encouraged by the fact that the Chinese Government is allowing churches to reopen and Christians to practice their faith publicly, the Pope closed his recent Asian trip by expressing a desire to heal the breach that has separated the Vatican and Catholics in China for more than two decades. 
He dispatched the Vatican's Secretary of State to Hong Kong to meet with the ailing Chinese Bishop Dominic Tang, presumably to discuss ties with Catholics in China.
But diplomatic visits may not be enough to reconcile the Vatican either with the estimated three million Chinese Catholics, nor with China's Communist Party leadership. 
For the past three decades, China's Catholics have existed in an anomalous situation. 
Their persecution by the party on one hand and their virtually unprecedented independence from the Vatican on the other have combined to create an almost distinct brand of Catholicism. 
A rapprochement with the Vatican will undoubtedly be complicated both by doctrinal and by political difficulties.
Vatican hopes to close brach that has separated Catholics in China
To many Chinese, moreover, the history of Christian missions is an unhappy tale of foreign domination. 
In the early days of the Christian mission to China, millions were converted to Christianity, but the church there remained tightly controlled by the missionaries. 
Of the 143 Roman Catholic bishops in China in the 1940's, only 20 were Chinese. 
During the early days of the Communist uprisings, missionaries were identified with the imperialism of Western nations, especially with America's ''gunboat diplomacy.''
Chinese animosity toward outside churches increased when millions of Christians fled the country after the 1949 revolution, and the Vatican urged Catholics who stayed on the mainland not to cooperate with the new Government. 
Later, the Government-sponsored Catholic Patriotic Association ordained bishops without Vatican approval. 
The Vatican censured the church in China and still considers those bishops ''validly, but illicitly'' consecrated.
At the same time, years of persecution and isolation, especially during the Cultural Revolution, forced Christians in China to develop an indigenous Christianity in a hostile environment. 
Regular public worship became impossible. 
Gung Binmei, the Vatican-appointed Bishop of Shanghai, was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1960, and is still in jail; meanwhile, the Vatican has refused to recognize Zhang Zhuishu, elected Bishop of Shanghai by the Chinese Catholics in 1960. 
Catholics continued to worship in Latin, unaware of changes in the church.
The official policy of Chinese Catholics is that the Vatican is responsible for the break in relations. 
When several Maryknoll priests met with the Bishop of Peking, Michael Fu Tieshan and other Chinese Christian leaders in January, a priest told the Rev. John Cioppa that he did not have ''gan ching'' - feelings of loyalty and affection - for the Pope, because the Vatican had ordered Chinese Catholics not to be patriotic. 
Further resentment is provoked by the Vatican's recognition of Taiwan.
Chinese Government officials and some Chinese Catholics also feel that foreigners are still meddling in their affairs. 
For instance, a pamphlet issued by the Roman Catholic bishop of Hong Kong telling Chinese Catholics how to celebrate the mass ''in situations of emergency and persecution,'' was seen as an attempt to interfere with the authority of bishops in China. 
Anglican Bishop Ding Guangxun, formerly head of the theological seminary in Nanking, told visitors this year that ''all missionary activities, including radio broadcasts beamed at China, are expressions of disrespect and unfriendliness.''
Clearly, both Christian and non-Christian Chinese are wary of anything that might tie the church to foreign influence. 
Bishop Michael (an irregularly consecrated bishop), responded coolly to the Pope's comments about closer ties and said Chinese Catholics would not surrender ''organizational independence'' to Rome.
But despite continuing tensions, both the Vatican and the Chinese feel the need to heal old wounds. 
Some Chinese Christians are actively seeking contacts with churches in the rest of the world. 
A delegation of Protestants visited the World Conference on Religion and Peace meeting in Princeton last year, and Chinese Catholics will be represented at a conference on the church in China in Canada this fall.
The theme sounded by Pope John Paul during his Asian trip was ''forget the past, look to the future.''
But he is likely to be extremely circumspect in his overtures to the Chinese Catholics. 
More than any other recent Pontiff, he knows what a church faces in a hostile society, having begun his own theology studies secretly in Nazi-occupied Poland. 
He may also know that if there is to be a rapprochement, it is likely the Vatican that will have to make the most compromises, such as endorsing the self-government of the Chinese church, or even accepting the bishops ordained without Rome's approval. 
Neither the Peking Government nor the Chinese Catholics - for reasons of patriotism or political expediency - are likely to do anything that would imply that the church in China is subject to Rome.
The Rev. Lawrence Murphy, M.M., president emeritus of Seton Hall University in New Jersey, who went to China with the Maryknoll delegation, agrees that future contact with Christians in China must be on Chinese terms. 
No one wants to repeat the missionary mistakes of the past, he said. 
Like many former missionaries, Father Murphy admits that the church did not always respect the values and beliefs it found in other cultures. 
''The mission enterprise was once colored by Western colonialism,'' he observed. 
''But today the view of mission in the world has changed.''

file: China_s Economy Takes Small Leap Backward.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's Communist Party Central Committee meets Monday to deal with economic problems that have grown increasingly serious since the country embarked on an ambitious program of restructuring its economy nearly a decade ago.
In the last year, as China has moved farther away from the Soviet model of socialism, the country has been racked by soaring inflation, bank runs by panicky depositors, corruption within the bureaucracy and a rising tide of worker unrest.
China's financial system is in disarray with an uncontrolled growth of the money supply, its currency is sinking rapidly in value against the dollar and a patchwork of free and controlled prices has created gluts in some areas and shortages in others for everything from industrial raw materials to daily consumer goods.
Salt, the most basic seasoning in Chinese food, is now being rationed in Beijing. 
Pork, sugar, eggs and cooking oil have been rationed for six months now and people in the capital are beginning to voice doubts about the benefits of the country's economic direction.
'There Are Problems'
''Of course there are problems,'' a Chinese economist said recently. 
''But to change from the old way to the new way has never been done. 
We are exploring a direction that nobody else has.''
These problems, however, have severely shaken China's leaders, according to Chinese academics who are familiar with policyy discussions, and the Communist Party chief, Zhao Ziyang, has lost some of his authority. 
Already, hints that the leadership will dramatically scale back various forms of economic experimentation and restructuring have appeared in China's press. 
The 175 members of the Central Committee who will meet Monday are to ratify this slowdown in reordering the country's economy.
Deng Xiaoping, the country's senior leader, told a group of Japanese economists this weekend that China's policies would be modified to cope with these concerns. 
''The difficulties we are facing now concern development and are different from those we had before,'' Mr. Deng was quoted by the official New China News Agency as saying. 
''The readjustment we are going through now is not a change of policy. 
Neither is it a change of development strategy. 
We are working out methods and measures for future progress after summing up our experiences and we are capable of overcoming the present difficulties, including combating inflation. 
The rate of development is now too fast.''
Â 
'The New Economic Order'
''The transition from the old economic order to a new economic order is now generally blamed to be responsible for most of the irregularities of Chinese society,'' China Economic News, a weekly review of economic and financial issues, said recently.
This new economic order, what China's newspapers are calling ''the new order of socialist commodity economy,'' has achieved much, particularly in recent years. 
The country's farmers, almost all of whom till their own land, are thriving. 
For the first time in Chinese history, farmers are benefiting from substantial economic growth. 
They are building new homes, buying consumer goods common in urban areas and are educating their children.
In urban areas, department stores are jammed with consumer goods, from televisions to refrigerators to cosmetics. 
Vegetables are available in the winter in the north and fish are sold at many inland markets.
What has invigorated agriculture is now being tried in other segments of the economy. 
But transforming the industrial, power, housing and service sectors of the economy into a system propelled not by planners but the efficiencies of the market has proved far more difficult than most Chinese economists had envisioned.
For the first time since China began this process, the difficulties of erecting a new structure while slowly dismantling the old are becoming manifest.
Â 
Industrial Growth Put at 17%
Industrial growth is continuing to roar along, with the rate of increase for the first six months of this year at about 17 percent, according to the State Statistical Bureau. 
But this growth, a level many Chinese economists believe is excessive, has fueled inflation and unhinged efforts by the central bank, the People's Bank of China, to impose discipline on the financial system.
Thirty-six percent more money was put in circulation in the first six months of this year than during the same period last year, a trend the bank hopes to end.
''With more currency in circulation, bank loans increased rapidly,'' the press agency reported. 
And, as inflation picked up, it said, ''people panicked.''
Much of the panic stemmed from the widespread belief that prices would, and indeed did, begin a steep climb for most consumer goods. 
Accustomed to relatively stable prices, China's urban consumers for the first time faced official inflation rates of 24 percent and widely acknowledged, but unofficial, rates closer to 50 percent.
Retail sales in many cities jumped 50 percent over those of a year ago. 
''As a result, the supply chain of goods began to falter and the amount of goods in stock became 'weak,' according to the statistics bureau,'' China Daily reported over the weekend.
Many economists, both Chinese and foreign, argue that a major element in any structural reform of the country's economy is the freeing of prices from centralized control so that goods and services are distributed by market forces. 
Mr. Zhao, the party leader, has pushed aggressively for what he calls ''price reform,'' regardless of the short-term pain it would bring.
But other members of the leadership have decided that uncontrolled inflation and the potential for urban discontent are problems too severe to continue with price reform at the moment.
Â 
Putting Off Price Reform
In a meeting this weekend with Valentin L. Pavlov, the chairman of the Soviet Union's State Committee for Prices, Yao Yilin, one of the five members of the Standing Committee of the Politburo said that any further freeing of prices would be put off for two years.
The prices of half of the raw materials, industrial and consumer goods and food - including grains, cotton and edible oils - are still subject to control, Mr. Yao said, according to the New China News Agency.
''China is not prepared to free the prices of these commodities, nor is it ready to restore the prices of those commodities that have already been freed from Government controls, because this is conducive to production and consumption,'' the agency quoted Mr. Yao as saying.
At the same time, China's currency, the yuan, has begun sinking in value on the black market. 
Last year, one dollar fetched about five yuan. 
Today, the same dollar is worth between eight and nine yuan.
Although the official rate of exchange, 3.7 yuan to the dollar, is fixed, the growing disparity between the official and black market rates has raised the concern of foreign investors, who are burdened with the artifical rate in computing their transactions with the Government. 
Effectively, foreign investors and traders who are bound to the official rates are paying double for Chinese goods.
Of growing concern to China's leaders as well is the mounting level of industrial unrest. 
Chen Ji, a senior official of the All China Federation of Trade Unions, said that there have been 49 strikes reported throughout the country in the first six months of this year with many more strikes probably going unreported.
''Since we have begun reforms,'' he said in an interview, ''we have new contradictions between prices and wages. 
Now factory directors earn more than workers, and some workers earn more than other workers. 
There are new problems we never met in the past.''

WASHINGTON, March 4 (Reuters) - Zhang Wenjin, a veteran of toplevel meetings between China and the United States, arrived today to take up his post as Peking's Ambassador to Washington.
Mr. Zhang is a former aide to Prime Minister Zhou Enlai and took part in the initial contacts with the United States that led to the signing of the Shanghai Communique in 1972.
Mr. Zhang replaces Chai Zemin, who had been Ambassador to the United States since 1979. 
On arrival at National Airport today, Mr. Zhang was met by Assistant Secretary of State Paul D. Wolfowitz. A State Department spokesman said such a greeting for a new Ambassador was ''not unprecedented.''
The two men met during Secretary of State George P. Shultz's trip to Peking last month.
Mr. Shultz said then that Mr. Zhang took part in all the Peking meetings and would be warmly received in Washington. 
Mr. Zhang, 68 years old, who is expected to present his credentials to President Reagan in a White House ceremony soon, speaks English and was formerly Ambassador to Canada and to Pakistan.
In July 1971 he flew with Henry A. Kissinger, then President Nixon's national security adviser, on his secret mission from Pakistan to Peking. 
That trip paved the way for Mr. Nixon's journey to Peking in February 1972 and the breakthrough in relations between the two countries.

file: CHINA_S GENIUS WITH VEGETABLES.txt
text:
ï»¿
FEI LO is the author of ''The Dim Sum Book: Classic Recipes from the Chinese Teahouse.''
Â 
By EILEEN YIN-FEI LO
V egetarianism in China is as old as Buddha. 
And the Chinese co ncept of elaborately arranged artistic banquets of many courses is as old as Confucius. 
Somewhere in time, felicitously and naturally, th e ideas came together. 
These days the vegetarian banquet, with beancu rd, vegetables and doughs artfully dressed to appear as something th ey are not, is common to such disparate parts of the country as Ca nton, Peking or Shanghai, whose cuisines are quite different.
One traditional center of vegetarianism is Hangzhou, whose name means ''City Across the Stream.''
Hangzhou is built surrounding the beautiful West Lake with its pavilions and palaces, its boats, its tree-shaded paths and gardens and its thickets of magnolias, camellias and azaleas.
Eileen Yin-Fei Lo discusses cooking vegetables the Chinese way
In the days when Hangzhou was a warm-weather resort for the wealthy of Shanghai, it had a tradition of specialty restaurants, a tradition that continues in a small way today, for it is in Hangzhou that one finds restaurants of many regions of China, including several fine Moslem eating places. 
It is in that city that the arts of carving melons and gourds into table decorations and arranging sliced foods on plates so that they resemble butterflies, roosters and birds flourish.
Hangzhou is also known for its restaurants serving temple food, the food of the Buddhist temples, vegetarian foods such as vegetables, soybean products and breads of grain.
One of these, more than 30 years old and perhaps its best, is the Spring Vegetable, on Yanan Street, just one short street away from the eastern rim of West Lake. 
On a recent trip to China I had the experience of eating in that restaurant a banquet that was as much an art exhibit as it was a meal. 
There were slices of beef that were actually kneaded dough, a fish constructed of mashed taro root, duck of bean curd and meatballs of minced vegetables. 
It was an artful feast, and a delicious one.
The Spring Vegetable is not the only vegetarian outpost in the resort city. 
Others include Kui Yuan Guan on Jiefang Road, justly famous for its vegetables and noodles; the Hangzhou Hotel Restaurant, perhaps the most sophisticated in the city; San Wai San inside the Hangzhou Botanical Garden, where the specialty is soup made with the vegetable called shuen chai, native to Hangzhou. 
But we were the first Westerners to come to the Spring Vegetable, we were told, and the restaurant wanted our banquet to be very special. 
And it was.
Much of the $30-per-person banquet was based on the soybean, one of China's most important staples. 
In most of the country it replaces the need for dairy products, providing more protein an acre, nutritionists tell us, than any livestock could produce. 
It is also quite versatile. 
The beans are seldom eaten as grown, they can be fermented, they can be ground into flour, they can be sprouted and those bean sprouts used as a vegetable accompaniment, they can be milled. 
When they are milled wet they form a spongy mass that when pressed dry and cooked become those bean curd cakes (called dau-fu by the Chinese, tofu by the Japanese) that are so popular these days. 
The bean curd skins are really a byproduct of boiling the soybeans, and are skimmed and dried and used often in soups.
The Spring Vegetable, just across the street from the Islam Food Shop, is a rather small restaurant, two floors high, and, like the majority of the restaurants in China, is somewhat short on decoration. 
It was obvious that the restaurant's effort goes into its food, which is as it should be.
We sat down around large round tables and after a sip of plum wine the first course came out. 
Actually it was a series of three cold platters of ''duck,'' ''chicken,'' and ''beef.''
Th e first was dried bean curd ski n rolled tightly and sliced across, dressed with sesame oil and quick ly deep-fried. 
It did indeed taste like pressed duck. 
The chicken w as likewise of bean curd skin, but skin that was rolled flat and then sliced so that it resembled slices of breast of chicken. 
The beef was a dough, kneaded, allowed to ferment, rinsed incold water, f lavored with anise and sugar and colored with dark soy sauce before frying. 
All the frying, by the way, was in peanut oil.
The second course was ''scallops,'' again made of fermented dough, flavored with garlic, vegetable stock and sugar and cut to resemble scallops. 
They were stir-fried with bok choy, the green stalk vegetable so widely used by the Chinese.
Three vegetable courses followed. 
First there were fresh bamboo shoots with soaked black mushrooms in a light soy sauce. 
Then came a chicken soup made of vegetable stock into which was put sliced bamboo shoots; then the soup was garnished with fresh roasted sesame seeds. 
Mushrooms and fresh water chestnuts in a thick sauce of soy and water-chestnut powder came next.
The sixth course was a platter of fresh bean curd cakes, their centers opened and filled with minced vegetables, and vegetarian spring rolls, filled with shredded bamboo shoots, mushrooms, water chestnuts and carrots. 
The skins of the spring rolls were made of dried bean curd.
The next dish was an imitation Chinese sausage, made of bean curd skins, tightly rolled, deep-fried, c olored wi th soy sauce and sliced diagonally. 
These were mixed with choy sum, a small stalk green vegetable, with sliced black mushrooms and fr esh tiny straw mushrooms.
Our palates were refreshed and sweetened with courses eight and nine. 
First came fresh sweet red dates coated with tapioca flour, then a sweet soup concocted of fresh water chestnuts cooked to tenderness, sweetened with rock candy and thickened with waterchestnut powder.
The highlight of the banquet was the 10th course: Our ''fish'' was presented. 
Its body consisted of taro root, (the poi of Hawaii) cooked until soft and seasoned with salt, pepper, sesame oil and sugar, then mashed. 
This was shaped like a fish. 
The head and gills were shaped out of fresh bean curd cakes. 
The tail and fins were finely cut dried bean curd skins. 
The aroma of the fish was nutlike (from the sesame oil dressing) and the platter was garnished with fresh, green coriander. 
It was a triumph.
The last two courses were almost anticlimactic, and would have been had they not been so good. 
There was a sub gum, which means a mixture of 10 ingredients, and it was sort of a reprise of stir-fried dried bean curd skins, slices of dough, vegetables and nuts. 
The finale consisted of a soup of fresh bean curd cut into small cubes, of vegetarian meatballs, chopped vegetables, bok choy and tiny fresh mushrooms.
That was to settle our stomachs, we were told, as were the cups of hot, steaming green tea, the Dragon Well tea for which Hangzhou is equally famous. 
It was altogether a splendid memory to take with us as we left on the train for Shanghai a couple of hours later.

One is the Po Lin Monastery on Lan Tau Island, a day trip by boat from Hong Kong proper, where Buddhist monks will prepare lunch (with advance notice). 
The second is the Chang Chung Koon Monastery in Castle Peak, the New Territories, outside of Kowloon, where Taoist monks do the same.

file: CHINA_S HIGH-TECH TROUBLES.txt
text:
ï»¿
UNABLE after a lengthy investigation to diagnose a malfunction in its $160,000 computer system, a Chinese institute in Shaanxi Province took the final, reluctant step of calling in a service engineer from Peking, 725 miles away. 
The American engineer, an employee of the small United States company that made the computer, quickly discovered the source of the problem: a rat. 
The animal had been foraying nightly into the computer room and chewing on a sensitive cable. 
The cable was replaced, the rat's droppings swept away and a six-inch-high wooden plank nailed across the doorway.
Then, because he was already there, the engineer was asked to take a look at one of the computer's terminals, which had not been acting just right. 
He removed the terminal's casing, leaving the power on to perform some tests. 
A cleaning woman responsible for keeping the equipment free of dirt was mortified to see dust clinging to the electronic circuit boards. 
She hurried over with a wet rag to wipe it away. 
The engineer recalls that he restrained her just in time to stop her from doing serious damage to herself and the terminal.
Lack of routine maintenance of American-made computer equipment by Chinese has led to forecast that Chinese will waste between $20 million and $85 million by noting taking care of computers they bought in 1984 (L)
This service call, made several months ago, was not all that bizarre by current Chinese standards. 
China has embraced computers virtually overnight, but the Chinese face bewildering problems in maintaining and getting used to them. 
''The average Chinese is simply not oriented to this technology,'' said a United States official here who monitors sales in this field. 
''It's like taking someone who's worked on a bicycle all his life and suddenly handing him a six-cylinder engine to work on.''
The Chinese and foreigners alike generally agree that technicians in China will ultimately be at least as good as anyone else at servicing computers. 
But in the short term, the problems of poor maintenance and underutilization are critical, given China's plans to buy billions of dollars worth of new computers in the 1980's, mostly from American companies.
China spent a conservatively estimated $425 million on foreign-made computers last year. 
A United States official here calculated that within three years of delivery the Chinese typically pay between 5 and 10 percent of the equipment's price on service that would be unnecessary if proper maintenance were practiced. 
The head of the China office for a large American computer manufacturer put the rate at 10 to 20 percent, by factoring in the costs of productivity loss suffered when a computer is down. 
Both put the corresponding percentage in the United States at well under 5 percent.
Put in their harshest terms, these estimates mean the Chinese are expected in the next three years to waste between $20 million and $85 million by not taking proper care of the computers they bought in 1984.
Official policy is to blame the Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976 for the nation's current technology lag. 
A recent Government book on modernization plans maintains that ''the 10-year turmoil stunted the intellectual growth of a whole generation.''
Whatever the root cause, the problem is vastly compounded by Chinese insistence - born of both personal pride and Government policy - on maintaining by themselves the computers they import. 
Then there are the other complications - outmoded but deeply ingrained work habits, training aimed at the wrong people, even China's climate.
LI YUXIANG, director of the General Office of the Computer Industry Administration, a branch of the Ministry of the Electronics Industry, conceded that maintenance is a ''big problem'' for Chinese computer users. 
To combat it, he said, the China Computer Technical Service Corporation (C.C.T.S.C.) - a Government agency with 3,000 employees - has set up 41 training centers across the country, with plans to build 10 more. 
The C.C.T.S.C. has service branches in nearly every one of China's 29 provinces, notes Mr. Li. The People's Daily, a Peking newspaper, puts the number of computer maintenance people in all of China at a scarce 20,000. 
For the most part, say foreign experts, their level of training is not yet high enough.
Representatives of computer companies here say that China's goal - to service its computers with its own maintenance corps - is unrealistic. 
They point out that relatively new buyers simply cannot be as efficient in diagnosing problems as the company that makes a particular model and regularly services it.
Chinese technicians sometimes have difficulty figuring out what to work on. 
''They will continue to take a minor problem and because they cannot diagnose it properly, they'll rip the whole machine apart,'' said a representative of an American computer company, who, like many officials interviewed for this story, asked not to be quoted by name. 
''That brings about many more problems than they ever started with,'' he said.
When they buy computers, and many other kinds of technology, the Chinese generally insist on receiving extensive service training from the manufacturer. 
But their intention is to rely on the manufacturer for service only when absolutely necessary.
The Chinese also tend to insist that any training they get from the manufacturer be conducted overseas because, in the words of David Fong, Hewlett-Packard's China sales manager, such travel is a ''lifetime opportunity'' for people who might otherwise never be able to visit a country like the United States or Japan. 
We've had people telling us they won't buy our computer unless they can have maintenance training in the United States,'' said a representative of another American company.
But this ultimate perk does not always go to the technicians who most logically should receive it. 
''Sometimes people who have nothing to do with computers are the ones sent overseas,'' said Mr. Fong. And one C.C.T.S.C. engineer said all his training in the United States was on an American computer model that he ''hadn't touched since returning to China.''
China's insistence on self-reliance even extends to a refusal, for the most part, to buy ''insurance contracts'' - special warranties that extend beyond a manufacturer's normal guarantees. 
Chinese customers are willing to spend ''tons of money'' for repairs, Mr. Fong said, ''but they cannot understand insurance buying,'' costly warranties that, he said, the Chinese view as buying only a technician's visit ''for chit-chat once a month to look everything over.''
Given the Chinese approach, many foreign sales representatives here say the best solution to the maintenance difficulties may be some sort of innovative contract that somehow combines instruction for the Chinese with warranty features that preserve a manufacturer's reputation.
WITH all this, there are also maintenance problems that are simply a reflection of poor operating conditions in China. 
Electricity here is subject to wide voltage surges and to blackouts, both of which can wreak havoc with computer systems. 
And the country can be extremely hot in summer or, in the north, suffer fierce dust storms when sands blow down from the Gobi Desert each spring. 
Chinese users are not always able to provide the special rooms and air-conditioning necessary to protect sensitive electronic equipment under such conditions.
Foreign experts here also cite the problem of old habits dying hard. 
For example, it is an article of faith, and the product of many long Government campaigns, that any machine should be turned off when not in use to save energy. 
Just as cars are frequently turned off when idling for more than a few seconds at an intersection, personal computers tend to be switched on and off many times throughout a Chinese workday. 
This wears down the equipment - and, according to most studies, does not save energy. 
But the practice continues, although most foreign officials here say that the Chinese have come around a bit and are at least leaving on their mainframe computers.
Apart from all these maintenance problems is the question of just how much use China is getting out of its computers. 
The Chinese have criticized themselves openly on this score. 
In an article last month, The People's Daily took up the issue, claiming: ''Many users buy their computers in a hurry without first making the necessary preparations and end up leaving their machines idle'' because they cannot find useful tasks for the machines. 
The article concluded that ''there is a serious wastage problem. 
. . Even according to optimistic estimates, only 50 percent of computers are in effective operation'' compared, the article maintained, with 98 percent in advanced nations.
There are anecdotes to support the newspaper's contention. 
An American salesman here recalls making a sales call to a Chinese institute and finding a $750,000 computer already on the premises - unused. 
The maker had gone out of business and the institute had neither the knowledge nor the spare parts to solve a repair problem. 
The institute bought a new computer from the salesman. 
It hums along next to the idle machine.
The Chinese have not, for the most part, been innovative with the machines they use, either. 
''In most other places of the world you might buy a computer for one or two reasons. 
Then two years later you are using it to do 16 other things,'' said David R. Keys, general sales manager of Control Data China Inc., a subsidiary of the Minnesota based Control Data Corporation. 
''I haven't seen much of that here.''
Mr. Keys and others say that the Chinese write very few of their own programs. 
They purchase them abroad, but often, for lack of funds, do not purchase the software updates that manufacturers periodically issue to help customers get optimum use out of programs they have already bought.
''Our level of application is comparatively low,'' acknowledged Mr. Li. He says that China is trying to solve this problem by distributing publications and organizing user associations.
Quite apart from trying to solve the maintenance problem, the Chinese are seeking to design and build their own machines. 
The Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party urged exactly such self-reliance in March, and China is planning a ''massive push in scientific and technological research to quickly narrow its technology gap with developed nations,'' according to China Daily, the English-language newspaper published in Peking.
Will they do it?
''Right now the Chinese are studying very hard,'' said a Japanese official with one of the large Japanese companies selling computers and telecommunications equipment here. 
But the consensus among foreign experts here is that for China - once the world's technological leader - self-reliance in computers is still decades away.

In a city bustling with high finance and low intrigue, Wang Guangying has drawn more than the usual curiosity. 
He heads the new Everbright Industrial Corporation, which is taking over a highrise floor in Hong Kong's gold-colored Far East Finance Center.
Mr. Wang, the brother-in-law of China's late President Liu Shaoqi, has described himself modestly as chairman of a private corporation set up to import millions of dollars of Western technology for China's modernization.
His genial refusal to disclose details about Everbright's assets and backers prompts an assumption that Mr. Wang is Peking's newest man of significance in town. 
His operation appears to be part of the latest Chinese strategy to keep Hong Kong prosperous by investing in its future.
China, alarmed by financial jitters that its claim to sovereignty over Hong Kong has touched off, is diversifying its economic presence in the city.
China, alarmed by the financial jitters that its claim to sovereignty over Hong Kong has touched off, is diversifying its economic presence while soft-pedaling its old threat to move in by 1997, when Britain's lease over most of the crown colony expires.
Â 
Mounting Indications Noted
''Infiltration has been heavy in recent years, but now it's coming to the surface,'' said one Hong Kong Chinese analyst.
''They're stepping it up, no doubt about it,'' a Western diplomat agreed. 
Mr. Wang, who brought some employees along from Peking, has said he also plans to hire Hong Kong Chinese for some jobs at Everbright. 
There have been other signs of increased activity besides the arrival of Everbright. 
China has spent $10 million to open another department store, in addition to several that already sell Chinesemade merchandise in Hong Kong. 
Kao Yunshan, chairman of the China Products Company, explained that the newest store was opened because ''it is China's wish to keep Hong Kong prosperous and stable.''
Wang Jianghua, who manages a textile subsidiary of the China Resources Company, a commercial concern run from Peking, said China was investing in the Hong Kong textile industry. 
Other Chinese officials said China might supply raw materials for a Hong Kong cement plant.
Â 
Visit From Shanghai Mayor
Wang Daohan, the Mayor of Shanghai, visited Hong Kong recently and paid a courtesy call on Sir Edward Youde, the crown colony's British Governor. 
Mr. Wang earlier had assured some Hong Kong journalists visiting Shanghai that their city could keep its market economy after China took over.
A Hong Kong newspaper, Ming Pao, reported from Shanghai that a trade official there had implied that China intended to encourage Hong Kong's prosperity by making investments and setting up factories in the colony.
China has long maintained a visible presence in Hong Kong. 
The Bank of China has a prominent building in downtown Hong Kong. 
The Hong Kong office of the New China News Agency operates like a Chinese consulate, representing mainland interests and issuing visas. 
Xu Jiatun, the former Communist Party chief of Jiansu province, was appointed director of the agency's office here last month, thus becoming China's ranking envoy in Hong Kong.
Â 
An Emphasis on Prosperity
In a panel discussion at the recent session of China's nominal parliament in Peking, Mr. Xu said, ''Both before and after the recovery of Chinese sovereignty over Hong Kong, appropriate measures will be taken to maintain its prosperity.''
The China Resources Company has handled deals in Hong Kong with mixed results. 
Last summer it became overextended in a major real estate project and had to sell the land back to the colony's government. 
Some Chinese provinces such as Guangdong and Fujian maintain their own trade offices in Hong Kong.
Hong Kong's economic stabilityII is important to China, which gets more than 30 percent of its foreign-exchange earnings through the colony. 
Each pronouncement from Peking on Hong Kong's future has set off financial tremors, eroding its profits.
The Hong Kong dollar has declined since last fall's Chinese-British talks on Hong Kong. 
The colony's currency plummeted 24 percent in relation to the United States dollar by early June, before staging a modest recovery.
Â 
Currency Accusations Made
Some Hong Kong economists accused the Bank of China of contributing to the slump by unloading local currency to buy United States dollars.
The bank's Hong Kong director, Jiang Wengui, denied speculating and complained that the Hong Kong government did not intervene in the currency market to stop the slide. 
He said that China's exports to Hong Kong, which exceed $5 billion a year, had lost 20 to 30 percent of their value.
Mr. Jiang's advice to shore up the Hong Kong dollar by dropping a withholding tax on local bank accounts was ignored by the Hong Kong authorities and was resented by some residents as interference.
Peking has avoided giving a timeta@ble for its takeover of Hong Kong. 
Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang said recently that the colony would be recovered ''at an opportune moment.''
A Chinese journalist in Hong Kong hinted privately that this could mean a delay until after 1997.
A dozen young Hong Kong professional people visiting Peking in May issued a statement to Chinese officials warning that, if China intended to take control in 1997, ''Hong Kong will lose its prosperity in a very short time.''

text:

China is displaying fresh irritation with the United States over what Peking feels is Washington's failure to bring about a quicker resolution of their longstanding differences on Taiwan.
Peking appears concerned that the abrupt resignation of Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. and Washington's preoccupation with the Lebanon crisis may be undercutting its efforts to get the Reagan Administration to end the delivery of aircraft and other weapons to Taiwan.
This unhappiness has become apparent in prominent articles in the Chinese press over the last week. 
The Chinese leadership also seems worried that conservatives in the United States are exploiting the vacuum created by Mr. Haig's departure to revive support for the Nationalist regime on Taiwan. 
Peking insists that Taiwan is a part of its territory and that the United States accepted this when it established diplomatic relations with China.
PEKING, July 13 - China is displaying fresh irritation with the United States over what Peking feels is Washington's failure to bring about a quicker resolution of their longstanding differences on Taiwan.U.S. 
Blamed for Strains
The recent articles, which appeared in People's Daily, Beijing Review, the magazine Fortnightly Talk and the Journal of International Studies, all blamed the United States for the strains in relations over Taiwan.
Taken together, they amount to the harshest criticism of the United States since before the visit of Vice President Bush early in May. 
Today, People's Daily devoted a full page to reprinting the 10,000-character article that appeared in the Journal of International Studies. 
The article ostensibly reviews American attitudes toward Taiwan over the last 140 years.
The article was also circulated in full by the New China News Agency, complete with 43 footnotes. 
It had already been excerpted in the last two issues of Beijing Review. 
Such historical scholarship is employed in the official press to give more weight to the leadership's views.
Â 
No Direct Comment on Haig
Though Peking has not commented directly on Mr. Haig's resignation, there has been apparent unease over the departure of a man whom one Chinese editor characterized earlier as China's best friend in the Reagan Administration.
The evident fear is that his successor, George P. Shultz, will concentrate on the crisis in Lebanon and other immediate problems, while neglecting the negotiations over the Taiwan arms issue that have gone on quietly through the United States Embassy here.
On Monday, People's Daily accused American conservative ''diehards'' of trying to undermine the talks and resurrect the old two-Chinas policy. 
The New China News Agency leveled similar accusations against the conservatives on Sunday.
Several Western diplomats here have noted that with a crucial Communist Party congress planned this autumn, China's foremost leader, Deng Xiaoping, may feel he is under mounting pressure from his own conservative critics to explain why his overtures to the United States have not halted its military sales to Taiwan.
Â 
Deng Could Force a Showdown
This could prompt Mr. Deng to force a showdown with Washington on the Taiwan issue, the diplomats speculate, to protect other vulnerable aspects of his foreign and domestic policies.
Today's article in People's Daily, as reprinted from the Journal of International Studies, charged that the United States had coveted Taiwan since the 1840's but had been too busy expanding across the American continent.
Japan's seizure of Taiwan in 1895 frustrated American designs and set the stage for the eventual conflict between the United States and Japan in Asia, the article said.
While the United States agreed that Taiwan would revert to China after World War II, it later began looking for ploys to control the island, the article went on. 
It charged that President Harry S. Truman used the Korean War as a pretext to send a fleet into the Taiwan Strait to prevent the island's reunification with China.
Â 
Taiwan Relations Act
With American influence declining in the world, the article explained, ''realistic United States statesmen'' changed their policy and acknowledged that there was only one China and that Taiwan belonged to it.
''It took the United States rather long to recognize such an obvious fact,'' the article said. 
''Nevertheless, better late than never. 
It is precisely on this point that China and the United States established diplomatic relations.''
However, it complained, some American politicians pushed through the Taiwan Relations Act, under which the United States kept supplying military arms, ''which means that it is unwilling to stop its interference in China's internal affairs.''
In a conclusion that capsuled the message, the article remarked: ''It is inconceivable that the Chinese people, who have paid such high prices for the ending of national humiliation, would tolerate for long the continuation of such a state. 
But it is conceivable what a difficult situation the United States will find itself in if it clings to its policy, which was already discarded in its heyday.''
Â 
Little Room to Maneuver
The future of Chinese-American relations depends on whether American policy makers are ready ''to learn from history, throw off their heavy burden and catch up with the tide of the times,'' the article ended.
Another commentary in Fortnightly Talk maintained that the visits of Vice President Bush and Senator Howard H. Baker Jr. of Tennessee, the majority leader, had produced no breakthrough on the Taiwan issue. 
It reiterated a contention made earlier by Chinese officials that ''there is not much room left for China to maneuver'' on a principle affecting its sovereignty.
While the Chinese hinted last spring that they might agree to seeing American arms deliveries to Taiwan phased out, the latest round of articles has not suggested any flexibility. 
China had formally protested the Reagan Administration's decision earlier this year to sell military spare parts to Taiwan but did not move to retaliate by downgrading diplomatic ties.
Peking has also signaled a chill in relations by reverting to its old characterization of the United States as a superpower together with the Soviet Union.
