file: CHINA_S LUXURY HOTEL BOOM.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Great Wall Hotel borrowed its name from China's ancient landmark and there the similarity ends. 
The operators of the new 22-story building, its exterior sheathed in reflective glass, say it is China's most modern hotel, which is hardly an exaggeration considering the state of hotels in this country.
The Great Wall Hotel, which opened the first 40 of its 1,007 rooms on Dec. 
10, is the biggest Chinese- American joint venture so far, involving an investment of $75 million and setting a new standard in the hotel boom in China.
The Westerners who descended on China after it opened its doors to foreign trade and tourism placed a strain on facilities that has yet to be resolved. 
Peking's Tourist Department reported last May that 456,000 tourists visited the capital in 1982, 2.4 times more than in 1978. 
Over the same period, Peking's hotel accommodations expanded by only 70 percent, to about 5,100 rooms.
Â 
Service Is Often Poor
At the height of the autumn season, tourists have been bused to other cities as much as 75 miles from Peking, or left sitting in airport lounges for lack of hotel space. 
Those who get into a hotel may confront bleak rooms, broken toilets, spasmodic hot water and indifferent service.
The reservation system is so chaotic that travelers seldom know where they will be billeted, and the hotel staff cannot tell callers who is registered. 
Restaurants and other facilities usually shut down early.
The dearth of comfort and courtesy has left a vacuum for foreign investors to fill. 
The pacesetter has been Peking's new Jianguo Hotel, a joint venture built by Clement Chen, a San Francisco businessman, for $22 million. 
The Jianguo, which looks like the Holiday Inn in Palo Alto, Calif., opened in 1982 and earned $1 million in its first 10 months.
Â 
Boom Spreads in China
A half-dozen other quality hotels, including the 2,000-room Lidu, are now under construction in Peking, and the demand has spread to other major Chinese cities.
Nanjing has the newly opened 37- story Jinling Hotel, with a revolving restaurant at the top. 
Canton's White Swan Hotel opened last February and a Hong Kong joint venture, the China Hotel, is expected to be completed shortly.
The Great Wall Hotel has tried to eclipse them with such novelties as an indoor swimming pool, a nightclub and a 24-hour coffee shop, as well as China's first computerized reservations system. 
The hotel's shiny steel pillars are reinforced to withstand earthquakes, and there is even a bomb shelter in the basement.
The Chinese employees wear sleek uniforms instead of the usual soiled white jackets. 
Their training program stresses knife-and-fork etiquette and the pronunciation of English tongue-twisters like cauliflower.
Â 
Ex-Bendix Official's Idea
The hotel was the idea of C. B. Sung, a Shanghai-born American businessman who was vice president of engineering and research for the Bendix Corporation until he resigned in 1974 and went into trade with China.
Through his California-based company, Unison International, Mr. Sung has advised or represented American clients like the American Motors Corporation, which has a $51 million joint venture to manufacture cross-country vehicles in Peking, and Parker- Hannifin of Cleveland, which invested $1 million to make rubber seals in China.
Mr. Sung, who has degrees from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the Harvard Business School, conceded, ''I know nothing about hotels, except for having stayed in them.''
But he saw the potential for a luxury hotel in China.
He joined with the Becket Investment Corporation, based in California, to create the E-S Pacific Development and Construction Company. 
As its chairman, he signed China's first joint-venture agreement, in October 1979, to construct the hotel in partnership with the Peking branch of the China International Travel service. 
The $75 million cost was financed through a consortium of Western banks led by the Nordic Bank of Scandinavia.
Â 
Dispute Over Construction
Problems developed after the ground was broken in March 1981. 
The American side favored a fast approach, in which construction pushed ahead while the detailed drawings were completed and materials purchased and shipped. 
This upset the Chinese side, which wanted the project to move in tidier stages.
Because of what was euphemistically called an incompatibility between Chinese and American construction practices, the American engineers were dismissed and the Chinese took over.
Mr. Sung declined to discuss the infighting. 
''This project has many problems like any pioneering project, so I don't need to rehash them, but I think we have learned a lot from them,'' he said.
The hotel met the Dec. 
10 deadline by opening the coffee shop and part of three guest floors while construction continued on the rest of the building.
The prices are the highest of any hotel in Peking. 
A double room ranges from $110 to $160 a day - three times what some other major hotels charge. 
A small pizza in the coffee shop costs up to $7, and a premium Scotch in the bar, up to $5. 
The customers pay because such treats are generally unavailable in China.
Â 
'Top People Are Spoiled'
Mr. Sung felt that the comparatively high prices would not deter Western businessmen. 
''Frankly, America's top people are spoiled,'' he said. 
''How can you ask them to stay in a hotel where they don't feel comfortable?''
In any case, the limited rooms are already full.
The secret of success in the hotel joint ventures lies in efficiency. 
The Jianguo Hotel, thanks to its smooth management by the Hong Kong Peninsula Group, has become the most popular with Peking's Western expatriate community.
By contrast, the more elegant Fragrant Hills Hotel, which was designed by I M. Pei, has deteriorated only 14 months after its opening. 
Its marble floors are scuffed and dirty, glass panels are smudged, and bathroom fixtures are broken or missing.
Mr. Sung felt that the emphasis on staff training would help the Great Wall Hotel avoid such pitfalls.

file: CHINA_S NO. 1 DEPARTMENT STORE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Once it was called Dai Sun and it was the biggest, most lavish department store in Shanghai, and therefore in China, rising 10 stories above Nanking Road, Shanghai's busiest, most Westernized shopping street.
The quality of its goods was impressive, its counters piled high with cigarettes from all over the world, Cuban cigars, American made cotton shirts, Swiss watches and German fountain pens. 
Its all-Cantonese staff, by all accounts, would have done Gucci proud with its studied haughtiness.
Today its name is No. 1 Shanghai Department Store. 
It is one of a postrevolution collection of 10 stores scattered throughout the city of 11 million and the closet thing in China to Bloomingdale's. 
In prerevolutionary days, Dai Sun was perhaps the most famous of four Shanghai department stores operated by the Cantonese-owned Sun Company. 
Today the others are the Numbers 2 through 4 Shanghai Department Stores.
Profile of China's No. 1 Shanghai Department Store
The giant rooftop red calligraphic neon sign reading, "Shanghai First Store," can be seen from most parts of the city, and the imposing granite building dominates the avenue of 300 shops, many of them Western feeling.
Though the store's most avidly watched attraction might be a collection of Sony television sets, radios and stereo equipment in a display window at the intersection of Nanjing (as Nanking is now spelled) and Zhejiang Roads, it carries few imports except Japanese radios, appliances and watches. 
Instead its five selling floors are stacked with Chinese-made goods ranging form kitchen hardware and ready-to-wear clothing to bicycles and sewing machines. 
The store is a one-stop introduction to one aspect of Chinese urban life because of its concentration of thousands of goods and thousands of people in a limited space.
On our trip to China, we had, in several cities, sought in vain for small, child-size versions of dark blue, quilted Mao jackets and for children's blouses. 
They were difficult to get, we were told. 
Sold out, we were also told. 
But Mrs. Ying Lai-Chu, our China International Travel Service guide, told us, "If you cannot buy it in peking, wait until Shanghai."
She was right. 
We bought blue cotton Mao jackets for our children for about $10 each and other items as well, including beautiful bolts of silk and embroidered silk scarves that would have been $50 or more each in the United States. 
We paid less than $10 and enjoyed walking around the cavernous place, which is open seven days a week form 8 A.M. to 8 P.M. It employs 2,200 salespeople and serves an estimated 100,000 customers a day, 200,000 on Sunday and national holidays.
The No. 1 Department Store has a cosmetics counter on the first floor where lipsticks in a variety of colors are displayed, and there is a Chinese-made brand of perfume called Butterfly. 
That first floor, or street floor, is the busiest, and it teems with customers everywhere. 
Some push, some wait patiently. 
Some shout. 
But the clerks are unfailingly courteous and helpful, and it is almost always possible to find somebody who speaks English.
Â 
* * *
Also on te first floor are T-shirts and jogging outfits with "Shangahi" printed in English across them, not very stylish ready-to-wear clothing, bed lines and blankets, sweaters and children's clothing, plain shirts, trousers and hats of what appear to be good quality cotton. 
The souvenir shirts and athletic outfits cost about $2 to $4 each, and souvenir duffel bags are about $5.
In the basement are bicycles. 
There seems to be a steady demand for the black-painted basic bicycles of China in Shanghai, which has three bicycle factories and two million bikes on the road. 
There are also sewing machines, radios, television sets and wristwatches hard by rows of decorvative thermos bottles and white enameled chamber pots. 
Most of the appliances are inexpensive by American standards, but, being in the $50-to$100 range, they are something the Chinese have to save for. 
They are intriguing to look at but not to buy. 
Chinese elcetrical current is not compatible with ours, and on a more esthetic level the appliances are a bit rudimentary.
Back on the first floor is the food, generally canned and dried items, favorit eChinese teas such as green Dragon Well, balck Bo Lei and lichee, Jasmine along with candies, biscuits and cookies. 
There is liquor such as Ng Gah Pei, a potent rice-based drink and the equally strong grain-based Mao Tai as well as Shao Shing wine and various brands of plum wine. 
United States customs rules forbid importing foodstuffs, but many Chinese products are available in the United States today, so if you must take home a culinary souvenir, try a tine of tea for under $1.
In the old Dai Sum there were elevators and escalators, as well as stairs, but the escalators were not working when we were there.
The store's second floor is stacked with bolts of cloth, brightly colored cottons, some of those lovely silks we bought and samples of the growing women's ready-to-wear clothing.
Men's clothing is on the next floor, along with women's overcoats and shoes for both. 
Most Americans, I would think, would reject most of the clothing on stylistic grounds, but women might have some interest in high, stiff-collared blouses of cotton or silk. 
There are no changing rooms for trying on clothes, but we noticed sales clerks carefully measuring customers before selling them garments.
The fourth floor is a vast housewares center with stacks of aluminum cookware, rice cookers and services of porcelain in various patterns including reproductions of such export-ware, the originals of which are much in favor among antiques collectors. 
There are also individual cups, bowls, dishes and platters and glassware.
Â 
* * *
When we inquired we were told it would be no trouble to pack dinner sets for shipment to the United States. 
Though much of this ware would be tempting to people interested in Chinese cuisine, the idea of carrying home a cast-iron wok from Shanghai just to save a few pennies does not make much sense. 
My wife did, however, find some decorative vegetable cutters that are not available in the United States. 
They cost about $2 each.
The price for a Canton ware look-alike 192-piece service for 10 was a bit more than $300, which we thought rather inexpensive, considering the number of pieces, We were told that the same porcelains were available in the tourists-only Friendhsip Stores at slightly higher prices.
The top selling floor, the fifth (the upper five floors are offices and storage space), was our favorite. 
It is the sports department. 
There are basketballs and soccer balls, sweatsuits and colorfully trimmed athletic clothing. 
This floor also contains the stationery department, with paper, inks and brushes used in calligraphy work, and there were children's toys, which are becoming increasely available in China.
The fifth is also the place for crafts. 
There are carved wood statues, jade and other stone carvings, decorative silk screens and wall hangings and examples of carved blackwood furniture. 
The furniture pieces are generally poor copies of antiques, but the painted silk screens are nice and range in price from $35 to $400.
We were told that prices are the same for identical items throughout China. 
This is not always so. 
Duplicates of a small pair of tables, which we had bought in Suzhou, were arrayed along the top of a display case and were more expensive than those we had bought. 
But generally the prices were about the same for the usual tourist purchases of such items as new cloisonne enamels, souvenir small-size hooked rugs and carved figurines. 
So comparison shopping should not be a major exercise, but it would not hurt to compare.
It is easy to buy. 
All items are marked with prices. 
You decide what you wish and notify a sales clerk. 
They roam about the store, write an invoice, take your money, deliver a copy of the invoice to a clerk who gets the merchandise, wraps it and delivers it to you - all rather quickly.
The No. 1 Department Store is always crowded - with customers, with gawkers, with foreign tourists - which is what makes it so interesting. 
Even for those who are just gawkers.

file: CHINA_S PRIESTS, STICKLERS FOR LATIN, DISAVOW VATICAN.txt
text:
ï»¿
Five masses were celebrated this morning in Holy Mary, Mother of God Cathedral, as has happened every Sunday since it reopened in November 1979. 
Hundreds of Catholics attended each mass, and many remained for religious instruction,
But the Catholicism that has come into the open again, after 13 years in the wilderness created by the Cultural Revolution and the ''Gang of Four,'' as the long historic period is called here for short, is no longer Roman.
Its priests, the youngest of whom are in their 50's, regard themselves as having been rejected by the Vatican and go their own way in a schism that the Vatican has preferred not to discuss in public. 
The Catholic Church in China no longer recognizes the authority of Rome and the Pope; Chinese priests regard themselves as ''holier'' than the Pope in ignoring the teaching of the Second Vatican Council (1962-65) and continue to sing the mass in Latin.
Article discusses Catholicism in Shanghai'Nothing Against the Doctrine'
''We do everything according to the spirit of the church and the Gospel,'' said the Rev. J. Berchmanns Sheng Pao-tse, speaking the now rusty French that all four of the cathedral's parish priests learned from their French Jesuit teachers.
Father Sheng, like the other priests here, is traditionalist not only in the language of the church but even in Chinese. 
The priests do not favor the Pinyin style of transliteration, which the Government has made official.
''We do nothing against the doctrine and ecclesiastical tradition,.''
Father Sheng said. 
''But the Vatican does not allow us to love our country,''
''Even before the liberation,'' he said, referring to the Communist victory in 1949, ''the Vatican said Catholics were not allowed to read our newspapers and Catholics should not go to work with the Government. 
The church teaches that you must love your fatherland and family.''
Â 
Pope's Speech Disparaged
The Vatican maintains diplomatic relations with the Nationalist Government in Taiwan, Father Sheng explained, and ordered priests here not to cooperate with their Government. 
He said he had heard about the speech of Pope John Paul II in Manila last month inviting a dialogue with China but added disparagingly: ''The Vatican speaks well, but we do not see real facts. 
The tongue is one thing, facts another.''
Despite the nationalism of the Catholic hierarchy, led by a conference of about 30 bishops under the direction of Bishop Aloysius Chang Kia-shu of Shanghai, who is 89 years old, the church suffered heavily during the Cultural Revolution and ceased to function. 
Bishop Chang, who was appointed after the break, is not recognized as a bishop by Rome, and the December 1979 consecration of the Bishop of Peking, Michael Fu Tieshan, was held invalid by the Vatican because the prelate was elected by parishioners.
Red Guards ransacked all churches, destroyed missals and priests' vestments, broke stained-glass windows and profaned the buildings by other uses. 
The 40 priests of the city and the nuns were driven from their parish houses and convents and put to work making umbrellas from 1966 until 1977. 
The missals, vestments and other religious objects that priests use today were hidden by parishioners; the clerical collars they wear are of soft cloth because the usual material is no longer available.
The priests said that the Government had made complete amends. 
''All churches are really free in China,'' Father Sheng said. 
Some of those attending mass today, including a small child, were wearing crosses. 
Last Christmas season, said the Rev. Joachim Lie, 17 people in their 20's received long-delayed baptism and about 20 children first communion.
Â 
Some Priests Are Jailed
A seminary is being prepared in Peking, the priests said, and for the first time priests not to be ordained by the Roman church will be trained. 
Not all Chinese priests accepted disobedience to Rome, Father Sheng conceded.
''After the liberation a few priests were against the Government and the country,'' he said. 
''They were put in prison, but after their release they were still against Government and country. 
I knew some of them, bit I don't know where they are now.''
Asked whether he appproved of the jailing of priests, Father Sheng said: ''These people stood against the law and the doctrine of the church, so they were punished and should have been. 
But we are Catholics, so we pray that God will help them repent for their sins.''
Father Sheng asserted that last year a French priest from Hong Kong visited and circulated a printed letter in Latin and Chinese signed by Agnelo Cardinal Rossi, prefect of the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, calling on priests and laymen not to attend church but to worship in secret.
Â 
Church Still Owns Properties
''The responsibility for the complicated situation is the Vatican's, not ours,'' said Father Sheng. 
He estimated the number of Catholics in China at three million. 
The church still owns extensive properties here, he said, and recently received from the Government full payment for arrears in rent accumulated during the Cultural Revolution and the ''Gang of Four,'' which are being used to pay for the renovation of the cathedral and other churches.
Protestant churches are also returning to life. 
A West German tourist reported that he was so jammed into a tightly packed, fervently singing flock of thousands this morning that he could not leave when he discovered that he, a Catholic, had entered a Protestant church by error. 
But the houses of worship whose congregations have disappeared, probably forever, serve other purposes. 
The many domes of the Russian Orthodox Church bear the wounds of crosses broken off, and the synagogue is a music conservatory.
Asked whether he thought Catholicism and Communism were compatible, Father Sheng shook his head and said: ''In China, we Catholics are not Communists. 
They are atheists.''

file: CHINA_S SONGBIRDS AND PEOPLE HAVE NEW REASONS TO SING.txt
text:
ï»¿
It is 5 o'clock on a misty, dewy and unusually placid August morning. 
Old men in shorts are filtering into city parks to walk their birds and young boys are crouching in the first high grass in decades in search of crickets.
As the old men walk, they swing hooded bamboo cages back and forth, left and right, simulating for their imprisoned songbirds the effect of the wind on a branch of a tree. 
To keep its balance, a bird must flex its muscles as its cage swings, thus getting exercise for singing.
James Sterba comment discusses return of leisure activities in China after Government authorized recreational pursuits for people
The boys part the grass in search of brownish-black crickets which will, when properly stimulated, fight one another. 
The proper stimulation, the old men tell the youngers, is a single mouse whisker carefully fitted into a shaved end of a chopstick.
These are traditional pursuits of leisure in China, and this summer they are the sunrise preoccupation in thousands of cities and villages across a land which, once again, has authorized leisure pursuits. 
After 32 years of what can only be called deep seriousness, a certain frolicsome spirit has returned.
With the Gang of Four dispatched to prisons for their heinous rule during the Cultural Revolution, with Mao Zedong relegated to a revised role as fallible mortal, and with Deng Xiaoping's subordinates in firm, if not entrenched control, the relaxation might seem logical.
It does not, however, seem permanent. 
There is already talk of repression of writers and artists, a renewed assault against recalcitrant Communist Party hacks and a revised campaign against a basket of evils, which will include anything the senior party leadership feels threatened by or simply does not like. 
In short, a crackdown by the party - whose 39 million dues-paying members make up a 4 percent minority of the population - looks inevitable.
But meanwhile, there is a marvelous new sensation in China of people goofing off instead of secretly loafing. 
Instead of hiding in back corridors and snoozing during lunch hours, workers are organizing card games and basketball games.
Theories about Chinese workers lacking energy are being quickly revised. 
In some city jobs, at least, workers do what they wish in their time off without fear of punishment. 
They are capable of enormous bursts of energy and enthusiasm. 
The animation and muscle used to slap a lunch-hour ace down on a card table - no gambling, of course, is allowed, wink wink - suggests that after 32 years of communization and force-fed dogma, there is still a lot of Chinese left in China's population.
A scientist walked into his office a few weeks ago and was told that he and his wife were going on a 10-day vacation at the nearby ocean resort city of Beidaihe. 
He is in his 50's and had never taken a vacation - unless, he jokes bitterly, one counts the 10 years he was forced to work as a peasant. 
His wife, from Shaanzi Province, had never seen the ocean. 
They had a wonderful time, and when they came back, he volunteered the following about China's current leaders: ''They're about the best we can expect. 
They're our best hope right now. 
I can't think of anybody who would not be worse.''
A bitter skeptic had become hopeful and grateful. 
He says he expects the party will resort to its methods of using fear to run his life, but this summer, at least, he is not so sure.
Listening to the old men who hang around the free markets where eggplants are sold and in the shade of the new highway underpasses where stories are swapped, one can learn a lot of cricket lore. 
Although revisionists say that two crickets can be provoked to fight each other by tingling their antennas with a mere feather, old connoisseurs of cricket fights contend that a mouse whisker is the only proper instrument of provocation.
Because most people could not afford the luxury of a mousetrap 30 years ago, getting a mouse whisker was not easy. 
A man who now works in a profession says that as a boy he lured an occasional foolish mouse under an old powdered milk can propped up by the end of a shoetree and baited with meat. 
He and his friends would quickly turn the can right side up and half fill it with water so the mouse couldn't jump out. 
They grasped the mouse with two sets of chopsticks, holding it up, and attempting to pluck out one or two whiskers.
The old men insist that cat whiskers are too stiff to work on cricket antennae. 
But youngsters won't listen, then and now, so there are a lot of stories about children trying to pluck a whisker from the family cat and ending up scratched.
Neither the keepers of crickets nor the keepers of birds would think of opening the cages and letting their prize pets scurry or fly away. 
The Communist Party, likewise, however loose and secure it feels this summer, is not likely to let its charges out of control. 
But in the summer of 1981, the cages at least seem to be getting larger.

file: China_s Trade Surplus Reaches a Record High.txt
text:
ï»¿
China registered a record $4.6 billion trade surplus last year, according to preliminary official figures released today.
The figure was more than three times the $1.4 billion surplus announced in October for 1981, and with China's considerable invisible earnings from services should mean an even bigger balance of payments surplus, according to foreign economists.
PEKING, Jan. 
29 (Reuters) - China registered a record $4.6 billion trade surplus last year, according to preliminary official figures released today.
The Government-run Economic Daily, quoting preliminary working statistics from the Ministry of Foreign Trade, said imports fell by 12.8 percent in 1982 to $17 billion, while exports rose by 3.5 percent to $21.6 billion.
The big surplus was in line with forecasts by foreign economists, who were expecting a drop in imports as a delayed effect of China's economic retrenchment program launched in 1979.
This policy change prompted cancellation or renegotiation of several major foreign contracts for heavy industrial equipment. 
The trade surplus has already led to rapid growth in China's foreign exchange reserves, which more than doubled in the 12 months ending last September to $9.23 billion.
China announced late last year that it planned to increase imports by one quarter in 1983 and Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang recently unveiled the long-overdue 1981-85 economic plan that provides for imports to grow faster than exports and for a $2.5 billion trade deficit in 1985.
But the sharp fall in imports last year meant China's total foreign trade decreased by $1.8 billion to $38.6 billion in 1982, a fall of 4.4 percent after an annual growth rate of nearly 30 percent in the previous three years.

file: CHINA_S UNHAPPY CHOSEN_PROTESTS REVEAL AN UNSUSPECTED DISCONTENT AMONG ELITE YOUTH AND FEARS ABOUT F.txt
text:
ï»¿
The pro-democracy demonstrations by university students over the last several weeks have revealed a depth of discontent among the elite of China's youth that was unsuspected until now.
That university students, the chosen young, should demonstrate in such numbers in favor of political principles closely associated in the minds of Chinese with the non-Communist West, particularly the United States, has raised disturbing questions among many here about the direction of economic and political change in China.
The largest rallies were in Shanghai last weekend, where close to 50,000 people were estimated to have gathered on Sunday alone. 
But they also occurred in Beijing and about half a dozen other cities. 
Today there were reports that 3,000 students demonstrated in the port city of Tianjin to show their solidarity with the Shanghai protests.
Marches in Province Capitals
In the provincial capitals of Hefei and Wuhan, several thousand students marched under banners calling for greater democracy and freedom. 
They also protested university living conditions, which are primitive by Western standards.
Students in Hefei in particular derided the elections to the local legislative people's congress as a sham, saying they did not even know the candidates they were supposed to vote for as student representatives. 
As the protests continued, local leaders agreed to postpone the elections to give the students an opportunity to run their own candidates.
But it was the five days of demonstrations in Shanghai that were the most visible sign of widespread student discontent. 
Even in the beginning, the demonstrations were large, with more than 10,000 students marching. 
Quickly, the protests grew until more than 50,000 students were packed into People's Square in downtown Shanghai.
Students carried banners with the words ''Freedom'' and ''Democracy'' in passionate red brush strokes.
Many of the students interviewed during the Shanghai protests, while unable to describe in any sustained fashion what they meant by greater democracy, fervently argued that they had no control over their lives and that the Chinese people had no say in how their country was run.
Repeatedly over the last year, China's top leaders, including Deng Xiaoping, the senior leader, have said political ''reform'' would accompany China's economic restructuring, a process that has drawn much of its character from Western economic and financial models. 
But, uneasy about the implications of political reform - a widely used but only vaguely defined term that seems to embrace some form of decentralization in economic and adminstrative decision-making -the leadership has stressed that real political change will take two or three decades to achieve.
Â 
Economic Controls Loosened
The economic liberalization, a loosening of central controls over the economy so that individual enterprises are free to prosper or flounder on their own without state support, is intended to envigorate an economy that functioned in only the most rudimentary sense in the three decades until 1980. 
Now, companies go bankrupt, raise money through stock issues and dismiss workers for incompetence, practices inconceivable just a few years ago.
Even the party theoretical journal, Hongqi, has urged that the work of John Maynard Keynes be explored. 
''Whether one is a Marxist or a non-Marxist,'' the journal said, ''and whether one is a supporter of Keynsianism or its opponent, one needs to study the doctrine of Keynsianism.''
But with this shifting economic orientation, many intellectuals have insisted that responsibility in the workplace must be accompanied by rights in the political sphere. 
If people are allowed to take individual risks for economic gain, they should also be able to express their views individually, and collectively through some form of electoral system, on the country's political direction.
In 1979, when a hint of intellectual liberalization surfaced, there was a brief explosion of free political expression that became known as the Democracy Wall Movement, named for wall posters calling for democratic rights that were plastered on a wall in downtown Beijing. 
Although at first endorsing the movement, Mr. Deng quickly reversed himself and ruthlessly suppressed it, jailing its leaders for ''counterrevolutionary acts.''
That crackdown, while firmly consolidating Mr. Deng's power over the party ideological apparatus, succeeded in cowing China's intellectuals.
Â 
Easing Controls on Intellectuals
But Mr. Deng was aware that he could not successfully increase China's openness to the West while intimidating the country's intellectuals, the very people needed to propel the country out of its economic backwardness. 
So in the last five years he has gradually eased controls on intellectuals. 
Indeed, there is now virtually nothing that cannot be discussed in academic journals, according to many intellectuals.
''Nothing is taboo,'' said a young graduate student at Beijing University who is a regular contributor to the journal Reading Books.
But even as this intellectual liberalization proceeds in the highest reaches of university life, the absence of substantive liberalization in the daily lives of Chinese has become increasingly apparent to students on Chinese campuses. 
Students have no decision in who their representatives to student councils are, have no role in picking student candidates to local people's congresses, a sort of local legislature, and no freedom to chose where they will work after graduation.
A professor at Beijing University said the Government could not react harshly against the students.
''What can they do?'' he asked. 
''If they attack the students, no one will ever trust them again. 
They cannot be committed to intellectual freedom on the one hand and attack students calling for democracy on the other.''
At the same time, many students realize the fragility of their positions, that university administrators can ruin their lives through bad job assignments upon graduation. 
As the demonstrations petered out, many students explained the calm by citing such pragmatic considerations over their future.
Â 
A Warning in Editorials
For the Government, of course, those concerns and the threats it can make to enhance those concerns are its best hope for containing future protests.
Today, for instance, China's leading newspaper, People's Daily, and other major newspapers warned in front-page editorials that those who deviated from Communist Party policies would ''have to eat their own bitter fruit.''
People's Daily noted Mr. Deng's efforts this year to ''invigorate party and state organs, bring into play the initiative of grassroots units and the masses, overcome bureaucracy and increase efficiency.''

file: China_s Waters And Mountains Of Eternity.txt
text:
ï»¿
The river forms a green gauze belt, the mountains are like jade hairpins.Â Â Â -Â Â Han Yu, a Tang dynasty poet
Â 
I'D timed my visit to coincide with the flowering of the osmanthus trees. 
So when I arrived in Guilin on a moonless night in early October after a one-hour flight from Hong Kong, I smelled the city of my forebears before I saw it. 
Even as I stepped off the plane, the pervasive sweet-orange scent made me shut my eyes both in reverie and in anticipation of what daylight would bring. 
The next morning, and every morning thereafter, I threw open my bedroom window to intoxicate myself, first with the delicate fragrance that suggested that I was in the Forest of Osmanthus Trees, as Guilin is translated, then with the unearthly scenery that convinced me that I was.
I was staying in my grandmother's house, a dignified half-timbered two-story brick and stucco house - sort of Chinese Tudor - that she had built in 1941 as a wedding present for my parents. 
Around the house ran a high, thick wall into which was built a row of small rooms that traditionally had no place in a Chinese house: a storage room for coal, a privy, a washroom with new shower, a kitchen and a larder. 
With the advent of modern plumbing, two bathrooms were installed inside the house, and my grandmother's home had the distinction of being the first in Guilin to possess Western-style toilets. 
Above and beyond the wall lay Guilin's totally improbable, impetuous mountains, some of them right in the middle of the city. 
I could see two of them from my bedroom terrace: to the left, Folded Brocade Mountain rose in layers of soft greens, grays and violets, like so many quilts piled one on top of the other; to the right, set on the river bank, the straight, proud shaft of Wave Restraining Hill was more than sufficient to contain the tranquil Li River, almost at a standstill now that it was the dry season. 
My grandmother had her house built close to and equidistant from the two mountains, not only for esthetic reasons but also for practical purposes: both contained caves that were natural air-raid shelters when the Japanese bombed Guilin during the Sino-Japanese War and World War II.
As I was a member of the four generations of Lis who lived under her roof, there was always a cousin, aunt or uncle to accompany me up some of the more famous limestone towers thrust up from their seabed 300 million years ago and carved to their present-day configurations by centuries of erosion. 
Luckily, the most famous had steps, requiring walking rather than scaling. 
So after a substantial breakfast of mi fen (rice noodles, a Guilin specialty), a cousin and I joined the crush of visitors - mostly Chinese from other provinces and several Americans and Japanese - who poured out of their tour buses to partake of the forces of nature from the pinnacle of Folded Brocade Mountain.
FROM its pergola-topped summit, Guilin's shan-shui - its otherworldly mountains, lakes and rivers - seemed straight out of a Chinese landscape painting. 
Scores of rocky crags and peaks soar straight up without warning from the verdant plain. 
The jade-green Li River meanders among them, dotted with rickety houseboats and the narrow bamboo rafts of fishermen using cormorants rather than nets to catch fish, looking like floating matchsticks from such a height. 
Gardens, walkways and pergolas embroider the edges of Banyan and Fir Lakes, all reasons why Guilin has for centuries been the destination of Chinese painter-poets in quest of immortalizing on silk, paper or stone the ''fragment of eternity'' to be found here.
Based on its dreamlike karst scenery, an abundance of myths and legends have grown up over Guilin's 2,000-year history, examples of which my cousin took pleasure in pointing out. 
Brooding yet indomitable, Old Man Hill sat facing away from the city in the direction of the sea, awaiting the return of his unfilial son. 
Piercing Rock's gaping hole was the result of a general's arrow shot in a contest of strength that re-established the allegiance of a rebellious tribe to the emperor. 
A kindly elephant who deserted the emperor's ranks to help Guilinese plow their fields during a time of famine dipped his trunk into the Li River to quench his thirst and is commemorated as Elephant Trunk Hill. 
I climbed Elephant Trunk Hill alone one morning, passing by the small Buddhist reliquary tower on its summit, the hilt of the sword thrust into the elephant's neck by a vengeful general. 
Taken altogether, the mountains of Guilin, one of China's major tourist cities, were once stones carried from central China by conscripted laborers to fill up the South China Sea. 
The laborers got only as far as Guilin, and the ''stones'' have remained here ever since, making Guilin the epitome of Chinese landscape when in reality it is a landscape unique to Guilin.
Guilin's importance as a commercial and cultural center began in 214 B.C., when the first Qin emperor built the nearby Lin Canal - one of the longest canals in the world and used today as an irrigation aqueduct - to connect the Yangtze and the Pearl Rivers, thereby establishing a north-south route for military transport and trade. 
From the Ming Dynasty (A.D. 1368-1644) to the 1950's, Guilin served as the capital of Guangxi Province, which, in southwestern China, was far from Beijing's administrative authority and cultural influence. 
Headquarters of an American Air Force unit in World War II, Guilin was described by Theodore White, then a foreign correspondent, as ''the most lovable and abandoned city in the Orient. 
For intellectual Americans there was always good conversation; for Americans of a more earthly sort there were women.''
For a group of Chinese liberals who took advantage of the province's reputation as a traditional thorn in authority's side, Guilin was a shelter from which to irritate Chiang Kai-shek's central government. 
For most of its history, Guangxi has been known for four things: its extreme poverty, its aversion to authority, the quality of its fighting men, and as a way station for opium shipments passing from India to neighboring Guangdong Province. 
Given the rebellious nature of Guangxi, it is not surprising that the Taiping Rebellion, which hastened the downfall of the decadent Qing Dynasty, began here, nor that the Northern Expedition, which my grandfather helped lead, had its starting point in the then capital of Guilin.
Even after the success of the Northern Expedition, which ostensibly stamped out warlordism and unified the nation, Guangxi, dissatisfied with the policies of Chiang's Kuomintang government, threatened more than once to secede. 
Even today the independent-minded province, a great many of whose inhabitants are members of several ethnic minorities, the largest of which is the Zhuang, is officially known as the Guangxi-Zhuang Autonomous Region.
IF Guilin's shan-shui as seen from its mountaintops seems straight out of a landscape painting, by riverboat it is a slowly unfurling horizontal scroll. 
The Li River cruise should not be missed, even though the return bus ride is long, bumpy and positively noxious with diesel oil fumes. 
It starts in Guilin, whose ''landscape is the best under heaven,'' and wends its way to Yangshuo, 50 miles downstream, a town that vies with Guilin for this accolade. 
Because it was the dry season, our boat didn't dock under Elephant Trunk Hill, the usual site, but at Yangdi, an hour away by bus. 
Here, where the hillocks resemble the horns of a goat, we threaded our way past vendors on the shore selling Mao caps and coolie hats, pomelos and panda bear pins, then past those on the river, their slender rafts loaded down with little bags of mandarin oranges or woven bamboo handbags, to reach our awaiting vessel, revving its engine and jockeying for position with a dozen other boats, all impatient to be on their way.
Once we had weighed anchor, river life flowed past like scenes from time gone by. 
Tiny villages of several houses apiece dotted the shoreline at distant intervals. 
A fisherman in a graceful bamboo boat sat motionless in the shade of a tall cliff waiting for a bite or more likely just to pass the time. 
A woman washed clothes by slapping them on the pebbly shore, while a throng of children played in the water, slicing it with their hands to see if the spray would reach our boat. 
A more serious youngster guided the family water buffalo into the river to give it a refreshing bath and a meal of duckweed from the river bottom.
The Chinese imagination takes pantheistic pleasure in giving a life and spirit to inanimate things, so our boat was fairly buzzing with botanical and zoological comparisons. 
Each twist and turn of the river, each new vista that appeared around the next bend, besides evoking sighs of delight or amazement, elicited a game that peopled the ''stone forest'' on our flanks with geological flora and fauna: here a mountain shaped like an apple, there a rock that looked like a turtle basking in the sun, and directly ahead Mural Hill - nine horses that nature had painted on the sheer face of a cliff, each in a different pose, though I could see only three with certainty.
BY midday, exercising our imaginations had whetted our appetites, and we scrambled down from the deck for lunch. 
Guangxi Province is renowned for the unusual animals - scaly anteater, bamboo rat, masked civet - that make their home in this hinterland and find their way onto restaurant tables here and in cuisine-conscious Guangdong. 
The highlight of our meal, however, was a quite commonplace though unquestionably fresh fish I had seen thrashing about in a net dropped over the side, hauled aboard just as our river safari got underway, and cooked in the tiny al fresco kitchen at the stern.
Green Lotus Peak, looking exactly like its namesake, announced our arrival in Yangshuo, a small but growing town that capitalizes on its proximity and resemblance to Guilin. 
Shaking out our sea legs, we followed winding paths lined with shops selling the usual scrolls and paintings, crocheted sweaters from Shanghai and embroidered nappery, ceramics and curios. 
Evidence of ''spiritual pollution'' abounded. 
Joanne's, a restaurant whose sign was written in English, invited us to try their ''best Irish coffee,'' while another establishment offered, also in English, a ''feast of menus - aren't you lucky!''
But the most interesting sign in our wanderings through Yangshuo, and certainly the most beautiful, was the single bold Chinese character emblazoned onto the side of a cliff: dai, which can mean many things, including bring and wear. 
The calligraphy is exquisite, a combination of painting and writing. 
Chinese calligraphy is, in fact, abstract painting, composed of structure, composition, rhythm, movement and balance and requiring of the calligrapher both tranquillity of mind and spontaneity of execution. 
''The artist must nourish in his heart gentleness and cheerfulness,'' a classic on Chinese calligraphy reads, ''the ideas must be harmonious. 
The heart should be quiet, honest, and sincere to the utmost, then the various aspects of human gladness and sorrow and every other thing, be it pointed, oblique, bent or inclined, will appear naturally in the mind and be spontaneously brought out by the brush.''
Some say the dai of Yangshuo comprises eight strokes; some say as many as 14. 
No one knows who put it there, or when. 
It was the attraction of these ambiguities - particularly after the straightforwardness of Yangshuo's appeal to the tourist dollar - that lent the huge ideogram a good part of its charm.
But it is not from Guilin's unearthly peaks or on the Li River's blue-green waters that one gathers a sense of the region or comes to feel the city's rhythm, but on the streets of the city. 
One morning at dawn, I walked along the Li River Promenade on my way to watch Guilin's elders practice the ancient art of tai chi in the small acacia-shaded park midway up Wave Restraining Hill. 
In the still-blue light of early morning, Guilin was alive with other forms of athleticism: people jogging, skipping rope, playing badminton, pedaling bicycles or huge tricycles that pulled wagonloads of people, produce, coal, bamboo or scrap iron. 
The trickle of cyclists became a steady stream as I entered the campus of Guangxi Teachers College, which in the 14th century was the palace of the emperor's nephew.
In the center of the campus, in the center of town, solitary Single Beauty Peak rose 306 knee-bending steps above Guilin, offering the sheerest climb, highest point, broadest and, after Folded Brocade Mountain, most breathtaking view. 
By midmorning I found myself on Zhongshan Street, the main thoroughfare and shopping street, where I bought a stone seal incised with my Chinese name, following the Chinese custom, albeit belatedly, of choosing one's mingzi, or first name, at the threshhold of adulthood according to one's own philosophy or experience. 
Still following the bicycle traffic, I crossed Floral Bridge, the tile-roofed and many-arched Song Dynasty beauty that leads to Seven Star Park. 
Inside the park are caves whose walls are lined with stelae that look like stone newspapers but really are poems carved in rock by visitors, dynastic and contemporary, inspired by Guilin's beauty. 
Deeper inside Seven Star Cave, stalactites and stalagmites re-enact the drama of Guilin's karst scenery above. 
The theatrical effect of colored lights ''coaching'' the rock formations to appear to be what they already resembled seemed melodramatic, besides robbing the imagination of a different interpretation. 
The same was true for Reed Flute Cave, a 15-minute motor scooter ride into the lush paddy fields and even higher peaks outside Guilin. 
According to legend, this technicolored grotto is a fragment of a heavenly crystal palace built at the beginning of time and hidden so that mortal eyes might one day gaze on it.
But after Seven Star Cave and the Li River cruise, I'd had enough of comparisons and associations, however apt, and wanted to see things as they were. 
The streets of Guilin were the place to find them. 
By late morning every thoroughfare wide enough for the simplest conveyance was a cacophony of bleating truck horns and ringing bicycle bells, a swollen river of cyclists unperturbed by close encounters with heavier transport and oblivious of pedestrians who ventured out into each intersection and managed each street as though it were a dare and an obstacle course combined. 
Such maneuvers would have been even more hazardous had the women's feet been bound, a former northern practice that the women of Guilin never had to tolerate.
I HAVE never seen, not even in Sicily, life lived so openly, so completely in the public eye as Guilin lives its daily life. 
For lack of adequate living space, personal life spills into the street in an almost Bruegelesque intensity. 
It is on the street that many Guilinese cook their midday meal and eat it as well, that they wash their dishes as well as their clothes, hanging clothes on ropes strung between trees to dry. 
Seamstresses hunched over treadle sewing machines make or repair clothing on the street; cobblers affix heels and soles on the street; bed quilts are sewn and shown to clients there; mattresses are dragged out of doors for a thorough wash and rinse there. 
Even the storefronts have no fronts: open barber shops, restaurants, pharmacies, shops of all kinds abound, testament to China's infatuation with private enterprise.
Toward dinnertime, the roads become passable; the populace retires indoors; the tinkle of bicycle bells sounds like music rather than a threat, and the mountains again predominate. 
For all the people who spill out of their Lilliputian dwellings onto the sidewalks and streets in daylight hours, Guilin seems smaller than its 400,000 population would suggest. 
Despite the influx of visitors and continuing construction of new buildings and repair of old ones, Guilin remains curiously rural. 
Even the several hotels, the three-stage 800-room Ramada Renaissance Hotel being the newest of the lot, do nothing to alter this impression. 
It is as if the primeval mountains that surround the city and rise right in its midst, like sentries, guard it against the march of progress elsewhere, preserving its aura of timelessness.
Â 
FLIGHTS, LODGING AND DINING
Â 
Getting There
Â 
C.A.A.C., the national airline, has direct daily flights to Guilin from major Chinese cities, such as Beijing, Shanghai and Canton. 
From Hong Kong there are daily flights via Canton on C.A.A.C., direct charter flights, and direct flights three days a week on Dragonair. 
There are also rail connections to Guilin from Beijing, Shanghai, Kunming, Zhanjiang and Nanning, as well as boat and bus service from Canton and Hong Kong.
Â 
Where to Stay
Â 
Several first-class hotels have been built in the last two years to help cope with the enormous influx of foreign visitors.
Ramada Renaissance Riverside, Yuanjiang Road; telephone 2611. 
Opened late last year, this 334-room hotel on the Li River will have 800 rooms and a shopping arcade when its two remaining phases of development are completed this year. 
The hotel has a heated indoor swimming pool, health club and Chinese, Continental and Japanese restaurants. 
A room with two double beds for double occupancy costs from $95 to $105; for single occupancy the rates are from $83 to $95. 
Reservations through Ramada Worldwide, 800-272-6232.
Holiday Inn Guilin, 14 South Ronghu Road; 3950. 
Situated in the center of town on Banyan Lake, this 259-room hotel has a ballroom, health club, banquet hall and telex. 
A double room, double occupancy, costs from $80 to $90; single occupancy is $75. 
For reservations call 800-465-4329.
Guilin Riverside Resort, Anjiazhou Road; 2291. 
This 236-room hotel with a river view from every room has both Western and Chinese restaurants, a swimming pool, tennis courts and a shopping arcade. 
A double room, double occupancy, costs $65 to $75. 
Direct reservations or through a travel agent.
Li River Hotel, 1 Shanhu Bei Road; 2881. 
Remodeled in 1986, this 360-room hotel is in the center of town on Fir Lake. 
At 14 stories one of the highest buildings in Guilin, it provides spectacular views of the surrounding landscape and has been the city's major tourist hotel for years. 
The price of a double room is $65 to $75. 
Direct reservations or through a travel agent.
Â 
Where to Eat
Â 
The best restaurants in Guilin are to be found in the best hotels, many of which serve both Western and Chinese (mostly Cantonese) cuisine. 
While not noted for the excellence of its cuisine, Guilin is nonetheless famous for the unusual nature of its regional offerings. 
Visitors who would like to try wild game dishes should specify their order a day in advance. 
There are also a number of good bakeries and noodle stands along Zhongshan Road, the main shopping street. 
For those who want to venture out on their own, two suggestions:
Yueyalou Restaurant, in Seven Star Park; 3622. 
Here you can have a vegetarian meal, or one of wild game, after visiting the park's six caves, bonsai garden and small zoo complete with panda.
Tonglai Guan Restaurant, Zhongshan Zhong Road; 3449. 
For the adventurous palate only. 
This restaurant just north of the Hotel Osmanthus Guilin is famous for its wild game, live examples of which are displayed in cages outside, and include pangolin (scaly anteater), bamboo rat, masked civet, snake and turtle.Â Â Â Â L.

text:

THE striking images of ''Yellow Earth,'' a Chinese movie about the forced marriages inflicted on teen-age peasant women before the Communist takeover, offer respite from a plot that bears the impress of the cultural arm of the Chinese Communist Party's Central Committee.
A group of farmers, chests bared, heads garlanded, pray for rain. 
Musicians with red drums and dancers in blue with white headbands make rousing recruiters for Mao Zedong's army. 
A wedding procession is seen far off as specks of red against the desert-brown landscape. 
The interior of a farmer's hut is so smoky it seems to be part of the earth. 
The guests at a wedding feast are served wooden fish; no real fish is to be had, but, as one explains, ''We must have fish with dinner.''
The movie, directed by Chen Kaige, which can be seen as part of the New Directors/New Films series tonight at 6 and tomorrow at 1 at the Museum of Modern Art, is not complicated, though the English subtitles seem designed to maintain the East's reputation for mystery.
The time is 1939. 
A Communist soldier comes to Shaanxi province to collect folk songs for adapting by the army. 
By luck, he settles in with a poor farm family, whose members -taciturn father, dull 10-year-old son and especially the pretty 14-year-old daughter - have the best voices in all Shaanxi and burst forth at inspirational moments, in the style of old Hollywood musicals. 
We see their hard lives and the life of their town through the soldier's sympathetic eyes.
The girl, who spends a lot of time carrying water from the river three miles away, falls in love with the soldier, who helps with the water. 
But he has to go back to the army, and she is sold into marriage. 
Her consciousness has been raised, however, and by the time he comes back for her, she has sailed daringly off on her own to find liberation, in the form of the People's Liberation Army, and the hills are alive with the sounds of ''It's the Communists who save the people.''
Love and Liberation YELLOW EARTH, directed by Chen Kaige; screenplay (in Mandarin with English subtitles) by Zhang Ziliang from a short essay ''Sanwen'' by Ke Lan; photography by Zhang Yimou; a World Entertainment Release.

file: CHINE TO BROADCAST CBS SELECTIONS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese national television network has signed an agreement with CBS to broadcast 64 hours of CBS television programming in China, beginning Dec. 
1. These will be the first regularly scheduled broadcasts of American television ever seen in China.
The programs will range from selected segments of ''60 Minutes'' to four animated ''Dr. 
Seuss'' specials to football, hockey and basketball games. 
Most will be broadcast in prime time. 
Included will be commercials from 10 major corporate sponsors, probably large international companies with an interest in the Chinese market, according to CBS spokesmen.
The agreement was described as a one-year arrangement, and not necessarily an exclusive one that would preclude the Chinese from negotiating with other networks as well. 
However, representatives of CBS and of China Central Television, the Chinese television network, said they expected an expanded American presence on Chinese television to evolve from this arrangement, which they consider only the first step in a long- term relationship with CBS.
Â 
'To Promote Understanding'
The agreement was signed yesterday at the CBS building, on 52d Street and Avenue of the Americas, in a news conference attended by a delegation from China Central Television.
''Our purpose in signing the agreement with CBS is to promote understanding between the Chinese and American people,'' Wang Feng, the director of China Central, said through a translator.
CBS officials said negotiations began more than two years ago, at the invitation of the Chinese. 
The agreement involves no exchange of payments; the only money involved will be that generated by the sale of advertising time, which CBS and China Central will share.
The China Central officials said that there were more than 45 million television sets in China, but that the number of viewers was much higher because so many people watch the programming on each set.
Â 
Reasoning Behind Choices
Chinese television, which is government-controlled, is run according to the Communist concept of television as a medium for ideological enlightenment rather than entertainment, and has heretofore resisted what is regarded as the corrosive influence of bourgeois values and trends.
''If you look at the programs they have chosen, they are really not controversial,'' said Joseph DiCerto, the director of communications for CBS/ Broadcast Group Worldwide Enterprises. 
''They were chosen because CCTV wants to provide additional programming that is informational and cultural rather than controversial.''
Many Communist countries buy Western programming to supplement their own government-controlled content.
Representatives of the Chinese station had screened hundreds of programs to make their choices. 
Selections from news programming include episodes from a series on aviation history called ''Air Power,'' Walter Cronkite's science magazine series, ''Universe,'' ''21st Century,'' a science documentary series, and ''World War II,'' a 12-part series.
Â 
Vietnam and Gardening
The ''60 Minutes'' segments are one on economic and social conditions in Vietnam, one on Chinese people living in Singapore, one on American gangsters, and one on English gardening.
Sports programming includes segments of New York Rangers ice hockey games, National Basketball Association games, probably from the 1985 N.B.A. playoff series; an ice skating special called ''Superskates'' and National Collegiate Athletic Association football, probably a Bowl game. 
Chinese officials said this would be the first football game ever broadcast on Chinese television.
However, some of CBS's most popular programs, such as ''Dallas'' and ''Falcon Crest,'' were absent from the list. 
CBS officials said that much of the network's prime-time programming had not been offered to the Chinese because CBS does not own the rights to many of those series. 
However, Chinese officials acknowledged that their choices had also been governed by their own sense of what would be appropriate for Chinese audiences.
The Chinese officials said that while individual programs from other nations had been seen on Chinese television, including some from Britain and Japan as well as the United States, the CBS programs would constitute the first extensive, regularly scheduled American programming.

China agreed today to accept substitutes for some products of the Toshiba Machine Company, partly resolving an eight-month dispute over Japan's decision to bar Toshiba from exporting to Communist states.
The Ministry of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade, however, continued to demand compensation for losses incurred by delayed or suspended contracts, the official New China News Agency reported.
Last May, the Japanese Government imposed a one-year ban on Toshiba Machine's exports to 14 Communist nations after disclosures that Toshiba had illegally supplied the Soviet Union with milling equipment used to produce ultra-quiet submarines.
The Chinese ministry said in a news release that the May ruling victimized China in 25 contracts involving Toshiba exports and that $900 million worth of Chinese contracts signed with other Japanese concerns were stalled because of tightened Japanese export restrictions.
The direct value of the Toshiba contracts has been put at $19 million.
Last month Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry offered to let Toshiba Machine, a subsidiary of the giant Toshiba Corporation, fulfill seven of the 25 contracts. 
The ministry said other Japanese concerns would supply the products promised under the other contracts.

China, embarrassed by the first successful hijacking of one of its civil airliners, today dispatched an official delegation for discussions with authorities in South Korea on the return of the hijackers as well as the plane, its crew and passengers.
Shen Tu, the director of the China's Civil Aviation Administration, left for Seoul with the delegation at 8 A.M. aboard a special plane. 
It will be the first such face-to-face meeting between the Chinese and the South Koreans, who were enemies in the Korean War. 
The two countries still do not have diplomatic relations, since Peking recognizes only North Korea, but they have quietly conducted trade through Hong Kong and other Asian countries.
PEKING, Saturday, May 7 - China, embarrassed by the first successful hijacking of one of its civil airliners, today dispatched an official delegation for discussions with authorities in South Korea on the return of the hijackers as well as the plane, its crew and passengers.105 People on Plane
The British-made Trident jet was on a domestic flight from Shenyang in Manchuria to Shanghai Thursday when it was seized by the Chinese hijackers. 
They shot and wounded two of the crew before forcing the plane, with 105 people on board, to land at a military airfield in South Korea.
Mr. Shen sent a telegram on Friday to Chol Yong Kim, director of the South Korean Civil Aviation Bureau, expressing ''deep concern'' for the passengers and crew.
''In order to deal with this matter,'' the telegram said, ''I will go to Seoul personally as quickly as possible. 
I earnestly hope you agree and will give assistance.''
The text of the telegram was released by the New China News Agency.
The Chinese aviation agency had announced that Mr. Shen would hold a news conference for foreign journalists Friday afternoon, but the session was canceled less than an hour before it was to have started. 
The agency would not explain the cancellation, though it appeared the Chinese had not expected the South Koreans to be ready to cooperate.
Â 
Foreign Ministry Statement
The Chinese aviation agency said details of the discussions would have to come from South Korea. 
China's intentions, however, were spelled out in a statement issued Friday by the Foreign Ministry.
The statement said, ''The Chinese side requests the South Korean authorities immediately return the aircraft together with all the crew members and passengers and hand over the criminals that hijacked the airliner to the Chinese side in accordance with related articles of international civil aviation conventions.''
The New China News Agency identified the leader of the ''group of armed thugs'' as An Weijian, but gave no other details. 
One unofficial theory was that the hijackers were the children of senior Communist officials. 
Ordinary Chinese cannot get airline tickets for domestic travel unless they are authorized by their work unit.
If the hijackers are returned to China, they are virtually certain to be tried, sentenced and shot, as happened to five hijackers who tried to divert an Ilyushin-18 airliner from Shanghai to Taiwan last August. 
They were overpowered and beaten up by the crew members and passengers. 
At least nine other Chinese have been sent to prison for complicity in that attempt.
Â 
Strict Security Measures
China, which joined the international antihijacking convention in early 1979, has set up tough security measures at its airports, including body searches and luggage inspection. 
As a result, there was amazement among some Chinese that the hijackers managed to smuggle weapons on board.
Chinese officials have denied or refused to confirm stories of other unsuccessful hijackings here, some of which have been reported in the Hong Kong press. 
These include purported attempts from Canton in October 1981, from Shanghai in July 1982 and from Hangzhou in January of this year. 
The destination of all previous hijacking attempts has been Taiwan.
China's discreet trade with South Korea through Hong Kong has been sharply cut back, possibly under pressure from North Korea, after South Korean exports alone, mostly of industrial goods, approached $140 million in 1981. 
But it is thought that some commerce continues through Hong Kong, Japan and other Asian middlemen.
There has also been occasional unofficial travel between China and South Korea involving businessmen, athletes and relatives.

Seoul to 'Abide' by Agreements
Â 
Special to the New York Times
SEOUL, South Korea, May 6 - South Korean Government officials said today that they would ''abide'' by international agreements on air piracy, but it was not clear if that meant they would give up the hijackers to Chinese authorities or put them on trial here.
Newspapers in Seoul that tend to reflect official thinking described the hijackers - five men and a woman in their 20's and 30's - as ''seekers of freedom.''
For the Seoul Government, the incident was regarded as a potential, if unexpected, political boon. 
Strongly anti-Communist, it has no diplomatic ties with Peking, but it has long been interested in a friendlier relationship, more than once seeking direct talks on a range of issues.
One possibility, foreign officials said, was that the South Koreans would use the hijacking talks as a wedge to open the discussion to other topics.

file: CHINESE AIDE LEAVES WASHINGTON WITHOUT FORMAL ARMS SALES PACT.txt
text:

The Chinese Defense Minister, Zhang Aiping, left here today without reaching formal agreement with Secretary of Defense Caspar W. Weinberger on United States military sales and assistance to China, according to Defense Department officials.
The chief Pentagon spokesman, Michael I. Burch, issued a statement saying discussions would continue on a technical level toward ''the possibility of agreements being reached in the future.''
Defense Department officials said Mr. Zhang and Mr. Weinberger had ''agreed in principle'' to the potential United States sale of antiaircraft missiles and antitank weapons to China. 
They also said China might buy military technology and possibly set up plants to produce weapons under license from American companies.
The officials cautioned, however, that no specific sales had been decided. 
The expression ''to agree in principle'' is often used in Asia to avoid specific or formal agreements but expressing a willingness to continue negotiations.
Â 
No Arms Sales Since '49
The United States has not sold weapons to China since the Communists took power in 1949. 
After that China and the United States were enemies in the Korean War, and formal diplomatic relations were established by President Carter only in 1979.
On Monday Mr. Burch said Mr. Weinberger and Mr. Zhang had ''reached agreement on a number of important matters'' but declined to say what they were. 
He suggested then that an announcement would be made before Mr. Zhang left Washington.
The Chinese asked for a news blackout over the negotiations because, officials said, they did not want to appear to be moving closer to to the United States. 
Mr. Burch said Monday that the Chinese had asked that the meetings be considered ''private'' and that Mr. Weinberger had agreed.
The officials said that a Chinese delegation of technicians and military officials had been in Washington since March and that several officials who came with Mr. Zhang had remained behind after he left. 
Mr. Zhang is continuing his visit with tours of United States military bases and visits to military contractors.
Officials said no specific agreements had been reached because the Chinese had not decided what arms they want and were exploring all possibilities. 
Mr. Zhang is expected to continue that search as he visits General Dynamics, Boeing and other arms contractors.
Â 
Interested in High Tech
In addition, officials said that the Chinese had been more interested in high technology but that the Americans had sought to steer them toward weapons more in keeping with the relatively rudimentary nature of the Chinese military forces.
The Chinese, who have limited amounts to spend, have long said they are more interested in buying technology than in arms themselves, but the Administration wants to sell weapons, the officials said. 
A compromise between those two positions has still not been achieved.
The initiative in forming a military relationship between the United States and China has largely come from the United States, both in the Carter and Reagan Administrations. 
Mr. Weinberger, in his public statements during a visit to China last fall, made clear that the Administration would welcome an anti-Soviet posture by China.
The Chinese, however, have made equally clear that they are not interested in allying themselves with the United States against the Soviet Union, with which they share a 5,000-mile border. 
Soviet military power along that border is much greater than China's.
The Nationalist Government in Taiwan has vigorously objected to possible United States arms sales to China. 
The Government in Peking, in turn, has strenuously objected to continued American arms sales to Taiwan. 
The Reagan Administration has slowed the sales to Taiwan but has refused to stop them.
Â 
'When They're Ready'
After Mr. Zhang left today for the remainder of his visit to the United States, one official said: ''We think they'll go back home and look over all their notes and then make a presentation to us. 
Maybe it will be just one system at a time, when they're ready.''
Officials said the Chinese evidently had a long list of weapons in which they appear interested but had not given the list to American officials. 
They also said that arms sales to China would be subject to Congressional approval and that a formal announcement might not made until it was time to notify Congress.
Among the weapons apparently high on the list of potential sales, the officials said, were Hawk antiaircraft missiles, which are supersonic, can reach to 60,000 feet and have a range of 25 miles.

text:
