file: CHINESE OFFICIAL URGES MODERATION.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's acting Prime Minister, Li Peng, opened the annual session of parliament today with a call to continue the economic and political initiatives that have dramatically affected the lives of the nation's one billion people.
But his call was tempered by an insistence that China should not go too far too fast.
''The Government should put reform at the center of all our undertakings,'' Mr. Li said, but urged officials to ''take into account what the state, the enterprises and the masses can tolerate.''
Mr. Li delivered his remarks, a review of the nation's accomplishments and prospects, at the opening session of the National People's Congress, China's lawmaking body. 
Attended by 2,978 delegates, the congress is to solidify the constitutional and legal bases of the country's economic restructuring, approve the appointment of new ministers and ratify the reorganization of parts of the Government.
For the first time in the four decades of Communist rule, constitutional protection will be accorded to private enterprise and the right of people to buy and sell the right to use land in what amounts to the re-emergence of private property.
Â 
Hard-Liners Are Quiet
Gone from this year's congress is the ideological breast-beating that dominated proceedings 12 months ago, when party hard-liners sought to whip up opposition to ''bourgeois liberalization.''
Instead, pragmatism, economic growth and Government restructuring are the new orthodoxy.
The public is being barraged with newspaper and radio coverage of the day's developments at the congress.

file: Chinese Plan Foreign Stock Listing.txt
text:
ï»¿
A Chinese company appears to be aiming to become the first to be publicly traded on an international stock exchange, through a listing in Hong Kong later this year.
Public trading of stock in Guandong Enterprises, which now is owned by the Guandong Provincial Government in southern China, apparently would mark the first time since the Communists came to power in China in 1949 that a Chinese company turned to a foreign stock market to raise capital.
Another China-controlled concern, Tian An Development Company, also is hoping to go public soon, according to a company official and market sources. 
K. C. Tan, an executive of Tian An Development, said that a planned issue of shares - to take effect after the stock becomes publicly listed - was 100 percent subscribed.
William Phillips, managing director of Baring Securities in Hong Kong, said that the primary reason for seeking new listings seemed to be that the two companies regarded Hong Kong as an efficient place to raise capital. 
But he added that the effort to be listed might contain a larger lesson as well, particularly after the recent turbulence in Beijing.
''It does appear that China means to carry on with economic reforms, albeit in a lower profile,'' Mr. Phillips said. 
''I think these two public listings are evidence of this.''
Chinese companies in recent years have experimented with issuing stock inside China, but the financial instruments often do not resemble shares elsewhere and do not carry with them the regulatory burdens that a publicly listed company must bear in foreign markets.
China already controls some companies that are publicly traded on the Hong Kong Exchange. 
But these companies, such as Ka Wah Bank and Union Bank, are longtime Hong Kong institutions that were recently acquired by Chinese interests, rather than Chinese companies that decided to go public.
Guandong Enterprises declined to comment. 
But K. K. Leung, a Hong Kong financier, said that Guandong Enterprises had purchased a company he owns, which in turn is in the process of buying Union Globe Development, a property company listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. 
Analysts said the result of the transactions, if regulators permit, would be that Guandong would inject some of its nearly $1 billion in assets into Union Globe and then sell shares in exchange for new capital.
Mr. Tan of Tian An Development could not say when the public listing of his company might occur. 
He said the issue of shares would take place through the vehicle of a related company, the Tian An China Investment Company, which would invest primarily in China.
A fund manager who has agreed to purchase Tian An shares said he understood that a Tian An listing -whether in the form of a new listing or acquisition of an existing publicly held concern - had been delayed by cautious regulators.
Tian An, for example, is less than two years old, while Hong Kong Stock Exchange rules normally require a publicly traded company to have a five-year financial track record.
E. R. Astin, Hong Kong's Commissioner for Securities, declined to discuss particular companies. 
But he said that in principle the same rules must be applied to companies of any national origin and that rules should not be relaxed when a company gains a listing by going through the ''back door,'' by buying a defunct company with a stock listing.
Mr. Astin said, however, that it would be ''highly material'' if a company was backed by the creditworthiness of a sovereign government, as Chinese companies appear to be.
''I don't think it's all political,'' said Teresa Ma, an analyst at Jardine Flemming Securities in Hong Kong, ''but there is an element of giving confidence to people in Hong Kong. 
People would say that at least China isn't against capitalist investment.''

file: CHINESE PREMIER, IN MAJOR SPEECH, ADOPTS HARD LINE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang told the Chinese people today that his Government's economic initiatives would continue. 
But he denounced ''pernicious'' Western ideas and demanded a tight rein on intellectual and artistic expression.
In the opening address to the National People's Congress, the country's legislature, Mr. Zhao acknowledged serious economic problems, including low productivity, widespread inefficiency, trade and budget deficits and runaway spending on construction projects.
The speech offered the first broad insight into both the Government's economic plans and the political temperament since the ouster of Hu Yaobang as leader of the Communist Party in mid-January in a campaign against Western ideas and values.
The 2,719 delegates to the People's Congress, gathered in the Great Hall of the People for a 16-day session, applauded as Mr. Hu strode onto the stage in his first public appearance in three months. 
On Tuesday a spokesman for the National Peoples Congress said Mr. Hu had been re-elected to the 157-member presidium.
The spokesman, Zeng Tao, also said the assembly would not name a new Prime Minister despite the fact that Mr. Zhao holds both the senior Government and senior party posts. 
Mr. Zeng said there would be no major changes in China's leadership at least until September, when a Communist Party congress is scheduled.
Â 
Many Difficulties Remain
Prime Minister Zhao, in his nationally televised address, said, ''We must be keenly aware that we still face many difficulties in our advance and that our work is not free from mistakes and problems.''
In addressing those difficulties, Mr. Zhao said, the nation must dramatically increase agricultural and industrial output, stem the increase in consumer spending and maintain Marxist political orthodoxy.
He said Government spending will be cut by 10 percent from last year's expenditures and investment in projects like hotels and office buildings will be reduced.
Nonetheless, Mr. Zhao insisted that China's economic initiatives, intended to infuse the economy with Western management techniques and market mechanisms, would continue, although he acknowledged that some would be slowed.
Since January, a group of hard-line party leaders, represented most prominently by the chairman of the National People's Congress, Peng Zhen, have spoken repeatedly about the need for caution in pursuing the economic program and have urged a reassertion of some traditional socialist economic practices, such as a renewed emphasis on central planning.
Â 
A Sartorial Contrast
Mr. Zhao, in a light gray suit, blue shirt and dark tie, provided a sartorial contrast to Mr. Peng, seated on his right in a dark blue, high-collared Mao jacket.
The Prime Minister urged the fulfillment of what he called the ''two major tasks'' for the coming year: to ''increase production and practice economy'' and to ''combat bourgeois liberalization,'' the catch phrase for Western political and ethical ideas.
In outlining the economic program, Mr. Zhao stressed the need to increase agricultural output, particularly grain production. 
Hard-line leaders have expressed dissatisfaction with with the growing number of peasants who, instead of rice and wheat, are growing vegetables or other crops that can be sold on the free market at higher prices.
Mr. Zhao devoted a significant portion of his speech to ideological questions and repeatedly denounced the intrusion of Western ideas into China. 
''Immense efforts must be made to eliminate the pernicious influence of this erroneous ideological trend,'' he said.

file: CHINESE PROVINCE HAS SEVERE FLOOD.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's populous southeastern province of Guangdong has begun recovering from severe floods that marooned 450,000 people and left at least 430 dead.
The floods, said to be the worst in Guangdong in 30 years, came after torrential rains early May 12. 
They affected over a million people in northern and western Guangdong and raised fears that Canton might be threatened.
PEKING, May 19 - China's populous southeastern province of Guangdong has begun recovering from severe floods that marooned 450,000 people and left at least 430 dead.
Today, People's Daily, in its first acknowledgment of the disaster, reported that the floodwaters were starting to recede and that stranded people were being evacuated. 
The official party newspaper did not say how many Chinese had died or been left homeless.
Fuller details, however, have appeared in the Hong Kong press, which reported on the casualties, and in a local newspaper, Canton's Yangcheng Evening News, copies of which reached Peking.
In Qingyuan County, less than 50 miles north of Canton, nearly 24 inches of rain fell in 13 hours, raising the North River to its highest level since 1949 and leaving some roads six feet under water. 
More than 4,000 soldiers and peasants were mobilized to reinforce the river's dikes.
Â 
46,000 Houses Collapse
The floodwaters inundated more than 286,000 acres of farmland, according to reports. 
The Yangcheng Evening News said 46,000 houses collapsed and 40 bridges were washed away along with telephone poles and smaller dikes. 
One account said Qingyuan and Yingde Counties were entirely under water. 
In all, 18 counties were affected.
The floods also swept away more than 20 miles of the main rail line between Canton and Peking. 
Rail traffic is not expected to be restored for two weeks, a local official said. 
Travelers arriving in Hong Kong reported being stranded on trains for 30 hours as the waters rose and landslides blocked the tracks.
Chinese television this week showed army units rescuing stranded peasants, some from rooftops. 
Military aircraft dropped tons of biscuits, clothing and candles. 
Helicopters also evacuated some people. 
Sailors in landing craft and rubber dinghies rescued others. 
More than 100,000 troops and civilians have been mobilized, according to one report.
The flood's effect has been felt in Hong Kong, where food prices jumped this week after the usual supplies of pork and vegetables were disrupted. 
Daily vegetable shipments from Guangdong dropped by more than a third over the weekend, and the Hong Kong authorities started ordering extra produce from Taiwan and Thailand.
Guangdong Province, whose population of 58 million exceeds that of Britain or France, is primarily agricultural, and the full impact of the devastation probably will not be known for some time.
Â 
Drought in Northern China
Other parts of Guangdong had floods last fall but recovered sufficiently to have a good harvest. 
The latest floods appear to be less severe than those in Sichuan and Shanxi Provinces last summer, when more than 1,000 Chinese were reported killed and up to a half million were left homeless.
Northern China, meanwhile, is having a drought. 
The authorities say Peking's water reserves are dangerously low, although rain in the last week has helped.
Guangdong's flood relief effort is being led by Yang Deyuan, a Deputy Governor. 
Li Xuan, a Deputy Minister of Railways, came from Peking to supervise the restoration of China's north-south trunk line. 
China's airline has sent extra planes to Canton to carry passengers and mail.
The New China News Agency, said Tuesday night in its first report on the flood, ''The water levels of rivers have been falling slowly in the past two days and surface water is subsiding.''
And in the province of Qinghai, People's Daily reported today, heavy spring snows last month killed 690,000 head of livestock.

file: CHINESE REPLACE LEADER OF TIBET.txt
text:

China has dismissed the Communist Party leader in Tibet and tightened security to prevent monks from staging new anti-Chinese protests, Westerners in the autonomous region said today.
Speaking from Lhasa, the Tibetan capital, the Westerners said that monks and hundreds of pilgrims filled the main square outside the Buddhist shrine Saturday night and chanted the Prayer of Truth.
They said police officers patrolling nearby did not intervene, although the prayer contained lines entreating the ''protectors of Tibet to drive the barbarians of the east from the land of the snows.''
The Westerners said the police began a crackdown on Nov. 
23 during a festival for Lhasa's goddess, the symbol for many Tibetans of their desire for independence from China.
The Communist Party leader, Wu Jinghua, a Chinese, was recalled to Beijing and dismissed for failing to stop a simmering revolt, the Westerners said.
A Communist Party spokeswoman in Beijing confirmed that Tibet had a new party general secretary as of Dec. 
1. She identified him as Hu Jintao, former party leader in Guizhou province. 
And she refused to comment on what had happened to Mr. Wu, who led the party in Tibet since 1985.
Â 
No Longer Separate
The Communist Government in Beijing took over Tibet in 1959 and forcibly incorporated it into China. 
Protests against Beijing's rule over the Himalayan region erupted periodically and notably in October 1987, in perhaps the bloodiest riots since the Dalai Lama, Tibet's Buddhist spiritual leader, to flee across the border to India.
Last March, monks again clashed with the police, and an unknown number were shot or beaten.
Residents in Lhasa said the city is tense with armed police circling the Johkang Temple, questioning people and checking identity papers. 
Foreign tourists had their passports checked and hotel rooms searched, the Westerners said.
The Westerners quoted informed Tibetans as saying more than 100 political prisoners, including at least 30 monks and nuns, had been transferred to other areas of China, perhaps to re-education centers.

file: CHINESE REPORT THEY BEAT BACK VIETNAM ATTACK.txt
text:
ï»¿
China announced Friday that its frontier guards repulsed a large-scale attack by Vietnam Thursday across their tense border after 10 hours of heavy combat.
A dispatch by the official New China News Agency from what it said was the front line in Yunnan Province, where another battle was reported a month ago, said that after the fighting, ''the invaders fled in utter confusion.''
It said Chinese troops, working in the rain, had fortified their positions in preparation for a new attack.
Â 
First Reported by Vietnam
The border hostilities were confirmed by the Vietnamese News Agency. 
It accused China of shelling Ha Tuyen Province, which abuts Yunnan, with artillery and rockets since early July, killing civilians and seriously damaging property.
Vietnam has accused China of creating border incidents to tie down Vietnamese troops and take pressure off guerrillas in Cambodia who are fighting Vietnamese occupation forces there. 
China supports the Cambodian guerrillas, while the Vietnamese, who invaded Cambodia at the end of 1978 and installed the regime of Heng Samrin, are allies of the Soviet Union.
Chinese newspapers and radio carried the first domestic reports of the fighting Friday morning. 
The armed forces newspaper, Liberation Army accused Vietnam of taking ''a new ferocious step on its wrong road against China.''
The initial dispatch of the New China News Agency Thursday night said a Vietnamese division with artillery support mounted an incursion into Malipo County in Yunnan at 5 A.M. Thursday local time. 
But it said the Vietnamese ran into stiff resistance from Chinese frontier guards, who stood their ground and inflicted heavy casualties.
Â 
Battle Reported Over
''Fierce fighting was still going on at sunset,'' the Chinese press agency said Thursday night. 
Its report Friday implied that the battle was over, at least for the time being.
A broadcast by the Voice of Vietnam, monitored in Bangkok today, repeated the Vietnam News Agency report that Chinese gunners had fired 5,000 artillery shells into two districts of Ha Tuyen Province this month. 
But it made no mention of the battle that China said took place Thursday.
The Vietnamese radio also said more than 200,000 artillery shells had been fired into Vietnam's six northernmost provinces from China in the last two months, wounding hundreds of civilians and destroying homes and property.
There was no way to confirm the accuracy of either version, since independent observers have not been allowed into the remote area. 
Similar recriminations have been traded off and on over the last three months. 
Foreign diplomats in Hanoi and Peking believe that reports on both sides tend to be exaggerated for greater propaganda effect.
The reports of border clashes have been circulated since early April, which is far longer than the duration reported in previous years. 
The tensions in the past coincided with Vietnam's spring offensive against Chinese-backed guerrillas in Cambodia and tapered off as the fighting there wound down.
Members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations reportedly told the United States and other ''partner'' nations at a meeting in Indonesia Thursday that the anti-Vietnamese coalition in Cambodia was ''working very well'' and causing serious military problems for Hanoi.
Â 
Frontier Guards Exhorted
Liberation Army Daily, which is read in the Chinese armed forces, contended today that hostilities with Vietnam were continuing. 
If the Vietnamese provoked border incidents, the newspaper said, ''we can do nothing but hit them back in self-defense and fight to the finish.''
It urged China's frontier guards, who operate as light infantrymen with artillery support, to defend every inch of Chinese territory and hit back hard at Vietnamese attackers. 
Liberation Army Daily is not permitted reading for foreigners, but the New China News Agency took the unusual step of circulating extracts of the article to give it greater authority.
Liberation Army Daily charged that Vietnam was committing fresh troops to its continuing border conflicts because it regarded China as the biggest obstacle to its aggressive ambitions of controlling Southeast Asia.
Â 
New Strains With Soviet
The latest reports of fighting come at a time when Moscow's support of Hanoi has caused new strains in Chinese-Soviet relations. 
On June 25, Liberation Army Daily accused the Soviet Union of inciting the Vietnamese to engage in ''armed provocations'' along the border. 
Otherwise, it said, ''the Vietnamese authorities could not have been so brazen in their outrages.''
Last week the weekly magazine Outlook called Vietnam's ''strategic alliance'' with the Soviet Union the root of tension and turbulence in Southeast Asia. 
Peking has charged that Moscow is using Vietnam as a forward base for its hegemonistic strategy in Asia and the Pacific.
Vietnam has leveled similar charges at China. 
On Thursday, Vietnam's Foreign Minister, Nguyen Co Thach, said China had launched an ''absolutely unprovoked attack'' at several points along their border. 
Mr. Thach, who was flying to Mongolia, another Soviet ally, for a visit, contended that Asia should guard against China's ''new expansionist designs.''
Â 
Terrain Is Rugged
The clashes along the Chinese-Vietnamese border are confined to a rugged terrain of densely vegetated mountains, limestone cliffs and narrow valleys and streams, which would normally restrict the scope of military operations. 
The reported fighting seems to be over the high ground that can dominate both sides of the border.
Friday's Chinese press accounts observed that Vietnam mounted a regimental-sized attack in the same area of Malipo County earlier on June 11. 
Chinese frontier guards said then that they repulsed six Vietnamese assaults that day, inflicting heavy casualties.
By contrast, the Vietnamese claimed to have retaken three Chinese positions dug a half mile inside Ha Tuyen province, capturing ''many'' Chinese prisoners and seizing 12 artillery pieces and 6 mortars.
The New China News Agency quoted Chinese military sources as saying the Vietnamese spent a month preparing for Thursday's attack, a period that would have given Chinese troops time to reinforce their positions.

file: CHINESE REPORTERS THWARTED IN TRYING TO COVER THEIR MAN.txt
text:
ï»¿
For the Chinese journalists following Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang, this has been a trying trip. 
They often look bewildered, both by their more aggressive American counterparts and by the maze of security precautions. 
Worst of all, they can't get near Mr. Zhao.
''At home, we talk to him freely,'' said Li Dan, a reporter with the Peking radio.
Chinese journalists following Chinese Premier Zhao Ziyang on his trip to US often look bewildered, both by their more aggressive American counterparts and by maze of security precautions; many Chinese reporters say Zhao has been isolated from Chinese press; photo (M)
The Chinese said they expected to be treated more as part of the official delegation. 
Their problems have been compounded, they say, by security precautions and by what they call the disorganized fashion with which the trip has been handled on the American side - a contrast to the sleek organization of the 1979 trip of the paramount Chinese leader, Deng Xiaoping.
''The Chinese Premier has been isolated from the Chinese press,'' complained Yuan Xianlu, Peking correspondent for People's Daily, the official Chinese Communist Party newspaper. 
''This time we cannot write anything. 
We don't know what has been going on.''
Â 
'Difficult to Get the News'
''I think if the President of your country visits China and you are treated the same way,'' he told an American reporter based in Peking, ''you will be very unhappy.''
''We know security is the number one thing and we try to understand,'' added Mr. Li. ''But it's very frustrating. 
Security is too tight.''
These views are echoed by others in the 38-member Chinese press contingent, including Zhang Yunwen, the Washington bureau reporter of People's Daily.
''It's very difficult to get the news,'' he said. 
''Our people in China should know everything about this trip, not just general description. 
We need more chances to have facts and details.''
Conceding his press corps' problem with competition, Mr. Zhao thanked President Reagan last week for giving the Chinese press a separate White House photo session so they would not have to get into a shoving match with the more experienced White House press corps.
''I think American journalists are more capable than Chinese journalists,'' Mr. Zhao told the President. 
''They have trained themselves through competition.''
If the Chinese are frustrated by their problems on tour, they are delighted with the performance of their Prime Minister.
''He has been very correct in his answers and quick in his responses to sensitive situations,'' Mr. Zhang said.
Â 
'The Ice Has Become Firmer'
Chen Hui, 56 years old, an editorial board member from China Daily, China's English-language newspaper, agrees. 
''At first both leaders were treading a little bit on thin ice,'' he said, ''but as the visit has progressed, the ice has become firmer and firmer.''
The reporters seem baffled by the news judgment of the American journalists, who often give equal attention to official meetings and pro-Taiwan demonstrations against Mr. Zhao.
By contrast, the Chinese have given short shrift, or no shrift, to such demonstrations in their reports.
The New China News Agency, the Chinese wire service, reported the demonstrations in Washington that drew between 600 and 800 protesters by saying ''they were just a handful of people.''
Mr. Zhang, in his stories, ignored the protests completely.
''It's not a big issue,'' said Mr. Zhang, 53. 
''When your friend, Mr. Reagan, visits our country, we will not put pictures of demonstrations side by side with the formal meetings. 
It's not appropriate to our standards of reporting.''
Â 
Defends Chinese Press
The Taiwan press covered those afternoon demonstrations live in Washington - the middle of the night for their viewers - and did not devote any air time to Mr. Zhao's official doings.
The Chinese reporters defend themselves against the criticism of some who call them propagandists.
''A lot of people from the West think our journalists are a propaganda machine, but I can't agree with such a view,'' said Mr. Zhang. ''In your country, journalists want to do something sensational in contradiction with the Government's policies. 
In our country, it's quite different. 
We don't feel we should argue or doubt our policies. 
What we should do is bring our people the facts.''
''We are more conscious of the impact of the press than American reporters,'' Mr. Chen said. 
''We are more conscious of repercussions that stories might make at home or abroad. 
We don't want to give the wrong impression to people who are not following events too closely.''

file: CHINESE STUDENTS LEARN WESTERN-STYLE MANAGEMENT IN BUFFALO.txt
text:

About 100 Chinese students at the State University campus here are learning accounting, organizational behavior and the intricacies of the free market system in a new experiment in the compatibility of Marxist economics and Western-style management.
The performers in this delicate balancing act are participants in a program that last December graduated China's first 39 American-accredited M.B.A.'s. 
The intent, its founders say, is not to preach capitalist ideology, but to improve Chinese management skills and, in the process, make China more productive.
''We are not teaching capitalism,'' said Frank C. Jen, a management professor at Buffalo who was born in China and is a founder of the program, part of the science and technology exchange that began in 1980. 
''We are teaching them a series of management techniques that will help them raise their standard of living.''
The idea for the Buffalo program, with courses in English and similar to most M.B.A. programs, grew out of shorter courses offered by a joint United States-China project, the National Center for Industrial Science and Technology Management in Dalian, a major seaport on the Bay of Korea.
Â 
Conflict in China Noted
Previously the Chinese had offered their students short courses in the Western style of management. 
But under the new program - three semesters in China and an intensive final semester of study here - the students return to their homeland with the equivalent of two years of Western training and extensive knowledge of the free market system. 
Awaiting them is an industrial system that is largely state-owned and that, despite some reforms, remains closely tied to the Communist Party.
University officials acknowledge the push and pull between reformists and hard-liners in China. 
Last year's pro-democracy demonstrations there and the Government's ensuing campaign against capitalism were ample evidence of the political conflicts.
''We want to allow the students to function as China exists today,'' said Joseph A. Alutto, dean of the university's School of Management. 
''We also want them to be able to adjust as China changes.''
Mr. Alutto said the Chinese Government had given every indication that it was happy with the M.B.A. program and that it intended to renew its contract with the university. 
Two more classes of students are expected to graduate before the current contract expires in 1989.
Â 
Western Techniques in China
From the outset, the primary concern among program supporters has been the sharing of power. 
They question the willingness of Chinese leaders to institute Western management techniques, even when they proved effective.
But Mr. Alutto, citing the advancement of earlier Dalian graduates, expects success from the M.B.A. program. 
In the short term, he said, graduates should advance rapidly as managers. 
The long-term outcome, he said, should be an increase in Chinese-American joint business ventures and greater interest in trade between the two countries.
Eager to capitalize on the potential for additional trade, the university has established a China Trade Center. 
Raymond G. Hunt, director of the center and associate director of the China M.B.A. program, said the center relied on the growing trust between the university and China and served as a conduit for companies that want to trade with China, and Chinese enterprises anxious to enter the United States market.
Â 
Obstacles and Frustration
''By providing China with proper management, we will help them to re-industrialize and in the long run promote bilateral trade,'' said Richard W. H. Lee, the United States Commerce Department's director of science and technology for East Asia and the Pacific.
The program has not been without obstacles and frustration. 
In addition to the loss of a student who chose to remain in the United States, there has been political resistance in China.
Mr. Alutto said the economic reforms adopted by the Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping had been supported by top managers and younger workers. 
The resistance has come from middle managers, the sector of management most heavily infiltrated with untrained people, many of whom are rewarded for service to the Communist Party.
Mr. Jen said he had told the Chinese at the program's outset: ''You can run a very good economic system. 
But if you want to reward Communist Party members who fought the long war, send them to management school.''
Mr. Jen and Mr. Alutto both agree that Marxism and Western management are not totally incompatible.
''China has to find her own destiny,'' Mr. Alutto said. 
''All we can do is provide the technology.''

file: Chinese Visitor Admires Home Built for Disabled.txt
text:

An official guest from China came to the Parrinos' home here in this Westchester County village today, and as he pushed himself from room to room in a wheelchair, he commented on the wide, smooth hallways and the picture-window views of the outdoors.
Features such as those, he told his hosts through a translator, could help disabled people like himself to forget they were restricted at all.
The visitor was Deng Pufang, the eldest son of China's pre-eminent leader, Deng Xiaoping. 
His public role as director in chief of the China Fund for the Handicapped, which is intended to aid disabled people in his country, stems from personal misfortune.
Nearly 20 years ago, during China's Cultural Revolution, Deng Pufang was paralyzed from the waist down in his senior year at Beijing University.
Â 
Active and Visible Spokesman
The cause was not accidental, but coincided with the period of political disfavor for his father, who at the time had been stripped of his post as Secretary General of the Communist Party and made a factory hand.
Red Guards came to Deng Pufang's room on the upper floor of a dormitory, where they attacked him and then either pushed him or forced him to jump to the ground.
Mr. Deng will probably never walk again, but the changing political fortunes of his father have allowed him in recent years to become an active and visible spokesman for the disabled in China and abroad. 
The connection to his father has apparently also allowed him, through treatment abroad, a measure of health not available to thousands of others who were victims of physical attacks in the Cultural Revolution.
The road that led Deng Pufang to Briarcliff Manor, at the start of his first trip to the United States, began with a meeting last year in China with Sandra Swift Parrino, chairwoman of the National Council on the Handicapped, an independent Federal agency.
Â 
Understanding and Respect
Mrs. Swift's eldest son became a quadriplegic shortly after his first birthday because of an illness that has never been fully diagnosed. 
When she and her husband, Dick, built a house in Briarcliff Manor, they designed it, wherever possible, to be accessible by wheelchair.
Mr. Deng, who is 43 years old, took a particular interest in the Parrinos' home. 
He and a variety of Chinese officials, in advance of a series of meetings this month in New York City, Washington, Florida and California, visited the Parrinos' home, where they asked questions about policies toward the disabled in this country. 
Mr. Deng later took a brief tour of the home, perhaps looking for ideas for his own home in Beijing, although an official in his position would be unlikely to concede such a thing.
The discussion on programs here ranged from centers for independent living to automated lifts in public buses, which caused Mr. Deng to ask who paid for such amenities. 
''There must be a conflict between your Council for the Handicapped and your Department of the Treasury,'' he said.
Mr. Deng, whose vigorous hand motions and square, deep jaw seemed to reflect the same determination as his father, listened intently and nodded when the executive director of the National Council on the Handicapped, Lex Frieden, described the ''subtle, psychological and often inadvertent'' ways that handicapped people face discrimination in this country.
That problem was no different in China, Deng Pufang said. 
The toughest battles faced by the disabled are often not against their own disability, he said, but against the reactions of others.
For that reason, Mr. Deng said he was urging a policy of four steps to treatment of the disabled, which he said could apply not only in his country but anywhere.
''First must come understanding of the disabled, and then respect,'' he said. 
''Then concern, and then help. 
Otherwise, if it's only the last two, then it is not really help at all, but only pity.''

file: CHINESE, MODERNIZING ARMY, RETIRE OFFICERS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The drive to professionalize China's armed forces took a step forward today with the announcement that 47,000 officers, about a tenth of the officer corps, will be retired before the end of 1986.
The announcement had political ramifications since the officers involved are mostly men who joined Mao Zedong's guerrilla forces before the Communists seized power in China in 1949. 
Although there has been an official retirement policy for 25 years, the practice had been to allow those who took part in the guerrilla struggle to remain in uniform until they died or voluntarily stepped aside.
Deng Xiaoping, the 80-year-old army veteran who holds pre-eminent political power, has made the remaking of the army one of his priorities. 
He wants to replace the poorly educated peasant boys who made the revolution by younger, better-trained men.
Chinese Government announces that 47,000 military officers, about 10% of officer corps, will be retired before end of 1986 in effort to professionalize country's military; political impact noted in light of fact that most officers joined Mao Zedong's guerrilla forces before Communists seized power in 1949 (M)Aim Is to Curb Army Influence
Mr. Deng has political as well as military objectives. 
By clearing the officer corps of revolutionary veterans, he hopes to curb the political influence wielded by the army in the past, often in favor of the so-called leftist policies Mr. Deng has discarded. 
He has also said that the army, which had a woeful experience in the 1979 war against Vietnam, must be modernized.
The New China News Agency said the officers being retired were men who joined up in the war against the Japanese occupation forces in the 1930's, or in the civil war against the Nationalists between 1945 and 1949. 
Most of them had achieved junior rank up to regimental level, the agency said, indicating that they were mostly the equivalent of majors, or less.
The retirees were said to be part of a larger group of 70,000 to 80,000 officers designated to retire in the next few years, the press agency said. 
Western military attaches said this suggested that a decision had been taken to retire officers as they reach the nominal retirement age of 60, except at higher command levels. 
An example is the commander of the armed forces, Yang Dezhi, a Deng appointee who is 75.
The move to purge the junior officer corps has been accompanied by pressure on veteran senior officers, thousands of whom have been retired since 1980. 
Late last year, Mr. Deng obtained the retirement of 40 officers on the command staff who held ranks equivalent to lieutenant general and higher.
The halting progress in carrying out the retirement policy appears to reflect resistance among those affected as well as constraints on Mr. Deng's own political power. 
At times he has sounded testy on the subject, as when he struck out in 1982 at officers whom he called ''undisciplined, arrogant, extravagant and lazy.''
When he was purged twice during the Cultural Revolution, between 1966 and 1973 and again in 1976-77, Mr. Deng was under army guard in provincial exile.
Â 
Better Pensions Offered
As compensation for retirement, there has been a drive to improve pensions and other benefits. 
The New China News Agency said today that 30,000 apartments had been built for retiring officers and that the Ministry of Civil Affairs, which cares for the retirees, had appointed a special staff to look after their needs. 
One point of strain has been an order that retiring officers vacate their army quarters.
Similar policies have been applied among the nine million party workers in civilian jobs. 
The Central Committee's Party Organization Department, in charge of personnel, said recently that 900,000 party workers over the age of 60 had retired, allowing 80,000 professionally competent middle-aged party workers to be appointed to responsible posts.
Mr. Deng has laid stress on promoting men in their 30's and 40's, saying that it is to them that China must look for leadership for the rest of the century. 
In the armed forces, General Yang has stipulated that division commanders should be about 45, with regimental commanders 40 or younger.

file: CHINESE-U.S. RELATIONS TAKE A MORE REALISTIC DIRECTION.txt
text:
ï»¿
If China's rhetoric can be believed, two of its fondest friends are the North Korean President, Kim Il Sung, and the ousted Cambodian guerrilla leader Pol Pot, whose notoriety has isolated them elsewhere. 
By contrast, the United States gets lumped with the Soviet Union as hegemonistic superpowers who pose the real threat to the peaceloving world.
But an old Chinese proverb counsels: ''Listen to what a person says and then watch what he does.''
This week Chinese Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang visits the United States as head of a Government that has distanced itself from Washington since diplomatic relations were established on Jan. 
1, 1979, but that nonetheless retains common interest on a range of issues.
In the last five years, perceptions on both sides have matured, sometimes painfully, into a more sober realism about the limitations as well as the potential of the relationship. 
Antagonisms persist over the future of Taiwan and lesser problems, even as interdependence increases on other fronts. 
Mr. Zhao, who is expected in Washington tomorrow and will see Mr. Reagan Wednesday, set a conciliatory tone for the visit last week when he spoke at a news conference of ''great progress'' in relations between the two countries.
For complex reasons, China welcomed strategic cooperation with the United States in 1979. 
The Vietnamese had invaded Cambodia, ousting Pol Pot's regime. 
Before retaliating with a punitive invasion of Vietnam, China wanted a link with the United States to discourage a comparable Soviet response on its northern border. 
The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan that year confirmed the value of such an alliance for Peking. 
The Chinese and American outlooks still coincide on the Cambodian and Afghanistan invasions, and converge on some other areas threatened by the Kremlin's ambitions. 
But the bilateral relationship suffered from an American failure to live up to China's grand expectations. 
Peking hoped that the severing of official ties between the United States and Taiwan would demoralize the nationalist regime there and force it to negotiate with the mainland. 
Instead, Taiwan has prospered, while enjoying new infusions of American military aid. 
Mr. Zhao said last week he would not press for an immediate end to arms shipments to Taiwan but indicated he would remind Washington of its pledge to phase the sales out. 
Peking also expected its friendship with the United States to produce a cornucopia of capital and technology for China's modernization. 
This was obstructed by high interest rates and tight controls on the export of computers and other sophisticated hardware. 
The lack of a quick technological fix from the United States was interpreted by China as a deliberate slight. 
Coziness with the United States also hurt China's standing with other developing countries, where American policies are not popular. 
This discovery produced a shift in late 1981 toward conspicuous nonalignment. 
China shelved strategic cooperation and revived its superpower label for the United States - a change owing in large part to the election of Ronald Reagan, whose campaign remarks in support of Taiwan upset the Chinese. 
Mr. Reagan's tough approach to Moscow also left China freer to moderate its hostility toward the Soviet Union and agree to talk about improving strained relations. 
The Chinese-American communique of August 1982 clarified the Reagan Administration's position on Taiwan but fell short of dissipating the ill will. 
By last winter, the Chinese seemed to see little prospect of getting along with Mr. Reagan. They were consequently surprised by his decision to relax substantially controls on technology exports, which involved reclassifying China from a potential adversary to friendly nonaligned country. 
This week, an accord on industrial cooperation by which both sides would facilitate private investment in China is due to be signed during Mr. Zhao's stay in Washington. 
A treaty defining investors' rights may be ready when Mr. Reagan visits Peking, probably in April.
Other aspects of the relationship have also expanded. 
Although bilateral trade declined in 1983 because the Chinese stopped buying grain to protest a temporary imposition of import quotas on its textiles, total trade is still expected to exceed $4.2 billion. 
That is four times the figure for 1978, before diplomatic ties were established. 
United States officials estimate that at least 120,000 Americans visited China in 1983, compared with fewer than 10,000 in 1978. 
Some 13,000 Chinese students and scholars are studying in the United States, up from virtually zero five years ago. 
Chinese delegations are visiting the United States at the rate of 200 a month, a tenfold rise over five years ago. 
China remains beholden to its self-image as a revolutionary nation. 
''The Chinese want to think of themselves as Communists,'' said an Eastern European diplomat. 
This may help explain why they claim to feel more comfortable with Kim Il Sung or Pol Pot than with President Reagan. 
But when Mr. Zhao comes to Washington this week, his baggage will be lighter with the absence of the old illusions about Chinese-American relations.

file: Christmas in China For Hockey Team.txt
text:
ï»¿
Harbin, Manchuria, is an unlikely place to spend a Christmas vacation.
An industrial city of 2.5 million people in northeastern China, Harbin is also China's winter-sports capital. 
The Brown University hockey team spent its Christmas vacation there, playing five games in nine days. 
The last game signaled the formal opening of China's National Ice Festival.
Brown had accepted the invitation extended by the New York-based People to People Organization on behalf of the Chinese Government. 
China has a national hockey team, which has had limited international exposure to date, and is looking for more.
Â 
Captain Lost to Injury
Brown won 2, lost 2 and tied 1 game during the team's stay. 
Two of the games, a 7-6 loss and a 3-3 tie with the Chinese national team, were televised throughout China. 
Three others were against club teams, sprinkled with players from the national squad. 
Brown also lost its captain, Tom Wallack, for the rest of the season with a knee injury suffered during one of the games.
Coach Herb Hammond, now in his fourth year at the Providence school, compared both the city and the hockey to his visit to Moscow in 1972.
''They've had 25 years of hockey in China, but only recently have they gone in an Olympics direction,'' he said. 
''They have a couple of coaches from Czechoslovakia in to help out. 
They want to go to Calgary in 1988 and play in the B or C pool.
''The Chinese play a noncontact type of hockey. 
They were very impressed by our desire to win. 
They called a lot of penalties, and we played short-handed almost all the time just because they haven't been exposed to our kind of play.
''Their equipment was really inferior, too, much like the Russians had 10 or 15 years ago. 
But they'll improve. 
They were all interested in trading pieces of equipment with us.''
Â 
Impressed by a Goalie
The Chinese national team was roughly comparable to a mediocre major United States college team, according to Hammond. 
Four or five of its players, including one of the goalies, would be capable of playing at that level, he said.
The cultural differences were striking and unforgettable. 
''We all lost weight,'' joked Hammond, recalling banquet dishes such as bear claw, sea slug and moose nose. 
As the only Westerners in the city, team members drew curious onlookers wherever they went. 
The Chinese were particularly intrigued by the Western modes of dress of Hammond's and the wife of an assistant coach, Mark Trivett.
Hammond said the crowds were quiet. 
''There was no emotion, no cheering at our games, even though there were 6,600 fans at each one,'' he said.

file: COMMERCIAL RENTS IN CHINATOWN SOAR AS HONG KONG EXODUS GROWS.txt
text:
ï»¿
A flood of immigrants from Hong Kong has pushed commercial rents in New York's Chinatown up to the levels of midtown, making the real estate in one untidy corner of Manhattan among the most expensive in the United States.
The demand for space is so strong, local real estate brokers say, that the operators of vegetable stalls near the bustling intersection of Catherine and Division Streets pay more rent per square foot than the owners of Tiffany & Company at Fifth Avenue and 57th Street. 
City officials describe the frenzy in the Chinatown real estate market as ''hysteria.''
''Everytime you turn around the prices have shot up again,'' said Michael Dirzulaitis, an assistant commissioner in the city's Division of Real Property, which has been involved in several development projects in Chinatown this year. 
''It's hard to believe that there is enough money around to keep it going, but there is.''
The pressures on Chinatown have been building for some time. 
But they have been given added urgency by the exodus of people and capital from Hong Kong in advance of the 1997 deadline for Britain to turn the colony over to China.
New York's Chinatown is not big enough to absorb much of Hong Kong's wealth. 
The largest real estate deal in the works in the neighborhood is about $18 million, tiny by Manhattan standards and modest even by those of other cities.
The money coming in from Hong Kong, however, is not the big fortunes, counted in millions of dollars, but nest eggs measured in the thousands - just enough money to stake a newcomer in business. 
In Chinatown, where newcomers are isolated from the outside world by language and culture and where severe zoning restrictions prevent the addition of space to accommodate a larger population, these sums are enough to run up the bids for every available nook.
Two decades ago, Chinatown was a neighborhood of 20,000 people, most of them men and most of them of Cantonese extraction, squeezed into about 35 square blocks at the foot of the Manhattan Bridge in the shadow of City Hall. 
The population is estimated now at 100,000 or more and is growing geometrically. 
If Chinatown were an independent municipality, it would rank as one of the fastest-growing communities in the United States.
With new arrivals squeezing in at a rate at nearly 2,000 a month, the district spread north through what was once a Jewish section on the Lower East Side and west across Little Italy, turning Yiddish into Mandarin and fettucine into won tons. 
The frontier of Chinatown has crossed into TriBeCa and SoHo, and new Chinatowns have blossomed in Queens and Brooklyn, bringing the total Chinese population in the city to about 300,000.
Â 
Hundreds of Entrepreneurs
Wherever they live, the immigrants are drawn back to downtown Chinatown to work and shop, creating an atmosphere of an old city market, with hundreds of entrepreneurs tending their own stalls or shops.
Bushels of live blue crabs, crates of bok choy and hordes of intense shoppers crowd the sidewalks of Canal Street, the central business district of Chinatown. 
Shopkeepers hawk wares from every available nook: batteries and audio tapes, scarves, T-shirts, jewelry and food of every description, from lobsters to doughnuts.
''We Chinese are very independent people,'' said Danny Li, owner of a chain of bakery shops and an investor in real estate and restaurants. 
''The first ambition for a Chinese person is to have his own business. 
It gives jobs to everyone in the family.''
On East Broadway, a new arrival sublets enough space under the awning of a fish store for a dozen open crates of vegetables. 
''He might pay the owner of the fish market $1,500 a month for a place to stand in front of the store window,'' said Kwok Ming Chan, a restaurant owner and real estate investor. 
(He describes the lease as if it were hypothetical. 
In the intimate, small-town atmosphere of Chinatown, where neighbors and partners often know each other's business, no one admits to knowing details.) Mr. Chan said that, to obtain the lease in the first place, a lease that might run for as little as two years or as long as five, he might pay $20,000 or more in ''key money,'' an illegal but universal - and universally acknowledged - fee assessed everytime a tenant moves in or renews his lease.
When the key money is amortized over the life of the lease, the operator of the vegetable stand might pay the equivalent of $275 a square foot a year for the privilege of selling his apples, snow peas and mushrooms. 
Some of the shops in the atrium of Trump Tower on Fifth Avenue, among the most expensive retail space in the city, pay little more than that.
Yet the competition is so fierce that retail prices at many of the stalls are considerably lower than those uptown. 
Apples that sell for 89 cents a pound on the upper West Side go for 33 cents on Henry Street. 
Snow peas cost a third of what they bring at greengroceries in other parts of the city.
''They can make a living only by working 14 hours every day,'' Mr. Chan said. 
''And everyone in the family must work, too.''
Despite the drab exterior of the neighborhood, Chinatown is not poor. 
''People have plenty of money,'' Mr. Li said. 
''If they do not have enough to open their own business, they work as waiters in the Chinese restaurants. 
You can put aside a lot when you work as a waiter. 
You have no time off to spend what you earn.''
The drabness comes in part from the compulsion to do business. 
''A few years ago, a group of us convinced the city to commit several million dollars to rebuilding the sidewalks and planting trees and shrubbery in the area,'' Tieh Chi Ho, an architect and developer, said. 
''But the merchants objected. 
They said the construction would drive away customers.''
When the Golden Pacific National Bank, one of the many banks in Chinatown, failed last year, Federal regulators who examined the books were surprised to find so many waiters with savings accounts of $20,000 or more, Mr. Chan said. 
He pointed to a vendor selling hot noodles from an aluminum pushcart on the corner of East Broadway and Pike Street. 
''He takes in $500 a day,'' Mr. Chan said. 
''One day soon he will have enough to lease a stall.''
Those who lack the capital for a pushcart settle for a cardboard box on which they spread a half-dozen mackerel or a dozen scarves.
Â 
Restaurants and Curio Shops
The customers who support this multitude of merchants come not only from Chinatown but also from the Chinese communities in Queens, the non-Chinese residents of the lower part of Manhattan and the tourists drawn to the hundreds of inexepensive restaurants and curio shops.
''With so many people passing by, the owner of a small stall can sell a lot of merchandise,'' Mr. Chan said. 
''You can watch him in the morning unload a truckload of goods to sell, maybe $2,000 worth, and by the end of the day it is all gone.''
But the day does not end until late at night, he added.
Mr. Chan and nine other stockholders hope to take advantage of the demand for space with a new shopping center they are building on East Broadway underneath the Manhattan Bridge on land leased from the city. 
It is one of the few sites available for new construction.
''Most of the real estate in Chinatown is owned by family associations with many members,'' said Irwin Liu, an American-born lawyer who with several partners founded a title insurance company on Pell Street in Chinatown. 
''It is very hard to get so many different people to agree on a plan for development.''
Â 
Density Limited by Zoning
When sites do become available, the new buildings that rise on them are limited to some of the lowest density zoning in Manhattan, in most cases reaching no more than six stories. 
One of the few projects planned to exceed that limit was derailed last month when the state's highest court, the Court of Appeals, halted a 21-story condominium project on Henry Street at Market Street. 
The court ruled that the city had failed to conduct thorough environmental impact studies.
The caps on new development have helped make every inch of existing space more valuable. 
The shopping center designed by Mr. Ho, to be known as East Broadway Mall, would house 101 shops and restaurants. 
The center would be far larger than any other shopping area in the neighborhood. 
''We have about 33 tenants so far,'' Mr. Ho said. 
''The store owners will pay a fixture fee to cover the cost of improvements in their space, and they will receive a lease of up to 25 years, which is unheard of in Chinatown.''
Mr. Chan said he expected the mall to touch off other development along East Broadway and nearby. 
''You won't recognize this area in two years,'' he said.

file: Communications to Tibet Cut And Foreigners Are Banned.txt
text:

Little new information was available yesterday about the situation in Tibet as telephone and telex communications were interrupted and travel there by foreigners was banned.
A State Department spokeswoman in Washington said ''everything is calm'' in Lhasa, the capital, as Tibetans marked the 37th anniversary of China's takeover of Tibet, but she acknowledged that reports from the area were ''fragmentary.''
The latest communication with an American consular officer visiting Lhasa occurred on Saturday, she said.
A Chinese airline official said a 10-day ban has been imposed on foreigners' travel to Tibet from Chengdu, the principal gateway to Lhasa, The Associated Press reported. 
Western travelers arriving in Chengdu from Lhasa yesterday said the Tibetan capital was quiet.
In Beijing, a Foreign Ministry spokeswoman said foreigners were being advised not to go to Tibet at this time ''because Lhasa has a special situation.''
At least 14 people have been reported killed in clashes between Tibetan nationalists and Chinese security forces in Tibet in the last two weeks.
Â 
Lhasa Is Virtually Sealed Off
It could not be confirmed that the communications blackout was ordered by the Chinese Government. 
A spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, Wu Zurong, would say only that the way to contact Lhasa was through the telecommunications bureau in Beijing.
The New York Times was unable Tuesday and yesterday to contact its correspondent, Edward A. Gargan, who reported from Lhasa on Monday. 
Mr. Gargan is chief of the Times bureau in Beijing.
A Washington Post correspondent, Daniel Southerland, who left Tibet late Monday to send an article from Chengdu, tried unsucessfully to return to Lhasa Tuesday and yesterday.
The Associated Press said its correspondent had been able to telephone reports from Lhasa on Tuesday but had not been heard from since shortly after midnight yesterday, New York time. 
United Press International received the last 10-minute telex message from its staff correspondent at 4 A.M.
Â 
Second-Hand Reports
The Associated Press and Reuters filed reports yesterday based on interviews with travelers arriving from Lhasa in Chengdu, who . told journalists that security officers visited several hotels in Lhasa around midnight Tuesday night and checked guests' passports. 
They said there were three roadblocks on the way to the airport.
The major American television networks said they did not have crews in the Tibetan capital. 
''They're making things very difficult,'' said Elizabeth Eynon, press representative for the ''CBS Evening News.''
ABC News said a producer and correspondent, Todd Carrel, left Lhasa on Tuesday.

file: Companies Find Profits In China.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE president of the Farmstead Telephone Group might be based in Glastonbury, but he is doing a lot of business in Beijing.
The Farmstead president, David M. Jastrembski, is overseeing the fulfillment of a telecommunications contract that is expected to bring his company $100 million. 
No one is more surprised by all this than Mr. Jastrembski, who a few years ago did not expect to be doing business in China at all.
Mr. Jastrembski is one of a growing number of Connecticut business executives who find that their overseas itineraries include China.
For years, major Connecticut companies like the United Technologies Corporation have had their own business dealings with China, but over the last few years, smaller companies have been getting involved, many through the efforts of the State Economic Development Department, which has made trade with China a priority.
There are about 200 Connecticut companies doing business with China, and about 20 of those in Shandong Province, with which Connecticut has a sister-city relationship. 
It is estimated that business with China represents about $150 million of the $6 billion that Connecticut does in export business annually, said the director of marketing for the State Department of Economic Development, David C. Driver.
The state's role in fostering such relationships dates back to 1980, after the normalization of trade relationships between the United States and China. 
State Economic Development Commissioner John J. Carson was the deputy commissioner then, and he recalls being skeptical when his boss, Edward J. Stockton, went to China and returned brimming with enthuasiasm. 
Since then, Mr. Carson has become a believer.
''The China relationship nicely combines two strategic market segments that Governor O'Neill has encouraged us to be involved with: small business and exporting,'' Commissioner Carson said. 
''That's one of the fundamental reasons why we are both excited about it and fairly active in the China trade business right now.''
He acknowledged that not all Connecticut businesses could benefit. 
The Chinese know precisely what they are looking for, he said, and are most keenly interested in companies that combine high techology with such industries as transportation equipment, including aviation; electronics; machine tooling, and instrumentation.
Until recently, the Economic Development Department functioned as a matchmaker, providing Connecticut companies with free consulting services to help them find the right market for their goods. 
But in the last legislative session, the General Assembly passed the Financial Capital Act, which will provide companies doing business overseas with low-interest loans, said Mr. Driver.
China is not the only country with which Connecticut deals. 
The Economic Development Department also oversees offices in Japan to aid Connecticut companies doing business in the Far East, as well as in West Germany, for European trade. 
The legislature has also passed a bill to establish the Connecticut Israel Exchange Commission, to encourage more commercial and cultural exchange with that country, he said.
In doing business with China, personal contact is key. 
To this end, the department has organized several trips to China, including an important mission last September led by Governor O'Neill. 
This was the first official visit by a Connecticut governor to the Far East, and in a country like China where government is all important, Mr. Driver said, his presence lent an invaluable stamp of prestige.
But, even when businesses cannot visit China directly, state officials take along brochures from Connecticut companies. 
This led to the $100 million contract for the Farmstead Telephone Group.
Mr. Jastrembski laughed when he recalled rebuffing repeated assertions by state economic development officials that the Chinese were very interested in buying the refurbished telecommunications equipment his company specializes in. 
In fact, it was not until he learned that the Chinese were ready to sign a contract that he became interested at all. 
Now, he plans to spend about 11 months a year in China.
Farmstead will be in charge of modernizing China's telephone system, a system that ''is about what ours was like in the 1930's and 40's,'' Mr. Jastrembski said. 
The agreement with China is expected to bring Farmstead, a company with fewer than 50 employees, about $100 million over the next decade. 
Also, through a joint corporation set up with China, Farmstead expects to do business with other countries as well, such as Australia and India.
''If it all comes to fruition, this will overshadow our operation here,'' said Mr. Jastrembski, conservatively enough, Farmstead had about $3.5 million in sales last year.
When he thinks about it all, Mr. Jastrembski still marvels.
''I think we've moved so fast not because of any brilliance on our part but because we happen to deal with a product China is interested in,'' he said. 
''China is trying to develop its infrastructure and a key element is telecommunications, so they are buying it now. 
We have the right product at the right price. 
That's the key to our success.''
Usually, Connecticut businesses dealing in China have to be prepared for delays that drag on for months, or even years.
The president of Bauer Aerospace Inc. in Farmington, Louis J. Auletta Sr., is optimistic that his current negotiations with the Chinese will lead to some lucrative contracts, but he expects it to take a while, he said.
His company, which has about $5 million in sales annually, manufactures test and ground-support equipment for the aircraft industry, and exports account for about 60 percent of its business.
Mr. Auletta is working with members of China's Civil Aviation Authority, which, he said, has a very modern fleet of aircraft, and is now seeking to begin servicing them independently, which is where his company would come in.
''As a result of my trip in September, we've had communications back and forth,'' he said. 
''I do foresee visiting China again in 1989 and '90. 
It is absolutely a long process. 
You have to establish trust and credibility early on. 
Visiting the country, your presence there is important. 
You also need to do good planning, and have patience and persistance to go along with it.''
But doing business with the Chinese is not for everyone. 
Just ask Anne Evans, owner of JAR Trading in Hebron, a tire business.
Ms. Evans, whose company expects to export about $39 million worth of tires this year to Europe, Africa, South America and the Far East, also went along on the Economic Development Department's trip. 
She discovered, though, that adding China to her export business would probably be impractical for a business her size, which has two full-time employees.
A potential for business with China exists if Mrs. Evans wants to become involved in having rubber companies manufacture tires to Chinese specifications.

text:

When the chairmanship of Hutchison Whampoa Ltd. passed quietly into the hands of Li Ka Shing, a powerful developer, on Jan. 
1, it was one more sign that local Chinese investors, many with official connections to the Chinese Communists, are challenging the British for control of Hong Kong's economy.
''What you have here is a new visibility for Chinese money and Chinese control of publicly controlled companies in Hong Kong,'' said William R.A. 
Wyllie, the ousted British chairman of Hutchison Whampoa, a major trading and industrial conglomerate based here. 
''The real wealth in this colony has been in Chinese hands. 
But they've always kept a low profile until just recently.''
Profile of Hutchinson Whampon Ltd (Hong Kong) chairman Li Ka Shing notes growing influence of local Chinese in Hong Kong economy
Mr. Li, the 52-year-old chairman of Cheung Kong Holdings Ltd., had acquired a controlling interest in the British holding company over the previous 15 months, but officially took charge this month. 
Cheung Kong has a market capitalization of about $2 billion and is projecting 1980 profits of about $200 million.
The core of Cheung Kong's activities is property development, one of the most lucrative fields in the 400-square-mile British colony where commercial rents typically are twice those of midtown Manhattan.
Â 
'A One-Man Organization'
''It is very much a one-man organization in the sense that one man controls it,'' said George C. Magnus, executive director of Cheung Kong. 
''It is kept extremely small and moves extremely fast. 
Because we know which way we want to go, we don't have to waste time with committees and all that.''
Mr. Li, a native of southern China's Chiu Chow region, seems to epitomize the newly aggressive Chinese property and shipping executives who operate out of this British enclave.
Although one of the richest and most powerful men in Hong Kong, Mr. Li has a passion for keeping out of the public eye. 
He has not granted a press interview since claiming the chairmanship of Hutchison Whampoa, saying only through an aide: ''All of what I should say I already have said.''
Associates say that Mr. Li was sent by his family to Hong Kong in 1940 to escape the Japanese invasion of China, and that he had originally hoped to become a scholar. 
But by 1950, he had opened a factory producing plastic flowers, toys and household items, and, in 1958, expanded into real estate.
The purchase of a controlling stake in Hutchison Whampoa represented a major expansion of Mr. Li's influence. 
The company engages in general trading, quarrying, ship repair and a variety of other fields in Britain, Australia, Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines.

Expanding on Other Fronts

His success is partially attributable to business connections that allow him to bridge the gulf between established British companies and a China bent on acquiring modern technology and management skills.
Mr. Li sits on the board of directors of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, which recently purchased a controlling interest in the Marine Midland Bank in New York State, and derives much of his support from the Hongkong bank. 
When he staged his first assault on Hutchison Whampoa in October 1979, for example, he was able to purchase a 22 percent block of the company's stock from the bank on favorable terms.
At the same time, Mr. Li is one of a handful of Hong Kong Chinese named to the China International Trust and Investment Corporation, an agency of the Chinese Government established in July 1979 to encourage foreign investment.
Although Mr. Li denies that he is acting as an agent for Peking, the so-called China connection is evident in many of his major deals.

Links to Chinese Government

Business associates and competitors alike say that a dominant factor in Mr. Li's success is his own personal business acumen.

file: COMPANY NEWS_INVESTING IN CHINA_ STILL HARD.txt
text:
ï»¿
When China opened its doors to capitalism several years ago, Western businessmen and financiers seized the opportunity as the opening of a vast new frontier. 
But they have found that the reality is not living up to the promise.
That view has now been buttressed by a leading international lawyer, Jerome A. Cohen, who is an expert on Chinese law and is widely known for his sympathetic attitude toward Chinese business practices. 
In an analysis, he and another lawyer, Stuart J. Valentine, said that foreign investors still confront severe problems in China, including exorbitant costs, unpredictable negotiating practices, unenforceable contracts and an uncertain legal environment.
The two lawyers, members of the New York law firm of Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison, offer a harsh assessment of Chinese attitudes toward international business ventures.
Â 
The Major Problems
These are among the major difficulties facing foreign investors in China, according to the two lawyers:
* The uncertainty about China's political direction, which will not become clearer until the new leadership is announced this fall.
* The inability of investors to repatriate profits, primarily because of China's low foreign exchange reserves.
* The extraordinary cost of doing business in China and the excess fees and charges on foreign businesses.
* The practice in China of ignoring the language of contracts and of regularly insisting on renegotiations.
* The continual interference of Government officials in foreign ventures.
* The inadequacy of China's laws and the constant recourse by the Chinese to internal rules that are unknown to the foreign investor.
* A hostile tax structure and tax administration that often prevent foreign investors from evaluating the profitability of a proposed project.
Â 
Businessmen Back Analysis
The analysis by Mr. Cohen and Mr. Valentine was presented at a discussion with Chinese officials last month and later made available to The New York Times by the authors.
Western business executives and diplomats here endorsed the analysis and pointed to the 50 percent drop in foreign investment in China last year as evidence of the harsh environment.
Despite moves by China last fall to address the problem, most foreign business executives say that the inhospitable investment scene has remained unchanged. 
One American diplomat said: ''Two years ago I would have 12 companies a day in my office looking for advice. 
Nowadays, I can go for a week and not see anybody.''
Despite repeated assurances by China's leadership that economic reform and openness to foreign investment will continue, the lawyers say that the threat of political instability overshadows investment decisions.
Even more troubling, according to the authors, is the country's financial limitations, the capriciousness of officials and the arbitrary application of regulations.
Foreign companies will have trouble converting earnings into foreign exchange for the repatriation of profits, according to the lawyers.
Â 
Discrimination Seen
''Next to foreign exchange problems,'' the authors found, ''perhaps the most widely aired complaint of foreign investors in China is the escalation of costs for the investors and their enterprises. 
Prices and charges often bear no relation to the quality of the goods or services provided. 
Many of the complaints are colored by the personal experience of the expatriate employees of foreign investors in China who feel that they are being consciously and systematically discriminated against.''
The authors cite higher prices paid by foreigners , solely because they are not Chinese, for airplane and rail tickets, for telephone use and at hotels.
''Until now,'' the authors contend, ''there has been a widespread belief in China that a foreign company is fair game for any costs and that no matter how many it is loaded down with it will nevertheless be able to earn a profit and retain its enthusiasm for China.''
That belief, they wrote, is reflected in the refusal of Chinese negotiators to disclose to an investor the true costs of labor, land use fees, utilities and raw materials.
Perhaps more serious for foreign companies, the two lawyers said, is contract negotiation. 
Chinese negotiators, they said, often refuse to permit foreign companies to write detailed contracts to protect their interests. 
And even after contracts are signed, the lawyers added, it is common for the Chinese to insist on renegotiation.
Â 
'New Rules' Imposed
''Sometimes government agencies will directly interfere with the performance of the contract by imposing new rules, conditions or fees that affect the profitibility of the venture,'' the lawyers said. 
''In practice, contracts concluded with Chinese entities lack legal enforceability.''
For example, a $25 million joint venture with an American company to open a hog farm in Guangdong province ran into trouble when the province's Government, which opened its own hog farm, imposed a quota on the joint venture's exports, It was ''a move that went against the joint venture agreement,'' the American Embassy said.
Similarly, China's tax laws constitute a formidable obstacle to any successful investment, the two lawyers said. 
''Foreign investors coming to China are faced by an increasingly complex web of tax legislation, regulations and rulings that appear to lack consistency in their interpretation and implementation from one locality to another,'' they said, ''and allegedly arbitrary taxation is frequently mentioned as a deterrent to investment.''

file: CONNECTICUT OPINION_ALL AROUND CHINA, MEMORIES OF HOME.txt
text:
ï»¿
IF everyone from Connecticut is
in China, who is home minding
the store?
This is a question I
have asked since going to Peking several months ago for a year's stay.
Word has it that 200,000 American tourists will visit China this year. 
Some quick arithmetic calculates that Connecticut's proportion of that group should be about 2,000, if one extrapolates directly from the state's proportion of the national population. 
Social scientists may tell us to consider income and other variables when accounting for tourism, so one might even project a larger share of tourists for Connecticut.
A quick, and very unscientific, sample seems to support the larger number.
On a basketball court at Peking University, my son thought he saw on a Chinese student a familiar T-shirt in red and black boldly stating, ''Bob's Surplus.''
Hadn't he seen that around Willimantic?
There was no such a place in Peking, was there?
Not at all. 
The student had been to Wesleyan University and the shirt was from Middletown.
The Columbia Law School graduate, studying Chinese law in preparation for a job with a San Francisco firm that specializes in Far Eastern matters hails from the Fairfield area. 
He speaks Chinese extremely well - and without a Connecticut accent.
When my wife and I, after an evening at the ballet in Peking, hitched a ride on a tourist bus so that we could get to a taxi stand (Pekingtaxis do not cruise), we struck up several conversations. 
Inevitably, I was asked where we were from. 
Connecticut?
The never-before-seen couple I spoke with, as if newly discovered family from home, were from North Haven. 
Oh yes, they used to visit the Coventry Bookstore before it closed and knew my home community well.
When I left the Peking University library one day and mounted my bicycle (there are three million bicycles in Peking), I saw a number of limousines and a reporter interviewing a distinguished, silver-haired gentleman. 
He looked familiar. 
Was it former Senator Ribicoff?
Sure, it was. 
He could not be campaigning for votes in Peking, could he?
No, he had left elective office, but was in China on a mission for a law firm. 
We spoke and shook hands. 
A photographer took photos. 
The scene reminded me of the Coventry Democratic smorgasbord at election time.
Who could be homesick when so many from home seem to be here?
And, I expect, more will come.
Last spring, I read that Connecticut companies were doing about $100 million of business a year in China. 
The State Economic Development Commissioner, John J. Carson, saw the world's most populous country as a golden opportunity for Connecticut companies. 
He remarked, ''China is essentially a new trading frontier. 
And many Connecticut manufacturers, especially in our high-tech industries, are producing just what Chinese industries will be purchasing in coming years.''
With China's current move toward modernization and its new economic reforms under way, it is not unlikely that even more Connecticut residents will find their way to the Orient.
So, the town meeting will convene in Tiananmen Square. 
It holds over a million people. 
While we don't quite have a quorum, it seems like we do.
Bruce M. Stave is professor of history and director of the Center for Oral History at the University of Connecticut. 
He is spending this year as Fulbright Professor of American History at Peking University.

text:
