As China moves toward an economy driven more by consumer demand than by central planners, its leaders have begun to recognize that greater consumer choice also requires greater consumer protection.
In what amounts to a crash course in consumer protection, a delegation of four Chinese officials is visiting consumer organizations, businesses and a government agency in the United States - a tour that is exposing them to everything from Ralph Nader's role in this country to a ''sneeze'' machine that tests the strength of paper tissues.
The primary mission of their visit is to gather information about consumer laws and codes, which they plan to translate and consider for use at home, they said.
Â 
More Goods, More Complaints
While washing machines, refrigerators and television sets are becoming commonplace in urban areas of China, so have consumer complaints about shoddy quality, according to Chinese Government reports.
In addition, consumer prices increased 19 percent last year, prompting panic buying of household goods. 
This summer, Prime Minister Li Peng warned that hoarding and speculation could threaten social stabilityI.
Officials of the China Consumers' Association, a four-year-old, quasi-governmental organization, arrived in New York last Tuesday. 
Their itinerary included visits to New York City's Consumer Affairs Department, the American Express Company, the New York Public Interest Research Group and the Consumers Union, which publishes Consumer Reports.
On Friday they canceled appointments in order to see the Statue of Liberty and other sights before heading to Washington.
The Chinese officials visited Consumers Union in Mount Vernon, N.Y., where they toured product-testing laboratories and marveled at the ''sneeze'' machine as well as another that pummels mattresses with a split bowling ball.
Â 
'Socialist Commodity Economy'
After a buffet lunch of seafood salad and carrot cake, Li Yanshou, president of the association, passed out a pamphlet about the organization and Li Yuanmin, the delegation's interpreter, read some of it aloud: ''The aim of the association is to protect the consumers' interests, to provide guidance on consumption and to promote the development of a socialist commodity economy.''
Other members of the delegation are the presidents of regional or city affiliates of the association: Xiao Di Sheng, from Beijing; Zhang Ruofeng, from Hebei province, and Zhang Xing Wu, from Heilongjiang province. 
Prior to becoming officials in the association, the men served as managers in Government agencies.
Ms. Yuanmin said the association, which has 865 regional offices, was created to help the billion Chinese consumers register their complaints and product preferences with Government agencies and factories. 
In addition, she said the association has a role in testing products, supervising quality control and developing consumer-protection regulations.
Any questions?
The Consumer Reports staff had many.
What is the association's annual budget?
About $60,000, Mr. Yanshou said, with almost half coming from the Government and the rest from individual contributions and an international grant.
Â 
Guiding the Consumer
How does the association ''guide consumers in having a correct understanding of the relationship between consumption and production and that between personal consumption and national consumption,'' as its brochure states?
After a prolonged discussion in Chinese, Bu Fanpeng, a vice consul of China's consulate in New York, who accompanied the consumer leaders and helped with translations, summarized their reply. 
''It's like propaganda,'' he said. 
Later, he explained that demand for many products far exceeded production capacity and that the association helps explain this problem to consumers.
How many consumers complain?
About 10,000 since 1984. 
''People are just realizing the importance of making complaints,'' Mr. Fanpeng said.
Are defective products recalled?
Well, not exactly, but individual consumers have the right to obtain repairs, replacements or refunds, Mr. Yanshou said. 
There is no hesitation to criticize Government-controlled factories, he added.
Their opinion of American consumers?
The delegation conferred again. 
''We have learned a lot,'' Mr. Yanshou replied.
Â 
'Who Is Ralph Nader?'
When it was their turn to pose questions, the Chinese leaders asked about the value of the magazine's product-testing equipment ($5 million), its circulation (3.7 million) and Consumers Union's connection with other consumer organizations (ad hoc).
In the course of the discussion, Rhonda H. Karpatkin, executive director of Consumers Union, mentioned the importance of Ralph Nader and organizations he founded.
The Chinese were puzzled. 
''Who is Ralph Nader?''
Mr. Fanpeng asked.
''You haven't heard of Ralph Nader?''
Mrs. Karpatkin said. 
''That's refreshing.''

'Nuclear Outlaw' Nations
''My information,'' Mr. Cranston said in a statement issued by his office, ''is that China has either engaged in serious nuclear trade negotiations with or actually has continued a series of nuclear exports to each and every one of these five 'nuclear outlaw' nations.''
He also charged that the information about the Chinese violations had been covered up by the State Department, particularly by Richard T. Kennedy, the department official who negotiated the 1984 accord. 
The Senator said the intelligence information showed that the Chinese actions contradicted Administration assurances that China supported nonproliferation policies.
He said Mr. Kennedy ''has systematically withheld, suppressed and covered up information - known virtually throughout the executive branch -which Congress might find worrisome as it reviewed the draft agreement now before us.''

text:

WHETHER New Year's Day is celebrated on Jan. 
1 according to the Gregorian calendar, in September or October as the Jews' Rosh ha-Shanah or in midwinter by Asians, foods serve as edible talismans to assure luck, happiness or prosperity in the coming year.
The notion, for example, that eating gold-colored food will put money in your pocket is common in Peru, where papas a la huancaina, a potato dish tinted with tumeric or with a saffron-colored spice called tadillo, is served on New Year's Eve. 
In China, dumplings made from golden egg pancakes, crisply gilded spring rolls and oranges are the aureate foods appropriate for the Chinese New Year's celebrations in midwinter.
The Chinese also value fish. 
A whole one is preferred, suggesting that prosperity has favored you with more than you can eat.
Pork is on the New Year's table in many cultures, connoting riches because at one time having a pig to slaughter guaranteed food for the coming year.
In Italy and the southern parts of the United States, pork is eaten in the form of sausage, stuffed pig's trotters (zampone), ham hocks or pig's knuckles, invariably accompanied by a dish of dried beans. 
The Italians eat lentils, or lenticchie, which since Roman times have represented coins. 
According to the cookbook author and cooking instructor, Anna Teresa Callen (''Anna Teresa Callen's Menus for Pasta,'' Crown, 1985 ), parsley decorates the dish because it was thought to ward off evil spirits. 
In the American South, greens are added to black-eyed peas or hoppin' John (black-eyed peas with rice). 
The symbolism is straightforward: the greens represented dollars and the black-eyed peas coins. 
Dried beans, garnished or plain, represent the changing over of years, for they can be stored through the winter and then be planted to create the harvest.
Sometimes a silver coin or trinket is buried in a dish of black-eyed peas or hoppin' John, providing an extra measure of good luck to the person finding it. 
The Twelfth Night cake or king's cake served on Epiphany in France will have coins or fava beans tucked inside. 
Similarly, the Spanish roscon de Reyes, a bread, is baked with a coin or small ceramic animal inside for luck. 
The Mexican version, a king's bread with nuts and raisins, is baked with a clay doll inside. 
These breads and cakes are round, symbolizing a whole year, much like the hallah baked for Rosh ha-Shanah.
When it comes time to ring in the New Year, you lift a glass - of Champagne, punch, eggnog or whatever -and propose a toast. 
Why toast?
The tradition in England and Wales was for slices of toasted bread to be soaked in the hot spiced ale called wassail and served with it.
In Spain, according to Penelope Casas, author of ''Tapas'' (Knopf, 1985), 12 grapes are eaten just before midnight on New Year's Eve, one for each chime of the clock. 
Good luck will come to those who finish the grapes before the final stroke.

The Dalai Lama, the exiled spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism, today dismissed China's offer to allow him to return to Tibet if he abandoned his campaign for independence. 
He said there was nothing new in the offer, which was made Monday, and indicated that he would not accept the restrictions.
''I have had that invitation from the Chinese Government since 1979,'' he said in London.

The 52-year-old spiritual leader, who fled to India in 1959 after Chinese troops put down a nationalist rebellion, has long been an outspoken advocate of human rights and independence for the people of Tibet.

He expressed a willingness to meet with the Chinese authorities, if there were genuine signs of improved treatment of Tibetans by the Chinese.
The Dalai Lama emphasized the need to solve the Tibetan problem through what he called ''the middle way - some kind of compromise.''

text:
ï»¿
The goods ranged from goat-hair scarves (khati) and yak-butter lamps (choekung) to dharma buttons and copies of the official Dalai Lama comic book.
They all sold well as the fourth annual Tibet Fair opened near the United Nations yesterday. 
It attracted those with considerable knowledge of the Himalayan land - a man from Virginia showed up to buy a study book for third-year Tibetan - as well as those with only a passing curiosity about the ''roof of the world.''
Strung along walls and piled on tables in a crowded room in the Eastside International Community Center, at 330 East 45th Street, exotic items beckoned buyers, many of whom said they were looking for Christmas ideas. 
Jewelry, dresses, sweaters, boots, hats, silver teapots, ornamental knives, scrolls, books, Buddha statues and ''I Love Tibet'' T-shirts all vied for a spot under the tree.
Many of the items were made by Tibetans, but many were not.
Â 
'Hey, Don't Buy That'
''Don't you just love this?'' said Helen Brill, holding up a red scroll with Chinese characters on it. 
''I don't know whether it's Tibetan, but it sure is beautiful.''
''Hey, don't buy that,'' a man whispered conspiratorially to his wife, who was admiring a silk scarf that had a ''Made in Beijing'' tag on the back. 
''The Tibetans don't like the Chinese.''
China annexed Tibet in the early 1950's and has run it as an administrative unit since a crackdown in 1959 that prompted the Dalai Lama - the Tibetan spiritual and temporal leader - to flee on horseback over the Himalayas into India.
The fair involved an odd mix of Tibetan serenity and American hustle. 
''Now wait a minute,'' hissed a woman who believed she had been overcharged. 
''I thought the Dalai Lama postcards were a quarter each and five for a dollar.''
The seller started to explain no, those were 50 cents each.
Â 
'A Sort of Uneasiness'
Then he shrugged and sold them, placidly, five for a dollar.
''The feeling is something different from a normal feeling for me,'' explained Jigme Sampho, who with his wife, Dechen, was selling hats and boots made by Tibetans living in exile in India. 
''There is a sort of uneasiness.''
But Mr. Sampho, who works for the Parks Department as a maintenance man in Central Park, added that the fair does come only once a year. 
And he said he was glad that people could come and learn something about the land where he was born.
Many said they did appreciate that chance. 
''I'm fascinated about Tibet,'' one woman said, ''but I've pretty well decided I'll never go there because of the altitude.''
Tenzing Chhodak sat selling posters, books and calendars underneath a large print of the Tibetan Wheel of Life, depicting what are believed to be the six stages into which human beings are continually reincarnated and from which, in order to attain enlightenment, they must escape.
These cycles are the realm of false gods; of titans vainly trying to battle their way into heaven; hell dwellers being administered hot-and-cold tortures; preta, or hungry ghosts, that symbolize greedy people; animals, guilty of ignorance, and humans, who alone among those in the six cycles are offered the chance to study and practice religion.
The fair, proceeds of which are contributed to Tibetan refugees in India, continues today from 11 A.M. to 6 P.M., and also Saturday, Dec. 
20.
Tibetans hold the fair both to raise money and to educate people about their land, said Tinley Nyandak, president of the New York-based Tibetan Association.
Mr. Nyandak said the region's Tibetan community, numbering about 160, is one of the smallest ethnic groups in the metropolitan area. 
Not quite the smallest, he noted: ''You know the Manchus?
There are only two Manchus in the whole Northeast, so far as I know.''

TUNG'S dances work their way along with a thoughtfulness and conviction that persuade one to follow. 
Such was the case Friday at the La Mama Annex, when Chen & Dancers presented Mr. Chen's new ''Longmen Mountain,'' one in a series of modern-dance pieces on old China.
Set to wonderfully primeval clangor and chants composed by Li Tai-Shaing, ''Longmen Mountain'' takes its title from the name of a Chinese grotto of the fifth century, a cave-temple that served Silk Route travelers and Buddhist pilgrims. 
Mr. Chen blends the elasticity and bold attack of Western modern dance with the flexed fingers and hands, for example, of ancient Chinese dance forms in work that is as much dance as drama.

file: DAVID HWANG_ RIDING ON THE HYPHEN.txt
text:
ï»¿
IN THE ETHNIC COMMUNITIES that spawned them, artists who manage to cross over into the mainstream from Harlem or Watts or Chinatown east or west call the journey ''riding on the hyphen.''
Pop musicians like Mexican-American Ricardo Valenzuela, who as Ritchie Valens topped the charts in the 1950's with ''La Bamba,'' were among the first. 
Today's crossover stars include the black American film maker Spike Lee, whose vaguely anarchist dispatches from the city (''She's Gotta Have It'') and the campus (''School Daze'') are propelled by a savvy populist energy.
David Henry Hwang - barely 30 and haunted by spirits often of his own invention - is riding on the hyphen into mainstream American theater as few Asian-Americans have before him. 
For the young playwright, the Broadway opening next Sunday of his ''M. 
Butterfly'' represents a breathtaking leap. 
With its scandalous and incredible plot, its flourishes of Chinese opera and flashes of nudity, its Western soliloquizing and reflections on East-West politics, its original music (by Lucia Hwong) interwoven with Puccini's ''Madama Butterfly,'' Hwang's play breaches just about every convention of the commercial theater.
Of the five new American dramas to open on Broadway in the 1987-88 season (a figure that baldly expresses many producers' hostility to the category), Hwang's is the only one to arrive without the benefit of development in the noncommercial sector. 
Moreover, the $1.5 million production, staged by the British director John Dexter and starring John Lithgow, is one of the most opulent ever given a nonmusical play on Broadway.
The source of ''M. 
Butterfly'' is a story that itself defies belief. 
Under the headline ''France Jails 2 in Odd Case of Espionage,'' a dispatch from Paris in The New York Times of May 11, 1986, told of Bernard Boursicot, a former French diplomat, and his lover, Shi Peipu, a star of the Beijing Opera, who had each been sentenced by a French court to six years in jail for spying for China. 
(Shi was subsequently expelled from France.) Their affair had begun in 1964 in Beijing, where Boursicot was stationed. 
It ended two decades later, after the opera star, accompanied by a child who had purportedly been fathered by the diplomat, moved into the Frenchman's Paris home and attracted the attention of the French counterespionage service. 
During the trial, the opera star was revealed to be a man.
The diplomat testified that this was shocking news to him. 
Paris buzzed.
So did the young playwright. 
''The story enabled me to pull together various concerns that I have about racism, sexism and imperialism,'' says Hwang. 
''The story was like a perfect little jar that could hold all these different subjects.
''I only knew Madame Butterfly as a cultural stereotype,'' he continues. 
''Like, sometimes you would say, 'Oh, she's pulling a Butterfly' - which meant someone trying to do a submissive-Oriental number. 
I was trying to think of a hook, a way to break the back of this spy story. 
One day it popped into my head: What did Boursicot think he was getting?
Well, he probably thought he was getting Madame Butterfly.''
Hwang, who lives in Los Angeles with his wife, Ophelia, would fit nobody's stereotype of the submissive Asian. 
He tends to augment his slight frame with the padded contours of Armani suits and speaks with considered precision, though his voice has a childlike pitch and often cracks when he is engaged by a subject.
In ''M. 
Butterfly,'' Hwang spins a complex yarn from the 1986 news report. 
His fantasy includes a slangy precis of the Puccini opera from an Asian point of view and an attempt to pair the story of the affair with a meditation on what might well have been going on within a French mission in China in the late 1950's and early 60's.
The spying gave the playwright a route into political issues he wanted to deal with. 
''It has real implications for the choices that were made,'' Hwang says of the affair. 
''People went to war, died, made political decisions through these personal things. 
We didn't consider Orientals to be our equals. 
We didn't figure after the Second World War that they'd come back and beat us at our own game. 
That sort of miscalculation also led us to believe that if we bombed Vietnam enough, they would all give in.''
''M. Butterfly'' begins a few years earlier than the true story. 
The diplomat, renamed Gallimard, meets the opera star, called Soong (played by B. D. Wong), at an embassy function where the singer performs Madame Butterfly's death scene. 
In a conversation over drinks, Soong scoffs at Gallimard's sentimental response to the opera. 
''Consider it this way,'' the singer says. 
''What would you say if a blonde homecoming queen fell in love with a short Japanese businessman?
He treats her cruelly, then goes home for three years, during which time she prays to his picture and turns down marriage from a young Kennedy. 
Then, when she learns he has remarried, she kills herself. 
Now, I believe you would consider this girl to be a deranged idiot, correct?
But because it's an Oriental who kills herself for an American - ah!
- you find it beautiful.''
Jack Viertel - one of the principal figures in bringing ''M. 
Butterfly'' to New York - was a dramaturge, working with playwrights on scripts, at the Mark Taper Forum in Los Angeles when he read the accounts of the French spy trial. 
Soon after, he called Hwang to suggest that the newspaper account had dramatic possibilities; the playwright told Viertel he'd already written the play, with the encouragement of Stuart Ostrow, an independent producer.
''It's one of the few plays that present a fascinating event - as in e Met a the blinding of the horses in 'Equus' - and then explain it in a way that's up to the fascination of the event, that isn't ultimately a disappointment,'' says Viertel.
Ostrow sent Hwang's script to John Dexter last year. 
The director's response was immediate and positive. 
Dexter - who had staged Peter Shaffer's ''Equus'' on Broadway in 1974, as well as such modern operas as Francis Poulenc's ''Dialogues of the Carmelites'' at the Metropolitan Opera - instantly recognized in David Hwang a powerful new theatrical voice.
''The language and the freedom with which he uses the stage, playing across time, space, geography - I suppose that was the appeal,'' says Dexter, whose staging of Alban Berg's ''Lulu'' will open at the Met a few days after ''M. 
Butterfly.''
''But mainly the language, which is extraordinarily funny and touching, never striking a false note. 
He has a great instinct for creating situa-tions in which theatrical magic can happen.''
DAVID HENRY HWANG, the son of a Shanghai-born banker and a Chinese pianist raised in the Philippines, began riding on the hyphen to mainstream prominence from the unlikely ''ghetto'' of San Gabriel, Calif., a middle-class enclave south of Pasadena.
''I knew I was Chinese,'' he says, ''but growing up, it never occurred to me that that had any particular implication or that it should differentiate me in any way. 
I thought it was a minor detail, like having red hair. 
I never got a lot in school to contradict that. 
My parents brought us up with a rather nice sense of self.''
Nothing in his past propelled him toward the theater; indeed, he assumed he would go into law when he went to Stanford University in the mid-1970's. 
But when he got there, he found himself searching for the meaning of ''Chinese-American.''
His parents' diverse histories didn't make the task easy.
''My father has always been interested in discarding the past,'' says Hwang. 
''He's never much liked China, or the whole idea behind China or Chinese ways of thinking. 
He's always been much more attracted to American ways of thinking. 
He feels Americans are more open - they tell you what they think - and he's very much that way himself.''
Hwang's mother brought to the family a tradition of Protestant fundamentalism. 
Her grandparents, who lived in the seaside village of Amoy, in Fujian Province, were converted by missionaries; her grandmother, Hwang says, was an exorcist. 
His mother's family migrated to the Philippines and there became wealthy merchants before coming to the United States in the late 1960's. 
Hwang's parents met at a foreign-students' dance at the University of Southern California and fell in love, but they couldn't marry until his father converted to Protestantism.
While at Stanford, Hwang started going to the theater, particularly San Francisco's Magic Theater, where Sam Shepard was bringing out his new work. 
On a lark, in 1978, Hwang attended the first Padua Hills Playwrights Festival in Claremont, Calif. 
- a workshop that has become a major playwrights' retreat - where Shepard, Maria Irene Fornes and others worked with fledgling writers.
There, Hwang began writing ''FOB'' (''fresh off the boat''). 
The play tells the story of a young, rich newcomer to California and his visit with Chinese-American cousins. 
But, in the kind of twist that was to characterize much of Hwang's subsequent work, that story is interwoven with one about Fa Mu Lan, the legendary heroine who figures in Maxine Hong Kingston's novel ''Woman Warrior,'' and Gwan Gung, the Chinese god of war introduced to American audiences by another Chinese-American playwright, Frank Chin.
''I read Maxine's book,'' Hwang says, ''and felt immediately excited by the possibility that you could interweave the hyperrealistic details of contemporary American life with the larger, mythical ghost story in the background.''
The naive in ''FOB,'' the son of a Hong Kong businessman, is treated with contempt by the kin who know what the future holds for him. 
''Coming to America, you're gonna jump the boat,'' an assimilated Chinese-American hisses. 
''You're gonna decide you like us. 
Yeah - you're gonna like having 15 theaters in three blocks, you're gonna like West Hollywood and Newport Beach. 
You're gonna decide to become an American. 
. . . You won't even know it's coming before it has you. 
Before you're trying real hard to be just like the rest of us - go dinner, go movie, go motel, bang-bang. 
And when your father writes you that do-it-yourself acupuncture sales are down, you'll throw that letter in the basket and burn it in your brain. 
And you'll write that you're gonna live in Monterey Park a few years before going back home - and you'll get your green card - and you'll build up a nice little stockbroker's business and have a few American kids before your dad realizes what's happened and dies, his hopes reduced to a few chattering teeth and a pack of pornographic playing cards. 
Yeah - great things come to the U.S. out of Hong Kong.''
No one who read ''FOB'' in its first drafts could fail to be moved by the blend of slice-of-life realism and yearning spiritualism - scattershot anger mixed with a sense of fathomless loss. 
It wasn't Hwang's first play, but John L'Heureux, his writing coach at Stanford and author of the novel ''A Woman Run Mad,'' was stunned by it.
''He came in and said he wanted me to give him a tutorial in play writing,'' L'Heureux recalls. 
''He showed me some of his first attempts; they were palpably bad. 
I told him to read Sam Shepard and to get some education. 
In the middle of the second week, he handed in a play. 
I couldn't believe it was by the same person.''
''FOB'' was first performed by students in Hwang's Stanford dormito-ry - part of the spring rites on cam-pus - under the young playwright's direction. 
At the same time, he sent it off to the National Playwrights' Conference of the Eugene O'Neill Theater Center in Waterford, Conn. 
- one of the country's most prestigious launching sites for new plays. 
In the spring of 1979, just weeks before he graduated from Stanford, he got the call: the O'Neill wanted the play. 
''Of all the moments in my career so far,'' says Hwang, ''just on a visceral level, that's probably been the most exciting.''
''The main thing I learned there,'' he says of that summer at the O'Neill, ''was how to filter criticism. 
You do this play and then everyone sits around and tells you how they would write your play if they were you. 
. . . I tended to take the bulk of the comments and do rewrites based on those lines, and I eventually threw them all out, because, yeah, there's a certain value in all this criticism, but you can't just swallow it all.''
HWANG FILLED A VAC-uum in New York, where productions of Asian-American plays were mostly limited to Tisa Chang's Pan Asian Repertory Theater and Wynn Handman's American Place Theater. 
In the early and mid-70's, the latter had produced Frank Chin's ''Chickencoop Chinaman'' and ''Year of the Dragon'' - angry plays by an angry young playwright. 
In Hwang, the producer Joseph Papp -on the prowl for new Asian-American work - found a different but no less compelling and personal voice.
'' 'FOB' reminded me of the 'greenhorns,' the Jews who came from Eastern Europe,'' says Papp. 
''Even though the cultures were strikingly different, it was the same notion. 
The principle of someone coming from the old country who didn't know how to behave himself was very much part of my own tradition. 
But this went further than that. 
'FOB' went into the traditions by suddenly moving into a more abstract, poetic existence in the context of a very naturalistic play.
''So I met him and liked him immediately,'' Papp continues. 
''He was trying to maintain his connection with his roots. 
I met his parents in Los Angeles. 
We went out for dinner. 
Naturally, his father selected a French restaurant. 
There was the son, holding on to tradition, and the father, very Westernized. 
David was looking for his past. 
That was very refreshing to me, because usually it's lost into the American culture or nobody can articulate it properly.''
''FOB'' opened at New York's Public Theater on June 9, 1980, directed by Mako, who had acted in the original Broadway production of Stephen Sondheim's ''Pacific Overtures.''
Starring in Hwang's play was John Lone, a Chinese actor trained in Asian opera techniques, with whom the playwright would be associated through several subsequent productions, and who would himself ride on the hyphen to stardom in Bernardo Bertolucci's ''The Last Emperor.''
Frank Rich wrote in The New York Times: ''Surely 'FOB' is the first show that has ever attempted to marry the conventional well-made play to Oriental theater and to mix the sensibilities of Maxine Hong Kingston and Norman Lear.''
Though ''FOB'' won Obie awards for both Hwang and Lone, the playwright found that not everyone was comfortable with his unboosterish portrayal of assimilation.
''My work has always been controversial within certain segments of the Asian-American community,'' says Hwang. 
''This is a community that is generally not represented well at all on the stage, in the media, etc. 
So on those few occasions when something comes along, everybody feels obligated to make sure that it represents his own point of view. 
And of course no artist can do that. 
. . . I find that sort of political criticism much more difficult and substantial than the esthetic criticism that I received at the O'Neill - that's nothing compared with being told that you've set the Asian-American back 10 years.''
Maxine Hong Kingston saw the Public Theater production of ''FOB.''
''The main question he asks is, What is a Chinese-American?'' says the novelist. 
''Is there a separate identity?
In 'FOB' there's a little bit of borrowing from Chinese theater, but it's not Chinese theater. 
He's searching, and he hasn't found it yet.''
Hwang achieved greater recognition with his next work, ''The Dance and the Railroad,'' which was commissioned by the Off Off Broadway New Federal Theater and moved to the Public in 1981. 
That play, set in 1867 during the construction of the transcontinental railroad, featured John Lone as a Chinese laborer more concerned with maintaining his operatic skills than with serving the white man, and Tzi Ma as another laborer whose heart is set on learning how to perform the role of a heroic warrior. 
While continuing to combine past and present, the playwright was also revealing another trait: a packed literary style that is never turgid.
Confident in Hwang's development as a playwright, Papp followed ''Dance'' almost immediately with a full-scale production of an audacious new work, ''Family Devotions.''
Mixing unembarrassed family portraits with a searching into the past, ''Family Devotions'' is a big, messy farce with a bleak, surreal coda. 
The centerpiece of the set is a pulpit, embellished with a neon cross, that is brought out daily for family prayer meetings. 
Here was Hwang skewering the Christian tradition that had obstructed his journey into the past.
''In this country, Christianity provides both a means of assimilation and a source of community,'' says the playwright. 
''Community for obvious reasons, because you have these Chinese churches and Korean churches. 
But you're also taking on what is perceived to be the religion of the society, doing something that's very acceptable by American standards -that is, you're buying into the great American cultural myth, and everybody's very happy. 
Except for your own soul, everybody wins.''
''Family Devotions'' is set in a home much like the one the playwright came from and revolves around a visit from a family elder who runs afoul of his sisters' efforts to convert him to Christianity. 
It also tells the stories of a wealthy father -a bank president who has found notoriety as a victim of a kidnapping -and his son (a thinly disguised stand-in for the author), who is leaving the family to go east and play the violin for the Boston Symphony.
''Chinese culture in general is not very religious,'' Hwang observes. 
''Confucianism is more a code of ethics than a religion, and ancestor worship is a way for parents to control you even after they're dead.''
The playwright's parents, Henry and Dorothy Hwang, were in the audience on the opening night of ''Family Devotions.''
''When he was a sophomore in college, he showed me a play and I said, 'Well, I send you to this expensive school and you write trashy stuff like this?'
'' recalls Henry Hwang, who was himself kidnapped in a bizarre incident about 10 years ago. 
''Two weeks later, he said it was going to be done in the dormitory. 
We went to see it, and I was moved to tears. 
But I felt dizzy after 'Family Devotions.'
I felt as if my life had been turned upside down. 
Of course, if the material is useful to him, he's welcome to it.''
With fame came a strong dose of self-doubt. 
''I was being put in a position for which I was not prepared,'' says the playwright. 
''At 23 or 24, I was asked to be some sort of spokesperson for Asian-Americans on various issues which I hadn't really thought out that well consciously. 
On the one hand, it was flattering. 
But on the other hand, growing up as a person of color, you're always ambivalent to a certain degree about your own ethnicity. 
You think it's great, but there is necessarily a certain amount of self-hatred, or confusion at least, which results from the fact that there's a role model in this society which is basically a Caucasian man, and you don't measure up to that.
''What was happening to me,'' he continues, ''was that that quality about which I was ambivalent was being thrust into the forefront. 
. . . It was no longer that I was a playwright per se, but that I was an Asian-American playwright, and my Asian-Americanness became the quality which defined me to the public.''
Hwang spent the next few years living a life of modest celebrity in New York - in 1983, the Public produced a pair of one-act plays of his under the collective title ''Sound and Beauty'' that were received with qualified praise - and traveling in Asia, Europe and Canada. 
In Toronto, he met Ophelia Chong, a Chinese-Canadian; they were married in Los Angeles and have lived there since 1985 with an aging Welsh corgi named Victor.
''Rich Relations'' was written during Hwang's Canadian sojourn, after a long bout with writer's block, and produced Off Broadway by the Second Stage in the spring of 1986. 
It was his first non-Asian play. 
It was also his first flop. 
Critics complained that he was rehashing old themes, and the playwright didn't disagree with the charge.
'' 'Rich Relations' was another attempt to write a spiritual farce,'' says Hwang, ''and it's about my family -except that they're not Asians. 
It was also an attempt to talk about resurrection, which was what I felt had just happened to me. 
Ethnic writers still have a kind of second-class cultural citizenship. 
. . . I've gotten a lot of mileage out of writing about Chinese-Americans. 
Whether that's good for my career in the long run is debatable.''
Hwang began writing for the movies and television as well as for the theater. 
He recently completed ''My American Son,'' about the Iran-contra affair, for Home Box Office and is at work on ''Seven Years in Tibet,'' a feature film set in India and Asia during World War II. 
All-out failure, he says, was the most liberating thing that had happened to him since the first strong flush of success with ''FOB.''
IT IS EASY TO SEE ALL OF Hwang's work as leading up to ''M. 
Butterfly,'' a play that is, at its root, a meditation on the ways the West misperceives the East and vice versa.
The composer Philip Glass, with whom Hwang was working on another project, recommended the playwright to Stuart Ostrow, who funded the research for ''M. 
Butterfly.''
By the time the play was ready to go into production, Jack Viertel had moved to New York to become a creative director for the Jujamcyn Theaters organization, which owns five Broadway theater houses. 
Viertel persuaded the company to invest in ''M. 
Butterfly'' and Ostrow to house it in a Jujamcyn theater when it came to Broadway. 
David Geffen signed on as co-producer. 
For a hugely risky work, ''M. 
Butterfly'' had garnered an extraordinary amount of mainstream support.
''This is a leap for a number of reasons,'' says Viertel. 
''One, it's a big play. 
It's the first play David's written that deals with history in a way that isn't totally imaginary or imagined; he's using the real world in a highly theatrical way. 
It's a much larger version of what he was doing in 'The Dance and the Railroad' -take an event and find the underlying social and political meaning of it.''
In ''M. 
Butterfly,'' as in all of his plays, Hwang searches in some of the darker corners of his own psyche. 
''As an Asian, I identify with Soong,'' he says. 
''As a man, I identify with Gallimard. 
That willful self-delusion is something I know I've experienced as a man; I've been good at self-delusion when I've wanted to be. 
The really sexist things Gallimard says are things that I know on some level work in my own soul and color my relationships with women. 
Pleasure in giving pain to a woman is not that far removed, I think, from a lot of male experiences.''
He recognizes the risks in moving into the political arena with so personal and stylized a work as ''M. 
Butterfly.''
During its pre-Broadway run in Washington, Hwang sweated out some negative criticism, reworking a few scenes and adding others to clarify the play without compromising his iconoclastic history lesson.
''The play might be seen as anti-Western, in the sense that it's saying that the West just hasn't looked at these issues,'' he says. 
''That's partly true, but it's very pro-American, too. 
It's saying, 'These are the facts of the situation, and if you would like to get along better in the world, then you had better look at the world more clearly. 
The East isn't going to go away.'
''

Xiang-Dong Kong
Xiang-dong Kong, a pianist, was born in Shanghai in 1968, and was one of the young musicians featured in Isaac Stern's 1979 film, ''From Mao to Mozart.''
Since then, he has completed his studies in his homeland and enrolled at Brigham Young University, in Utah. 
Earlier this year, he won the gold medal at the Gina Bachauer International Piano Competition, which sponsored his New York debut recital Oct. 
15 at Alice Tully Hall.
Mr. Kong proved especially impressive in works that demand outgoing, bravura playing - Liszt's ''Rhapsodie Espagnole,'' Grainger's wild-eyed paraphrase on Tchaikovsky's ''Waltz of the Flowers,'' and the sober, incisive and fiery Second Sonata by Robert Muczynski.
In these, he played with great energy, and a sense of rhythmic liquidity. 
Yet, even in the densest, loudest passages, every strand of the musical texture was clear and well-placed, and matters of phrasing and coloration appeared carefully considered.
This deliberation worked less well in a Haydn Sonata (Hob. 
XVI:50), Chopin's Polonaise-Fantaisie (Op. 61) and a Rachmaninoff Etude-Tableau (Op. 33, No. 8), all of which he played more gently. 
His sound was delicate and lovely in these, and there were some fine coloristic ideas. 
But there was also a tendency toward rhythmic squareness - the opposite of what made the brighter works so successful.
Â 
Arax Davtian
Arax Davtian, a soprano from Armenia who has been singing at the Bolshoi Opera in recent seasons, made her way easily through a demanding debut program last Sunday afternoon at Weill Recital Hall.
Ms. Davtian has a large, powerful, rich-toned voice and a commanding presence. 
She was most striking in arias by Verdi (''Pace, Pace'' from ''La Forza del Destino,'' and ''Ecco l'Orrido Campo'' from ''Un Ballo in Maschera'') and Bellini (''O Quante Volte'' from ''I Capuletti e i Montecchi''), and her renderings of contemporary songs by Tigran Mansurian and Edward Mirzoyan were quite moving.
She was also an effective Mozart singer, after a fashion. 
To this listener's taste, her heavy but well-controlled vibrato is better suited to music of later vintage; yet, once one got used to the dimension of her voice, her renderings of ''Come Scoglio'' from ''Cosi Fan Tutte'' and a pair of Mozart songs turned out to be fairly persuasive.
Also on the program were songs and arias by Beethoven and Glinka. 
Diana Mkrtchian was the excellent accompanist. 
Her handling of the operatic reductions were particularly pleasing.
Â 
Edith Murano
Edith Murano, a pianist from Argentina, favors a dry, lightly pedaled sound, and an approach to phrasing that can seem clipped and edgy. 
But her ideas are often original enough that one can overlook the more quirky aspects of her style - as well as the fact that her renderings are not always note-perfect.
At her North American debut, on Thursday evening at Weill Recital Hall, she played Beethoven's ''Pastorale'' Sonata and Prokofiev's Sonata No. 3 daringly, with razor-like rhythms and a tempestuous energy that often threatened to careen out of control, but never did. 
She also offered the United States premiere of Virgilio Mortari's Serenata, an attractive, neo-Baroque suite, which she played with clarity and incisiveness. 
Her opening pair of Bach Preludes and Fugues was less impressive. 
And her closing Chopin group was a mixed success. 
A Barcarolle (Op. 60) and an Impromptu (Op.51) were nightmarishly overwrought, but the Andante Spianato and Grande Polonaise Brillante (Op. 22) was played with a soulful, almost improvisatory approach that offset the frequent wrong notes in exposed places.

text:

THE YEARS OF MACARTHUR Volume Three: Triumph and Disaster 1945-1964. 
By D. Clayton James. 
Illustrated. 848 pp. 
Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. 
$29.95. IN last volume of D. Clayton James's biography of Gen. Douglas MacArthur (1880-1964), the greatest military figure of his day turns to peace and revives the energies of the Japanese to develop a modern state. 
He then returns to war, in Korea, and, after a period of defeat, fashions the Inchon landings, one of the outstanding military feats of the century. 
He is honored to the point of idolatry, but then his reputation is eroded, and his judgments about the Korean War are proved wrong by a powerful offensive by Communist Chinese armies. 
Contemptuous of President Truman, impudent toward the Joint Chiefs of Staff, MacArthur is removed from command.
This book and its two predecessors form one of the best military biographies of our time. 
The only comparison I can make is to Winston Churchill's ''Marlborough.''
In its presentation of the Duke's bickering with allies, his victory at Blenheim in 1704 and his final retreat into the shadows, that book evokes the same atmosphere of Greek tragedy.
Mr. James's book is abundantly researched and scrupulously fair to all the eminent figures who march through its pages - Truman, Dean Acheson, Gen. Matthew B. Ridgway, Emperor Hirohito. 
I regret that the author could not devote more space to the training and tactics of the Chinese troops, for it was that preparation that turned a United Nations parade to Korea's Yalu River into a stunning defeat.
A single exchange he cites between two other American generals reveals the nature of Washington's difficulties in dealing with the hubristic commander in Korea, especially after the success of the Inchon operation, which MacArthur carried out despite the misgivings of many senior officers. 
General Ridgway, then the Army's deputy chief of staff and shortly to be MacArthur's successor, asks Gen. Hoyt S. Vandenberg, the Air Force chief of staff, why the Joint Chiefs did not simply ''send orders to MacArthur and tell him what to do.''
To which the Air Force general replies, ''What good would that do?
He wouldn't obey the orders. 
What can we do?''
MacArthur had emerged from World War II as one of the great captains. 
Given the task of ruling occupied Japan, he was adept at bringing that country back into the family of nations. 
Understanding and liberal in his approach to Japan's economic and political problems, he nursed, cajoled and ordered a sick society back to health. 
The most professional of soldiers, he was thought too conservative for the job. 
But he encouraged the formation of unions, fought the giant business conglomerates that had run Japan and oversaw the country's almost miraculous recovery.
Mr. James demonstrates that MacArthur was a mass of contradictions. 
The soldier of splendid gifts also yearned for the Presidency and pursued it with singular ineptitude. 
The actor in him won the allegiance of politicians, publishers and businessmen, but he was also capable of great strategic and tactical operations in war. 
Mr. James makes a valiant effort to get to the real man, but he is only partly successful. 
Throughout his life, MacArthur spewed out speeches, communiques and statements, but like Robert E. Lee, he kept his inner self locked up.
MacArthur's dismissal by Truman in 1951 and the events that led up to it provide the most fascinating part of this excellent volume. 
After the North Korean invasion of South Korea in June 1950, MacArthur, directing poorly trained Americans and a frightened South Korean Army, held the line around Pusan with grim determination. 
After he planned and carried out the Inchon landings - of which Gen. Walter Bedell Smith remarked, ''I don't like the man, never did, but that was a great feat of arms'' - things began to go wrong. 
In his last communique about a victory, he claimed that his general assault after the landings should ''for all practical purposes end the war.''
But on Nov. 
25 the Chinese, who had intervened locally earlier, struck with two armies of 180,000 and 120,000 men. 
''We face an entirely new war,'' MacArthur said.
He was correct. 
But from that point on, his quarrels with Truman, whom he undoubtedly underestimated, and the Joint Chiefs grew more intense. 
He felt that even in this new situation, he was being denied the reinforcements he needed. 
The American and Allied buildup of NATO forces in Europe irritated him.
At the time of the Chinese intervention, the United Nations, under whose authority MacArthur operated, had begun a series of peace initiatives. 
In one of those public statements that even today set the teeth on edge, MacArthur made ''an arrogant challenge to the pride of Communist China,'' voicing his readiness to meet with the enemy Commander in Chief. 
It was also a challenge to Washington, and Truman decided MacArthur had to go because of an act ''totally disregarding all directives.''
The general had compounded previous errors by sending a message to the House minority leader, Representative Joseph Martin, declaring that he was fighting Europe's war with arms while diplomats fought it with words and ending with the slogan ''There is no substitute for victory.''
The order for his relief from command came on April 10, 1951. 
Even then some hesitated. 
Gen. Omar Bradley, then Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, wrote that MacArthur had ''stretched but had not legally violated any JCS directives.''
But to Truman, alarmed by the weakening of European support, the message was clear. 
So MacArthur went.
His departure provoked a political firestorm at home. 
In retrospect, however, it was remarkably short-lived. 
The general was showered with praise. 
He had abundant opportunities before Congress and the public to make his case. 
Then, in 1952, he flirted with Presidential politics but got nowhere. 
Another general, Dwight D. Eisenhower, took the stage.
MacArthur lived a full life until the end. 
He was much loved by many, scorned by others. 
But as few have done, he left his mark on history, not only as a soldier but as an unwilling sacrifice to the dominance of civil power in our Republic.

ON JAN. 
3, 1986, THE READERS OF THE ASIAN EDITION of The Wall Street Journal were treated to an arresting full-page advertisement. 
Topped by a smiling photograph of S. B. (for Shien Biau) Woo, the Lieutenant Governor of Delaware, who is also the state's highest-ranking elected Democrat, the highest-ranking Chinese-American official in the United States and a physicist, the ad posed two questions. 
''Are you thinking of investing in the USA?'' it asked. 
''WHY NOT DO AS THE AMERICANS DO!''
The wily Americans, Woo's text explained, incorporated their companies in the benign business climate of Delaware, established trusts there and founded Delaware banks and holding companies.
Shortly after the ad appeared, Woo himself was in the Orient, personally extolling the virtues of his state. 
With the Delaware Secretary of State, Michael E. Harkins, in tow, the Shanghai-born official traveled to Taiwan, Hong Kong, China, Indonesia, Singapore and the Philippines, tirelessly drumming up business with the help of a bilingual pamphlet that resembled something dreamed up by the National Lampoon back in the days when it was funny. 
''We Protect You From Politics,'' ran one passage. 
''By incorporating secretly, in the event of an emergency in your home country, such as insurrection or invasion by a hostile power, your company can temporarily or permanently move its domicile and be protected by the laws of The State of Delaware (for additional fees).''
The text went on to explain the many and subtle beauties of Delaware trust law, described the state as an investor's paradise and expounded on the wonders of the Port of Wilmington, a major point of entry for bananas and Volkswagens.
Strange as Woo's campaign may have seemed to an American, it worked. 
In the United States, Woo may be virtually unknown outside his adopted state, but in the Far East he is famous, and many doors fell effortlessly open before him. 
''We all know a lieutenant governorship isn't worth a hill of beans,'' he says, ''but they don't.''
If all goes according to plan, Delaware will shortly become the proud possessor of the only steel mill in the Western hemisphere partly owned by the Peoples' Republic of China.
Meanwhile, half a world away, Delaware's Governor, Michael N. Castle, was a man with all the delightful problems that accompany a booming economy and a healthy budget surplus. 
His state has long been known, not always favorably, as a corporate haven, a kind of American Liechtenstein - ''a pygmy state,'' fumed the late William L. Cary, a former chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, ''interested only in revenues.''
As recently as January 1988, the state lived up to its reputation when it passed legislation requiring anyone raiding a Delaware corporation either to acquire a whopping 85 percent of its stock in a single transaction or to suspend such efforts for a tedious three years. 
The precise effect of this legislation is unclear, especially because the S.E.C. immediately challenged its constitutionality, but it's typical of Delaware's tradition of tender concern for the well-being of its corporate children.
It is not a concern widely shared by other states in the Middle Atlantic region. 
Indeed, sympathetic observers of what is often called ''the Delaware design'' have long been known to express amazement that large, sophisticated neighbors like Pennsylvania and New York haven't found a way to compete with Delaware for the incorporation business.
''Surprisingly,'' notes one legal study, ''much of the difficulty of these large states appears to be . . . because of their legislatures.''
The large states persist in viewing corporation laws as complex moral and political problems rather than - as in happy Delaware - a way of making everybody rich.
Delaware has long boomed as a corporate venue; it now booms in other ways as well. 
The unemployment rate, at 3.3 percent of the work force, is the second lowest in the nation; only New Hampshire's is lower. 
Indeed, Delaware has become a net importer of labor, with more than 21,000 out-of-state commuters, most of them from Pennsylvania, Maryland and New Jersey. 
Downtown Wilmington, only a decade ago dominated by the stone mass of the Du Pont Building, the vacant lots of failed urban renewal schemes and a huge junkyard, now boasts a new skyline whose crown jewels are the 12-story Hercules Plaza (the junkyard still visible from its windows), the handsome mirrored facility of the Chase Manhattan Bank and the new 23-story Manufacturers Hanover Plaza.
In just seven short years, Delaware in general and Wilmington in particular have become a major financial center, a development that has brought the state some 15,900 jobs, 9,616 of them directly involved in the operations of out-of-state institutions like Manufacturers and Chase - jobs that would once have been domiciled mostly in New York. 
Moreover, Wilmington is the nation's largest depository of privately owned gold, largely because Delaware charges no sales tax on precious metals transactions - nor, for that matter, on anything else.
The absence of a Delaware sales tax is comparatively old hat. 
Of more interest is the fact that the state averaged an annual revenue growth of 7.7 percent over the past five years - more than double the rate of inflation -despite four consecutive cuts in the personal income tax that reduced the annual bite to an estimated 4.1 percent. 
Some have called the state a supply-side miracle. 
Others, perhaps more temperate in their judgment, suggest that the Delaware miracle is what happens when conservative Republicans like Michael Castle and Pierre S. du Pont 4th end up in the Governor's office.
In many ways, they are less ideological than pragmatic. 
Their policies have reflected the concerns of the well-educated professional class -the members of the state's unusually powerful bar association, the Ph.D.'s from Du Pont, the executives in the booming banks - that forms such an important part of the Delaware constituency. 
Like many of their generation and accomplishments, Delaware's Governors have been liberal on matters of civil rights, pragmatic on social policy, deeply concerned about education and fiscally conservative. 
''In Delaware, there isn't a lot of difference between the Democrats and the Republicans,'' says Governor Castle, who used the occasion of his latest State of the State message to utter some fairly tart words about the Federal Government and its abdication of its responsibilities. 
''I'm more of a Governor than I am a Republican.''
Delaware may not be easier to govern than, say, New Jersey, but it's certainly very different. 
In a state with 644,000 inhabitants occupying only 1,982 square miles -''Three counties at low tide,'' says Castle, ''and two counties at high'' - obtaining a consensus is fairly easy. 
''Everybody knows everybody else,'' one official explains. 
This doesn't necessarily mean that everybody is interested in looking after everybody else. 
''I'm not very proud of it, but we have the highest infant mortality rate in the country,'' Castle says. 
Delaware also has one of the highest rates of black teen-age pregnancy, and its welfare benefits are the second lowest in the mid-Atlantic region, after West Virginia. 
''The Delaware miracle?'' says the Rev. Otis Herring, the president of the Ministers' Action Council. 
''I wait to see it.''
SURROUNDED BY the dark paneling and antique china of the executive conference room on the 12th floor of the Carvel State Office Building in downtown Wilmington, Castle and his aides contemplate their handiwork and discuss a dilemma. 
With money pouring into the state coffers from the economic boom, Delaware sailed out of fiscal 1987 with an unencumbered surplus of $85 million. 
Castle wants to devote the money to long-term projects, to his new highway trust fund, to his welfare reform, to his overcrowded prisons and environmental programs.
Unfortunately, the legislators in the state capital of Dover also want to spend the money. 
''Day-care centers,'' says Castle. 
''People want to put their names on buildings. 
This whole day-care thing has gotten out of hand.''
At the same time, there is talk around the big table of granting a tax break to venture-capital firms. 
''I don't see anything wrong with giving a tax break to a business that isn't even here yet,'' says Castle, ending the debate. 
Someone points out that the whole question is moot, since Delaware will be at the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean in a mere 7,000 years. 
''Yeah, well,'' says Castle. 
''That's the trouble with us politicians. 
We always think in the short term.''
Down on the 11th floor, Lieutenant Governor Woo contemplates the handiwork resulting from his 1986 swing through Asia. 
Woo's office estimates that the Lieutenant Governor's efforts have led to an annual $1 million in incorporation fees from Oriental companies. 
The Ambassador of the People's Republic of China came to call; Wilmington and Ningbo, a port city near Shanghai, were designated as ''Friendship Cities,'' and the Lieutenant Governor was on the lookout for some Ningbo shipping business. 
With Woo pinch-hitting as interpreter, a local company won an important polypropylene contract from the People's Republic, and a refinisher of 1840's furniture landed a $1.5 million joint venture to build a furniture plant. 
And while Woo is looking forward to a rich harvest of Hong Kong flight capital in anticipation of the British pull-out from the colony in 1997, in the short run he can look forward to restarting the moribund Phoenix Steel Corporation mill using money advanced by a Hong Kong investor together with the China International Trust and Investment Corp., the second largest financial institution in the People's Republic.
IT WAS IN DELAWARE, IN 1802, on the banks of the Brandywine River, that Eleuthere Irenee du Pont de Nemours erected his first gunpowder mills and laid the foundation of the nation's largest chemical company. 
Evidently a man of iron nerve, he built his personal mansion overlooking his works, the most explosive site in North America. 
Soon, however, the estates of his heirs were spread all over the northern arc of the state, and the du Ponts occasionally seemed to harbor the illusion that they owned the place.
With 25,400 employees, the Du Pont company easily remains the largest in the state, far ahead of Hercules Inc., the chemical and plastic concern (2,700), the British-owned ICI Americas Inc. 
(3,600) and the General Motors plant (4,200). 
''Until the out-of-state banks began to come in around 1981,'' says one local banker, ''three institutions ran this state. 
One was Du Pont, of course. 
Another was the Wilmington Trust. 
And the last was the corporate law firm of Richards, Layton, & Finger.''
The firm's legendary Aaron Finger, who died in 1969, was regarded as one of the most formidable corporation lawyers in the United States, a voice that was respected, sometimes feared, and often heeded. 
And thereby hangs a tale.
Once, in Delaware and many other states, the life of a corporation was limited to a specific term (in Delaware, 20 years, after which it had to be incorporated again) and for highly specific purposes. 
The method of incorporation was via a special act of the Legislature, which offered rich possibilities for bribery. 
In 1875, the Legislature passed a general incorporation law that permitted the founding of corporations ''for religious, charitable, literary and manufacturing purposes, for the preservation of animal and vegetable food, building and loan association, and for draining low lands.''
Then, in 1896, New Jersey adopted its own incorporation statute, the most liberal in the land. 
In New Jersey, a corporation could be eternal. 
It could carry on operations anywhere it pleased, it could merge and consolidate its operations as it pleased, and within the bounds of the law it could revise its charter by a simple vote of its board of directors, without consulting the pesky and unpredictable stockholders.
Needless to say, companies raced to New Jersey; by 1902, its income from filing fees and the franchise tax was so great that it abolished the property tax. 
Delaware, quick to sense an opportunity, was not far behind with its own General Corporation Law of 1899, which was ballyhooed as even more liberal than New Jersey's, to say nothing of cheaper, but Delaware was wasting its breath. 
New Jersey remained the premier incorporation state until 1913, when the outgoing Governor, Woodrow Wilson, persuaded the Legislature to outlaw trusts and holding companies.
Most of Wilson's law was repealed in 1917, but by then the damage was done; Delaware, which had nothing against trusts and holding companies, also had most of the business. 
By 1929, corporate fees and taxes provided 42.5 percent of state income. 
Still, nothing lasts forever. 
By 1945, with more than 30 other states having liberalized their own corporate statutes, only 16.3 percent of Delaware's revenue came from the corporations it sheltered. 
By 1955, the figure was down to 7.2 percent.
Clearly, something had to be done. 
In 1967, when corporate filings had reached a new low, the General Corporation Law was revised under the guidance of a committee put together by the Secretary of State's office. 
It was an unusual but very tidy arrangement, rather as though the nation's defense contractors were to draw up the military budget. 
Few dissenting voices were heard in Delaware. 
''You can't trust the Legislature to do a lot of things,'' says former Governor du Pont, ''but you can rely on it to keep the corporation law up to date.''
With a little help from its friends, of course.
SHOULD YOU DECIDE TO incorporate in Delaware, the state makes it easy for you with a booklet entitled, appropriately enough, ''Incorporating in Delaware.''
It comes complete with handy fold-out forms, and it is a gold mine of useful tips. 
Should you be at a loss for a precise reason for incorporating in Delaware - or if you have reason for lying low when the subject is raised - the booklet suggests that you simply state: ''The purpose of the corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which corporations may be organized under the General Corporation Law of Delaware.''
The minimum filing fee is $50. 
For an additional $100, the state will incorporate you on the day you hand in your papers; $50 gets you incorporated within 24 hours. 
''We respect your privacy,'' Woo's pamphlet reminds us. 
''You don't have to tell us the details of your business; you don't have to list who's on your board or who's holding office; and you don't have to use your name and address -just use your Delaware agent's.''
The job can be done in a matter of moments. 
''The fact is,'' says Carolyn McKown, the vice-president of Corporate Agents Inc., a Wilmington specialty firm, ''it's real easy to get incorporated in Delaware, no matter how you do it. 
We can do an incorporation in about three minutes.''
Buying a used car should be so simple. 
''No waiting!'' trumpets the C.A.I. advertisement in the state booklet. 
''Just call us toll free . . . and our friendly, professional staff will form your corporation while you are on the telephone via our direct computer link to the Delaware Corporation Department. 
(Have your VISA or MasterCard ready.)''
Once you have received your certificate, the advantages accrue immediately. 
For example, you can hold meetings of your anonymous board by telephone, saving yourself much bothersome expense. 
Your profits, if earned outside Delaware, will be exempt from state taxation. 
You can pay dividends, if any, out of either your annual profits or your accrued surplus from past operations. 
(New York allows dividends to be paid only from the surplus, meaning that you have to establish a track record. 
Delaware is uninterested in your track record.) Other states allow outraged stockholders to sue board members for glaring misjudgment, an increasingly common (and successful) practice that has led insurance companies to withdraw their protection - which in turn has caused many candidates to decline the honor of a company directorship, creating a small crisis in the nation's boardrooms. 
In 1986, however, Delaware allowed its corporations to reimburse their directors for many kinds of court-ordered money damages, which solved the problem quite nicely.
Moreover, if a charter is properly written, companies can change their by-laws without stockholder approval, a handy power to have when defenses are being put in place to repel a raid. 
And when it comes to corporate raiding, Delaware is by no means immune to those irrational moralisms and political acts that so bedevil the Legislatures of its larger neighbors. 
In 1987, when the Texas oilman T. Boone Pickens Jr. was trying to accumulate an ominous block of stock in the Boeing Company, long a loyal Delaware corporation, he uttered many eloquent words about the state and even traveled to Wilmington. 
(''I was surprised that he was so charming,'' says Governor Castle.) Around that time, the thinking of the Legislature in Dover was sharpened when Hercules Inc. abruptly sold its share of a joint venture for $1.5 billion - meaning that Hercules, with all that money on its books, was now itself a prime takeover target. 
In January 1988, the incorporation statute was amended to forbid any holder of 15 percent of a Delaware company's stock from effecting a merger for three years unless the board of directors approved, two-thirds of the stockholders overrode a negative board decision or the raider managed to acquire 85 percent of the company's unencumbered stock in a single purchase.
Still, anyone can make laws, and states seeking a share of the Delaware pie have amended their incorporation laws in a so-called ''race to the bottom line'' as they strive to accommodate the needs of corporate America and, not incidentally, pick up some of Delaware's handsome fees. 
Notwithstanding, companies have continued to flock to Delaware, whose continued pre-eminence in the field resides largely in the hard-to-duplicate depth and expertise of its powerful legal profession and, not least, in its unique Chancery Court, modeled on a royal institution that was abolished in most of the rest of the United States at the time of the Revolution. 
''I think a lot of my predecessors were Anglophiles,'' says the present Chancellor, William T. Allen, only the 19th person to have occupied the post in nearly 200 years.
His decisions - like those of his predecessors - will be cited by courts and lawyers far from Wilmington as the definitive word on the subject. 
Everything that happens in the Chancery Court is potentially worth millions of dollars to the arbitrageurs who bet heavily on the outcomes of the various battles, which accounts for the fact that the Chancellor's diminutive and almost makeshift courtroom - it seems to have been furnished from the catalogue of a third-rate store specializing in providing liturgical furniture to impoverished storefront churches - is sometimes thronged with local lawyers in the pay of the nation's investment community.
At crucial moments, the lawyers bolt for the phones; at least one lawyer has been known to boast of reporting to his masters directly from the courtroom, by means of a concealed cellular phone. 
Yet for all the vast sums involved, no Delaware judge has ever been convicted of corruption. 
''I think it's because we're so small,'' says Allen. 
''If somebody started getting rich at this job, the rest of us would notice.''
In the midst of the slightly hallucinatory Delaware miracle, it's easy to forget that it was not always thus. 
In 1978, Irving S. Shapiro, then the chief executive officer of Du Pont, flatly advised other companies not to locate in the state. 
For one thing, the personal income tax was a confiscatory 19.8 percent. 
''When I first came to the Legislature in 1963,'' says State Senator Herman Holloway Sr., ''we used to hope that a du Pont would die so we could balance the budget with the inheritance taxes.''
To Pierre du Pont, who was elected Governor in 1976, the problems were enormous, but the causes were simple. 
''In 1976, we were the classic liberal basket case. 
High tax rates. 
Second highest unemployment rating in the country. 
Lowest bond rating. 
When I first got here, I wondered if I could actually run this place. 
When I was a Congressman in Washington and we needed money, we always said we could take it out of the Defense budget. 
But Delaware didn't have a defense budget.''
Du Pont, an improbably handsome patrician Republican of the bluest blood, immediately adopted a classic remedy. 
''I decided I could only do two or three things a year, but I was going to get them done,'' he says. 
High on his list were balancing the budget and cutting taxes. 
''Pete du Pont is a little like Mike Dukakis,'' says a banker close to the situation. 
''He got lucky. 
He can take credit for someone else's success.''
What happened next is a little confusing, at least in its details; victory has many fathers. 
Du Pont, his first tax cut on the books, was deep in his 1980 re-election campaign when the Chase Manhattan Bank came to call. 
''They wanted to move in their credit-card operation,'' says the banker. 
''They said they could live with our situation, but they needed the usury law [the state law that set a cap on interest rates] repealed. 
They did not meet with a good reception.''
Other Wilmington businessmen persuaded Chase officials to pay calls on the Governor and on Irving Shapiro of Du Pont. 
Mr. Shapiro regarded the Delaware usury laws as absurd.
In early 1981, with Governor du Pont safely re-elected and the future tax cuts therefore assured, the Legislature passed a remarkable law called the Financial Center Development Act. 
The new law permitted out-of-state banks to set up shop but prohibited them from engaging in retail banking that could take away customers from local banks - a move that assuaged the anxieties of Wilmington Trust. 
It also required them to bring in at least $25 million in capital within their first year of operation and to hire at least 100 employees. 
But it offered them a remarkable tax advantage. 
A bank generating less than $20 million in income within the state boundaries would pay a tax of 8.7 percent, while a bank that earned more than $30 million would pay only 2.7 percent on anything over that amount.
Business flocked in. 
Chase was joined by Manufacturers Hanover, Chemical Bank, Citicorp, Bankers Trust Company, J. P. Morgan & Company, E. F. Hutton & Company, J. C. Penney Company, Montgomery Ward & Company and the Bank of New York; other banks moved in operations from as far away as Michigan and Texas. 
E. F. Hutton established a trust company; J. C. Penney and Montgomery Ward set up consumer-credit operations. 
''We had no idea it was going to be so successful,'' says Governor Castle. 
In Wilmington and its suburbs, construction boomed. 
In a state the size of Delaware, the prospect of 10,000 new banking jobs and 7,000 new jobs in support industries, many of them held by minorities, was no small event.
''Electricity in Delaware costs roughly half as much as it does in New York,'' says William E. Pike, the executive vice-president of Morgan's Delaware operations. 
''We have found that Delaware productivity is 20 percent higher per employee, at a minimum. 
There's a completely different political environment here. 
In New York it sometimes seems that the environment is not very hospitable. 
In Delaware, they couldn't have been more welcoming and helpful. 
You can't move Wall Street to Delaware, of course, but there's no reason to keep all those back office operations in lower Manhattan.''
WHAT DOES IT all mean?
To former Governor du Pont, whose Presidential ambitions are clearly not dead but sleeping, the Delaware miracle is a triumph of sound conservative principles and supply-side economics. 
He regards the Delaware model as easily exportable to other states, once they come to their senses.
Others are not so sure. 
''I don't understand supply-side economics,'' says Irving Shapiro, now a lawyer with Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom, ''and I don't think Pete du Pont does either. 
But as a businessman I can tell you it doesn't work.''
To some, the Delaware phenomenon is a result of luck, good timing, a regional boom (especially in financial services) and increasingly predatory tax policies in other states. 
''We are a very small place with a very large industrial base and a long head start in corporation law,'' says one local banker. 
''You can't duplicate that sort of thing. 
I can't believe how complacent everyone is.''

text:

A daughter of Deng Xiaoping, in an article published on the Chinese leader's 80th birthday, today described for the first time her father's ordeal as a political outcast during the Cultural Revolution.
Mr. Deng operated a lathe in a tractor factory, lived in a brick house with no heat, grew cabbages and beans to feed his family and read Marx and Lenin late into the night, the article said.
The description of Mr. Deng's humiliation at the hands of Mao Zedong and his followers was provided by one of Mr. Deng's five children, identified only as Mao Mao. 
A 3,000-word article under this name filled a half-page of the Communist Party newspaper People's Daily today.
Daughter of Deng Xiaoping, in article published on Chinese leader's 80th birthday in Chinese Communist Party newspaper People's Daily, describes for first time her father's ordeal as political outcast during Cultural Revolution; article says Deng operated lathe in tractor factory, lived in brick house with no heat, grew cabbages and beans to feed family and read Marx and Lenin; article does not identify Deng by name, but officials confirm article refers to him (M)
No mention of Mr. Deng's birthday was made in the article, and there were no official celebrations.
Â 
Deng Not Identified by Name
The article did not identify Mr. Deng by name, but Chinese officials confirmed that the article clearly referred to him. 
Mao Mao appeared to be a nickname, and the daughter's real name was not known.
Mao Mao took up the story after 1967, when Mr. Deng and Liu Shaoqi, who was then President, were purged as would-be capitalists.
The article said: ''It had already been two years since my father was kept in custody after being labeled the nation's second biggest capitalist roader. 
Now he suddenly got the order that he was being sent to Jiangxi Province.''
Mr. Deng's family was scattered. 
His older son, Deng Pufang, a physics student, was disabled after persecution by Red Guards at Peking University, and his other son and three daughters were being ''reformed'' in the countryside, the article said.
Â 
Couple Kept Under Guard
''Only my father's stepmother lived with my parents in Peking,'' Mao Mao wrote. 
She said her mother, her father and his stepmother were flown to Nanchang, the capital of Jiangxi Province in south-central China, and were taken to a closed infantry academy nearby, where they lived for three years in a two-story brick house.
The family had a kitchen and dining room, a sitting room and two bedrooms. 
''The rest of the rooms were for people sent to guard my parents,'' Mao Mao wrote.
''The only able-bodied worker,'' she said, ''was my 65-year-old father, so menial jobs such as cleaning the floor and splitting firewood were done by him. 
They looked after each other, loved each other, shared together.''
Mr. Deng's wife, Zhou Lin, was often bedridden, the article said. 
There was no heat. 
''Father used to bathe in cold water every day,'' the article said.
Â 
'They Lived Frugally'
In spring, the family planted beans, cabbage, peppers and squash, the article went on. 
''Every day Father spent time in the garden. 
My grandmother raised a few chickens. 
Because Father was labeled a capitalist roader, my parents got only small allowances for their daily needs. 
They lived frugally.''
After supper, they listened to news on the radio, Mao Mao said. 
''They got permission to bring with them the family library. 
Father would read into deep in the night, many works by Marx, Engels, Lenin and Stalin, and also history books.''
Mao Mao described her father as an introspective man who ''day after day, month after month, year after year'' would walk in the courtyard, meditating.
In 1971, the disabled Deng Pufang was allowed to join his parents, the article said. 
He is now an official of China's Fund for the Handicapped.
Â 
Jobs in a Tractor Factory
At their request, Mao Mao wrote, Mr. Deng and his wife were given jobs in a tractor factory, where Mr. Deng, who had learned the trade as a youth, operated a lathe. 
Armed guards went with him to the factory.
When he was told of the death in 1971 of Defense Minister Lin Biao, accused of plotting to kill Mao Zedong, ''Father was very excited,'' the article said. 
''He uttered one sentence: 'Even heaven won't tolerate Lin Biao.'
''
Soon after, according to Mao Mao, conditions improved and the guards were removed.
In February 1973, Mr. Deng was summoned back into China's Government. 
He was purged again in 1976 and 1977 before Chairman Mao's death and the overthrow of the so-called Gang of Four, radicals led by Mao's widow, Jiang Qing. 
But Mr. Deng eventually regained power, becoming the highest leader in China.
