text:
ï»¿
A decade after he lectured America's foes from the podium at the United Nations, Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan brought some of the same style into a meeting this week with China's pre-eminent leader, Deng Xiaoping.
The issue, once more, was the United Nations - specifically, China's overwhelming record of voting against the side taken by the United States.
As the United States representative to the United Nations under President Ford from 1975 to 1976, Mr. Moynihan gained a reputation for taking the offensive against critics of the United States and its allies and for assailing those critics for what he characterized as hypocrisy.
At a meeting with Mr. Deng on Tuesday in the Great Hall of the People, he used less flowery language than he often used in the General Assembly. 
But his remarks on the Chinese voting record were a departure from the bland exchanges that usually result when visiting Western politicians are ushered in to see the Chinese leader.
Sen Daniel Patrick Moynihan, in China with Congressional group, complains to Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping about China's overwhelming record of voting against side taken by United States at United Nations; notes State Department tally of last year's General Assembly session shows China and United States on opposite sides 86 percent of time; official New China News Agency, in its report of meeting, says Deng acknowledged that 'certain problems' exist between two nations (M)
The New York Democrat was one of seven senators at a 75-minute meeting with Mr. Deng. The group was headed by the majority leader, Bob Dole, Republican of Kansas.
Â 
Tally of Assembly Votes
Mr. Moynihan entered the session with a State Department tally of last year's General Assembly session that showed China and the United States on opposite sides 86 percent of the time when a for-or-against vote was taken. 
He said at a news conference later that he had told Mr. Deng that this put China ''in the same column'' as the Soviet Union and the countries espousing nonalignment, with patterns of voting overwhelmingly against the United States.
Mr. Moynihan said he had chided Mr. Deng for what the Senator called China's ''two United States policy,'' a friendly attitude in direct relations between Peking and Washington, and a sharply different posture at the United Nations.
This was a play on China's longstanding allegation that the United States follows a ''two China policy,'' treating Taiwan as a separate state while recognizing Peking as the Government of the mainland. 
In the Shanghai communique in 1972, the United States accepted that Taiwan was part of China.
Mr. Deng, who celebrated his 81st birthday last week, appeared to be in a genial mood as he greeted the Americans. 
Reporters who were admitted to the opening minutes of the session were struck by the Chinese leader's apparent robustness and his deep tan. 
He recently spent a month at the Chinese leaders' retreat at Beidaihe, a seaside resort 165 miles east of Peking, where he is said to swim in the sea twice a day.
Â 
Visitors Do Most of Talking
In a break from the usual practice, the Chinese leader left most of the talking to the visitors. 
That allowed the Americans to raise matters ranging from Taiwan to China's policy on nuclear proliferation and the increasing expense faced by American businessmen living and working here.
From the senators' accounts at the news conference, Mr. Moynihan's seemed to have been the most sharply worded of the American statements.
In its report of the meeting, the official New China News Agency said Mr. Deng had responded to the senators' views by saying, ''Certain problems do exist between us, but as long as we have the desire to develop relations, these problems can be solved and solutions can be found.''
Mr. Dole, in a statement, said the two sides ''had similar views on most issues, and even when we didn't, we disagreed in an open and friendly way.''
Asked for his account of Mr. Deng's response, Mr. Moynihan chuckled. 
''He looked at his watch and indicated that it was time for the meeting to end,'' the Senator said.

file: Deng Is Quitting the Central Committee.txt
text:
ï»¿
Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, will not be a member of the new Central Committee of the Communist Party, delegates to the party congress said today.
Mr. Deng's expected departure from the Central Committee, which debates and approves policy, means that he will apparently also have to quit the Standing Committee, or inner circle, of the Central Committee's Politburo, the body that rules the country, But Mr. Deng is expected to remain a forceful presence behind the scenes, relinquishing little of his actual authority.
Diplomats and knowledgeable Chinese agree that Mr. Deng, who is 83 years old, will stay on as chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces, in keeping with Mao's dictum that ''political power grows out of the barrel of a gun.''
Â 
Chairmanship Eliminated in 1982
The Central Committee seat would be the first party post that Mr. Deng has given up since he eliminated his job as deputy party chairman at the last party congress in September 1982. 
The party chairmanship, which was created for Mao in 1945, was also abolished with its deputy slots.
Mr. Deng's refusal to accept the mantle of chairman then underscored the shift to a more collective leadership and left the General Secretary as the top official of the Communist Party, which has 46 million members. 
Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang is now the Acting General Secretary.
Mr. Deng was twice purged from the Central Committee, in 1966 and in 1976, when he ran afoul of leftists in the Cultural Revolution, but each time he returned to power. 
Since 1978, he has been the most powerful man in China, despite his unwillingness to assume formal leadership posts. 
He declined to succeed Hua Guofeng as Prime Minister when Mr. Hua was forced out in September 1980.
Word of Mr. Deng's decision to step down from the Central Committee emerged during a series of strictly controlled interviews today with four delegates to the party congress.
Pressed by foreign reporters, Lu Guangqiu, a prosperous 44-year-old chicken farmer from Hangzhou, blurted out his astonishment that Mr. Deng's name had not appeared on the list of potential candidates that was presented to delegates of the congress.
''I never thought I wouldn't find Deng's name on the list,'' Mr. Lu said to the foreign reporters who crowded around him.
Â 
Wants the Aged to Retire
Mr. Deng, who designed China's economic resurgence over the last decade, has called on all the party's elderly leaders to retire in favor of younger leaders. 
At the last party congress in 1982, he became chairman of a Central Advisory Commission newly created to get aging Communists to step aside, but he failed to get many of his contemprories to follow him.
Today, the presidium of the congress, a body of 187 delegates composed of the party's elite, approved a list of 172 names to be elected to the new Central Committee by the congress at large, according to the Government-controlled New China News Agency. 
The election, which is little more than a formality, is expected to occur on Sunday.
The list of 172 names represents a sharp drop in the size of the Central Committee from its current 209 members. 
It was unclear why a decision had been made to pare it down, unless its size has been found to be unwieldy.
Â 
'New Nucleus of Leadership'
There had been some speculation, particularly among Eastern European diplomats, that Mr. Deng would remain in the Politburo. 
Several Chinese familiar with the deliberations of the congress said today that it was clear now that Mr. Deng would leave the Central Committee.
Yet foreign diplomats and Chinese alike agree that even outside the Central Committee Mr. Deng will continue to exercise great influence over the formulation of policy. 
As one Western analyst here put it, referring to Mr. Deng's favorite hobby, ''he could become president of the bridge association and he'd still run the show.''

text:

On her first trip to SoHo the other day, Deng Lin, a Chinese artist who is accomplished in the brush-and-ink tradition that has flourished in her country for more than a thousand years, circled warily around a huge and complex Frank Stella wall piece at the Leo Castelli Gallery on Greene Street. 
She paused meditatively in front of a simpler floor piece by Ellsworth Kelly, composed of two flat semicircular planes. 
And she looked with a certain fascination at a pair of massive steel plates by Richard Serra, standing upright in precarious tension.
''Some American art is more about architecture and industry than feeling,'' said Miss Deng, who is the daughter of Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader.
No doubt about it, these bold and ambitious American works are in sharp contrast with the traditional art of Miss Deng, who specializes in pine trees, plum blossoms and wisteria vines done with vivacity and great delicacy by means of a brush wielded freehand with water and ink.
Â 
'A Simple Medium'
''It's a simple medium in which you can express strong passions,'' she said, through an interpreter. 
Though her medium is a conservative one, Miss Deng is credited by its aficionados with bringing a highly personal sense of freedom and vitality to it, a tendency perhaps inherited from her father, who has pursued a program of liberating and revitalizing the Chinese economy.
Miss Deng was in New York for the opening of her first show here, at the Hefner Galleries, 1020 Madison Avenue, at 78th Street (through Oct. 
29). She was accompanied by Long Rui, a leading Chinese landscapist who works in the same manner and shares the show with her. 
The two were not novices at contemporary American art - they had seen it in Paris, Tokyo and even in Beijing, where Robert Rauschenberg's work has been shown at the National Gallery.
''We do respect the ideas and creativity of American artists,'' said Miss Deng, who said she felt that sculpture was more developed in the United States than in Europe.
''Chinese artists know more about Western artists than the West knows about them,'' Miss Deng said. 
At Castelli, they admired the brushwork and colors in Roy Lichtenstein's vast canvas, ''Forest Scene With Figures.''
At the Phyllis Kind Gallery, Miss Deng was bemused by the oil paintings of Jim Nutt, whose distorted faces, she felt, had ''a touch of Picasso.''
''But for myself,'' she said, ''I'm much more interested in the results coming from paper and ink.''
Later, at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Mr. Long found a de Kooning that he said he would like to take back to China.
But of some of the work they looked at - or did not - their reactions were more negative. 
They did not, for example, cotton to Bruce Nauman's ''Hanging Carousel,'' a kinetic work at Sperone Westwater, in which the skinned carcasses of animals (in replica) swing around a video monitor on which a man is seen skinning a fox.
''Does such work sell?''
Miss Deng wondered. 
''Would anyone buy it for his home?''
Nor did they appreciate the art of Kenny Scharf, seen at the Tony Shafrazi Gallery, a kind of watered-down Pop that comments on the consumerism of American life.
Â 
Painted, 'but Not Made'
''It's too bright, too garish,'' Miss Deng said. 
''There's too much going on. 
I like things to be painted, but not made.''
And she was not interested in visiting the Whitney Museum of American Art to see the work of Robert Mapplethorpe, whose photographs deal explicitly with parts of the male anatomy.
''Any form of art can be seen in China,'' said Lisa Lai, Miss Deng's interpreter. 
''Even nudes, if they're not too unhealthy.''
As part of her painting career, Miss Deng - who is 47 years old, married and, in the new Chinese way, the mother of only one child - serves as president of the Society for the Excellence of the Fine Arts in the Orient, an organization that is run by artists and is devoted to the wider recognition of brush-and-ink painting. 
The group organizes exchange exhibitions with other countries, and has even had one with Taiwan.
As a recognized artist, with solid academic training, Miss Deng is given a stipend by the Chinese Government, and she is allowed to sell her work abroad, although political opponents of her father recently accused her of charging exorbitant sums for her paintings in Hong Kong and not accounting for the money.
Â 
'A New Freedom'
At a luncheon for Miss Deng and Mr. Long given Thursday by the China Institute, on East 65th Street, the two were asked if there was underground, or black, art activity in China, as there has been in Russia. 
''There was in the 60's and 70's during the Cultural Revolution, but it has disappeared in the last five years or so,'' Mr. Long said. 
''There is a new freedom now, and artists no longer feel a hesitancy to say things out in the open.'
Though she declined to talk specifically about the Cultural Revolution, the 10-year campaign against artists and intellectuals carried out in the last decade of Mao Zedong's rule, Miss Deng and her family suffered greatly. 
In one incident, a brother, Deng Pufang, was thrown out of a window by Red Guards and suffered permanent paralysis. 
He now leads the Chinese organization for the disabled.
Miss Deng's own career was severely blighted.''I had a tough experience,'' she said, through Miss Lai. 
''It changed my personality.''
In general, had being the daughter of Deng Xiaoping helped or hindered her?
''We're in two different areas,'' Miss Deng said. 
''He runs the country and I'm an artist.''

file: Diaper Import Quotas Under Fire.txt
text:
ï»¿
Thousands of parents are likely to pay more for diaper services as a result of import quotas the United States has quietly imposed on plain cotton diapers from China.
The quotas, which were fixed after a textile trade pact signed with Beijing on Dec. 
20, illustrate the complexity of trade issues and the trade-off involved in using protection as an instrument to preserve jobs.
The action was taken to placate the domestic textile industry, which has long complained about the job-destroying effects of imports. 
The industry is pushing legislation to set quotas on all textile and apparel products entering the United States.
Â 
Only 60 Jobs Involved
Only 60 jobs at diaper plants in South Carolina are involved. 
But the action seems likely to raise prices charged by diaper services around the country, as they face higher prices for diapers. 
It has also prompted criticism on environmental grounds because it may encourage more use of disposable diapers.
If use of disposable diapers increases, layoffs at diaper services may outstrip the number of jobs the cloth-diaper quotas are meant to preserve. 
At the same time, of course, the number of jobs at companies that make disposable diapers would presumably increase.
Environmental, consumer and free-trade advocates are the leading critics of the curbs. 
''They will mean higher prices, a switch to disposables and more environmental problems,'' said Mark Silbergeld, director of the Consumers Union's Washington office. 
''I'm not sure how much they can really help the domestic industry.''
Â 
'Destroys Their Credibility'
Representative Ron Wyden, Democrat of Oregon, criticized the Administration's trade policy as inconsistent. 
''For guys like me, fighting in the trenches for free trade,'' he said, ''this sort of protectionist action to help a grand total of one company destroys their credibility.''
The Reagan Administration says the curbs are necessary. 
Gary Holmes, a spokesman at the Office of the United States Trade Representative, said the domestic industry ''told us they were being killed by imports.''
Only one company in this country makes the thick-ply diapers that compete with Chinese diapers as the mainstay for hundreds of services. 
The Gerber Products Company of Fremont, Mich., a $1 billion-a-year baby-products concern with a small plant in Pelzer, S.C., makes Curity brand diapers as part of its Soft Care Apparel division.
Sixty of the 400 jobs at the plant are related to production of the heavy Curity diapers used by diaper services, said a company spokeswoman.
About a year ago the Government imposed temporary quotas, following a surge in imports in 1986. 
Meanwhile, Gerber raised prices twice -12 percent effective Oct. 
15 and 15 percent May 1 - increasing prices to around $9 a dozen. 
Diapers from China now cost roughly the same.
For many diaper services, the cost of diapers is about one-fifth the cost of doing business.
With Chinese diapers limited and prices higher for domestic diapers, some services now plan to increase their rates. 
''Within two months we will raise prices 6 percent, our first increase in two and one-half years,'' said Brian Smithson, president of Baby Diaper Service of Seattle, which calls itself the largest service in the country. 
That increase would work out to 50 cents on top of the $9 it now costs to provide the 80 diapers an average baby uses in a week.
Paul J. Anderson, president of Babyland Diaper Service of Portland, Ore., said that over the next two years diaper prices could go up by an additional 25 percent. 
''When you have only one supplier, you're at their mercy,'' he said.
Although shipments of diapers are normally measured in dozens, the quotas are fixed by weight. 
China this year is barred from sending the United States more than 1.27 million pounds of diapers, of which 270,000 pounds will go to Pro Diaper. 
A dozen diapers weigh approximately three and a half pounds.
Â 
Many More Jobs at Stake
Mr. Anderson maintained that many more American jobs are at stake than the 60 in South Carolina to be protected under the quota policy.
At least 40,000 people are employed by diaper services, including drivers, office and sales personnel and people who launder and package diapers for customers.
According to importers, the Chinese diapers, made in Nanjing, Shanghai and Beijing, are thicker, more durable and more absorbent than the South Carolina diapers.
A Gerber official who asked not to be identified acknowledged that the Chinese diapers were thicker, but added that Gerber was working on a comparable product. 
90% Come From China Diapers are also imported from South Korea and Mexico, but far more come from China. 
In 1986 diapers from China totaled 894,000 dozen, up from 45,000 dozen in 1985, according to Knox H. White, an associate of the Greenville, S.C., law firm of Haynsworth, Marion, McKay & Guerard, who sought the quotas in representations before the Office of the United States Trade Representative and the Commerce Department. 
The Chinese sales accounted for 90 percent of the one million dozen diapers taken by diaper services in 1986.
''This was a classic case of an import surge,'' said Mr. White, who represents a number of textile companies. 
Mr. White has some powerful allies in Washington, including Senator Strom Thurmond, the ranking Republican on the Judiciary Committee, and Representative Butler Derrick, a Democrat on the Rules Committee. 
Both are South Carolinians. 
The quotas have become all the more controversial because of the timing. 
Only recently have analysts begun to see at least a tentative consumer shift away from disposable diapers back to cloth diapers.
Â 
'Worst of All Worlds'
So trade policy, as public policy experts note, appears to be undercutting environmental policy. 
''We try to solve our trade problems only on a political basis,'' said Clyde V. Prestowitz Jr., a former counselor to the Commerce Secretary. 
''The result is that we get the worst of all possible worlds. 
We pay the cost of protection and get no benefits from it.''
Establishment of the first new diaper services in years - Diaper Fresh in Las Vegas, Nev., and KC Diaper Service in Baton Rouge, La. 
- is cited as one illustration of the revival of cloth diapers.
Because Beijing was a party to the restraints, it has not protested. 
Chen Ming Hui, commercial attache at the Chinese Embassy here, said, ''We will abide by the agreement, but of course we are opposed to any more restrictions.''
Â 
Visions of 'Mount Diaper'
Long before the Chinese came to the scene, the domestic industry had been hurt because of the popularity of the disposables, made chiefly by Procter & Gamble, Kimberly-Clark and Weyerhaeuser. 
Today this product, made of plastic, bleached paper and chemicals, accounts for about 85 percent of the country's diaper changes and racks up annual sales of $3.5 billion.
Nearly 18 billion disposable diapers were dumped into trash cans last year, accounting for 3 percent to 4 percent of all the waste going into the nation's landfills, according to Carl Lehrburger, manager of recycling programs for the Energy Answers Corporation, an Albany resource recovery concern.
A Washington State legislator, Georgette Valle, who has introduced a bill that would require that disposable diapers be biodegradable by 1990, said, ''Someday I will look out my window at Mount Rainier and there will be another mountain - of disposable diapers.''

China's fashion industry is perking up, adapting some of its classic styles for Western taste.

The same updating has been given to the full-length kung pao, or palace robe. 
It comes in such shades as sky blue, has a diagonal fastening banded in pale pink and is appliqued with large flowers.

You've promised to knit a sweater for someone you're fond of, but you've put it off too long.

file: Distinctions Blur as Deaf Actors Share a Stage.txt
text:
ï»¿
As soon as the powerful-looking Akahira Yonaiyama moves across the stage, speaking in Japanese sign language as he goes, the blur of simultaneous translations begins.
Mr. Yonaiyama is a star of the Japan Theater of the Deaf; as he plays his part in a rehearsal, a speaking member of the cast interprets the sign language into spoken Japanese. 
At the same time, Mr. Yonaiyama's lines are being spoken by another actor in English - and immediately translated into American sign language. 
In the actual performances, though, the only spoken words are in Japanese.
When Mr. Yonaiyama's American co-actors from the National Theater of the Deaf in Chester, Conn., speak or sign their roles in the Tokyo International Theater Festival here, the whole process is reversed. 
The festival continues through Wednesday; the theaters of the deaf will perform in Osaka for one night.
Â 
'Somehow, It All Works'
''When you think about it, it should all be a confusing mess,'' the American group's artistic director, David Hays, said during a rehearsal. 
''But somehow, it all works.''
In fact, it does, and the success of this largely deaf cast from India, Japan, China and the United States seems to prove that sign language is less of a barrier on stage than the spoken word.
Although spoken Japanese and English have about as much in common as sashimi and hot dogs, American and Japanese sign languages share fundamental concepts.
''I think it must be easier to understand English sign language than English itself,'' the 36-year-old Mr. Yonaiyama said through a sign-language translator.
The deaf actors in the American and Japanese acting companies were soon chatting, and by late afternoon during one recent rehearsal it became clear they were already on each other's wavelengths.
Â 
Festival Is in Ikebukuro
The festival is in the Seibu Theater in Ikebukuro, a jammed commuter hub and shopping area in northwest Tokyo. 
The Japan Theater of the Deaf, a small company founded eight years ago, opens its part of the program with a Kyogen, a traditional Japanese comedy often performed during the intermission of Noh, or dramatic, plays.
The American actors perform improvisations based on spoken and sign-language suggestions from the audience, with Mr. Yonaiyama and another deaf Japanese actor, Tetsuya Izaki. 
Both trained with the American group in Connecticut.
The highlight of the program is ''In a Grove'' by Ryunosuke Akutagawa, a tale of rape, betrayal and suicide that was the basis of Akira Kurosawa's film ''Rashomon.''
The story is told through the testimony of a woodcutter, a priest, a policeman, a bandit and others involved in a bizarre encounter in the woods. 
The one-at-a-time nature of the testimony - in which each of the participants gives a different version of the truth - helps to simplify the problem of multiple translations.
Â 
Selecting the Play
''I chose the play because the testimonies are individual, and the parts can be developed,'' said Mr. Hays, a former set designer for George Balanchine who first came to Japan in 1960 as a technical adviser to the Kabuki theater.
But Kabuki is one thing to the Japanese, and deaf actors are another. 
It is rare to see physically disabled people on the subways and buses in Tokyo; physical handicaps are viewed here as a family stigma, and the disabled are often kept at home.
That is changing slowly in Japan, and Mr. Hays and his troupe are trying to speed the process. 
''When we first planned to come here, agents told me that Japanese would not come to the theater to see deaf actors,'' Mr. Hays said. 
''They would be afraid that if they were seen, people would assume their families had someone at home in the closet.''
Â 
Popular Actress Appears
So far, the crowds have been encouraging. 
And this performance has an added drawing card: Tetsuko Kuroyanagi, an immensely popular actress and talk-show host, who has become a major force behind the Japan Theater of the Deaf. 
She appears in one of the few speaking roles.
Along with her are a few actors and actresses from theaters of the deaf struggling to begin elsewhere in Asia. 
Among them is Wang Ling, a young business school graduate from Beijing who is fulfilling the dream of his late father, Wang Zhentai.
When the National Theater of the Deaf went to China in 1986, Wang Zhentai spoke in Mandarin as the company performed in sign language. 
He then started a theater of the deaf in China and brought several Chinese performers to the National Theater's summer school in Connecticut. 
He died last August, shortly after returning to China, and his son picked up the effort as a tribute to him.
Â 
Winning Recognition
''The Chinese bureaucracy is so huge, and they had never heard of a theater for the deaf before,'' Wang Ling said. 
But he has begun to win recognition for the group, and he persuaded the Chinese authorities to allow a young deaf factory worker, Yang Ling, to join in the Ikebukuro festival.
An actor and an artistic director from India, which uses the American sign-language system, are also involved.
''I've never seen anything quite like this,'' said the artistic director of the Indian group, Zarin Chaudhuri, an actress from Bombay.
''Yesterday it looked impossible,'' she said. 
''Today it is all coming together.''

file: DOWN THE YANGTZE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Christopher S. Wren is The New York Times Peking bureau chief. 
By Christopher S. Wren ANY WORTHY undertaking in China starts with a meeting, and a voyage aboard the East Is Red No. 46 was no exception. 
Once the river steamer had pulled away from the dock at Chongqing in the early morning drizzle and swung into the cocoa-colored waters of the Yangtze, the ship's loudspeaker asked passengers in each cluster of cabins to dispatch a representative to the small dining room on the second deck.
Because it was my first trip down the Yangtze, I asked if I could sit in. 
''There's nothing secret about it,'' shrugged Hu Yuchun, the chief steward. 
So I joined 14 other passengers around the table. 
Tea was poured. 
''We need the help of the passengers to make this trip smooth and peaceful,'' said Mr. Hu, a tall, earnest young man in a white jacket and horn-rimmed spectacles. 
Everyone nodded at being asked to do his part to get the vessel to Wuhan, 851 miles downriver.
Mr. Hu rattled off the statistics in the flat drawl of his native Sichuan province. 
The East Is Red No. 46 was 252 feet long and 50 feet wide. 
Its mighty twin diesel engines propelled it at a speed of 16 miles an hour, but the Yangtze's current was so swift that it sailed downstream at 21 miles an hour and back upstream at only about 10 miles an hour. 
It was carrying 850 passengers, not quite full capacity, and Mr. Hu asked that they not leave watches and other valuables lying about, throw trash overboard or sit on the railings; he also cautioned against shining flashlights at night because it would confuse the helmsman.
This was not just any boat excursion. 
A voyage down the Yangtze offered a look at a China in the midst of what may be the most massive peaceful transformation of the 20th century. 
The agricultural communes we would pass were being dismantled to encourage greater peasant initiative on a household basis. 
In the countryside and towns, private enterprise, once prohibited, now burgeoned. 
Our ship was a microcosm of this changing China. 
An increasing minority of the passengers who take this river trip travel for pleasure, and many of the rest are traveling to enrich themselves, taking advantage of a relaxation of restrictions that accompanied the de-mythification of the late Chairman Mao Zedong.
The upper reaches of the Yangtze remained closed to foreigners, no doubt because the Government was embarrassed at the persisting pockets of rural poverty. 
But between Chongqing and Wuhan, the country was moving from a spartan garrison society toward a more dynamic mixed economy. 
A traveler who changed boats at Wuhan to continue down the lower Yangtze to Nanjing or Shanghai would see signs of China's doors opening anew to foreign investment and commerce.
The Yangtze, at the heart of this transition, is to the Chinese, who call it the ''Long River,'' what the Mississippi is to Americans - and more. 
Like the Mississippi, the Yangtze courses through the nation's heartland, delineating distinct regions, customs and dialects. 
Geographically, it runs from west to east, dividing northern from southern China. 
Historically, it was a cradle of Chinese culture and later became the prominent route by which the Western colonial powers pried open the decaying empire of the ineffectual Ching Dynasty in the 19th century. 
Today, a third of China's one billion people live in the fertile basin watered by the Yangtze.
Nearly 4,000 miles in length, one of the world's longest rivers, the Yangtze begins as a clear mountain stream fed by the glaciers of the Tibetan plateau in western Qinghai province. 
But as it drops more than 17,000 feet and cuts eastward past eight more provinces to join the East China Sea, its clear waters turn muddy with silt, some 500 million tons a year, that gives the Yangtze its distinctive brown hue.
By the time it meets the Jialing River at Chongqing in southeast Sichuan, the Yangtze is also fast becoming a sewer. 
Less than a third of the 100 million tons of industrial waste dumped annually from Chongqing into the Yangtze gets treated. 
No sooner had we boarded the East Is Red No. 46 than my fellow travelers began flinging the dregs of their teacups over the side of the boat. 
As we churned downriver, some backwaters frothed with the suds of unabsorbed detergents and other effluents.
Â 
HE EAST IS RED No. 46 was one of 110 steamers dubbed with the same revolutionary motto that have plied the Yangtze. 
Other reminders of the old Maoist fervor lingered. 
A sign atop the boat ticket office in Chongqing proclaimed in fat red characters, ''Long Live Mao Zedong's Thoughts,'' which in the revised ideological exegesis now means the collective wisdom of the Communist Party and not really Mao Zedong's thoughts.
Deng Xiaoping, the man behind the new reforms in China, was born in the Sichuan countryside 100 or so miles from Chongqing. 
The wooden, hand-lettered sign he made to hang over the entrance to the Chongqing Youth Palace of Culture has been a weathervane of his political career. 
Twice, when Mr. Deng was demoted into official disgrace for his reformist notions, the leftists pulled down his calligraphy. 
Twice, it has been hung back up.
Mr. Deng's impact has been more obvious along the steep winding streets of Chongqing, which was the capital of the Nationalist Government during World War II. 
The air-raid shelters tunneled into the embankments to provide protection from the heavy Japanese wartime bombing have been converted into workshops. 
On the sidewalks, small private businesses repaired shoes, sewed clothes, served up steaming noodles laced with fiery peppers and rented out comic books for a penny apiece. 
Peasants in rough denims noisily hawked juicy oranges, wriggling river eels, and fresh vegetables still moist with the morning dew. 
Such farmers' markets were suppressed as the ''tail of capitalism'' under Chairman Mao. 
Now they provide Chongqing with nearly a third of its pork and half of its vegetables.
Chongqing's gray industrial skyline overlooking the river, which tempted comparisons with less prosperous Pittsburgh, soon gave way to a view of snug farmhouses with tiled roofs and terraced fields diligently exploiting every inch of soil. 
Navigational lights anchored in small gray dinghies churned against the river current. 
The river banks were scarred at intervals by the detritus of small mines and factories that splattered ugliness across an otherwise pastoral landscape.
From our steamer's wheelhouse, the foghorn blasted and a loudspeaker squawked at slower barges and sampans to pull over and yield way.
''The Yangtze River is more complicated than the Mississippi,'' declared Xu Guilin, the ship's captain, though he had never seen the big American river himself. 
''We have memorized everything - the light signals, the rocks.''
Before receiving me in his cabin on the bridge, Mr. Xu took the trouble to change from the customary sailor's garb of shorts and sandals into a new gray pinstripe suit with dark shirt and maroon tie. 
He had slicked back his thick black hair and thrust his feet, without socks, into leather shoes without laces.
Mr. Xu grew up on the river. 
At 13, he shipped out as a cabin boy. 
He became a river sailor at 18 and captain of a ship at 41. 
Now he was 49 and sailed four round trips a month between Chongqing and Wuhan, which left him little time at home. 
Snapshots of his family were tucked under the glass top of his desk, along with a large magazine picture of Deng Xiaoping in an army uniform.
The most treacherous shoals were dynamited out of the Yangtze in the 1950's, but the muddy water has remained unpredictable, particularly as the river swells with the accumulation of melting snow in spring and heavy rain in summer. 
''When there are high tides and floods, it is difficult to navigate,'' said Mr. Xu. The trickiest section, he reported, was the Yangtze Gorges, a spectacular 120-mile stretch of sheer canyons and small ragged peaks that attracts tourists to the Yangtze. 
''I steer the boat myself in the most difficult sections,'' Mr. Xu said.
By mid-afternoon, the passengers, many of whom were bound on business great and small, had acquiesced to the ship's routine. 
Some lay on their narrow bunks reading or sleeping. 
Others leaned over the railing, played cards on the bleached deck or gobbled rice with chopsticks from enameled bowls. 
One man washed his white shirt and hung it out in the passageway where it flapped wetly against passers-by. 
Curiously, the airy top deck was reserved for the crew; the paying passengers were billeted in the gloomier quarters below.
The accommodations ranged from second class, which cost $44 for a bed in a small cabin for two, with a fluorescent bulb overhead and hot water in thermos flasks, down to fifth class where a bunk for $10 came with 23 roommates. 
The boat had no first class, whether because it was deemed inappropriate for a society marching toward Communism or because none of the quarters could be called deluxe. 
Sleeping space on the deck for the 2 1/2-day journey to Wuhan cost only $8.50.
Some Tibetans camped in one of the passageways: six men and a shy woman, all with heavy coats, necklaces of coral and turquoise and cheeks ruddy from exposure to the sun. 
One said that they came from western Sichuan and were going to Wuhan, but he didn't know enough Chinese to explain why. 
They kept sullenly to themselves for the entire trip.
The second-class cabins were filled mostly with a delegation of elderly cadres, or party and Government functionaries, who were getting a free trip down the Yangtze as one of the rewards for agreeing to retire and let the middle-age generation move ahead. 
They wore drab garments, of the kind preferred under Mao, and the women wore their graying hair bobbed severely short.
The crowd seemed livelier down below. 
(One can move from second down to lower classes, but not the other way around.) A young man with glasses was returning to Wanxian, a town 200 miles down the river. 
The ship cost more than the bus from Chongqing and took the same time, 11 hours, he said, but here you could walk around.
A gaunt, unshaved cadre named Lu was attending a family-planning conference in Nanjing, on the Yangtze. 
It was his second visit. 
The first had been 35 years ago, as a young soldier in the Communist forces that captured Nanjing from the Nationalists. 
He extended a twisted hand to show where shrapnel had torn it. 
''But I couldn't sightsee because we were too busy fighting and we went through too fast,'' he said. 
This time, Mr. Lu planned a more leisurely look around.
I asked if he was satisfied with how China had turned out. 
''There have been great changes so far, but it is still not enough,'' Mr. Lu said. 
''The reforms are correct and the policy is correct. 
The cadres at the top understand the reforms and the grass roots understand them. 
But there is no direct link, because the middle-level cadres still don't fully understand them.''
A squad of soldiers lugging dirty-looking rifles filed aboard the ship at Peiling, the first of half a dozen stops down to Wuhan. 
For most Chinese, traveling down the Yangtze is purely business. 
At Peiling and elsewhere, a few officials got on carrying small black vinyl portfolios that are as much a status symbol for cadres as the metal fountain pens in their breast pockets. 
But China's broad masses, as ordinary folks get called, staggered under the weight of canvas bags, gunnysacks, cardboard cartons, bedding and the odd slab of raw meat, sometimes all swinging together from bamboo shoulder poles.
At Wanxian, a county seat west of the great gorges, the East Is Red No. 46 was scheduled to tie up for the night rather than run the worst stretch of river in the darkness. 
Wanxian, perched on a bluff atop a wide stone staircase, had been one of the treaty ports forced open a century or so ago, when Western colonialists vied with one another to control the Yangtze. 
Many years ago, a British gunboat shelled the town to retaliate for some local resistance, a fellow traveler told me. 
During the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution, Wanxian saw new violence when rival Red Guard factions shot it out with guns stolen from Sichuan's armament factories. 
NOW WANXIAN, LIKE most of rural China, was succumbing to Peking's new mandate to ''get rich through labor; getting rich is glorious.''
As the passengers disembarked to wander up the winding streets, they were beset by local sellers of homemade baskets and wicker chairs. 
The chief steward, Mr. Hu, passed the word that any passenger coming back loaded with wicker furniture would pay a freight charge.
Most of Wanxian's shops had closed by 7:30 P.M., but a score of young men hung around a hardware store, wistfully watching a romantic movie on one of the small black-and-white television sets for sale. 
The lilting song of the heroine, who kept fluttering her eyelids as she leaned against a tree trunk, echoed down the dark street into the dingy Beautiful Taste Spring Restaurant, where patrons were wolfing down the last of the fried fish and rice.
A display of large propaganda cartoons across the street told passers-by that they, too, could own a television set and even a refrigerator if they worked harder and saved. 
There were cartoons warning about extravagance, notably in weddings. 
In one, a greedy young woman informed her dispirited fiance, ''I want everything but your mother.''
In another, a bride- to-be with her mother sat at a negotiating table presenting a young man and his father with a set of demands: color television set, electric fan, bicycle and wedding banquet. 
A sort of dowry system, previously condemned as feudalistic, was clearly still a problem in Wanxian.
Passengers straggling back to the ship before the midnight curfew had to wait while seven peasants in patched denims lurched aboard with large flat wicker baskets containing scores of baby chicks intended for the market in Fengjie, downriver. 
They arranged the baskets in the passageway and hunkered down beside them for the night. 
Using the boats for private enterprise was not permitted under Chairman Mao. 
Besides, most peasants were too poor to buy a boat ticket.
Mr. Hu said that the peasants were most numerous in the autumn, when oranges and tangerines ripened along the Yangtze. 
The farmers got a high price for their fruit down in Shashi, Wuhan and even Shanghai - because they moved it faster than the state transportation network. 
Peasants were permitted to bring aboard chickens, ducks and live fish; but reasons of sanitation, Mr. Hu said, ruled out pigs or sheep.
At Fengjie, the tired peasants got off. 
Each man slid his bamboo pole under two baskets and, as if balancing on eggs, slowly climbed the long steps to the city gate. 
Wanxian's vaguely European architecture, introduced by colonial merchants in the 19th century, had looked romantic after dark. 
By cold daylight, the buildings seemed worn and gritty in the old river town near the entrance to Qutang, the first of the great gorges.
The sheer canyons loomed abruptly overhead on either side like high-rise apartment buildings, leaving a channel for the ship barely 100 yards wide. 
For the next few hours, we rode the quickening brown river past cliffs capped with lush foliage and rock spires shrouded in clouds. 
Their bizarre shapes had given rise to centuries of fanciful interpretations. 
We sailed past Fairy Maiden Peak, the Lion Wearing a Silver Medal and the Peak of the Jade Screen. 
Shafts of sunlight penetrated the morning mist.
Between gorges, isolated farmhouses were perched on the hillsides. 
Some were striped red and white like barber poles to mark the shoreline when fog hung over the river. 
The steep slopes held rows of citrus trees. 
A sharp valley at the Wu Gorge defined where Sichuan ended and Hubei Province began.
Small sampans with sails moved slowly upstream, the boatmen sometimes standing and rowing with their long oars. 
The trail worn by the trackers, men who once labored like draft animals hauling barges through the gorges, disappeared underwater when the Gezhouba Dam was thrown across the Yangtze a few years ago. 
Still, we passed other men pulling their sampans upstream with long ropes from the rocky shore as if nothing had changed.
In the second-class lounge, a grizzled, retired Red Army veteran named Liu sat in a fat armchair by the window, taking in the scenery. 
He needed little encouragement to reminisce about how he had joined the Communist guerrillas in North China's Shanxi province in 1935. 
His family was so poor that ''I had no other choice.''
He was 15 when he went off to war, Mr. Liu recalled. 
''It was hardest against the Japanese in the early 1940's. 
We never had enough to eat and we were always fighting. 
We would take some millet and potatoes and black beans and cook them together. 
Those were bitter years.
''I never expected to live this long. 
We always thought that we would die in the next 24 hours.
''We captured our weapons from the Japanese. 
Later we used them against the Kuomintang,'' he said, referring to Chiang Kai-Shek's Nationalist Government. 
''The Japanese were much harder to fight. 
When we fired, the Kuomintang troops would run away.''
He returned home after 15 years. 
''My mother and father were very happy to see me. 
They had no letters from me, and thought I was dead. 
Neighbors came from miles around.''
After the Communist victory in 1949, Mr. Liu said, the leadership ''Put me in a factory and make me a leader.''
He retired recently and, as an old party man, receives his full salary plus a bonus and other perquisites.
Mr. Liu went on: ''My three sons said to me, 'Your life hasn't been so easy, so we want you to enjoy your remaining years. 
Travel and see the country. 
You deserve it.'
''
The veteran party man was too old to be coy about Mao Zedong: ''Chairman Mao had the right idea when he launched the Cultural Revolution. 
He did it to combat revisionism, but it became confused because of the Gang of Four.''
Mr. Liu employed the approved epithet for Mao's widow, Jiang Qing, and three other imprisoned leftists, who have been blamed for all the ills that befell China during Mao's final decade.
''Everybody makes mistakes, and Mao Zedong was no exception,'' Mr. Liu said. 
''Later, he made some wrong decisions. 
But without Mao, there wouldn't be any Communist Party. 
And without the Communist Party, we wouldn't be here today.''
AFTER XILING, THE last of the three great gorges at Nanjinguan, the landscape flattened out. 
The river widened from a few hundred yards to more than a mile and a half. 
The boat headed for the locks of Gezhouba, China's largest hydroelectric dam and the first built to harness the powerful Yangtze.
The Gezhouba was conceived by Chairman Mao in the 1950's to solve both China's energy shortage and the Yangtze's seasonal flooding. 
Construction began in 1970, when it was considered better to be Red than expert, and the revolutionary amateurs made such a mess that the project was halted two years later.
The Yangtze was finally dammed in 1981, after China's experts were summoned back from tending pigs and cleaning toilets. 
When the dam is fully completed, in four years, it will generate 14.1 billion kilowatt hours a year of electricity and transmit it as far as Shanghai, Peking and Canton.
It took an hour for the boat to be lowered 65 feet to float through the lock. 
The Gezhouba will have cost about $2.4 billion by the time it is finished, but no tolls are charged, on the principle that the dam belongs to the people.
To further solve the country's shortage of energy, a hydroelectric power dam four to five times bigger than Gezhouba has been proposed 25 miles upriver in the Xiling Gorge. 
Its construction would not only impair the beauty of the three Yangtze Gorges by raising the water level farther; it would also mean relocating up to 1.4 million Chinese, whose ancestral roots in the Upper Yangtze Valley go back centuries. 
The Government has been nervous about ordering such a massive displacement of its citizens. 
WITH THE MOST exciting part of the voyage over, a few frictions surfaced. 
Most of the staff spoke Sichuanese, a dialect that other Chinese passengers had trouble understanding. 
One man asked an attendant for glue to put stamps on a letter. 
She thought he wanted ink, and snapped back that there wasn't any.
Complaints about the poor food were more numerous. 
As waibin, or foreign guests, my wife and I were in a separate dining room where for $7 a day, 5 to 10 times what ordinary Chinese might pay, we were served a plethora of undistinguished dishes of meats, vegetables and rice. 
In the mess hall below, less coddled travelers had to buy meal coupons and then line up, sometimes for 45 minutes, before getting rice, bean noodles and vegetables.
Some passengers seemed content. 
A tall young army officer from Peking remarked later that his eight- bunk cabin was like home - better - because a hot shower and toilet were just down the passageway. 
He reminded me that most Chinese still make do without the luxury of indoor plumbing and hot-water taps.
With dusk, the tree line on the wide flood plain faded into the horizon. 
A fisherman effortlessly cast his weighted net. 
Lights twinkled on the buoys marking a channel on the broad river. 
A cool wind blew up, drawing the travelers out of their stuffy cabins.
A trio of salesmen from Chengdu leaned against the railing. 
They were traveling to Wuhan, then to a foreign trade exhibition in Canton. 
''It's fun to travel around when you are young, but when you get older, you want to settle down and raise a family,'' one of them said. 
He was already 30, with a wife in Chengdu. 
''I've been traveling for five years, but next year I hope to stop.''
He complained that he couldn't live on his travel allowance, which amounted to barely $1.30 a day. 
''Our leaders know that life is hard for us, so sometimes they try to give us a little more. 
It still doesn't cover the expenses, so I have to pay out of my own pocket sometimes.''
I asked why he didn't set up his own business, as the Peking Government is encouraging young Chinese to do in order to alleviate unemployment and provide more consumer services. 
''Oh no, then you don't have a work unit,'' he objected, referring to the state enterprises providing lifetime tenure and womblike welfare benefits, however badly an employee works. 
''And besides,'' he added, ''you can't quit your work unit without permission.''
The next morning, the passenger delegates were summoned to a last meeting. 
''Give us your opinions and suggestions in order to help us improve our work, in order to meet the demands of the broad masses,'' implored Mr. Hu.
A man with glasses and a graying crew cut stood up. 
''The guiding ideology of the boat's crew is correct,'' he announced. 
''They have acted according to the promises they made at the start of the journey, including maintaining sanitation, delivering drinking water and being responsible in their service work.''
This man knew his way around a criticism session.
''However,'' he said, only then going into complaints about the food, ''I know that it is impossible to satisfy everybody's tastes since we come from all over the country. 
But it seems there is not a suitable taste for people from the north, and the quality of the food should be improved.''
Others took up the litany, a few opening compliments followed by danshi, meaning ''however.''
Danshi, the staff should learn standard Chinese. 
Danshi, there should be a television set on board. 
Danshi, the meal coupons were too flimsy and easy to lose. 
Danshi, the boat's store should sell film and better souvenirs.
Another speaker complained that his cabin loudspeaker was broken, so that his group missed the announcements, light music, Peking opera and comedy patter that were broadcast from dawn till dark.
Mr. Hu explained that the boat had a wireless operator, but that perhaps he didn't know how to repair the loudspeaker. 
If he's happy, he may be willing to try. 
If he's not, he may refuse.
With a glance toward me, Mr. Hu plunged to the crux of the problem: foreigners sometimes ripped out the wires when the loudspeaker began blaring at 6:30 A.M. Mr. Hu pointed out that trains didn't suffer this vandalism because their loudspeakers were imbedded in the ceiling, where the foreigners couldn't reach them.
This led to a request that I, as a waibin living in Peking, add my suggestions about the voyage. 
I thanked them for having been hospitable and praised the stunning beauty of the gorges.
However, I continued, and they all nodded, I was upset to see so much trash bespoiling such a renowned river. 
Why didn't the boat install more trash baskets and mount a tidiness campaign?
The young attendant taking down all the comments scribbled furiously in her ledger and I got a flattering round of applause.
I left the meeting quite smug about my contribution. 
I leaned over the railing to watch the river I was saving when an empty soy sauce bottle flung from the crew quarters swished past my head and into the water. 
I wondered how many books of suggestions the boat had filled and where they got stored. 
AT WUHAN, THE East Is Red No. 46 ended its voyage and prepared for the trip upstream the next day. 
Travelers who wanted to continue to Nanjing or Shanghai had to go to the downtown ticket office and queue up for passage on another boat. 
My wife and I decided to stay in Wuhan because we were told that the lower Yangtze would be anticlimactic.
Wuhan, a center for heavy industry, had been a proletarian bastion for Chairman Mao, who was fond of swimming in the Yangtze. 
In July 1966, the 72-year-old leader refuted rumors of his ill health by plunging into one of history's most celebrated swims. 
For more than an hour, he floated down the Yangtze nine miles at the head of 5,000 young swimmers from Wuhan. 
Then he returned to Peking and unleashed the cruel chaos of his Cultural Revolution.
Wuhan used to re-enact Chairman Mao's swim every July, sometimes employing little red flags mounted on rubber inner tubes. 
Nobody wants to do it anymore. 
As our boat trip had suggested, revolutionary hardship is a notion whose time has come and gone in present-day China. 
The Yangtze still flows eastward to the sea, as it has throughout China's history, but now it bears peasants with baskets of baby chicks, intent on exploiting the party's latest maxim that getting rich through labor is glorious.

file: DROP IN DRUG COST MAY ALLOW ALL-OUT ATTACK ON A PARASITE.txt
text:
ï»¿
A drug that takes only a single dose to effectively treat all forms of schistosomiasis, a debilitating parasitic disease that infects one in every 20 people in the world, has fallen so sharply in cost that the World Health Organization now believes it can be used for an all-out attack on the scourge.
Dr. Kenneth E. Mott, the director of the W.H.O. program to fight the disease, said the drug, praziquantel, ''is the greatest advance'' in treating parasitic diseases since chloroquin was developed in World War II as the chief weapon against malaria.
The cost of a single dose of praziquantel has been reduced to $1.40 for adults and 74 cents for children, who make up 60 to 70 percent of the victims of the disease. 
Only four years ago a single adult dose cost about $4.20. 
The single dose appears to offer two to three years' defense against reinfection by the disease, which attacks such organs as the intestines and liver. 
Although the disease is not often fatal, it is so debilitating that it has become an economic drain on many underdeveloped countries.
World Health Organization program director Dr Kenneth E Mott says cost of drug praziquantel has dropped so sharply that organization now believes it can be used for all-out attack on schistosomiasis, dibilitating parasitic disease that infects one in every 20 people in world; Bayer Drug Company makes drug, which takes only single dose to effectively treat all forms of the disease (M)
The cost reduction was announced July 1 by the Bayer Drug Company, which makes the drug.
Like other drugs used to treat schistosomiasis, praziquantel does not kill all the parasites in a person's body but reduces their number until the symptoms disappear. 
Unlike malaria parasites, those for schistosomiasis cannot multiply in the body. 
Once their population is reduced it remains low unless the victim is infected again.
Â 
Snails Harbor the Parasite
Freshwater snails are the parasite's hosts for part of its life cycle, just as mosquitoes are hosts for malaria. 
The disease is prevalent in hot, humid climates and has become more widespread as irrigation projects have enlarged the habitat of the snails.
At one time the World Health Organization tried to control the disease by waging all-out attacks on the snails. 
But these efforts, including a drive in China, proved disappointing as the snails quickly returned.
Now health officials are focusing their efforts on drug treatment and prevention of exposure to the parasite. 
They are doing this by reducing the discharge of human waste into bodies of water and keeping people away from such waste, whether they are swimming, fishing, washing or planting rice.
Eggs excreted from infected humans hatch into free-swimming parasites propelled by tiny hairs as they seek out a snail. 
If they fail to find a snail, they die within 12 hours. 
However, enormous numbers of eggs are produced by severely infected people. 
Inside the snail, the parasite subdivides thousands of times. 
It emerges into the water in a form with forked tail and seeks out the skin of a human being.
Â 
Three Types of the Ailment
Traveling through the bloodstream, the parasites evolve into male and female worms that mate and can remain joined for many years, producing a steady stream of eggs. 
In two forms of schistosomiasis, the worms lodge within the walls of blood vessels lining the intestines and the eggs are discharged with the feces.
One of the three types of the disease occurs in Africa, the eastern Mediterranean, the Caribbean and South America. 
The other is Asiatic. 
The third form, which is found in Egypt and much of the eastern Mediterranean and Africa, lodges in blood vessels of the bladder. 
Blood in the urine is a typical symptom and the eggs are discharged through the urine.
There are now relatively simple ways to test for the prevalence of eggs in urine or stool samples. 
But it is the eggs remaining in body tissues that cause severe immune reactions leading to lethargy and other symptoms.
Some drugs are effective against only one or another of the three forms but praziquantel attacks them all.
Health officials believe it is possible that the parasites may eventually develop resistance to the drugs, and for that reason some specialists see a vaccine as the long-term solution. 
While many laboratories are working on various aspects of the vaccine problem, the obstacles seem so great that a practical vaccine seems many years away.
Â 
Other Drug's Success in Brazil
Praziquantel grew out of research by the Merck Company in the 1970's and was then developed as a drug by Bayer. 
Since then it has been subjected to numerous tests and the cost has finally become low enough for mass administration. 
It is also effective, he said, against liver flukes and tapeworms.
Dr. Mott's optimism regarding large-scale attacks on schistosomiasis is based in part on experience gained in northeast Brazil, where seven million people have been treated with oxamniquine, a specific drug for the disease there. 
A 30-fold drop in the number of cases found by autopsies has been reported from the University Hospital in Bahia.
The beneficial effects of praziquantel are so obvious, Dr. Mott said, that ''riots'' have occurred in areas of the Sudan where supplies ran short. 
In Egypt the United Nations Children's Fund is participating in administering the drug to 30,000 residents of a single district. 
The disease has been eradicated in some of China's southern provinces.
The Chinese are using pyquiton, their own form of praziquantel. 
While 44 species of wild and domestic animals in China have been found to carry the Asian form of the disease in the same manner as humans, they do not appear to play a role in maintaining it as a threat to the human population, Dr. Mott said.

file: DRUG SMUGGLERS_ NEW BREED OF ETHNIC GANGS.txt
text:
ï»¿
As the Mafia's role declines, the multibillion-dollar heroin trade in New York is increasingly being conducted by criminal organizations that together sound like a United Nations of drug smugglers, including Chinese, Thais, Pakistanis, Indians, Iranians, Afghans, Nigerians and Israelis.
Last year, for example, Federal officials had to scour the city for eight translators of the African language Twi to assess wiretaps of a ring of heroin smugglers from Ghana.
Since January, more than a dozen Israelis have been arrested for drug trafficking, and officials say there are at least four major Israeli criminal organizations stretching across Asia, Europe and North America.
More than any other ethnic group, law-enforcement officials say, overseas Chinese with contacts in Bangkok, Hong Kong and throughout the UnitedVStates have developed large, sophisticated but little-understood international drug trafficking organizations. 
The Chinese groups, the Federal Drug Enforcement Administration estimates, are now responsible for more than 30 percent of the heroin entering the city.
Yet few police departments and Federal agencies charged with fighting drug traffickers have recognized the rise of organized crime outside the Mafia and begun to learn the languages, cultures or even the identities of new groups that could eventually pose as severe a threat as the well-known Mafia families.
''These groups are posing a major challenge to law enforcement,'' said Robert M. Stutman, the special agent in charge of the Federal drug agency in New York. 
''We now are dealing with languages and cultures we don't have real depth in. 
Even in Chinese there are a number of dialects that are very different, and agents with a knowledge of Chinese are few and far between.''
For decades the Mafia dominated the importation and processing of heroin. 
Its involvement stems from the 1930's when, at the end of Prohibition, bootleggers had the capital, experience and overseas contacts to turn their smuggling operations to narcotics.
Until the late 1960's, they were able to dominate a business that bought Turkish opium, processed it into heroin in laboratories in Marseilles or the Corsican underworld and sold to distributors in poor inner-city neighborhoods.
Although most Mafia leaders proclaimed their disdain for the drug business to one another, many, including Vito Genovese, the head of one of New York's five mob families, became heavily involved.
Â 
Shift From Turkey
But in the early 1970's, a crackdown on opium production in Turkey shifted the source of heroin increasingly to Mexico, Southeast Asia and areas in Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran -places where the Mafia did not have extensive contacts. 
In addition, the growth of international air transportation made it easier for groups in source countries to bring the drug into the United States themselves.
Finally, officials say, it was the Mafia's involvement in the drug business that led to the most damaging Federal cases against the Mafia, including the pizza connection trial that ended in the conviction of the former chief of the Sicilian Mafia and 16 other defendants for operating a drug smuggling ring from Siciliy to Brazil to the Middle West.
''The people who join the mob now are second- and third-generation and don't have the values their predecessors had,'' said Ronald Goldstock, the director of the New York State Organized Crime Task Force. 
''They are, in effect, yuppies. 
The ties that bind them together are financial. 
When they join and find they are not doing as well as they thought they would, it is much easier for them to break and turn informant.''
Together, these factors have opened up the heroin market to a new generation of high-level traffickers, made up largely of ethnic groups from opium-source countries or with trading contacts around the world.
In the last two years increasing numbers of major heroin cases in New York have involved organizations of Chinese, Pakistanis, Israelis and West Africans.
Â 
New Set of Problems
Law-enforcement officials say a recent flurry of cases against these groups are ''test bores'' into worlds they do not completely understand. 
It may take years to explain fully how these groups are organized, they say, how they make contacts with street drug distributing organizations in New York ghettos and how they take their profits out of the country.
In many ways, Mr. Goldstock added, organized crime among Chinese immigrants today resembles organized crime that developed with the mass migration of Italians at the turn of the century.
''They prey on their own with extortion and protection rackets, in a culture where people don't go to the police and where most police don't speak the language,'' Mr. Goldstock said. 
To the outside world, he added, the organizations seem mysterious and impenetrable.
Evidence abounds that groups of ethnic Chinese from Thailand, Hong Kong, Malaysia, Taiwan and China - some of whom may have long been involved in illegal gambling and other enterprises - are shipping large quantities of heroin into the country. 
Since January 1986 Federal agents have seized more than 200 pounds of heroin in New York, worth hundreds of millions of dollars, after it had been shipped by Chinese groups in furniture, musical instruments and air-conditioners.
Often it is just an odd tip or a bit of luck that leads to unraveling a smuggling organization. 
Last July, for example, the Thai police told Federal agents that a shipment that might contain heroin was heading to the United States, addressed to ''Joe Wong'' in Queens.
Â 
Shipment Followed
The agents discovered the shipment on a Seattle dock, watched its delivery to an apartment in Flushing, Queens, and eventually linked it to a chef in a neighborhood Chinese restaurant.
The four crates contained fine teak furniture, carved with ornate reliefs of jungle scenes and packed with 15 kilograms of pure white heroin worth more than $30 million on the street. 
In the end, the case resulted in more than a dozen arrests in New York, Thailand and China and the seizure of drug labs in Amsterdam.
Â 
Dispersed Expatriots
On a smaller scale, law-enforcement authorities have become increasingly aware of heroin trafficking by Israeli criminal organizations that had been active in smuggling, credit card fraud and other crimes at least back into the 1970's.
Like the Chinese, the Israeli criminal gangs are drawn from a dispersed population of expatriots who live and conduct business in Asia, Europe and the United States. 
Many are made up of Sephardim, immigrants whose families came to Israel mainly from Arab countries.
Many are believed to have met one another in Israeli prisons, officials say. 
As with the Chinese and other groups, officials say, Israeli criminals are only a tiny part of larger ethnic communities in the United States and in other countries.
The Israeli organizations caught the attention of Federal authorities in 1979, with the gang-related slaying and dismemberment of two Israelis, Eli and Esther Rubin, in Los Angeles. 
Authorities believe that there are now at least several hundred around the world who may affiliate with one another for criminal activities and that there are at least four large organizations with members on several continents.
Â 
Special Caution
In the last two months, authorities arrested 11 people in Brooklyn, including nine Israelis, and accused them of importing heroin from Thailand to New York through Canada. 
Two Israelis were arrested on drug charges in Detroit and three were arrested in Atlantic City in possession of five pounds of heroin.
According to officials involved in the Brooklyn case, the Israelis showed a remarkable sophistication in counter-surveillance. 
The drug traffickers would sometimes spot Federal agents' unmarked cars circling a block, and often they would protect one of their dealers by following his car at a distance with a second car to make sure no one was on his trail.
In the last three years, authorities have also seen a rise in trafficking of Southwest Asian heroin by Pakistanis, Afghans, Iranians and by West Africans who ship the drug through their homelands. 
In one case last fall in which 29 people, mainly immigrants from Ghana, were charged with heroin trafficking, the Justice Department had to find 8 to 12 translators who understood the Twi language to staff a telephone wiretap 24 hours a day.
And this week alone, Federal narcotics agents seized five pounds of heroin from Pakistani smugglers in one case, and in another case arrested four Indians who were charged with smuggling 10 pounds of heroin from their native land to Kennedy International Airport in shampoo bottles.

The Netherlands, under pressure from China, said it would reconsider its decision to export two submarines to Taiwan, a Foreign Ministry official said today.
The official said that the Peking regime had threatened to reduce relations with the Netherlands to the lowest possible level if the submarines and a variety of nuclear power station components were exported to Taiwan.
Netherlands reconsiders its decision to export two submarines to Taiwan following warning from Peking
''The Chinese Government has pointed out that it regards the export order as a rejection of the 1972 communique in which the Netherlands recognized that Taiwan was a province of China,'' he said. 
''That communique was the basis for full diplomatic relations between the two countries.''
The official said that the Dutch Ambassador in Peking, Johannes Kneppelhout, had been summoned to the Chinese Foreign Ministry last week to receive the warning and a Chinese representative had been received at the Foreign Minister here at the same time.

Former President Richard M. Nixon, asserting that Chinese leaders had ''misunderstood and misjudged'' President Reagan's views on the Taiwan issue, called today for an early meeting between Mr. Reagan and Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang of China to create better trust between Peking and Washington.
In a speech tonight at a dinner of the National Council on United States-China Trade, Mr. Nixon said their meeting should take place before Mr. Reagan has a meeting with Yuri V. Andropov, the Soviet leader.
''I believe that most of the misunderstandings and suspicions which have characterized recent developments could be dispelled by a faceto-face meeting in the near future,'' he said.
WASHINGTON, June 1 - Former President Richard M. Nixon, asserting that Chinese leaders had ''misunderstood and misjudged'' President Reagan's views on the Taiwan issue, called today for an early meeting between Mr. Reagan and Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang of China to create better trust between Peking and Washington.
''Before a summit meeting with our potential adversaries takes place, it is vital that a meeting be scheduled with our friends,'' he added.
At the time of Secretary of State George P. Shultz's visit to Peking last January, Mr. Zhao said he agreed in principle to visit Washington, but no date has been set.
Â 
'Speaking as an Old Friend'
Mr. Nixon, whose visit in 1972 was the first by any President to China, said that ''speaking as an old friend, there has been a disturbing tendency in statements emanating from Peking to question the good faith of President Reagan on issues like Taiwan and the tennis star.''
The reference to the tennis player was to Hu Na, who was given political asylum this year.
''This does a disservice both to China's and to our own interests,'' Mr. Nixon said, in one of his infrequent public appearances in Washington. 
''We had vast differences which we bridged over by quiet diplomacy in 1972. 
More resort to quiet diplomacy could prevent that bridge from falling into disrepair in the next ten years.''
''Speaking candidly, I believe some of our Chinese friends have misunderstood and misjudged President Reagan's position on the Taiwan issue.''
Mr. Nixon also said he saw no reason for concern in the event that China and the Soviet Union improved relations. 
''A war between two major powers in the nuclear age would inevitably escalate into a world war,'' he said. 
''Consequently, it is in the interest of the United States, for China, and the Soviet Union to try to reduce tensions between them which could result in war. 
It is equally in China's interest for the United States and the Soviet Union to try to reduce tensions between them which might result in war.''
Mr. Nixon also called for a further loosening of restrictions on trade with China. 
''It is my personal belief that the present policy is unnecessarily restrictive,'' he said. 
''China should be treated the same as other friendly, non-allied countries like India, which incidentally, unlike China, has close relations with the Soviet Union. 
It is time to remove United States agencies from the straightjacket which requires them to treat China like an adversary.''
