file: EAST GERMANY STEPS UP CONTACTS WITH CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
With a visit to Peking planned next month by its party leader, East Germany is stepping up a reconciliation with China that appears to have the cautious blessing of the Soviet Union, according to scholars and Bonn officials.
Since 1982, when the Soviet Union made its first overtures to China, East Germany has been quietly mending the relations that were ruptured two decades earlier in the course of the ideological confrontation between Moscow and Peking.
The visit to China in the latter half of October by the East German leader, Erich Honecker, 74 years old, is expected to consolidate relations and possibly open the way for other Eastern European Communist chiefs to follow. 
Poland's leader, Gen. Wojciech Jaruzelski, and Hungary's leader, Janos Kadar, are the main candidates.
For Mr. Honecker, the steady opening to China is a strand in a larger strategy of gaining recognition for East Germany as a sovereign and autonomous country. 
The timing of the China trip felicitously offsets an apparent veto by Moscow on a long-planned milestone visit to West Germany.
Although there is broad agreement that Mr. Honecker has a green light from Moscow for his China trip, some analysts detect potential signs of low-level tension between the Soviet Union and its Eastern European allies over renewed ties with Peking.
Â 
Pressure on Moscow
The Chinese, according to this line of reasoning, want to use their improved relationship with Eastern Europe as a lever for putting pressure on the Soviet Union to wrest concessions from Moscow. 
In a speech in Vladivostok in late July, the Soviet leader, Mikhail S. Gorbachev, put fresh emphasis on seeking better relations with China, but several Eastern European allies are well ahead of Moscow in this regard.
The East German contacts reached a high point last December when Horst Sindermann, a Politburo member and president of the East German legislature, visited Peking and was received by Hu Yaobang, general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Conspicuously, Mr. Sindermann recalled that German Communists and the Communist movement in China have hoary connections, including a friendship struck between Mr. Hu and Mr. Honecker in the 1950's when they were the leaders of their countries' respective Communist youth groups.
In June, Margot Honecker, Education Minister and wife of the East German leader, followed Mr. Sindermann's path to Peking, and in the same month China's Foreign Minister, Wu Xueqian, came to East Berlin. 
It was the highest-level Chinese delegation sent to Eastern Europe since the 1961 split with Moscow.
As trading partners, the East Germans are interested in China's vast market, and the Chinese see in the German Communist state a source of high-technology. 
Yet, at the political level, some political analysts express doubts that the Honecker visit will produce a resumption of party-to-party ties.
Nonetheless, East Germany has abandoned anything resembling ideological polemics with China, and its state-controlled press has reported with interest and even a touch of enthusiasm on the Chinese economic experiment and its free-market mechanisms.
For their part, the Chinese have virtually exculpated the East Berlin Government from complicity in such issues as the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan or the domination of Cambodia by the Vietnamese.
In Bonn, a senior adviser to Chancellor Helmut Kohl welcomed the Honecker visit to China, saying that the East German was going as ''a door-opener for Moscow.''

file: Economic Scene_China_s Fight Over Ideology.txt
text:
ï»¿
YESTERDAY was National Day, the 36th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China, and the Cantonese were firing off skyrockets and firecrackers, strolling and shopping, and eating up a storm.
The saying here is, ''The Cantonese will eat anything with four legs except the table.''
Or, for that matter, anything without legs. 
One of the local delicacies is called ''tiger fighting dragon.''
It is actually a combination of cat and snake.
This year the two-day National Day holiday followed a couple of days after the Moon Festival and everyone has been enjoying the long break. 
The Canton hotels are crowded, especially with many Hong Kong Chinese who have come back in droves to visit their families on the mainland. 
The stores, most of which are open, are mobbed. 
Children are having a ball racing up and down halls and corridors and through restaurants, laughing and shrieking, but apparently never crying. 
Their Chinese parents let them carry on as they please; with the one-child policy, teachers here say the children are getting spoiled.
There is a certain amount of economic pride connected with the celebration. 
Monday night the Governor of Guang Dong Province, Ye Zhen-Ping, told a large reception: ''This is the last year of the sixth five-year plan, and by the common effort of all the people, the plan we establish can be fulfilled and overfulfilled.''
China, he said, had now ''basically realized'' its aim of trying to get on an upward financial and economic trend. 
''We firmly take the economic reforms as our first priority,'' he added, ''and we will go on firmly, step by step.''
But, as though to demonstrate that the reformation of China still has a way to go before ''groupthink'' is over, the major local newspapers, Renmin Ribao, Guengzou Ribao and Nanfang Ribao, all played the leading speeches here and in Peking on page 1 and used identical pictures.
Deng Xiaoping's open door policy and four modernizations of industry, agriculture, science and technology, and national defense coexist with important remnants of old-style Marxism and what the Chinese call Mao Zedong thought, and others would call Stalinism.
In public, the fight between the two ideologies is muffled. 
Some old-style Marxists seek to push their cause by pretending there is no conflict between Dengism and Maoism. 
For instance, an editorial in Guangnung Daily states: ''In Deng Xiaoping's opinion, strengthening the second civilization'' -that is the new code word for the regime's objectives - ''requires ideological and political education as well as the development of socialist education, science and technology and culture.''
As though to scold Mr. Deng's disciples and those business types who are denounced here as ''capitalist roaders,'' the editorial says: ''We must unswervingly adhere to the four cardinal principles of leadership of the Communist Party, socialist road, people's democratic dictatorship, and upholding of Marxism, Leninism and Mao Zedong thought.''
Deng's response to the challenge is to put his own people on the Politburo and the Central Committee, and retire the old guard.
A little of the conflict at the ideological level does break into the open, however, at least symbolically. 
A new film, called ''Xiangshi Inn,'' which was previewed in Peking in July but has not yet been released, has already stirred up a storm of controversy among the politicians and intellectuals. 
It takes up the contemporary economic reforms, but without a happy ending.
The film, which was made by a leading director, Dong Kena, a 56-year-old woman, is about a young woman who is sent by the Government to take over and modernize an inn in a mountain village in southeast Hunan Province. 
But the former female manager of the inn tries every trick in the book, with the support of the county Communist Party secretary, to drive the young newcomer away. 
Finally, the new woman quits in despair and departs with her lover, an unmarried truck driver. 
(In the short story from which the film was made, her lover was married to a mad woman.) The movie critic of China Daily, Cheng Fang-Ming, who called ''Xiangshi Inn'' ''probably the best film of the year,'' drew the political-moral lesson for his readers: ''Obviously,'' he said, ''the sad ending implies that people sometimes must fight against the established order to succeed in rural economic reconstruction.''
The film's director said in an interview that ''one reason the film stirs heated response is that we produced it at the right time.''
But, here in Canton, in the midst of this holiday, the issue posed by ''Xiangshi Inn'' seems very remote. 
All day long the holiday-makers have been ogling, and buying, clothes and trinkets, refrigerators and stereos and other durable goods with which the stores are amply stocked. 
It is the consumer revolution that seems to be firmly in the saddle although, elsewhere in the country, Marxist and Maoist thought may die hard.

file: Economic Scene_Complexity And Control.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE decision of the Central Committee of the
Communist Party of China to give greater
freedom to capitalist-style market forces and independence to a million state-owned enterprises may be the most damning indictment thus far of the failures of central planning and rigid controls of Communist states.
The Chinese, under Deng Xiaoping, are moving further along the capitalist road, without calling it that. 
The announcement said China would continue to adhere to Communist principles. 
Deng, unlike his predecessor, Mao Zedong, does not believe in great leaps forward or cultural revolutions; even after the reforms, some central planning will remain for key industries, such as steel, coal, cement and fertilizers, and there will be a mixture of collectively and privately controlled enterprises.
Leonard Silk (Economic Scene) column on move by China to give greater freedom to capitalist-style market forces and independence to many state-owned enterprises; says action may be most damning indictment thus far of failures of central planning and rigid controls of Communist states; sketch (M)
Yet a genuine overhaul of the centrally controlled system seems to be in the works. 
Strikingly, the Chinese declaration said the most crucial change would be in the price system, switching from fixed to flexible prices, responsive to changes in supply and demand. 
And the Chinese stress their determination to promote competition and provide greater economic incentives to producers to meet the needs of consumers, to increase productivity and to innovate.
The changes in China's economic system could have a far more powerful effect on the Soviet Union than earlier experiments in Hungary, Yugoslavia and other Communist countries because of China's huge population and the strategic threat Peking represents to Moscow.
For what the proposed changes in the Chinese system imply is acceptance by a group of top Communist leaders that the complexity of developing and operating a modern economy is incompatible with the methods of central planning and control practiced in the Soviet Union, and still preached as orthodoxy through much of the Communist world.
A new book, ''The Idea of Economic Complexity,'' by David Warsh, a reporter on The Boston Globe, serves to demonstrate that economic development involves not just greater wealth or new technology but a higher degree of complexity, with economies consisting of a greater and greater number of ''separable, analyzable parts.''
Growing complexity, in economic terms, means an increasing number of different jobs, different businesses, different machinery, different goods and services; it also means, with greater and greater division of labor, greater interdependence, nationally and internationally.
On the surface, it might seem that greater complexity would require greater control for an economy to work efficiently. 
But the reverse is true, as the experience of capitalist and Communist countries demonstrates. 
The gap between living standards in Western and Communist economies, as Mr. Warsh notes, grows greater every day. 
There are 26 centrally planned economies that, with nearly 40 percent of the world's population, produce slightly less than 20 percent of the world's goods.
But the Communist countries account for nearly 40 percent of the world's military spending. 
This huge outlay on arms helps to retard the Communists' economic development and exacerbates tensions among themselves and with the West.
''The prospect for the knitting together of these two blocs through extensive foreign trade is not bright,'' Mr. Warsh says. 
He doubts that two such different systems can really coexist peacefully when the gap between them - material and technical - keeps widening. 
''Given the exceedingly precarious balance of the arms race,'' he says, ''it seems to me that all the questions really worth worrying about grow out of this great inequality.''
China's decision to try a new route to narrow the gap in income and living standards is thus important not only for its own development, and possibly that of the entire Eastern and world economy, but also for international peace. 
That would be particularly important if China should succeed in moving forward in industry, as it has in agriculture, and establish a model for the Soviet Union.
But resistance to capitalist-style economic change is strong in the upper reaches of the Soviet political ruling class, the bureaucracy and the military. 
Partly. this resistance seems rooted in the habits of the oldest Communist regime in the world, partly in fear of the political consequences of the lifting of repression. 
Yet the Soviet system may be mired in endless stagnation if its leaders continue to resist the lessons that the Chinese - and many Soviet economists - have been learning about the complexities of modern economic systems and how to deal with them.
''The chief advantage of time,'' said Henri Bergson, the French philosopher, ''is that it prevents everything from happening at once.''
To this, the economist Jagdish Bhagwati of Columbia University adds, ''The chief advantage of economic theory is that it prevents us from considering everything at the same time.''
There's a second corollary, which Mr. Warsh's book inspires: Growing complexity requires greater simplicity, independence of decision-making, and interdependence within and among nations. 
There remain problems, including air and water pollution, congestion, crime, disease and the arms race, which require cooperation and control. 
Capitalists as well as Communists still have things to learn.

file: Economic Scene_Where China Is Booming.txt
text:
ï»¿
THIS Special Economic Zone, an area marked out to attract foreign investment through special tax programs and other incentives, is the most spectacular success story of China's open door policy.
While not without its problems, the growth of Shenzhen, which lies just across the water from Hong Kong and is connected to the New Territories of Hong Kong on its southern border, can be seen in a number of ways: Since 1979, its population has mushroomed to 350,000, from 20,000; it has signed more than 2,300 foreign investment agreements valued at more than $1.6 billion; it has attracted more than 30 percent of all foreign investment in China; it has seen the number of businesses grow to 400, and is planning 307 more; its electronics industry has grown from one company employing 300 to 60 companies employing 13,000; its total output has increased 29-fold, and its per-capita output has climbed to almost $2,000 a year in a country where the average has been less than $100 a year.
In addition, Shenzhen is expected to become the principal support base for offshore oil exploration in the South China Sea, and it is likely to become a major exporter of food, textiles and petrochemicals.
As for this zone's problems, a key one is a black market in currency. 
Three kinds of money circulate in this area - China's renminbi, its foreign exchange certificates and Hong Kong dollars. 
The three currencies, which can be used for purchasing only certain kinds of goods, provide opportunities for a great deal of wheeling and dealing.
Zhang Hongyi, the general manager of the Bank of China's Shenzhen branch, says the black market in money is the alternative to a black market in goods. 
He suggests that the goods black market would come into being without the money black market because of China's effort, which he regards as necessary, to run a dual-price system. 
One set of prices is for domestic goods, with many subsidies to support the standard of living of poor people; the other set applies to imported goods. 
But there is no way to raise an impregnable wall between the two.
Some people here maintain that the three-currency system, complicated as it is, is a valuable stimulant for business activity. 
But Mr. Zhang does not agree. 
''It's not good for the country,'' he says, ''to allow foreign currency to circulate.''
And he added that the disorderly currency system helped bring on the huge scandal on Hainan island involving Government officials who imported cars at one rate; sold them inland at far higher prices because of monetary differences, and then turned the profits back into foreign exchange for importing more cars.
This scandal, plus other criticism, Shenzhen officials say, will still not deter them from policies that have brought such prosperity to the people.
''We know from experience that the closed door policy did not work and we will not go back to it,'' one official said.
The open door does not mean just an effort to put out the welcome mat to foreign money and technology. 
The Chinese are also trying to bring people here with whom they wish to make friends, regardless of their politics or even their past connections with Taiwan or South Korea. 
Many are scientists, economists, business people and politicians from the United States.
For example, Ken Jernstedt, a 68-year-old member of the Oregon State Senate, who has been a test pilot at Republic Aviation and a Coca-Cola dealer, is back in China for the first time since World War II, when he helped defend the Burma Road as a member of Gen. Claire Chennault's Flying Tigers.
Mr. Jernstedt, who specializes in Pacific Rim affairs in the Oregon State Senate and has maintained close ties with Taiwan, was a bit wary when he and his wife were invited by the Chinese Government for an expense-free trip. 
But he wanted to see his old base in Kunming in Hunan Province, where the Third Pursuit Squadron, in which he was a flight leader, was based.
When he got back to Kunming, he was astonished to find the walled city gone, replaced by one with wide avenues, rows of trees, modern hotels and a population that had tripled.
Asked why he thought the Chinese had invited him, he said: ''I don't think they want anything out of me directly. 
The primary reason is they want to build better relations with the United States and the State of Oregon.''
He said they were interested in buying logs, and Oregon had plenty to sell. 
''They'd rather have the logs than our finished lumber,'' he added. 
''It's the difference in price.''
China is struggling to conserve foreign exchange.
''I'm a believer in free trade,'' Mr. Jernstedt said. 
''I like Reagan's attitude. 
The world is going through a kind of leveling, and this Chinese economy is not going to grow completely unless they have outlets for their goods.''

text:

Lo Chengxun, whose 10-year sentence as an American spy was disclosed in Peking yesterday, was one of several Chinese or Hong Kong journalists and officials who have informal license from the Chinese Government to maintain contacts and exchanges with foreigners in Hong Kong.
In that sense, Mr. Lo belonged to a system that includes meetings over lunch and a constant round of cocktail parties and receptions involving foreign diplomats and journalists on the one side and Chinese presumed to be well-informed of the policies of the Peking Government on the other.
On the Chinese side, those people include editors and journalists like Mr. Lo attached to Hong Kong's three pro-Peking Chinese newspapers. 
They also include officials of the Hong Kong branch of the official New China News Agency and employees of the Bank of China and other Chinese commercial offices in Hong Kong.
Lo Chengxun, whose 10-year sentence as an American spy was disclosed in Peking yesterday, was one of several Chinese or Hong Kong journalists and officials who have informal license from the Chinese Government to maintain contacts and exchanges with foreigners in Hong Kong.System No Longer as Important
The system of informal contacts and exchanges, still in existence but no longer as important in these days of China's more outgoing foreign policy, seems useful both to the foreigners, including many Americans, and to the Chinese Government. 
Even though the Chinese involved are known not to divulge information that has not already appeared in the official Chinese press, foreigners find the meetings helpful in interpreting policies of the Peking Government.
Most of the diplomats and journalists assume that their meetings with the editors and others are routinely reported to the authorities in Peking, who are interested in gathering information about individual specialists on China and on Western attitudes toward the country. 
The system of contacts is also widely regarded as part of China's ''united front'' work, a series of activities by which the Peking Government builds ties with foreigners and with Chinese outside China proper.
Mr. Lo, though he did not speak English, was a prominent and highly valued participant in this system. 
It was well-known in Hong Kong that Chinese-speaking diplomats and journalists frequently sought him out. 
A lively, affable man who spoke with the accents of his native Guangxi, Mr. Lo was regarded as a pragmatic thinker who generally favored a greater political openness in China.
Hong Kong newspapers reported last fall that Mr. Lo, who was known in Hong Kong by the name Lo Fu, had been arrested while traveling in Guangdong Province with his family. 
The newspapers said that during that trip in May 1982, Mr. Lo was suddenly called to Peking. 
After that, the papers said, his family heard nothing from or about him except for a brief handwritten note to his wife that arrived a few weeks later.
Similar incidents have been reported involving other Hong Kong residents, who are considered Chinese nationals by the Peking Government.
The Chinese police have detained members of human rights groups based in Hong Kong who were traveling in China to collect information about dissidents. 
One of them, Lau San-ching, disappeared in Canton after visiting the relatives of some human rights activists who had been arrested in that city.
Another case involves Hanson Huang, a 1976 graduate of Harvard Law School who went to China in 1979 to teach law at Peking University and work as an adviser for the China International Trust and Investment Corporation, a Government body that arranges business contracts with foreign companies.
According to reports gathered in Hong Kong and published in The Wall Street Journal and SPEARHead, a magazine published in New York that monitors human rights in Asia, Mr. Huang called his mother in Hong Kong early in 1982 to tell her that he was moving out of his hotel room. 
There has been no word of him since, and it is assumed he is under arrest.

file: EMBASSY SECRUITY_ PROBLEMS EXIST FOR U.S. AROUND THE WORLD.txt
text:
ï»¿
Some of the security problems that have arisen at the American Embassy in Moscow are present in a number of other American missions around the world, according to Administration officials, intelligence experts and current and former American ambassadors.
Missions in China, Eastern Europe and other areas with a large Soviet presence have been particularly vulnerable, American security officials said. 
But they said there were also problems in certain Middle Eastern and African countries.
Americans serving in friendly countries where internal security regulations are more relaxed are also susceptible to Soviet and other subversion, they said.
Security lapses elsewhere have not drawn the same attention as those in Moscow, the specialists acknowledged, although many of the problems have existed for decades and are considered as serious. 
Nor has the attention directed at the problem in Moscow been duplicated elsewhere.
Â 
'Problems Are Widespread'
''What the incident in Moscow should awaken us to is that the problems and vulnerabilities are widespread,'' said Adm. Bobby R. Inman, retired, a former Deputy Director of Central Intelligence, who headed a special State Department advisory panel that investigated embassy security in 1985.
''While the Soviets most skillfully exploit them, they are not the only ones trying,'' he added, ''and vulnerabilities are at least as large if not larger in other places where the guard is not so high.''
An Assistant Secretary of State for Diplomatic Security, Robert E. Lamb, acknowledged that hostile espionage is a global problem confronting United States diplomatic facilities.
''Moscow has a threat level unmatched in the world, but there are other places that are just as vulnerable,'' he said. 
''Espionage is a worldwide problem and not confined to just hostile countries.''
Â 
Break-Ins in Eastern Europe
In discussing security problems in Eastern Europe, the officials said that embassy buildings in Prague, Budapest, East Berlin and Sofia, Bulgaria, are next to buildings that is some cases are owned by the host government. 
American investigators have turned up evidence of break-ins in buildings in Eastern Europe and electronic bugging.
Outside the Eastern bloc, the least acknowledged but the most serious security problems are at American facilities in China, according to intelligence officials.
When Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigators visited the three Beijing embassy buildings last year, they discovered a maze of tunnels from the basements to other buildings. 
Doors to the tunnels were locked but did not have alarms. 
One tunnel led into the basement of the Czechoslovak Embassy, said one committee staff member who went on the trip.
The consulate in Canton, meanwhile, is considered impossible to protect, since it is situated on several floors of a high-rise hotel and even ''secure areas'' where only Americans are allowed are guarded by the Chinese police, not American marines.
Â 
Many Local Employees
American installations are also made vulnerable by the extensive use of local employees. 
While West Germany, France and Britain hire an average of one local employee for every three of its own officials, the average number of local employees at American posts far exceeds the number of Americans.
Last December there were 10,766 Americans and 15,327 local employees working full-time at American posts around the world. 
In some countries, the difference was dramatic. 
In Japan, for example, local employees numbered 407, compared with 269 Americans. 
In France there were 583 local employees and 291 Americans, and in Morocco 268 locals and 96 Americans.
Local employees outnumbered Americans even in some posts in Eastern Europe. 
In Czechoslovakia, for example, 46 locals worked for 27 Americans, while in Poland there were 119 locals and 52 Americans.
In Moscow, 210 Russians worked at the American Embassy, but all have been withdrawn.
Â 
Many Natives Used in China
Because of language and cultural barriers, American posts in China employed 336 locals and 155 Americans.
The United States can hire its own local employees in countries with large numbers of Soviet officials, such as Cuba, Nicaragua, Iraq and Syria, but it is assumed that some of them are intelligence agents and that all must report to their governments.
In November 1985, for example, the State Department issued a strong protest when Nicaragua subjected local employees of the American Embassy in Managua to several hours of intense interrogation. 
American diplomats in both Baghdad, Iraq, and Damascus, Syria, have reported problems with electronic surveillance.
Government investigators assert that the problem of socializing between American embassy staff members and local employees and residents is more widespread than is generally acknowledged by many officials.
Â 
'Sleep NATO'
''The basic rule, especially in the Eastern bloc, is 'Sleep NATO,' but that's not always followed,'' a former Foreign Service officer said.
American officials working at the United States Interests Section in Havana and the embassy in Managua have been sent home in recent years after they were caught dating local women. 
In Havana, investigators believe there was a serious intelligence loss because of an incident three years ago.
It is common practice for the Soviet intelligence services and their surrogates to use their nationals to seduce Americans in countries outside the Eastern bloc, where there is a tendency to be less suspicous and where socializing may not be forbidden.
Â 
Bill Would Ban Locals
In many emerging nations, where salaries are low, local employees have been particularly susceptible to offers to spy for Soviet-bloc governments and, to a lesser extent, ostensibly friendly countries.
This month, Representative Jim Courter, Republican of New Jersey, submitted a bill that would ban all local workers from American posts in Eastern Europe.
Although the State Department opposes the bill, it is working on a plan that would eliminate local employees from sensitive areas of American offices in Eastern Europe. 
It is also investigating regulations that would further prohibit socializing.
Reducing the number of local employees would require budgeting enormous resources to substitute Americans in many jobs. 
It would also shrink significantly the services offered to Americans abroad.
Â 
Locals Called Vital
Extensive renovation or replacement of more than 100 embassies to deter terrorism and espionage, as recommended by the Inman panel, would be even more expensive.
But despite the concern about the widespread use of locals, many diplomats argue that on the whole they benefit the Foreign Service.
They provide valuable services that in some cases could not be duplicated by American contract employees, according to State Department officials. 
And without local employees, they say, American embassies could turn into closed fortresses with little connection to the populace.
The officials say that native employees know how to resolve problems with local bureaucracies, know the language and dialects and often provide insight into culture and politics.
Â 
'Tremendous Benefits'
''There are tremendous benefits to being surrounded by foreign nationals, and if one is careful the benefits outweigh the liabilities,'' one Foreign Service officer said.
''There's a lot of sentiment in Congress for building new embassies when you're saving lives, but not for espionage,'' Mr. Lamb said, referring to the readiness of Congress to make embassies more secure against terrorism. 
''If this Government is going to make embassy security a priority, this Congress can help.''
Mr. Lamb is expected to raise this and other issues in testimony before the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on International Operations on Wednesday.

file: ENDANGERED SPECIES_ BIRD_S NEST SOUP.txt
text:
ï»¿
Nothing that a Chinese host can put on a table has more cachet than a bowl of viscous bird's nest soup. 
For centuries, it has been a delicacy throughout the Chinese world, a dish famed for its ability to keep people young and healthy.
But bird nests are becoming increasingly scarce. 
While the shortage is not yet a crisis, Chinese connoisseurs are obliged to pay more each time they bargain for nests - up to $1,000 a pound for top-quality nests.
''The price will definitely continue to increase,'' Stephen Tam, owner of the Cheong Loong Swallow's Nest store, said as he sorted the dozens of varieties of nests in his small shop here. 
''Most places the birds live have been developed into farmland or towns, and that reduces the number of birds that are left.''
In addition to the encroachment of humans on the birds' habitat, pollution is eroding some of the cliffs where they live and build their nests. 
Meanwhile, rising prices are leading the ''harvesters'' of nests to become more aggressive, sometimes snatching nests as soon as they are built, or grabbing nests that have eggs in them.
The nests used to make the soup belong to a kind of swallow, which builds on rocky cliffs or inside caves in several countries in Southeast Asia. 
Most of the nests today come from Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam or China.
The nests are not, as most Americans assume, a thatch of twigs and grass such as a robin might manufacture. 
Rather, they are made of the birds' saliva, which hardens into cementlike threads. 
When collected, the nests contain liberal amounts of feathers and even droppings, but are carefully washed and cleaned until they are white strips that look more like sponges than nests.
While swallow saliva soup may not send tingles across a Western palate, the Chinese rave over it. 
It is usually cooked with crab meat, shrimp or ham to make a gelatinous soup that is renowned principally for its healthfulness .
''The taste of the nests is nothing great,'' said Fok Kam Tong, head chef at the Man Wah Restaurant in Hong Kong's Mandarin Hotel, where a bowl of bird's nest soup ranges in price from $14 to $38. 
That is why crab and other embellishments are added, he said.
But bird's nest soup has virtues other than mere taste. 
''It's very good for you, very nourishing,'' Mr. Fok added. 
''It's good for women, for their skin, so they don't look old. 
But it's not just for women; it's good for everybody.''
Mr. Fok disputes the pessimists who say that bird's nest soup could eventually disappear. 
While scarcity of the proper nests is a concern, he and many Chinese food experts say, the resulting price increase would make it even more prized as a delicacy.
''If it becomes more expensive, it will be even more popular in Hong Kong,'' said Sunny Lan Kun Ying, a salesman at Yuen Wo Bird's Nest store near Hong Kong's business district.
Not according to the owners of the small Hong Kong shops that sell bird nests, who say most people are being priced out of the market. 
The cost of bird's nests has more than doubled in the last few years, they say, making it more difficult to afford a nest for a daughter with a skin blemish or a son who is about to take an important examination.
Some kinds of nests are becoming particularly rare, such as the red ones called ''blood nests.''
These have a reddish tinge that chefs say derives from blood in the birds' saliva. 
It is even better for one's health than regular bird nests, they say.
So, while regular bird nests sell for about $500 for a catty - a Chinese unit of weight amounting to just over a pound - the best-quality blood nests sell for nearly $1,300 a catty at the most exclusive shops.
Meanwhile, the swallows are seeking more and more remote locations to build their nests in places where humans will not intrude. 
They must avoid not only youths who scamper along the cliffs or climb bamboo scaffolding to cave ceilings, but also monkeys that have been trained to climb the rock walls and retrieve nests.
''The swallows are very careful,'' said Mr. Fok, the chef. 
''They will never build a nest where it is easy to get to.''

file: EX-PRISONER TO SEE CHINA, BY INVITATION.txt
text:
ï»¿
John T. Downey came home to Connecticut a decade ago after spending more than 20 years in a Chinese prison on charges of being an American spy.
This week, for the first time since his return, Mr. Downey will go back to China. 
He said his 18-day visit was a gesture of good will that had attracted the attention of the White House.
''If I had one strong conviction coming out of there it was that a solid relationship between the two countries was very important to our national interest,'' Mr. Downey said at his New Haven law office.
John T Downey, who returned to Connecticut 10 years ago after spending 20 years in jail in China on spy charges, will visit China for 18 days by invitation from Chinese Government; Downey says he hopes trip will be viewed as good-will gesture by Chinese; photos (S)
''It just seemed to me that maybe this was the time to go back,'' he said. 
''I'm hoping it will be seen as a good- will gesture by the Chinese.''
Â 
'Interest and Curiosity'
Mr. Downey, 53 years old, said he was ''looking forward to it with great interest and curiosity, but no trepidation.''
In 1952, at the height of the Korean War, Mr. Downey was 22 years old - fresh out of Yale University and working for the Central Intelligence Agency - when his plane was shot down over the mountains of Manchuria.
He was captured and sentenced to life imprisonment. 
He spent more than 20 years in prison before he was released in 1973 as relations between the United States and China began to improve.
Mr. Downey resumed his life almost as if the 20-year gap had never existed.
After his return, he went to Harvard Law School, got married and began practicing law with occasional forays into Connecticut Democratic politics.
Â 
A Race for the Senate
Last year he ran for the United States Senate but lost the Democratic nomination to Representative Toby Moffett, who in turn lost to Senator Lowell P. Weicker Jr., the Republican incumbent.
Speaking this month to the Western Connecticut Retired Officers Association in Westport, he said his experience in China was ''not one I would like to repeat.''
But he said it had convinced him that America society was ''the best hope for mankind.''
Mr. Downey said he began thinking about a return visit last winter when problems cropped up in United States- China relations over such things as arms sales to Taiwan and textile quotas.
''It just kind of set off alarm bells,'' he said.
He sounded out people who were familiar with China, such as Vice President Bush, a former chief of the United States Liaison Office in Peking.
They were enthusiastic about the idea of a visit but did not know how the Chinese would react, Mr. Downey said. 
They suggested that he get in touch with the Chinese on his own, which he did in March with a telephone call to the Chinese Embassy and a follow-up letter from his wife, Audrey, who was born in China but raised in Taiwan.
Mr. Downey, who will leave Wednesday with his wife and 3-year-old son, John, is going at the invitation of the Chinese People's Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries, which he described as an unofficial arm of the Chinese Foreign Office. 
The Chinese are not paying his way, he said.
Â 
A Chat With the President
Earlier this month, Mr. Downey discussed his trip at a meeting in Washington with Mr. Bush, who took him to the Oval Office for a brief chat with President Reagan.
Mr. Downey also had lunch with a staff member of the National Security Council for a background briefing. 
Despite the meetings, he said, his visit will be ''strictly private.''
Mr. Downey said he expected to find many changes since 1973. 
''The fact we are going is a sign of that,'' he said.

A Chinese boycott of American agricultural products last year cut American exports to China by more than a third, according to preliminary Government figures released today.
Huang Wenjun, a spokesman for the Ministry of Foreign Economics and Trade, also said at a news conference that China's total foreign trade reached $40.14 billion in 1983, up 2.2 percent from 1982, despite what he called a sluggishness in demand.

Mr. Huang said China's exports to the United States had remained at the 1982 level, while its imports from the United States dropped 38.3 percent.

Curbs on Farm Products
The sharp drop in China's imports came after China refused to purchase United States grain and other agricultural commodities in retaliation for American quotas placed on the purchase of Chinese textiles. 
A new textile agreement was reached last August, but China failed to meet its commitment to buy a minimum of 6 million tons of grain annually under a long-term purchasing agreement extending through 1984.
Last month, the Chinese Embassy in Washington told the United States Government that China would make up its obligation by buying the remaining 2 million tons of grain for delivery in 1984. 
It bought only 4 million tons last year.
The United States Embassy here said Friday that China imported $1.8 billion worth of American goods in the first 11 months of 1983, while exporting $2.1 billion in Chinese products.

Climb
Despite Washington's imposition of controls on Chinese textiles, sales of Chinese clothing and accessories to the American market climbed 25 percent in the first 11 months of last year, to $713.9 million.

file: FAMILY CELEBRATES YEAR OF THE RABBIT WITH FEASTING, SHANGHAI STYLE.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE week before celebrating the Lunar New Year, which begins tomorrow, San Yan Wong, his wife, Rosanna, and his mother-in-law, Kwai Wu Chui Fung, began searching the markets of Chinatown for the appropriate foods. 
For the start of the year 4685, the Year of the Rabbit, the Wongs had decided to celebrate as they had in Shanghai.
More than 23 years have passed since Mr. Wong, a former restaurateur and now a partner in the Asian American New York Land Corporation of Flushing, had celebrated in Shanghai fashion; for Mrs. Wong it had been 16 years. 
Both had left Shanghai and married in Hong Kong before settling in New York.
''Our children had never had a true Shanghai New Year,'' Mrs. Wong said in their apartment in Chinatown's Confucius Plaza overlooking the Manhattan Bridge. 
''We wanted them to have some of the things we had.''
Their children, Lily, 14 years old, Joseph, 12, and Lisa and Lucy, their 7-year-old twins, were enlisted in the preparations.
The refrigerator holds a surfeit of seafood for the New Year's Eve dinner: two sea bass to be cooked in Shao-Hsing wine, the wine of Shanghai; two pomfret flown in from China for marinating in soy sauce and sugar in the Shanghai manner; clams for cooking in a Shao-Hsing sauce, and shrimp for stir-frying in a sweet red dressing. 
In Shanghai, fish signify plenty, clams gold and shrimp happiness, Mr. Wong said.
Mrs. Kwai, whose husband, Kwai Tak Yui, is visiting Shanghai this New Year, insisted that the apartment be swept, scoured and vacuumed in keeping with tradition, because it is bad luck to clean on New Year's Day. 
At least one new item of clothing has been bought for each child, and envelopes of ''lucky money'' have begun appearing under the children's pillows.
Tonight a New Year table for visitors is to be set up in the living room, with dishes of peanuts (symbols of birth); watermelon seeds (a wish for many sons); gold-foil wrapped chocolate coins (riches); candied lotus seeds, kumquats and dates (plenty); a pomelo, or Chinese grapefruit (abundance); oranges (life's sweetness); tangerines (good luck), and water chestnuts (many children).
On the living room wall is a picture of Chai Sun, the god of fortune, surrounded by five slogans, wishes for a successful and healthy New Year, in gold calligraphy on bright red paper.
In Shanghai, children customarily knock on doors seeking lucky money, Mrs. Wong said. 
When people answer their doors, the children cry, ''Chai Sun doh!'' and present pieces of red paper with the same words, ''The god of fortune arrives!''
This means the children are entitled to some lucky money. 
Although this tradition is not followed in New York, the Wongs plan it this year for their children, a niece and four nephews, who will come to the Wongs' door wearing red for the New Year.
The New Year's Eve dinner is to have 12 courses, ''a very good number,'' explained Mr. Wong, because it is the number of signs in the zodiac.
Â 
The family will also spend New
Year's Day together. 
''Here in New York we usually go from house to house,'' Mr. Wong said. 
''We see other people. 
It is not like that in Shanghai.
But this year we will all stay at home together as we used to in Shanghai.
We must be together for dinner and for the games - dice, dominoes and for mah-jongg.''
Preparation of the New Year's Eve dinner started early this morning with Mrs. Kwai cutting, slicing, chopping and mixing in the kitchen. 
Later she was joined by Mrs. Wong and Mrs. Leung Li Man, the mother-in-law of Mrs. Wong's second-oldest brother, - ''number 2 sister-in-law's mother,'' as Mrs. Wong puts it.
At dinner time, the dishes will begin to go to the dining room table - yueh e choi (a combination of hair seaweed, dried oysters, fried bean curd and bean sprouts), which signify togetherness and agreement; cold vegetarian ''duck'' wrapped in dried bean curd; vegetarian ''beef'' made from fermented high-gluten flour; noodle soup with Shanghai pickled cabbage, and a Shanghai New Year's dish, dried bamboo shoots and bacon.
There will be chi ma tong yuen (boiled glutinous rice dumplings filled with sweet sesame-seed paste) and a soup of egg dumplings and tiny meatballs with long bead-thread noodles symbolizing longevity. 
These dishes will be followed by boiled chicken dressed with Shao-Hsing wine, the sea bass and pomfret, the clams and the shrimp.
There will be ''gold bars'' of bean curd wrapped around pork, chives and bean sprouts; lin gau (Shanghai rice cakes) with spinach; shoots of the snow pea plant with shredded beef, and finally a sweet soup of red beans flavored with rock sugar.
Sixteen dishes are to be put on the table in the course of the meal, and offered to heaven and the family's ancestors before any are tasted.
''To our good health,'' Mrs. Kwai will say.
''Gung Shi Fat Chai,'' Mrs. Wong will say, intoning ''Happy New Year'' in the dialect of Shanghai.
''May our house be filled with gold and jade,'' Mr. Wong will say.
And then the family will eat.

file: FARE OF THE COUNTRY_FALL IN SHANGHAI_ TIME FOR CRAB RUSH.txt
text:
ï»¿
Shanghai's annual crab rush begins with a frenzy in mid-September, continues unabated through October, and then subsides for another year. 
But during those six weeks virtually everyone in Shanghai, it seems, wants to eat nothing but the freshwater da zhai xie, or hairy crabs.
People line up at markets for the crabs, which are sold in the hand-woven bamboo baskets in which they are kept after being pulled from the water. 
Local people have been known to pay merchants to tell them when the first shipments of da zhai xie are to arrive. 
And after the crabs are bought, they are brought home to be steamed and eaten with shaoxing wine, the sherry-like beverage of Shanghai. 
Throughout the Shanghai region, late September and all of October are times for crab parties, time to have friends over for a feast of hairy crabs and wine.
Shanghai's crab craze is similar to the mussel madness each fall in Brussels and across Belgium, the quests for shad roe and soft-shell crabs each spring in the eastern United States, the need for crayfish each September in Finland. 
It is fascinating to watch people, mostly women, line up impatiently in Shanghai's many morning markets just to buy the crabs.
Nor will just any crabs do. 
Only the gray-blue crabs of Jiangsu Province, from the lake known as Yangcheng (west of Shanghai) are acceptable. 
And people will pay enormous prices, as much as 45 yuan (about $15) a pound for them.
Because of the demand, unscrupulous merchants have been known to place other crabs, such as those from the Yangtze River where it passes close to Anhui Province, in among the da zhai xie. 
Careful shoppers can be seen sorting through the baskets, to examine each crab individually. 
The distinguishing feature of the da zhai xie are hairlike bristles along their legs - thus their name - and the people of Shanghai know that.
So intense is the demand for the hairy crabs each fall that markets have developed in places other than Shanghai. 
In Hong Kong and the United States, immigrants from Shanghai await air shipments of the crabs, and in New York's Chinatown people will pay as much as $20 a pound for live da zhai xie.
For the markets the Chinese Government has printed brightly colored posters that show the crabs, red after being cooked, hairy legs sticking out. 
When I was in Shanghai during the crab craze last year I saw posters that read, ''Autumn is here, the chrysanthemums are blooming and the crabs are fat.''
Others read, ''This is the season to eat the crabs.''
Still others described the roe in the female crabs as ''fat and thick,'' and the meat as ''soft and tender, full of vitamins.''
It is difficult to trace historically the annual demand for da zhai xie; the three characters translate as ''big gate crab.''
The people of Shanghai say there is no religious or mythological significance to the hairy crab. 
Some suggest that it is an extreme manifestation of the appetite for crabs throughout Asia, where crustaceans are generally held in higher esteem than in other parts of the world.
In the waters of and around Thailand, Malaysia and Vietnam many species of crab exist: The so-called zebra crabs and blue swimming crabs of Thailand, the mangrove crab of Malaysia and the monkey-god crab of Vietnam are all highly prized as food.
Attention is given the hairy crab not for its history, but for its consumption, the traditions that concern how and when they should be eaten.
The body of the perfect hairy crab is ''the size of a rice bowl,'' according to the people of Shanghai, three and a half to four inches in diameter. 
The male crab has bigger claws and more bristles along its legs, and weighs about 11 ounces; the female, with smaller claws and little bristle, is about 8 ounces.
Early in the season the female crabs are much higher in demand, for they are fat with roe, their shells are softer and their meat sweeter. 
Later, as the males grow, their bodies become plump and their meat sweeter. 
The crabs are never seasoned when cooked. 
Occasionally a traditional Shanghai dipping sauce of vinegar, soy sauce and ginger will accompany them, but most often they are eaten just steamed.
The only exception to simple steaming is toward the end of October when the crabs are smaller and harder and their meat is not as tender or as sweet. 
Then they may be eaten as ''drunken crabs,'' steamed after being marinated in shaoxing wine.
Part of the art of the Shanghai table, after the crab has been consumed and all its meat plucked out, is to reconstitute the body so that it looks whole.
So much a part of Shanghai life is the hairy crab that it transcends the table. 
The way the crabs are marketed, their legs and claws bound tightly against their bodies, has meaning in the financial markets.
In Shanghai and in Hong Kong, when business dealings are most difficult, when money supplies are tight, when property transactions are moving slowly, the condition is said to be ''da zhai xie.''
I have eaten hairy crabs in the Ru Yi, a fairly new restaurant in Shanghai atop the Shanghai Friendship Store on Nanjing Road (these were steamed and accompanied by a bottle of cold Seagull Beer), and in the Lubolang Restaurant inside the mid-city enclave known as Shanghai's Old Town.
Neither of these restaurants has a listed telephone number. 
It is best to book tables through the Shanghai branch of the China International Travel Service, telephone 217200. 
The office is quite close to both restaurants. 
In both cases, the cost was about $15 to $16 each, the price of one crab the same as the normal price of a full meal for two or three people. 
But that is an indication of how greatly they are prized.
In Hong Kong, where the desire for hairy crabs increases each autumn - and where copies of the Shanghai posters are to be found in virtually every one of its Shanghai-style restaurants - the Wu Kong (27 Nathan Road, Kowloon; telephone 3-667244) is famous for da zhai xie. 
''We cook them the way they do in Shanghai,'' said the restaurant's manager, Bill Kong. 
And so they do.
Last fall, my husband and I paid about $18 each for four da zhai xie in Wu Kong, a small basement-level white marble restaurant entered from Peking Road. 
The crabs had been steamed to redness, and with them we drank glasses of shaoxing wine.
As we ate, more hairy crabs were inching about in a nearby holding tank illuminated with bright, emerald green lighting, waiting like the precious creatures they are, to give enjoyment.

file: FARE OF THE COUNTRY_JAPAN_S FUCHA RYORI, A MEAL FIT FOR A MONK.txt
text:
ï»¿
The vegetarian dishes of Japanese Zen temples are prepared in a manner that reveals and enhances the purity, simplicity and freshness of the ingredients. 
This cuisine, called shojin ryori (which means a method of cooking in which one pursues the pure way of the Buddha), has developed mainly within the Rinzai sect of Zen, with its emphasis on meditative practices and sudden enlightenment, brought to Japan from China in the 12th century. 
In Rinzai temples, preparation of the food is a kind of religious discipline, and during the meal, to which each monk brings his own utensils, one must not speak and must sit formally and adhere to various other rules.
The Tokyo restaurant Bon serves another type of shojin cooking, called fucha ryori. 
A feast to be eaten together by all the monks of a temple after a special day of meditation and discussion, fucha ryori is a product of the more recently imported Obaku sect of Zen, brought from Ming China in the mid-17th century by a Chinese monk, Yinyuan, and other refugees from the Manchus. 
The sect's headquarters are in Kyoto, at Manpukuji Temple. 
Obaku Zen incorporates elements of Pure Land Buddhism, in which salvation depends on simple faith rather than rigorous and self-denying disciplines, and this somewhat more relaxed approach to Zen is reflected in the fucha cuisine. 
In its complexity of flavor and form, the food reveals its Chinese sources.
One Chinese element traditionally associated with fucha ryori is the harmony of spirit created by each of the guests taking food from a common dish onto his own plate. 
Perhaps due to the fastidious nature of Japanese eating habits (at home each member of a family always uses his own pair of chopsticks; guests are given disposable ones) this custom is not observed at Bon.
As in other styles of Zen cooking, the meal represents a balance of the six tastes (bitter, sour, sweet, hot, salty and faint or delicate) and the five methods of food preparation (boiling, grilling, deep frying, steaming and serving raw). 
These correspond, more or less, to the five directions (east, west, north, south and center), the five colors (green, white, black, red and yellow, also represented in a Zen meal) and the five elements (wood, metal, water, fire and earth) that structure the Chinese cosmology. 
In a complete fucha meal, the selection of dishes -both the food and the ceramic, bamboo and lacquer utensils in which it is served - mirror this harmony.
On entering the serene and elegant Japanese house occupied by Bon, all of these compexities fuse into an atmosphere that is purely Japanese. 
Bon opened 14 years ago in the quiet residential district known as Hakusan. 
Twelve years before that, the mother of Furusawa Kazuaki, the proprietor, opened the original Ryusen Bon not far away, preparing food to serve at various temple functions. 
The family built the Hakusan house as their residence and there prepared temple meals to send out.
The house is a fine example of traditional Japanese domestic architecture, scarce in Tokyo since World War II, with mud-plastered walls in earth tones complementing the tatami mats. 
The sliding glass doors that form one wall of each private dining room are framed in wood, not aluminum, and look out on a luxuriant and extensive garden, unexpected in the middle of the city.
I visited Bon in one of Tokyo's rare blizzards. 
The snow, weighing down the branches of trees and shrubs in the garden, reflecting, as the sky grew dark in the late afternoon, the light of a stone lantern, made a delightful setting for the meal. 
My companions and I stepped into the room set aside for us, already warmed in preparation for our visit by a charcoal brazier and a charcoal-burning hearth with an iron tea kettle - and a hefty electric heater. 
The calligraphy scroll in the alcove, written in bold strokes by the head of the Obaku sect, extolled the pleasures of listening to the song of the boiling kettle, comparing it to the wind in the pines - a common conceit in Chinese poetry.
A full course fucha meal (about $45 to $55) is almost indescribably elaborate, consisting of the following elements: the thick foamy tea of the tea ceremony, a tiny appetizer often given the form and color of some seasonal flower or foliage, a clear soup with a few perfectly shaped pieces of mushrooms or bamboo shoots afloat, kuchi-kawari (literally a change of flavors - a vegetable dish, varying monthly in method of preparation and ingredients according to the season) and unpen (a fragment of cloud - thickened soup made with leftover vegetables).
These are followed by nimono (boiled things - a dish of seasonal vegetables cooked in a transparent but richly flavored stock), sesame tofu (a rich and silky smooth substance, similar to bean curd in texture but redolent with sesame seeds ground to a paste in a mortar), agemono (fried things - tenpura), a hearty miso soup containing vegetables and tofu, freshly made pickles, rice and fruit. 
The ingredients and preparation as well as the utensils change seasonally, however, so guests will find a different meal at different times of the year.
Among the dishes we sampled was a warm kuzu (arrowroot) jelly containing a sweetened kumquat, said to be especially good for the throat on raw winter days.
There was also sashimi made of konnyaku (a root called devil's tongue), a firm but slippery gray substance, one of many characteristically Japanese foods valued as much for its texture and consistency as for its elusive flavor. 
Then we had a dumpling made of lily root dipped in buckwheat batter and lightly fried and a shell of yuzu (citrus junos, one of the most fragrant of Japanese citrus fruits - always translated as citron but in neither appearance nor flavor resembling the heavily candied fruit we see at Christmas) in which nuts have been cooked in miso (fermented bean paste) and preserved for months until all the flavors blend. 
This was followed by a tenpura selection crowned by a fragile spray of enoki mushrooms on their long slender stems, resembling (not by coincidence) the snow-frosted branches outside.
A somewhat more limited selection, called aka-zen (red tray) because all the dishes as well as the tray on which they are brought are made of vermilion lacquer, may cost $40 to $45. 
The golden miso soup in which slices of white turnip and brilliantly colored mustard greens float must have been chosen to enhance the red lacquer bowl. 
A smaller selection, which makes a good lunch, the hangetsu fuchidaka (half-moon tray), is simplified by presenting several of the fucha courses in a partitioned half-moon shaped lacquer box (about $30).
The restaurant consists of five private rooms, which can accommodate up to 50 guests at one time. 
Each room can seat up to 10, but two rooms can be joined together to handle larger parties. 
Beer is about $3, sake $4.25. 
Only Japanese is spoken by the staff.
Bon, 4-37-19 Hakusan, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo (telephone 947-1525), open from noon to 8 P.M., closed Tuesday. 
It is best to reserve a day or two in advance, and it is customary but not essential to order when the reservation is made. 
From July 25 to the end of August, Bon moves to Karuizawa, a mountain resort in Nagano Prefecture, and the Hakusan branch closes. 
The address of the Karuizawa branch is Tsukushigaoka Building, Kariyado, Karuizawamachi, Nagano Prefecture (02674-5-4480 or locally 5-4480).

file: FARE OF THE COUNTRY_WHY DIM SUM IS _HEART_S DELIGHT_.txt
text:
ï»¿
FEI LO teaches regional Chinese cooking and nutrition at the China Institute in America in New York. 
She is the author of ''The Dim Sum Book: Art of the Chinese Teahouse'' to be published in the spring.
Â 
By EILEEN YIN-FEI LO
T o the people of southeastern China, particularly those of Canton, and Hong Kong, dim sum is far more than food. 
It is a custom rooted in history and mythology. 
It is brunch with tea. 
It is the Chinese equivalent of the business lunch. 
It is the core around which families gather.
Eileen Yin-Fei Lo discusses Chinese custom of brunch with tea, called dim sum
In Cantonese the words dim sum mean ''a dot on the heart,'' or more broadly, ''the heart's delight,'' and the seemingly unending dishes of beautifully shaped dim sum that are carried or wheeled by as you sit in a teahouse sipping green or black tea do indeed bring a sense of wonder and joy.
On the mainland of China itself, dim sum is virtually unknown outside the area around Canton - and, of course, the British colony of Hong Kong that adjoins it - although in cosmopolitan Shanghai there are both dim sum teahouses and a few Shanghai-style dim sum dishes. 
In Peking there are steamed breads and small buns that are similar, but they are not consumed in the tradition of the dim sum teahouse. 
Rather, they are meals themselves or accompaniments to courses.
The atmosphere of the teahouses in which dim sum is served is often as important as the food. 
In a little teahouse such as Hing Wan on Queen's Road in Hong Kong's central district, you sit beneath a ceiling hung with bird cages. 
They belong to elderly wealthy men who cling to the tradition of carrying their birds while taking a walk before tea. 
You might prefer to indulge in a restaurant on Nathan Road in Kowloon called the International, which seats 1,500 people on each of three floors; nevertheless customers must wait for seats on Sundays.
And what is worth waiting for?
The following are perhaps the most famous of the many dim sum:
- Har gau (shrimp dumplings), crescent-shaped dumplings filled with shrimp and pork.
- Fung ngan gau (phoenix eyes), which look, as intended, like women's eyes - almond-shaped and dotted with minced shrimp and egg whites.
- Fun guor (rice noodle fruit), half-moons filled with ground pork, mushrooms and shrimp.
- Siu mai (cook-and-sell dumplings), basket-shaped dumplings that earn their name by being the first made, the first sold, the first eaten.
- Char siu bau (barbecued pork), steamed or baked buns filled with chunks of roast pork - known to many Americans.
- Siu lung bau (soup dumplings), made with gelatin, shrimp and pork so that when they are steamed, the gelatin becomes soup inside the dumpling.
- Nor mai gai (lotus leaf rice), pillow-shaped masses of glutinous rice into which have been folded mushrooms, chicken, pork, shrimp and Chinese smoked pork sausage, the whole then wrapped with dried lotus leaves and steamed. 
The leaf imparts a slightly sweet aroma and taste.
- Jook (thick rice soup), or congee, as the Cantonese call this soup, which resembles porridge because of the preserved eggs and pork, or pieces of chicken, that are usually added.
- Yeung hai kim (stuffed crab claws), claws around which chopped shrimp are mounded, then deep-fried.
- Chun guen (spring rolls), tiny log-shaped fried rolls filled with pork, shrimp, water chestnuts, bamboo shoots and scallions. 
They are not to be confused with that American invention, the larger egg roll.
- Woo gok (dumplings fashioned from mashed taro root and stuffed with pork and mushrooms) are football-shaped and deep-fried until crisp and brown.
- Lor bok goh (turnip cake), a translucent cake of turnips, ginger, shrimp and rice powder that is cut into slices and pan-fried before serving.
And there are many more, all to be discovered in serendipitous fashion. 
Waitresses traditionally wheel the dim sum in on carts in such restaurants as King Bun in Hong Kong's central district and the venerable Luk Kwok on Gloucester Road. 
You select by pointing or asking for what you want as you drink one of several varieties of tea - green, black, jasmine, chrysanthemum or oolong.
The tea has been important since the eighth century, when Lu Yu, China's historical master of the beverage, wrote his ''Classic of Tea.''
It set down for the first time how tea leaves should be grown and processed, how the product should be brewed and steeped, how it should be served. 
He wrote that tea is a drink for body and soul, a mental stimulant, perhaps even an aid toward eventual immortality.
T he beginnings of the dim sum meal go back to the Sung Dynasty, when travelers on the highways of southern China in the 10th century would stop at small roadside teahouses to refresh themselves with tea and light meals. 
It was centuries before the practice took root and the Chinese of the south devised the small bite-sized foods that became stylized into dim sum.
These days you will see businessmen discussing what is most dear to them, sales clerks around a table chattering, family groups of three or more generations clustered together for a Sunday morning reunion, all enjoying dim sum, perhaps the most inexpensive of Chinese meals.
One of the more memorable dim sum meals I have had recently was in the 1,000-seat Maxim's Palace in the new World Trade Center extension of Hong Kong's Excelsior Hotel. 
It is a huge barn of a restaurant hung with gold and red dragons supported by green-painted pillars around which curl gilded phoenixes. 
Maxim's Palace is busy and noisy and the wagons of dim sum come by at an almost breathtaking rate.
First we had har gau, those delicious moist shrimp dumplings, then bowls of jook filled with chunks of preserved eggs. 
We also had a specialty of Maxim's Palace, gum yueh gau - or golden fish - which is a dumpling sculptured in the shape of a goldfish and stuffed with shrimp and pork.
Next came slices of fried water-chestnut cake, with siu mai, those basket-shaped ''cook-and-sell'' dumplings; and another specialty, gun jing ngau yuk kau, tiny beef meatballs.
Before finishing with sweet egg custard tarts we had kim ding guen cho, pigs' feet and egg cooked with shredded ginger and black, sweet rice vinegar. 
Wonderful!
One pays for dim sum by the plate. 
Each preparation comes on a different sized and shaped plate - round, oval, deep and saucerlike, in bamboo steamers, in metal fluted pastry tins. 
And when it is time to pay the bill the waiter simply counts the plates and matches price to size and shape. 
Most dim sum cost from 50 cents to 75 cents for three or four dumplings. 
For only a few dollars a party of four can snack to their heart's content. 
Or even their heart's delight.

THE CHINESE EMPEROR
By Jean Levi. 
Translated by Barbara Bray. 
341 pp. 
San Diego: A Helen and Kurt Wolff Book/ Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. 
$18.95.
OF the many stupendous stories that constitute the record of China's past, perhaps none is more moving and powerful than that of the rise and fall of the Qin (Ch'in) dynasty in the late third century B.C. Emerging from obscurity on the bleak northwestern borders of the known world, the small state of Qin, over several centuries, gradually developed an economic base, a harsh legal system and a military machine that made it a potent force among the much larger territories of the old Chinese multistate system.
By devious intrigue, by negotiation and by savage fighting the Qin rulers slowly overwhelmed their rivals. 
In 221 B.C., with the collapse of his last enemy, the ruler Qin Shihuang (Shih Hwang-ti) was able to declare himself the emperor of the first great unified Chinese empire, founder of a dynasty that was to last for 10,000 generations. 
In 206 B.C., wracked by internal rebellions and factional succession struggles, the Qin dynasty disintegrated.
Though many details of this story are lost, its general structure was shaped shortly after the Qin collapse by a Chinese historian of genius, Sima Qian (Ssu-ma Ch'ien), who lived from 147 B.C. to around 90 B.C. In a group of interconnected chapters in his ,great ''Historical Records'' (some of which may have been drafted by his father, Sima Tan) Sima Qian depicted the characters of the men, and a few of the women, who made Qin the terrible state that it became. 
His biographies of the merchant, king-maker and statesman Lu Buwei, of the ruthless bureaucrat Li Si, the Emperor Qin Shihuang, the eunuch Zhao Gao, the romantic assassin Jin Ke, have been regarded ever since - rightly - as masterpieces of both historical narration and of literature.
Jean Levi's ''Chinese Emperor'' is the first major attempt to create a historical novel out of this rich material. 
Mr. Levi, a Sinologist who was born and educated in France and studied at the University of Beijing and the University of Fudan as well as in Shanghai during the Cultural Revolution, won the Goncourt Prize for historical fiction for ''The Chinese Emperor.''
It is an ambitious and at times extremely powerful book, where moments of ghastly violence are interspersed with flickers of rare beauty. 
Mr. Levi does not admit to the title of novelist, nor does he claim that of historian. 
His goal, he tells us in his afterword, is just ''to create an atmosphere, and suggest certain ways of looking at human and political relationships, rather than revive or reconstruct a bygone age.''
The atmosphere Mr. Levi evokes is one of an archaic and murderous bureaucratic state that destroys the individual in its search for an impossible precision where all deviance from the state's norms will be obliterated. 
It is this aspect of the Qin world, Mr. Levi writes, that ''fascinated me as a mirror of the present day.''
Mr. Levi does not attempt to say whether this is an indictment of certain Western capitalist bureaucracies, or of the Soviet Union. 
But he does imply a harsh indictment of the People's Republic of China when he notes that the political organization established by Qin Shihuang and his chief minister Li Si ''endured for more than twenty centuries in various avatars - of which the present regime is the latest.''
''The Chinese Emperor'' has a deceptively simple-looking structure. 
Of the three main parts into which it is divided, the first concentrates on the minister Lu Buwei as he ruminates on his life and awaits his final fate at the Emperor's hands; the second is centered on the minister Li Si; while the third charts the descent of Emperor Qin Shihuang via paranoia and melancholia to his eventual illness and death. 
But Mr. Levi weaves the stories together imaginatively; one artificial but effective device is to have the Emperor in his study reading the dossier prepared on Lu Buwei by Li Si, as he tries to decide how to treat his former favorite. 
It does not betray too much of the plot to say that he graciously gives Lu Buwei the time to commit suicide. 
(Li Si, Lu's nemesis, was later to be cut in half at the waist on the orders of the first Emperor's successor.) SOME of the best imaginative passages in the book are Mr. Levi's reconstructions of the Qin Emperor's reflections on time and mortality as his power rises to its apogee: ''He began to reflect on the futility of all the maneuvering he had just been reading about. 
These people thought that they were playing tricks with time, but in fact they were only the dupes of history.''
In a particularly fine passage, rendered into beautiful English by the book's translator, Barbara Bray, we see the Emperor alone at his desk with the bureaucratic reports he loved to read, ''cut off from the world and the cycle of days and nights, yet conscious of the passage of time through the crystal sound of the drops of water that marked the flight of the hours. 
It seemed to him then that his mind, detached from contingency, took on a singular sharpness. 
. . . His gaze wandered amid the clouds of smoke rising from the perfume burner, then he saw them as bronze mountains, contorted slopes, vertiginous gorges.''
Or, as the Emperor reflected on his own approaching death even as he searched with mounting passion and expense for the elixir of immortality that his Taoist advisers promised him: ''A slight tremor of the earth, the collapse of a mountain, and the world, after a faint quiver at its disappearance, would continue on its way like a cart that has dropped a bit of dung.''
In these and other passages of equal grace, Mr. Levi weaves a veil of introspection around this melancholy, all-powerful man. 
The most dramatic and terrifying happenings are mostly drawn from various sections of Sima Qian's ''Historical Records'': the ghastly battles, the Emperor's secretive meanderings, the hideous punishments handed out to criminals and enemies. 
From Sima Qian also comes the satanic figure of Lao Ai, who won the Empress Dowager's love by shoving his vast erect member into the hub of a cartwheel and cavorting among drunken guests at one of Lu Buwei's parties. 
And it is to Sima Qian that we owe the unforgettable vision of the mounds of fish carried along by Li Si to hide the otherwise all too obvious fact that his Emperor had not only died but was decomposing.
But Mr. Levi does not only draw on Sima Qian. 
He has read widely in Chinese sources and makes excellent use of the ''Records of the Warring States'' (the ''Zhanguo ci''), the early chronological record of the apparently endless wars of the major Chinese contenders for power in the pre-Qin period. 
He also uses the voluminous writings of the legalist philosopher Han Feizi (Han Fei Tzu), amusingly rendered by Mr. Levi as Han Negation, as well as Taoist medical tracts, and of the recent archeological finds in China. 
Most important of these latter - though the millions of Chinese and foreign tourists who have gazed in awe at Qin Shihuang's terra cotta army buried near his tomb may find it hard to agree - are the legal and bureaucratic documents dating to around 217 B.C. unearthed by Chinese archeologists during 1975 at tomb number 11 in Yunmeng County of what is now Hubei Province. 
It is these documentary finds that allow Mr. Levi to reconstruct the bureaucratic mentality of the Qin state.
Because a source is old and in Chinese, of course, does not mean it is necessarily accurate, and this simple reminder is most important in the case of Sima Qian. 
Not only did Sima Qian love a good story, he had no scruples about recreating prolonged dialogues between leading historical figures of which he could not possibly have had any knowledge. 
He just followed his judgment as to what the characters would have said. 
Other hands then confused the issue by emending and adding to Sima's own text during the Han dynasty, so we cannot be sure at all times which passages are in fact his, and which were inserted later to bring additional opprobrium on the fallen Qin ruler, who was anathema to later generations of Confucian scholars because of his burning of books and burying alive of scholars.
THERE is also an aspect of the Qin experience that Mr. Levi gives us little of - the world of humor. 
For jokes and puns still bubbled at the heart of all that Qin terror. 
In William Dolby and John Scott's ''War-Lords,'' in the rendering of some of Sima Qian's section called ''Jesters,'' one can see how that great historian tried to lighten his own bleak vision of the immediate past that had brought such powers and yet so much misery in its wake. 
My favorite Qin jester is ''Twisty Pole.''
It was Twisty Pole who suggested to Emperor Qin Shihuang that he fill a gigantic game preserve with wild animals, so that if anyone dared to invade Qin, the Emperor could simply order the gazelles and deer to butt the enemy with their horns and drive them back whence they came. 
And it was Twisty Pole, according to Sima Qian, who applauded the plan of the Emperor's son to coat the entire length of the Great Wall with lacquer. 
To think of lacquering the wall, said Twisty Pole, was an act of genius, because all the enemies would slither and slide as they tried to climb over it. 
The only problem might be building a drying-room large enough to hold the wall while the lacquer dried to the requisite sheen. 
Even amid all that mayhem simple people could laugh at their tyrants. 
Let every reader try and remember this to avoid getting too harsh a picture of Chinese culture from Jean Levi's fearsome and remarkable book.
Â 
THE CRADLE OF DEMOCRACY
PARIS
The Qin bureaucracy invented in the third century B.C. in China by men lusting for power continues to this day, according to Jean Levi. 
He sees modern dictatorships mirrored in the Qin dynasty, the subject of his first novel, ''The Chinese Emperor,'' and speculates that the system of rule drifted into Russia via the Mongols and permeated both Czarist and Communist regimes before returning to China via the 1948 Communist revolution, in imitation of the Russians.
Qin-invented bureaucracy also affects the individual, Mr. Levi said recently in an interview, ''even in modern democracies. 
But their constraints on the individual are more veiled, subtle, presented for the individual's well-being. 
The political news I watch on French television all echoes that.''
Men still lust for power because ''power is a drug. 
The taste for power comes with power. 
Mao Zedong did not make a revolution to take power, he became a dictator through the Communist Party system.''
Mr. Levi, a friendly, soft-spoken 39-year-old, was born in Paris of an Italian father and Hungarian mother. 
He joined the French Government's National Center for Scientific Research in 1979 and wrote about ancient China.
The publishers of his four scholarly nonfiction works were not interested in his first novel, but his friend Mary McCarthy contacted her French publisher, Albin Michel, and, ''thanks to her,'' Mr. Levi said, it was published in France in 1985.
In 1986 he gave the book to some friends in China, ''but I don't think they were satisfied with it,'' he said wryly, referring to the bureaucracy currently in place.
Over tea in his Left Bank apartment, where he lives with his Chinese wife, whom he met in Paris, a daughter, Celia, 5, a son, Silvio, 2, his mother and two black cats, he talked about his latest project: ''I am working on my next novel about China, to show the other side - revolt - that there is resistance to bureaucracy. 
No order is perfect.''
ALINE MOSBY
Â 
MORE ABOUT THE QIN
One great virtue of Jean Levi's novel may well be that the atmosphere it weaves is so compelling it will bring readers back to the various sources to try and sort out fact from fiction for themselves. 
Mr. Levi's afterword gives a good many of the Chinese leads, as well as paying due homage to Edouard Chavannes's great 1890's French translation of the historical annals sections of Sima Qian's work. 
But the general reader may also be interested to know that much of the key material is also available in English.
Fifty years ago, Derk Bodde produced a fine annotated translation of Sima Qian's biography of Li Si, which he published as ''China's First Unifier,'' and he followed this up with masterly translations of Sima Qian's biographies of three other major Qin actors - including Lu Buwei and the assassin Jing Ke - under the title ''Statesman, Patriot and General in Ancient China.''
J. I. Crump, nearly 20 years ago, translated ''The Records of the Warring States,'' so one can read a flowing English version of the source that offers the most important alternative interpretations of Qin's rise to power.
Burton Watson has published extensive and admirable further translations of Sima Qian, as have William Dolby and John Scott in a little book published in 1974 in Edinburgh which they entitled simply ''War-Lords,'' but which is not limited to military figures.
