In Hong Kong's colonial system of government, a relative handful of Britons have complete control, even though 98 percent of the city-state's five-million-plus residents are Chinese.
Yet with the negotiations over Hong Kong's future just under way, begun two weeks ago when Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher of Britain met in Peking with Chinese leaders, the vast majority of the British crown colony's people want to retain the British administration without any real changes for the foreseeable future, according to public opinion polls.
Under the present setup, the Governor, Sir Edward Youde, in consultation with the executive and legislative councils, makes all policy decisions. 
Though there are some Chinese members of the two councils, they are all appointed by the British administrators, not elected by the populace.
HONG KONG, Oct. 
6 - In Hong Kong's colonial system of government, a relative handful of Britons have complete control, even though 98 percent of the city-state's five-million-plus residents are Chinese.
The system of government is, in many ways, as contradictory and anomalous as Hong Kong itself - a colony in an anticolonial era. 
For example, when Mrs. Thatcher was in Peking, Hong Kong was engaged in its largest exercise of democratic expression in its history, the election of representatives to so-called city district boards. 
These boards have been established as a vehicle for gathering views from the people on matters of public concern.
Â 
Reluctance to Vote
Despite a big get-out-the-vote effort by the Government, only 12 percent of the two million people eligible to vote bothered to exercise their privilege.
''The Government is pushing people to the polls,'' acknowledged Joseph Cheng, a professor of political science at Hong Kong's Chinese University and a leading critic of the Government. 
''It is the people who are reluctant to vote.''
There are several reasons for the apparent political apathy in Hong Kong. 
With more than 40 percent of the population immigrants and the colony's future uncertain, there is a sense of impermanence to Hong Kong that makes people less inclined to be politically active.
Moreover, even the Government's harshest critics describe British rule as a ''benevolent dictatorship.''
In the mid-1970's, for instance, the Government established statuatory holidays. 
In 1979 and 1981, rent control legislation was enacted. 
In both cases, social programs were enacted by government fiat that the labor unions were too weak to push for and the business community resisted, according to political experts.
Â 
Hands-Off Government
In addition, Hong Kong is renowned for its brand of hands-off government with low taxes, and public-sector spending and services, while expanding, is kept to a minimum.
Because of the Government's limited scope, some residents are not particularly anxious to have a voice in shaping its activities. 
''The Government does very little for us,'' said Shirley Woo, a 25-year-old office worker, who did not vote in the district board elections. 
''Why should we care about it?''
Rising wages and living standards afforded by Hong Kong's rapid economic growth and a policy of giving the Chinese elite appointed positions in Government have also blunted demands for a more democratic system.
However, the portion of Hong Kong's population that is seeking more direct participation in Government, though still a minority, is growing. 
About 60 percent of all residents are under 30 years old, and their levels of education and expectations are higher than their parents, many of whom were refugees.
Â 
Talks on Hong Kong's Future
One force that should heighten political awareness, analysts say, is the Peking-London negotiations over the future of Hong Kong after 1997, when the lease covering 90 percent of the colony's land runs out.
China has stated that it will reassert its sovereignty over all of Hong Kong by 1997. 
Britain says that the 19th-century treaties that created the colony are still valid, though they can be altered.
For years, it has been understood that the Peking leadership would not permit Hong Kong to become an independent, self-governing state, or ''a third China,'' Taiwan being the second. 
This has allowed Britain to run Hong Kong without opening the Government up to elected representatives from the local Chinese community.
Now, one likely compromise in the British-Chinese talks appears to be a long transition period, up to 40 years, during which the British presence is gradually phased out. 
Presumably, local Chinese would then be phased in. 
''It's very clear that there will be a transition period,'' Mr. Cheng said. 
''There can be no excuse for keeping local Chinese out anymore.''
Â 
System Characterized as Relic
As a first step, Mr. Cheng thinks that there should be elected representatives on the legislative council within five years. 
Many British Government officials here agree. 
In private conversations, they are among the first to characterize the present system as a relic of a bygone era. 
But first, they emphasize, an agreement must be worked out with China, preferably within a year to restore business confidence by removing uncertainties about Hong Kong's future.
So for the time being, the British administration must remain as the reassuring symbol of the ''stabilityI and prosperity'' in Hong Kong that Peking and London agree are key objectives of the current negotiations.
''This benevolent dictatorship isn't 100 percent what I'd like, maybe not even 80 percent,'' said Ronald Li, chairman of Hong Kong's Far East stock exchange. 
''But 60 percent is better than a lot of the alternatives.''

text:

Britain's tabloids had a field day today insuring that remarks attributed to the Duke of Edinburgh about Chinese ''slitty eyes'' and how ''ghastly'' he had found Peking would become the longest-remembered happening of the royal tour of China by Queen Elizabeth II.
The most sophisticated headline was in The Daily Mail, which asked, ''Does Britain Need a Terracotta Duke?''
Under it was a photograph of a grim-faced Queen inspecting the terra cotta warriors guarding the imperial tomb of the Chin Dynasty emperor near Xian and a heading that said, ''They're tall, dignified, ceremonial and above everything else, they are silent.''
There was also a cartoon of the Queen's husband with a gag over his mouth.
Â 
A Barrage of Puns
Headline writers on other newspapers let loose with a barrage of outrageous puns to show why British diplomats on a tour that had earlier been heralded as ''historic'' were now choking with embarrassment.
''Philip Gets It All Wong,'' screamed the front page of The Sun, a mass-circulation tabloid, which was illustrated with a photo of the Prince retouched so as to give him darting Fu Manchu eyebrows and eyelids. 
''Prince Philip torpedoed the royal visit to China,'' the newspaper reported.
''Great Wally of China,'' cried The Daily Mirror, using a British colloquialism applied to bumblers and buffoons. 
Taking a more somber line, the newspaper Today's front page declared simply, ''Philip Drops a Clanger.''
Reporting from Peking, the BBC found some consolation in the fact that the Chinese press had ignored the remarks, which were made in Xian in conversation with a group of University of Edinburgh students.
Â 
Chancellor of University
The Prince, who is the university's chancellor, was reported to have asked one of the students how long he had been in China. 
When the young man replied that he had been there six weeks, the Queen's husband then wisecracked, ''If you stay here much longer, you will go back with slitty eyes.''
Asked by one of the students how he had found the Forbidden City, the Prince seemed momentarily confused about where that was. 
His wife's response - that she had found it fascinating and wished she could have spent more of her time in Peking visiting it -appeared to refresh his memory. 
''Oh yes,'' he was quoted as having said. 
''But Peking was ghastly.''
A journalist then repeated the Duke of Edinburgh's remarks to a British diplomat. 
''Thank you for spoiling my evening,'' the diplomat replied.
Michael Shea, the Queen's spokesman, was rushed in to explain that the Prince's remarks had been entirely jocular and that ''the Duke of Edinburgh is in no way disparaging of the Chinese people.''
Â 
A Pained Expression
Wearing what was described as a pained expression, the spokesman went on to try to explain the statements. 
He said: ''It's a well-known physiological fact that people in different parts of the world have eyes that are differently shaped. 
My eyes are round.''
Asked today, when the royal party stopped in Kunming, about the uproar over his remarks, the Prince commented offhandedly that he thought it had been ''a little tactless'' of the Edinburgh students to repeat them.
Queen Elizabeth II is the first British sovereign to visit China, but a distant ancestor, George III, sent an envoy to Peking in 1792, an occasion that became the first of many embarrassments and misunderstandings in relations between the two countries. 
The Chinese assumed the envoy had come to pay homage on behalf of George III to the reigning Ming emperor and to make Britain a tributary state.

text:

After a long climb out of the American basement rec room, the game of Ping-Pong is spinning toward acceptance as a sport in this country.
The impetus is the decision to include table tennis as a game in the 1988 Olympics. 
The American effort to compete against the two national teams that dominate the sport, China and Sweden, will be helped by a $1.2 million grant from the United States Olympic Committee, one of 37 full shares of the profits from the Summer Games last year in Los Angeles.
As the United States Open Table Tennis Championships got under way in this resort's cavernous convention hall this week, with more than 600 players from 30 countries rocketing shots at each other across dozens of green tables, promoters were savoring the chance to boost the game from summer-camp obscurity to the hot-ticket mass following it enjoys in other nations.
China's 'Most Popular Sport'
One of the first things the United States Table Tennis Association did with the Olympic money was to hire a Chinese couple to coach the American men's and women's teams.
Ai Liguo moved to the United States last year from Peking with his wife, Li Henan. 
Ai, 43 years old, was a player on the Chinese team that won the world championship in 1961. 
Miss Li was the coach of the world championship Chinese women's team.
''We had good jobs and high social position in China,'' Ai said during a break from his scrutiny of the strokes of the hundreds of American players participating in the Open. 
Ai was chief editor of Sports News, which he described as the leading sports publication in China.
''My wife was very famous because table tennis is the most popular sport in China,'' he said.
Â 
Second Behind Soccer
The top-rated American player is Eric Boggan, a 21-year old New Yorker who is ranked 33d among the best male players in the world.
''Our problem in America,'' said Tim Boggan, Eric's father and a vice president of the International Table Tennis Federation, ''is that there are something like 19 million Americans who play table tennis, but only a few thousand take it seriously. 
In China there are two million officially registered players - players who compete seriously at the sport - and the unofficial figure is probably more like 12 million.''
The game is the only livelihood of about 40,000 Chinese players, he said.
By contrast, he pointed out, only a few American players are able to squeeze a living from it. 
Eric Boggan plays for a club team in West Germany, said his father, a professor of English at Long Island University whose other son, Scott, 23, is ranked the third-best American player.
Ping-Pong is estimated to be the second most popular participatory sport in the world behind soccer, but it has never attracted much of a following in the United States, even though most Americans have played the game.
Until the 1950's, when Europeans dominated the game, table-tennis competition was seen as battle between players with special offensive or defensive skills. 
Long battles over points tended to pitch two players ranging far from the table, one killing the ball while the other returned the smashes with unerring, looping shots. 
Or else the opponents engaged in an exchange of chopping, spinning shots and single points could involve dozens of individual strokes.
''Now techniques have changed and the game is much faster,'' said Tim Boggan. 
''The Japanese introduced a racket in the 1950's with a sponge layer that rocketed the ball. 
In the 1960's the Chinese used a sponge paddle with a layer of rubber that gave their shots both speed and spin.
''With the new rackets the day of long rallies came to an end and now the game is attack, attack, attack,'' said Boggan, smiling. 
''The quality of the rubber paddles allows for so much speed and hop on the ball that the defensive player doesn't have a chance.''
The International Federation is studying ways to slow down the game, he said. 
One proposal is to raise the net by a half-inch; another is to force single players to serve cross-court as doubles players are made to do.

text:

In the middle of a recent weekday afternoon, in a large, immaculately maintained cinema off the Ginza, there were only two dry eyes in the house - mine. 
They really didn't count, since the film I was watching was in Japanese, supplemented from time to time by dialogue in Mandarin Chinese translated by Japanese subtitles.
The house wasn't packed. 
However, the people who were there sat rapt while a small, rambunctious Chinese boy, who could have studied acting at the knee of Gary Coleman, chewed the scenery that wasn't being chewed by a panda cub named Hoa Hoa. 
The film was ''The Panda Story,'' the latest in a series of sentimental Japanese movies about animals that, at least until now, have done nothing but make money.
Though Japan is riding the crest of one of the greatest economic booms the world has ever seen, serious film makers are not receiving many of the benefits.
The venerable Akira Kurosawa, now 78 but tireless, must look for financing outside his own country. 
His ''Kagemusha'' came to fruition only through the support of George Lucas and Francis Coppola, tax-paying citizens of a large debtor nation. 
Serge Silberman, the French producer responsible for Luis Bunuel's final masterworks, produced ''Ran,'' Mr. Kurosawa's majestic reworking of ''King Lear.''
Now Steven Spielberg is in the process of producing Mr. Kurosawa's next film, tentatively titled ''My Favorite Dreams.''
Nagisa Oshima, who shook up the censors at home and abroad with his sexually explicit ''In the Realm of the Senses,'' made his most recent film outside Japan - in France. 
With the exception of Shohei Imamura, who is now completing ''Dark Rain,'' an epic about the atom-bombing of Hiroshima, and the handful of new social satirists exemplified by Juzo Itami (''Tampopo''), serious film making appears to be languishing.
Instead, the nation that gave us the classic films of Kenji Mizoguchi, Yasujiro Ozu and Mikio Naruse, which were produced in the 30's, 40's and 50's (though unseen in the United States until the 60's and later), has developed an insatiable appetite for kitsch.
Kitsch is certainly not an exclusively Japanese passion. 
If it can be defined as anything that's both too much and not enough, whether the subject is art, architecture, literature, fashion, food or movies, the passion is clearly international.
Kitsch is Sylvester Stallone's musculature, the Liberace museum in Las Vegas and possibly even those Presidential campaign pitches that are designed to melt the heart but often melt the head. 
It's music in elevators. 
It's the music you hear when the airline reservations clerk puts you on hold. 
In Tokyo, it's the music with which almost every office pacifies you while you're waiting to be passed on by the secretary to the person you're calling.
In the major cities of the world, from Cairo to New York and on, kitsch is also the top-of-the-hotel restaurant that revolves to give the diner a 360-degree view during a 60-minute repast. 
The turntable of the restaurant atop the New Otani Towers, which was built in anticipation of the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, may be getting rusty. 
Its discreet lurches make some people seasick. 
Yet the night view of Tokyo is as significant as it is spectacular.
The skyline is aglow with huge, brightly lit signs for Toshiba, Sony, NEC and the other wizards of electronics responsible for revolutionizing American home entertainment. 
Tokyo takes on the aspects of some great 47th Street Photo in the sky.
Japanese kitsch is conspicuous consumption, such as the sort of casual jacket a suburban father might wear on late autumn weekends to rake the leaves, only the one on display here is made of waterproofed, olive-colored silk, instead of poplin, with a mink lining to keep dad warm. 
The price: $10,725. 
Kitsch is also conspicuous consumption in terms of the occasional film budget.
One of the most expensive films ever produced by a Japanese company, and apparently one of the year's biggest box-office flops, is the $40 million ''Dun-huang,'' based on Yasushi Inoue's novel set in an ancient city of Buddhist cave temples in China.
The project was one long cherished by Masaki Kobayashi, who became interested in it in the late 60's. 
In spite of, or maybe because of, his formidable reputation as the director of the three-part, nine-hour ''Human Condition,'' among his other internationally recognized works, Mr. Kobayashi was never able to raise the financing. 
The fear was that he would be too fussy, too intellectual and would run over his budget.
When the project finally came together, it was put into the hands of a director who, according to someone who worked on the film, was thought to be good in his handling of horses and camels. 
I have not seen the film. 
The horses and camels may look great, but the reviews were caustic and the public did not break down the doors the day the film opened.
It's one of the oddities of the current Japanese film scene that, in spite of the general apathy, ''Dun-huang'' may not actually lose much money. 
The film was a joint venture of Daiei, a production company, with Marubeni, a huge trading company with offices all over Japan, and Dentsu, a production company with interests in publishing and advertising.
An accepted practice in such cases is for the companies involved to require their employes to buy tickets to these show-business ventures sight unseen. 
When the numbers of employees, plus the members of their families and their friends, run into the tens of thousands, the size of the captive audience can make the difference between a hit and a flop.
Another practice that is helping producers of Japanese films to cut their losses is the advance-discount purchase plan. 
Some time before a film opens, the public is given the opportunity to buy tickets at discounts of 20 percent. 
This is a sizable saving when a first-run Tokyo movie ticket sells for 1,500 yen (approximately $12 at the current rate of exchange), and going up to 1,700 yen at the end of this year.
The Japanese film industry is not declining to quite the same degree as the industries in France and Italy, but it's far from healthy. 
Theater attendance was down to 143,935,000 last year from 185,324,000 in 1973, and though box-office receipts were up, most of the increase could be attributed to the 300 percent rise in ticket prices between 1973 and 1988. 
Cable television is still limited to hotels and a few choice apartment houses. 
Japanese television stations present nowhere near as many films as American stations. 
Everybody, however, has his video cassette recorder, and movie rentals are cheap and popular.
That Japanese movie producers should lean toward sure-fire pop hits is not hard to understand. 
They are fighting fire with fire in a highly competitive market in which American films take nearly half of the annual receipts.
It also isn't difficult to understand why Japanese audiences are so taken at the moment by animal kitsch, of which ''The Panda Story'' is a gooey if harmless example:
A pretty, 20-year-old Japanese zoo worker, played by a pop star named Saori Yagi, is sent to north central China as part of a joint Chinese-Japanese team whose mission is to save pandas. 
She becomes friendly with a tirelessly cute little Chinese boy and, with him, helps to raise a motherless baby panda to an age when the panda must be turned back into the wilderness to find its own bamboo.
Though I could guess at some of these plot twists, I am indebted to Alan Booth, the film critic for The Asahi Evening News, for explaining a number of the film's subtleties in his cheerfully jaundiced review. 
(Among other things missed by the non-Japanese-speaking critic is the information that pandas are black as well as white because they are in mourning for a young woman who gave her life to save a panda cub.) Preceding ''The Panda Story'' in release was the hugely popular ''Hachiko,'' based on the true (pre-World War II) story of a dog that used to wait each night outside the railroad station for the return of his master, a Tokyo professor. 
One day the professor died on the job and was taken home by a different route. 
The faithful dog refused to believe his loss. 
For years he returned to the station each evening, only to be disappointed again.
When the dog finally died, local citizens erected a statue of him that sits today, as he once sat, outside the Shibuya station in Tokyo. 
The film was a bigger hit than ''Love Story.''
In addition to ''Hachiko'' there have been ''The Antarctica Story,'' about the rescue of some huskies inadvertently abandoned after a Japanese expedition to Antarctica, ''Chatran,'' dealing with the marvelous adventures of an anthropomorphic cat, and ''Oracion,'' which I saw without benefit of English subtitles, inflight, en route to Tokyo.
''Oracion'' seems to be about a small boy, dying of some dread but not disfiguring disease, and a horse that is being groomed to win a Japanese derby. 
It's full of scenes set in great wide-open spaces (juxtaposed with hospital room scenes), lots of pretty sunsets and shots of horses frolicking freely on broad, grassy plains.
Such films obviously touch on current Japanese longings, especially for space in a tiny country where much of the land is too mountainous to be habitable, and where 10 percent of the population of 120 million lives in crowded, though remarkable tranquility in and around Tokyo. 
Pets mean space, room in which to roam. 
In most Tokyo apartments, a litter box would be an odoriferous intrusion. 
Japan has money to burn, but even fortunes can't buy much space in a city where nine square feet of land was recently valued at $255,000.
The Japanese find themselves in a maddening position. 
Japan is a rich society, and only rich societies can afford to indulge themselves with animals as pets. 
People in poor countries, or even in poorer sections of rich countries, regard animals as creatures that must earn their keep. 
Unless they can herd sheep, bark at prowlers, catch rats or pull the plow, they are just so many more mouths to feed. 
They are luxuries.
People here can afford virtually every conceivable appliance and labor-saving electronic gadget, which, if it wasn't invented by the Japanese, was perfected by them.
What they don't have is room to swing a cat.

file: FILM_S FAR EAST CONNECTION_ Janet Yang_Bringing Hollywood Hits to China_s Moviegoers.txt
text:
ï»¿
JANET YANG remembers clearly the first time she saw an American movie in China. 
It was called ''Nightmare in Badham County,'' and it was about the horrors and injustices heaped upon two women trapped in a backwoods town in the American South.
''At the end of the movie, people came running up to me and said, 'It's so terrible that you have to live in such a place,' '' Ms. Yang said.
That was in 1980. 
Today, if the sophistication of the Chinese about the United States and American films is vastly improved from the days when ''Badham County'' was a hit, it is in part because of Ms. Yang, the head of Far East Operations at MCA Inc., the parent company of Universal Studios.
Since 1985, the 31-year-old native of New York has been spearheading the joint effort of three of Hollywood's biggest studios - Universal, Paramount and MGM/UA - to sell their films in China.
Ms. Yang is one (almost surely, the one) Hollywood executive who can discuss Chinese history in fluent Mandarin as comfortably as she can take a meeting, as they say here, with Steven Spielberg.
Both skills come in handy, since she must explain the ways of Hollywood to the Chinese as she promotes the long-term business potential of China to entertainment moguls who usually measure success by overnight box-office reports.
It is a slow, somewhat frustrating process, subject to all the financial, political and cultural hurdles that might be expected when the decadent capital of Western entertainment meets the world's largest workers' state.
But two years after Universal and Paramount joined forces to become the first American studios since the 1949 Communist revolution to strike ongoing distribution deals with the Chinese - MGM/UA joined the consortium later - China's appetite for blockbuster Hollywood movies, as for many things foreign, seems to be growing as it opens itself to the rest of the world.
Under the guidance of Ms. Yang, the three studios are selling China some of the most popular films in their libraries. 
''Love Story'' opened last winter to packed houses in Beijing, where a movie costs about 8 to 15 cents. 
''Spartacus'' and ''Roman Holiday'' drew huge crowds later in the year. 
''In the Heat of the Night'' is scheduled to open early in 1988. 
And in the works are titles ranging from ''To Kill a Mockingbird'' and ''North by Northwest'' to ''National Velvet,'' ''Earthquake'' and ''Airport.''
CULTURAL aspects aside, the studios are dealing with China primarily to see if it will develop into the huge and profitable market that peddlers of everything from airplanes to toothpaste have dreamed of since the Ping-Pong diplomacy of the early 1970's.
So far, China is mostly promise and little payoff, at least as far as motion pictures go. 
Studios have long been wary of doing business there because the China Film Corporation, the Government-controlled agency that oversees movie imports, resisted arrangements to pay for American films on the basis of their box-office popularity.
Now, under the compromise agreement struck by Universal, Paramount and later MGM/UA, payment is based on a formula involving the number of prints that go into distribution. 
In negotiating the deal a few years ago, the Chinese also agreed to pay for movie rights in hard currency. 
Still, financially speaking, China is a market that can only be justified on its long-term potential.
Ms. Yang declined to give the revenue figures to date for her Chinese venture. 
''If we were in this to make money in 1987, we wouldn't be in it at all,'' she said.
WHETHER or not the project pays off for Universal, Paramount and MGM/UA, it has already proved to be a dream come true for Ms. Yang. For years, she says, China and film have been her two passions.
Her parents came to the United States from China as students in the late 1940's, and stayed on after the Communist takeover at home. 
Ms. Yang was born in Queens, and raised on Long Island and in Scarsdale, N. Y. Her father is an engineer; her mother has worked at the United Nations.
As she grew up, she says, she thought little about her Chinese heritage. 
But in 1972, the year that President Nixon started the process of normalizing diplomatic relations with China, Ms. Yang went with her mother to visit relatives in a number of Chinese cities. 
The trip sparked an intense curiosity in the 16-year-old.
''It was a very moving experience,'' Ms. Yang said. 
''All of a sudden, I felt an intense connection to this great mass of people.''
The feeling stayed with her at home; she pursued Chinese studies at Brown University in the mid-1970's and briefly in graduate school at the University of Michigan.
In 1980, with the help of a former professor, she landed a job as a translator and editor at the Chinese Foreign Language Press in Beijing (where she saw ''Nightmare in Badham County'').
Her time there gave her a much deeper understanding of China, and a new passion - film, an interest she says she first developed through friendships with some young Chinese directors.
After 15 months in Beijing, Ms. Yang returned to New York, where she tried, with little success, to sponsor some Chinese film festivals in American cities.
Film and China were still the constant themes in her life, she says, when she enrolled in Columbia University's graduate business school in 1982. 
After receiving her M.B.A., Ms. Yang worked for a year with a small San Francisco company, World Entertainment, distributing Chinese films in the United States.
One day while she was at World, she got a call from Charles S. (Skip) Paul, president of MCA Enterprises, an MCA subsidiary. 
Mr. Paul said he was going to China to try to distribute some films, and wondered if Ms. Yang had any contacts she could share.
As Ms. Yang tells it, she naively admitted to Mr. Paul that she had never heard of MCA but was happy to supply him with a few names. 
The two stayed in touch, and within a few months, he offered her the job of helping Universal Studios set up its deal with Paramount and the Government of China.
In the two years that she has been head of MCA's Far East operation, she says, she has learned that Hollywood and China - seemingly an unlikely match - have a lot to offer each other. 
''One thing that's very apparent to anyone who goes to China is the tremendous and overwhelming curiousity about American culture,'' she said.
American films were popular in China during the 1930's and right up to 1949, the year of the revolution. 
Widespread distribution ceased when Mao Zedong took power, although a few films trickled in whenever the politics of the day allowed.
Through it all, Ms. Yang says, the allure of Hollywood and the power of its imagery persisted. 
''The love for American movies is an incredibly powerful thing,'' she said. 
''Even when America was public enemy No. 1, that thread was never broken.''
During the 10 years of the Cultural Revolution, ended in 1976, foreign films virtually disappeared in China. 
Indeed, only eight films, in all, were sanctioned for viewing, Ms. Yang says. 
Called ''Revolutionary Model Operas,'' they had names such as ''The Red Detachment of Women,'' and concerned themselves with the efforts of the proletariat to cast off the shackles of oppression.
UNTIL the Universal-Paramount deal and Ms. Yang's efforts, the only American films widely seen in China were sold by independent producers under ad hoc arrangements. 
Although occasionally a well-known film like ''Superman'' might get limited distribution, most of the Hollywood movies that found their way to China were low-budget and were useful for making propaganda points. 
''Badham County,'' for example, was a 1977 ABC television movie.
In contrast, ''Love Story,'' one of the most popular films distributed by Ms. Yang, does not carry any more of a social message in China than it did when it opened in the United States 17 years ago. 
If ''Love Story'' illustrates anything, Ms. Yang says, it is that films with simple plot lines play best in China.
''What works well is a good story,'' she said, adding that Chinese audiences ''want to know what is going to happen. 
They don't want too much left up to the imagination.''
They also apparently do not want anything too current. 
The newer films might contain cultural and social references that the average Chinese moviegoer could not connect with.
Beyond that, older films are more popular with both sides, because there is less likelihood that they will draw fire from those Chinese who see politically touchy subjects in them. 
''We don't want to give them a film where a few years from now someone will ask what that was doing on the screen,'' Ms. Yang said.
There is another reason, too, that the best of the studios' newer films are not going to China now: There is not yet enough money to be made. 
''An 'E.T.' or a 'Jaws' is too valuable a property,'' Ms. Yang said. 
''The fee structure still has to evolve to absorb those films.''
Besides distributing films, Ms. Yang also sells television programming to Chinese Central Television. 
The programming includes dramatic shows like as ''Columbo,'' ''Marcus Welby, M.D.''
(both from MCA/Universal) and ''Family Affair'' and ''Star Trek'' (from Paramount). 
She also is trying to sell American companies advertising time on those shows - aired from 8 to 10 P.M., China's prime time - and in movie theaters.
As sending motion pictures to China becomes less of a novelty, Ms. Yang may soon move on to a motion picture production and development job within MCA, leaving the Far Eastern operations in the hands of the company's normal international distribution arm. 
But wherever she ends up, she said, ''I'll always be a China person.''

China complained yesterday that Moody's Investors Service assigned too low a rating when the nation issued its first international bonds last October.
Moody's rated the 300-million-mark issue A-3, or lower than the Aa rating that Chinese officials said it deserved. 
The newspaper China Daily quoted a Finance Ministry spokesman in Beijing as saying it was ''unbelievable'' that China's bonds were rated lower than those of India and South Korea. 
Chinese officials said Moody's analysts were in their country only eight days.
Stephen Taran, a senior analyst at Moody's, said, ''It is our policy not to comment on the reaction of issuers to our ratings.''

The World Bank announced today that it had approved a $231.9 million interest-free loan to China for road-improvement and tree-harvesting projects.
Road-improvement projects in Sichuan and Shaanxi provinces will be aided by a $175 million loan, the bank said.
It said A $56.9 million loan would be used for a tree-harvesting project that hopes to salvage about two million acres of trees damaged by a forest fire in May 1987.
The loan, made through the International Development Association, the bank's concessionary lending arm, is for 35 years, including a 10-year grace period.

China will need $20 billion to finance offshore oil exploration and production by 1990, a prominent Hong Kong banker said here today.
Michael Sandberg, chairman of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, told delegates to an oil conference here that ''if drilling is initiated early in 1982, at least $10 billion will be required to fund exploration and production by 1985, followed by another $10 billion by 1990.''
Michael Sandberg, chairman of Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corp, predicts that China will need $20 billion for oil exploration by 1990
China is expected to call for bids from foreign oil companies early next year to exploit its offshore oil resources in the South China Sea and the southern Yellow Sea.
The chairman of Hong Kong's largest bank said that the Pacific Basin banking community could manage financing packages or loan syndications for the venture.
China must develop its offshore oil to finance its modernization programs, Mr. Sandberg said. 
It is also in the strategic interests of the Pacific Basin nations to see China expand its oil production to lessen dependence on Middle Eastern sources, he added.
The Middle East provides 70 percent of the area's oil consumption of 25 million barrels a day.

file: FINDING SUCCESS IN THE CHINESE MARKET.txt
text:
ï»¿
BY the end of its first year in business, Sun Associates Inc. in Elmsford, an international trading and consultant company, had one customer but nevertheless managed to gross $7.5 million. 
Four years later, Sun Associates, still with the same single customer, has quadrupled sales to post figures of $28 million gross this year.
''It helps when your customer is the People's Republic of China, with one-quarter of the world's population,'' said Robert C. Sun, the company's founder and president. 
Mr. Sun, an electrical engineer, spent 16 years in International Business Machine's development laboratory in Poughkeepsie as a computer designer and engineer of future systems before starting Sun Associates in 1982.
''The development lab was an exciting place to work,'' he recalled. 
''We started working on the design of the I.B.M. model 3081, the big computer, in 1970 and it was not until 1980 that the first one was shipped. 
All our projects were 5 or 10 years down the road. 
I liked my job very much but when I saw that a new era was beginning for China, I felt strongly that I was in exactly the right spot to take advantage of it. 
China wanted modernization, I knew they would need high-tech computers, my specialty, so I decided to start a business directed to the China market.''
Mr. Sun, who is 51, was born in Zhejiang, China, but moved to Taiwan with his family in 1949 when the Communists came into power in China. 
Two years after he graduated from Chengkung University in Taiwan, he won a scholarship for graduate study at the Steven's Institute of Technoloy in Hoboken and set out for New Jersey.
''My father, who is also an engineer, encouraged me to come to the United States,'' he said. 
''I found the teaching here very different from Taiwan. 
The atmosphere was much more stimulating. 
Professors encouraged creative, original thinking.''
Before being recruited by I.B.M., Mr. Sun worked for Western Union, and later for CDS Communications. 
''My wife and I liked it so much here that we became American citizens as soon as we could,'' he said.
However, when Mr. Sun was invited to visit China in 1972 by Premier Zhou Enlai, he accepted with alacrity.
''I was part of a group of 28 overseas Chinese who made the first return into Communist China,'' he said. 
''I was very anxious to see my former home and my grandmothers, who were still living there. 
We were all also very anxious to see what was going on in China first-hand.''
Soon after he returned to the United States, he took part in a seminar at the State University of New York at New Paltz, on trade with China. 
''I was very impressed with the predictions made concerning the increase of trade with China,'' he said. 
''Here is a brand new opportunity, I thought. 
It is my time to try it. 
I have been very lucky in choosing the right field and the right time.''
Capitalizing the company start-up himself, Mr. Sun, drawing on his knowledge of computer technology for the power industry, put together a sophisticated package including hardware, software, training and maintenance of equipment for Chinese power stations. 
He won his first contract for 11 systems from the Ministry of Water Resources and Electric Power in the People's Republic of China.
''Vast problems occur in China when the power fails,'' he said. 
''If electicity is kept constant, productivity is increased; on the other hand, when it is disrupted, productivity dips considerably. 
The Chinese Government's emerging power industry is anxious to expand its power networks throughout the country.''
Mr. Sun strengthened the capabilities of his company with the addition of Robert S. Lin. Mr. Lin, who is 47 and Sun Associates vice president, comes from a background similar to Mr. Sun's.
''I was born in Fujian, in the south of China,'' he said. 
''My father was a businessman. 
When I was 9 years old, the Communists took over. 
We went to live in Taiwan, where I went to school and eventually studied engineering. 
I had a scholarship for graduate work at McGill University in Canada and stayed there for one year before transferring to the University of West Virginia, where I finished my master's degree. 
I became involved with nuclear power and it became my specialty.''
For a decade, Mr. Lin worked on the design of the Clinch River nuclear power plant in Tennessee, only to see the project terminated by Congress.
''One billion dollars and 10 years' work went down the drain,'' he recalled. 
''It was very frustrating. 
When friends introduced me to Mr. Sun and he described his company to me, I joined the company happily. 
I wanted to have some control over my own destiny.''
Using first-hand knowledge of current technology in the power industry, Sun Associates delivered 11 of what is known in the industry as SCADA/AGC systems based on a DEC Super-Mini processor to ten regional power stations in China in the fall of 1985.
''We had to develop a special Chinese character set for the display-generation equipment,'' said Mr. Lin. ''It was an expensive project that we financed ourselves. 
The Chinese character terminals and printers were integrated into the system to meet the requirements of the Chinese end-user. 
It was a complex task.''
The contract that sent the special VAX computer system to China also brought 50 Chinese engineers to the United States for training by Sun Associates.
''Training the engineers in the use of the VAX computer system was part of the package deal we made with our customer, the Chinese Government,'' said Mr. Sun. ''In China, computers are installed in various regional power bureaus and will be operated by the people we train here. 
We built classrooms and a computer laboratory here in Elmsford to give the engineers hands-on experience. 
The courses are conducted in Mandarin by our in-house engineers, who are Mandarin-speaking specialists in communications, hardware maintenance, software programming and other areas of computer science. 
It is not a simple business staffing such a school.''
Sun's training program must also prepare students to perform substantial portions of the maintenance and troubleshootings on their machines in China; students must also have the ability to diagnose problems that demand the attention of Sun's maintenance staff.
''We keep a maintenance staff and a huge inventory of spare parts in China,'' said Mr. Sun. ''As part of our agreement, we supply free maintenance service for all the systems for a full year.''
Two groups of students have already completed the 12-week training course in Elmsford. 
A third group has just begun the same intensive course.
''The training program has received high praise from the top officials of the Ministry of Water Resources and Power,'' said Mr. Sun. ''I believe it is what gives us the edge over our competitors - training engineers on the spot. 
We are competing with the Japanese, the French and the English for a share of the huge China market.''
Sun also serves as China representative to Westinghouse Systems Ltd. of the United Kingdom. 
''We helped Westinghouse win one of China's largest contractor awards for 1986-1987,'' said Mr. Sun. ''It calls for Westinghouse to supply energy management systems to four power centers and development systems to two energy research institutes in China. 
We provided Westinghouse with a formal introduction to the Ministry of Water Resources and Electric Power and we negotiated on their behalf at numerous liaison meetings in Beijing, the United States and the United Kingdom.''
Sun is supplying equipment, training and maintenance for the project and as the sub-contractor will supply a large portion of the hardware and integration for Westinghouse Energy Management Systems. 
Wen Xinguang, one of the engineers now being trained for the Westinghouse project, will go to England for additional training before going back to China.
''I find this course very interesting and very challenging,'' he said. 
''In two or three years, China will be very different. 
Since the People's Republic was founded, the Government has placed great importance on developing its power industry in the entire country.''
Mr. Wen and his group are billeted at the Elmsford Motel, where arrangements have been made to allow them to cook their own meals. 
Weekends are spent sightseeing. 
''We work them very hard from Monday to Friday,'' said Mr. Sun. ''On the weekend, they need a change of pace. 
We show them whatever we can of the United States. 
We have been on numerous trips to places like Niagara Falls, to museums, to Washington, and we have even had a tour of a supermarket. 
Local people have been very generous in inviting our students to dinner in American homes. 
Cultural exchanges, we feel, are very important.''
Mr. Sun, a charter member of President Reagan's Republican Presidential Task Force, has served as host to many official Chinese delegations visiting the United States.
''I am very happy to be an American citizen,'' he said. 
''But I have a very personal interest in the modernization of the land of my birth.''

file: FIREWORKS AND ICE FOR CHINATOWN_S YEAR OF THE PIG.txt
text:
ï»¿
''One should rise before the cock's crow and explode firecrackers in the courtyard to ward off demons.''
So wrote Zong Lin of the New Year in the fourth-century text ''Records of Annual Festivals in Central China.''
No cock crowed yesterday. 
No demons loomed. 
Still, it began as it has for more than a century in Chinatown: A crackle here and there; slowly, one rat-a-tat-tat echoing against another. 
Then hundreds and thousands of tiny explosions collapsing into a thunderous din that resounded from the brick walls of six-story red-brick tenements. 
An odor of cordite hung in the air.
Edward A Gargan highlights Chinatown's celebration of Year of the Pig
The Year of the Pig, 4681, stumbling over snowbanks in the narrow streets, arrived in Chinatown yesterday, a neighborhood struggling with the woes of an economically depressed garment industry and troubled by recurring gang violence. 
But yesterday was a day for Chinatown to forget its difficulties and embrace the optimism brought by the year's first new moon.
At noon, a huge lion's head, trailing a paper tail in brilliant reds and blues, undulated in a small circle before a mound of exploding fireworks. 
To the thump of a large drum, the lion dancers, sponsored by the Chinatown Community Young Lions, a youth group, slowly veered up Mott Street, halting in front of restaurants and shops.
''We stop at all stores and restaurants to bring good luck,'' said Victor Soo Hoo, a director of the Young Lions, who brandished an immense ceremonial sword. 
''We usually have a wagon for the drum, but not with the snow. 
People will carry it this year.''
Â 
Pandemonium in the Snow
On the corner of Mott and Pell Streets, Lorina Lee and her sister Sandra stood on a solid mound of snow watching the semiorganized pandemonium before them.
''It's noisy, it's exciting,'' said Lorina, who was wearing a nearly luminescent blue-silk brocade jacket. 
Amid the festive cacophony of drums, cymbals and fireworks, Lorina, who works at a Chinatown branch of Citibank, said that she was worried about the area.
''I deal with owners of garment factories,'' she said. 
''Things aren't so good. 
I can't see it getting better.''
A New Year's custom in China that has endured here is giving hongbao, red envelopes that contain money, to family members. 
Shortly after midnight on New Year's Day, according to tradition, junior members of the family pay ceremonial respect to their elders and the elders, in return, give money.
To the New Year's greeting ''Gong xi fa cai'' (''Happy and prosperous times'') little children gleefully retort, ''Gei wo yige hung bao lai'' (''Give me a red envelope'').
And always there are feasts. 
The rest of the year rice is primary in Chinese meals, with cai, meat and vegetables dishes, secondary. 
But at New Year's, this custom is reversed and cai becomes primary.
''We've been eating all week,'' said Perry Hong, a camera hung around his neck. 
After taking a snapshot of a dragon swooping toward a pile of exploding firecrackers, Mr. Hong pointed to 14 family members, including uncles, cousins, brothers and sisters who came in from Brooklyn for the day. 
''Everybody likes to throw firecrackers at the dragons,'' he said.
Everywhere the dim sum restaurants, like the Silver Palace on Bowery and No. 1 on Canal Street, were teeming. 
Carts piled with duck feet, steamed shrimp balls, cold spiced pork slices and myriad other delicacies trundled past tables filled with families in their finest holiday dress. 
A special New Year's dessert, ba bao fan, a ball of sticky rice laced with sugared candies, appeared.
As the dragon from the Ho Nan Shau Lin Golden Dragon Team started down Mott Street toward Chatham Square, it paused before the Mayflower Tea Parlor, where a waiter came out to throw firecrackers. 
At Lee's Good Food, where ducks and finely barbecued chickens hung on skewers in the window, a man in an apron stood and watched the dragon bow and soar.
Not everyone on the streets of Chinatown could claim Chinese ancestry, however. 
Eleven-year-old Shay Silvestri came from Long Island wearing her own blue dragon headdress made of cardboard, Styrofoam balls, tin cans and layers of blue and green crepe paper.
''Every year I come here,'' she shouted over the rattle of fireworks. 
''I made this mask first for Halloween, and I thought I'd use it for New Year.''

file: FIRST CHINA EUROBOND OFFERING.txt
text:
ï»¿
A syndicate of 10 Western banks, led by Deutsche Bank, West Germany's largest commercial bank, has initiated the first Eurobond issue ever guaranteed by the Bank of China, even though nearly $100 million of pre-revolution Chinese government-backed bonds are still in default.
German bank officials said the banks were seeking to improve their position in the emerging market for bank services in China. 
Several large German banks, including Deutsche Bank and Dresdner Bank, the second largest, have expanded their activities in China in recent months.
Syndicate of 10 Western bank, led by West Germany's Deutsche Bank, has initiated first Eurobond issue ever guaranteed by Bank of China even though nearly $100 million of pre-revolution Chinese government-backed bonds are still in default (S)
Investment bankers say the lack of a settlement of old defaults still prevents the Chinese from raising money in dollars or pound sterling. 
But the Bank of China, which handles the country's foreign exchange dealings and overseas banking, has issued more than $150 million of Government-backed, yen-denominated bonds in the Japanese domestic market in the last year.
Deutsche Bank said Merrill Lynch International was the only United States-affiliated partner in the syndicate, which includes banks from West Germany, Britain, France, Japan and Switzerland.
The bond issue is the latest indication of China's apparent willingness to resurrect capitalist cash-raising practices under its new economic policies to help finance development.
Â 
Stock Offerings
Over the last year, several stock offerings, including a recent $385 million issue for the construction of a rail line in northern China, have backed up repeated reports in Chinese newspapers that the Government is considering reviving the nation's stock markets, which were closed after the Communists came to power in 1949.
The United States Foreign Bondholders Protective Council, a New York-based group set up in the 1930's to guard the interests of foreign securities holders, has records showing that more than $30 million of Chinese debt, including government bonds, is owed to American investors.
But John Petty, chairman of the Marine Midland Bank and the council's president, said the council did not oppose the Deutsche Bank bonds.
Â 
'Outstanding Problem'
Mr. Petty said the ''outstanding problem'' relating to American investors involved a 1919 issue of $5.5 million of dollar-denominated Chinese government treasury notes that were sold in the United States but never honored.

text:

China and Taiwan today concluded their first face-to-face negotiations in 37 years, with Peking agreeing to allow the Nationalist Government to reclaim a cargo plane flown to the mainland by its pilot, who defected.
The agreement, after three days of talks here, will also involve the return of two crewmen who were flown to China on the plane by the defector.
During talks on Saturday and Sunday, representatives of the airlines of Taiwan and China disagreed on where the transfer of the plane should occur. 
China wanted Taiwan to pick up the plane, a Boeing 747, on the mainland, while Taiwan said China should fly it to Hong Kong.
Today China agreed that a crew from its national airline, the Civil Aviation Administration of China, would fly the plane and the two crewmen to Hong Kong. 
Another meeting was scheduled for Tuesday to work out the details.
Â 
First Talks Since 1949
The talks have been the first direct contact between Taiwan and China since the Nationalists fled the mainland for Taiwan after losing a civil war to the Communists in 1949.
The Nationalists, who say they are China's rightful Government, had until now shunned all contact and had rebuffed initiatives by China to set up commercial, postal and communication links with the eventual goal of reunification.
Both sides have said the talks did not have political significance, but were a business matter between two airlines, not Governments.
But political commentators said they believed Taiwan's decision to negotiate directly must have been approved by President Chiang Ching-kuo, whose Government has been criticized by some legislators for rejecting all contacts with China.
Western diplomats in Peking have said that China, which views Taiwan as a Chinese province and has hopes of gaining its agreement to a new relationship, scored a victory by getting Taiwan to negotiate, whatever the outcome of the talks.
Â 
A Desire to Appear Reasonable
China has sought to appear reasonable and it was in its interest to reach an agreement quickly to avoid the impression that the two crew members who want to return to Taiwan were being held hostage, according to the diplomats.
Zhang Ruipu, the head of the Chinese delegation, said today that China had accepted Taiwan's proposal as a gesture of sincerity.
''We always maintain that there is no problem that cannot be solved between fellow countrymen through friendly and sincere discussions,'' he said in a news conference.
Chung Tsan-jung, the head of the Taiwan delegation, said China's concession was ''not a victory but a right'' of Taiwan.
The China Airlines cargo plane, which had left Bangkok bound for Hong Kong, landed in the southern Chinese city of Canton on May 3.

Father Is in Sichuan
Mr. Wang said in a news conference in Peking that he had defected in order to be reunited with his 82-year-old father in the central province of Sichuan.

In Taipei, a spokesman for China Airlines, Larry Lin, said the carrier did not regard the outcome of the talks as a victory ''because the release of all three crewmen, including Wang Hsi-chueh, is our final goal.''

''I hope he is allowed to visit Hong Kong to clarify the situation,'' he said.

file: FIVE AMERICANS AND A CHINESE REACH FINALS IN CLIBURN PIANO COMPETITION.txt
text:
ï»¿
Six pianists, all males, five of them Americans and one from China, were chosen last night as the finalists of the Van Cliburn International Piano Competition. 
They are the survivors of the 39 pianists from 17 countries who started competing on May 17 for the richest prize that any musical competition in the world has to offer - a $12,000 cash award, a recording contract and two years of solo and concerto appearances in the United States, Europe and the Far East.
The judges, aided by a computer, selected the finalists shortly before midnight last night. 
They are: Zhu Daming, 29 years old, from China. 
Jeffrey Kahane, 24, from Piedmont, Calif. 
Andre-Michel Schub, 28, from New York. 
Santiago Rodriguez, 29, from Columbia, Mo. 
Christopher O'Riley, 25, from Jamaica Plain, Mass. 
Panayis Lyras, 27, from New York. 
Over a hundred people waited patiently at the Ed Landredth Auditorium
Eighth in series on Van Cliburn International Piano Competition notes 1981 finalists and briefly describes their playing styles
This is the eighth of a series of occasional articles on the Van Cliburn International Piano Competition. 
The world-famous piano contest will end Sunday with the winner on the way to a major career.
of Texas Christian University until John Giordano, chairman of the jury, read the names of the finalists. 
In the audience were all 39 of the competing pianists and their host families. 
The families were more excited than the contestants, who received the news of success or failure with stoic professionalism. 
The six finalists were brought to the stage, where they embraced one another. 
A photo session followed, climaxed by pictures of the contestants in Texas hats. 
Mr. Zhu, for one, was obviously amazed at this example of American folk ways.
In reading the names of the finalists, Mr. Giordano emphasized that the order in which the pianists were called to the stage had no relation to the actual scores the jury had given. 
The pianists were called forth by the number that they originally had drawn, starting with the lowest. 
Before the competition started, each pianist had drawn a number, giving him the order in which he would play. 
Mr. Zhu had the lowest number of the finalists (No. 5) and Mr. Lyras was highest (No. 36).
Â 
How Judges Operated
Each of the 11 judges had submitted a ballot with a numerical rating for each contestant, with 100 being the top score. 
The computer averaged the scores, breaking down the results to four decimal places. 
When the printout was studied last night, it was clear that four pianists were well above the other eight semifinalists. 
But for the fifth and sixth places there was a triple tie. 
According to the rules of the competition, a less than twopoint difference between two contestants is considered a tie. 
Three pianists were within two points of each other for the last two places.
Thus a vote was taken and fed into the computer. 
The judges were asked to list the three names in order of preference, No. 1 being the highest rated. 
''Don't forget,'' Mr. Giordano emphasized. 
''No. 1 is the best, No. 3 is the worst.''
When the votes were put into the computer, the last two finalists emerged. 
It was close. 
Each of the three was within a single vote of the others. 
The two-point rule does not apply to a tie-break.
The selection of the finalists was greeted by the public and the professionals around here with general approbation. 
It is when the winner is named on Sunday that there may be howls of outrage. 
Each of the three leading contestants has a fervent following.
Among the young pianists in the competition who did not make it to the finals, the favorite by far is Mr. Kahane. Seven or eight of them were discussing the level of talent in the competition the other day, and it was unanimously agreed among them that Mr. Kahane is the most poetic and elegant of all. 
They will be terribly disturbed if he does not win first prize.
Â 
Judges Leaning Toward Two
But it is believed, on very good authority, that the judges are leaning toward Mr. Shub and Mr. Rodriguez, who are neck and neck. 
The next three days will of course decide the issue. 
With solo recitals and chamber music out of the way, the finalists now have to play concertos. 
With the Texas Little Symphony, all will be heard in a concerto by Mozart or early Beethoven. 
With the Fort Worth Symphony, they will play a major 19th-century concerto. 
Leon Fleisher will conduct.
Each of the finalists has a sharply etched style, and they differ considerably from one another. 
Mr. Zhu, trained entirely in China, does lack experience in Western music, but his instincts are remarkably sure and he learns with incredible speed. 
He has a blazing technique, draws a resonant sound from the piano and approaches music in a very serious manner.
Mr. Kahane is indeed the poet that his colleagues believe him to be. 
A prize-winner in the 1977 Clara Haskil International Piano Competition in Vevey, Switzerland, and high up in the 1980 American National Chopin Competition in Miami and the Chopin International Piano Competition in Warsaw, Mr. Kahane studied at the San Francisco Conservatory and the Juilliard School. 
He does not rely on powerhouse technical effects, though he has a glittering technique. 
It was characteristic of his style that in his recital he played a perfect performance of Chopin's Variations Brillantes (Op.12), and later he received a deserved standing ovation for his performance of the Dvorak Piano Quintet. 
But he did have a bit of trouble with the big sonorities of the Schumann Fantasy. 
Many believe him to be the most sensitive, refined pianist in the finals.
Â 
Self-Described Romantic
Mr. O'Riley has been a finalist in the 1975 Three Rivers Competition in Pittsburgh and second-prize-winner in the 1980 Montreal International Piano Competition. 
He grew up in Pittsburgh and was trained at the New England Conservatory. 
He describes himself as a Romantic pianist. 
Mr. O'Riley likes big sonorities, and attacks the keyboard energetically. 
When he played the Brahms F-minor Piano Quintet, he all but made a little concerto out of it. 
He is a pianist with temperament and a big style.
The one pianist who went out of his way in his programming was Mr. Lyras. Greek-born, he came to the United States when he was 12, and attended the High School of Performing Arts in New York and the Juilliard School. 
He has won first prizes in the 1976 University of Maryland International Piano Competition and the 1978 Three Rivers Piano Competition. 
In 1980 he won the Silver Medal at the Arthur Rubinstein International Piano Competition in Tel Aviv. 
Where everybody else stuck close to repertory staples for their recitals, Mr. Lyras played such things as three Medtner ''Fairy Tales'' and the ''Islamey'' of Balakirev. 
His inclusion of the Balakirev piece suggested a pianist with virtuoso instincts, and Mr. Lyras did play the old warhorse with technique to burn. 
He is a well-schooled, utterly dependable pianist who brings logic and power to his playing.
Of the two front-runners, it is a classic case of Apollo and Dionysus. 
Mr. Schub was born in Paris but came to the United States as an infant. 
He started to play the piano at 4, studied at Princeton University and the Curtis Institute of Music, won the 1974 Naumburg Competition and was awarded the Avery Fisher Prize in 1977. 
Mr. Schub is an Apollonian player. 
He is an elegant pianist and, as his performances of two of the Paganini-Liszt etudes showed, a supreme technician. 
His fingers have been well brought up and have been taught never to associate with a wrong note.
Â 
Plays With Immense Authority
He plays with clarity, intelligence and immense authority. 
Yet he is a cool pianist. 
Proportion to him is more important than color. 
He refuses to make a play for the audience, and he performs miracles of virtuosity in a detached, aloof manner.
Mr. Rodriguez is the Dionysian pianist. 
He was born in Cuba, came to the United States at 9, received a degree from the University of Texas at Austin, and studied at Juilliard. 
In 1976 he won the Maryland International Piano Competition and took second place in the Naumburg Competition. 
In 1977 he was a finalist in the Leventritt Competition.
Mr. Rodriguez is a crowd-pleaser, a virtuoso, a colorist, a dashing, cocky performer who has thought out every element of his interpretations. 
Fortunately he is much more than a technician. 
His interpretations have had taste at all times, and his virtuosity is always employed for legitimate musical devices. 
In the Preliminaries, he played the first book of the Brahms ''Paganini'' Variations, and it was a stunning performance, one of the best this listener has ever heard. 
He was also remarkably effective in the Stravinsky ''Petrushka.''

The live coverage is part of a 90-minute special on the competition, made possible by International Business Machines Corporation. 
In New York, the telecast will start at 7:30 P.M.

Flash flooding along China's eastern coast has killed thousands of people and left tens of thousands homeless so far this year, and a drought in the country's central and southern grain belts has damaged millions of acres of crops.
Over the last four days, more than 200 people have died and 450 more were listed as missing in floods that engulfed parts of the coastal province of Zhejiang, news reports said.
At the same time, a heat wave continues to grip the Chinese heartland, from Jiangsu Province, across Anhui and Hubei Provinces, and into Jiangxi Province. 
Officials say 65 million acres of grain have been devastated by temperatures of 100 degrees and higher.
More than one-fifth of China's 296 million acres of farmland have been hurt by drought this year, with 24 million acres damaged by floods.
Natural disasters are a common feature of life in China, and their effect is accentuated by poorly constructed homes, bridges and dams; inadequate flood-control devices, and rudimentary road networks in rural areas - all of which hamper rescue efforts.
This year, the effect of the flooding and the heat wave is more severe, and many Chinese speak fatalistically about the cataclysms that every 12 years seem to accompany the Year of the Dragon.
''It's the dragon year,'' said a man who returned from Hebei Province on Sunday. 
''In 1976, there was the big earthquake, and the Chairman died,'' he said, speaking of the previous Year of the Dragon, when a catastrophic earthquake in Tangshan killed 100,000 people, and Mao Zedong died.

Five counties in the central part of Zhejiang Province have been struck by flash floods, said The People's Daily, the official newspaper of the Communist Party. 
In a torrential rainstorm on July 29 and July 30, the paper said, nearly 700 people were reported missing, almost 17,000 houses were destroyed, the banks of 100 reservoirs crumbled, and 305 bridges collapsed.
China's central television station showed scenes of devastation, including towns with flooded streets. 
Fallen trees and other debris were shown sweeping past crumbling houses in a muddy torrent. 
Troops were sent to the region.

Oil Wells and Granaries

Half the cities and counties in the province were struck by the storms, which flooded 1,000 oil wells and inundated grain stores, factories, shops and schools.
In the south and center of China, a stubborn heat wave parched paddy fields and withered rice stalks, damaging or destroying large portions of the year's first crop.
Officials in Hubei, one of the provinces hardest hit by the drought, reported that more than half the arable land in the region shriveled under the absense of rain and that two-thirds of the peanut and sesame crops were lost for the year.
''The drought is not only happening here in China,'' said Fan Yongxiang, the chief meteorologist at the Central Meteorological Bureau. 
''It's a global one.''
Mr. Fan suggested two possible causes for the dry spell. 
The first was an increase in sunspot activity earlier in the summer. 
Sunspots, which run in 11-year cycles, lead to strong electro-magnetic disturbances on earth.
The other was the global increase in temperatures attributed substantially to the greenhouse effect, in which an excess of carbon dioxide and other gases, produced primarily by the burning of carbon-based fuels, collects in the atmosphere, trapping heat and causing a gradual warming of the planet. 
Although the greenhouse effect's functioning has yet to be definitively established, there is a consensus among specialists that it is the cause of hotter temperatures on earth.
A spokesman for the Chinese Agriculture Ministry said the drought is the second this year in the region. 
The first occurred in April and May.
Xu Yuchang, a spokesman for the relief department of the Ministry of Civil Affairs, said more than 1 billion yuan, or about $270 million, has been allocated for relief work in drought- and flood-stricken areas.

text:

China's parliament approved a new lineup today of Government leaders who are widely seen as committed to its ambitious program of economic restructuring.
As the National People's Congress approved the new leaders, men who in general are slightly younger and better educated than the previous leadership, it also voted to give constitutional protection to private enterprise and to the selling of land use rights, activity that is tantamount to selling land itself.
Last Saturday, the congress approved Li Peng, a 59-year-old Soviet-trained engineer, as Prime Minister. 
The congress, which meets annually, has been marked by a degree of open discussion not seen since the founding of the People's Republic in 1949, but its real power is essentially confined to ratifying decisions already made by the Communist Party's Politburo.
The official New China News Agency described the new group of state councilors, the equivalent of a cabinet, and ministers as ''a group of technocrats, who are younger in age, pragmatic and enthusiastic in the reform.''
''China is rejuvenating its leadership, making it professionally more competent as a measure to insure the continuity of its current policies for reform and the opening to the outside world,'' the press agency said.
Western diplomats here generally subscribed to that view, saying that the new group of officials reflects a continuing shift toward a more nuts-and-bolts and less politically motivated government.
Among the most prominent appointments made today was that of Qian Qichen, 60, as Foreign Minister. 
He succeeds Wu Xueqian, 66, who was named a Deputy Prime Minister and who is expected to retain overall control over China's foreign policy apparatus.
Mr. Qian, who has spent nearly all his career in the diplomatic ranks, has been heavily involved with the Soviet Union, where he was stationed for a total of 10 years, and with Eastern Europe. 
He has been a Deputy Foreign Minister since 1982.
Other significant appointments include the naming of Li Guixian as a state councilor and governor of the country's central bank, and Li Tieying as Minister of the State Education Commission..
Neither man brings visible experience to his new position. 
Li Guixian is a chemical engineer who has been a senior party bureaucrat, and Li Tieying, an electrical engineer who studied in Czechoslovakia, has worked in the electronics industry and as a senior party official in the provinces.
Qin Jiwei, 73, a veteran military man, was named Defense Minister. 
He replaces the ailing Zhang Aiping, 80. 
The party's Central Military Commission, headed by Deng Xiaoping, has most of the military power in China.
Altogether, three Deputy Prime Ministers, two fewer than there were previously, were appointed: Yao Yilin, Tian Jiyun and Wu Xueqian; 11 state councilors, down two from before; and 41 ministers, down from the previous 45. 
The slight shrinking in the number of senior posts is evidently part of an effort to streamline the cumbersome governmental apparatus.
Both constitutional amendments approved today are intended to give legal weight to the continuing remolding of the economy. 
By granting constitutional legitimacy to private enterprise, a radical step here,the leadership has given recognition to the need to protect the most rapidly growing segment of the economy.

file: FOR CHINA_S CUISINE, A RETURN TO GLORY DAYS.txt
text:
ï»¿
''THE food in China used to be very good, but it was set back by the Cultural Revolution,'' said Zhou Zhi Bin. 
That observation is particularly noteworthy because the man who made it is one of Shanghai's oldest master chefs. 
Western visitors to China have been saying the same thing for years.
In a period of increasing openness and contact with the West, Chinese chefs have begun to acknowledge the poor quality of the food in a country once as famous as France for its culinary heritage. 
In an effort to repair the damage, master chefs have been called out of retirement and foreign chefs have been invited to demonstrate Western cooking.
A desire to regain their culinary stature is not only a matter of national pride for the Chinese; it makes creasing number of privately owned restaurants, those owned by the state face stiff competition: as the Chinese become more affluent they demand better food. 
It is often difficult to get reservations in the best restaurants. 
And foreign visitors expect to eat equally well in dining rooms serving Chinese and Western food.
The Cultural Revolution, which extended from 1966 to 1976, is rightly blamed for the state of disrepair into which Chinese culinary artistry had fallen. 
Like so many of his peers, Mr. Zhou spent six years in that period working in a rubber factory.
But the Cultural Revolution does not bear full responsibility. 
Between 1950 and 1958, China had virtually no training program for chefs. 
As a result of these two barren periods there is a shortage today of competently trained chefs in their late 30's, 40's and even 50's. 
Most skilled chefs are in their 60's, 70's and 80's. 
In the late 1970's Mr. Zhou and other professional chefs were ''rehabilitated,'' returned from the countryside and factories to the professions for which they had been trained, but the rehabilitation was short-lived. 
These older men were soon forced to retire to make room for the young people who were coming back from ''retraining'' in the countryside. 
Speaking through an interpreter, Jie Zhi Zhong, manager of the new Sichuan restaurant in the Jinjiang Hotel, one of Shanghai's most famous old hotels, explained: ''It was the Government's policy to replace old people with young people. 
But the young people couldn't produce the best food as their fathers had done because they did not have the proper training. 
Eventually, the restaurants and hotels took things into their own hands and invited old chefs back to supervise and to teach.''
Mr. Zhou was called back to the Jinjiang, where he had begun his career 50 years before. 
This time he would train the young generation of chefs, who until a few years ago learned most of what they knew from books.
''Now, leaders of the Government at various level are giving full attention to the art,'' Mr. Zhou said, ''and we are focusing our attention on training young chefs. 
The cooking schools have improved and the chefs are going there for theoretical training. 
We understand Chinese cooking is not of the finest quality at this moment, but the food is improving.''
One of Mr. Zhou's pupils nodded in agreement. 
''Self-taught by books,'' as he put it, Lu Da Ming went to the hotel in 1974. 
''Because of Mr. Zhou,'' he said, ''I am learning the traditional dishes and I am learning much faster, especially the things you can only learn by experience. 
We all hope the old chefs will have long life and stay healthy.''
The better food in China is being cooked by chefs who have had the advantage of training under the old master chefs: Li Cheng Heng, for example, the Sichuan chef at the Golden Flower Hotel, a joint venture operated by the Chinese Government and a Scandinavian company in Xi'an.
Mr. Li, 42 years old, was also a victim of the Cultural Revolution, but he had been trained by a master chef from the age of 12. 
He gives full credit to his old teacher, who eventually became a chef at several Chinese embassies abroad, an honor accorded only to the country's best.
As evidence of the Government's renewed interest in its culinary experts, chefs like Mr. Li have been sent to Europe and America to demonstrate Chinese cooking and to work at foreign restaurants. 
The Sichuan Pavilion in New York is one of the first of these restaurants to employ its entire kitchen staff from China.
Wong Lin Chou, a gracious, sophisticated older man who speaks fluent English, was also called out of retirement, in this case to add polish to the state-run Mei Leung restaurant in Shanghai. 
At one time Mr. Wong owned an import-export business; he knows about dealing with Westerners and about the fine points of old-fashioned service. 
During the Cultural Revolution he was forced to work in a candy factory. 
In 1984, he said, the restaurant hired him to ''greet foreign guests and to teach the dining room staff how to speak English and how to conduct themselves.''
He appears to have had an effect: the service at Mei Leung was several cuts above that in many of the other restaurants visited on a recent trip to China. 
''The cooking art is picking up,'' said Ge Xian-E, vice principal of the City Restaurant and Service School in Shanghai. 
''The central Government is paying attention.''
Speaking through an interpreter, she said: ''There was a large culinary demonstration in the Great Hall of the People in Beijing in 1983, and similar demonstrations have been held throughout the country. 
The status of cooks has been raised from simple worker to master, and the system of accrediting cooks at varous grade levels, which had been stopped during the Cultural Revolution, has begun again.''
To improve the quality of middle-aged chefs, schools like the one in Shanghai are also retraining them.
Miss Ge said the quality of that training is very high: ''Most of the teachers are the creme de la creme.''
It is certainly good enough to attract some foreign students studying at Chinese universities in Shanghai.
Full-time students at the school must pass an examination to enter.
To graduate, they must design and prepare a banquet. 
The course is two years for senior high school graduates and three years for students above the junior high school level. 
American chefs are being invited to China to share their culinary secrets, among them Jasper White, chef and owner of Jasper's in Boston, and Lydia Shire, executive chef at the Four Seasons Hotel in Los Angeles.
''They want to elevate the status of the chef by having important American chefs go into the kitchens with big Chinese chefs,'' Ms. Shire said. 
''It strengthens what they are trying to do.''
The American chefs are also teaching the Chinese how to prepare Western food. 
''The Chinese have lost a whole generation of chefs and especially those who knew anything about Western food,'' Mr. White said. 
''One morning we had eggs and sausage for breakfast, and the eggs were deep-fried. 
Having us do cooking demonstrations is part of an effort to satisfy their guests, both tourists and businessmen.''
