By CLIFFORD D.MAY
W ith travel, there is generally a tradeoff: The more exotic the destination, the more arduous the journey. 
But hard traveling need not be regarded as just the price one pays to get far away. 
On the contrary, those who truly subscribe to the view that it is better to go than to arrive also know that it is when the going gets rough that the excitement really begins.
I understood these rules subliminally at best when, along with seven friends (three other Americans, two Englishmen and two Pakistanis), I recently found myself in Islamabad contemplating a long weekend excursion into Pakistan's remote northern region. 
Within this area, three of the world's great mountain ranges - the Himalayas, the Karakorams and the Hindu Kush - converge, and eight of the world's 10 tallest mountains rise.
Highlights of traveling in Pakistan's remote northern region
The hub of the territory is a city called Gilgit, long ago a far western outpost of Tibetan Buddhism and an important trading center on the ancient Silk Route. 
More recently, Gilgit has been popular with European tourists on the overland route to the Far East; the war in neighboring Afghanistan has virtually put an end to that traffic, however.
Beyond Gilgit lies Hunza, the isolated valley that some say provided the inspiration for Shangri-La in James Hilton's ''Lost Horizon,'' and a place opened to foreigners without special permission only within about the last year. 
Finally, there is the Karakoram Highway, the artery that links these places, two narrow lanes joining Islamic Pakistan with China.
Around 1 o'clock on a Thursday afternoon we boarded a twin-engine Fokker 27 at the airport in Islamabad and settled back for what had been described as the breathtakingly scenic flight to Gilgit, 371 miles to the north. 
A tape recording of a sitar played softly. 
Tea and cakes were served with quiet grace by the hostess.
Through the window we watched the landscape grow rugged. 
On the highest peaks, among smudges of evergreens, the snow shone so brightly that it seemed to be lit from within. 
But the mood that was coming upon us was to be disturbed before we had even drained the tea from our cups. 
The ride suddenly became bumpy and islands of darkening cumulus clouds came into view ahead.
''Ladies and gentlemen,'' said a metallic voice, interrupting the strains of the sitar, ''we are sorry to tell you that due to bad weather we are having to turn back. 
Inshallah, we shall land in Islamabad momentarily. 
Please fasten your seat belts.''
The eight of us moaned. 
The other 40 or so passengers - none of them tourists, judging from the long dark veils draped over the women and the soft, flat-topped felt hats worn by the men - appeared neither surprised nor troubled by the news.
We had two choices: We could return to the hotel and hope for better luck on tomorrow's flight. 
Or we could attempt to reach Gilgit by road. 
Since the weather had already been unseasonably rainy for some days - and since the pilot prudently makes no attempt to maneuver through the tall mountains when it's even cloudy - we decided to go by land.
We hired a minibus and driver and were soon passing through fields carpeted with fresh hail. 
A light rain fell as we continued at a slow but steady clip to Hazara, in the North-West Frontier Province east of the Indus River, an area believed to have been settled by soldiers left behind by either Genghis Khan or Tamerlane.
No signpost marked the point, in the village of Havelian, where the road merges with the Karakoram Highway, constructed by the Pakistanis and the Chinese over a 20-year period. 
It is said that one life was lost for every kilometer of road. 
At the peak of the effort, 15,000 Pakistanis and 1,000 Chinese were working on the KKH, with little in the way of modern machinery.
The rain had just about stopped when we came to the village of Besham in the early evening. 
A queue of trucks lined both sides of the road, an indication of trouble ahead. 
We stopped to inquire at the local musafir khana, a sort of Pakistani truck stop, a squat cinder-block building containing rows of wooden cots, each strung with rope. 
In front of the building, tea brewed on a charcoal fire under a dim gas light.
''I'm afraid it is not possible for you to go any further,'' the man tending the fire told us. 
''The mountain is still moving.''
The leader of our group, Lieut. 
Col. Muhammad Akram Khan - a founding member of the Adventure Foundation (Pakistan), a nonprofit organization modeled on Outward Bound - explained that the recent rains had caused a landslide and the road could not be cleared because mud and rock were continuing to fall. 
''We should be able to get through in the morning,'' the colonel consoled us.
We went to a nearby guest house to pass the night. 
But when we moved out again just after dawn the trucks were still parked along the roadside. 
We pressed on until we could see the road disappear into a thick, smooth slab of mud that began high on the slope above and ended in a gorge several hundred feet below. 
We turned to Colonel Akram in despair. 
''Come now,'' he said. 
''We're not turning back yet.''
We grabbed our hand luggage and followed the colonel on a zigzagging trail down the steep, rocky mountainside. 
A line of men, some carrying boxes or trunks, some herding goats, trekked both ahead and behind us. 
Through the middle of the narrow gorge below ran a shallow stream, a small tributary of the Indus River, which splashed over smoothly rounded boulders. 
Before crossing the gorge, we looked up and listened attentively: Each time the rocks began to roll, people above whistled and yelled out a warning.
We crossed one at a time, as quickly as we could manage without losing our footing on the slick stones. 
Then, relieved that no rocks had made contact with our skulls, we began the long, tiring climb up the other side. 
The slope was so steep that we had to grab bushes for support. 
At one point, a goat just above us stopped, refusing to go farther despite the urgings of its herder and the whacks he was applying with a switch to its rump. 
The exasperated herder finally picked the goat up in his arms like a child and carried it the rest of the way up to the road. 
On the far side of the gorge, too, was a line of trucks that had been waiting since the day before. 
Colonel Akram told us to catch our breaths while he went off among them. 
Within minutes he was back, sitting next to the driver in a small Toyota diesel pickup. 
''Okay, it's arranged,'' the colonel said. 
''This man will take us at least part of the way to Gilgit. 
There will be a phone up ahead. 
I will arrange for other transport to be sent down to meet us.''
We piled ourselves and our luggage into the back and sped off along the serpentine road, high above the Indus River. 
The open cargo bed provided an unobstructed view and an extraordinarily heightened sense of speed. 
The faces of my companions - and probably my own as well - became pale as we swung from side to side, tightly grippling the railing and bouncing painfully on the metal floor.
The steep mountain slopes in which we were cradled were barren and eerily desolate. 
Only occasionally would we catch sight of a tiny plot of cultivated terraces, some no more than a few feet wide. 
Goats browsed among sparse brush nearby. 
And, looking carefully, we would invariably make out one or two small houses, constructed of the same gray stone as the mountains to which they so precipitously clung.
Until the completion of the KKH just four years ago, this area had been almost entirely cut off from the rest of the world. 
The lateral valleys beyond the road are still known as ''Yaghistan,'' which loosely translates as Land of the Unruled. 
In other words, they are tribal territory beyond the control of the Pakistani Government. 
We had been told that the people of Yaghistan could be quite hospitable; they could also draw and quarter you, more or less with impunity.
At a settlement about 50 miles from Besham our driver stopped: He didn't want to be too far away when the road was finally cleared. 
Colonel Akram arranged for us to switch to a small taxi with a canvas-enclosed bed containing two parallel wood benches on which passengers could sit facing one another. 
An assistant to the driver stood on a platform at the rear of the car, scanning the mountaintops for signs of a rockslide.
A little after 1 o'clock the car suddenly jolted and screeched to a halt. 
I had a vision of all the little headlines I had seen in newspapers over the years reporting a ''Bus Plunge'' in places very much like this. 
Luckily, we had not been going fast when the tire blew. 
The spare tire that the driver had brought along did not inspire confidence. 
It was covered in bulging patches, evidence of the many times it had been repaired.
A half hour or so farther down the road we met up with two Toyota jeeps that had set out from Gilgit following the colonel's phone call. 
We packed ourselves into these vehicles and contnued on, riding high above the silty Indus, its bone-colored sand beaches unmarred by human footprints.
At Chilas, a village about 4,000 feet above sea level, we stopped briefly at a small stone hut, another musafir khana, for milky tea, dal maash - a local dish made from yellow lentils and spices - and tandoori roti, flat round bread baked in deep stone ovens.
O n the road once more, the colonel pointed out Nanga Parbat, the Naked Mountain, with its snow-covered 26,660-foot peak. 
Finally, in the early evening, we entered Gilgit, where donkey carts rolled down the narrow streets and where the tiny stone shops in the bazaar were still crowded. 
It is said that long ago the people of Gilgit were fire worshippers. 
Then, beginning in the eighth century, China, Tibet and Arabia conquered the area in turn. 
Today the population of about 25,000 includes people of many ethnic groups: Pathans, Kashgaris, Chitralis, Tshins, Kirghizis and Hunzakuts.
We spent the night at a guest house and rose at 4:40 on Saturday morning to the sound of the muezzins calling the faithful to prayer. 
Because we were now about a day behind schedule, and because the weather looked fairly clear, we decided to set out again immediately, hoping to make it to the Chinese border and back - a round-trip excursion of a little more than 300 miles - by nightfall.
We headed out of town over the 100-year-old British-built suspension bridge that spans the Gilgit River and disappeared into a tunnel roughly carved through a mountain. 
We returned to the KKH, which twisted through bleak, infertile mountains where rare Marco Polo sheep and ibex are said to dwell. 
We neared Rakaposhi, the southernmost peak of the Karakorams, whose 25,550-foot peak was buried in clouds.
Our unofficial but well-informed guide for this part of the journey was the local police superintendent, Ali Ahmad Jan, who happened to be an old college chum of one of our fellow travelers, Syed Husain Mahmud, a freelance photographer. 
Superintendent Ali had blue eyes and a bushy blond moustache. 
His ancestors, he said, were either early Greek or Persian invaders, he wasn't sure which; he could trace only about 900 years of his family's history in this area.
It was fully light by the time we reached the Hunza Valley shortly before 6. 
We came around a turn and there, just ahead of us, three seasons seemed to coexist. 
The mountain summits were white and wintry. 
Just below them was a layer of autumnal red-brown rock. 
And down beside the river, stretched an alluvial plain, lush with pinkblossomed apricot trees, tall, swaying poplars, and neat, Lilliputian green pastures surrounded by sturdy stone fences.
The narrow Hunza Valley is not only fertile, it is also exceptionally rich in semiprecious stones. 
It is said that years ago, when soldiers of the British Empire fought there, the bullets removed from them would often turn out to be garnets coated with lead.
Until as recently as 1974, Hunza was a separate kingdom ruled by the hereditary Mir of Hunza. 
Not long after Hunza's incorporation into Pakistan, the last Mir ''died of heartbreak,'' Superintendent Ali told us. 
I asked him how he knew. 
''Oh well, he was a relation,'' the Superintendent said. 
''It happens that my mother was the Mir's sister and the Mir's wife was my auntie. 
My father and uncle simply exchanged sisters, you see.''
The people of the Hunza Valley -which is surrounded by 21 peaks more than 20,000 feet high - are famous for good health and longevity and a number of books have been written about ''Hunza health secrets.''
One does indeed see many robust old Hunzakut men and women about, but as far as I was able to ascertain there has never been any proof that these people represent a medical marvel.
The villagers of the Hunza Valley are remarkable in other ways, however. 
Hunza is said to be a basically cooperative society with little difference in wealth from family to family. 
Fruit - the apricot in particular - is the staple of the diet. 
Although alcohol is widely prohibited in Pakistan, the Hunzakuts freely - if discreetly -drink a concoction known as ''Hunza water,'' varieties of wine and brandy distilled from mulberries and grapes. 
In contrast to the people farther south, many Hunzakuts have pink-white skin, and green or blue eyes. 
Women do not hide their faces as most Pakistani Moslems do; instead they cover only their hair with a colorful scarf draped over a sort of pillbox cap.
We stopped for a brief breakfast of green tea, sheep liver fried in apricot-pit oil, porridge, potatoes, chicken, phiti - brown bread made from unrefined wheat - and jam, then quickly resumed our journey. 
In places, the shoulders of the road were piled high with snow, cleared after recent avalanches. 
Elsewhere, the mountain slopes were covered in scree, rock pulverized to a fine powder by the force of glaciers over centuries.
One of the largest glaciers in the world outside the polar regions is the 30-mile-long Batura Glacier, which we approached at about 9:30. 
This is normally as far as foreign visitors may go, but we had earlier applied for and received permission to proceed the remaining 60 miles to the border.
T he road followed the course of the clear and shallow Hunza River through a deserted landscape of dry, rocky soil, wild willow and scrub. 
About noon we came to Kara Jilga, the point where the road begins a steep climb to the Khunjerab Pass. 
The countryside was snowcovered; the river was frozen and bluish icicles hung from the rocks. 
Dark, hairy yaks trudged along in the distance, leaving a shadowy trail in the otherwise unbroken whiteness.
Finally, the road flattened out and we drove up to an unimposing wooden sign indicating that China lay beyond. 
The elevation was 15,072 feet, said to be the highest point on any paved road in the world. 
Although I was wearing several layers of clothes, I shivered with cold and my breathing was labored. 
Moving about in the snow to keep warm, I soon became dizzy and light-headed.
''When the Karakoram Highway was completed, the road gang from China and the road gang from Pakistan played volleyball right across the border here,'' Superintendent Ali told me. 
I said I thought I would drop dead if I attempted such exercise at this altitude. 
''As a matter of fact, that's just what did happen to one chap,'' he noted.
We could not spend long in the cold, rarified atmosphere of the pass. 
We climbed back into the jeeps and headed south, stopping for a snack about 5 P.M. and arriving in Gilgit just before 9.
Our plan was to fly out Sunday afternoon. 
No plane had made it to Gilgit in the last few days, but the sky was clear and we were hopeful. 
We attended a polo match after breakfast; Gilgit happens to be the place where the sport originated.
The plane did not arrive, however, and we reluctantly began the long and arduous trip by road back to Rawalpindi. 
By Monday morning we had somehow made it to the airport, more or less on schedule and more or less ready for the long flight back to New York.
Although I don't think any of us would have been prepared to make the trip again right away, we were all pleased to have done it. 
In part, that's because we had learned something about the rules of travel and did not doubt that the destination had been exotic enough to justify the hardships we had endured. 
Equally important was another rule that we were just beginning to recognize: few memories are more savored than those of a risky journey successfully completed.
Â 
Guide for visitors to Gilgit
The Basics The round-trip excursion fare via Pakistani International Airlines from New York to Islamabad is $2,470 in first class, $1,285 economy. 
(For stays of less than a month no visa is required.) The easiest and least expensive way to get to Gilgit is by air. 
P.I.A. has a flight that leaves Islamabad for Gilgit daily if the weather is clear. 
The Government-subsidized fare is very reasonable, about $26 each way. 
A car and driver can be hired in either Rawalpindi or Gilgit for about $10 a day plus five cents a mile. 
The best time of year to go to northern Pakistan is spring or fall. 
Days are warm, but evenings can be quite cool, especially at high altitudes. 
Rain is likely in July and August. 
Exhibition and practice polo matches are held in Gilgit (as well as in many villages in the region) at almost any time of year, but the regular season begins in late spring and ends in the fall. 
In Gilgit, the best known hotels, such as the Rakoposhi Inn and the Hunza Inn, charge about $35 a night for a double occupancy room. 
Less expensive but still quite decent accommodations are also available. 
Making Arrangements Further information can be obtained and arrangements made through the Tourism Division, Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, Government of Pakistan, College Road, Shalimar, 7/2, Islamabad, and the Adventure Foundation (Pakistan), a nonprofit organization modeled on America's Outward Bound. 
The Adventure Foundation's main goal is to introduce indigent youth of Pakistan to sporting activities in wilderness areas of the country, but A.F.P. representatives are also beginning to organize excursions for American groups on a select basis. 
Contact the A.F.P. at No. 1 Gulistan Colony, College Road, Abbottabad, Pakistan.

text:
ï»¿
For 17 years, Beate Gordon has been a sort of cultural detective. 
She travels to Asia each summer, ferreting out virtuoso performers of traditional arts and arranging for them to tour the United States.
The assignment, for the Asia Society,seems tailor-made for the 63-year-old Mrs. Gordon, whose background is as exotic as her work. 
Born in Vienna of Russian parents, both pianists, she was reared in Japan and studied dance, drama and music. 
She speaks six languages: German, French, Spanish, Japanese, English and Russian.
Her latest find, eight Mongolian musicians and dancers - the first such troupe ever to tour this country - will appear at the Asia Society, on Park Avenue at 70th Street, tomorrow through Friday.
They are the 34th group, from 13 countries, that she has brought over. 
Typically, they were assembled after some digging by Mrs. Gordon. The program will include khoomei - a technique in which a singer emits a long, low ''szzz sound,'' as she put it, ''with overtones'' - an art she had known about, but only glimpsed in the concert to which she was invited in Ulan Bator.
Â 
Khoomei Is Heard
''So I went to the conservatory of music,'' she recalled, ''I simply marched myself in, and talked to the receptionist. 
She was very charming. 
She ran out and came back with the man who had sung khoomei the night before!
So in the reception room he sang and I really could hear and watch how the muscles worked.''
The other artists chosen by Mrs. Gordon include players of a two-stringed fiddle, mouth harps and flutes, and an ''upper body'' dancer who performs with bowls of milk.
Mrs. Gordon, who formerly worked for the Japan Society in New York and now directs the Asia Society's department of performances, films and lectures, has many tales to tell.
There was the time a monsoon delayed her arrival in Purulia, India, and she slept on a mat in a hut until drums woke her at 2 A.M.; performers who had learned she was there were emerging from the forest to play for her.
Or her trip to the heights of Lhasa, Tibet, when she walked very slowly, as cautioned, but ignored advice not to laugh or talk - both qualities that seem natural to the impresario, whose enthusiasms break through a cordial reserve. 
So she blacked out, then had to carry around bags of oxygen while auditioning performers.
Â 
The Struggle for Authenticity
Speaking in her small office overlooking Park Avenue, Mrs. Gordon cited a pervasive problem: convincing cultural ministers and performers that she wants authentic, classical art, not tourist entertainment; genuine costumes, not glitter.
''What I often am shown,'' she said, ''are forms that have been changed to become more accessible, not just for foreigners but often even for their own audiences.''
In Tibet she heard ''La Paloma'' played by a 75-piece orchestra. 
In Burma, someone crooned with a microphone. 
They sang ''I love coffee, I love tea'' in Suzhou, China. 
And in the Chinese province of Fujian, she saw an anti-smoking puppet show.
''Can you imagine expecting this,'' she asked, showing a replica of a centuries-old Fujian hand-puppet in a glass case near her desk - a woman's figure wearing an intricately embroidered silk gown - ''and seeing a panda and a monkey?
The monkey's pipe kept growing bigger and bigger. 
They thought, 'Americans would love this.'
''
Â 
Missing the Point
Sometimes she seems to have made her point only to suffer dismay when the performers arrive in this country. 
''I have spent hours,'' she said, ''begging Indian dancers to bring their beautiful silk saris woven with gold and silver thread, only to be told that they had special costumes made for the States with hand-sewn sequins.''
Mrs. Gordon, whose research includes visits to museums and lots of questions to village elders, learned early to find a key person to put her in touch with performers. 
''You meet a patron of the arts in Madras, or a critic in Bombay who can open doors for you,'' she said.
Detecting probable anachronisms comes with experience, she said. 
For instance, she saw something amiss in South Korea when a dance that she knew originally represented the instrospective struggles of a Buddhist monk was performed by 50 people.
She spotted another alteration when dancers in Burma formed a boat with their bodies. 
There she drew on what she knew of China -that ''you might make movements of a boat, rocking side to side, or show water with a long blue scarf, but never something realistic like that.''
Â 
A War Intervenes
Mrs. Gordon, an only child, moved to Japan with her parents in 1929, when her father, Leo Sirota, played concerts there and stayed on to teach at the Imperial Academy. 
She attended a German school near Tokyo until Nazi teachers arrived, hardly the place for a Jewish child. 
She switched to an American school, and later moved to the United States to attend Mills College in Oakland, Calif.
Mrs. Gordon lost contact with her parents during World War II. 
While still a Mills student, she worked for the Federal Government, monitoring Tokyo Radio. 
Later she wrote broadcasts beamed to Japanese soldiers in the field - the counterpart, she notes, to Tokyo Rose.
After a stint as a researcher in New York for Time magazine, she became a civilian employee of the Army as a way to rejoin her parents in Japan. 
Assigned to Gen. Douglas MacArthur's headquarters in Tokyo, she wound up writing the womens' rights section of Japan's postwar Constitution.
She also met Lieut. 
Joseph Gordon, an interpreter, whom she later married. 
They have a daughter, Nicole, a lawyer, and a son, Geoffrey, a playwright. 
Mr. Gordon, who taught Chinese and Japanese, then switched to real estate, retired a couple of years ago and began accompanying his wife on what until then had been solo travels.
Pursuing old ways, Mrs. Gordon notes their swift passage. 
In the year since her first visit to Lhasa in 1985, she said, ''it changed from a sleepy village to a small town with a completely modern hotel, a new theater and even yakburgers.''
''With the inroads of Western culture,'' she added, ''it's wonderful to see that in some places, a lot of the original is left.''

The espionage case against a retired Central Intelligence Agency analyst began in 1983 with a tip from a Chinese defector, Government sources said today.
Prosecutors have said in court documents that the analyst, Larry Wu-Tai Chin, had admitted to Federal agents that he was a spy for the Chinese. 
According to a motion filed by prosecutors today, Mr. Chin was impressed at the agents' knowledge of his activities, so much so that he speculated aloud that his principal Chinese contact might have defected to the United States.
The motion did not disclose whether Mr. Chin's suspicions were accurate, but intelligence sources said today that the case arose from information provided by a Chinese official who fled to the West.
The prosecutors' motion, filed in Federal District Court in Alexandria, offers a rare glimpse into the techniques used by F.B.I. agents to elicit admissions from a spy suspect. 
It describes the dramatic moment on Nov. 
22 when two F.B.I. agents confronted Mr. Chin in his Virginia apartment with what the bureau says was evidence of 30 years of espionage activity.
Â 
Talk of Double Agent
The document filed today said that Mr. Chin first denied the charges, then offered to be a double agent for American intelligence and finally gave details of his career as a spy for the Chinese beginning in 1943.
Mr. Chin has pleaded not guilty. 
His attorneys have moved to suppress his statement to the agents on the ground that the F.B.I. violated his constitutional right to counsel and that he had been coerced.
The document filed by prosecutors today was a response to this motion.
It quotes Mr. Chin as questioning whether the agents had sufficient evidence, asking, ''How do I know you're not bluffing?''
In response, prosecutors said, Mark Johnson, an F.B.I. agent, described a September 1983 trip to China in which Mr. Chin was said to have met with Ou Qiming, described as his Chinese handler. 
Mr. Johnson said that Mr. Chin talked to Mr. Ou of the possibility of recruiting a fellow C.I.A. employee as a spy. 
He also mentioned his marital difficulties.
Â 
'Only Ou Knew'
Mr. Chin then told the agents, ''You have details that only Ou knew,'' according to the motion.
''Chin said the details about his wife were only known by Ou and asked where the agents obtained their information,'' the motion said. 
Mr. Chin, it said, ''speculated that Ou had defected.''
The Government sources, who asked not to be identified, would not comment on whether Mr. Ou was the defector they said was involved in the case.
Mr. Chin worked for nearly 30 years for the Foreign Broadcast Information Service, an arm of the C.I.A. that translates and interprets broadcasts and publications. 
Administration officials have said that because of his language skills Mr. Chin was also used by other sections of the C.I.A. and had access to virtually every classified intelligence document on the Far East for a period of years.
The F.B.I. said in an affidavit filed last month that from 1961 to 1967, Mr. Chin met with Mr. Ou and others while visiting Hong Kong. 
He was paid money and given an address in Canton where he could send correspondence, the F.B.I. said.
Â 
Contact in Canada
In 1976, the F.B.I. affidavit said, Mr. Ou gave Mr. Chin procedures to be used to reach Chinese agents in Canada. 
According to the F.B.I. statements, Mr. Chin would take documents home from work hidden in his clothes and briefcase and then deliver them to agents of the Chinese in Canada.
The motion said that when the agents appeared at Mr. Chin's apartment and identified themselves, Mr. Chin said, ''Why sure, come on in.''
They sat at the dining room table and said they were investigating ''the passage of classified information to the Chinese Intelligence Service.''
Mr. Chin denied any involvement in the case, the motion said.
Mr. Johnson of the F.B.I. read details of Mr. Chin's 1982 trip to Peking. 
''Chin appeared surprised with the detailed information,'' the motion said.
The agents then said they had been investigating the case a long time, the motion said. 
It continued: ''They had come to offer him a chance to explain what happened. 
They told him if he didn't want to talk to them that they would get up and leave and present the case to the Department of Justice.''
According to the motion, Mr. Chin said, ''Maybe I should seek legal counsel.''
Â 
Not Arrested at First
Mr. Johnson said Mr. Chin was not under arrest and was free to call an attorney, the motion said. 
The F.B.I. agent identified himself as an attorney.
After being confronted with the details that he thought only Mr. Ou could have known, Mr. Chin offered to confirm or deny what the agents knew, the motion said. 
They refused this offer. 
According to the motion, Mr. Chin said ''it would take a long time for him to tell everything'' and that he wanted to think it over and decide the following day whether to cooperate.
The agents then told him, ''This was his only chance to cooperate,'' the motion said.
After a pause, Mr. Chin offered to work as a double agent for the United States. 
The agents said they were not authorized to approve such an arrangement and they could only relay what he had to say to their supervisors.
''He said he would start with an outline and go back and fill it out,'' the motion said. 
''He then began with 1943.''

The Chinese Foreign Minister arrives here tomorrow on a fence-mending mission that could pave the way for a new phase of friendship between India and China.
The visit by Foreign Minister Huang Hua is the first by a senior Chinese official since Prime Minister Zhou Enlai came here in 1960. 
Within months of that visit, the relationship deteriorated over Chinese territorial claims.
Chinese Foreign Minister Huang Hua arrives in New Delhi (India) in effort to improve relations between India and China
A border war in 1962 ended in defeat for India and the Chinese seizure of a piece of territory in northeastern Kashmir known as Aksai Chin. 
The border dispute has kept the two countries apart although India took the first step toward reconciliation in 1976 by sending an ambassador to Peking after an absence of 15 years. 
In 1979, the Indian Foreign Minister visited Peking.
Foreign Minister Hua of China was scheduled to come here last year after Prime Minister Indira Gandhi had returned to power, but he canceled the trip when she accorded recognition to the Soviet-backed Cambodian Government.

Border Dispute No Stumbling Block

India has said that the proposal is unacceptable and wants talks confined to the Aksai Chin area. 
The area is now crossed by a major Chinese highway linking Tibet and Xinjiang.
Indian officials do not expect any dramatic developments to come out of Mr. Hua's visit.

file: HOLLYWOOD RETURNS TO CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
For the first time since the Communists took power in 1949, two major American film companies, Paramount Pictures and Universal Pictures, will distribute American films in China.
The films will be shown in 3,000 major theaters and 20,000 smaller theaters in Chinese cities and the countryside. 
Ticket admissions in China, which has a population of one billion, were estimated to be about 25 billion in 1985.
The two studios signed an agreement with the China Film Corporation of Peking, which controls the exhibition and distribution of all films in China. 
The financial arrangements of the deal were not disclosed, but Charles S. Paul, president of MCA Enterprises, which represented Universal, said that the initial financial value of the transaction was secondary.
''The primary impact will be cultural and strategic,'' he said. 
But he added that the financial structure of the agreement set a precedent for other more profitable arrangements.
Â 
Problems With Deals
Until now the major American movie studios have stayed out of the China market. 
The Chinese would only agree to make deals on a flat-fee basis, which Mr. Paul said was not attractive to the American companies. 
He also pointed out that China does not have stringent copyright laws, which protect against unauthorized duplication and distribution of original properties. 
However, China is working to improve those laws as a means of attracting foreign business.
As a result, although the Chinese show films from many countries around the world, only American films produced by independent companies have been shown in China for a flat fee, as well as a small number of films that were produced by independent companies, but distributed by major studios. 
For example, ''Superman'' and ''Rambo'' have been licensed for a lump sum, reportedly between $10,000 and $20,000 each.
''We asked for a percentage of the box office gross, or what is known in the U.S. as a rental fee,'' Mr. Paul said of the recent negotiations. 
''They refused.''
However, he added ''that the payment would be related to the popularity of the film, though not precisely a percentage of box office, as is the case in the United States.''
Â 
Seeking a Profit
''A rental fee arrangement is crucial,'' Mr. Paul said. 
''It gives the Chinese access to huge film libraries. 
And it gives us access to a huge audience, on terms that can eventually be profitable for both partners.''
From his Los Angeles office, Yongming Lu, the business manager for China Film, said his company would soon begin selecting films from the studios' libraries and dub them into Chinese, with the intent of exhibiting 8 to 10 films annually from the major American studios. 
Mr. Lu said that the Chinese, who are avid moviegoers, produced more than 140 films a year at the country's 15 production studios. 
In addition, he said that the Chinese showed about 50 foreign films a year.
Not only do the Chinese flock to theaters, but the country has more than 160,000 projection units, which are groups of people who travel around the countryside exhibiting films in informal settings. 
Admissions can range from the equivalent of about 15 cents to one penny. 
In some places admission charges are paid in commodities, said Mr. Paul, who recalled visiting a community where some moviegoers paid with eggs.
Last year, China Film, together with the Motion Picture Association of America, the industry trade group, organized a festival of five American films, of which the most popular were ''Kramer vs. Kramer'' and ''On Golden Pond.''
The other films were ''Coal Miner's Daughter,'' ''Star Wars'' and ''The Turning Point.''
Noting the strong audience response for ''Kramer vs. Kramer'' and ''On Golden Pond,'' Mr. Paul, who spent several months in China, said: ''Those films involved family issues and respect for elders. 
People could relate the problems and issues in the family structure.''
Until the war of 1949, the American majors showed their films in China and had offices there. 
Some companies, such as the MGM Entertainment Company, even owned theaters in Peking, Shanghai and other major cities, but after 1949 they withdrew.

The one clear reaction to the Chinese-British talks over Hong Kong's future has been in the colony's financial markets.
In the two trading sessions since discussions between Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and Chinese leaders ended last Friday, prices on the Hong Kong stock markets have fallen by more than 9 percent. 
In addition, the Hong Kong dollar dropped to its lowest level against the United States dollar since the local currency was allowed to float in late 1974.
''There has been nothing in the talks to give any comfort to Hong Kong investors and people,'' said Lawrence Chui, a director of Jardine Fleming & Company, an investment firm. 
''The reaction in the markets is what you would expect.''
HONG KONG, Sept. 
28 - The one clear reaction to the Chinese-British talks over Hong Kong's future has been in the colony's financial markets.
Yesterday, stock prices, as measured by the Hang Seng index, fell 83.74 points, the second-largest one-day decline this year. 
Today, the index retreated 23.96 points, closing at 988.66. 
The trading volume was extremely heavy both days, nearly twice the average daily volume last week.
Â 
Exchange Rate Declines
The United States dollar closed yesterday at $6.20 (Hong Kong), up from $6.11 on Saturday. 
After opening lower this morning, the local currency closed at about yesterday's level, largely because of Hong Kong dollar purchases by the Government, dealers say.
As a barometer of reaction to the British-Chinese talks, the weakness of the local currency is viewed as less significant than the stock market drop because the United States dollar is now unusually strong against all major currencies.
Stock market analysts cited three reasons for the big declines in share prices. 
First, the British-Chinese joint statement on Hong Kong, released last Friday, was less specific than many investors had hoped, giving only a general assurance that both sides wanted to maintain the ''stabilityI and prosperity'' of Hong Kong.
The differences of opinion between the two sides appear to be greater than many in Hong Kong had expected. 
Britain has made it clear that it considers the 19th-century treaties, which established its rule in Hong Kong, still valid. 
''Britain keeps her treaties,'' Mrs. Thatcher emphasized yesterday, though she added that theyzcould be ''modified.''
Â 
Chinese Seek Sovereignty
For its part, Peking has stressed that it must regain sovereignty over all of Hong Kong. 
Britain controls Hong Kong under a 99-year lease of 90 percent of the colony's land, which expires in 1997.
''The market was not expecting a sharp difference of views over the treaties,'' said Barry Yates, research director of Hoare Govett Far East Ltd.
The third factor in the big declines has been concerted selling by wealthy Chinese investors in Hong Kong, several market participants believe.
''It is not in the big guys' interest to see confidence or the stock market go higher at this time,'' one executive said. 
''This is a way of showing Peking and London that prosperity in Hong Kong is a very fragile thing.''
The stock markets are watched as a key indicator of business confidence in Hong Kong. 
Real estate issues represent about 40 percent of the market capitalization. 
Real estate prices, in turn, are viewed as an index of how much people want to live in Hong Kong and set up offices and factories here. 
Though still high, property values have, on average, declined 30 percent during the past year.
The Hong Kong stock markets are notoriously volatile. 
Analysts were reluctant to make specific predictions about the market outlook. 
Most agreed they would probably fall further in the near future, though they observed that the markets could stabilize and even turn up if the big Chinese investors decided to step in.
''They don't want to see things go down too much,'' one securities executive said. 
''After all, they do have the most to lose.''

file: HONG KONG SAVORS ITS INTERLUDE.txt
text:
ï»¿
IT was lunchtime in one of this British colony's finest Chinese restaurants, a plushly carpeted aerie overlooking Victoria Harbor. 
Clear skies in the wake of the annual typhoons made for a picture-postcard view of junks and freighters and Navy frigates from the United States; behind them, grey-green mountains stretched into China.
Below, in the central district, where skyscrapers produce an aura of an Asian Manhattan, sidewalks pulsed with the energy that has turned this patch of territory into one of the world's most important financial and trading centers. 
In the restaurant, the tables were filled with Chinese and Americans and Europeans brought together by the deals in the textiles, toys and electronics that pour out of the industrial districts of Kowloon, the teeming city across the harbor.
Lunchtime talk was mostly of discounts and freight rates and currency fluctuations, but three middle-aged Chinese at a corner table paused between servings of steamed prawns and beef Szechuan-style to take up a matter that has become almost all-consuming among the colony's middle class: how to obtain foreign passports or other papers that would allow them to emigrate more easily. 
An intense-looking man with gold-rimmed spectacles explained how an acquaintance recently acquired a Fiji passport. 
The man's companions chuckled, then asked for details.
A year after Britain formally agreed to surrender sovereignty over Hong Kong to China on July 1, 1997, the mood in the business community is a mixture of confidence and caution. 
With the removal of the uncertainties that arose during the sometimes bitter negotiations between London and Peking, the economy is back to a healthy growth rate. 
This year, growth was about 4.5 percent, down from the 9 percent growth rate achieved on record export levels in 1984 but a major improvement over the early 1980's, when fears of a unilateral Chinese takeover and a recession in the United States combined to bring about a slump.
The stock market, too, has achieved a four-year high. 
Parcels of luxury real estate, which fell to a fraction of their values in 1983, are once more fetching record bids. 
A decline in exports overseas has been offset by a leap in the colony's traditional staple, trade with China.
The 1984 agreement has played a major part in this, assuring investors that they have at least a few years in which business will be played by the old rules, or by something close to them. 
For the last two decades, Hong Kong has been a place where investors could pour capital into hotels, office blocks and cross-harbor tunnels and retrieve it with a profit in as little as three to five years. 
Almost everybody agrees that there is that much time, perhaps more, before the shadows of 1997 cast a pall.
Despite the inevitable crowding in this 404-square-mile territory, most of the 5.5 million inhabitants are not likely to have any choice but to stay. 
Most potential destinations, including Britain, have made it plain they could not handle an influx of refugees. 
For these people, the handover could be a nightmare - a plunge from a freewheeling society that is relatively affluent by Asian standards into one that could mirror that of China which, despite China's recent reforms, is still considered repressive and backward by most in Hong Kong.
In the past 12 months China has been energetic in trying to calm anxieties, at least insofar as they relate to the maintenance of the colony's standard of living. 
It has worked with Britain on complex technical issues such as the establishment of an independent Hong Kong shipping registry. 
It has expanded its already substantial investments here, moving on at least two occasions to save major locally owned enterprises from collapse. 
Beyond this, it has lost no opportunity to voice its determination to keep the territory prosperous. 
The message was repeated over and over during the two-week visit here earlier this month of Ji Pengfei, the former Chinese Foreign Minister who is in charge of the Peking Government's Hong Kong Office. 
That agency has responsibility for drawing up the constitution, under which the territory will operate as a ''special administrative region'' of China after 1997. 
NEVERTHELESS, talk of eventual emigration is common among merchants, brokers and lawyers, and without them, Hong Kong could swiftly turn into an expensive drain on Peking. 
Thoughts of leaving are perhaps inevitable, since more than three-quarters of the Chinese families in Hong Kong either fled or are descended from people who fled China after the revolution succeeded in 1949. 
''Remember, most of us are refugees from Communism in the first place,'' said Martin Lee, a British-trained lawyer.
Lately, Mr. Lee, who is 47 years old, has been leading a local outcry over statements from Peking that there should be no ''democratization'' of local political processes in advance of 1997. 
The British agreement with Peking refers to an elected legislature after 1997, and to the appointment ''by election or through consultations'' of a Chinese chief executive to replace the British governor.
The apparent balking at political change has raised concerns about Peking's willingness to honor other guarantees in the 1984 accord. 
These include commitments to preserve Hong Kong's ''capitalist'' system for 50 years after 1997, along with its stock market, its convertible currency and its free port.
Nevertheless, some local executives say that arguments about prospects for the territory after 1997 obscure the fact that Hong Kong even now is moving more into China's economic orbit for reasons that have little to do with the 1984 accord. 
At the end of 1984, the territory was still the world's largest exporter of clothing, fur garments and toys, and nobody here sees much danger of those markets disappearing. 
But official figures suggest that these boom industries of the 1970's are gradually yielding their dominance and that Hong Kong is re-emphasizing its historic role as the gateway to China, but this time on a much larger scale.
Hong Kong suffered a 5 percent decline in the manufacturing work force this year, but offsetting that has been an impressive 10 percent jump in employment in the wholesale, retail and service sectors - with much of the gain in businesses that are profiting from the rapid economic growth spurred by Deng Xiaoping's ''modernization'' drive in China.
The executives here say that this basic shift in the Hong Kong economy involves more than just the slowdown in economic growth in the United States, the colony's largest export market. 
They point out that Hong Kong also faces growing competition from other Asian countries, including China, that have low-cost labor, and that the colony is having difficulty moving from low-technology industries into more sophisticated fields. 
THESE trends make the China trade increasingly important. 
In the first nine months of 1985, that trade leapt by 33 percent over 1984, to a total of 88 billion Hong Kong dollars, or $11.3 billion United States dollars, more than a quarter of the colony's total trade. 
While more than half the total was accounted for by ''re-export trade,'' goods that pass through Hong Kong on their way to and from other markets, there was also a more than 50 percent leap in Hong Kong's own exports to the mainland. 
How significant the trend is for Hong Kong can be measured from figures that show total trade with China in 1979, at the beginning of Mr. Deng's reform program, to be barely 17 billion Hong Kong dollars, roughly 15 percent of the total expected this year.
Without the increase in trade with the mainland, the territory would almost certainly have been in a mild recession this year, a point that Peking's Mr. Ji made during his visit, reminding audiences that Hong Kong was becoming increasingly dependent on China's prosperity.
China is making that point in other ways. 
At a choice site near the Hong Kong waterfront, work will begin soon on a new building designed by I.M. 
Pei as the local headquarters of the Bank of China, Peking's foreign exchange bank. 
Apart from the personal gratification involved for Mr. Pei - his father was the bank's first Hong Kong manager in the 1930's -the building's triangular glass towers and its height, at 70 stories the tallest in the colony, will make for a powerful symbol. 
The new headquarters nearby of the locally controlled Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, giant of the territory's banking industry, stands only 47 stories and has been pilloried for a skeletal appearance that one local critic compared with ''an oil-cracking plant.''
Peking has also been pumping in large amounts of money to save Conic Investment Ltd., a major manufacturer of televisions, radios and electronic components, and to prop up the failing Ka Wah Bank, which was founded by local Chinese. 
In both cases, Peking's money men consulted local experts closely before making their moves, and won plaudits for their sophistication.
''We're not dealing any longer with the baggy-suited chaps in sandals,'' one British financial official observed. 
''They still come, of course, but more and more we're seeing people who could hold their own anywhere, in tailoring or know-how.''
There are now more than 300 Chinese-owned enterprises in the territory. 
Many of these are part of China Resources Holdings Ltd., the huge trading and investment enterprise that is the mainland's answer to traditional British ''hongs,'' family-controlled conglomerates like Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd. and Swire Pacific Ltd., whose dominance of business in the territory has faded rapidly in recent years before the challenge of local Chinese entrepreneurs. 
One reason for this, critics of the British say, is that they have been slow to adjust to new circumstances - including the importance of the China market.
But lately, even the hongs have been altering their approach. 
Since Jardine's moved its legal address to Bermuda in 1984, a largely symbolic move that deeply angered Peking, the British-owned companies have shown a new sensitivity to politics and geography. 
One example came last month, when Swire's announced that it would make a public offering of up to 25 percent of the equity in Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd., a 70 percent-owned subsidiary that has been the company's most profitable holding. 
Analysts said the move was a response to the formation of a new Hong Kong-registered airline, Hongkong Dragon Airlines Ltd., in which Peking has a substantial stake.
By admitting Hong Kong investors to part-ownership of the airline, Swire's chairman, Michael Miles, evidently hopes to give the carrier a local presence that will protect it once Peking controls Hong Kong's Kai Tak Airport, where Cathay is based. 
But the view among airline industry watchers here was that the move could be a case of too little, too late.
Dragonair's chairman is Sir Yue-kong Pao, the Hong Kong shipping magnate who has been developing close ties with Peking, and its appeal to China has been enhanced by its announcement that it will train Chinese flight crews. 
Cathay Pacific has operated in Hong Kong for 39 years and has numerous Chinese employees, but none among the 500 people it employs in its cockpits.
In some ways, the airline's dilemma epitomizes the problems facing many of the British companies that once ruled the roost here. 
The sons of Britain's upper classes who have long enjoyed the fast route into the companies' executive suites have proven no match for the nimble Chinese entrepreneurs in recent years. 
Jardine's, largest of all the ''hongs,'' has seen its assets shrink by more than a quarter in the past few years.
In the meantime, the influence of American companies has risen sharply, to the point where there are now more than 15,000 Americans living here, employed by about 800 American companies with local offices, factories or joint ventures.
For the foreigners, 1997 poses less of a problem. 
Privately, many Britons say they will return home before then. 
Americans tend to be more sanguine about the prospects - but they, too, have passports that permit a relaxed view.
Â 
THE RICH FOLK GO A'COURTING IN PEKING
HONG KONG -In the year since Britain signed the agreement under which Hong Kong will revert to China in 1997, local millionaires have been conspicuously courting Peking's favor. 
One name that crops up frequently is that of Sir Yue-kong Pao, known as Sir Y. K., chairman of the Worldwide Shipping Company, whose maritime interests, real estate, and other holdings have made him one of the colony's richest men.
The shipping magnate - the ''Sir'' comes from a knighthood bestowed upon him by Queen Elizabeth - rarely gives interviews. 
But associates say that he believes that China's official guarantees will matter less than the personal relationships that leaders here can build up with the top men in China, and the degree to which they can ''educate'' the Peking elite in the things that make Hong Kong tick. 
To this end, Sir Y. K. has become a frequent visitor to Peking and his native town of Ningbo, east of Shanghai, and has more than once been a guest of China's pre-eminent leader, Deng Xiaoping, in the Great Hall of the People.
Along the way he made a major contribution to the construction costs of Peking's newest luxury hotel, the Zhao Long, whose opening last month was the occasion for one of Mr. Deng's rare appearances at a public function outside the Great Hall. 
Sir Y. K. has also pledged nearly $16 million for the establishment of a university in Ningbo.
None of this is much different from the courting of the British establishment that has been going on for decades among prominent Chinese in Hong Kong. 
What has disturbed some people here is Sir Y. K.'s political stance. 
Along with Li Kaxing, another wealthy businessman, Sir Y. K. was appointed by Peking to participate in the drafting of the basic law that will govern Hong Kong after the transition. 
It is an open secret that one of his first moves in the drafting committee was to speak against direct elections.
Few here see this as a conspiracy. 
Rather, many believe that wealthy citizens like Sir Y. K. find themselves, paradoxically, sharing Peking's anxieties about popular government. 
People like Sir Y. K., it is believed, fear that elected legislators might usher in an expensive social welfare program. 
Apart from a huge public housing program that has provided homes for more than half the population, Hong Kong currently has only a rudimentary welfare system. 
Taxes are at levels low enough to be the envy of entrepreneurs throughout Asia.
