THE REVISION OF HISTORY IS A NEVER-ending process. 
Each generation, it is said, rewrites history in the light of its own experience. 
But when the historical event is defeat in war, as Japan experienced in World War II and the United States experienced in Vietnam, the impulse to ignore or explain away or tidy up the defeat is particularly strong.
In such cases, history is an embarrassment. 
If the defeat is marked by widescale atrocity on the battlefield or by initial aggression of the defeated power - as in Japan's case - the embarrassment is that much more humiliating, and the impulse to sanitize it is that much stronger. 
A country is apt to go through a period of amnesia, when its citizens simply do not want to think about the downbeat side of its recent past.
The loss of memory can go on for years. 
Sometimes, after the period of amnesia, history re-emerges in a distorted fashion. 
Its embarrassments are not as clearly recalled as its heroics or its near-victories. 
A country's own suffering is better remembered than the suffering it caused.
Inevitably, there are questions: What should succeeding generations be taught about the darker periods, what weight should those times be given?
On a recent trip to Japan, I explored such questions with a number of Japanese educators and writers and government officials, for I expected that the problems the Japanese face, and perhaps the solutions they have found, 40 years after World War II, might tell us something about America's memories of its own dark periods. 
IN A SPARE, UNADORNED CLASSROOM AT HIROSHIMA University, across from the only structure on the campus to survive the atomic blast, a frail Asian scholar named Humio Kobayashi began his lecture in a course titled ''Comprehensive View of War and Peace.''
Speaking softly, he opened with a challenge.
''You are,'' he said, ''ignorant of your country's aggressive past. 
You are not responsible for that ignorance, because you have been forced to be that way. 
But if you are to have a true concept of peace, you need a historical context.''
An unrelenting two-hour discourse on the bellicose instincts of the Japanese nation in the 20th century followed. 
With quiet intensity, Professor Kobayashi spoke of Hiroshima, with its military port of Ujina, which became the chief military depot for the invasions of China in 1894 and 1931; of the victory over Russia in 1904 and 1905 that validated Japanese imperialism in Korea and originated the prejudice against Korean people by the Japanese, which endures today; and of the atrocity at Nanjing in 1937 that showed the Japanese potential for barbarism.
In a hushed classroom, Professor Kobayashi drew his conclusion: ''It is said that over 200,000 people were killed in the atomic-bomb attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. 
. . . But this tragedy of Hiroshima happened as a natural course of events. 
From 1931 to 1945, we Japanese killed more than 10 million Chinese, the majority civilians. 
Have you heard about that?
''Some say, 'But that was different. 
Chinese are different from us.'
Even some survivors of the atomic bomb here sometimes say that. 
Of course, atomic bombings can not be countenanced. 
But there was a reason. 
Japanese were the aggressors, and so it was inevitable that they would end up as victims.''
At the end of two hours, two graduate students, both of whom had been born in the 1960's, when Japan's era of economic growth took off, approached the front of the classroom to discuss their trip to Nanjing the year before with Professor Kobayashi. 
The first student spoke softly of walking along a road near a site where reportedly 10,000 Chinese had been slaughtered by Japanese soldiers. 
The area had recently been excavated and human bones were clearly visible. 
As he spoke of his shame, the youth's voice cracked, and he concluded quickly with the hope that the students in the class could see this for themselves.
The professor was not surprised by the young man's reaction.
''When I take students to China . . . students who were brought up in affluence,'' Kobayashi said, ''who have never seen poverty anywhere and don't know it exists, who have lived entirely in a peaceful Japan, they go through culture shock. 
This is what I can do as an individual. 
All educators must share this kind of mission, for if this present trend of beautifying the seamy side of our history continues, history could repeat itself.''
T HERE IS A SENSE now that Japan has arrived at a historical bench mark, at which economic power alone begins to seem hollow. 
Concerns about the ''Japanese soul'' are moving to the fore. 
For the first time in 40 years, basic institutions are being questioned; among them, education is one of the most hotly debated.
Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone has declared that the postwar era of Japanese history is now at an end. 
Forty years after Japan's humiliation, a new era, unassociated with that humiliation, must begin. 
All institutions, especially those imposed upon Japan after its defeat, must now undergo a ''total re-evaluation.''
Using accountants' parlance, he asserts that it is time ''to settle accounts'' and ''to close the books.''
A new educational system must match the social changes and the cultural developments of the last 40 years. 
To that end, he has formed the Provisional Council on Educational Reform. 
From its early draft proposals, the commission -whose members are, for the most part, conservative and nationalistic - is clearly looking for ways to strengthen traditional values and moral education.
But all this talk of new societies, of reviving traditional values, of reinforcing moral education, make some Japanese nervous indeed. 
It is, they say, merely a code for reviving prewar imperial values: what Nakasone is really up to is a master plan for the remilitarization of Japan; for scrapping the peace constitution with its total renunciation of war; for teaching a patriotism that is dangerous.
The controversial novelist Kenzaburo Oe feels, for example, that talk of a new era is nothing short of an attempt to nullify the lessons of World War II and to undermine the unique Japanese vision, molded in the ashes of defeat. 
That vision was of a world without nuclear weapons, in which Japan would be the world's spiritual leader. 
For Oe, whose work examines the spiritual emptiness of a nation fixated upon material wealth, the authenticity of Japan's spiritual leadership is rooted not only in the wretchedness of a nuclear holocaust, but also in the honest acknowledgment of the Nanjing massacre as a poisonous seed.
The official visit of Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone in August to the Yasukuni Shrine for the Japanese who died in World War II only served to exacerbate fears of a new militarism and a state Shintoism. 
Although the Prime Minister tried to put the worries to rest, the symbolic move aroused condemnation at home and abroad. 
In its first official reaction, China attacked the visit, contending that it ''pandered to and has actually emboldened those in Japan who have always wanted to deny the aggressive nature of the war and to reverse the verdict on Japanese militarism long condemned to the dustbin of history.''
Then, in September, on the anniversary of the Mukden incident in 1931 that led to the Japanese invasion of Manchuria, more than 1,000 students marched in Peking, shouting anti-Japanese slogans and protesting Nakasone's visit to the shrine. 
Again, the Japanese seemed to be caught out at the virulence of the reaction. 
Just this month, bowing to Chinese sentiment, Nakasone canceled his intended second visit to the Yasukuni Shrine. 
Nonetheless, two weeks ago, the topic of a revival of militarism arose at talks between the Foreign Minister of Japan, Shintaro Abe, and the Foreign Minister of China, Wu Xueqian.
Americans might take offense at Nakasone's official homage as well. 
In a prominent place at the Yasukuni Shrine, a letter from a 15-year-old Okinawa boy is displayed. 
He was embroiled in the battle for Okinawa - one of the bloodiest of World War II - in which 12,000 American soldiers died. 
''I wear the uniform of the Iron Blood Imperial Corps to demolish the United States and Great Britain,'' the letter, in graceful calligraphy, reads. 
''There will come a time when Okinawa sees victory.''
Three years ago, worries about militarism surfaced in Japan in a curious way. 
Over a period of four months, torrid headlines charged that the Ministry of Education was out to ''water down,'' ''prettify,'' ''sanitize'' or otherwise ignore the unpleasant facts of modern Japanese history. 
Extraordinarily, the controversy became a serious diplomatic flap, when China and Korea leaped in with emotional official protests.
At issue was a pattern of textbook revisions that made historical embarrassments more palatable. 
In Japan, the education ministry validates all textbooks for use in elementary and secondary schools. 
It is called the authorization procedure, and is justified on the notion of insuring a standard level of excellence in the schools.
Authorization systems of this sort are scarcely unheard of in democratic countries. 
In Germany, the 11 states approve school texts, and each state has specific guidelines for sensitive subjects, such as how to deal with the Third Reich. 
In France, the Ministere de l'Education Nationale decides what French schoolchildren should be taught about the French debacle in the Algerian war and the weak resistance during the Nazi occupation. 
An old saw about French education holds that at any given minute in the school year one can know the precise page of the precise textbook that every sixth grader in France is studying.
The Japanese position that its own authorization system has only to do with standards of excellence foundered, however, when, in 1982, it came to light that the newly authorized high-school textbooks used semantics to obscure painful historical memories. 
Just as the United States' invasion of Cambodia was presented as an ''incursion'' and the invasion of Grenada was painted as a ''rescue mission,'' so the Japanese invasion of China in 1931 had been recast as an ''advance.''
Still worse, the Nanjing massacre of 1937 had become an episode of ''mob confusion,'' during which ''innumerable civilians and soldiers were killed'' -no mention by whom, no mention that fatalities numbered between 200,000 and 300,000. 
The Chinese Government was outraged, and the official Peking Review charged that, in distorting historical facts, the education ministry sought to ''obliterate from the memory of Japan's younger generation the history of Japan's aggression against China and other Asian countries so as to lay the basis for reviving militarism.''
In Korea, where Japan tried systematically for 40 years to merge the Korean identity into the Japanese empire, the Government was livid at the new ''updating'' of history. 
Not only had the annexation of Korea in 1910 become an ''advance'' of Japanese forces, but the March 1 uprising of Korean resisters in 1919 had become a ''riot.''
The outlawing of the Korean language became ''education in the Japanese language.''
Koreans were ''conscripted'' rather than forcibly impressed into service. 
Prayer to the Japanese spirits at Shinto shrines was ''encouraged,'' not required. 
The last Korean king simply ''resigned.''
No mention was made of the fact that during World War II young Korean girls from the countryside were forcibly packed off to the front lines to serve as ''wartime ladies of consolation'' for Japanese troops.
Within the conservative education ministry, there was consternation at the virulence of the official Chinese and Korean protests. 
Privately, the intrusion from abroad was deeply resented: ''How would you feel if another country complained officially that the teaching of Pearl Harbor in your schools was inaccurate and provocative?'' asked Teiichi Sato, until recently the head of the textbook division at the ministry.
But diplomacy takes precedence over education and, because both China and Korea made Japan's remorse about the past a ''principle of major importance'' in diplomatic relations, Japan capitulated. 
Good relations with her two neighbors are just too important for the future. 
The Japanese promised to reinstate the words ''aggression'' and ''invasion'' to its future history texts.
Japan also promised to rectify 14 of the 19 changes demanded by Korea. 
(As yet, it has not agreed to deal with ''wartime ladies of consolation.'') The tone of national regret was evident in a note to the Korean Government. 
Acknowledging ''the great pain'' Japan had inflicted on Asian peoples, the Government pledged itself ''not to repeat such past deeds.''
Today, resentment over the meddling from abroad lingers at the education ministry.
''We are in transition, trying to go beyond the psychology of the postwar era,'' said Isao Amagi, formerly the vice minister of education. 
''The American attitude after the war was that everything before the war was wrong. 
After the war, we were cut off from the past. 
We cannot deny history, good or bad. 
But we have a long history on our back. 
While we must be aware that the Chinese and Korean people still hold anti-Japanese feelings, we don't want to exaggerate past bad events.''
Akio Nakajima, the senior division chief in charge of textbooks for elementary and secondary education, was more blunt: ''For 30 years, we have criticized ourselves severely. 
This should pass. 
There is no need for continuous cleansing now. 
We must see history from a more neutral point of view.''
In searching for a ''neutral point of view,'' Nakajima and others at the education ministry are struggling with the subtle problems of the defeated nation, while they try to find the right emphasis for certain historical embarrassments.
Clearly, education must avoid propagandizing, which was so evident in imperial Japan. 
Then, education was a tool of indoctrination. 
History textbooks for children began with the divine origins of the Emperor at Ise, and every school had a copy of the Imperial Rescript on Education, defining the virtues of the good Japanese citizen: filial piety, affection for friends, love of parents, respect for elders and obedience to the Emperor. 
Regularly, the Imperial Rescript was read at school functions; once, when it was misread, the bumbling principal committed suicide to atone.
After World War II, American occupation authorities censored Japanese school books, blacking out whole sec-tions of text. 
After the occupation, new texts rarely referred to the Emperor, and the Russo-Japanese War was described in a paragraph. 
In that lesson, the picture of a victorious Japanese admiral outside Port Arthur was replaced with a photo of President Theodore Roosevelt adjudicating the 1905 Treaty of Portsmouth between Russia and Japan in New Hampshire.
In effect, Japan was cut off from its cultural heritage. 
Historical heroes vanished from the texts, and the pendulum swung toward a ''scientific'' approach to history, one not so very different from the new genre in this country called ''Vietnam revisionism.''
Social structures and economic forces, rather than the acts of individual men, were said to move history. 
But, in the opinion of many educators, the pendulum swung too far. 
Now the problem of the education ministry is to find the correct median point between imperial propaganda and the influences of American conquerors. 
It is trying to rehumanize Japanese history. 
''We need more heroes now, not just political and wartime heroes, but cultural heroes,'' said Isao Amagi. 
''We must teach young people what those heroes did and how they served the nation.''
What about historical villains?
Upon this tender point, it is very hard to get any forthright opinion at all, much less a consensus. 
The prime candidate would seem to be Gen. Hideki Tojo who, as the Japanese Prime Minister at the time of Pearl Harbor, symbolizes to Americans the bushido spirit of Japanese military fanaticism in World War II. 
But he is scarcely mentioned in the textbooks. 
Masanori Komiya, a 19-year-old honors student at a superior Tokyo high school, knew of Tojo only as ''a bad politician'' who failed to control the military. 
When pressed for reasons for the war and for names of those who might be accountable, he blurted out: ''We don't have anything inside of us that compels us to ask our fathers why. 
Nothing to suggest blame or placing responsibility.''
In his inability to identify culprits, young Komiya was, to some extent, exhibiting an essential Japanese trait. 
In a country long ruled by consensus and factions, responsibility is seldom placed on individual leaders.
I was struck by this fact during an interview with Ryotaro Shiba, perhaps Japan's best-known historical novelist, who is something of a cross between Bruce Catton and Gore Vidal. 
Referring to Tojo as ''the midget who held the magic stick of supreme military power,'' Shiba said: ''He was a ghost - or a skeleton. 
It is a waste of time to look for answers in him. 
It is important to try to define the magic that lay in the policies then, and to see how those policies of collective leadership were executed.''
Japanese bridle at the association of Tojo with Hitler, for time has softened the once-harsh attitude toward Tojo. 
(For years, Tojo was disdained and ridiculed for his bungled attempt at suicide when American G.I.'s ar-rived at his home to arrest him.) ''The Germans could blame everything on Hitler,'' said Teiichi Sato. 
''His discrimination policy was his own. 
In our case, leadership was collective. 
Everyone has to bear the burden of the past.''
When everyone is guilty, individu-als are exonerated. 
Historically, the acceptance of collective guilt took the form of a statement on Aug. 
28, 1945, by Prince Higashikuni, who was the Prime Minister of a caretaker Government for the first two months after the war. 
Known as the ''confession of a hundred million people,'' it implicated every Japanese citizen in the war and in the defeat. 
Higashikuni felt that collective confession was the first step toward reconstruction of Japan.
Some trace this unwillingness to consign political blame back to the imperial system. 
Only the Emperor could declare war, thus the political leadership behind him was absolved. 
And yet, in this, the 60th year of Emperor Hirohito's reign, few are ready to castigate the kindly old man. 
Instead - again a matter of emphasis - it has become a hallowed verity in Japan that the Emperor, not the Americans, graciously ended the Pacific war by breaking a deadlock between the fanatics and the doves in the war cabinet with his vote for the nation's surrender.
Meanwhile, in Aichi prefecture, Gen. Hideki Tojo is buried alongside the six other men executed by Americans as war criminals. 
The inscription on the sepulcher reads: ''The Tomb of Seven Martyrs.''
Other potential villains are even less likely to be recognized: Nobusuke Kishi, Tojo's minister of commerce and industry, who was tried as a Class A war criminal and sentenced to three years in Sugamo Prison, is known as a leader of the Reconstruction Era in Japan who signed the United States-Japan Security Treaty. 
Between 1957 and 1960, he was Japan's Prime Minister. 
Today, the 89-year-old statesman wants to eliminate Article 9 from the Japanese Constitution. 
That article renounces war as an instrument of national policy. 
Old voices, even from the old militarist past, are still respected.
A T SOPHIA UNIVERSITY, Prof. Masao Kunihiro turned over his politics and economics class to me, so that I might ask his students a few questions.
Virtually every student in the class of 200 said that he had been taught nothing of Japanese history from 1930, or only the sketchiest details. 
The emphasis was on ancient eras and the Middle Ages. 
By the time a teacher reached the Meiji Era, which commenced in 1868, the pace of instruction started to pick up speed. 
Many students told of their teachers' ''running out of time'' at the end of the school year, just before reaching 1930, and of being instructed, if students were interested, ''to read the rest of the book'' on their own. 
Not a single student could remember having been asked a question relating to modern Japanese history on the all-important college entrance examinations they had taken.
Thus, it became clear that all the questions about what cast to give events such as the Nanjing massacre, Pearl Harbor, the invasion of China, the atomic bombs and the colonization of Korea, are really moot. 
As a practical matter, history from 1930 is simply not taught. 
Teachers consider the post-1930 period too fraught with political awkwardness. 
Nor is there much interest in the 30's among scholars in Japanese universities. 
(This contrasts sharply with Germany, where scholarship on the 1920's and 30's is voluminous.) As a result, young Japanese have virtually no notion of how Japan got into World War II, what major leaders were responsible, or whether Japan's cause was righteous or immoral. 
The cataclysm simply happened in the ''flow of history.''
It was something like a typhoon, which could not have been stopped and for which no one, least of all Emperor Hirohito, was held to be responsible.
One hears a great deal about Japanese ''peace education.''
But there is an irony to this; the curriculum is superficial, inconsistently used and lacking in grounding or follow-up. 
What instruction does exist emphasizes Japan as the victim of the war. 
''Peace education days'' are designated by the dates of American attacks on Japanese areas: June 23 in Okinawa, the day the battles ended there; May 29 in Yokohama, when the city received its most devastating bombing; July 7 in Kofu, for the same reason, and, of course, Aug. 
6 in Hiroshima and Aug. 
9 in Nagasaki.
In response to official pressure, the graphic detail with which the bombings at Hiroshima and Nagaski were once described in school texts has been watered down over the years. 
Recently, there has been a sharp decline in visits by schoolchildren to the frightfully realistic Peace Memorial Museum in Hiroshima. 
Such visits, students told me, are strongly discouraged now by high-school administrators, who prefer instead that students visit Kyoto or Nara, the graceful ancient capitals of Japan where an affluent young citizen can learn lessons of Japan's culture and past. 
Atomic bombs are downbeat. 
''The trend now is to emphasize the upbeat side of our modernization,'' novelist Kenzaburo Oe commented, ''Japanese are supposed to talk of Toyotas, not Toyota traffic.''
A current high-school text in wide use, written by three well-known Tokyo University professors, devotes part of only one sentence to the nuclear events. 
It reads: ''While the Japanese Government was trying to deal with the Potsdam Declaration, on Aug. 
6 in Hiroshima and Aug. 
9 in Nagaski, the United Stated dropped atomic bombs.''
There is nothing written about the special nature of the devastation, and there is no picture. 
By contrast, a 1953 text contained a bizarre Goya-esque painting of humans at the epicenter -next to copious details of the holocaust.
The way in which textbooks handle the atomic blasts is at the heart of the case of Prof. Saburo Ienaga. 
In 1963, Ienaga, professor emeritus of the Tokyo University of Education, submitted a revised version of his Japanese history for authorization to the education ministry. 
It was not approved. 
Of the 300 complaints leveled by the ministry, Ienaga considered two-thirds of them to be political in nature. 
Two offending pictures dealt with Hiroshima -a mushroom cloud and the demolished city. 
These, Ienaga was told, were ''too gloomy'' for children. 
Another showed a war casualty with a gruesome artificial arm standing next to a sign asking for donations. 
Underneath, the author's caption read: ''We should never have this kind of victim in war again. 
That is why we have the Peace Constitution.''
The ministry objected, said Ienaga, because the picture was ''too cruel for children.''
In 1965, Ienaga sued the Government. 
Twenty years later, his case is still in the courts. 
It is famous now in Japan, and behind the professor is a nationwide organization that claims more than 20,000 adherents. 
Its purpose is to destroy the authorization system. 
Of the controversial picture of the maimed casualty, Ienaga commented: ''The education ministry camouflages its control with this talk of what is suitable for children. 
Their objection to that picture is an excuse. 
That picture is not cruel. 
I was restrained. 
I could have used other pictures.''
Ienaga withdrew for a moment to his library and returned with a picture book, opening it to a double-page spread depicting bodies strewn across a field after the firebombing of Tokyo by United States planes, resembling somewhat the photographs of My Lai:
''One picture of a maimed victim?
Compared to the enormity of war, that one picture is nothing.''
Often, throughout modern Japan, one feels a visceral revulsion of war, even though there is no thorough understanding - or any widespread attempt to understand - the causes of war. 
For the most part, one hears only: ''It must never happen again.''
''That is the kind of promise my adolescent son would make,'' a social psychologist at Keio University said. 
''It is a promise made and quickly forgotten.''

text:

King Hussein of Jordan and an Arab League delegation arrived in China today, hopeful of winning Chinese support for a Middle East peace compromise.
King Hussein and the delegation arrived from Pakistan, where they dined with President Mohammad Zia ul-Haq during a 17-hour stopover en route from Moscow.
The tour is aimed at winning support from the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council for the Arab League peace plan agreed upon at Fez, Morocco. 
King Hussein will travel to the United States this month.
PEKING, Dec. 
5 (UPI) - King Hussein of Jordan and an Arab League delegation arrived in China today, hopeful of winning Chinese support for a Middle East peace compromise.
China's new Foreign Minister, Wu Xueqian, met the delegation, and talks with senior Chinese officials were expected to begin Monday.
Â 
'There Are Many Questions'
At a 15-minute airport news conference in Islamabad, King Hussein raised the possibility of a compromise between President Reagan's plan for Middle East peace and the eight-point plan drafted by Arab heads of state at Fez.
''This is what we are attempting to ascertain during the coming phase and hopefully the situation would become clearer as we proceed and progress,'' King Hussein said. 
''There are many questions we would like to receive answers to.''
King Hussein did not specify on which points in the Reagan plan the Arabs would seek clarification. 
China has consistently supported the Palestine Liberation Organization and opposed Israel. 
The Arab League's eight-point proposal calls for a full-fledged Palestinian ''state'' on Israelioccupied territory, while Mr. Reagan's plan calls for a Palestinian ''homeland'' linked with Jordan.
Â 
Held Talks With Andropov
King Hussein is believed to be exploring the attitude of world leaders toward an affiliation between Jordan and the P.L.O. 
In Moscow, King Hussein and the Arab delegation held talks with the new Soviet Communist Party leader, Yuri V. Andropov, who said the Reagan plan was useless.
King Hussein was asked in Islamabad how he would procede now that Mr. Andropov had rejected the Reagan plan and Washington had opposed the Fez plan.
''Our mission has been to explain the eight-point Fez plan,'' the King said. 
''This is what we have concentrated upon throughout our visits so far, and once we have a complete picture we will put it together to see where do we go.''

file: HU_S OUSTER_ DENG_S ROLE__Did He Drop Protege Or Was He Forced_.txt
text:
ï»¿
The abrupt ouster of Hu Yaobang, China's Communist Party chief, raises the question whether the move was engineered by Deng Xiaoping, the country's paramount leader, or was forced on Mr. Deng by increasingly powerful hard-liners in the party.
State Department officials sought today to play down the importance of the dismissal of Mr. Hu, long the protege of the 82-year-old Mr. Deng and apparently his choice as successor.
''Deng has now got to find a new successor, but there is evidence that he decided he wasn't ready to retire and didn't like feeling being pushed out by Hu,'' one official said.
But a number of academic specialists disagreed, contending that Mr. Hu's ouster could be a serious setback to Mr. Deng's plans to create a more orderly political system and modernize the country's economy.
''This has to be seen as a serious development and one that runs counter to much that Deng was attempting to change over the past eight years,'' said Michel Oksenberg, a professor of political science at the University of Michigan who was the China specialist on the National Security Council under President Carter.
Among the effects of Mr. Hu's ouster, Mr. Oksenberg said, could be the disruption of Mr. Deng's plans to insure an orderly succession and to reassure the country's intellectuals that the Communists will not slip back into the political struggles of the Cultural Revolution.
Mr. Oksenberg, like other academic experts, acknowledged that he had been caught by surprise by the dismissal of the 71-year-old Mr. Hu, a leading advocate of introducing more market forces in China's economy and loosening the Communist Party's tight political controls.
Â 
Protests by Students
Mr. Hu's ouster came after a wave of demonstrations by students demanding greater democracy and after resistance by hard-line Communist officials to Mr. Hu's efforts to offer more freedom. 
But exactly what caused Mr. Hu's downfall remained uncertain, Mr. Oksenberg and others said.
''I think the student demonstrations were only a pretext, the straw that broke the camel's back,'' said Merle Goldman, a professor of Chinese history at Boston University. 
''His fundamental problem was that he had alienated the conservatives, who put pressure on Deng.''
As an example of the political changes that Mr. Hu championed and that annoyed the hard-liners, Mrs. Goldman recalled that in 1984 he overturned a decision to have the Communist Party present a pre-selected slate of officers at a national writers conference.
Instead, after some writers appealed, Mr. Hu told the gathering to vote by secret ballot, and several outspoken liberals were elected, including Liu Binyan, China's most popular and widely read author.
Â 
'It's a Great Shame'
Mr. Liu, whom Mr. Deng attacked by name earlier this week for helping foster the liberal mood in which the student protests took place, was a close friend of Mr. Hu. He had told associates that only Mr. Hu protected him from earlier reprisals for his frequent writings about corruption among party officials.
Roderick MacFarquhar, a professor of government at Harvard University, said Mr. Hu's ouster raised the question whether a Communist nation such as China ''can liberate itself'' to pursue the kind of rapid economic growth that has transformed the other countries of Asia.
''The rights and wrongs of what happened to Hu are not as important as the institutional question,'' Mr. MacFarquhar said. 
''What Deng has done is undermine the succession process which he had so laboriously set in place. 
It's a great shame, because China is now no further along than it was under Mao. 
When Deng goes, struggle will break out again over the succession.''
Mr. Hu, who joined the Communist Red Army guerrillas as a 14-year-old and took part in the Long March, was like a son to Mr. Deng, Mrs. Goldman said. 
He served under Mr. Deng as a youthful army political commissar in the late 1930's and they were purged together in the Cultural Revolution.
But Mr. Hu also had a brusque, impetuous personality that often brought him into conflict both with hard-liners in the party and some intellectuals, who found him uneducated.
Â 
Resistance in the Army
A State Department official said today that there had been indications for a year that Mr. Hu was in trouble and might not end up as Mr. Deng's successor. 
Mr. Deng had been expected to give up his post as head of the party's Military Affairs Commission at a scheduled party congress next fall. 
But there were reports that senior army officers did not get along with Mr. Hu and would not accept him on the military commission, the official said.
''It's possible Deng decided Hu wasn't up to his shoes and then saw the reaction to the student demonstrations as a neat opportunity to get rid of Hu,'' he added.
The official recalled that Mao Zedong had turned on several of his supposed successors, including Liu Shaoqi, then the head of state, and Lin Biao, the military commander who was actually designated the successor in China's Constitution during the Cultural Revolution.
Mr. Oksenberg agreed that Mr. Deng may have been outraged by Mr. Hu's failure to curb the student protests, which spread to at least 11 cities. 
But he said it was difficult to discern whether Mr. Deng had acted under pressure from the hard-liners or just moved dramatically, as he has done inthe past, to assure his own authority.

text:
ï»¿
Paul Goldberger is the architecture critic of The New York Times.
Â 
The architect I.M. 
Pei, creator of the East Building of the National Gallery in Washington, the New York City Convention and Exhibition Center and some of the most conspicuous skyscrapers of the last decade, does not normally design relatively modest 325-room, low-rise hotels. 
But few of the small hotels he would be likely to disdain as unworthy of his time are intended for a hillside 25 miles outside of Peking, and so when the Government of China invited him to design such a building in 1978, he did not say no. 
He returned to China - where he had been born in 1917 - and began to produce what in short order became the most eagerly awaited piece of architecture in recent Chinese history. 
The building is called Xiangshan (meaning ''Fragrant Hill'') Hotel, and it will not be entirely completed until this spring, when it will serve as a luxury hotel mostly for foreign visitors. 
Its first wing opened last October, before a gathering of Chinese dignitaries and Americans, including Pei's friend Jacqueline Onassis, at whose behest he had designed the John F. Kennedy Library near Boston. 
Fragrant Hill resembles neither that building nor the National Gallery, nor any of Pei's other well-known works; it is no exaggeration to say that it is a mix of Chinese and Western architectures the likes of which have never been seen in China or anywhere else. t is too soon for a formal critical evaluation of Fragrant Hill, which is impossible in any event without a visit to the building, which this critic has yet to make.
Paul Goldberger profiles architect I.M. 
PeiBut no visit is necessary to explore the other aspects of this building that make it a project of compelling international interest: the process by which I.M. 
Pei designed it, the role it plays in the evolution of Mr. Pei's own work, the unusual blend of Chinese and Western technology that built it, and, beyond this, its effect on contemporary Chinese culture in general.
''The Fragrant Hill Hotel initially seems unimpressive. 
It even appears strange,'' is how Renmin Ribao, the People's Daily, began its description of the building. 
If the newspaper's unnamed critic is typical, the Chinese were clearly bewildered, for Pei's building neither derives entirely from any of the traditional Chinese styles which they have long known, nor is it altogether in the sleek, boxy Western style that the Chinese - like the people of the developing nations, especially the Middle East - have recently begun to find appealing as a badge of increasing sophistication.
Renmin Ribao's writer went on to speak of the facade of Fragrant Hill as ''severe,'' but then listed respectfully the varied architectural effects to be found within the building, and the overall conclusion was a positive one. 
What was fascinating -almost as much, in a sense, as the building itself - was the extent to which the review underscored how new and even perplexing the very idea of architecture is to the Chinese. 
There has been virtually no serious Chinese architecture since the People's Republic was founded, and the landscape is a mix of ancient imperial and religious structures, hovels and banal modern buildings constructed quickly and cheaply. 
Until recently, the Government chose to expend neither time nor money exploring the notion of architecture as an expression of cultural values; it regarded buildings primarily as shelter. 
The Pei hotel, in a sense, is modern China's first attempt to see building as something more than that - as something symbolic of a culture's aspirations.
For I.M. 
Pei, the hotel is also an attempt - and this is perhaps the most important part of it all for Pei - to lead the Chinese toward some sort of modern architectural vernacular, or common language of building, that might be used in other projects elsewhere in the country. 
What he was seeking was a building that would ''feel'' Chinese and yet modern at the same time.
''The Chinese have to find such a vernacular if they are to build towns and cities that are decent - that do not look like the dreary structures the Russians put across the landscape,'' Pei told an interviewer on his return from China. 
''The urgent problem for them is to find some sort of building-type that they can afford to build with their limited resources that will still respect their culture.''
The origin of the project was in a visit Pei made to lecture in China in 1978. 
It was his second trip there since he had left his homeland to study architecture in the United States in the 1930's; he had led a group of American architects to China in 1974, soon after China had begun to invite travelers from the West. 
By the time of Pei's second visit, the Government's effort to modernize China had begun in earnest, and the Chinese were actively negotiating with Western real-estate developers and hotel operators to create several Western-style skyscraper hotels in Peking.
Although Pei's reputation in the West had been based on his skyscraper designs - such as the John Hancock Tower in Boston and the Texas Commerce Tower in Houston - as much as anything else, he found himself disturbed by the idea of tall buildings in Peking. 
''The early conclusion of the Government and the city planners was that there had to be skyscrapers, simply because there were not enough sites in Peking with Page 30 modern utilities to spread the needed number of hotel rooms out in lower buildings,'' he said recently. 
''But I wasn't sure that was right - I urged the Chinese to move cautiously, to remember that they could do great damage to their city. 
Once they create skyscrapers, they could never again recapture Peking as it was, and I wanted to ask if there weren't some alternatives.'' few months later, Pei was asked to discuss the question of planning Peking with high Chinese officials, who were seeking outside advice without seeming to be turning over control to others. 
Pei, as a native-born Chinese with an international reputation - and as a man of extraordinary diplomacy and tact - was an ideal figure for the Chinese Government to rely on. 
He sought to reassure the Chinese of the importance of their own heritage, telling them that the highly technological Western culture that he himself had so relied upon throughout his career was not by itself the answer to their needs. 
By the time of his second visit for the project, Pei had become firmer in his view that while tall buildings might be acceptable in Western cities or in already built-up Far Eastern cities such as Hong Kong and Tokyo, they would be a mistake in Peking, with its important historic core of low buildings and unobstructed vistas. 
The municipal government - acting both on his advice and on a growing realization of the enormous construction costs of tall buildings - decided to ban skyscrapers from the historic center of Peking.
''It was just in time,'' Pei recalls. 
''By then, a Japanese group was beginning work on a 60-story building.''
The Chinese invited Pei to take on a project of his own in Peking, and to select a site. 
By then, he had established himself as a critic of dense center-city development - ironically, in view of how much of his work in the United States consists of such projects - and he chose to build a new hotel at Fragrant Hill Park, a rural area near Peking that had long had a small and rather primitive resort hotel.At Fragrant Hill, there could be no thought of the skyscraper construction that Pei found so inappropriate to Peking.
It is a site of unusually beautiful trees, many of which are quite old, and it is nestled in a cradle of mountains. 
The land at Fragrant Hill is another world altogether from Peking, or from any community at all; though it is but 45 minutes by car from Peking, it gives the impression of being a distant wilderness.
Because Fragrant Hill is a place apart from the hurly-burly of a city, it could serve easily as a kind of laboratory in which to experiment with the issues of design that were on Pei's mind. 
As part of his search to find a kind of new Chinese vernacular, an architecture that would look neither Western nor ancient Chinese, he considered especially earlier Western styles that had served well as vernacular architectural styles. 
He looked very hard at Georgian architecture, he says, and went to China with slides of London to prove the point that Georgian architecture makes so well - that an architectural language can be rich and complex, yet capable of being used not only for grand public buildings but for small private ones.
Pei took to China a group of architects from his office in New York and encouraged them to travel about in search of traditional Chinese vernacular styles. 
The team, which ultimately included Preston Moore and Kellogg Wong, his associate part-ners, and his son C.C. 
Pei as the associate in charge of design, reassembled in New York and began the design process.
Pei is involved in determining the basic design concept for most of the projects his office creates, but his interest in Fragrant Hill was so intense that he remained active through every stage of the design process. 
''It is the first time I ever saw him actually sitting at a drafting table,'' said a Pei associate. 
''I.M. really wanted to be in the middle of this, all the time.''
Spurred on both by Pei's enthusiasm and by the tight schedule the Chinese had set, the team completed a design in about three months, considerably faster than normal for so complex a project.
The design Pei created strives to evoke traditional Chinese forms without literally imitating older architecture. 
It is not surprising that the Chinese found it a bit severe: the exterior seems cool, and at first glance the building design calls to mind the architectural vocabulary of Western modernism that is Pei's normal language.
The Fragrant Hill Hotel is low and sprawling, much in the manner of many Western suburban office buildings. 
Its facades, however, employ the traditional Chinese materials of white stucco and gray tile, and such details as the design of the windows are taken, sometimes literally and sometimes with variation, from Chinese precedent.
The building is organized around several courtyards, one of which is treated essentially like a Western atrium and covered with a glass and metal frame. 
The other courts, however, are open to the sky and treated in the manner of traditional Chinese gardens - they are miniature landscapes, organized around specially crafted rocks, and their goal is no less ambitious than to create a metaphorical model of the universe. 
Unlike those in traditional Chinese buildings, the gardens at Fragrant Hill are
Pei Jump
fairly similar to one another; they are intended as parts of a larger whole, and they are all seen by the architect as subservient to the larger landscape that surrounds the building.
''I saved every tree that I could,'' Pei said. 
''That led to the building twisting and turning, but, in the end, the trees came back to bless us -the whole site became an instant garden.''
The rocks in the Fragrant Hill garden were not molded by human hands over a long period, as are those of the classic Chinese gardens. 
They were, instead, imported to the site from the so-called ''Stone Forest,'' a huge deposit of weathered limestone, 1,500 miles from FragrantHill in the province of Yunnan. 
The site is well known to the Chinese, and Pei himself first learned of it when he saw a photograph of it in a travel brochure. 
He was so enamored of the landscape of rock that he looked into means of transporting the huge stones, and tried to persuade the city government that moving them would cost less, in the end, than crafting rocks by hand closer to home. 
He won that dispute, and a kind of instant rock garden was created by bringing in rocks from Yunnan to the site.
The precedents in Chinese architectural history come almost entirely from central China, far south of Peking, and this explains in part why the northern Chinese found the building a bit perplexing. 
Peking and the immediate vicinity of Fragrant Hill offered Pei little that was useful in terms of architectural precedent - much of the architectural heritage of northern China has disappeared, and the remaining structures are mostly palaces and temples, buildings with the traditional gold tile roofs and red columns. 
The roots of that style are both royal and religious, and as such, it is not a style that either Pei or the Chinese Government officials would have been comfortable translating into a hotel.
So Pei went south to his family's home city, Suzhou, where the houses of a 19th-century merchant class - including the residence of the Pei family, which contains a celebrated garden - are still intact. 
There he rediscovered the plum-shaped windows, simple gray tiles, the stucco, and the cool, ordered formality that represent as significant a part of China's architectural heritage as the gold tiles and pagoda roofs that have by now, to Western eyes, become something of a cliche. 
And so it was to this other Chinese architecture, geographically distant from Fragrant Hill but in his view symbolically more appropriate, that Pei turned - moving, in a sense, to his own past for his inspiration.
The building that resulted appears in photographs to be serene and self-assured, with a sense of texture to it that is absent from much of Pei's sleeker Western work. 
The texture comes not from traditional ornament, but from Pei's mix of white stucco, trelliswork and gray tile set in geometric patterns around each window opening. 
These elements, along with the diamond-shaped pieces of tile set into the facade, function as a kind of abstract ornament. 
(Pei says of the gray tile that it is ''a unique Chinese material - but I have used it in a Western way.'') Glass, a material Pei has used extensively in his Western work, is absent except in small window openings and the roof of the central court, and its scarcity emphasizes the sense one has of this as a traditional masonry building.
Indeed, the only element that lends a Western sleekness to the facade is the stark white color of the stucco -which did not come about precisely in the way Pei had intended. 
His design had called for the stucco to have a natural finish of white but with a hint of gray to it. 
Yet sample after sample of the stucco refused to yield the proper tone. 
Finally, the decision was made to paint the facade instead - and the Chinese mixed a tone similar to Pei's favorite paint color, ''seed pearl,'' from the American manufacturers Pratt & Lambert.
The color change was but one of many last-minute adjustments that made the process of constructing Fragrant Hill entirely different from the way such a project would proceed in the West. 
Everything was more ad hoc: There were frequent substitutions of materials of a sort that would rarely be proposed in a large-scale, high-design project in the West. 
And it is rare that a graphics designer would have to explain to a hotel manager what kind of silverware and glassware had to be ordered for a restaurant, as Tracy Turner, who designed all of the graphics, signs and menus for the hotel, had to do. 
Miss Turner, who spent four months in Peking devising a system of signs in both English and Chinese and finding manufacturers to make them up, said that she had a particularly odd conversation with the hotel's assistant manager, who, when confronted with a list of 25 basic items of tableware needed for a Western-style banquet, ''threw down his hat on the table and exclaimed, 'How can you keep track of all this?
We eat with two chopsticks, and, when we throw a banquet, our idea is to add 25 more dishes, not utensils!'
''
Miss Turner also devised a logo for the hotel that is Western in its general look, but is based on a four-part leaf found on the site of Fragrant Hill. 
Each part of the leaf contains a Chinese character, and the hotel's name, in Roman type, is set to the left of the leaf. 
Miss Turner also designed a T-shirt with the hotel logo, and managed to convince the hotel's shop manager to print 15,000. 
One size sold out almost immediately - to the construction workers, it turned out.
I.M. Pei had ordered that as many elements of the hotel be made in China as possible. 
Still, his own authority was, in general, more restricted than on a Western project. 
He could not give orders to a general contractor, in part because protocol would not permit it and also because there was no general contractor in the first place.
The government of the city of Peking was the official client of the hotel, and a department called the Peking First Service Bureau, which is in charge of hotels, directly supervised construction. 
But there was no clear line of authority, and some problems and disagreements were referred to the Mayor of Peking for resolution.
''We could not give orders - only advice, and the Chinese do not make decisions lightly,'' Pei says. 
''We had to meet with group after group and go through committee after committee. 
The approval process is very cumbersome and time-consuming. 
It is something like the community boards in this country, a kind of grass-roots representation. 
The workers got to have their say, and Peking's architects were given a chance to review the design, and they asked every possi-ble question - and it was not only, 'Why do you need this gray tile here?' but also along the lines of, 'Why should someone from America tell us how to build in China?'
But we tried our best to explain what we were trying to do, and in the end the architects came to be very supportive.''
Although the long and complex bureaucratic process necessary for approval of the original design and of any proposed changes made for frequent delays, the size and energy of the work force tended to offset this. 
The crew averaged between 400 and 500 workers (as opposed to the no more than 200 who would raise such a building in the West) and at times there were as many as 1,500 workers on the site. 
''The Chinese were capable of incredible bursts of effort,'' Pei says. 
''Things would seem to move very slowly, and then they would suddenly all come together at the last minute.''
There was occasional friction between the Chinese workers and the security guards, and at one point near the hotel's opening it broke out into a scuffle that even led to a brief work stoppage. 
The actual construction process, however, mixed Western-style technology and Chinese hand labor. 
Large-scale machinery was used where it was absolutely necessary, but because the amount of it the Chinese possess is limited, pieces of machinery remained only briefly at the site and sometimes were replaced by horse carts. 
Some things went very fast - an entry road Pei thinks would have taken a Western crew three weeks to build was finished in less than a week. 
Elements of the building that required skilled labor moved with painful slowness - but were usually completed to high standards. 
Chinese craftsmen made a set of reproductions of a French chair that Pei had specified for the lobby, and the architect later compared them happily to the original.
Portions of the work at times had to be redone because the Chinese, inexperienced at this kind of construction, did not always proceed with each part of the building process in its most logical order. 
In some cases, for example, walls were plastered before electrical work was finished, requiring the plasterer to come back and duplicate his work after the electrician had finally finished. 
And decorative elements such as fine carpets were often brought in while painting was still going on.
But there is no doubt, at least in I.M. 
Pei's mind, that the effort of Fragrant Hill was worth it. 
When he speaks of this project, Pei, a man who normally makes his enthusiasms public but keeps his passions private, displays no restraint. 
''It was a marvelous experience,'' he said not long ago. 
''The Chinese have never been challenged as this project has challenged them. 
We have begun to learn about building in China. 
We still have a lot to learn - but I am elated.''

file: IDEAS & TRENDS_FOR JAPAN, EVEN THE WAR TAKES A BACK SEAT TO TRADE.txt
text:
ï»¿
AS ALWAYS in this season, Japan is consumed with memories of its suffering at the end of World War II. 
Wednesday was the 41st anniversary of Hiroshima's nuclear destruction. 
Yesterday thousands of people gathered for remembrances of the Nagasaki bombing. 
On Friday, Japanese will pause to recall the day in 1945 when the Emperor told them to ''endure the unendurable'' by surrendering.
Little - virtually nothing, in fact - is said on these occasions about how much suffering was inflicted by Japan, especially on its Asian neighbors. 
But Asia does not easily forget, and recent events underline how shadows of the war continue to influence this country.
This summer has brought new flare-ups of old disputes over Japan's sensibilities, including what it teaches its youth about the war.
A Government-authorized history textbook plays down Japanese atrocities such as the murder of tens of thousands of Chinese civilians in Nanjing in 1937. 
Until the Education Ministry ordered revisions, the manuscript had referred primly to the massacre as the ''so-called Nanjing incident'' and made no mention of casualty figures.
For its part, the ministry acted only after the Chinese denounced the book as an attempt by some Japanese to ''distort their dishonorable history.''
A fresh controversy swirls over whether Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone will repeat his diplomatic gaffe of Aug. 
15, 1985, when he made an official visit to Yasukuni Shrine in central Tokyo.
Â 
A Symbol of Militarism
In prewar Japan, Yasukuni was the home of state Shintoism and a powerful symbol of militarism. 
A visit to Yasukuni is equated in some circles with a desire to send Japanese troops on the march again. 
While the link is tenuous, it is still enough to set off alarms in Asia, especially in China.
Peking's attacks last year were so strong that they unsettled Mr. Nakasone. It seems likely that to avoid the risk of giving further offense the Prime Minister will forgo a trip to the shrine this week.
In dealing with Asia, Japan often succumbs to what at first appears to be a war-induced guilt complex. 
It spends considerable energy trying to convince wary neighbors that it means no harm, either with its gradual but steady military buildup or with its relentless exports. 
This policy, however, serves a purpose. 
Japan's goal as a prosperous trading nation is to stay on good terms with everyone; it is obviously bad business to make the customers distrustful.
Compared with West Germans, the Japanese indulge in fewer self-reflections on their wartime responsibilities. 
Rather, the imperative here is to pick oneself up quickly after a disaster and to resume life without unproductive dwelling on the past.
''Japanese so easily forget about their past,'' said Kiyoko Takeda, a professor of social and intellectual history at Tokyo's International Christian University.
As early as 1957, Japan felt sufficiently comfortable to choose a convicted war criminal, Nobusuke Kishi, as Prime Minister. 
There were protests from the political opposition.
But they lacked the sting of the recent furor in Austria over Kurt Waldheim, who, whatever the truth about his past, was convicted of nothing.
Many Japanese, perhaps most, assume no moral blame for their country's expansion across Asia in the 1930's. 
It certainly was no worse, they say, than decades of European and American colonialism; its failings were political miscalculations that led to a ruinous war.
Â 
Fear of Retaliation
A similar concern nags at Japan these days as it registers countless victories in trade and high finance. 
Too much success may invite retaliation, and that worry is one reason why Mr. Nakasone now calls for more Japanese imports and fewer exports.
''Unless we change,'' said Naohiro Amaya, a Government economic adviser, ''we will get a storm from outside.''
Still, some Japanese despair of knee-jerk reactions to outsiders' complaints. 
They suspect these attacks are occasionally disingenuous. 
The South Koreans, for instance, have attacked the new Japanese textbook far less forcefully than they did in a similar dispute in 1982, when, coincidentally or not, they were angling for a big aid package from Japan.
It is time to stop apologizing, many Japanese say. 
The conservative new Minister of Education, Masayuki Fujio, bemoaned his country's ''Yasukuni allergy,'' for which he blamed the postwar American Occupation.
''It's wrong to think that prewar Japan was all bad and Occupation-period policies were perfect,'' he said.
In a remark that caused considerable stir, Mr. Fujio was also quoted as saying, in somewhat rough language, that ''those guys'' who attacked the textbooks ''should look back themselves to see if they didn't commit similar acts in world history.''
Not surprisingly, China and South Korea took umbrage. 
Mr. Fujio insisted he was misquoted, but, in another display of Japan's edginess toward its neighbors, the Government issued a formal apology nonetheless.
Correction
A Tokyo dispatch in The Week in Review on Aug. 
10 misstated the dispositon of the case against Nobusuke Kishi, who was Commerce Minister in the Japanese Cabinet during World War II. 
Although imprisoned from 1945 to 1948 as a suspected war criminal, Mr. Kishi was never convicted.
Correction-Date:Â December 7, 1986, Sunday, Late City Final Edition

file: IN CHINA, A NEW _100 FLOWERS_ DRIVE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Chinese intellectuals who associate the ''Hundred Flowers'' campaign of 1956 with the Communist Party's most notorious betrayal of the principle of intellectual freedom have been faced with a new version of the campaign in the past few weeks. 
The new version comes complete with the slogan that continues to chill many of those who were punished for speaking out 30 years ago.
The slogan, ''Let a hundred flowers blossom, let a hundred schools of thought contend,'' is firmly associated with Mao Zedong, who used it in a series of speeches in early 1956 to start what was ostensibly to be a broadening of intellectual debate. 
When this prompted an outpouring of criticism from the intelligentsia, some of it directed against Communist rule, Mao responded with a campaign the following year that sent thousands of people to labor camps.
In later years the slogan became so controversial - despised by party theoreticians, who associated it with dissent, and distrusted by intellectuals - that it was excised from the official volume of Mao's speeches and writings that covered the period of the ''Hundred Flowers'' campaign. 
By reviving it now, the party apparently hopes to spur new efforts on behalf of the country's modernization campaign, and to do so in a way that depicts Mao, who has been heavily criticized in recent years, in a more favorable light.
Â 
A Series of Anniversaries
Westerners who watch Chinese politics have been intrigued by the new campaign for another reason, which is that 1986 offers the party leadership a number of vexatious anniversaries. 
In addition to the 30th anniversary of the ''Hundred Flowers'' campaign, the year holds the 20th anniversary of the onset of the Cultural Revolution and the 10th anniversary of the death of Mao.
The difficulty confronting party propagandists trying to popularize the ''Hundred Flowers'' idea is essentially the one they faced when the slogan was new. 
Like Mao, they have been concerned with spurring intellectual activity that could be socially useful.
But it has also been clear that the kind of free thinking they have in mind is to be limited to professional endeavors in the arts and sciences, and not to spill over into free political debate, which has remained proscribed under the program of social and economic relaxation adopted by the current top leader, Deng Xiaoping.
Â 
Regulation vs. Freedom
Western critics have often contended that the distinction is impossible to sustain in a society where virtually every human endeavor is subject to party regulation. 
Nonetheless, the insistence that people's minds should range freely in matters related to their work, while holding within approved parameters when considering the personalities and policies of their rulers, is one that Mr. Deng has steadfastly upheld.
Mr. Deng's attitudes are illuminated by his remarks about the events of the ''Hundred Flowers'' campaign, which took place when he was the party's General Secretary. 
In recent years he has said that the idea was a good one, but that the party's political enemies abused it for what a 1980 party document described as ''a wild attack on the party and the nascent socialist system.''
Although this justified a counterattack, Mr. Deng has said, the 1957 crackdown and his own role in it were excessive.
In the current campaign, efforts have been expended to present the ''Hundred Flowers'' idea as directed from the first at scientists. 
An article in a party-controlled journal, Beijing Review, said an important impetus for the 1956 campaign came from events in the Soviet Union, where the 20th Communist Party congress that year was the occasion for Nikita S. Khrushchev's ''secret speech'' denouncing Stalin.
The speech marked the end of the tyranny in Soviet genetics of Trofim D. Lysenko, a Stalin protege, and made the Chinese leadership realize that genetics here - and science in general - were in thrall to Soviet models, the journal said.
Â 
Special Freedom for Scientists
The idea that scientists above all should be intellectually unbonded is important to the reform-minded leaders around Mr. Deng, who believe that technology will carry China out of its backwardness into the next century.
The Beijing Review article, and others, have offered assurances to scientists that they will not again be labeled as ''rightists'' or ''counterrevolutionaries'' for reaching conclusions that conflict with political preferences.
In practice, this is likely to be difficult. 
An illustration of the complexities comes from the bitter controversy raging over whether the country should proceed with a hydroelectric dam across the Yangtze River. 
A number of scientists have criticized the plan, saying it would be an ecological disaster, but several political leaders have made it plain that they favor going ahead.
Still more vexing are the questions that arise in the performing arts. 
A number of those who took the policy at its word, following their creative instincts, have found themselves in trouble, with avant-garde plays canceled within days or novels condemned for ''bourgeois'' tendencies.
Predictably, the reception accorded the new ''Hundred Flowers'' campaign has been cool. 
A Peking University professor whose experiments in free speech during the 1957 campaign earned years of harassment said this week that he and many of his friends were ''profoundly grateful'' for the much wider academic freedoms that have developed under Mr. Deng.
''But when the party speaks of 'a hundred flowers,' we are cautious,'' he said. 
''There are memories that do not fade.''

file: IN CHINA, IN MONGOL STEPS, HORDES OF BACKPACKERS.txt
text:
ï»¿
At dawn, when a crescent moon lingers on the horizon, the donkey carts are on the move in this old Islamic town. 
Through an open doorway in a whitewashed wall, the murmurings of young boys reading the Koran filter into an alley. 
Old men in leather boots gather silently on a nearby bench, watching the sun spreading a wash of pink across the distant Pamir peaks.
For more than 2,000 years Kashgar has lived by its own rhythms, absorbing only as much as it has cared to from the alien tides that have flowed through the town.
The Chinese first made their power felt here in the Han dynasty, in the third century B.C. The Russians were a pervasive influence for a century and a half before World War II, and in between the dusty streets were trod by Tibetans, Mongols, Indians and British, among others.
Because the town stands at the furthest fringe of the deserts that cushion China from the west, it has always attracted conquerors, adventurers and traders. 
But none has made more than a passing impact on the Uighurs, a Turkic-speaking people who migrated from the western perimeter of Mongolia and who had been predominant in Kashgar for at least eight centuries when Marco Polo passed through in 1275. 
Today they account for about 90 percent of the town's population of 180,000.
Â 
Geography Has Been Ally
Geography has been the Uighurs' ally. 
It is more than 2,000 miles from here to Peking, most of it desert. 
Travelers from the capital take two days to arrive by plane, longer if flights are canceled because of sandstorms that sweep the Gobi and Taklamakan, the vast seas of dune and scrub that cover much of the Xinjiang Uighur Autonomous Region in which Kashgar is situated.
As if nature's isolation were insufficient, the Communist authorities declared the town closed to foreigners in the 1950's, an edict not lifted until 1983.
Whether approached from the east, across the desert, or from the west, across the 25,000-foot mountains that run like a shield across China's Central Asian frontier, Kashgar has always provided respite to the traveler. 
Now, once more, it is opening doors to strangers, and doing so in the tradition of Uighur friendliness that has impressed virtually every sojourner except Polo, who found the local merchants mean.
A few days here furnish vivid memories of free donkey cart rides, of spontaneous invitations to private weddings, of friendly chatter at dusk in the precincts of the Id Kah mosque, where the muezzin's cry has been heard for 1,000 years.
''Hospitality is a part of our culture,'' said Abdullah Shakir, a carpet salesman encountered in the Hong Kong Bazaar, so named for its profusion of inexpensive goods. 
#20,000 Visitors Expected This year, with the opening to foreigners of the Karakoram highway that crosses the mountains from here to Pakistan, officials expect 20,000 foreign visitors. 
Backpackers, in particular, are arriving in force.
The local foreign affairs director, Abdullahjan Dawud, a Uighur with Chinese subordinates, says the town is the most authentic of all surviving Uighur towns in Xinjiang, whose population of 13.5 million includes a diminishing proportion of Uighurs, now about six million.
''Kashgar,'' said Mr. Dawud with a smile, ''is keeping to its ethnic characteristics.''
This was a polite way of saying that here, unlike the Xinjiang capital of Urumqi, the Uighurs have managed to maintain their culture and religion without major inroads by the Chinese.
The sense of being carried back across the centuries comes most vividly on Sundays, when the citizens of Kashgar and outlying villagers mingle at the weekly market. 
In a clearing off a poplar-lined road that enters the town from the west, as many as 70,000 people crowd together to trade, to eat and to gossip. 
Most travel by donkey, some by horse or camel. 
Whole families ride together.
Officials say the market accounts for 30 percent of the commerce, an underestimate that serves the pretense that Kashgar's economy is predominantly Goverment-controlled.
Every Uighur need is met. 
Whether it is bolts of silk, top boots fashioned from yak hides, or camels - available for as little as $100 for a high-mileage specimen, as much as $450 for an animal that is still breaking in - the Uighur trader retains the shrewdness that sat ill with Marco Polo. 
Hours can be spent haggling over a few dollars.
Â 
Bargaining Can Be Cantankerous
As a customer, the Uighur is no less narrow-eyed. 
Beyond the market's five-cent haircuts and its silk-clad tumblers performing in the open air, traders gather beside a dusty track where draft animals are taken through their paces.
Old men with fierce countenances and jutting beards spend an hour or more testing camels and horses. 
When the animal has been rated the bargaining begins, often in the most cantankerous way.
During Mao Zedong's Cultural Revolution, which began in 1966, the market was disbanded. 
But the Uighurs revived their trading in a cemetery beyond the town and, in the late 1970's, saw their entrepreneurship embraced and Mao's brand of Communism condemned.
Mao's 40-foot statue still gazes solemnly northward from a plinth on the Chinese side of town, but a local Uighur official says quietly that it is there solely as ''a reminder of our worst times.''
Mao is only one of the alien influences whose course in Kashgar is run. 
Not far from the market is the yellow stucco compound that served as Britain's most remote diplomatic outpost in Asia until it was closed in 1950. 
Once celebrated for its watercress sandwiches, it is now a crumbling relic that serves as a cheap hotel. 
Across town, the Neo-Classical buildings of the old Russian consulate have been transformed into a higher-class guesthouse.
Â 
Past Contacts Recalled
To the Chinese the buildings are redolent of imperialism. 
Uighurs, by contrast, seem pleased to recall past contacts with foreigners. 
A walk in the maze-like alleyways of the old Uighur city is virtually guaranteed to produce invitations into courtyard homes that hide behind high mud walls.
Inside, guests are seated on raised platforms covered with the richly colored carpets for which the region is famous, and, over cups of thick black tea, invited to discourse, among other subjects, on Islam and carpet-making.
A common topic is the matter of relations between Uighurs and Chinese. 
Barely five years ago the town was convulsed with riots that erupted after Chinese youths killed a young Uighur and lost one of their own in revenge.
Uighurs say relations have improved greatly since. 
''After Mao, things were certain to improve,'' said an Uighur doctor who works among Chinese. 
''We still lead our separate lives, but we have learned to co-exist. 
''

file: IN CHINA, MILLIONS USE FUEL PRODUCED FROM WASTES.txt
text:
ï»¿
PEKING CHINA, a land where almost no natural resource goes overlooked, has mounted the world's largest and most determined effort to generate substantial quantities of methane gas for rural household use by fermenting human and animal wastes.
The program has advanced well beyond the experimental stage, and millions of backyard fermentation tanks on communes and farms are supplying up to 35 million peasants with fuel for cooking, lighting and heating that would be otherwise difficult to obtain.
China's experience in producing ''zhaoqi,'' or marsh gas, was described by Zhang Jigao, a prominent agricultural engineer, at a recent seminar in Peking entitled ''The Changing Rural Habitat.''
The seminar, sponsored by the Aga Khan Foundation, brought experts from nine countries together to share locally developed technologies.
Christopher Wren describes program in China which uses human and animal wastes to generate methane gas for fuel
''We now have built seven million tanks, which we call digesters. 
Their main use is for living - cooking three meals a day and heating hot water,'' explained Mr. Zhang, who is affiliated with the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences.
The notion of extracting energy from human and animal wastes may strike Americans and Europeans as bizarre, but the Chinese cannot afford to overlook any potential fuel source. 
A recent survey on the use of energy in rural China, where more than 800 million peasants live, found that about 70 percent of the households lack enough fuel.
The gleaning of firewood, straw and weeds, which account for threequarters of the energy consumed in the countryside, is not only a time-consuming chore but has also contributed to soil erosion in many regions.
Recognizing that China does not have sufficient conventional fuel for its needs, Yu Qiuli, a Deputy Prime Minister, told a session of the State Energy Commission in Peking last month that the energy shortage in rural areas should be met by building more methaneproducing digesters, as well as by reforestation.
Chinese studies on producing methane gas from wastes contend that the fermentation system also improves rural sanitation and produces an organic fertilizer rich in nitrogen, potassium and phosphates. 
The New China News Agency reported last week that the digesters were providing 40 million tons of fertilizer matter as a byproduct.
Nightsoil, as human wastes used to fertilize crops are euphemistically called, has often been used in poorer countries, but it also poses a health hazard for both farmers and consumers. 
In an interview, a Chinese public health specialist here said that with proper fermentation in the digesters, bacteria and parasites were killed, making nightsoil safe.
The conversion idea is not new in China. 
In 1936 Zhou Peiyuan, a well-known Chinese scientist, constructed an underground hydraulic pressure tank in Jiangsu Province for cooking and lighting. 
An indoor tank in Hebei Province, built a year later, is still reportedly in operation. 
Similar digesters have been tried in other countries, notably India, with less success.
The technology has been widely introduced in China only within the last decade and has been kept intentionally simple. 
The peasants dig a pit in the backyard and construct a fermentation well of concrete blocks or rocks and cement. 
The tank is then buried, except for a removable concrete cap tightly fitted on top.
A feedstock pipe slants down into the tank from the nearby latrine and pigsty. 
On the opposite side is a storage chamber into which fertilizer is pushed under gas pressure. 
Mr. Zhang said that the feedstock often consisted entirely of human wastes, though straw and other crop stalks might be added.
Once the cap is closed, the contents are left to ferment under pressure for a month to 40 days. 
Because gas pressure building within the fermentation tank could be unstable, the process requires careful tending, though Mr. Zhang insisted that ''acidity and temperature control has been well mastered in China.''
Â 
Temperature Is Important
The methane gas produced by the fermentation is later drawn through a hose into the farm kitchen for cooking with stove rings adapted to function at low pressure. 
After the gas is spent, the remaining waste is pumped out and carted to the fields for fertilizer. 
Then the process is started again.
The system's efficiency depends heavily on the climate because fermentation will not take place in the tank below 50 degrees Fahrenheit. 
Not surprisingly, most of the digesters -about five million - have been built in Sichuan, a southern province with a generally mild winter.
Mr. Zhang also said that digesters were operating nearly year-round in Guangdong, another southern province. 
The current cost of building a medium-size digester of eight cubic meters, to provide fuel for a family of four or five, is about $56, with communes and farm households generally sharing the cost.
Â 
Zhaoqi Is 'Easier to Manage'
The New China News Agency estimated that 68.3 billion cubic meters of methane gas could be generated annually if just half of the human and animal waste in rural China were put to use. 
Larger digesters have been tried in some urban areas, particularly Shanghai. 
But Mr. Zhang noted, ''The main purpose of zhaoqi is for the farmer. 
It is easier to manage there and we save on pipes and accessories.''
As energy costs rise, the digester has become more attractive to the third world as an alternate fuel source. 
A Western economist familiar with process estimated that China's digesters were already supplying the energy equivalent of 4 million tons of oil.
The Chinese experience has caught the attention of some officials in the United Nations Development Program. 
And Roger Carmignani, an energy specialist from the World Bank who attended the seminar in Peking, remarked, ''It is apparent that developing methane production is one of the most efficient ways of solving the problem of rural energy resources.''

file: In China, Nucleus of Eugene O_Neill Admirers Stages Festival.txt
text:
ï»¿
The brooding face of Eugene O'Neill stared out from the window of the Yaxipai motorcycle dealership on Zhongshan Road. 
Farther on, his face appeared on the rough brick wall of a herbal medicine shop.
Throughout this city that hugs the south bank of the Yangtze River, huge blood-red posters, stark with a stern portrait of the American playwright, declared the arrival of the Nanjing-Shanghai O'Neill Theater Festival.
''It's a triumph for us,'' said the chairman of the English department at Nanjing University, Prof. Liu Haiping, who is the organizer of the festival and an accompanying conference on O'Neill's work in honor of the playwright's centenary.
''We were told at first that it would be impossible to have a conference on such a figure as O'Neill,'' Professor Liu said. 
''Only with someone like Tolstoy could a conference be devoted to an individual artist. 
I told them that O'Neill's influence was growing and that he had a direct relation to China.''
Â 
Discussion and Debate
Professor Liu won the day and last week on theater stages around town the Tyrone family quarreled and agonized, the Emperor Jones ruled and the Mayos were transplanted to a southern Yangtze River village. 
During the day, scholars from three continents discussed, debated and applauded O'Neill's vast dramatic work.
When Cheng Jianxun strode onto the stage of the Qianxian Drama Theater as the unshaven James Tyrone in ''A Long Day's Journey Into Night,'' the Chinese audience remained riveted to the drama, silent and attentive, a departure from the usual noisy crowds that attend Chinese theatrical performances.
The production, staged by the drama troupe of the Nanjing military command of the Chinese Army, is believed to be the first by an army theater group of an American play, and it was also the first time ''Long Day's Journey'' had played in China.
But the road to the production, indeed to the festival and conference, was not easy. 
For Professor Liu, it was an exercise in patience, stubbornness, and the conviction that it was important for China to explore the complexities of O'Neill's tragic vision.
Â 
A Year at Harvard
Mr. Liu, who was banished to work on a farm during China's Cultural Revolution, was a professor of modern English and American drama at Nanjing University but had never seen a production of the plays he taught until he spent the 1983-84 academic year at Harvard University.
