He returned to the United States in 1986 to read a paper on Taoism in O'Neill's plays at a conference on the playwright at Suffolk University in Boston.
''Actually, the idea came during a conference on O'Neill in Boston in 1984,'' Professor Liu explained in an interview. 
''One of the professors said, 'Why don't you hold a conference on O'Neill in China so we can see your country and bring O'Neill to China?'
It seemed a joke to me at the time.''
As time passed, though, the idea gripped his imagination and Professor Liu approached the administrators of the university with his project. 
Even after he persuaded the administration that O'Neill warranted the attention of Chinese scholars and dramatists, the school told the professor that without money, approval could not be granted.
''There was actually a Catch-22,'' he remembered. 
''In order for me to get money, I had to get approval from the university. 
But to get approval from the university, I had to get funding for the conference.''
This was February 1987.
''So I sat down at my typewriter and sent letters to major U.S. foundations and joint venture companies in China,'' he said. 
''One letter came back with a positive response. 
They gave us $1,000. 
But that was a start.''
Â 
Lack of Money
''We had no money in the beginning,'' he said. 
''We had to save on stamps because international postage is very expensive. 
But then the Amity Foundation in the United States provided $8,000 and another $8,000 came from the China Fund.''
As money came in, the attitude of the university changed and permission was granted for Professor Liu to go ahead. 
In the end, the more than 30 scholars from Japan, the United States, Sweden, Belgium and Britain who traveled to Nanjing were all required to pay their own way, Professor Liu said.
For Professor Liu, who has just published a book on China's treatment of O'Neill since the 1920's, the growth in interest in the playwright reflects a profound step in China's intellectual and dramatic landscape.
Â 
Alternative to Ibsen
''Eugene O'Neill was fairly popular in the 1920's,'' Professor Liu said. 
''China had established its own drama, huaju, by then. 
Although Ibsen was the most influential playwright then, people wanted someone different from Ibsen. 
O'Neill was the second most important playwright mainly because of his Expressionistic work 'The Emperor Jones.'
''When the director Hong Shen saw a performance of 'The Emperor Jones' he was impressed by the techniques and came back to China and staged a production here. 
He restaged the Emperor Jones as an army official who stole rations from his men and ran away. 
He used the drums the same way the original production did. 
It was the first introduction of Expressionism onto the Chinese stage.
''After that, Cao Yu - one of China's best-known playwrights -argued that China didn't know how to use Expressionism. 
In an influential article in the 1930's, he said that we should learn from O'Neill's one-act plays, that we should start simply.''
From the 1940's until 1979, O'Neill vanished from the Chinese stage, buried by war, revolution and political orthodoxy. 
''After 1979,'' Professor Liu said, ''he emerged as one of the most-read playwrights.''
''One reason for this revival of interest is that those of us of the younger generation see him as very modern,'' he said. 
''He has absorbed a lot of European influence: Nietzsche, Freud, Schopenhauer. 
Graduate students like to write about O'Neill because he is seen as contemporary, not a classic playwright like Shakespeare. 
And though O'Neill's Expressionism is old in the West, it is still very new here.''
''Further, there is a newly released enthusiasm about America,'' he continued.
The limits of Chinese understanding of O'Neill, however, was discussed in one of the papers delivered at the conference. 
Zhao Yu, a graduate student at Nanjing University, noted that two of the plays - ''Desire Under the Elms'' and ''Mourning Becomes Electra'' - are ''beyond the horizon of expectation of Chinese readers because of different esthetic standards.''
Â 
The Meaning of Tragedy
''As Chinese tragedians are concerned about the happiness of man in the present world, all the problems they put forward usually are solved right within the plays,'' Ms. Zhao said. 
''But this is not the case in 'Desire Under the Elms' and 'Mourning Becomes Electra.'
In China, it is a rule that tragedies, especially classical tragedies, end in happiness.''
Long Wenpei, a professor of literature at Fudan University in Shanghai, was enthusiastic about the revival of O'Neill in China, however. 
''Human nature is no longer off-limits for us,'' he exclaimed. 
''O'Neill is a real writer who looked at the meaning of life.''

file: In China, Signs of a Power Struggle.txt
text:
ï»¿
The orthodox Marxists who have dominated politics and culture in China for more than five months are coming under increasing attack from other Communist Party members who support the economic and social changes introduced by the country's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping.
Western diplomats here infer that a serious struggle for power is under way within the country's leadership four months before the party's 13th National Congress is scheduled to begin in October. 
The congress, normally held every five years, charts the country's direction and names its new leaders.
''Clearly there is a major struggle going on,'' a senior Western diplomat said. 
''Now it seems that the reformers led by Zhao are coming out on top.''
Zhao Ziyang is both Prime Minister and Acting General Secretary of the Communist Party.
Â 
Warnings on 'Leftism'
Since the former party chief, Hu Yaobang, was forced to resign in January, a coalition of ideological hard-liners has clamped down on freer expression in the press, the arts and in universities and has opposed those who advocate Western political ideas. 
The hard-liners also have sought to rein in components of the economic modernization pushed by Mr. Deng and Mr. Zhao.
Now, in newspaper editorials, public statements and private meetings, supporters of the policies of Mr. Deng and Mr. Zhao are warning of the dangers of leftism and ossified political views.
''The conservatives don't have any credible alternative,'' a Western European diplomat said. 
''They don't have any economic program.''
A Communist Party member who identifies closely with those who support change said: ''What do the conservatives want?
They want to go back to the 50's. 
Who wants that?
Nobody.''
Â 
A Sign of Change
One sign that the hard-liners may be on the defensive, according to diplomats here, was Mr. Zhao's choice of Wan Li, a Deputy Prime Minister, as Acting Prime Minister, and Hu Qili, a senior Politburo member, as temporary party head when Mr. Zhao visited Eastern Europe two weeks ago.
Both men are regarded as strong proponents of economic change. 
Prominent party conservatives were overlooked for the temporary appointments, according to these diplomats.
Still, some diplomats said, it is by no means certain that Mr. Zhao and his supporters have regained the political initiative necessary to dominate the upcoming congress. 
With Mr. Hu's political demise, a new party leader must be named and a new Politburo must be formed. 
The faction that controls the Politburo, diplomats here say, can set China's economic and ideological course through the end of the decade.
The diplomats pointed out that the inner workings of the Communist Party leadership remained tightly guarded. 
Their conclusions came from close readings of newspapers and scrutiny of public statements.
Â 
Accounts of Crime for Profit
Western diplomats are divided about whether Mr. Zhao and his supporters have beaten back the hard-liners. 
The articles championing the benefits of economic innovation have coincided with a crackdown on illegal publications and criticism of some private business practices.
In recent weeks, China's papers have been full of accounts of illegal dealings by private businessmen and brazen crimes for profit. 
In an economic climate that encourages making money, a diplomat said, unequal wealth and crime are easy targets for hard-liners who believe that innovations not only depart from true Communism but also induce social disorder.
In their counterattack, the so-called reformers have equated strident leftism with poverty. 
The phrase ''socialist poverty'' revives memories for many Chinese of the hysteria and social upheaval of the Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976, when Mao Zedong and his allies maintained that ''eating socialist grass'' was better than partaking of capitalist food.
''As poverty is not a characteristic of socialism, it is imperative to develop productive forces,'' Shanghai's party secretary, Rui Xingwen, said in a recent speech.
Â 
Support for 'Open Policy'
For such advocates, this means strengthening programs intended to loosen central controls and relying more on market forces to stimulate production.
Even the party's theoretical journal, Red Flag, which has become an outlet for hard-liners in the last six months, defended economic change recently. 
''Without reform and the open policy,'' the journal said in a major editorial, ''our socialism would have stagnated or ossified and socialist construction with Chinese characteristics would be nothing.''
For the first time in six months, a vague program for separating the Communist Party from the state's administrative apparatus is being discussed. 
This week, Mr. Deng told a Yugoslavian visitor that ''political reform is the order of the day and will be the major topic for discussion at the 13th National Congress.''

file: IN CHINA, _CAPITALIST ROADERS_ CAN NOW CRUISE IN CADILLACS.txt
text:
ï»¿
China, amid some ceremony, acquired a fleet of Cadillac limousines today.
At a formal handover, Chinese officials lined up to accept the 20 dark blue limousines, described in Cadillac brochures as ''the car of the stars,'' each equipped with a built-in television set, refrigerator and bar.
It was the kind of occasion that left Westerners with memories of Mao Zedong's China shaking their heads in disbelief. 
The ceremony was held only a short bicycle ride from the stadium where Mao's enemies were once paraded in duncecaps as ''capitalist roaders.''
China acquires fleet of 20 Cadillac limousines, each equipped with built-in television set, refrigerator and bar; stretch version festooned with red bunting, stands at steps of 29-story skyscraper that makes its own debut as symbol of China's new directions; executives of General Motors and O'Gara Coachworks, Los Angeles-based company, attend ceremony in Peking; photo (M)Parked Next to Skyscraper
An extended-wheelbase, or ''stretch'' version of the car, 18 feet long and festooned with red bunting, stood at the steps of a 29-story skyscraper that was making its own debut as a symbol of this country's new directions. 
The building, the tallest in Peking, was specially cleaned up ahead of its official opening to allow speech making by executives of General Motors and O'Gara Coachworks, a Los Angeles-based company that delivered two similar, armor-plated vehicles for use here by President Reagan last year.
Beyond a wrought-iron railing separating the building from a broad avenue that sweeps across Peking, hundreds of people returning from work stopped to gaze. 
Their comments, initially, at least, were a public relations executive's dream.
''Magnificent!
The most beautiful cars I've ever seen,'' said Huang Liang, a 25-year-old construction worker as he watched from the saddle of his Flying Pigeon bicycle. 
''How much do they cost, three or four thousand yuan?''
At the official rate of exchange, his estimate came to just about $1,600.
Told that the version of the limousine that had caught his eye sold in the United States for $39,000, an amount it would take him 115 years to earn at his construction job, he was dismayed. 
''That's a laugh,'' Mr. Huang said, with an expression of surprise. 
''Tell me you're joking.''
Chinese officials were evasive when asked who would use the cars. 
Even under Mao the most powerful figures in the country were chauffeured around in impressive limousines, but the vehicles used then were almost exclusively the Chinese-made Red Flag cars that looked like a cross between a Soviet Zil and a Cadillac of the 1960's. 
The Red Flag has now fallen into disfavor as unreliable and unwieldy, and Western engineers have been consulted on ways to improve it.
Â 
Deng Said to Favor Mercedes
Deng Xiaoping, the man who succeeded to Mao's power and who has proclaimed Western-style economic changes, is believed to favor a Mercedes-Benz for his own travel. 
One official at the handover ceremony today said ''state leaders'' would be among those using the Cadillacs. 
Others said that the main reason for buying the cars was to provide the comfort expected by ''foreign guests'' and that it was ''unclear'' if officials like Mr. Deng would use them.
''It will depend on the opportunities,'' said Rong Yiren, chairman of the China International Trust and Investment Corporation, which bought the cars.
Although General Motors executives described the Cadillacs as the first ever delivered to China, Mr. Rong knew better. 
He acknowledged after the ceremony that he had driven one in the 1940's, when his family was one of the richest in China, owning a string of textile mills near Shanghai. 
When the Communists took power in 1949, most of the family fled to Taiwan or the United States, but Mr. Rong, now in his late 60's, remained.
In Communist eyes that made him a member of the ''national bourgeoisie,'' which meant Mr. Rong was honored as a patriot until 1966, when Mao unleashed the Red Guards.
When the Cultural Revolution ended, Mr. Deng redeemed him and appointed him to his present position, where he channels Chinese investments abroad and foreign investments in China.
At the ceremony, wearing an immaculately tailored gray suit and blue button-down shirt, he could have passed for a top executive in any boardroom. 
But the crosscurrents that flow behind the scenes of Chinese politics were represented in the mixture of high-buttoned Mao-style tunics and loose-fitting, open-necked shirts worn by his companions, some of whom seemed ill at ease during the florid speeches by the Americans.
John Grettenberger, general manager of General Motor's Cadillac division, suggested that the limousines should be seen as a symbol of the new era in China. 
Like the country, he said, the cars had ''an enduring tradition,'' but they also had a ''sophisticated future.''
Arthur W. Hummel Jr., the American Ambassador, assured the gathering that ''dollar for dollar, I think you will find that the Cadillac will give you a smoother ride than any other car.''
Â 
Lining Up for a Ride
After Mr. Rong accepted a set of gold keys from Mr. Grettenberger, dozens of Chinese officials lined up for a demonstration ride. 
Officials who ride bicycles to work and live in apartments with no hot water disappeared behind darkened glass windows into a world of air-conditioning, plush seats and iced drinks. 
Later, they rubbed shoulders with Cadillac dealers from New Jersey, Florida and Illinois at a lavish reception in one of the city's new Western-style hotels.
Before leaving the ceremony, Mr. Rong was asked if he was concerned about a revival of the attitudes prevalent during the Cultural Revolution, when anyone owning or using Western-made luxuries was liable to be punished by Red Guards.
''The Cultural Revolution was bad,'' he replied.

file: IN HONG KONG_ OF THE NEWEST, 10 OF THE BEST.txt
text:
ï»¿
Hong Kong is a city of ceaseless conspicuous wonders. 
It supports the world's biggest neon sign, the 328-foot-long Citizen watch sign atop Elizabeth House in Causeway Bay. 
It has the densest concentration of Rolls-Royces, 580, or one for just about every mile and a quarter of Hong Kong road, according to Asia Magazine. 
Its new stainless steel subway carries 1.2 million people a day over its 16-mile length. 
It has the world's longest escalator ride, a 700-foot moving stairway in its Ocean Park recreation center. 
Its Star Ferry boasts a 9-cent harbor ride. 
It is the largest exporter of clothing, watches and toys in the world.
As if all of that weren't sufficient, Hong Kong also has perhaps the best collection of restaurants anywhere. 
To be sure, there may be better individual restaurants in other cities, though even that opinion might occasion some argument in Hong Kong, but there is no place that boasts so many good restaurants.
Not only is the eating wonderful in Hong Kong, so are the varieties of its restaurants, their vitality and their restlessness. 
The restaurant scene is one of constant change. 
Last year I made two trips to Hong Kong, the last just before the end of the year, and in the eight months between those visits scores of new restaurants were opened, this in a city that boasts more than 20,000 restaurants as it is. 
Each time I go to Hong Kong I try as many new places as I can to determine if they are indeed new, exciting, yet true to their Chinese culinary heritage, and each time I find many that please.
Following are 10 of the best of Hong Kong's new restaurants, all of them opened in the last year. 
Unlike what I found on some earlier visits, these restaurants are not all in East Tsimhatsui, that burgeoning enclave of malls, hotels and restaurants in Kowloon. 
Some are in Kowloon proper, and some are on the developing waterfront on Hong Kong Island, across Victoria Harbor from Kowloon.
As with virtually all restaurants in Hong Kong, they are not expensive. 
Such delicacies as shark's fin soup and bird's nest soup can, of course, run up your bill, but for two to three courses of the foods mentioned below, dinner should not be more than $15 to $20 a person. 
The food is the thing; the more rare the more expensive. 
Nor is elegance a sole index of price. 
Such restaurants as Lai Ching Heen and Ziyang Szechuen are decorated in good taste and can be a bit more expensive, but food in far less glossy places can cost as much or more.
All of these restaurants are open from about 11 A.M. to 11 P.M., but those noted as serving dim sum will customarily open several hours earlier, usually about 8 A.M. As important as being new is the fact that these restaurants represent all of the four regional cuisines of China.
Perhaps the most outlandish is the North Sea Fishing Village (first and second basements, Auto Plaza, East Tsimshatsui; telephone 3-7236843), which has a full-size Chinese junk moored in its center. 
On the deck of the junk is a sushi bar at which fresh raw octopus, abalone, conch, lobster and many varieties of raw fish are prepared. 
Sushi, while not common in Hong Kong, is becoming more well known. 
The Chinese call it yueh sang, which translated literally means live fish. 
Tanks of live turtles, crabs and lobsters are piled on the deck of the junk as well.
The restaurant's specialty is the freshest of seafood, and on the junk sit many tanks of filtered water in which swim sea bass, garoupa and pomfret. 
You select your fish; it is netted and cooked as you wish. 
The best method, in my opinion, is to have it steamed with shredded ginger, mushrooms and scallions. 
The restaurant is also fine for dim sum, that traditional Cantonese brunch of different kinds of dumplings and scented tea.
For elegance and Cantonese cookery raised to the level of high art, Lai Ching Heen (Regent Hotel, Salisbury Road; 3-7211211) has few competitors. 
This restaurant on the basement level of the hotel, which sits on the border between East Tsimshatsui and Kowloon proper, is all gray velvet walls and antique Chinese blackwood furniture. 
The table setting consists of a square plate of green jade, a holder of carved green jade that contains a spoon of silver with a jade handle and ivory chopsticks banded in silver and a condiment dish, also of green jade.
Do not miss roast suckling pig in Lai Ching Heen, a dish served nouvelle style, glistening, cross hatched and crisp, or other Cantonese classics such as steamed crab with its roe or roasted pigeon with freshly ground spicy Sichuan peppercorns. 
And all the while enjoy the traffic of the harbor as it passes by your window.
Outstanding examples of the cooking of the people of Chiu Chow, many thousands of whom live, and cook, in Hong Kong, are found at City Chiu Chow Restaurant (East Ocean Center, 98 Granville Road, East Tsimshatsui; 3-7245383). 
The food of the Chiu Chow, who live on the southern coast of China, is one of sharp tastes. 
They use much garlic and white vinegar in their cooking and season the food with a sauce of tangerine juice and ground chili peppers. 
A specialty of the Chiu Chow is pomfret fish, smoked in tea leaves; this restaurant does it superbly. 
Another specialty is large crabs from the China Sea, boiled then served at room temperature so that they can be cracked and eaten in the style of a New Orleans crab boil. 
A custom here is to have Iron Goddess tea before and after the meal, initially to cleanse the palate, finally to cut the pungency of what has been eaten and to help you digest it. 
The tea, widely available, even in the United States, is also known as Ti Kuan Yin.
In Kowloon, one of best of the new is the Ziyang Szechuen Restaurant (45D Chatham Road South; 3-687177), the brainchild of Allan Koo, whose two previous Hong Kong restaurants were Italian and named Valentino and Leonardo. 
Why?
''Because I spent so much time in Italy. 
Italian food is family-style food. 
I like spaghetti,'' says Mr. Koo, all of whose reasons seem sensible.
Ziyang has gray suede and pink marble walls, caged parakeets that chirp incessantly, a guitarist nightly, chairs from Italy that cost Mr. Koo $200 each, and Sichuan food of an exceptionally high order. 
We had wonderful fried dumplings, thinly sliced loin of pork in a garlic, soy and vinegar sauce, bean threads dressed with hot peanut and sesame sauce, prawns in searingly hot chili and dry-fried shredded beef, a difficult dish to make because it often resembles used shoelaces. 
Not here.
The Shing Tao Restaurant (6-8 Jordan Road, Jordan House; 3-7243832) divides its menu equally between Sichuan and Peking cooking. 
It is just off Nathan Road, in the traditional back lot of Kowloon, away from much of the Tsimshatsui glitter, but its food is worth the trip.
When you sit down, a plate of peanuts that have been stewed in cinnamon, eight-star anise and Sichuan peppercorns is put before you to nibble on while you consider the menu. 
We had Yunnan ham with fresh honey in steamed buns, duck smoked in tea leaves and camphor and as a final course Mongolian-style grilled beef. 
A curved cast-iron grill that looks like one side of a waffle iron is placed over a small fire in the center of the table. 
Beef is placed on the grill and cooks in seconds. 
This is then dipped into a bubbling mixture of soy sauce, wine, sugar, white pepper and peanut oil and eaten with shredded leeks. 
A spectacular dish.
A fashionable, though tiny, establishment in Kowloon that is serving some of the best Shanghai food in Hong Kong is the Wu Kong Shanghai Restaurant (27 Nathan Road, Alpha House; 3-667244), a white marble place entered from Peking Road, just around the corner from its nominal address. 
The restaurant is the creation of Bill Kong and his chef, Wu Chow, who was born in Shanghai and has been cooking the food of his native city for 30 years.
The food is classical Shanghai in execution: so-called drunken pigeon, the bird marinated in Hsao-Shing wine before being lightly braised; tiny shrimp poached with egg white and sauteed quickly so that they look like a snow drift; eel, shredded so that it resembles pasta, then braised with bean sprouts and minced garlic in wine vinegar and soy sauce.
Across the harbor, on Hong Kong Island, many new restaurants have opened in recent months. 
Most of them are Cantonese, as are most restaurants in Hong Kong, but one of the best is the East Ocean Seafood Restaurant (25 Harbour Road, third floor, Harbour Center; 5-8938887), where, as its name suggests, the menu is heavily accented with fish and seafood. 
The restaurant's strength lies in elaborate, banquet-quality preparations, and even though you might not want to indulge in a 10-course binge, a selection from the banquet menu is advised.
We had, for example, whole prawns steamed with garlic and served in small bamboo steamers; double-boiled whole shark's fin cooked with wintermelon and Yunnan ham and octopus fried with snow peas and fresh ginger. 
Then as a respite from seafood we were served a whole chicken that had been marinated in Grand Marnier, fried, then presented with a bit of lemon juice and Sichuan peppercorns and sea salt, ground together. 
It was outstanding.
In Hong Kong Central, up the slope from Queen's Road, is the West Villa Restaurant (1-5 On Lan Street; 5-212196), which is one of Hong Kong's best fowl, bird and game restaurants. 
The dishes are classic (but often overlooked) Cantonese. 
For example, you can eat, as we did, partridge cooked in a closed porcelain jar with sugar cane, Yunnan ham and ginger, a striking preparation. 
We have had pigeon stuffed with shark's fin, then braised, and crab meat with beaten egg whites, a snow white mountain of softness bordered with bright green flowers of broccoli.
The chef, Peter Tang, cooks what he calls ''the food of the home'' and says he pays ''obedience to the old masters'' of Chinese cookery, those master chefs called Mon See Fu, and when he cooks such delicate things as eel, first double boiled, later steamed in hollowed bamboo, his respect for elegance is understood. 
There is a similarly named restaurant on the Hong Kong waterfront, the West Villa Admiralty Restaurant (18 Harcourt Road, ground floor, Admiralty Center; 5-298333), which is said to have several partners in common with the other West Villa. 
Whether it does or not, the restaurants are totally different, the West Villa Admiralty specializing in Shanghai cuisine.
It serves drunken shrimp, a rare delicacy consisting of live shrimp marinated in rice wine, then slowly cooked in the wine in their shells. 
The restaurant cooks shredded beef with fermented black beans and fresh shallots, makes quite a rich wintermelon soup filled with duck meat, shrimp, fresh lotus seeds and frog legs and steams Hong Kong's native fish, the garoupa, with scallions and fresh sliced ginger.
Finally, there is another of those new and elegant Cantonese restaurants, the Tao Yuan Restaurant (23 Harbour Road, third floor, Great Eagle Center; 5-738080) near the new Hong Kong Arts Center. 
It looks out over the harbor, and on its tables are pink cloths and table settings that are adequate copies of Ching Dynasty porcelain.
The Tao Yuan has wonderful dim sum in the morning, then in the afternoon it becomes a place to eat minced quail, mushrooms, cucumbers, water chestnuts and celery wrapped in cool lettuce leaves, crisp goose with sweet plum sauce, scallops stuffed with mashed taro root, then fried, and hot bouillon into which are dropped puffy fried vegetable fritters.
This is the sort of food being cooked in Hong Kong. 
It is inventive, yet true to its Chinese roots, and is extraordinarily well prepared by a growing band of young Hong Kong-born and Hong Kong-trained chefs. 
It is food worth making a trip more than halfway around the world to taste.

file: IN MARCO POLO_S FOOTSTEPS.txt
text:
ï»¿
Westerners who live in China are accustomed to being told how fortunate we are. 
But for us there is a company of foreigners still more to be envied, those who journeyed here before the Communists closed the outlying reaches of the country to the world. 
One has only to read the accounts of Somerset Maugham, who visited here in 1921, or of Peter Fleming, who was here in 1935, to know the beguiling possibilities of a China where travel was less hindered.
As the Government has extended its list of ''open'' areas, this chagrin has eased. 
Most of the regions newly accessible to foreigners are in the Chinese heartland, but one of them has made possible a journey to an area remote even by the standards of those who explored the country before 1949. 
With the opening on May 1 of the Karakoram Highway, Peking licensed any foreigner to relive one of the most daunting experiences of Marco Polo, the most fabled China traveler of them all.
It was during his confinement in a Genoese prison that Polo dictated his account of his travels to a cellmate, Maestro Rusticello, a fact that has made the adventurer's precise route from Venice to Khanbalik, the modern Peking, a matter of scholarly dispute. 
But it is certain that his path, by horse and camel, led over the towering mountain passes, some more than 16,000 feet, that admit to China from what is now its western frontier with Afghanistan and Pakistan. 
It is over this terrain that the Karakoram Highway runs, a 795-mile triumph of engineering that was built over a period of 18 years before 1978 by army road crews from China and Pakistan.
The story of the Karakoram is of the road, a narrow strip of asphalt and graded gravel that runs through forbiddingly rocky lowlands, along sinuous corniches extending hundreds of feet above stony riverbeds and up into the crystal freshness of three of the world's highest ranges, the Pamirs, the Himalayas and the Karakorams. 
It is a tale, too, of Kashgar, a town of biblical simplicity that is the road's starting point on the Chinese side, of the unaffected friendliness of upland people who live much as they did in Polo's time, and of the lovely mountains and orchards of the Hunza Valley of northeast Pakistan.
On the day the highway opened the Chinese reserved the few four-wheel-drive Jeeps in Kashgar for dignitaries attending ceremonies in the Khunjerab Pass, the 16,072-foot border point with Pakistan. 
Accordingly, our party of eight - five reporters, a New York banker based in Peking, and two of our wives - resolved to spend time exploring farther east in the sprawling Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. 
This introduced us to the arid fastnesses of the Gobi and Taklimakan Deserts, nearly 2,000 miles of sand and scrub that fill most of the terrain between Kashgar and Peking.
At the searing oasis of Turpan, where summer temperatures reach 125 degrees, we measured the rigors that confronted the traders, adventurers and marauders who journeyed along the Great Silk Road, the romantic thoroughfare that linked the Mediterranean of imperial Rome to the China of the contemporaneous dynasty of the Han. 
At Gaochang, a ruined city outside Turpan, sacked by Mongols not long before Polo ventured across the Taklimakan, we gazed westward across the desert from ancient ramparts and knew how the desert got its Turkic name, meaning ''Enter, and you won't return!''
We reached Kashgar on a Saturday evening, marveling at our first aerial view of the 2,000-year-old town with its poplars, its wheat fields and its vines. 
After the biscuit-brown expanses of sand that stretch like a ruffled carpet before the Tien Shan Mountains buffering Xinjiang from Soviet Kirghizia and Kazakhstan, the greenness was like cooling air. 
Looking down on the shaded forecourts of the mosques, we understood how Peter Fleming felt - ''Few people can ever have enjoyed a bath more than we did'' -when he arrived here in a camel train after a five-month journey from Peking in 1935.
It is a safe bet that none of the 244 Chinese cities and towns now open to foreigners provides a less altered appearance to contemporary travelers than Kashgar. 
No Japanese taxis here, only donkey carts that, unsprung, carry visitors through the mud-walled back streets of Yumlakshakulbishe, heart of the old town. 
In back alleys and courtyard homes hidden behind whitewashed walls, the curious can find the unchanging rhythms of life among the Uighurs, who constitute 90 percent of Kashgar's population of 180,000 and about half of the 13 million people in Xinjiang.
In two days we were invited to a wedding, to a courtyard school where youngsters recited the Koran, and to an evening with a Uighur doctor living in the spacious home his family has owned for more than 200 years. 
Sitting beneath the stars, cross-legged on a carpeted platform over cups of thick black tea, we spoke, in Chinese, of the matters that preoccupy Uighurs' minds. 
Our host, who had doffed the Uighur's long cotton coat and boots for a dusty business suit, told us that relations with the Chinese, who established their influence here as early as the third century B.C., have improved radically since Peking scrapped the tyrannical policies of Mao Zedong.
The Uighurs, who once had an empire of their own, are essentially a trading people now, a talent displayed in Kashgar's sprawling Sunday market. 
All pretense of a collective economy is abandoned as a gigantic crowd gathers in an open area beyond the town. 
Among sellers of cart wheels and camels, we met a gregarious Uighur, Abdullah, who had learned English working with the British in India before World War II. 
He led us to the bazaar in the center of town, where a wily trader relieved us of $300 for a muted old Xinjiang carpet of the kind that graces virtually every Kashgar home.
You cannot be in Kashgar long without being drawn toward the mountains, their snowy flanks shimmering in the haze to the north and west of town. 
At noon on our third day, we paid our bills at the old Russian Consulate that does service as the Kashgar guesthouse and headed for Pakistan. 
Leaving behind our Peking interpreter, who lacked the pass necessary for Chinese entering border zones, we boarded a Toyota Landcruiser driven by an impetuous young Chinese and headed for the Pamirs. 
In the next 48 hours the driver's insistence on daredevil driving was virtually our only vexation. 
About 25 miles down the road, at the village of Upal, we came across reminders of the earthquake hazard that has plagued the area for centuries. 
In August last year a major quake hit the Keshi prefecture, leveling several villages and killing dozens of their inhabitants. 
The tomb of Mahmoud Keshgeri, the 11th-century Turkic scholar who is thought by some to have been the author of the world's first dictionary, was destroyed but has been already been rebuilt, a shimmering edifice of painted white tiles on a rise looking to the Pamirs. 
In the village, naked boys splashed in a river yards from the remains of mud-walled homes.
In the Pamir foothills, the scope of the road building began to strike home. 
Led by the Engineering Troops of the People's Liberation Army, who did the bulk of the blasting, leveling and bridge-building on both sides of the frontier, the crews spent years in regions of burning heat and numbing cold, using pack horses to carry equipment where no vehicle had ever been, menaced by avalanche, landslide or explosion. 
Often, charges had to be placed hundreds of feet up sheer cliff faces, hand-drilled into the rock by men suspended from ropes.
In all, 408 men died, many of them buried beneath simple cairns. 
Although the largest number of these were Chinese, most of the serious mishaps occurred on the Pakistan side, where the graduated plateau that carries the highway for long stretches inside China gives way to more intimidating going. 
In the Hunza and Indus River valleys, the road clings to precipitous mountainsides, with only occasional posts to keep vehicles from plunging into the riverbeds below. 
During the spring runoff, in April and May, subsidence from above is a constant threat.
In the worst cases, hundreds of tons of rock plummet down the mountainside, obliterating the highway and any bridge standing in the way. 
Road crews from Pakistan's Frontier Works Organization, which deploys 10,000 soldiers for road maintenance, are usually on the scene within an hour, but it can take days to clear the rubble, and slides can recur at any time.
Our worst moment came an hour after crossing the Pakistan frontier at Sust, above the Hunza Valley, when the American-made Willy's Jeeps we had transferred to at the border halted before a pile of rock four or five feet high that had been washed across the road by a torrent of water from a nearby glacier. 
While we dismounted and forded our way across 100 yards of rubble, our Pakistani drivers amazed us by challenging the pile with their four-wheel drive and regaining the unshattered continuation of the road. 
Two hours later a major landslide at the same spot closed the road for 48 hours.
A lesser worry was altitude sickness. 
Of the total of 36 hours of driving between Kashgar and Islamabad, nine are spent at altitudes above 10,000 feet, and those, either side of a night stop at Taxkorgan, 250 miles from Kashgar, are spread over the better part of a day. 
We traveled with an amateur dispensary that included tablets for altitude sickness prescribed by an Australian doctor in Peking. 
But none of us took the pills, and perhaps as a result each of us suffered to some degree from heavy limbs, headaches and labored breathing.
Between myself and my wife, Jane, a smoker, the odds for trouble seemed to lie with her. 
But it fell to me, a 41-year-old nonsmoker, to suffer most. 
The trouble started over lunch by a lake in the lee of Muztagata, one of a number of peaks along the highway that hover around 25,000 feet. 
While Jane prepared a meal - canned baked beans and sausages brought from Peking, supplemented by chocolate - I set out to photograph a passing camel. 
We had risen 8,000 feet in five hours since leaving Kashgar, and now, at 12,500 feet, I began feeling dizzy. 
But the symptoms eased overnight in Taxkorgan, at 14,000 feet, and when we reached the peak, 2,000 feet higher, I felt no more than listlessness and a minor headache. 
We were amply rewarded for the physical discomfort. 
Although there are long stretches of nearly barren road, even they offer unexpected relief. 
In a rocky section two hours out of Kashgar, where the road crossed a bridge over an icy brook, a heavily laden camel stood tied to a lean-to made of rocks. 
Smoke curled upward from a chimney, and beside the door stood a weather-beaten old man, white beard falling to his chest, in ankle-length coat and boots. 
This was a trader taking a rest on the way to Kashgar, much as Polo and his caravan must have paused on their journey through this region in 1275.
Elsewhere, habitation took the form of felt-lined yurts, the circular tents favored by the armies of Genghis Khan. 
The Uighur and Kirghiz herders of these uplands, mostly nomads, migrated more than 1,000 years ago from areas to the northeast, near Mongolia, but little in their customs has changed. 
Unlike ethnic Chinese, who are often wary of admitting strangers to their homes, herders' families came forward in greeting when our Landcruiser pulled up, inviting us into the rug-lined comfort of the yurts and offering mugs of fermented yak's milk or tea.
Our stop in Taxkorgan offered another reminder of the ethnic tides that have swept across the old Silk Road. 
After hours of rough driving the road emerged into a landscape of green pasture stretching to the mountains, reminiscent of Ireland's County Galway. 
By a river of crystal-clear water, a group of herders' children were taking the last rays of the sun, dangling their feet over the bank. 
Turning smiling faces to the camera, they were a revelation - blue eyes, proud noses, features wholly European.
This was our first glimpse of the Tadzhiks, a people of Persian origin said to have migrated at about the time that the armies of Alexander the Great pushed eastward from Greece. 
Contemporary Taxkorgan, a few streets of whitewashed homes with an army barracks and blaring loudspeakers, is no more than a century old. 
But closer to the Soviet frontier, 20 miles distant at this point, lie the ruins of an earlier town of the same name, leveled by earthquakes, that was mentioned as the ''gateway'' to China by the mathematician and geographer Ptolemy when writing in the second century.
China demurred for several years before acceding to Pakistan's suggestion that the highway be opened, and one reason was probably the proximity of the road to Afghanistan. 
The Wakhan Corridor, the eastern finger of Afghanistan, meets the Chinese frontier about 50 miles southwest of Taxkorgan. 
The corridor has been occupied by a heavy concentration of Soviet troops since 1979, and it is a fair assumption that the Chinese have fortified their own defenses. 
The only clue we saw was the unsignposted road that breaks westward toward the Wakhan, its surface rutted by trucks.
Another reason for the Chinese to demur was obvious at the Pamir guesthouse in Taxkorgan, used until recently by the Pakistani and Chinese travelers who were the only permitted users of the road. 
Although an effort had been made to upgrade the 160-bed hotel, its washing facilities consisted of an outhouse and a galvanized steel tank with ice-cold water outside each room. 
When one of our party opened a door off his room and spied a bath, the Tadzhik room attendant swiftly locked it. 
The baths are to be activated when running water is available, but nobody was sure just when.
The road, hitherto washboard gravel, turns to asphalt shortly before the Chinese border post at Pirali, and is paved thenceforth all the way to Islamabad. 
In our case, the relief from the gravel was offset quickly by a bureaucratic snafu at the Chinese border post, when our banker friend was found to have an invalid exit visa. 
As usual with foreigners in China, a lengthy discussion and expressions of good will were enough to surmount the problem, and we were soon under way for the final stretch to the frontier proper, at the pinnacle of the Khunjerab Pass.
There, beside a stone plinth recording the official commissioning of the road, we gathered for a group photograph. 
The heavy winter clothing we had brought with us proved superfluous in the brilliant sunshine but the altitude made itself felt in other ways, mainly on our breathing. 
Two days later, overnighting between Gilgit and Islamabad, we could only marvel when a party of British mountaineers enroute to K2, at 28,250 feet the world's second highest mountain, told us that they planned to ascend the mountain's unconquered northwest ridge without oxygen.
In the Kirghiz language Khunjerab means ''Valley of Blood,'' a name the pass earned centuries ago from the activities of the Khanjut brigands who made a livelihood attacking caravans. 
The worst dangers to be faced in our passage, and thereafter through 500 miles of driving to Islamabad, came not from brigands, though even 20 years ago they had not entirely disappeared, nor even from landslides, but from a still more deadly hazard, the Pakistani driver. 
Times beyond number, we stiffened as our Jeep approached a blind corner on the highway to find the entire roadway filled by a careering truck or bus.
The heavy vehicles are mostly British Bedfords with custom-made superstructures that have been extravagantly painted and filigreed, a popular Pakistani folk art. 
Designs include wrestling lions, iridescent peacocks, mountainscapes and mosques. 
High above the Indus, on our fourth day out from Kashgar, we followed a lavishly decorated truck with a rhyming Moslem couplet inscribed in Urdu on its rear door. 
''Oh God, protect me and those who travel with me,'' it began. 
On the Karakoram Highway, with an 800-foot drop beside us, we too felt the need of Allah on our side. 
Three weeks after our journey, a Bedford truck carrying 47 people swerved off the highway near Chilas, south of Gilgit, killing 11 in its plunge into the Indus.
Fortunately, we had fortified ourselves for this last, most taxing part of the journey with a day's rest at Karimabad, in the heart of the Hunza Valley. 
It was a tossup between Kashgar and the Hunza for the highlight of the trip, for in the lee of 25,550-foot Mount Rakaposhi we found what must be one of the loveliest spots in Asia. 
Viewed from Baltit, a medieval village situated hundreds of feet above the valley floor, the Hunza in spring is a carpet of pink and white blossoms, rising to the green of terraced fields on the mountains' lower slopes, and above all the pristine whiteness of the peaks. 
Here, two hours' drive from the bleakness of the Khunjerab, is a vast orchard of apricots, peaches and plums, nurtured by a people renowned for their longevity and their gentle hospitality. 
For at least 1,000 years this has been a stronghold of the Ismailis, the Moslems of Persian origin whose spiritual leader is the Aga Khan, and it was among Ismailis that we relaxed at the $7-a-night Tourist Park Hotel. 
We felt we had found much that was best among them in our young guide, Irfanullah Baig, who charmed us with his chiseled good looks, his porcelain blue eyes and his intense loyalty to the race-horse-owning multimillionaire who is the sect's current leader, Prince Karim Aga Khan. 
''He has his faults, of course,'' he said. 
''But he is ours, and we love him.''
At Baltit, we found traces of the ''great game'' played out between Russia and England for a century and a half after 1800 for dominance in the strategic fastnesses of Central Asia. 
At the 600-year-old Baltit fort, home until 1948 of the mir of Hunza, traditional ruler of the valley, the aging caretaker scurried forward to a dusty mantelpiece and snapped to attention as he displayed the item that seemed to delight him most of all - a sepia-colored photograph, duly autographed, of Field Marshal Lord Roberts of Kandahar, hero of the Indian Mutiny of 1857, who visited the fort after British-led troops marched up the valley in 1891 in furtherance of Britain's policy of controlling the Himalayan passes.
Lower down the valley, at Gilgit, there were reminders of the price that great powers have paid for their efforts to entrench their influence in the region. 
Outside the town, in a shaded grove, stands a granite monolith surrounded by 88 concrete tombs, each containing one of the Chinese who died in building the Karakoram Highway. 
A mile or two away, near the bazaar on the northern side of town, protected by barbed wire, are the crumbling remains of the old British cemetery. 
There, on tablets shattered by vandals or overgrown with weeds, are inscriptions to pioneers ''most cruelly murdered'' in the Pamirs, to missionaries who fell victims to typhus, and to mountaineers killed while tackling Himalayan peaks.
As we drove southward toward Islamabad, rarely losing sight of the torrents of the Indus, one tablet in particular kept coming to mind. 
It was simple in its grief, yet a powerful reminder of how the harshness of geography in these parts has so often triumphed over man. 
''In loving memory of our only son, Harold S. Eldred,'' the inscription read, ''Captain, Sikh Pioneers, Kashmir Infantry, accidentally drowned while fording the Indus, Dec. 
1, 1929, aged 33. 
'Until the day breaks and the shadows flee away.'
''
Â 
THROUGH THE KHUNJERAB PASS -
Planning Few trips in China fall easily into place, but this is one where careful preparation can be especially important. 
Particularly on the Chinese section of the highway, limited hotel space, Jeeps and air service create potential bottlenecks. 
Although Pakistan, too, has only recently begun to develop the route for tourism, matters there are somewhat easier.
The journey can begin from either end of the highway, in Kashgar or Islamabad, but uncertainties of transport on the Chinese side make it easier, for the time being, to begin in Kashgar. 
Barring serious landslides, the entire 795-mile distance from Kashgar to Islamabad can be covered in approximately 36 hours of driving. 
In our case, with a day's rest stop in Karimabad, in the Hunza Valley, and an afternoon's layover in Gilgit, the journey took five full days, with eight to 12 hours' driving on each of four days.
Travel arrangements must be made separately for each side of the border, since Chinese and Pakistani vehicles are currently permitted to serve only their own section of the highway.
Â 
When to Go
For now, the highway is open to travel by nationals of countries other than China and Pakistan from May 1 to Oct. 
31 each year for group travel and from May 1 to Nov. 
30 for individuals. 
Eventually both countries hope to keep the route open year round, but currently problems with snow clearance and general road maintenance dictate the limited season.
Â 
Visa Requirements
A standard Chinese tourist visa is accepted for entry and exit at the frontier post at Pirali. 
In the first weeks after the highway's opening, Pakistan required special visas for those making the journey, but this has now been dropped for all but two categories of traveler - journalists and nationals of countries that do not enjoy 30-day visa-free entry to Pakistan for tourist reasons. 
In the case of Americans and most Westerners, no visas will be required by Pakistan regardless of whether your trip begins in Kashgar or Islamabad.
Â 
Group Tours
A number of American companies specializing in China are offering Karakoram Highway trips. 
Mountain Travel (1398 Solano Avenue, Albany, Calif. 
94706; 415-527-8100 or 800-227-2384) is offering two 23-day group tours departing June 14 and 22 next year that are priced at $3,575 a person, based on double occupancy, not including round-trip air fare from the United States. 
However, the price for the trip does include extensive travel inside China, besides the Karakoram Highway. 
Lindblad Travel is planning to include the highway on its trips to the region next year (1 Sylvan Road North, Westport, Conn. 
06881; 203-226-8531 or 800-243-5657).
Â 
Independent Travel
Costs can be considerably lowered by making arrangements yourself, but where the Chinese side of the journey is concerned this may be difficult to arrange from outside China, and commitments made by the China International Travel Service can be infuriatingly unreliable. 
The large numbers of backpackers making the journey in May in both directions proved, too, that for those willing to accept delays of days at a time - and to entrust themselves to the public buses that run on either side of the frontier - the journey can be made with practically no advance preparation.
Agencies to contact in China include the Peking branch of the China International Travel Service (domestic bookings, 755272) and the branch in Urumqi, capital of Xinjiang (25794). 
In all probability, direct contact with Urumqi through the international operator will be more effective. 
The Urumqi branch can make bookings on the five weekly flights between Urumqi and Kashgar, a three-hour leg on a twin-engine Antonov-24 that is one of the major potential bottlenecks; if sandstorms ground flights, a common occurrence, the only other means of covering the Urumqi-Kashgar leg is by public bus or minibus, a three-day journey across the desert. 
By minibus, the cost is about $600.
Jeep or minibus bookings from Kashgar to Sust, on the Pakistan frontier, are another potential bottleneck, since there are fewer than 20 vehicles available for the journey in Kashgar. 
The standard rate for a Toyota Landcruiser between Kashgar and Sust, where the highway crosses into Pakistan, is about $350. 
Here again, the best contact is the Urumqi office of C.I.T.S., which will seek reservations by telephone through the travel service's Kashgar branch. 
Most C.I.T.S. officials answering the telephone in Urumqi speak English.
For arrangements on the Pakistan side, the easiest course is to contact one of Pakistan's best-known travel agencies, Travel Walji's Ltd. 
(Walji's Building, 10 Khayaban Suhrawardy, Box 1088, Islamabad; 828324 and 826621, telex 5769 WALJI PK or 5836 WALJI PK). 
Arrangements can be made for a Jeep or minibus for all or part of the journey on the Pakistan side, including having a vehicle waiting at the Pakistan frontier on your arrival from Kashgar. 
The company will also book hotel rooms and air flights, including the crucial Islamabad-Gilgit leg, which cuts 15 hours of driving off the journey for those who decide to forego the journey through the Indus Valley. 
Walji's drivers are excellent, and the company's other services impeccable. 
Costs vary according to vehicle and distance, but for a jeep journey over the entire length of the highway on the Pakistan side will run about $325, regardless of the number traveling.J.

text:
ï»¿
He was seated at a table in the prison dispensary, dressed in a white dustcoat. 
From the anguish in his eyes and the awkward way he rose to his feet, it was plain he was no ordinary doctor.
What brought Zhao Guomin to the Shanghai Municipal Prison was not medicine but murder. 
On Dec. 
28, 1968, he and four other men beat to death the 38-year-old scientist who was head of the Shanghai Pharmacological Institute in a case that was swallowed up for a time in the general tumult of the Cultural Revolution.
Now 43 years old, Mr. Zhao has about 18 months of an eight-year prison term still to serve, and he counts himself a lucky man. 
''I could have been executed,'' he told a visitor. 
Tears welled in his eyes as he spoke of his victim's family and of the travails of his own wife and son as they await his return.
Article describes conditions at Shanghai Municipal Prison, China, where many young people arrested during country's Cultural Revolution remain incarcerated; some efforts have been made by Government of Deng Xiaoping to help prisoners prepare for better life (M)
Mr. Zhao's story is one of many in the forbidding edifice at 147 Changyang Street in central Shanghai that have their origin in the ''10 years of calamity,'' as the Cultural Revolution is officially known. 
When Mao Zedong set out in 1966 to turn Chinese society upside down, he unleashed forces that shattered hundreds of thousands of lives, and the legacy is still felt in every corner of the nation's life.
A tour of the Shanghai prison is a sobering affair. 
More than 60 percent of the 3,700 inmates are under 35, men and women who belong to what Chinese call the ''lost generation'' of youth whose education and family life were uprooted when the Cultural Revolution closed schools, set children against parents and licensed mayhem against anybody standing for the established order.
Â 
Cultural Revolution Is Blamed
''What we have here in many respects are the victims of the Cultural Revolution,'' said Wu Jichen, the prison's deputy governor, as he led a visitor through workshops and classrooms that cluster around granite cell blocks built by the British between 1903 and 1923. 
''They belong to a generation that was told by the Gang of Four that education was useless, so they grew up without culture, without any sense of right and wrong.''
''What we try to do is to engage in a process of remolding, to try and help the inmates distinguish what is right from what is wrong, what is beautiful from what is ugly, what is lawful from what is not.''
Similar accounts have been offered for many years in Chinese jails, but officials acknowledge now that much of what was said in the past was false or at least exaggerated. 
The picture that has emerged since the ascent of China's current leader, Deng Xiaoping, is one in which the country's vast network of jails and labor camps, indeed the entire legal system, was fatally prejudiced by arbitrariness and brutality.
Not all of this has changed. 
In two years, under a crackdown on crime begun by Mr. Deng, thousands of people have been executed, some within days of their offenses. 
The central authorities' insistence on a broader use of the death sentence has led to thousands of executions since the autumn of 1983, nine in Peking on one day in January alone. 
Troubling questions remain about the fairness of court procedures, including limited opportunities for defense.
Â 
Greater Effort Visible
Nonetheless, a visit to the Shanghai prison suggests that greater effort has been made under Mr. Deng to give substance to Mao's instruction that prisons be turned into factories, farms and schools where inmates can prepare for a better life. 
A visitor passing through workshops where prisoners make clothing, electrical components and ornaments has the impression of generally healthy men and women unafraid to talk about their yearning for life outside.
The prison sits off a busy street, shielded by a succession of three steel doors, by guards with automatic rifles and by a 20-foot granite wall topped by glass shards. 
According to Mr. Wu, the deputy governor, sentences range from 20 years to six months, with ''seven or eight'' inmates under suspended death sentences that can be commuted for good behavior after two years.
The case of Dr. Zhao suggests that there is still much that is arbitrary in the sentencing. 
As he told it, he was press-ganged into joining an ''investigation team'' that came to the pharmacological institute to press charges of spying against the party secretary. 
Because torture was to be involved, the team wanted a doctor present, but as things progressed Dr. Zhao became an accomplice in the beating.
Dr. Zhao said the death was covered up at the time, but the case was reopened at the widow's instigation after the overthrow of the so-called Gang of Four - Jiang Qing, who was Mao's wife, and her associates - in 1976. 
Two of the five assailants were tried, and Dr. Zhao received the stiffer sentence. 
After two years at hard labor and two more in another prison, he was assigned to the dispensary. 
On his release next year, he expects to be reassigned to medical work in Shanghai.
Â 
Song Shows New Attitude
Against this, other sentences seem relatively severe. 
Chen Jingcai, conductor of the prison orchestra, is serving a 15-year term for ''molesting women'' while interviewing them for posts with a Shanghai ensemble. 
Since there is a charge of rape under Chinese law, his offense evidently was less severe. 
Now he spends his days teaching prisoners the violin, flute and other instruments and rehearsing lusty renditions the ''Ode to Joy'' movement of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony and American songs such as ''Oh!
Susanna'' sung with Chinese words.
Even in the orchestra, prisoners are expected to work at remolding attitudes. 
Zhao Derong, a former glassmaker serving a four-year term for stealing bicycles, exercises his strong tenor in a prison ballad he composed, ''Don't Worry About Me, Mother.''
In the refrain, he sings of his wish to study hard, learn skills and ''make my contribution to the motherland.''
Work is the center of prison life. 
Inmates labor eight hours a day, six days a week for three yuan, or $1.07, plus monthly bonuses of up to 20 yuan. 
All are required to attend classes and to work toward at least a junior middle school certificate, the equivalent of 10th grade. 
Each block has a television set, a library and a Ping-Pong table. 
A half-hour family visit once a month is permitted, and about a fifth of the prisoners are allowed to go home for a couple of days each year.
At night, two inmates are locked into each of the cells, which measure about 8 feet by 5 and have steel doors and a sliding peephole that opens from the outside. 
Bedrolls stacked against the wall are laid on concrete floors. 
Regulations pinned to the wall forbid discussion of crimes and sentences between cellmates and command them to ''seriously repent'' their wrongdoing.
According to Mr. Wu, the deputy governor, the last time anybody escaped was in 1975, clinging to the underside of a delivery truck, and he was caught in hours. 
Although guards are unarmed, officials say none have been attacked in memory. 
''What we aim for is to achieve the kind of relationship doctors have with patients,'' said Mr. Wu. ''You can see for yourself, there is no hostility between wardens and prisoners.''

file: IN THE VILLAGES OF CHINA, BUSINESS RIVALRY BLOOMS.txt
text:
ï»¿
A hand-cranked telephone still stands between Ma Tianying and his hopes of becoming the richest peasant in his village in Sichuan Province.
Mr. Ma runs his own small sawmill, repairs trucks and tractors and makes prefabricated housing slabs. 
Last year he and his family earned the equivalent of about $6,000, making him the second wealthiest resident of the village of Chengbei.
But Mr. Ma, a stocky man whose business attire is a T-shirt and baggy blue trousers held up by an old army belt, has yet to catch up with Zhang Daishen. 
She got a head start in turning out the prefabricated concrete that is in demand because of the housing boom touched off by recent changes in agricultural policy.
Agricultural specialist in China has estimated that as many as 70% of China's peasants are economically superfluous and Chinese Government, hoping to better utilize peasants, is encouraging them to stop tilling soil and set up small workshops, service trades and specialized occupations that will keep them gainfully employed; photos; map (M)
Miss Zhang earned about $6,800 last year and installed the village's first and only private telephone.
Â 
Rivalry Is Encouraged
Miss Zhang and Mr. Ma personify the kind of rivalry that the Chinese Government likes to encourage. 
The country's agricultural output has soared since 1979, when a new policy let farmers keep whatever they could grow beyond a quota set by the state. 
But the new productivity has revealed the extent of underemployment that long existed among China's 800 million peasants.
Because China has too many farmers and too little arable land for them to cultivate, the Government wants more peasants to stop tilling the soil and set up small workshops, service trades and specialized occupations like raising livestock that will keep them gainfully employed in the countryside.
Du Runsheng, a leading agricultural specialist, estimated three months ago that as many as 70 percent of China's peasants were economically superfluous. 
The cities could not afford to absorb them, he said, so new jobs must be created for them in rural areas.
Mr. Du, who heads the Rural Policy Research Center of the Communist Party's Central Committee, said at a news conference that he envisioned a strategy of shifting 30 to 40 percent of China's rural labor force out of traditional farm work and into sideline occupations and small industries.
Â 
A Policy for Development
''In a situation of surplus rural labor,'' Mr. Du said, ''this may be a proper way to increase employment and people's incomes, to raise their cultural level and to speed up rural development. 
In short, this is a policy for comprehensive development of the countryside.''
A directive since issued by the Cabinet-level State Council and the party's Central Committee has made clear that Mr. Du's views are more than academic. 
It urged that by the end of the century 40 percent of the rural labor force, or about 200 million peasants, should be performing jobs not in the fields.
The directive noted that 31 million peasants already worked in commune- run enterprises and that two million others had set up their own businesses.
Chengbei village, set in the rolling hills and bright green rice paddies of Ziyang County in Sichuan, has benefited from the changes. 
The village head, Zhang Chenming, said that his community had 395 households with 1,584 people, but only 61 acres of farmland, which is a fraction of the meager national average of a quarter acre per person.
Â 
No More Handouts
Before the 1979 changes, Mr. Zhang said, the village was crippled by leftist egalitarianism and so poor that it relied on annual state subsidies of grain and money. 
After the land was contracted out to individual households, the peasants began working harder and the handouts stopped. 
Last year Chengbei's annual per capita income reached about $230, which is nearly three times the income in 1979.
''The responsibility system is like an elixir for the people,'' Mr. Zhang said. 
''In the past, we all ate from the same big pot. 
Now we have broken the iron rice bowl.''
Mr. Ma, who is 45 years old, earned 55 cents a day under the old commune system. 
When the new policies let him stop, he set to work for himself repairing tractors and machinery, then took up making concrete housing slabs. 
He borrowed about $3,000 from the state bank and later invested $4,000 that he had saved. 
Recently, he built a large new three-story house with his workshops on the ground floor and two rooms for each family member on the upper floors.
Â 
Success Is Not Resented
Now that peasants are allowed to go into long-distance hauling, Mr. Ma bought a secondhand truck and plans to buy a couple more so that he can compete with the state-run transportation companies.
Asked if the neighbors resented his success, Mr. Ma said, ''No, because all of us are trying to become well-off.''
Mr. Ma said he also wanted to get a telephone, to let him compete better with Miss Zhang. 
She insisted her rival was actually her brother-in-law, Liu Zifu, who broke away from her business to set up a workshop of his own.
''At the beginning, our family was the only one making building materials here,'' she said. 
''Later on, some people learned from our example. 
Now more than 20 households are doing the same job.''
Miss Zhang, who is 36, started out as a fieldhand, earning only work points from the commune. 
She also pulled a handcart carrying charcoal and coal. 
Now, she said, she employs 10 other villagers in her enterprise, which makes asbestos tiles as well as concrete slabs, and raises poultry on the side. 
She has not hired her husband, Lu Ziling, who works as a purchasing agent for the local marketing cooperative and earns far less than she does.
Â 
Phone a Status Symbol
''We have very serious competition now,'' said Miss Zhang. 
''I try to offer lower prices and better quality.''
To solicit orders from the provincial capital of Chengdu, 50 miles away, Miss Zhang bought a black telephone with a hand crank. 
The installation cost about $140, nearly as much as an average Chinese peasant earns in a year.
The telephone is a status symbol in Chengbei, where there is no one else to call. 
But Miss Zhang explained that ''it does provide a lot of convenience for business.''

text:
ï»¿
A group of Indian pilgrims who for the first time in 22 years were permitted to visit a lake sacred to Hindus in southwestern Tibet have returned with descriptions of monasteries that were destroyed in China's Cultural Revolution.
The 13 worshipers who entered Tibet through the Himalayas traveled 300 miles by horse, mule and truck in a region that has rarely been visited by outsiders since the Chinese conquest of Tibet.
As part of efforts to thaw relations between India and China, Peking permitted pilgrims to travel to the lake, which is known as Manasarowar in India and as Mapam in Tibet. 
The deep blue lake, at an altitude of 14,000 feet, is considered holy by both Hindus and Buddhists. 
Before the Chinese invasion, eight large monasteries housing thousands of monks ringed the slopes around the lake.
Indian pilgrims, permitted for first time in 22 years to visit sacred areas of Tibet, see ruins of temples destroyed in Chinese Cultural Revolution
The travelers had cameras with them but said they were frequently discouraged by their guides from photographing the vandalized sites.
Â 
Buddhist Palace Is Destroyed
The travelers said that the gompas, as they are called, were all empty shells, having been systematically blown up. 
''Our Chinese guides told us that the destruction had all been the work of the Gang of Four,'' one of the travelers said, referring to Mao Zedong's radical associates who have been blamed for the excessses of the Cultural Revolution.
The traveler added that the same guides did not permit the pilgrims to make close inspection of the ruins. 
One gompa, measuring nearly half a mile in length, had been reduced to rubble.
The summer palace of a Buddhist order was also destroyed. 
However, one of the Indian visitors said local residents had apparently salvaged some ancient prayer stones and built ramshackle chapels. 
Above one ruin there flew a solitary prayer flag that had apparently been recently put in place, attesting to the tenacious hold of the religious culture even in the absence of monks.
According to the pilgrims, the group's guides, both Chinese and Tibetans, said several times that they had heard reports that the Chinese Government was preparing to rebuild the religious buildings.
The travelers said that they were kept at a distance from settlers but that they spent some time in the town of Taklakot, now known officially in Tibet as Burang. 
It is a settlement where local herdsmen exchange yak wool for food smuggled in by Nepalese traders, and Tibetans live in huts of stone.
Flags flew from official buildings, the visitors said, but they saw no pictures of Mao or any other revolutionary figures. 
''My impression,'' a young traveler said, ''was that the authorities had given up doing anything for the local people and that the Tibetans were living as hard a life as they had for centuries.''
There was no sign of the kind of rich ceremonial life that dominated the lives of local people. 
There were no communes and no schools, the travelers said, and there were no temples and no monasteries, just high gravel expanses without vegetation and some hardy goats, sheep and people.
In their trek the Indian pilgrims came upon the remains of Shershung, where fairs used to be held on days of the full moon. 
The site is now rubble, the travelers said, marked only by burial mounds of inscribed prayer stones.

An organization of more than 400 American companies forecast today that trade with China would increase by $1 billion next year from the $6 billion estimated for 1984.
The National Council for U.S.-China Trade also said that American companies formed 31 ventures with Chinese partners in the first nine months of 1984 - more than the total of the preceding four years.
''We're quite upbeat,'' Christopher H. Phillips, president of the council, commented in an interview.
''Having lived with this thing for the last 12 years, we've learned to avoid extremes of euphoria and pessimism,'' he said. 
''But because of what the Chinese themselves are doing, the situation now is more encouraging than it's ever been.''
National Council for US-China Trade forecasts that trade with China will increase by $1 billion in 1985 from $6 billion this year; says American companies formed 31 ventures with Chinese partners in first nine months of 1984--more than total of preceding four years (M)
The council, formed after the Nixon Administration's opening to China in 1972 to promote commercial links, today has a membership of 430 companies. 
Its president, Mr. Phillips, is a former diplomat and banker.
Â 
Direct Investment
The group placed at $700 million the value of direct American investment in China. 
Much of this - $588 million - is committed to offshore oil exploration. 
But, Mr. Phillips said, ''the tempo is picking up'' in direct investment outside the oil sector.
In recent months Peking has taken these steps:
- Promulgated a law to protect patents, which takes effect next April 1.
- Opened 14 coastal cities to foreign investment, in addition to the four originally designated Special Economic Zones.
- Decentralized government control over local enterprises to encourage more efficient management.
- Shortened the approval process for foreign investment.
- Allowed foreigners greater access to the domestic Chinese market.
Â 
New on the Scene
Among companies that are starting new ventures are the McDonnell Douglas Corporation, the Foxboro Company, Admiral International, the AVX Corporation, the Fedders Corporation and the Midland-Ross Corporation.
McDonnell Douglas plans to assemble passenger planes in Shanghai. 
On the outskirts of Shanghai, Foxboro will make instruments to control industrial processes. 
The R.J. 
Reynolds Tobacco Company has just entered its second joint venture to produce cigarettes, at a plant in Xiamen in Fujian Province.
The American Motors Corporation is already producing four-wheel-drive vehicles in Shanghai. 
The Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Company makes Scotch tape and other products in Shanghai. 
And the Gillette Company makes razor blades in southern Manchuria.
Â 
Trade Surplus for China
American exports to China should top $3 billion next year and grow faster than China's exports to the United States, according to council projections. 
China had a surplus of about $400 million in trade with the United States this year but that is expected to be wiped out in 1985.
Most of the rise in American exports will come in manufactured goods and high-technology products, Mr. Phillips said.
Machinery sales to China, for example, have been rising steadily. 
This year they will approach $1 billion, accounting for about 30 percent of total American exports to China.
Next year, the council notes, a number of large contracts will raise the figure further. 
It cited equipment orders for the Eastman Kodak Company's $100 million color film factory in Fujian Province, orders for machinery for the huge open-pit coal mining project under way in north China, and orders for oil well pumps, drill bits and other oil equipment to support offshore exploration.
Also likely to swell the export totals next year are sales of passenger aircraft and helicopters.
Â 
Commodity Figures
American commodity exports, while remaining significant, are expected to shrink as a proportion of total exports. 
Grain sales should be somewhere between $500 million and $1 billion, even in the absence of a long-term agreement.
Under a 1980 grain agreement which expires at the end of this year, Peking was committed to purchasing 6 million metric tons of wheat or corn annually. 
As of late November, China had purchased only 4.4 million tons for 1984. 
It had been short 2.2 million tons of its commitment for 1983.
The council foresees continued growth of Chinese exports here. 
Textile sales, which accounted for nearly one-third of Chinese exports in 1984, will continue rising, especially as the Chinese shift toward higher value- added textile products, the council forecast.
The two-way trade with China of nearly $6 billion this year was almost three times the value of goods the United States and the Soviet Union exchanged in 1984.
