file: INQUIRY SET ON CHINESE TEXTILES.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Commerce Department said today that it is investigating whether Chinese textiles and apparel exported to the United States are being illegally subsidized.
The department said it started the countervailing duty investigation Monday. 
It was set off by complaints filed last month by several domestic textile and apparel groups that the Chinese textiles are subsidized through dual exchange rates and therefore can be sold in this country below their real production costs.
US Commerce Department probes whether Chinese textiles and apparel exported to US are being illegally subsidized through dual exchange rates; investigation poses novel legal issue because it is first brought by department against a non-market economy, one in which prices are set by government order and not by market forces (M)
An example of a dual exchange rate, variations of which are used by a number of countries, is one in which a nation employs one exchange rate for trade payments and another for tourism. 
If a trade rate artificially undervalues the dollar, the price of goods might not reflect their actual cost.
The investigation poses novel legal issues because it is the first brought by the department against a non-market economy, Commerce Secretary Malcolm Baldrige said. 
The department considers a non-market economy one in which prices are set by government order and not by market forces, often the case in Communist- bloc countries.
The Commerce Department said in a release that the law requires it to investigate ''where the U.S. industry alleges subsidies and provides information to support its allegations, as in these cases.''
The complaints come at a time when Reagan Administration is engaged in an effort to expand trade between the two countries.
The Commerce Department said that a Nov. 
3 hearing will consider the issues of whether the countervailing duty law covers non-market economy countries and whether dual exchange rates can in fact be considered a subsidy in cases where the exchange - in this case Chinese currency - is not freely convertible into dollars and the exchange rate for payment of exports and imports is set arbitrarily by government order.
The department said it will decide by Dec. 
6 whether, and to what extent, textile products from China are subsidized. 
If the textiles are found to be subsidized, importers will have to post bonds in the amount of estimated duties for all goods named in the case that enter the United States on or after the date the preliminary decisions are published.
Â 
1,000 Categories of Imports
The Commerce Department's investigation covers the bulk of the Chinese textile exports to the United States. 
Last year, the United States imported about $870 million worth of textiles that are the subject of the current investigation. 
More than 1,000 separate import categories, as the department classifies them, are being studied.
The complaints were filed by the American Textile Manufacturers Institute, the American Apparel Manufacturers Association, the Amalgamated Clothing and Textile Workers Union and the International Ladies Garment Workers Union.

file: INTERNATIONAL REPORT_DRAGONAIR, A GNAT THAT ROARS.txt
text:
ï»¿
Dragonair, a 22-month-old airline that owns one plane and leases another, has a burning ambition. 
It wants to become a major international carrier.
Standing in its way is Cathay Pacific Airways, which has everything Dragonair does not: passengers, profits and prospects.
Regarded as among the world's best airlines, along with other Asian carriers such as Singapore Airlines and Thai Airways International, Cathay Pacific has expanded rapidly in recent years and now uses Hong Kong as the hub of 494 flights each week, on 22 aircraft. 
Most of the flights are within Asia, but it also serves destinations ranging from Amsterdam to San Francisco. 
More than 4.3 million passengers flew Cathay last year.
Â 
Byzantine Struggle
The battle is more than just for business: It is a prime example of the Byzantine struggles in Hong Kong for China's patronage before Beijing resumes control of this territory in a decade's time.
''Cathay Pacific is the image of Hong Kong past, and we're the image of Hong Kong future,'' said Stephen H. Miller, the feisty general manager of Dragonair, formally known as Hong Kong Dragon Airlines Ltd.
Seven weeks ago, many analysts might have agreed with that assessment. 
Dragonair was viewed as having Beijing's backing, through the crucial web of relationships known in Chinese as ''guanxi,'' the key to getting what you want in China. 
Of the Chinese businessmen associated with the airline, the most prominent is Sir Yue-kong Pao, a shipping magnate who is one of Dragonair's largest backers and is serving as chairman. 
He has good links with Beijing and is often mentioned as a future candidate for governor of Hong Kong. 
Meanwhile, Cathay Pacific, with its crew of 100 percent non-Chinese pilots and flight engineers, was seen as being British-backed.
Then abruptly, at the end of January, China's investment bank, the China International Trust and Investment Corporation, purchased a 12.5 percent stake in Cathay Pacific for $245 million (United States).
Dragonair's managing director, Helmut Sohmen, likened the Cathay move to ''pushing panic buttons,'' but in the airline industry it was seen as a brilliant maneuver that robbed Dragonair of its status as the fighter in Beijing's corner.
Dragonair has hardly wilted under the pressure. 
On New Year's Eve, it announced that it had placed firm orders for two of the McDonnell Douglas Corporation's new long-haul planes, the MD-11 - even though Dragonair as yet has no long-distance routes.
Then, shortly after the China International investment in Cathay, Dragonair's shareholders announced they would double the paid-up capital, to $51 million.
Cathay formerly was 70 percent owned by Swire Pacific, a Hong Kong conglomerate that in turn is controlled by John Swire & Sons, a diversified London concern. 
The remaining 30 percent was owned by the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation. 
However, last year, the two owners decided to make a public offering and issue stock.
Traded on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, the issue was 52 times oversubscribed, a measure of Cathay's premier role in the territory - and of the profits that are anticipated. 
In 1985, the last full year for which figures are available, Cathay Pacific earned $100 million on revenues of $965 million.
For the present, Dragonair is losing money - reportedly $500,000 a month - although Mr. Miller, the managing director, said that when two more planes are in service later this year the airline could break even.

file: IS CHINA IMPEDING WESTERN REPORTERS_.txt
text:
ï»¿
Several Western broadcast news organizations, including the British Broadcasting Corporation and a CBS crew led by Walter Cronkite, have experienced difficulty with the Chinese Government in negotiating to film stories there in recent months. 
In each instance, the Chinese have requested substantial payments in return for permission to do the stories.
The British Broadcasting Corporation, which has produced a large number of documentaries in China during the last eight years, has not filmed there since January. 
It was then that the Central Broadcasting Administration of China -one of several Chinese bureaucracies that handle requests from Western news organizations - demanded a large sum from the BBC for permitting it to film a series of stories in China during 1981.
Discussion of difficulties encountered by western broadcasting groups in China focuses on high fees demanded by Chinese
It is common for broadcast crews filming in China and elsewhere to pay their hosts for direct services rendered, including hotels and meals, technical support, transportation and interpreters. 
However the BBC put the Chinese request for fees in another category.
Â 
Against Lump Fees
''We did not agree to the principal that we should give lump sums for unitemized services,'' said Dina Lee, a correspondent for the Far Eastern Economic Review who speaks Chinese and regularly negotiates on behalf of the BBC.
In the current edition of The Listener, a BBC publication, Aubrey Singer, managing director of BBC radio, suggests an explanation for the practice of seeking fees.
''The Chinese are building a new television centre in Peking,'' Mr. Singer writes. 
''To do this they need foreign currency and they have to persuade their government that they can be a foreign currency earner. 
Under the new Chinese economic rule this would qualify them to spend foreign currency. 
Seen in this light, the reasons for the policy become all too apparent.''
Â 
Cronkite Has Difficulty
Mr. Cronkite and his crew flew to China last month to do three stories for the CBS science series ''Universe'' and also ran into some difficulties. 
Two of the stories were completed, but the crew was unable to get permission to go ahead with the most coveted one: a report on the acclaimed panda project near the central China city of Chengtou.
When one of the CBS producers decided to try filming pandas at the Peking Zoo, she was told that it would cost CBS $80 for each minute of filming. 
A second CBS producer who went to film pandas at a zoo in Chengtou was told that a Japanese crew had recently paid $30,000 to film there. 
According to Jonathan Ward, producer of ''Universe,'' both CBS producers declined to pay, and ultimately were permitted by the Chinese to shoot without any additional cost.
John Fisher, a producer for New Cinema Ltd. of Ontario, Canada, also faced a request for payment during his early negotiations to do six one-hour programs in China.
''They said they wanted an administrative fee that was exorbinant - in the hundreds of thousands of dollars,'' said Mr. Fisher. ''We took the position that we wouldn't pay a fee for the license to shoot, but we were certainly prepared to pay for any services rendered.''
An agreement covering what Mr. Fischer calls ''fair and reasonable costs'' was finally reached.
Â 
A Product to Sell
''The Chinese want as much hard currency as they can get, and they believe that they have a commodity that has a value on the open market'' Mr. Fisher explained. 
''It's very capitalistic, but by and large they haven't had a lot of experience in this area, and they really don't know what to ask for.''
ABC News had such difficulty getting approvals for a documentary it had planned on the performing arts in China that the project was finally abandoned after more than six months of discussions.
The ABC ''Close Up'' unit intended to do a documentary about the performing arts in China and how they reflect the country's political situation. 
During the early discussions last fall, according to Dick Richter, senior producer of the ABC unit, the Chinese seemed enthusiastic about the project. 
Then the delays in approvals began.
''It became apparent that the Government was becoming more restrictive in terms of freedom of expression in the arts,'' Mr. Richter said. 
Finally in March, an agreement was reached and plans were made for ABC producers to do a survey trip, to be followed by four weeks of shooting.
Â 
Untenable Restrictions
The survey trip began, but according to Mr. Richter the Chinese imposed untenable restrictions. 
''They told us we couldn't film on this street or that, that we couldn't talk to anyone outspoken or turn on cameras without permission. 
They also wanted to charge us extra for almost everything, even shooting in the street.''
The project was shelved last month.
Not all Western producers have experienced difficulties, however. 
Peter Larkin, foreign editor for CBS News, said that his relations with the Chinese have never been better. 
The only time that CBS did agree to a fee, Mr. Larkin said, was for exclusive United States rights to a Chinese special report about the so-called Gang of Four shortly before their trial began last winter - just as the network might pay for historical footage from a library.
During that same winter period, CBS News was able to produce 32 stories in China, including a large number about the trial. 
''We've never had to pay fees for any of them,'' said Mr. Larkin. ''We have explained that it is not our policy to pay for stories. 
They understand the distinction between news and stories from which we could derive a profit.''

file: IS PEKING_S LIBERALIZATION REALLY OVER_.txt
text:
ï»¿
From a small room below street level in a student hostel at Hong Kong University, there is likely to issue, any day or evening, the crackling of broadcasts from China, the murmur of a cultivated Central European voice dictating Communist propaganda into a tape recorder, the noble lines of a Bach sonata for violin solo played by an accomplished musician or the barking of a robust German Shepherd dog.
The nameplate says ''1. 
La Dany,'' which gives no clue except to those in the know, because Father Laszlo Ladanyi of the Society of Jesus works anonymously. 
Those in the know are toilers in the same vineyard as the priest - students of contemporary China. 
Father Ladany, as he now spells his name on his personal stationery, is a leading practitioner of the craft of China-watching, widely respected even by those who do not always share his conclusions.
Analysis of current political climate in China focuses on seeming shift away from liberalization of past several years
In a field where backbiting is not uncommon, Father Ladany could listen in on the private conversations of his colleagues without embarrassing them. 
''He is pre-eminent,'' said Robert Elegant, a veteran journalistic China-watcher before he turned novelist. 
''His track record is better than anyone else's.''
On the other end of the spectrum from Mr. Elegant, whose admiration for Communist China has always known limits, are China's former friends, the countries of the Soviet camp. 
''Most of their embassies in Peking are on my mailing list,'' said the priest contentedly, puffing on a pipe that had gone cold.
Father Ladany's mailing is the oldest journal of China-watching, China News Analysis. 
Now a fortnightly, it was founded in 1953; the current issue is No. 1,204. Except for 76 quarterly issues devoted to Vietnam, the journal is the work of Father Ladany. 
Each issue is a seven or eight-page essay devoted to a single theme, rather than a newsletter giving snippets of current news. 
''My files go back 30 years,'' said the gaunt and grey-haired Jesuit.
At 67, the Hungarian intellectual is slightly weary because nothing seems to happen that hasn't happened before, but also intellectually alert, because he does not appear to have abandoned hope that something new and better might come along. 
''When I want to write about a subject, I read the files and then go for a walk and think, 'What's new now?'
''
Father Ladany's views are remarkably free of ideology, Communist or Roman Catholic. 
Having spent 41 years in China and Hong Kong, he sees events through the prism of millennia of ebb and flow in the history of the Middle Kingdom. 
In a long afternoon of conversation, the priest-historian betrayed neither adulation for a hero nor hatred of a villain. 
''Only one thing is certain in China,'' he said. 
''Every few years, the whole system changes. 
Between dynasties, it takes 50 to 100 years until the new emerges,'' he continued. 
''We are in that period. 
The Chinese think like that; you Americans don't. 
In your system, everything changes every four years.''
His disabused view has put Father Ladany occasionally at odds with his fellow China-watchers and subscribers, but he is taken seriously even by those who disagree, and the journal, sold by subscription only at $135 a year, is self-supporting. 
''He has been unfashionable at times,'' an American China-watcher said, ''because he is usually right.''
While the opening of the United States Embassy in Peking has reduced the number of American China-watchers in Hong Kong, the United States Consulate General continues the work. 
Its Chinese staff members are free from restrictions that affect all Chinese working for embassies in Peking. 
They point out the nuggets of new information and interpretation that appear in Chinese media, while those in Peking are under evident instructions to be no more than clinically neutral translators.
'A Very Nervous System'
American diplomats in Peking think Father Ladany too pessimistic; he finds many Americans interested in China insufficiently skeptical and too eager to believe the facade presented by a regime that represents one billion prospective customers. 
Presently, Father Ladany believes that the liberalizations instituted by Deng Xiaoping have already run their course and have in most respects already been reversed. 
''The whole population must say that nothing has changed,'' the priest said. 
''Before, everything was all wrong; now, everything is all right. 
They must say the reversal has not taken place.''
In Father Ladany's apparent view, a Stalinist regime can reverse course publicly only when the leadership has been unseated; leaders still in power cannot admit to having been unsuccessful or wrong.
The priest believes that conservative pressures, coming largely from the military, have forced Mr. Deng to abandon his liberal positions. 
''The Russian system is stupid but stable,'' he remarked. 
''The Chinese are always intelligent but Utopian and unrealistic. 
It is a very nervous system.''
Father Ladany has a staff of five Chinese who help him to read about 15 Chinese newspapers, monitor broadcasts, read the publications of the Hong Kong Communist community, which he considers the most enlightened, liberal and avant-garde of the Chinese party, and to receive Chinese visitors who have left for exile. 
He sees few foreigners, he said, because they either ''discover China as if they were Columbus'' or, ''like Germans, take down all the data when they visit a commune, multiply it by the number of communes and think they know China.''
Nothing in early life predisposed Father Ladany for his present calling. 
The son of a physician, he was born in Budapest, obtained a doctorate in law and studied the violin at the conservatory until he discovered his priestly vocation. 
He was sent by the Jesuits to Peking in 1940 to study Chinese, not at his request, was ordained in China in 1946 and left in 1949. 
His order imposes no other priestly functions on him, he said, ''because we believe God created the whole world and not only church buildings.''
He began to publish his journal anonymously and divided his name into two parts because in the early years he still had close relatives in Hungary. 
He returned there for a visit in 1976 and came back with his violin, a 19th century Italian instrument, which he had left with relatives when he joined the church. 
Life has rarefied his musical taste to unaccompanied Bach only. 
He thinks in Chinese and English now, he said, having forgotten some Hungarian. 
It appears fluent, as are his German, French, Italian and Latin.
Father Ladany charitably did not discuss his critics, but in a note delivered after the conversation, he recalled with delight that Simone de Beauvoir once wrote that his journal was ''une publication venimeuse (poisonous).''
He believes that China will survive all Utopian experiments. 
''China has a vitality which is well beyond that,'' he said.

file: ISAAC STERN IN CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
THEY call it ''From Mao to Mozart - Isaac Stern in China,'' and the title of this delightful film that opens today for a five-day run at the Symphony Space gets the general idea across.
Our American violin virtuoso, a remarkable, cheerful and cherubiclooking man, visited that calisthenics-smitten nation, marveled at the extraordinary nimbleness of mind and body, shrugged his shoulders and observed, ''On the other hand, they can't play Mozart.''
Mr. Stern by no means deprecates his hosts in this account of his visit to China in June 1979. 
Indeed, he marvels at the talent developing there, and his love for the musicians and students he met overflows in his singularly expressive and good-humored way. 
This is a film that will teach you something about China but more about Mr. Stern. For those who have not met the man behind the violin before, it offers insights into his deeply humanistic approach to music.
He took something to China that is not prevalent there: the realization that the music must come from the heart and soul rather than from the instruments alone. 
The director of a conservatory of music in Shanghai - an older man who suffered during the Cultural Revolution - explains how young Chinese set great store by technical skill. 
They want hard pieces, loud and fast, to demonstrate how well they can use instruments. 
And in so doing, they miss the point of the music itself.
Mr. Stern and David Golub, the pianist who often appears with him, are seen in performance; negotiating for a piano to replace the unusable one they found in Shanghai; getting a tourist's-eye view of China.
The film, which has been nominated for an Academy Award in the best-documentary category, produced and directed by Murray Lerner, with Allan Miller as artistic supervisor. 
It is a beautifully made documentary that does not presume to tell all about China or Mr. Stern but does give us a most enjoyable record of a productive visit.
From Mao to Mozart - Isaac Stern in China (Movie)

file: ISRAEL AND CHINA QUIETLY FORM TRADE BONDS.txt
text:
ï»¿
While reports surfaced last week about secret exchanges between Israel and the Soviet Union, a far more intense and lucrative relationship has been quietly developing between Israel and China, according to Israeli officials.
The Chinese in the last seven months have shown an increasing appetite for Israeli skills in agriculture, solar energy, manufacturing, advanced technology, robotics, construction, road building and arms manufacturing, say Israeli officials familiar with the trade. 
Some deals have already been struck and many others are pending at one stage or another, according to recent Israeli press accounts.
Â 
Chinese Drive for Development
The Chinese interest in Israel - a country with which Peking has not had diplomatic relations and whose policies it regularly denounces in international forums - is seen by Israeli experts as one more manifestation of China's new economic policy, which is aimed at achieving rapid industrial development by adopting Western methods and technology from any country willing to sell it.
Israeli officials say intense and lucrative relationship has been quietly developing between Israel and China; Chinese, in last seven months, have shown interest in Israeli skills in agriculture, solar energy, manufacturing and advanced technology, robotics, construction, road building and arms manufacturing; some deals have already been struck and many others are pending; Chinese interest in Israel--with which it does not have diplomatic relations--is seen as manifestation of China's new industrial development and economic policy (M)
The extent to which the Chinese have been willing to develop economic ties with Israel despite the absence of diplomatic relations was demonstrated just a few weeks ago, Israeli officials said. 
In the past, virtually all Israeli academics or businessmen who wanted to visit China had to hold dual citizenship, so they could travel on the passport of a country with which China had diplomatic ties, such as the United States. 
The Chinese would not issue visas to holders of Israeli passports.
Â 
New Precedent Reported
But according to Israeli Government sources, a delegation of nine representatives from various Israeli industries - most of them owned by collective farms - visited China at the end of May and early June at the invitation of the Chinese authorities.
These Israelis, Government sources said, were given visas on official Israeli passports, and their delegation was led by Shmuel Pohoryles, director of the Israeli Ministry of Agriculture's Joint Agricultural Planning and Rural Development Authority.
''The fact that Israelis entered China without having to hide their identity is a major step forward for us,'' a senior Israeli official said.
Â 
'I Don't Know Anything'
Asked to comment on the trip, a spokesman for the Ministry of Agriculture said: ''I never heard of the thing. 
I don't know anything about it. 
This fellow won't talk to you about it. 
You can interpret that any way you want.''
The Israeli Foreign Ministry has been equally tight-lipped on the subject. 
A routine request by a reporter to meet with the senior Foreign Ministry official dealing with economic relations in the Far East was turned down.
But one very senior Israeli official, speaking only on the condition that he not be identified, said: ''The Chinese know that we have developed systems, in agriculture and irrigation for instance, which they are very interested in acquiring. 
Israeli businessmen are trying to expand relations. 
We were one of the first nations to recognize China and we are very interested in reaching better relations, politically and economically. 
We have never had any reason for hostility. 
On the contrary, we are two ancient peoples.''
Now, in order to facilitate Israeli-Chinese economic relations, the Israeli Foreign Ministry has decided to reopen its consulate in Hong Kong in the next few weeks. 
The consulate was closed in 1975 because of budgetary cuts and an absence of contacts with China.
Israeli officials say the Hong Kong consulate will be used as the main point for diplomatic and economic contacts between Israel and China.
Last week there were reports of secret contacts with the Soviet Union in which, according to the Israeli radio, the Russians proposed an arrangement under which diplomatic relations with Moscow might be restored.
Israeli officials have no illusions that the Chinese, who have thousands of workers in the Arab world, will recognize Israel in the near future. 
But they hold out the hope that they could have the kind of relationship with China that it has with the many African nations that do not formally recognize Israel but nonetheless maintain covert diplomatic contacts and engage in trade.
Â 
New Consul Is Designated
Israel has said its new consul in Hong Kong will be Reuven Merhav, a highly respected former head of the short-lived Israeli diplomatic mission in East Beirut and a man with experience in sensitive assignments such as in Iran. 
Mr. Merhav is to take up his post in the next two weeks.
Even in the absence of an Israeli consul in Hong Kong, Chinese and Israeli businessmen have had no problem making contact.
According to a report several weeks ago in an Israeli political weekly, Koteret Rashit, the basic thrust of which has been confirmed by Israeli officials, Chinese provinces and economic development companies have submitted more than 70 project proposals to Israeli companies since last December. 
The projects range from the construction of residential neighborhoods to the export of high-technology hardware. 
The original go-betweens were Jewish businessmen working out of Peking, Hong Kong, Europe and Australia, but now the Chinese are said to be increasingly approaching Israeli companies directly.
Â 
'Hungry for Know-How'
''The Chinese are hungry for know-how, ideas and investments and are prepared to buy anything under the right economic terms,'' said Koteret Rashit. 
''Information on such projects is transferred from China to Israel on facsimile machines.

text:

''Gung Hay Fat Choy!''
400 pupils roared yesterday at the Edward Hart Elementary School in Flushing, Queens.

Â 
A Time for Ethnic Sharing

Yesterday's event was one of the first celebrations of the Year of the Rabbit, which, on the lunar calendar, begins on Thursday. 
For Chinese, Koreans and other Asians, the 60th day of the Gregorian calendar used in the West is the first day of year 4685.
The Rabbit is one of 12 animals whose names are given successively to each year. 
As the Year of the Tiger dwindles to its final courageous days, people born in the Year of the Rabbit can begin to take comfort in the positive nature of the traits said to be possessed by them.

Â 
Proclamation by Koch

The celebration continued last night with a dinner at the Flower Drum restaurant given by the Chinese Chee Yue Community Association, an organization dedicated to helping new immigrants.
Today at P.S. 
130 in Chinatown, students who six months ago were in mainland China will perform the Silk Ribbon and other dances.

On Saturday the drum and bugle band of the New York Chinese School will march in Mott Street.
Â 
Classical Dances Performed

21's celebration of the year of the Rabbit, a high point was two Chinese classical dances, adeptly performed by 29 dancers chosen from 120 who had auditioned.

file: Japan Quietly Recalls World War II Surrender.txt
text:

Japan's past militarism and its present-day diplomacy converged today as the country paused to recall its surrender 42 years ago to end World War II.
Hoping to avoid ruffling his country's unsettled relations with China, Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone conspicuously stayed away from a Shinto shrine associated in many minds with Japan's wartime aggression, which included an invasion of China.
Mr. Nakasone touched off a diplomatic storm in 1985 when he became the first postwar Japanese leader to make an official visit to the Yasukuni Shrine, which honors the 2.5 million Japanese soldiers killed in wars over the last century. 
The overwhelming majority died in World War II.
Soon after the Nakasone visit, China denounced him as having ''pandered'' to those who wanted to expunge Japan's war guilt, which had included an invasion of eastern China and atrocities against civilian populations.
To keep from offending Beijing further, the Japanese Prime Minister did not go to Yasukuni last Aug. 
15.
His decision to stay away again today assumed added significance because relations between Japan and China have reached their lowest point since the two countries restored normal ties in 1972.
The decline began with the ouster last January of Hu Yaobang as China's Communist Party leader. 
Mr. Hu had advocated close ties with Tokyo, and since his departure Beijing has maintained anti-Japanese statements.
Â 
A Turn for the Worse
Matters took a turn for the worse in late spring when Japan's Deputy Foreign Minister, commenting on critical comments made by Deng Xiaoping, the Chinese leader, said in off-the-record remarks that Mr. Deng may have ''become a man above the clouds.''
When his comment became known, the Japanese official, Kensuke Yanagiya, was forced to apologize to China. 
He later left office in what was officially described as a ''voluntary retirement.''
Four decades after the war, Chinese criticism of Japan often evokes the specter of old militarism. 
And as demonstrated today by Mr. Nakasone's avoidance of the shrine, Japan tends to step gingerly here.
Still, what seems to be a growing number of Japanese also believe that they should not have to keep apologizing for a long-ago war, and that they have as much right as anyone else to honor their war dead. 
This is a view that Mr. Nakasone has often taken.
''It is only natural,'' he said in 1985, ''that people should give thanks to those who gave their lives for the country. 
Othewise, who will give his life?''
Reflecting this attitude, most of the Prime Minister's Cabinet - 16 of 20 members - went to pray today at Yasukuni even though he himself did not. 
In addition, about 200 members of Parliament from the ruling Liberal Democratic Party paid a visit, including at least two men who hope to succeed Mr. Nakasone this fall, Noboru Takeshita and Shintaro Abe.
The shrine is a short walk from the Nippon Budokan, a martial-arts hall behind the Imperial Palace. 
There, at the stroke of noon, Emperor Hirohito bowed before an altar set in a field of chrysanthemums and led his country in a remembrance of the moment exactly 42 years ago when he called on them to surrender.
As usual, the Government-sponsored memorial service was attended by Mr. Nakasone and other senior officials, and by relatives of the 2.3 million Japanese soldiers and 800,000 civilians who died in the war. 
Also as usual, the ceremony was boycotted by left-wing opposition parties, which held their own gatherings elsewhere.
The strong Japanese penchant for tradition and fixed procedure was much in evidence at the Budokan, where the rituals have changed little since they began 25 years ago. 
There was certainly nothing different in the remarks of the Emperor, who showed his 86 years as he went to the stage.
''I mourn the war dead and pray,'' he said, reading from a prepared text.
''Even now,'' Hirohito said, using the identical phrases he has uttered many times, ''my heart aches when I think of the many people who fell in the war and of their bereaved families.''

A Cabinet minister who caused a stir with recent comments about Japan's wartime role embroiled himself in fresh controversy today by saying that the Japanese invasion of China five decades ago was not a war of aggression.
The remarks of the Cabinet minister, Seisuke Okuno, created serious political and diplomatic problems for Prime Minister Noboru Takeshita, and produced opposition calls for Mr. Okuno's resignation or ouster.
As he did last month, Mr. Okuno played down Japanese wartime aggression, first on Monday during parliamentary debate and again today while talking with Japanese reporters.
Discussing Japan's military attacks against China in the 1930's, Mr. Okuno, who is director general of the National Land Agency, told reporters: ''I don't want to describe it as an aggressive war because both many Japanese and Chinese were killed.''
On Monday, answering questions in Parliament, he said that Japan ''had no intention'' of invading China. 
In fact, Japanese troops overran much of eastern China, killing several million people in the process.
After World War II, an Allied tribunal in Tokyo convicted Japanese leaders of war crimes, and sentenced seven to death, including Prime Minister Hideki Tojo. 
The verdicts, Mr. Okuno said Monday, were a case of ''victors' punishment on the losers.''
But he insisted that that he wished ''to establish friendly Japan-China relations,'' adding, ''I have never spoken ill of China.''
Nevertheless, his insistence on repeating comments that China has labeled offensive put Mr. Takeshita in a bind, especially since the Prime Minister hopes to visit Beijing this summer.

When Japan's Foreign Minister, Sosuke Uno, visited Beijing last week, he was rebuked by his Chinese counterpart, Qian Qichen. 
Mr. Qian was quoted as complaining about a Cabinet member who had ''made remarks that lack good manners.''
Â 
Official Position Stated
On April 22, after visiting the Yasukuni Shrine for Japan's war dead, Mr. Okuno said that ''Japan fought the war in order to secure its safety.''
He added: ''The white race had turned Asia into a colony. 
Japan was by no means the aggressor nation.''
Today, the Government's main spokesman, Chief Cabinet Secretary Keizo Obuchi, told a parliamentary committee that Japan's official position continued to be that it indeed was an aggressor in World War II. 
But he added that he would find out the ''true intention'' of the 74-year-old Mr. Okuno, who during the war was a prefectural director of the Kempeitai, the notorious secret police.

file: JAPAN_S OIL FIND IN CHINA COULD STIMULATE TRADE.txt
text:

An oil discovery off China this year by a Japanese drilling company, part of the first major foreign oil exploration in Chinese territorial waters since the Communist revolution, appears likely to galvanize trade between the two nations, trade officials said here.
The discovery, announced by the state-owned Japan National Oil Corporation, which has been drilling under a joint-production agreement with China, offers the prospect of the first significant Japanese production of Chinese oil since World War II.
The oil strike comes at a critical time for China, which is beset by inflation for the first time since the Communist revolution in 1949. 
China, under the leadership of Deng Xiaoping, is also troubled by shortfalls in onshore oil production that threaten to undermine plans for industrial expansion and are also causing a serious lack of foreign exchange.
Japan's discovery of oil off coast of China may stimulate trade between two countriesTrade Tripled in Three Years
Oil is the key to Chinese-Japanese trade, which has nearly tripled to more than $9 billion a year in the three years since China and Japan concluded a long-term, $20 billion trade agreement in early 1978.
China exports its oil primarily to Japan; it shipped eight million tons here last year. 
These exports help pay for imports of vital Japanese industrial plant and equipment. 
China's long-term development plans appear to hinge on oil production, which totaled 106 million tons last year.
''Oil and the foreign exchange that China obtains abroad, mostly from Japan, are the keys to Deng's plans,'' said a trading house executive. 
''Without these to help him, Deng's plans to open the economy at least halfway to Western enterprise could crumble.''
Â 
Also Crucial to Japanese
Industry executives here say that the oil is also crucial to Japan in the long run. 
The oil, found under Pohai Bay at Japan National Oil's No.1 well, where drilling began last year, is light, low in wax content and ideal for Japanese refineries that are designed to process Arabian light grades, not the heavy, waxy oil supplied to Japan from such Chinese onshore fields as Daqing.
Japanese planners have sought for 20 years to diversify supply sources away from the Middle East, which still supplies threequarters of all oil consumed by Japan. 
Japan has virtually no domestic oil, and nearby Pohai offers a secure source of the type that Japan has so far lacked.
The Japanese Government, which finances the national oil company, and about four dozen Japanese concerns that are minority partners with the state company in the Pohai Bay exploration stress security of supply, not profit, and are offering China attractive terms.
Â 
Seismic Surveys Completed
The discovery came just after dozens of Western companies had completed seismic surveys in the South China Sea at their own expense. 
They are expected to tender bids for the first joint production opportunities that China will offer in that part of its 2,800-mile coastline, and the Atlantic Richfield Company and the Philips Petroleum Corporation have already reported such an agreement.
Japanese and French concerns, led by the Compagnie Fran,caise de Petroles, went ahead with China faster in Pohai Bay than private Western companies elsewhere along the coast. 
Their rapid success in finding oil suggests that Western estimates in the 1970's of offshore Chinese reserves of close to four billion tons may be conservative.
Oil is not expected to flow from Pohai Bay until about 1984. 
But Japan National Oil is scheduled to sink five wells in Pohai Bay this year, and some unofficial Japanese estimates put reserves there as high as 10 billion tons.
Â 
Hopes May Be Too High
Press reports here have put the likely yield from the field found by the Japanese at 300,000 to 400,000 barrels a day, or between 15 million and 20 million tons a year, with Japan to pay all costs and receive 42.5 percent of the oil. 
But one Japanese executive described the forecasts as ''perhaps wishful thinking - it's just too early to tell.''
American geologists in Peking believe that Pohai Bay's oil is scattered in rich but small pockets and that the oil-bearing strata have been disrupted -and made hard to tap - by earthquakes in the region. 
If the warnings are justified, then Japanese hopes may be pitched too high.
Reports from Peking say that Deputy Prime Minister Gu Mu has forecast that China's onshore production may drop by 10 million to 20 million tons a year by the mid-1980's. 
Tokyo executives said that the new finds offshore were timely, to make up for this possible decline, and because of the tentative shelving by China of $1.5 billion worth of contracts for industrial plants from Japan.

file: JARDINE MATHESON_S HEIR-ELECT_ Brian M. Powers_An Asian Trading Empire Picks an American _Tai-Pan_.txt
text:
ï»¿
Struan and Company (was) the greatest house in Asia, and so rich and powerful that the other China traders had named it in awe and jealousy The Noble House - noble because it was first in riches, first in largess, first in trade, first in clippers, but mostly because Dirk Struan was Tai-Pan, the Tai-Pan among all the tai-pans of Asia.
- ''Tai-Pan,'' by James Clavell
Â 
Â 
IT is not power so much as magic that swirls about the tai-pan of the Jardine Matheson group - a legacy of opium and intrigue that goes with being the ''big boss'' of Asia's famous trading company. 
Chronicled as Struan and Company in James Clavell's novels, Jardines is more than an international conglomerate; it is a legend.
At least nine streets in Hong Kong are named for tai-pans at Jardines, which has towered over the British territory for 145 years, dealing in opium and silk in the last century and everything from ice cream to investment banking today. 
The tai-pan of the Noble House - or the Princely Hong, as Jardines is also known - inherits the mantle of William Jardine, the first tai-pan, a shrewd Scotsman nicknamed by the Chinese ''iron-headed old rat.''
Most of the tai-pans - whose arrivals in earlier days sometimes were greeted by cannon salutes - come from branches of the same family tree, serving in the Hong Kong hot seat before retiring to London or the family estate in Scotland. 
So Hong Kong gasped at the announcement that a 37-year-old American investment banker, with just 14 months' experience at Jardines, is set to become its next tai-pan.
Brian M. Powers is a 6-foot 2 former football player, sandy-haired with a hint of gray, who looks a bit too affable to be tai-pan. 
But he can rake the landscape with his speech: Ideas and quips and analyses fly through the air like shotgun pellets. 
And for years - ever since his first job at a New York law firm - he has set himself apart from others with his long workdays, even in offices where absurd hours were the norm.
On his wedding day eight years ago, Mr. Powers was busy with a real-estate transaction and had to rush to the church at the last minute - only to discover that he had left the ring behind. 
The bridal party watched aghast as he searched his pockets before racing back home to get the wedding band.
Last fall, during negotiations on a Jardines sale of some of its American oil interests, he flew to San Francisco for the day to try to get a better price - a move that worked and that impressed the man who counts most at Jardines: Simon Keswick, the current tai-pan and a distant relative of William Jardine.
''People in Hong Kong think they work very hard,'' Mr. Keswick said in his office 48 floors above Hong Kong's bustling central district. 
''I think Brian has demonstrated that people in New York work even harder.''
And so the 45-year-old Mr. Keswick (pronounced KEH-zick) announced earlier this month that he would relinquish his position of managing director of the Jardine companies to Mr. Powers. Mr. Keswick will remain as chairman, but, he says, he will spend more time outside Hong Kong than in it. 
He calls Mr. Powers the ''heir-elect,'' and says he already regards Mr. Powers as tai-pan.
THAT may be a bit premature, so long as Mr. Keswick is still in town. 
But the expectation, within Jardines and without, is that moving vans will appear sometime over the next year or so at 35 Mount Kellett Road, the residence of the tai-pans, on the Peak on Hong Kong Island. 
Mr. Keswick, the whispers say, will retain the title of chairman from London, just as his uncle, Sir John Keswick, did two decades ago.
Mr. Powers will presumably inherit the keys to the Mount Kellett Road home, as well as to the tai-pan's second residence at Shek O, along the water. 
He apparently will also assume a seat on the board of the Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation and the coveted position as steward of the Royal Hong Kong Jockey Club.
But most of all, there is Jardines to command. 
As managing director, Mr. Powers will head up a network that sells cognac in Japan, operates the renowned Oriental Hotel in Bangkok; runs Pizza Huts in Hawaii and 7-Eleven stores in Malaysia; oversees ship management in the Pacific, construction in China and investment banking throughout Asia.
The empire - with 1986 revenues of $1.3 billion and after-tax profits of $61 million - employs 61,000 people in 22 countries and includes Jardine Matheson Holdings, Jardine Strategic Holdings and controlling interests in the Hongkong Land Company, Mandarin Oriental Hotel Group, and Dairy Farm International Holdings.
To this may be added some large American company. 
Mr. Powers says the group is looking for acquisitions in the United States and Britain, though he says this could be a single $2 billion deal or a string of $100 million purchases. 
Mr. Keswick says he would like a major American presence, and he adds that Mr. Powers might want to return to the United States in five years or so and run the American wing of Jardines.
But familiarity with the American market was not the reason for choosing Mr. Powers. Indeed, his nationality may even have worked against him a little, in the clubby world of British-run Hong Kong companies. 
His Yankee frankness has ruffled some feathers here, he acknowledged. 
''The business style is different,'' he said. 
''The Brits are much more civilized than Americans.''
And though Mr. Powers has joined the Jockey Club and he and his wife have dutifully entertained at their home on the Peak, their presence in Hong Kong's social circuit is subdued. 
''I like Hong Kong,'' he said, ''but I work very long hours and I'm very committed to my job.''
But if Mr. Powers has not always displayed proper enthusiasm for drinking port, no one doubts his mastery of law and finance. 
Those skills seem to have been key to his meteoric rise, after arriving at Jardines in April 1986 as ''chief strategist.''
The conglomerate was then in the process of slimming down - after some disastrous investments in real estate, shipping and oil.
Rivals for power within Jardines had their own credentials, but they could not compete with a financial alchemist at a time when the group was so absorbed by financial matters. 
Mr. Powers immediately set to work planning a restructuring of Jardines that included spinning off subsidiaries and creating a complex web of corporations that own each other. 
He also registered some more of the group's assets in Bermuda, in the belief that foreign-registered corporations might fare better when China takes over Hong Kong in 1997.
That grasp of finance and corporate strategy seems to have impressed many people in Hong Kong, in and out of Jardines. 
''Maybe U.S. financial people are more on the ball than British people,'' mused one British executive at Jardines. 
''Nobody here has the financial know-how to take all those companies apart and register them elsewhere and watch those share prices rocket.''
FOR Brian Powers, the road to becoming tai-pan began in Massapequa, L.I. 
The second-youngest of four children, and the son of a stockbroker, he devoted most of his energy in high school to football. 
He even turned down Yale initially to go to Holy Cross because of its more rigorous approach to athletics. 
He transferred to Yale after two years.
''When he played football, his favorite position was defensive end,'' his wife recalled. 
''I think that's because reading the other side is what he finds fun and intriguing about a situation.''
An economics major, Mr. Powers graduated with average grades and then went to the University of Virginia Law School, where he excelled. 
He graduated near the top of his class and, after a year as a teaching fellow at Stanford Law School, he became an associate in the New York law firm of Debevoise & Plimpton. 
He is remembered there as a hard worker and a quick study who was fortunate to specialize in mergers and acquisitions just as the wave of mergers was beginning in the United States.
After two years at Debevoise & Plimpton, Mr. Powers accepted a job as an attorney with the Ford Foundation. 
However, almost immediately he was put in charge of a large investment portfolio that included venture capital and real estate.
One of his first acts was to foreclose on two big real estate developments in the belief that the Foundation could run them better than the developers. 
Colleagues noticed that. 
Some thought him brash. 
Most - including his boss, Jon L. Hagler -were impressed. 
''I haven't seen a better negotiator,'' said Mr. Hagler, who now runs a Boston investment firm. 
''He had it all.''
Mr. Powers was at the Ford Foundation when James D. Wolfensohn, an Australian-born financier, gave him a call. 
Mr. Wolfensohn was planning to set up a New York investment bank, and had heard about Mr. Powers from a Debevoise & Plimpton partner. 
So after four years at the foundation, Mr. Powers joined Mr. Wolfensohn, becoming his right-hand man at James D. Wolfensohn Inc.
SOON after the firm opened, a man named Simon Keswick called. 
He was in the New York office of the Coudert Brothers law firm, and wanted to know if Mr. Powers could come by that evening to help structure a deal. 
With characteristic bluntness, Mr. Powers asked the tai-pan: ''This is a terrible question, but who are you?''
From that inauspicious beginning, a relationship grew between the two. 
Mr. Powers handled more and more Jardines business, including an extremely complex sale of sugar interests in Hawaii that included a leveraged buyout with commercial and government financing. 
''That was an extraordinary piece of work,'' recalled Mr. Wolfensohn.
Indeed, it was one of the accomplishments that led Mr. Keswick at the end of 1985 to ask Mr. Powers if he would like to come to work for Jardines. 
Mr. Powers's initial response was that he was happy at Wolfensohn and that his wife, Paula, had a job in New York and was not mobile.
Mr. Keswick persisted, and Mr. Powers finally arrived in April of last year, with a seat on the board and a mandate to direct financial strategy. 
Paula Powers, who was teaching at Columbia Law School, was willing to move to Hong Kong, and both parents thought it was the ideal time for their son, Jeremy, to live abroad. 
Mr. Powers has so far not studied Chinese, but six-year-old Jeremy is learning the local dialect and already knows important words like ''su tiu,'' which means french fries.
Mr. Keswick seems to have raised the possibility of succession with Mr. Powers when he was first hired, but both say that no commitment was made. 
There were a number of other candidates: David J. Davies, the head of the Hongkong Land Company until he resigned last year rather than see it dismantled; Martin G. Barrow, board member and head of a key subsidiary until he was promoted out of both positions earlier this year, and Nigel Rich, the current chief executive of Hongkong Land.
As the new tai-pan, Mr. Powers will face a number of challenges. 
Despite diversification, a large share of the company's assets remain in Hong Kong. 
The property market and business climate here are extremely sensitive, even though Beijing has promised that it will allow Hong Kong to maintain its capitalist way of life for at least 50 years after 1997.
Then there is the rise of a new breed of competitor in Asia: local entrepreneurs who in the last two decades have built their own conglomerates to challenge British interests. 
In Hong Kong, such Chinese entrepreneurs as Sir Y.K. 
Pao and Li Ka-shing have often outmaneuvered Jardines in the last decade.
These entrepreneurs are not only rivals but also potential threats, for Jardines could become an acquisition target. 
One reason they have gained on British interests is that they know the market better - and that could be all the more true when Jardines is run by a man who is a newcomer to the region.
Nor is it clear exactly how much control the Keswicks will continue to exert. 
The family is the company's largest shareholder, with about a 10 percent interest. 
Simon's older brother, Henry Keswick, is a former tai-pan now living in London who remains deeply involved in Jardines.
''I think the Keswicks will still pull the strings from London,'' said William Phillips, the managing director of Baring Securities Hong Kong Ltd. 
Others say Jardines will still be run out of Hong Kong, but that there will be constant consultations.
Mr. Powers may want to keep an active chairman. 
He says he approves of separating the top job, to spread the power. 
Otherwise, he says, there is a risk for the tai-pan that ''if things go reasonably well, you can easily believe you're God.''

text:

After Jardine Matheson, the Hong Kong trading company, disclosed last Wednesday that it planned to move its legal residency to Bermuda, The Hong Kong Standard likened the shock to hearing that the Queen of England was emigrating to Australia.
Jardine Matheson & Company Ltd., after all, helped found the British Crown Colony in 1841, only nine years after the company itself was born in Canton, China. 
Jardine has long since outgrown its opium-running origins to become a major conglomerate with investments in Asia ranging from real estate to financial services to shipping. 
More than any other company, it epitomized Hong Kong's commitment to free-wheeling capitalism.
Article examines impact on Hong Kong of disclosure by Jardine Matheson & Co Ltd that it plans to move its legal residency to Bermuda; full details of relocation decision will not be known until company's annual report on May 14, but number of Hong Kong business people and other analysts have concluded that Hong Kong Government's characterization of legal relocation as only 'a commercial decision' is not far off; illustration (M)
The full details of the decision to move will not be known until the company's annual report is issued to the stockholders on May 14. 
The decision will then come up for approval at a general meeting in June.
But in the few days since the jolting announcement was made, a number of Hong Kong business people and other analysts have concluded that the Hong Kong Government's characterization of the legal relocation as only ''a commercial decision'' is not far off.
There are potential psychological ramifications, say the analysts, but they believe that it will not touch off a hemorrhage of business confidence in Hong Kong's future after 1997, when China intends to reclaim sovereignty.
''Nobody wants to pull out of Hong Kong,'' said one United States businessman. 
''There is too much money to be made. 
There are no sales in Bermuda.''
In making the unexpected announcement, Jardine's chairman, Simon Keswick, acknowledged that the plan to set up a parent holding company in Bermuda reflected the prevailing uncertainty over what will happen to businesses when Hong Kong reverts to Chinese sovereignty.
Mr. Keswick, who came from Britain to take over as chairman less than a year ago, said that as an international corporation allocating its investments, Jardine found it ''undoubtedly a disadvantage to have to deal with questions regarding the long-term future of Hong Kong.''
As a British-run business, Mr. Keswick said, ''we wish to remain as long as possible under that jurisdiction.''
As Mr. Keswick noted, Jardine is not physically pulling out of Hong Kong in changing its legal registration. 
The head office and fixed assets will remain in the colony and business activities here will continue.
But the Bermuda connection is meant to ensure that Jardine continues to operate under British laws after Britain's lease over most of the colony expires in 13 years. 
One business analyst described the plan as ''a legal maneuver on where the tax will be paid.''
In practical terms, this means canceling the company's shares issued in Kong Kong and replacing them with equal new shares issued in Bermuda. 
Jardine's Hong Kong stock is now valued at about $5 billion (Hong Kong), or $641 million (United States).
Mr. Keswick linked the decision in part to an 80 percent drop in his company's net earnings last year over those of 1982, caused by financial jitters over the colony's future.
Jardine's announcement has already affected the colony's equities market. 
Last Thursday, the Hong Kong stock market plunged more than 61 points in the worst one-day loss this year. 
On Friday, it slipped nearly 43 more points, to close at slightly over 1,014 points on the Hang Seng index. 
The Hong Kong dollar has been unaffected because it was pegged to the United States dollar following its fall to a record low of 9.5 Hong Kong dollars to the United States dollar last September.
A local architect who follows the stock market suggested that ''now is the time to buy. 
The stocks are cheap and they'll come up again.''
Â 
Political Reaction Sharper
Politically, reaction has been even more negative, since the decision came while Britain and China remain engaged in sensitive and secret negotiations on a Hong Kong agreement before the September deadline set by Peking.
Several members of the colony's Legislative Council called Jardine's plan bad news. 
One council member, Selina Chow, told reporters ''this is definitely a manifestation of the lack of confidence of some of the business community in Hong Kong's future.''
Stephen Cheong, another member, said that ''the damage to the delicate flower of confidence has been done.''
The Chinese Government, apparently caught off guard, has been conspicuously silent. 
But the leftist Hong Kong press, which tends to reflect Peking's thinking, has criticized Jardine's plans and questioned its motives. 
The daily newspaper Wen Wei Po contended that the ''unwise'' decision could not have been made without the collusion of the British.
Other analysts do not fault Jardine for refusing to wait until China and Britain announce their plans for the transition of authority in Hong Kong. 
The secrecy surrounding the talks, which resume in Peking on April 11, prompted Hong Kong's legislative council to vote last month to open its own debate on the colony's future. 
Peking has objected to such a public voice.
Â 
A 'Justifiable Question'
''What Jardine has done is to raise a very justifiable question,'' said a Western resident of Hong Kong. 
''Under which law are we going to operate once China takes over this place?
How can we stay here to play a game whose rules are not known to us?''
Chinese officials have promised that Hong Kong can operate with its own political, economic and legal system as a special administrative region after it reverts to Chinese sovereignty. 
The Foreign Minister, Wu Xueqian, was quoted in a recent magazine interview as saying that China would ''scrupulously implement'' the agreement that it reaches with Britain.
The major concern now is that other companies, seeing Hong Kong's most prominent firm register an apparent lack of confidence in the future, may decide to follow suit and look for their own bases outside Hong Kong, a move that could dampen further investment in the colony. 
Particular attention is focusing on Swire Pacific, another company that originated as Jardine's major rival nearly a century and a half ago.
Another question is whether Peking may be angry enough to retaliate in some way against Jardine's business ventures in China. 
Such vindictiveness could also hurt China's credibility with Hong Kong investors, the analysts say.

The American Motors Corporation expects to sign an agreement later this week with China to jointly produce Jeeps in Peking and export some of them to other nations in the Far East.
The four-wheel-drive vehicles are to be produced by the Peking Jeep Company, a joint venture of Peking Auto Works and A.M.C., which is the smallest of the American automobile companies and the only manufacturer of Jeeps. 
Production is expected to reach 40,000 vehicles a year, which are to be sold in China and other Asian countries.
''This is probably the largest individual joint venture in China,'' said A.M.C.'s chairman, W. Paul Tippett, at a briefing last week before he left for China for the scheduled signing. 
He added that negotiations for the project had been in progress for more than four years and had been initiated by A.M.C., which sought access to the potentially huge Chinese market. 
It also wanted a low-wage area to manufacture vehicles to compete with Japanese companies in overseas markets.
SOUTHFIELD, Mich., May 2 - The American Motors Corporation expects to sign an agreement later this week with China to jointly produce Jeeps in Peking and export some of them to other nations in the Far East.
A.M.C. executives had hoped to withhold public announcement of the agreement until the actual signing, they said, to avoid angering Chinese officials and possibly endangering the accord. 
They declined, in fact, to comment today on reports appearing in Ward's Auto World, a trade publication, that said the formal announcement of the agreement was due shortly. 
However, last week, company officials, in advance briefings for reporters, said the signing was planned for Thursday in Peking.
The Chinese-made vehicles are not intended to be sold in the United States, Mr. Tippett said. 
The A.M.C. agreement, if it is signed, will be the first joint production agreement in China by an American auto manufacturer, an agreement that could result in the start of actual production this year or next.
Nevertheless, Volkswagen of West Germany has a preliminary contract to start making a new-model car in 1988 in a joint venture at a plant in Shanghai, where Chinese auto production is centered. 
The Ford Motor Company has been attempting to set up a joint venture to produce trucks and tractors.
A number of other American companies have established themselves in China, including the R.J. 
Reynolds Tobacco Company, which has been producing cigarettes there, and Avon Products Inc., which is marketing cosmetics. 
The largest single-project agreement apparently is a $230 million coal-mining development to be undertaken by the Occidential Petroleum Corporation.
Peking Jeep will be in a factory owned by Peking Auto Works, which now produces about 20,000 units a year of an older-design, fourwheel-drive vehicle based on a 1954 Soviet design for a Soviet Army jeep. 
A.M.C. will invest $8 million in cash and $8 million in technology for a 31.4 percent share of the $51 million joint venture. 
A.M.C.'s share could rise to as high as 49 percent under the terms of the agreement.
The initial plan for the joint venture, Mr. Tippett said, is for A.M.C. to update the existing Chinese 212 model with A.M.C.'s new four-cylinder engine and other engineering improvements intended to make the vehicles more fuel-efficient and to increase their carrying capacity. 
The engine is to be manufactured largely in China.
Within a few years, Mr. Tippett said, the objective is to develop a new vehicle, based in large part on A.M.C.'s CJ7 Jeep, the company's basic model.
''This is important to the Chinese and to us,'' Mr. Tippett said. 
He noted that, in China, autos are largely confined to urban areas while four-wheel-drive vehicles are necessary for the primitive rural road system. 
''The Chinese view transportation as one of their top five priorities in terms of economic development,'' Mr. Tippett added.
For A.M.C., he said, the venture gives the company an inside position in what could develop into a vast market for utility vehicles for all types of use in rural areas. 
It also gives the company a pool of 4,000 factory workers at the Peking plant whose pay averages 60 cents an hour, compared with about $12 an hour in labor costs in Japan and more than $20 an hour in the United States.
The average-equipped Jeep manufactured by American Motors in the United States sells for $11,500. 
Mr. Tippett did not indicate what the price of the vehicle built in China will be.
Â 
President to Be From A.M.C.
The president and chief operating officer of Peking Jeep will be an A.M.C. executive, although the chairman will be Chinese. 
''Basically, we plan to run it,'' said Mr. Tippett, who added that 8 to 10 A.M.C. executives would be permanently assigned to Peking with others visiting as needed. 
None of the American executives of the venture have yet been named, he added.
Mr. Tippett also said that officials of Renault, the French auto company that controls 46.4 percent of A.M.C.'s stock, had not been involved in the Chinese negotiations, other than to approve the transaction at the board level.
The agreement was initialed about a month ago, while a delegation from China was visiting here, he said. 
The formal signing was put off so that it could be done in the Great Hall of the People in Peking and publicized from there, Mr. Tippett said.
(In Peking, reports had circulated that a deal with American Motors was near for the venture, but there had been no official comment.)
Â 
Long-Term Strategic Move
The joint venture, Mr. Tippett said, will permit competition with Japanese companies that now sell 97 percent of all the 100,000 fourwheel-drive vehicles purchased in Pacific basin countries each year. 
A.M.C. now sells 2,000 to 3,000 of its Jeeps in the Pacific area, out of a total of 91,000 jeep-type vehicles sold in this country and abroad last year. 
''This is a long-term strategic move by A.M.C.,'' he said. 
''It will be a long time before there is much in the way of profit, but the opportunities seem very great to us in the long run.''
Mr. Tippett said Chinese officials would handle distribution and sales within the country while A.M.C. would use its own marketing channels for export.
Mr. Tippett said the only restriction on bringing profits back to the United States was that they not represent a drain of hard currency on China. 
Sufficient export sales of the vehicles should satisfy that requirement, he added.

Politicians, movie actors and leaders of industry shielded their eyes from the glare of flashbulbs and the sparkle of costumes Wednesday night at the Textile Museum here.
''The entire resources of NBC, Procter & Gamble and the Chinese and Italian Governments are assembled here,'' said John Houseman, the actor. 
He smiled and added: ''What more do you want?''
The party at the museum was held to unveil 30 of the costumes designed by Enrico Sabbatini of Italy for ''Marco Polo,'' a 10-hour mini-series that will be shown on NBC-TV for four nights beginning on May 16. 
The series is being sponsored by the Procter & Gamble Company. 
RAI-Radio Televisione Italiana, in cooperation with the Chinese Government, produced the film.
Politicians, movie actors and leaders of industry shielded their eyes from the glare of flashbulbs and the sparkle of costumes Wednesday night at the Textile Museum here.Mongolian Court Gown
''They are an inspiration - the colors, the simplicity,'' said Ulla Wachtmeister, wife of the Swedish Ambassador, Count Wilhelm Wachtmeister, as she touched a sweep of embroidered blue silk on a Mongolian court gown.
''That looks like something Diane Keaton would wear,'' said another guest as she looked at a mannequin that was wearing an intricate layer of Persian shawls, overskirts and petticoats.
''If you really want a good room, go to where the duck and the pig are,'' shouted another guest in the noisy room, referring to the pieces of Peking duck and roast suckling pig, wrapped in miniature pancakes, that were being served.
Lee Kimche, former director of the Institute of Museum Services, said the costumes were of ''museum quality.''
She said she had been meeting with officials of RAI-Radio Televisione Italiana to discuss the possibility of showing the costumes in other cities.
Â 
A $7,000 Embroidered Robe
''I'm so intrigued with this kind of detail,'' said Mary Jane Wick, wife of Charles Z. Wick, director of the International Communication Agency, as she looked closely at the ornately embroidered dragons on a ceremonial robe. 
The robe, with the help of gold-leaf embroidery, cost $7,000.
Robert Mulholland, president of NBC, admired the costume of a woman of Tabriz. 
After he was told that an ornate clasp on the mannequin's outfit was an antique safety pin, he quipped: ''I thought it was a chastity belt.''
George Clifford, a Washington writer, added: ''They don't have a thing in 44 long.''
It took Mr. Sabbatini three years to design 4,000 costumes and 3,500 handmade shoes, ranging from Mongolian boots made of goat fur to silken court slippers, for the series. 
He said he had made two trips to China, where he visited museums and talked with historians in an attempt to re-create the 13th century. 
He returned to Rome with thousands of square feet of silks, cottons and cashmeres and more than 1,000 furs. 
He said: ''The embroideries were done in China, the hand-hammered armor was made in Italy and the jade was hand-carved for the Mongol belts and the breastplate of Kublai Khan. 
Even the undergarments are authentic.''
Burt Lancaster, who plays Pope Gregory X in the series, said the costume he wore weighed 80 pounds. 
''We had a papal delegate working with us to authenticate details,'' he said, ''and he told us the materials in our costumes were much richer than what the Pope himself wears today.''
Mr. Houseman, who plays the Patriarch of Venice, recalled: ''Sabbatini kept draping me in more and more of the stuff. 
He virtually built the costume on me.''
Leonard Nimoy plays the role of Kublai Khan's regent. 
He said that ''the character does have a bit of a problem - he has a healthly lust for women and has 30 wives and 400 concubines.''
The $25 million film tells the story of the 20-year journey of Marco Polo, who was played by Ken Marshall. 
The actor was not able to attend the party.
Some of the filming was done at the Great Wall of China and in Peking's Forbidden City. 
Inner Mongolia, Fez and Marrekesh in Morocco were other location sites. 
The series had 180 speaking parts and used 5,000 extras, including two regiments of the Mongolian Cavalry.
Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr., was billed as one of the party's hosts, along with Chai Zemin, the Chinese envoy to the United States, and Rinaldo Petrignani, the Italian Ambassador. 
But the Falkland Island crisis prevented Mr. Haig from attending and Assistant Secretary of State Robert D. Hormats extended Mr. Haig's regrets to the gathering.

Carter Brown, the director of the National Gallery of Arts, and his wife, Pamela; George Stevens, a television producer, and his wife, Elizabeth; William Cafritz, a Washington businessman, and his wife, Buffy; Ambassador Ashraf F. Ghorbal of Egypt; Commissioner Barbara Thomas of the Securities and Exchange Commission, and Grant Tinker, chairman of the board of NBC.

text:
ï»¿
South Korea continued tonight to hold a Chinese torpedo boat that drifted into its waters with six dead crew members, killed in what some reports described as a mutiny after some crewmen tried to defect.
The South Korean Government made no direct response to a Chinese request for the return of the naval vessel and its crew ''as soon as possible.''
(China and South Korea were reportedly holding talks on the return of the boat and crew through officials they maintain in Hong Kong.)
Â 
2 Reportedly in Hospital
Two crew members, reportedly shot but not critically wounded, were in a hospital in the South Korean port of Kunsan, on the Yellow Sea. 
A total of 10 or 11 other crewmen were also believed to have been taken to Kunsan, but their whereabouts could not be determined. 
Their boat was apparently offshore.
South Korea continues to hold Chinese torpedo boat that drifted into its waters with six dead crew members, killed in what some reports described as mutiny after some crewmen tried to defect; two crew members, reportedly shot but not critically wounded, are in hospital in South Korea, and South Korean Government makes no direct response to Chinese request for return of vessel and its crew 'as soon as possible'; photo (M)
It was not clear whether any of the sailors sought political asylum in South Korea or preferred to be sent home.
South Korean officials seemed to deal cautiously with the episode, which threatened to undercut recent attempts by the two countries to pursue friendly contacts even though they have no diplomatic relations.
Â 
'A Simple Scuffle'
A statement issued tonight in Seoul by the Minister of Culture and Information, Lee Won Hong, did not mention a mutiny or any deaths.
''It was determined, based on facts so far obtained, that casualties aboard the Chinese torpedo boat were due to a simple scuffle among the crewmen and that no political reason was involved,'' Mr. Lee said.
Officials interviewed by telephone from Seoul declined to give details. 
But several foreign diplomats in South Korea described the incident as a mutiny that seemed to have begun on Friday when some Chinese crew members tried to defect to Taiwan.
Â 
Demand by Crewman
A Western diplomat said available information suggested that one crewman had held a rifle and demanded that the vessel - apparently part of a naval exercise in the Yellow Sea - be diverted to Taiwan. 
The Japanese press, citing unidentified sources, reported that at least two Chinese crew members sought political refuge.
No details were available about who shot whom or what happened after the gunfire ended.
But according to Mr. Lee and other officials, the torpedo boat's engines failed during the incident, and the vessel drifted into South Korean waters, where it fired flares to signal it was in distress.
By then the Chinese Government had become aware that one of its boats was missing and was heading toward South Korea. 
China alerted the Seoul Government through the South Korean Consulate in Hong Kong, diplomats said.
Â 
Sighting by Fishing Boat
On Friday night, a South Korean fishing boat sighted the torpedo boat and towed it to Hawangdung Island, 45 miles west of Kunsan. 
From there, survivors and the bodies of slain crewmen were taken to the mainland.
Through American diplomats, South Korea sent a ''stern protest'' to Peking over the entry of three other Chinese military ships into South Korean waters. 
The three ships apparently followed the torpedo boat, and one was said to be a missile destroyer.
A Government statement issued this afternoon in Seoul said the three ships had returned to international waters after warnings and a ''show of force'' by the South Korean Navy and Air Force. 
The nature of the ''show of force'' was not clear, but diplomats said no shots had been fired.
China later acknowledged that its vessels had entered South Korean waters. 
But it said they had done so ''inadvertently'' while searching for the stricken boat and had turned around once they realized the error. 
Peking did not respond directly to a South Korean demand for an apology.
Â 
Seoul Plays Down Episode
By tonight, Mr. Lee's statement dropped all references to the three intruding ships and his Government's earlier protest.
It appeared to reflect a decision to play down the episode after an evening of meetings by senior officials, including Prime Minister Lho Shin Young and Foreign Minister Lee Won Kyung. 
A decision on a matter of this importance almost certainly had the imprimatur of the South Korean leader, President Chun Doo Hwan.
The fact that South Korea had not said after more than 24 hours what it would do with the Chinese boat suggested to some diplomats that officials in Seoul were weighing political as well as diplomatic consequences.
The closest parallel to the situation was a hijacking in May 1983 in which six Chinese seeking asylum in Taiwan forced a Chinese airliner on a domestic flight to land in South Korea. 
In that incident, senior Chinese airline officials visited Seoul to negotiate the return of the airplane, a journey regarded by South Korea as a political coup.
Diplomats said Seoul may hope for similar gains this time.
Â 
Trade Is an Open Secret
Both China and South Korea have given signs of wishing to ease the deep bitterness that has divided them since they fought during the Korean War. 
Trade between them is more or less an open secret, with most goods passing through Hong Kong.
South Korea expects China to attend the Olympic Games in Seoul in 1988. 
It also regards Peking as a moderating influence on North Korea. 
A fundamental assumption in Seoul is that Chinese pressure has been a main reason for the mildly improved climate between two Koreas over the last 15 months.
In the 1983 hijacking, South Korean courts convicted the six Chinese but handed out mild sentences. 
Last Aug. 
13, adhering to a pattern set in previous defections, South Korea ignored China's objections and allowed the hijackers to go to Taiwan, where they were given homes and jobs.
