file: LAW FIRMS CAPITALIZE ON CHINA TRADE BOOM.txt
text:
ï»¿
In keeping with the rapid expansion of United States trade with China in the last few years, five American law firms have now established what amount to permanent offices in Peking.
The new legal interest in China was underscored last month when Jerome Alan Cohen, who is widely regarded as the foremost American authority on Chinese law, resigned as professor of law and associate dean at the Harvard Law School to accept an offer as a senior partner at the New York firm of Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison.
Mr. Cohen, 51 years old, had been intensely courted by at least two other major Wall Street law firms, including Coudert Brothers, for whom he had worked as a consultant on American-Chinese trade over the last 10 years. 
He had also been one of the leading candidates for dean of the Harvard Law School last spring.
5 American law firms establish permanent offices in Peking (China)
Mr. Cohen took a two-year leave of absence from Harvard to help Coudert Brothers set up an office in Peking after the normalization of relations with China in 1979.
Â 
A Doubling of Trade
American trade with China last year amounted to $4.8 billion, more than double the 1979 figure. 
American trade with the countries of East Asia as a whole has also climbed rapidly in the past decade and reached $139 billion in 1980, more than the total of the United States' imports and exports with Western Europe, which amounted to $114 billion, according to the Department of Commerce.
''But American law firms were very slow to take note of this trend,'' Mr. Cohen said in an interview. 
Officially, China still does not permit Western legal firms to have offices in Peking. 
This is partly because of Chinese suspicion about what the foreign lawyers are doing and partly because of a shortage of housing and office space.
There is intense competition among foreign businessmen, bankers, lawyers and journalists for hotel rooms in Peking. 
Mr. Cohen will use a suite at the Peking Hotel that he got when he was working for Coudert Brothers in 1979.
Â 
Seminars Paid Off
Coudert Brothers was able to secure permanent rooms there because Mr. Cohen gave a series of legal seminars to officials of the Peking city government, which runs the Peking Hotel.
In this stay, Mr. Cohen will give a course for a Chinese Government ministry on United States contract, investment and trade law.
The other American law firms that have offices in Peking are Baker & McKenzie of Chicago, Graham & James of San Francisco and Heller, Ehrman, White & McAuliffe of San Francisco.
Stanley Lubman, a partner with Heller, Ehrman, said he now spends one-third to one-half his time in China. 
Mr. Lubman, who speaks Chinese, said that, from 1979 and 1980, a series of laws issued by the Chinese Government on taxation, foreign investment and joint ventures had made it easier to do business with China.
Â 
Legal System Is Different
But he cautioned that lawyers should not expect the Chinese legal system to be as complete and relatively free of ambiguities as United States codes.
In negotiating any deal with the Chinese, he said, it was his experience that ''it is a matter of shrinking the American contracts and stretching the Chinese ones.''
''The Chinese contract,'' he said, ''will emphasize what should be done, the American contract will also emphasize what happens if the project isn't done, and that's where the big differences come up between us.''
Both Mr. Cohen and Mr. Lubman began to study Chinese law in the early 1960's with grants from the Rockefeller Foundation. 
At the time, Mr. Cohen recalled, China and the United States were bitter enemies, and his wife and friends thought ''I was losing my mind.''
''It's a wonderful thing to study,'' his wife, Joan Leobold Cohen, counseled him, ''but this is a field that has absolutely no practical application. 
We'll have to live off our academic salary.''

text:

HALLS OF JADE, WALLS OF STONE Women in China Today. 
By Stacey Peck. 
Illustrated. 315 pp. 
New York: Franklin Watts. 
$15.95.
STACEY PECK, a professional interviewer who has worked for the Sunday magazine of The Los Angeles Times, traveled in China for two months in late 1983, recording conversations with Chinese women. 
As she acknowledges, she lacked the background in Chinese culture and language that would have enabled her to move beyond the official progam arranged for her by her host organization, one of China's major newspapers.
The women with whom Mrs. Peck was allowed to meet included a large proportion of officials, model workers and others trusted by the Communist Party. 
Many of the intellectuals and artists mentioned the foreign studies of their children or their own travels outside of China, usually an indication of privilege or status; the peasants she was taken to see were so well off that her interpreter exclaimed, ''Their living conditions are better than mine!''
Despite its limitations, however, this collection is noteworthy as the largest group of interviews with Chinese women to be published since the Cultural Revolution of 1965-76. 
In today's more relaxed climate, even what is said to an American stranger in official meetings is frequently interesting.
Many of the women speak of the improvement in their lives over those of their mothers and grandmothers before the Communist victory, but their complaints about men who do not share the housework and child rearing, about stereotyped attitudes toward the capabilities and talents of both sexes, and about women's lack of political power will sound quite familiar to Western women. 
In openly discussing such problems, the women Mrs. Peck interviewed were not departing from the official position of the All-China Women's Federation, a Government organization whose English-language publication, Women of China, often contains even more outspoken statements on the status of women than those included here.
Very different in tone are the interviews conducted with Chinese in the United States. 
A temporary expatriate tells Mrs. Peck, ''You interviewed many women in China, and I don't think they would lie to you but . . . some questions they might not answer at all or just omit certain information.''
One of the best interviews was conducted with a computer scientist in Los Angeles who speaks of claiming her father's corpse after his ''persecution to death'' during the Cultural Revolution: ''At the door to the morgue a policeman said, 'Your father was a reactionary, so you are not allowed to cry when you see him.'
Then they took me into the room, and I saw him for the first time since he had been arrested.''
The same woman describes her 10-year marriage to a man from whom she was separated because of their state-assigned jobs, an all too common situation in China: ''We tried very hard to work in the same city so we could live together. 
But we never could, so he's really a stranger to me. 
. . . We only saw each other on our twelve-day vacations every year, but I do know he's a nice person and very honest.''
In a final section, Mrs. Peck interviews several of the long-term foreign residents of Peking; she is apparently unaware that the reason they are often unexpectedly disappointing informants has to do with the unusual adaptations they have had to make to survive in China for so many years. 
Although she does speak with one more recent arrival, it would have been more useful and quite easy, even within the modest framework Mrs. Peck has chosen, to interview a few of the hundreds of Western students who have spent several years at the major universities, many of whom have no language barrier and have formed deep friendships with the Chinese. 
Their anecdotes might have given a sense of what the women of China would have said in a less official context.

file: Liuqiying Journal_In the Good Earth, Did Envy, Too, Bear Fruit_.txt
text:
ï»¿
Yin Yongcheng, a beige snap-brim cap planted firmly on his head, walked among his orange trees, their fruit harvested now, and wondered about the future.
''I'm not sure I can go on,'' Mr. Yin said, scanning the 11-acre orchard that prickled the otherwise barren mountain like a four-day growth of beard.
A slight man who has worked the soil of this part of the northern province of Shaanxi much of his life, Mr. Yin has become a minor cause celebre in China. 
The People's Daily, the official organ of the Communist Party, has portrayed him as an aggressive agricultural entrepreneur who has reached the brink of failure, undermined by the rigid bureaucratic attitudes of village officials and ill-disguised local jealousies.
The plight of Mr. Yin, who in many ways represents the direction agriculture in China must go if it is to modernize, points also to the obstacles faced by the country's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, and Zhao Ziyang, the leader of the party, in their effort to insure the compliance of localities with national policy.
Â 
Encouraged by Changes
For Mr. Yin, of course, the cosmic problems of China's agricultural policies are at most a remote concern. 
Rather, it is the health of his mountain where his trees grow and the antagonism of the village head, Yin Jinxue, and the township boss, Zhao Qiwen, that preoccupy him.
''I was a farmer,'' the 38-year-old Yin Yongcheng explained. 
''Like everybody else, I grew paddy rice, some corn, cotton, peanuts. 
We were organized into a collective. 
Nobody had their own land at that time. 
That was 1983.''
''I'd heard about the reform policies and was encouraged,'' he continued, referring to the national policy, begun in 1978, of disbanding collective agriculture and distributing land to individual households.
An agricultural school in nearby Hanzhong had started planting orange saplings on a hillside above the village in 1982. 
Mr. Yin said that it seemed to him that by taking care of those trees and planting more saplings and some grape vines a profitable fruit farm could be built.
The problem, of course, was that for a single individual to control so much land was almost unheard of.
''I went to talk to Yin Jinxue,'' Mr. Yin said. 
''I told him that this area is poor land and wasn't being used. 
I said I just wanted to try it. 
They decided to let me try.''
On June 30, 1983, Yin Yongcheng signed a contract with the village to care for the existing orange trees and expand the orchard further. 
With loans from the local agricultural bank, he hired workers and over the next four years transformed the hilltop into a flourishing orchard.
This year, for the first time, his trees and vines produced a good crop and he began repaying his loans. 
But this year also his problems with local officials began. 
''I need to build a pond to irrigate the trees,'' Mr. Yin said. 
''I put forward the plan to the village and the township for a loan to go ahead. 
I asked for 28,000 yuan,'' or about $7,500. 
''They would not provide the money.''
As a result, Mr. Yin was prepared to abandon the orchard until a reporter from The People's Daily arrived in the village this fall. 
It is here that accounts differ. 
According to The People's Daily, local officials refused to make the loans to Mr. Yin because he had only a 10-year contract, the maximum permissible, and were afraid the money would not be repaid. 
At the same time, the officials would not consider extending the contract.
An unidentified village official was quoted as having said, ''Maybe on the ninth year of the contract we'll discuss whether Yin will be allowed to prolong his contract.''
When questioned again recently, the officials seemed evasive. 
Zhao Qiwen, the township leader, blamed the backwardness of the region. 
''We started to carry out the system of contracts and individual responsibility four years later than other places,'' he said. 
''We had no idea what difficulties we would meet.''
Yin Jinxue, the village chief, said: ''Even if The People's Daily hadn't come the problem would be resolved. 
It took time because it needed the two sides to discuss it.''
But Yan Kejian, an official in the foreign affairs department of nearby Hanzhong city, the agency that supervises contacts between foreigners and Chinese in this region of Shaanxi Province, conceded that the two local leaders were less than candid. 
''They didn't tell the truth,'' he said.
Â 
Villagers Called Resentful
Yin Yongcheng said some of his problems also stemmed from the resentment among villagers that he was better off than they were. 
Where once an old ramshackle mud brick house stood on the mountain ridge, he has built a five-room red brick home that, though plain, seems less bound to the soil than the mud houses in the village below.
''My grandfather was landlord of this village,'' Mr. Yin said. 
Then, with a sigh, he continued. 
''I heard people saying that I was another landlord, that things were going back to the way they were.''
Next year, Mr. Yin said, he hopes to double the crop of oranges. 
But whether the orchard can, in the long run, survive without the irrigation pond that local officials do not seem willing to let him build, he said he did not know.
For The People's Daily, the newspaper that speaks for China's leadership, Mr. Yin's problems are the truest test of whether the country will move ahead.
''The problems he has encountered are faced in varying degrees by others who contract to run enterprises,'' the paper wrote. 
''We hope that the telling of Yin Yongcheng's story will attract widespread thought and discussion.''
Mr. Yin is still waiting for his loan.

file: MACAO PLANS FOR A FUTURE UNDER CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
Not quite two years after Britain and China fashioned a formula for the return of Hong Kong to China, Portugal and China have agreed to open negotiations on a similar deal for Macao, the oldest European enclave on the China coast.
The talks will begin at the end of June in Peking and are expected to conclude more quickly than those on Hong Kong, which took three years.
Compared with the frenetic British colony that lies 40 miles away across the mouth of the Pearl River, this has always been a quiet and unstressful place, and so it is proving as the China talks approach.
Unlike Hong Kong, which went through a stock market plunge and associated jitters on the road to agreement with Peking, Macao's 400,000 people, only about 12,000 of them Portuguese, are generally sanguine about the prospect of returning to Chinese sovereignty sometime in the next 10 to 15 years.
'Hope for the Best'
''I wouldn't say that people here like the idea, but they accept it and hope for the best,'' said the Rev. Domingos Lam, the vicar general of the colony's Roman Catholic Church.
Father Lam has more to worry about than most, given the repression experienced on the mainland by priests who insist on their loyalty to Rome. 
But even on this score he is optimistic, saying he doubts the Communist authorities of the future will require him to remove the oil paintings of popes and bishops that line the upper gallery in the 18th-century villa that serves as the church's main office here.
''If they ask for that, they may as well tell me to get out,'' the chain-smoking priest said, chuckling. 
''I will simply tell them, 'No!'
''
Besides the Catholic Church the mainland rulers have much else to contemplate as they prepare for their negotiations with Portugal's chief delegate to the United Nations, Ruy Barbosa Medina, who will head Lisbon's delegations in the talks.
Macao's largest source of revenue is its 24-hour casinos, which draw more than three million Hong Kong gamblers a year onto the ferries and high-speed jetfoils that cross the choppy waters between here and Hong Kong.
Although gambling and licentiousness have raised their heads in China, the authorities repeatedly crack down on what they call the threat to China's ''spiritual civilization.''
In Macao, unless there is a radical change in the colony's economic fortunes, they are not so much a threat to the way of life as the pillar of it.
Â 
Peking Seems Little Bothered
So far, Peking seems little bothered by the colony's ways. 
Tens of thousands of mainlanders make their way here each year, and it is easy to spot the short haircuts and baggy suits of the typical Communist officeholder among the pleasure-seekers at the Lisboa's ''crazy Paris show.''
Along with this, the authorities in Kwangtung Province, beyond the archway that straddles the border with China, have boosted the mainland's stake in the Macao economy, to the point where Communist-owned banks, construction companies and trading houses account for 10 to 20 percent of local business.
Partly to protect the economic upswing Macao is experiencing, Peking has sketched out the agreement it expects from the talks. 
The basic pattern will be the same as those for Hong Kong, which provide for the extension of the British colony's capitalist system and the laws that underpin it for 50 years after the handover in 1997. 
But a Peking political newsweekly, Outlook, recently spoke of the need to meet the ''specific conditions of Macao,'' implying that there may be some special provisions here.
Portuguese and Chinese opinion leaders hope that one difference will be the timing of the transition. 
With 1997 barely a decade away, they say, Macao is far less prepared for the autonomous existence envisioned in the Hong Kong formula.
''We will need more time,'' said Joaquim Marinho de Bastos, the Portuguese lawyer who is the colony's tourism director as well as the leader of its Social Democratic Party, which has majority support among the Portuguese officials, professionals and businessmen.
Â 
Few Chinese Officials
Mr. Marinho noted that the administration here remained almost entirely in Portuguese hands, unlike Hong Kong, where the bureaucracy is predominantly Chinese and has begun to yield some of its most important posts to local people.
China is unlikely to want Macao back before 1997. 
Hong Kong, which has 5.5 million people and is one of the world's most important economic centers, weighs far more heavily with Peking than the six square miles of Macao.
A recovery date for Macao that preceded Hong Kong's would risk the confidence that British and Chinese officials are trying to develop in the British colony. 
''If things went wrong here, it could have a devastating effect in Hong Kong,'' Mr. Marinho said.
An important role in the bargaining over Macao's future is being played by wealthy Chinese businessmen who have fostered close ties with Peking. 
The most important is Ma Man-kei, a multimillionaire in banking and real estate, who makes his priorities clear in the portraits that adorn his office above an antiques shop on the Praia Grande promenade. 
A large photograph of Deng Xiaoping, the Chinese leader, dwarfs a much smaller shot of the former Portuguese President, Antonio Ramalho Eanes.
Mr. Ma has already helped obtain revisions to investment rules on the mainland, and Portuguese officials, including some who have not always trusted him, say they believe he can perform a similar ''educating'' role for Macao.

file: MACAO WILL REPORT TO CHINA IN 1999 UNDER PORTUGAL PACT.txt
text:
ï»¿
China and Portugal reached agreement today on returning this small gambling haven, a Portuguese colony for 430 years, to China in 1999.
The agreement means that Portugal, which here became the first European power to establish a beachhead on the Asian mainland, will be the last colonial power to leave.
Macao, a dot on the South China coast 40 miles southwest of Hong Kong, is home to 420,000 people, 97 percent of whom are ethnically Chinese. 
The enclave is sprinkled with casinos and massage parlors and has a reputation as Hong Kong's playground. 
The economy depends on the 4.2 million tourists who visit each year, mostly from Hong Kong.
'The Holiday Is Finished'
''We have had a long summer holiday, but the holiday is finished,'' the Rev. Domingos Lam, the Roman Catholic Vicar General of Macao, said today. 
''Everything will change.''
The agreement, which followed nine months of negotiations, was announced in a brief statement by negotiators in Beijing. 
The terms of the accord were not disclosed, and apparently will not be, at least until it is initialed in Beijing on Thursday by chief negotiators for both Portugal and China. 
[A Portuguese diplomat in Beijing said the accord would be signed next month by Prime Ministers Mario Soares of Portugal and Zhao Ziyang of China.] But reports in Macao, Beijing and Lisbon agree on major aspects of the agreement. 
The accord is similar to the one by which Britain will return Hong Kong to China in July 1997.
According to these reports, Macao will return to Chinese control on Dec. 
20, 1999. 
Like Hong Kong, Macao will be guaranteed 50 years of noninterference in its way of life and capitalist system. 
A committee of Portuguese and Chinese negotiators will resolve other issues, such as the political institutions and legal system.
''I think the agreement can be considered a fairly good one,'' said Carlos Monjardino, the acting Governor. 
''But for now there is no significant reaction here.''
Indeed, most people interviewed here seemed relatively unconcerned about the agreement. 
In part, this reflected the lack of information about the accord. 
In part, many people said, it also reflected the view that there is not much that residents can do about it, whatever they think. 
'Small People Cannot Go'
''We have worries, but what can we do?'' asked Danny Cheung, whose small shop here sells traditional medicines and bird nests used to make soup. 
''We are not millionaires, or we could fly to another country. 
We are small people; we cannot go.''
Mr. Cheung and several others interviewed said they doubted that China would continue for long to tolerate the gambling casinos and strip shows that are the enclave's economic foundation. 
But a senior Government official here said that the gambling would definitely continue, and other analysts note that China would face substantial economic pressure if it closed the casinos -which supply 20 percent of economic output here and a large proportion of government revenue.
''The mind-set here is entirely different from China's,'' said the 36-year-old well-dressed owner of a small shop. 
''But I'm not worried. 
I have a green card to go to the United States. 
I figure I have 10 more years here.''
#1999 Is Considered Distant Many people here stressed that 1999 was still very distant, and that much could happen before then.
''I'm not anxious about 1999,'' said C. K. Lo, a pawnbroker. 
''My main worry is whether I can find a meal today.''
Macao's economic dependence on vice has caused problems for China before. 
Soon after the Portuguese revolution of 1974, some Portuguese officials traveled to Beijing to suggest that the colony be returned to China. 
They were rebuffed. 
Chinese officials said they wanted Macao back but not just yet. 
Apparently they were unsure how to reconcile Communism with blackjack, and afraid that if they interfered the jitters would spread to Hong Kong and disrupt that territory's economy.
Although Macao, which was permanently settled by the Portuguese in 1557, has the architecture and relaxed atmosphere of Portugal, and shop signs must be in Portuguese as well as Chinese, the Portuguese influence is minimal. 
Only 3 percent of the population speaks Portuguese, and almost no one knows streets by their official Portuguese names. 
Instead, they are known by their Chinese names.
A Portuguese official here said that his country had insisted in the negotiations on favorable trade arrangements as parthedding its colonies - such as Angola, of Macao. 
No formal trade concessions - such as increased purchases by China of Portuguese exports - were adopted, but an informal understanding was reached, the official said. 
Issue of Dual Nationality A more contentious issue was the rights of some 80,000 ethnic Chinese residents of Macao who hold Portuguese passports. 
China refused to regard them as dual nationals, and at one point last week Portugal reportedly threatened to suspend the talks because of disagreements on the subject.
But China is reported to have agreed that while it would regard dual passport holders as solely Chinese nationals, they could retain their passports and claim Portuguese nationality while traveling outside China.
The agreement also serves Portugal's interest in allowing it a more gracious departure than it experienced from its other colonies. 
Portugal was widely criticized in the mid-1970's for shedding its colonies - such as Angola, Mozambique and East Timor - without adequately preparing them for self-government. 
In the final years of its stewardship, Portugal is trying to increase its role in Macao, and is considering leaving a ''farewell gift'' such as an airport or other major project for Macao.

file: MANDARINS, MARTYRS AND REVOLUTIONAIRES.txt
text:
ï»¿
ANCESTORS
900 Years in the Life of a Chinese Family.
By Frank Ching.
Illustrated. 528 pp. 
New York:
William Morrow & Company. 
$22.95.
Shortly after Frank Ching arrived in the People's Republic of China in June of 1979 to set up The Wall Street Journal's first Beijing bureau, he found himself embarked on an odyssey of personal and historical discovery that lasted nearly a decade. 
Beginning with an exploration of his immediate ancestry, his quest, by the time he finished, had drawn him back to the Song Dynasty (960-1279) on a seemingly endless trail of family genealogies, dynastic records, local gazetteers, oral histories and other historical and literary works in both Chinese and English. 
The result is ''Ancestors: 900 Years in the Life of a Chinese Family,'' a stunning accomplishment in which, by recounting individual lives of members of his own clan, Mr. Ching brings to life the last nine centuries of Chinese history and culture as almost no other work in the English language has done. 
But, equally important, Mr. Ching's long narrative of personalized Chinese history reveals to us the myriad ways in which, despite the defiant ''antifeudal'' rhetoric of the Chinese Communist Party, both Mao's tumultuous socialist revolution and Deng's unprecedented capitalist counterrevolution share common roots with China's past.
Among other American correspondents in Beijing, Frank Ching quickly acquired a reputation for being not only a thoughtful journalist, but for having the best Chinese sources. 
Those were the days when unauthorized contact with a tourist, a businessman or even a visiting scholar from abroad was often enough to cause serious trouble for a Chinese. 
Association with Western journalists - who were viewed by the Government as little more than thinly camouflaged spies - often caused arrest and ruination. 
But, being a Chinese-American, Frank Ching, who was in any event a paradigm of civility and discretion, was able to slip quietly away from the pack of other newly arrived American reporters and disappear on his own into the other side of that stark divide which, in the minds of most citizens of the People's Republic, still separated them from ''foreigners.''
To those of us whose alienness kept us so bound within the confines of the foreign community, Mr. Ching's aunts and uncles, some of whom were rumored to have high positions in the Chinese party hierarchy, seemed like unimaginably forbidden and exotic sources.
Mr. Ching's family contacts doubtless helped him unravel the events that propelled Chinese life during those first years of political reform in Deng Xiaoping's China; his reporting was indeed excellent. 
But, as we now learn, these family connections ended up having consequences of far more significance for him than simply providing a little extra information for his regular dispatches, or even for the kind of obligatory post-tour-of-duty book many of his colleagues wrote on returning home. 
For Mr. Ching, finding his contemporary relatives led to a rediscovery of a long-lost family that stretched back for more than a millennium and that ultimately unsealed for him not only his family history but the history of his native land.
Returning to his native country was an awakening for Mr. Ching, who left mainland China as a 5-year-old and who had grown up beyond the borders of the land and culture in which his own family and clan had for centuries been so deeply immersed. 
His reconnection with lost family members in post-Mao China made him aware for the first time not only of his clan's fate in the People's Republic, but also of the distinguished part it had played during the dynastic period as well. 
In fact, it was not until his return to China that he found out about his own father, who until then had remained an elusive figure for Mr. Ching. A prominent Shanghai lawyer and supporter of republicanism in the 1920's and 30's, by the 40's the elder Ching had become discouraged by war and revolution, and finally sent his family to Hong Kong, where Frank Ching was born in 1940, as part of that great diaspora of refugees that fled China before Mao's ''liberation'' in 1949. 
The family returned to Shanghai in 1942, but then left again in 1946.
Having stumbled on a genealogical history (''zong pu'') of his clan, Mr. Ching began research that soon resulted in a domino effect: the discovery of each successive generation of the illustrious Qins (the name ''Ching'' is simply a different transliteration of the character for ''Qin'') only set Mr. Ching off in search of its predecessor.
Reading this family genealogy is like visiting a Confucian ancestral hall that every great family in ancient China once maintained as a means of keeping up a connection between the living and the dead, and where each tablet placed in memory of a departed member is able to speak. 
As Frank Ching, who left The Wall Street Journal in 1983 to complete this book, takes us back through the generations of his own kinsmen, one has the sense of being in a moving time capsule, on a biographical tour of Chinese history, which is ineluctably moving forward toward present time. 
Returning to his hometown, Wushi in Jiangsu Province, one of the main seats of high literati culture in ancient China, Mr. Ching began his expedition of familial archeology by searching out and finding the grave of his Song dynasty ancestor, the poet Qin Guan, who lived from 1049 to 1102. 
From then on, he guides us through generation after generation of Chinese life, so that as we meet scores of long-departed family members, each in his way emblematic of the time and culture in which he lived, we feel almost as though this is a cautionary tale meant to illustrate the vicissitudes of Chinese culture and politics. 
The list includes Qin Kui, the infamous chief councilor of the Song dynasty in the 12th century, who was alleged to have sold out the country to marauding Jurchen tribesmen; Qin Yubo, the just Yuan Dynasty (1279-1368) official who ultimately became the patron god of Shanghai; Qin Jin, the celebrated Ming dynasty (1368-1644) minister to the Jiajing Emperor; and Qin Yong, philosopher and stubborn Ming loyalist; Qin Songling, a Qing dynasty (1644-1912) official par excellence and keeper of the Imperial diary for the Kangxi Emperor; Qin Huitian, illustrious official and minister of punishments under the Qianlong Emperor - and, coming closer to remembered time, Qin Guojun, Mr. Ching's grandfather and highly esteemed district magistrate; Qin Jiajun, Mr. Ching's half-brother and a Communist martyr who died with Mao's Fourth Army in 1942 while fighting the Japanese; and finally Qin Liankui, Mr. Ching's father and 20th-century Shanghai pioneer of legal reform. 
Each generation added its chronicle to the family genealogy.
Getting a meaningful overview of Chinese history, particularly dynastic history, has never been easy for Westerners. 
Specialists, professors and graduate students have tended to approach it in segments, so that their research often misses the marvel of its sweep and cultural continuity. 
On the other hand, generalists and students in introductory college courses who have little background, are forced to confront its enormity as a whole, so that its three millenniums end up appearing as little more than a repetitive, blurred, not to say dull, cycle of emperors and rising and falling dynasties. 
By allowing members of his own family to speak for the times in which they lived, Mr. Ching has personalized the vastness of this historical panorama, thereby allowing his readers to become generalist and specialist at the same time. 
By focusing on the microcosms of individual lives, he makes history immediate, and by stringing these generational portraits together, he also succeeds in highlighting those themes and cultural and political traits that have endured right down to the era of Deng Xiaoping.
For instance, Mr. Ching's depiction of Qin Songling, a scholar-official and member of the prestigious Hanlin Academy who lived from 1637 to 1714 during the Qing dynasty and who served under the Kangxi Emperor when the Qin clan was at the height of its glory, presents not only a telling portrait of life at that time, but a reminder of how hauntingly similar the fates of officials then could be to their contemporary Communist counterparts. 
Qin Songling, like Deng Xiaoping, was twice disgraced, dismissed from office and then rehabilitated. 
In a way that is also suggestive of the present, Mr. Ching describes how Songling served on a project to write an official history of the previous Ming dynasty, in which, because the emperor was offended by the incorrect use of Ming loyalist reign titles favored by the enemies of the Qing, earlier compilers had been executed. 
Moreover, even the family members of these unfortunates, considered tainted by their association with the accused, were extirpated as traitors in an orgy of persecution.
The custom of giving enemy designations to all the family members of any accused individual foreshadowed all too accurately the later Communist practices during the Anti-Rightist Campaign and the Cultural Revolution when the ''bad'' class or political ''background'' of any individual was grounds for cashiering all their kith and kin. 
Moreover, when Songling was first digraced and removed from office on a trumped-up charge of tax evasion, he readily accepted guilt, evincing the same kind of contrition and willingness to submit to government authority that was characteristic of so many party officials accused of ideological crimes during more recent times. 
One can see in the insistence on orthodoxy and the admissions of guilt and self-confessions of each period how deeply the notion of obedience to one's ruler has been inculcated into the Chinese psyche, and how fundamental the idea of an inviolable ''correct'' or ''orthodox'' political line has always been in Chinese politics.
The unpredictable ups and downs of Qin Songling's career in government are a mirror of the present in other ways as well. 
We are reminded how the absolute power of emperors, constrained by little more than whatever moral restraint each ruling member of the imperial family chose voluntarily to exercise, cast the die for future patterns of leadership. 
Mao Zedong was every bit as imperial in his way as the most autocratic of emperors. 
And we are reminded how parlous public service in China is even now, bearing out the old adage that ''keeping company with the emperor is akin to keeping company with a tiger.''
Indeed, what comes through most clearly in Mr. Ching's portraits of his relatives who served so many dynasties and emperors, are the manifold ways in which both republican and Communist history of our century share cultural genes with China's past. 
During both those periods, one is struck again and again by the fate of just bureaucrats and officials who because of the paranoia or caprice of a ruler are tarred with the brush of unorthodoxy and treason and defrocked. 
Whether animated by devotion to the Confucian notions of loyalty and obedience, or the Communist notion of party discipline and hewing to the ''correct line,'' officials throughout Chinese history have been deeply imbued with a sense of political conformity that has led them to bear their humiliations and defrockings in a way that is almost unimaginable to Westerners.
From this tour of Mr. Ching's gallery of historical profiles, we can see how the ''self-criticisms'' demanded of intellectuals in the Maoist era grew organically out of the compulsory admissions of guilt expected by the emperors of officials accused of wrongdoing. 
We see also how deeply rooted are the traditions of rank and hierarchy, intolerance of diversity, and the stress on the Confucian virtues of obedience, loyalty and filial piety. 
And we cannot help but note how factional struggle, political infighting, informing, intrigue, the humiliation of adversaries, the absolute and arbitrary power of supreme leaders have always been the heart and soul of Chinese politics. 
Finally, we are made abundantly aware how ill-equipped all this traditional political culture now makes China to deal with the Western ideas of democracy and human rights. 
By way of criticism, it must be said that in poring through all the family genealogies, ancient ''veritable records'' of departed emperors, and so forth, Frank Ching sometimes succumbs to a weakness characteristic of many Chinese dynastic historians - namely, an overemphasis on the compilation of detail and fact. 
While Mr. Ching's research is impressive, we are often left yearning for the kind of interpretive connective tissue that helps make an abundance of fact more meaningful. 
In this respect, we wish Mr. Ching had allowed himself to be more present in his work, and had played the role not only of dispassionate chronicler of his family, but of interpreter. 
For what keeps his narrative moving is precisely our knowledge that the Qin clan does finally culminate in such a curious way, namely in the guise of its newest genealogist, the expatriate Frank Ching himself. 
And so, we are left wanting to know more about him; what he got out of this unusual project, how it made him see his homeland and its history differently, and how he now feels about these fathomless layers of family records he has unearthed. 
As it is, we are left with tantalizingly little by way of his own sensibility and thoughts.
But never mind. 
''Ancestors'' is a tour de force in its own right. 
It not only leaves one with a new appreciation of Chinese history, but reminds one that while China may have been one of the most revolutionary societies in the 20th century, it has in many ways been one of the least rebellious. 
Deeply steeped in its own history and conservatism, even Mao's monumental paroxysm of militant socialism was finally unable to detach the vast nation from its past. 
While Mao still lived and his socialist ideology was still being blared from every media outlet in China, Chinese and foreigners alike most often drew attention to the ways in which the society had changed. 
But now that the Great Helmsman has gone, and the process of de-Maoification has begun, what books like ''Ancestors'' bring out in bold relief is the continuity that still surges on through Chinese history like a powerful if sometimes unseen subterranean current.
Â 
NEW RELATIVES AND OLD
HONG KONG
When Frank Ching was researching his family's history for ''Ancestors,'' he was so immersed in his work that he dreamed vividly about relatives he had never known or met. 
''In one very clear dream, I was asking my father, whom I never really knew, to tell me about my grandfather, who died 30 years before I was born,'' Mr. Ching said in a recent interview. 
''It was very intense.''
After beginning his research, Mr. Ching realized that ''trying to discover my family origins was a very Chinese characteristic.''
And he found that he shared with his father an interest in politics combined with a resolve not to become a politician.
Even while he was working on ''Ancestors,'' Mr. Ching never quite put away the present for the past. 
When he finished his book, he began writing a political column for the leading English-language newspaper here. 
A member of a small band of progressive reformers in Hong Kong, Mr. Ching, who is married to a Chinese lawyer, believes that before Britain returns the colony to China in 1997, colonial officials should set up a strong, representative government because the territory might need the protection of democratic institutions even from the new, more liberal China.
Mr. Ching underscored his point with an anecdote of a friend from Beijing who, a few years ago, came to Hong Kong on business. 
''On the phone he talked about how things had changed in China and he said he was eager to see me because we could now speak openly and freely,'' Mr. Ching recalled. 
Then he threw back his head and laughed: ''I met my friend later and he told me he had to say all those things because there was someone in the room with him.''

text:
ï»¿
A year ago Feng Lanxiu seemed a discouraging prospect for marriage. 
She was totally deaf and unable to speak even in sign language, and she was still being cared for by her parents.
Now Miss Feng, who is 34 years old, has a doting husband who kids her gently about not yet producing their first child. 
Her husband, Liu Jinli, 32, also cannot hear or speak. 
He met Miss Feng and married her last July through an unusual matchmaking service.
Profile of matchmaking of handicapped people in China
In this Manchurian city, an agency run by amateur marriage brokers tries to find spouses for physically handicapped people who in traditional Chinese society were long considered unmarriageable.
Hong Zhiguo, director of the city's Society for the Disabled, said regular employment had been found for 92 percent of Harbin's 6,000 handicapped adults. 
Their disabilities have been turned to advantage sometimes. 
Many of those who are deaf work in a local truck assembly plant where the noise does not disturb them.
Â 
46 Have Registered
This reduces the burden on their families, Mr. Hong said, but does not guarantee the disabled an independent life. 
So early last year his society set up its marriage service.
About 100 people have visited the bureau so far and 46 have registered. 
Two couples got married last July, and a third couple is preparing for marriage. 
Three other couples are courting and expect to wed, Mr. Hong said, ''so basically we have a success rate of 25 percent.''
The introductions are arranged by Li Shuqing, a staff member, every Monday and Wednesday morning in her small office, which is over a bottlecap factory. 
''The job of matchmaking is new to us; we have no experience at all,'' Miss Li acknowledged.
With the decline of traditional family-arranged marriages, Chinese cities have enjoyed a boom in matchmaking centers. 
But Miss Li said her responsibilities went well beyond the simpler task of bringing ordinary people together.
Â 
'This Job Is Delicate'
''Because marriage is a major event in the life of young people, it is concerned with their happiness or bitterness,'' she said. 
''So I know that this job is delicate. 
They are disabled physically but not mentally, and they have this desire for marriage and happiness.''
Miss Li said her handicapped clients made good marriage partners because ''they may be more considerate and careful than normal people.''
But because they are self-conscious about asking for a spouse, the first tense visit to the matchmaking office often includes anxious relatives and even translators for sign language.
''They fear that it will be difficult to find a partner or that they won't find someone, so they come together with their parents,'' Miss Li said. 
''We tell them that is it normal and natural for young people to marry and there should be no problems.''
''They are very shy at the first meeting,'' she said. 
''They don't talk much. 
They may arrange the next meeting by themselves, at a park or movie theater, and then report back to us.''
Â 
Handicaps Are Also Paired
In addition to trying to match hobbies, interests and family backgrounds, Miss Li said she also usually paired physical handicaps, reasoning that those sharing the same problems would be more sympathetic to a partner's needs.
But sometimes weeks of effort by Miss Li end in failure. 
She recalled introducing a 25-year-old man, ''crippled in both arms but good-looking,'' to a 25-year-old woman who could not walk and got about with a hand-cranked tricycle. 
Both were working hard to become foreign language translators, he in Japanese and she in English, so Miss Li decided that ''in my opinion, they were a very good match.''
But she could not negotiate the stairs to his second-floor apartment, and she worried that he would not be able to carry a child. 
''So they didn't make it,'' Miss Li said with a sigh.
On another occasion Miss Li introduced two deaf people who were each married before and had a child. 
''At their first meeting they got along very well, but then it broke down,'' Miss Li said. 
The two people worried that if their children quarreled, they could not hear it and family harmony would be upset.
Â 
Problems After Marriage
''Sometimes we feel discouraged, but the difficulties of the disabled are bigger than ours,'' Miss Li said. 
''So we try to persuade ourselves to be patient and to keep working.''
While the office is also prepared to mediate problems that may develop after marriage, the couples so far seem to have made their own adjustment. 
Shao Kuihe, a husky 30-year-old, is proud of saving $750 in preparation for his marriage to Sheng Lijuan, who is 28. 
Neither can hear nor speak. 
Mr. Shao explained in sign language through an interpreter that he and Miss Sheng communicated by writing messages and watching the shape of each other's mouth.
Once a couple decides to marry, the office refers them to specialists at a Harbin medical college to determine whether they should have a child. 
Mr. Hong said heredity was not involved in the disabilities of the couples matched so far.
The matchmaking service is open to those who are blind as well as to those who are deaf and mute or handicapped in some other way. 
It has not turned down anyone for being too disabled.
''We do have some severe physical cases, but if the problem lies within the bounds of the marriage law, we will try our best to make it possible,'' Mr. Hong said. 
''For some people, we have to tell them in advance that their case will be difficult, so they must be patient.''

HONG KONG In Hong Kong, where making money is a national pastime, nothing is more applauded than a consummate deal, and no individual is more revered than the businessman who can make one. 
Most revered of all is Fung King Hey, an immigrant from China whose formal education stopped at about the eighth grade. 
Widely recognized as king of the deal makers, he has built a real estate, securities and banking empire larger than any other in Asia.
Mr. Fung and Merrill Lynch & Company are planning to sign a deal early next month which, although beneficial to both parties, has clear advantages for Mr. Fung's Sun Hung Kai Securities and Sun Hung Kai Bank. 
And it advances what some people believe is a rather eerie company motto: ''With our feet in Hong Kong, with our back against China, with our face towards the Asia-Pacific region, with our eyes open, we scan the world.''
Colleagues describe the financial wizard in terms that suggest science fiction rather than high finance. 
Physically, he could have been designed by a graphic artist: a pencil-thin body which seems to be powered by a dozen glasses of water a day, an angular head and spare features with hardly a wrinkle after 60 years.
Profile of Fung King Hey, Hong Kong entrepreneur, describes his new deal with Merrill Lynch & Company
Mr. Fung does not grant interviews, but his efforts to stay out of the limelight have been thwarted by his deals, which have brought much attention his way. 
Those deals are considered here to exemplify a business encounter of the most ingenious kind.
''He is an exceptional businessman,'' said Robert Fell, Hong Kong Commissioner for Securities. 
''He has a keen sense of timing and he is not afraid to take chances. 
He has made some mistakes, but he is very clever.''
The latest development, under which Merrill Lynch is acquiring 25 percent of Sun Hung Kai Securities and 15 percent of the Sun Hung Kai Bank, could make Mr. Fung the largest individual shareholder in Merrill Lynch & Company, parent of the United States' largest securities firm.
The arrangement, said William R. Arthur, chairman of Merrill Lynch International, ''will greatly strengthen our ability to serve individuals, corporations, institutions and governments throughout the Pacific region.''
But it is Mr. Fung who is being congratulated on this side of the world for pulling off a classy deal. 
He personally will make $60 million, and it gives him possibly the largest foothold of any Hong Kong businessman in the United States market. 
Through it, his companies are expected to gain considerable foreign expertise, security and clout.
The Merrill Lynch agreement, which has been valued at $81.5 million, calls for Merrill Lynch to buy 20 percent of the outstanding stock of Sun Hung Kai Securities directly from Mr. Fung. Sun Hung Kai Securities has assets of $478 million and reported 1981 aftertax profits of $32.6 million.
Merrill Lynch will also buy 17.3 million shares, or 10 percent, of the outstanding stock of Sun Hung Kai Bank directly from Mr. Fung. Formerly known as Sun Hung Kai Finance, the bank received its license only two months ago. 
The bank has assets of about $760 million and its aftertax profits were $12.5 million in 1981.
Mr. Fung will be paid in Merrill Lynch convertible debentures, which if exercised will give him 4 percent of Merrill Lynch. 
No decision has been made yet on whether or when Mr. Fung might convert his debentures.
In the same deal, Compagnie Financiere de Paris et des Pays-Bas, known as Paribas, will sell some of its holdings in Sun Hung Kai Bank to Merrill Lynch, cutting its holdings in the bank to 25 percent from 30. 
By reducing Paribas' holdings, the bank can now offer higher deposit rates than allowed by top-tier banks, which include banks with foreign bank holdings of more than 25 percent. 
But Paribas will lift its holdings in the securities firm to 10 percent from five and with Merrill Lynch, it plans a limited tender offer for another 10 percent of Sun Hung Kai Securities.
By bringing Merrill Lynch into the bank and the securities firm, Mr. Fung took care of his obligations to Paribas and his plans for expansion into the United States while realigning operations and eliminating the need for numerous foreign partnerships.
''Even before Banque de Paris et des Pays-Bas became a minority shareholder in 1978, Sun Hung Kai had already mapped out a strategy for cooperation in Europe, America and Asia,'' said Mr. Fung through the buffer of executives who isolate him from the press. 
''Objectives were set for the desirable distribution of share holdings. 
After that, it was a question of waiting for the right opportunity. 
When this presented itself, Sun Hung Kai was able to reach agreement with Merrill Lynch almost immediately.''
Sun Hung Kai is expected to end a five-year-old joint venture with ACLI International, a commodities brokerage house owned by Donaldson Lufkin Jenrette, a rival of Merrill Lynch's, and end a nine-monthold arrangement with Bear, Stearns & Company to market United States securities.
ALTHOUGH there are no figures to substantiate the claims, Bear S terns and Sun Hung Kai, which controls 25 percent of the trading in H ong Kong stocks, were said to be the largest brokers of United S tates securities in Hong Kong last year.
Bear Stearns will stay in Hong Kong, but the partnership will be dissolved because ''obviously there would be a conflict,'' said Michael Tarnapol, general partner of Bear Stearns. 
In Hong Kong it is felt that Bear Stearns was just an interim step for Mr. Fung, who wanted an American link to market United States securities.
Mr. Fung has not just been working on strengthening ties to the United States market. 
Mr. Fung, who had a money-exchange business in Canton before the Communist takeover and began his China trading ventures in 1978 with his Sun Hung Kai China Ltd., is considered the chief China link in Hong Kong. 
There are no other businessmen quite as well connected with China trade as Mr. Fung or with a company big enough to handle the trade on a large scale.
In Hong Kong, it is felt that although Merrill Lynch was able to get a foothold in Hong Kong, it wanted China trade connections and broader access to Southeast Asian markets. 
Sun Hung Kai China has liaison offices in Peking and Shanghai, and it enters joint undertakings with American and European multinationals mostly in equipment and technology projects.
Mr. Fung, who lives in Hong Kong's exclusive Victoria Peak area, is quiet and unassuming, say people who know him. 
He loves European antiques and has an exceptional memory, but he is most excited by a deal, his associates relate. 
The deal, not the money, interests him. 
He is, some say, embarrassed by his wealth and prefers to ride in a Cadillac than in the Rolls Royce that serves as his company car.
Yet he is not a traditional Chinese businessman. 
His son is in training on the company's board, but Mr. Fung recruits managers from all over the world to run the company while he plans for the future and does his deals. 
He does not get involved much in day-to-day operations, but delegates authority and likes innovation. 
He is considered a gentleman and not vindictive, but most executives here are careful not to offend him - in word or deed - because his business empire is so vast that they will have to deal with him sometime or other.
In style, Merrill Lynch and Sun Hung Kai seem well suited. 
In Hong Kong, Sun Hung Kai was the first to market stocks to the man in the street. 
Stock markets had been exclusive clubs. 
No one offered shares to taxi drivers and hawkers until Sun Hung Kai set up retail brokering operations.
A trial-and-error businessman, Mr. Fung came to Hong Kong after the Communist takeover to take advantage of trade opportunities. 
In one of his earliest efforts, he tried to ship tropical fish to Taiwan. 
But en route he became so seasick that he was unable to keep the oxygen bubbling through the containers holding the fish. 
When he arrived, the fish were dead. 
Undaunted, he loaded the ship with bananas for the return trip, but bad weather delayed it and the bananas rotted.
During the Korean war, he made money selling supplies to Macao. 
When refugees began pouring into Hong Kong from China in the 1950's, Mr. Fung with two partners began a property concern, which prospered until 1967 when riots inspired by the Cultural Revolution soured Hong Kong business. 
He fled to Canada.
After returning to Hong Kong, in 1969 he began building the Sun Hung Kai empire with the formation of Sun Hung Kai Securities and Sun Hung Kai Finance. 
His retail-brokering operations were helped by a credit plan that allowed small investors to finance stock purchases through Sun Hung Kai Finance. 
Most of these investors do not speak English so the firm does stock research in Chinese. 
Because Mr. Fung also does not speak English, he has developed an entire department that translates, interprets and analyzes documents, publications and research in Chinese.
Sun Hung Kai Securities was the first non-banking financial Asian institution to enter the Eurobond market, and with Marsh & McLennan, it began an insurance brokering and consulting business. 
Last year it established a joint venture with West Germany's A.E.G.-Telefunken to set up a link between China, Germany and Hong Kong. 
''Mr. Fung makes wonderful deals,'' said David K.P. 
Li, manager of the Bank of East Asia. 
''He's a natural.''

text:

In preparing for the visit of Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. to China next week, the Reagan Administration is moving toward decisions that will give more of a military cast to Chinese-American relations.
Specifically, according to American officials, there is strong pressure to remove China from the list of Communist countries subject to special export controls. 
This would allow for the transfer of military technology such as the engine and electrical equipment from the new F-16 fighter plane and for the sale of TOW antitank missiles.
Â 
Common Anti-Soviet Front Sought
A number of officials see this as a way of strengthening a common anti-Soviet front, but some also see the prospective offer as an effort to induce Peking to accept the sale of an advanced type of fighter plane to Taiwan.
Military aid for China considered as Haig prepares to visit Peking
It is the prospect of this sale to Taiwan, and the concern that ''Taiwan not be allowed to get in the way of the Chinese-American strategic consensus against Moscow,'' as one Chinese diplomat put it, that has activated Chinese lobbying.
Ambassador Chai Zemin held two dinners last week for Reagan aides and State Department officials. 
While circumspect in these talks, the Chinese said they were concerned that the pro-Taiwan lobby in the Republican Party would succeed in turning the clock back in the relationship between the United States and China and that selling the FX fighter to Taiwan would damage relations most of all.
The National Security Council met today in the White House to consider whether the Chinese were bluffing, what negative reactions might be expected from Moscow and Tokyo and what could be done for Taiwan to keep the Republican right wing happy. 
The council also intended to work out the objectives of the Haig mission.
Officials said earlier that no specific decisions on sales of military equipment would be made, but that there was a consensus to transfer more arms and technology to both China and Taiwan. 
The major decision on China is expected to come in proposed visits by Defense Secretary Caspar W. Weinberger to China or by Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang to the United States.
In interviews, American officials have discussed these elements:
- Government experts are still reacting to a remark by a visiting Chinese military delegation last year that China wants the same kind of security relationship with the United States that Egypt has. 
In the absence of a more specific Chinese explanation, the Americans have taken this to mean the desire for military credits and the F-16 plane. 
The Chinese have long held the public position that they do not want an explicit security relationship with any country.
- Pentagon officers, reversing their judgment, have concluded that Taiwan does not need the advanced FX fighter, which is still on the drawing boards. 
The officers have come around to the view that China does not pose a major threat to Taiwan and that China is more important to the United States than Taiwan. 
But the officers do not want to make this judgment public for fear of a fight with conservatives.
- Chinese diplomats are stressing their policy of seeking an ''evolutionary'' reunification, which they say would leave Taiwan ''autonomous'' with its own government, armed forces and economy and possibly give its ruling Nationalist Party a role in Peking.
Â 
Key Issue Is Export Controls
The major specific issue for the White House meeting today was to be the largely symbolic, but important question of the export control category in which China should be placed.
It could continue to be treated in the same category as the Soviet Union, meaning restrictions on exports of materials with potential military applications. 
It could be put a special category with Yugoslavia, in which exemptions can be made for items of a military use. 
Or it could be placed in the general category with Britain and India, with virtually no restrictions.
In any event, when it comes to exports of potential military items, the Commerce Department makes the decision case by case, regardless of the category.
There is virtually total agreement in the Government that China should not be treated the same way as the Soviet Union. 
A typical statement, from the State Department, was: ''It is nonsense to treat China like an unfriendly state like Russia and be prepared, in principle, to sell anything to a state like India which buys arms from and has a friendship treaty with Moscow.''
Â 
Only Nonlethal Equipment Allowed
A related decision is what to do about China's standing on the munitions control list, or list of actual weapons, which is administered by the State Department. 
As of now, China is restricted to nonlethal equipment such as trucks and radios.
If the United States were to go ahead and actually sell arms and transfer the technology to build weapons, the most likely candidate seems to be the antitank missile. 
The Chinese prefer buying the technology and producing the weapons more cheaply themselves.
As an economy measure, for example, they are understood to seek only the engine and the electrical equipment of the F-16 so that thay can install these components in a plane they would design themselves. 
But in the case of the antitank missiles, they have told the United States that they need them now and that it would take too long to produce their own.
In the meantime, the Chinese have made clear that they want the Haig visit to be a success, and that they regard him as the one in the Administration who best understands their situation. 
Administration officials say the Chinese have been the ones pushing for the visit, urging that it take place soon, and saying that unless policies are satisfactorily clarified soon, there could be retrogression in the relationship.

text:
ï»¿
There once was an extraordinary monkey who could be found only in the opera until he came to America and scampered about in a circus, which is something he would never do back where he came from.
If the story is to be told properly, the ''once was'' should be changed to the present tense, because this is happening now under a big tent at Lincoln Center where, through Jan. 
9, the Big Apple Circus is bringing a taste of the Far East to Manhattan's far West Side. 
It is a story about a Chinese clown in the guise of China's legendary Monkey King who is having the time of his life in a role he has studied for 30 years and will probably never repeat when he goes home.
The Monkey King has been a favorite of Chinese readers and operagoers for nearly 500 years. 
He is the hero, in his own mischievous way, of the entertaining novel ''A Record of a Journey to the West,'' based, in a manner barely more than coincidental, on an actual pilgrimage by a monk to India, home of Buddhism. 
In the novel, the adventurer is the Monkey King, a formidable and impish simian endowed with extraordinary powers. 
He can, in one leap, vault thousands of miles. 
He can chew up one of his own hairs and spit it out in the shape of an army of monkeys.
Buddha assigns him to bring back some scriptures from India, and the journey is marked by fabulous contretemps, all of them characterized by the Monkey King's irrepressible urge to be a prankster. 
His story has become a staple of Chinese opera, which incorporates acrobatics and clowning in a way that might bring confusion to devotees of the Metropolitan Opera.
The fact that the Monkey King is capering about under the Big Apple's big top, next to the Metropolitan Opera House, may also cause some consternation among devotees of the Beijing Opera. 
In China, the Monkey King has never appeared in a circus, only in opera. 
By further coincidence, almost fictional in itself, it was an appearance by the Monkey King in a program by the Beijing Opera at the Met more than half a dozen years ago that helped spark the world debut in the part at this year's Big Apple Circus by Yang Xiao Di, master acrobat and clown of the Nanjing Acrobatic Troupe.
This company of 25 performers is a main element in ''The Big Apple Circus Meets the Monkey King.''
Its members spin plates with a skill that puts to shame the most dexterous hash-slinger. 
They ride a bicycle en masse in numbers that make rush-hour subway cars seem empty. 
Mr. Yang has been made the centerpiece as a Monkey King who serves both as performer and as something of a master of ceremonies.
To the Chinese all this is more revolutionary than it may sound to a jaded American audience accustomed to having characters and performers appearing outside the roles they are associated with. 
In China, where tradition persists somehow through the most tumultuous of changes, one might easily believe that employment of a Monkey King in a circus is the sort of thing only an American would dream of.
''When I told the Chinese I wanted a troupe and a Monkey King, there was a sort of shock and surprise,'' said Paul Binder, founder and director of the Big Apple Circus. 
''Then Xu Shu Er, the Minister of Culture and an actress herself, said, 'I don't see why not.'
That informed everyone that that nut from New York was preparing something different.''
For Mr. Binder, this was a major step in his effort to stage an unusual show that would be particularly meaningful on both sides of the International Dateline. 
''I wanted to do a collaborative show, one in which we could question differences between two cultures,'' he said, explaining that he had wanted to do it ever since he saw a performance by an acrobatic troupe from Shenyang on television in Washington in 1962.
In the summer of 1986, he went to China as a guest of the Government and was shown nine troupes, eight of them first rate and the other presented to let him know that the balance sheet on acrobatics was not entirely one-sided.
''The Chinese had honed in on the Nanjing troupe, and I felt that this one had a youth and energy about it, a sense that the troupe really wanted to do this job,'' he recalled.
The Chinese selected Mr. Yang to be the Monkey King from members of the Nanjing company. 
''When we met him in Nanjing, we knew within 10 minutes that we spoke the same language of presentation and entertainment,'' Mr. Binder said.
Mr. Yang, who passed his 43d birthday in New York last month, was born in Shanghai. 
''When I was a child, I started learning acrobatics from a famous teacher, Pan Ying, who had many students,'' he said. 
''Pan Ying trained people for acrobatic troupes and for the opera. 
My father, who was a chef, wanted me to concentrate on the opera but I liked doing the funny parts.
''So, by accident, I studied the acrobatics. 
I performed on the teeterboard and the swing, learned martial arts, juggling tridents and learned walking on a rolling globe. 
My teacher often explained Beijing Opera to the students. 
This is the first time I play the Monkey King.''
Mr. Binder interpolated: ''They told me he had studied the part for 30 years. 
I was leery. 
I saw more acrobatics than I wanted in the role. 
I kept saying I was concerned about the delicacy of gesture. 
He didn't worry. 
He kept saying he understood the difference between Chinese and Western clowning. 
Don't worry.''
Mr. Binder did worry. 
''I wanted him more accessible to American audiences. 
In Beijing opera, the Monkey King is more soberly colored as befits a black sheep of a monkey. 
The character is more complex.''
At Lincoln Center Mr. Yang appears in a saffron suit, wearing a leopard apron, red kerchief, dark tie and yellow headgear. 
His Monkey King face is elaborately and loudly yellow with a heart-shaped motif in red that surrounds his eyes and converges below the mouth. 
His nimbleness comes in a mischievous package that seems even more charming because he is 5 feet 2 inches tall.
Mr. Yang explained why he is especially happy about his temporary reign on the Monkey King throne, which will end after the Big Apple Circus's tour of the Northeast planned for late this spring.
''When I return, I will not keep the Monkey King role,'' he said. 
''I will return as a face in the crowd and there will be no problem,'' Mr. Yang said, adding, as though to be sure no one could construe modesty and dedication to ensemble work as prideless humility, ''Even before I did this, I have been quite well known in China. 
I am also a director of the troupe and I train newcomers. 
You might say that, even in China, I am a famous clown.''

To Carl Guardino, owner of the Sea King Sea Food Market here, the problem of East-West trade barriers is no longer simply the stuff of international summits.
Mr. Gzardino has taken a decidedly microeconomic approach to the issue: to sell seafood to his increasingly Oriental clientele, he has posted the Japanese names of all the fish he stocks.
''I can also say, 'Thank you very much' in Japanese and 'What else do you want?'
'' Mr. Guardino said.
To Sara Small's third-grade class, the Far East does not seem too exotic anymore. 
Among the 18 students in the class at the Greenvale Elementary School in Eastchester, two are from Korea, five from Japan, one from China and another from Thailand.
Although their numbers are small, Asians are the fastest-growing group in the suburbs of New York City, according to planning officials in Westchester, northern New Jersey and Long Island. 
In several counties, they are also the racial group with the highest average income and the highest average level of education.
Planning officials say the growing Asian population is concentrated in some of the most affluent communities in the suburbs, including Great Neck, L.I., Fort Lee, N.J., and Scarsdale in West-chester. 
These communities are also known for the quality of their schools, something that is a high priority among Asian residents.
''Most of my customers ask me first thing, 'How about the school?'
'' said Han Chung, a Korean-American real-estate agent who works in Scarsdale. 
''As far as Koreans are concerned, the first thing is schools.''
Sociologists say the influx of Asian-Americans into New York City's more affluent suburbs is, to a large extent, simply a result of increased immigration. 
They point out that between 1970 and 1980, Asian immigration to this country increased dramatically as a result of liberalized quotas. 
#10-Year Growth Rate: 200% While the Asian population in New York City roughly doubled during the 1970's, according to United States Census data, in the suburbs it tripled.
A recent report by the Westchester County Department of Planning shows that during the 1970's, the county's Asian population increased by 200 percent, to more than 15,000. 
A similar jump was recorded during the same decade in both Suffolk and Nassau Counties. 
No more recent data are available, but many local officials say the trend is continuing.
In Bergen County, where the Asian population more than tripled during the 1970's, planning officials say they expect the growth rate to remain high through the 1980's. 
''I think it may be even faster,'' said Jim Hulsizer, supervising planner for the Bergen County Planning Board.
Many of the Asians living in the suburbs are temporary residents, such as Japanese business executives and their families, who will return after a three- or four-year stint here.
In Hartsdale, where Japanese executives for many years have brought their families, there is now a Japanese hair salon complete with Japanese editions of Cosmopolitan magazine. 
The late-night commuter train to town ''we call 'the Orient Express,' because there are so many Japanese fathers on it,'' said Mikiko Taga, a Japanese journalist who lives in Scarsdale.
Much of the growth is also due to the increasing affluence of Asian-Americans who, in a pattern well established by other immigrant groups, seek to escape the crowded city.

The acting Chinese party leader, Zhao Ziyang, said today China must intensify the restructuring of its economy along Western lines if it is to escape poverty.

He also declared that Government offices needed to be completely overhauled and called for the creation of a civil service system.
''We must be soberly aware that we still face a great many problems and difficulties, many more than we anticipated,'' Mr. Zhao told the 1,936-member congress. 
''There are not a few failings in our work of leadership.''
Mr. Zhao's speech marked the first party congress China has held in five years. 
Leaders who have gathered from around the country will spend the next week discussing and approving plans for the Government and the economy, which has already undergone the biggest changes in any Communist nation.
Before adjourning, the congress will also elect a new Central Committee, which in turn will name members of the new Politburo that will rule China.
It was the first time that the party, which was founded in secrecy in Shanghai in 1921, has opened its congress to foreign reporters. 
As copies of Mr. Zhao's address were handed out in six languages, spokesmen said China was permitting foreign reporters to attend as part of its efforts to become more open to the world.
The congress started this morning with Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, striding into the auditorium of the Great Hall of the People to applause from the delegates. 
He was followed onto the dais by the rest of the leadership, including the former party chief, Hu Yaobang, who was removed in disgrace in January after a tide of nationwide student protests. 
Mr. Deng, who looked tan and fit, was praised by Mr. Zhao for ''his courage in developing Marxist theory'' and ''his foresight and sagacity.''
For two and a half hours, Mr. Zhao read his 32,000-word report to the congress, sitting and pausing to sip tea from a white ceramic cup. 
As he spoke, some delegates appeared to nod off. 
Chen Yun, an 82-year-old member of the Politburo's standing committee, left the dais supported by two nurses in the middle of the speech.
While reaffirming the nation's adherence to socialism, Mr. Zhao said China would accelerate the introduction of many economic and financial methods integral to Western capitalist economies.
''Some of the things we have introduced in the process of reform such as expanded markets for means of production, funds, technology and labor service and the issuance of stocks and bonds are phenomena which are not peculiar to capitalism,'' he said. 
''Socialism can and should make use of them, trying in the meantime to minimize their negative effects in practice.''
The 68-year-old Prime Minister also called for a thorough reordering of China's pricing system, so that market forces would regulate supply and demand.
Whenever Mr. Zhao or his supporters discussed the need for pricing changes over the last year, party hard-liners blocked his proposals by labeling them capitalist. 
The opponents object to having market forces govern the decisions of industrial managers, a traditional role of state planners. 
Today, Mr. Zhao appeared to have imposed his position on the party.
''We should gradually establish a system under which the state sets the prices of a few vital commodities and labor services while leaving the rest to be regulated by the market,'' he said.
While the state should have a role in industrial policy, he said, other mechanisms besides free prices, like taxes, bank credit and other new financing arrangments, would also influence industrialization.

To Maintain Private Sector

A growing class of private entrepreneurs has emerged in both urban and rural areas. 
Orthodox Marxists in the leadership have voiced opposition to the growth of individual private enterprise because of its unabashed capitalist nature.
''Practice has proved that a certain degree of development of the private sector promotes production, stimulates the market, provides employment opportunities and helps in many ways to meet people's needs,'' Mr. Zhao told his fellow Communists. 
''It is thus a necessary and useful supplement to the public sector.''
Mr. Zhao spoke repeatedly and with unusual bluntness of problems of leadership, corruption in the party and a bureacratic style in Government.

Resistance to economic restructuring has been most pronounced among the party organizations that oversee many industries and rural areas.

He said a state administrative college would be established.

Mr. Zhao concluded his address by attacking widespread imperiousness and corruption in the party, which he said meant that ''members of a party in power tend to become divorced from the masses.''

China's foremost movie studio director has publicly assailed a senior Communist official for interference in the work of the Xian Film Studio and the arts.
The director, Wu Tianming, who has become the patron of China's tiny young generation of innovative filmmakers, denounced Mao Shengxian, the head of the propaganda department of the party in Shaanxi province, as a bureaucrat driven to control the political content of China's best movies.
''He is a typical bureaucrat,'' Mr. Wu said in an interview here. 
''He doesn't understand films but he wants to control film making. 
He's a bureaucrat who is influenced by leftist thinking. 
He is a conservative and ossified thinker.''
It is virtually unheard of for a well-known Chinese artist or intellectual to criticize an official in the Communist party to a Western reporter. 
Last year, for instance, when several prominent intellectuals were expelled from the party for supposedly advocating the spread of Western values, none of them spoke out against the party officials who had had them removed.

Over the last year, many of China's artists have expressed their despair over the policies of Communist Party officials toward the arts, which became more stringent after last winter's pro-democracy student protests. 
Painters have been deprived exhibition space, movies have been kept in their canisters and publishers have refused to print novels and works of poetry.
Mr. Wu's comments, the first by a prominent Chinese artist to attack a party official directly, appear to reflect a growing confidence among some artists that they have the prestige and support of at least some leaders in Beijing to speak out.
Named director of the Xian Film Studio in October 1983, Mr. Wu in October won the grand prize at the second Tokyo International Film Festival for his film ''The Old Well.''
As studio head, he has shepherded virtually every politically controversial and avant garde Chinese film into production in the last four years and has supported and protected young directors who have sought to go beyond the bounds of conventional propagandistic movie making.
But last winter, after Liu Binyan, a nationally known investigative reporter for People's Daily, was expelled from the party, Mr. Wu said his troubles with the propaganda bureau of the Shaanxi province Communist Party began.

''For a long time I have had contradictions with the propaganda department of the provincial party.

''But I opposed him,'' Mr. Wu continued. 
''He actually has no qualifications to be a leader in the arts.''
Â 
Almost Complete Control
The provincial propaganda bureaus are charged with overseeing cultural and publishing activities in their respective provinces in addition to their activities in publicizing decisions made by the central leadership. 
As part of their work, officials, or as they are called here, cadres, are sent to fill posts in universities, news organizations, film studios and official art groups where they often exercise almost complete control over the substance of these groups' work.
Mr. Wu said the Shaanxi propaganda bureau, at Mr. Mao's direction, had sent three groups of officials to review the work of the studio. 
The first of the investigation teams, Mr. Wu said, appeared last winter, stayed for one month and issued a report stating that Mr. Wu was ''without selfishness.''
