'To Check on Our Finances'
''In July, he sent another group of people to check on our finances,'' he said.

The use of the word ''reform,'' a broad term referring to the modernization efforts pushed by the country's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, and the party leader, Zhao Ziyang, is often used by Chinese managers and intellectuals to describe the process of draining away purely political criteria in decision making.

Mr. Nakasone touched off unexpectedly harsh denunciations in Peking when he made an official visit to the Yasukuni Shrine on Aug. 
15, the anniversary of Japan's surrender in World War II.
China's official press agency said a week later that the Prime Minister's action had ''pandered'' to Japanese who wanted to deny their country's guilt for World War II. 
Last month, students marched through Tian An Men Sqare in Peking, chanting ''Down with Nakasone'' and other anti-Japanese slogans in one of the biggest protest demonstrations there in years.
Japanese newspapers reported today that Mr. Nakasone hoped to avoid prolonging the controversy by calling off another visit to Yasukuni scheduled during a fall festival at the shrine next week. 
His intention was said to have been relayed Tuesday night to members of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party by Takao Fujinami, the chief Cabinet secretary and main Government spokesman.
Â 
Shadow of the War
The controversy, although rooted wholly in symbolism, demonstrates the extent to which Japan's wartime aggression shadows its latter-day foreign relations. 
Other Asian countries continue to look warily for possible signs of revived Japanese militarism, and Tokyo reacts with open edginess every time the issue arises.
Officials here are especially uneasy when the complaints come from China, to which Japan owes much of its cultural heritage.
The Yasukuni Shrine, near the Imperial Palace grounds, honors the spirits of nearly 2.5 million Japanese soldiers who gave their lives for their country in the last century. 
Among those whose souls rest there, however, are convicted war criminals like Japan's Prime Minister in the early 1940's, Hideki Tojo.
In current political debate, officials who go to Yasukuni tend to find themselves accused as militarists by anti-Government critics.
For years, governing-party politicians sought to deflect such charges by insisting that their visits were made as private citizens. 
But Mr. Nakasone, an ardent nationalist, added considerable fuel to the dispute on the Aug. 
15 anniversary by becoming the first postwar Prime Minister to state that he had gone in his official capacity.
Â 
'Thought It Only Natural'
''I thought it only natural to pay homage to those who fought for their country and fell in the war,'' he said early this week in an appearance before Tokyo-based foreign journalists.
Mr. Nakasone, 67 years old, was in the Japanese Navy in World War II. 
He saw little combat, serving mostly as a payroll officer, but his experiences and Japan's crushing defeat helped shape many of his nationalistic views.
On the visit to the shrine, however, he apparently underestimated the depth of feeling in China, which puts its war dead at more than 20 million. 
The sensitivity resembled that shown three years ago when China denounced what it said were distortions in Japanese textbook accounts of Japan's wartime occupation of Manchuria.
For Mr. Nakasone, the criticism may have been especially troubling because he prides himself on having presided during a period of uncommonly cordial relations between the two countries.
This warmth has recently been undermined, however, by a growing trade imbalance heavily in Japan's favor. 
China's trade deficit with Japan was $1.2 billion in 1984, a figure that soared to $4 billion in just the first eight months of this year.
The students who demonstrated in Peking last month attacked not only Mr. Nakasone but also Japan's growing commercial presence, shouting, ''Down with the second occupation!''
The twin issues of trade and charges of a revival of militarism are likely to arise in talks that Japan's Foreign Minister, Shintaro Abe, will hold with China's leaders starting Thursday.

text:

THE Chinese film ''Wild Mountains'' takes place in a rustic paradise fraught with problems that might be found anywhere: troubles about money, ambition, get-rich-quick schemes, idle gossip and marital discord. 
It concerns two married couples, the younger of them separated. 
Hehe (Du Yuan) has come to live with his brother Huihui (Xin Ming) and sister-in-law in a hut that is within clear view of the place where his beautiful wife Quirong (Xu Shouli) lives with their baby. 
Hehe and Quirong have quarreled about his dissatisfaction with simple peasant life and his eagerness to see the wider world.
For all its emphasis on crude simplicity, ''Wild Mountains'' seems conceived as a commercial entertainment, and an enjoyable one at that. 
The hard, chore-filled life of these peasants is presented with a glowing romanticism. 
And even at the end of each exhausting day, the characters retain their cheerfulness and good humor. 
The film's homespun humor (''Filthy!
We could grow crops on you!'') is delivered with a certain urbanity, by actors who seem markedly more sophisticated than the characters they play. 
None of this diminishes the film's rueful intelligence or its picturesque charm.
In ''Wild Mountains,'' which was directed by Yan Xueshu, the scenery is the real star. 
The camera often takes time out to roam the landscape, which is quite spectacular. 
And the beauties of nature are celebrated at every turn, as is the work ethic. 
Quirong labors long and hard with her little son strapped onto her back, an arrangement that must be made doubly taxing by the baby's diaperless apparel. 
Guilan, Huihui's childless wife, cares for barnyard animals and teases her husband about the pigpen, which is the closest thing to an outhouse that the family has. 
Hehe argues with his brother about the peasant's lot and helps to dream up moneymaking ideas, the loveliest of which involves silkworms. 
Perhaps the worst plan, which is Hehe's alone, is to raise a passel of flying squirrels, on the theory that their droppings have medicinal value.
''Wild Mountains'' eventually takes Hehe and Guilan on a trip to a small city, where they marvel at the souvenirs, the television and the other signs of modern civilization. 
This way of life impinges only indirectly on their mountain existence, but it signals a dissatisfaction that has far-reaching effects for all four principals. 
''Wild Mountains,'' acted in a hearty, life-affirming spirit that suits the direction, demonstrates considerable wisdom in presenting a discontent that could turn up anywhere, and the forces that may set it in motion.

text:

Growing numbers of Vietnamese have been arriving in Hong Kong by boat in the past few months, crowding into refugee camps with thousands of other Vietnamese, most of whom have only a slim chance of finding new homes outside the chain-link fences of the bleak compounds.
So far this year, more than 1,500 Vietnamese refugees, most of them poor farmers and fishermen from north Vietnam, have landed in Hong Kong, four times the number of arrivals during the same period last year, according to Govennment figures.
Waves of refugees have been arriving in Thailand and Malaysia as well, and the Thai authorities have pushed some boats back out to sea.
Hong Kong has so far resisted such an extreme measure, but a recent newspaper survey revealed that 65 percent of those polled here want any new refugee boats turned away. 
And the Governor of this British colony, Sir David Wilson, said last week that Hong Kong is reconsidering its policy of allowing all boat people to land.
'Compassion Fatigue'
The Governor said resettlement countries are experiencing ''compassion fatigue,'' and are simply not prepared to accept all the boat people Hong Kong is sheltering.
Relief officials said people have been fleeing Vietnam in greater numbers this year because the country's economy is near collapse, and crop failures threaten famine in some areas.
The new swell of immigrants has left Hong Kong with a total of 10,400 Vietnamese refugees - a Vietnamese refugee population second only to that of Thailand, according to Nigel J. French, the Hong Kong Government official in charge of refugee policy.
Refugees sail north to Hong Kong from the northern Vietnamese port of Haiphong, a 500-mile journey through the South China Sea that takes about 15 days with good luck and fair weather. 
Refugees from the north, Mr. French said, are poor people with few skills, no foreign languages and no ties to countries outside Vietnam.
''More and more we have the men, women and children nobody else wants,'' Mr. French said.
Â 
Barracks-Like Buildings
A teacher at a closed camp on Hei Ling Chau, a tiny rocky island that was once the site of a leper colony, said there are children there who had never seen a dog or walked on grass.
Hei Ling Chau is about an hour's boat ride from central Hong Kong, and a recent visitor was asked to send picture postcards of the city because most of the refugees had only caught a glimpse of it as they landed.
The camp's barracks-like cinder-block buildings house 2,900 people in spaces meant for 2,400. 
Two meals a day and a snack are served and there is one toilet for every 90 people.
''We try to take the children on field trips, to see what real life looks like,'' said Nilda Bernardo, a teacher with World Relief, which runs programs in Hei Ling Chau.
''Sometimes we take them into a flat there so they can see what a kitchen and a living room and a bedroom look like,'' she said.
Christopher Bale, the director of the Oxfam relief agency in Hong Kong, said the three closed camps, surrounded by high steel fences and supervised by prison guards, are ''just barely adequate for short-term stays, but there are almost 5,000 people who have been living in these places for three years, and 3,000 who have been in them for more than five years.''
Â 
'No One Has Asked to See Us'
Bao Ntuyen, a 12-year-old from Haiphong, said he had been living in Hei Ling Chau for four years and no resettlement official had ever interviewed him or his uncle, a farmer who has no ties to anyone outside Vietnam.
''No one has asked to see us,'' the boy said, ''so we are learning English. 
We want to go to a free country, somewhere where they play football.''
Hong Kong has had a continuous flow of refugees since 1975, but the numbers had begun to drop, from a high of about 8,500 arrivals in 1981 to only 1,200 in 1985. 
But by 1986 the flow of refugees began to increase once more.
Hong Kong now plans to build a fourth closed camp to handle the increasing numbers of Vietnamese. 
In addition to the closed camps, Hong Kong has one ''open'' camp, where about 3,000 refugees who arrived before mid-1982 may come and go freely and hold jobs in the community.
Â 
Ethnic Chinese Resentment

Critics are seeking to delay a regulation that the Reagan Administration says would improve its ability to monitor imports of textiles and apparel.
The critics claim that the regulation - which the Government issued Aug. 
3 and is to take effect Sept. 
7 - would strand $500 million worth of foreign-made textiles and apparel that American companies have already ordered.
They say that would cause substantial financial difficulties for retailers and other businesses, as well as apparel shortages and price increases of up to 20 percent for consumers. 
It also could cause China to take retaliatory trade measures, they say.
US textile and apparel importers seek delay in Federal regulation--announced on Aug 3 to take effect Sept 7--changing Customs Service's country-of-origin rule as it applies to textile import quotas established through bilateral agreements; say it would strand $500 million worth of foreign-made textiles and apparel that American companies have already ordered and cause substantial financial difficulties for retailers and other businesses, as well as apparel shortage and price increases of up to 20 percent; say China might also retaliate (M)
The proposed measure would change the Customs Service's country-of-origin rule. 
It applies to textile import quotas established through bilateral agreements.
Under current regulations, if parts of a garment are made in one country and shipped to another for assembling and then shipped to the United States, they are counted against the import quotas of the second country.
For example, if sleeves or other parts of sweaters are made in China, but sewn together in Hong Kong, they have been counted against the textile import quotas of Hong Kong rather than China.
The Administration proposal would apply the country-of-origin designation to the country where the fabric originated - in the example above, China rather than Hong Kong. 
That could reduce the amount of Chinese textiles that ultimately find their way into this country, since China has a smaller quota than Hong Kong, which has been trading longer with the United States.
Â 
Varied Group of Opponents
The measure's opponents include retail industry groups, textile importers, agricultural interests and members of Congress who contend that the proposal is ill-conceived and motivated largely by the re-election concerns of the President and two of his Senate allies, Senator Jesse Helms, Republican of North Carolina, and Senator Strom Thurmond, Republican of South Carolina.
But Federal officials, along with some members of Congress and domestic textile manufacturers, offer two reasons for the regulation. 
One is to prevent fraud and evasion of textile quotas established by bilateral trade agreements. 
The other is to protect American textile manufacturers and workers against a burgeoning volume of less-expensive imports.
Although the proposed change would apply to each of the 36 nations with which the United States has bilateral textile trade agreements. it would most sharply affect those in the Far East.
According to Government and industry figures, four countries - Taiwan, Korea, Japan and China - and the colony of Hong Kong together supply nearly 60 percent of the textiles and apparel imported by the United States. 
The proposed regulation would also require inspection of shipments of textile imports at their United States port of entry rather than at their destination.
Rules now allow textile shipments that enter the country through one port but are bound for another location to be sealed, bonded and shipped to their destination before the Customs Service makes its inspection.
Walter C. Lenahan, Deputy Assistant Secretary of Commerce, who directed the Government group that drafted the rule, said Government statistics show that in 1983 the Customs Service seized about $5 million worth of textiles that were imported fraudulently.
By contrast, the estimated value of illegal goods seized so far this year is close to $28 million. 
This year, special textile squads were assigned to the ports of New York and Los Angeles, where 75 percent of the imported textiles enter the country.
The proposed rule was praised by James H. Martin Jr., president of the American Textile Manufacturers Institute. 
Mr. Martin is also vice chairman of Ti-Caro Inc., a Gastonia, N.C., company that manufactures yarn and industrial sewing thread.
''It clarifies the fact that the intent of the bilaterals have been stretched, even to the point of fraud in some instances,'' he said. 
''We're not against imports, but we feel that trade should be orderly, above-board, and fair.''
Â 
Called 'Administrative Overkill'
However, critics such as Sim Gluckson, chairman of the textile and apparel group of the American Association of Exporters and Importers, contend that as a fraud-fighting device, the new policy ''amounts to administrative overkill.''
He said: ''It's a very bad regulation that will be extremely disruptive to the fall and winter retail season.''
Mr. Gluckson, president of a New York-based knitwear company, said that because textiles and apparel are bought six to nine months in advance, the proposed rule would likely mean that shipments already ordered by companies would not arrive in time. 
''Contracts have been signed. 
Letters of credit have gone out, dates of shipment have been arranged,'' he said. 
''And now this. 
It's thrown the whole industry into confusion.''
At least a score of senators and representatives have complained in letters to President Reagan that the regulation ''would suddenly make illegal widespread methods of textile and apparel production which are absolutely legal under present U.S. law and which have been legal for many decades.''
Â 
Concern About China
Others, including Senator Bob Dole, Republican of Kansas, expressed concern that the measure would sour the United States-China trade relationship. 
About 11 percent of the textiles imported by the United States last year came from China.
The official New China News Agency has said that the proposed regulation would ''adversely affect the textile exports of the Chinese mainland for Hong Kong.''
The comments by the news agency have raised concern among agricultural interests that China might limit or ban imports of American grain or other commodities in retaliation.
Last year, China banned purchases of several United States exports, including wheat and cotton, when the two countries could not agree on ceilings for textile and apparel imports.
Finally, several critics assert that the rule change was pushed primarily to help the re-election chances of the Carolinas' Senators and the President's own re-election campaign.
The charges of political motivation were denied by Mr. Lenahan and by Senators Helms and Thurmond.
The textile industry nationwide employs about 2.4 million people, according to the industry, with North Carolina, New York and South Carolina, respectively, the top three states in textile-related employment.

Countries Sign Agreements

The first thing to strike a visitor's eye as he alights from the military plane are two huge signs that proclaim in bold white Chinese characters on a flaming red background, ''Recover the Chinese Mainland'' and ''Destroy the Communists.''
Military transport remains the only way of reaching Quemoy and its sister island, Matsu, because the offshore islands, just a few miles from the mainland, remain fully military areas and are customarily referred to by Nationalist officers as ''the battlefront.''
The last exchanges of gunfire took place 23 years ago, and the Communist gunners stopped their every-other-day barrages of shells loaded with propaganda leaflets in December 1978, a few days before the United States broke diplomatic relations with Taiwan.
Nationalist islands of Quemoy and Matsu continue propaganda warfare with mainland China

Slogans, Music and News
Moreover, both sides still fill the airwaves with propaganda slogans, propaganda music and propaganda news for as much as 20 hours a day.
''We are soldiers and we obey our commanders,'' replied a psychological-warfare officer when asked whether after more than three decades of unceasing propaganda bellowed at the limited audiences on both sides of the Formosa Strait the words and music had not suffered from repetition.

The United States' two members of the International Olympic Committee and a senior State Department official said yesterday that the presence of many allies of North Korea, including the Soviet Union, would serve as a deterrent to the possibility of disruptive actions by North Korea during the Seoul Olympic Games.
North Korea announced yesterday that it would not attend the Games unless it could be co-host of them. 
The deadline for accepting the invitation to the Games is Sunday, and of the 167 countries invited, 153 have accepted, including the Soviet Union.
''The world will be there,'' said one of the members, Anita DeFrantz, an attorney in Los Angeles and a former United States Olympic rower. 
''Over 150 nations have accepted the invitation to the Games. 
With North Korea not there, if anything untoward happens, my sense is people will know where to look. 
I am also confident that the security will work.''
Robert Helmick, the other I.O.C. member and the president of the United States Olympic Committee, said the South Koreans have ''one of the best security systems in the world.''
He also said that United States Government officials monitoring the situation in South Korea have assured him that athletes competing in the Games have no reason to fear.
Â 
'Total International Outcast'
Those views were underscored by Edward J. Derwinski, an Under Secretary of State, who said North Korea would become a ''total international outcast'' by attempting to sabotage the Games or destabilize the region before they start, Sept. 
17.
''Any act of sabotage could accidentally inflict losses on many of their cohorts,'' Derwinski said from Washington, referring to North Korea's allies. 
''Their mere presence almost guarantees safety for everybody.''
Derwinski allowed for the possibility that South Koreans might sense a lingering concern because of questions surrounding the midair explosion of a Korean Airlines jet in late November near the Burma-Thailand border.

But because of the record number of countries planning to attend and their expectation of successful Games, he doubted North Korea would attempt any disruptive action either during the Games or in the eight months preceeding them.

Appeal to North Korea
Meanwhile, yesterday in Seoul, members of the organizing committee appealed to North Korea to reconsider its decision not to attend.

16 presidential elections in South Korea and never resumed.

Cuba Is Exception

file: NORTH KOREANS SAY KIM IL SUNG GREETED VISITORS.txt
text:
ï»¿
North Korea reported today that its leader, Kim Il Sung, greeted a foreign group this morning. 
The report, also carried by the Chinese press agency, was apparently intended to dispel rumors that Mr. Kim had been killed.
But confusion over the fate of the North Korean leader persisted amid reports in South Korea that his Defense Minister had seized power.
The North Korean press agency said Mr. Kim had ''warmly met'' a visiting Mongolian delegation at the airport in Pyongyang and then joined his guests in reviewing a military honor guard. 
Thousands of people were on hand, the report said.
Austrian Says He Saw Kim
United Press International reported that an Austrian trade representative who attended the airport ceremony said that he had seen Mr. Kim and that the North Korean appeared healthy.
U.P.I. also said the North Korean press agency had released a photograph of Mr. Kim shaking hands with the Mongolian leader, Jambyn Batmunh, that was shown on television in Japan.
A spokesman for South Korea's Defense Ministry, Lee Heung Sik, issued a statement this afternoon that acknowledged the reports that Mr. Kim was alive but did not confirm them.
''We are closely watching such North Korean moves,'' Mr. Lee said, ''to determine whether they are a result of serious power struggles that are going on inside the North or represent a sophisticated form of psychological warfare to hide a scheme for military provocation.''
In either case, he said, South Korean armed forces were maintaining ''intensive vigilance against the North.''
Earlier in Seoul, the Government-run Korea Broadcasting Service, quoting South Korean Defense Ministry sources, said North Korean loudspeakers at the border had announced that ''full power'' had been assumed in the North by Defense Minister Oh Jin U. The account was especially confusing because it followed recent reports that Mr. Oh was in a coma after a car accident.
The South Korean service carried the reports of Mr. Kim's presence at the airport as the main item on its noon broadcast, followed by the accounts of the loudspeaker announcements. 
That suggested that greater weight was being placed on the report that Mr. Kim, 74 years old, was still alive.
U.P.I. quoted the Austrian trade representative in North Korea, Wolfgang Entmayer, as saying of Mr. Kim: ''I saw him with my own eyes, and he seemed to be in good health and smiling. 
He was walking on his own, and there was nothing unusual about it.''
U.P.I. said the interview was conducted by telephone from Peking.
Mr. Entmayer said that a military band and honor guard had been present for the arrival of the Mongolian delegation, and that roads leading from the airport to downtown Pyongyang had been lined with ''the usual crowds'' waving flags and cheering. 
''Nothing extraordinary has occurred here that I know of,'' he said. 
''There has been nothing unusual on television or radio.''
On Monday, unconfirmed reports circulated that Mr. Kim had been assassinated or that a power struggle was under way in that Communist nation.
South Korean Government officials and news agencies continued to report Monday night that Mr. Kim may have been shot. 
And the Defense Minister, Lee Ki Baek, told a National Assembly committee that ''serious signs of an emergency in North Korea'' suggested that Mr. Kim had died or that a power struggle was in progress.
But other Government officials and foreign diplomats expressed uncertainty about the reports and said it was premature to draw firm conclusions.
''There are factors pointing to his being dead,'' a Western diplomat said. 
''But the factors pointing to the contrary are more solid.''
Â 
No Word on Kim's Son
Nothing was said about the whereabouts of Mr. Kim's son, Kim Jong Il, 43 years old, whom Mr. Kim has designated as his successor in the last few years. 
The designation of the younger Kim, referred to in the North as the ''Dear Leader,'' created the merchanism for the first dynastic transition in a Communist country.
Mr. Lee, who has been the most outspoken South Korean Government official in discussing the Kim matter, told members of the National Assembly that on Saturday morning the Government received intelligence reports from Japan saying Mr. Kim had been killed by soldiers a day or two earlier. 
These military men defected to China, which has thus far rejected North Korea's demand for their repatriation, he quoted the reports as saying.
In its editions today, The Korea Herald, a Government-controlled English-language daily, reported without elaboration that a story was circulating that Mr. Kim had been shot on a train. 
Other accounts said he had died in a car accident.
Â 
'A Severe Power Struggle'
''Judging from information gathered from various sources, North Korea is suffering from a severe internal power struggle,'' Mr. Lee said.
Mr. Kim has ruled North Korea since it was formed in 1948 after the postwar division of the Korean Peninsula.
To North Koreans, he is known as the ''Great Leader,'' and his image is ubiquitous, on everything from statues to lapel pins.
Mr. Lee repeated earlier assertions that North Korean loudspeakers along ''front-line areas'' of the Korean demilitarized zone announced Mr. Kim's assassination on Sunday. 
He said some loudspeakers had announced, ''Let's embrace the Dear Leader Kim Jong Il as leader of the nation.''
At some points along the DMZ, North Korean flags were flown at half-staff and funeral music was played, he asserted, and a portrait of Mr. Kim decorated with white flowers was seen.
Â 
Says It May Be a Ploy
The Defense Minister also said he could not rule out the possibility that the ''loudspeaker blasting may be part of North Korean psychological warfare against the South.''
In Tokyo, the Japanese news agency Kyodo reported that a senior official in Hanoi had said Vietnamese representatives in Pyongyang were saying that Mr. Kim had died.
There was countervailing evidence, however, culminating in the reports that Mr. Kim had met the delegation from Mongolia.
United States military officials said American soldiers at the truce village of Panmunjom in the DMZ had reported no unusual activity on the northern side of the border. 
North Korean flags were flying at full staff today, and North Korean guards at Panmunjom behaved normally, they said. 
According to Bill Fullerton, a civilian spokesman for the United States Eighth Army in Seoul, regular busloads of tourists visited the DMZ today.
''As far as our soldiers can tell, everything was the way it was before,'' Mr. Fullerton said. 
He and other officials acknowledged, however, that American troops patrol an area that is only about a mile long -a fraction of the 151-mile-long border. 
It was possible, they said, that the loudspeaker broadcasts had occurred out of earshot of the Americans.
Â 
'Honestly, Truly Don't Know'
One foreign diplomat said an American intelligence officer monitoring the Pyongyang radio from Seoul on Sunday morning heard an announcement that Kim Il Sung was dead. 
This was followed by funereal music, he said. 
But this report was not repeated, the diplomat added, and since then broadcasts have been routine.
''We honestly, truly don't know what has happened,'' he said.
North Korean diplomats in Peking and New Delhi strongly denied the death reports and accused South Korea of inventing them. 
''The South Korean side always spreads such fabrications,'' the North Korean Embassy in Peking said.
There were few signs on Seoul streets that anything unusual had occurred, let alone something that could have huge importance for South Korea as well as the North.
The national police were put on special alert, and busloads of officers filled some downtown streets. 
But the police presence is normally thick and has been especially so in recent weeks after large anti-Government demonstrations.
South Korea's armed forces were said to be kept to a normal state of readiness, as were the 40,000 United States soldiers stationed here.
Â 
North's Borders Tightly Sealed
Determining political developments in North Korea is extremely difficult because that country has tightly sealed its borders, revealing little of itself to outsiders, even Communist countries.
There have been periodic reports in recent months of unhappiness among North Korean military officers with the Kims' plans to transfer power from father to son, and several political analysts in Seoul said today that the displeasure might have spilled over. 
Close allies of Pyongyang, notably the Soviet Union and China, have also hinted at dissatisfaction with the transition plan.
Another possibility, the political analysts said, was that certain officers had disapproved of Kim Il Sung's recent tilting toward Moscow in the balance that his country traditionally has sought to achieve between the Soviet Union and China. 
The North Korean leader made a visit to Moscow late last month, an unusual trip in that he made the journey by plane. 
Mr. Kim is known to have a strong aversion to flying and in the past had traveled the nearly 4,000 miles from Pyongyang to Moscow by train.
The two Koreas share one of the world's most heavily fortified borders, and, unlike the two Germanys, they are implacable enemies. 
In the South, Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il are depicted as almost demonic personalities, and their pictures are rarely seen.
Several political analysts said the developments in the North could also affect South Korean politics. 
The Government of President Chun Doo Hwan has begun a crackdown on dissidents, and the possibility of unrest north of the DMZ may make the political opposition think twice before further challenging the Government's authority.
Â 
North Korea At A Glance
Â 
Government
Â Â In the four decades since he was installed by the Soviet forces that took over from occupying Japanese, Kim Il Sung has been the absolute ruler of North Korea, running the country almost like a personal fiefdom. 
The national ideology, while officially Communist, is primarily based on the glorification of Mr. Kim's thinking. 
In recent years Mr. Kim has elevated his son, Kim Jong Il, to a position of almost equal influence and has named the son to be his successor.
Â 
History
Â Â Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and retined control until the end of World War II. 
Korean customs and nationalism were brutally suppressed. 
The Cairo Declaration of 1943 called for a free and independent Korea after the war, but Stalin accepted a 1945 American plan for two military zones to be established after the Japanese surrender, divided along the 38th Parallel. 
Free elections were to be held.
After the Japanese surrender, political exiles came home. 
In the South, Syngman Rhee returned from the United States; in the North, the anti-Japanese resistance leader, Kim Il Sung, returned from the Soviet Union.
With Soviet backing, Mr. Kim was named head of the new Government of the North, which was proclaimed the Democratic People's Republic of Korea in September 1948. 
Mr. Rhee became the first leader in the South, which had been founded a month earlier. 
American forces were pulled out of the South in June 1949.
Â 
The Korean War
Â Â The Korean War began on June 25, 1950, when North Korean forces invaded the South. 
Seoul, the South Korean capital, was captured after four days. 
United States troops returned, at the request of Seoul, at the end of June. 
Responding to a United Nations call, 16 other nations sent military contingents to the defense of the South.
In October 1950, the North Korean capital was captured, and in November, the allies reached the Yalu River on the Chinese border. 
Peking had committed troops to the fighting in October, and they were able to push the South Korean and United Nations forces back to approximately the 38th parallel.
Fighting continued back and forth until an armistice was signed at Panmunjom in July 1953.
Â 
Military Strength
Â Â Counting all branches, North Korea has approximately 785,000 troops, according to the International Institute for Strategic Studies. 
By comparison, South Korea has 622,000 troops. 
United States forces in South Korea number approximately 40,000.
Â 
Geography and People
Â Â North Korea has a population of about 20 million, about half that of South Korea. 
Its area is 46,540 square miles, somewhat larger than the South and about the size of New York State.
Â 
Resources
Â Â Seventy percent of the mountainous Korean Peninsula is forested, and most of the best timber is in the North. 
Iron ore and coal deposits are concentrated in the North. 
Rice and corn are the major crops, and extensive efforts have been made to reclaim land for agriculture.

file: NUCLEAR ALARM STIRS HONG KONG ACTIVISM.txt
text:
ï»¿
A NUCLEAR plant under construction in China just 30 miles from Hong Kong is generating enormous heat in this crowded British territory. 
The project, which is not scheduled for completion until 1992, has already aroused a political typhoon and caused tension between Hong Kong and its vast neighbor to the north.
No one in Hong Kong paid much attention to China's proposal to build the nuclear plant at Daya Bay when it was first discussed early in this decade. 
But in the last several months, after the accident in April at the Chernobyl plant in the Soviet Union, Hong Kong residents have been distressed at the prospect of such a facility on their doorstep.
Perhaps even more fundamentally, the situation raised new doubts about whether China can be trusted after it absorbs Hong Kong in 1997. 
If China does not heed the British colony's wishes now, some say, why should it pay attention to such concerns after the territory becomes a part of the motherland?
A Chinese official in Hong Kong grimaced at that logic. 
''A lot of resources already have been committed to the project,'' he said. 
''China says, 'Why should we give it up because of a lot of people who don't know about nuclear power?'
It's a very difficult situation for China.''
Of course, Hong Kong has been gripped by political events in the past. 
In the late 1960's the colony was shaken by riots sponsored by admirers of Mao Zedong, the late Chinese leader. 
But Daya Bay marked the first time that many Hong Kong residents had signed a petition or taken a controversial stand.
The Hong Kong Government, led by a British-appointed governor, is also in an awkward position. 
At first it refused to release a 1984 study it commissioned to examine the Daya Bay proposal. 
Later the Government backed down and released part of that report. 
This unusual concession to public opinion hurt the antinuclear campaign; the report strongly favored the plant.
''A lot of people think if they can't get the plumbing right in Peking, how can they get nuclear power right,'' said Peter B. Harris, chairman of the political science department at Hong Kong University. 
Like many others, he believes that concern over the Daya Bay plant has forced Hong Kong for almost the first time to take a substantial interest in politics. 
Normally apathetic Hong Kong residents have rallied against the project, and 20 percent of the territory's 5.5 million residents have signed a petition objecting to it.
''The middle class woke up,'' explained Albert W.Y. 
Chan, a social worker and politician. 
Mr. Chan says that Daya Bay has for the first time created a political system based on mass participation, not small interest groups.
Professor Harris agrees: ''There are signs that a political consciousness is beginning to emerge for the first time. 
In politics, you've taken the cork out of the bottle, and you won't be able to put it back again.''
Â 
British Engines
''Hong Kong people are quite reluctant to take a stance, especially on a political issue,'' explained the Rev. Fung Chi-Wood, a 30-year-old Anglican who is leading the campaign against the Daya Bay plant.
Despite the protests and opinion polls showing that most Hong Kong residents favor a halt or delay in the construction of the plant, neither Hong Kong's Government nor Britain's seems to have done anything to dissuade China. 
Indeed, some Hong Kong residents charge that Britain has accepted the risk to Hong Kong because a British company will supply turbines for the $28-billion plant.
Pushed into a defensive alliance, Britain, China and Hong Kong all assert that the plant will be safe, that it is sufficiently far from Hong Kong and that it will be the cheapest source of power. 
Southern China is desperately short of electricity, to the point that industrial growth must be curtailed, and Hong Kong is expected to face a shortage in the next decade. 
While 70 percent of Daya Bay's output will be sold to a Hong Kong utility, some will be left to ease the shortage in the area around Canton, China.
The Daya Bay protests may not be enough to stop the nuclear plant, but they are likely to reverberate through Hong Kong's emerging political system. 
Proponents of direct elections to choose territorial leaders say their movement has gained support as a result of the nuclear controversy.

file: OF FIG LEAVES, ART AND OTHER DISPUTES_Hong Kong_ Uproar Over Film Censorship.txt
text:
ï»¿
FROM REMOVING FIG LEAVES on Italian masterpieces to censoring films in Hong Kong to protecting antiquities in Israel, culture the world over provokes heated debate.
Following is a roundup of reports from 12 Times foreign correspondents about cultural issues that have sparked controversy and discussion in their countries. 
In addition to reflecting the inextricable connections among art, money and politics, their reports show that countries throughout the world are struggling to maintain their cultural heritage and that television - its control, programming and funding - is an increasingly important concern.
The Government here is facing sharp criticism after its admission that it has been censoring films for the last 34 years without legal authority to do so. 
The Government, which is headed by British officials appointed by London, apparently censored films that it believed would offend China, Hong Kong's vast northern neighbor.
The admission, which came only after a report in The Asian Wall Street Journal, has provoked bitter accusations that Britain is more interested in placating China than in protecting the interests of the 5.5 million residents of this territory, which reverts to China in 1997. 
Supporters of direct elections here are concerned that if Britain is unwilling to stand up to China on artistic matters, it is unlikely to introduce democracy in the territory in the face of apparent opposition from Beijing.
The fact that censorship took place was not new, although many residents apparently were unaware of it until the recent publicity storm. 
What was new was the realization that the Government knowingly censored films without any legal right to do so.
''Such an abuse of power for so long is a shocking state of affairs, and is contradictory to the spirit of rule by law,'' said the Chinese-language Hong Kong Daily News. 
The English-language South China Morning Post lamented that the incident undermined ''the confidence-building process so vital to Hong Kong.''
At least 21 films were banned outright by the Government, but certain scenes were apparently cut from many others. 
Some films reportedly were even sent to the Xinhua News Agency office in Hong Kong, China's unofficial representative in the territory, for editing. 
The banned films included an array of little-known titles, mostly from Taiwan and Vietnam, both of which are strongly critical of the Beijing Government. 
One 1974 Hong Kong film that was banned portrayed a group of young people who escape from China to the territory.
Hong Kong, clearly embarrassed by the reports, issued a statement confirming that films had been censored ''on the grounds that they might damage good relations with other territories.''
It also noted that the censorship had never been challenged in court. 
In any case, the row seems likely to be settled through new legislation that will grant the Government clear authority to ban films.

file: OF MONKS AND MARTIAL ARTS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The vivid frescoes seem startling in a 1,500-year-old Buddhist temple. 
On one wall, monks fight with feet and clenched fists in a cloistered garden. 
On the opposite wall, more monks spar with swords, staves, cudgels and other ancient weapons. 
The stones of an adjacent hall have been stamped down into 48 indentations, a legacy of centuries of practice in the martial arts that have left the floor pitted up to seven inches deep. 
Shaolin Monastery, nestled on the barren slopes of Song Mountain in central China's Henan Province, was the home of Chan Buddhism, a Chinese sect that gave rise of Zen Buddhism in Japan. 
But it is even better known as the cradle of wushu, an ancient fighting skill that has evolved into Chinese kung fu and influenced Japanese karate and Korean taekwondo.
Christopher Wren article on visiting Shoalin Monastery in central China's Henan Province; photos (M)
During the Tang Dynasty 13 centuries ago, the monastery had 500 fighting monks along with 1,000 more prosaic monks who tilled several thousand acres of communal farmland. 
The monastery then fell on hard times. 
It was burned three times, most recently in 1928 during a struggle between rival warlords. 
It was vandalized during the Cultural Revolution, and its remaining monks dispersed to secular labor. 
Several years ago, Shaolin Monastery reopened and now has 20 monks ranging in age from 16 to 76 years. 
The revival of historical interest in Shaolin Monastery is ironically the result of the popularity of China's first kung fu movie, ''Shaolin Temple.''
(Buddhist monasteries in China are usually called temples.) The film followed the formula of revenge and mayhem that has been a staple of the Hong Kong film industry and was shot on location.
The monastery's reputation derives from an incident in 618 A.D., when the Tang Dynasty Emperor Li Shimin, hearing of the martial arts developed at Shaolin Monastery, appealed for help in defeating Prince Zheng in a battle at nearby Luoyang, then the imperial capital. 
Thirteen warrior monks who responded to the Emperor's call helped win the victory, opening the way for the unification of China. 
(With a license that Hollywood might envy, the movie had the monks winning the campaign by themselves.)
The introduction of fighting skills at Shaolin Monastery has been attributed in legend to the Indian monk Bodhidharma, who went to the monastery in 527, three decades after it was founded by Batuo, another Indian monk. 
Bodhidharma allegedly spent nine years in contemplation, facing the wall of a cave on Song Mountain above the monastery. 
For exercise and protection from wild animals, he taught himself self-defense and later passed the skills along to his disciples.
Actually, the ancient martial arts probably originated even earlier as Buddhist monks learned to fend off brigands and other predators. 
Variations of their refined techniques subsequently reached Japan, Okinawa, Korea and other Asian countries that developed their own distinct fighting styles.
Chinese wushu goes well beyond the ''empty-hand'' fighting of the more familiar karate of Japan or taekwondo of Korea because it incorporates 18 ancient weapons, such as nine-sectioned chains, hinged sticks, staves and swords. 
Chinese wushu, like the more contemporary kung fu, has no belt gradings but can take up to 10 years to master. 
It is taught in China for physical exercise and health rather than self-defense. 
The best known of its styles is taijiquan, called tai chi in the West, which has been vastly slowed down to emphasize flexibility and serenity.
Shaolin Monastery has become a tourist attraction, with the government allocating more than $1.6 million for its restoration. 
The monastery, a few miles from the county seat of Dengfeng, is about four hours by car or tour bus from Henan's provincial capital of Zhengzhou, itself an overnight train ride from Peking, 400 miles to the north. 
The monastery can also be reached from Luoyang.
The monastery is entered through its elevated ''mountain gate,'' reached by a flight of 16 broad stone stairs. 
Under the curved tile roof hangs an elegant gold leaf inscription with the three Chinese characters for Shaolin Temple, written in the 18th century by the Qing Dynasty's Kangxi emperor. 
Stately cy press and ginkgo trees planted by the monks centuries ago rise above the reddish walls. 
More than a dozen buildings, including the Heavenly King (Tianhuang) Hall and a library of Buddhist scriptures, were burned down by the warlord Shi Yousan during the civil fighting in 1928. 
It was said that the monastery burned for 45 days.
Fortunately, the last row of buildings inside the monastery was not destroyed. 
The largest is the Hall of a Thousand Buddhas, in traditional red brick with a curved blue-gray tile roof. 
It contains what are regarded as the finest surviving frescoes in China, painted during the Ming Dynasty, covering more than 3,000 feet of wall. 
They show in intricate detail 500 ''arhats,'' or Buddhist saints, worshipping Buddha amid clusters of billowing clouds. 
No two faces or figures look alike.
A martial arts enthusiast may be more intrigued by the green brick floor, with its 48 indentations in four symmetrical rows about one yard apart. 
The depressions were formed over the centuries, when the monks learned to strengthen their fighting stance by pressing their feet down on the bricks. 
Nearby, a rack of weapons displays a vicious-looking collection of spears, halberds and tridents.
To the east is the White Robe (Baiyi) Hall with its equally famous frescoes of the martial arts, only slightly damaged by graffiti and wear. 
Along the southern wall, 34 monks in colorful open jackets, sleeves rolled up, spar in bare-fisted pairs before a small but intense audience of scholars and spectators. 
On the northern wall, other monks show off their skills with the 18 ancient weapons.
Another wall fresco depicts the 13 warrior monks coming to the aid of the Tang emperor. 
There are additional frescoes of a barehanded monk subduing a dragon and a tiger. 
The origin of the art is obscure. 
The robes and pigtails of the onlookers suggest that the frescoes were painted early in the Qing Dynasty, which overthrew the Ming emperor in 1644 and was itself finally toppled in 1911.
Shaolin's monks today go about their duties with shaved heads and coarse gray robes, oblivious to the stream of tourists. 
But they also have tales to tell. 
Fu Yun, now in his 60's, recalled how the monastery had 300 monks when he joined as a child novice in 1930. 
In those days, he said, the monks practiced wushu six hours a day as a respite from meditation. 
''The basic lessons in wushu were to keep us fit,'' said Fu Yun. 
He was forced to go home to work as a farmer in 1949 but returned after the Communist authorities adopted a greater tolerance for religious belief after the repressive Cultural Revolution.
To the disappointment of many visitors, the monks no longer perform wushu. 
''I can still play but not very well,'' Fu Yun confessed. 
''To be good at wushu, you must be obedient and willing to bear suffering and hardship.''
Chuan Qing, a 24-year-old monk from eastern China, said he was not interested in wushu because ''it is very hard to do.''
For the monks, who rise at 3 or 4 A.M. and subsist on vegetables and rice, life is not much more glamorous than that in other Buddhist monasteries in Asia.
Shaolin's traditional martial arts are being preserved at the nearby town of Dengfeng, where a sports school specializing in wushu opened two years ago. 
Its 140 or so pupils practice wushu every afternoon following their academic classes. 
The pupils, some of whom are only 10 or 11 years old, frequently stage fighting displays for foreign tourists on the packed dirt of their outdoor practice field.
Visitors to China do not have to travel all the way to Shaolin Monastery to see wushu. 
In any major Chinese city, simply rise at dawn and head for the local park, where some young people practice before going off to jobs or classes. 
In Shanghai, for example, there is early morning wushu practice along the Bund, or waterfront promenade. 
Just head for the clatter of swords and staves.

file: OLD NEW YORK IS BEING UNEARTHED ON ELLIS ISLAND.txt
text:
ï»¿
Under the Great Hall on Ellis Island, the door through which millions of immigrants entered America, archeologists last year discovered the skeletons of two American Indians.
They are believed to be Munsees, a local branch of the Delawares, who gathered oysters around the island before the arrival of Europeans.
''Somehow it is very appropriate that the only remains we find on Ellis Island represent the one group that was here before the waves of immigrants that came to make America,'' said John Belle, the main contracting architect for the Ellis Island restoration project for the National Parks Service.
The Indian remains are to be interred on the island before the Great Hall opens to the public as a national museum of immigration in 1992.
Preserving Historic Graffiti
Mr. Belle said the discovery of the skeletons was one of a series of finds that offered new insights into Ellis Island and the 12 million immigrants who passed through the red brick building.
Historians have spoken of the Babel of tongues that rose and fell when thousands of immigrants crowded the cavernous Great Hall in the early part of this century.
Today, conservators are working to preserve the surviving traces of that hubbub - snatches of graffiti scribbled on plaster walls or carved in wooden windowsills.
''They used pencils, penknives and the same blue chalk that doctors used to mark comments on people's coats,'' said Christy Cunningham, a paintings conservator contracted by the Parks Service. 
''Some are just names, dates and villages of origin. 
But there are also sketches of the boats they came over on, with flags flying and steam billowing out of the funnels.''
The 25 areas of graffiti selected for preservation speak of America's multinational roots. 
There are scrawls in Arabic, Armenian, Chinese, French, German, Hebrew, Hungarian, Polish, Greek, Italian, Russian and Serbo-Croatian. 
Some are prosaic. 
''If there were no mosquitoes, one would probably be healthier,'' reads a scrawl in Hungarian. 
Others are more discursive. 
''Thinking of home brings tears,'' one writer scribbled in Chinese on the marble wall in a men's room. 
''Lucky just to arrive in Flowery Flag country. 
I expected peace with no worries. 
Who knew the immigration guards would detain us?
Left locked up without any reason. 
How can we change these harsh laws?''
''Let's devote ourselves to return to China and kill our enemies,'' the man concluded. 
''When I have the opportunity to see my father, brothers, wife and children, I will be overjoyed and tell about my Western journey.''
An Italian immigrant wrote in the men's room: ''Women make men suffer because they are venomous and loose and don't look after their husbands.''
Two graffiti in obscure Armenian dialects continue to puzzle translators.
Â 
Impression Owed to Acoustics
Mr. Belle, an immigrant from Wales, believes he has solved the mystery of why the Babel of tongues had so impressed visitors to the Great Hall.
''The wall plaster is reinforced with horse hair to give it body,'' he said.
This 19th-century construction technique - mixing wet plaster with horse hair purchased from slaughterhouses - was also used in the construction of Carnegie Hall and several Broadway theaters.
''Sounds were clear as a bell in the Registry Room,'' Mr. Belle said, using the formal name for the Great Hall.
The acoustics are also good because of the fine workmanship of the vaulted ceiling of the main hall. 
Constructed around 1917 by the Guastavino Brothers, the same tile contractors who built the ceiling of Grand Central Terminal, the ceiling is almost perfectly intact today.
''We inspected every tile with a rubber hammer,'' said Mr. Belle, who is managing partner of Beyer Blinder Belle Architects and Planners of New York. 
''Less than 40 tiles out of the thousands had to be repaired or replaced.''
Â 
Finding Old Manhattan
On the outside of the main building, contractors digging trenches for power lines have uncovered evidence that supports a theory that much of today's Ellis Island was created by landfill produced when the New York subways were dug at the turn of the century.
''Two feet under the front lawn, we found pottery, silverware, plates and lanterns from the 1820's and 1830's,'' said Michael Alderstein, Parks Service project manager for Ellis Island. 
''As we dig through Ellis Island, we find old Manhattan.''
From the late 1700's to the early 1830's, Ellis Island was also used as an execution ground, largely for sailors convicted and hanged for piracy or mutiny.
When the human bones were unearthed below the building foundations, some restoration workers speculated that they might be the remains of executed convicts.
However, John Pousson, staff archeologist for the Parks Service, said that during the time the northern end of Ellis Island was used for executions, the remains of executed convicts were usually sold or donated to medical schools.
Furthermore, he said, examinations of the teeth show they have a wear pattern characteristic of American Indians.
''There are no cavities, which indicate that these are not Europeans,'' he said.

file: OLYMPIC PROFILE_CHINA_S MASTER TECHNICIAN OF THE ART OF HIGH JUMP.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's best prospect for the Olympic gold in track and field hardly looks like a world- class athlete. 
With his Nike shirt worn inside out, wire-rimmed spectacles and hunched back, 21-year-old Zhu Jianhua is plugged into his Sony Walkman, nonchalantly watching a pre-Olympic competition from the bleachers, as he waits for his event.
Nicknamed ''Bean Pole'' in his native Shanghai, Zhu's frail, long- legged 6-foot-4-inch, 152-pound frame marks him as a high jumper. 
In a backward flop style that combines the agility of a gymnast with the speed of a runner, his featherweight body sails across the 7-7 1/4 (2.33- meter) bar with the ease of an airplane at takeoff.
Profile of Zhu Jianhua, China's master technician of art of high jump, who is competing in Olympic games; photo (M)
Though he has set the world record three times - at 7-9 1/4 (2.37 meters) and 7-9 3/4 (2.38) in China's preliminaries and national championship last year, and 7-10 (2.39) at a West German track meet in Eberstadt in June - the ultimate test of Zhu's athletic prowess will be the men's finals in the high jump on Aug. 
11.
Can he handle the pressure of international competition, particularly against the two-time United States Olympic bronze medalist, Dwight Stones?
As the leading athlete of the first full Chinese team to join the Olympic Games, Zhu bears the additional pressure of ''winning for the motherland.''
For a nation with a weak sports tradition, once dismissed as the ''sick man of Asia,'' Olympic medals carry the symbolic weight of China's struggle for recognition as a world economic power.
''We have three objectives,'' Hu Hongfei, Zhu's 59-year-old coach, said in his native Shanghai dialect. 
''First, to bring in at least the bronze, second, to bring in the gold, third, for Zhu to break his own world record.''
Â 
Has Stones's Respect
According to Stones, now 30, Zhu is ''technically the best high jumper around; he'll probably be the first to clear 8 feet.''
But, Stones added, world-record high jumpers don't necessarily perform well in the Olympics.
''The Olympic record was significantly below the world record in 1972 and 1976,'' Stones explained. 
''Every time Zhu broke the world record, the competition was held under ideal conditions. 
Eberstadt was a synthetic environment with only 4,000 spectators; a fantastic facility, where high jumping was the only event. 
The Olympics is a one-time competition with special pressures. 
There will be distractions - the 1,500 final, 400 relay final and other premier track events that same day, the crowds; it will be a long competition that could last five hours.''
Stones emphasized the importance of mental preparation in managing the lengthy hours between jumps.
''Zhu is 21 years old; this will be his first Olympics,'' Stones said. 
''This is my third Olympics on the facility where I made my best mark - 7-7 3/4.''
Â 
Zhu's 'Bad Luck'
Once before, Zhu buckled under pressure. 
At the first international track and field championship in Helsinki last year he finished third, clearing 7-6. 
Only two months before he had set his first world record on his home turf in Shanghai.
''It was bad luck,'' Zhu said of the world championships. 
''I was nervous and did not know how to handle the psychological pressure of international competition.''
Â 
Is he nervous about the Olympics?
''No. I've paid my dues,'' he said in a conversation conducted in his Shanghainese dialect.
''Comparing oneself to others increases anxiety,'' Hu said. 
''When Zhu was a child, I told him that the goal was to raise his own personal record among the best high jumpers in his age group; I never pushed him to be first in competition. 
I tell Zhu that he must aim high, keeping in mind his own record and the world record. 
The opponent is the bar, not the competitor.''
Â 
'Long Lower Limbs'
Hu, a former middle-distance runner who describes himself as a ''so-so athlete determined to succeed as a coach,'' first spotted the 10-year-old boy's ''long lower limbs, the stuff of a high jumper,'' at a school playground, and has been training Zhu since.
''The unity of their coach-athlete relationship is remarkable,'' said Harry Sneider, Stones's coach, who also has plaudits for Zhu's technique. 
''Zhu's speed conversion, the ability to convert horizontal speed into vertical lift, and his use of the swing leg are marvelous. 
He's also got the best flexibility of any jumper. 
Zhu has maximized the use of his physique to achieve extraordinary results.''
''Zhu needs to develop endurance, though, through weight lifting,'' said Stones.
''Stones has his technique and I have mine,'' said Zhu, who only takes 10 rapid-fire steps to the bar, before his speedy flight up and over.
The competitive styles of both Zhu and Stones are as dissimilar as their personalities, perhaps a reflection of the dichotomy between East and West. 
Stones is outgoing and talkative, with a reputation for ''psyching out'' his competitors, whereas Zhu appears introspective and mellow as he competes against his own standard.
Mobbed by reporters after he had won the pre-Olympic competition, Zhu handled the press with aplomb, and simply walked away when he'd had enough.
''For every half-hour I speak, Zhu only says two words,'' said Hu.
Fans come up to Zhu and say ''Youre No. 1,'' or ''Good luck,'' and Zhu understands and looking genuinely pleased, murmuring a humble ''thank you,'' the only two words he knows in English.
Zhu's public reserve masks the determination of a professional athlete, which was evident at a young age. 
At one time suring his childhood, Zhu continued to high jump, despite a painful wound from a splinter on the sole of his foot. 
Zhu was a sickly youngster who suffered from frequent fevers and respiratory problems, and as the pampered youngest son of five children, he was discouraged from sports by his parents.
He also suffered from ''fear of height,'' ducking the bar instead of going over it, whenever the height was raised, not an uncommon phobia among high jumpers, said Hu. 
How Zhu performs on that one day of the Olympic competition, however, will depend on his ability to handle the distractions and his detractors; how he manages his energy level; whether he can endure the August heat, all while carrying the weight of Chinese and world expectations.
Can he put it all together?
''Only Zhu himself knows,'' said Hu.

file: OLYMPIC PROFILE_TIMING WAS FINALLY RIGHT.txt
text:
ï»¿
Before the Olympic Games began, many gold medals were predicted for China in men's gymnastics. 
The Chinese were favored to win the team gold medal; their star, Li Ning, was favored to win the individual all-around gold medal; and Li, Tong Fei and Lou Yun all were expected to win medals in various of the individual apparatus finals.
Once the competition began, the raves for China were tempered by the entirely unexpected performance of the men of the United States team. 
They not only won the team gold medal, but their Peter Vidmar took the lead, just ahead of China's Li, in the preliminary standings for the individual all-around medals.
Profile of Japanese gymnast Koji Gushiken, who has won gold medal in all-around individual competition despite fact that he placed fifth before start of event; Gushiken's career and background traced (M)
With all the hubbub about Vidmar and Li, not much notice was paid to the little man with the ancient-looking face who stood in fifth place as the all-around competition began Thursday night. 
Koji Gushiken of Japan was known as one of the world's best gymnasts, but there were four other world-class performers ahead of him - not only Vidmar and Li, but Tong and Bart Conner of the United States.
And in this sport where thousandths of a point can make a difference, there is very little margin for error for someone in fifth place trying to move up. 
So Gushiken gave six very nearly error-free performances, scoring a 10 on his vault, 9.95 on his horizontal bar and rings routines, and 9.90 on the other three events, and overtook Conner, Tong, Li and Vidmar to win the gold medal.
Â 
Vidmar Not Surprised
Most observers were astonished. 
They thought that if anyone was going to overtake Vidmar in the finals, it would be Li. 
But Vidmar wasn't surprised.
''No, no,'' said Vidmar, whose silver medal was the first medal for an American in Olympic all-around competiton. 
''I remember at the '81 world championships, everyone was talking on and on about the Russians and the Chinese, and Koji got third in the all-around. 
At the '83 world championships, everyone was talking about the Russians and the Chinese, and Koji got second in the all-around.
''He just moved up to the right spot today,'' Vidmar said. 
''He has good timing.''
Gushiken might dispute that. 
He is 27 years old, aged by the standards of his grueling sport. 
And good timing hasn't been a highlight of his 16-year career, judging by what he said, through a translator, in the interview session after his victory.
Gushiken, who is from Osaka and now lives in Tokyo, where he teaches at the Nippon Physical Education College, would have been at a prime age for Olympic competition during the Montreal Games, in 1976. 
But in each of the two years before those Olympics, he suffered a serious injury - first a ruptured Achilles' tendon, then a broken ankle. 
Each time, he said, it took him six months to recover, and another six months to reach top competitive form.
''I was only ranked 13th in Japan when the Montreal Olympics came,'' he said. 
''So I could not go.''
Â 
Disappointment in 1980
When it was time for the Moscow Games, he was back at the top, but his country joined the boycott led by the United States.
''I was very disappointed in Japan's boycott of the 1980 Olympic Games because I was a member of that team, and I had trained so hard and perservered through so much for that,'' he said.
''I left Japan this time with determination to win sort of double gold, making up for the one I missed in Moscow.''
He also made up a bit for the lost glory that once belonged to Japan in men's gymnastics. 
After winning their first team medal, a silver, in 1956, the Japanese went on to dominate Olympic gymnastics from the 1960 Games, in Rome, through the 1976 Games in Montreal. 
Japan won each of those five team gold medals, and Japanese men won 10 of the 15 individual all-around medals - three golds, four silvers and three bronzes.
Since then the Soviet Union, which had been Japan's closest competitor ever since 1956, has dominated men's gymnastics. 
The Russians won the team gold in Moscow and were heavily favored to win the world championships last October, although the Chinese slipped past them by a fraction of a point.
In those world championships, Gushiken took the silver all-around medal behind the Soviet Union's celebrated 17-year-old, Dmitri Bilozerchev. 
But the relative youth of the Chinese men, and the relative old age of Gushiken, were considered strikes against him here.
And fifth place after the preliminary scores (computed from each individual's scores in the team competition) was not the best place from which to launch a medal run. 
''I knew I was in fifth place but the difference was only 17-hundredths of a point,'' he said. 
''So if I take each exercise very carefully and do it my best, I knew I could win.''
Gushiken did not edge into first place until the fifth rotation, when he earned a 9.95 on the horizontal bar while Vidmar earned a 9.90 for his vault, putting Gushiken .025 of a point into the lead.
Either man could have won on the sixth and final rotation. 
Up first on the floor exercise, Gushiken scored a 9.90, which meant that Vidmar needed a 9.95 or 10 on the parallel bars to beat him. 
Bit Vidmar bobbled his dismount slightly and got a 9.90.
As soon as he saw that score, Gushiken burst into tears, knowing he had won.

text:

The State Department has assured the Los Angeles Olympic Organizing Committee that foreign athletes and officials traveling to the 1984 Summer Olympic Games will be allowed into the country without visa problems.
Peter V. Ueberroth, the president of the L.A.O.O.C., said Friday that he had received ''reassurance'' on the sensitive question from Secretary of State George P. Shultz at a meeting in Washington Thursday. 
During the course of his visit, Mr. Ueberroth said he had also had met briefly with President Reagan (''It was a social thankyou visit''), whom he described as being ''very helpful'' with plans for staging the first Summer Olympics in the United States since the 1932 Los Angeles Games.
No Federal funds are being used to assist Los Angeles's $500-million effort, but Mr. Ueberroth said the Reagan Administration had assigned Michael K. Deaver, deputy chief of staff in the White House, to work with the organizers on law enforcement.
The State Department has assured the Los Angeles Olympic Organizing Committee that foreign athletes and officials traveling to the 1984 Summer Olympic Games will be allowed into the country without visa problems.
The biggest expense problem to be resolved between now and the opening ceremonies on July 28, 1984, remains negotiating contracts with 54 independent police departments and protecting thousands of athletes, officials, members of the media and visitors, Mr. Ueberroth added.
Â 
Several Topics Addressed
During a luncheon meeting with editors and reporters of The New York Times, Mr. Ueberroth answered questions on a variety of sports and political issues related to the Los Angeles Olympics. 
Some of the more significant were these:
- China's decision to cut off all cultural and sports exchanges with the United States for the remainder of this year in response to the United States having granted political asylum to the Chinese tennis player, Hu Na, had left the Los Angeles organizers ''vulnerable'' to a possible Chinese boycott in 1984. 
''The Olympics are a political event,'' Mr. Ueberroth said, describing the Chinese situation as ''very sensitive.''
He said he is hopeful that the People's Republic of China and Taiwan, which is to send athletes and officials to the Games under name Chinese Taipei Olympic Committee, would both compete. 
From an original plan to send only 30 athletes, mainland China's most recent estimate for 1984 is now at 385, Mr. Ueberroth said.
- The international governing body for soccer, the Federation Internationale de Football Association (FIFA), last week approved the sites proposed for the Olympic soccer tournament (including stadiums at Harvard University, Annapolis, Md., Stanford University and the Rose Bowl in Pasadena). 
But because of an eligibility dispute with the International Olympic Committee over the definition of amateur players in soccer, Mr. Ueberroth indicated there was still a possibility that FIFA could withdraw its sanction for soccer in the 1984 Olympics, and perhaps even stage a substitute tournament.
- A site for the shooting events still has not been found, since the I.O.C. rejected Las Vegas, Nev., as an alternative. 
''We're trying to find a solution,'' Mr. Ueberroth said. 
The possibility of the Olympic shooting events being staged outside the host country has precedence. 
''If worse comes to worse, they won't hold it anywhere,'' he said.
- The Los Angeles Raiders of the National Football League have until April 28 to decide whether they will build luxury boxes in the Coliseum, for which the Los Angeles Olympic Organizing Committee will pay the Raiders $3 million.''My guess is he won't build them,'' Mr. Ueberroth said, referring to Al Davis, the Raiders' managing partner.
- The United States is ''dead last'' in understanding that sports can influence young people in a positive way. 
''It hasn't dawned on us,'' Mr. Ueberroth said, citing the 1980 boycott of the Moscow Olympics and the reluctance to ''share our athletes'' with less developed countries as examples of recent United States negativism at the international level.
- Even without government assistance, the L.A.O.O.C. still envisions finishing in the black, with income from television ($210 million), cash ($140 million), tickets ($90 million), interest and a coin program covering its commitment. 
Mr. Ueberroth, however, has cut his original estimate of a $21 million profit to $8 million.
Mr. Ueberroth said a nationwide ticket policy that would give individuals 60 days in which to file their requests would be announced soon. 
Historically, many Olympic events are not sold out; but in the event of any sellout, a computer will select winners randomly from requests.
Appointed in March 1979, after being recruited at the last minute by the search firm of Korn-Ferry, Mr. Ueberroth left the financial comforts of the second-largest travel corporation in North America, First Travel, which he founded 20 years ago, to head the 360-member organizing committee. 
Committed to financing the games privately for the first time made Mr. Ueberroth an early target in I.O.C. circles, particularly after the administrative and financial foulups at the 1980 Winter Olympics in Lake Placid and Denver's aborted plans to stage the 1976 Winter Games.
Â 
Lake Placid Is Recalled
Foreign delegations are most seriously concerned about such matters as security, transportation and their treatment upon their arrival here. 
Some delegations had criticized the housing, transportation and services provided by the organizers in Lake Placid.
Mr. Ueberroth said his trip to Washington was designed to explain to Administration officials ''the Olympic Games and what they're about.''
''I just want to be sure as we move along we're not passing up chances for international friendship,'' he said. 
John Caulfield, of the visa affairs department, said making entry to the United States easier for foreign Olympic athletes had been discussed. 
''In general, it is quite reasonable that we would take steps to facilitate the entry of members of foreign delegations,'' Mr. Caulfield said. 
''The Olympics is different from an occasional golfer or player from the North American Soccer League.''
The success or failure of the Los Angeles Olympics, Mr. Ueberroth said, would be measured not in dollars and cents, but in how well the city embraced the games. 
''Things go better when people like it,'' he said.
''I think the best sporting event in this country is the New York City Marathon, because the people embrace that event,'' said Mr. Ueberroth, a San Jose State University graduate, who tried out for and failed to make the United States Olympic water polo team in 1956.

file: ON SOVIET-CHINA BORDER, THE THAW IS JUST A TRICKLE.txt
text:

This bustling Central Asian city is barely 100 miles from China, yet for 20 years it has had virtually no contact with the other side of the frontier.
Centuries of trading, intrigue and war have given way to silence, broken only by the propaganda broadcasts that each side beams at the other across the towering Tien Shan range. 
On July 1, however, a small beginning was made on restoring some of those ancient ties when the two countries reopened two border points that have been sealed since the ideological and territorial rift between them broke into the open in the 1960's.
The opening of the barriers for local trading, at a mountain pass at Turugart, 130 miles east of here, and another at Korgas, 470 miles to the northeast, will not extend to passenger traffic, and thus will not relieve the forced separation of tens of thousands of families that straddle the border. 
Nor will it mean any major increase in trade, since the major country-to-country traffic, which will more than double this year, passes through rail points thousands of miles farther east.
OSH, U.S.S.R. 
- This bustling Central Asian city is barely 100 miles from China, yet for 20 years it has had virtually no contact with the other side of the frontier.
Nonetheless, it is a symbolic step in the overall effort by Moscow and Peking to improve relations. 
Two rounds of talks since last October, the first in Peking and the second in Moscow in March, have failed to produce any major steps toward resolving their differences, and manifestations of good will have been limited to such things as reopening minor border points, stepping up trade and reviving sports and scientific exchanges.
Â 
Soviet Officials Wary
Local officials here and in Frunze, capital of Soviet Kirghizia, adopt a wary tone when discussing the border reopenings, reflecting the ambivalence that has characterized Government pronouncements in Moscow since the unproductive round of talks in March. 
Sopubek B. Begaliyev, chairman of the Kirghizian state planning committee, mentioned the border points only in passing while reviewing the state of affairs in the republic for visiting reporters, and added cryptically, ''You can say this is some evidence of improved relations.''
A similarly noncommittal view was expressed by Karybek M. Moldobayev, first secretary of the Frunze party committee, who dismissed suggestions that the gradual improvement in ties was of particular importance to Kirghizia, given its proximity to China and the memories of border clashes that have occurred during the years of enmity. 
The clashes, mainly in 1969, never reached the intensity of the fighting on the Amur and Ussuri rivers in the Far East, where the death toll was considerable.
''As part of the Soviet state, Kirghizia will benefit along with other parts of the republic,'' he said. 
Hardly a year ago, when Leonid I. Brezhnev was making little headway with his appeals to China for a turn toward improved ties, visitors here found a more emphatic attitude. 
Then local officials spoke openly of the ''threat'' that they said China's military presence posed to Kirghizia, and they recounted how conditions on the other side of the border caused tens of thousands of refugees to pour across the frontier into Kirghizia at the height of China's Cultural Revolution in the late 1960's.
Today, such matters are approached more discreetly. 
Asanbek Tokombayev, head of the republic's radio and television service, recalled the border skirmishes as ''small-scale matters'' that had long since been forgotten, and described border tensions in general as ''a thing of the past.''
Other officials questioned on the matter said they attached little importance to China's historical claim to Soviet territory on the north side of the Pamir Mountains, part of a much wider Chinese position that places about 580,000 square miles of Soviet territory in the category of land seized from imperial China under ''unequal'' treaties with the Russian czars.
Â 
Slight Interest in China
Mr. Tokombayev said that the border reopenings were not sufficiently interesting to audiences here to warrant sending film crews to monitor the event. 
Indeed, he said, there was little general interest here in what was going on in China, apart perhaps from the people of Uighur, Kazakh or Kirghiz origin who had been residents of China until the 1960's but had taken up residence here and become Soviet citizens.
He said he was ''unsure'' whether China was still broadcasting radio propaganda in the local languages, ''but we do not listen, anyway.''
He denied knowledge of Soviet propaganda transmissions, but Western monitoring services have confirmed that Soviet stations in Alma-Ata, Tashkent and elsewhere in Central Asia continue to vaunt the higher Soviet standard of living in shortwave programs transmitted across the mountains in Uighur and Kazakh.
Almost everywhere, officials questioned on the matter said that the greatest threat these days came not from Peking but from Washington, and President Reagan's program of modernizing United States nuclear arms. 
This is the standard line in Moscow. 
But on the streets of Osh, an industrial city of half a million that sits amid one of the most fertile agricultural areas in Central Asia, ordinary people tended to reverse the view.
''United States?'' a gold-toothed fruit vendor in the Osh bazaar said, as an American reporter sampled one of his melons. 
''Excellent,'' he said, giving a thumbs-up sign.

text:
