To trim, as usual.
PEKING, March 6 - The passengers aboard C.A.A.C. 
Flight 1506 from the southeastern city of Fuzhou arrived in Peking on schedule, but their luggage did not. 
The passengers waited for nearly an hour before an airline employee explained that heavy air cargo had been piled on top of the luggage.
When the luggage finally appeared, the employee murmured a rare apology to an American traveler. 
''I know that C.A.A.C. is bad,'' she said.
Her admission would not be challenged even in China. 
The official Chinese press has taken up the incessant complaints about the surliness, incompetence and sloth of the Civil Aviation Administration of China, as the state airline is officially called. 
Now it is promising to undo its reputation as arguably the world's worst major airline.
A new directive issued recently by the airline's officials announced it had embarked upon a shake-up under the slogan, ''A people's airline for the people.''
According to People's Daily, incompetent managers and employees who do not shape up will be dismissed.
Â 
Delays to Be Announced
From now on, the party newspaper said, there should be no more rude and uncivilized behavior, bad meals, rough baggage handling and soliciting of gifts. 
It said the airline planned such startling changes as announcing flight delays honestly and feeding stranded passengers.
The campaign has been remarkable so far for the skepticism that it has evoked. 
''We'll see,'' a Government official in Peking said. 
''Deeds are more eloquent than words.''
Other veteran travelers recalled earlier pledges. 
In August 1980, the airline promised to improve after newspapers exposed cases of mismanagement, surly service and disrespect for passengers, including an argument in which one employee spat in the face of an African Ambassador's wife.
A year ago, Shen Tu, the airline's director general, admitted at an international conference of travel agents in Peking that his airline had ''many aspects which are far from satisfactory, such as deficient management, low efficiency and poor services, which caused difficulties and unpleasantness to our passengers.''
Mr. Shen added, ''We have the confidence to overcome them.''
Â 
Airline Earned $100 Million
Any Western airline that arbitrarily canceled flights, refused to make connecting or return reservations and was generally slovenly would most likely go bankrupt. 
But the Chinese airline earned $100 million in profits last year, thanks to a monopoly on air travel inside the world's most populous country and such practices as charging foreigners two-and-a-half-times the fare for Chinese.
The airline also restricts competition on regional flights. 
It has only five direct flights a week between Peking and Hong Kong, and applicants for a seat have to wait up to two weeks. 
C.A.A.C., which manages every aspect of civil aviation in China, refuses to let other airlines share the lucrative route. 
British Airways was finally granted the right to carry Hong Kong passengers once a week on its London-to-Peking run.
Flights on the Chinese airline are seldom full because a few seats are saved in case an important party or Government official shows up at the last minute. 
Overbooking, however, was resolved on at least one flight by setting up canvas stools in the aisle.
Â 
Many Need an Explanation
The airline treats flying as a privilege, and ordinary Chinese need a letter of explanation from their work unit to get a ticket. 
Sales offices tend to ignore telephone reservation requests, but appearing in person is not much better. 
A Chinese traveler reported lining up at the airline's Canton's office only to have the ticket window slam down for lunch. 
It was 10:55 A.M.
The airline has made some improvements in the last few years. 
It has upgraded its fleet of 160 or so aircraft by buying some Boeing and Douglas jetliners, although aging Soviet-made Ilyushins, Tupelovs and Antonovs still fly the provincial routes. 
The airline's pilots, trained in the Chinese Air Force, are competent, though a Western airline official said ''they do come in a little fast.''
A European military attache compared his landing in Canton to ''a strafing run.''
The Chinese, like the Russians, do not disclose air crashes unless foreigners are involved. 
In the worst incident reported, an airliner slammed into a mountain near Guilin in April 1982, killing all 112 people aboard. 
According to Hong Kong reports, an air controller gave the wrong altitude to the plane's pilot.
Â 
Combs for Souvenirs
Safety briefings are nonexistent on the airline's flights, and flight attendants approach their responsibilities with sometimes engaging innocence. 
A first-class traveler on a flight to Urumqi recalled how the flight attendants lounged in the spare seats eating tangerines and never offered her one.
One duty of the flight attendants involves distributing key rings, plastic combs and other inexpensive souvenirs. 
Small nail clippers were doled out on one trip, and the bored passengers set to work.
The airline tolerates an almost unlimited amount of hand baggage stuffed into overhead compartments and piled along the aisles. 
On one Shanghai-to-Hong Kong flight, a shipment of live crabs broke loose, and they scuttled under the seats.
Occasional defects in maintenance are more serious. 
A Western airline representative found a Chinese ground crew washing out and reusing disposable filters. 
When a Chinese pilot discovered problems with an engine last December, he took off from Hong Kong with his passengers aboard and flew over to Canton, where the repairs could be done more cheaply, before arriving in Peking eight hours late.
An Ilyushin-18 caught fire on its approach to Canton in December 1982 because a passenger was smoking in the lavatory. 
Some airport fire trucks had not filled their water tanks, and 23 people died in the blaze.
Â 
Hijackers to Be Resisted
One policy unlikely to change became apparent after an internal flight was hijacked to South Korea last May. 
Mr. Shen, the director general, said at a subsequent news conference that crews had been ordered to resist hijackers ''if the safety of the passengers is assured.''
Until now, the airline's attitude has been that disgruntled passengers could take a train, or walk. 
After the hijacking last spring it banned air travel for everyone except ranking officials, military officers and foreigners until X-ray security devices could be installed at airports.
Its wholesale cancellation of flights left stunned travelers crowding aboard trains. 
The situation has since returned to normal, which People's Daily said at the Peking airport meant ''filth, chaos and rudeness.''

text:

I cannot say quite when I first heard of Trebitsch Lincoln. 
He is one of those types, notorious in their own day, who sink rapidly into obscurity after their deaths, sometimes hovering briefly in the footnotes of history. 
I believe that the outline of Trebitsch Lincoln's bizarre story was recounted to me some years ago in Jerusalem by the editor of the Encyclopedia Judaica, Geoffrey Wigoder, whose encyclopedic knowledge of such historical byways is unrivaled. 
From him I heard, with incredulity, of the birth in 1879 of Ignacz Timotheus Trebitsch in a small provincial town in Hungary, of his conversions from Judaism to various sects of Christianity and then to Buddhism, of his wanderings from Hungary to China, of his adoption of the name Lincoln (the first of more than a dozen noms de guerre), of his election to the British House of Commons and of his activity as a German spy in both world wars. 
But, in spite of the fantastic nature of the tale, little remained in my memory save a dim recollection that the man was somehow mixed up in something scandalous (like the man who fixed the World Series in 1919).
Late one afternoon in August 1984 I was imprisoned in the Bodleian Library at the University of Oxford by heavy rain - a not unusual occurrence in Oxford in August. 
Having no work at hand, and it being too late to order up further books from the stacks, I took to browsing among the supremely boring items Bodley's librarian chooses to make available on the open shelves. 
My eye fell on the hundred or so red and green volumes of the ''Index to the General Correspondence of the Foreign Office'' -enthralling reading matter, at any rate for a historian on a wet afternoon. 
For reasons the psychological mechanics of which are still not clear to me, I decided to look up the name Trebitsch Lincoln. 
I started to read while waiting for the storm to pass. 
That was more than three years ago, and the tempest has not abated yet.
Searching at random I came across entries for Trebitsch in almost every year between 1921 and 1938. 
These were frequently of a piquant nature, tantalizing by reason of their brevity. 
Thus the entry for 1923: ''LINCOLN, Trebitsch (alias Patrick Keelan) Activities in connection with Chinese deputation to General Ludendorff respecting Sino-German relations.''
Or for 1924: ''LINCOLN, Trebitsch (alias Trautwein) Alleged sale of bogus German military plans to French authorities.''
As I moved into the volumes dealing with the 1930's, the arena of activity appeared to shift. 
1931: ''Initiated as Buddhist priest.''
1937: ''Japanese propaganda activity.''
1938: ''Activity in Tibet.''
At 7 P.M. the library closed and I was thrust out into the rain. 
Cycling away, I pondered the meaning of the frequent changes of name, the apparent movement from Europe to the Far East and the seeming combination of religious and political intrigue. 
As I considered the matter further during that weekend, it seemed wise to dismiss the man as a colorful but unimportant confidence trickster or adventurer. 
But the next week, finding myself in the Public Record Office (the British national archive) in Kew, I resolved to check the Foreign Office files to find out whether the apparently sensational entries in the index were reflected in the Government documents themselves. 
Long experience with such materials (many of which are shredded by Government ''weeders,'' whose destructive capabilities would on occasion put even Lieut. 
Col. Oliver North to shame) had taught me to be highly skeptical of finding anything at all. 
To my amazement I found that the index entries were the tip of a vast iceberg of British Government documentation on Trebitsch Lincoln stretching back to 1906. 
The contents, however, did not quench my curiosity. 
If anything, they increased my perplexity. 
For they opened a window into a world of such exotic and convoluted conspiratorial activity that it seemed impossible to disentangle truth from rumor, propaganda stunts or psychological warfare.
I returned to Oxford more puzzled than ever, bemused as to why several governments had involved themselves with this man for more than three decades and wondering whether it was really worth my while to try to find out. 
I had half resolved to banish Trebitsch Lincoln from my mind altogether when a second chance discovery embroiled me deeper in his affairs. 
Once again it occurred in the Bodleian Library, to which I had returned with the intention of devoting myself to my more conventional scholarly vocations. 
Passing one day through Duke Humphrey's reading room, the ancient heart of the library, I happened to recall that I had read somewhere that the Bodleian had recently acquired the archives of some missionary society; Trebitsch, I remembered, had briefly served as a missionary in Canada around the turn of the century. 
I made inquiries and was directed across the road to the hideously ugly pile known as the New Bodleian, where modern historical papers are kept. 
It was a long shot. 
After all, hundreds of missionary societies had existed and it seemed unlikely, to say the least, that any documentation about an obscure missionary who had worked briefly in Montreal around 1900 should turn up in Oxford eight decades later.
I found that the papers of the London Society for the Promotion of Christianity Among the Jews had recently been deposited in the New Bodleian and were open to readers. 
The society had maintained a Canadian section, of which a few bundles of papers were extant. 
To my astonishment I found that they included a detailed and highly circumstantial account of the short career in the society of the ''Revd. 
I. T. Trebitsch.''
These contemporary papers gave a vivid picture of his spiritual wrestlings as well as of certain financial irregularities in his early life.
For the first time I felt I had begun to penetrate beyond the curtain of bluff and bombast behind which Trebitsch, in his later career as spy, concealed his real self from scrutiny. 
True, these papers by themselves were not the key to the mystery of his personality. 
But they persuaded me that here was a problem in historical psychology that it would be worthwhile to unravel. 
What was at first curiosity had by now grown into genuine interest; eventually, I must confess, it was to develop into a virtual obsession as I stripped away veil after veil shrouding the truth about Trebitsch.
Over the next year I transformed myself from historian to detective, scouring archives, plaguing librarians and carrying my inquiries to more than a dozen countries. 
I was able to persuade the recalcitrant Hungarian authorities to make available to me Budapest police records disclosing Trebitsch's early career as a juvenile criminal. 
Using the admirable provisions of the Freedom of Information Act, I obtained hundreds of pages of photocopies drawn from the case files of the F.B.I., the C.I.A. and other American intelligence agencies. 
A loophole in the much more strict British laws governing access to official records enabled me to see closed Home Office records (including some Scotland Yard and M.I.5 papers) concerning Trebitsch.
So I was able to build up an authentic and verifiable picture of his life - surely the most extraordinary life in the history of modern espionage. 
But one fundamental aspect continued to elude me. 
Apart from a few snippets of data garnered from archives of the Budapest Drama Academy, I possessed little reliable information about Trebitsch's youth. 
How would it be possible for me to explain his later development without some examination of the formative influences on his character of his family and early surroundings?
For a time I ignored the problems, comforting myself with Evelyn Waugh's airy dismissal (in his autobiography, ''A Little Learning'') of the common notion that the events of early childhood determine the patterns of adult life. 
Would it really be helpful, after all, to know whether Freud was toilet-trained at the age of 1, Einstein moonstruck at 2, or that little Niccolo Machiavelli unscrupulously manipulated the affairs of his playmates at 3?
Even if such information were available, would not such an approach risk falling into the trap of hindsight - of seeing a false significance in trivial events merely because of their superficial connection with adult characteristics?
Nevertheless, this gap in my evidence bothered me and I was at a loss as to how to deal with it.
It happened that I had been corresponding for some time with John Greppin, an expert in Armenian linguistics who teaches at Cleveland State University in Ohio. 
The subject of our correspondence was the ethnography of Palestinian gypsies. 
In October 1984, when I went on temporary assignment to Jerusalem, I wrote to Mr. Greppin to give him some trivial information on the local gypsies. 
Meanwhile, I had found out that a younger brother of Trebitsch Lincoln had emigrated around 1910 from Hungary to the United States and had settled in Cleveland, where he established a Hungarian socialist newspaper. 
Beyond that I knew nothing, but I thought it worth asking Mr. Greppin whether it might be possible to trace any descendants of this man who might still live in Cleveland. 
What Mr. Greppin (whom I have never met) made of such a strange request I do not know. 
But he is evidently a person of tolerant spirit and rare resource. 
For by return mail I heard that in Cleveland he had indeed located a woman, then in her late 80's, who was Trebitsch Lincoln's niece. 
She not only responded to my many questions, but also very generously gave me a copy of a manuscript about her father, her notorious uncle and the Trebitsch family, which she had set to paper when she was a college student in the 1920's.
A little later a no less miraculous coincidence brought me further help. 
One evening, at a concert in the Jerusalem Theater, I happened to meet my old friend Elizabeth Eppler, a noted authority on the history of the Jews in Hungary, who had recently settled in Jerusalem. 
When I mentioned that I was writing a book about Trebitsch Lincoln, she responded by fishing out of her handbag the address of another niece of his, then in her 90's, whose daughter, she informed me, was one of her greatest friends. 
She also said that living in London was an equally venerable nephew of Trebitsch.
When I returned to England shortly afterward, I had the pleasure of meeting these people. 
Both of them could remember their uncle with remarkable precision and clarity. 
Since they had known him well (and in the case of the nephew had even worked with him during Trebitsch's short-lived career as a Rumanian oil company promoter), their testimony was invaluable. 
Moreover, through them I was introduced to Trebitsch's granddaughter, who, over lunch in the charming restaurant that she and her husband ran in Greenwich, provided me with more vital information.
By combining the new evidence given me by Trebitsch's relatives with what I already knew from other sources, I was in a position to attempt to draw at least the outlines of an account of his childhood and adolescence - and of the relationship of his early experiences to the wayward odyssey of his adult life.
My quest for the truth about Trebitsch Lincoln carried me even farther from my usual beat. 
I little expected, when I first looked up Trebitsch's name in the Bodleian Library, that a year or so later I would be immersed in the records of the Special Branch of the Shanghai Municipal Police, let alone that these documents would furnish me with the last crucial set of clues that would enable me finally to unravel the mystery of Trebitsch Lincoln.
I discovered exactly how he moved from a bohemian student life in Budapest to a Presbyterian mission house in Montreal; how he got himself elected Liberal Member of the British Parliament for Darlington; how his speculations in Rumanian petroleum ended in disaster; how he defrauded his English benefactors and set himself up as a double (or rather a triple) agent during World War I; how he fled to the United States, was arrested, escaped from jail in Brooklyn and baffled and exasperated the police as he eluded capture, cheekily issuing taunts and challenges to his would-be captors through the New York press; how he returned to Europe and emerged as a member of the rightist German revolutionary government of Wolfgang Kapp in 1920; how he encountered the young Hitler, who had rushed up from Munich to join in that putsch; how, after the collapse of the coup, he combined with German, Hungarian and Russian reactionaries to form the ''White International,'' a right-wing equivalent of Lenin's Red International dedicated to the cause of revolution everywhere; how he then betrayed his fellow conspirators, fled to China, appointed himself abbot of a Buddhist monastery and became deeply immersed in political intrigues in Tibet and north China; and how finally, in the last and most extraordinary phase of his life, he re-emerged in the eerie twilight of wartime Japanese-occupied Shanghai in his old role as an undercover agent, this time for both the Nazis and the Japanese.
Beyond tracking the picaresque story of a man who could bamboozle David Lloyd George, J. Edgar Hoover and Heinrich Himmler, I tried to achieve another level of understanding. 
The core of the mystery seemed to me the enigma of Trebitsch's inner life. 
What, if any, were his true loyalties?
What was he really up to?
Did his conscience sit easy as he labored for the Axis while his son was tortured by the Japanese in Java and his brother was murdered in Auschwitz?
Drawing on my multifarious sources, I was able to reconstruct this hidden dimension of personality and to explain the messianic delusion that ultimately engulfed him.
The later part of Trebitsch Lincoln's life was governed by a severe manic depressive psychosis that produced alternating rhythms of gloom, pessimism and paranoia on the one hand, and of supernal omnipotence, euphoria, gregariousness and elation on the other. 
The cycle of moods found expression in periods of monkish withdrawal and despair, followed by manic phases of hyperactivity, prophetic claims and compulsive political folies de grandeur. 
The messianic manic-depressive syndrome provides the key to an explanation of Trebitsch Lincoln's life, and in particular of the link between his inner construction of the world and external reality. 
But he cannot be simply dismissed as a madman. 
On the contrary, the remarkable thing about him - and the most telling commentary on the world in which he lived - is that he was able to operate on a plane of apparent rationality throughout his career as a confidence trickster. 
Otherwise, how could he have been elected to the British Parliament?
Otherwise, how could he have been appointed a member of the German Government?
Otherwise, how could the most senior figures in the Buddhist hierarchy in China have accepted him into their midst with affection and pride?
During World War II, even the chief Gestapo agent in the Far East, SS Col. Joseph Meisinger (a hard-bitten Nazi who was to be executed in 1947 for war crimes, and who boasted that he trusted no one - ''Sometimes I even have doubts about myself!''), accepted Trebitsch's fantastic pretensions with a naive credulity. 
Meisinger recommended Trebitsch's recruitment to his ring of agents and became embroiled in a bitter controversy over the issue with the top echelons of the Nazi security apparatus in Berlin. 
Far from being a disadvantage, Trebitsch's specific form of madness thus thrust him insistently forward in the world of the great dictators - a world where madness had gained an ascendancy over large portions of humanity.
Trebitsch Lincoln died in Shanghai in October 1943. 
Yet, even in death, he retains a capacity to astound, and I suppose it is possible he may yet rise from his grave in the Shanghai Municipal Cemetery, in the form of a posthumous cache of papers, to contradict everything I have found out about him. 
Notwithstanding that faint possibility, I felt, by the end of my researches, that my archival burrowings and merciless badgering of witnesses, along with some outstanding strokes of good fortune, had yielded the closest accessible approach to the true history of a false messiah.

text:
ï»¿
INTELLECTUALS AND THE STATE IN MODERN CHINA A Narrative H istory. 
By Jerome B. Grieder. 395 pp. 
New Y ork: The Free Pres s. 
$22.50.
CHINA'S INTELLECTUALS Advise and Dissent. 
By Merle Goldman. 
276 pp. 
Cambridge, Mass: Harvard University Press. 
$22.
FOR ordinary mortals who have not acquired through study or practice the art of deciphering Chinese thought and politics, such matters can seem forbiddingly unfamiliar or quite simply impenetrable. 
The Confucian heritage sounds impossibly archaic and the Marxist-Leninist present is hardly inviting. 
In the past 30 years, debates about philosophy and politics have usually been conducted in code: Today's leaders and issues wear the disguise of figures and events from the past, from a literary and historical culture unknown to most people in the West. 
Those brief moments during which the Chinese have spoken en clair, such as the Hundred Flowers campaign of 1957 and the Democracy Movement of 1978-79, have riveted our attention but ended almost as suddenly as they began.
Roger Garside reviews Jerome B Grieder's "Intellectuals and the State in Modern China," and Merle Goldman's "China's Intellectuals"
So we still need interpreters - though many books by China specialists thicken the mystery instead of dispelling it. 
Not so Jerome Grieder's ''Intellectuals and the State in Modern China.''
Convinced that China's modern history is not an item of intellectual exotica but ''something that belongs to all o f us,'' Grieder set out to write about China's intellectuals from the middle of the 19th century until the Communist victory in 1949, in a manner that would be intelligible to the general reader.
The result is no facile work of popularization. 
It will make demands upon the stamina of any reader. 
At times the author overestimates the layman's capacity to absorb detail, and Grieder's style can be wordy, even portentous. 
But his broad learning and vitality of spirit make him an excellent narrator and companion for this eventful journey. 
This is intellectual history in the sense defined by Joseph Levenson: ''The history not of thought, but of men thinking.''
Grieder engages the reader emotionally as well as intellectually as he recounts the fate not only of ''men thinking'' but of ideas living, and dying, in modern China. 
It is worth noting in this regard that neither America nor Europe has in modern times been through an identity crisis of the intensity the Chinese have endured since the middle of the 19th century.
Grieder makes a major contribution to our understanding of the intellectual adjustment China has had to undergo in the face of overwhelming pressures from outside and massive economic imbalance within. 
He shows us that many of the most difficult and sensitive issues that confront China today faced Chinese intellectuals 50 or 100 years ago. 
Pragmatism in conflict with dogma, pluralism versus an ideological monopoly, how to absorb the best of foreign culture without destroying China's own sense of identity, how to devise political and legal institutions that will balance freedom and order, how to modernize the economy - all these are themes of the book as well as issues in Peking today.
''Intellectuals and the State in Modern China'' provides sketches of the lives of the protagonists, and with deft economy Grieder evokes the conditions of the China they have inhabited. 
But he concentrates on their sense of themselves, their values, philosophies and proposals for reform or revolution. 
He conveys the agonizing of those who wanted to save the imperial system but realized it could not be done by drawing on the resources of traditional philosophy. 
Men like the early Communist leader Chen Duxiu icons of inherited culture with verbal violence. 
We hear the quieter voice of the liberal pragmatist Hu Shi calling on China to adopt a different strategy, to choose pluralism instead of totalitarianism.
Since the death of Mao Zedong, China has been engaged in a sober reassessment of its socialist revolution, and it is enlightening to look back now with Grieder at what Hu Shi wrote. 
''Civilization is not created wholesale,'' he cautioned in 1919. 
''It is created bit by bit and drop by drop. 
Progress cannot be achieved all at one go, of an evening.''
After the traumas of the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, such words must sound more persuasive to Chinese ears now than they did in the 1920's. 
But in those days, as Grieder points out, in a nation with no tradition of tolerance for a party of loyal opposition, and at a time of growing anarchy, it was not surprising th at China's leaders should have been drawn to authoritarian political forces, Chiang Kai-shek at one pole and the Communist Party at the other. 
Events in the 1920's and 1930's were pressing, and people were too impatient for Hu Shi's ''drop by drop''philosophy.
Nevertheless, from Grieder's account, Hu Shi emerges as a thinker no less radical than his Communist contemporaries: China must ''accept without prejudice the scientific-industrial world culture and the spiritual civilization that underlies it,'' he said, and declared that ''the only way to have democracy is to have democracy.''
In one of those connections that make his book so stimulating, Grieder moves from Hu Shi in the 1920's to Wei Jingsheng, the most radical activist of the Democracy Movement of 1978-79, and places them both in the line of those who have struggled for a pluralist China.
But Grieder does not deal with the period after 1949 in any detail. 
Our understanding of the continuities between the old China and the new is thereby impoverished. 
So few of those who study the new China possess his combination of boldness, historical perspective and ability to relate Chinese thought to the world outside. 
Intellectual history of the post-l949 period has been largely in the hands of craftsmen, not artists.
Merle Goldman is a fine artisan. 
In the serried ranks of Sinologists, there is no more skillful code breaker than she. 
Her earlier book, ''Literary Dissent in Communist China,'' chronicled literary developments up to the Great Leap Forward at the end of the 1950's. 
In her new book, ' 'China's Intellectu als: Advise and Dissent,'' she has broadened her focus to inc lude not only literary writers but philosophers, historians, journal ists and scientists.
The most valuable part of this book is the chapter in which she interprets the veiled debates that took place in the early 1960's, in the aftermath of the disastrous Great Leap Forward. 
With scholarly precision Goldman indicates how intellectuals, enjoying the patronage of powerful Communist Party leaders opposed to Mao, expressed an amazing array of heterodox ideas, reopening questions that seemed to have been settled by the Communist victory in 1949.
She presents the playwright Wu Han calling for the breakup of collective farms, eminent historians speaking of the need to unite the country around common goals, and philosophers like Liu Jie arguing that the Confucian ideal of human kindness produced in China an evolutionary rather than a revolutionary process. 
No one to my knowledge has researched and written so comprehensively on this aspect of the period. 
But the rest of the book is disappointing. 
Its title leads one to expect an intellectual history; one finds instead a history of the bureaucratic politics of the intellectual culture.
Merle Goldman is so preoccupied with Lenin's question ''Who: Whom?'' that she presents intellectual ideas and values as functions of these bureaucratic politics, whereas we have abundant evidence that there is an autonomous life of the mind and spirit in China.
This has been plain to see each time the lid has been lifted on post-1949 China: during the Hundred Flowers campaign and the Cultural Revolution, and in the years since Zhou Enlai's death in 1976. 
A volcanic eruption of poetry has provided evidence that traditional patterns of expression are being married to contemporary thought and feeling. 
For an intellectual history to be published today without a proper examination of that evidence - let alone of the earlier evidence - is just not good enough.
That is not all. 
Goldman has not developed the vital connections between what has happened in this later period and the point at which Grieder stopped. 
The social context in which Chinese intellectuals operate is all but invisible. 
Finally, Goldman's acknowledgments and notes on sources confirm what the text itself makes clear: Discussions with Chinese played no significant part in her study.
Such detached and dispassionate writing is sometimes regarded as ''scientific.''
Certainly it is justifiable if one is writing about molecules or plants, neither of which have been known to die for their ideas. 
But when transposed to the realm of people, this approach becomes unscientific; it filters out too much of the essence of our untidy lives.
Oh, ye watchers of latter-day China, open your doors and bring into your studies other men's emotions, suffering and dreams!
Nations and their politics are not made by power play alone.

text:

When Secretary of Defense Caspar W. Weinberger arrives in China on Sunday for a five-day official visit, he will be introduced to an army that was at one time considered the world's best light infantry but has been overtaken by progress.
China's People's Liberation Army, with over 4.2 million men and women under arms, is largely obsolete, lacking sophisticated antitank and antiair craft missiles and electronic communications gear, among other modern necessities.
The army, which was born as a guerrilla band 56 years ago, remains mired in its traditional dual role of defending the country and ''serving the people,'' as the old Maoist slogan put it.
Â 
Soldiers Still Harvest Rice
Its soldiers still routinely fix roads, plant trees, raise pigs and harvest rice. 
Yu Qiuli, the army's political commissar, declared recently that the armed forces had contributed 100 million work days of public service over the last four years.
Yet an effort has now begun to transform the army into a more modern fighting machine. 
''The P.L.A. is no longer in the era of millet plus rifles,'' a commentary in the official newspaper People's Daily said last May. 
Mr. Weinberger, who is making his first visit to China, according to a Pentagon spokesman, is scheduled to review an armed forces honor guard on Sunday in Peking. 
On Tuesday he is to visit the elite Third Division of the Peking Garrison, and two days later he is to visit an aircraft factory in Xian and inspect a naval vessel in Shanghai.
The Chinese leaders are expected to ask Mr. Weinberger about the Reagan Administration's decision to liberalize its export to China of dual-use technology - primarily civilian computers and other hardware that can be adapted for military purposes.
Â 
U.S. Offer Remains Open
Washington's offer, made two years ago, to consider Chinese requests for United States weapons remains open, though some Western military observers here doubt that the Chinese will present Mr. Weinberger with a specific shopping list, for two reasons.
The Chinese leadership is thought to be concerned that its purchase of American arms might give the Reagan Administration a pretext to sell more weapons to the rival Nationalist regime on Taiwan. 
This issue remains a key sticking point in Chinese-American relations, since Peking interprets the joint communique of August 1982 as committing Washington to phase out its military deliveries to the Nationalists.
But China is also too poor to re-equip the world's largest army with foreign weapons. 
Mr. Yu was quoted by The Beijing Review in August as saying:
''We have never pinned our hopes for modernizing our military equipment on imports. 
China is a big country with a big army. 
We cannot afford to buy all the weapons we need. 
Even if we could afford it, it is hard to acquire really advanced weapons of important military value.'
Â 
Foreign Arms Used as Prototypes
The Chinese seem interested in acquiring small quantities of foreign arms that could become prototypes for eventual weapons of Chinese manufacture. 
Some Western diplomats expect the Defense Minister, Zhang Aiping, to raise this issue with Mr. Weinberger, if only in an inconclusive way, though they point out that it would be faster for China to buy the arms than the production technology.
But the indications are that China, which canceled a multimillion-dollar deal with British Aerospace earlier this year, wants to do things cheaply. 
The Chief of Staff, Yang Dezhi, assured army delegates to the National People's Congress in June that ''we will mainly rely on our own efforts to improve our weapons and equipment while introducing advanced techniques from other countries.''
Statements by Chinese military leaders, articles in the official press and analysis by Peking-based diplomats and military attaches indicate that the problem of modernization of the army extends beyond arms alone to basic tactics and leadership competence.
The army's arsenal consists of copies of Soviet weapons mostly predating 1960, when the Soviet Union stopped its military and economic assistance to China. 
Light weapons like the Chinese version of the Kalashnikov assault rifle are highly enough regarded to make China a major arms seller to developing countries.
Â 
Military Aircraft Outdated
But heavier equipment is badly out of date. 
The Chinese Air Force uses copies of Soviet combat aircraft that go back to the MIG-15 of Korean War days. 
Its more modern Shenyang jet fighters, painstakingly updated from the MIG-19 and MIG-21, were described by one United States analyst as ''the world's most advanced obsolete aircraft.''
China has obtained some MIG-23's from Egypt to copy and its version is now believed to be in production, but even this new plane is no match for supersonic fighters like the Soviet MIG-25 or the American F-16.
The Chinese T-59 tank is likewise copied from the old Soviet T-55. 
A newer Chinese model, the T-69, has a gun stabilizer for high-speed firing, infrared searchlights and a laser range-finder, but it remains inferior to the T-72 that spearheads Soviet armored units.
Lacking self-propelled artillery, China has tried to mount heavy 122-millimeter guns on some of its armored personnel carriers, straining their suspension systems. 
Its antitank weapons resemble first-generation Soviet models dating back at least two decades.
Â 
Troops Still Move on Foot
The Chinese Army still basically moves on foot. 
Of the 200 or more divisions it is estimated to have, only 11 are armored and three are airborne. 
The Chinese have mechanized three to five infantry divisions, though it is unclear whether all their battalions are included. 
By comparison, the 45 or so Soviet divisions positioned along China's northern borders are all motorized.
The Chinese Navy has at least one nuclear-powered submarine capable of firing ballistic missiles from underwater. 
Presaging a move away from the traditional role of coastal defense, two Chinese naval vessels made a nonstop 6,000-mile voyage into the South China Sea and Western Pacific earlier this year. 
But the navy remains old-fashioned.
A military attache from a North Atlantic Treaty Organization country who has watched Chinese ground military tactics said, ''It is just like World War I with trenches.''
The Chinese Army is now trying to transform its old strategy of static defense, which is vulnerable to armored and airborne assault, into what the Liberation Army's daily newspaper has called an ''active defense.''
As some Chinese officers describe it, this means combining fixed defensive positions with mobile forces for counterstrikes and guerrillas for harassment behind enemy lines. 
Wu Xiuquan, head of Peking's Institute of International Strategic Studies, told visiting American members of Congress in August that China was also prepared to use nuclear weapons against an invader.
Â 
'Combined Operation' Maneuvers
Last year, the Deputy Chief of Staff, Zhang Zhen, said that tank battles would be emphasized over set-piece infantry warfare and that officers would be trained to use more sophisticated weapons. 
The press has disclosed ''combined operation'' maneuvers that coordinate infantry, artillery and armor with supporting signal and engineer units.
There has also been talk of slimming down the swollen forces by 10 percent or more and relieving them of nonmilitary duties. 
More than 20 divisions, by one estimate, are being transferreed from the army to a newly formed paramilitary People's Armed Police whose duties range from guarding public buildings and embassies to manning frontier posts. 
It was reported last month that a 30,000-man army construction unit was being demobilized and reformed as a construction engineering corporation in Peking.
One of the toughest challenges is to rejuvenate the upper echelons of the army, which have been dominated by aging guerrilla veterans too conservative to accept change. 
A plan to restore military ranks, which were abolished in 1965, has yet to be put into effect, partly because there would be so many elderly generals.
Â 
Higher Education Required
Other steps have been taken to create a younger and more professional officer corps. 
Mr. Yang, the Chief of Staff, reported in June that officers would no longer be chosen from the enlisted ranks but must graduate instead from military academies. 
The Political Commissar, Mr. Yu, told The Beijing Review that ''we have made it a rule that officers above the platoon level must have received a college education.''
The military has ranked last in China's ''four modernizations'' campaign, behind industry, agriculture and science and technology. 
The army's military budget this year has been put at 17.87 billion yuan - less than $9 billion - which is about the same as those of the last two years, though some programs like nuclear weapons and missile development have been tucked away in the budgets of ostensibly civilian ministries.
China's leader, Deng Xiaoping, has reportedly persuaded the army leadership to accept this low priority, arguing that industrialization will create a base for the domestic production of sophisticated weapons.
Â 
Technical Renovations Cited
''We have devised and produced our own atomic and hydrogen bombs, long-range guided missiles and other sophisticated strategic weapons for self-defense,'' the Communist Party journal Red Flag said last year in encouraging the army to stretch out the equipment that it already has. 
A few days ago, Mr. Yang, the Chief of Staff, said at an army meeting on arms production that over 12,000 technical renovations had been made on Chinese wapons in recent years.
But Mr. Deng has also maintained his grip over the armed forces by retaining the chairmanship of the party and state military commissions, while giving up other Government and party posts. 
He has installed in key slots senior officers who, if not enthusiastic about his policies, are at least unwilling to oppose them. 
Five of the commanders of China's 11 military regions have been replaced in the last year.

Bo Yang is a mild-mannered, bespectacled scholar who scribbles Chinese characters on notebooks in his small study, and infuriates people throughout the Chinese-speaking world.
Taiwan once labeled Mr. Bo a Communist agent, and imprisoned him for nine years. 
On the Chinese mainland, the authorities this year banned his books and condemned him for insulting the Chinese people. 
And in Chinatowns in the United States, as well as Hong Kong and Southeast Asia, Mr. Bo's acid pen has earned him bitter criticism as well as adulation.
Mr. Bo is a Chinese Voltaire, a social critic who is prolific, biting, and read. 
A stocky 68-year-old man with thick glasses and a bump below his knee where Taiwanese interrogators broke his leg to elicit a confession, Mr. Bo is best known for his scathing criticisms of his own people and culture.
''The Chinese people continue to grow increasingly base and despicable,'' Mr. Bo writes in a notable essay, ''The Ugly Chinaman,'' that was first published nearly three years ago. 
He complains that Chinese people are too conformist, too loud, too cruel, too crass, and, above all, too willing to tolerate injustice.
Â 
'A State of Ugliness'
''How is it possible for such a great people and great nation to have degenerated to such a state of ugliness?''
Mr. Bo writes elsewhere in the essay. 
''Not only have we been bullied around by foreigners; even worse, for centuries we've been bullied around by our own kind - from tyrannical emperors to despotic officials and ruthless mobs.''
Such vitriol is finding a larger audience. 
Mr. Bo says that some 120,000 copies of ''The Ugly Chinaman'' have been sold in Taiwan, and at least five editions were published in China in 1986 before Beijing banned the essay this year during the nationwide crackdown on intellectuals. 
There have been two translations into English, and the Chinese version has been published in periodicals in Hong Kong, Los Angeles, New York and other cities.
''Bo Yang's name is well known on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, in America and in Southeast Asia,'' said T. K. Tong, chairman of the Department of Asian Studies at the City College of New York. 
''I'd say he is the leading writer in Chinese literature today.''
Dai Tien, a literary editor and newspaper columnist in Hong Kong, said that what sets Mr. Bo apart is his criticism of Chinese culture. 
''Traditionally, Chinese writers have always written nice things about their own people,'' Mr. Dai said. 
New Book Completed Now Bo Yang has just completed a new book, to be published in October, that expands on the theme of ''The Ugly Chinaman.''
The main essay in the book was published in September in Hong Kong and Los Angeles, and is attracting considerable attention. 
The essay focuses on the reason why Mr. Bo continues to drum away at what he regards as the shortcomings of the Chinese people. 
Only when the Chinese acknowledge the flaws, he believes, will they be liberated of them.
The latest essay, a blend of history and fiction, is nominally about the brutal destruction of a town by a Chinese warlord 1,200 years ago. 
As the warlord and his soldiers slaughter the townspeople, the local queen utters a terrible curse on the Chinese people: they will be weak and disunited and suffer constant tragedy. 
When the warlord asks when the curse will end, the queen answers, ''The curse will never be lifted, unless the Chinese people wake up to the fact that they have been cursed.''
Bo Yang, sipping tea in the living room of his spacious apartment in a Taipei suburb, explained: ''I want to make people think about why we are so weak. 
We have to wake up to it.''
If his writing style is bold and contentious, Mr. Bo seems quiet, almost diffident, in conversation. 
He works in a study overlooking the green hills outside of Taipei, his desk crammed with books and papers and unfinished articles. 
Surrounding the desk are shelves groaning with books, including about 55 volumes of fiction, essays and history that he has written himself. 
The shelves also accommodate the poetry published by his wife, Jeanette Chang Shiang-hua.
Â 
Novels Attack Communism
Born in Kaifeng, China, as Guo Yidong, the author is today known mostly by the pseudonym Bo Yang. 
He came to Taiwan after the Communist victory on the mainland in 1949, and in the 1950's he wrote many novels attacking Communism.
In the 1960's he began attacking the Nationalist Government on Taiwan, and in 1968 he was arrested and accused of being a Communist agent. 
The prosecutor demanded the death penalty, but he was released after serving nine years and 26 days in prison.
''In prison a day is like a thousand years,'' Mr. Bo wrote in one of the many poems drafted during his imprisonment. 
He also wrote several history books while incarcerated, and he says that it was during this time that he concluded that there was no moral difference between the Communists on the mainland and the Nationalists on Taiwan.
A common Chinese culture, based on Confucianism and spiced with cruelty and intolerance, afflicts both Taiwan and the mainland, he says. 
It is changing, he concedes, but too slowly.
''I have discovered that God has predestined people like me to go to jail, whether the jail be in Taiwan or on the Chinese mainland,'' he writes in ''The Ugly Chinaman.''
''Why does speaking the truth lead to such unfortunate consequences?
My answer is that this is not a problem of any particular individual, but of Chinese culture as a whole.''

text:

THERE is the shock of ''deja vu'' about the the Guangdong Yue Opera Troupe of China, which gave its first performance in the Beacon Theater on Saturday night. 
The opera troupe, which is performing 10 operas in Chinese until July 18, is presenting a style of musical theater that developed only recently in Chinese history - a mere 200 years or so ago, which makes it a bit younger than European opera and a bit older than grand opera.
As in a deja vu, the opera ''Searching the School,'' seemed intimately familiar. 
There was the young woman, unjustly condemned; the sensitive man, unwittingly causing her harm; vaudeville pieces of comedic dialogue between a folksy man and a mannered scholar; mime out of a silent movie; a woman disguised as a man.
THERE is the shock of ''deja vu'' about the the Guangdong Yue Opera Troupe of China, which gave its first performance in the Beacon Theater on Saturday night.
The shock was that, as in a deja vu, there was something strange, as if the scene were watched from the outside: and so it was. 
It derived from folk traditions in the south of China, and used folk instruments - including the erxian, a two-string guitar - and an elegant microtonal folk-song style, a heightened speech, in which pitch and duration extend the expressive sounds of words. 
It was also created with formalized gestures: the placing of fingers in the air, the motion of hand against face and the explicit darting of eyes were used, along with the stock situations, to express an inner life.
Then, too, there were the costumes, peach, lime and violet robes and headgear; the women's hairpieces, long black locks divided into parts and adorned with shells and beads; and the sets, gauzy drapes, ocean backdrops and eloquently simple light effects.
And if the plot unfolded familiarly, it was also always surprising, taking place in a different realm: A woman is flying her kite; the string breaks. 
A man finds it and writes a poem upon it; when the kite is returned, the poem seems incriminating; she is beaten and imprisoned. 
In 19th-century opera she would have to have an illegitimate son to be so condemned; instead a gust of wind and a poem carries her to her fate.
The opera, then, fascinated, even while long stretches of dialogue could be understood only by the largely Chinese audience, which could also read the Chinese script flashed on a small screen near the stage.
Hong Xiannu, as the woman, Chilian, created a minutely detailed performance that at times made her transformation into a man and her shifting emotions seem uncanny. 
Now in her 50's, she is reportedly a classic actress in this form. 
She was abused by the Cultural Revolution, rehabilitated, abused because of her connection with the Gang of Four and rehabilitated again. 
With such experience must have come some knowledge of incriminating poems and wind gusts.
Her daughter, Hong Hong, played the same role in some scenes, giving the uncanny another twist. 
Huang Zhiming, as the schoolmaster Xie Bao, was also a theatrical master, mixing seriousness with exaggeration. 
Chen Xiaofeng was the stolid yet sensitive scholar Zhang Yimin. 
Ye Weixiong was Qiong Tai.
The operas scheduled vary from the fantastical to the military and, judging from the first, the Guangdong Yue Opera might well provide a fascinating experience - at least once.

text:

A former foreign leader and frequent visitor here once asked Deng Xiaoping about the best strategy for regaining office. 
''Be patient,'' Mr. Deng said, laughing. 
It was advice born of experience. 
Few leaders have been as far down as Mr. Deng was between 1966 and 1973 and again between 1976 and 1977, when Mao Zedong and his cronies reduced the disputatious little man from Szechuan to the status of an ordinary worker. 
The Red Guards called him a ''Napoleon'' for his imperious ways, but the nickname proved more apt than they imagined.
Like the French Emperor returning from exile on Elba, Mr. Deng came back, in his case to a new hold on power beyond any he had known.
Last week, seven years after he gained control of the Communist Party, China's pre-eminent leader made his boldest move yet to outmaneuver those who oppose his ''open door'' reforms.
At a special conference, more than 130 high-ranking veterans of the party's days as a peasant guerrilla force were gently shunted aside in favor of middle-aged officials selected for their loyalty to Mr. Deng's vision of a modernized, competitive future.
The resignations were the culmination of a campaign that has already resulted in the forced retirement of more than a million civil servants and tens of thousands of military officers.
Almost all the retirees were in their 70's or 80's and had marched with Mao. 
Among the more prominent were Marshal Ye Jianying, 88 years old, one of the five men who sat with Mr. Deng on the Politburo's Standing Committee, China's inner circle; Deng Yingchao, 81, the widow of Zhou Enlai and the country's highest-ranking woman, and Wang Dongxing, 72, the former head of Mao's bodyguard. 
Surprisingly, two Cabinet members, Defense Minister Zhang Aiping, 75, and Culture Minister Zhu Muzhi, 69, were also removed.
In part, the retirements - 64 from the Central Committee, 10 from the Politburo - were designed to bring new vitality into the overaged hierarchy. 
But by pressing for the departure of dozens of leaders with ties to the party's inward-looking obscurantist past, Mr. Deng was also attempting to slay the Maoist dragon once and for all.
It seemed an appropriate time. 
After six weeks at a seaside retreat, Mr. Deng returned to the capital for his 81st birthday on Aug. 
24 with a walnut tan. 
But his age is beginning to show. 
He has developed a minor speech impediment and a miniaturized aid in his left ear has only slighly improved his hearing. 
He banters about going to see Hong Kong after China gets the colony back in 1997, but virtually everyone assumes that the post-Deng transition cannot be far away.
Because he trod carefully in securing his power after 1978, Mr. Deng is in a hurry now. 
At the Party Congress in 1982, the first under his control, he pulled nine of his allies onto the Politburo, but was left with a rump of holdovers from the Mao era who continued to snipe at his reforms. 
In 1983, the policies came under heavy pressure during a ''spiritual pollution'' campaign that was blatantly anti-Western, and it was several months before Mr. Deng mustered the political muscle to suppress it.
At that time, he and his allies devised an expedient for consolidating their position: the special conference now in session. 
Only two such meetings have been held since the party's founding in 1921, one in 1937 to approve the policy of a ''united front'' with Chiang Kai-Shek's nationalists against Japan, and another in 1955, when Mao needed the party stamp on his ouster of a major rival, Gao Gang, and Gao's associate, Rao Shushi. 
One of the keynote speakers on that occasion was Mr. Deng.
The 1982 party Constitution envisaged special conferences for the discussion of ''major problems that require timely solution.''
Although they have never been used for wholesale political housecleaning, the Dengists used their Central Committee majority to deem that the phrase covered the need to ''rejuvenate'' the committee, a task that would normally be handled by the next Party Congress in 1987.
That they were sensitive to mumblings about irregular proceedings was implied by a constitutional exposition that Hu Yaobang, the General Secretary, offered the conference's opening session.
This week, Mr. Deng will unveil the list of those he has recruited to the Politburo. 
At the top will be two men who have emerged under his stewardship as heirs-apparent - Hu Qili, 56, favored to succeed the unrelated Hu Yaobang as General Secretary, and Li Peng, 57, the insiders' choice to take over from Zhao Ziyang as Prime Minister.
Â 
Economic Growth
Both are university-educated, tough and economically literate, particularly the Soviet-educated Mr. Li, who impressed his hosts on a tour of the United States this summer.
Beyond their talents, the new elite inculcated by Mr. Deng will have the advantage of the vaulting popularity of his reforms. 
Statistics released at the conference showed that since they took hold in 1980 there has been an average annual growth rate of 10 percent, against a best rate of 2 or 3 percent under Mao.
There have also been huge leaps in basic living indices - a 600 percent increase in retail shops and services, a 120 percent rise in retail food sales, an 85 percent increase in the income of peasants and a gigantic leap, to 15 million, in the number engaged in private business.
But to describe the strengthening of Mr. Deng's hand on the Central Committee as ''a guarantee'' of the reform policies, as the People's Daily did in its editorial, is to discount party history.
The contest between the Maoist levelers and those such as Mr. Deng, who see Communism as a means of making China rich and strong, has deep and bitter roots, and there is the example of the immediate post-Mao period to show that majorities evaporate rapidly when sentiment shifts in the innermost councils of power. 
The Dengists are stronger, but the opposition is still there.

ABC-TV's final Mutual of Omaha Spirit of Adventure Series for the season, ''Uncovering China's Hidden Wildlife,'' is a splendid production that serves to remind us that man, this planet's ultimate predator, now holds the fate of so many less fierce and less adaptable creatures in his hands.
The show, which will be broadcast July 19 at 5 P.M. Eastern time, abounds in brilliant footage of many of China's rare or endangered species whose habitat ranges from rain forests to the snow-capped Himalayas. 
One sees a Manchurian tiger stalking and killing a deer, and another tiger giving birth. 
One watches researchers working with the rare and wondrous white flag dolphin, a fresh-water mammal once common in the Yangtze River, whose ranks have been reduced to about 100 animals living in captivity. 
And one also observes a brief glimpse of the courtship ritual of the red-crowned crane, a huge bird - total population about 1,000 - that summers in Siberia and winters on the coast of the Yellow Sea in China. 
It is comforting to learn that their population has doubled since 1949.
There is also a fascinating sequence showing Chinese alligators bursting free of eggs and scuttling toward the water while their mother looks on. 
These alligators, now listed as critically endangered, have a chance of maintaining a toehold on Earth if a breeding program being conducted at a research station in Anhui Province is successful.
Other rare creatures in the show include the caribou and yak, the Asian elephant, the Himalayan black bear and the Mongolian moose.
A short but telling segment is devoted to villagers busy burning and clearing land for agriculture, part of the enormous effort to feed the country's more than 1.2 billion inhabitants, an endeavor taking place all over the world that is, along with highways, factories and homes, gobbling up the habitat that the creatures man would protect must have in order to survive and flourish.
Devotees of the Mutual of Omaha series will be pleased with its return to the Panda Reserve at Woolong, where, one learns, a giant panda cub born in captivity last October is doing well. 
The endangered giant panda's habitat has been reduced to a few hundred square miles of high-altitude bamboo forest and there are less than 1,000 of the animals living in the wild. 
(The current Eastman Kodak Colorama display in Grand Central Terminal celebrates the arrival of two giant pandas at the Bronx Zoo. 
These animals, on loan from China, will remain in New York City until the end of October.) The show is a brilliantly photographed but grim account of the destruction or corruption of wild places, as well as a celebration of man's efforts, however belated, to correct the wrongs and lessen future occurrences of them. 
One truly happy note is sounded in the story of China's Pere David's deer. 
There are records of these animals in China's history as far back as 6,000 years. 
Early in this century, when they were nearly extinct, a few of them were brought to an estate in England where they prospered. 
Some of the descendants of those animals have been successfully reintroduced into China. 
Pere David was a Jesuit missionary and naturalist who ''discovered'' the deer in 1865 within the Imperial Park near Peking.

The American official, who asked not to be identified, confirmed a report from Pakistan, but provided no independent details on the test.
A Pakistani with close ties to the Government of President Mohammad Zia ul-Haq said in Islamabad that the missile was launched at a test range in the Thar Desert of southern Pakistan on April 25. 
He said the missile was capable of reaching Bombay and New Delhi and was of ''home design,'' but produced with Chinese help.
Support for China Connection
Another Administration official asserted that China was helping Pakistan with its missile project. 
A Pakistani Government spokesman here said he had no information on any missile program or the reported test.
Development of such a weapon would not violate any international agreement on nuclear arms.
Before the confirmation of the test firing, Defense and State Department officials had discounted the report from Pakistan and said the report might have been propaganda to warn India that Pakistan could produce surface-to-surface missiles capable of carrying nuclear warheads.
According to an annual survey by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London, Pakistan has had few missiles until now. 
The army has multiple rocket launchers, which are used like artillery, its air force is armed with air-to-air and air-to-surface missiles, and the navy has surface-to-air missiles.
Â 
India Announces New Missile
In February, Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi announced that India had successfully fired a surface-to-surface missile 150 miles into the Bay of Bengal. 
The Indian missile is capable of carrying a nuclear warhead, but India denies it possesses any nuclear weapons, even though it exploded a nuclear device 14 years ago, American officials believe that Pakistan can also build nuclear weapons at its test site at Kahuta, southeast of Islamabad. 
But President Zia has repeatedly assured the United States that it has no nuclear weapons program.
Concern over the Pakistani nuclear program led Congress last year to threaten a cutoff of $4.2 billion in American assistance to Pakistan over six years until the President certified in December that Pakistan ''does not possess a nuclear explosive device.''
The Indians, who have been at war with Pakistan three times since both countries gained independence from Britain in 1947, have long suspected that neighboring Pakistan was secretly building nuclear weapons. 
In 1984, American officials revealed that Indira Gandhi, the Indian Prime Minister at the time, rejected a recommendation from her senior advisers that she order an Indian air strike against Pakistan's nuclear development site at Kahuta.
Â 
A Reference to '2 Stages'
The Pakistani report of the missile firing said Pakistan had components for 42 missiles and made reference to ''two stages'' to the missile, but from an analysis of the details provided, it appears that the two stages are actually two separate missile systems: one, 20 feet in length with a range of 50 miles; the other, a 32-foot missile with a 186-mile range.
If these are accurate specifications, neither missile could reach Bombay or New Delhi from Pakistan.
On the basis of other characteristics provided in the report from Pakistan, the missiles closely resemble two Soviet-made short-range missiles known in the West as Scud and Frog. 
The more powerful Scud has been exported to several foreign countries by the Soviet Union, and it is possible that Pakistan has been able to procure some of them.
Most missiles today, because of the reduction in size of nuclear weapons, can be used with either conventional or nuclear warheads. 
However, both the Scud and the Frog were specifically designed by Soviet specialists to carry nuclear warheads.
Of the two missiles, only the larger and more powerful Scud has the range and accuracy to reach major Indian installations. 
If one of the missiles described in the report is a Scud, it can be modified to extend its range at the expense of accuracy and warhead size.
Iraq has a large supply of Scuds and has already twice modified them to increase their range to hit targets deep in Iran with conventional warheads.

text:

Haji Baz Gul, the owner of Arms Store No. 1 in Darra Adam Khel, an hour's drive south of here, said he was not worried about peace breaking out in neighboring Afghanistan.
''We're very happy when peace comes to this part of the world,'' he said, while all around his shop in the arms bazaar sellers and customers were test-firing pistols into the air. 
''But we believe in God, and he will make some other business for us.''
''God will send customers from another part,'' he continued. 
''I'm not afraid.''
He directed a questioner's attention to his photograph in a recent issue of National Geographic, and was pleased to present the range of his merchandise. 
Mr. Gul's principal stock in trade is no longer the locally made rifles, shotguns and pistols that are part of the business and leisure wear of all the adult men in this tribal area of North-West Frontier Province.
Â 
Ammunition at 9 Cents a Round
In addition to various versions of the Soviet AK-47 rifle, the arms dealer said he supplies the guerrillas with ammunition, at 9 cents a round, and such weapons as Chinese and Soviet rocket-launchers and rockets, Soviet, Chinese and American land mines, and machine guns, largely Soviet-made.
His main customers were represented by a silent, unsmiling man sitting next to him in the rug-covered rear of his shop.
''He's bought for 30 million rupees,'' or $1.7 million, over the years, the dealer confided. 
''He still owes 10 million. 
He pays in rupees, sometimes dollars. 
Dollars very good.''
The man, according to Mr. Gul, is a buyer for one of the seven political parties that make up the Peshawar-based alliance of the Afghan insurgent movement. 
The man neither confirmed nor denied the arms dealer's identification.
Mr. Gul said the Afghan was buying quantities of the principal rifle of all parties in the Afghan war: the Soviet-designed AK-47, or Kalashnikov, automatic rifle. 
It is used by the Soviet Army, its Afghan Government allies and all the insurgent groups.
Mr. Gul carries the weapon in three versions: the original Soviet model, which sells for about $1,400; the rifle produced in China under license, at $1,150, or a copy made by the local arms makers. 
The local copy costs about $400, and according to those who have used it in combat, it is not worth even that.
A neighbor, an arms dealer on a smaller scale, said prices for AK-47's took a dip last month when the Soviet Union said it was ready to withdraw its troops from Afghanistan within a year. 
But he seemed relieved to report that after a few days of reflection the Afghan fighters became less sure that peace was near, and the price has reached its old level.
''Business is very good,'' said Mr. Gul. ''We don't believe in war. 
We believe in God.''
The United States, through the Pakistani military, supplies most of the insurgents' weapons. 
The arms are for the most part of Communist manufacture, because they are compatible with the equipment the Moslem fighters capture from their enemies. 
Smuggling or Trade?
The unlicensed manufacture of arms and smuggling of arms and everything else are deeply anchored traditions in the tribal areas around Peshawar. 
The sway of the Islamabad Government is severely limited in the zones governed by the tribes, and smuggling, said Peshawar's customs collector, Salim Malik, is not against their canon.
''I call it smuggling,'' he said. 
''For them, it's trade. 
Nowhere in the Koran is it said you can't do this.''
He threw up his hands and looked heavenward, in despair that seemed real.
Since the tribal areas are, in effect, duty-free zones where the national customs service has no access, they have always been a smuggler's paradise. 
But the Soviet military presence in Afghanistan has made things much more acute, said Mr. Malik.
A wide range of consumer goods are smuggled into the tribal areas, and from there they find their way into all parts of Pakistan. 
In addition to goods from Western Europe and Communist and non-Communist Asia, large quantities of Soviet household goods, notably refrigerators, are sold in Pakistan at rock-bottom prices.
''They're really killing us,'' said Mr. Malik, referring to the damage the Soviet dumping of goods was having on Pakistan customs revenues.
The vast bazaar at Bara, in a tribal area a short drive south of here, sells almost exclusively imported goods that have never passed through Pakistani customs. 
The same is the case at a smaller market in this city. 
Japanese electronics, West European toiletries, dishes and housewares, textiles from all over Asia are openly sold, alongside guns and narcotics.
A dealer in the Peshawar bazaar, whose specialty is kitchen utensils and housewares, gave this explanation:
On regular shopping trips to Europe and Asia, he and his colleagues buy large consignments, to be shipped to Singapore. 
There they are shipped by sea to the Soviet Union. 
The goods proceed by rail across the Soviet Union, by road to Kabul, and on bonded trucks, ostensibly for transshipment through Karachi, to the Pakistani border.
But Pakistani customs controls only a narrow strip at the border post at Torkhan. 
Shortly beyond it, the trucks leave the main Khyber road to deliver their cargoes to various markets in tribal areas. 
Because the Government in Islamabad, like its British colonial predecessor, has never been able to dominate the border tribes, it sees no choice but to close its eyes.
The alternative would be the risk of tribal warfare. 
Occasional kidnappings reinforce the tribal assertions of autonomous power in their regions.
Customs tries to limit the trade by checkpoints on the highways leading out of the border regions and confiscations of imported goods that have not passed through customs. 
But for $30 extra, a Soviet refrigerator or air-conditioner will be safely delivered to Lahore or Karachi.
In the Bara market, Naseeb's Arms and Crockery Dealers sells Chinese and Italian kitchenwares on the shelves, pistols in the showcases and rifles leaning in racks along the walls.
The shop next door has no name. 
It sells guns, loaves of black opium and cakes of grayish-brown hashish, openly displayed. 
''No heroin, no heroin,'' the shopkeeper volunteered.
Local people said the assertion would not stand up to inspection.

WASHINGTON, June 16 (AP) - The Reagan Administration served notice today that it had no intention of complying with Peking's demand that Pan American World Airways be replaced by another carrier for flights to China.

Dan McKinnon, chairman of the Civil Aeronautics Board, said Pan Am was selected more than two years ago for flights to China and ''we intend to stick by Pan Am.''
