IF you've ever wondered why the names of so many computer products use nonstandard capitalization or punctuation, like WordStar, Compute! and dBASE, now we have an answer. 
It's a conspiracy to improve our typing skills.
At least that's what occurred to me in a moment of whimsy while using IntelliType, a thorough and often entertaining series of typing lessons for owners of Amiga computers. 
The program is described as ''the first typing tutorial for adults.''
IntelliType guides the learner through 30 lessons of warm-ups, drills, tests and analyses. 
Each lesson takes about 45 minutes, and at the end of the course you should be well on the way to becoming an accomplished touch typist.
An initial diagnostic test establishes your current level of ability. 
After that, the program may suggest that you start with a more advanced lesson. 
I chalked up a score of 47 words a minute with 97 percent accuracy, and so was moved ahead to about the middle of the course. 
After working through a lesson or two, I was told that I needed more work on capital letters, and I was drilled by having to type passages of words full of capital letters.
Especially valuable are the three bar charts that sum up your strengths and weaknesses at the end of each lesson. 
The first analyzes your accuracy, the second your speed (in both cases, for each key), the third your susceptibility to common typing errors like transposing, skipping or adding letters.
So why is this program specifically for adults?
Well, starting with the fourth lesson, much of your practice consists of retyping passages from the story of Ted and Laura, a couple whose amorous adventures are more silly than salacious, though salacious enough, and whose dialogue contains an improbably high percentage of hard-to-type words. 
There are also spies and car chases.
IntelliType is a product of Electronic Arts, 1820 Gateway Drive, San Mateo, Calif. 
94404, and costs $49.95 for the Amiga. 
If it is not available at your dealer, you can order it directly from the company at (800) 245-4525.
In this age of computer ubiquity, efficient typing is a valuable skill, and the computer is the perfect machine on which to learn. 
But what do microprocessors and hard disks have to do with a 5,000-year-old system of writing?
Chinease, a new program from China Books and Periodicals, is a series of lessons that uses I.B.M. 
PC-style machines to teach the meaning, pronunciation, history and proper way of drawing 80 Chinese characters. 
As the characters are shown on the screen, the learner is shown how to draw them onto paper.
Many people would enjoy learning a smattering of the calligraphy for esthetic reasons alone. 
In addition, Chinese-Americans might find Chinease a pleasant way of keeping themselves, or their children, in touch with their heritage.
I ran a demonstration disk that gives a sample of the lessons. 
The program uses simple animation attractively, and the Chinese characters are quite beautiful.
The demonstration disk is $5. 
The full course comes on three disks, and costs $67.50. 
Either may be ordered from China Books and Periodicals, 2929 24th Street, San Francisco, Calif. 
94110. The phone number is (415) 282-2994.
''Ahoy!'' magazine has been around about four years for those Commodore 64 and 128 enthusiasts who have more than a casual interest in their computers. 
Now it has a spinoff, ''Ahoy!'s AmigaUser,'' for owners of Amiga computers.
''AmigaUser'' is a quarterly, at $2.95 an issue, with more than a passing resemblance to its parent publication, which is published eight times a year. 
In the first issue, there is a list of the two dozen ''best'' Amiga games, two pages of computer-generated art contributed by readers, reviews, technical columns and features on graphics, sound and communications, complete with programs you can type in at your own keyboard.
Generally, the magazine assumes that the reader commands a fair amount of computer knowledge, somewhere between advanced beginner and intermediate. 
For anyone who matches that description, it is well worth taking a look.
''Ahoy!'s AmigaUser'' is published by Ion International of New York.

Detained Without Bail

7, Mr. Chi ''indicated that the buyers of the stolen missiles, who are individuals associated with the Chinese mission to the United Nations, were being cautious about the methods to obtain and to transport these stolen missiles.''

file: PLUMBING CHINA OIL RESERVE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Years of arduous negotiations with China are finally starting to pay off for some of the largest oil companies, yielding contracts to explore and drill in areas off the Chinese coast that may hold the largest untapped reserves in the world.
Already, the Atlantic Richfield Company, the British Petroleum Company and the Occidental Petroleum Company have been granted rights to drill there, and the Exxon Corporation said yesterday that it expected to have a contract soon.
''This is the longest virgin coastline in the world, and we think it holds tremendous potential,'' said Paul Ravesies, the president of the Arco International Oil and Gas Company, the division of Atlantic Richfield that is at work in the Chinese waters.
Although it had long been thought to hold large reserves, the continental shelf off China was not evaluated by geologists from outside China until 1981. 
It was then that Atlantic Richfield, B.P., Exxon and a handful of other companies were invited by Peking to perform seismic and geological studies of the area; the companies spent more than $200 million on the research.
Western oil companies, after years of negotiations with China, are beginning to win contracts to explore and drill in country's offshore waters, which may hold largest untapped reserves in world; Atlantic Richfield, British Petroleum and Occidental Petroleum have contracts, and Exxon expects to have one soon; production could begin in '88, although large-scale production is probably at leat 10 years off; China's energy shortage, which is handicapping its industrial development, is said to be incentive to quick development; map (M)Estimates on Reserves
The size of the reserves is still undetermined. 
But Russ Hill, a spokesman for British Petroleum in London, said yesterday that the best estimates were that the offshore area in China could yield 30 billion to 100 billion barrels of oil.
Even at the low end of that range, the Chinese reserves would surpass the proven onshore and offshore reserves in the United States, which last year totaled 29.8 billion barrels.
''Our thinking is that offshore Chinese reserves represent at least another North Sea, and perhaps more,'' Mr. Hill said. 
The North Sea, which has some of the world's richest offshore oilfields, is currently estimated to have 10 billion to 30 billion barrels of reserves. 
''What we're looking at in China has very, very attractive potential,'' he added.
Mr. Hill and other oil industry executives said the companies currently holding contracts to drill in Chinese waters might begin producing oil as early as 1988. 
But they added that large-scale production was probably at least 10 years away.
Last August, 33 oil producers from the United States, Canada, Britain, Japan and other countries bid for rights to drill off the Chinese coast. 
British Petroleum, the first company to win drilling rights on the basis of the bidding, announced its contract in May. 
Occidental said last week that it had also received a contract.
Atlantic Richfield, which conducted its negotiations with the Chinese before the other companies submitted bids, was awarded a drilling contract last September. 
Arco has drilled two exploratory wells in the South China Sea, and has reported finding large volumes of natural gas in one of them.
Exxon, the world's largest oil company, said yesterday that it expected to be awarded drilling rights soon. 
It declined to confirm a report that a contract would be signed on Aug. 
23, but a company spokesman, Chet Bushnell, said Exxon was ''optimistic'' that a contract ''will be finalized in the near future.''
Western experts maintain that China, which is finding its industrial development handicapped by an energy shortage, has a vital need to develop its offshore oil reserves quickly. 
China is now the world's sixth-largest oil producer, pumping about two million barrels daily from onshore wells. 
But the productivity of those wells has begun to decline.
''Even if their reserves are as big as the optimists suggest, China won't be another Saudi Arabia,'' said Selig Harrison, a senior associate with the Carnegie Endowment for Peace and a specialist in Chinese energy development. 
''Because of their enormous population, their energy needs are going to cover most of the production.''
Nevertheless, Mr. Ravasies, of Atlantic Richfield, said he expected the Chinese to ''export as much oil as they can.''
Mr. Harrison also said offshore oil production could benefit China's economic development by giving it a sorely needed commodity that could earn foreign exchange.
United States oilmen have been attempting to persuade Peking to open up its coast for exploration and drilling since the late 1970's.
The negotiations, only now yielding drilling contracts and joint ventures, have involved a variety of oilfield equipment and services concerns, as well as the major production companies. 
Officials of these companies say that in all cases, China has insisted that its own geologists, construction companies and field personnel be taught offshore techniques so that a foreign presence in Chinese waters would be only temporary. 
At the same time, American oilmen say dealing with Chinese officials has often been a slow, bureaucratic process. 
That stands in stark contrast to the free-wheeling business environment of an industry where transactions are often closed on the basis of a single phone call or a handshake.
For example, the Hughes Tool Company, a major United States manufacturer of drill bits for oil wells, said it began discussions with Chinese officials in 1978. 
These discussions led to the opening two months ago of a drill-bit factory in China in which Chinese workers, using parts provided by Hughes, will assemble finished bits.
But Hughes said its agreement provided that beginning next year, the Chinese would begin manufacturing some of the parts themselves, and that by 1985, the Chinese would be making the entire bits.
Â 
Focus on Technology
''Their main interest is in the technology,'' said Robert Lockhart, president of the Hughes Trading division of the company. 
''They want to do it themselves.''
Another American concern, the Baker Marine Company, a Texas concern that makes drilling platforms, said it had been holding disucussions with China since 1980. 
Although these discussions have not brought Baker any new orders, the company did build a rig for an American oil production company with the help of the Chinese in 1981.
Steven Griffin, a Baker spokesman, said the company was offered the use of a Chinese shipyard in exchange for employing Chinese engineers and construction workers. 
''It was an exchange that allowed the Chinese to look over our shoulders and get some hands-on experience,'' he said.

Communist Party organization of ousted Pol Pot regime in Cambodia announces that it is disbanding

Although this is the largest guerrilla faction in the country, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations as well as Western countries like the United States are more sympathetic to the smaller non-Communist Khmer People's National Liberation Front headed by Son Sann, who once served as Prime Minister under Prince Norodom Sihanouk. 
A third group owes nominal allegiance to Prince Sihanouk.
Other nations have expressed a revulsion toward the Pol Pot faction, which still enjoys United Nations recognition, because it was accused of committing widespread atrocities against its own people after it took over Cambodia in 1975.

30 and subsequently circulated here, accused Mr. Son Sann of trying to amass government authority for himself and said it had agreed to study a further coalition proposal for two months.

'Scrupulous Discussion' Cited

text:

Pope John Paul II named 25 new Cardinals today, including two Americans and a Lithuanian whose nomination was said to reflect a determination to strengthen the Roman Catholic Church inside the Soviet Union.
The two Americans elevated to the rank of ''prince of the church'' were Archbishops James Aloysius Hickey of Washington and Edmund Casimir Szoka of Detroit. 
As with all the others named today, they are considered conservatives on matters of doctrine who follow the Pope's line on major church issues. 
[List of new Cardinals and sketches of Americans, page 4.] Several American bishops who by tradition might have been expected to be made cardinals were ''notably excluded,'' said a senior Vatican official, who added that this was a matter of practical constraints rather than a policy decision. 
#5 Active U.S. 
Cardinals Altogether five American archdioceses will now be headed by cardinals, compared with eight when the Pope was elected in 1978. 
Los Angeles, St. Louis and Philadelphia have often been headed by cardinals but are not now. 
In addition, there are now four American Cardinals who are retired and one in the Vatican.
The Lithuanian named today, Bishop Vincentas Sladkevicius, has been free to perform his church duties only since 1982, having spent the previous 25 years under virtual house arrest in an rural village. 
The 67-year-old Bishop, the son of peasant farmers, is Apostolic Administrator of Kaisiadorys.
When the new Cardinals are officially installed on June 28 at a ceremony called a consistory, Bishop Sladkevicius will become the first Lithuanian Cardinal in several centuries and only the second Cardinal now resident in the Soviet Union. 
John Paul named Julijans Cardinal Vaivods of Riga, Latvia, in 1983.
Â 
'A Surprise' for Moscow
Asked if the Soviet authorities had been advised about the Bishop's designation as a Cardinal, the Vatican spokesman, Joaquin Navarro-Valls, said, ''It was a surprise for them.''
The nomination of cardinals is one of the most important exercises of a Pope's authority because they elect his successor after his death.
Moreover, the College of Cardinals forms the most important governing body in the Catholic hierarchy. 
It can be called by a Pope to review policy on specific issues, as it was in 1982 when it examined a scandal touching on the Vatican Bank.
In another appointment important to the church's relations with Communist nations, the Pope elevated Bishop John Baptist Wu Cheng-chung of Hong Kong, the British Crown Colony that is due to revert to Chinese sovereignty in 1997. 
No Catholic cardinals have been allowed to function in mainland China since the Communist authorities made Chinese Catholics break with the Vatican in the 1950's.
Commenting on the new Lithuanian and Chinese Cardinals, Mr. Navarro-Valls said, ''These are not symbolic appointments, but they are options for the future.''
The Cardinals named today come from 18 countries, and most lead important archdioceses, including Vienna, Montreal, Genoa, Naples and Sydney. 
Also elevated today was Archbishop Laszlo Paskai, who as Primate of Hungary is in a post traditionally held by a Cardinal.
Today's papal announcement, which came at the end of a High Mass in St. Peter's Basilica, had long been expected because in recent years many cardinals have died or reached 80, the age at which they are ineligible to vote in the conclaves electing new popes.
Pope Paul VI set the age limit in 1975. 
He also ruled that there should be no more than 120 ''electors.''
The number of electors had dropped to 97 cardinals, and the Pope named 24 new cardinals of voting age today. 
The limit will be exceeded for less than a month until another Cardinal reaches his 80th birthday.
Â 
John Paul's Fourth List
This is the fourth time John Paul has named a group of cardinals, and he has now chosen 85 of the 161 members of the College of Cardinals, including a majority of the electors.
Making the announcement, John Paul said, ''The entire church takes joy because once again it sees underlined in their choice its own universality.''
He noted that the new cardinals include prelates from every continent.
The Pope has often expressed his intention to internationalize the hierarchy. 
But after today's nominations, Italians will still constitute by far the largest national group in the College of Cardinals; they have 23 electors, just three fewer than when John Paul was elected the first non-Italian Pope in 455 years.
The Cardinals named today included three Archbishops holding senior Vatican posts and a senior Vatican diplomat. 
Their nominations indicate that important changes in the Vatican leadership will be made soon, because they are not likely to remain in their current jobs, Vatican officials said.
Â 
Two Older Men Elevated
In addition, John Paul exercised a traditional perogative by elevating two older men in recognition of their life work. 
They were Archbishop Jacques Martin of France, 79, who is now retired after serving as head of Prefect of the Pontifical Household for many years and the Rev. Hans Urs von Balthasar of Switzerland, 82, an influential Swiss theologian.
The Pope again confirmed today that there is a Cardinal whose name he has kept secret since naming him in 1979.

file: POPE OFFERS A SPECIAL MASS FOR THE CATHOLICS OF CHINA.txt
text:

Pope John Paul II said an unusual mass in St. Peter's Basilica today on behalf of the Roman Catholics of China and afterward called on about 40,000 people in St. Peter's Square to pray that China's Catholics might again enjoy normal links with the center of their faith.
On Saturday, the leadership of the Chinese Catholic Church that is supported by the Government denounced the Pope, saying his recent assertion that Chinese Catholics were being persecuted was ''vicious slander'' and blasphemy.
Church sources noted the exceptional character of the Pope's actions today, pointing to the rarity of his saying a mass in St. Peter's except on holidays or other special occasions.
In a day marked by tributes to victims of political repression, John Paul also paid homage to Archbishop Oscar Arnulfo Romero of San Salvador, who was assassinated by right-wing terrorists two years ago. 
The Pope called once more for ''a just solution of the grave problems that torment'' El Salvador.
Pope John Paul II said an unusual mass in St. Peter's Basilica today on behalf of the Roman Catholics of China and afterward called on about 40,000 people in St. Peter's Square to pray that China's Catholics might again enjoy normal links with the center of their faith.
In the afternoon, the Pope visited the Ardeatine Caves outside Rome and prayed at the graves of 335 civilians, including 73 Jews, who were slain there by the Nazis in 1944.
Â 
Prays for China Every Day
A senior Chinese priest here said the Pope was very concerned over the fate of the church in China, where the Government has fostered the creation of a so-called Patriotic Church that denies the authority of the Vatican and where all other Catholic activity has been surpressed since the early 1950's. 
The priest reported that the Pope said a special prayer for China every day.
In his homily, the Pope said bishops and priests all over the world were devoting a mass to China today in response to a call he issued in January. 
The Pope's mass was broadcast live to China by the Vatican radio; since he became Pope, John Paul has ordered mass to be broadcast to China every Sunday.
Although the Roman Catholic Church faces difficulties in all Communist countries, the Catholics of China are generally believed to constitute the most repressed church.
Since it took power in 1949, the Communist regime has treated Catholics, especially priests, as agents of a hostile foreign power, and an unknown number of bishops and priests have been in prison for more than 30 years. 
The Vatican has no diplomatic relations with Peking, and a papal repesentative below ambassadorial level is accredited to the Nationalist Government in Taiwan.
Â 
15 Cardinals in Attendance
Four priests of Chinese origin said the mass with the Pope today, and Chinese were given special access to the basilica, which was filled with worshippers. 
Fifteen cardinals attended, to underline the importance of the mass.
In implicit recognition of the Peking regime's success in isolating Chinese Catholics, the mass was said in Latin, with only some readings and chants in Chinese. 
Because of the break with the Vatican, the Patriotic Church, the only one that is allowed to hold Catholic services in China, has not recognized the innovations of the Second Vatican Council and holds masses in Latin only.
The liberalization in China in recent years has profited the Patriotic Church, which was also persecuted during the Cultural Revolution, but has brought little relief to those Catholics who have stayed away from the pro-Government churches. 
But under the liberalization an unknown number of bishops and priests have been freed from labor camps.
Last November, however, about 20 Catholics, including about half a dozen released priests, were arrested in Shanghai on vague charges of helping organize pilgrimages and giving information to foreigners.
Â 
Peking Published Attack
In anticipation of today's special mass, the Peking Government on Saturday published an attack on the Pope by pro-Government clerics, It described the arrested Catholics as ''counterrevolutionaries in religious clothing.''
Few specifics are known about the Catholics who remain faithful to Rome or about the ''underground church'' in which many are believed to participate. 
Laymen and priests of Chinese origin who have visited China and have been allowed to visit relatives outside the big cities have reported a fervent faith among Catholics faithful to Rome and clandestine masses in private homes, particularly in villages.
The Patriotic Church is believed to exist only in big cities. 
No priests have been ordained since the early 1950's, when there were about 2,600 Chinese priests. 
How many survive, how many are at liberty or how many still consider themselves bound by their vows is not known. 
One well-known priest, Bishop Ignace Gong Pinmei of Shanghai, has been in a hard-labor camp for 26 years.
Similarly, no one knows how many Catholics there are. 
Their number was 3.2 million in 1949. 
Recent visitors report many secret baptisms and say many Catholic families still bring up their children in the faith.

text:

The White House announced today that President Reagan and Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang of China would hold a meeting in the United States this year.
Administration officials said Mr. Zhao's visit to the United States would probably take place in June or September. 
They said today's announcement had been timed to coincide with Secretary of State George P. Shultz's visit to Peking.
In Peking, Mr. Shultz said at the end of his four days of talks with Chinese leaders that his visit had established a new atmosphere of mutual trust and had ''set the stage for renewed advances'' in relations. 
(Page 9.)
WASHINGTON, Feb. 
5 - The White House announced today that President Reagan and Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang of China would hold a meeting in the United States this year.
Officials here view Mr. Shultz's meetings in Peking as aimed at signaling that after a period of considerable difficulties, relations between the two nations are back on track.
White House officials said tonight there was a possibility that President Reagan would visit China, perhaps even this year. 
''Nothing is ruled out, including a visit this year,'' one official said.
Â 
Invitation Disclosed by Zhao
Mr. Zhao said Friday that he had accepted Mr. Reagan's invitation to visit the United States but made the plan sound somewhat tentative by adding that he hoped the trip would take place even though ''the obstacles in our relations cannot be removed.''
He said the Taiwan problem remained the main obstacle to better relations.
Administration officials conceded that there were ''various problems'' in the United States-Chinese relationship and said the planned visit was intended, in effect, to permit continued efforts to improve the ties between the two nations despite some strains. 
In the last two years, the key difficulty has been caused by American military sales to the Chinese Nationalist regime on Taiwan.
One Administration official said that despite ''difficulties'' in the relationship, the planned visit was intended to underscore the ''steadiness'' in the two countries' ties. 
The official noted that ranking Administration officials, including Vice President George Bush, Treasury Secretary Donald T. Regan and Mr. Shultz had visited China, and Defense Secretary Caspar W. Weinberger was tentatively planning to go.
Administration officials said details of Mr. Zhao's trip had been worked out by Mr. Shultz. White House officials said Mr. Shultz had presented a letter from Mr. Reagan to the Chinese Prime Minister inviting him to visit this country.
''The President has invited Premier Zhao Ziyang of the People's Republic of China to make an official visit to the United States in 1983,'' the official statement said. 
''The Premier has accepted the invitation and will meet with the President on a date to be mutually agreed upon.''
The visit by Mr. Zhao ''is just a continuing part of the relationship between the U.S. and China,'' one official said. 
He added: ''I don't see this as a dramatic announcement. 
There's been a steadiness in the relationship.''
Mr. Reagan and Mr. Zhao met at the economic conference of industrialized and developing nations held in Cancun, Mexico, in October 1981. 
Officials said today's announcement was unrelated to Mr. Reagan's offer earlier this week to meet with the Soviet leader, Yuri V. Andropov, ''whenever and wherever he wants'' to sign an agreement to ban all intermediate-range, land-based nuclear missiles.
One official said the Taiwan issue was ''difficult for this Administration'' because President Reagan himself had had a long commitment to a continuing United States relationship with the Nationalist regime. 
Taiwan was recognized by Washington as the legitimate seat of the Chinese Government until 1972.
Â 
'Political Trouble' Held Likely
One Administration aide speculated that Mr. Reagan would have ''some political trouble'' in the United States if he visited China, especially among Taiwan's traditional supporters in the Republican Party and in conservative quarters. 
Officials insisted, however, that this would not deter Mr. Reagan from visiting China, possibly even this year.
The Reagan Administration has been seeking a meeting with the Chinese Prime Minister for over a year and a half. 
It was originally viewed under Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. as a way of demonstrating ties between Washington and Peking in the East-West context against Moscow.
Problems have centered on the continuing American ties to Taiwan. 
Last August these were resolved in large part in a so-called Taiwan communique that included a promise by the United States to phase out arms sales to the Nationalists in return for China's pledging that it sought reunification of Taiwan with the mainland by peaceful means only.
Â 
'Back to Correct Relationship'
An Administration official said today that before the communique, ''we didn't have a normal relationship with China.''
Relations were ''very difficult and sticky,'' largely over the Taiwan issue, he said. 
''Now we're back to a correct relationship,'' the official said.
It appears that the general aim in the Administration is to seek to use high-level bilateral meetings to cast Chinese-American relations into a firm long-term mold, while at the same time accepting the frictions within the relationship.
Officials have acknowledged that over the last two years the Reagan team has undergone a shift in its thinking about China. 
Initially Mr. Reagan's advisers saw Peking as a diplomatic counterweight to Moscow.
Now officials indicate that expectations about the relationship have been lowered. 
Although China is viewed as an important strategic anchor, holding almost 50 Soviet Army divisions on its borders, it is also seen as a struggling Asian economic power lagging far behind Japan.

text:

As Elizabeth II touched her right foot to the ground here this evening, she became the first British sovereign to enter China.
With a smile and a wave of her gloved hand, the Queen, in a wide-brimmed white hat and a lemon-yellow dress, emerged from the door of her plane and walked down a flight of steps to receive two bouquets of red and white flowers, each clutched by a young Chinese girl and boy.
On the concrete tarmac, beyond the dour, gray cement terminal, China's Foreign Minister, Wu Xueqian, led a delegation of officials in greeting the Queen. 
''I extend a warm welcome to your majesty on behalf of President Li Xiannian,'' Mr. Wu said.
''I'm very glad to come to China,'' the Queen replied.
Prince Philip, the Queen's husband, who arrived half an hour earlier, stood with Chinese officials as his wife stepped onto the red carpet to begin her six-day visit.
The visit comes not quite two years after the two countries agreed on the future of the British Crown Colony of Hong Kong, and during a time of increasing British-Chinese trade. 
Four years ago, Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher paid a state visit.
Â 
Flowers and Flags
After the brief welcoming ceremony at the airport, the Queen rode in a black Mercedes-Benz down the airport road lined with carefully pruned willow and poplar trees, past fields and small brick homes, into the capital, where streets were festooned with flowers and flapping British and Chinese flags.
She was then taken to the state guesthouse, where hundreds of children on a platform, wearing elaborate costumes, were singing and waving colored pennants as her limousine drove into the compound.
During her stay in China, the Queen, 60 years old, is to meet with the Chinese leader, Deng Xiaoping, as well as President Li and Hu Yaobang, the party General Secretary, and Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang. 
But the bulk of her visit will be devoted to touring historical monuments.
Although she is the first British sovereign to visit China, her ancestors made repeated efforts to approach the Chinese. 
The first British monarch to try contact with China, Queen Elizabeth's great-great-great-great-grandfather, King George III, was soundly rebuffed by the 11th Qing emperor, Pianlong, who imperiously lashed the King for seeking to send an ambassador to the Chinese court.
Â 
'The Blessings of Civilization'
''You, O King, from afar have yearned after the blessings of our civilization, and in your eagerness to come into touch with our converting influence have sent an embassy across the sea,'' the Emperor wrote.
''I have ever shown the greatest condescension to the tribute missions of all states which sincerely yearn after the blessings of civilization, so as to manifest my kindly indulgence. 
I have even gone out of my way to grant any requests which were in any way consistent with Chinese usage.
''I do not forget the lonely remoteness of your island, cut off from the world by intervening wastes of sea, nor do I overlook your excusable ignorance of the usages of our celestial empire. 
But the demands presented by your embassy are not only a contravention of dynastic tradition but would be utterly unproductive of good result to yourself, besides being quite impracticable.''
Although George III was deterred, the guns of his granddaughter Victoria's warships opened China not only to England but to other Western powers as well. 
Memories of that humiliation have been interwoven both in the political history of modern China and in the country's relations with the West.
Â 
The Suspicion Remains
The China that welcomed Elizabeth II today echoes little of the 19th century, although there remains a fundamental suspicion of foreigners, a distrust that confines non-Chinese to insular, guarded compounds. 
But it is a China that has overcome foreign invasion, civil war, disastrous economic policies and the bloodbath of the Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976.
It is a China grappling with the future, a China strenuously trying to escape the stultifying bonds of tired bureaucracy by encouraging free, or comparatively free, economic enterprises. 
It is becoming the age of the Chinese consumer.
But the relics of China's past are what the Queen will be shown, a past sundered by Mao's revolution.
No events were scheduled for the Queen today, who arrived with a large retinue, including the Mistress of the Robes, a lady-in-waiting, the Master of the Household, a medical officer, a chief inspector of Scotland Yard and other assorted assistant dressers, private secretaries and an equerry-in-waiting.
During their four nights in Peking, the Queen and Prince Philip will stay in the elaborately restored state guesthouse west of the Gate of Heavenly Peace in the city's center.
The formal arrival ceremony is to take place on Monday outside the walls of the Forbidden City, once the residence of the Emperor Qian Long.
Queen Elizabeth is to spend three days sightseeing in and around the capital, including the Forbidden City, the Great Wall, and the tombs of Ming emperors.
Then the Queen is to visit Shanghai, which was shelled by British ships in 1842 in a campaign to force the Chinese to buy opium sold by British merchants. 
She will also go to Xian and on to Kunming in southwestern China and Canton. 
The Queen is to sail from Canton next Sunday for Hong Kong aboard the royal yacht Britannia.
Correction
A Peking dispatch Oct. 
13 on Queen Elizabeth's visit to China misidentified the Chinese emperor who ruled at the time of George III. 
The emperor was named Qianlong, and he was the fourth ruler in the Qing dynasty.

file: REAGAN AND THE WORLD.txt
text:
ï»¿
After less than three weeks in office, the Reagan Administration finds itself in a political confrontation with the Soviet Union and facing potential crises in Poland and El Salvador even before it has had time to put together a comprehensive program for dealing with the dozens of other foreign policy problems demanding answers.
What about China and Taiwan?
Should Israel and Egypt be pressed to negotiate on Palestinian autonomy?
When should arms control talks with the Russians be resumed?
What can be done about Afghanistan?
How should Namibia and South Africa be dealt with?
What about Iran, now that the hostages are home?
The list is long.
Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. has tried to take charge of the foreign policy machinery only to discover how slowly the system can move. 
He has had to deal with budget cutters threatening America's ability to use foreign aid as a policy tool; he has had to argue with agricultural interests that want to end the grain curbs against Moscow even as Soviet troops remain on alert around Poland, and he has had to try to insure that the Administration speaks with one voice.
There has been little foreign policy comment from the White House, which has been preoccupied with getting its economic recovery program started. 
President Reagan, in his few remarks on foreign affairs, has demonstrated a lack of expertise.
Bernard Gwertzman's discussion of probable U S foreign policy under Reagan Administration presents overview of likely relations with different nationsPriority Given to Tough Talk
The Reagan Administration's perception of the world military balance as moving dangerously in the direction of the Soviet Union has given priority to tough talk about building up defenses and standing up to the Russians, the like of which has not been heard in Washington since John F. Kennedy came to office 20 years ago, worried about a ''missile gap,'' wars of national liberation and Cuban subversion.
There has been considerable discussion in diplomatic circles about a new cold war, but that seems to be an exaggeration for the moment. 
Anatoly F. Dobrynin, the Soviet Ambassador, may have been deprived of his parking privileges in the State Department basement, but he was highly visible a week later sitting next to Mr. Haig at a Washington Press Club dinner.
Despite the polemical exchanges, highlighted by Mr. Reagan's charge that the Russians reserve the right to ''commit any crime'' to advance their goals, both sides seem to want to leave the way open for eventual discussions.
For diplomats and journalists looking for a checklist of priorities and goals, it has been frustrating. 
Mr. Reagan has so far produced nothing like Jimmy Carter's blueprint of 1977: a Panama Canal treaty, Middle East negotiations, a strategic arms limitation treaty, a Rhodesian settlement and normalization of relations with Cuba, Vietnam and China. 
Instead, this Administration, as it struggles with the issues, has produced certain attitudes that will presumably affect substance.
Â 
Administration's Likely Views
From listening to Mr. Haig and his top aides, these points can be made with some authority about the Reagan Administration:
- It will openly criticize Soviet behavior around the world. 
It wants to insure that Moscow understands that it cannot have ''business as usual'' unless it subscribes to a international code of conduct, as yet undefined.
- It regards human rights as a proper subject for diplomatic discourse, but the emphasis will be on the violations committed by terrorists and Washington's adversaries, not by countries friendly to the United States, such as South Korea.
- It will seek to avoid public disputes with allies by consulting intensively on all problems and trying to confine disagreements to diplomatic channels.
- It has no fascination for developing countries, which Mr. Haig has referred to as ''the so-called third world.''
Those that cooperate with the United States will be rewarded wherever possible, as when tanks were sold to Morocco recently. 
Soviet penetration of Africa and Asia will not be regarded as inconsequential.
Despite its acerbic exchanges with the Russians in its first week in office, the Reagan Administration has moved cautiously. 
It deliberately avoided being drawn into the emotional outpouring against Iran in the days after the hostages' return.
Â 
Minimum Revenge Toward Iran
Recognizing that long-term American interests favored keeping the door open to future contacts with Iran, the Administration limited itself to the minimum retribution. 
It said it would not sell arms to Iran, a decision dictated as much by a desire to remain neutral in the Iran-Iraq war as by the rough treatment of the hostages. 
It also advised caution in future trade.
Yet Mr. Reagan, in his most considered foreign policy remarks, ruled out ''revenge'' although he was ambiguous about what the United States might do in a similar situation elsewhere.
The Administration's main concerns have focused on the continuing tensions surrounding Poland and El Salvador. 
Both involve the risk of military involvement, the first by the Soviet Union and other Warsaw Pact forces if the Polish situation disintegrates internally; the second, if guerrillas backed by the Soviet Union and Cuba step up efforts to oust the moderate junta now in power.
In both cases, the Administration deeply hopes that the crises can be avoided but has gone ahead with contingency planning in case they cannot. 
It is already clear that a Soviet move into Poland would create a breakdown in East-West relations, with even such countries as France imposing an economic boycott on the Russians. 
Mr. Haig's first message to Foreign Minister Andrei A. Gromyko repeated the West's warning about the dire consequences to East-West relations if there is intervention in Poland, and the Secretary of State sent copies to all the allies.
Â 
Bogged Down in Salvador
In El Salvador, the hope is that increased American aid will allow the army to prevail. 
There is already concern on Capitol Hill that the United States might be drawn into ''another Vietnam,'' this time close to home. 
A French diplomat worried the other night that the United States would become as bogged down in El Salvador as the Russians seem to be in Afghanistan.
In keeping with the Administration's caution, it has not disclosed exactly what it would do if the crises exploded in Poland or in El Salvador.
The Reagan Administration seems to lack a senior conceptual thinker in foreign policy. 
Neither Mr. Haig nor Richard V. Allen, the White House national security adviser, seems comfortable developing broad schemes. 
They seem more at home with pragmatic decisionmaking.
Nevertheless, they bring to their positions certain ideas, and they have inherited certain realities, that will inevitably influence policy. 
Following are summaries of some of the basic problems the Administration must deal with in three major areas.
Soviet Union
The Administration sees the Soviet Union as dangerous, untrustworthy and antagonistic to Western interests. 
But it recognizes that it must deal with the Russians. 
The problem is when to talk and what to say. 
There seems little interest at the moment in reviving the cultural exchange agreements that were suspended or canceled when Moscow intervened in Afghanistan, but there seems to be a recognition that American public opinion, American strategic interests, and allied concerns all compel resumption of certain arms control negotiations.
Last week the Administration said it ''strongly supported'' the decision by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization in December 1979 to go ahead with the deployment in Europe of 572 new American missiles, while at the same time pursuing negotiations with the Russians on reducing each side's missiles in Europe.
The European allies have always put considerable stress on seeking arms control arrangements with the Russians. 
With the second strategic arms limitation treaty virtually dead, the negotiations on theater nuclear forces have become even more important in European eyes, even though the chances for an early agreement seem slim.
The Reagan Administration, despite its opposition to the second strategic arms accord, is publicly committed to resuming the quest for a ''real'' strategic arms agreement, and one of the studies now under way in the State and Defense Departments is about how to approach such negotiations - whether to try, for instance, to amend the second treaty or to begin negotiating a new one.
Mr. Haig said at his confirmation hearings that strategic arms limitation was ''an urgent and important task'' but that ''we acquire breakthroughs in negotiations with the Soviet Union in arms control only when they perceive that the alternative facing them is a willingness on the part of the United States to match or better what they are willing to deploy.''
Both he and Mr. Reagan have repreatedly stressed that there can be no arms control negotiations without reference to Soviet actions elsewhere - the so-called linkage theory.
Thus, if the Polish crisis worsens, there is no chance of any arms control negotiations, officials assert. 
But even if Poland remains relatively calm, the Administration must decide on a timetable for probing Soviet intentions; it is unclear what it would link to such talks to make them possible.
China
Given the Administration's stated antipathy toward the Soviet Union, it would seem logical to expect it to move rapidly toward a closer relationship with Peking, Moscow's main adversary, in order to build on the framework erected by the Carter Administration when it formally normalized relations on Jan. 
1, 1979.
If Mr. Carter had been re-elected, it is fairly certain that his Administration would have moved toward a much closer military arrangement with Peking to offset the Russians in Afghanistan and elsewhere, despite concerns by some in the State Department that this might damage relations with Moscow.
But such a policy by this Administration has been hampered by Mr. Reagan's preference for what Peking considers a two-China policy. 
The President's campaign statements indicated that he believed the United States should have a more official relationship with Taiwan, which since 1979 has had only unofficial links with the United States.
Those campaign statements produced two sets of responses. 
Taiwan was enthusiastic and has been lobbying privately and publicly for more access to official circles in Washington and for the right to buy the F-16 jet, an advanced fighter that the Unites States has refused to sell to the Nationalist Chinese.
Peking, however, was angered by the statements. 
State Department experts believe that Peking is considering curbs on its growing contacts with the United States if the Adminstration does not stop talking about Taiwan and if it fails to follow the path charted by the Carter Administration.
In particular, China wants the Administration to declare the normalization communique of 1979 to be the basis of relations, and not the Taiwan Act passed by Congress. 
China would also like a sign that the Administration is interested in building on the security links with China that were begun in the previous Administration.
The Administration affirmed, in a little-noticed statement last week, that it would live up to the normalization agreement, but it did not commit itself on security arrangements. 
Some American officials believe that Peking was probably pleased by the cordial Washington welcome recently given to the South Korean President, Chun Doo Hwan, and the pledges by Mr. Reagan to keep 39,000 American troops in South Korea and to maintain security ties in East Asia. 
Indirectly, that increases stability in an area threatened by a growing Soviet military presence.
Mr. Haig said in his confirmation hearings that ''the challenge of this decade'' for the United States is to provide Peking with the incentive to maintain good relations with Washington while not provoking the Russians to the point that East-West relations are permanently damaged.
Middle East
There are two aspects to this problem that demand answers. 
The first, the direct result of the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan, concerns the American security role in the Persian Gulf area. 
The Carter Administration, while talking of the dire threats to world security, moved very gingerly. 
It refused to offer Pakistan more than what amounted to symbolic aid and would not give an ironclad security guarantee for fear of antagonizing India.
Mr. Reagan has talked of having an American military presence in the region, but as Mr. Haig said at his confirmation hearings, it is difficult to find a country that would accept a permanent garrison of American troops. 
Any that might, such as Israel, would taint those forces in the eyes of the rest of the region. 
The key countries in the area are Iran, Saudi Arabia and Iraq, and the United States has diplomatic relations only with the Saudis.
Any long-term policy must consider ways of increasing American influence in the region, but experts are quick to point out that at the recent conference of Islamic nations in Taif, Saudi Arabia, the emphasis was not on ridding Afghanistan of Soviet troops, but on the traditional concern of ending Israeli domination over the West Bank and Jerusalem.
Mr. Haig, aware that Israeli elections are to be held this summer, is in no rush to plunge into the complexities of the EgyptianIsraeli negotiations on Palestinian autonomy. 
He seems to think it is better to wait until after the elections, when it is likely that the Labor Party, which is believed to be more flexible than Menachem Begin's governing Likud, will be restored to power. 
But as so often happens in the Middle East, the best laid plans may come to naught.
President Anwar el-Sadat of Egypt is pressing to come to Washington in the next month or so, and that means that Mr. Begin cannot be far behind. 
This will force the Reagan Administration to begin to develop a negotiating strategy for the region. 
So far it seems to have given surprisingly low priority to that task.
Until there is some progress toward resolving the Palestinian problem - meaning, at the minimum, self-rule in the West Bank - there will continue to be problems in dealing with Iraq and to a growing extent, Saudi Arabia. 
Relations with the Saudis may be further strained if another dispute arises in Congress on whether to supply them with additional equipment for the F-15's that were sold to them after a grueling fight in 1978.

file: REAGAN ARRIVES FOR VISIT TO CHINA AND TALKS WITH SENIOR LEADERS.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Reagan arrived here today for a six-day visit to China and quickly plunged into meetings with senior Chinese leaders.
After landing at Capitol Airport, Mr. Reagan drove to the Great Hall of the People for a 21-gun salute and a half- hour meeing with President Li Xiannian. 
This evening, he is to exchange toasts of friendship with President Li at a dinner also attended by Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang, who visited the United States in January.
Wu Xueqian, the Chinese Foreign Minister, was on hand to greet Mr. Reagan at the airport and travel with him to the eastern court of the Great Hall for the 21-gun salute, a review of the Chinese honor guard and an exchange of national anthems.
Pres Ronald Reagan arrives, Peking, for six-day visit to China and quickly plunges into meetings with senior Chinese leaders; is met at airport by Foreign Min Wu Xueqian and is given 21-gun salute outside Great Hall of People; meets with Pres Li Xiannian; is to attend dinner with Pres Li and Prime Min Zhao Ziyang; is scheduled to appear on Chinese national TV three times during visit; illustration (M)
White House officials, excited and optimistic about the trip, attached significance to the fact that President Li, instead of inviting Mr. Reagan to a large dinner, will go to the guest house where Mr. Reagan is to stay to act as host at a small dinner for only 40 Americans and Chinese.
Mr. Reagan is due to meet with China's paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping, on Saturday. 
The meeting, scheduled for 90 minutes and to be followed by a working luncheon at the Great Hall, is expected to cover issues relating to the Soviet Union, which are considered to be the most sensitive and important topic on this trip.
Aides said Mr. Reagan hoped to advance the Chinese-American relationship to the point of reaching a mutual understanding about the importance of what is perceived as a Soviet threat in Asia and elsewhere around the world.
American officials said that perhaps the most extraordinary gesture was Chinese willingness to let Mr. Reagan appear on national television three times during the visit.
The televised appearances include a speech on Friday in the Great Hall to an audience of scientists, business officials and other community leaders, an interview with Chinese journalists on Saturday, and, on Monday, a question- and-answer session with students at Fudan University in Shanghai.
The meeting with Mr. Deng is to serve as the culmination of eight hours of conversation with Chinese leaders. 
Most of the time is to be spent with Prime Minister Zhao, the head of government, with whom Mr. Reagan got along well in January.
Mr. Reagan will also have an hourlong session with Hu Yaobang, general secretary of the Communist Party, who is regarded as a second heir-apparent, along with Mr. Zhao, to the paramount leadership after Mr. Deng.
The sightseeing aspect of the trip is intended to focus on three themes. 
In Peking, the emphasis is to be on the relationship between the United States and China.
In Xian, the stress will be on visions of Chinese history offered by the archeological excavation of the tomb of Shih Hwang-ti, the first emperor of the Chin dynasty, who built most of the Great Wall during his reign in the third century B.C.
In Shanghai, China's biggest city and manufacturing center, Mr. Reagan is to emphasize the growing economic relations with the United States by touring a factory set up by the Foxboro Company of Foxboro, Mass, manufacturers of industrial-process control equipment.
Â 
Visits to Rural Areas Planned
Visits to a farm, a rural market and a commune are also planned in Xian and Shanghai.
Before leaving Peking on Monday, Mr. Reagan is to sign various agreements, including a treaty that eliminates the possiblity of double taxation for American corporations operating in China.
White House officials now say they expect Mr. Reagan to witness the initialing of a treaty on nuclear cooperation, rather than signing the treaty himself. 
The treaty would permit American companies to bid on the construction of nuclear reactors in China.
The general terms were agreed on last week, according to White House officials. 
The text of the initialed agreement is to be reviewed by the State Department legal specialists and by the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency and the Department of Energy in Washington.
Â 
Congress Is to Be Consulted
Administration officials said Congress would be consulted because the treaty would entail a pledge by China to honor the terms of an American law requiring guarantees and safeguards for the use of reprocessed nuclear fuel at reactors built with American help. 
Congress wants such fuel to be kept under strict control and not to fall into the hands of a country that might use it for nuclear weapons.
Administration officials said that if neither the Senate nor the House of Representatives moves to block the treaty, it would be ready for signature after 60 days of its being initialed.

file: REAGAN BARS ROLE IN ASKING TAIWAN FOR MAINLAND TIES.txt
text:
ï»¿
Deng Xiaoping, China's paramount leader, urged President Reagan on Saturday to prod Taiwan into steps toward political reunification with the mainland, but Mr. Reagan rebuffed the overture, American officials said.
Later, in an interview on Chinese television, Mr. Reagan said:
''We believe that this is a problem of the Chinese people on both sides of the strait to work out for themselves. 
We do not believe that we should involve ourselves in this internal affair.''
An American official said Mr. Reagan had used virtually the same language when Mr. Deng sought to involve the United States as a broker to get talks going with Taiwan on such issues as postal links, family visits, fishing rights, technical exchanges and trade.
Â 
Official Talks Concluded
The 100-minute meeting of the two leaders concluded Mr. Reagan's three days of official talks in Peking.
American officials report Deng Xiaoping, China's paramount leader, urged Pres Reagan to prod Taiwan into steps toward political reunification with mainland; Reagan, in later interview, says problem should be worked out by Chinese themselves; American official says Reagan used virtually same language when Deng sought to involve US as broker to get talks going with Taiwan on such issues as postal links, family visits, fishing rights, technical exchanges and trade; photo(M)
The American officials said Mr. Reagan had declined to put pressure on Taiwan or to act as a broker. 
Apparently alluding to recent experience in Lebanon, the officials said the White House feared that initial dealings on ''a tangential issue may lead you down a slippery slope'' to deeper involvement. 
Although both sides wound up their talks with optimistic dinner toasts hailing the potential for Chinese-American trade, disagreements on foreign policy were underscored when Chinese television for the second day in a row censored Mr. Reagan's indirect criticism of the Soviet Union. 
(Page 10.)
Â 
Protest Ordered by Reagan
This time it came in a taped interview with a television reporter. 
On Friday, television excised portions of a videotaped speech in which Mr. Reagan attacked the Soviet downing of a South Korean airliner and the stationing of troops on the Chinese border. 
The White House had expected both the speech and the interview to be broadcast in full, possibly even live.
Mr. Reagan ordered his spokesman, Larry Speakes, to issue a public protest over the censorship of his views on foreign policy and free enterprise.
''We regret the fact that statements by the President which would have given the Chinese people a better understanding of our country and its people were not included in Chinese media coverage of the speech,'' a White House statement said.
A Chinese spokesman said it would have been inappropriate for China to broadcast Mr. Reagan's attack on another nation over state television.
Among the censored portions were comments by Mr. Reagan about American values, freedom, the worship of God and the principle of law. 
When a White House official was asked whether the President had compounded differences with his remarks, the official burst out angrily:
''We stand for something and, God damn it, I don't care where we are, we're going to say so.''
Despite policy differences, Mr. Deng said, his talks with the President had produced ''much progress.''
American officials said neither side had changed established positions on issues.
''The most important progress is that I met the President the first time,'' Mr. Deng said, indicating that he attached significance merely to having the President visit China.
When the two leaders, sitting together at the start of a 55-minute working luncheon, were asked whether there had been any diplomatic breakthroughs, neither chose to answer.
On Monday, the two sides will sign a tax treaty and an extension of a cultural accord, and initial a nuclear power pact.
With the official discussions over, Mr. Reagan began the sightseeing part of his six-day visit to China with a 45- mile drive through the flat, dusty farmlands to see the Great Wall winding over hills northwest of Peking. 
The stone wall, 3,500 miles long, 26 feet high and 18 feet across at the top, was built originally to provide a protective perimeter against hostile nomads.
Â 
Reagan Calls Wall 'Awe-Inspring'
Surveying the battlement, Mr. Reagan called it ''awe-inspiring'' to think the wall had been built by hand.
''It is something walking up,'' he said, holding Mrs. Reagan by the hand and peering at the horizon. 
''Imagine walking up carrying boulders.''
''How would you like to have one in Washington?'' a reporter asked.
''Around the White House,'' the President joshed, drawing a circle in the air.
On the drive to the Great Wall, people dressed in baggy blue cotton outfits lined the sidewalks of the Avenue of Eternal Peace as the motorcade sped out of the city center. 
Bicyclists craned their heads, but there was no visible commotion or show of emotion.
At some intersections, the crowds were three to six deep. 
People looked down from balconies, peered through factory gates, stood on prefab concrete slabs, sat on sewer pipes or dirt mounds, and even stood around near the barbed wire fence of what was apparently a prison.
There were no flags, no cheering and no jeering. 
Occasionally a hand waved.
A camera crew for the Reagan-Bush re-election campaign committee traveled with Mr. Reagan, taking shots for possible commercials.
Saturday was Mr. Reagan's most varied day in China so far. 
It began with the taping of the television interview followed by recording of his regular Saturday radio broadcast, the meeting and luncheon with Mr. Deng, the visit to the Great Wall, some politicking with members of the American community here, and a dinner for Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang in the Great Wall Hotel.
The setting provided the most successful theme for the talks so far. 
At the dinner, Mr. Zhao said there was ''great potential'' for active economic and technical cooperation.
''The common interest of maintaining world peace and bringing benefit to the people of both countries requires that our two sides transcend the difference of social system and ideology and work for expanded cooperation based on equality and mutual benefit,'' he said.
Â 
Satisfied With Technology Flow
Mr. Deng told Mr. Reagan that he was ''reasonably satisfied'' with the flow of American technology, but wanted it speeded up, an American official reported. 
In his radio broadcast, Mr. Reagan said trade with China would mean ''more jobs'' for Americans.
But Mr. Deng told Mr. Reagan that the Taiwan issue limited the pace of improvement. 
The Chinese have said that they would allow Taiwan to keep its political, economic and social structure, and today, as an apparent inducement, Mr. Deng added that it could keep ties with the United States. 
But Mr. Reagan declined to help.
On issues such as Central America and American missile deployment in Western Europe, American officials said Mr. Deng told Mr. Reagan that his policies were disrupting relations with Western allies and other friendly countries. 
According to the officials, Mr. Reagan replied that the Atlantic alliance was holding together.
The American officials contended that Mr. Deng had ''concurred'' in the American arms buildup. 
They said that, even though the Chinese had ''a different agenda'' on foreign policy, it was ''not inimical to ours.''
An official said Mr. Deng reported that China's improvement in relations with the Soviet Union was ''glacial.''
Mr. Deng greeted Mr. Reagan and his wife warmly before the talks began and invited Mrs. Reagan to ''come by herself independently'' on another visit and ''bring your grandchildren along.''
Age appeared to be on Mr. Deng's mind as they bantered.
''You look very healthy and strong,'' he told Mr. Reagan. ''Today we are in the same age group, we are in our 70's. 
But in three months I will be 80.''
The President, who is 73, demurred.
''Along about after the 70's, it doesn't matter much really,'' he said. 
''I will be there shortly myself.''
Mr. Deng persisted.
''It is not a good thing to enter the 80's,'' he said. 
''I am sure when you reach 80, you will certainly be much stronger than I am now.''
The President again disagreed.
''Oh, no,'' he said.
After a few more pleasantries, reporters were ushered out and the two leaders continued their talks in private.

text:

President Reagan said today that the pledge by the United States to gradually reduce arms sales to Taiwan was based on ''the full expectation'' that China would abide by its promise to seek reunification with Taiwan by peaceful means.
Seeking to reassure the Nationalist Government on Taiwan and its American supporters that the Chinese-American communique issued today did not undermine the security or well-being of Taiwan, Mr. Reagan said in a statement that ''we have paid particular attention to the needs and interests of the people of Taiwan'' in agreeing to the communique.
''My longstanding personal friendship and deep concern for their well-being is steadfast and unchanged,'' he said.
Â 
Taipei Expresses Regret
In Taipei, the Nationalist Government expressed ''profound regret'' over the United States-Chinese communique. 
In a sharply worded statement, the Foreign Ministry said the communique was ''in contradiction of the letter and the spirit'' of the Taiwan Relations Act, which provides for continued United States arms sales to Taiwan. 
(Page A13.)
WASHINGTON, Aug. 
17 - President Reagan said today that the pledge by the United States to gradually reduce arms sales to Taiwan was based on ''the full expectation'' that China would abide by its promise to seek reunification with Taiwan by peaceful means.
The communique, the result of 10 months of negotiations between Peking and Washington over the issue of continuing American arms sales to the Nationalists, contained a statement by the Chinese Government that its stated position of seeking peaceful reunification of Taiwan with the mainland was a ''fundamental policy to strive for a peaceful solution to the Taiwan question.''
In response, the United States said in the communique that, taking that statement into consideration, ''it does not seek to carry out a long-term policy of arms sales to Taiwan, that its arms sales to Taiwan will not exceed, either in qualitative or in quantitative terms, the level of those supplied in recent years since the establishment of diplomatic relations between the United States and China and that it intends to reduce gradually its sales of arms to Taiwan, leading over a period of time to a final resolution.''
But John H. Holdridge, Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs, told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee this afternoon that there was ''no time frame'' for phasing out the arms sales to Taiwan and that the United States had rejected Peking's efforts to secure a specific commitment for ending such sales. 
The arms sales amounted to $835 million in 1980, the high point in recent years.
Â 
Some See Contradiction
The Administration's stated willingness to reduce arms sales to Taiwan drew criticism from members of Congress today, some of whom said it seemed to contradict the Taiwan Relations Act, adopted in 1979, in which the United States undertook to supply Taiwan with sufficient defensive arms even though there would no longer be official diplomatic relations. 
Some senators, like John H. Glenn, Democrat of Ohio, noted that Mr. Reagan as a Presidential candidate in August 1980 had promised not to impose new restrictions on Taiwan.
In January 1979 the United States established diplomatic ties with Peking and severed those with Taiwan. 
Mr. Holdridge, under attack from Mr. Glenn and some others at the Foreign Relations Committee, said particular significance should be attached to China's inclusion of the words ''fundamental policy'' in describing its peaceful approach to the Taiwan question.
A senior official said the Chinese had agreed to include the terms ''fundamental policy'' as a concession in the last weeks of the negotiations that were concluded in Peking on Sunday.
Mr. Holdridge said that the Chinese characters for those words carry the connotation ''of unchanging and long-term.''
Another State Department official said the Chinese characters, ''@dazheng,'' which translate as ''fundamental,'' literally mean ''great'' and ''governing'' and are used only to describe major policies.
American officials have never been sure why the Chinese made the Taiwan arms issue so important. 
They have speculated on internal splits within the Chinese leadership with opponents of Deputy Chairman Deng Xiaoping trying to undermine his policy of close relations with the United States by pressing the Taiwan arms issue to the limits. 
Because of this, Washington went out of its way to try to reach an agreement on a document that would be ambiguous enough to satisfy the Chinese leadership without seriously compromising the Taiwan Relations Act.
Reactions on Capitol Hill were mixed. 
Mr. Reagan, who had campaigned on a strong pro-Taiwan plank, which has been significantly modified since he took office, invited about 30 members of Congress to an afternoon meeting to explain that he had not undercut Taiwan.
Not all conservatives were critical. 
Senator S.I. 
Hayakawa, Republican of California, said, ''There are enough ambiguities in the agreement so that no one should be seriously offended, no one should feel sold out.''
Â 
Baker and Goldwater Differ
Senator Howard H. Baker Jr., the majority leader, said he was pleased with the document, but Senator Barry Goldwater, Republican of Arizona, the Senate's leading supporter of Taiwan, said it was ''a bad agreement.''
As a result of the communique, the Administration will send to Congress either on Wednesday or Thursday official notification of plans to extend co-pro@duction of F-5E fighters between the Northrop Corporation and Taiwan, a decision that was announced last January, but that was delayed in being carried out because of Washington's desire to secure at least tacit approval from Peking, which it says it has done in the communique.

President Reagan will seek support at the economic summit meeting here for a United Nations resolution threatening Iran and Iraq with an arms embargo if they refuse negotiations to end their war, White House officials said today.
The resolution would be the centerpiece of the Administration's strategy for forging a united posture on gulf policy among the leaders of the seven major non-Communist industrialized nations. 
Their talks begin here Monday.
Officials said that the decision to pursue the measure in the General Assembly was made out of the recognition that Mr. Reagan would be unable to secure a unified position among the summit nations' leaders for increased military action in the Persian Gulf to keep its sea lanes free from attack.
''Realistically, it is the only thing,'' said a senior White House official here.
Â 
Reagan May Lift Sanctions
On another matter that may arise at the summit meeting, ostensibly on economic matters, the White House indicated that Mr. Reagan could be near lifting economic sanctions against Japan. 
The President imposed the sanctions April 18 on a range of Japanese consumer electronics products in reprisal for what Washington called Tokyo's failure to live up to a trade agreement. 
The accord was intended to help the semiconductor industry in the United States.
Indicating that the United States and Japan could be close to resolving the trade rift, the White House spokesman, Marlin Fitzwater, said the President is reviewing new data on whether Tokyo is opening its semiconductor markets and on whether it continues to sell the chips in third countries below cost, a practice known as ''dumping.''
The senior White House official said that there was some support within the Administration for the President to lift the sanctions while here, but that Mr. Reagan has not made a final decision.
On policy in the Persian Gulf, officials said that the United Nations resolution envisioned by the Administration would be similar to one that has been stalled in the Security Council.
Â 
Iran Arms Embargo Threat
The thrust of that measure is to warn Iran and Iraq that unless they agree to a ceasefire, withdraw to international borders, and negotiate a compromise, they would be subject to a United Nations-approved arms embargo.
White House officials said the President's attempt at seeking support here for a new initiative was regarded as a way of getting such a measure out of the Security Council. 
The endorsement of the leaders attending the summit meeting, one senior aide said, would bring new pressure on the Chinese, which the Administration has accused of selling missiles to Iran, and which has opposed such a resolution thus far.
''The Chinese would not want to stand alone on this,'' the aide said.
The Administration had stepped up public criticism of China as Mr. Reagan arrived here on Wednesday. 
Frank C. Carlucci, the President's national security adviser, said the United States was ''obviously displeased'' that the Chinese were selling missiles to Iran, and that the practice added ''new dimensions'' to the threat in the Persian Gulf.
Â 
Gulf a Key Issue
Mr. Reagan's discussion of the Persian Gulf has emerged as a key political issue at the summit talks in the wake of an Iraqi missile attack on the American frigate the Stark, in which 37 sailors were killed. 
In the atmosphere of heightened tension since that attack, the United States is preparing to allow 11 Kuwaiti tankers to fly the American flag and to provide naval escorts for those vessels in the gulf.
Although Administration officials declined to discuss what Mr. Reagan will seek in the talks in the way of gulf policy, aides here said he had decided to pursue a new United Nations resolution following a review of options submitted after a meeting Friday of top foreign policy and national security advisers.
On Wednesday, Mr. Carlucci cautioned against Mr. Reagan seeking support for increased military involvement in the region, saying that the nations attending the summit meeting had ''varying capabilities.''
He noted, for example, that Japan's and West Germany's Constitutions prohibit such military involvement.
Administration officials have also expressed uncertainty about France's support for such a plan, noting that country's reluctance to engage in what might be perceived as a joint exercise led by the United States.
Similarly, Italy's Foreign Minister, Giulio Andreotti, indicated Wednesday that his caretaker Government was not interested in such a plan after meeting with a high Iranian official.
Â 
Japan Weighs Contribution
Â 
TOKYO, June 4 (Special to The New York Times) - Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone hinted today that Japan might consider requests for financial contributions to international efforts in the Persian Gulf war.
But Mr. Nakasone said he wanted first to discuss the matter at the Venice summit conference.
A newspaper report today quoted an unidentified senior Foreign Ministry official as saying that Mr. Nakasone was prepared to offer financial help to protect oil tankers in the gulf ''if money can solve the problem.''
Asked about the report, Mr. Nakasone pointedly did not repeat the argument that Japan was unable to take such action. 
Instead, in remarks to foreign journalists, he took a noncommittal stand.
In their public comments, Ministry officials have noted repeatedly that Japan's Constitution prevents Tokyo from getting involved, even financially, with military operations far from Japan's shores.
Correction
Because of an editing error, a Venice dispatch yesterday on United States plans to seek a resolution threatening Iran and Iraq with an arms embargo if they refuse talks to end their war misidentified the body in which the measure is being sought.
Â 
It is the United Nations Security Council, not the General Assembly.

STEVEN R. WEISMAN
TACOMA, Wash., April 19 - President Reagan told a group of lumber industry executives today that he would seek to ease trade barriers to American exports when he travels to China next week.
''You know, as I do, that occasionally the interests of diplomacy and the interests of American industry sometimes seem to collide,'' Mr. Reagan added. 
''I see it as our job to reconcile the two.''
Pres Reagan, without offering specific examples of trade difficulties with China, says he will seek to ease trade barriers to American exports when he visits China next week, speech to group of lumber industry experts, Tacoma, Washington (M)
The President offered no specific examples of the trade difficulties with China. 
But Administration officials have been upset that China has failed to meet its commitment on grain imports. 
China, on the other hand, has run into American roadblocks in increasing high-technology imports and also exporting textiles to the United States.
Mr. Reagan said ''we were in a kind of period of strain'' over textile and high-technology products, but that the strain had eased. 
He said further that China had promised to meet its full quota of grain purchases this year and make up for the shortfall it incurred last year. 
The President made his comments during a visit to the log export facility operated by the Weyerhaeuser Company.
For the second consecutive week, Mr. Reagan found himself on the defensive with a public audience about high interest rates. 
Asked by a dock worker why the rates were so high, he said that in part it was because of the heavy demand for borrowing that resulted from the economic boom, and in part because money markets were being ''unnecessarily pessimistic'' that there would be a resurgence of inflation.
The President said ''I have a hunch'' that if the Congress joined his Administration in ''whittling away at the deficit,'' interest rates would go back down.
Mr. Reagan flew here from Washington this morning, and afterward flew to Santa Barbara for a brief weekend at his ranch. 
On Easter Sunday Mr. Reagan is to leave for overnight stops in Honolulu and Guam before arriving in Peking on Thursday. 
He will be in China for six days before returning via Fairbanks, Alaska.
At the Weyerhaeuser headquarters in a lush campus-like setting, Mr. Reagan heard from local business leaders that trade with China and other nations in the Pacific was absolutely essential to the local economy. 
In response, he promised to press the need for trade in traveling to China, adding that he would do everything up to putting a ''Buy America'' sticker on his suitcase.
