file: RUSSIANS AND CHINESE TO EXCHANGE VISITS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Soviet and Chinese Foreign Ministers will exchange visits next year in a further effort to broaden talks between the two nations, according to Soviet officials here.
The officials said Foreign Minister Wu Xueqian was expected to travel to Moscow in May for meetings with his Soviet counterpart, Eduard A. Shevardnadze, who would return the visit later in the year. 
It would be the first exchange of Foreign Ministers in more than 20 years.
The Soviet officials presented the plans as evidence of growing momentum in the relations between Peking and Moscow. 
For months Soviet diplomats in Peking have been saying privately that the United States has an eroding position here and that China is moving toward an ''equidistant'' relationship between the two superpowers.
Western diplomats take a more cautionary view. 
On the plan for the Foreign Ministers to exchange visits they note that the two nations have already exchanged visits at the more senior level of Deputy Prime Minister in the last 12 months, and that efforts to improve relations have been continuing in twice-yearly meetings at the Deputy Foreign Minister level since 1983.
Â 
Meetings at U.N. Session
The two Foreign Ministers have met in each of the last two years during the fall session of the United Nations General Assembly, each time without any significant breakthrough on the three issues that China has called obstacles to better ties. 
These are Moscow's backing for the Vietnamese occupation of Cambodia, the Soviet presence in Afghanistan and the Soviet military presence on China's border.
''It's not an avalanche,'' one Western diplomat said of the planned talks between Mr. Wu and Mr. Shevardnadze. ''It's just another step in the process of developing a high-level dialogue, only this time they'll be doing it at home instead of in New York.''
Other diplomats said it was probably a mistake to pay too much attention to issues like Cambodia and Afghanistan, which were unlikely to yield progress at any time soon. 
While dramatic improvements in relations were unlikely, the diplomats said, the two countries had already made progress in matters of trade, Soviet assistance in the modernization of Chinese industry, and scientific, cultural and sports contacts.

file: SAILOR_S LAMENT_ WHAT DID THEY DO TO SHANGHAI_.txt
text:
ï»¿
Once Shanghai ranked among the world's rowdiest ports of call, with a licentiousness that outstripped even its own reputation.
A sailor on shore leave found no lack of diversion, from gambling casinos like Delmonte's or Farren's to nightclubs and dance halls like Ciro's or Roxy's, which normally closed at 6 A.M. but would stay open later if the patrons requested it.
Sleazier sport was found in the countless dives, opium dens and brothels near the waterfront. 
Beggars tugged at the jackets of carousers prowling the red-light district off Fuzhou Street and sailors settled quarrels with knives in ''blood alley,'' under the indifferent gaze of hard-eyed young prostitutes.
Once among world's rowdiest ports of call, Shanghai has been turned into one of most prudish by Communist morality
Muggings were commonplace. 
And the practice of bashing a tipsy sailor unconscious and sending him out involuntarily on another ship occurred often enough to spawn the expression ''to be shanghaied.''
But Asia's most notorious dens of vice closed down after the Communists took over Shanghai in 1949. 
Some 30,000 prostitutes were packed off for re-education and several hundred thousand opium addicts were detoxified. 
The old racecourse was razed to make way for a people's square and park, with only some bleachers left to evoke the thrill of a bet on the right horse.
Â 
Communist Morality
Communist morality has turned Shanghai into what may well be the world's most prudish major port of call. 
''If it was paradise, it was only for adventurers,'' said Gu Yiping, director of the Shanghai International Seamen's Club. 
''For other people, it was hell. 
Our Shanghai people suffered a lot.''
Mr. Gu is responsible for entertaining sailors when they reach China's biggest port after a long voyage. 
His club, which was founded in 1950 as the seamen's home, works hard to provide wholesome fun.
There are cheap tickets to local operas and acrobatic shows. 
There are volleyball and basketball games. 
There are tours of local factories and communes. 
There are trips to the zoo. 
The club even hosts get-acquainted parties where arriving sailors can get to know other arriving sailors.
''Recently we sent some chefs to American ships to let them have a taste of Chinese food,'' said Mr. Gu, who explained that it was not easy to ferry Chinese cuisine across the harbor. 
The chefs, who were used to cooking with gas, were also upset to find the galleys equipped with electric stoves.
''But we solved this difficulty,'' Mr. Gu reported. 
''That was a specific demonstration of our friendship with American friends.''
The seamen's club, which is housed in the elegant old Russian Consulate on the waterfront where the fetid Suzhou Creek pours into the muddy Huangpu River, hardly lacks for business.
Â 
Visited by 30,550 Seamen in 1981
Shanghai now handles 85 million tons of cargo a year. 
Last year 30,550 seamen from 85 countries sailed in on 1,135 foreign vessels, Mr. Gu said. 
His club tallied up 90,000 separate visits. 
It is now expanding by building another 12-story building next door.
Sometimes the seamen get a bit out of hand. 
In a brawl last August about 20 sailors demolished the ground-floor bar at the respectable Shanghai Mansions Hotel just down the street from the seamen's club. 
One Shanghai resident described it as a ''Hollywood-style punchup'' with policemen being flung through plate-glass windows when they arrived to restore order.
Municipal authorities reacted by closing down the coffee shops and bars of Shanghai's three major hotels. 
Now a sailor can get a drink only in the paneled bar of the seamen's club, which opens at 5 P.M. and closes at 11 P.M. The bar serves ice cream sodas and pineapple ice cream along with alcoholic beverages.
The bartenders keep a solicitous watch over their charges. 
''We are not capitalists,'' Mr. Gu said. 
''We don't try to make them drink too much. 
We want to preserve their health. 
We want to love and protect them. 
The majority of seamen understand our rules.''
Mr. Gu, who was never a sailor himself, has no nostalgia for the bad old days. 
Today a seaman rarely gets robbed in Shanghai, he said, while ''it was a common scene before liberation.''
He added, ''I saw such rascals myself.''
The ban on prostitution extends even to casual fraternization between foreign seamen and local women.
''After liberation the prostitutes were given medical treatment and were taught special skills to make a living, so they could find jobs and get married,'' Mr. Gu recalled. 
''Of course most of these people were innocent. 
There was nothing for them in the countryside so they came to the city, but there was no work for them here.''
Â 
Ideological Journals in Library
If seamen stay ashore too late to get back to their ships they can sleep in one of the club's 40 tidy beds for about $4.50 a night. 
Before retiring they can visit the club's reading room, which is stocked with copies of Beijing Review, China Reconstructs, Social Sciences in China, and other publications of an ideologically uplifting nature.
Mr. Gu led a visitor on a tour of the club's facilities, which include a table-tennis table, three billiard tables, a chess room and two small restaurants. 
The hall displays photographs from the recent 12th Communist Party congress. 
There is also a shop selling guitars, stuffed animals and local souvenirs, all at prices that Mr. Gu said were cheaper than in the hotels.
''We don't intend to make money deliberately,'' he explained. 
''We make just enough to support ourselves.''
The employees outnumbered the seamen in the club, but Mr. Gu explained that it would get busier later that evening. 
Outside the bedrooms a sailor in dungarees slouched in a chair staring glumly into space. 
In one restaurant a half-dozen other men lingered over their cups of coffee.
Mr. Gu acknowledged a risk that the seamen might import their own Western decadence into Shanghai. 
He said that the club ran regular education sessions for its employees to inoculate them against bourgeois contamination.
''We have an open door policy but we can resist their way of life,'' explained Chao Bufa, an earnest young staff member. 
A large display case in the foyer, lit up like a jeweler's window, offered lost items for sailors to claim when they next reached port. 
As proof of Shanghai's vaunted new incorruptibility, the display included, along with some umbrellas, sunglasses and dolls, a disposable all point pen.

file: Salem_s Spell Goes Beyond Witchcraft.txt
text:
ï»¿
Jim McAllister, who calls himself the unofficial historian of Salem, Mass., conducts guided tours of his adopted hometown. 
''There are four reasons why people come to Salem,'' he said. 
''Maritime history. 
Architectural history. 
Nathaniel Hawthorne. 
And witches.''
As Mr. McAllister noted, there's a lot more than witchcraft to Salem, though a visitor might be forgiven for thinking otherwise. 
Every other Salem shop window seems to sport dark-robed mannequins wearing pointy hats and looking like leftover sorcerers from an early Disney animated cartoon, while gothic letters scream the attractions of the Witch House, the Witch Museum and the Witch Dungeon.
Yet this tidy little town of 38,000 on the North Shore, 15 miles from Boston, has much else to recommend it, including a cluster of handsome early houses in Colonial and Federal styles, many open to the public; the birthplace and other memorabilia of the great 19th-century novelist, and the impressive collection of maritime historical material in the Peabody Museum of Salem.
Lately a new item has been added to the list of attractions - Asian export art, especially as displayed in the stunning Asian Export Wing that opened this spring in the Peabody Museum. 
The new wing houses a collection of the arts and crafts that were created in Asia for markets and avid consumers in Europe and America. 
Most of this material was exported from China, but Japan, India and other East Asian countries also played a part in the trade.
With four galleries devoted to Chinese export porcelain alone, and significant display space for Chinese silver and gold wares the Asian Export Wing has already become an important center for study and research by scholars and collectors. 
Beyond ceramics and precious metals, there are galleries of period furniture produced in the workshops of Canton and India, as well as fans and screens, shawls and fabrics, lacquerware, enamels and ivories, nearly life-sized figurines of Chinese merchants and other memorabilia.
The wing's stairwells, illuminated by skylight, are hung with paintings and drawings of Asian scenes by Western artists, most notably George Chinnery's detailed views of early-19th-century Hong Kong, Canton and Macao. 
Pacific rim may be the latest jargon from the West Coast, but wandering through the galleries of the Peabody's new wing one has the distinct impression that those old Salem sea captains and merchants, the Crowninshields, Derbys and Bowditches whose ships roamed the East in search of fortunes, would have felt at home with the term.
Among the oldest museums in the country, the Peabody was established in 1799 as the East India Marine Society. 
One of its purposes, according to the museum's original charter, was to form ''a museum of natural and artificial curiosities,'' which the members, a dauntless group of Salem entrepreneurs and master mariners, would collect on their voyages.
First settled in 1626, Salem had become one of the leading commercial centers of the 13 Colonies by the time of the Revolution. 
A few years after the Revolution, Salem ships were trading with China and, under charter to the Dutch East India Company, with Japan. 
Until the last East India vessel was taken out of service in 1880, Salem vessels sailed to China for tea and silk; to Calcutta for textiles, hemp and jute; to East Africa for hides; Arabia for coffee, and Sumatra for pepper.
Right from the start, then, Asian exports were an obvious focus for the Peabody Museum collections. 
In 1984, a merger with the the China Trade Museum in Milton, Mass., tripled the size of the Peabody holdings in export art. 
The China trade museum had been established in 1964 as a scholarly labor of love by Dr. Crosby Forbes, now curator of the Peabody's Asian export collection. 
Indeed, some of the pieces from the China trade museum, now in the Peabody, were from his or his family's collections. 
On a recent tour of the new wing, he pointed to a display of ornately handsome silverware, heavy with decoration and complete down to the ''pseudo-London'' hallmark: ''My mother was horrified to discover the family silver wasn't Georgian at all,'' he said. 
''Instead it's a Chinese imitation.''
Designed by the Boston architects Kallmann, McKinnell & Wood, the interior of the new wing soars with a thoroughly modern sense of light and space, even as it reflects the sober proportions of the original museum building, the Federalist-style East India Marine Hall, built in 1824 of gray granite.
The variety of the collection sometimes borders on the bizarre, as in the early-18th-century carved ivory secretary, lavish with intricate and ornate decoration, or the reverse painting on glass of ''The Apotheosis of General Washington,'' in which the first President grimly clenches his false teeth as angels attempt to pull him heavenward. 
Travelers in 19th-century Asia were apparently just as attracted to expensive souvenir kitsch as modern tourists are.
The wing also performs a useful didactic function, with clear explanations of the processes of porcelain manufacture, for instance, or of the market forces that drove this youthful nation's trade with the countries of East Asia.
Just down Essex Street from the Peabody Museum is the Essex Institute, established in 1821 as a center for the study of Essex County, one of the early areas of British settlement on this continent. 
The institute library is a scholarly resource, with information and documentation in both published and manuscript form. 
The museum in the same building may come as something of a disappointment after the glories of the Peabody, but it has much to recommend the diligent, including one of the few known portraits of a youthful and Byronesque Nathaniel Hawthorne.
The period rooms are the work of George Francis Dow, one of the first and best-known workers in historic restoration. 
They are maintained not because they are considered particularly accurate but because they indicate something of the romantic view of the past that obtained among historians earlier in this century.
The Essex Institute also maintains several historic houses, some of which are open to the public, a few by appointment only. 
On the grounds of the institute are the John Ward House (1684, with later additions), with its Elizabethan gables and mullioned windows, and the gambrel-roofed Crowninshield-Bentley House (1727), a first-rate example of the Georgian Colonial style. 
Guided visits to these can be arranged at the main desk of the institute; not open but still worth looking at from the outside are the Andrew-Safford House, with its striking three-story, columned portico on the garden side, built in 1818 and 1819 for a Salem merchant made rich by Russian furs; and the more soberly handsome Gardner-Pingree House (1804), one of the masterpieces of Salem's great Federal period architect, Samuel McIntire. 
(The Gardner-Pingree House is currently undergoing a major restoration that is expected to be finished by June 1989.) There are several other McIntire houses in Salem, but just one is currently open to the public and only by appointment. 
Visits to the Peirce-Nichols House at 80 Federal Street (1782, remodeled by McIntire in 1801), thought to be McIntire's first major commission, can be arranged through the Essex Institute. 
Information about McIntire and a discussion of his Salem houses is available in ''Architecture in Salem,'' a survey of the town's buildings from earliest times to the present by Bryant F. Tolles Jr., with Carolyn K. Tolles (Essex Institute, 1983; $9.95), available in the institute's bookshop and at the Peabody.
Outside the Essex Institute a red line painted on the sidewalk marks the Salem Heritage Walking Trail. 
Following it along Essex Street and across Hawthorne Boulevard will bring you to the broad expanse of Salem Common, also known as Washington Square, lined on all sides with Federal-period brick mansions. 
Like Chestnut Street at the other end of town, Salem Common is the quintessence of a prosperous old New England town; as impressive as the individual houses are, the full impact comes from seeing them together in their original setting. 
The heritage trail continues across the common and down to the waterfront where another group of historic houses clusters around the House of Seven Gables, once owned by Nathaniel Hawthorne's Ingersoll relatives and the model for the house in the novel. 
With the exception of the Ingersoll place, the period buildings (among them Hawthorne's birthplace), set in a waterfront garden looking across the harbor toward Marblehead, were collected from other sites by the House of Seven Gables Settlement Association (508-744-0991). 
The $4 fees ($2 for those aged 6 through 17) for visiting the houses, which are accessible only through guided tours, go to support the association's settlement house nearby. 
The houses, although sometimes heavily restored, are nonetheless rare examples of 17th-century domestic architecture. 
The site is open through Labor Day from 9:30 A.M. to 5:30 P.M., and the rest of the year from 10 to 4:30.
Heading back toward the town center along the waterfront, walkers will come to the Salem Maritime National Historic Site (508-744-4323), with the Custom House, built in 1819, where Hawthorne worked as surveyor of the port of Salem between 1846 and 1849; Derby Wharf, once the focus of the maritime empire of Elias Hasket Derby, a prominent China trade merchant and said to be America's first millionaire, and Derby House (1762), a gambrel-roofed brick mansion built as a wedding present for Elias when he married Elizabeth Crowninshield. 
Both the Custom House and Derby House (guided tour only, three times a day) are open to the public from 8:30 A.M. to 6 P.M. (5 P.M. after Labor Day). 
There is no admission fee. 
Derby Wharf, a half-mile-long, grassy verge extending into the harbor, makes a fine site for a picnic or just a quiet rest stop.
There is at least one witch in Salem. 
Her name is Laurie Cabot and she has a shop on Essex Street opposite the Essex Institute beneath a sign that proclaims ''Official Witch of Salem.''
If spells and incantations are part of her product line, it is not immediately apparent, but the shop does sell amulets and souvenirs, incense and packaged herbs.
Â 
STAYING, SIGHTSEEING AND DINING IN SALEM
Â 
Museums and Tours
Â 
All addresses are in Salem.
The Peabody Museum (161 Essex Street at East India Square; 508-745-1876), is open Monday through Saturday, 10 A.M. to 5 P.M.(Thursday until 9); Sunday, noon to-5. 
Admission is $4; $3 for senior citizens, and $1.50 for those aged 6 through 16.
The Essex Institute (132 Essex Street; 508-744-3390) is open Tuesday through Saturday, 9 A.M. to 5 P.M. (open Monday June 1 through Oct. 
31); Sunday, 1 to 5. 
Admission is $3; $2.50 for seniors, and $1.50 for children 6 through 16. 
The cost of tours of the historic houses (June 1 through Oct. 
31 only) and the institute galleries vary from $3.50 to $5.
Derby Square Tours (508-745-6314) are run by Jim McAllister Thursday through Sunday until Labor Day; after then special tours can be arranged. 
His regular tours leave at 6 P.M. from Old Town Hall in Derby Square, last for approximately 75 minutes and cost $4, $2 for children between 7 and 17.
Â 
Where to Stay
Â 
The Salem Chamber of Commerce (82 Derby Square, 01970; 508-744-0004) can provide a list of area accommodations with prices.
The Hawthorne Hotel (18 Washington Square West; 508-744-4080) is at the corner of Essex Street and Hawthorne Boulevard. 
Double rooms average $98 a night. 
At the other end of Essex Street, on the corner of Summer Street, is the Salem Inn (7 Summer Street; 508-741-0680). 
Prices here go from $79.28 to $100.42 for single or double rooms.
Many bed and breakfasts are in historic Salem houses. 
The most famous is the Nathaniel Bowditch Guest House (2 Kimball Court; 508-745-7755) the birthplace of the navigator. 
Unfortunately, only one bedroom is currently available, at $75 for two with Continental breakfast.
Â 
Where to Eat
Â 
The North Shore is not known for good eating places although the situation is improving.
Signs of a new order can be found at the Courtyard Cafe on the ground floor of the Salem Inn (7 Summer Street; 508-741-4086) where in good weather diners have the option of eating in the patio garden. 
Lunch entrees range from $4.95 to $6.95; dinner prices are from $10.95 to $18.95. 
The chef and owner, Anthony Young, is commited to using fresh and, when available, local ingredients, especially in a variety of crisp summer salads.
Tea is served in the quiet lobby of the Hawthorne Hotel from 3 to 5:30 P.M., weekdays only. 
A pot of tea is $2 and for $3.75, one can choose from a selection of such goodies as banana bread, strawberry bread and a warm cheese tart.
For outside dining with a view of the water, there are several options at Pickering Wharf, the development of shops and restaurants west of the Salem Maritime National Historic Site. 
Among them are: Topsides Seafood Grill (508-744-8500); Victoria Station (508-745-3400), and the Chase House (508-744-0000). 
At all three, main courses run from around $7.50 to $18 or $20 for dinner.
Finally, there is Fragata (21 Congress Street; 508-745-5776), a Portuguese restaurant with moderate prices. 
The menu offers a number of robustly flavored seafood stews. 
Dinner, including two copious courses and a glass wine, costs about $18 a person.
Â 
Shopping
Â 
Both the Peabody Museum and the Essex Institute have first-rate museum shops, with a good selection of books on local and maritime history, Asian arts and anthropology, and jewelry, reproduction Canton ware, ceramics, posters, toys and games.
Asia House (18 Washington Square West; 508-745-8257) has a small but well selected collection of Asian antiques. 
Prices range from $65 for a little blue and white porcelain saucer to $4,000 for a Burmese bronze ceremonial drum. 
Open Tuesday through Saturday, noon to 5 P.M.
Chocolates made by Ben Strohecker's Harbor Sweets can be tested at various locations but the chocolate factory is at 85 Leavitt Street (508-745-7648), near the Palmer Cove Yacht Club, where visitors are welcome Monday through Friday (except holidays) during business hours.
The Alden Merrell Cheesecake Company, (19 Congress Street; 508-744-2820) is renowned locally for their lush cheesecakes ($4.55 for six-inch plain), dense carrot cakes ($4.30 for a six-inch cake).

file: Savoring the Distinctiveness of Korean Art.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE WEST HAS LONG been familiar with the art of China and Japan, but Korean art remained relatively unknown until the mid-1970's. 
Viewed as a mere imitation of its two neighbors, the culture was generally overlooked. 
One effort to correct this situation is an exhibition of 100 works - ''From the Land of Morning Calm: Korean Art at the Brooklyn Museum.''
The exhibition, which opened recently and continues until Jan. 
4 testifies to the distinctness of that culture, maintained throughout a 5,000-year history of occupations by China and Japan as well as internal feudal turmoil.
The Brooklyn Museum's permanent collection of Korean art is modest in number compared to those of the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston and the Newark Museum. 
But, according to Robert Moes, the Brooklyn Museum's curator of Oriental art, its 250 pieces constitute the most comprehensive Korean art collection in this country, because it includes folk art - an area that is not represented either in Boston or Newark. 
''The Brooklyn is the only American museum that has a collection of folk art - it is seldom seen outside of Korea,'' Mr. Moes said. 
The museum's first Korean holdings were brought over in 1913 by Stewart Culin, then its curator of ethnology. 
But when Mr. Moes came to Brooklyn in 1973, he found no Korean art on display; it was all stored in the basement. 
A year later, part of the Japanese wing was renovated to include a small Korean gallery.
This exhibition, which ranges from scholarly and noble art to folk art, consists of items from the collection chosen as fine and characteristic examples of their genre. 
One-fourth of the installation is devoted to folk art.
Koreans developed an earthy artistic style. 
For many centuries, Korea was a cultural crossroads where Chinese and Japanese traditions converged - a bridge to Japan from mainland Asia. 
But although China was a major influence, the culture of Korea has individuality.
''Unpretentiousness, directness, spontaneity and joy are the qualities that give Korean art its compelling appeal as well as its uniqueness,'' Mr. Moes said. 
''Japanese art and Korean art are as different from Chinese art and from each other as are the languages and personalities of the three peoples.
''One of the charms of Korean art is the use of colors,'' he continued. 
''They use very bright mineral greens with red and blue, and jarring combinations, completely different from the color schemes of Chinese and Japanese works. 
The Koreans' love of colors and naivete comes through, even in the more official forms of art, in spite of the heavy overlay of Chinese style.''
The earliest work in this collection, which ranges from the Bronze-Iron Age to the mid-20th century, is a bronze belt hook from the Han Dynasty (A.D. 108-313). Excavated at the Lo-lang Chinese colony in northwest Korea, it is shaped like a horse, and its full, rounded forms and firm posture show the influence of early Chinese nomads of Central Asia.
The exhibit also contains celadon porcelain of the Koryo Dynasty (918-1392), which was for a long time the only form of Korean art that the Western world admired. 
One example of this work is a 12th-century wine vessel, considered one of the finest pieces of celadon ware in the world. 
The ''Ewer With Lid'' has several notable features: Its lustrous glaze is kingfisher blue, ''a rare color found on only the best 12th-century celadons,'' Mr. Moes said. 
Its round body is incised and carved with lotus petals and ornamental motifs. 
Slips of black were applied on the eyes of a small butterfly which sits on the lotus-flower lid. 
These tiny dots were applied with the point of a brush.
A ceramics industry has always thrived in Korea. 
Celadon porcelain was an official art form, produced for the aristocracy. 
Common people used functional, glazed-stoneware pottery - known as punch'ong, which means light blue - that was plain or simply decorated.
Representative of the refinement of this functional art is a Yi Dynasty (1392-1910) white porcelain storage jar. 
''The energy is extraordinary,'' Mr. Moes said of the 17th-century jar, which is in the exhibit. 
''It is Korean folk ceramics at its best. 
The shape is powerfully round and the simple, iron-brown painted dragon motif is bold. 
The freedom and naivete of the dragons have led some to suggest that they were painted by children.''
During the Yi Dynasty, the technique of Chinese literati (scholarly) paintings was redefined, and artworks depicting scenes of everyday life were popularized in Korea. 
A 17th-century six-panel silk-screen painting, ''Kuo Tzu-i's Banquet,'' is a Korean painting based on Chinese style. 
The figures, composed of thin, even lines, are lavishly filled in with bold, vibrant colors, creating a happy scene.
Folk-art motifs of animism and mythical creatures, based on the ancient beliefs of Korean shamanism, were used as auspicious symbols to bring long life and good fortune. 
Images were boldly drawn and almost abstract, as seen in a 19th-century hanging-scroll painting known as ''Tiger and Magpie.''
Tiger-and-magpie paintings were one of the most popular Korean folk-art themes - the tiger was a symbol to repel evil and the magpie represented good fortune.
According to Mr. Moes, it is in Korean folk art that one finds a pure indigeneous form: direct, volatile and with little pretense or over-refinement. 
A hanging-scroll painting in the exhibition, ''Spirit Shrine'' (1811), exemplifies these characteristics. 
''It has a rugged kind of beauty - colors are so vivid and forms are so direct, full of vitality and wit,'' he said.
Among the antiquities in the show is a fourth-century Kimhae gray stoneware jar with a coil-like surface, which resembles American Indian pottery. 
Also on exhibit are a pair of polychromed wood figures, known as altar attendants, that typify 18th-century folk sculpture with its rich color combinations - harsh juxtaposition of mineral green, orange-red and a bright blue that is uniquely Korean.

file: SCANDAL BLIGHTS HAINAN HOPE.txt
text:
ï»¿
The cranes in the harbor are mostly idle, the berths for the heavier vessels empty. 
Guards sit drowsily at the gate in the tropical heat. 
Beyond the breakwater, rusty freighters ride at anchor, outnumbered by high-fantailed junks.
A mood of blighted hope has settled over the capital of Hainan Island. 
A backwater for 1,000 years, known best for its pirates and its exiles, the island is on the downside of a short-lived boom. 
In Haikou, where 20th-century luxury had brought little to most people but motorized rickshaws and 40-watt bulbs, there were a few heady months last year when the port became one of the busiest on the China coast.
This spring, the bubble burst. 
Instead of prosperity for the island's 5.8 million people, many still living in homes of mud and thatch, there was scandal - a $1.5 billion web of skulduggery that sent tremors all the way to Peking. 
Nothing like it has struck China since the Communists came to power in 1949. 
It is still not clear how deep the political consequences may run.
Â 
A Showcase of Reform
The seeds were sown in March 1983, when Deng Xiaoping and his fellow reformers granted the island a range of tax and duty exemptions previously limited to four Special Economic Zones, smaller trade-and-investment areas along the South China Sea. 
By making the island a showcase for Mr. Deng's ''open door'' economic reforms, Peking hoped to end the poverty that had become synonymous with Hainan's name.
New men were drafted from the mainland to manage the anticipated flow of investment in the island''s fisheries and plantations. 
But these required years of development, and the pressure was for quick returns. 
The island's top officials opted for a shortcut. 
Instead of investment, they went into luxury imports - goods that could be resold, at high profit, to China's inland provinces.
The decree granting duty exemptions specified that imports were to be for local use, and warnings came from the provincial capital, Canton, and from Peking. 
But the local men persisted. 
Over a 14-month period, until last March, they authorized the import-for-resale of 89,000 cars and light trucks, nearly 2.9 million color television sets, more than a quarter of a million videotape recorders and 122,000 motorcycles, along with a wealth of cosmetics, food and toys.
Â 
Mercedes Limousines
By Chinese standards, the scale was grotesque. 
The motor vehicles arriving here and in the harbor at Sanya, a resort town on the island's southern coast, exceeded the total imported by the rest of the country in a year. 
Many were in the luxury class, including 20 Mercedes-Benz limousines that sell for more than $50,000 in Hong Kong. 
Harbors were choked, and navy landing craft from the island's west coast were chartered to ship vehicles to the mainland.
Temptations to join in were overwhelming. 
Among nearly 900 institutions on the island that went into the car business was the island's principal newspaper, The Hainan Ribao, which turned a $1.4 million profit, its first in years, from the resale of 400 Toyota vans.
In the end, 27 of the country's 29 self-governing regions, some of them 2,000 miles away, bought some of the tainted goods, paying as much as 300 percent of the original import price. 
When Peking clamped down, a team of 100 investigators sent to the island discovered that in order to exploit the import loophole, local agents had mounted the biggest black-market currency operation in the country's history.
The agents had raised 4.2 billion yuan in loans from local branches of two Peking banks, equivalent to $1.5 billion at the official rate of exchange. 
They took the money to the mainland, principally to the Special Economic Zone at Shenzhen, outside Hong Kong, where they traded it at black market rates to trading companies granted foreign exchange allowances to import technology for the country's modernization.
Â 
'Red Packet' Bonuses
When the dust settled, more than 2 billion yuan, equivalent to $700 million, was unrecoverable. 
Much of it had been paid out in special ''red packet'' bonuses to employees at participating institutions, including 800 yuan each for reporters and editors at The Hainan Ribao. 
The island's physical culture commission used its profits to build a stadium. 
Other government agencies commissioned new office buildings.
Only three officials were arrested, among them the chief editor of The Hainan Ribao, Guan Xin, accused of pocketing a 10,000-yuan commission. 
Senior officials who initiated the scheme, pleading that they had made no personal profit, got off lightly. 
For having made ''serious mistakes'' and for having turned ''a deaf ear'' to warnings from higher levels, the two top government officials on the island, Lei Yu and Chen Yuyi, were transferred to lower-ranking jobs. 
The island's party boss, Ao Enxu, received a reprimand.
For many on the island, the scandal was a body blow. 
A settled part of China since the Han Dynasty, 2,000 years ago, it had been neglected by generations of rulers in Peking. 
Even after the Communists took power there was still little effort to improve the economy. 
In some years the island's entire output was worth less than that of some of the more prosperous counties on the mainland.
The injection of money from the import boondoggle raised hopes that matters were turning for the better. 
Instead, a clamp has been placed on all new investments, particularly those involving foreign exchange, while investigators unravel what occurred. 
The effects are visible everywhere in abandoned construction sites, deserted restaurants that were booming last year, and empty rooms where trading companies have disappeared.
Â 
Rusting Vehicles
Outside Haikou, thousands of new Japanese cars and trucks sit in muddy lots, rusting in the sea air. 
In the hinterland, along sinuous roads that run through thick groves of rubber and papaya trees, signs of the bubble are evident in the Honda motorcycles and Toshiba refrigerators that sit by village homes. 
But mostly the mood is one of disillusion, as though the island must resign itself to becoming a backwater once again.
The malaise is palpable at the island's tourist headquarters in Haikou. 
Plans for a rapid increase in the number of visitors - 24,000 came last year, all but 750 of them overseas Chinese - are in doubt because of a construction halt on many of the 18 new hotels.
Liu Min, deputy manager of the office, admits to feelings of resentment at the officials who allowed it all to happen. 
''After the scandal, investors are hesitating to put money on the island,'' he said. 
''They seem doubtful of the stabilityI of our policies.''
He paused, and added: ''It is all a great pity. 
For generations people on the mainland thought that we on Hainan were like monkeys, strange people who were not like them at all. 
Now we have a lot more persuading to do.''

EACH month, 20,000 Russian language copies of Scientific American magazine are snapped up as soon as they hit the streets in the Soviet Union. 
In Peking, the circulation of Discover magazine, published in the United States by Time Inc., is expected to go above 100,000 by 1986. 
In Shanghai 50,000 translated copies of the American publication Science News are printed each week.
The popular science journals of the United States are being circulated to the far corners of the earth as foreign governments, including the Soviet Union and China, recognize their education value in keeping pace with the explosive growth of high technology elsewhere.
Article on popularity of science journals of the United States, which are being circulated to far corners of the earth as foreign governments, including Soviet Union and China, recognize their education value in keeping pace with explosive growth of high technology elsewhere; Jonathan Piel, Scientific American's president, says in capitalist countries, foreign edition is a joint effort with local publisher who arranges for translations, production and distribution; Scientific American appears in Moscow as In the World of Science, with a subtitle indicating that it is a Russian-language version of Scientific American; foreign editions also appear in Chinese, French, German, Italian, Japanese and Spanish; illustrations and photos (M)
Ironically, such foreign language editions are proliferating as the Reagan Administration seeks to stem the overseas flow of high technology information.
Scientific American, for example, is now published in eight foreign languages. 
Jonathan Piel, Scientific American's president and editor, said foreign publishers may occasionally substitute an article of local interest for one that appears too parochial for its audience or that would raise political problems.
For example, the Russian edition, produced by Mir Publishing in Moscow, did not use an article on the controversy over the Reagan Administration's missile-defense program that was published in the United States edition last June. 
This, Mr. Piel suspects, may have been because the article included information on Soviet antisatellite and space surveillance systems whose publication in the Soviet Union might be illegal or might be taken as confirmation of Soviet military strategies.
On the other hand, an article in the August issue entitled ''The Climatic Effects of Nuclear War'' was included when that issue was reproduced in full as the October issue of the Moscow edition. 
The Moscow edition appears monthly under the title, in Russian, ''In the World of Science,'' with a subtitle indicating that it is a Russian-language version of Scientific American.
Foreign editions of the magazine also appear in Chinese, French, German, Italian, Japanese and Spanish, as well as the original English. 
According to Mr. Piel, in capitalist countries the foreign edition is a joint
effort with a local publisher who
arranges for translations, production and distribution. 
In China and the Soviet Union
the arrangement is by contract
with a governmental institution,
such as the Institute for Scientific and Technological Information in Chongqing. 
In each
country articles are farmed out
to bilingual specialists in the
subject of the article and their
translations are then polished
by an editorial board. 
While the quality of color
reproductions in the Soviet edition is not up to the standards of
the American one, it is remarkably good compared to other
Soviet publications. 
In contrast
to the numerous advertisements
in the American edition, advertisements in the Russian edition are chiefly limited to those promoting other products of the Moscow publisher.
On the other hand, the Chinese edition of Discover routinely carries advertisements for such products as Marlboro cigarettes. 
In view of the current Chinese emphasis on catching up with the West, James B. Hays, publisher of Discover, said he hopes that American manufacturers of computers and other such items will also place advertisements.
Â 
Collapse of Connecticut Bridge
Under the contract between Discover and the Chinese, revenue from such advertisements would go to the American magazine. 
In view of the present trend in China toward free enterprise, Mr. Hays said he also expects Chinese concerns to place advertisements. 
Revenue from them would go to the publisher in Peking.
The Chinese edition of Discover, which sells for the equivalent of 30 cents, first appeared in 1983 and includes high-quality full-color photographs on heavy paper, usually with English text, intermingled with Chinese text and illustrations.
It appears quarterly and the Chinese editors select only part of what is published in the United States edition. 
Articles in recent issues have dealt with such subjects as the collapse of the Mianus River bridge on the Connecticut Turnpike, with diagrams to illustrate the suspension system that failed.
Â 
Pirated Editions of Science News
Science News, published in Washington by Science Service, appears in a Chinese edition that is essentially pirated, although the magazine cooperates by sending each issue to Peking. 
According to Edward G. Sherburne Jr., the American publisher, the Chinese publisher has available 200 scientists and engineers qualified to translate articles on specific subjects, and the translator is identified at the end of each article.
Science Digest appears in Danish, Italian, Norwegian and Swedish, and until recently a Portuguese edition was published in Brazil. 
Science Digest is published by the Hearst Corporation, some of whose other publications, such as Cosmopolitan, also appear in foreign languages.
Last year, according to John Wrede, president of McGraw-Hill Publications Company, individual issues of four McGraw-Hill magazines were translated into Chinese in a joint venture with China Consultants of Hong Kong. 
They were Aviation Week and Space Technology, Chemical Engineering, Power, and Textile World. 
From 1979 to 1983 the same consortium published in Chinese a journal, American Industrial Report, containing selected articles from American journals.
Â 
Science 85 in Italian
Before Science 85 was born in 1980 as Science 80 (it changes its title annually) it was approached by an Italian publisher interested in producing an Italian edition. 
According to Allen L. Hammond, the editor of Science 85, the Italian press run is now 40,000. 
It uses photographs and color separations provided by Science 85, which is published by the American Association for the Advancement of Science.
In recent years popular science magazines have proliferated in Italy, as they have in the United States, with six started in recent years, Dr. Hammond said. 
Half, however, have already gone out of business, he added.
''We don't want to make investments abroad,'' Dr. Hammond said. 
His magazine grants a license rather than sharing profits. 
A Japanese magazine uses a great deal of material from Science 85, which is also negotiating for two other foreign outlets whose identities have not been disclosed.
Soon after the magazine appeared it discussed with the Chinese a possible edition there, and some issues were translated. 
But, according to Dr. Hammond, it was decided that the content was better suited to a college-educated American audience than to one in China.
Psychology Today has contracted to provide publishers of Dutch, German and Italian magazines with exclusive rights to its articles. 
Earlier arrangements with Japanese and French publishers have ended, although the French still buy a number of articles, according to Patrice D. Horn, the editor.

text:

YOU have to say this for ''Tai-Pan'': it's ridiculous - but in a big way. 
It's two hours of Super Comics: Bearded Brutes!
Busty Belles!
Bloody Blades!
Exotic Settings!
Colorful Costumes!
A Beheading!
A Castration!
A Typhoon!
The movie, which opens today at the Criterion Center and other theaters, is taken from James Clavell's best seller of the same name, part of his million-page saga about Western traders in mid-19th-century China.
We meet Tai-Pan, which means, loosely, the boss trader (Bryan Brown in a rolling Scottish accent), as he is being chased out of Canton by the Emperor, who is displeased with foreigners bearing opium. 
Tai-Pan is so strong that he can demolish a boatful of rough-looking Chinese attackers single-handedly, but when it comes to white men, he has trouble one on one. 
Anyhow, he gets the British Government to take over the island of Hong Kong so he can set up shop. 
Yes, he's the man to thank for all that duty-free stuff.
Tai-Pan has two virtuous and handsome sons in their 20's, one by his Glasgow wife, the other by a former Chinese concubine. 
He also has a Chinese mistress about a third his age (Joan Chen, being unbearably cute) who occasionally tries on a Scottish burr and often takes off her clothes. 
And he has a bitter enemy (John Stanton), who has a pathological son on whom he dotes and a ninny of a daughter for whom one of Tai-Pan's handsome, virtuous son falls.
The Cast of Thousands is all dressed up, and there's no end of posing, strutting, milling and glowering. 
There's also a lot of scenery, shot in China, Macao and Hong Kong by the reliable Jack Cardiff. 
As for the acting, the screenplay does not make that easy. 
The lines often seem to have been cribbed from an English-language primer: ''I am proud to be British, but I am also proud to be Chinese.''
''This is not the Mary Sinclair I know.''
Only Norman Rodway as a dissolute but good-natured artist manages to bring a bit of life to his role.
The director, Daryl Duke, shows an infallible talent for accentuating the obvious. 
He is abetted by Maurice Jarre's music, which can be very noisy. 
But not noisy enough to cover lines like ''I'll use the devil to break you and, by God, break you I will.''

file: SCURVY RASCAL SEES IT THROUGH.txt
text:
ï»¿
FLASHMAN AND THE DRAGON By George MacDonald Fraser. 
320 pp. 
New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $16.95.
AT the heart of good history, even the most rarefied and scholarly history, is a naughty little secret: good storytelling. 
A history that isn't implicitly a colorful, twisty yarn is at best fodder for other specialists - and not particularly nourishing fodder at that, for a historian's richest insights generally come when he asks himself what it would have been like to have been there, to have confronted the personalities, conditions and conundrums of which history is made. 
The British novelist and screenwriter George MacDonald Fraser understands all this, but he works from the opposite direction: at the heart of his vivid storytelling is plenty of solid history. 
In creating his justly celebrated Flashman novels, of which the rousing ''Flashman and the Dragon'' is the eighth, he seizes on a historical milieu and then hurls himself into it - or rather he hurls his dastardly alter ego, Sir Harry Flashman V.C., the self-avowed lecher, blackguard and coward whose military and amorous exploits Mr. Fraser has been chronicling since 1969.
Flashman's putative memoirs are set amid the great intrigues and upheavals of the Victorian era, from the Indian Mutiny to the Crimean War, and without Mr. Fraser's scrupulous regard for history they would probably read like third-rate Ian Fleming, meandering accounts of blood and villainy leavened only by the occasional roll in the hay. 
But Mr. Fraser's enthrallment with history is infectious. 
He coaxes its remotest figures to life, footnotes with zeal, corrects his hero's memory when it strays from documented fact (and the ever-so-slight straying adds to the memoirs' verismo), and gives the old soldier an admiring slap on the back wherever his observations prove most pungent.
''Flashman and the Dragon'' sets us down in China at the height of the 14-year Taiping rebellion (1850-64), during which a fanatical Christian army (led by a Cantonese madman whose hallucinations of holy conquest began shortly after he flunked his civil service exams) battled the Manchu dynasty in the bloodiest civil war the world has ever known. 
Flashman enters the fray in customary fashion, enticed by a lissome blonde into running guns to the Taipings. 
Thereafter, we find him lying and lovemaking among scurvy Christian soldiers, Manchu cutthroats and the odd Yangtze River pirate queen; marching northward to Peking alongside Lord Elgin (whose father had stripped Greece of the marbles that bear his name); and playing secret paramour to the Imperial Yi Concubine, who would later rule as the last Empress of China.
But there are longueurs and passages of meretricious vulgarity. 
Mr. Fraser is not above composing paeans to ''the satin gleam of bums, bellies and boobies in the candle-shine.''
And his narrative structure is irritatingly slack. 
His most delicious characters - a concupiscent giantess in a steel collar, for instance, or a portly rebel kingpin whose suave cruelty reminds one of Sydney Greenstreet - no sooner captivate us than they're dropped from the novel forever. 
Mr. Fraser even abandons the fascinating Taipings about two-thirds of the way through, the better to concentrate on their more vaguely sketched (though equally vicious) enemies. 
For readers who, like me, take pleasure in the tapestry of correspondences and cross-references that careful novelists weave, Mr. Fraser's linear doodling looks lazy.
Still, history creates correspondences of its own, and Fraser exploits these beautifully. 
It's great fun to find Chinese Gordon, the future martyr of Khartoum, looting a Manchu palace while cooing, ''What pleasure to look at a gift for a dear one at home, and think of the joy with which it will be received.''
And Mr. Fraser's historical perspective doesn't stop at Victorian celebrity-spotting. 
His vibrant descriptions of life among the Taipings pointedly remind one of the Khmer Rouge, or the Maoist Chinese before them. 
And he uses his portrayal of the Yi Concubine to construct a masterly portrait of eroticism and power. 
As much as Flashman adores her, he is also repulsed by her, by ''the sudden capricious change from hellish scheming to playful mischief, from the cold, unspeakably cruel calculation that meant dreadful death for men she'd never seen, to happy high spirits demanding crackling with cherries, and a tea-leaf pillow because her eyes were tired.''
Flashman himself has deepened. 
True, he still dubs any man with skin darker than the full moon a ''nigger''; and yes, he remains a rat with women, a liar with men and a poltroon perfectly willing to kowtow to savages when braver souls would rather die. 
But one grows fond of Flashman, fond of the delight he takes in the world's absurd propensity to mistake him for an honorable man, fond of the way his cynicism balances with a genuine amazement at the wonders he beholds. 
He is no longer merely the serviceable mock-up of a Victorian cad that he was when Fraser adopted him from his previous incarnation as the bully in Thomas Hughes's ''Tom Brown's School Days.''
The hero of ''Flashman and the Dragon'' is a man of our era, a man who brings a subtle 20th-century sensibility - and a wickedly eloquent tongue - to the beauties and barbarisms of 1860's China. 
He would make a terrific historian.

file: SECRECY IN A DISMISSAL BY STANFORD FUELS ACADEMIC FREEDOM DISPUTE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Stanford University's expulsion of a graduate student, on the basis of a secret report by faculty members who investigated his anthropological work in China, has touched off a dispute about academic freedom.
The student, Steven W. Mosher, was dismissed from Stanford's doctoral program by an 11-0 vote of the anthropology department last February, with no reported dissent. 
But the secrecy surrounding the decision and conflicting accounts of the charges against the student have raised questions over whether Stanford had bowed to pressure from Peking to retaliate against Mr. Mosher.
Mr. Mosher, 34 years old, conducted research in a village near Canton in 1979 and 1980. 
He was one of the first American scholars allowed to work in China after normal relations between Peking and Washington were restored.
Stanford University's expulsion of a graduate student, on the basis of a secret report by faculty members who investigated his anthropological work in China, has touched off a dispute about academic freedom.Work Led to Chinese Ban
He gathered a highly unusual collection of local police and government documents that the Chinese consider secret, and he later published an article in a Taiwanese magazine that described a campaign to force many women to undergo abortions as part of China's birth control program.
The Chinese were angered by Mr. Mosher's activities, and soon after his departure, whether by coincidence or not, banned all further field research by American academics. 
In conversations with other American scholars, Chinese officials also began accusing Mr. Mosher of a long list of charges, including spying, smuggling and immoral conduct with a woman. 
Several of the scholars reported the charges to Stanford.
Stanford then set up a three-member investigating committee that reported that Mr. Mosher had engaged in ''illegal and seriously unethical conduct'' in China. 
But the anthropology department has refused to release the 47-page committee report on which the vote to expel Mr. Mosher was based, contending that it ''contains information that may be injurious to innocent parties.''
In a statement this spring responding to critical letters and editorials, Donald Kennedy, president of Stanford, termed the dispute over Mr. Mosher ''one of those unfortunate cases in which we find two important social values in collision.''
He said the university would like to be able to release the information to answer questions about ''possible infringements on academic freedom or about the operation of political influence.''
''But an equally strong set of values attaches to the need for privacy,'' he went on, saying that the information might be ''damaging'' to other people.
A spokesman for the university said Mr. Kennedy had not read the investigating committee's report.
Â 
Ex-Wife Said to Be a Source
Although members of the anthropology department have offered differing accounts of the charges against Mr. Mosher, several professors said the critical evidence had been supplied by his former wife, Maggie So, a Chinese born in Hong Kong.
In the spring of 1980, after a bitter quarrel over Mr. Mosher's demand for a divorce, Miss So went to the United States Consulate in Canton, where she accused him of bribing local officials to obtain documents, the anthropology professors said. 
She complained that Mr. Mosher's actions were endangering her relatives who still lived in the village, they said.
In early 1982, after the couple were divorced, the professors said, she repeated her accusations to the Stanford investigating committee, calling collect from France. 
One professor said Miss So had also charged Mr. Mosher with financing his operation by smuggling Chinese antiques to Hong Kong, though other professors said this was untrue. 
Miss So's current whereabouts are unknown.
Â 
'Abolutely False,' He Says
Mr. Mosher derides Miss So's information as ''absolutely false and unsubstantiated slander'' from a ''scorned woman who vowed to ruin me.''
In a telephone interview from Taiwan, where he now lives, Mr. Mosher said he had been dismissed because of Chinese anger over the abortion article and pressure from American China scholars eager to please Peking.
Stanford has denied both charges. 
Clifford R. Barnett, the chairman of the anthropology department, insisted that the department had been fair and had, for example, excluded China specialists, who might have appeared to be subject to pressure from the Chinese Government, from the investigating committee and the departmental vote.
Â 
Stanford Widely Criticized
The university, however, has been widely criticized for its handling of the case. 
Editorials in The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal questioned the need for secrecy and suggested that Mr. Mosher might have been expelled to mollify the Chinese. 
Arthur Wolf, a Stanford anthropology professor, said all department members had received critical letters from groups that oppose abortion.
Several professors at such universities as Harvard, Brown and Yale, who asked not to be named to avoid cooler relations with colleagues at Stanford, have raised questions about how much authority a university should exercise over students' actions off campus. 
They pointed out that Harvard University, along with some other Ivy League schools, had adopted a policy of limiting disciplinary action to offenses connected with a student's academic record or behavior on campus.
Irving Louis Horowitz, the editor of Society magazine and a professor of political science and sociology at Rutgers University, said there was a serious question whether Stanford could withhold a degree from a student without making public the charges against him.
Â 
Quality of Work Termed Issue
''The issue is not whether Mosher's a nice man but the quality of his work,'' said Mr. Horowitz. ''I've read his manuscript,'' he added, referring to Mr. Mosher's proposed dissertation, ''and I'd be glad to have him as a graduate student.''
''I think Stanford felt they had to deliver a head to the People's Republic,'' Mr. Horowitz charged. 
''If Mosher had done the same things in the Soviet Union, he'd be a hero.''
He noted that many American academics disliked the Soviet Union but had a favorable attitude toward China.
Thomas Grey, a professor at the Stanford law school and one of the three members of the investigating committee, disputed Mr. Horowitz's contention. 
''We were aware from the beginning that the Sinological community had a bias in this, so we kept them out,'' Mr. Grey said.
''I certainly didn't have any ax to grind,'' he added, ''and it took a lot of time away from my work at the law school.''
As an indication of Stanford's sensitivity, Norman K. Wessels, dean of the School of Humanities and Sciences, has appointed a panel of three scholars, including one from outside Stanford, to hear a threepage grievance Mr. Mosher has filed against the school. 
Mr. Wessels asked the panel to recommend how he should deal with the case and requested a report that could be published.
Â 
Student Says He May Sue for Libel
Mr. Mosher, who has the investigative committee's report on the charges against him, has not released it. 
He has said he might sue Stanford for libel and that releasing the report himself would undermine his case.
Mr. Barnett, stressing that he had tried to insure a fair investigation, said the department had rejected a number of unsubstantiated accusations made by Peking and by fellow China scholars, including the charge that Mr. Mosher was a spy and that he illegally imported a van into China and gave it to village officials.
Still, Mr. Barnett asserted that some of the Chinese charges, including one that Mr. Mosher traveled without authorization into Guizhou Province, which is closed to foreigners, indicated a pattern of questionable behavior.
One Stanford professor said Miss So's evidence had been corroborated at least in part by Richard Williams, who was the United States Consul General in Canton when Mr. Mosher was in China. 
Mr. Williams, now deputy consul general in Hong Kong, said by telephone that it ''wouldn't be appropriate'' for him to comment on the case.
To support his contention that Stanford bowed to pressure by China scholars, Mr. Mosher cited a letter from Kenneth Prewitt, president of the Social Sciences Research Council in New York, to Stanford after he talked with Chinese officials late in 1981.
The exchange program between China and the United States ''could be harmed if the American scholarly community took no action on what the Chinese regarded as improper behavior by Mosher,'' Mr. Prewitt warned.
Stanford itself has conducted an active exchange program with China.
Â 
Abortion Campaign Described
In a book, ''Broken Earth: The Rural Chinese,'' to be published in September, Mr. Mosher paints a portrait of apathy, corruption and poverty among China's peasants and village officials.
He also describes, as he did in the article published in Taiwan, a campaign in his village in the spring of 1980 to force abortions on pregnant women who were not permitted to have children under Peking's strict birth control rules. 
At a family planning meeting he attended, he wrote, a local official told the pregnant women, ''None of you have any choice in this matter.''
''The two of you who are eight or nine months pregnant will have a Caesarean,'' Mr. Mosher quotes the official as saying. 
''The rest of you will have a shot that will cause you to abort.''
In a nearby village, Mr. Mosher asserted, a woman seven months pregnant who had no sons had an ordered abortion and was found to have been carrying twin boys.
The woman's husband, Mr. Mosher wrote, went in a fury to the home of the official who had ordered the abortion. 
''Seizing the man's two sons, aged 8 and 10,'' he wrote, ''he heaved them into the courtyard well and then leaped in himself. 
All three drowned.''
The magazine article, published in May 1981, brought accusations from Peking that its content, and its publication in Taiwan, was an attack on China. 
And the head of Mr. Mosher's dissertation committee at Stanford, the anthropologist G. William Skinner, wrote Mr. Mosher that he was ''appalled at your irresponsibility and insensitivity'' in not concealing the identity of the women facing abortions. 
Concealing subjects' identity is a canon of anthropological ethics.
Â 
Chinese Had Been Complaining
Chinese officials had already been complaining to American scholars about Mr. Mosher, and Stanford decided to set up the investigating committee. 
When it began its work in October 1981, however, it lacked proof. 
The committee head, Prof. Jane F. Collier, wrote to Zhao Fusan, a deputy director of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, appealing for evidence. 
''Much of the information we have received on these charges,'' she said, ''has been indirect and secondhand, consisting of reports by American scholars of complaints made to them by Chinese officials.''
Mr. Zhao's response only reiterated the allegations that had been gossiped about, said Mr. Barnett, the anthropology department chairman.
But in December 1981, Miss So began making her accusations to Stanford, according to several professors familiar with the investigative report.
Mr. Mosher asserts that Miss So had little first-hand knowledge of the village, though she had cousins there, because she visited him infrequently. 
Instead, she was either finishing graduate school at the University of California at Berkeley or working out of Hong Kong for an import-export company.
Â 
'I Will Ruin You'
''Matters came to a head in March 1980,'' Mr. Mosher said. 
''She came to the village and I said I wanted a divorce.''
''She replied, 'You can't, I will ruin you,' '' Mr. Mosher said. 
About the confidential documents, Mr. Mosher insists he was given access to them legally after three Chinese officials from Peking visited the village shortly before his arrival in 1979 and ordered the local authorities to cooperate with him.
The documents included land registers, household registers and class status registers, giving a social and economic profile of each peasant going back to the 1940's. 
Mr. Mosher also obtained crime reports prepared by the local secret police. 
Scholars say no American had ever gained access to such material.
Mr. Mosher said he did give his Mazda van to the village and turn over to his wife's cousins a house he built. 
But his only other gifts, Mr. Mosher said, were dinner invitations to peasants who helped him.
Â 
Gifts Held Improper
Professor Barnett concedes that anthropologists routinely provide their research subjects with money or gifts in exchange for their information or time. 
But, without elaborating, he asserted that Mr. Mosher ''went way over the line'' with his gifts.
Before he was expelled, Mr. Mosher had planned to give all his documents to the Hoover Institution on War, Revolution and Peace at Stanford. 
An official of the politically conservative institution said he had already turned over some materials on education and a microfilm file of the local county newspaper, a valuable tool for scholars.
Unfortunately, the film he took was of such poor quality that it is unusable, the official added.

file: SEEING CHINA LIKE A CAPITALIST.txt
text:
ï»¿
From the inside of a 23-foot 3-inch-long blue-black Fleetwood Brougham Cadillac stretch limousine with a 5-liter V-8 engine, vinyl roof, whitewall tires, air-conditioning, push-button (and tinted) windows, color television, AM-FM radio, dual refrigerators, bar stocked with Gorham lead-filled crystal glasses, lace antimacassars on the backs of the red plush seats, driven by a young chauffeur in a new blue uniform with bright brass buttons, the Peoples' Republic of China seems like a different country.
As one pulls out of the Great Wall Sheraton Hotel in Peking, where the Union Car Rental Company has just opened for business with a fleet of 20 new Cadillacs and 26 Mercedes-Benzes, and turns onto North Donghuan Road through the flow of crowded buses, bicycles, donkey carts and curious pedestrians, one feels as if one were hardly in China at all, but rather sitting in the soft seat of a wide-screen movie theater back in the United States watching a travelogue.
As the dusty earthbound world of China slides silently by outside with nothing more than the sound of the air-conditioner inside, it is hard not to be struck once again by the magnitude of change that has been taking place in China these last few years. 
Looking out over the enormous shining metal hull of this so-American car as it navigates through the sea of traffic, the familiar Cadillac emblem on the hood seems like a contemporary version of the figureheads that were once carved on the bows of the great clipper ships that first opened trade between China and the West.
Although one hardly notices the flotillas of limousines that clog the streets of the great cities of the West, it still comes as a shock to see these hallmarks of western capitalism -the first imported entries of their kind in China - in what had once been a heartland of the Communist world.
Now, if one wishes to tour Peking and its environs from the inside of a Cadillac (pronounced in Chinese as ''Kah-dee-lah-kuh'') Fleetwood Brougham limousine, all one has to do is call 5005566, extension 2339, at the Great Wall Sheraton and ask for Comrade Wang Shaojun or Comrade Wu Wei at Union Car Rental's polished red granite counter in the lobby. 
For about $35 they will meet you at the airport, and for $115 a day, they will rent you a limousine from 8 A.M. to 6 P.M. (75 free miles) complete with driver.
''Now that China has adopted a policy of opening to the outside, we want to be able to provide the best car and the best drivers possible for our foreign V.I.P. guests,'' said Wang Shaojun, a young woman in a gray flannel suit who is the company's assistant general manager. 
''To do this, our head, Mr. Yong Yiren, decided to import these cars. 
Our intention was to become something like Avis. 
But, since there are problems in China with foreigners driving their own cars without Chinese licenses, for now we must provide chauffeurs.''
Mr. Yong, a former Shanghai industrialist, is the chairman of the board of the China International Trust and Investment Corporation.
When I ask Miss Wang whether she feels that there are any contradictions between China's previous committment to Spartan egalitarianism and these luxury cars, she replies matter-of-factly:
''Formerly people might not have been able to accept these kinds of things, and might have become angry. 
But now, everything has changed and we're more open-minded. 
We believe China should develop and look to the future on all fronts.''
Since Peking is still far from accustomed to such high-class livery, and since the city has just recently become swamped with taxis, business for Union Car Rental has been somewhat slow in starting. 
As recently as two years ago, when a serious taxi shortage left throngs of angry Western businessmen stranded outside their hotels late for important meetings, a car rental service would have had no trouble finding clients regardless of cost. 
But now, as the city's taxi fleet has suddenly swollen to epic proportions -14,000 in Peking compared to 11,000 medallion cabs in New York, but with rates about three-fourths the cost of the limousines -Union Car Rental finds itself with much unanticipated competition. 
During its first few weeks, it rarely had more than four or five cars rented at a time. 
But with so many foreign businessmen arriving to check out the China market, and with many heads of state paying official visits to Peking, Yong Yiren's gamble may yet pay off handsomely. 
Who can say exactly what it is that kindles a yearning for limousines among contemporary Americans?
Whatever it is, they bring it with them to China.
What C.E.O. of a large Western multinational would feel comfortable arriving for a banquet at the Great Hall of the People in a Toyota cab, much less one of the old mental-hospital-green Shanghai sedans, taxis that still ply the street, albeit in waning numbers?
What foreign businessman who has been trying to hammer out a difficult new joint venture agreement with an immovable Chinese counterpart would not sometimes dream of arriving in a glistening new stateside limo at the No. 2 Peking Steam Turbine Factory in hopes of gaining a little needed face and jolting the comrades into a needed concession?
Or what wealthy tourist might not be tempted by the whimsical idea of throwing a reception for friends with French Champagne on the Great Wall, all arranged by Union Car Rental or Great Wall Sheraton's food and beverage service, or of taking a limousine excursion to the Ming tombs, complete with a catered picnic banquet (about $10 a boxed lunch) all set up and waiting at the tomb of his choice when he arrives?
Indeed, Cadillac limousines are only the most recent addition to a whole new layer of luxury services that are appearing in China, making travel for wealthy foreigners easier and earning dollars and other Western cur-rencies for China at the same time. 
Luxury foreign-managed hotels are opening in most of China's major cities. 
Deluxe German-made train cars are now available to foreigners on certain rail lines. 
Luxury air-conditioned cruise ships have long since been plying the China coast and the Yangtze River. 
Club Med has just opened a resort on Kunming Lake at the Summer Palace outside Peking, and will soon finish a club in Shenzhen across the border from Hong Kong. 
And while deluxe services are not generally available to local Chinese since they are enormously expensive and must be paid for in foreign currency, they are emblematic of the direction in which Chinese society is heading as a whole.
Wondering what had happened to the old notion of self-reliance, which had once been painted on almost every wall, chimney and billboard in China, I asked Miss Wang, the assistant manager, what had become of all the old Red Flag limousines. 
With their wooden dashboards, curtains in the back windows and chrome characters for Red Flag (Hongqi) written after Mao's own hand emblazoned on the rear trunks, these 100 percent Chinese-made automobiles had once plied the streets of Peking without competition from foreign interlopers.
''Red Flag cars are somewhat backward,'' she replied unenthusiastically. 
Then, brightening a little, she continued: ''They have stopped making the old models. 
But I hear that they are now trying to design something more up to date which will include mechanical parts from your Lincoln company.''
Like so many other hallmarks of Maoist China, these Red Flag limousines will now doubtless vanish almost as fast as portraits of the chairman himself. 
For, alongside the newly arrived Fleetwoods and the Mercedes, these clunky-looking automotive behemoths from China's era of socialist self-reliance do indeed look like throwbacks to another age.
While Mao still lived, I used to watch curiously as high-ranking officials were whisked, shrouded behind curtains, through the then nearly car-less streets of Peking to what then seemed to me to be mysterious and forbidden destinations. 
In a land that was supposed to have purged itself of all distinctions of rank and privilege, these limousines were among the few visible if anomalous symbols of a social privilege that endured even through the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution.
Indeed, as these strangely forboding conveyances sped by on the street, one could even then feel a gust of imperial China blow past. 
The hauteur of those modern-day officials -their Maoist slogans notwithstanding - harkened back to a time when high officials and members of the imperial family made no pretense of ''being at one with the masses,'' and would pass through the streets of their capital in curtained sedan chairs.
One night this spring, as I took a short cut home through the underground parking garage of the Great Wall Sheraton Hotel, I happened upon three or four of these old socialist war horses parked off to the side on slowly deflating tires. 
As I passed, I saw that these relics of an earlier time were so covered with the dust that blows down each spring onto Peking from the steppes of Mongolia, they seemed almost to have become interred in their parking spots. 
And when I came up from underground to the front of the hotel, where the Union Car Rental's fleet of new Cadillacs stood ostentatiously parked near a modern fountain, I felt a little like an archeologist who has just emerged from an ancient tomb where he has happened upon the ceremonial relics of a culture that was all but lost. 
That night, as I slept eight floors above the abandoned cars, I dreamed of home in California and the giant condors, which like Red Flag limousines are also an ungainly but very native species that has been brought to the edge of extinction by evolutionary pressure from the modernizing world around them. 
And in my dream I saw several battered old condors silhouetted against the cobalt blue sky staring down from their thatched nests in tall pine trees onto gleaming rows of predatory Cadillac Fleetwoods below.
In the morning, when I went downstairs to have a cup of imported coffee and a croissant with Swiss jam, this image still burned in my mind like the outline of a light in the dark long after it has been turned off. 
When I left the hotel, I found myself drawn back once again to the underground parking garage where the Red Flags still rested under their coats of dust like mothballed warships. 
Whatever it is in human beings that makes us lament the passage of time - as things may be improving around us - was at work on me.
Besides the exhilaration I usually felt at watching China come alive, I now also felt a sense of wistfulness over how rapidly this country, which I had first come to know over 10 years ago, was changing. 
And as I drove away from the ultramodern hotel in a new Japanese taxi through streets newly choked with traffic past scores of new high rise buildings, I knew that my state of mind was not only caused by the fact that Red Flag limousines were vanishing into history, but also that China itself was being transformed; that just as the country had frequently passed from one dynastic period to another during ancient times, so now it was irrevocably passing from one era into another.
