file: Seoul Olympic Rings Include Some Made of Barbed Wire.txt
text:
ï»¿
Every airport has security checks for departing passengers. 
The one here even forces arriving visitors to walk through metal detectors after they leave the plane.
Outside the main terminal at Kimpo International Airport, soldiers carrying automatic rifles march in solemn lockstep past tourists searching for the taxi stand. 
In central Seoul, streets are awash in easily detected plainclothes police officers, who stand on street corners and at the entrances to underground passageways, all looking as if the last time they smiled was 1985.
Even at its most quiet, South Korea does not suffer from lax law enforcement. 
But with only six months until the Sept. 
17 opening of the Seoul Summer Olympics, security has become a national preoccupation.
Few days pass without a warning from one official or another that Communist North Korea will try to disrupt the Games through terrorism. 
Such polemics are not new. 
But they have assumed added significance after the destruction of a South Korean airliner as it flew over the Thailand-Burma border last Nov. 
29.
Seoul, supported by key allies like the United States and Japan, blames North Korea for the plane's destruction, which killed 115 people. 
As proof, it produced a televised confession from a young woman captured a few days later, who said that she and a male accomplice had acted under instructions from North Korean leaders.
And now that North Korea's leaders in Pyongyang say that their athletes will stay away from the Summer Games, the South worries that more violence may lie ahead.
''Some people feel that the threat is greater before the Olympics than during,'' said Kim Un Yong, vice president of the Seoul Olympic Organizing Committee. 
That theory is based on an assumption that Pyongyang wants to scare participants away, but would be reluctant to act once its principal allies, the Soviet Union and China, are in Seoul running after medals.
Â 
Full Military Alert
The Games themselves are shaping up as the most heavily fortified sporting event in history.
South Korea's armed forces of 620,000 and its national police force of 120,000 are to be placed on full alert to protect the estimated 34,000 athletes, officials, journalists and technicians who will form the ''Olympic family.''
More than 30,000 specially hired security guards are scheduled to be posted at the 34 competition sites and at dozens of training areas, hotels and other potential targets.
In addition, United States officials say that the 40,000 American soldiers stationed here will be on alert.
The Pentagon plans a full-scale show of military force, a reprise of deployments carried out during the Asian Games that took place in Seoul in September 1986.
Under this strategy, one aircraft carrier, and possibly two, will cruise off the South Korean coast, with each carrier having 6 to 10 escorting vessels. 
Surveillance by reconnaissance aircraft and intelligence satellites will be increased. 
Air Force planes may be flown in from Japan, and Marine amphibious battalions based on Okinawa are to be made available.
Â 
Special Watch on Airport
South Korean forces intend to watch Kimpo airport extra closely. 
As a precaution, athletes and other participants will be steered on arrival to a special terminal. 
Officials are still haunted by memories of 1986, when a bomb exploded at the airport, killing five people, just a week before the Asian Games opened. 
As usual, the South blamed the North, but no evidence has been produced.
At the Olympic Park, security will be equally intense. 
By official count, 117,000 gadgets - including television cameras, metal detectors and X-ray machines said to be able to detect plastic explosives - will be put into use.
The Athletes' Village, which is nearing completion, will be surrounded by three concentric fences, and a separate electrified fence will ring the entire Olympic Park. 
For good measure, police dogs will be used to sniff out explosives, and troops toting machine guns will patrol key locations.
Some officials wonder if they may be overdoing it. 
South Korean police officers and military men are not known for mild-mannered behavior. 
There is concern that the atmosphere could become oppressive by the time the Olympic flame is lighted.
To soften their image, the security forces recently began assigning women to Kimpo duty. 
True, the women smile a bit more than the men. 
But they are not conspicuously gentler, judging from the way they slam hand-held metal detectors against bodies. 
161 Nations to Participate South Korea is encouraged by the commitment of nearly every Communist nation to attend the Seoul Games, especially the Soviet Union and China. 
In all, a record 161 countries say they will come, the only exceptions being North Korea, Cuba, Nicaragua, Ethiopia, the Seychelles and Albania, which habitually declines participation.
''The more nations that participate, the more that a terrorist country has to lose,'' said Hwang Kyu Wong, director general for security at the Olympic organizing committee. 
''Any country that might want to disrupt the Games must be isolated from the diplomatic community.''
In Calgary, Alberta, a few weeks ago, the committee's president, Park Seh Jik, said Soviet and Chinese athletes might be asked to arrive a few weeks early to reduce the terrorist risk.
Still, more hawkish South Koreans insist that even a Soviet and Chinese presence may not be enough to deter Pyongyang if it feels cornered during Seoul's greatest public-relations coup. 
Skeptics include former President Chun Doo Hwan.
''North Korea will try to use all the instruments of violence in its arsenal,'' he told foreign reporters before stepping down in late February. 
''There is no evidence that they have changed their heart.''
Security aside, Seoul has shifted into high gear now that its pre-Olympic day count has dipped below 200.
Â 
A Calmer Political Scene
South Korea's roiled political scene of last summer and autumn has entered a period of calm following the first genuine presidential elections since 1971. 
The new national leader, Roh Tae Woo, took office to little protest, and there is no reason to anticipate trouble, although in volatile South Korea one makes such statements at one's peril.
As ever, South Koreans view the Olympics as an affirmation of their arrival as a global economic force. 
Except for Mexico in 1968, theirs is the only developing nation to host the Games, and they have prepared with a vengeance.
All told, the country has invested $3.1 billion over the last seven years, most of it going to speed up projects technically unrelated to the Games, such as new subway lines, an airport expansion and a cleanup of Seoul's Han River.
Some major Korean corporations, whose arms were blatantly twisted by the Government to become Olympics sponsors, are having doubts about whether they will get their money's worth in terms of future sales. 
But officials at the organizing committee remain bullish. 
They predict that earnings from television rights, special lotteries, licensing fees and the like will put them $271 million in the black, a profit greater than that of the Los Angeles Games four years ago.
Perhaps more significantly, South Korean officials want the Olympics to be a springboard for improved relations with China and the Soviet bloc, a significant shift in priorities for a fiercely anti-Communist government. 
Newspapers are filled almost every day with stories about South Korean trade opportunities with Eastern Europe and with Beijing. 
President Roh goes so far as to talk about establishing diplomatic ties with China during his five-year term.
Although that seems overly optimistic, it would be quite a coup for Seoul, given the fact that China fought side by side with North Korea during the 1950-53 Korean War. 
Such a development would further isolate Pyongyang, officials here say.
Everything always comes back to North Korea in the end.
For the record, South Korea says it still wants the North to come.
Pyongyang had insisted on serving as an equal co-host to the Games. 
But the International Olympic Committee, with Seoul's concurrence, is willing to go no further than to have all or part of five events held in Northern territory: table tennis, archery, women's volleyball, soccer and cycling.
That's the final offer, the committee says, and it has set May 17 as its absolute deadline.
But ''absolute deadlines'' on this matter have come and gone before. 
Mr. Roh told an interviewer last month that he would leave the door open ''until the eve of the opening ceremony.''
But there is no sign that South Koreans would shed tears if - and more likely, when - North Korea stays home.

file: SEOUL PLANS LINKS TO EASTERN BLOC.txt
text:
ï»¿
South Korea, whose Government is as fiercely anti-Communist as any to be found, has mounted a full-scale diplomatic offensive to improve relations with Soviet-bloc countries and China.
The atmosphere in Seoul was almost giddy last week when officials announced that Hungary would set up a trade office here next month to complement a South Korean office that opened in Budapest in mid-December. 
Poland, Yugoslavia and East Germany are all considering similar operations.
While the level of South Korean trade with the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe is small - $240 million last year - it is growing fast. 
And with the Soviet bloc saying it will take part in the Olympic Games here this year, Government leaders and exporters here talk expansively about business, tourism and cultural opportunities.
Quietly, South Korean conglomerates like Samsung are also exploring investment possibilities in Vietnam. 
Meanwhile, officials have trained their sights more sharply on their most important target, China.
Â 
China Trade Is Strong
They have stopped whispering about the size of their trade with China, long an open secret, and brag that it exceeded $1.5 billion last year and should top $2 billion in 1988. 
That, they say, is more than twice the level of China's trade with its ally, North Korea.
Perhaps more important, some officials say, hope now exists for eventual diplomatic relations with Beijing, an ideological enemy since the two countries fought in the Korean War.
''It is only a matter of time,'' said Park Soo Gil, an Assistant Foreign Minister. 
''North Korea is the only factor standing in the way.''
The South's long-stated objective, opposed by the Government in Pyongyang, is for ''cross-recognition'' by the four major powers in the region. 
This means formal acceptance of the North by the United States and Japan, and recognition of the South by the Soviet Union and China.
Â 
Normal Chinese Relations
During South Korea's recent presidential election, Roh Tae Woo, the victorious ruling party candidate, predicted that normal relations with China would be arranged during his five-year term. 
But some experts caution against over-shooting the mark.
''I'd rather de-emphasize the political meaning in our short-term dealings with China,'' said Kim Dal Choong, who heads an institute on East-West relations at Yonsei University.
The rush to deal with Communist nations has given some South Koreans pause on ideological grounds. 
Seoul has no formal relations with any Communist country, and has preached the evils of Communism insistently.
Park Young Jin, a senior Education Ministry official, has said hat textbooks may now have to be revised to give students ''a true picture of Communist societies.''
Â 
North Korean Isolation
Such considerations aside, officials say that they now have an opportunity both to isolate North Korea from its natural allies and to reduce a bit the North Korean dependence on the United States, which absorbs 40 percent of this country's exports.
Seoul's emphasis comes at a time of rising tensions with Washington over demands that South Korea open its markets wider to American beef, tobacco and insurance companies.
Resentments deepened last week when the Reagan Administration announced that it would end special trade preferences for South Korea and other powerful East Asian economies. 
Although the action came as no surprise here, it reinforced a conviction among Koreans that they must do more to diversify their markets.
Some South Koreans worry that if North Korea feels it has been painted into a corner, it might be more prepared to consider terrorism to disrupt the Olympics. 
But Mr. Park said the South's diplomatic and economic advantages - the North has the military edge - could force Pyongyang to adopt accommodating policies.
Correction
Because of an editing error, an article on Feb. 
5 about a South Korean effort to improve relations with Communist countries misstated the trade relationship between the Koreas and the United States. 
It is South Korea, not North Korea, that depends heavily on trade with the United States.
Correction-Date:Â February 25, 1988, Thursday, Late City Final Edition

file: SHANGHAI JOURNAL_A City in Misery, Betrayed by a Taste for Clams.txt
text:
ï»¿
Lu Guiying, a portly woman in a white apron and cap, stood glumly outside her restaurant, her arms folded across her chest.
''This week, all of a sudden, business is down,'' she said. 
''We used to take in 1,000 yuan a day; now we're making less than 500,'' a sum equivalent to $135. 
''People think they're going to get sick here.''
Everywhere in Shanghai, life is stalling as this city of 12 million confronts its worst epidemic of hepatitis-A, an inflammation of the liver, in more than a decade. 
City officials report that as many as 20,000 people may have contracted the illness and the numbers are expected to grow.
''Some people predicted that there would be a problem with hepatitis near spring festival,'' said Dr. Yan Zuyan, referring to the approach of the Chinese Lunar New Year on Feb. 
17. ''Nobody thought it would be this serious.''
The English-language China Daily described the rapid spread of the disease as causing ''public panic.''
Â 
Hospital Wards Are Overflowing
Hospitals in Shanghai are filled with patients, with wards overflowing and beds jammed into hallways and corners. 
Schools, now empty of children for the spring festival holiday, have been converted into isolation wards for thousands of bedridden patients. 
Pharmacies have exhausted their supplies of banlangen, an herbal cold remedy.
Dr. Yan, a pediatrician who is director of the No. 4 People's Hospital here, said the spread of the disease had been spurred by Shanghai's tremendous overcrowding. 
The disease, while not fatal, is debilitating and highly infectious. 
Victims often lose their appetite and taste, suffer nausea and have pain in the liver area.
''The housing problem here is very serious,'' Dr. Yan said. 
''One thing we try to do is isolate patients at home. 
But many people live in crowded conditions and this is very difficult.''
Like all large Chinese cities, Shanghai suffers from an acute shortage of housing so that often three generations of a family crowd into a single one- or two-room apartment.
The outbreak of hepatitis-A began two weeks ago, Dr. Yan said, when shipments of what are now believed to have been contaminated clams arrived in Shanghai from nearby clam flats east of the city.
''About 90 percent of the patients we have identified have eaten this sort of shellfish,'' Dr. Yan said. 
Why the clams were contaminated remains unclear, according to Dr. Yan and an official from the municipal health bureau. 
However, it is common practice in China for cities and towns to dump raw sewage into rivers and harbors. 
''People like shellfish in this city and this province,'' Dr. Yan said. 
''They only dip the clams in boiling water for a moment, not really long enough to kill the virus.''
Â 
Many Lack Immunity
The disease has spread rapidly, Dr. Yan said, because much of the city's younger population does not have an immunity to the virus.
People who once have hepatitis-A, he explained, cannot get it again. 
They are not immune to the more serious hepatitis-B, which is caused by a different virus.
''There was an outbreak of hepatitis five years ago,'' Dr. Yan said, ''but it was not very severe and not many people were infected and got immune.''
At his 350-bed hospital, Dr. Yan showed a visitor an obstetrics ward that had been transformed into an isolation area for hepatitis patients.
Patients, bundled in layers of sweaters and jackets against the leaden cold that hung in the unheated building, lay quietly on iron-framed cots in the hall of the ward. 
Nurses and doctors wrapped in surgical gowns and masks moved among the beds quickly, dispensing a bit of medicine here and there.
''There are no bedside tables,'' Dr. Yan pointed out. 
''Conditions are not so ideal here. 
We are very crowded.''
In the city itself, residents are more wary of what they eat, what they touch. 
An official from the city health bureau, Zhang Zhuen, declined to shake a visitor's hand. 
''I used to shake the hands of foreigners,'' he said. 
''Now I don't think it's a good idea.''
Mr. Zhang said the city had mounted a ''propaganda'' campaign to encourage citizens to wash their hands frequently and not to eat shell fish. 
''We destroyed all the clams that came in once we realized they were one of the causes,'' he said. 
''But people still must be careful.''
''We've told people to pay attention to personal sanitation,'' he said. 
''We've also said that people should not visit their relatives because the disease is very infectious. 
And we've told people to be careful to clean their cooking utensils.''
Shanghai's water and sewer system, often rudimentary in many areas, is more than 60 years old in the central part of the city and clean drinking water is sometimes hard to find.
According to the city's health statistics, the illness has largely been confined to young adults in their 20's and 30's, Mr. Zhang said. 
For the most part, he said, older people have developed immunities from previous epidemics and younger children tend not to eat shellfish, thus reducing their exposure to the virus.
Â 
Medicine Is Sold Out
At the Ruijin herbal pharmacy downtown, a pharmacist said that there were no supplies of banlangen to be had in Shanghai. 
''We're completely sold out,'' she said, leaning on a counter displaying various types of ginseng.
Down the street, Wang Yafang emerged from a store with her two daughters, 7 and 8 years old. 
''I'm not too worried,'' she said. 
''I gave the children banlangen and they're all right.''
At the restaurant, Mrs. Lu surveyed the empty tables as other workers drifted onto the street to warm themselves in the sun.
''We can only try our best,'' she said. 
''One of our workers caught hepatitis and is in the hospital. 
We had inspectors from the city come in to check the restaurant. 
I've never seen a situation like this before. 
But I'm not worried for myself. 
Not at all.''
A young man also in a white apron eavesdropping on her comments laughed. 
''Of course she won't get sick,'' he said. 
''Look how chubby she is. 
She's too healthy.''

file: SHANGHAI_S EX-CAPITALISTS BACK ON JOB.txt
text:
ï»¿
Two Mercedes-Benz cars and a British Ford of recent vintage were parked in the enclosed courtyard of the wellmaintained villa in what was once the French Concession in this most cosmopolitan of Chinese cities, and the two men who were seated in armchairs in what was once the drawing room looked as if they belonged there, or in the rear seats of the cars, despite their regulation Mao suits.
There are no privately owned automobiles in China. 
They and the villa have been assigned to the Shanghai Federation of Commerce and Industries, an anachronism that unites the surviving former capitalists of China's capital of industry, commerce and banking.
Now that China pursues its program of ''the four modernizations,'' the former men of means have been recalled from the menial jobs that they had been given to meet foreign businessmen and potential investors and to employ their once-scorned skills to attract badly needed foreign capital and technology.
Henry Kamm profiles Chinese construction company's general manager and chairman, Han Zhiming, and Liu Jingji respectively
It is not only their skills that have been enlisted. 
To advance ''the four modernizations,'' 1,300 members of the federation have ''invested'' their private fortunes in the Patriotic Construction Company, which was formed in 1979.
Â 
'Contribution' Proposed
''After the 'Gang of Four' was smashed, a lot of our money was returned to us with interest,'' said Han Zhiming, the 69-year-old deputy general manager of Patriotic Construction. 
''There was no way of spending it. 
We suggested that we could make a contribution to the 'four modernizations.'
We could contribute to socialist construction.
''We have relatives abroad and in Hong Kong and Macao,'' he explained. 
''They could help us introduce new equipment and technology to China.''
By voluntary contributions, Mr. Han asserted, the company raised 57 million yuan, the equivalent of about $38 million. 
Mr. Han, the former owner of a cotton mill, contributed 400,000 yuan, or about $268,00, as did the other deputy general manager present, Zhang Chensheng, once the owner of a cigarette factory.
The two men of wealth - with which they can buy very little because necessities are rationed and luxuries are available only for foreign currency - said they were far from being the biggest ''investors.''
Chen Yuaching and Liu Jingji, both former textile industrialists, invested 2 million yuan each. 
Mr. Liu is the company's chairman and managing director.
Â 
Shareholders' Return Is Limited
The allocations are investments in name only, because no matter how the affairs of the Patriotic Construction Company may flourish, its shareholders receive only the 6.84 percent annual interest that the funds would earn if they were left in bank accounts. 
In five years, the shareholders can decide whether to withdraw their capital and return it to the bank or commit it for five more years.
The surviving personal fortunes derive from the properties that the men operated until the Communist takeover of the Government in 1949. 
Until the Cultural Revolution of 1966, the former capitalists continued to draw interest on the equities that the Government granted them after their concerns were taken over. 
Payments stopped in 1966 and bank accounts were confiscated, to be returned beginning in 1978.
Mr. Han and Mr. Zhang conceded with embarrassment in the presence of the officials who monitored the interview that the total expropriation of their equities in 1966 had not been undone by China's present leadership.
''After 1967, there was no more exploitation by capitalists,'' said Mr. Zhang. ''The enterprises were transformed through socialism.''
Mr. Zhang, a large man who wears gold-rimmed, tinted glasses, has a son who has been studying engineering at Ohio State University since last year, a rare privilege for a person of ''capitalist'' family.
Â 
Company Will Build Apartments
The Patriotic Construction Company's principal project is to be two 15-story apartment towers containing 180 flats, to be sold to overseas Chinese who would like to provide for their families here. 
The housing shortage is Shanghai's principal social problem. 
Piledriving for the foundations has been completed, but as is the case with many capital projects in China, construction appears to have been stretched out and the target of completion by the end of next year seems unlikely to be met.
The company also plans to build houses for former capitalists disposessed in the past. 
It has invested in 29 neighborhood projects in the food and service sectors, aimed at providing work for the masses of young people returning from banishment to the countryside during the Cultural Revolution. 
These people have been added to the ranks of youths finishing high school who can find neither employment nor access to higher education.
The two former capitalists said that they had learned that exploitation of the many by the few had been wrong and declared that they had come to believe that Communism was China's best hope. 
Asked if he was a member of the Communist Party, Mr. Zhang said: ''The requirements are high, and I am not under consideration.''

file: SHARON FESTIVAL TO PROMOTE CULTURES OF ASIA AND INDONESIA.txt
text:
ï»¿
INSTEAD of the traditional harvest festival so customary in New England in autumn, a procession of dancers garbed as ferocious Chinese lions will converge upon the Sharon Town Green on Saturday. 
Their huge papier-mache heads bobbing up and down, they will dance to the clamor of bells, gongs and whistles that marks the beginning of a daylong festival promoting the cultures of Asia and Indonesia.
The festival will feature Indonesian dances, Indian shadow puppet shows, Asian food and crafts booths and demonstrations of Chinese cooking. 
The event is sponsored by the East-West Fusion Theater of Sharon, with a matching grant from the State Commission on the Arts.
Although the East-West Fusion Theater has toured nationally and in Canada since it was formed four years ago, the festival will mark the group's formal debut in its hometown, said the company's artistic director, Teviot Fairservis Pourchot, an actress.
''Because we do not have our own performing facility, many of our events have had to be private,'' she said. 
''This is a way for us to introduce our work publicly and share it with the local community.''
Based at the Center for East-West Studies, a nonprofit organization based in Sharon, the group brings together artists and scholars from around the world to create an international form of theater based on the traditions of Asia and other non-Western cultures. 
The company uses acting, dance, music, masks, puppetry and techniques of Asian theater.
In addition to mounting performances, the East-West center is a resource facility for people studying China, India, Indonesia, Japan, the Pacific Islands and the Soviet Union, Mrs. Pourchot said.
''We're hoping the festival will make people aware of the center and the resources we have here,'' she said. 
''We have a library, a costume collection and a collection of artifacts, which are available for research. 
For us, it's really important to be seen as that kind of a resource.''
Mrs. Pourchot said she was also hoping the event would encourage people who have lived abroad to share their experiences. 
Among the area residents who will be on hand are the authors Charlotte and Harrison Salisbury, both of Taconic, who have traveled extensively in China and written about their experiences. 
They will give the keynote address at noon, Mrs. Pourchot said.
Throughout the day, there will be many exhibits on the grounds of the Sharon Playhouse, including demonstrations of the Japanese tea ceremony, shiatsu message, karate and Asian costumes. 
Chinese cooking will be demonstrated by Danny Lee, a master Chinese chef at New York's Culinary Institute of America. 
Food booths will also sell Chinese, Indian and other international delicacies, and there will be a tea tasting, pottery and paper-folding demonstrations.
Also throughout the day and into the night, a number of theatrical performances will feature international artists, including the Chinese opera performer Kuang-yu Fong of Taiwan, the Indonesian dance expert Deena Burton and the Music for Homemade Instruments Ensemble, a New York-based ensemble.
The members of the East-West Fusion Theater will also present plays, including a comic Chinese opera, ''The Black Bowl''; ''Animal Tales of India,'' Indian folktales staged with authentic costumes and masks; ''The Ramayana,'' the famous Hindu love story of Prince Rama performed in West Javanese masked dance; ''The (Balinese) Frog Prince,'' the story of a frog who turns into a prince, and ''Traditional Japanese Comedies and New Fusions,'' which includes comic plays and dances from the Kabuki and Kyogen repertories.
At dusk, there will be a candlelight procession and prayer for peace and in the evening, a performance of ''The Magic of the Orient,'' a tribute featuring authentic dance and costume, Mrs. Pourchot said.
The festival will coincide with other exhibits on display at nearby sites, including ''Faces of China,'' an exhibition by the photographer Tom Zetterstrom now on display at the Hotchkiss Library, and ''Contemporary Asian Artists,'' an exhibit of work by Japanese and Korean artists on display at the Sharon Library.
Most of the events will be held at the Sharon Playhouse and its grounds, with the opening and candlelight processions on the Town Green.
In addition to the Saturday festivities, East-West Fusion Theater will present ''The Orient Express,'' four plays from the four cultures, on Oct. 
12 and 13 at 3 P.M. at the playhouse. 
In the event of inclement weather, all activities will take place in the Sharon Center School.
Admission to the exhibits is free, but performances are $5 each. 
A ''passport'' ticket entitling the bearer to all the performances except ''The Magic of the Orient'' is $12.50 for adults, $10 for the elderly and $5 for children. 
Families may purchase a special ticket for $30, which entitles admission to two adults and up to four children.
For further information and tickets, write East-West Fusion Theater, P.O. 
Box 141, Sharon, Conn., 06069 or call 364-5220.

file: SHOPPER_S WORLD_HONG KONG_S STREET OF _GREEN TEMPTATION_.txt
text:
ï»¿
Each morning just before 10, every day of the year, four blocks of Kowloon along Canton Road are transformed into a street lined with jade, a path called the Jade Market by Hong Kong's Western population but referred to by the Chinese as Jade Street. 
For a shopper it is a seductive wonderland of green temptation with more than 300 dealers sitting along Canton Road from Jordan Road to Saigon Street, under jerry-built awnings or large umbrellas, on camp chairs or on their haunches, unfolding tables, cloths or racks of red satin- backed cards all displaying jade rings, necklaces, bracelets, pendants and carvings. 
One man sits on a curb in front of a towel on which are piled stacks of black-green jade carvings; another perches on a padded folding chair behind a glass-covered display case filled with what he swears is nothing but the finest of deep apple-green imperial jade. 
A woman ambles up the street with several dozen red, white and green jade necklaces suspended from her wrist and forearm, stopping whenever someone shows interest. 
Children watch the jade while their parents go off for tea or some food in one of the two narrow alleys that cut through Jade Street, Ningpo Street and Nanking Street.
In the street, ignoring the traffic, are other jade peddlers, dealing among themselves with a ritual so old that nobody can remember its origin. 
They bargain with their hands, but their hands are under cloths, white or black. 
One man or woman will hold a piece of jade in one hand while the other hand is hidden. 
The prospective buyer will put his hand under the cloth. 
Then they will speak. 
The seller might say ''yat'' and extend three fingers. 
Yat designates a unit of 100 and three fingers means three units, or $300. 
The buyer will grab, perhaps, only one finger, which means he is offering $100. 
And so it goes, hands under cloths with units of 1,000 designated by ''teo,'' units of 10,000 by ''tso.''
Jade Street is the world's only open-air bazaar devoted entirely to the gem that the Chinese regard with some degree of veneration. 
A beautiful woman is often called a woman of jade, and a handsome man is said to have a countenance of jade. 
Every Chinese baby is presented either with a tiny jade wrist bracelet or with a ''pi,'' a circular, smoothly polished piece of jade with a hole in the center, a tiny doughnut of jade, if you will, that has been for centuries a symbol of heaven. 
Confucius is said to have suggested that jade's smoothness represented gentleness of character, its varying colors and texture wisdom and nobility, its solidity for one's duty towards one's neighbor.
Jade ornaments as symbols of wealth, rank and power were commonplace in the imperial courts of China and the emperor's accouterment, his scepter, sword, throne and altar, even his sandals, were usually of highly prized, ornately carved jade. 
A flat stone, shaped octagonally, with a hole in its center, is often worn as a good luck talisman, to ward off evil spirits
Its mythology notwithstanding, jade is a highly regarded stone among all people, and to shop for it in the Jade Street bazaar is an extraordinary experience.
You cannot help but be goggle-eyed as you watch the jade sellers unpack their stones and ornaments from satchels, schoolbags, cookie tins, food containers and plastic bags, and spread them out for inspection.
Know a bit about jade before you go, resolve to bargain hard and long mainly because that is more than half the fun of shopping in Jade Street, and make up your mind that you will spend no more than $20 or $25, and you will have a rewarding time. 
Bear in mind that some of the imperial green jade might be chemically color-enhanced (genuine imperial green jade is the most desirable), that the men and women who sell jade know a good deal more than you do and will give away nothing.
A bit about jade: What is known as jade is either jadeite or nephrite. 
Jadeite comes in differing grades of red, called ''fei'' by the Chinese, or green, called ''tsui.''
Green is most highly prized; when it is deep apple, pure in color, with no traces of either deep bottle green or white, and almost transparent, it is considered to be the finest. 
It is not unusual for a tiny stone of imperial jade to sell for as much as $10,000.
Nephrite, which can be pale green but is mostly creamy white or off-white, is often called mutton fat and is best for carving. 
But jade can come in shades of brown, rust, almost yellow, peach, almost blue, gray and black. 
Some black and gray jade, deeply carved into bracelets are highly thought of by the Chinese, and often family members who have died are buried with jade bracelets of these colors on their wrists. 
Such pieces are called, appropriately, Dead Jade.
The traders along Jade Street will tell you ''Chinese jade, Chinese jade,'' but that is usually jade from Burma that has been imported into the People's Republic, carved, then shipped to Hong Kong for sale. 
North Burma remains the source of most fine jade.
Perhaps more than any other jewelry stone, jade is sold most often on esthetic appeal alone. 
Its marbled texture; the way green will blend into black or into white; whether the dragon and phoenix design, the yin and the yang of Chinese culture, are carved to satisfaction; whether carving is new or old, or merely looks old, all of these enter into one's purchase. 
And so should they for the tourist, the casual buyer.
As you wander along the narrow sidewalk, with jade hawkers both right and left, look for what pleases. 
Think what would look best hanging from a gold chain around your neck, what would look best sitting on a carved teak stand on your mantel, then either make an offer or ask a price and make a counter-offer. 
That is when the fun begins. 
I remember seeing what I considered a nice piece of carved jade, of a light green with some dark mottling. 
I asked the price.
''Three hundred fifty dollars, Hong Kong,'' replied the seller. 
This was the equivalent of about $50 in American money.
''No,'' I said, and began walking away.
''How much?'' called the seller.
''One hundred,'' I called back.
''No,'' he said, shaking his head with great sadness.
''Okay,'' I said and continued walking.
''OKAY!'' he called after me.
Back I went and bought the carving for $100 Hong Kong, a little more than $15 U.S. 
And I was satisfied. 
Did I get a bargain?
I thought so. 
Did the seller make a profit?
I'm sure he did. 
Were we both happy?
I'm pretty sure we were. 
And that is the essence of shopping along Jade Street.
Â 
How to find the Jade Market
That part of Canton Road called Jade Market or Street is convenient from both sides of Victoria Harbor. 
From Hong Kong island the Jordan Road Ferry (fare about 10 cents) will deposit you about two blocks from the intersection of Jordan and Canton roads. 
From the Kowloon Star Ferry Terminal the No. 9 Bus (fare about 9 cents) will drop you off at the corner. 
A taxi will cost about 65 cents and all you need do is tell the driver Jade Street. 
The new Hong Kong subway will also take you there for about 30 cents. 
Get off at the Jordan Road station and Jade Street is just at the top of the stairway. 
The market is open formally from 10 A.M. until 2 P.M. daily. 
But you can begin shopping as early as 9:30. 
By 2 P.M., however, most of the dealers have finished for the day and are in the teahouses.F. 
F.

file: SHOPPER_S WORLD_JAPAN_S ANCIENT ART OF LACQUERWARE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Joao Rodriguez, a Portuguese missionary, wrote of finding a varnish of unsurpassed quality, like ''smooth shiny ivory,'' applied to everything from jewelry to armor in an island kingdom east of China during the 16th century. 
Early traders, dazzled by this rare lustrous coating that was produced from the sap of an indigenous tree of the sumac family, christened it with the name of the land of its origin -Japan.
Today fine lacquerware can be seen in shops all over Japan and in museum collections in Tokyo. 
It's also possible, and rewarding, to visit the handful of rural towns, like Wajima on Japan's western coast, where old networks of small factories and craftsmen survive.
In an age of plastic, few younger Japanese use wooden lacquerware in daily life. 
But among older and wealthier Japanese - for whom the warmth and glow of a simple soup bowl can evoke deep cultural values - the mystique lives on.
One connoisseur is Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone, whose gift to the visiting President Reagan in 1983 was a lacquer chest of drawers embossed with a powdered gold maki-e, or sprinkled painting, of butterflies. 
It was produced in Wajima, a small town on the Sea of Japan and the home of Japan's most renowned regional variety of lacquer.
When he returned from his mission to open trade with Japan in 1854, Commodore Matthew C. Perry brought lacquer gifts for another President, Millard Fillmore, and noted in his report that it was ''one art in which they excel the world.''
Perry added, ''It is said, however, that the best specimens are never sent out of the kingdom.''
The oldest known Japanese lacquer, found on wooden implements excavated near Fukui on the coast of the Sea of Japan, dates from 2400 B.C. Buddhist and feudal artisans began producing sophisticated decorative styles around A.D. 500, copying Chinese and Korean masters at first, then inventing their own techniques, most notably gold and silver maki-e.
By the time the priest Rodriguez arrived in Japan, lacquer was ''the most universal art in the kingdom,'' applied to tableware, helmets, beaded armor, chopsticks, temple art, furniture and miniature boxes, called inryo, which were hung from sashes.
The coating adhered to wood, metal, rock, bamboo and even stiffened linen to produce feather-light teacups. 
The aging of milky crude lacquer produced a black tint. 
Chemicals were added to make other colors - red, yellow, green and Prussian blue. 
Embossing, etching and inlays of ivory, shell, metal and stone evolved.
When exported, gaudy Japanese lacquer became the rage in the salons of Europe and America. 
Marie Antoinette, for one, amassed a huge collection.
The industrial revolution and the end of feudalism in the mid-19th century brought an end to the golden age of lacquer. 
Export markets were soon flooded with cheap mass-produced lacquer products.
Today the industry is segmented. 
Lacquered plastic, said to account for $20 million worth of the lacquer business a year, has replaced wooden lacquerware on most Japanese tables.
As for traditional lacquer, there are still some masters, like Gonroku Matsuda, 89 and deemed a living national treasure, who create works rarely seen in public for an elite clientele. 
Mr. Matsuda, who lives in Tokyo, combines the skills of woodworker, embellisher and painter to fashion decorations and furniture fit for the Imperial household. 
His powdered gold maki-e and glossy gold-flecked nashi-ji, or pear-skin, surfaces are extraordinary.
A walk through the National Museum of Modern Art in Tokyo provides a primer on the tradition Mr. Matsuda represents. 
A Matsuda crane poised on gold foil legs seems to rise from a shimmering thicket of willow leaves on a decorative box. 
Its wings are formed of bits of varnished quail eggshell. 
On a glossy black table large molten birds swirl in a golden sun.
''Properly made,'' Mr. Matsuda has said, ''a lacquer article will last almost forever.''
Other craftsmen, found mostly in remote areas of northern and central Japan and along the Sea of Japan, produce traditional lacquer art - on a more modest scale - that can be used as well as admired. 
The best known of these towns is Wajima, which produces a durable red and black lacquer called Wajimanuri as well as fine designs of maki-e and chinkin, etchings usually filled with gold powder or foil. 
Kazuo Yamagishi, 30, one of a younger generation of Wajima craftsmen, compares the patina of the lacquer process to the effect of severe weather on the people and landscape of the Noto Peninsula, a curl of land in the turbulent Sea of Japan where Wajima sits. 
He doubts whether outsiders can fully appreciate his art's subtlety.
''The most common question Westerners ask is why do you have to paint it so much?''
Mr. Yamagishi said recently. 
''You must live in Japan and experience the seasons to understand the art of lacquer,'' he added.
Mr. Yamagishi makes boxes and tea containers with chinkin designs in the home of his father, Mori, a bowl latherer, whose shop is near the churning Sea of Japan. 
In winter, snow drifts surround it. 
During the typhoon season, waves splash over the sea wall across the street.
For Mr. Yamagishi, the difficult technique and muted beauty of fine lacquer embody traditional values that are still a way of life in this wind-buffeted region. 
He etches common road-side grasses and flowers with steel styluses on polished lacquer. 
It's a modern touch that sets his chinkin work apart from more traditional depictions of cherry, plum and pine. 
Once tamped with crushed gold, the patterns resemble negative images of sumie (ink paintings).
The Omukai Kokudo Company, which produced the chest given to President Reagan, operates two of the dozens of small lacquerware factories in Wajima. 
Modern technology has done little to speed up the process. 
Companies employ craftsmen and contract with others to work at home.
After cutting and shaping the wood, latherers dry it and smoke it in ovens for as long as five years. 
Zelkova wood is used for round objects, warp-resistant cypress for flat ones.
The tough finish of the typical wan, or soup bowl, results from about eight coats of lacquer, some laced with baked clay, which are each slowly hardened and buffed with ash, whetstones and water. 
Strips of cloth, glued underneath the primer coats, strengthen fragile edges. 
Finer pieces may have as many as 60 coats of lacquer and take a year to complete.
The lacquer hardens by slow chemical oxidation of the varnish in damp rooms or compartments. 
The hardening takes from about eight hours for thin primer coats to four days for the finishing layer of lacquer.
Traditionally, Japanese lacquer -which contains from 40 to 90 percent more of the main hardening ingredient, urushiol, than other Asian lacquers - was favored. 
But an imported Chinese variety is now used.
Leveled during World War II to make more room for food crops, most of the lacquer trees were never replaced, according to Masato Nakayama, the director of a cooperative representing 8,000 manufacturers.
The cheaper Chinese product remains the choice of all but a few artists, like Mr. Matsuda, who represent a small percentage of Japan's annual $40 million wood lacquer industry, Mr. Nakagawa said.
The cultivation of a lacquer tree is itself painstaking. 
A tree takes 15 years to reach maturation and then produces small amounts of top grade sap in the summer and early fall for about six years before it must be cut down to start again.
In the Omukai workshop, painters wearing nylon clothing apply the last coats of lacquer in glass-encased rooms. 
A piece of lint can destroy months of work.
In two adjoining tatami rooms, craftsmen paint shimmery designs on finished pieces with various brushes. 
Hair from the forelegs of mice is said to be best for fine detail work. 
Maki-e specialists sprinkle gold dust from pencil-thin bamboo tubes on wet lacquer drawings. 
Others use gold-laced paint. 
A chest similar to the one made for President Reagan would cost about $2,000, according to company officials.
During a visit to the small shop, next to the plant, which sits on a narrow lane a few blocks from the sea, the company's president, Mitsugu Omukai, 66, the mayor of Wajima, or his son, Minoru, may appear, and guests may be treated to Japanese tea and rice jelly sweets while browsing. 
Mr. Yamagishi has some works on display.
Now visitors can also observe the lacquer process at the company's new factory and showroom near City Hall across town.
Besides Wajima, the Ministry of Industry and Trade recognizes 16 towns where the lacquer tradition survives. 
Yamanaka, for example, produces a clear lacquer that highlights the wavy grain of native zelkova wood and cherry. 
Kamakura and Murakami specialize in Chinese-influenced carved vermilion lacquer on chestnut wood.
Some varieties of multihued, mottled or pitted lacquers resemble swirls of latex, tortoise shell and bark. 
Among other places noted for lacquer are Tsugaru, Kyoto, Kanazawa, Kiso and Hida, which makes a caramel-like lacquer.
In Tokyo, Wajimanuri and other varieties of regional lacquer are sold at the Japan Traditional Crafts Center in Minami Aoyama. 
The center employs staff members who speak English and will show, on request, videotapes on lacquer and other folk arts, some of which have English narratives. 
Two tapes focus on the work of Mr. Matsuda, who was trained in Kanazawa, and Taiho Mae, a chinkin master from Wajima who died in 1977.
The Omukai company has a shop on the first floor of the same building, where prices are the same as in Wajima.
Yujiro Sahara, an adviser at the traditional craft center, which is run by an association that promotes crafts, suggests visiting smaller shops in Tokyo where, because of special arrangements with craftsmen and smaller commissions, prices are apt to be lower than in large department stores. 
The cost of top-quality lacquer in shops like Omukai and the crafts center in Tokyo can range from about $30 for a black or red soup bowl with matching cover to more than $1,000 for a large low table with an ornate gold-embossed design. 
A decorative tray costs about $100, and boxes range from $150 for a small gold-etched one to about $200 for a larger, gold-embossed one that can be used to store documents. 
A set of five small tea coasters sells for about $20, a vase for about $190.
Neither shop ships to the United States, and the craft center warns that fragile lacquer can be damaged in transit. 
The Omukai factory in Wajima and larger department stores like Takashimaya and Mitsukoshi, both in Tokyo's Nihombashi district, will, however, arrange shipping on request.
Dealers say that lacquerware should be kept in the shade away from dry air and wrapped loosely if stored. 
In museums, lacquer pieces are displayed next to a glass of water. 
During the winter, lacquer shops use humidifiers to keep the air moist. 
The traditional crafts center has an expert in the repair of scratched or damaged lacquer on its staff.

With a $10 membership, you can receive a 10-percent discount on purchases. 
Free admission.

The Omukai Kokudo Company shop on the first floor of the same building as the craft center is open from 11 A.M. to 7 P.M. every day but Thursday.

Kuroeya (Nihombashi district), a shop carrying many regional lacquers, is open from 9 A.M. to 5 P.M. every day but Saturday.

Wajima: A visit to the Omukai factory can be arranged by calling the company's shop in Tokyo or the plant directly for an appointment with an English-speaking guide.

file: SHOPPER_S WORLD_VINTAGE TEAS IN A TAIPEI SHOP.txt
text:
ï»¿
TERRY TRUCCO is a Tokyo-based writer.
Di Yung-zu may be the most hospitable merchant in Taipei. 
Dressed in an old T-shirt, Bermuda shorts and sandals, he greets his customers warmly, bowing, smiling, offering a cigarette and patting a chair.
Briefly he disappears to fuss with his teapots. 
But within moments he returns to present his visitor with a thimble-size china cup filled with a flowery jasmine brew.
Shopper's World describes tea merchant in Taipei
The customer is admonished to savor the tea, hold the warm liquid in the mouth, then swallow it slowly, allowing it to caress the throat. 
''Tea is very, very healthy,'' he says, sipping from a cup of his own. 
''It improves the blood circulation, settles the stomach and helps you sleep.''
When the last jasmine drops are gone, Mr. Di produces a pot of oolong, the blend for which Taiwan is famous. 
Then just as his guest thinks it is time to leave, out comes a sampling of Chinese green tea, rich and tangy. 
All are delicious and making a selection is difficult. 
The customer leaves laden with three large tins.
For more than 40 years Di Yung-zu has held impromptu tea parties each day at his humble shop, the Hua Yei Tea Company. 
Tea is the staple drink for this country's 18 million people, and Taiwan's capital supports an estimated 1,000 tea establishments, old and new, large and small.
What distinguishes Mr. Di's enterprise is its appearance, which immediately marks it as a traditional Chinese tea shop. 
A neat, handpainted sign labels the place, and with no front windows or doors, customers enter by walking past an old-fashioned wood-framed display case of tea jars and tins.
The place, Mr. Di says proudly, has changed little since the day it opened in 1939. 
Even then he made no attempt to be up to date, equipping the shop with the dim lighting, bright-colored tins and traditional wooden tea crates used for decades.
''Many young people think tea has to be displayed in a more modern style,'' Mr. Di says, holding a worn, rust-colored teapot, which is more than 200 years old and still in daily use. 
''But I've kept my store this way for historical reasons, for the same reason some people collect antiques.''
Styles of clothes may change, he adds, ''but the tea doesn't change.''
For someone with an eye for tradition Di Yung-zu made a brilliant real estate decision. 
Though Taiwan's brisk economy has replaced many older buildings with gleaming skyscrapers, Di Yung-zu's part of town has stubbornly remained the same. 
According to one longtime resident, the area has changed little since the days of the Japanese occupation, which lasted from 1895 to the end of World War II.
The business pace is also in harmony with that of old Taipei. 
Hours are long, stretching from 8:30 A.M. to 7 7 P.M. every day except Sunday. 
But the pace is unhurried and informal, leaving Mr. Di ample time to discuss tea with his customers.
A slender, white-haired man with tea-stained teeth, Mr. Di has spent all of his adult life in the tea trade. 
Though he was not born to the business, at the age of 15 left his family's farm for Taipei, where he was apprenticed to a tea merchant.
When Mr. Di was 29 he bought his present shop and a few years back unofficially retired, turning the business over to his daughter-inlaw, an efficient-looking woman with a grown daughter. 
He still lives above the shop, and every day he comes down to chat with customers, read the newspapers and play with the neighborhood children.
He also purchases his own tea, patronizing farmers in Taiwan's northern and central regions. 
''I never owned my own mountain like some tea merchants, because this way I could select the tea I thought was best. 
Even when it all comes from the same mountain, the quality can differ, he says.''
The tea drunk in Taiwan today has a provenance as distinguished as its flavor. 
As Mr. Di says, tea cultivation in China is believed to date back to prehistoric times. 
The first of these leafy evergreen tea plants grown in the Taiwan mountains were originally imported from the China mainland, probably by the vast waves of immigrants who arrived during the Ming and Manchu dynasties.
W ith its balmy climate, ample rainfall and mountainous terrain, Taiwan proved a rich breeding ground for tea. 
Last year the island produced more than 25,000 metric tons, a 3 percent increase over the previous year.
Tea plants, which are related to the camellia family, can grow to a height of 30 feet, though when cultivated they are usually pruned to three to five feet. 
More importand than climate is site. 
The finest tea comes from the upper mountain reaches, with the quality dipping as one moves down the hill. 
At the top, tea receives the proper amounts of sun and dew, Mr. Di says, while tea grown on flatlands often suffers from too much of both.
The harvest season is vital for a quality brew, too. 
For most teas, the finest is harvested in the spring, though choice oolong tea is gathered in the summer. 
Additional caches of tea are cut in early autumn and November.
All these factors help determine the tea's price, and good tea can be expensive. 
Di Yung-zu's tea sells by the gram; 600 grams -a bit more than a pound - of the finest can cost as much as $80. 
The same amount of a lesser grade can sell for as little as $5. 
Tins cost about 50 cents extra.
If the tea is not packed in tins, it is measured into thick paper bags, never plastic, says Mr. Di. He has weighed tea for years on the type of iron scale seen in small shops all over Taipei. 
It is important to keep the tea away from light and heat, which is why the Hua Yei Tea Company's leaves are stored in old metal-lined pine boxes. 
Mr. Di has more than 50 of these brown trunk-size crates. 
''Wood keeps the temperature moderate so the tea's color won't turn,'' he says.
There are hundreds of teas, but the basic types in Taiwan are jasmine, tiehkuanyin, assam, oolong, daffodil, green tea and yen tea. 
The tea's color depends on the method used to process it. 
Black teas, such as assam, are fermented before firing. 
Oolongs are partially fermented, and green teas not at all. 
Even within a broad category like green tea, which the Chinese call bao chung, dozens of varieties exist.
The shop also sells what is best described as old tea. 
Tucked away in some of those wooden crates is tea dating back to the days when Mr. Di opened the shop. 
It is quite costly: 600 grams for $770. 
It hasn't much flavor. 
But many people believe in its medicinal effects - calming nerves, cleansing the system and releasing excess body heat. 
There is also an old myth that it can treat cancer.
How can a customer identify choice tea?
A hearty sniff helps. 
''The better teas all smell good,'' says Mr. Di. Still, the smell won't tell you if the tea comes from the mountaintop.
Almost as he spoke, two middle-aged women entered the shop, headed for the yen tea bin, scooped up a handful and held it to their noses. 
And how is the best tea brewed?
Mr. Di says you simply cover the bottom of your teapot with leaves, add boiling water and let the brew steep for two or three minutes. 
The leaves can be used again the same day and should yield almost as much flavor, provided the second brew is allowed to steep six or seven minutes.
Technically, any tea brought into the United States has to be submitted to a Food and Drug Administration examiner, but travelers have reported that Customs officials have allowed them to bring in a tin without question.
Â 
If you go
The Hua Yei Tea Company is at 96, Section One, Kai Fang Street in the northern section of Taipei. 
The phone number is 3114918. 
The shop willingly accepts both United States dollars and Japanese yen. 
If he is there, the retired owner, Di Yung-zu, a seasoned businessman, quickly looks up the exchange rate in the day's newspaper as a courtesy to customers. 
T.T.

file: SHULTZ ON CHINA_ ACCENTING THE POSITIVE_News Analysis.txt
text:
ï»¿
Despite some tough language in China's official commentary on Secretary of State George P. Shultz's four-day visit to Peking, there seems to be considerable agreement by American and Chinese officials on what Mr. Shultz did and did not accomplish there.
In interpreting the results of the Shultz mission, however, the two sides appear to be practicing what one of Mr. Shultz's aides today called ''half full, half empty diplomacy.''
The aide meant that Peking persists in seeing the same ''cup'' of relations as half empty that the Americans see as half full.
Mr. Shultz was informed of the New China News Agency commentary when he awoke this morning. 
He read the text along with senior advisers, Paul D. @Wolfowitz, the Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian Affairs, and Thomas Shoesmith, Mr. Wolfowitz's deputy. 
The commentary said Mr. Shultz's visit had helped Chinese-American relations ''to some extent'' but unless the Taiwan issue was resolved ''mutual trust between China and the United States is out of the question.''
SEOUL, South Korea, Feb. 
7 - Despite some tough language in China's official commentary on Secretary of State George P. Shultz's four-day visit to Peking, there seems to be considerable agreement by American and Chinese officials on what Mr. Shultz did and did not accomplish there.
The initial American reaction was one of relief that it had not closed the doors to improved relations, and was less negative than some early news accounts suggested. 
One aide, in talking to reporters, said, ''We don't see anything startling: in fact, there are some positive things in it.''
Â 
Shultz Limits Claims of Success
This assessment, of course, was in keeping with the traditional American approach to Chinese relations. 
Every secretary of state leaving China has described the results in a more positive way than have the Chinese. 
For instance, Cyrus R. Vance in 1977 said some progress had been achieved, only to have the Chinese call the visit a failure. 
Alexander M. Haig Jr. 
In 1981 was exuberant about moves in the strategic field, only to have the Chinese lash out at the Reagan Administration, and to suspend military contacts.
Mr. Shultz has limited his claims of ''success'' to having achieved a better understanding of each other's position, more mutual trust and a laying of groundwork for closer ties in the future. 
He did not claim any breakthroughs on Taiwan or anything else.
The reason Mr. Shultz's party was not unhappy about the press agency commentary was that much of it meshed with what the Americans were saying about the visit. 
These points were made by Mr. Shultz's aides:
- The two sides agreed that the visit improved relations ''to some extent'' by allowing a full airing of differences, even though problems remained.
- The press agency said the two countries were ''close in their analyses of the current international situation as well as in their views on the issues of Afghanistan, Cambodia and arms control.''
That was an even more positive statement than Mr. Shultz had made at his farewell press conference and was the first time publicly Peking said it agreed with Washington on arms control matters.
- The press agency commentary did not take issue with two potential developments made public by Mr. Shultz. The first was that the two sides had agreed to hold talks on ways of bringing about closer military relations. 
The second was that Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang had agreed to come to the United States and a date would be worked out. 
The White House said he had agreed to come this year, but Mr. Shultz was not that specific.
- Even though the Chinese raised the Taiwan issue repeatedly during the talks with Mr. Shultz, the press agency article quoted Mr. Shultz correctly as saying that he and President Reagan fully intended to live up to last August's communique calling for phased out arms sales to Taiwan.
The article went on to list what it said were violations of agreements on Taiwan, such as officials attending Taiwan receptions in Washington and the setting up of a new Taiwan office.
''Obviously, the point they are making is that Taiwan is a problem in relations,'' one American said. 
''We know that.''
What is unknown, of course, is whether the Chinese side will seek to focus so heavily on Taiwan and other problems such as the difficulty of getting licenses to buy certain advanced technology so as to prevent relations from developing further.
Mr. Shultz and his aides who sat through the long hours of talks insist the Chinese made it clear they wanted to advance the relations, even though differences persisted.
Â 
Felt Chinese Were Ill Informed
As a longtime mediator, Mr. Shultz believes that with patience and trust most problems can be solved, or at least ought to be. 
As he made clear on the plane flying here from Peking, he came away from the talks feeling that the Chinese side was not as well informed on American policy as it should have been and this, in his view, created distortions. 
One reason, some of his aides said, was that the former Chinese Ambassador, Chai Zemin, spoke no English, and was not able to become closely enough involved in Chinese-American relations in Washington.
The new Chinese Ambassador to Washington, Zhang Wenjin, is an old American hand, speaks fluent English, and was involved in the opening of relations in the early 1970's. 
Mr. Shultz's hope is that Mr. Zhang will become involved in such matters as licensing problems for exports, and can better appreciate the political realities in Washington that makes it impossible for any administration to renounce the Taiwan Relations Act, which obliges the United States to provide for Taiwan's defense.
It is assumed by the Americans that the Chinese harp on the differences to make clear they remain independent in their foreign policy - something crucial to their relations with the Soviet Union and the third world. 
And the Chinese may feel, American officials say, that by stressing the problems they can bring pressure on Washington to make compromises.

text:
ï»¿
Secretary of State George P. Shultz indicated today that he might meet with the Soviet Foreign Minister, Andrei A. Gromyko, at an East-West conference on disarmament in Stockholm Jan. 
17.
Several Western European nations, especially West Germany, have been urging that the 35-nation conference on developing safeguards against surprise attacks be begin with foreign ministers present. 
Mr. Shultz, at a breakfast meeting with reporters, indicated he would not oppose that effort, although he declined to say specifically that he would meet with his Soviet counterpart.
''It seems to be shaping up as a meeting to which foreign ministers will go,'' he said. 
''If that's the way it emerges, then the United States will be represented.''
State Sec George P Shultz indicates that he might meet with Soviet Min Andrei A Gromyko at East-West conference on disarmament in Stockholm Jan 17; several Western European nations are urging that 35-nation conference begin with foreign mins present; other points made by Shultz outlined (M)
Such a meeting would be the first high-level Soviet-American encounter since the chilly exchange between Mr. Shultz and Mr. Gromyko in Madrid on Sept. 
9 after the Soviet Union shot down a South Korean passenger airliner. 
The tension between Moscow and Washington has worsened with the deployment of American medium-range nuclear missiles in Western Europe and the Soviet suspension of the talks in Geneva on medium-range missiles.
Â 
Kohl Backs Deployment Schedule
In Bonn, Chancellor Helmut Kohl said he favored adhering to the deployment schedule for the American missiles as a way to to persuade the Soviet Union to return to the Geneva talks. 
(Page A13.)
In Geneva, Soviet and American negotiators met for 3 hours and 35 minutes in the current round of talks on limiting strategic, or long-range, weapons. 
They agreed to meet again next Tuesday. 
(Page A10.)
Â 
Joint Decision Expected
As for the Stockholm meeting, Mr. Shultz said he and other North Atlantic Treaty Organization foreign ministers would decide whether to attend when they met in Brussels next week. 
He said his attendance would not depend on whether Mr. Gromyko was coming. 
An aide said later that while there were no arrangements for Mr. Shultz to meet Mr. Gromyko in Stockholm, ''it would be logical'' for that to happen.
The United States is reported to have privately suggested to Moscow various possible topics for talks, such as technical exchanges or navigation agreements to prevent events like the Korean jet incident. 
But Administration officials are skeptical that much can be done while the state of health of Yuri V. Andropov, the Soviet leader, remains uncertain.
When asked about Mr. Andropov, Mr. Shultz replied: ''He's obviously ill. 
How ill he is and what is his illness, I don't know. 
I know that statements are issued in his name. 
There's all sorts of speculation. 
Obviously we follow these matters closely. 
But what we have to do is not try to base our policies on what we think may be happening there, but base our policies on what we think is right for us.''
In his wide-ranging one-hour session with reporters, Mr. Shultz made these other points:
- Recent conciliatory statements by the Nicaraguan Government were ''good to hear'' and ''vastly different'' from what the Sandinista junta was saying six to eight months ago. 
But Mr. Shultz said there is ''always a question of whether there is a reality behind the words.''
- Planning continues for the visit of Zhao Ziyang, the Chinese Prime Minister, to the United States in January, and for President Reagan's visit to Peking in April. 
Mr. Shultz said he assumed the visits would take place despite Chinese objections to two Congressional measures that referred to Taiwan as the Republic of China. 
The Administration has since reaffirmed its position that the Peking Government ''is the sole legitimate Government of China.''
- The Salvadoran Government risks erosion of its support unless it can take some action quickly to curb right-wing death squads and bring suspected killers to trial. 
Unless improvement from the current ''grave'' situation is made by January, Mr. Shultz said, it would be ''very difficult'' for him to report to Congress that progress on human rights was being made in El Salvador.
- Supplies of American-made cluster bombs to Israel will depend on working out a satisfactory agreement on their use, an indication that the Reagan Administration is looking for tighter restrictions to insure that such weapons are not used in areas with heavy civilian populations.
Â 
Conditions on Sale and Use
During this week's visit to Washington by Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, the Reagan Administration indicated that it was ready to consider resuming supplies of such weapons. 
Those shipments were suspended 18 months ago as a sign of Administration unhappiness over Israel's invasion of Lebanon.
In response to a question about the cluster bombs, Mr. Shultz said: ''What we have said is that the suspension on sales of cluster munitions will be lifted if there is a satisfactory agreement on usage. 
We will have to see whether such an agreement can be made in the course of our meetings. 
I assume there's interest. 
If there's no interest, why, that's fine.''
Several times, he defended President Reagan's agreement with Mr. Shamir to set up a new American-Israeli political-military group as a necessary move to offset ''the buildup of Soviet arms and troop presence in Syria.''

file: SLAYING WAS ORDERED FROM TAIWAN, LAWYER SAYS.txt
text:
ï»¿
A lawyer for the family of a Chinese writer who was slain here asserted today that the identification of the killers as leaders of an underworld gang with good political connections in Taiwan showed the killing had been ''ordered and planned by powerful figures in Taiwan.''
The lawyer, Jerome M. Garchik, asserted that Chen Chi-li, leader of the gang, had links to a number of officials in Taiwan, including a son of President Chiang Ching-kuo.
Mr. Chen was named last week by the Federal Bureau of Investigation as mastermind of the slaying of Henry Liu, who was shot in his home in nearby Daly City on Oct. 
15 shortly after publishing a critical biography of President Chiang and his family.
Lieut. Thomas G. Reese of the Daly City police said the department was still uncertain about a motive. 
Taiwan has denied any involvement in the incident.
President Chiang's son, Chiang Hsiao-wu, is Deputy Secretary General of the National Security Council on Taiwan, a powerful umbrella security agency, and was formerly head of the China Broadcasting Corporation, where he had contact with a number of movie stars and singers. 
Mr. Garchik contended that some of the performers were members of the underworld organization, known as the Bamboo Gang.
Â 
Political Repercussions
The killing appears to have touched off political repercussions in Taiwan.
Since the Nationalist Government maintains tight political control over Taiwan with a highly effective police network, many Chinese assume the gang must have had good relations with the Government to survive, said a Chinese scholar at Stanford University. 
The Bamboo Gang has grown rapidly in recent years and has been heavily involved in extortion, gambling and prostitution.
The scholar, who asked that his name not be used because of fear of retaliation by Taiwan or the gang, said President Chiang appeared to be above suspicion in the killing.
On Nov. 
13 the Taiwan Garrison Command suddenly began a major crackdown on the gang, arresting more than 300 members, including Mr. Chen and Wu Tun, another suspect in the killing. 
Among those detained was a senior police official in the city of Kaohsiung and a former officer of the Garrison Command who now serves as head of the Prominent Merchants Club, a private club run by Mr. Chen, according to accounts in the Taiwan press.
Â 
'Looking for the Answers'
Paul Mao, a spokesman for the San Francisco office of Taiwan's unofficial mission in the United States, the Coordination Council for North American Affairs, said today that his Government had begun the crackdown on the Bamboo Gang and other underworld groups precisely to find out what was the extent of their power and political connections. 
''We are looking for the answers,'' Mr. Mao said.
Both Lieutenant Reese and an agent of the F.B.I. familiar with the case said they had been told by various Chinese about a friendship between Mr. Chen, the gang leader, and President Chiang's son. 
''I've heard about it, but I'm not at liberty to comment on it,'' Lieutenant Reese said.
Mr. Garchik, in a news conference, said several other unresolved questions suggested the involvement of the Taiwan authorities in the killing. 
For example, he noted that Mr. Chen himself had come to San Francisco, even though he is the head of a gang with perhaps 4,000 to 10,000 members. 
Mr. Garchik also said Mr. Liu had never written about the Taiwanese underworld and had no connection to it.
''There is no other explanation than a political assassination,'' Mr. Garchik said.
In addition, Mr. Garchik pointed out that Taiwan has recently banned two magazines that reported on Mr. Liu's writings and killing and noted that the head of the Government Information Office in Taiwan last week had threatened to sue anyone who said anything critical about Taiwan.
Mr. Garchik contended that the killing and recent identification of the suspected killers had serious international implications. 
''We feel this is a case of international terrorism, and if Taiwan doesn't extradite these criminals, they will be harboring terrorists,'' Mr. Garchik said at a news conference here.
Â 
State Department Is Silent
A State Department spokesman in Washington said the department would have no comment at present because the case is a criminal matter and is being handled by the F.B.I.
Mr. Chen and two of the others named by the F.B.I. as the killers fled to Taiwan after the shooting. 
A fourth man identified as the driver of the car used by the killers, David Yu, a business executive from San Gabriel, near Los Angeles, was arrested at his home but then released last week because of insufficient evidence, the police said.
On Monday the San Mateo County District Attorney's office near here issued an arrest warrant for Mr. Chen, which is being forwarded to the United States Attorney's office in San Francisco to obtain Federal warrants for illegal flight from justice, a first step in trying to extradite Mr. Chen. However, the United States does not have an extradition treaty with Taiwan, with which it broke diplomatic relations in 1979.
Â 
Statement Is Demanded
Mr. Garchik, who represents the Committee to Obtain Justice for Henry Liu, demanded that Taiwan make it clear whether it would cooperate in extraditing the suspects.
Lieutenant Reese of the Daly City police said the police were close to getting warrants for the other suspects. 
''We know how it went down,'' Lieutenant Reese said of the slaying, which took place in Mr. Liu's garage.
The incident comes as the Reagan Administration is taking a heightened interest both in international terrorism and in the new development of Asian crime gangs in the United States.

file: SOVIET AIDE HINTS AT A CUT IN TROOPS ON CHINESE BORDER.txt
text:
