A key member of the Central Committee of the Soviet Communist Party has told a group of Japanese journalists that talks with China could result in a pullback of troops from the Soviet-Chinese border.
Participants in a conference of Japanese and Soviet journalists being held here confirmed today that the Soviet official, Viktor G. Afanasyev, who is the editor of Pravda, the party newspaper, made the remark on Tuesday during a meeting at Pravda's offices.
The suggestion was similar to one that a Chinese official was reported as having made to Western journalists in Peking during a background discussion last month after the resumption of Soviet-Chinese negotiations.
Â 
Efforts at an Accommodation
Kyodo, the Japanese news agency, quoted Mr. Afanasyev as having said: ''It is possible that the two sides might promise each other a reduction of military forces in border areas.''
A reporter for the agency later said the quotation was accurate. 
(Although the United States has deliberately not been voicing public concern about the improvement of Soviet-Chinese relations, Washington officials say privately that they find the trend worrisome. 
Page A7.)
MOSCOW, Nov. 
17 - A key member of the Central Committee of the Soviet Communist Party has told a group of Japanese journalists that talks with China could result in a pullback of troops from the Soviet-Chinese border.
The indication that the Soviet Union might consider troop reductions along the frontier in the context of a general improvement of the relationship was not in itself new. 
But it attracted attention in the context of the change in the Soviet leadership and the renewed Soviet overtures to the Chinese.
Â 
Unusual Warmth for Chinese
The new Soviet leader, Yuri V. Andropov, signaled his attitude when he greeted the Chinese Foreign Minister, Huang Hua, with what appeared to be unusual warmth at a reception that followed Leonid I. Brezhnev's funeral on Monday. 
The next day Mr. Huang met with Foreign Minister Andrei A. Gromyko for 90 minutes in what was the highestlevel discussion between the Soviet Union and China since their Prime Ministers met in 1969.
The Soviet press has also given unusual prominence to Chinese condolence messages, printing them with those from the Soviet-bloc nations.
On Tuesday, Pravda and Izvestia, the two principal Soviet newspapers, published excerpts from an interview that Mr. Huang gave to the New China News Agency. 
In it, he said:
''Peace and friendship between China and the Soviet Union fully correspond not only to the interests of both peoples and both countries, but also to the interests of peace in Asia and the whole world.''
Western diplomats assessed the remark about a possible troop pullback as another carefully considered signal. 
Mr. Afanasyev, as the principal conveyor of official news to the Soviet people, is close to the Kremlin leadership. 
When he met with an American editor two weeks ago, he spoke in general terms about the new contacts with China and did not mention the possibility of troop reductions.
In his talk with the Japanese, he said that he thought Soviet troops ''will eventually withdraw'' from Afghanistan and that he did not think the issue could be settled militarily. 
The remark was not inconsistent with Soviet policy, which has called for a political settlement, but its timing seemed significant.
Mr. Afanasyev was quoted as having said that a senior Soviet official, whom he did not identify, had been conducting discussions on Afghanistan with ''concerned'' parties, including Pakistan. 
This appeared to be a hint that the Kremlin had been making a hitherto undisclosed bid to find diplomatic maneuvering room over the issue. 
Western proposals for an international conference have been repeatedly rejected.
The editor's remarks appeared to be fashioned as a response to the demands that China has made a condition for a return to normal relations. 
The demands, restated in recent months, are for a reduction of troops on the border, a Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan and an end to Soviet backing for the Vietnamese-installed Cambodian Government.
Mr. Afanasyev's remarks, as reported by Kyodo, also included references to the new political situation here. 
According to Kyodo, the Pravda editor alluded to some kind of power struggle after the death of Mr. Brezhnev. He did not elaborate, but Kyodo quoted him as having said that Mr. Brezhnev's chief of staff, Konstantin U. Chernenko, ''had the possibility'' of succeeding Mr. Brezhnev.
However, the Pravda editor was quoted as having said that ''many responsible, sincere men'' had chosen Mr. Andropov instead. 
The editor said vacancies would be filled in the two key bodies in the Soviet power structure, the Politburo and the Secretariat of the Central Committee, which together make up the Soviet leadership group. 
These additions are expected to be announced next week. 
However, Kyodo said, Mr. Afanasyev did not expect major changes of top figures because Mr. Andropov is ''a man of prudence.''

file: SOVIET AND CHINA SIN FIVE-YEAR TRADE PACT.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Soviet Union and China agreed today to almost double trade over the next five years, a move that diplomats assessed as a notable step in the revival of relations.
The Tass press agency said that Yao Yilin, a Chinese Deputy Prime Minister, and Ivan V. Arkhipov, a Soviet First Deputy Prime Minister, had signed an accord under which the volume of trade is projected to reach $3.5 billion by 1990. 
It is expected to be $1.8 billion in the current year.
In 1982, before relations began to improve, exchanges between the two countries were down to $300 million.
Chinese Deputy Prime Min Yao Yilin and Soviet First Deputy Prime Min Ivan V Arkhipov sign agreement to almost double trade over next five years, to total of $14 billion, move that diplomats say is notable step in revival of relations (M)
Over the next five years, during which trade is expected to total $14 billion, the Soviet Union is to supply machinery, equipment, transport, raw materials and chemicals in exchange for Chinese agricultural and industrial raw materials and consumer goods.
Moscow has also agreed to assist in building seven new plants and in modernizing 17 others in the fields of electric power generation, metals, machinery manufacturing, coal, chemicals and transport. 
Some of the industrial establishments to be modernized were built with Soviet aid during the 1950's, before the political break between the two countries.
Although the Soviet Union's trade with China is still far below exchanges with Moscow's Eastern European allies and even with some Western European countries like West Germany, Finland and Italy, there has been a major upsurge in recent years.
The trend has gained further impetus under Mikhail S. Gorbachev. In several statements since assuming office in March, the new Soviet leader has called for a ''serious improvement'' in relations with China.
The attention paid to Mr. Yao, who is in the Soviet Union on an eight-day visit, reflected the warming trend. 
The signing ceremony was shown on television, and Mr. Yao was shown laying a wreath at the Lenin Mausoleum.
The publicity given the wreath-laying was considered notable since Soviet-Chinese relations have been limited largely to the governmental level rather than the party level, which among Communist countries is considered more important. 
Although Mr. Yao's visit is at the governmental level, the wreath-laying ceremony seemed to signal at least a symbolic nod to the Soviet party.
There is no indication whether Mr. Yao will meet with Mr. Gorbachev, who was in Minsk today.
But even if the two officials meet, diplomats said, real reconciliation remains a considerable way off. 
China has not abandoned its three demands as conditions for improved political relations - that the Soviet Union withdraw its troops from Afghanistan, reduce its military presence along the Chinese border and stop backing the Vietnamese occupation of Cambodia.
Moscow has shown no readiness to meet any of these demands, and has followed the economic liberalization measures in China with skepticism.
Nonetheless, Soviet-Chinese relations have changed considerably since Leonid I. Brezhnev invited China in 1982 to end the estrangement that began around 1960. 
The two sides have held regular political consultations since then, and have reduced the level of public criticism of one another.
The steady expansion of economic contacts has been the most important measure of the warming process.
Diplomats believe that the possibilities for large increases in trade are in any case restricted by the needs of the two sides, which are mostly for the sort of technology and equipment that only the West can provide.
The more intriguing question is whether the Soviet Union and China will prove ready anytime soon to restore relations at the party level. 
Since Mr. Gorbachev came to office, Chinese officials have referred to him and other Russians, including Mr. Arkhipov, as ''Comrade,'' a term used among fellow Communists. 
Mr. Yao's homage to Lenin seemed another small step.

file: SOVIET ANNOUNCES DECISION TO TRIM ITS AFGHAN FORCE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Mikhail S. Gorbachev said today that the Soviet Union would withdraw six regiments from Afghanistan by the end of the year, and asked that the move be matched by a reduction of Western aid to the guerrillas.
In a televised speech from the Pacific coast city of Vladivostok, he also gave a noncommittal response to President Reagan's recent letter on arms control, and called for closer relations with China.
Western diplomats said the troop withdrawal would cut Soviet forces in Afghanistan by 6 percent. 
The number of soviet troops in Afghanistan is estimated at 120,000, and the number of Afghan guerrillas as high as 30,000.
Â 
Call for Verification
Mr. Gorbachev said the six regiments would be withdrawn in such a way as to make possible verification by ''anyone interested,'' presumably meaning American spy satellites. 
[In Washington, the Reagan Administration indicated it did not attach great importance to the announcement. 
In another move, the State Department proposed to a visiting Soviet official that the foreign ministers meet in mid-September to begin planning for a summit meeting. 
Page A7.] In the Vladivostok speech, Mr. Gorbachev said Mr. Reagan's reply on arms control had been delivered over the weekend. 
The letter ''sets one thinking'' and is being studied with ''responsibility and attention,'' Mr. Gorbachev said.
He said the Soviet reaction would depend on whether the American positions ''meet the principle of equal security'' and ''make it possible to reach effective joint solutions in the field of ending the arms race and preventing its spread to outer space.''
In Washington last week, officials said Mr. Reagan was prepared to delay deployment of space-based missile defense systems for up to seven years on condition that the Soviet Union agree to deployment after that period. 
Western diplomats said the fact that Mr. Gorbachev did not criticize or reject the latest American offer was a positive sign. 
But they cautioned that the Soviet Union was likely to have reservations since the offer was contingent on the continued development of space-based defenses.
On Afghanistan, Mr. Gorbachev said that the withdrawal of the six regiments ''must be answered'' by a reciprocal curtailment of Western aid to the guerrillas fighting Soviet and Afghan Government forces.
It was the first announced withdrawal of Soviet troops since they entered Afghanistan in December 1979.
Western diplomats said the withdrawal of the six regiments - one armored regiment, two motorized rifle regiments and three antiaircraft artillery regiments - was a token gesture that would not significantly reduce Soviet influence in Afghanistan, but might improve the climate for efforts to reach a political settlement.
Â 
Contingent on Western Response
Mr. Gorbachev indicated that no additional withdrawals would occur without a cutback in Western support for the guerrillas. 
If aid continues, he said, ''the Soviet Union will stand up for its neighbor.''
In the 1985 fiscal year, the United States gave the Afghan guerrillas $280 million in aid, mostly in the form of small arms, ammunition, support equipment and clothing, according to American officials.
Mr. Gorbachev said, ''The Soviet Union is striving to speed up a political settlement, to give it another impetus.''
He said that the Soviet Union and Afghanistan had worked out a timetable for the withdrawal of all Soviet forces, and that this schedule might be speeded up if a political settlement were worked out. 
He said there had been progress in indirect United Nations-mediated talks between Afghanistan and Pakistan.
At a round of talks in June, the Afghans said their agreement with the Soviet Union provided for a phased withdrawal over a four-year period. 
Pakistan and the United States called such a drawn-out schedule unrealistic.
Â 
View on Summit Talks Affirmed
On a second meeting with President Reagan, Mr. Gorbachev insisted that the talks should promote progress in arms control and help reduce tension.
The Soviet leader said he could not agree with the view that the accords reached at the first summit meeting in Geneva could ''be reduced simply to the promise of having more meetings.''
''No,'' Mr. Gorbachev said. 
''The main thing on which we agreed last time with President Reagan, and what we signed, is a consent to strive for normalization of relations and for improvement of the international situation and to speed the course of talks on the reduction of armaments.''
On the issue of medium-range missiles, he insisted that any proposed elimination of Soviet missiles in Europe would mean just that - elimination - and not the transfer of such missiles to Asia.
Mr. Gorbachev spent considerable time on the issue of Soviet-Chinese relations. 
He said these had noticeably improved in recent years, and offered talks on additional measures aimed at transforming what he described as the world's longest land frontier into a ''line of peace and friendship.''
Troop Cuts Offered to China He proposed talks on reductions in Soviet and Chinese land forces and noted that the two nations had similar priorities in developing and modernizing their economies. 
He suggested that the two countries might discuss the best ways of achieving these aims.
''Why not support each other?''
Mr. Gorbachev said.
He disclosed that the Soviet Union and China were working out an accord to renew joint water management projects in the Amur River basin on their border. 
Such a program had been worked out in the 1950's, but was canceled when the two countries began to drift apart.
Mr. Gorbachev said the Soviet Union was also preparing a ''positive reply'' to a Chinese proposal to renew construction of a railroad linking the Xinjiang Uighur Autonomous Region of China and the Soviet republic of Kazakhstan. 
Such a project was also begun in the 1950's.
The Soviet leader added that Moscow had offered to train Chinese astronauts for a joint space mission. 
Relations in Pacific Basin Reviewing political and economic relations in the Pacific basin, Mr. Gorbachev said, ''We clearly realize that that the United States is a great Pacific power with legitimate economic and political interests in the region.''
But, since the mid-1970's, he went on, the United States has conducted a military build-up that is turning the Pacific Ocean ''into an arena of military-political confrontation.''
During the same period, according to the Pentagon, the Soviet Union has also strengthened its forces in the Pacific.
To reduce tension, Mr. Gorbachev proposed, as a long-term objective, a conference of Pacific nations that would work out an agreement for cooperation similar to the 1975 Helsinki accord in Europe.
Even before such an ambitious undertaking, he added, the Pacific nations might come together to consider confidence-building measures and the nonuse of force, similar to measures now being worked out by the European nations in Stockholm.
He said such an Asian-Pacific security conference might be convened in a Soviet Pacific city, possibly even Vladivostok, which as a naval base is among Soviet cities now closed to foreigners. 
He said the Soviet Union might consider ending this restriction.
''We would like it to be our widely opened window to the east,'' he said, drawing an apparent analogy to the construction in the 18th century of the city of St. Petersburg (the present Leningrad) as a ''window to the west.''
Among other diplomatic initiatives, Mr. Gorbachev called for an improvement of relations between the Communist countries of Indochina - Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos - and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, a regional grouping made up of Burnei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand.
Mr. Gorbachev also proposed Soviet-American negotiations aimed at a reduction of Pacific naval forces, particularly nuclear-armed ships, and limitations on the deployment of antisubmarine weapons.
He suggested that the United States consider removing some or all of its military forces from the Philippines.
''If the United States gave up its military presence, say, in the Philippines, we would not leave this step unanswered,'' he said.

file: SOVIET PREMIER HINTS AT OVERTURE TO IMPROVE RELATIONS WITH CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
Prime Minister Nikolai A. Tikhonov said in an interview published here on Sunday that the Soviet Union is ''not going to keep from concrete steps'' toward improved relations with China, but that the process ''must not be one-sided.''
Mr. Tikhonov did not elaborate on the steps he had in mind. 
But his remark, in prepared answers to questions submitted by the Japanese newspaper Asahi, appeared to be the most positive signal from Moscow in several years on the frosty relationship with Peking.
Diplomats said it was not clear whether Mr. Tikhonov was giving an advance signal of a breakthrough or was summoning up the possibility of a rapprochement as a lever in the Soviet bid for improved relations with the United States. 
Since Washington and Peking began normalizing relations in 1971, all three capitals have engaged in feints and maneuvers of this kind.
Soviet Union's Prime Minister Nikloai Tikhonov hints at overture to improve relations with China
The Soviet Prime Minister coupled his comments on China with a review of Soviet-American relations and the situation in Poland. 
He urged the United States to abandon the ''language of power and diktat'' and to accept a ''smoothing'' of relations, and he said that it was ''staggering how reckless'' the United States and its allies were being in using the Polish situation to sour international relations.
But it was his comments on China that seemed to strike a fresh note. 
The 75-year-old Prime Minister balanced his overture to Peking by saying that ''the Chinese leaders, as is known, persistently follow in international affairs a course of animosity toward the Soviet Union, its allies and its friends.''
But even this formulation was milder than most that Soviet leaders have used in the two decades since the two nations fell into a rancorous dispute over ideology, territory and other issues.
Â 
'All This Cannot Be Ignored'
Mr. Tikhonov also alluded to the role that the closer relations between the United States and China have played in the equation by saying that ''there exist also other forces in the world that are pressing in every way for a further worsening of Soviet-Chinese relations.''
But it was his reference to possible improvement in the relationship that caught the eye of diplomats. 
Embassies here and in Peking have been alert to the possibility of a thaw since Moscow approached Peking last fall with a proposal that they revive talks about a new relationship that were broken off after the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan in late 1979.
''We have proceeded and continue to proceed from the view that there are no problems in Soviet-Chinese relations that could not be decided on the basis of equality and in the spirit of mutual understanding,'' Mr. Tikhonov said. 
''We are not going to keep from concrete steps that would meet vital aspirations and interests of the Soviet and Chinese peoples.''
''But this process must not be one-sided,'' he said. 
Any move to improve relations is likely to confront obstacles. 
Among them are the border dispute that led to armed clashes in 1969 and the Soviet role as the principal backer of Vietnam, which is in a state of tension with China over the Vietnamese occupation of Cambodia and other matters. 
In recent years the Kremlin has made a number of approaches to Peking seeking better ties, but the initiatives foundered each time.
Â 
'Scaring Themselves Stiff'
An indication of the Kremlin's perspective came in an article two weeks ago in the Government newspaper Izvestia, in which a commentator, Aleksandr Bovin, pointed to recent strains between Washington and Peking and predicted that the relationship would ultimately founder on differences in ideology and global interests. 
In the meantime, he said, ''as long as Americans are scaring themselves stiff with the 'Soviet threat,' they will always be haunted by the nightmare of normalization in Soviet-Chinese relations.''
Mr. Tikhonov's remarks on relations with the United States broke no fresh ground but were notable for continued stress on the need for the ''constructive dialogue'' that the Prime Minister advocated in a speech three weeks ago. 
Since then, Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. and Foreign Minister Andrei A. Gromyko met in Geneva for talks that produced no breakthroughs on arms control, Poland and other issues.
Mr. Tikhonov said ''a smoothing of Soviet-American relations'' would lessen international tensions and the risk of war, but added, ''Regrettably, there are so far no signs that things are moving in a favorable direction.''
Mr. Tikhonov also said that the American military buildup was futile. 
''Washington will not gain anything either by striving to introduce in diplomacy the language of power and diktat,'' he said.

file: SOVIET SEEKS STATUS IN GATT.txt
text:
ï»¿
Faced with falling foreign trade volume and declining oil prices, the Soviet Union has recently made public its interest in becoming an observer at the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
At an unusually candid news conference here recently, Mikhail Pankine, who heads the Soviet Foreign Ministry's Department for International Economic Organizations, said Moscow viewed it as ''essential'' that it be granted such status, and be allowed to observe a new round of world trade talks expected late this year or early next year.
But diplomats here, headquarters of the 90-member GATT, which works to expand and liberalize world trade, say there is little chance that the Soviet Union would gain such observer status anytime soon. 
They said industrialized nations such as the United States and the European Economic Community would block the consensus decision needed for Soviet membership or observer status, for political as well as economic reasons.
'System Isn't Compatible'
''The fundamental thing is that the GATT is an organization for free trading countries and one which is geared on the free, open market system,'' one Western diplomat said. 
''The U.S.S.R., on the other hand, is so enormous that there's some fear that it could skew the whole system. 
Their system isn't compatible with the GATT anyway, and their form of state subsidies wouldn't lend itself to GATT discipline.''
A nominal precedent exists for letting a state-trading nation such as the Soviet Union join the GATT, since Soviet-bloc allies Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and Rumania have long been members, and China already has observer status. 
But there the comparisons end, the diplomats say, because the four Warsaw Pact nation's economies are too small to make a difference, and China has already begun major economic reforms more adaptable to the GATT structure.
''First of all, China is actually seeking to return to membership in the organization, since it was in fact a founding member,'' the diplomat said. 
''Their economy, though one of state trading, is in a state of change and flux so I think that if negotiations with them do begin, it will be partly because people forsee a change in the Chinese system, and believe that membership in the GATT would encourage that, whereas we don't believe letting the Russians in would change anything.''
Â 
Way to Expand Foreign Trade
For the Soviet Union, joining the GATT would conceivably be one way of expanding its foreign trade, still regarded as minor in comparison to the United States, Western Europe and Japan. 
And such expansion could also shore up exports that declined dramatically last year.
According to the new report of the United Nation's Economic Commission for Europe, Moscow's exports to the Comecon countries stagnated last year, while exports to market economies plummeted by a staggering l4 percent. 
The report blamed winter disruptions of production and transport of Soviet raw material and fuel exports in early 1985, and the decline in world oil prices toward the end of the year.
The continued drop in oil prices could cost the Soviet Union between $4 billion and $5 billion in hard currency this year, or about 25 percent of its export earnings, the report noted. 
That is seen as a major factor that could spur the Soviet Union to move more aggressively into the world trading system by trying to join GATT.
Â 
Push to Soviet Union
''You can see the effects in the decline of oil revenues and how this could clearly be giving a push to those inside the Soviet Union who have been arguing for the advantages of getting into the trading system on a bigger scale,'' the diplomat said.
But besides the economic considerations cited by diplomats here, several envoys spoke of political considerations as well. 
The primary concern among Western nations, they said, is that Soviet entry into the GATT - one of the few United Nation specialized agencies they have refrained from joining - could politicize an agency that has so far largely avoided overly political debates.
''Clearly, the relationships with the Soviet Union are different, and many countries would be reluctant to have them join,'' another Western diplomat said. 
''There is the question of whether they would act in a political manner, rather than an economic manner, like they do in the General Assembly.''
Â 
'Different Size of Fish'
He continued, ''The East European nations which are already members don't tend to do that. 
They haven't been digested well by the GATT, but they're so small that we can handle it. 
The Soviet Union is a different size of fish altogether.''
The Soviet Union has yet to apply formally for observer status, which would be a stepping stone to membership, but it has been sounding the waters at the organization for three years. 
Nevertheless, some Western diplomats suggest that though the Soviet Union might see membership as ''essential,'' there is little likelihood of it being granted.
''Given the size of their economy, they couldn't avoid becoming a major player,'' one diplomat commented. 
''If we let them in, I don't think the GATT could continue to function as it has. 
We believe in fact that the GATT would cease to function as we know it.''

file: SPEAKING PERSONALLY_A FRIEND FROM CHINA FINDS SIMPLE PLEASURE.txt
text:
ï»¿
I REMEMBER thinking, as I stood on the platform waiting for my Chinese guest, that there wasn't a single bench to sit on in the whole station, and I was tired. 
I hadn't stopped rushing for hours, what with dusting my entire collection of Chinese spoons and rice bowls, making up the guest bed, hiding the grandchild's toys and preparing to act nonchalant once Hu Shiguang arrived. 
I had it all worked out to join our mutual Chinese friends for dinner out in our own special restaurant, so I wouldn't have to spend hours in the kitchen. 
My aim was to return his hospitality in Beijing, and give him a day in the countryside at peace with the world.
I searched for the train's headlight, checked my watch a dozen times, and I think I worried that train into view around the curve. 
Shiguang bounced out of the open door with a shout of, ''Hello, Penny!'' and I knew he meant his big smile. 
He was carrying a backpack and a bunch of carnations. 
We really did throw our arms around each other, he, the diminutive Chinese, I, the overstuffed American. 
''How have you been, Da Jie?'' he asked - he has always called me ''Big Sister'' because I am older than he - and we got to talking about everything that had happened to us since we had last met, as I drove us home.
''I have a dog, a big, black dog my neighbor threw away!'' he said. 
It is unheard of for a Chinese on the mainland to have a dog. 
''I called him Reagan, so everybody knows he is mine,'' he chuckled. 
''And I am learning to drive. 
My roommate bought a car for $150, and he is teaching me. 
I need a driver's license as proof of address, so I will be permitted to have a library card.''
I thought to myself, what extraordinary process of logic brought him to that conclusion?
New York University had brought him to the United States to teach Chinese poetry for one year. 
''But the students clamored for language lessons instead of poetry, and so I was drafted into a new vocation,'' he said, smiling wistfully. 
''They are all A.B.C.'s (American-Born Chinese) and they don't know the language. 
It's a difficult job for me.''
I knew that Shiguang was almost prevented from coming here, because he was the only person in Beijing who could translate the ancient poets into modern Chinese.
My husband, Jimmie, came outside to greet us and we all migrated to the backyard where Jim was whip-cutting the edge of the vegetable garden. 
Shiguang automatically squatted and proceeded to pull weeds. 
There he was, smack in the middle of all those vegetables - Chinese, of course - bok choy, snow peas, long beans - in his pin-striped pants and shiny black shoes.
''You enjoy weeding, Shiguang, a city boy like you?''
''Of course!'' he answered. 
''I am a human being.''
''Would you harvest the snow peas, if I get you a bucket?''
I asked.
''Of course!'' he said again. 
So I set about fixing the raspberries and we worked in silent rapport. 
Then we recalled his months of forced labor on a farm, during the Cultural Revolution.
''Is it true, Shiguang, that the farmers would steal your crops if you didn't post a lookout?''
He laughed. 
''They would steal anything you turned your back on, even a little piece of wire!''
''But you were all one people - why would they do that?''
''The peasants were very intolerant of the mass of intellectuals that got dumped in their midst. 
They told us, 'You have money to buy food!
Why should you be growing it?'
We were torn from our homes and families, separated from our work, but we were rich in their eyes, and envy makes a dangerous bedfellow.''
I eventually found the courage to ask him a question:
''Shiguang, I am giving a barbecue in late August for my father's 85th birthday, and I don't dare attempt to plant the back wall like I used to, because of my surgery. 
Would it appeal to you to stick in a few plants for me?''
''Of course!''
His ever-faithful reply. 
We took off in the car for the best nursery around, knowing it was late in the season for such a project, and he was delighted to see shed after shed of impatiens and begonias of so many colors.
Shiguang hand-picked 36 six-packs of coordinated colors and I watched him tenderly place them in the car. 
He unloaded everything in the shade, to await the next morning for planting.
During dinner, our friends' college-age niece volunteered to help, so we picked her up bright and early the next day. 
I had a surprise in mind for both of them and took them to the Scarsdale Women's Club Book Drop, where they thumbed through the stacks like bees checking blossoms. 
She emerged with a handful of books on shells, gems and household pets, all subjects for her art classes; he took an armful on contemporary American literature, necessary for his forthcoming book in Chinese.
In three hours the whole job was done, and marvelously, too. 
Shiguang organized the work. 
He dug the holes, and Zhen Rong planted the flowers, everything by color.
After I had fixed my favorite Chinese dinner - shredded chicken and zucchini with fish flavor - we relaxed with two symphony orchestras on television. 
Then Jimmie asked Shiguang if he had ever played computer games, to which he replied excitedly that he had wandered into an arcade once, and would like to try again. 
So my ''Little Brother'' and my giant husband banged mercilessly at the computer keyboard - forgotten was the culture gap, the exhaustion from the garden work, even the hour of the night, for they played until 1 A.M., like young boys.
The next day Hu Shiguang made ready to leave and pumped both our hands by way of ''thank you.''
''It's friendship across the oceans once again, Da Jie, isn't it?'' he said. 
I hugged him goodbye so no one could see the tear caught in my eyelash. 
Penny Stamm of Scarsdale is a member of the Westchester Chapter of United States-China Peoples' Friendship Association.

file: SPORTS OF THE TIMES_Graceful, With Strength_.txt
text:
ï»¿
LOS ANGELES First they made history, then they
were history. 
The American
women's volleyball team won a silver medal Tuesday night and yesterday began planning a reunion, when all of them will have scattered to the corners of the earth.
The players talked about their plans with tentative optimism, but their coach, Arie Selinger, spilled out his doubts about the future of volleyball in America, his decision to step down as American coach, and his bitterness with some people's perception of him as a tyrant.
While an all-star collection of players was celebrating America's first gold medal in women's basketball, the close, cohesive 10-year volleyball effort (''I've got 11 sisters,'' Debbie Green had said) came up one medal short.
In these Summer Games, we have seen a few Americans sulk over not setting world records and brood about silver medals, but there was no all-or- nothing bravado from Arie Selinger and his players, no cheapening of America's first volleyball medal.
''We did our best, we gave it our all,'' Flo Hyman said yesterday. 
''The competition was intense. 
We accomplished a lot. 
We're proud of our silver medal.''
Volleyball's Team America brought a beautiful sport to the public consciousness, but in the end it was defeated by a deserving Chinese team in three crushing games Tuesday night.
History will make them one of the most unusual teams in American sports history. 
They came together in a suburb of Houston nearly a decade ago, and they moved to Colorado Springs and then to Coto de Caza, Calif., becoming the Jeannie Appleseeds of a sport that flourishes in the Orient.
Since 1975, they traveled to China
and Japan and the Soviet Union,
they trained together to the exclusion of college degrees and full personal lives, and as their era ended yesterday, they proudly said it had all been worth it.
''Nobody put a ball and chain on us,'' said Sue Woodstra, the captain, who is 27 years old, has been playing volleyball 11 years, and will never wear the national colors again.
They are old now - 9 of the 12 players at least 24 years old, well into the age when the body no longer thinks it's fun to dive onto the floor, landing on one shoulder, while trying to flick a hard rubber ball back into the air with the fingertips.
''The Chinese have 10 million players,'' Miss Woodstra said. 
''You see what you're up against.''
On Tuesday night they were up against Lang Ping, the best Chinese spiker, an athletic combination of lace and steel. 
Flo Hyman, the worldly and talented American spiker, has described volleyball players as ''graceful, with strength,'' and Lang Ping and her always-positive teammates were more graceful, more strong, than the Americans.
The Chinese work 358 days a year, with a national volleyball program extending into every province, since the government decided to join the world sports powers in the mid-70's.
''Friendship first, competition second,'' the Chinese used to say, but in the regime of Deng Xiaoping they changed their motto to ''Break out of Asia and advance on the world.''
On Tuesday night they advanced on the net of Team America - more agile, more subtle, more aggressive than the home team. 
The scores were 16- 14, 15-3, 15-9.
The two teams had met last Friday in the final match of the first round, with the loser knowing it would meet Japan in the semifinal round. 
Selinger admitted yesterday that he had wanted to avoid Japan, and that he had motivated his players for the supreme effort against China the first time, ''to go at least for the silver.''
If Selinger was working with his players' minds, his counterpart from China was no ''Ned-in-the-third-reader,'' as Casey Stengel used to call novices. 
After losing to the United States, Yuan Weimin had accused his players of being ''qing xu bu wen ding'' - emotionally unstable in Mandarin.
''The players felt regret on our part,'' Miss Lang said Tuesday night through an interpreter. 
''Afterward, the coach did not criticize us. 
He told us last Friday was important but this one is the tough match.''
After the victory over Peru in the
semifinals, Selinger and Miss
Hyman said they felt an important part of their mission had been accomplished. 
They had brought volleyball to national television, they had interested new fans and even some new journalists, who hadn't known a spiked shot from a spiked drink. 
But if their mission was accomplished, a second-guesser asked, didn't that detract from their gold-medal effort?
''I didn't want to make it too hard,'' Selinger said. 
''Had we won the first game, I think the Chinese would have been in a tense situation. 
Maybe, it could be, that when we lost the first game, maybe at that particular time our players said, 'We've already won the silver,' but I doubt it.''
They were proud of their silver yesterday, the last trophy this team will win. 
The team is breaking up. 
The older players will become coaches, get their degrees, stay with the game in some capacity. 
Selinger said he would step down as coach and try to gain funding for a private, amateur volleyball base, rather than work through the United States Volleyball Association. 
He defended the ''conscious decision'' to build this team ''at the top of the pyramid'' for the 1980 Summer Games that America never attended, at the risk of not building a junior program, and he acknowledged that behind the disbanding team, the cupboard is bare.
''I think at this point, we should not maintain a national team but look for the future,'' Selinger said. 
''It will be difficult to come up with a team for four or eight years. 
I'd look to go back to basics. 
We have very little at the younger ages.''
Then some bitterness surged out of Arie Selinger, a 47-year-old Polish Israeli-American, who was rescued from a ''death train'' on its way to a Nazi camp in 1945. 
He criticized articles by one Los Angeles reporter who, he claimed, had made him sound more driven, more intense, than he deserved.
''It was working on the minds of my players,'' Selinger said. 
''They found themselves in an emotional bind.''
Yesterday the players admitted the team had willingly worked
four or five hours a day with few weeks off for the past decade. 
Sue Woodstra said: ''Arie is very determined. 
If you know his background, you know what he's been through. 
He demands a lot from his players - but no more than we can deal with.''
For Arie Selinger to be the Captain Queeg of Coto de Caza, the Darth Vader of volleyball, he would have had to show some kind of mania for a gold medal, but it never surfaced, not in victory, not in defeat.
He talked about the social value of a sport that encourages athletes to be ''graceful, with strength.''
And when the time came to accept a loss to a deserving Chinese team, in the last time these 12 women will ever be together as a unit, volleyball's Team America was graceful and it was strong.

text:
ï»¿
LOS ANGELES
It was a short, short time ago, the
way history is measured in China,
that sports were relegated to providing exercise and an example of social propriety. 
In the time when China was closed and turbulent, the sports slogan of the cultural revolution of 1966 was ''Friendship first, competition second.''
Such a short time later, China has brought 227 athletes to these Summer Games, and Lu Jindong, the assistant chef de mission of the Chinese delegation, was able to tell a news conference yesterday: ''If we win 10 gold medals, I'll be a happy, happy man.''
This is a great leap forward for a nation that has not participated in an Olympics since 1952 and has never won a medal, but China is one of the emerging nations of the Olympic movement. 
Its ambitions were clear yesterday when Mr. Lu revealed that China would consider applying to be host for the Summer Games of 2000.
Mr. Lu also said that athletes who win gold medals will be given a grant of approximately $2,000, hastening to add that it would be ''an award, a scholarship,'' and that ''it's more important that they not think of the rewards, however.''
From outsider to would-be Olympic host in a few decades would be a staggering turnaround, but China has questioned many other values. 
Since the reign of Deng Xiaoping began in the late 1970's, the sports slogan has been: ''Break out of Asia and advance on the world.''
In advancing on the world, they have sent a team that includes their best-known athlete, Zhu Jianhua, the world-record holder in the high jump, as well as Wu Shude, a weight lifter, Li Ning and Tong Fei, two gymnasts, Li Kongzheng, a diver who has rebounded from laser surgery for a detached retina, and volleyball and gymnastics contenders.
The Chinese appearance here is
part of the great upheaval of the
1980's that has brought in western culture and technology, including the news report from Peking the other day that blue jeans are now acceptable in China.
''Critics say that blue jeans represent the bourgeois life style,'' commented the English-language China Daily of Peking. 
''This really is farfetched because blue jeans used to be worn by hard-working American cowboys who had little to do with the bourgeoisie.''
It was only 18 years ago that intellectuals were sent into the countryside for re-education. 
At a reception for the Chinese team in General Lee's Restaurant in Chinatown the other day, Minnie Gan, a Chinese national who was educated in Christian schools and is now living in this country, recalled how she was sent to a farm in the late 60's to correct her thinking ''because I was an intellectual.''
Competitive sports was never a high priority for the Chinese yet it was further diminished during the Cultural Revolution. 
Xin Yun-Zhang, a 23-year-old physicist student from Peking who is now studying at the University of California at San Diego, drove up to cheer the arrival of the Chinese team in Chinatown last week. 
In very good English, he recalled how values had changed since he was young.
''Under the rule of friendship first, competition second, sports was a meeting, a party,'' he said. 
''That's not bad, that's good, people came together, but it wasn't encouraging the quality of sports.''
There were examples of teams or individuals being declared the winner because of superior attitude, or results being ignored for fear of embarrassing the losers.
He recalled a childhood when according to official teaching, ''the United States was imperialist and the Soviet Union was, how do you say it, revisionist.''
He only vaguely heard of the Olympics and said ''I didn't know that Chinese could send a team.''
But not long after the death of Mao Zedong in 1976, the young student recalled, ''they taught us about the Greek soldier who ran so far that he died after delivering his message'' - the origin of the marathon race.
Since rejoining the Olympic movement in 1979, China has entered world competition, learning technique and attitude. 
The other day at a workout of the Chinese male volleyball team at the Long Beach Arena, the dozen players wore varied outfits and smiled often and patted each other on the back. 
The body language was of friends or comrades, not of teammates expected to bring home a medal or face disgrace.
Every so often, Shen Keqin, an
older player at 26, gave a few
slap handshakes to teammates, and once, after plunking a serve for a point, he did a little strut and a wiggle that reminded a couple of American observers of Jimmy Connors.
''We get used to these expressions maybe more from the Japanese than from Americans,'' Shen said through a translator.
Asked whether he had yet observed an American-style high-five, he smiled and replied: ''That is the ultimate expression of a wonderful job, when you are very satisfied. 
Therefore, most of the time, we do not do it.''
Shen was asked if his view of competition had changed since his childhood in Maoist China. 
He said: ''Friendship and competition are in first place but friendship is still the most important.''
Later, after Shen had left, a Chinese journalist based in the West, who had translated the interview, offered another view of the shift in sports values: ''Friendship is still more important,'' he said, ''but the best way to show respect for somebody is to compete hard in sports.''
The role of athletes is still evolving. 
Zhu Jianhua is given larger portions of meat to sustain energy in his tall, slender frame, yet Zhu feels the need to share his rations with his fellow dormitory students. 
Zhu is allowed to train in his home of Shanghai rather than in the sports centers in Peking.
Xin Yun-Zhang, the young physicist from Peking living in San Diego, said ''all China will watch closely to see what happens here.''
He said he thought his homeland was becoming more expectant of results, but he added: ''The difference is expression. 
Here, the athletes are making more money, they are millionaires. 
In China, you are valued more that people will respect you. 
There is privilege in a different sense.''
Now there are rising expectations, the prospect of small grants for winning gold medals, and the hope from Mr. Lu, the assistant chef de mission:
''Friendship and understanding, peace through the world Olympic movement,'' he said, adding, ''This is a chance to learn from other nations.''
Also, he said, ''our athletes have been preparing in order to win glory for our nation.''

The faculty council at St. John's University in Queens voted yesterday to reproach the president, the Rev. Joseph T. Cahill, for removing the Asian studies program from the Liberal Arts College and the Graduate School and making it a separate entity more directly under his control.
''The liberal arts faculty council hereby expresses its concern and displeasure at the removal and the manner of removal of the Asian studies program from St. John's College and the Graduate School,'' faculty representatives declared in their statement.
By its vote, the faculty registered its disapproval, but it has no power to change the president's action.

The faculty council at St. John's University in Queens voted yesterday to reproach the president, the Rev. Joseph T. Cahill, for removing the Asian studies program from the Liberal Arts College and the Graduate School and making it a separate entity more directly under his control.
Asked before the vote why he had taken the action, Father Cahill said through a spokesman that it was ''an administrative decision made to insure the viability of the center's academic programs.''
But faculty members throughout the university asserted that the president should have sought their approval before acting. 
The vote stems from a longstanding dispute between the administration and the faculty over how to treat the study of China. 
The Asian studies program has become the arena for the conflict.
The administration continues to maintain ties formed in earlier years with Taiwan. 
Some faculty members feel this jeopardizes the academic integrity of the program.
While programs at other universities have been increasingly open to scholarly links with China, the mainland government, St. John's has not.
Directors of the program have served in the Taiwan government, there have been publishing ties with Taiwan and money from Taiwan has supported the program and helped build its headquarters.
The differences between Father Cahill and the faculty came to light last Memorial Day weekend in connection with a conference on Chinese literature in which scholars from China participated.
Â 
Asian Scholars Are Summoned
Three weeks later, the Asian studies faculty was summoned to meet with Father Cahill in his private dining room in Alumni Hall. 
''He called my conference 'diabolical,' '' said Jeffrey C. Kinkley, the professor who organized the conference and invited scholars from both China and Taiwan. 
Dr. Kinkley's observation was corroborated.
''Father Cahill has no recollection of making a statement like that,'' Martin Healy said on behalf of the president, who refused to speak to a reporter, but agreed to respond to questions submitted to Mr. Healy, the university's public-relations spokesman.
Last fall, Father Cahill appointed Yih-Young Chen as a vice president of the university and director of Asian studies. 
Dr. Chen until then was director of a bureau in Taiwan's Ministry of Education. 
He has a doctorate in computer science from Tulane University.
Dr. Peter Nosco, who was associate dean for Asian studies until his removal after he had approved plans for the literature conference, Dr. Kinkley, who has a doctorate from Harvard in East Asian languages, and several other young scholars were hired in recent years, signifying an apparent intention to upgrade the program.
The Asian studies program was established at St. John's in 1959, and its first director was Paul K.T. 
Sih, who headed it until his death in 1978.
Dr. Sih had served Taiwan in its embassy in Rome, according to his autobiography. 
He took great pride in the building that was erected in 1973 to house the Asian studies program.
It is a pagoda-like structure with a yellow tile roof, contrasting with the nondescript, boxy buildings that make up most of the rest of the campus in Jamaica, Queens, overlooking the Grand Central Parkway.
Asked where the money had come from to erect the building, Mr. Healy said he would not release the names of donors, but Dr. Chen said the structure was ''a gift from the Republic of China,'' Taiwan.
In the mid-1970's, the program was prodded to give up its authority to grant doctorates, after a review by the State Education Department.
One of the outside reviewers, Charles O. Huck, a professor at the University of Michigan, said recently that ''the whole operation seemed pro-Taiwan,'' and that objective scholarship in that atmosphere would have been ''impossible.''
The program continues to offer bachelor's and master's degrees. 
Although the university press stopped operating in the 1970's, St. John's published a biography of Chiang Kai-shek under its imprint in 1981.

file: STAKES HIGH, CHINESE TENNIS DEFECTOR SPEAKS OUT.txt
text:
ï»¿
Hu Na, a 19-year-old Chinese tennis player who defected here last summer, says one of the reasons she decided to act was her feeling that Chinese officials were trying to coerce her into joining the Communist Party.
Miss Hu, who spoke in her first interview since seeking political asylum last July, also said she feared becoming caught up in a factional political struggle in China.
She recalled that on one occasion she became particularly upset when her team captain told her that whenever she lost a tennis match it would be a sign ''I had not sufficiently studied Marxist-Leninist thought.''
Until this week Miss Hu had remained in seclusion in San Francisco since her defection during the 32-nation Federation Cup tournament in Santa Clara, Calif.
Â 
Leader Demands That She Return
In the interview, which was conducted in Washington, Miss Hu expressed frustration over what she said was the Reagan Administration's delay in deciding whether to grant her asylum, and indicated she was worried that the Government might bow to pressure from Peking to block her request.
SAN FRANCISCO, March 19 - Hu Na, a 19-year-old Chinese tennis player who defected here last summer, says one of the reasons she decided to act was her feeling that Chinese officials were trying to coerce her into joining the Communist Party.
Miss Hu's case has become a serious issue in United States-Chinese relations, which have already been strained by Peking's unhappiness over United States arms sales to Taiwan, quotas on Chinese textile imports and restrictions on the sale of American technology to China. 
China's paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping, has taken the unusual step of personally demanding Miss Hu's return in meetings with several United States officials, according to a ranking State Department official, and the Chinese Foreign Ministry has warned that cultural exchanges between the two countries could be adversely affected if she is granted asylum.
To add to the pressure, this week the Chinese Consulate here made public the texts of two letters from Miss Hu's parents pleading for her return. 
One was addressed to Miss Hu, the other to Secretary of State George P. Shultz. Both were originally delivered to Mr. Shultz while he was in Peking last month for talks.
Miss Hu, a tall, graceful woman, suggested in the interview that one reason for Peking's intense efforts to obtain her return was that she had often played tennis with Wan Li, a member of the Standing Committee of the Chinese Communist Politburo and a close associate of Mr. Deng. Mr. Wan, she said, liked to play doubles with her and had often lectured her on Communist ideology after their matches.
Â 
Effect on Family Feared
Edward C.Y. 
Lau, Miss Hu's lawyer in San Francisco, said Miss Hu did not want to hurt relations between China and the United States and was worried about the effect her actions would have on her family. 
Her father is an army basketball coach and her younger brother is a star junior tennis player.
But Mr. Lau said that because of the Government's procrastination over her efforts to gain asylum, he had decided to let Miss Hu end her seclusion and tell her story. 
Last weekend he took her to Washington, where she met with several senators and represenatives who have expressed interest in her plight. 
These included Representative Stephen J. Solarz, Democrat of Brooklyn, chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on Asian and Pacific Affairs, who invited her to play tennis at his house with Zbigniew Brzezinski, President Carter's national security adviser, last Saturday.
Miss Hu is not sure what she will do if she is finally granted asylum. 
She says she recognizes she is not nearly as good a tennis player as Martina Navratilova, the Czechoslovak defector, and though she has been offered tennis scholarships to two small colleges she speaks only a few words of English and has not been to school since she began playing tennis full time at the age of 14.
In the interview Miss Hu said she had decided to defect after the Communist Party leader of the tennis camp where she had trained wrote her a letter virtually demanding she join the party. 
She said he had frequently advised her, ''The Communist Party has raised you and you owe your success to the party.''
Â 
'I Didn't Feel Safe'
But she was afraid he only wanted to use her as a model for other young Chinese and as a pawn in his own factional battles in the party. 
She recalled that China's world champion table tennis player, Zhuang Zedong, who had risen to be Minister of Sports during the Cultural Revolution, was sent to a labor camp after the downfall of his sponsor, Jiang Qing, Mao Zedong's widow, in 1976.
''So I didn't feel safe,'' Miss Hu said. 
''You never know when one faction is going to be replaced by another.''
Miss Hu's case presents an embarrassing situation for the Reagan Administration, which risks offending either the Chinese or the President's conservative supporters in the United States. 
Her application for asylum also raises the question of whether the United States has one standard for dealing with defectors from the Soviet Union and another for those from China.
A State Department official familiar with Miss Hu's case said it had touched off prolonged wrangling between the China desk, which opposed the request, and the Bureau of Human Rights and Humanitarian Affairs, which favored it. 
The Human Rights Bureau won the argument and made a favorable recommendation to the Immigration and Naturalization Service last November. 
But some officers on the China desk have continued to lobby out of channels with the Immigration Service, the official said. 
By law, the Immigration Service makes the final determination on requests for asylum, though it usually follows the recommendation of the State Department.
Mr. Lau said the Immigration Service had repeatedly assured him since early January that a decision on Miss Hu's request was imminent. 
But last week, Mr. Lau said, the Immigration Service submitted further questions to the State Department about Miss Hu, and the State Department official said the Immigration Service itself was now divided over what to do.
Â 
Other Requests Pending
The Immigration Service appears to be worried that granting Miss Hu asylum would set a precedent that could affect the more than 1,000 pending applications from other Chinese citizens now in this country. 
That figure is about 10 percent of the 10,000 or so Chinese on extended visits here, mostly students and scholars. 
So far fewer that than a dozen of these requests have been approved.
Last July, at a hearing before an Immigration Service judge in San Francisco for a Chinese meteorologist, Xia Yuren, a State Department official advised the judge that the Chinese scientist would not be in danger of persecution if he was deported to China. 
Mr. Xia, who had come to the United States to conduct research at the New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, had applied for asylum after jumping out of a window at the Chinese Consulate in San Francisco, where he had been taken by the Chinese authorities.
The State Department official, Lawrence L. Arthur, chief of the Asylum Division of the Bureau of Human Rights and Humanitarian Affairs, said in written testimony that he was sure Mr. Xia was in no danger because the State Department had checked with the Chinese Embassy in Washington.
In response, Chalmers Johnson, a professor of political science at the University of California at Berkeley and a specialist on China, told the judge that if a Foreign Service officer gave similar assurances about a Soviet defector after getting in touch with the Soviet Embassy he would probably be ''fired on the spot.''

While diplomats negotiate and nations go to war over international boundaries, stamp collectors remain unaffected by the winds of change. 
Nowhere is that better found than in the treatment of China. 
In stamp catalogues there are two Chinas.
The Scott Standard Postage Stamp Catalogue begins its China listings with the 1878 issues of the Imperial Maritime Customs Post. 
The large and small dragon issues have been the subject of intensive study and award-winning exhibits. 
The Imperial Chinese Post issues of 1898 were overprinted in 1912 to serve as the first issues at the time of the Chinese revolution.
The Communist revolution led by Mao Tse-tung changed the political geography of China in 1949. 
But in the catalogue, the China listings are the ''Republic of China (Taiwan)'' including the provincial issues and a separate section for ''China (People's Republic).''
Pre-Communist China listings end with Scott number 1006. 
The first Taiwan stamp is assigned N1007, while the first People's Republic stamp is assigned N1, the treatment normally accorded the issue of a new nation.
This arrangement reflects philatelic reality. 
While the issues of China have taken on increasing popularity, most serious collectors emphasize the early issues and continue their collections with the stamps of Taiwan and China.
The China Stamp Society is the major specialist group in this country devoted to the stamps and postal history of China. 
The society's quarterly journal is entitled ''China'', emphasizing the unified collecting approach. 
Information on the society can be obtained from Mr. Frederick deRidder, Secretary, The China Stamp Society, 100 Font Boulevard, San Francisco, Calif. 
94132.
Much of the challenge and the frustration encountered by collectors of Chinese stamps and covers stems from complexity of Chinese characters. 
The identification of Chinese stamps and cancellations is the subject of a new study by Michael Rogers of Winter Park, Fla. 
''The English-Chinese Philatelic Dictionary & Identification Key'' is a 59-page, 8 1/2 by 11-inch publication that unravels much of the mystery in understanding these characters.
The guide includes a dictionary that translates 300 philatelic terms, dates and colors, a section that translates Chinese characters and another that identifies and locates the towns and provinces.
Guides to the two Chinese systems of year numbering - essential in dating covers - and conversions of Chinese names using the three major translation systems plus an index for character identification and a locator map complete this comprehensive work. 
It is available for $11 from Michael Rogers, Inc., 340 Park Avenue North, Winter Park, Fla. 
32789.

Each is offered for $1 or will be sent free of charge with the Dictionary & Identifier.
The China area offers new issue collectors the dual advantages of some of the loveliest issues found anywhere and the existence of two postal entities to maintain a steady flow of new material. 
Despite their political differences, the historical, cultural and social similarities of China and Nationalist China are evident in their new issues.
China does lean more towards industrial and political themes, while Nationalist China emphasizes the great traditions of Chinese culture. 
But there are common themes, such as the 1984 Summer Olympics and the veneration of Sun Yat-sen.

Hospitals Issue
A United States commemorative stamp honoring this nation's public hospitals was issued Friday by the United States Postal Service. 
Peter E. Voss, vice-chairman of the Postal Service Board of Governors, was the principal speaker at the first day of issue ceremony conducted at New York's Bellevue Hospital Center which is celebrating its 250th anniversary this year.
The history of public hospitals dates back to the almshouses in 16th century England. 
The closing of religious institutions in the 1530's by Henry VIII made care of the sick a public responsibility. 
Acts of Parliament subsequently placed on local communities the responsibility for physically and mentally ill, aged and homeless.
The almshouses and workhouses brought together the poor, the sick and the petty criminals. 
The able-bodied were forced to earn their keep, while those who could not work were housed in cheap, often-unhealthy quarters.
By the 1700s, voluntary hospitals supported by charity and run by prominent citizens began to flourish in England. 
These institutions attracted distinguished physicians through the social contacts of board members. 
They also offered medical teaching facilities.
The American colonies adopted this dual system of hospitals. 
The earliest public almshouse to evolve into a hospital was opened in Philadelphia around 1731. 
It eventually became Philadelphia General Hospital. 
In New York City, the House of Correction, Workhouse and Poorhouse opened in 1736. 
That facility was the forerunner of today's Bellevue Hospital Center, a complex that is one of the largest hospitals in the country. 
With the closing of Philadelphia General in 1977, Bellevue became America's oldest active public hospital.
The Public Hospitals stamp follows a growing pattern caused by the need to limit the number of commemoratives issued each year while still recoginzing deserving institutions and organizations. 
The Postal Service's announcement and selection of a first day site singled out Bellevue on the occasion of an important anniversary, but the stamp is a generic salute to public hospitals.
In contrast, a 1964 commemorative singled out the Mayo brothers, who founded the Mayo Clinic in Minnesota. 
These are the only two United States stamps issued to honor health institutions in this country.
The sterile modern design by Uldis Purins of Newton, Mass. is an abstract presentation of a hospital with the familiar blue and white ''H'' road sign that leads motorists to hospitals. 
The artist demonstrates an ability to produce attractive traditional work in the 1985 Public Education issue.

The Cardinal Spellman Philatelic Museum will conduct its annual Philatelic Literature Fair and stamp bourse next Saturday and Sunday. 
The museum is one of the few of its kind in the United States. 
It is located at 235 Wellesley Street, Weston, Mass.
The museum was founded in 1963 through a generous gift to Cardinal Spellman from the estate of Mrs. Mabel Gilman Corey.

Because the same expertizing techniques and tools can be applied in a variety of situations, the Opinions books are useful to most collectors interested in the examination of stamps and covers and in the condition factors that affect their value.

On March 7 the Marshall Islands released two high-value definitives as the fourth section in its current maps and navigation series. 
A $2 issue depicts two atolls in the Radak Chain. 
A $5 stamp shows a map of Bikini atoll.
In addition to the atolls on the $2 issue, a depiction of Mercator's terrestrial globe is depicted. 
Mercator is credited with solving the problem of displaying the earth as a flat surface, using a cylindrical projection that is cut open. 
The navigational aid on the $5 is one-half of a stick chart, the first half having been shown on a previously-issued 20-cent issue.
Each stamp in the series illustrates a map of one or more atolls that make up this trust territory administered by the United States on behalf of the United Nations. 
By agreement with the United States Postal Service, the Marshall Islands began issuing its own stamps in 1984. 
The less than 100 stamps issued to date note the history of the region, as well as depicting native scenes, fish and birds.
