Prime Minister Yu Kuo-hwa of the Chinese Nationalist Government urged Hong Kong's Chinese residents today to resist the prospect of Chinese Communist rule and promised to help those wishing to move to Taiwan.
Mr. Yu made the remarks in a message to the people of Hong Kong coinciding with the initialing of an agreement between London and Peking under which the British colony is to be handed over to mainland government in 1997. 
The Chinese Nationalist Government has said that it will not recognize the accord.
''We urge the Chinese residents of Hong Kong and Kowloon more vigorously to pursue their struggle against Communism for freedom,'' Mr. Yu's message said. 
''We will assist and support this struggle using various methods and via different channels.''
The Kowloon Peninsula is part of the Territory of Hong Kong.
The message said that Hong Kong and Kowloon Chinese should take part in as many local elections as possible to increase their strength and enable them ''to deal with Chinese Communist ambitions for control, and thereby to help protect and secure freedom and democracy.''
Other than mentioning elections, Mr. Yu did now say how he thought the people of Hong Kong might wage a ''struggle against Communism.''
He also offered to help Hong Kong Chinese prepare to settle in Taiwan.
The message said the Taiwan authorities would grant would-be immigrants one-year multiple entry visas, the right to deposit funds in Taiwan's offshore bank and take them out again and make ''appropriate arrangements'' allowing their children to come to Taiwan to study.
He said even more benefits would accrue to ''dedicated anti-Communists'' or ''patriotic'' Chinese. 
He did not specify who would qualify, but a Government official said Mr. Yu was referring to people who risked persecution for past anti-Communist activities in Hong Kong.
Mr. Yu and a Foreign Ministry spokesman, Wang Chao-yuan said the Nationalist Chinese Government on Taiwan considered the Hong Kong agreement invalid on the ground that the Peking Government was illegal.

file: TAIWAN DENOUNCES OVERTURES BY PEKING FOR TALKS.txt
text:
ï»¿
Taiwan today denounced as a ''trick'' Peking's latest overtures for talks and its plans to celebrate on Oct. 
10 the 70th anniversary of the overthrow of the Manchu dynasty and founding of the Republic of China by Sun Yat-sen.
Sun Yun-suan, the Chinese Nationalist Prime Minister, said in an opening speech of the 68th session of the Legislative Yuan, which claims to represent the mainland, that Peking would have to renounce Communism before Taiwan would consider reunification talks. 
The speech was broadcast and was monitored here.
The Taiwanese response came after a flurry of interest among diplomats and journalists in comments made in July by Deng Xiaoping, senior deputy chairman of the Chinese Communist Party, to a Hong Kong editor about the possibility of the Nationalists' sharing power with the Communists in governing a unified China.
Taiwan denounces Peking's overtures for talks and Peking's plans to celebrate 70th anniversary of overthrow of Manchu dynasty
It also came after suggestions by Senator Mark O. Hatfield, Republican of Oregon, during a visit to Peking last month, that President Reagan use his influence with Nationalist leaders to get them to start talks with the mainland. 
The White House is said to be considering the idea.
Â 
Help of 'Friends' Welcomed
Peking, which used to insist that reunification be dealt with only among Chinese, responded to Mr. Hatfield's suggestion by saying that China welcomed the help of all Chinese and ''other friends'' to bring Taiwan back into the fold.
Mr. Deng's remark on sharing power was reportedly made on July 18 during an interview with Cha Leung Yung, president and chairman of the Hong Kong newspaper Ming Bao. 
The newspaper's monthly magazine supplement printed a text of the interview on Aug. 
25. In it, at one point, Mr. Deng stressed that ''upholding the leadership of the Communist Party is the most important.''
''Under the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party,'' he continued, ''the whole of China was unified, except for the Province of Taiwan. 
Has the Kuomintang unified China?
The K.M.T. ruled China for 22 or 23 years - let us say 22 years. 
However, it never unified China. 
The Chiangs - both father and son - failed to do so. 
The Chinese Communist Party has unified the mainland of Chi na.''
The two Chiangs he referred to are Chiang Kai-shek, the Nationalist leader, who died in 1975, and his son, Chiang Ching-kuo, who assumed the role of President of the Republic of China in 1978.
Â 
Past Cooperation Recalled
''Thus, the Chinese Communist Party wants to persist in its leadership and to be good in exercising leadership,'' Mr. Deng said. 
''It has not been good in exercising leadership in the past. 
In the past, the K.M.T. and the C.C.P. cooperated twice, once during the northern expedition and again during the war of resistance against Japanese aggression. 
The K.M.T. and the C.C.P. can cooperate for a third time. 
They can compete with each other. 
They can even lead together.''
Mr. Deng then went on to talk about the ''gross mistakes'' the Communists made in the past. 
But, he said, the party was capable of self-criticism, adding: ''It is meaningless to boast about oneself. 
If a woman is not beautiful and wants to pose as a great beauty, she will look ugly. 
It is important to know one's limitations, but it is not easy to do so.''
Chinese officials have in the past offered to allow Taiwan to remain autonomous, keep its capitalist economic system and keep its army. 
But some diplomats here could not recall any occasion when Mr. Deng or other Communist officials had used the phrase ''lead together.''
Because the comment was made to a Hong Kong Chinese, some diplomats here believed that it was a serious overture by Mr. Deng, since residents of Hong Kong have been used in the past not only as gobetweens for trade but also as transmission belts for messages.

file: TAIWAN FLIER DEFECTS TO CHINA WITH JET.txt
text:
ï»¿
A Taiwan air force pilot has defected to China with his reconnaissance aircraft, the New China News Agency reported today.
The pilot, identified as Maj. Li Dawei, flew his U-6A jet on Friday from Hwalien Airport in Taiwan and landed in Fujian Province on the mainland 3 hours and 35 minutes later, the agency said.
When he landed, the 33-year-old major reportedly implied that he had been influenced by the defection of Huang Zicheng, another Nationalist air force major, who flew his F-5 jet fighter to China in August 1981.
PEKING, April 23 - A Taiwan air force pilot has defected to China with his reconnaissance aircraft, the New China News Agency reported today.
Major Huang, who went by the name of Peter Z. Huang in Taiwan, received a reward equivalent to $360,000 and a commission in the Chinese Air Force, among other honors. 
He is now a deputy commander of an aviation academy on the mainland.
Â 
Peking Upset by Defections
Peking has been angered and embarrassed by recent defections of some of its citizens abroad, including Wu Yungkeng, a Chinese Air Force pilot who flew his MIG-19 jet fighter to South Korea last October. 
He has been received as a hero in Taiwan.
China also objected recently to the American decision to grant political asylum to a prominent tennis player, Hu Na, and in retaliation has suspended sports and cultural exchanges with the United States for the rest of this year.
The official New China News Agency reported that Major Li said he had left Taiwan because he was dissatisfied with what he called its social corruption and the rule of the Nationalist authorities. 
He said he had often listened to radio broadcasts from the mainland and had learned about Major Huang's flight to China.
''I decided to cross over, convinced that only the Government on the mainland can make our Chinese nation strong and prosperous,'' the press agency quoted Major Li as having said.
Â 
Born on the Mainland
Major Li was identified as having been the leader of the first flight of the observation squadron of Taiwan's First Air Force Group. 
The New China News Agency indicated that he had been trained in Taiwan and had been assigned to the island of Quemoy, among other posts.
The agency said that Major Li was born on the mainland in Fuyang County, Anhui Province, and that his wife and daughter, as well as his parents, lived in Taiwan. 
It did not say when his family left the mainland, but he appeared to have been born at least a year after the Communists took power.
When Major Li landed in Fujian on Friday, ''he was accorded a warm welcome by the local army men and people,'' the press agency quoted Chinese military sources in Fuzhou as saying. 
It gave no further details of his flight.

file: TAIWAN MAGAZINES PLAY _MICE_ TO THE CENSOR_S _CAT_.txt
text:
ï»¿
For Antonio Chiang, editor and publisher of The Eighties, advertising is not a concern. 
''We have never had an advertisement in our magazine,'' Mr. Chiang explains. 
''No one would dare.''
Most of his writers use pseudonyms. 
Some are so wary of being identified with the magazine that they will not meet editors at its offices, up five flights of stairs in an apartment building here.
Attention is being focused on small group of dissident magazines in Taiwan, one of which is The Eighties, because of case of Henry Liu, Chinese-American dissident writer who was slain in California in October 1984; Liu wrote for some opposition magazines and similar publications in Hong Kong and US; Antonio Chiang, editor and publisher of The Eighties, comments; photo (M)
The Government licenses and controls the newspapers in Taiwan. 
So about a dozen dissident magazines like The Eighties provide ''the sole window for the opposition to present its ideas to the public,'' one Western official said.
Attention is now being focused on this small band of defiant publications because of the case of Henry Liu, a Chinese-American dissident writer who was slain in California last October. 
Two weeks ago, the Taipei Government announced that two members of a Taiwan gang had confessed to the killing. 
More significant, though, was the disclosure that senior officials in the Defense Ministry's intelligence bureau were also implicated. 
One of them has been arrested.
Â 
Extensive Accounts of Case
Mr. Liu wrote for some of the opposition magazines in Taiwan, including The Eighties, and for similar Chinese- language publications in Hong Kong and the United States. 
The opposition magazines are printing the most extensive accounts of the Liu case available in Taiwan.
Last week, for instance, Mr. Chiang's magazine published three reports dealing with the activities of Taiwan gangs, contacts between the intelligence agencies and organized crime, and American press reports on the Liu case.
The Government banned the issue. 
The Taiwan Garrison Command, the internal security force, confiscated 10,000 copies of the magazine, two thirds of its circulation. 
The authorities never say precisely why they ban a specific issue, figuring that to do so amounts to free advertising. 
Mr. Chiang suspects it was because of the three Liu articles.
An outlawed issue of The Eighties is hardly novel. 
In fact, Mr. Chiang's main distribution problem is how to outsmart the police. 
Since The Eighties, the first of the dissident magazines in Taiwan, was first published in June 1979, nearly a third of its issues have been banned. 
The Government has also ordered the magazine to suspend publication for one-year stretches five different times.
Â 
'Cat-and-Mouse Game'
The latter circumstance explains why Mr. Chiang's magazine uses three names, the other two being Asian and Current. 
If the magazine is outlawed for a year in one name, he changes the name and continues publishing. 
''We play a constant cat-and-mouse game with the authorities,'' he said.
The situation is much the same for the other opposition magazines. 
For example, 30 of the last 93 issues of Progress, a popular weekly, have been banned. 
Among the magazines, a circulation of 15,000 or more is considered impressive; with Taiwan's population of 19 million, that is like a circulation of 175,000 in the United States.
The Eighties is widely regarded as the most professional and least polemical of the group. 
It says it has a diverse readership, mainly middle-class intellectuals, including some younger Western-educated members of the ruling Kuomintang.
''The Eighties is rather moderate,'' said Hu Fu, a professor of political science at National Taiwan University. 
''It is more rational and reasoned than the others.''
Â 
Editor Given Credit
The magazine's reputation is attributed largely to its editor. 
''Antonio Chiang is just head and shoulders above everyone else in the opposition press,'' a foreign diplomat said.
Mr. Chiang, 40 years old, is the dean of the dissident editors. 
He says he is all too familiar with Government harassment, shoestring budgets and a work regimen that finds him sleeping on an office cot two nights a week.
''I see my family only on weekends, usually,'' he said. 
''To my two children, I am a voice over the telephone.''
Unlike several of his peers, Mr. Chiang has a journalistic, not political, background, having spent 10 years as a political reporter for China Times, a newspaper with a circulation of more than a million. 
Mr. Chiang said he had been frustrated there because as a native Taiwanese, as are 85 percent of the island's people, he felt his opportunities for advancement were limited. 
The former mainlanders, who took control of Taiwan in 1949, still hold most of the top jobs in business and Government.
Besides, Mr. Chiang said, ''It is almost impossible to work for press freedom within the party-controlled newspapers.''
Â 
The Press as Propaganda
The publishers of the major dailies, such as China Times and the United Daily News, are typically senior members of the ruling party. 
Although there has been a gradual relaxation of censorship in recent years, the Government still views the press as a vehicle for its propaganda.
Government officials say the grounds for banning are fairly clear. 
The main ones concern positions regarded as subversive, including publicly advocating Communism or the overthrowing the Government, and ''agitation,'' especially if it is designed to ''drive a wedge between native Taiwanese and former mainlanders.''
Dissident editors contend that the guidelines are vague, and often point to one banning reports that will ''confuse the opinion of the public.''
And the list of items deemed subversive has included pictures of Chinese Olympic athletes.
Anything that might be considered embarrassing to senior members of the Kuomintang is also off-limits. 
The last issue of Mr. Chiang's magazine printed excerpts from the diary of President Chiang Ching-Kuo about his experiences in Russia during his youthful infatuation with Communism. 
Any reference to the President's early Communist-adoring days tends to bring the Garrison Command running, Mr. Chiang says.
Â 
Censorship Is Defended
The Government says its censorship powers are justified because the dissident magazines are often irresponsible. 
''They print things that are just completely made up,'' said James C. Y. Soong, director of the cultural affairs department of the Kuomintang Central Committee.
One magazine wrote that he and two other fast-rising young men in the ruling party had been invited to President Reagan's inauguration in Washington, but that the invitations were withdrawn because of the Liu death. 
Mr. Soong says, and American officials confirm, that the three were never invited in the first place.
Mr. Chiang and other editors point out that Taiwan does have libel laws, which is how democratic governments usually protect citizens from irresponsible journalism.
In the last several months, Government harassment of the opposition magazines has increased and a handful have folded.
Even so, the editor of The Eighties is guardedly optimistic that the Government may ease a bit after the slaying of Mr. Liu.
''The Government has to do something to improve our international image, ''Mr. 
Chiang says. 
''Things may loosen up now. 
I hope so.''

file: Taiwan May Soon Approve Visits to the Chinese Mainland.txt
text:
ï»¿
After 37 years of banning all contact with mainland China, Taiwan seems close to allowing some of its citizens to visit their ancestral cities and villages on the mainland.
Before the end of the year, aged veterans of China's civil war, who fled to the island of Taiwan after the Communist victory in 1949, may be able to visit relatives on the mainland they have not seen for nearly four decades.
Officially, Taiwan's chief spokesman, Shaw Yuming, has announced only that the Government is considering an end to the ban on visits to the mainland. 
But other Government officials and the Government-controlled press say the basic decision has already been made and only details remain to be worked out.
Announcement This Month
''The Government is now trying to work out the details of travel to the mainland, with Hong Kong as the intermediary,'' one official said today. 
An announcement could come later this month, he said.
The possibility of allowing visits to the mainland reflects the growing realization on Taiwan that its policy of forbidding any contact with China becomes less tenable as China gains influence and respectability throughout Asia. 
Taiwan officials also acknowledge that without a change of policy they would have to cut off relations with Hong Kong, which now is Taiwan's third largest trading partner, after the British colony returns to China in 1997.
In addition, there has been domestic political pressure for a more relaxed policy toward the mainland. 
Both the main opposition group, the Democratic Progressive Party, and a new political party, the Anti-Communist Patriotic Union, have pressed the Government to allow informal contacts with the mainland.
Â 
Direct Visits to Hong Kong
Already this summer, Taiwan relaxed its travel rules by allowing its citizens to visit Hong Kong directly. 
In the past, Taiwan citizens were generally allowed only to stop over in Hong Kong on their way to or from other destinations. 
Even so, 220,000 Taiwan citizens visited Hong Kong last year.
The Government allowed its citizens to visit Hong Kong even though it is an open secret that once in the territory many people from Taiwan arrange surreptitious visits to the mainland.
China encourages such visits, because of its desire to woo Taiwan into accepting some kind of reunion with the mainland. 
Representatives from China in Hong Kong facilitate visits to home villages for people from Taiwan, and they do not mark their passports.
Hong Kong trade statistics also show that some $955 million in trade between Taiwan and China passed through the territory last year. 
So far this year, such trade is running at 60 percent higher than last year's rate.
Â 
Age to Be a Factor
It is not clear who would be allowed to visit the mainland under the rules that apparently are now being drafted. 
Some newspaper articles in Taiwan have suggested that anyone would be allowed to make the trip who was not employed by the Government or military. 
But a Government official said today that permission would probably be restricted to those at least 55 years old, who have relatives on the mainland.
The pressure for change comes not so much from the youthful opposition to the Government as from elderly refugees from the mainland.
When Chiang Kai-shek fled the mainland in 1949, he took with him some two million people, including 600,000 soldiers. 
Many had to leave their families behind in the turmoil and want to see their relatives before they die.

file: TAIWAN REJECTS AS PROPAGANDA PEKING_S OFFER OF TALKS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese Nationalists in Taiwan said today that a Communist offer to begin talks on reunification aimed at sharing power in China was a propaganda ploy.
Â 
A spokesman for the Nationalist Government said the offer contained not hing new and was intended to subjugate the people on Taiwan.
''The only way to bring about national reunification is to abandon the Communist system,'' James Soong, a Foreign Ministry spokesman, said in Taipei.
The Communist offer had been put forward here by Ye Jianying, who as chairman of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (Parliament) is China's nominal head of state. 
Stressing nationalism and patriotism, he urged the ruling Nationalist Party in Taiwan to ''forget previous ill will and join hands.''
Chinese nationalists in Taiwan call Communist reunification offer "propaganda plug"
It was the first time that the Communists had offered publicly to share power in a reunified China with the Nationalists, who took refuge in Taiwan when they lost control over the mainland to the Communists in 1949.
Â 
Offer Made Through Press Agency
Mr. Ye made the offer in an interview with the New China News Agency, the Government's press service. 
He said: ''People in authority and representative personalities of various circles in Taiwan may take up posts of leadership in national political bodies and participate in running the state.''
He repeated earlier offers to allow Taiwan to maintain its autonomy as a special administrative region, keep its prosperous economic system, and continue its economic and cultural ties abroad. 
He said Taiwan could also retain its own armed forces.
Mr. Ye did not say how much power the Communists would allow the Nationalists to share. 
At a reception today, marking the 32d anniversary of China's Communist regime, senior officials said the details could be the subject of preliminary talks preceding formal negotiations. 
They said they were ready to entertain a counteroffer from Taiwan.
Western and Eastern diplomats here viewed the Communist proposal as a sincere but politically calculated offer designed to isolate the Nationalists in international eyes in general and in United States public opinion in particular if they rejected the offer.
Â 
Toast by Prime Minister
In a toast at the National Day reception, given for foreign diplomats in the Great Hall of the People, Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang said Mr. Ye's proposal ''fully reflects the common desire and fundamental interests of the Chinese people of all nationalities, including our compatriots in Taiwan.''
He added:
''We are pleased that a relaxed atmosphere has set in across the Taiwan Strait. 
We hope that all our compatriots in Taiwan will, in a spirit of patriotism, make contributions to an early realization of the great unity of the whole nation.''
According to the New China News Agency, an editorial in tomorrow's issue of The People's Daily, the official party newspaper, will say, ''We hope men of insight among the Taiwan authorities and also Chiang Ching-kuo will actively respond.''
Chiang Ching-kuo is President of the Republic of China, the state established by the Chinese Nationalists in Taiwan, and the son of Chiang Kai-shek, who ruled China from 1926 until the Communist takeover in 1949 and then headed the Nationalist regime in Taiwan until his death in 1975.
Â 
Concern Over 'Two Chinas'
The Communist offer of talks implied concern that sentiment on Taiwan was moving toward the creation of an independent nation that could result in two Chinas. 
Mr. Ye said:
''We hope that the Nationalist authorities will maintain their one-China position and their opposition to 'two Chinas' and that they will put national interests above everything else, forget previous ill will and join hands with us in accomplishing the great cause of national reunification and the great goal of making China prosperous and strong, so as to win glory for our ancestors, bring benefit to our posterity and write a new and glorious page in the history of the Chinese nation.''
Mr. Ye said that any Communist-Nationalist accord coming out of Peking's offer would be the third rapprochement between the parties. 
The first was from 1923 and 1927 when the two parties formed a united front against regional warlords and the period from 1937 to 1945 when they united to counter the Japanese who had invaded and occupied large parts of China. 
B oth periods dissolved into civil war.
An army general at today's reception here said that, in offering to allow Taiwan maintain its 400,000-member army, Peking was giving the Nationalists insurance against any worries they might have about betrayal. 
After 32 years of propaganda, the Nationalists are afraid of contact with the mainland, he said.
Â 
Downgrading of U.S. 
Ties Possible
Other Chinese officials have told diplomats in the last two days that no new arms aid from the United States to Taiwan would be tolerated. 
One senior official was reported by Western diplomats to have said that Mr. Ye's message had been designed, in part, to prepare Chinese public opinion to accept, if necessary, a downgrading of relations with the United States if it decided to supply more arms to Taiwan, especially advanced fighter planes.
Mr. Ye's offer of reunification talks reiterated and expanded on conciliatory gestures made on Jan. 
1, 1979, when the United States recognized the Communist Government here as the sole legitimate government of China and abrogated a defense treaty with Taiwan.
Mr. Ye, in calling for a free exchange of mail and visits by relatives and tourists, scholars and athletes, said Taiwan's socioeconomic system would remain unchanged, as would its way of life and its economic and cultural relations with other countries. 
He added:
''There will be no encroachment on the proprietary rights and lawful right of inheritance over private property, houses, land and enterprises, or on foreign investment.''

file: TAIWAN SEEMS UNEASY ABOUT ZHAO_S VISIT TO U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
The visit of Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang of China to the United States has aroused unease in Taiwan that it may portend new setbacks when President Reagan visits Peking in April.
Officials and newspaper editorials have expressed satisfaction that Mr. Reagan reaffirmed United States commitments to the island when he met with Mr. Zhao. But worries remain that Mr. Reagan will be maneuvered by Peking into giving ground later.
James C. Y. Soong, the Taiwan Government's chief spokesman, said: ''We in the Republic of China have confidence in the Reagan Administration. 
President Reagan has, on many occasions, assured us that he will not betray his old friends and allies.''
But Mr. Soong conceded in an interview that Prime Minister Zhao's trip ''has caused serious concern'' in Taiwan.
Â 
'Moving Closer and Closer'
Other officials have taken note of the new momentum in Chinese-American relations marked by Prime Minister Zhao's visit. 
''In the short term, I don't think that Zhao's visit will hurt relations between Washington and Taipei greatly,'' said Chang Hsiao-yan, the Foreign Ministry's ranking specialist on American affairs, ''but in the long term, it will hurt us. 
It gives more of an impression that the United States and mainland China are moving closer and closer.''
Even Mr. Zhao's low-key approach has caused some trepidation in a capital that scrutinizes every contact between Peking and Washington for potential damage. 
The United States severed diplomatic ties with the Nationalist Government on Taiwan five years ago in order to establish full diplomatic relations with Peking.
''I think Zhao has become smart in taking a different approach,'' said Mr. Chang, who observed that Mr. Zhao muted Peking's usual complaint about United States arms sales to Taiwan. 
''He understands that if he takes a high profile in dealing with the United States, he will not get what he wants.''
Officials in Taipei said they did not expect any particular Chinese-American breakthrough during the visit, and Mr. Chang emphasized a common view that ''we will attach more importance to Reagan's trip in April.''
Â 
Flurry of Local Activity
The Nationalist Government has tried to offset the attention given Mr. Zhao's visit to the White House with a flurry of local activity intended to reinforce an image of continuing American support. 
Four United States senators and more than 20 members of Congress are being accorded red-carpet treatment in visits to Taiwan this month.
The semiofficial Institute of International Affairs opened a four-day conference on Tuesday that focused on the Taiwan Relations Act, which Congress passed in 1979 to guarantee that unofficial American relations with Taiwan would continue.
Chang King-yuh, the institute's president, insisted that the conference was not meant to coincide with Mr. Zhao's visit to the United States, despite widespread speculation to the contrary. 
But a Government official confirmed that the invitations to the visiting American members of Congress were deliberately scheduled.
''We had the timing in our mind,'' the official said. 
''When we learned Zhao Ziyang was visiting in January, and it was recess time in Congress, we invited some people from Congress at the same time.''
Taiwan's President, Chiang Ching- kuo, and Prime Minister Sun Yun-suan have been among the top officials entertaining the visiting Americans. 
The visitors have included Senator Arlen Specter, Republican of Pennsylvania; Senator Mark O. Hatfield, Republican of Oregon; Senator Thomas F. Eagleton, Democrat of Missouri, and Senator Frank H. Murkowski, Republican of Alaska.
Â 
Senators Offer Assurances
The four senators were quoted as offering various assurances that the United States commitment to Taiwan would not diminish. 
Mr. Murkowski said that the United States should provide Taiwan with better combat jets if Peking deployed more advanced jets. 
Taiwan officials express bitterness that the United States has been unwilling to sell sophisticated FX jet fighters because it would offend Peking.
The conference on United States Congressional-executive relations and the Taiwan Relations Act was attended by 40 ''renowned scholars,'' as the local press describes the local and American participants. 
The conference featured speeches by Senator Murkowski, Representative Tom G. Loeffler, Republican of Texas, and Representative Thomas A. Daschle, Democrat of South Dakota.
Mr. Chang, the institute's director, told the session he hoped the Congress would ''ultimately enhance relations between the United States and Taiwan, regardless of the nonexistence of diplomatic relations.''
The China Times, one of Taiwan's largest newspapers, summed up the reaction to Mr. Zhao's visit in an editorial on Wednesday. 
''We do not believe that President Reagan and his Administration will consciously betray or do things that harm the Republic of China,'' it said.
It then went on to caution that the Chinese Communists ''are the most treacherous group in the world.''
''Any gentleman will fall into their trap,'' the editorial said, ''if he is careless while negotiating with them and makes irrecoverable mistakes.''

file: TAIWANESE SEEM UNMOVED BY U.S.-CHINA ACCORD.txt
text:
ï»¿
Patrick Lin presented the view apparently held by most Taiwanese on the agreement between Washington and Peking in which the Reagan Administration agreed to limit future arms sales to Taiwan.
''Nothing will change as a result of this communique,'' said Mr. Lin, who runs a small electronics plant in Hsinchu, 40 miles south of here. 
''And it was no surprise.''
Like many Taiwanese, Mr. Lin noted that the communique, which was released Tuesday, was simply further evidence of Taiwan's isolation from other governments, its need for self-reliance and the necessity of diversifying its arms supplies.
Taiwanese seem unmoved by US-China accord
The 18 million people on this island have become accustomed to being spurned by other nations, at least diplomatically and politically. 
In 1971 the People's Republic of China displaced Taiwan, formally known as the Republic of China, in the United Nations. 
In 1979 the United States withdrew its diplomatic recognition of Taiwan and recognized the mainland as the ''real'' China. 
Today only 23 nations maintain official diplomatic relations with Taiwan.
Â 
Living Standard Improved
Yet none of these political setbacks have had much effect on the day-to-day lives of the people of Taiwan. 
The nation's economy has recorded one of the highest growth rates in the world over the past two decades, greatly improving the Taiwanese standard of living.
''People here have lived through so many of these diplomatic events in the past that they are numb to them,'' observed Diane Ying, the editor of Tien Sia, an influential monthly magazine that covers economic and social affairs.
Public reaction to the joint communique was also softened by a barrage of advance warning in newspapers. 
Almost every day for three months the Taiwan papers carried reports on the coming communique and what it might contain.
The Taipei stock market index has advanced steadily in the two days since the communique was released, apparently because the American concession to China was less than had been feared.
Â 
Trade With 140 Countries
Taiwan's strength is its economy. 
It has trade relations with more than 140 nations, and Taiwan's rapid growth, political stabilityII and well-educated, diligent workers have made it an attractive place for foreign investment. 
''The communique should not alter the economic dynamism or the climate for investment here,'' said Carter Booth, general manager of the Chase Manhattan Bank in Taiwan and president of the local American Chamber of Commerce.
Though the immediate effects may be few, the Reagan Administration's agreement to gradually reduce arms sales to Taiwan is taken as a sign that the nation cannot rely on the United States for its security as much as it has in the past. 
''This is a reaffirmation of Reagan's hands-off policy toward Taiwan,'' said Charles H.C. 
Kao, an author and commentator. 
''Taiwan has no choice but to buy arms elsewhere.''
This is a course the Government has so far resisted. 
It has argued, for example, that buying fighter planes now from other countries would involve the costly maintenance of two logistics systems. 
In addition, given Taiwan's diplomatic isolation, that would be difficult politically, Government officials say.
Â 
'Fulfill Our National Policy'
For more than three decades Taiwan has been ruled with a firm hand, under martial law, by the Kuomintang, the Nationalist Party, which has the avowed aim of recovering the mainland. 
The ruling members of the party are mostly men in their late 60's and 70's who fled to Taiwan with Chiang Kai-shek when the Communists triumphed in 1949.
The joint communique predictably brought calls from President Chiang Ching-kuo, Mr. Chiang's son, for redoubled efforts to ''fulfill our national policy of anti-Communism and national recovery.''
Yet even Taiwanese who express little fondness for the Kuomintang, and who still resent the mainlanders' control of their island, believe that the threat from China is real and that Taiwan should maintain a strong defense. 
Moreover, they distrust recent overtures from the mainland for a ''reunification,'' despite assurances from the Communist leadership that Taiwan could retain its economic and social system.
Â 
Argument Against Reunification
On these issues there is little dissent, publicly or privately. 
Most people agree with the assessment of James C.Y. 
Soong, a senior Government official: ''Ultimately the issue here is way of life. 
If there is a reunification and the Communists take control, can we maintain our way of life?
Everyone here doubts that.''
The implicit argument against reunification anytime soon is Taiwan's relative prosperity compared with the mainland. 
In 1981, the per-capita income in Taiwan was nearly $2,400, compared with about $300 on the mainland. 
In addition to Taiwan, people point to the economic dynamism of the other offshore nations of East Asia that are predominantly Chinese, Singapore and Hong Kong. 
''Clearly the mainland has the wrong formula,'' one local banker said. 
''Taiwan may not be paradise, but why should we want to join with the Communist mainland?''
Taiwan and the mainland will, by all accounts, remain separate for the foreseeable future. 
But many Taiwanese do not rule out the eventual possibility of reunification. 
''If we could reunify under an economic system that is basically the one we have now,'' one Taipei lawyer said, ''it would be possible I think.''
He noted the mainland's recent experiments with capitalism, such as the so-called special economic zones in Guangdong and Fujian provinces, as evidence that ''the Communists are making concessions to reality.''
He added, ''They are slowly coming our way.''

file: TAIWAN_S EMBARRASSMENT OF RICHES.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE China News, a Taipei newspaper, published a long editorial this month with a stark headline lamenting the ''Worrisome Financial Situation.''
It captured the concern throughout the island over Taiwan's grave economic distress.
The problem?
Taiwan's economy is mired in success, generating so much wealth from exports - mostly to America - that no one knows what to do with the cash. 
That is creating financial and political difficulties that might seem humorous from afar but that are taken very seriously here. 
So seriously that the Government is loosening its strict currency controls to allow the private sector access to some of its foreign-cash hoard.
The nation's huge foreign-exchange reserves, accumulating at a rate of more than $1 billion a month, are at the center of the Worrisome Financial Situation.
At last count, those reserves topped $44 billion. 
That means that this little island of 19 million people, with a per-capita income one-fourth of America's, has more foreign exchange reserves than the United States ($36 billion), Japan ($41.7 billion), Britain ($18 billion), Canada ($2.9 billion) -or indeed any country other than West Germany, which sits upon a $52.9 billion reserve.
''The buildup has been extraordinary,'' said Frederick C. Copeland Jr., Citicorp's top officer in Taiwan. 
''Before you know, it'll be $50 billion or $60 billion.''
The growing pile of foreign funds has has been an embarrassment to Taipei as it negotiates with the United States in an attempt to keep American goods and financial services out of Taiwanese markets. 
''They give the U.S. this song and dance about how poor little Taiwan can't afford more imports - then it produces these monstrous foreign exchange reserves,'' said a Western analyst here.
But the huge reserves carry other political liabilities, too. 
The Taiwanese read of the huge accumulation and wonder why their own streets have not been resurfaced and why more money is not spent on the nation's social welfare system. 
And while Taiwan's economic growth of about 11 percent this year has created new jobs - the island reports an unemployment rate of only 2 percent, though economists say it may be a bit higher - and raised the standard of living, an opposition politician running in the legislative elections this month touched a raw nerve in the Government by proposing that the billions in foreign exchange be divided among the inhabitants of Taiwan: $2,200 per person.
Then there are the economic drawbacks. 
Because Taiwan's central bank generally requires exporters and other private parties to turn in foreign currency in exchange for local currency, there has been an explosion in the money supply. 
It is growing at a 44 percent annual rate (compared with 14 percent in the United States). 
''We have too much foreign exchange, and it creates the potential for inflation,'' said Steven H.C. 
Wu, an official in the Government's Industrial Development and Investment Center.
The local currency glut exacerbates a broader problem: Taiwanese people save more money than they can reasonably invest. 
They salt away about 32 cents of every dollar, but invest only 16 cents. 
There are few productive investments on Taiwan - building vacancy rates are high, for example, and there is no need for new offices or hotels. 
Private investment fell 8.8 percent last year, and is up only a little this year.
So Taiwan overflows with cash. 
Some banks even turn down big deposits, for lack of adequate lending or investment opportunities.
It is this mix of international and domestic difficulties that has prompted the Government to move part of its foreign currency stockpile into private hands. 
The process is delighting American and other foreign banks here. 
They hope to get some lucrative business in recycling the export dollars, just as Western banks recycled petrodollars earned by oil-exporting nations a dozen years ago. 
But that may not happen soon. 
So far, Taipei has taken only these steps:
* Corporations and individuals can now hold $5,000 in foreign currency each year. 
An investor simply takes Taiwanese currency worth $5,000 to the bank and receives the foreign currency, which can be kept under a mattress or invested overseas. 
But most foreign investments still must be arranged through a Taiwan bank and are limited to a small number of highly reliable instruments, such as United States Government bonds.
* The capital requirement for a Taiwanese company planning to invest abroad has been cut by 60 percent, from the equivalent of $1.39 million to $555,000. 
This allows smaller companies to get the foreign exchange necessary to open a branch or build a plant overseas.
* Companies no longer need to turn over all foreign income as it is received, but can balance foreign receipts and expenses and turn in net foreign receipts each quarter. 
This reduces the paperwork for both the company and the central bank, and allows businesses to manage foreign exchange for short periods.
* A ban on the sale of gold has been lifted. 
As gold is imported for sale, foreign-cash reserves and local currency liquidity are sopped up.
In general, the private sector will probably use the currency in the same way the Government has: It will invest in foreign securities, mostly Government bonds and notes. 
Some of the money will also be used for investments in plants and equipment abroad, officials say.
With all this, the Government has also come up with another ploy to reduce official foreign currency reserve figures. 
It is asking private banks to hold on to foreign exchange instead of immediately sending it to the central bank. 
As a result, several billion dollars appears to be in the hands of the banks - on top of the $44 billion in official reserves. 
The banks are far from happy about this, because the new Taiwan dollar is rising, causing big losses for those who hold American currency. 
(Taipei acceded to the rising exchange rate because of American pressure, but analysts doubt that the rise will be enough to choke off Taiwan's exports.) THE relaxation of controls reverses nearly four decades of strict currency rules - regulations that have been in effect since the Nationalist Chinese forces led by Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek fled mainland China and took refuge on the island of Taiwan.
According to Mark Mobius, a Taipei investment manager, Taiwan's tendency to keep a tight grip on its foreign cash originates with the experience of Chinese Nationalists in the late 1940's in Shanghai. 
The stock market there, then the biggest in East Asia, collapsed as the Communists captured more and more of China, and eventually the Communist Government seized financial and physical assets. 
Capital fled the country, and many investors lost all.
Now many American investors are eager to buy Taiwanese securities -they are relatively cheap and Taiwan's growth is expected to continue at a brisk pace. 
But Taipei still keeps foreign investors at arm's length because of the memory of the 1940's. 
''When you go to an official who lived through that, and say that if you lift capital controls you'll get more money coming in than going out, they'll reply, 'Not in my experience,' '' said Mr. Mobius.
The tight controls only became a major problem this year, as the export-generated reserves swelled. 
Just a year ago, Taiwan - and Singapore, Hong Kong and South Korea, the other newly industrialized Asian countries variously known as the Four Tigers or the Gang of Four -were facing what for them were severe economic difficulties. 
Taiwan's economic growth rate tumbled from 10.9 percent in 1984 to 4.7 percent in 1985, while Singapore suffered its first recession in 20 years. 
South Korea and Hong Kong also experienced tough times.
But with the exception of Singapore, which is slowly emerging from recession, they are now booming. 
The reason: exports, mainly to the United States. 
The tonic this year was the rise in the Japanese yen and in European currencies. 
That has allowed the Four Tigers to snatch export business from Japan and Europe all over the world - everything from toys to cars.
Today, Taiwan, the 40th-biggest economy by population, is the world's 10th-biggest exporter. 
The nation generates 58 percent of its economic output for exports, 47 percent of which go to America. 
WHILE American manufacturers are appalled by these trade successes, some American financial houses are attracted by what they see as a new opportunity, as capital controls are eased. 
If Taiwan does not know what to do with all of its cash, they have a few ideas.
Bond salesmen and financial advisers have been streaming into Taipei, making visits to the central bank and commercial banks. 
They are getting some business, but for the most part they are working at building relationships. 
Though the controls are only being relaxed at this point, there is the firm prospect that they will be lifted entirely over the next few years. 
That could create significant opportunities for foreign fund managers who have hitherto found Taiwan largely a closed market.
''It's a question of keeping your ear to the ground and keeping up with regulations,'' said Kwok Lap-chiu, general manager of the Security Pacific National Bank in Taiwan.
American banks would like to act as fund managers, offering international investment services to Taiwanese clients in the private sector, but that is not yet permitted. 
So far, foreign banks are still limited to buying and selling securities for the central banks, at very thin margins.
The central bank has been so conservative in its investment policy that its returns have been low. 
More than 80 percent of the reserves are invested in United States dollar-denominated instruments, overwhelmingly Treasuries.
As the dollar sank over the last 22 months, the central bank did not do nearly as well as it would have had it invested in yen or Deutsche marks. 
The central bank reports that it earned 7.84 percent on reserves between July 1985 and June 1986, down from 9.39 percent a year earlier.
The lackluster performance has not gone unnoticed. 
Taiwan's normally cozy political system has recently allowed some criticism of the central bank's handling of its foreign funds: The Control Yuan, a Government agency that is supposed to function as a watchdog, has discussed the matter on several occasions, according to minutes of the meetings.
So besides alleviating inflationary and international trade pressures, the Government's move to ease currency controls may deflect these criticisms.
Still, the issue remains a ticklish one in Taipei. 
An interview on the subject with the central bank was canceled an hour before it was to take place. 
The Finance Ministry - after inquiring about the topic - refused to arrange an interview.
American banks may get more of an opportunity to manage some of Taiwan's hoard. 
But the pace will be measured. 
''We want to go step by step,'' said Wang Chien-shien, vice minister of economic affairs. 
''We want things to go smoothly.''

The issue of illegal drugs has got so out of hand in the United States Senate race in Florida that the Coast Guard has answered a political distress signal.
Paul A. Yost, Commandant of the Coast Guard, has asked Gov. Bob Graham, the Democratic senatorial candidate, to withdraw a television commercial showing Mr. Graham conversing with Coast Guard personnel about Federal budget cuts that have hampered their operations against drug smuggling.
The commandant said in a letter to the Governor that the commercial, which he described as ''both improper and misleading,'' had dragged the Coast Guard into partisan politics.
The Graham campaign refused to withdraw the commercial, which criticizes his Democratic opponent, Senator Paula Hawkins, for voting for the budget cuts, and charged that it was Mrs. Hawkins who had drawn the Coast Guard into politics. 
Coast Guard officials acknowledged that Mrs. Hawkins, among others, had complained about the commercial, but they denied that she had applied political pressure.
Meanwhile, the Hawkins campaign is refusing to withdraw a television commercial that her aides concede is factually incorrect. 
The narration says Mrs. Hawkins ''travels to China and meets personally with Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping'' to stop the export of the drug methaqualone.
Hawkins aides have acknowledged that the Senator and Mr. Deng never discussed drugs when they met at a state dinner in 1981. 
Nor did the Chinese leader respond to her letter on the subject in 1982. 
Details aside, they say the point of the commercial is to show that Mrs. Hawkins is no newcomer to the drug issue.
Correction
Because of an editing error, the Talking Politics column yesterday misstated the political affiliation of Senator Paula Hawkins of Florida. 
She is a Republican.

file: TANZICHONG JOURNAL_COMRADES IN DEATH_ MAO AND A VICTIM.txt
text:
ï»¿
Waggling a 10-foot bamboo pole, Huang Renhe shooed his ducks into a newly plowed paddy field, a pebble's toss from the house that stands on the site where Liu Shaoqi was born 88 years ago.
''He was a good man,'' Mr. Huang said, holding the rod of weathered bamboo behind his back.
''Vicious,'' ''pernicious,'' ''a scab,'' is what Mao Zedong called Liu Shaoqi more than 20 years ago before ordering him dismissed as China's first President and banished to political oblivion and death.
In the violent decade of the Cultural Revolution that ended in 1976, Mr. Liu's birthplace was sacked and destroyed by rampaging young people called Red Guards, their zealotry spurred by Mao's attacks against China's ''No. 
1 capitalist roader.''
Today, a new house built in ocher-colored mud with rough thatched roofing stands on the site of the Liu birthplace. 
The structure is gradually becoming a political shrine.
Â 
The Buses Still Come
There is, to the south across a clump of round hills, another shrine at Shaoshan, the native village of Mao and the most hallowed political site in China. 
Twenty years ago, tens of thousands of Red Guards, crimson banners flapping, trooped daily to Shaoshan, many on foot, to pay homage to the leader of the Chinese revolution.
The Red Guards are gone now; they no longer exist. 
The daily train from Hunan's capital, Changsha, is not quite full. 
But on the village common, a patch of pavement ringed with souvenir stands and tiny eateries with names like Patriotic Restaurant, buses still arrive, disgorging Chinese and Western tourists alike.
Despite Mao's torment and ultimate destruction of Mr. Liu after decades of tension between the two men, an accommodation of political purpose unhindered by history has settled on this small swath of central Hunan that links these two villages. 
The bitterness of that time has been covered over by the current orthodoxy that decrees that the two men were, after all, comrades and friends.
For Mr. Huang, who lives with his ducks, his wife and three sons in Lojiatang village across the paddy fields from Mr. Liu's old house, the past is not so clear.
''When the Cultural Revolution came, Comrade Liu was criticized,'' said Mr. Huang, 60 years old. 
''We thought he worked for the revolution for most of his life. 
Why for this time was he not good?''
''In 1961, Liu came back here,'' Mr. Huang said. 
''At that time it was very difficult economically. 
We did not have enough to eat. 
Those were the worst years we ever had. 
Even before liberation we could get enough rice to eat. 
When Liu Shaoqi came back, he investigated. 
He saw the peasants eating grass and eating rice husks and he cried. 
If he had not come back in 1961, many people would have died.''
''We only knew Liu Shaoqi was dead in 1980,'' Mr. Huang continued. 
''There were rumors he was dead before that. 
Some people believed those rumors. 
I myself thought he was dead.''
Â 
Death Comes in Prison
In 1969, 11 years before any public announcement, Mr. Liu died alone in a special prison in Kaifeng. 
''The party Central Committee,'' Mr. Huang said, ''they killed him.''
At the new Liu house, there is no mention of Mao's persecution of Mr. Liu, no mention of his denunciation by the Red Guards, of his wife's humiliation in a show trial for political crimes. 
A plastic sign in the entryway puts the blame for Mr. Liu's death on Jiang Qing, Mao's wife, and Lin Biao, once designated as Mao's heir, both now labeled ''counterrevolutionary elements.''
But the memory of Mr. Liu as a victim of Maoist excess remains. 
In cars and minibuses, an increasing number of people journey here, said Peng Ying, a guide at the house. 
''Yesterday,'' she said, ''I sold 1,100 tickets.''
A short walk away, a sprawling complex of whitewashed buildings, their roof corners flipped up in a traditional Chinese manner, is nearing completion. 
Some time next year, photographs, documents and whatever personal effects remain from Mr. Liu's life will be scattered through these buildings as a memorial to China's President. 
The cluster of buildings is larger than a similar memorial hall built for Mao over the hills in Shaoshan.
Twenty years ago, Shaoshan was thick with the passion of revolution, Wen Huikang said, ''I was a guide in Mao's house during the Cultural Revolution,'' Mr. Wen said. 
''I worked all day except to eat and sleep. 
I worked eight hours a day. 
You had to carry a thermos of water, and it was difficult to go to the restroom. 
We were open 24 hours a day. 
At the height, there were 56,000 people a day. 
The Red Guards would line up for four or five hours.
''I said very simple things, like: 'Here is Mao's bedroom. 
This photograph was taken in 1914.'
If you spoke too slowly the Red Guards would complain and say you didn't like Mao Zedong.''
#600,000 Visitors in a Year After 1967, Mr. Wen said, the number of visitors began to decline slowly, and by 1979, three years after Mao's death and the re-ordering of China's economic and political policies, the number of visitors had fallen to a mere 200,000 a year.
Since then, however, there has been a steady growth in the number of visitors to Shaoshan. 
Wu Dawei, the head of the Communist Party propaganda unit in Shaoshan, said that about 600,000 people trod the cement floors of Mao's childhood home last year and that he expected the number to rise this year.
Despite a re-evaluation of Mao in 1980 that decreed that he had made serious mistakes in his later life, there is little in Shaoshan to suggest that the Communist Party chairman led his country to the brink of starvation and chaos for nearly two decades until his death in 1976.
Those years are but scantily covered in the rambling memorial hall filled with photographs and writings of Mao. 
It is an unsullied past on view, absent the political tumult of his later years. 
Even Jiang Qing, the movie actress whom Mao married in 1939 and who became one of China's most powerful figures during the Cultural Revolution, is not visible.
''This museum is dedicated to Mao's life, so pictures relevant to Mao's life have been put up,'' Mr. Wu said. 
''Pictures of Jiang Qing were not put up because they are not relevant to Mao's life.''
And almost gone from Shaoshan too are the once ubiquitous Mao buttons, disks of plastic and bamboo emblazoned with Mao's image that were once produced in the hundreds of millions. 
The nearby factory that manufactured the badges says that there are only a few hundred remaining in storage and that there are no plans to make more.
In Tanzichong, surrounded by freshly plowed rice paddies, a solitary souvenir seller peddles yellow and white hand towels. 
A strip of red Chinese ideograms read simply, ''Visit to Comrade Liu Shaoqi's house.''

file: TEACHER CALLS CONFINEMENT IN CHINA A _NIGHTMARE_.txt
text:
ï»¿
An American teacher who was expelled from China after being accused of spying said today she had undergone a ''nightmare'' experience. 
She arrived home Friday night to a greeting of tears, flags and flowers.
Lisa Wichser, exhausted from a 36-hour journey that began with a flight from Peking, looked pale and her voice quavered as she greeted her parents, brother and sister at Indianapolis International Airport.
Miss Wichser, who proclaims her innocence, told reporters today that her week-long detention in China had been ''a nightmare, something I don't understand.''
She had been in China two years collecting material for a thesis on agricultural changes in China since 1969. 
She is working on a doctorate in economics at the University of Denver.
INDIANAPOLIS, June 5 (AP) - An American teacher who was expelled from China after being accused of spying said today she had undergone a ''nightmare'' experience.Awakened by Telephone Call
She said she was awakened around 1:30 A.M. on May 28 by a telephone call from one of the attendants in the hotel where she lived, saying there was an urgent cable from the family.
A few minutes later, she said, she answered a knock on her door and found five or six uniformed members of the Chinese Public Security Bureau, accompanied by the bright lights of several television cameras.
''I had no idea what was going on,'' she said. 
''They came in and searched my room. 
I asked them what was going on. 
They alternated between saying, 'You know what you've done' and 'You'll know in a while.'
''
Miss Wischer said she had been taken to a cement room in a detention center with a barred window, where her requests to to get in touch with United States Embassy officials or her friends were repeatedly denied.
Miss Wischer, a 29-year-old teacher of English and economics, was accused of stealing secret documents and spying. 
She was held until Thursday, spending three days in solitary cofinement, and then was released and ordered to leave within 48 hours.
In Washington, a State Department spokesman, Alan Romberg, said the department had voiced ''serious concern'' to China over its handling of the case.
In San Francisco, on her way home, Miss Wichser said, ''I am not a spy. 
I have never been a spy. 
That's ridiculous.''
Asked if she still hoped to marry Yi Shigong, 31, an economics student who had tutored her, Miss Wichser said, ''I certainly hope so; I sincerely hope so. 
The Chinese have not foreclosed that possibility.''
Chinese sources familiar with the case say Mr. Yi is now in jail. 
As Miss Wichser came off the plane members of her family held aloft small American flags. 
Her brother, Eric, brought roses from his garden.
Miss Wichser said earlier she had not been mistreated by Chinese officials, and that despite her recent experiences, ''I have very strong and positive feelings toward the Chinese people.''
She said that while she was a prisoner she had been interrogated three times a day for about two hours at a time. 
Miss Wichser said she had a roommate at one point, and that she spent much of her time composing a ''confession'' requested by the Chinese.
''They called it a confession, which meant I was to title it 'My Confession,' '' she said, adding that the document consisted of her name and background, a history of her studies in China and a detailed identification of papers taken from her hotel room.
''They weren't state secrets,'' she said. 
Miss Wichser told a reporter on the flight from Peking to Tokyo that she did not know she had violated any laws until the Chinese explained them at her interrogations. 
''The Chinese never clearly publicize their laws,'' she said. 
''Now I know and I would not do it again.''

file: TEAHOUSE REGAINS ITS GLORY.txt
text:
ï»¿
Only in Newport, where the social arts function with the force of great money, could the event planned for today transpire: at the behest of the First National Bank of Chicago, China's Ambassador to the United States has consented to come here to honor the restoration of a teahouse built almost 70 years ago for Alva Vanderbilt Belmont.
As the teahouse glows in stained and lacquered shades of jade green and red in the afternoon light, a United States Navy band is to play, with Deputy Secretary of State Walter J. Stoessel Jr. and Claiborne Pell, the senior United States Senator from Rhode Island, in attendance. 
A uniformed squadron of the Newport Artillery Company will aim its cannon to sea and fire 19 times from the lawn of Marble House, the Vanderbilt mansion built for $11 million in 1892. 
His Excellency Chai Zemin, the Chinese Ambassador, is to cut a ribbon opening the teahouse to the public. 
And a troupe of balloons will float off on the ocean breeze.
NEWPORT, R.I. 
- Only in Newport, where the social arts function with the force of great money, could the event planned for today transpire: at the behest of the First National Bank of Chicago, China's Ambassador to the United States has consented to come here to honor the restoration of a teahouse built almost 70 years ago for Alva Vanderbilt Belmont.
Thus is an extraordinary restoration of a singular little building to come to its official end. 
It is thought to be the only structure of its kind east of San Francisco. 
Almost $500,000 and a year and a half of work by craftsmen in 15 specialties has gone into the restoration by the Preservation Society of Newport County.
A sad and coincidental footnote is that the society's director, Paul E. Molitor Jr., will not be on hand to celebrate the completion of the project he supervised. 
After an interview at the site on Sunday and a dinner party that night at Bailey's Beach, the 36-yearold Mr. Molitor apparently drove to the top of the Newport Bridge over Narragansett Bay. 
His car was found there just before midnight with its lights on, according to Detective Sgt. William E. Eckert Jr. of the Rhode Island State Police. 
Mr. Molitor's body was pulled from the bay on Monday afternoon, Sergeant Eckert said.
''I think he was just despondent,'' said John G. Winslow, president of the society. 
''It was a personal thing. 
He was very enthusiastic about the teahouse. 
He devoted most of his time the last two or three years to it.''
Compared with the piles of brick, stone and marble that the money barons of the 19th century built here as summer ''cottages,'' the teahouse is as bright and fanciful as a cut jewel. 
Mrs. Belmont, who was divorced from William K. Vanderbilt and married O.H.P. 
Belmont, may, in fact, have intended it as a temporary adornment for the lawn of Marble House, which became hers by the divorce.
The architects and researchers in the restoration project cannot be sure of her intent in the year 1913. 
But in the same way that mansions such as Marble House have been saved for the public by donations from the rich, a fond memory has interceded to preserve the teahouse, which had been boarded up and left to the vandals and the salt air for decades.
It happened this way, Mr. Winslow said: The late Frederick H. Prince of Chicago, whose fortune came from railroads and Armour & Company, owned the Marble House after the Vanderbilts did. 
When Harold S. Vanderbilt, a son of Mrs. Belmont, provided the funds for the preservation society to purchase the estate from the Prince family in 1963, the society restored the mansion but had no money for the teahouse.
But William Wood-Prince, Mr. Prince's stepson and heir and a director of the First National Bank of Chicago, remembered courting his wife in the teahouse. 
He gave $50,000 toward restoring it. 
Other money was raised. 
And when the project neared completion, the First National Bank of Chicago, which has business interests in China, prevailed on Mr. Chai to lend his office to the occasion.
That is how things work on that level in Newport. 
But on another level, at the teahouse, the work of restoring the obliterated Chinese calligraphy, the paintings of 12th- and 15th-century Chinese garden scenes, the chopped-off copper figures of dragons, lions and dogs on the roof, the broken terra-cotta roof tiles, the crumbled plaster of paris moldings, all proceeded by hand, tediously and inch by inch.
The teahouse had been designed for Mrs. Belmont by the New York architectural firm of Richard Howland Hunt and Joseph Howland Hunt. 
Documents in the firm's archives indicate that someone from the firm went to China to study and sketch pavilions there, and the resulting design, according to Mark Weber, a consultant hired by the society to research the history of the teahouse, ''is a composite image,'' and perhaps ''the most significant example of American chinoiserie architecture in America.''
''The French term chinoiserie,'' Mr. Weber added, ''can only properly be used to mean European decoration whimsically applied in the Chinese manner, not to Oriental work or strict copies of it.''
Mrs. Belmont called her little building ''the Teahouse,'' he said, but it was actually an imitation of Chinese temple architecture.
Many of the original architectural drawings, along with records of the pavilion's cost and the number and identity of the original craftsmen, were lost. 
The restoration had to proceed from old photographs, from intuition, from copying existing parts to reproduce missing pieces.
Jeffrey L. Staats, the supervising architect for Donal Simpson Associates of Newport, discovered that Mrs. Belmont had cut corners. 
Spruce and pine had been used instead of the mahogany and teak called for in the original specifications. 
Instead of elaborate lacquer work and varnish, only a single coat of paint was used. 
The teahouse was built with ungalvanized nails. 
And the paintings inside were done on plywood.
Before restoring the paintings, Christy Cunningham, who specializes in frescoes on wooden panels, had to restore the surface of the vandalized and peeling plywood. 
She had to make such carved inscriptions as ''L.S.D.'' and ''Joey Loves Sarah'' disappear. 
It took her a year.
Arnold Cyr, the coppersmith who hand-hammered a new dragon's head and parts for a lion and a dog for the roof, discovered to his amazement that the coppersmith who had originally done such beautiful work had not scratched his name inside the copper sheeting. 
On the new work, Mr. Cyr said, ''I put my name inside.''
Only one defect now remains in the teahouse. 
Should the Chinese Ambassador look up, he will see that the characters on the bottom of the bronze lanterns tell of the reign of the emperor in which the lanterns were made. 
But the characters are Japanese, as was the emperor. 
The lanterns were made in Japan.

file: Technology Exports to China.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Western allies and Japan have agreed to a major relaxation of the rules under which they export high-technology products to China. 
Such sales totaled $6 billion in the year ended Sept. 
30, up from $1 billion in the fiscal year 1984.
The move to expand and expedite exports will add new categories of goods eligible for transfer to the Chinese, who have long chafed under rules that have been applied without distinction to Eastern Europe, the Soviet Union and China.
The regulations are those of the 15-member Coordinating Committee, consisting of the NATO allies and Japan but excluding Iceland, that screens exports to prevent the transfer of technology with military applications.
Â 
Categories Not Specified
The decision was announced today in China in a brief statement by Vice President Bush, just before he left Peking for Chengdu. 
Mr. Bush did not say what categories of goods are newly authorized for shipment to China and a Commerce Department official here said the department could ''not get into specifics.''
It was understood, however, that the decision permits the export of 27 categories of computers and medical equipment, but no military hardware. 
It was unclear today whether the decision would permit the export of minicomputers and semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
''We feel it is an improvement,'' a spokesman for the International Business Machines Corporation said in a statement. 
''We don't know the details yet, but we are confident that it will improve our ability to market to China.''
I.B.M. has the largest presence of any American computer maker in China and stands to be the biggest beneficiary of relaxed guidelines. 
It already has a Chinese subsidiary.
Mr. Bush said that about 80 percent of the committee's work involves China and that about half the high-technology items requiring the group's licenses would be affected by the relaxation.
Â 
Easing a Trade Backlog
He said the move would ease a major backlog in United States-China trade, a source of increasing frustration among the Chinese. 
China has complained repeatedly about its inability to buy American and other Western technology for its modernization program.
The Vice President said the decision, made a month ago in Paris, where the Coordinating Committee is based, required a 30-day waiting period that has just ended. 
The multinational liberalization takes effect immediately.
The United States has also taken its own steps to speed up the processing of licensing applications for China, including the formation in July of a China Team Center.
The Acting Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Trade Administration, William T. Archey, told Congress last week that by the end of September the department had reduced processing times for Chinese sales to 1983 levels even though the caseload had risen by 162 percent.
In 1983, 2,800 export licenses were approved for China with the total rising to more than 8,000 in the 12 months ended Sept. 
30.

WASHINGTON, June 3 (AP) - The Pentagon says that it is reviewing its regulations on the transfer of technology in line with President Reagan's directive calling for a more liberal approach to trade with China.
Asked whether the thrust of the Reagan directive called for more liberal trade with China, Mr. Welles replied, ''That is my understanding.''

file: TEXT OF CHINA_S STATEMENT.txt
text:
ï»¿
Following is the text of a Chinese statement on the case of John F. Burns, the Peking bureau chief of The New York Times, who was expelled yesterday. 
The statement was read in Peking by Xu Hui, an official of the State Security Bureau, to A. M. Rosenthal, executive editor of The Times, and Warren Hoge, the newspaper's foreign editor.
The Burns-McNally case is a grave one. 
They disregarded the laws of China, deliberately violating the law governing aliens entering into and exiting from the People's Republic of China. 
They broke into a military restricted zone of our country and took numerous photographs of classified objects.
Such demeanor obviously constitutes an act of spying and intelligence gathering which will not be tolerated by any sovereign state and needless to say is also a regrettable incident.
We attach great importance to friendly relations between China and the United States and are loath to see such a relationship impaired.
Since the beginning of the Burns and McNally case, while upholding the sovereignty of the law of China, we have acted with the utmost restraint and have sought earnestly to deal with the matter satisfactorily within the limits permitted by law and restricted to the least possible publicity.
It is out of such considerations that we did not investigate and affix criminal responsibility of the two persons through judicial procedures, which we could have done according to the nature of their offense.
Thus the penalization has been greatly mitigated. 
We hope this is taken notice of by the U.S. side.
We have made a decision to expel Burns from the territory of the People's Republic of China today.
We will only release a brief news item, without making public the details of the case.
We will adhere to this attitude unless we are faced with a difficult situation, in which case we will have to act against our will.

text:

Following is the text of the official English translation of China's reunification proposal to Taiwan, which was made public here today by the Foreign Ministry:
PEKING, Sept. 
30 (AP) - Following is the text of the official English translation of China's reunification proposal to Taiwan, which was made public here today by the Foreign Ministry:
1. In order to bring an end to the unfortunate separation of the Chinese nation as early as possible, we propose that talks be held between the Communist Party of China and the Kuomintang of China on a reciprocal basis so that the two parties will cooperate for the third time to accomplish the great cause of national reunification. 
The two sides may first send people to meet for an exhaustive exchange of views.
Official text of China's reunification proposal to Taiwan
2. It is the urgent desire of the people of all nationalities of both sides of the straits to communicate with each other, reunite with their relatives, develop trade and increase mutual understanding.
We propose that the two sides make arrangements to facilitate the exchange of mail, trade, air and shipping services and visits by relatives and tourists as well as academic, cultural and sports exchanges and reach an agreement thereupon.
3. After the country is reunified, Taiwan can enjoy a high degree of autonomy as a special administrative region and it can retain its armed forces. 
The central Government will not interfere with local affairs on Taiwan.
4. Taiwan's current socioeconomic system will remain unchanged, so will its way of life and its economic and cultural relations with foreign countries. 
There will be no encroachment on proprietary rights and lawful right of inheritance over private property, houses, land and enterprises or on foreign investments.
5. People in authority and representative personages of various circles in Taiwan may take up posts of leadership in national political bodies and participate in running the state.
6. When Taiwan's local finance is in difficulty, the central Government may subsidize it as is fit for the circumstances. 
7. For people of all nationalities and public figures of various circles in Taiwan who wish to come and settle on the mainland, it is guaranteed that proper arrangments will be made for them, that there will be no discrimination against them and that they will have the freedom of entry and exit.
8. Industrialists and businessmen in Taiwan are welcome to invest and engage in various economic undertakings on the mainland, and their legal rights, interests and profits are guaranteed.
9. The reunificiation of the motherland is the responsibility of all Chinese. 
We sincerely welcome people of all nationalities, public figures of all circles and all mass organizations in Taiwan to make proposals and suggestions regarding affairs of state through various channels and in various ways.
We hope our compatriots in Taiwan will give full play to their patriotism and work energetically for the early realization of the great unity of our nation and share the honor of it.
