The Senate tonight defied threats of a Presidential veto and approved legislation that would place stringent quotas on textile imports from 12 countries, most of them in Asia.
The vote was 60 to 39. 
A similar version was passed last month by the House, and now a conference will have to reconcile the two measures.
Senator Daniel J. Evans, a Washington Republican who led the fight against the bill, said he was ''absolutely convinced'' that President Reagan would veto whatever bill comes out of the conference and that Congress will sustain the veto. 
A two-thirds vote is needed to override a veto, and supporters of the bill failed to get that much in either chamber.
'Fruitless' Debate Is Seen
''The debate has been interesting, worthwhile and useful,'' Mr. Evans told reporters, ''but it will turn out to be fruitless.''
Sponsors of the measure maintain, however, that Mr. Reagan will ultimately decide to sign the legislation because a veto would hurt Republicans in key Southeastern states in next year's elections.
''The textile industry in this country is in crisis,'' argued Senator Strom Thurmond, a South Carolina Republican. 
''Unless something is done to stop these massive imports, we won't have a textile industry in a few years.''
The textile bill is the first trade measure to pass Congress since the lawmakers returned from their summer recess alarmed by the loss of jobs to foreign competition.
Â 
Other Legislation Afoot
Many other bills are working their way through the legislative process, partly because Democrats believe they can use the trade issue against the Republicans in Congressional elections a year from now.
The bill adopted today would slash textile imports by 30 percent from the two largest sources, South Korea and Taiwan. 
Products from Hong Kong would be cut 14 percent. 
Imports from nine other countries would be frozen at their 1984 levels; these countries are China, Japan, Pakistan, Indonesia, India, the Philippines, Thailand, Brazil and Singapore.
Under pressure from the State Department, the Senate altered its original bill to be less restrictive toward China. 
The Administration is concerned that a sharp cut in Chinese imports would harm relations between the two countries and provoke retaliation against American manufacturers trying to sell their goods in China.
The House bill is harsher toward China than the Senate version.
Other industries are also looking for help against imports. 
The bill passed today, unlike the House bill, includes a clause protecting the domestic shoe industry from foreign competition. 
Under that provision, imports would be limited to 60 percent of the American market.
Senators from copper-producing states added an amendment today that would direct the Administration to initiate trade talks with copper-exporting countries in an attempt to limit their share of the American market. 
That amendment won the votes of Pete V. Domenici, Republican of New Mexico, and Jake Garn, Republican of Utah, for the final bill.
Today's debate reflected long-standing, strongly held views on the textile issue that frequently divided along regional lines. 
Lawmakers representing states that make cloth, such as the Carolinas, and produce apparel, such as New York, supported the legislation.
But legislators from states that could lose exports if there is foreign retaliation, primarily agricultural states, tended to oppose the bill. 
They were joined by West Coast Senators who fear that a decline in trade with Asia would harm their region's ports and transportation industry.
Sponsors of the measure argued that the textile and apparel industries have lost 200,000 jobs since 1980.
''Families are being deprived of a living,'' Mr. Thurmond said. 
''We've got to turn it around.''
The lobbying coalition behind the bill was particularly effective because it combined labor and management forces that have fought each other in bitter organizing battles throughout the textile industry.
Opponents of the bill said the loss of textile jobs reflected automation and productivity as much as foreign competition. 
And protectionism, they said, would be ''counterproductive,'' in Senator Evans's words, because it would cause the loss of jobs in other sectors of the economy.
Some of the strongest fears were voiced by farm state lawmakers, whose constituents depend heavily on exporting grain. 
Max Baucus, a Montana Democrat, made a typical comment when he said that the bill ''says to agriculture that we're going to kiss you good-bye, it's all over, we're going to send you down the drain.''

GENEVA, July 25 (Reuters) - The United States and China resumed negotiations in Geneva today on a textile agreement, trade sources said, with both sides optimistic that a pact could be reached to replace the one that expired last December.
When earlier talks failed to produce a new accord, Washington unilaterally imposed textile import restrictions and Peking threatened to reduce its purchases of United States farm products. 
Near-record harvests in China are expected this year.
American farming interests hope the textile dispute ends soon, but American textile manufacturers are seeking tighter restrictions.

file: THANKSGIVING_ WHEN CUISINES MEET, IT_S A CHANGEABLE FEAST.txt
text:
ï»¿
Thanksgiving, in our house, is a changeable feast. 
It is American to the extent that it is observed on the day set aside for it, occasionally Italian in flavor simply because that is the ancestry of my husband and old feasts die hard, and quite often Chinese in taste because that is what I know and what I cook.
It wasn't always so. 
Thanksgiving, American Thanksgiving, came upon me in 1959, the year we were married and I came to New York to live. 
That November my husband told me we were going to his mother's for Thanksgiving dinner and I asked what Thanksgiving was.
Eileen Yin-Fei Lo discusses meeting of Italian and Chinese cuisines for Thanksgiving feast
He told me about the pilgrims and the Indians and corn and turkeys and how the day originally had been a day of thanks on the part of the pilgrims for their continued well-being.
''Oh,'' I remember saying, ''that is like the 24th day of the 12th month in China, when my mother used to say thank you to Tsao Chun.''
''Oh?''
I remember him answering. 
That day, the culmination of the New Year celebration, which is China's most important holiday, was our traditional day of thanksgiving for a year enjoyed, for harvests that were successful. 
During the year a picture of Tsao Chun, also known as the Kitchen God, drawn on rice paper, was tacked above our kitchen stove, a vantage point from which he observed our family at table, which as we all know is when truth comes out. 
At any rate, on that 24th day of the 12th month his job is to report to the Jade Emperor on the family he has been living with.
So we would smear honey on Tsao Chun's lips and put him on a tiny bamboo throne, then join him in a thanksgiving feast of sweet cakes, candied fruit and sweetened glutinous rice before setting fire to his picture so that, through the wisps of smoke, he would rise upward and say only sweet things about us. 
That was our thanksgiving.
''Ours is a bit different,'' said my husband, and as he described it I thought to myself that it certainly was. 
He mentioned that we would certainly have turkey, but that there would be important Italian additions to the feast. 
To wit, an antipasto of such things as freshly smoked salami, peppers that had been roasted atop the oven that morning and dressed with olive oil, and chunks of hard cheese called locatelli; a thick chicken broth with chicken; a green salad; followed by the roast turkey and everything that would go with it, including dressing; followed by cold celery and fennel to cool the palate, then dates and nuts. 
Dessert would come a few hours later, after Uncle Frank's accordion music and the penny poker game.
That, I thought, was certainly more elaborate than what we did for the Kitchen God. 
My goodness!
It was also the first turkey I had ever eaten. 
I had never even seen a turkey until I went to Hong Kong from Canton, where I was born, and those that had been imported for the Christmas holidays of the British in the crown colony always looked so skinny and stringy that I refused even to taste them. 
Did I wish white meat or dark?
I was asked. 
Well, everybody knew that white meat is essentially tasteless, so I chose dark. 
And it was pleasant, I remember, but not at all special, and frankly I guess I couldn't understand what all the fuss was about.
The roasted peppers were, however, utterly wonderful, and I told my mother-in-law so, which made her feel a little better than she had when I suggested that turkey was dull. 
She also liked it when I told her I liked the chicken broth.
We did make the Thanksgiving Day dinners for years later, watching it move from in-law to in-law. 
And then my husband's family scattered and soon Thanksgiving Day was a day for my immediate family. 
We had turkey for a couple of years mainly because I enjoyed figuring out ways to creatively use the leftover turkey meat. 
I curried it, made Shanghai-style pastries with turkey as the filling, stir-fried it with celery, carrots, scallions and onions, all of which tasted better than the roasted turkey, I thought.
Thanksgiving kept meaning turkey because my husband and my three children said that at Thanksgiving you had to have turkey. 
That of course was nonsense and one year I listened to them ask for a turkey as they always did but I gave them a duck.
And a very special duck it was, a classical Chinese preparation called Tea-Smoked Duck. 
First I steamed it whole with ginger, eightstar anise and cinnamon sticks, then I smoked it with Dragon Well tea, that magnificent green tea from Hangzhou, roasted it briefly in the oven, then deep-fried it, whole, to give the skin the texture of parchment. 
Instant success!
And from then on there was no longer talk of Thanksgiving turkeys simply because tea-smoked duck tasted better.
After that came a couple of years of roasted fresh ham, a huge ham into which I slipped slices of garlic and basted with soy sauce and sugar for about nine hours, and with which I served snow peas and black mushrooms. 
It was also successful and wonderful as a leftover stir-fried with vegetables. 
Then, a couple of years ago, we started going to the home of our friends, the Perlines, for Thanksgiving. 
And the culinary character of our Thanksgiving changed still again. 
It was back to turkey, but before the turkey there was always a matzoh ball soup, and later on a flan, because Irving makes the best there is, and a wonderful chocolate sponge, cherries and whipped cream Black Forest Cake made by Frieda, the lady from Germany who came in to help the Perlines out. 
Now what sort of traditional Thanksgiving Day feast is that?
We do enjoy it very much, however, as much for the company as for the food, because Thanksgiving for the Perlines is sort of an open house and each year, it seems, there are others joining the regulars for dinner - students, relatives, friends who have dropped by. 
And that is a fine Thanksgiving too. 
Do I contribute?
Not really, except to say a few quiet and private words to Tsao Chun about the Perlines' very nice kitchen, so he can mention it upstairs.
Eileen Yin-Fei Lo teaches Chinese cooking and nutrition at the China Institute in America, in New York, and is the author of the forthcoming, ''The Dim Sum Book: Art of the Chinese Teahouse,'' Crown Publishers.

file: THE BEST OF HONG KONG_Four Hotels in the Grandest Manner. . .And Food Fit for Emperors.txt
text:
ï»¿
There are nearly 20,000 restaurants in Hong Kong, a city where it may seem that every resident is a self-styled gourmet and that everyone eats out as often as possible. 
The result is some of the very best cooking in the world, be it French, Italian or Vietnamese.
But why go to Hong Kong to eat foreign dishes when the territory's five million Chinese are mostly from Canton (Guangdong)?
Although Americans associate Cantonese food with thick, saccharine, orange-red sauces, it is considered by many the best Chinese food in the world. 
The key culinary words are harmony and simplicity: the subtle and the delicate play off the rich and spicy.
Hong Kong chefs, however, do equally well with food from other Chinese regions, so whether you choose to sample their talents in the hundreds of simple restaurants throughout the city or in the hotel dining rooms that you will love despite their amazing pretentiousness, you will be forever spoiled for most Chinese food in the United States, particularly what passes here for Cantonese.
From the jade and silver of Lai Ching Heen in the Regent Hotel, to the glazed tile walls and tile floors of the Hoi Tin Garden Restaurant in the fishing village of Lei Yue Mun, from the red lacquer and gold at the Shang Palace in the Shangri-La Hotel to the less than spotless tablecloths in the second floor Tin Fat Restaurant, Hong Kong food will astonish your senses.
Some of the most expensive meals are in restaurant hotels, but unlike the United States, most of the diners in them are local people. 
Hong Kong is a rich territory and, as the promotional literature for it says: ''Money is something of which most Chinese are proud and much of it is spent on lavish dining and entertaining.''
Meals in some of the most elaborate settings are easily more expensive than the costliest meals in New York. 
The great delicacy is anything made with sharks' fin and it is not unusual for a single dish to cost $200.
First-time visitors should not be put off by tales of dinner checks fit for an emperor. 
On a four-day eating tour that covered eight restaurants, there were meals that cost only $10 a person as well as one that was $60.
If, however, you are put off by less than impeccable linens you may have to confine yourself to the most expensive restaurants, where Western fastidiousness is practiced. 
But be prepared to pay for the jade and silver serving pieces.
A few words of practical advice: napkins are offered in some restaurants, but damp terrycloth washcloths before the meal are more common. 
A 10 percent service charge is added to bills; if the service warrants it, add another 3 to 5 percent. 
Don't hesitate to ask your waiter for advice. 
By the same token don't let him intimidate you into ordering dishes that cost more than you want to spend. 
But be sure to let him know that you don't want ''safe'' choices like sweet and sour pork. 
Chinese beer, particularly Tsing Tao, is usually the most appropriate accompaniment to the food. 
Most restaurants are open every day for lunch and dinner, closed only for Chinese New Year and public holidays.
Â 
SHANG PALACE
It is difficult to say where we ate the best food: different restaurants excelled at different dishes. 
And certainly if price is no object and conspicuous consumption is your cup of tea, you cannot go wrong at the aptly named Shang Palace.
Don't let the ornate decoration fool you. 
Despite copious quantities of imperial red lacquer and 22-carat gold leaf, carved lacquered elephants, gold tableware, impeccable linens and personalized matches for all who have made reservations, the food is exceptionally well prepared.
The meal began with a small whole suckling pig, the most succulent I have ever eaten. 
The usual maraschino cherry eyes were replaced by tiny lighted red bulbs. 
Served in the style of moo shi pork, scallop-edged steamed breads are used instead of wraplings, each to be spread with a delightful sweet and slightly spicy plum sauce, the scallion bundles wrapped with strips of hot red pepper.
Every dish was a picture, all of it served under silver domes in the French fashion.
A dish of crab and bamboo fungus, which has a texture not unlike a mushroom, had that subtle, delicate flavor for which Cantonese food is famous.
Pan-fried chicken with soybean and chili, though a simple mixture of green pepper, scallions, garlic and chicken, rose above the ordinary with a bit of hot red chili and black bean paste. 
Cantonese food has its own hot peppers.
Seasonal vegetables were an exotic mixture of hairy seaweed, black fungus with the rich taste of earthy wild mushrooms served in soybean skin. 
I am an unabashed fan of Chinese sweets and I thought the coconut cream soup with tapioca was delightfully refreshing.
For two, this superb dinner cost $75. 
The restaurant also offers a dim sum lunch.
Â 
(Shang Palace, Shangri-La Hotel, 64 Mody Road, Kowloon, Hong Kong; telephone 3-7212111. 
Lunch and dinner seven days. 
American Express, Diners, MasterCard, VISA.)
Â 
LAI CHING HEEN
If Shang Palace is exuberantly ostentatious, Lai Ching Heen is subtly ostentatious. 
Instead of imperial red and gold, it is jade and silver. 
The chopsticks are ivory and silver. 
The setting spells money. 
Like the Shang Palace, the service is flawless and instantaneous.
This was our first meal in Hong Kong and thus my first encounter with the much touted and very expensive sharks' fin soup. 
Although it is adored by the Chinese because of its texture, Westerners are not always taken with it, because it is bland and slippery. 
But if, like me, you are wild about the tapioca pudding you will love the soup with its extremely delicate flavor.
Topping off the well-prepared food is a glorious view of the harbor. 
Dinner for two is about $100.
Â 
9Lai Ching Heen, the Regent, Salisbury Road, Hong Kong; 3-7211211. 
Open for lunch and dinner seven days. 
Visa, American Express, Diners.)
Â 
FOOK LAM MOON
To veteran visitors the name Fook Lam Moon conjures up expensive meals, and if you insist on having abalone you can ring up a bill that will make the Four Seasons or the Quilted Giraffe in New York look like bargain basements. 
One abalone dish is more than $300; there is an entire page of abalone. 
There's another page of shark's fin dishes, which start at $180. 
But there is also exquisite golden deep-fried chicken for $18.
Garoupa, a fish with pristine white flesh that is extremely popular in Hong Kong, had just come out of the pond. 
Served with spring onions, it was very moist and delicate, as was the lobster in garlic sauce.
The food at Fook Lam Moon is quite sophisticated and while the setting is not as glamorous as the hotel restaurants it is attractive with a newly redone pale pink and green color scheme. 
As in so many Chinese restaurants, the lighting is far brighter than you would expect.
Dinner for two was $120.
Â 
(Fook Lam Moon, 31 Mody Road, Shop A Tsimshatsui, Kowloon, Hong Kong; 3-688755. 
Open seven days for lunch and dinner.
Â 
American Express, Visa, Diners
Club, MasterCard.)
Â 
YUNG KEE
If you want to see what restaurants were like in Hong Kong 40 years ago, a trip to Yung Kee is a must. 
Crowded and noisy, done up in gold and red, with less than spotless tablecloths, it is still an especially good choice for lunch, though there is less of a crush before noon or after 2.
The specialty is thousand-year-old eggs, exceedingly good with pickled ginger. 
But all the Cantonese food is an example of how light such cooking can be, even when it is as rich as golden-skinned roast goose with a delicate plum sauce. 
Here is the place to try fried rice as it should taste, flavored with salted fish rather than barbecued pork.
Judging from what we tried, you probably cannot go wrong with anything you order. 
Lunch for two wasIt was enough for a dinner.
Â 
(Yung Kee Restaurant, Yung Kee Building, 32 Wellington Street, Hong Kong; 5-221624.
Open seven days for lunch and dinner. 
Visa, American Express, Diners.)
Â 
HOI TIN GARDEN
If really fresh fish is your passion, be sure to take a trip to Lei Yue Mun, a tiny fishing village just a four- or five-minute ferry ride from Hong Kong. 
About 30 fish stalls line your route to about 14 restaurants. 
You choose from a vast assortment of exotic fin fish and shellfish and they are delivered to the restaurant of your choice, where your order is cooked in the simplest fashion in the plainest surroundings.
The preparation of the food is sublime: abalone steamed with soy sauce and ginger; clams steamed with spring onions, soy and oil; scallops with their roe in black bean sauce. 
Dinner for two was $45.
Â 
(Hoi Tin Garden Restaurant, 53-59 Praya Road, Lei Yue Mun.
Open seven days for lunch and dinner. 
No credit cards.)
Â 
TIN FAT
After hearing so much about Chiu Chow cooking, I had to taste it before leaving Hong Kong. 
In this country it is the least known of all Chinese food. 
Chiu Chow is in Guangdong Province, but the food is much gutsier than Cantonese. 
It is distinguished by its use of large quantitites of garlic and oil, and fish sauce in place of soy sauce.
The Chiu Chow restaurant I visited is nothing to look at. 
The menus are in Chinese. 
The staff speaks no English. 
Find someone who speaks Chinese to take you. 
It's worth it.
Sharks' fin soup was much richer and thicker than the Cantonese version and was served with dark vinegar that provided an appealing tang. 
Steamed lobster with Mandarin-flavored honey, stir-fried whelk with garlic, chili and black beans were very savory. 
Rice congee instead of steamed rice was served with the meal. 
Dinner for two was about $45. 
Menus do not show prices.
Â 
(Tin Fat Restaurant, 9 Des Voeux Road, West, Hong Kong; 5-481739. 
Open seven days for lunch and dinner. 
No credit cards.)
Â 
LUK YU
Everyone who has been to Hong Kong will tell you to go to Luk Yu for dim sum. 
People who live there will tell you not to bother. 
But because we were tourists we went.
We made sure, however, to go when the regulars were not around because we had been told that when the restaurant is busy no one pays attention to strangers.
Luk Yu, which opened in 1925, looks like an old English restaurant in the colonies with its overhead fans and highly varnished wood wainscotting, its wooden-backed booths, enormous stained-glass windows, marble floors and spitoons at each booth. 
There are glass tops on each white tablecloth. 
The present location is not the original.
This is a place where you are expected to wash out your cup and the tips of your chopsticks in a basin of tea, just as they still do in China for sanitary reasons. 
It is a place where the waiters shuffle along on slippered feet, and the women who carry the dim sum dishes sing out their wares as they pass.
Dim sum are not much different from what you will find in a good dim sum parlor in the United States: pork buns, sui mai filled with pork, har gao with shrimp, steamed beef rolls made with rice flour.
You don't have to speak Chinese to come here in the morning because you can motion to the women carrying the food and look at what is being served. 
In the afternoon, however, you must order from a menu, which is in Chinese without translations. 
Dim sum are $1 or less apiece.
Â 
(Luk Yu, 24 Stanley Street, Central Hong Kong; 5-232973.)

file: THE CHINESE STUMBLE ON THE ROAD TO PERSONAL FREEDOM.txt
text:
ï»¿
For more than five years, at a pace that has astonished people who knew Mao Zedong's China, the makers of the country's ''second revolution'' have proceeded to dismantle the rigid system imposed by Mao. 
Deng Xiaoping has established the elements of a society that takes man largely as is, instead of trying to remold him. 
Energies have been liberated that have placed one of the world's poorest nations on a fast track toward modernity.
In attempting this, the 80-year-old Mr. Deng has confronted complexities that would baffle a lesser politician. 
Not least has been the need to strike a balance between what he calls ''liveliness'' - freedom, in Western parlance - and social order. 
After 2,000 years of tight social and political constraints, any relaxation inevitably carries the risk of incipient chaos as people adjust to the idea of a society that encourages individual initiative.
Article on riot in Peking following China's elimination from World Cup soccer play by Hong Kong and concern it has raised about Deng Xiaoping policy of increasing personal freedom in China; photo (M)
Last week, the difficulty of maintaining that balance was clearly demonstrated. 
The occasion was a soccer match between China and Hong Kong, played at the 80,000-seat Workers' Stadium in Peking. 
A surliness grew in the crowd as Hong Kong won, 2 to 1, eliminating China from the 1986 World Cup playoffs in Mexico. 
After the final whistle blew, the visiting team was pelted with garbage and soda bottles and thousands of discontented fans took to the streets in an orgy of vandalism and menace.
Outside the stadium, buses were halted and taxis overturned. 
At least 30 policemen were injured; 127 rioters were arrested. 
But unlike soccer riots in Europe, South America and Africa, there was a distinctive element to this one: For an hour, any foreigner within reach of the mob was liable to assault.
Without regard to nationality, Russian, Canadian, Japanese and Rumanian passers-by were halted and their vehicles were pounded with rocks. 
Many were spat upon by tormentors who chanted ''Foreigners!
Foreigners!''
The Government reacted swiftly, and with rare candor. 
Newspapers, including the People's Daily, the principal Communist Party organ, ran full reports on the mayhem. 
Ambassadors who raised the matter at the Foreign Ministry received apologies. 
At an emergency meeting of the Peking party apparatus, officials described the rioters as ''ignorant and barbaric'' people who had brought shame on the country. 
''Due punishment'' was promised, for some at public trials.
But the official reaction went farther, indicating deep political resonance. 
Party officials were quoted as saying that the riot displayed ''serious weakness in the party's ideological work and in the work of educating people, particularly young people, in the necessity of abiding by the law.''
Mr. Deng kept silent, at least in public, but there was little doubt that he would insist on exemplary punishments, if only to protect the wider policy of relaxation. 
The Chinese leader has made it plain that he understands the link between the economic freedoms he has promoted and the broader social and even political flexibility that people demand as their prosperity increases. 
Already, the Chinese have far greater leeway in the conduct of their private lives and in the discussion of public policy than they ever had under Mao. 
At the same time, Mr. Deng has insisted that the ''stabilityI'' that enhances economic progress will remain primary, and that any ''liveliness'' that threatens progress will be suppressed.
In these terms, he explained the harsh retribution meted out in 1979 and 1980 to leaders of the ''democracy wall'' protests in Peking, the most prominent of whom, Wei Jingsheng, is serving a 15-year jail term. 
In Mr. Deng's view, the criticisms posted on the wall brought into question the party's right to rule, and thus raised the specter of chaos.
By contrast, when several hundred people known as ''re-settled youths'' occupied the steps of the Peking party headquarters last month, seeking the intervention of ''Comrade Xiaoping'' in a bid to regain the right to live in Peking, the protest was allowed to continue for a week, and ended in mediation and concessions.
The differing responses can in some respects be traced to the conclusions Mr. Deng drew while he was in political purgatory during the Cultural Revolution. 
Forced to wait on tables and run a lathe, he saw at first hand the unworkability of a system in which party doctrine and state decrees excluded individual thinking. 
But the mob frenzy he witnessed during the Maoist upheaval left him profoundly hesitant to relax social controls too rapidly. 
In the soccer riot, he may have seen evidence that his policies have already gone too far. 
Even Westerners are shocked by their first encounters with black-market money-changers, street-corner hooligans and other ''bad elements'' who have sprung up in the more benign climate of recent years.
Opponents of Deng policies have long argued that ''opening to the world'' in terms of investment and trade will inevitably expose the country to the more noxious aspects of Western culture. 
The soccer violence provided them with fresh grounds for dissent.
If the riot offered other material for reflection, it lay in the suddenness with which mass frustration can be turned against foreigners. 
This, too, seemed likely to provide fresh worries for Mr. Deng, who has labored hard to convince the West that the xenophobia that Maoist zealots stirred so viciously during the Cultural Revolution is a spent force.
Westerners who live in China or visit here would generally agree that in good times the Chinese are as pleasant a people to live among as any. 
But the mob outside the Workers' Stadium was a reminder of less benign passions that still persist.

text:

The city's first Chinese-American candidate for a judgeship was proposed yesterday by Mayor Koch.
Randall T. Eng, 35 years old, inspector general of the Correction Department since March 1982, was proposed for a post in Criminal Court.
Born in China, he came to the United States when he was 5 months old and was brought up in Queens. 
Mr. Eng is a 1972 graduate of the St. John's University Law School. 
After eight years in the Queens District Attorney's office, he moved to the Correction Department in 1980.
The Mayor's counsel, Patrick F. X. Mulhearn, said research had determined there have been no Chinese- American judges in the city. 
Mr. Mulhearn said Mr. Eng's appointment, which must await a hearing Sept. 
14 by the Mayor's committee on the judiciary, would leave four court vacancies to be filled by appointment.
This year, there have been 26 Criminal Court and Family Court appointments, along with 9 interim appointments to the Civil Court, where full terms are filled by election.

file: THE CLAN THAT CHANGED CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE SOONG DYNASTY By Sterling Seagrave. 
Illustrated. 532 pp. 
New York: Harper & Row. 
$22.50.
No mater whether you love them or hate them, Charlie Soong's six children make good copy. 
There were three sons and three daughters, and between them they carved out a permanent niche in the steamy politics of the Chinese republic in the years from its founding in 1911 to its fall in 1949. 
The three sons were educated at universities in the United States, two at Harvard and one at Vanderbilt, and became vastly wealthy. 
The eldest, T. V. (Tse-ven) Soong (by common practice all three were referred to by the initials of their Chinese given names) became a major figure in Nationalist Chinese, Kuomintang Party politics, serving at intervals as Finance Minister, Foreign Minister and governor of the Central Bank of China; his younger brothers, T. L. (Tse-liang) and T. A. (Tse- an), were powerful as bankers, industrialists and company directors.
Charlie Soong's three daughters, all also American-educated, had even more dramatic fates through their marriages - the eldest, Ai-ling, started out as Sun Yat-sen's secretary and went on to marry H. H. Kung, a wealthy industrialist, Oberlin College and Yale University graduate, and lineal descendant of Confucius; the middle daughter, Ching- ling, married Sun Yat-sen, and after his death in 1925 became an influential exponent of the liberal-radical cause, and eventually a vice chairman of the People's Republic of China; the youngest daughter, May-ling, married Chiang Kai-shek.
Given the remarkable lives of these six siblings, and the presence of such strong American-Chinese connections, one would have assumed that the Soong family would long since have been the subjects of massive, popular biographies. 
Yet such has not been the case. 
There has been a scattering of biographical sketches of the three daughters, the best-known being Emily Hahn's ''Soong Sisters'' (1941); but there is virtually nothing authoritative on the three sons, nor on Ai-ling's husband, H. H. Kung, except for the biographical entries in Howard Boorman's ''Biographical Dictionary of Republican China,'' and the painfully acquired details of the family's financial manipulations collected by Parks Coble in his admirable 1980 study, ''The Shanghai Capitalists and the Nationalist Government, 1927-1937.''
Sterling Seagrave, in ''The Soong Dynasty,'' has boldly decided to fill in the gap and to tackle the whole family at once, including the founding father, Charles Jones (Chiao-shun) Soong. 
His book is vigorously polemical, sharply biased and engrossing to anyone who has ever attempted to filter through the mass of detail and conjecture, fact and rumor and bare-faced lying that fill the bewildering hodgepodge of sources we must draw on for studies of modern China.
Mr. Seagrave, who grew up on the China-Burma border and is the author of ''Yellow Rain,'' a book on acid rain, has a thesis, and he presents it clearly. 
He believes that the lives of the Soongs only make sense if they are studied in the context of their ''long involvement with and dependence upon the Shanghai gangster underworld,'' and adds that ''such a biography did not exist earlier because the Soongs did not want it to.''
Until the 1970's, he thinks, an ''unwholesome'' interest in the Soongs, or ''a less than religious attitude toward the Chiangs, in particular, was enough to jeopardize a journalist's livelihood.''
THERE may be some truth to this latter assertion, certainly during the 1950's, and some historians also felt obliged to keep away from politically dangerous ground in the same years. 
Even the current dangers of writing slightingly about Chiang Kai-shek were dramatically underlined in October by the murder of the Chinese-American journalist Henry Liu in California; members of a powerful criminal syndicate in Taiwan known as the Bamboo Gang are under indictment in the case. 
But more important, most historians kept away because there was such a paucity of available sources that they despaired of ever being able to reconstruct an accurate account. 
The records had been laundered too thoroughly in Taipei and Peking, and concealed or blurred in the United States. 
As to the connections of the Soongs and Chiang with the ''Shanghai gangster underworld,'' that record had been partially reconstructed by the careful researches of Y. C. Wang, Pichon Loh, Jonathan Marshall and Parks Coble. 
But by its very nature, the record was likely to remain impossible to document fully, as long as the financial dealings of the Soongs in the United States and elsewhere remained protected by discreet bankers, cautious bureaucrats and the danger of libel suits.
Mr. Seagrave refuses to be daunted by such worries and hurls himself into the fray with flags flying. 
His book is fast-paced and jammed with racy details and incident, for the Soongs, as he tells us, ''passed through life like a team of pickpockets through a carnival crowd, doing what they did best, while the rubes watched geeks bite heads off live chickens.''
Bluntly put, he is convinced that the Soong family defrauded both the Chinese people and the American taxpayers (who provided loans and lend-lease) out of hundreds of millions, perhaps billions, of dollars; and that they held onto a great deal of this money after Chiang's regime collapsed in 1949, since it was safely stored in American, Brazilian and other banks.
A lot of people have believed some variation of this, and the discreet language of the diplomats reinforces it. 
A member of the United States Embassy staff noted in 1936 that Ai-ling Soong received ''a moderate but invariable commission on all purchases of military planes,'' while the British ambassador wrote that Ai-ling's husband, H. H. Kung, had such a ''preference for his own interests over those of his country'' that he was ruining the economy. 
Gen. Joseph W. Stilwell was mystified and angry over the disappearance of huge amounts of lend-lease supplies in World War II; and immense American loans, many of which passed through the hands of T. V. Soong, his brothers or his brother-in-law, were never adequately accounted for. 
May-ling Soong's extravagance and demands became legendary. 
Only Ching-ling escaped this unflattering attention; she was blamed instead for being soft on communism.
When Mr. Seagrave links his story to the newly documented estimates of the Soong-Chiang connections with organized crime in Shanghai, he is at his most interesting but also in the greatest danger of overstating his case. 
He is right that there was a tight link between Chiang and the Shanghai Green Gang racketeers who controlled opium, prostitution and the labor force on the docks and in the factories; these criminals were protected by the foreign powers in China - the French simply made the head of the Green Gang the chief of detectives in the French Concession, so that all other criminals stayed away - and Chiang needed money from opium sales for his own militarization program.
The trouble is in estimating the importance of this in the history of Nationalist China as a whole. 
Here, Mr. Seagrave is confident: there was a ''grand strategy'' between Chiang and the criminals in both Canton and Shanghai during early 1927, and later that same year the revolution in Wuhan was ''subverted by the Green Gang until it collapsed from within.''
Still later, ''The Nanking government was quite simply a Trojan horse, painted in bright colors by the Soong clan.''
Inside this horse ''were hidden the generals, secret policemen and Green Gang leaders who actually yielded power in China.''
Similar forces, he believes, lay at the heart of the New Fourth Army Incident of 1941, when a Nationalist attack on Communist troops prompted the collapse of the United Front against the Japanese.
If this is in fact true, why has it not been better known by the public?
Mr. Seagrave has several explanations, among them the power of Henry Luce's pro- Soong news network, the public-relations skills and lobbying of the Soongs themselves, the obstinacy or lethargy of State Department veterans like Stanley Hornbeck, the incompetence and ignorance of Franklin D. Roosevelt, and Harry S. Truman's reluctance to act. 
Again, there is some truth in all these aspects of the case - the difficulty is in knowing how to evaluate the separate elements. 
Luce certainly backed the Soongs and Chiang with Time, Life and all the other resources at his command, but those resources were still finite, and there were other news media that could have carried different stories.
The Soongs also had their own coterie of influential friends in the Congress and among the Presidential advisers. 
But many sensible officials were suspicious of them and doubted their competence. 
Hornbeck may have been, in Mr. Seagrave's rather splendid encapsulation, ''one of those basking hamadryads of the State Department who, having reached a place in the sun, lie coiled in wait for any creature that might disturb its repose,'' but he was not in a position to muzzle all criticism. 
At the governmental level, Mr. Seagrave has been persevering and ingenious in getting what he could through the Freedom of Information Act from the Federal Bureau of Investigation and other files on the Soongs, but the inconclusiveness of these reports leaves open the question of whether there was systematic purging of material - for example, by the Treasury Department - and whether the Presidents were at fault in not following up certain leads as to the Soongs' wrongdoing.
Much of the drive of Mr. Seagrave's book comes from his assumption that the Soongs were at the center of things much of the time, and he sets the scene skillfully by depicting the founding father of the clan, Charlie Soong, as also being a founding father of the republic. 
Sun Yat-sen and Charlie Soong, writes Mr. Seagrave, were linked in ''one of history's great conspiracies. 
Together they bamboozled the Manchus and brought the Empire to the edge of collapse - when all that was needed was a final nudge.''
This, I fear, is just not true. 
Mr. Seagrave has done a fine job in ferreting out a great deal of detail about Charlie Soong's education in the United States, the development of his business empire through the printing of Bibles and the manufacture of noodles, his role as a fund-raiser for Sun Yat-sen's insurrections and probable connections with various secret societies such as the Red Gang. 
These sections of his book are fascinating. 
But it is too great a leap to conclude from this that Charlie Soong helped bring the Manchu dynasty to ''the edge of collapse,'' just as it is too much to conclude that it was the Soongs who brought down China's republic. 
In both cases, complex economic and social forces and hundreds of other major actors were what brought about long-term political change. 
Without the Soongs, one can be pretty sure, things would not have been very different.
NEVERTHELESS, Charlie Soong is the most rounded character in Mr. Seagrave's gallery - ''somewhere between pimp and patrician.''
''With Sunday school at one extreme, Red Gang at the other, Charlie led a tidy double life,'' and the chapters that analyze him make a valued addition to our knowledge of the Chinese experience in America and the rise of a modernizing Chinese business class in Shanghai. 
With the children, Mr. Seagrave is less successful, and he can never quite divorce them from stereotype. 
Ching-ling is just too good, Ai-ling too ruthless, May-ling too petulant, T. V. too bumbling, to command our full attention or win our belief. 
Mr. Seagrave warns us squarely at the outset that he had trouble with the family, since, ''like the Cheshire Cat, the Soongs were visible only when they wished to be. 
They hid by being obvious. 
They had a public plumage that was so praiseworthy it dazzled the eye. 
Once this image was established, it became practically impossible to observe their actual movements, to record their true habits and personalities, or other aspects of character easily discernible in ordinary people.''
If Mr. Seagrave has not been totally successful in recording those true habits and personalities, he has nonetheless ruffled the plumage most thoroughly, and the eye is no longer dazzled. 
The only way his more dramatic charges will be countered or substantiated is if more evidence is dug out or made available, and I think this book will stimulate many scholars to try just that. 
The process will be all to the good, for our understanding of both Chinese and American politics during the first half of this century.B
'Lying Low' Out of Prudence These days, Sterling Seagrave's life has almost as much intrigue as his study of the Soong clan. 
He, his wife and their twin 16-year-olds, are, as he put it, ''lying low'' in a country whose name they prefer to keep secret. 
''It's not fear, it's discretion,'' he says, recalling that a journalist who wrote a book critical of Chiang Kai-shek's family was shot to death last fall. 
''I thought it would be prudent for me to fade into the undergrowth for a few months and not go on the author's tour. 
If the true story of the Chiang regime became well known in America there might be radical changes in how the Government deals with Taipei. 
That gives me very good reason to be cautious.''
The book was conceived 15 years ago, but its roots stretch back to the author's childhood as the son of a surgeon on the China-Burma border. 
There, he says, ''I would hear lots of things about the Soongs and Chiangs which didn't jibe with what I saw in Life magazine.''
One bonus of writing the book was traveling again to Asia. 
''I like the people and I like the way it smells there,'' he said. 
''It makes me feel at home.''
Someday, he hopes to make a trip there in a 41-foot, ocean-going sloop he is building. 
- Joseph Berger

text:
ï»¿
The down business is up. 
Thanks to the bitter Canadian winter weather blowing south to the United States, Canada's makers of down winterwear, major suppliers for the American market, are reporting surprisingly good sales despite the recession and record high world prices for the little puffs of feathers.
''Given inflation, people are looking for real value at today's high prices,'' said Russill H. Morin, president of the Canadian Down and Feather Products Association. 
''And they are finding it in down.''
Andrew Malcolm comment discusses how cold weather conditions have helped sales of down products
They are also finding a radically different, more fashionable and costlier product than consumers knew not so many years back when down was something worn only by geese, ducks and a few hunters in reversible red and green vests.
Now it has become a $100 million-a-year industry in Canada alone, has started a lucrative surge in international sales and has seen several Asian countries begin their own down industries to serve the exploding market in North America and Japan.
Â 
2 Million to the Ounce
Down, whose tiny resilient filaments number 2 million to the ounce, has long been popular as a pillow-filler and, in Europe, for bed comforters. 
It was warm and lightweight. 
But its bulk and perceived image as masculine, ''outdoorsy'' and unfashionable confined sales to the sporting goods sections of most North American stores.
There is considerable dispute about which one of Canada's many private clothing companies first combined new colors, better design and a stylish stitching pattern to make the first women's down coat. 
But there is no dispute that it happened about five years ago here in Winnipeg, the old prairie riverboat town that has the lowest mean temperature of any Canadian city.
''You don't care what you look like in Winnipeg in the winter,'' said Mr. Morin, who lives in Toronto, ''you just want to be warm.''
Consumers can now buy a complete line of down-filled products, from coats, mittens and parkas to comforters, sleeping bags, lounging slippers and the high-priced down skiwear made by Mr. Morin's company, Russill H. Morin Ltd.
Winnipeg's down manufacturers, such as Victoria Squire and Miami Fashions, cite many reasons for down's sudden success without largescale advertising. 
They include inflation, changing tastes toward more outdoor activities, acceptance of more pragmatic clothing, down's impressive insulation power and the strength of a fad that first introduced many to the comfort, practicality, light weight and warmth of some slightly used feathers.
Â 
'It Lasts a Lifetime'
''You use down one time,'' Mr. Morin said, ''you'll never go back to anything else. 
And it lasts a lifetime, too.''
The basic quality of down, however, owes nothing to man. 
Its many water-resistant filaments, naturally arrayed in clusters like a ripe dandelion pod, trap warm air next to the body yet allow the garments to ''breathe.''
The best down comes from the breasts of geese. 
One mature, 10-pound goose might produce eight ounces of feathers. 
But that includes only two ounces of down. 
The down, however, costs $54 a pound in December, which is a lot more than the entire rest of the bird is worth.
The problem is that feathers and down are a byproduct of the meat industry and there has never been that overwhelming a demand for goose and ducks in North America. 
So, according to Mr. Morin, a number of Canadian farmers are raising geese, selling the meat frozen to European outlets at little more than cost, and making money off the byproduct.
Still, the farmers are far from meeting the market's demands. 
For many years, the world's major feather supplier has been the Orient, primarily China, whose birds produce half the world's supply. 
Last year Canada imported some 2 million pounds of feathers, or 80 percent of its needs.
Â 
Prices Have Soared
But three years ago, China realized that it could create some domestic jobs and reap more foreign exchange benefits by founding its own down clothing industry. 
So it slashed down exports by half, sending down's price up. 
In 1970 down cost $4.25 a pound. 
In 1975 it cost $7.10. 
In 1978 the price tripled to $24, and it has doubled again since.
The feathers arrive at Canadian processors in burlap-wrapped bales in 40,000-pound container loads. 
They are washed, blown dry and blown sorted for shipment to Canad ian clothiers, who have been scrambling to provide th e best designed, most fashionable fabrics to wrap aroundthe feathers.
''There is a wider array of colors now than ever before,'' said Jeff Black, vice president of merchandising for Victoria Squire Inc., where 250 workers are already sewing next winter's down jackets. 
''The U.S. demand is growing all the time. 
''We've been increasing our production 25 percent a year since 1977.''
''We're pushing the more tailored look,'' said Murray Waldman of Miami Fashions Ltd., known in New York as the Canadian Garments Company. 
''Down is becoming more fashionable all the time.''
'People Will Remember the Cold'
''We've had two mild winters,'' Mr. Waldman noted, ''and people forget about the cold. 
Then, wham, comes this winter and our sales are way up. 
The boost will carry over to next year, too. 
People will remember the cold.''
The problem for Canadian and American down clothiers is competition from Asia, primarily Korea and China, where wages are but a fraction of North America's.
''I just came back from China,'' Mr. Waldman said. 
''They make a coat for half our costs. 
They're paying about 25 cents an hour. 
We pay $5.''
Thus, a domestic down coat might cost $250 to $300 at retail today, while Chinese coats, he said, might sell for $150 to $180 and cost the stores only $75 wholesale.
''Our challenge is to make our coats look that much more expensive than the imports,'' he said.

THE TSAI FUNG DANCE COMPANY was founded in 1982 with the aim of expressing Chinese tradition in modern dance and music. 
Some of the dances performed by the company on April 25 at Pace College's Schimmel Center had the look of uneasy hybrids. 
But there was also authentic theater, much of which tended to occur when Jiang Qi was on the stage.
A former member of China's Central Song and Dance Company who is now dancing with the Joffrey II, Mr. Jiang moves with the kind of magnetic exuberance and strong, clear focus that one would expect from a dancer who has performed in such new Chinese dance operas as ''The Red Detachment of Women'' and ''The White-Haired Girl.''
But the neatness of his dancing and the quietness of his charm insured that the occasional acrobatics in Mr. Jiang's ''Yellow River'' never looked like audience-pleasing tricks. 
Instead, the solo impressively evoked the river in all its pounding grandeur and playfulness, as well as depicting the swimmers who live along its banks, as it was intended to do. 
Named after the waterway considered the cradle of Chinese civilization and the symbol of the nation, ''Yellow River'' is set to Ying Chong-Jong's comparably refined Yellow River Concerto.
Based on the legend of the origins of face-painting in the Peking Opera, Mai Mei-Jiun's ''Double Image'' tells the story of a king who is so handsome that he has to wear a ferocious mask when he goes to war. 
Miss Mai, artistic director of the company, works in bold, strong images that can be seen as vibrant, stylized abstractions and traditional narrative elements.
Lu Yu was superb as Lan Ling, the handsome king, projecting smiling serenity and a ritual fierceness. 
The cast was completed by Xue Wei-Xin, as his warrior spirit, David Foresman and Wayne Williams as his soldiers, and Tobi Arrington, Naoko Katakami, Dyane Neiman and Susan Richardson as his enemies. 
''Double Image'' is set to a score by Tan Dun.
Miss Mai's ''Awakening'' was a similar piece of narrative, though it had good performances from Miss Katakami, Mr. Lu and, in particular, Mr. Jiang. The program was completed by Miss Mai's ''The Cicada Speaks,'' set to an evocative score by William Bolcom, and ''Ocean Series,'' by Mr. Xue, the company's resident choreographer. 
Unlike ''Yellow River'' and ''Double Image,'' these interminable impressionistic group works seemed to have been choreographed out of a compulsion to create rather than to express.

text:
ï»¿
The Encyclopaedia Britannica said today that its new Chinese version preserved the reference work's objectivity despite disputes over Stalin, Taiwan and the Korean War.
The 10-volume edition, a joint project of Encyclopaedia Britannica and the state-run Encyclopedia of China, is going on sale in China this month.
''Everybody started out from different sides of the ideological fence, and we were able to find a common ground,'' Frank B. Gibney, vice chairman of Encyclopaedia Britannica Inc., said at a news conference today. 
''We don't feel the Encyclopaedia Britannica has been compromised at all.''
Earlier, the company's chairman, Robert Guinn, met with Hu Yaobang, the Communist Party General Secretary, at the Great Hall of the People. 
Mr. Hu praised the publishers of the two countries, saying the encyclopedia was a ''very good thing,'' the official New China News Agency reported. 
Mr. Hu gave Mr. Guinn an autographed copy of the encyclopedia.
Some 500 Chinese scholars worked with the Encyclopaedia Britannica staff to compile the encyclopedia, Mr. Gibney said. 
The project took six years.
Work began after Deng Xiaoping, the Chinese leader, heard about an encyclopedia from a smaller country and lamented that China did not have its own, Mr. Gibney said.
Â 
'The Inevitable Problems'
Encyclopedia of China was producing a 75-volume encyclopedia, and Encyclopaedia Britannica suggested its encyclopedia be published in Chinese as an interim measure, he said.
''To satisfy the inevitable problems of differences of opinion, we had an editorial review board'' of Americans and Chinese who discussed areas of controversy, he said.
For the encyclopedia, almost 2,500 new articles were written by Chinese scholars. 
Many adjectives were deleted from the articles to make them objective, Mr. Gibney said.
One difference arose over the Korean War, he said. 
The Chinese insisted that South Korea started the war, and the Americans maintained it was begun by North Korea. 
The experts agreed on an entry that reports on fighting, but does not address the question of who started the conflict, Mr. Gibney said.
He said the only disagreement that was not resolved concerned Stalin. 
An article about the Soviet leader's approach to Communism and his political and economic policies was cut, leaving only a bare biographical sketch.
Â 
Assessment of Mao
One factor in the Soviet-Chinese split in the late 1950s was disagreement over Stalin's role as an international Communist leader, especially as compared with Mao Zedong.
In the encyclopedia, Mao is portrayed as a great leader who made serious mistakes, a version that conforms with China's current political line.
In the encyclopedia, Taiwan, which is led by the Nationalist Government that fled China after losing the civil war to the Communists, is described as a Chinese province under separate administration by the Nationalists.
Both the Nationalists and Communists claim authority over all of China, including Taiwan.
Because the Chinese experts had access to Communist Party archives, their work was more complete than past Encyclopaedia Britannica entries on China. 
Some of the work has been incorporated into the English version of the encyclopedia, company officials said.

text:

He had just plopped down on the grass, wrapped the line around his big toe and popped the cap off a cool bottle of Peking Five Star beer, when the fish hit.
Lao Li grabbed for his pole, but it was too late. 
The fish jerked him, toe first, into the lake. 
For six hours, the fish pulled him through the water, almost drowning him several times. 
It was dark before he crawled back on shore, wrapped the line around a big tree and began coaxing the fish to the bank.
James Sterba's describes fishing for sport in China; notes Chinese fish stories match scope of foreign anglers' tales
When he saw it, Lao Li almost fainted. 
It must have weighed 900 pounds. 
It was a grass carp so big, well, it was big enough to saddle up and ride home. 
When it saw Lao Li, the giant carp winked, as if to an old friend. 
Then, with a whoosh of its tail, the carp surged into the deep, tearing the tree out by its roots just before the line broke.
Of course, it's a fish story. 
It was told by a Mr. Wei, not Mr. Hemingway, in China, not America. 
Fishing is as honorable a way of enduring the 20th century in China as it is anywhere. 
And the ones that get away in China are as cunning as the ones that bellyflop off the hooks of fishermen in any lake or stream the world over.
Fishing is one of the few forms of recreation a man here can engage in once table tennis elbow sets in. 
While China maintains recreation centers for young people, workers generally live in cramped housing in crowded cities in which leisure time pursuits are limited to exercise in parks, comparing songbirds, playing cards or Chinese chess, talking with relatives or neighbors, or preparing for the next day's work.
Here in Peking, a day license to fish in the lake at the Summer Palace costs less than a dollar. 
The government grows fish there to sell to restaurants. 
It harvests them in late autumn with nets, but fishermen are allowed to catch them in the meantime and are charged less than the market price per pound for the fish they catch and choose to take home.
Legend has it, of course, that the big ones are too smart to be landed. 
There is said to be a bass out there so big that it eats water buffalo for breakfast. 
There are also said to be fish in that lake tagged by emperors of the Manchu dynasty.
A young computer scientist who fishes there regularly says that the way to catch grass carp is to use grass as bait. 
The problem with grass as bait is that it tends to come off the hook too easily. 
But one retired official in town secretly cultivates a kind of grass that stays on the hook. 
He is the envy of all the younger fishermen at the Summer Palace lake.
In America, that kind of grass is known as crabgrass. 
It has a solid, flat stem that stays on the hook. 
In short, it has body. 
For the Chinese bass that inhabit the lake and nearby reservoirs, crickets, worms and frogs are the preferred bait.
Chinese fishermen do not mount their fish. 
That is too expensive. 
Instead, they make fish prints. 
What they do is rinse their prized catches off in vinegar to remove the slime. 
Then they paint one side of the fish with ink and press the fish onto a piece of rice paper. 
The result looks like a Chinese painting of a fish. 
Then they wash off the fish and prepare it for the frying pan.
Peking's growing foreign community includes a substantial number of fishermen who find that they can make friends around the lake more easily than in working circumstances.
When Chinese and foreign anglers get together to compare gear, the conversation quickly evolves from techniques and locations into yarns about the big ones that got away. 
Any Chinese can match his foreign counterpart on this subject, fish for fish.
A young composer named Shao Lun, for example, swears that he caught a monster grass carp last summer, made a fish print of it for his collection, and then had second thoughts about eating the fish. 
It was still alive, and it seemed to look him in the eye. 
So he threw it back. 
Shao Lun insists that the fish was so grateful that it now allows him to catch it every Sunday.

file: THE GOOD WOMAN OF BENXI, A SUCCESS.txt
text:
ï»¿
Guan Guangmei, former peasant and former meat counter clerk, is a ''phenomenon'' to her fellow Chinese.
The determined 37-year-old woman has captivated the imagination of theorists of economic reform, infuriated defenders of Communist orthodoxy and become one of the most talked-about people in China - all because she succeeded in an enterprise where many had failed.
Over the last two years, Miss Guan, a member of the Communist Party, has leased eight bankrupt or financially shaky grocery stores from the city government here and transformed them into flourishing, profitable operations. 
Her markets now account for one-third of the non-staple food sales and one-half of all profits produced by food stores in this city of 1.4 million people in northeastern China.
Â 
'This Is Reform'
On the ground floor of the Dongming Shangchang, or Eastern Brightness Store, Miss Guan, efficient and brusque in a sober gray polyester pantsuit, drew the tips of her fingers along a gleaming white tile counter. 
Her barely perceptible nod of approval stirred smiles from the white-hatted women behind the counter, which was stacked with pyramids of cellophane-wrapped candies and jars of preserved apples and apricots.
''This is reform,'' Miss Guan said flatly. 
''I have the power to run this enterprise.''
For several weeks, newspapers around the country have broadcast the exploits of Miss Guan almost in storybook fashion. 
''Inside the Guan Guangmei phenomenon,'' promised a headline on page 1 of a national newspaper. 
Boasted another, ''Benxi produces Guan Guangmei!''
In the prestigious and influential Economic Daily, a two-week debate of sorts has raged over whether her success and methods are truly ''socialist'' or are, in fact, blatantly ''capitalist.''
Â 
A Rare Debate on Issues
And although anonymous commentators, editorialists and letter writers who support Miss Guan heavily outnumber her detractors, the extended discussion of the ''Guan Guangmei phenomenon'' is a rare instance of public exchange over issues that are at the very core of China's modernization effort. 
To be sure, the degree of official and public support for Miss Guan suggests strongly that her example is being used not only to champion the need for economic reform but also as a way of smoking out the ideological opposition.
Benxi's Communist Party branch has held a series of meetings over the last year to assess Miss Guan's endeavors. 
Her critics within the party, according to The Economic Daily, have attacked her for a variety of sins.
One party member who has worked for a quarter of a century in one of the stores now leased by Miss Guan accused her of ''disliking the supervision of the party and for being good at dancing.''
Another party member contended that Miss Guan ''plays down the role of political education,'' while a third charged: ''The leasing system of Guan Guangmei takes advantage of the situation to benefit herself. 
It has the character of exploitation.''
Â 
China's Current Dilemma
These criticisms, even the denigration of her ballroom talents, are fundamental to China's current dilemma: how to invigorate an economy that is resisting virtually all stimuli under a blanket of bureaucratic incompetence and corruption, while preserving a necessary patina of socialist ideology. 
That Miss Guan dances well raises the question of whether she is polluted with bourgeois values just as much as her high salary may imply she is a capitalist.
''They're not used to these things, so they oppose us,'' said Miss Guan of her critics. 
''Some workers are used to administration from above and the iron rice bowl. 
They think socialism means everyone should have rice to eat, whether they work or not. 
This kind of thinking is a real problem.''
Miss Guan, whose short black hair is beginning to show the first strands of gray, grew up in a rural area near this grimy town driven by steel mills. 
After graduating from high school in 1968 in the midst of the political hysteria of the Cultural Revolution, she worked on a commune near her home where she was eventually chosen as a production team leader in charge of 340 people. 
In 1971, she was transferred to Benxi, where she sold pork at the Xiaofang grocery store. 
Two and a half years later she was named head of the foodstuffs department and, shortly thereafter, became assistant manager of the entire store.
Â 
Seeks Better Standard of Living
''When we worked in the fields, life was very difficult,'' Miss Guan said, the words tumbling out at a speed rivaling the patter of a disk jockey. 
''So I thought, once we got enterprises going, we could make the country rich. 
I wanted to make it more successful but couldn't. 
Back then, I wanted to make the countryside rich.''
Her biggest disillusionment came, she said, when she was trying to turn the Xiaofang store around. 
''Even if you had talent you couldn't do well because the country didn't give you power,'' she said. 
''As assistant manger, I couldn't do anything because they wouldn't listen to me. 
We had no power.''
In 1984, the city of Benxi announced that private individuals could lease enterprises and run them as they wished. 
That decision, Miss Guan said, changed her life.
''I thought, by using this leasing method I could improve other enterprises,'' she explained. 
''I started looking at losing enterprises. 
I looked at the Guangming food store in 1986, which had consistently lost money for six years.''
Â 
Using Wage Incentives
''It lost money for lots of reasons,'' she said, ''Primarily because the managment was no good.''
In April of that year, Miss Guan leased the Guangming store. 
''The leaders were no good, so I demoted them,'' she said. 
''By the end of the year, the workers had bonuses.''
Her strategy at the Guangming store, she said, was typical of her management techniques at other stores. 
''There was a tremendous amount of waste,'' she said. 
''Internal management was terrible. 
Goods sat around. 
Nobody cared if they were sold or not. 
I set targets for every worker. 
If they didn't meet the target, their wages were cut.''
The combination of rising wages and tough discipline worked wonders on the work force. 
Jiang Xiu-e, a young clerk who confessed she had once had a notorious reputation for a quick tongue and nasty manner with customers, said that after Miss Guan leased the store, she ''told me that if I didn't change my behavior, I would be heavily penalized.''
She added, ''I didn't believe her at all.''
Â 
A Turning Point
But one day, after a raucus argument with a customer, Miss Guan cut 20 yuan, or about $5, from Miss Jiang's salary - about one-quarter of her monthly wage. 
''From that very day, I began to be more cautious with customers,'' Miss Jiang said. 
''Finally, I began to see that customers were actually reasonable. 
It's strange, isn't it?
Now I get the highest monthly bonus of the 220 workers in the store.''
The Economic Daily chronicled the transformation of one of Miss Guan's stores, as described by a frequent customer. 
''I live next to the Guangming grocery store,'' the customer was quoted as saying. 
''The store was dirty and disorderly. 
When you asked for something, no one would answer, and if they did you'd get a very cold response. 
One day, I went to the grocery store and found it had been whitewashed and the floor had been cleaned. 
A salesperson who had always quarreled with me in the past greeted me with a smile, saying, 'We have a new stock of bread, would you like some?'
''
Painfully aware that her success would breed both envy and criticism, Miss Guan canvassed the entire Communist Party hierarchy of Benxi looking for allies. 
In 1985, she stumbled on Li Ming, then the 35-year-old director of the political research office of the city's party branch and a fervent proponent of economic reform and experimentation. 
With the blessing of the city's party secretary, she wooed him away and installed him as the assistant general manager of her operation.
''I was looking at leasing and thought this was the way to promote reforms,'' Mr. Li said. 
''I said, 'If we go according to the Guan Guangmei model, profits will go up dramatically.'
I was interested in going to an enterprise and experimenting in a real environment. 
This was a way for me to be closer to real life.''
Â 
Burgeoning Success
With his help and the party's support, Miss Guan steamed ahead, leasing a total of eight stores and creating a holding company to oversee the venture. 
In two years, she earned more than 44,000 yuan, a sum equivalent to about $12,000 - 50 times what China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, earns. 
Much of her earnings she ploughed into Government-required ''risk funds,'' a rainy-day account in case her stores fail, and into extra bonuses and awards for workers. 
Still, she said, she is probably the wealthiest person in Benxi.
Despite her wealth, Miss Guan's achievements have earned her recognition as a national model worker, as well as the ''May 1 Labor Award'' and the ''March 3 National Woman's Award,'' both accolades usually conferred on exemplary factory workers. 
And just last week, she was elected by the Benxi Communist Party as a delegate to the 13th Party Congress to be held in Beijing this October.
''There are many outsiders who object to this,'' Miss Guan said. 
''They think I make too much money. 
Lots of people didn't understand me. 
'Why do you want this trouble?' they said. 
But I said I must do this to make the country better.''

TIM POLLAK and Alain de Pouzilhac represent the new breed of international ad executives.
Mr. Pollack is president and chief executive, and Mr. de Pouzilhac chairman worldwide, of HDM, a joint-venture agency with about $1.4 billion in billings and 53 offices in 23 countries in Europe, North America and Asia. 
The third man in their troika is Shinzo Ueno, senior executive vice president in Tokyo.
Mr. Pollak and Mr. de Pouzilhac were in New York yesterday for meeting after meeting - and even a meeting to plan a meeting of 56 managers later this month in Beijing. 
For Mr. Pollak, the trip will be his fifth to Asia this year.
The reasons for these meetings are not always major ones, perhaps just the celebration of a refurbished office that presents a good occasion to show the flag.
Indeed, Mr. Pollak said he had just returned from Beijing, where HDM is the only multinational full-service advertising agency.
''We're a new kind of venture and China is a new kind of adventure,'' he said. 
''Having an office in China is absolutely consistent with what HDM is all about.''
Mr. de Pouzilhac added: ''China is so big as a market you can't be important in that area without an office there. 
It's proof that we are a worldwide company.''
What brought Mr. Pollak to China most recently was to install Candy Wong as the new general manager. 
Ms. Wong, of Cedar Rapids, Iowa, is a Chinese-American who formerly worked for Young & Rubicam, the American partner in the HDM joint venture. 
Her staff of 18 is made up of one Singapore resident of Chinese descent and 17 Chinese.
The other two partner agencies in HDM are Eurocom, based in Paris, and Dentsu, in Tokyo. 
Like Y.&R., they are the biggest agencies in their main areas of operation.
HDM was formed last July by combining two joint ventures of Y.&R., one with the French and one with the Japanese. 
There were no duplicate offices except in Los Angeles, where they were merged. 
And if there were a place to expect friction to develop and productivity to decline, it would probably be this newly merged office.
Instead, the opposite happened. 
Two offices that had previously not experienced growth have since their merger grown 20 percent.
Mr. Pollak and Mr. de Pouzilhac had never met until after the merger. 
But they had several things in common besides their age. 
(Both are now 42 years old.) Both began their advertising careers with Doyle Dane Bernbach, one in New York, the other in Paris. 
They find an appreciation of creative work a common bond.
Mr. de Pouzilhac talked yesterday about the creative scene in Europe, where, he noted, over the last three years the copywriter has been replaced by the art director as the dominant creative force.
The reasons are simple enough. 
Satellite television, which crosses national borders, and language barriers now require advertising that emphasizes the visual rather than the vocal. 
Mr. de Pouzilhac said that many TV commercials were now being planned with voice-overs replacing dialogue, so that different languages could easily be dubbed in. 
The dubbing is done locally after the satellite transmission is received.
Europe is awaiting 1992, when the tariff barriers are scheduled to fall and, with few exceptions, the Continent is to become one big market. 
It will be a market with more than 330 million people and media spending is expected to boom in broadcasting, where advertising has been limited in a number of countries.
''Clients feel that if they're not in a number of countries by then, they'll be dead,'' Mr. de Pouzilhac said.

text:
