Pertti Karppinen, the Finnish singles sculler who is a three-time Olympic champion, won his race in the consolation finals of Olympic rowing Friday. 
It placed him seventh in the competition.
The 35-year-old Karppinen was eliminated from medal consideration Thursday when he finished sixth and last in his heat of the semifinals.
He won the Olympic single-sculls gold at Monteal in 1976, at Moscow in 1980 and at Los Angeles in 1984.
Karppinen rowed past Iouri Iaanson of the Soviet Union to win the consolation finals by a half-second in the last 50 meters. 
His time, 7:34.37, was far off the pace of 7:03.25 for 2,000 meters turned in by the heat leader, East Germany's Thomas Lange, and Karppinen's repechage time of 7:14.91.
Karppinen said that rowing has been hard for him this year, but that he will continue to train for the world championships and the next Olympics if he can ''regain the gladness'' of sculling.
Karppinen finished last in a semifinal heat Thursday that was won by Peter-Michael Kolbe, a four-time world champion. 
Kolbe's time was 7 minutes 1.76 seconds.
The Finn's reclusive manner and the lack of a common language have killed most conversations in the past. 
But as Karppinen contemplated his future after the defeat, Kolbe dug deep into his weak Norwegian for words of consolation.
''I managed to get a message over in Norwegian,'' said Kolbe, also 35. 
''I felt very sorry for him finishing last. 
It really does feel like a tearful goodbye.''
In other the consolation finals, Kurt Bausback of San Diego, Calif., and Ed Ives of Hamilton, Mass., were ninth in men's coxless pair. 
Angie Herron of Alpena, Mich., Sherry Cassuto of Seattle, Wash., Jennie Marshall of Boston and Anne Martin of Cambridge, Mass., were ninth in women's quad sculls. 
Dan Lyons of Wayne, Pa.; Robert Espeseth of Philadelphia, and Jon Fish of Bellmore, L.I., the coxswain, were 11th in coxed pair.

22 (AP) -The United States lost to the Soviet Union, 4-2, today and was eliminated from the tournament.

Water Polo
China Is Routed By U.S., 14-7

The Americans (2-1) started slowly against the Chinese (0-3), showing flashes of brilliance and then allowing their opponents to score easy goals.

Wrestling
Hungarian Wins Gold by Default
SEOUL, South Korea, Sept. 
22 (AP) -The Soviet Union collected four gold medals in the five-day Greco-Roman tournament, which ended today.
Italy, Bulgaria, Norway, South Korea, Poland and Hungary each earned one gold. 
The United States had one bronze.
In the final matches at Sang Mu Gymnasium, Andras Sike of Hungary won the gold when Stoyan Balov of Bulgaria withdrew because of an injury with 2:22 remaining in the second period in the 126-pound class.
Balov took the silver. 
Charalambos Holidis of Greece won the bronze, beating Yang Changling of China, 6-1.
Levon Djoulfalakian of the Soviet Union led Kim Sung Moon of South Korea, 8-1, in the first period and scored a 9-3 triumph for the gold medal in the 150-pound class.

The bronze went to Tapio Sipila of Finland, who beat Petrica Carare of Rumania, 7-4.
The Soviet Union took the day's second gold when Mikhail Mamiachvili, unleashing quick and powerful throw techniques, easily beat Tibor Komaromi of Hungary, 10-1, in the 181-pound class.

In the day's most fiercely fought match, Kim Sang Kyu of South Korea overcame a 0-5 first-period deficit to win 6-5 and earn the bronze.
Aleksandr Kareline took the the Soviet Union's fourth gold, the third of the day, when he defeated a Bulgarian, Ranguel Guerovski, 5-3, in the 286-pound class. 
Ranguel took a 3-0 lead with a quick throw and led by 3-2 after the first period.
Tomas Johansson of Sweden took the bronze with a 3-0 victory over Hassan Elhadad of Egypt.
Â 
Cycling
American Qualifies In Match Sprint
SEOUL, South Korea, Sept. 
22 (AP) -Connie Paraskevin-Young would just as soon not carry the hopes of the United States team on her shoulders. 
The expectations she has for herself are heavy enough.
The three-time world champion moved a step closer to earning a medal when she qualified tonight for the semifinals of the match sprint.
Standing between her and a shot at the gold is the 1987 world champion, Erika Salumiaee of the Soviet Union.
Paraskevin-Young and Salumiaee have been rivals for a long time but they have not faced each other since the world championships in 1986. 
She lost to Salumiaee, 2-0, in a two-of-three semifinal match.
Christa Rothenburger-Luding of East Germany, is in the running for the Olympic gold. 
The American lost to her, 2-0, in the world meet last year.
Â 
Tennis
Edberg and Mecir Advance in Singles
SEOUL, South Korea, Sept. 
22 (AP) -Stefan Edberg of Sweden and Miloslav Mecir of Czechoslovakia advanced to the third round today, edging closer to a repeat of their Wimbledon semifinal 10 weeks ago.
Edberg, the men's favorite in the first Olympic medal competition in tennis since 1924, swept Augustin Moreno of Mexico, 6-2, 7-6, 6-0. 
Mecir took four sets to beat Jeremy Bates of Great Britain, 6-3, 4-6, 6-1, 6-4.
Moreno took the Swede to a tiebreaker in the second set, but Edberg won it, 7-2, and blazed his way through the third set.
Mecir was his usual mixture of waywardness and brilliance against Bates, dropping the second set and almost letting the Briton back into the match in the fourth after taking a 4-1 lead.
Â 
Equestrian

text:
ï»¿
A GENERATION gap has formed in diving; the age of world-class talent has been dropping precipitously, so that suddenly veterans with two decades of training - and the maturity and grace that come with it - are finding themselves upset by tiny acrobats barely half their age.
The authors of this innovation are the Chinese, who in the last two years have loosed a childrens' brigade of spinning, grinning - and winning - divers.
They include 14-year-old Chen Xiaodan, who in May at the McDonald's International meet in Boca Raton, Fla., upset the defending Olympic silver medalist, Michele Mitchell of the United States. 
The year before at the same meet, Mitchell had just barely held off two other 14-year-olds.
''When I saw these little girls for the first time I said, 'What is this?''' said Mitchell, who is 26 and on the 1988 American Olympic team. 
''Every meet we go to they send different teams.''
Diving is one of the sports in which China has made dramatic progress since returning to international sports in the late 1970's. 
The three medals - I gold, I silver and I bronze - that Chinese divers pocketed at the Los Angeles Games contributed to the 32 medals over all the nation wona fter a three-decade absence from the Olympics. 
Since 1984, Chinese divers have only grown stronger. 
The program that produces them offers a paradigm of Beijing's emergence as the newest sports power.
In the four Olympic events (men's and women's 3-meter springboard and 10-meter platform), Chinese are favorites to sweep both women's gold medals; to strongly contend for both men's golds, and to take home the majority of silvers.
When people ask how have they done it, they are usually asking, What is their secret?
As far as any one factor has made the difference, it is the sports system that Beijing has put in place since the close of the Cultural Revolution, which is similar to that in many Communist nations.
The Chinese sports system is wide-cast and elitist, designed to net promising athletes from the largest talent pool on earth - a population of more than one billion - then measure progress in training, promoting the best and rejecting the average.
In the United States, if a youngster wants to learn an ''amateur'' Olympic sport like diving, his or her parents seek out a private program, like Ron O'Brien's Mission Bay club in Boca Raton, Fla. 
As long as parents can pay, O'Brien, who is the Olympic diving coach this year, and his staff presumably continue to train a youngster.
In China, diving coaches fan out from 3,400 part-time sports schools to recruit their charges. 
It is a rigorous meritocracy, beginning with strength and flexibility tests to detect aptitude in kids who have probably never seen a swimming pool. 
There is also some preselection based on the body type coaches believe makes good divers; short, compact, perhaps with hyperextended elbows, that is, elbows that touch when the arms are raised above the head, making for a less splashly entry in the water.
''We have set up selection criteria for most sports: the average height, weight, ratio of upper body to lower body, and circumference of various limbs,'' said Dr. Gao Chongxuan of the National Research Institute of Sports Science in Beijing. 
''In the West, your primary schools have pools, a gymnasium, even their own tennis courts. 
We don't have enough facilities, so we have to select athletes who've never played sports before.''
The ultimate sign of success is that there are fresh faces among the Chinese at nearly every meet. 
It's hard to highlight the country's top candidates for Seoul (who will be chosen by coaches rather than at trials) because there's no guarantee last year's world champion hasn't been shocked in training by a youngster who only began climbing the diving tower a few season ago, Tong Hui, who won the men's 10-meter World Cup in 1987, witnessed the same year as 13-year-old named Xiong Ni move up from the provinces to joint the national team in Beijing. 
That year, Xiong finished sixth in the McDonald's International. 
This year at the same meet he upstaged American Matt Scoggin for first.
Xiong, whose dives have nearly the same degree of difficulty as those of Greg Louganis, is one of a crew of Chinese putting pressure on the double-gold medal-winner of 1984. 
Early this year, China's top springboarder, Tan Liangde, ended a six-year victory streak Louganis had enjoyed. 
And he has since beaten Louganis again.
It takes one's breath away to see 5-foot-3-inch, 105-pound Xiong in a handstand at the very lip of the 33-foot platform, as tall as a three-story building, before the plummets into a blue abyss. 
This does not seem like a sport for kids. 
In the United States it is unheard of for divers of such tender age to perform the complex somersaults and twists of top-notch dives. 
Wendy Lian Williams, a 20-year-old University of Miami junior who finished fifth on platform at the McDonald's meet and will compete in the event at Seoul, said, ''I'm young for American diving, but I get to these meets and I feel old.''
Much of the credit for introducing extreme youth to the sport belongs to Xu Yiming, the head national coach in China, whose system emphasizes fast spinning and clean entries. 
Small bodies seem to have an advantage in both areas, and small means young. 
The Chinese are masters of the ripped entry, an almost splashless finale that sounds like fabric being torn, which is created when a diver locks his wrists and hits the water with hands flat, drilling a hole through which the entire body follows.
In the late 1970's, Xu, who had been a national champion in the arly 1960's before his career was idled by the Cultural Revolution, became a fixture at international competitions, along with his video camera. 
He focused the camera on the world's top divers, as well as on modern pools, weight training gear, even locker rooms. 
Back in Beijing, Xu, an authorization, nuts-and-bolts coach, had his athletes analyze and imitate the techniques of the world's best divers.
But at big international competitions the Chinese for years did not live up to their potential. 
They lacked mental intensity, or just the confidence that comes from international experience.
The Chinese have learned from their competitive misfires. 
Beginning at the 1986 world championships, the current crop of female prodigies began maturing. 
Gao Min, then 16, won the springboard title and has remained the world's best ever since. 
In the 1987 Xu Yanmei, 16, won the World Cup platform title. 
Both World Cup women's silver medals went to Chinese.

Gymnastics can be pretty and figure skating can be elegant, but for many people, no sport matches the esthetic and athletic beauty of diving. 
A good dive is easy to recognize, and television's slow-motion replays make a good dive even more enjoyable.
For years, the best divers were Americans. 
Now the best, or most of the best, are Chinese. 
They should dominate the four Olympic events, the men's and women's 3-meter springboard and 10-meter platform.
Of the 12 medals in the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, the United States won 8 and China 3. 
Of the 12 in the 1986 world championships in Madrid, China won 7 and the United States 4. 
Ron O'Brien, the United States Olympic coach, said he would be happy if his team won five medals in Seoul. 
Look for the Chinese to win seven or eight medals, the United Sates three or four and the Soviet Union one.
Of those American medals, two (probably gold) should come from Grey Louganis, who won both men's events in 1984. 
Now, at the age of 28, he is no longer unbeatable and his motivation and physical soundness have wavered, but he usually dives well when it counts and he remains the best diver in history. 
His main opposition will come from the Chinese: Tan Liangde on the springboard and 14-year-old Xiong Ni off the platform.
In the women's springboard, Kelly McCormick, the American silver medalist in 1984, must face 18-year-old Gao Min and Li Qing of China. 
In the women's platform, Michele Mitchell, the 1984 silver medalist, and Wendy Lian Williams, the other American, will contend for medals with Xu Yanmei of China and Elena Miroshina of the Soviet Union.
In springobard, the men do 11 dives, the women 10. 
In platform, the med do 10, the women 8. 
About half the dives are more or less basic and required.
Each diver does all his dives in the preliminaries. 
Then the 12 leaders in each event advance to the final, where preliminary scores are thrown out and all dives are repeated.
The diver tries to fill all requirements of his dive (somersaults, twists, body position, etc.) and finish with a vertical entry and minimal splash. 
Scoring is done by seven judges from different nations. 
After watching a diver's approach, takeoff, action in the air and entry, they give him from 0 points to 10 (for a perfect dive).
To minimize prejudicial scoring, the high and low score on each dive are thrown out. 
The five remaining scores are added, then divided by three-fifths, then multiplied by that dive's degree of difficulty.
The dives are clustered into six groups: forward, back, reverse, inward, twisting and (from the platform only) armstand. 
Four body positions are used; straight (body not bent, like a swan dive), pike (body bent only at the waist, like a jackknife), tuck (knees tight against the chest) and free (no restrictions).

text:

-------------------------------------------------------------------- RICHARD F. SHEPARD is a reporter for The Times.
Â 
By RICHARD F. SHEPARD
Our 17-day tour of six cities in China left me with an incredible jumble of luggage in impressions of what I saw and sensed. 
Indeed, I have come to only one firm conclusion: Our most satisfying stopover was in the remote city of Kunming, a gracious metropolis 6,200 feet above sea level with such a temperate climate that it is known as ''the city of spring.''
Kunming?
Kunming the favorite place in a trip that included the imperial splendors of Peking, the fantastic antique treasures of Xian, the rejuvenating urban tempo of Shanghai, the resort loveliness of Hangzhou and the peculiar loveliness of Canton?
Absolutely.
Although the name Kunming meant little to many on our trip, it was familiar to my generation, the one whose war was the Big One of the early 1940's. 
Kunming is in southwest China, 1,900 miles by plane from Peking, several hundred miles south of Chongqing, which, under the spelling Chungking, was China's wartime capital.
Richard Shepard describes his visit to remote Chinese city of Kunming
Kunming was the terminus of the Burma Road over which American aid was sent for China's fight against the Japanese. 
It was there that Gen. Claire L. Chennault's Flying Tigers (later the American 14th Air Force) had their base, and it was there that Gen. Joseph W. Stilwell, the peppery and knowledgeable Vinegar Joe who was commander of the Chinese Army until his disagreements with Chiang Kai-shek led to his ouster, established the liaison headquarters between Americans and Chinese. 
The Japanese menaced Kunming but never captured it, and thousands of American G.I.'s passed through this city, then bulging with troops and refugees from Japanese occupation.
By the account of some of those who remember Kunming in those fighting days of their youth, Kunming was a city in a beautiful setting, but a place of crowded, poor hovels and narrow streets. 
The Burma Road still terminates at Kunming, but almost everything else, except the eternal countryside, has changed.
We landed at the airport, which the guide who met us there said was built in 1943 by the Americans, and went by bus into the city. 
Kunming today offers a delightful prospect to the newcomer, particularly after the flat and dry plains of Peking. 
Surrounded by gently rising mountains and pleasant hills, with a large lake on its southwestern quarter at the foot of the beautiful, wooded Western Hills, it has the flavor of a French provincial or colonial city, with broad avenues lined by low-lying buildings and trees and flowers.
In contrast with formal Peking, it immediately strikes one as being somehow more relaxed, although the bicycles and tooting buses and trucks are certainly not leisurely. 
The Gallic flavor is subtle, perhaps enhanced by the knowledge that until World War II there was a French influence in Kunming, which was linked to Indochina, only 500 miles away, by a railroad built by the French in 1910.
Kunming is not a city steeped in ancient Chinese history; although the past there is traceable for 2,000 years, the city grew as a late bloomer in the 19th century and particularly since 1948. 
It is nothing like San Francisco, yet, whether because of its equable climate or its great local pride in its very difference from other Chinese cities, a comparison with the city by the Golden Gate springs to mind. 
Kunming, the capital of Yunnan province, is home to more than a million people and is a commercial and manufacturing hub, but its aura is that of a provincial center, making its own way in the world.
We stayed in the Green Lake Hotel, a modern and efficient establishment in the city's northwestern area. 
Across the street was Green Lake Park, its charming lake lined with drooping willow trees and dappled in the bright spring tints of peach and plum trees. 
Early in the morning Green Lake Park is alive with people doing exercises, playing badminton, jogging and bicycling to work. 
As is the case with many Chinese parks, there is an entrance fee of a few cents that seems to keep no one out.
Just behind the hotel, across the street from the park, a quick turn from the main roads plunges the sightseer from Kunming's modern, spacious face into a tangle of streets lined with cramped and old houses teeming with residents who use public toilets and spend their leisure outdoors. 
In the morning, sidewalk stands sell dumplings and porridges from steaming pots. 
One wonders how such a cheerful, wellmannered, well-scrubbed, healthy-looking and neatly dressed population can issue from such homes, but it does.
The strains of ''Old MacDonald Had a Farm'' emanate from a temple building that is now a school. 
The words, in Chinese, drift over the dilapidated area from the lusty throats of youngsters, the same ones who greet you in English after school, giggling, with ''Hello, how are you, goodbye.''
English, in schools and in the thronged sections of bookstores where grammars are sold, is a popular language these days in Kunming, as it is in all of China.
Kunming is a stroller's city rather than one in which historic markers are found at each step. 
We visited Kunming University, where students of English in the Foreign Language Institute each took a tourist in tow and, with remarkable fluency, quizzed us about life in America and fielded the most touchy questions about China, such as evaluating Mao Zedong (early Mao was good, later Mao not so good, said one student), and speaking of their ignorance about what their future would be after graduation, since assignments to jobs in China are made by committees with which little bargaining may be done. 
They queried us about our ages, our incomes, the Central Intelligence Agency, American attitudes toward China and our abysmally scant knowledge of Chinese history. 
It was one of the most intellectually stimulating afternoons we enjoyed in China.
At night we went to the massive and older Kunming Hotel in the center of town for a lamb banquet. 
The hotel is built in the heavyset style called ''Socialist realism'' in which the idea is to present a profile of no-nonsense solidity rather than elegant grace. 
Every dish of the 40 or so served at the banquet was made of lamb, from the eyes rearward. 
There were hors d'oeuvres, soup, entrails, tail, tongue, all steamed, roasted or otherwise cooked. 
The lamb itself was not particularly succulent, but the flavor of a dish depended strongly on the sauce that accompanied it, prepared from such ingredients as ginger, garlic and other spices. 
The reaction of most of the diners was ''very interesting.''
Through friends in New York we visited two elderly members of the medical college's faculty, relatives of the New Yorkers, who cooked us a banquet-size dinner with such Yunnan specialties as potato-chiplike chips made with goat's milk, cucumbers stuffed with beef and duck eggs.
Our tour visited Kunming's center of traditional Chinese medicine and saw patients receiving acupuncture in rooms adorned with spittoons (spitting is an officially deplored but common Chinese habit), at the hands of doctors, most of them women. 
The surroundings were less than inspired, but the treatment seemed to please the patients. 
Another room found patients being treated by a ''breathing machine'' that involved an electric wire that barely touched the arm and has been in use since last August. 
It was difficult to get a translation of the details about its operation, but it seems to be designed to treat high blood pressure. 
A woman told us that since undergoing these treatments she has regained her health and no longer needs pills.
Kunming is merely the centerpiece of the treats for the eye and ear that surround it. 
Yunnan is the home of more than 20 of China's minority peoples, whose presence antedates the appearance of the ethnic Chinese. in this region. 
The minority peoples, among them the Hui, Yi, Bai, Hani and Miao, speak their own languages and wear colorful jackets and headdresses that bloom flower-like in the drab standard dress of the city's strollers. 
A museum in Kunming displays the costumes, farming implements, carriages, urns and bowls that illustrate the ancient ways of life of these minority nationalities.
The minority peoples were very much in evidence at Shi Lin, the Stone Forest, which lies 60 miles southeast of Kunming, in the general direction of Vietnam. 
The three-hour bus ride there immerses the visitor in a panorama of rare magnificent beauty, past brilliantly green rice paddies that contrast with the bright red of the clay hills under a sky that was sparkling blue, a spectacle that even the most deft Impressionist painter would be hard put to capture on canvas. 
The journey goes past the railroad, over which a steam engine chugged pulling a train of old coaches toward Vietnam, and through endless fields and paddies where the labor is all by hand and water buffalo and through several lively marketplaces in small towns.
The peasants represent China Immemorial: They are gnarled and workworn but not badly dressed, and their children look hearty and healthy in contrast to what old China hands recall of pockmarked, disease-ridden children of years ago. 
Their brick houses in this region seem to have been only half built, with the tile roofs rising from the entrance in a graceful curve but then ending suddenly at the back wall, which drops vertically to ground level.
The Stone Forest is one of the great natural wonders of the world, 12,000 acres of towering rock formations, thousands of craggy pillars formed millions of years ago by rain water that eroded the thick limestone by dissolving and splitting it. 
This veritable forest of stone resembles nothing so much as an abstract nightmare of downtown Manhattan, with pinnacles that tower as high as 99 feet. 
The rock assumes strange silhouettes to which the imaginative Chinese have attached names, such as Lotus Peak, Pavilion Commanding the Entire Scene of Stone Forest and Sword Peak. 
A path, about a mile long, wends through the forest, whose stony grayness is relieved by growths of trees and bushes and streams and ponds, and the visitor may take a long route or be satisfied with a shorter one.
We stayed at the Stone Forest Guesthouse, which caters mostly to foreign visitors, 20,000 of whom arrive annually (the largest contingents these days, in order, are Japanese, Americans, Australians and Overseas Chinese from Hong Kong, which is more than 500 miles to the east). 
The guesthouse is a rural affair, two or three two-story buildings with entrances from an outdoor walkway. 
It has only 97 rooms, each fitted with mosquito netting that must be unfurled at bedtime and can pose a minor problem to a stranger who had the feeling he would never be able to fight his way free of the skein should emergency arise. 
The rooms are moderately spacious and have private bathrooms with high-sided tubs but no showers. 
The travel season reaches its peak between March and October, and lodging, with meals, costs about $20 a day.
At night visitors can go to Shi Lin Village, a commune hamlet of rice and tobacco farmers who are members of the Hani minority people. 
The Hani, well aware that visitors mean income, sell shoulder handbags, vests, belts and embroidered items that they have made themselves. 
At night a company of 30 handsome young Hani men and women from the Five Trees Production Team visited the guesthouse, and staged a thrilling performance of folk dance and song for us, far better than the ponderous, overstuffed, over-refined folk-art performance we had seen in Peking. 
The oldest member of the troupe was 36 and the youngest 14, and they danced to the music of native instruments, strings with long handles and drum-like bottoms, flutes, cymbals and mouth organs, nothing that resembled anything we have in Western music.
The music was surprisingly sweet - one half-expected a cacophony of unpleasant squawking - and the short, dark and pretty dancers were smiling and loose-limbed as they did a rattlesnake dance, a weaving song and a harvest dance. 
The men did a tiger-hunting dance, ferocious yet humorous, with two of them confronting the audience under a tiger-like skin. 
At evening's end, each group of visitors was asked, almost commanded, by the home team of performers to retaliate with some song of their native lands. 
The French visitors rousingly launched into ''Frere Jacques'' and more recent and more romantic melodies. 
A band of Italians lustily sang of amore. 
Our small but staid group of Americans, taken by surprise, managed to croak a few verses of ''Old MacDonald Had a Farm,'' but with none of the style of the Kunming school children. 
Then everyone had tea or went to bed.
Closer to hand, only a half hour from Kunming, are the Western Hills, a picturesque range that stretches along the western bank of Dian Chi, or Shimmering Lake, a large (more than 100 square miles) body of water southwest of the city. 
The Western Hills are four hills, and as seen from the lake their contour resembles, to the vivid imagination that is a Chinese staple, a langorous sleeping beauty whose hair trails down to the water. 
Actually, the hills are increasingly high as one walks up them on steps and paths that stop at various temples along the way. 
The climb can take three hours, but our bus went farther up than most and left us at the foot of the last 300 steps.
As we walked, we passed small shrines, such as one with a large figure of Guanyin. 
Many Chinese still believe they are insured of fertility if a coin affixed to the wall of the shrine does not fall down. 
This is somewhat strange in light of the official policy that demands tight family control: one child per family. 
There are turtles that one touches for longevity and figures that will bring good health - longevity and good health are not necessarily in the same package. 
At the Dragon Gate, on the summit, there is an unparalleled view of the big lake and of Kunming in the distance.
There is much else to see at Kunming, from the Yuantong Mountain Park in the city with its zoo and gardens to the impressive Qiongzhusi temple built 600 years ago with its collection of 400 clay figures of disciples of Buddha made over a seven-year period by a Sichuan sculptor during the Manchu period (China's last dynasty). 
You can see the Burma Road, a prosaic thoroughfare that today does not give evidence of the times when it was a lifeline for China. 
But in Kunming and its environs, the sightseeing is not in works made by man, not in temples or museums or institutions. 
The sight to see is China itself, a China in which man makes his way between heaven and earth, bending to both in such awesomely attractive surroundings that one wonders how he can intrude his own affairs into it.

file: The View From_ The National Theater for the Deaf_Bringing Change, One Play at a Time.txt
text:

AS a young Chinese man sat on a sunny deck and described his plan to continue his father's effort to form a theater troupe of deaf performers in China, a dozen American actors - most of them deaf - climbed and swung over a section of metal scaffolding in a shady yard nearby, exercising before a rehearsal.
Those activities were all in a day's work at the National Theater of the Deaf in Chester, where a company that was established to produce lively and unusual theater has also increased opportunities for deaf people and helped give hearing people a new view of the deaf, in this country and abroad.
''Our profession is theater, but the theater is so strong, it can create social change,'' said David Hays, who founded the theater in 1967 and is its artistic director.
The National Theater for the Deaf operates from a big renovated mill and a small office building, both on the banks of Pattaconk Brook. 
The 12-member acting company includes only two members who can hear; they speak aloud during the company's performances, which blend spoken language with signing. 
Audiences are composed mainly of hearing people.
On its annual tours, the company has given nearly 5,000 performances, in 50 states and 26 countries, in small towns and big cities. 
''We have not missed a gig,'' said Mr. Hays, who recalled that a couple of times blizzards caused cancellations, because the audiences were unable to reach the theaters, but that the company never canceled first.
Â 
'King of Hearts' Tour
The company members limbering up on the scaffolding were preparing to rehearse ''King of Hearts,'' with which the company will tour 22 states during the 1988-89 season, with four performances in Connecticut. 
The company has performed works ranging from tragedies to farces; ''King of Hearts'' is based on the French film of the same name, directed by Philippe DeBroca.
The company also splits up at times into two Little Theaters of the Deaf, which perform mainly for children. 
It performs in Chester at Christmastime; conducts free storytelling sessions every June on the Chester green, and each summer conducts a four-week professional school for deaf theater personnel from America and abroad.
Wang Ling, an ambitious 20-year-old from Beijing, came to the school this year for help in carrying on his father's dream. 
All over America and in other places as well - including Australia, England, India, Japan and Sweden - are theaters of the deaf that were formed with help and instruction from the company.
The company is financed through its performance fees, private donations and the Federal Government. 
''We took on Federal support with the idea that we were theater people first,'' said Mr. Hays. ''We are not social workers here, but we are proud of the power of our profession.''
For one thing, said Mr. Hays, company performances have removed the stigma from signing and have shown it to be a rich, expressive language. 
''We brought sign language out of the closet,'' he said.
The company also brought sign language to Chester, which became the troupe's permanent home - it was originally part of the Eugene O'Neill Theater Center in Waterford - in 1983. 
Since then, many shopkeepers and other residents have learned to sign.
Â 
'Total Communication'
Mr. Hays also said that the company's use of sign language has brought about a change in educational methods. 
Until recently, many schools for the deaf discouraged their students from signing, but now more schools use what is called total communication, which includes both signing and speech. 
And, Mr. Hays said, ''The N.T.D. helped blow open the job market.''
''When we started this company, there were few job opportunities for deaf people, but the understanding of deaf people's abilities has opened up jobs for the deaf,'' he said, adding that now, young deaf people are ''growing up aware'' that they can pursue various careers.
He said role models like the company's performers helped produce the recent successful protests at Gallaudet College in Washington, D.C., the world's only liberal arts college for the deaf. 
This spring, Gallaudet students staged protests when Dr. Elisabeth Ann Zinser, a hearing woman who did not know sign language, was appointed president of the school. 
The protests brought the resignation of Dr. Zinser and the appointment of Dr. I. King Jordan, Gallaudet's first deaf president.
Now, Mr. Hays said, he hopes the N.T.D. can help lead deaf people in China - where they are often shunted into factory jobs - ''up and out.''
He is lending a hand to Wang Ling, who seeks to continue the project his father, who is now dead, began after working with the company in China.
In 1986, the N.T.D. became the first American theater company to tour China. 
Accompanying the company performers in Beijing and six other cities was Wang Ling's father, Wang Zhen-Tai, a Chinese actor who spoke in Mandarin as the company signed on stage. 
He was so impressed with the company that he decided to start a theater of the deaf in China. 
He visited factories where groups of deaf employees had amateur theatrical groups and auditioned the performers.
Last summer, he brought four young Chinese performers to the N.T.D.'s professional school for training. 
Mr. Wang died of heart disease soon after he returned to China, but his son vowed to carry on, and wrote Mr. Hays to tell him of his plan. 
Mr. Hays wrote back, cautioning Wang Ling - then a business student at Beijing International Business College - -against devoting himself to an endeavor for which he might not be suited. 
But Wang Ling persisted, working his way through the Chinese bureaucracy in search of money and support. 
''He's up against old, experienced bureaucrats, but he can swim upstream,'' said Mr. Hays.
Wang Ling said he was starting the Chinese theater partly out of respect for his father. 
Also, he said, ''It's a very meaningful thing to do. 
China needs an organization like that.''
On his return to China, Wang Ling will try to arrange for a young deaf actress to be released from her factory job for two weeks so that she can join the National Theater of the Deaf at the International Theater Festival in Tokyo, Aug. 
14-18. Mr. Hays and Wang Ling feel that her participation will spur support for a Chinese theater of the deaf.
The National Theater for the Deaf will perform at the festival with the Japanese theater of the deaf - a troupe that the N.T.D. helped to start. 
The American company has toured Japan several times, often staying with teachers and performers in the Japanese troupe. 
''I feel like we're neighbors,'' signed Sandi Inches, an N.T.D. performer who is deaf, as she explained through a sign language interpreter how much she looked forward to the August event.
N.T.D. performers said they were also looking forward to working on ''King of Hearts,'' which will open this fall in Denver and reach Connecticut next winter, with performances Jan. 
20 (Kingswood Oxford School, West Hartford), Feb. 
16 (University of Connecticut, Storrs), Feb. 
19 (Southern Connecticut State University, New Haven), and Feb. 
24 (University of Bridgeport, Bridgeport).
The plot deals with a World War I soldier who finds himself in a town whose inhabitants have all escaped from a mental hospital. 
''But it's not an insane asylum story,'' said John Eisner, a hearing actor with the company. 
''The story is about love, and the importance of people to other people.''
Mr. Hays is looking beyond a Chinese theater of the deaf, a Japanese festival and another successful tour. 
He said he wanted the company to do a feature film and to build a television series around a pilot show, ''The Light Princess,'' which it performed for Connecticut Public Television last year. 
He noted that the company plans to perform at a festival in Jerusalem this year and also to tour South America.
And, he said, he would like the N.T.D. to tour South Africa. 
''South Africa is now cut off to American artists, but I wish artists were free to travel in both directions,'' he said, noting that South African artists performing in America have been effective in drawing attention to South Africa's apartheid policies.

file: THE WORLD_BEIJING IS GLIDING EVER MORE WESTWARD.txt
text:
ï»¿
IF not capitalism, at least a capitalist ethic is seeping into the marrow of China.
Everything Western, everything from the capitalist world outside, is copied, studied and worried about. 
In those areas of Guangdong province near Hong Kong, it is impossible to find a television station tuned to Chinese broadcasts. 
The slam-bang frivolity of Hong Kong TV blares from urban homes and farmers' huts. 
In Beijing, the city seems to lurch to a halt at six o'clock on Sunday night when Mickey Mouse cartoons are shown for 30 minutes. 
''It's done in a way even adults can appreciate,'' an older Chinese man said somewhat solemnly.
Spurring this has been the Government's increasing tolerance of freer economic activity. 
Last week, Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang said that his countrymen would have to embrace even greater economic changes if China's general backwardness was to be overcome. 
Indeed, the China that Prime Minister Zhao described in his opening address to the 13th Communist Party Congress is the China that Mao Zedong loathed and sought to prevent from materializing: a China that permits private enterprise at home, on the farm and in the cities. 
And far from stifling rich peasants, closing down small private industries, suppressing individual entrepreneurs, as Mao deemed essential if China was to truly become a socialist country, Mr. Zhao said they should flourish.
In short, the Prime Minister called for the further introduction and expansion of a vast array of economic practices that smacked more of capitalism than socialism, or at least socialism along the lines practiced in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. 
Across China, farmers, managers of small workshops and factories, restaurant owners, even physicians who have small private practices have eagerly grabbed the chance to improve their lives by making as much money as they possibly can.
Mr. Zhao talked of stocks and bonds, of commercializing the housing market, of stimulating private industry and leasing state enterprises to individuals. 
He urged regulating China's money supply through credit policies in the manner of the Federal Reserve Bank in the United States. 
He called for a sweeping reform of tax policies, piece-rate wages, free market pricing and free competition among enterprises.
But burdened by a legacy of revolution and socialism, Mr. Zhao hastened to disavow the apparently capitalist aura of his program, instead fashioning a schema that sought to preserve ideological rectitude without stifling his policy objectives. 
His solution, widely hailed in the Chinese press, was simply to say that China was in the primary stages of socialism where just about anything in the economic realm is acceptable.
Still, Mr. Zhao's championing of Western economic practices hardly means that China is on the verge of shucking off its socialist manacles in favor of fast, freewheeling capitalism. 
Indeed, the most severe critics of the Chinese regime are inclined to view the economic reform program created by the country's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, and pursued now by Mr. Zhao, as doomed. 
The core of the problem, these critics contend, is that the Communist Party, which intrudes into virtually every cranny of Chinese life, is unlikely to willingly relinquish its control of society and the economy.
Fang Lizhi, an astrophysicist who headed the country's prestigious University of Science and Technology in Hefei until he was summarily fired last winter for supporting college students' calls for greater democracy, explained the problem in an interview published in the West German news magazine Der Spiegel.
''In China, the party does not want to manage only politics,'' he said. 
''It wants to control everything, including the way of life and the thoughts of the people. 
Today, factories are being managed by managers, but the party cadres keep wielding the power. 
Peasants enjoy the free-market system, but the cadres tell them: 'You still need our rubber stamp, you still have to buy us off!'
There lies the root of the new corruption. 
In order to create a true economic democracy in China, one ought to abolish political controls. 
That is exactly what the party fears most.''
Yet it is far from clear how successful Mr. Zhao will be in encouraging his fellow Communists to extricate themselves from the management of day-to-day affairs in favor of technocratic managers, profit-oriented bankers and bottom-line manufacturers. 
Many western observers believe that the economic reforms of Mr. Deng and Mr. Zhao are at a critical juncture. 
They can move forward, away from socialism and toward a more Western economy, if the party gives up substantial amounts of its power. 
Or, their reforms can flounder in the hands of a party that holds power and refuses to let go.

file: THE WORLD_Facing The Facts About Cambodia.txt
text:
ï»¿
AS the outlines of an international settlement for Cambodia start to become clear, accelerated by the Chinese-Soviet talks last week in Moscow, there is suddenly a swell of anguished murmuring about the Khmer Rouge.
Having used their years in power to carry out barbarities and wholesale killings, the Khmer Rouge have been resuscitated by China with the assistance of the non-Communist countries of Southeast Asia and the acquiescence, at the very least, of the United States. 
Preoccupied elsewhere, Washington has been content to follow the Asian nations' lead.
When the aim was to punish the Vietnamese for their 1978 occupation of Cambodia, to tie them down and get them to withdraw, Pol Pot's soldiers were a convenient and efficient instrument. 
But now that the ideal seems close to reality - the Vietnamese are promising to pull out by March 1990 - this cat's-paw has, as in some grim fairy tale of moral retribution, put on gristle and flesh and become a tiger.
Americans estimate Khmer Rouge strength at between 28,000 and 60,000 hardened soldiers, lavishly equipped by China - the most powerful part of the Cambodian resistance, dwarfing the 16,000 of Prince Norodom Sihanouk and the 9,000 to 11,000 of the Khmer People's National Liberation Front of Son Sann. 
Appealing to nationalism, they can say they have fought most of the battle against the invader.
But they now spend almost as much time fighting their putative coalition partners as they do fighting the Vietnamese-backed Government of Hun Sen, repeating a pattern that preceded their defeat of an American-backed Government in 1975. 
The result then was mass murder and the deaths of an estimated 1.5 million, or 20 percent of the population.
So suddenly a lot of analysis in Washington and elsewhere is being based on a triumph of hope over experience - about how the Khmer Rouge may not be so strong or dedicated after all; about how much progress the non-Communist resistance has been making; about how nicely they will mesh with the soldiers of Mr. Hun Sen; about how Prince Sihanouk has matured and deepened and found his hour at last.
Ten years ago, the Khmer Rouge crumbled in the face of Vietnam's invasion. 
Most of the cadres fled toward Thailand, many trying to pass as refugees, in part to avoid being slain by those they had ruled. 
China, faced with the crushing of an ally by a Soviet-backed Vietnam, and Thailand, suddenly faced with Vietnamese troops on its border, refused to accept Hanoi's victory. 
With the help of the Association of South East Asian Nations, Beijing and Bangkok supported the Khmer Rouge as Cambodia's legal government and revived them with arms, food and cash as the best way to hound the Vietnamese.
Â 
A Decent Interval?
Now that the Vietnamese say they will leave, American policy is to work to keep the Khmer Rouge from returning to sole power. 
But senior officials say there is no clear or detailed idea of how to do it. 
Some Western and Asian diplomats believe the Chinese formula for a settlement - a four-party government and army, headed by Prince Sihanouk and made up of equal parts of his forces, Son Sann's, the current Government's and Pol Pot's - will only provide a decent interval before a collapse into a renewed civil war pitting the Khmer Rouge against the rest.
Â 
'A Sad Denouement'
A senior Western diplomat here described the Cambodia problem as an anachronism, the residue of a 10-year-old squabble among powers that are themselves changing rapidly. 
In the current talks, he said, ''one can see the outline of how this can be resolved as an international problem, and relations can be normalized all around'' among the outside powers. 
But whether such an agreement would prevent a new bloodletting in Cambodia is another question. 
''It could drag on and be a very bloody struggle, but a local one, like Africa,'' he said, in which the major powers are uninvolved and uninterested.
Does the world send 300,000 Cambodians in camps along the Thai border back home to that?
''That would be a sad denouement,'' the diplomat added. 
''At worst, there could be a complete return to power by the Khmer Rouge.''
There seems a parallel to the 1930's, when the European democracies decided to do business with Hitler despite what they knew or had read in his autobiography, because reasons of state seemed to demand it and because of a conviction that the realities of power would civilize or temper him. 
That was an error the world promised never to make again. 
In the case of the Khmer Rouge, this argument goes, the moral questions are even sharper, for there is the evidence of the killing fields, not just their promise.
In Bangkok in November, Senator Bob Dole, the minority leader, illustrated the quandary. 
Asked if the United States had done enough to beef up the non-Communist forces, he said a recent meeting between President Reagan and Prince Sihanouk ''again demonstrated our commitment.''
He added that he thinks American officials feel ''that the Khmer Rouge has forfeited any right because of the genocide they perpetrated on their own people.''
But why is it American policy to include the Khmer Rouge in a coalition government?
Could he talk about the contrast between historical experience and national interest?
The Senator sighed. 
''You have to recognize the fact that the Khmer Rouge are one of the four,'' he said. 
''But I don't believe, based on the conversations we've had, that they're going to emerge as the rallying point for the Cambodians.''
Senator Arlen Specter, a Pennsylvania Republican also on the trip, spelled out the contradictions. 
''To the extent there can be a force to compete with the Khmer Rouge we want to accomplish that objective,'' he said. 
''And if it were within our power to eliminate the Khmer Rouge we would certainly do that, but that's just not a reality. 
Our concern is that they will emerge as the dominant force, and if that were to happen, it would be very contrary to our ideas of human rights. 
So our efforts are to minimize their influence as much as possible.''
Yet Washington has done rather little, and that rather lately, to support the non-Khmer Rouge resistance. 
A senior American official said that for a long time he didn't believe there was a Vietnam syndrome, but that he had recently changed his mind. 
It is not simply reluctance to prosecute a sustained undeclared war, he said. 
It is an aversion to Indochina itself, a belief that any United States involvement there spells only trouble. 
Another Western diplomat said: ''Southeast Asia has not been a focus of concern among top-ranking U.S. officials for a very long time. 
I don't know what they imagined was going on here.''

file: THE WORLD_With Lasting Doubts, India Fosters Hopes of Better Ties to China.txt
text:
ï»¿
MORE than half a century ago and two decades before he became India's first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru had a dream. 
Friendship between China and India, he told a conference of anti-colonial parties in 1927, would form the core of a new pan-Asianism, a base on which to build a new order in the East.
But long before the dream died on a snowy Himalayan battlefield in 1962 in a short, sharp border war, Nehru and Mao Zedong had chosen separate roads. 
Nehru and Mohandas K. Gandhi took the difficult democratic path, robbing Indian Communists of their dream of capturing the independence movement, as Ho Chi Minh had done in Vietnam. 
Mao, on the other hand, was crafting a rigid brand of Marxism. 
Led in these separate directions, Asia's two giants strayed apart, and then the 1962 border war ended the era of amity with finality.
This week when Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi, Nehru's grandson, makes a trip to China - the first visit by an Indian Prime Minister in 34 years - no one in India expects a revival of Nehru's heady dreams of brotherhood. 
But there are cautious hopes that progress can be made on the still-unresolved border dispute and that cultural ties and improved air links will be initiated. 
More than anything, however, Indian officials and intellectuals want a better atmosphere and more contact to follow Mr. Gandhi's visit to Beijing, Shanghai and Xian.
India is tiptoeing toward East Asia, uncertain what its relationship should be with the world's most rapidly growing economies, or with China in transition. 
In New Delhi - unlike other Asian capitals, Moscow or Washington - there is little fascination with the Pacific Century. 
There is, instead, a continuing preoccupation with the West.
Â 
Appearing Too Friendly
''Despite Nehru's romanticism for Asia, and China in particular, our tradition in political terms has been Western,'' said S. Nihal Singh, an author and columnist. 
Mr. Singh added that Prime Minister Gandhi was making the trip to Beijing against the wishes of some of his advisers, and amid fears in his own party that no Indian leader can yet afford to appear too friendly to the Chinese.
''The feeling is still very strong in this country that we got a beating at the hands of the Chinese in 1962,'' said Nikhil Chakravartty, editor of the left-wing magazine Mainstream. 
He said that the Government has not done enough to educate Indians about the need for give and take in settling the border dispute. 
Instead, Mr. Gandhi is pushed by his own supporters into promising not to give away ''one square mile'' of Indian territory. 
The two border areas in question, in mountain terrain, are nearly impossible to demarcate accurately in any case, Indian scholars say. 
Both countries may have to settle for a rational compromise based on who is in control of what parts of ground.
When the Soviet leader, Mikhail S. Gorbachev, was in New Delhi last month, he pointedly remarked on several occasions that there was no problem in Indian-Soviet relations, even though no one had suggested publicly that there was. 
Mr. Gorbachev's comments were interpreted here as an assurance that Moscow's planned rapprochement with China, possibly involving a Sino-Soviet summit next year, would not affect the Moscow-Delhi link. 
But Mr. Gorbachev also made it clear that he would welcome warmer Indian-Chinese ties.
''If Gorbachev makes up to China,'' Mr. Chakravartty said, ''this is an important signal to India not to let itself be left out. 
India could be the only country in this part of the world not to have better relations with the Chinese.''
Â 
Comparing Two Giants
An Indian focus on China invites comparisons between the two Asian giants, the world's most populous nations: China with a billion people and India with 800 million.
In the days of Communist repression and the Cultural Revolution, India could feel more secure in the rightness of its chosen path. 
A free people and a free press have thrived here. 
A mixed economy has opened avenues to development policies of the left and right. 
Poverty and overpopulation were the curse and preoccupation of both nations.
But China has changed and in recent years it can point to many achievements - in agricultural development, rural industry, medical care and, despite criticism of Beijing's methods, population control. 
Now a Chinese citizen is healthier, lives longer and has access to as many or more consumer goods than does the average Indian. 
China is also working hard to integrate itself into the booming East Asian economies.
Lately, India has been close to Vietnam and almost alone outside the Soviet bloc in recognizing the Vietnamese-backed Government in Cambodia - a distinction that has cost it friends in the region but one that has given it a limited interest in Southeast Asian affairs.
Southeast Asia will be discussed on Mr. Gandhi's trip, Indian officials say, especially the problem of Cambodia, and how to get Vietnam's troops to leave. 
But will that whet India's appetite for more contact with the East?
''Not really,'' Mr. Singh said. 
''India has always been ambivalent to Southeast Asia.''
A more active interest in Southeast Asia, many Indians believe, can come only when India feels more comfortable with China - a relationship that will now have to be rebuilt step by step.
Â 
A HISTORY OF CONFRONTATION
In 1962, a dispute over a road built by the Chinese on territory claimed by India and a set of border clashes led Chinese to attack. 
Chinese routed the Indians in Arunachal Pradesh and seized territory in Ladakh. 
After a month of fighting, China declared a unilateral cease-fire.
Fighting broke out between Indian and Chinese troops in 1967 at the Nathu La Pass on the Sikkim-Tibet border. 
Two years later, Indians accused Chinese of firing on patrol in Lip Lekh.
In 1986, India asserted that Chinese troops entered valley of Sumdorong Chu in Arunachal Pradesh, where Indian intelligence post had been set up earlier without Chinese objections. 
Tens of thousands of Chinese and Indian troops confronted each other at height of crisis, which was defused after diplomatic contacts.

file: THE WORLD_WORDS THE CHINESE WERE WAITING TO HEAR.txt
text:
ï»¿
IN 1967, factions of zealous Red Guards fashioned a monstrous statue of their idol, Mao Zedong, and mounted it on a pedestal in front of the Beijing University library. 
Last month, in the dark of the night, the statue was toppled and carted off by workmen.
While statues of Mao have been demolished in many towns and cities, the removal of the statue at Beida, as the university is called, seemed to carry a broader message. 
In the weeks before the statue's fall, China's officials had engaged in more public discussion than China has heard since Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic from atop the Gate of Heavenly Peace in 1949. 
Tearing down the monument to Mao at the university suggested to some professors a release from intellectual bondage, just as China's officials were gingerly testing the once-dangerous waters of public debate.
Even though the scope of discussion has widened considerably in the past year, criticism of Government and Communist Party policies is elliptical at best. 
In private conversations, some Chinese people, intellectuals more than others, are more candid in their appraisal of their Government. 
Still, nowhere in China can one find the stringent critiques that have become commonplace in the Soviet press.
At Beijing's universities in recent weeks, though, there was undisguised enthusiasm over a speech given by a non-Communist economist several weeks ago at a national political forum that serves - theoretically, at least - as a consultative body to China's Parliament. 
The address was never published in China, but a copy was circulated hand to hand.
What was so special about an unpublished speech?
Is it another example of how the Chinese Government carefully controls the sparks of free expression?
Not exactly. 
Many people here said they could not recall a public forum being used to etch so sharply and frankly the serious problems that preoccupy so many Chinese.
The speaker, Qian Jiaju, a 79-year-old member of one of China's minuscule non-Communist parties, hammered on serious problems many Chinese feel are being ignored by the Government: official corruption, the decline of education, the relentless surge in consumer prices and inequities in the justice system.
''Some party members and state cadres have abused the power in their hands by engaging in malpractices for selfish ends, embezzling public funds and receiving bribes,'' Mr. Qian told the delegates.
Periodically the official press reports cases of corruption, but these cases are always portrayed as deviations from a general climate of official probity. 
A Beijing University professor who read Mr. Qian's speech said the debunking of this official line was important.
Mr. Qian called for the dispassionate enforcement of law and pointed to the disparity in justice dispensed in China's courts. 
''A certain governor of Jiangxi Province was sentenced to two years in prison for wasting several hundred thousand dollars in public funds on his mistress,'' he said. 
''A criminal was sentenced to life in prison for stealing watermelons. 
Can we say that laws are strictly enforced?''
Mr. Qian also called for changes in China's education policies, which, he declared, have essentially failed. 
''Instead of decreasing, the number of illiterates has increased somewhat,'' he said. 
''The status of China's primary school teachers and their remuneration are still among the lowest among all professions. 
In real terms, the wages of both university and primary school teachers are less than one-tenth of what they were in old China before the anti-Japanese war.''
Inflation is encouraged by the chaotic mixture of controlled and free-market pricing, Mr. Qian said. 
He argued that as harsh as it seems, all price controls should be lifted. 
''This means a major surgical operation on China's economic structural system,'' he said. 
''However, this operation is inevitable if China is to lead its economy toward handling its affairs literally in accordance with objective economic laws.''
The Beijing University professor said that he was troubled by Mr. Qian's economic proposals, but that it was time such things were said. 
''Of course, they couldn't publish this sort of speech,'' he said, acknowledging that the fact that it was given at a public forum was significant, but certainly not an indication that freedom of expression was imminent. 
''But he said it, and we've all read it,'' the professor said. 
''Some things are changing. 
Look, they've pulled down Mao.''

file: THEATER_An Actor Gives New Direction to China_s Stage.txt
text:
ï»¿
YING RUOCHENG IS FAMILIAR to American audiences as the prison warden in Bernardo Bertolucci's new film ''The Last Emperor.''
However, in China, he is now primarily known not for his acting ability, but as the nation's Vice Minister of Culture. 
In this powerful post he is presently at work on a broad reform of the performing arts.
Mr. Ying's ministry is putting into effect a new policy that grants autonomy to the state-run theater companies in the selection of repertories, the hiring of people and the management of finances. 
This ''structural reform'' is a departure from the controls which have been in force since the Communist Party took power in 1949.
At the Ministry of Culture compound Mr. Ying strode into the reception hall for a recent interview as if he was coming on stage. 
The walls of the hall were hung with traditional scrolls, but the minister was attired in a tailored blue blazer over a red cashmere sweater, gray slacks and a red tie. 
His strong Manchu features, resonant voice and fluency in English reminded one of his commanding performance as the Mongol Emperor Kublai Khan in ''Marco Polo,'' the 1982 NBC television mini-series.
As an actor, director and translator of Shakespeare, Sean O'Casey, Arthur Miller and Tennessee Williams, Mr. Ying looks to the adaptation of Western plays as a means of introducing Chinese audiences to modern theater.
Encouraged by the success of his Chinese productions of ''Death of a Salesman'' - in which he played Willy Loman - and ''Amadeus,'' Mr. Ying said he hoped to find time to stage ''Evita,'' which he thinks time to stage ''Evita,'' which he thinks ''would have a very strong message for the Chinese.''
He believes that ''Death of a Salesman,'' which played to capacity houses for three months, was a breakthrough. 
He said that Chinese audiences found they could relate to Willy Loman and his shattered dreams, having experienced the disappointments and pain of the Cultural Revolution.
Does he dare to present Tennessee Wilby traditional Chinese mores?
The 58-year-old minister, a founder of Beijing's People's Art Theater in 1950, nodded vigorously: ''Certainly 'Glass Menagerie' and another play which I think would go down very well in China, 'Cat on a Hot Tin Roof,' but I would think twice before putting on, say, 'Clothes for a Summer Hotel' '' (one of Williams's lesser plays about F. Scott Fitzgerald and his wife, Zelda, after she became schizophrenic).
Among foreign playwrights, Eugene O'Neill and Bertolt Brecht have exerted the greatest influence on the modern Chinese theater. 
Mr. Ying thinks that Chinese playwrights are becoming less interested in Brecht's Marxist ideology and more interested in his dramatic art. 
Recently they have been writing more plays that do not dwell on the familiar social concerns. 
One such work is ''A Dream of China,'' which is simply the love story of a Shanghai girl and a young American scholar.
Mr. Ying lit a cigarette and held it between thumb and forefinger as he fielded questions from a delegation of the Center for U.S.-China Arts Exchange about the campaign against ''bourgeois liberalization'' launched by the Communist Party last January. 
In the clamp-down on cultural life that followed, theater companies reacted by culling the more controversial plays from their repertories. 
The playwright Wu Zuguang was among the prominent intellectuals who were denounced and expelled from the party.
Mr. Ying was not sympathetic to the intellectuals accused of publicly criticizing the Socialist system, which he said could have caused a ''major upheaval.''
But he went on to insist that there had been significant progress in the last months toward a freer cultural life. 
The 13th party congress, which concluded in early November, reaffirmed the policy of ''openness,'' he said. 
''Very few people will now stand up and say 'I do not agree with the 13th congress,' that we should control the artists more. 
I don't think that is going to happen.''
''Old habits of thought die very hard,'' he said. 
''And since we have had a long history of state-directed propaganda in art, to break away from that tradition takes time on every level. 
I'm not saying this only about the ministry, or the politbureau, but on every level including the audience.''
Turning to the current theater scene, Mr. Ying said: ''We are now saying clear and loud that a work of art which arouses controversy is not a bad thing. 
Let's not shy away from controversy.''
He suggested that Americans will appreciate the change in policy when they see ''Uncle Doggy's Nirvana,'' the controversial play written by Liu Jinyuan, which is being taken to New York later this year for the International Festival of the Arts. 
The play tells of an old peasant who suffers through years of enforced collectivization, becomes disillusioned, burns his house and runs off, leaving to his children the task of building a new world. 
The play was performed in September at the first China Arts Festival, but only after being held out for a time by the complaints of conservative ideologues. 
It was first performed in Mr. Ying's own theater.
Mr. Ying said the ministry was now preoccupied with the structural reform of the performing-arts companies which number 380,000 and range from serious theater to acrobatic troupes. 
He said that most of these subsidized companies were overstaffed and overage, with people in their 70's occupying dressing rooms. 
There are 8,000 self-styled dramatists in the Theater Association. 
Mr. Ying said that the companies would be decoupled from the Government and made as autonomous as possible.
Under this new program the groups would be free to fire and hire as they please. 
Until now, anyone accepted into a group could expect a ''cast-iron rice bowl'' for life. 
The groups would continue to be subsidized but funds would be allocated according to merit rather than evenly, as now. 
They would be encouraged to run their own sideline enterprises, such as selling cassettes, and to seek private support. 
''With reform in the economic fields we now have quite a number of millionaires and some of them are willing to sponsor certain artistic efforts,'' Mr. Ying said.
''The theater groups should be able to chose their own plays,'' Mr. Ying said, but he added: ''That, of course, is a sensitive area. 
In a Communist country, ideology is always controlled by the party, by the propaganda department. 
In other words, censorship.''
He said that China did not have a Government body, as did the Russians, to censor productions. 
But in China, he observed carefully, people are understandably cautious, given the repressions of the past. 
During the Cultural Revolution Mr. Ying and his theater company of 250 were denounced and exiled to the countryside from 1968 to 1971 to plant rice while being ''re-educated.''
''There is a lot of self-censorship,'' Mr. Ying said. 
''A theater company is very cautious about putting on a controversial play and that is one area which we are determined to reform. 
We think there should be healthy criticism. 
But it should be limited to the literary and artistic merits of a work. 
We do not seek consensus.''
The ''model play'' - the propaganda revolutionary opera imposed as the sole model for the performing arts during the Cultural Revolution by Jiang Qing, Mao Zedong's wife - will no longer be required, Mr. Ying said. 
''We will not condemn a play and then persecute the writer.''
Earlier, however, Mr. Ying made it clear that the Government would be free under its new program to withdraw subsidies from a group if it was felt that it was not working properly.
At the Shanghai People's Arts Theater, one phase of Mr. Ying's program has already gone into effect. 
The director, Sha Yexin, said that for the first time in 40 years some of the untalented members of the company will be let go and new actors brought in. 
''We will break the cast-iron rice bowl,'' he said.
Mr. Sha's theater, one of the three major state theaters in Shanghai, stages six to eight plays a year, two of them foreign. 
Mr. Sha selects the plays for the company in consultation with a group of five members of the troupe and he says that none have been forbidden since he became director in 1985. 
The repertory for 1988 includes a new play ''Confucius, Jesus and John Lennon,'' written by Zong Fuxian, one of China's most talented playwrights; O'Neill's ''Marco Millions,'' to commemorate the playwright's 100th anniversary; ''Love Story of an Angel,'' a new play; ''Faust,'' and dutifully, a play that is being written reflecting on the reforms of the party congress.
Mr. Sha introduces his new plays discreetly. 
There is no advance newspaper advertising. 
Notice of a forthcoming performance is passed by word of mouth. 
The play is tried out in this manner to avoid that little danger that it might ''spark a fire,'' according to Mr. Sha. Presumably, the fire would come from party cadres who could raise political or other objections. 
In China, there are no professional critics who attend performances and review plays in the media soon after.
Audiences in the major state theaters in Shanghai and other cities tend to come from the elite. 
One evening in Shanghai, ''The China Dream'' was seen by this writer in a university auditorium before an appreciative capacity audience composed mainly of students. 
Xi Meijuan, the star of the People's Art Theater, played the lead role as the Shanghai girl, and Ye Mang wore a blond wig as the American scholar. 
The mass of the Chinese people witness the performing arts in smaller ''collective theaters'' in the cities and countryside.
During the last five years the growing popularity of movies and television has drawn audiences away from the theaters and almost halved the number of appearances by the performing-arts troupes. 
The companies most affected are those that stage the ancient traditional Peking Opera -which is described as being in crisis because young people will not attend - and also the provincial opera, folk dance and acrobatic troupes. 
In Guangzhou city proper, which neighbors Hong Kong, some 90 percent of the households have television sets, mostly color.
The mass audience for film has proven a mixed blessing for movie makers. 
Censorship of movies by the Film Bureau is tighter than the constraints imposed on the theater or publishing. 
The release of the popular film ''A Small Town Called Hibiscus'' was held up earlier this year until the ending was altered. 
In the original film a madman appears exclaiming that China will suffer another Cultural Revolution in six or seven years. 
The madman scene was retained but his prophecy was cut by the censor.

The fact is, the idea of a sister-state relationship between Oregon and Fujian Province in China had bad luck from the start, and the burglary of the Chinese cultural center and its historic displays here was just another hardship along the way.
''A couple of years ago, the Chinese we do business with asked us if we could do something like that,'' said William Mulholland, an engineer from Cult Creek, Ore., who says he proposed it to Gov. Victor G. Atiyeh of Oregon. 
''They heard about this sister-city thing between some places over here and some there, and they wanted something like it.''
The sisterly relationship has no diplomatic or legal status but is rather a device to promote trade. 
It has caused debates in several American Western cities and states over whether to establish such agreements with China or with Taiwan.
Article on Chinese Arts and Cultural Center in Oregon City, Ore, which has been suffering hardships, most recently burglary of its historic displays; center was opened in attempt to create sister state relationship between Oregon and Fujian Province; drawing (S)
The Governor, a conservative Republican, was cool right from the start of setting up shop with Peking, Mr. Mulholland said.
''He just didn't have any interest in it,'' Mr. Mulholland said. 
''So I went to the Legislature and they passed a resolution, 88 to 2. 
Then that same day, the Governor signed a proclamation saying he wanted to work with Taiwan.''
Both Taipei and Peking claim to be the legitimate Government of China, and both sides recognize Taiwan as a province.
Â 
Cultural Center Opened in July
The Taiwan proclamation was announced last June 16. 
Then, in July, without approaching anyone for help, Kafung Francis Yap of mainland China arrived in Oregon to open the Chinese Arts and Cultural Center.
He and his wife, Amy, came to this pulp and textile center in northwestern Oregon from London, where they had lived for 10 years. 
They have a 7-year- old girl and a 6-year-old boy.
Mrs. Yap, who said her husband was away on business for 10 days, described him as an authorized representative of the Fujian Advertising Corporation of Fuzhou, Fujian, and the Peking Advertising Corporation of Peking. 
She also said he was an agent for the Ka Fung Advertising Company, which sells television and print advertising in China.
The couple soon received from China a substantial amount of Chinese art, which was to be the display that would attract American visitors whom the Yaps said they hoped to meet, both to establish business contacts and to attract students to exchange programs.
Â 
Early American Settlement
The Yaps set up shop in Oregon City, which is 10 miles south of Portland, the state's largest city, because someone in China determined that Oregon City was the first major American settlement in the Pacific Northwest and thus should be the place for a Chinese cultural center.
Mr. Yap rented a store at 1015 Seventh Street here, two blocks from the old mansion on a bluff above the Willamette River from which Dr. John McLoughlin ran the Oregon Territory a century and a half ago. 
Dr. McLoughlin, who laid out Oregon City in 1842, was the chief agent of the Hudson's Bay Company and an influential figure in the early development of the Pacific Northwest.
The Chinese Arts and Cultural Center is surrounded by service stations and small stores on a heavily traveled street; no parking is allowed in front of it, and very few people pass on foot.
The first official notice of the center came on Oct. 
28, when Mr. Yap reported to the Oregon City police that the center was burglarized while he and his wife were in China.
Â 
176 Items Reported Stolen
The burglars entered through an unlocked bathroom window, bypassed a simple burglar alarm and carried off 176 items, including agate vases, statues, paintings and porcelain.
The items were covered by a $50,000 insurance policy, Mr. Yap told the police, but he said he doubted that this was enough.
When the burglary report was filed, Mr. Yap began to get public attention for the first time. 
Agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Customs Service visited him, as did Douglas V. Frengle, manager of the International Trade Division of the Oregon Department of Economic Development.
But the public did not visit the center, nor did representatives of the industrial concerns that Mr. Yap sought to attract. 
The burglary wiped out most of the artifacts on display, and the Oregon City police recommended that the others be stored in a more secure place. 
Now the former display rooms are vacant, except for office equipment.

Communist officials from Tibet today accused the Dalai lama, its exiled spiritual leader, of fomenting the recent Tibetan rioting.
It was the first time since Tibetan Buddhist monks in Lhasa demonstrated for independence a month ago that officials from China's Government in Tibet talked about the protests to foreign reporters. 
The officials spoke at a news conference held in conjunction with the 13th Communist Party Congress being held in Beijing.
The Tibetans, who are attending the 13th party congress as party delegates also asserted that the Dalai Lama dispatched assassins and saboteurs to Lhasa in 1985 and 1986. 
They offered no evidence to support their charges.
Unrest Blamed on Dalai Lama
''In 1985, the Dalai Lama sent people to conduct explosions,'' said Doje Cering, the Chairman of the Government of the Tibet Autonomous Region. 
''In 1986, the Dalai Lama sent back people to engage in assassinations in Lhasa.''
Mr. Doje blamed the unrest in Lhasa on the Dalai Lama. 
''We have conclusive evidence to show that the Lhasa riot early this month was instigated and engineered by the Dalai Separatistk clique,'' said Mr. Doje. He did not offer proof of his assertion.
Earlier this month, the Dalai Lama said he favored civil disobedience against Chinese rule but not violence and asked his Tibetan supportrs to press their campaign peacefully.
Â 
Violence Is Disavowed
''Violence is not the proper way at all,'' the spiritual leader said at his headquarters near the Indian town of Dharamasala.
The Dalai Lama blamed the rioting on what he termed Chinese repression and Tibetan discontent.
China involved Tibet in 19550 and suppressed an independence rebellion in 1959. 
That year, the Dalai Lama fled to India with thousands of Tibetans and took up residence in Dharamsala. 
Beijing maintains that Tibet is an integral part of China.
Over the last two years, there have been fragmentary reports from Tibetans in India that armed Tibetan exiles had infiltrated back into Tibet for acts of sabotage. 
But there had been no confirmation of these reports and until now the Chinese Government did not comment on them.
In late September and early October, protests led by Buddhist monks turned violent when police attacked the demonstrators. 
A Chinese police station was burned and at least nine Tibetan protestors were killed when armed police fired into the crowd.
Today, the Tibetan officials attending the party congress denied that the police fired on protestors.
Despite reports from travelers that curfews have been imposed in Lhasa and that heavily armed Chinese police patrol the streets, Communist officials in Tibet said that Lhasa had returned to normal.
Â 
Foreign Journalists Expelled
During the disturbances a month ago, 15 foreign jounralists were expelled from tibet. 
Today, Mr. Doje said that Tibet was not closed to froeign reporters but that they had to apply for permission to go there. 
Many journalists based in Beiging have been rebuffed in such efforts.
The Tibetan Communists are among nearly 2,000 delegates to the party congress, which will announce the party's new Central Committee tomorrow. 
It is expected to be smaller and younger than the current Central Committee.
The new Central Committee, to be pared down from 208 to 172 members, will be missing many of the old Communist revolutionaries, including china's senior leader Deng Xiaoping and President Li Xiannian. 
Several Chinese have said that the committee has been reduced in size because it is expected to meet more often and will be less unwieldly.
On Monday, the newly constituted committee will gather to elect the party's ruling Politburo, currently made up of 20 members. 
And the following day, Tuesday, a new Standing Committee of the Politburo, the most powerful organ in the country, will be named.
Only Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang, who is expected to be named party head, is thought to retain his seat.
