file: TRACKING DOWN ORIENTAL INGREDIENTS.txt
text:
ï»¿
FOOD is an important part of the New Year festivities this week in Chinatown and throughout the city as Chinese, Vietnamese and other Asian families gather to celebrate the start of the Year of the Tiger on Sunday.
Many non-Asians will want to join in by preparing their own versions of holiday meals. 
A good way to start is to visit Chinatown. 
The scene on and near Canal, Mott and Mulberry Streets, where the sights, sounds and smells recall the street markets of Hong Kong, can be as informative as it is bewildering. 
It's a good idea to peruse the ingredients section of any good Chinese cookbook beforehand.
Several large general stores sell an array of kitchen and table wares along with an enormous variety of preserved and processed foods. 
These are excellent places to begin.
One such is Kam Man, 200 Canal Street, and its sister shop, Kam Kuo, 7 Mott Street. 
They have such items as woks, steamers, rice bowls, cleavers and, of course, chopsticks, as well as vast selections of canned and bottled goods and sweets for the New Year. 
Kam Man also has roast pork, duck and chicken; Kam Kuo has frozen fish, such as dace and yellowfish from Hong Kong, and a fresh selection of unusual produce, such as bamboo shoots and yellow chives.
Pearl River Emporium, 13-15 Elizabeth Street, sells Chinese kitchen implements and has a whole section of dried and canned foods from China, Taiwan and Hong Kong. 
From Wing Woh Leung, at the corner of Bayard and Mott Streets, come packaged sweets, including sugared red melon seeds, lotus seeds, lotus root, coconut and melon pieces, all part of the traditional New Year table. 
Sacks of red rice (for luck) and glutinous rice (for pastries) are stacked next to small packages of lemongrass, lemon leaves, sweet and salty tamarind snacks, minced pork to flavor congee (Chinese rice porridge) and dried, salted fish.
Along with the food and kitchen equipment at the Chinese-American Trading Company, 91 Mulberry Street, are shelves of amusing plastic dishes in the characteristic shapes and decorations of Chinese porcelain, a great idea for a Chinese-style picnic. 
Chinese earthenware cooking pots are a major offering here, along with teas and the roots and spices for preparing Chinese herbal medicines.
Fresh meat and fish is often top quality in Chinatown and prices are frequently lower than in other sections of Manhattan, although not necessarily at this time of the year.
The Yee Fat Trading Company, 28 Mott Street, and Hyfund Company Seafood Market, 75 Mulberry Street, like many Chinatown fish markets, have tanks full of live carp and buffalo fish. 
Yee Fat also carries fresh meat and produce, and Hyfund has vegetables. 
Many of these shops have exotic ingredients - frozen pangolin, which is akin to the armadillo, imported from China was available recently at Hyfund.
Fresh white Peking ducks from Long Island are at the butcher shop at 88 Mulberry Street. 
It is best to order them in advance. 
All come plucked and cleaned of intestines but with other innards intact.
Bayard Meat Market, 57 Bayard Street, has tripe and duck feet as well as less exotic cuts of meat. 
Like many Chinatown meat markets, this is also a good source for Smithfield hams, which take the place of Chinese Yunnan hams in many Asian recipes. 
Another notable butcher shop is Gin Ray, 55 Mott Street, where there is a particularly good selection of roast duck, barbecued spareribs and barbecued pork.
Many food shops offer similar selections of roast and barbecued meats. 
One of the best is Noodle Town, 28 1/2 Bowery, with luscious dark red chunks of barbecued pork, broad sides of roast pork, bright orange roasted squids, duck wings in soy sauce and wine sauce, stewed chitlings or pigs' intestines, and roast ducks, squabs and chickens.
Dried Beef King, 89 Bayard Street, is a new shop offering a favorite Chinese snack food - strips of dried meat in a variety of sweet and spicy flavors, including oyster and fruit.
The quality of Chinatown's fresh fruits and vegetables is generally very high. 
A particularly good source is Sun Kwong Lee, at 71 1/2 Mulberry Street, which has many of the specialty Chinese items that cannot be found in other parts of the city, such as silk and hairy squashes, bitter and winter melons, water chestnuts and lotus root.
Another good produce source is Johnny Yip, a farmer from Easton, Md., who sets up his van on Mulberry Street, halfway between Canal and Bayard, every weekend, to sell fruits and vegetables, many of which come from his own market garden.
A good introduction to Chinese sweets and pastries is available at Lung Fong Chinese Bakery, 41 Mott Street, with delightful cookies in the shapes of chickens, fish, lions and fat friendly-looking Buddhas. 
Sesame buns, fried sweets and a deliciously oily, sticky rice pancake stuffed with a layer of sweet bean paste are among the other offerings.
Rice noodles in various shapes and sizes are a treat at the Fong Inn Pastry Corporation, 46 Mott Street, and Sun Hop Hing, 4 Bowery, which also make fresh bean curd and tofu.
Ewa Import Inc., 24 Mott Street, which has porcelain and ceramic table items, also carries preserved and dried Chinese ingredients, such as dried bird's nests, dried shark's fins and the prized white jelly fungus. 
Although intended for medicinal teas and broths, many of these ingredients can be used in cooking.
The teas at Ten Ren Tea and Ginseng, 176 Canal Street, are not herbal, although the shop, as its name indicates, also sells ginseng root. 
Teas are the stars, however, ranging from a superb first-grade green oolong ($100 a pound) to teas for as little as $4 and $5 a pound.
While shopping in Chinatown, don't forget the other Asian cuisines. 
Wing Woh Leung, at the corner of Bayard and Mott Streets, has an excellent selection of ingredients for Thai, Vietnamese and Philippine preparations, in addition to its Chinese selection.
The Thai and Oriental Grocery, 81 Bayard Street, is a hole in the wall crammed with Thai foods and prepared takeout dishes. 
And Thuan-Nguyen (also called the Sun-Win Trading Company), 82 Mulberry Street, has a first-rate selection of Vietnamese ingredients.
In recent years, a significant Asian community has grown up in the Flushing section of Queens. 
Around Main Street, Roosevelt Avenue and Northern Boulevard, Chinese, Korean and Japanese food shops are mingled with restaurants serving the cuisines of those countries.
Nippan Daido U.S.A. 
Inc., 137-80 Northern Boulevard (Union Street), has a vast selection of mostly Japanese and Korean items, fresh fish, meat and vegetables as well as packaged, processed and preserved foods. 
Royal Oriental Food, 142-38 Roosevelt Avenue, and C & K Food Company, 135-21 Roosevelt Avenue, also have large selections of fresh and processed Asian foods.
At the Taiwan Supermarket Company, 37-17 Prince Street (38th Avenue), the emphasis is on Chinese foods, teas, beverages and some cookware, while Flushing Meat Market Inc., 135-07 Roosevelt Avenue, a branch of Jing Cheong Meat Market on Mott Street in Chinatown, is a pristine shop with butchers and clerks who are well-informed about a large assortment of meat and poultry and willing to butcher anything to Asian or Western specifications.

file: TRANSLATING BASEBALL INTO CHINESE.txt
text:
ï»¿
When C. W. Post's baseball team opened a six-game exhibition series with Chinese squads here last week, something happened that the American players didn't expect: They lost.
In fact, the Pioneers, the regular-season champions of the New York Metropolitan Conference, lost twice - by 6-4 on June 3 to Peking, and by 4-3 the next day to a Sichuan Province team.
Since then, Post has bounced back with three victories. 
The final game, against Peking, will be played here Tuesday.
C W Post College baseball team, playing exhibition series with teams in China, lost first three games but bounced back with three victories; final game is to be played on June 11; American team members comment on difficulties they have in using Chinese-made baseballs; photo (M)
Aside from the surprising skill shown by their hosts, especially in base-running, the Post players have advanced many reasons for their defeats in a country where baseball is hardly the national passtime. 
These range from jet lag and overconfidence to questionable umpiring and strange ball parks.
However, perhaps the most interesting problem cited by the Americans in their first two games was a bagful of slippery, lumpy, seamless spheres of varying sizes: Chinese baseballs.
''This is a weird feeling, especially if your hands are wet with sweat,'' said Rick Wohlmacher, a C. W. Post pitcher from New Hyde Park, L.I., squeezing one of the Chinese balls in his palm. 
''I couldn't grip it, I had no control.''
Wohlmacher, one of the team's top pitchers the past two seasons, walked five and gave up four hits and five runs in 5Y innings before being relieved in the first game against Peking.
Â 
American Baseballs Used
The Chinese approved a switch to American baseballs in the third game, at Tianjin. 
C. W. Post responded by scoring four runs in the first inning on back-to-back home runs by the captain, Mike Alfano, and Joe Cioffi. 
Post went on to punch 11 hits in the 7-4 victory at Tianjin, 137 kilometers east of Peking.
The second game at Tianjin was played with a Chinese ball, which Alfano, the third baseman, said ''doesn't really carry - it''s softer.''
Nevertheless, Alfano, who has been drafted by the Atlanta Braves, hit two home runs, and his team won, 10-6.
The next day Ron Lupo, a pitcher from Commack, L.I., got a return match against Sichuan. 
In his first outing against that team, with the Chinese ball, Lupo, noted for his control, walked nine. 
The second time, with an American ball, Lupo went the distance in an 8-3 victory, walking only three and throwing five strikeouts.
Â 
Chinese Aggressive Runners
Apart from the controversy over the Chinese balls, which clearly seems to have generated more humor than hostility here, the Post players say they are highly impressed with the Chinese style of play. 
In particular, their hosts are extremely aggressive on the basepaths, and appear to get their way. 
The Chinese teams have stolen 26 bases in 35 attempts over the 5 games played so far. 
Post has stolen only three bases in nine attempts. 
In the 8-3 loss to Lupo, they stole 12 bases in 13 attempts.
''They run no matter what the score is,'' said Coach Dick Vining of C. W. Post. 
''There''ll be a man on second with no outs and they'll try to steal third.''
Post's sports information director, Bill Huffman, noted that the Chinese ''love to build runs,'' and are fond of bunting and sacrifice hitting. 
''They think of their baserunner as a resource,'' Huffman said. 
''They think, 'We've got to get this guy across the plate.'
There are no ego trips.''
Â 
Hitting Is Limited
On the other hand, the Chinese are simply not long-ball hitters. 
They have not hit any home runs in the series; their American opponents have hit six.
The fences at Peking's all-dirt Fengtai Field, one of the few baseball diamonds in China, are a Ty-Cobb distance from home plate - about 400 feet down the line and 450 feet to a billboard in left-center field that reads in Chinese, ''Friendship first, competition second.''
The games at Peking have each drawn no more than a few hundred onlookers, but this appears to be because the field is in the southwest suburbs and is difficult to reach by public transportation. 
At the more centrally located stadium in Tianjin, last Thursday's game drew 2,000 spectators.
Baseball once enjoyed some popularity in this country, but was banned at the start of the cultural revolution in 1966. 
It is now being officially encouraged, and Liang Youde, an official with the Peking Institute of Sports research, said China has ambitions to turn out a good team for the 1986 Asian Games or 1988 Olympics at Seoul, or at least in time for the 1990 Asian Games, which are being hosted by Peking.
Â 
Kuhn Is Encouraged
''You can look at the Taiwanese, the Japanese and the Koreans, and you don't have to use your imagination to think that the Chinese will do sensationally at baseball if they just hang in there for a while,'' said the former major league commissioner, Bowie Kuhn, who was sitting in the stands last Saturday with the president of the Los Angeles Dodgers, Peter O'Malley.
Kuhn said his interest in promoting baseball in the world's most populous country dates back to 1974, when the head of the United States Mission in Peking, a former Yale baseball player by the name of George Bush, saw a game and contacted the commissioner.
''George called and said, ''They're playing baseball over here,'' Kuhn said of Bush, now the Vice President.
As C. W. Post prepares for its final match, team members have alluded to one other possible reason for their resurgence after such a slow start here. 
Two Pioneer pitchers who have had problems this past season with tendinitis, Lou Burmester and Mike Juman, have experimented with acupuncture treatments here and both say they are very pleased with the results.
''It was painless and pretty effective,'' said Juman, who is from Merrick, L.I. 
''After acupuncture, I pitched pretty well, as a matter of fact.''

file: TRAVELS OF AN EXASPERATING MAN.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE QUESTION OF HU
By Jonathan D. Spence.
187 pp. 
New York:
Alfred A. Knopf. $18.95.
In the 1540's, St. Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Society of Jesus, exhorted his followers to apply their senses to reading scripture. 
They were to begin by conjuring an image of the place in which a biblical event took place: the room in which Christ held his Last Supper, the garden where Judas gave his kiss, the house in which Mary waited after the Crucifixion. 
Once this image was fixed, the other senses - hearing, smell, touch, taste - were to be added one by one until the ''imaginative representation'' was complete.
Jonathan Spence cites this prescription in the most recent of his books on Chinese history, ''The Memory Palace of Matteo Ricci,'' to illustrate the tradition out of which Ricci, a 17th-century Jesuit missionary to China, created his ''memory system,'' but it might equally serve to describe the kind of attention Mr. Spence himself brings to the historical record. 
Even when his chosen avenue of approach is at its most abstract - using the ''memory palace,'' for example, as a way into the complex mind of Matteo Ricci - Mr. Spence never fails to anchor his subject securely in the material world. 
He applies his senses to the discovery of particulars of landscape, color or smell that allow him to evoke the past in all its diversity and bring it into the present.
In ''The Question of Hu'' his preoccupation with making history palpable seems to take on a new dimension. 
More than any other of Mr. Spence's historical works, the new book reads like a novel. 
As the footnotes amply attest, however, it is a narrative constructed scrupulously from what can be documented. 
Mr. Spence is careful to cite his authority for the least detail - even the source for the length of a ''truly magnificent beard'' sported by one of the chief characters is duly noted and dated.
The hero of the story is an exasperating little man named John Hu, a Chinese convert to Christianity whose life was unremarkable in nearly every respect save one: in 1722, at the age of 40, he traveled halfway around the world to Europe. 
Since the time of Matteo Ricci, many Western missionaries had visited China, but in 1722 only three Chinese were known to have visited France - and only one returned to tell the tale. 
Hu hoped to write an account of Europe and its customs for his own countrymen, but this ambition proved impracticable, since he spent most of his three-year sojourn abroad in an insane asylum.
Hu went to Europe as the copyist-assistant of Jean-Francois Foucquet, a Jesuit missionary returning home after 22 years in China. 
Father Foucquet had devoted a lifetime to proving that the ancient Chinese religious texts, such as ''The Book of Changes,'' were originally handed to the Chinese by ''the same true God that Christians worship.''
By giving the Chinese ''the key to their own classical writings,'' he hoped to open the way for the spread of Christianity in the East. 
Hu's task was to copy out quotations from the 4,000 volumes Father Foucquet had amassed in order to demonstrate his theory.
Hu did little copying, however; his exuberant response to the new world, added to his inability to speak the language or assimilate the culture and act accordingly, entangled him in repeated difficulties. 
To the Europeans, he appeared to be mad: on his first trip by coach, he leaped from the moving vehicle to stuff his mouth with blackberries growing at the roadside; he gave his new suit of fine coffee-colored cloth to a beggar; he marched through the streets of Paris beating a drum and waving a small flag with the message ''Men and women should be kept in their separate spheres'' written on it in Chinese characters. 
Hu was beaten and locked up to discourage him from pursuing these activities, but he repeatedly escaped and persisted. 
Finally, Father Foucquet requested that Hu be committed to the hospital for the insane at Charenton, outside of Paris.
The title of Mr. Spence's book refers to the first question Hu asked when, after more than two years' incarceration, he finally was able to speak to someone in his own language: ''Why have I been locked up?''
But ''The Question of Hu'' also addresses the larger question of how we define madness and to what degree the madhouse was an instrument of social control. 
''The Question of Hu'' must also be read as the question of ''who?''
- a subtle and complex evocation of the way in which identity is bound up in culture. 
Perhaps the most important question ''The Question of Hu'' asks, though, is: what does it mean to interpret another culture?
In the same way that he used Ricci's memory palace as a metaphor for the writing of history, Mr. Spence uses Hu's story to examine the act of ''translation.''
Mr. Spence's choice of a narrative style resembling that of fiction allows him to draw these questions from the material itself, without imposing answers. 
In so doing, he offers us an interpretation directly opposed to that Hu's employer, Father Foucquet, sought to apply in giving the Chinese the ''key to their own classical writings.''
Mr. Spence's delicate but nevertheless ambitious approach makes him one of the most original and exciting historians writing now.

text:

American officials reported increasing concern today about rising tension between India and China as a result of a buildup of Indian and Chinese troops in a disputed, mountainous border region near Bhutan. 
The State Department has urged both sides to keep the situation calm, officials said.
The tense atmosphere developed when China began sending additional troops into the area about two weeks ago, a State Department official said. 
Then India followed suit. 
Since last weekend, the situation has become ''more threatening,'' he said, as more soldiers have been moved in, along with logistical support, to make a total of about 30,000 troops on both sides, according to American estimates.
Most of those troops were in secondary lines of defense, one official said, with relatively few facing each other on the ridge line that marks the border.
The region, which was fought over by China and India in 1962, is dominated by mountains 14,000 to 16,000 feet high, which preclude mechanized warfare. 
One specialist said only foot soldiers can fight there, and extensive combat is possible only during short periods of the year because of the weather.
This is one of those periods, shortly after the snow has ended and before the monsoon rains begin. 
A longer period of suitable weather follows the end of the rains, in late summer. 
That is when the 1962 battles were fought.
The United States has made diplomatic approaches to both India and China in an effort to dissuade them from attacking each other, a State Department official said. 
But Washington has little influence on the issue with either country.

text:
ï»¿
Dear Director,
''The Music Man'' was intended to be a valentine and not a caricature. 
Please do not let the actors - particularly Zaneeta, Mayor Shinn and Mrs. Shinn, who takes herself quite seriously - mug or reach for comedy effect. 
The Del Sarte ladies also should be natural and sincere, never raucous, shrewish or comic per se. 
The humor of this piece depends upon its technical faithfulness to the real small-town Iowans of 1912 who certainly did not think they were funny at all.
Â 
Faithfully,
Â Â Meredith Willson
WHEN MEREDITH WILLSON jotted this note to future directors of ''The Music Man'' in the mid-50's, he wasn't thinking of Wang Xingna, an exuberant operatic tenor who hides his bald spot under a lumpy blue beret, as the flimflam musical instrument peddler Harold Hill. 
And he wasn't thinking of Li Zhigang, a barrel-chested man of no uncertain presence, as the slightly pompous Mayor Shinn, who never quite gets around to delivering the Gettysburg Address to his farm-town constituents. 
Meredith Willson, it can be said, wasn't thinking of Chinese theatergoers.
''For an American audience, I know exactly what to do,'' said George C. White, the president of the Eugene O'Neill Theater Center in Waterbury, Conn.,, who is in Beijing to stage ''The Music Man,'' the first professional production of an American musical in China.
''I have to play this a lot more broadly for a Chinese audience because the subtlety is lost here,'' he explained, slouching in a cramped folding wooden seat as he scrutinized his cast gallivanting across the stage of the Central Opera Theater. 
''They don't have the context. 
They don't understand small-town Iowa in 1912.
''If we don't play it for laughs, it won't go,'' he continued. 
''Take Mayor Shinn. 
He's very big here. 
He shouldn't be so pompous. 
But here, we have to play it very broadly.''
Mr. White arrived in China last month with a choreographer, music director, costume designer, two producers, bolts of cloth, scores and scripts to transform a corps of Chinese opera singers and ballet dancers into a Broadway song-and-dance show that he hopes will span the cultural gulf between quintessential Americana and Chinese views of life and notions of entertainment.
He also brought with him Rodney Marriott, a tall, animated fellow with a thatch of blond hair and a beard a bit like an unraveling Brillo pad, to direct a production of ''The Fantasticks'' with players from the Central Opera Theater, which also supplied the singers for ''The Music Man.''
Unlike ''The Music Man,'' which will play only in Beijing, ''The Fantasticks'' will tour several cities in China in coming months.
''The Music Man'' grabs for middle-American values the way the Mississippi River reaches for the Gulf. 
It is the tale of Harold Hill, a smooth-talking, fast-walking seller of trombones, cornets and clarinets who arrives in River City, Iowa, intending to fleece yet another small town with grandiose promises of the new, the wonderful, the unexpected. 
The musical stirs provincial gullibility with down-home common sense, slick hucksterism with apple-pie earnestness. 
In the end, of course, the Music Man is sold the kettle of small-town virtues by a proper librarian, and River City learns to dream a little.
For China, where over the last 37 years Communist rule has ripped the countryside apart, forced millions of families from their homes, triggered widespread starvation and battered its people with rampaging, violent political campaigns, one would expect little lightheartedness left. 
But since 1979, when a dramatic series of economic reforms were introduced, life in the countryside has been reinvigorated and cities have begun to bustle with a growing sense of self-assurance.
Still, entertainment in China remains a very mixed duffle of didactic and maudlin films, traditional Peking and provincial operas playing to increasingly aged audiences and a small but growing number of Western operas and ballets of world-class quality. 
Hong Kong pop music blares from twin-speaker boom boxes in shops and markets while stately polkas played by dowdy orchestras pull couples onto the floors of dance halls across the country.
Into this cultural landscape parachuted Mr. White and his staff. 
And the question that hangs over the red brick rehearsal halls here is whether China is ready for the busy, boisterous ''Music Man'' and the slapstick, illusory, romantic ''Fantasticks.''
''After the Cultural Revolution, people like comedy and singing and light opera,'' said Zou Dehua, the director of the art committee for the Central Opera Theater and its leading soprano, referring to the Cultural Revolution, the decade of political upheaval and torment that ended in 1976. 
''I think audiences here will accept American musicals very well. 
Young people got on to pop music very quickly.''
Nonetheless, the politicized atmosphere that has pervaded the arts during the current upheaval in China's leadership has crept up on the production of the American musicals in recent days. 
Li Guangxi, a prominent opera star here and a member of a political body called the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, has urged the Chinese Opera Theater, the country's most prestigious operatic organization and the hosts for the American musical productions, to stage more Chinese operas and fewer Western productions.
China Daily, the country's English-language newspaper, quoted Mr. Li as complaining that theater directors did not appreciate Chinese opera and that the Central Opera Theater had not produced a Chinese opera in two years. 
''Although some established writers do not approve of the present situation,'' Mr. Li was quoted as saying, ''they are too old to create modern operas. 
For the young, who are fresh with new ideas, it is easier for them to look to the West for inspiration.''
Mr. Li, who is a candidate for the presidency of the Central Opera Theater, said he would require more Chinese operas to be performed. 
''Most of all I want to make the theater well known to the world by performing our own operas,'' he said.
The day Mr. Li's pronouncements appeared, a bit of glumness hung over the Americans here. 
Mr. White, who rarely refrains from opining on anything, said it was a time to be quiet. 
''Let's just go on,'' he said.
And go on they have. 
In the slightly dank rehearsal hall Rodney Marriott was running his troops through the abduction scene in ''The Fantasticks.''
An actor doing his best to whoop like an American Indian bundled a girl on his back and scooted off stage right.
''Stage left, stage left,'' hollered Mr. Marriott, his right hand jerking up to push at a brush of hair that wouldn't stay out of his eyes. 
''Stage left always means left facing the audience.''
A translator quickly explained the new terminology.
''This is the longest-running show in the history of American theater,'' Mr. Marriott said during a break in rehearsal. 
''This is about illusions about young love, the illusions children have about parents, illusions about the theater. 
It's amazing how universal this is.''
Still, he said, turning opera singers into players in a musical required not only imbuing an appreciation of American humor but breaking established operatic modes. 
''These are opera singers who've never really had to dance, act, sing,'' Mr. Marriott said. 
''They're having to learn how to dance, to move. 
They're really going hard, six, seven hours a day.''
For both ''The Fantasticks'' and ''The Music Man,'' translating American repartee, assumptions and humor into a recognizable Chinese form brought with it considerable obstacles.
'''We want this to be relentlessly American,'' Mr. White said, ''right down to blond and red wigs. 
If you're going to do it, do it all the way. 
But how do you translate, 'What is the sin in sincere'?''
Translating the script of ''The Music Man'' - which will be known in China as ''The Musical Instrument Peddler'' - into Chinese took six months, according to Li Shirong, the deputy director of the Central Opera Theater. 
Then the Chinese script was sent back to the United States, where it was retranslated word for word into literal English. 
''We wanted to see what we had,'' Mr. White said.
Every day, changes are made in the script - to make it more colloquial, to make it more accessible to the Chinese, to make it truer to Meredith Willson's original text. 
Where the Willson script reads, for example, ''Cubebs, tryin' out, tailor-mades like cigarette feends [slam] and braaagin,' '' (which even English speakers may find rather cryptic) the Chinese version read something like, ''foolishly making tricks, learning to take drugs, secretly smoking marijuana cigarettes and heroin, degenerating into a drug addict.''
''We changed that,'' Mr. White said flatly.
Elsewhere in the play, Mayor Shinn rises to address townspeople and attempts to recite the Gettysburg Address: ''Four score and seven years ago. 
. .''
In colloquial Chinese, there is no precise rendering of ''four score,'' so Li Zhigang solemnly intones in Chinese, ''On the Fourth of July, 1776. 
. .''
More importantly, however, the phrase ''four score and seven years ago'' summons up a welter of images in the American mind. 
In the Chinese mind, even the date is little more than one of 365 that year during the reign of Qianlong during the Qing Dynasty.
Yet another line quotes a townsman, Oliver Hix, as saying in the Chinese version, ''If the banking business was correct most of the time, you wouldn't be able to keep your rice bowl.''
But beyond these problems of language, Mr. White and his colleagues as well as his Chinese counterparts believe that the larger impact of the musical will hit home.
''It's so funny,'' said Mr. White, during an afternoon rehearsal, as actors and singers careened across the stage. 
''It's like the old Durante. 
Everybody wants to get into the act.''
Paulette Haupt-Nolen, the artistic director of the O'Neill, is the musical director of the production. 
A slim white baton with a battered handle seems never to leave her right hand.
''Is the boom, boom, boom added?'' she asked her Chinese counterpart, Gao Weiqun, the music director of the Central Opera Theater, during a run-through of the train scene, in which traveling salesmen heading for Iowa swap tales of the trade and of the legendary Music Man. 
In the Chinese translation, Ms. Haupt-Nolen said, ''There are more words than the beat, so the rhythm of the train is always changing.''
Suddenly the run-through collapses. 
A bewildered Ms. Haupt-Nolen looks about, finally lowering her baton. 
''What happened now?'' she asked.
Mr. White stood up quickly, his arms flailing, urging, ''Keep going, keep going.''
Frantically the Chinese translator, Liang Lili, tries to get the train scene moving.
''It always takes twice as long with the translation,'' Mr. White said. 
He sighed a bit and sat down.
Li Shirong, a rail-thin, soft-spoken man, said that the musical presented real difficulties for the opera singers.
''Frankly speaking,'' he said, ''the singers at the beginning are not accustomed to it. 
They have to get used to singing and acting and dancing at the same time. 
This is not like traditional opera, where you walk a few steps, sit down or stand up and then sing an aria.''
Wang Xingna, a 47-year-old operatic tenor, was chosen by Mr. White during casting last October to play Howard Hill, the Music Man. 
''I studied opera at the Central Conservatory of Music,'' he said, during a pause in a rehearsal. 
''I started singing professionally in 1958. 
During the Cultural Revolution there was no opera. 
We went to the countryside.''
When the Cultural Revolution ended, Mr. Wang was first assigned to a film studio as a musician and singer and did not come to the Central Opera Theater until 1979. 
Since then, he has played Alfredo in ''La Traviata'' and Don Jose in ''Carmen'' as well as parts in ''Madama Butterfly'' and ''I Pagliacci.''
''This is totally different,'' he said. 
''The style, to get the style, the music, the action. 
All Chinese actors have trouble playing and singing and jumping around.
''Originally, I'm a tenor,'' he continued. 
''Now I'm singing baritone. 
So it's a bit hard to sing. 
I have so many spoken lines I cannot use the technique I know. 
I have to find a new way to speak clearly and to project my voice further. 
In classical opera I only need to stand and sing. 
Here there is a lot of movement. 
Now I am moving into new areas.''
And how will the Chinese audience respond to the slickster Harold Hill pushing his instruments on an Iowa town?
''Maybe people will say I don't do the right thing,'' Mr. Wang said with a laugh. 
''But I dare say most people will like me. 
This is closer to the people, this kind of music.''
Onstage, Lynn Britt, the choreographer, was tugging dancers about, moving furniture. 
''Bom, bom, bom,'' she said, popping the beat. 
The dancers moved about her, bit by bit with more confidence.
''To think,'' observed Mr. White, clutching the railing of the pit and tugging the lapel of his ''lucky'' gray jacket in mock despair, ''we have to open in only six weeks.''
Replied Ms. Haupt-Nolen. ''Cross your fingers.''
Correction
An article in the Arts and Leisure section last Sunday about a Beijing production of ''The Music Man'' gave an incorrect location for the Eugene O'Neill Theater Center. 
It is in Waterford, Conn.

text:
ï»¿
AN INSULAR POSSESSION
By Timothy Mo. 
593 pp. 
New York: Random House. 
$19.95.
TIMOTHY MO has sent his craft up a crowded river. 
A few years ago C. Mary Turnbull, a historian at the University of Hong Kong, charted the many novels set in Hong Kong and found well over a hundred. 
Most, she thought, were of little account, though the public obviously thought differently of the panoramas offered by James Clavell, whose ''Tai-Pan,'' published in 1966, sprawls across much the same riverscape as Mr. Mo's remarkable effort, ''An Insular Possession.''
Mr. Clavell was never content to let his ship slide into quiet waters, however, and in the end he was false to the history he tried to tell. 
Mr. Mo is more confident, his hand steady on the tiller, his sense of when to allow boredom to descend over a quiet colonial day precisely calibrated.
''An Insular Possession'' is many things. 
Foremost, it is a fine book. 
Mr. Mo's third novel, the result of five years' work, fascinates much as a great, highly illustrated encyclopedia will fascinate, with odd bits of information competing with long, sustained passages of action, description and pure narrative for the reader's attention. 
Mr. Mo is particularly good with water: in rivers, in the sea, from the sky, in waste and in food. 
''Rain distresses the river's grey surface, making it seethe like an oil painting attacked by a strong reagent,'' he writes. 
''It is quite a light rain - 'hair-fine' rain, in the local patois â¦ and from the shelter of the balcony seems like a rolling mist.''
He enjoys language, plays with it, takes risks, sometimes fails, but page after page rolls on, a controlled flood of metaphor.
Mr. Mo ties Hong Kong to London with the image of his great river, which as it reaches the sea is ''yellow-brown, the colour of tea as drunk in London.''
The river is much like the British Empire, which ''succours and impedes native and foreigner alike; it limits and it enables, it isolates and it joins.''
The river is the highway of commerce that makes possible a triangular trade no less vicious than the one that had tied an earlier British Empire together - the trade in slaves, molasses, rum and horses that linked Africa to the West Indies and the whole to the mainland colonies of North America. 
This triangular trade is based on opium: slave-grown cotton is carried from the New World to England, where wage slaves turn it into cloth. 
The cloth is carried to India, sold to brown men who produce from the poppy a much prized drug. 
Though the practice is illegal, there are Chinese who will exchange silver for opium, thus to finance the tea that flows back from the East to comfort and stimulate the English factory hands, ''so that drug of a kind is at work at all corners of the triangle.''
It is into this trade that two young Americans obtrude. 
Gideon Chase, still in his teens, hails from New England; his friend Walter Eastman hails from the South. 
Eastman is interested in the daguerreotype and senses how photography will change our perception of reality; Chase, who learns Chinese from a Jesuit priest, becomes an interpreter and translator for the British, so that their reality is filtered through his language. 
Chase and Eastman break with the American traders who are prepared to go along with the British in promoting the opium trade. 
They found an irreverent newspaper, The Lin Tin Bulletin and River Bee, which competes against the stern voice of the British, The Canton Monitor: ''The only measures which have ever proved efficacious against the insolence of the Chinese have been those inspired by a manly and determined firmness.''
From the opposing newspapers, and through opposing views of what is best for the Chinese and for the future of commerce in the region, the reader learns of the range of Western visions of the East.
But more is going on here than a panoramic exploration of Canton, Macao and Hong Kong between 1833 and 1841. 
Mr. Mo's approach is, at first, maddeningly circular. 
His story appears to move in fits and starts, told largely in the present tense, yet interspersed with oracular observations, as from the outside. 
It is moved on (and at times retarded) by long passages from the competing newspapers, by letters, chunks apparently ripped from gazetteers - in short, told through all the historian's customary primary sources, from eyewitnesses to memoirs. 
He is, one discovers, letting us know that the Chinese novel proceeds differently, for as an essay in Mr. Mo's Lin Tin Bulletin tells us, a Western novel moves by virtue of its plot, ''a veritable engine which advances the tale along its rails to a firm destination,'' while ''the native novel â¦ moves in a path which is altogether circular,'' being made up of separate episodes joined only by the loosest threads.
Mr. Mo supplies an appendix that mixes his fictional characters with the several historical figures that walk upon his stage. 
Through it we learn that young Gideon Hall lives to become a world-famed scholar who, in 1881, prepares a translation of ''The Dream of the Red Chamber,'' sometimes called the first Chinese novel (which, in fact, was first translated in part by an English consul in China and published in Hong Kong in 1892). 
Thus Mr. Mo links young Chase's pursuit of an understanding of the Chinese language -which he must learn in order to serve as go-between in a world of British plenipotentiaries and naval officers and Cantonese compradors - to the emergence of a body of scholarship about China in which two contending views of the novel, one about time and the other about distance (as Chase observes in another context), are given concrete example. 
MR. MO also has fun with stereotypes. 
The first Chinese we encounter is ''grinning Ah Cheong,'' valet to a second-rate artist and first-rate womanizer who plays a central role in Mr. Mo's (or Eastman's) exploration of how painting and photography, in parallel to Western and Chinese ideas about the novel, shape different realities. 
Ah Cheong speaks as the condescending literature of the past required: ''Mastah Eastman just now come chop-chop say you plomise give him sketch-y lesson today, you no lemember bimeby?''
This bit of nonsense soon passes, and Mr. Mo returns to his rich vocabulary (the artist, we learn, has ''plenilunar buttocks''), the point made.
What most appears to fascinate Timothy Mo is a central question of empire. 
He knows that many of the British merchants who promoted the opium trade were in all other respects kind men, generous even, Christian to a fault. 
He is not satirical, he is genuinely puzzled. 
How is it, he wonders, letting Chase speak for him, that good men do bad deeds?
Or that bad men do good deeds?
And how, between cultures and between generations, is one to find the language to define such deeds?
How could the missionaries go up the China coast on the opium clippers, distributing Bibles with the drug?
Mr. Mo seems to conclude that we cannot know. 
In passages from Chase's unpublished autobiography, he has Chase explicitly reject all iron laws, whether of Malthus or of Marx. 
He reflects on language (''What is a dictionary but a photograph of the river of language at a given moment?''), on how language diverges as well as divulges, isolates as well as unites. 
In the end, it is clear, Chase and Mr. Mo feel that historical truth is as the river, ''the surface of the waters half-transparent, brittle, yet in the end opaque to our discernment, while beneath that glassy roof the fish flutter, tantalisingly, half-glimpsed as an idea or memory struggling to the surface of our thought.''
History is not melodrama, it simply is.
Â 
THE VIEW FROM BOXING
The afternoon before the Hagler-Leonard fight, there was so much commotion in the London office of Boxing News that Timothy Mo had to close a door for a telephone interview. 
Mr. Mo has worked at Boxing News for 11 years, a fact his American publishers don't mention.
The 36-year-old author, a former bantamweight boxer himself, was born in Hong Kong to an English mother and a Chinese father. 
He moved to England at the age of 10 and was educated at Oxford. 
He held one or two ''proper'' jobs in journalism before settling at Boxing News, where he spends a day and a half each week. 
''I wouldn't want to write fiction seven or even five days a week,'' he said, ''so the job is a blessed relief.''
He had the idea of doing a large novel about the classic colonial period in Hong Kong ''from the age of 15 or 16,'' but he didn't feel ''ready to write it'' until he solved the problems of ''representation in visual images or prose'' about five years ago.
''If you are a gymnast or a skater, you get boldness points for the difficulty of what you are trying to do. 
So many modern novelists write small novels perfectly. 
So many English writers write well within their abilities. 
I'm aiming for sweep and ambition.''
Mr. Mo appreciates being compared to V. S. Naipaul and Paul Scott, who number among his favorite writers, along with Thomas Mann and Doris Lessing. 
He and Mr. Naipaul share the same British editor, Diana Athill. who bought their first novels - both small, comic colonial gems -exactly 20 years apart. 
Mr. Mo's ''Monkey King'' will be published here late this month.
In its subject matter and skillful use of multiple voices, documents and letters, ''An Insular Possession'' is reminiscent of Scott's ''Jewel in the Crown,'' which Mr. Mo admires. 
'' 'An Insular Possession' is the only one of my books I would like to consume,'' he said. 
''As a writer I quite like all three of them, of course, but I think it is a cracking good read. 
In England it was found overcerebral, some said too sophisticated, even though it was a best seller.''
Â Â - EDEN ROSS LIPSON

text:
ï»¿
When Jimuya, a herdsman in Inner Mongolia, sold the wool sheared from his 200 sheep last spring, half of the $320 that he earned went to buy a locally made Swan television set.
Mr. Jimuya, who like many Mongolians uses only one name, took the 12- inch black-and-white set back to his two-room house in the rolling grasslands of Siziwang Banner, or County. 
The herdsman rigged the television set to a windmill generator turned by the incessant wind that sweeps down from Mongolia.
At night, when his sheep, horses and cattle have been settled down, Mr. Jimuya joins his wife, four children and elderly parents on the family's kang, or heated-brick sleeping platform, to find out what is happening in the world outside.
Article on introduction of television to peasants living in Mongolia, many of whom make TV sets their first major purchase under new agricultural responsibility system which rewards them for working harder; illustration; map (M)
''I'll watch whatever programs the others watch - news, features, films,'' Mr. Jimuya told a journalist who had driven two hours across the prairie to find him. 
The family's favorite nights are Tuesday and Friday, Mr. Jimuya said, because the television station in Hohhot, the regional capital of Inner Mongolia, broadcasts in Mongolian then instead of Chinese.
Â 
A Reward of New System
Mr. Jimuya is one of many peasants across China who made a television set their first major purchase under the new agricultural responsibility system, which rewards them for working harder. 
Some fellow herdsmen bought color television sets, Mr. Jimuya said, but he frugally limited himself to a black-and-white set because he is saving to build a new house.
About 200 million Chinese watch television, the official New China News Agency reported last January, making them the world's largest television audience. 
The Ministry of Radio and Television said in September that television reached nearly 60 percent of China's population, which means 600 million people.
Whatever the audience, factories cannot turn out enough television sets. 
China plans to produce more than 4.6 million sets this year. 
In the first nine months, 823,400 color sets were manufactured, a jump of 160 percent over the comparable period last year, but this lagged behind consumer demand.
The impact has been most obvious in the countryside, where television antennas sprout from mud-brick houses on dirt roads. 
In Guangdong Province in southeastern China, many peasants have put up UHF ''fishbone'' antennas to bring in sassy television shows from Hong Kong, despite periodic campaigns by the authorities to pull them down as conduits of bourgeois pollution.
Â 
Prime-Time Physics
But elsewhere, peasants who once went to bed when the sun set now spend evenings mesmerized in front of prime- time physics lessons, reports on the harvest output, Chinese operas, teleplays that act out the Government's latest injunctions and sports events like the triumphs of China's abiding heroines, its female volleyball team.
The Communist Party recognized in a directive a year ago that radio and television were effective tools for keeping in touch with the masses. 
Last December, Wu Lengxi, the Radio and Television Minister, admitted that Chinese television should be livelier, though he made clear that it would eschew the violence and sex found on Western television. 
''While clearing away cultural contamination,'' he said, ''we should try our best to meet the people's cultural needs.''
Over a cup of Mongolian milk tea flavored with salt, Mr. Jimuya explained why a fifth of his income so far this year was spent on a television set. 
''Television has become a fashionable thing, and everybody wants to have one, even here,'' he said. 
''With television, I can see what's happening in the outside, how other areas of China are using the responsibility system.''
Â 
Hasn't Changed the Routine
The arrival of a television set has not changed the family routine much, he said, since herdsmen usually stayed up late. 
Before, his family gathered around a radio, which, like the overhead light, was powered by the windmill generator he acquired last year.
Mr. Jimuya said he set no viewing rules for his children, who rise early to walk several miles to primary school at the Sandan Production Brigade. 
His oldest daughter is boarding at a secondary school in Siziwang, 45 miles away.
''The children watch television every night,'' he said. 
''I let them watch it until the end of the program. 
They are interested in whatever there is on television.''
The local channel goes on at 6:45 P.M., with the news starting at 7 P.M. It stays on until 10:30 or 11 P.M. There are no programs in the daytime, when everyone should be working.
The signal comes in clear from a transmitter that was built on a hill about a mile away to relay the programming from Hohhot. 
Before he bought a television set, Mr. Jimuya said, he used to hike over to the relay station after dinner to watch its monitor with his friends. 
Now other herdsmen who still lack sets will drop in on his house at night, sometimes traveling by horseback.
Â 
A 69-Year-Old TV Fan
The most avid viewer may be Mr. Jimuya's father, Arenchinkache, 69 years old, a white-bearded herdsman whose weathered face and bandy legs show the years spent in the saddle. 
''I like to watch because every evening brings so many things that are fresh and new,'' Mr. Arenchinkache said.
On rare occasions when the wind drops, the television set runs on electricity stored by the generator. 
The Jimuyas forgo watching television in the summer, when the family lives in a yurt, or felt tent, to follow the livestock across the grasslands.
Except for television, their traditional life is mostly unchanged. 
They eat one large meal a day, with mutton and milk heated on a stove fueled by animal manure because the prairie has no firewood. 
The family sleeps on bedrolls thrown across the kang, which is warmed by pipes from the adjacent stove.
In television, Mr. Jimuya and other peasants in remote parts of China have discovered horizons that they never knew or, for that matter, thought much about.
''When I listen to the radio, I can only listen,'' Mr. Jimuya said. 
''But when I watch television, I can see with my own eyes how things are changing in the other parts of the country.''

text:

''The Unruly Dragon'' flows along like its subject, the Yellow River in China. 
It's long and it's muddy, but it has lots of bright flashes of color. 
The Yellow River, or Huang Ho, starts in the Tibetan highlands and empties out in Bo Hai Bay off southeast China after twisting and turning 3,300 miles. 
Some 120 million Chinese, Tibetans, Mongols and Moslems live along its banks, a great many of them, one thinks, worried about disaster. 
In the last 50 years, ''The Unruly Dragon'' reports almost casually, floods, crop failure and starvation have taken the lives of more than 4 million. 
The figure of 4 million is hard to comprehend; we can't imagine misery that vast. 
The problem is, ''The Unruly Dragon'' can't quite imagine it, either.
The hourlong film, at 10 o'clock tonight, is presented by ABC News. 
Presumably, that means it's a news documentary. 
In fact, it's not a news documentary; it's a travelogue. 
The Yellow River moves endlessly through gorges and canyons, past ancient stone dwellings and giant Buddhas carved out of hillsides. 
Meanwhile, we hear a flute. 
Then the film returns to a studio, where Jim Laurie, the chief Asia correspondent for ABC News, attempts to put what we see in perspective. 
That's a tough job. 
Mr. Laurie, through no fault of his own, is reduced from reporter to tour guide. 
He points to a map: This is where we've been; here's where we're going. 
Then we return to the Yellow River.
''The Unruly Dragon'' is a hybrid - a cross between ''National Geographic'' and the evening news. 
It's pleasant and watchable, but it's also like the proverbial Chinese dinner: You've eaten but you don't feel full. 
The Japanese Broadcasting Corporation made the film as a co-production with China Central Television, and then, it seems, ABC became involved. 
The network, which recently disbanded its ''Close-Up'' documentary unit, is apparently searching for new cost-effective ways to present news.
Thus the film we see tonight: no questions, no answers, no interviews; Mr. Laurie is the narrator for a film made by someone else. 
The production almost certainly costs a lot less than a ''Close-Up'' documentary. 
That's fine; there's nothing wrong with a network saving money. 
Nevertheless, a different price is paid. 
''The Unruly Dragon'' slips into that vast, wishy-washy, though not necessarily unpleasant, area where we're not sure if we're watching entertainment or news. 
Tibetan monks beat gongs; Moslems celebrate a marriage (the sequence is charming); Mongols gallop on horseback. 
It's beguiling, but where are we?
The ''Close-Up'' unit would have told us. 
Mr. Laurie can't do it alone.
He does try, though. 
In one sequence, we see two rams butt heads while villagers stand and watch. 
Ram head-butting, apparently, is a traditional sport. 
''And the ramming of the rams might also be seen as symbolic of something else,'' Mr. Laurie says from the studio, ''the clash of cultures and the clash of ancient beliefs against the encroachment of modern life.''
How's that again?
What is the ramming of the rams supposed to mean?
One problem when a network news department uses someone else's film is that it's got to find meaning where none may exist. 
The ramming of the rams is just the ramming of the rams. 
It's not symbolic of anything except, perhaps, a headache. 
Mr. Laurie, however, is being forced to verbally connect all the random footage. 
Just after we see the rams (they're somewhere near the mouth of the river), we see Tibet. 
Nomads are tossing paper charms to the winds while they watch a horse race. 
Then there's a race on yaks. 
It's terrific footage. 
It's unlikely you've ever seen yaks thunder down the homestretch before. 
At the same time, the yak race, and most of the rest of the film, is so blatantly picturesque that we're sure the Japanese crew that made ''The Unruly Dragon'' was led on an official tour. 
That may be fine, too; it's one way of seeing China. 
On the other hand, this kind of production forces Mr. Laurie into a spoilsport role. 
The Tibetans on horseback seem to be having a wonderful time; they're wild and fierce and free. 
But then Mr. Laurie says that at least eight people were killed in rioting in Tibet last month, and that ''unrest has now spread to the Yellow River lands.''
Then we see yaks.
It doesn't add up. 
Mr. Laurie, who is properly performing his journalistic duty, is saying one thing, but the pictures say something else. 
''The Unruly Dragon'' has a fuzzy context. 
When it visits a Moslem area, we see a song festival that attracts some 100,000 people, many descended from Turkish tribes that settled long ago near the river. 
Singers sing, and Mr. Laurie says the songs indicate that ''a great pride is shown in the ethnic diversity of China.''
Then he adds, ''It should be noted, though, these Moslem singers sing in Mandarin Chinese.''
We don't know what to make of that. 
Does it mean something imporant or not?
One wishes Mr. Laurie had been at the song festival himself so that he might have told us.
''The Unruly Dragon'' often looks lovely and is never less than exotic, but it's like being on a boat ride where we keep seeing attractive vistas - it's great to see them for a while, but as the boat ride goes on they lose meaning. 
When we're back at the dock, we're not quite sure where we've been. 
ABC News is offering an excursion. 
It's nice, but you may wish that the folks from ''Close-Up'' were along.

text:
