file: U.S.-CHINA TIES_ LOWER EXPECTATIONS_News Analysis.txt
text:
ï»¿
As Secretary of State George P. Shultz begins his visit to Peking, the prevailing view in the Administration, according to many officials, is that China is decades away from becoming a true global power, and that the United States has little to gain now in trying to play off China against the Soviet Union.
Over the last two years, officials acknowledged, the Reagan team has gone from the extreme of thinking of Peking as a major diplomatic counterweight to Moscow almost to the other extreme of simply seeing China as a struggling Asian giant lagging far behind Japan.
For the Administration, China remains an important strategic anchor, holding almost 50 Soviet divisions on its border. 
Because of this, a key Administration official explained, ''We will try to develop the relationship with them, but not oversell it and not pay a high price for it either.''
WASHINGTON, Feb. 
1 - As Secretary of State George P. Shultz begins his visit to Peking, the prevailing view in the Administration, according to many officials, is that China is decades away from becoming a true global power, and that the United States has little to gain now in trying to play off China against the Soviet Union.
Administration officials believe that the necessary price to preserve China as an anchor was paid last August with the promulgation of the Taiwan Communique, which included an American promise to phase out arms sales to Taiwan in return for China's promise to pursue peaceful reunification with Taiwan.
Â 
Demythologizing of China
This new thinking in the Administration represents what some officials called a demythologizing of China, a substantial lowering of expectations, a sense that China and the United States cannot do very much very fast for each other - sentiments reciprocated in full measure by Chinese officials.
Accordingly, American officials said that Mr. Shultz is bearing no surprises, concessions or gifts. 
There is nothing to break the deadlock over Chinese textile exports to America, nor any major breakthroughs on requests for high technology, and above all, nothing new on Taiwan. 
He will be bringing only an old list of military items Washington would ''consider'' selling and sale approvals for computers, semiconductors and laboratory measuring instruments Peking requested some time ago.
Officials said the aims of the five-day visit, which begins Feb. 
2, are to put the relationship on a firmer long-term footing, to discuss mutual opposition to Soviet involvements in Afghanistan and Southeast Asia and to set up other meetings on defense and trade. 
If the trip is successful, a visit by Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang to Washington could follow and maybe early next year, President Reagan could go to Peking.
Â 
Triangle Turned on Its Head
Throughout the 1970's, the United States was at the apex of the great power triangle, maneuvering with Moscow and Peking to capitalize on their antagonism, seemingly in control, almost always retaining the diplomatic initiative. 
Now, with Washington's relations with China and the Soviet Union nearly frozen and with Peking and Moscow now beginning to deal with each other again, the triangle has been turned on its head.
In this inverted triangle, Peking and Moscow are maneuvering in ways that officials and outside experts feel could weaken and certainly will complicate American foreign policy.
Administration officials comfort themselves with the thought that a lowering of Chinese-Soviet tensions is not contrary to American interests, and that their courtship is not likely to go far.
There is also comfort drawn from the sense that while President Nixon constructed triangular diplomacy as a strategic device to reposition major pieces on the global chessboard to contain the Soviet Union, Moscow and Peking appear to be using the inverted triangle essentially as a tactical device to court Washington.
Â 
U.S. Trade and Technology
Mainly, both want American trade and technology. 
But while Moscow is seeking arms limitation treaties with Washington, Peking is looking for American arms.
But American relations with both Peking and Moscow are at a 12-year low, and Administration officials say there is little disposition toward making compromises with either of them that might produce a major breakthrough.
''There is a degree of unavoidability to this,'' said Helmut Sonnenfeldt of the Brookings Institution and one of the framers of triangular diplomacy in the Nixon Administration. 
''Compared with the moves we were able to make with Peking and Moscow in the early 1970's, there probably isn't as much room for maneuver. 
The issues are harder.''
To Richard C. Holbrooke, a high-ranking official in the Carter Administration, the issues are harder in good part ''because of the inaction and insensitivity of the Reagan Administration.''
''Toward Moscow, the Administration concentrated on ideological rhetoric and took over a year before getting to the table on arms control,'' he said. 
''Toward Peking, they dragged their heels to the point where even when they settled some central issues in the Taiwan Communique, the atmosphere had been poisoned.''
It was former Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. who brought about the Taiwan Communique. 
One of President Reagan's campaign pledges in 1980 was to improve relations with Taiwan.
Â 
Linking U.S. and Soviet
Now, as described by officials in the State Department, the Pentagon and the White House, the view at the top is that China is a large and important Asian country with an almost hopelessly outdated conventional military force, and its influence is restricted essentially to Asia.
Mr. Shultz's estimate of China was said to be relaxed to the point where he turned down his Asian experts twice before agreeing to make the trip.
State Department experts argued that China was going through a particularly important leadership transition, from older to younger leaders, and that this was the time to shape attitudes.
In their judgment, new attitudes in the Administration toward China were being mirrored by new Chinese attitudes toward the United States.
But what troubled some senior Administration officials, much more than it disturbed the experts, was Peking's maneuvering with Moscow and Peking's return to the formula of ''double hegemonism,'' or speaking of the Soviet Union and the United States as equal threats to peace. 
''They wanted to get our attention,'' said one official, ''and they did.''
Â 
'They Pulled Back Somewhat'
The State Department let the Chinese know of the Administration's unhappiness about the yoking of Washington and Moscow: Washington would not look kindly on providing new dual-use technology, technology that could have military and civilian applications, as long as Peking maintained an anti-American profile.
Chinese diplomats reacted quickly, calling in their American counterparts and reporters to reassure them of Peking's intentions. 
''They understand that it's one thing to get our attention, and another to go too far, and they pulled back somewhat in their public rhetoric,'' said an Administration official.
The State Department's Soviet experts also began expressing concern about the talks between Peking and Moscow. 
While granting that Chinese-Soviet detente was not in the offing, they worried about perceptions in Europe and elsewhere. 
Western European diplomats are not as comfortable as the Administration is with perceptions of the diplomatic initiative passing from American hands to Soviet and Chinese hands.

file: U.S.-CHINA TRADE DOWN 5.5_.txt
text:
ï»¿
Trade between the United States and China in 1982 fell slightly, for the first time in six years, to $5.2 billion, according to figures issued today by the United States Embassy here. 
The total was down 5.5 percent from the record high of $5.5 billion in 1981.
The value of American exports to China declined 19 percent last year, to $2.9 billion. 
By contrast, Chinese exports to the United States rose 20.5 percent, to $2.3 billion, with the most significant gains being in petroleum products and clothing.
PEKING, Feb. 
2 - Trade between the United States and China in 1982 fell slightly, for the first time in six years, to $5.2 billion, according to figures issued today by the United States Embassy here.
China continued to run a deficit in trade with the United States. 
The gap was $628.4 million last year, but this was 63 percent less than 1981's $1.7 billion deficit. 
The last time China had a modest surplus in trade with America was in 1977.
China's Ministry of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade reported last Saturday that China achieved a record surplus of $4.6 billion last year in overall foreign trade. 
Chinese exports rose to $21.6 billion while imports remained virtually constant at $17 billion.
Â 
Statistics May Help Shultz
The United States, China's third-largest trading partner after Hong Kong and Japan, accounted for 13 percent of Chinese trade volume last year.
The trade figures, which the American Embassy released shortly before the arrival in Peking today of Secretary of State George P. Shultz, seemed likely to help him in his meetings with Chinese officials this week. 
China has complained about Washington's restrictions on the transfer of American technology and on the importing of Chinese textiles by the United States.
Following the failure of the two countries to reach a new agreement on Chinese textiles last month, Washington imposed unilateral curbs freezing the imports at previous levels. 
Peking had been holding out for a larger share of the American market.
The latest statistics show that Chinese exports of clothing and accessories jumped 49 percent last year, to $619.9 million, accounting for more than a quarter of total Chinese sales to the United States. 
Textile fibers and yarns and fabrics declined slightly. 
But China evidently expanded its textile exports far more than the previous agreement had envisioned.
Â 
Some U.S. 
Products Banned
China retaliated against the curbs by announcing last month that it would ban future imports of American cotton, soybeans and synthetic fibers. 
But these categories of American exports had already fallen sharply, according to the 1982 trade figures, because the Chinese no longer needed them after several record harvests. 
Thus Peking's ban was mainly a symbolic gesture.
The latest American statistics indicated some shifts in the pattern of China's commerce with the United States, which has climbed sixfold from the $97.5 million level of a decade ago, when the two countries resumed normal trade relations.
With its record harvests, China has cut back on buying some American farm products. 
But China has bought more of the technology that is wanted for its current modernization drive, as well as lumber and fertilizer, which are in limited supply in China.
Agricultural exports to China from the United States declined last year in all categories except corn, which tripled in value, reaching $189.4 million.
Â 
Wheat Value Shows Decline
Wheat sales to China, because of depressed prices, dropped by $222.3 million, although the tonnage of shipments increased. 
Wheat remains the largest American commodity sold to the Chinese, with a value last year of $1.05 billion.
China has agreed to buy at least 6 million tons of grain annually from the United States. 
In the fiscal year 1982, China purchased 9.2 million tons, up from 8.4 million tons the year before. 
Western agricultural experts expect China to buy 9 million more tons during the present fiscal year.
Last year, China earned $198 million by selling crude oil to the United States, compared with virtually nothing in 1981. 
China's sales of other petroleum products rose 36 percent, to nearly $400 million.
Chinese purchases of American coal-cutting, mining and welldrilling machinery jumped more than 53 percent, to $45 million. 
Office machines and computers rose even more sharply, by nearly 64 percent, to account for $36.2 million of China's imports. 
Scientific instruments from the United States also grew 18 percent, reaching $65 million.

file: U.S.-PEKING RELATIONS CALLED DELICATE.txt
text:
ï»¿
The prospect of American military sales to Taiwan is producing a ''very delicate moment'' in relations between the United States and China, former Vice President Walter F. Mondale said today.
His assessment, Mr. Mondale said, was based upon private talks with Chinese leaders, principally Deputy Prime Ministers Deng Xiaopeng and Wan Li, over the last few days here.
Speaking to reporters at a news conference concluding his four-day visit as a guest of the Chinese Government, Mr. Mondale said: ''I cannot deny, based on my discussions, that the current disputes surrounding the potential arms sales to Taiwan - the potential advanced fighters and the rest - is creating a very delicate moment in our relationship.''
Â 
Delay in Delivering Computers
Mr. Mondale said that an additional, although ''not fundamental,'' irritant for the Chinese was continuing American delay in delivering several large computers that the Carter Administration had promised, including one that China wants for a census next year.
Prospect of American military sales to Taiwan produces "very delicate moment" in relations between US and China
The computer sale, arranged when Mr. Mondale made an official visit to China in 1979, remained ''seemingly tied up in red tape,'' he said. 
A member of Mr. Mondale's party here said privately that Mr. Deng had specifically asked what happened to the computers when he met with Mr. Mondale this morning.
Mr. Mondale's appraisal of Chinese-American relations was reminiscent of a statement by Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. a week ago that the arms sales issue had raised ''a very worrisome specter'' for Washington and Peking in their future relations.
Mr. Mondale indicated that prospective military sales to Taiwan came up in his meeting with Mr. Deng as well as with some other officials, but he declined to give any details of the Chinese remarks beyond saying that ''they were very general in nature and very similar to statements that have been made public on the issue.''
Â 
Arms Sales Called 'Litmus Test'
In several officially sanctioned press commentaries recently, the Chinese Government has called the military sales issue a ''litmus test'' of American respect for China's soveriegnty and has said that China would have to ''pull back'' from its developing relationship with the United States if the Reagan Administration went ahead with the sales to Taiwan.
But Peking has carefully avoided spelling out what the consequences would be, evidently to avoid limiting its options by its own public statements. 
Many diplomats here feel that Mr. Deng would have to retaliate in some fashion to protect his flanks from remaining political opponents in the bureaucracy and army, but the diplomats disagree on how serious the consequences might be.
Two senior officials of the Reagan Administration who visited China recently insisted that the Chinese did not bring up the Taiwan arms issue with them. 
Treasury Secretary Donald T. Regan said last week that his meetings here were purely economic. 
Under Secretary of State Walter J. Stoessel, Jr., told reporters two weeks ago that his talks with Chinese officials centered on general issues of world politics rather than specific issues like Taiwan.
But Mr. Mondale said today that the question of the sale of American advanced arms to Taiwan ''was discussed very seriously'' during his visit and that ''there is no question that the Chinese are very concerned about the issue.''
Â 
Report of Decision on Sale
News reports from Washington have said that the Reagan Administration has ruled out selling the highly advanced F-16 jet fighter-bomber to Taiwan and has decided instead to supply the F-5E Tiger with an improved electronics and weapons systems, as well as the F-5G Tigershark, a substantially newer high-performance aircraft that is still less potent than the F-16. 
The State Department has denied that any decision has been made.
Since Taiwan already assembles the basic F-5 fighter, some Pekingbased diplomats speculate that Washington might try to convince Peking that these newer versions are merely replacements for present aircraft and did not represent qualitatively new technology.
But after his talks here, Mr. Mondale said that ''the Chinese will be looking at the capability of the plane and not the number or the name described.''

file: UNABASHEDLY, THE BUSINESS OF HONG KONG IS MONEY.txt
text:
ï»¿
A foreign banker new to Hong Kong tells of how, shortly after being posted here, he decided to close the office at 8 o'clock every night so his Chinese staff could spend more time with their families. 
He was taken aside and politely but firmly told to discard that notion, since nothing would be more likely to foment an office revolt than limiting working hours.
Hong Kong's reason for being seems to be unabashedly, singlemindedly to make money. 
That is its philosophy, its ideology, its worldview. 
The traditional New Year greeting here is, ''Happy New Year, and may you make a fortune.''
Negotiations between officials representing Hong Kong, Great Britain and China begin to discuss the future of colony
''Hong Kong is the last truly capitalist place on earth,'' said Jimmy D. McGregor, a former top Government official who is director of the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce.
Â 
Concern About the Future
What people in Hong Kong fear now is that this model of unfettered capitalism may be altered as a result of the negotiations between China and Britain over the British colony's future.
''People here are very worried, very concerned,'' said Joseph Cheng, a political science professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong. 
''We do not want our economic system drastically changed and our living standards lowered.''
The first round of talks on the future of Hong Kong took place in Peking last Thursday and Friday, when Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher of Britain and Chinese leaders met. 
As expected, the initial discussions produced only a general statement that further negotiations were planned, with the goal being an agreement that will maintain ''the stabilityI and prosperity of Hong Kong.''
Mrs. Thatcher arrived in Hong Kong today to meet with the colony's leaders.
Peking says it will reassert its sovereignty over Hong Kong when the 99-year lease on the so-called New Territories, accounting for 90 percent of the colony's land, expires in 1997.
Though the lease does not run out for another 15 years, Hong Kong's future status must soon be clarified. 
Many property mortgages and other business contracts run a 15-year term. 
Already, business leaders say, investments are being delayed. 
If the matter is left unresolved, it could seriously hurt Hong Kong's economy.
The key issue is not sovereignty itself, but who actually runs Hong Kong. 
No one here seems to care whose flag flies above the citystate. 
''The Union Jack isn't all that pretty anyway,'' one British expatriate said.
At the same time, there is almost universal resistance to China's playing any genuine part in running Hong Kong, even under a joint administration. 
''All indications are that the leaders in Peking are quite ignorant of what makes Hong Kong work and how capitalism operates,'' said Lawrence Chui, 34 years old, an investment manager.
Â 
'Close to Independence'
''We want something that is very close to independence,'' said Christine Loh, chairman of the Hong Kong Observers, a group of politically active Chinese professionals.
For the foreseeable future, most agree that the British, as symbols of the economic status quo, will have to retain the key administrative posts in order to maintain business confidence.
In many ways, Hong Kong is already independent. 
Although the colony is administered by a Governor appointed by Britain, and a council that he appoints, London is not consulted before Government decisions are made. 
The real objective of the negotiations with Peking, one British diplomat said, is to ''replace the fiction that Hong Kong is part of England with the fiction that it is part of China.''
One industrialist pointed out that Hong Kong's political and economic system is entirely different from that in England. 
''And thank heaven for that,'' he added with feeling.
Government in Hong Kong, though growing, is small. 
The economy is freewheeling and largely untouched by public-sector regulation.
Â 
Maximum Tax Rate: 15%
To anyone who has been perturbed about having so little of a paycheck left after the tax collectors get through with it, one statistic tells much about Hong Kong: the maximum rate of taxation on personal income is 15 percent. 
For corporations, the ceiling is 16.5 percent.
Most governments today are plagued by huge deficits, but Hong Kong runs a surplus. 
Personal wealth and living standards have risen sharply in recent years. 
In the decade 1971-81, per-capita income more than doubled, even though the population increased by 1.1 million, to 5.1 million.
Hong Kong's system of winner-take-all capitalism results in vast disparities in wealth and circumstances. 
Rolls-Royce and Mercedes Benz sedans are a common sight, but so are squalid squatter tenements that house roughly 600,000 people, more than one-tenth of the population.
Much of the squatter problem, however, is a result of Hong Kong's openness to immigrants. 
It has taken in more than three times as many Indochinese refugees as its larger, richer East Asian neighbor, Japan. 
Also, Hong Kong absorbs 65,000 people a year from China.
Â 
Immigrants' Goal: The Peak
The immigrants come because of the promise that hard work will pay off in a better life for them and their children. 
The animating myth of Hong Kong has long been that the noodle-shop owner on the waterfront can, if he has enough courage, brains and luck, someday live on the Peak, where Hong Kong's millionaires reside. 
And it is not always a myth.
There are rags-to-riches stories here that would have made Horatio Alger's jaw drop. 
Nearly all the superrich of Hong Kong are Chinese. 
Take Yue-kong Pao, the billionaire shipping magnate whose assets include probably the largest fleet of privately owned ships in the world.
''He started with one beaten-up rust bucket,'' said a crusty old Scot who has been around long enough to know. 
Mr. Pao was in Peking last week, seen on television with Mrs. Thatcher and the rest of the British delegation at official receptions. 
These days he is properly referred to as Sir Yue-kong, having been knighted in 1978 by Queen Elizabeth.

text:
ï»¿
LOVE MUST NOT BE FORGOTTEN By Zhang Jie. 
207 pp. 
San Francisco: China Books & Periodicals. 
Cloth, $16.95. 
Paper, $8.95.
ZHANG JIE, the author of this collection of six short stories and a novella, is one of the foremost women writers in China. 
In the summer of 1982 she toured the United States as a member of the official Chinese Writers Association and so charmed her American hosts that one of them, the noted poet and essayist Annie Dillard, devoted half of her book ''Encounters With Chinese Writers'' to a lavish description of Ms. Zhang's winning character, though not much about her writings. 
In China, at age 50, she enjoys a degree of pre-eminence chiefly for her controversial novel ''Leaden Wings'' (1981), a roman a clef that deals with government bureaucracy and its manifold problems. 
The work won not only a prestigious prize in China but a translation award in West Germany. 
Ms. Zhang has also been hailed as China's first feminist novelist for her fearlessness in ''lashing out at male supremacy, hypocrisy, corruption, bureaucracy, nepotism, and other malpractices holding up China's advance,'' as Gladys Yang tells us in her preface to this book. 
These stories give the Western reader a true sampling of such social issues and, to some extent, of the author's real-istic art.
Reading contemporary Chinese fiction may be an ''acquired taste'' (a condescending remark perhaps unintended by Ms. Dillard in her book mentioned above) presumably because of its usually pervasive political ideology. 
But in these stories we do not see ''politics in command.''
Rather, it is the portraits that loom large; vivid and life-size, they are drawn on a human scale and deal with the familiar human problems of love, marriage, divorce, work, emotional sacrifice and death. 
The stories collected in ''Love Must Not Be Forgotten'' clearly show a feminist sensibility; the author unmistakably identifies with the women characters featured in three substantial stories. 
The title story reveals, through the familiar form of a discovered diary, the unbelievably romantic ''secret'' of a woman's lifelong devotion outside her marriage to a married man with whom she has never ''once even clasped hands!''
In the second story, ''Emerald,'' two strong-willed, educated women devote their lives to a handsome weakling; one of them, the story's heroine, suffers infamy and torture when she takes the blame for her lover's alleged petty crime during the Cultural Revolution and later secretly bears him an illegitimate son. 
The novella, titled ''The Ark,'' depicts three divorced women living in a rundown apartment, victims of shattered romantic illusions, all having to cope with everyday problems in a male-dominated society. 
Despite its sprawling, unstructured narrative, ''The Ark'' is also the most authentic and universal story in the volume.
Surely no American reader needs to acquire a Sinological taste to savor the following description in the novella of a typical Sunday morning in the women's apartment: ''A large pile of dirty dishes had collected in the sink over the past two days, and not a single clean bowl remained in the cupboard. 
. . . The water quickly turned murky, with a layer of oil bubbles floating on the surface. 
. . . They always seemed so busy, yet how was it that they never seemed to do anything properly?''
However, unlike the usual Chinese prototypes, these women all smoke and swear (the striking earthiness of their Chinese curses is less intense in the uninspired English translation). 
Even in Socialist China, it still takes courage to write like that.
On the other hand, the stories about men are weak: two - ''An Unfinished Record'' and ''Under the Hawthorne'' - deal with older males, one dying and the other hospitalized in a sanitarium. 
A third story, ''The Time Is Not Yet Ripe,'' is a mild satire about a party bureaucrat frustrated in his maneuvers to bar a nonparty friend from promotion. 
Only one story deals with the younger generation; ''Who Knows How to Live'' focuses on a heavily idealized portrait of a young woman bus conductor who handles with exemplary ease the obnoxious advances of one young man and gently accepts the friendship of another. 
WHEN the story ''Love Must Not Be Forgotten'' was first published in 1979, Ms. Zhang, like one of her characters in ''The Ark,'' came under fire from some conservative critics who accused her of glorifying a married woman's love for a married man -something that apparently does not meet with the socialist ideal of correct human behavior. 
It is a reflection of the liberalizing trend since then that in her more recent stories she is able to cut through such ideological hypocrisy and delve into the unhappy aspects of marriage and divorce. 
In defiance of all rosy visions, Ms. Zhang's fiction appears to deny that women are liberated in post-Liberation China. 
If her feminism does not evince the expected militancy, she nevertheless shows a respect for genuine emotions, particularly those of women. 
Indeed, one could conclude that Ms. Zhang is as much a romantic as she is a feminist.
But with all such outpourings of the heart, Zhang Jie is unable to exercise control over her narratives. 
I have read these stories in both Chinese and English and must admit that the original texts are as sentimental and full of descriptive cliches and overblown prose as can be found in the somewhat toned-down translations (some by such well-regarded translators as Gladys Yang and W. J. F. Jenner).
Despite the eminence Zhang Jie now enjoys, there are more outstanding practitioners of fictional art in China - both male and female - especially among the young generation. 
Though contemporary Chinese literature is taught in some colleges in this country, Western bias has precluded its broader exposure to the general public. 
As a result, China Books & Periodicals' initiative in launching with this book a series on New Chinese Fiction should be applauded. 
Perhaps time is still not ripe for contemporary Chinese literature from China and Taiwan to compete with modern Japanese and South American works in the American market. 
(The latter now exert a powerful impact on many young Chinese writers.) With the publication of this volume (and a similar collection, ''Chrysanthemum & Other Stories'' by Feng Jicai last year), a beginning step has at last been taken to introduce current works of Chinese literature to Americans.

text:

In the three and a half years since Vietnam invaded Cambodia, a stalemate has developed between Hanoi and most other governments around the world, which have adamantly refused to accept the invasion's legitimacy or results.
Vietnam, with as many as 200,000 troops in Cambodia, maintains a government in Phnom Penh and says it liberated the country from the atrocious rule of Pol Pot. 
It defends its occupation as a necessary defense against China and has often termed its action ''irreversible.''
With China's aid, however, Mr. Pol Pot's guerrillas still opppose the Vietnamese from strongholds on the Thai border. 
The United Nations continues to seat Mr. Pol Pot's representative in the General Assembly. 
An international conference on Cambodia has demanded that Vietnam withdraw its troops and let the United Nations supervise a Cambodian election. 
And since 1979 Vietnam's critics - including the United States, much of Western Europe, Japan and, not least, the non-Communist Association of Southeast Asian Nations -have denied it economic aid.
Vietnam is seen mounting full-scale diplomatic effort aimed at advancing its views on invasion of CambodiaVietnamese Initiative Sighted
Recently international pressure, threats, frustration and diplomatic initiatives have shown signs of jiggling the Cambodian chessboard. 
One of the most closely watched of these developments has been the growing evidence that Vietnam is starting a full-scale diplomatic initiative designed to advance its view on the Cambodian question.
Whether Vietnam's efforts can succeed is unclear. 
But that they have already made a mark became clear last week when most of the Asean foreign ministers announced that they welcomed - though in some cases skeptically - a proposed tour of non-Communist Southeast Asian nations later this summer by Vietnam's Foreign Minister, Nguyen Co Thach.
Whether that announcement in turn prodded the three major factions of anti-Vietnamese Cambodians to talk again of uniting after years of suspicion and hatred is also not certain. 
Diplomats in Bangkok, however, said Thursday that after a year of effort a formal coalition had been arranged among Cambodia's former chief of state, Prince Norodom Sihanouk; his former Prime Minister, Son Sann, who commands a few thousand Cambodian guerrillas, and the Pol Pot group, which commands as many as 30,000 troops and has avoided Vietnam's attempts to destroy it.
Today, in a statement monitored here, the Vietnam press agency denounced Asean's pledge of support for the coalition of resistance groups. saying ''the Asean countries are doing only harm to their organization.''
Â 
U.N. Vote Due in September
The effect of these developments on Cambodia may not be known until September, when the General Assembly will again vote on whether to seat a Cambodian Government that does not govern. 
By then, Vietnam's critics hope, Mr. Pol Pot will have gained more standing through formal ties with nationalist leaders who are untainted by his murderous record.
It is largely in anticipation of the United Nations session in September, as well as out of an interest in any shift in Hanoi's attitude concerning Cambodia, that Western and Asian officials have been carefully following the Vietnamese diplomatic initiative.
Since last fall Vietnameese officials, and particularly Mr. Thach, have argued that Vietnam is sincerely interested in peace and that Hanoi remains its own master despite its military and economic dependence upon the Soviet Union.
Â 
Vietnam Cites China
Vietnam has consistently asserted that it wants to withdraw its troops from Cambodia but that it has not done so out of fear that the Chinese would fill the vacuum and reinstate Mr. Pol Pot.
And fundamentally, perhaps, Hanoi has been saying that it needs Western economic aid. 
These arguments, though eliciting skepticism in some quarters, have led to increasing contacts between Hanoi and its critics. 
These contacts have been mostly with Mr. Thach, a diplomat who earlier this year was appointed to the Vietnamese Politburo. 
Through such contacts, some Western diplomats believe, Vietnam's goal is to end its isolation.
After Vietnam's defeat at the United Nations last fall, Hanoi has pressed its arguments wherever it could - during a visit to Japan by the Mayor of Ho Chi Minh City, in the United Nations during debates over humanitarian aid to Vietnam, to visiting delegations of American war veterans and to reporters.
Â 
France Sending Credits
Last year, President Francois Mitterrand of France indicated that $23 million in French credits that had been held up under his predecessor would be given to Vietnam despite France's continuing opposition to Vietnam's presence in Cambodia. 
France has since sent high-level delegations to Hanoi.
In February, Indochina's foreign ministers, meeting in Laos, issued a low-key statement suggesting that Thailand might help reduce the tension caused by the presence by warring troops on its border with Cambodia. 
Thailand replied that it had no interest in dealing on strictly bilateral terms with Vietnam, and it responded cooly to a proposal that it join Vietnam in disarming Cambodian guerrillas.
In April, Mr. Thach visited West Germany, France, Sweden and Belgium, all of which have provided economic aid to Vietnam but none of which approves its Cambodian policy. 
Chinese and most Western diplomats later called the visit a flop, since Mr. Thach's Chinese-Cambodian arguments were blandly received, and he came away with no new financial commitments. 
Mr. Thach, however, said in an interview in Hanoi last month that, despite differences ''on our military presence in Cambodia,'' the European foreign ministers ''understood better than before.''
Â 
3-Step Plan for Peace
Last month Mr. Thach summoned the Western ambassadors in Hanoi to brief them on his European trip and to outline a three-stage plan for peace in Cambodia. 
In the first stage, he said, Hanoi would unconditionally withdraw some troops.

By HENRY KAMM
BANGKOK - In Southeast Asia, where for more than a century the only dynamic forces were alien - Europe first, America, Japan and China later - a new power has come into being since 1975. 
Its actions and, perhaps even more, its assumed intentions are sending shivers down the spines of statesmen and politicians, as well as ordinary citizens.
Even neighbors who do not subscribe to a simplistic ''domino theory'' see in Vietnam a cause for worry. 
Hanoi has gobbled up Laos and Cambodia, the two neutralist states that served as buffers between the Communist world and pro-Western nations in the region and its armed might encircles the large northeastern bulge of Thailand.
AN-A
Last week, Secretary General Kurt Waldheim of the United Nations concluded a four-day visit to Hanoi and Bangkok persuaded that both Governments were willing to talk but that neither was ready to make the concessions that would give negotiations a chance of success.
If that were not enough to frighten Southeast Asians, Vietnam has also teetered from its neutrality between the two principal Communist powers and fallen entirely into the Soviet camp, grievously offending China. 
Soviet warships come and go in Vietnam's ports, and military transport planes regularly overfly anti-Soviet countries to deliver tools of war to Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos.
From these realities, differing conclusions have been drawn, but even those who believe that Hanoi's goals of dominance do not reach beyond the borders of former French Indochina have been shocked by Hanoi's bald aggression in Cambodia. 
Few in Asia set stock by Hanoi's pretensions to humanitarian concern when it overthrew the brutal regime of Prime Minister Pol Pot; until Phnom Penh broke relations, Hanoi ritually praised Cambodia as a brotherly nation. 
Vietnam's easy resort to military force has convinced many that a power of such bellicosity constitutes a menace to the non-Communist countries, whose small armies tend more to be bases of political power than military bastions. 
Whether Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines and Burma, which deeply distrust China, share the belief of Thailand and Singapore that Vietnam is, by its own design and with Soviet complicity, out for regional conquest has not been the issue since the invasion of Cambodia. 
A consensus exists that all in the region must be on guard.
In this context, Vietnam's brief incursion into Thai border villages in June provoked a demonstration of unity in support of Thailand. 
Even countries that feel uneasy in finding themselves on the same side as China were impressed by clear signals that Vietnam, for the first time using military might against a non-Communist nation, wanted its readiness to do so understood. 
What frightened many political leaders was that Hanoi made no attempt to describe the incursion as an act of hot pursuit or a local action by a unit commander. 
Vietnam made clear that it felt its anger over Bangkok's cooperation with the Pol Pot remnants entitled it to use armed force to teach Thailand a lesson on Thai soil.
Bangkok's fear of Vietnam's bellicosity is real, even if the premise that Hanoi desires to annex Thai territory may not be. 
The Government's hard line is matched by a popular perception of Vietnam as menacing and the continued disgorging of tens of thousands of refugees from the Vietnamese domain hardens this belief. 
Premier Pham Van Dong's olive branch visit to Thailand and other Southeast Asian countries three months before the full-scale attack on Cambodia in January 1979 is viewed as characteristic of Vietnamese duplicity. 
Thailand has aligned itself closely with China in adamant opposition to recognition of the Vietnamese puppet government in Cambodia, in strong support for the Pol Pot regime and in a border policy that favors the Pol Pot remnants in their enclaves. 
Its insistence that international food aid must be channeled to Pol Pot forces as well as to bona fide refugees has engaged Bangkok in angry controversy with international organizations.
Thailand finds encouragement in this policy, whether intended or not, from the United States. 
Although Washington never recognized the Pol Pot regime in power, American policy shifted, after Vietnam dislodged it, to backing its right to hold Cambodia's seat in the United Nations. 
The United States made clear that, between two governments it does not recognize, it prefers the one that has China's support, no matter how atrocious its human rights record, over the one backed by Moscow. 
Whatever chances may have existed for a reversal of the American policy - a shift might help the survival of Cambodians by encouraging Vietnam to adopt a more humanitarian attitude toward distribution of international food aid - have been vitiated by the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. 
In the present mood toward Moscow, it is unlikely that Washington will confer even implicit recognition on the conquest of a nation by a Soviet ally.
Non-Communist Southeast Asia, the United States and the rest of the West appear firmly entrenched in attitudes toward Vietnam that parallel China's. 
But Vietnam's position is equally firm and the balance of forces in Cambodia makes it unlikely that Hanoi will yield in its insistence that the situation is irreversible. 
The highest Vietnamese leaders emphatically made that point to Mr. Waldheim. This leaves Thailand and the other Southeast Asian nations behind it supporting a force whose hopes cannot go beyond resisting strongly enough to survive and continuing indefinitely a war it cannot win without active Chinese intervention against Vietnam. 
Hanoi's actions have set off reactions that seem to assure it of lasting hostility in the region and have made Southeast Asia an arena of Soviet-Chinese conflict.

file: VIEWS OF SPORTS_IN CHINA, A NEW PASTIME, THOUGH NOT QUITE NATIONAL.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE North China air was a cool 55 degrees and the silver poplar trees were budding. 
A slight breeze puffed swirls of dust up from the athletic field. 
The players were already warming up, woolen winter underwear peeping out from under the cuffs of their baggy pants. 
Their movements were awkward and a constant laughter belied their nervousness.
This was the first baseball game to be played in rural Shanxi Province, several hundred miles west of Peking, since the sport was banned following the 1949 revolution. 
Some baseball equipment had been found locked in a closet in the field house of the agricultural university where I was teaching.
''Must have been left here by some American missionaries,'' said the student who had brought the equipment to my office. 
Several cloth softballs, their wrappings yellow with age, rocked gently on my desk. 
The dry climate had also preserved the stubby baseball gloves and kept the slim bats from rotting.
First we talked about getting up a game. 
But, as so often happens in China, politics threatened to get in the way. 
Baseball had been introduced to China by American missionaries in the 19th century. 
Because of this association with the West, the Chinese Communists had denounced baseball as a bourgeois and decadent sport. 
Although the Chinese government was now seeking rapprochement with the West, change comes slowly to backwater regions like Shanxi Province. 
The student hemmed and hawed, unwilling to take responsibility for organizing the game. 
And so it fell to me. 
I scheduled the game for the following Sunday, telling only selected friends. 
If threatened by the authorities for playing baseball, they could always say they did it to please me, a visiting American English teacher who could not be punished for political mistakes.
So it was that one nippy afternoon a few years ago, baseball returned to Shanxi. 
Two dozen players gathered on a rutted yellow dirt field at the back of the small campus. 
A major road cut by the field, leading to a college store and a gate, beyond which peasants sold their produce in an open market.
One elderly player, a retired gym teacher, had umpired a few games in the 1940's, and could still say ''ball'' and ''strike'' in English. 
He explained the rules, or what he remembered of them, to the other players. 
And by dribbling lime powder from a paper bag, he marked off a rough diamond on the school athletic field.
My team batted first. 
A powerful tractor driver named Zhang from Manchuria stepped into the batter's box. 
He swung hard at an inside pitch and met it squarely. 
The bat, brittle with age, split in two and rifled back over our heads. 
Zhang stared at the stump of wood left in his hand and then took off for third.
''No!
No!,'' we screamed from the sideline. 
''Run to first!''
Zhang wheeled sharply and charged diagonally across the diamond. 
He collided with the pitcher. 
But scrambling on his hands and knees, he made it to first and stood up triumphant, yellow dust billowing from his once blue clothing.
The next batter, a graduate student named Liu, sauntered up to the batter's box. 
He spat on the ground and mashed the spittle into the earth. 
Then he deliberately twisted his blue Mao cap around so the brim covered the nape of his neck. 
''I saw an American player do this on television,'' he said.
Liu hit a grounder. 
He rounded first just as the first baseman caught the ball. 
Liu headed for second, the first baseman chasing after him with the ball. 
Meanwhile, Zhang had stopped at second, probably assuming that players progress only one base at a time. 
Liu barreled into him. 
They took the first and second basemen down with them.
A wheat specialist named Mei was up next. 
He said he was an old hand, having played baseball in missionary school in the 1940's. 
He was very short, and by crouching down he practically eliminated his strike zone. 
He got to first on a walk.
By now the game was attracting quite a crowd. 
Peasants and students were swarming onto the field. 
In China, when people see a line, they stand behind it. 
So here they stood on the edge of the infield. 
When our team took the field, I played shortstop. 
I tried to explain to the hundreds of people standing between second and third that this was dangerous. 
But the sight of a tall foreigner waving his arms and speaking Chinese only caused the crowd to swell.
A line drive was hit to third. 
I dove into the crowd, knocking over bicycles and trampling on feet in a frenzy to get the ball. 
But it seemed to have vanished. 
Finally someone tapped me on the arm. 
It was an old peasant woman tottering on bound feet, her cracked lips spread wide in a toothless grin. 
Her hands were raised to me as if offering tea. 
But she was proffering the softball instead.
The old woman was luckier than a student who was beaned a short time later by a pop fly. 
As the ball plummeted down, the crowd in the outfield scattered as if being strafed by a fighter plane. 
But one student hesitated for a moment and the ball thudded down on her. 
She fell to the ground clutching her head to ward off any further attacks. 
After that, people decided that maybe it was wise to move to the sidelines.
The game continued for four more innings. 
The most dramatic play was made by a boiler repairman playing right field who stopped the ball from rolling into the outhouse cesspool. 
The final score was 10-10; all the runs scored on errors.
For several days afterward, we nervously awaited a reaction from the authorities. 
But no wall posters appeared condemning baseball. 
At the weekly political study session, the game was not mentioned. 
In China, no reaction means tacit approval. 
We began playing baseball every Sunday afternoon.
Soon, the workers in a nearby herbal-medicine factory organized a team and challenged us. 
Then a chemical fertilizer plant got up a team and joined the competition. 
By summer, 10 teams were battling each other. 
And with each game, more baseball equipment kept turning up. 
It was like the equipment I had seen on my desk in the early spring, old and worn after having been locked away, presumably forever.

file: VISITORS STUDY U.S. MODERN DANCE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Merce Cunningham walked through his Manhattan studio yesterday as an international group of choreographers waited to watch class there. 
''Can't we meet him?'' the choreographers asked hopefully. 
They had seen Mr. Cunningham's company perform in their home countries, but to meet the choreographer himself was a special dream. 
When Mr. Cunningham stopped and talked informally with them, it was the climax of an extraordinary six-week exploration of American modern dance that began in North Carolina.
Representing countries from Argentina to Zaire that have comparatively little or no modern-dance tradition, the choreographers have been participants in the just-ended International Choreographers Workshop sponsored by the American Dance Festival and the United States Information Agency at the Duke University campus in Durham, N.C., where the festival is based.
There, over the past six weeks, 15 choreographers from 12 nations went to dance programs presented by the summer festival, which included everything from performance-art pieces and ballroom dancing to the work of leading American modern-dance choreographers.
They took part in the classes presented by the festival, which also trains young dancers - classes that ranged from anatomy to high-energy upheavals taught by Pooh Kaye, an experimentalist choreographer. 
And they were encouraged to create their own pieces during the project, working often with festival students and with music by composers participating in the festival.
Â 
'Different Directions'
Participants in the three-year-old project are selected on the recommendation of cultural experts and American Embassies around the world, 19 of which submitted 40 nominations for this summer's workshop. 
''The purpose is to give people from other countries an opportunity to enhance their idea of American culture,'' Stephanie Reinhart, head of the workshop, said. 
''And what could be a more wonderful vehicle than American modern dance?
We are trying here to give the choreographers an overview of the many different directions of modern dance.''
Alejandro Carlos Cervera, a soft-spoken young choreographer from Argentina who became known at the workshop for his colorful T-shirts, got just that from the project. 
''I think it's great that in one place there is African, classical and jazz dance,'' he said. 
''There are no walls here.''
Some aspects of American culture were familiar. 
At a homey potluck dinner given by a local family, Marion D'Cruz of Malaysia belted out ''Bye Bye Blackbird'' and ''Fascination'' as one of the family's neighbors accompanied her on the piano. 
That morning Dr. Yang Meiqi of China had demonstrated Chinese traditional dancing, which she teaches as a dean at the Guangdong Dance College in Canton. 
That night she danced a decorous Charleston.
Gopal Dubey brought his expertise as a leading interpreter of Chhau dance in Bihar, India, to bear on the workshop experience. 
Dr. Yang wondered if rigid teaching methods in China could benefit from a dose of the exploratory spirit of American modern dance. 
Reyes de Lara, an experimentalist from Spain, spoke of finding new steps in Spanish dancing. 
''I'm not an investigator of new movement,'' Mr. Cervera observed. 
''My work is abstract. 
But dramatic things start to come out and make the dance more theatrical. 
I suppose that is my history and the history of my country. 
In countries that are troubled, it is harder to keep things abstract. 
You feel you have to comment. 
Reality comes out.''
At one point, Dr. Yang asked Charles Reinhart, festival director, why dancers swing their limbs in the Jose Limon style. 
''Why not?''
Mr. Reinhart answered. 
It was a revelation. 
For Lin Hsiu-wei of Taiwan, there were other revelations. 
''It's very interesting to find your own nature in movement,'' she said, talking of Miss Kaye's classes. 
''Before, when I choreographed, I always set the movement like a computer. 
Now I want to do everything new.''
Miss Kaye was a figure of some controversy. 
''The kinds of things Pooh Kaye shows in her class are very hard for Chinese to accept,'' Dr. Yang said, speaking through an interpreter, Shuo Pang. 
''I think she is very good at developing a body self, but art is not only for creating some movement for bodies. 
And some of her movements the Chinese have already developed. 
I talked with her very frankly. 
I asked her to come to China.''
The workshop left some feeling a little wistful. 
Dr. Yang hopes to establish China's first university modern-dance department. 
''But there is a serious problem of teachers,'' she said. 
''I wonder if the American Dance Festival would have the generosity to provide teachers to my college.''
Sharon Kinney, an American choreographer who served as workshop coordinator, sighed as she talked of the project. 
''I wish there could be a program like this in another country,'' she said. 
''I'd like to be in it.''

file: VOTING IN TAIWAN IS A SIGN OF GAINS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Kuomintang's particularly one-sided victory in Saturday's elections for the national legislature represents an acknowledgment by the voters of Taiwan that the ruling party has progressed in three related areas of social change, officials said today.
The areas are referred to here as democratization, Taiwanization and rejuvenation.
Democratization, officials said, means expanding the scope of elections and increasing freedom of speech and political activity. 
Taiwanization refers to bringing more native Taiwanese, who comprise 85 percent of the island's 18.5 million people, into positions of responsibility in the Government and the ruling party. 
Rejuvenation is adding new blood to the ranks of the Kuomintang, the Chinese Nationalists, led by Chiang Kai-shek, who fled to Taiwan in 1949 after the Communists took control of China.
Kuomintang's one-sided victory in elections for national legislature represents acknowledgment by voters of Taiwan that ruling party has progressed in democratization, Taiwanization and rejuvenation, officals say (S)
There has been gradual progress on all three fronts, despite occasional setbacks.
In the elections Saturday the Kuomintang won 62 of the 71 seats that were at stake. 
Most of the seats in the 371-member legislature are held by lifetime members elected on the mainland in 1947, who still nominally claim to represent districts in China.
Â 
Lifetime Members Dwindling
However, the 71 ''supplementary'' seats decided by election this year compare with 11 in 1969, when the first such elections were held here. 
The lifetime members, whose average age is 77, are often inactive and their numbers are being reduced by deaths at a rate of more than one a month.
Most of the elected legislators are native Taiwanese. 
Today, in fact, more than 70 percent of the Kuomintang's two million members are Taiwanese- born and only 5 percent are 75 years of age or older.
''The stereotype that the Kuomintang is a party of old people from the mainland is simply not true,'' said Chen Li-an, a top party official.
Amid the trend toward social change of recent years, there have been some notable exceptions. 
The most striking example came in 1979, in the aftermath of anti-Government demonstrations in the southern city of Kaohsiung. 
Some of the dissidents involved in the demonstrations were punished with stiff jail sentences, inordinately severe in the view of many people.
Fang Su-min, the wife of one of the jailed dissidents, handily won a seat in the legislature in the elections, in an expression of personal and political sympathy. 
''That issue still has not died,'' one Kuomintang member conceded.
Â 
Dissidents Treated Harshly
Many people here say the Government has sometimes dealt too harshly with dissidents. 
But most also note, as a businessman put it, that ''in terms of personal, economic and political freedom, this is heaven compared to what you will find on the other side of the Formosa Strait,'' meaning the mainland.
With the opposition divided, foreign diplomats here say they believe that the main arena for political debate and pluralism will increasingly be within the ruling party itself.
With this development, one diplomat said, there is often ''a significant split between the younger members of the party and the elders.
''The young Kuomintang members,'' he said, ''are just as critical of the elders as people outside the party.''
One of the key splits is over the pace of social change, an area in which the Nationalists were certainly not overly ambitious when they ruled the mainland. 
Still, the influence of the younger generation is evident.

file: Washington WatchClyde H. Farnsworth China, Soviet Trade Cases.txt
text:

WASHINGTON THE Commerce Department and the United
States International Trade Commission are
gearing up for major decisions on low-priced imports from China and the Soviet Union that could set a pattern in trade with centrally planned economies.
The textile industry's politically explosive case against China says that Peking's textile monopoly receives subsidies of more than 40 percent on exports to the United States because of a dual exchange rate benefiting exporters.
The domestic industry, still smarting from recently negotiated import quotas on Chinese textiles that it regards as too liberal, wants countervailing duties imposed by the Commerce Department that would practically halt the imports. 
China is the fourth-largest textile supplier to this country after Hong Kong, South Korea and Taiwan.
The State Department and other agencies fret about the broader political consequences. 
Washington and Peking have taken a number of steps since the late 1970's to improve relations. 
The cutting off of its textile trade would hardly be seen by Peking as a friendly act.
Experts believe that the case, which was prepared for the industry by a former Commerce Department official, John D. Greenwald, now with the Washington law firm of Verner, Liipfert, Bernhard & McPherson, will reach the decisive stage next April at about the time President Reagan is scheduled to visit China. 
That will also be in the heat of a political campaign that promises heavy involvement of the textile lobby, one of the most potent because of the large labor force it represents. 
Employers as well as unions filed the complaint.
Some in the Administration are urging the Commerce Department to dismiss the case, arguing that quotas are the only equitable way of dealing with centrally planned economies.
The ferroalloy industry's case against the Soviet Union involves two sizable shipments into New Orleans this year of a product known as 50 percent ferrosilicon, used in the deoxidation of steel.
The argument is that the 11,000 tons have suddenly raised imports of this sparsely traded product from 5 to 13 percent of the domestic market and are therefore causing ''market disruption.''
The Russians went from zero to 8 percent of the United States market within a three-month period.
At the urging of the National Security Council, the United States trade representative, Bill Brock, asked the trade commission to make a finding on whether the shipments constitute disruption. 
The commission's preliminary ruling may come before the end of the year.
Here, too, the penalty could be higher duties. 
The Russians already pay a 13 percent tariff on the 50 percent ferrosilicon. 
No duty is currently levied on the product if it comes from countries with whom the United States has normal trading relationships.
Competing With Exhibits
''Retaliate,'' came the order from the United States command at the Geneva-based International Labor Organization, and soon officials were wheeling into the assembly models of geothermal power plants, tractors and earth-moving equipment. 
A lightweight firefighter's suit drew cheers. 
It was made of the same material as the spacesuits of astronauts. 
Washington's decision was in response to a propaganda offensive undertaken by the Russians to try to convince third-world delegates of Moscow's industrial leadership.
''The Soviets would usually give them a couple of glasses of vodka, then show them movies of Soviet industries that were 20 years behind the American industries,'' said Barbara Dunkak, a Labor Department international affairs officer. 
Added her boss, Robert Searby, Deputy Assistant Secretary of Labor for International Labor Affairs, ''We're in a competition.''
Trucking Immunity Battle
The chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee, Bob Packwood, Republican of Oregon, took the unusual step of walking across to the House to personally urge Representative James J. Howard, Democrat of New Jersey, to withdraw an amendment that would upset the delicately balanced trucking deregulation package. 
The amendment would extend antitrust immunity for single-line freight rates two years, to July 1986. 
Mr. Howard said he could not oblige.
Senator Packwood decided he could play rough as well. 
He returned to the Senate and introduced a bill that would totally deregulate trucking by 1987.

file: WEINBERGER ARRIVES IN CHINA AND GETS A MIXED WELCOME.txt
text:
ï»¿
Secretary of Defense Caspar W. Weinberger arrived in Peking today to a Chinese welcome that was at once cool and warm.
At a banquet tonight, Defense Minister Zhang Aiping made clear that his Government had limited interest in military cooperation with the United States, saying in a toast, ''We will not attach ourselves to any big power or bloc of powers.''
Mr. Weinberger rose to propose ''an enduring relationship,'' saying that ''close United States-China relations and cooperation in the strategic area serve both our national interests.''
Defense Secretary Caspar W Weinberger arrives in Peking in his first trip to China; proposes 'an enduring relationship' between US and China (M)
Neither Mr. Zhang nor Mr. Weinberger mentioned the Soviet Union by name. 
Earlier in the day in Tokyo, Mr. Weinberger called the Soviet regime ''a corrupt government'' that had exhibited ''paranoia'' and ''total barbarity'' in shooting down a South Korean passenger plane with the loss of 269 lives on Sept. 
1.
Â 
Words Reflect Feelings
A senior official traveling with Mr. Weinberger said later that the choice of words was not calculated but reflected the Pentagon chief's feelings about that episode. 
The official said Mr. Weinberger believes that the image of Soviet behavior should not be allowed to fade. 
In his speech at the banquet this evening, Mr. Zhang recalled that the Chinese had been subjected to the miseries of foreign aggression, a reference to European, American and Japanese forces in China in the 19th and 20th centuries.
''That's why we treasure our independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity,'' Mr. Zhang said. 
He said that, while China is still a developing country, ''We do believe that with our own efforts, with our own initiative and our own hands, we will be able to achieve the modernization of our country.''
But he said that China would be willing to cooperate to speed up the modernization of Chinese armed forces. 
Mr. Zhang spoke without a text and his remarks were translated into English.
Â 
Shared Strategic Concerns
In reply, Mr. Weinberger spoke from a prepared text, saying that ''the United States and China share many important strategic concerns.''
He said he hoped his visit would be the basis for ''exchanges and cooperation between our two armed forces.''
He added that the Reagan Administration's ''new policy on technology transfer provides the means for us to contribute in a responsible way to China's modernization, including defense modernization.''
The Reagan Administration in June decided that China could acquire American technology, including that for weapons and military equipment, on the same basis as other friendly nations.
Officials accompanying Mr. Weinberger, however, said that a specific agreement on technology transfer had not been worked out. 
The United States, they said, wants written assurance that China would not pass along American technology to other nations.
Â 
'An Enduring Relationship'
Mr. Weinberger, repeating the theme of ''an enduring relationship,'' said that ''candid exchanges of views will enable us to avoid the kinds of unjust criticism of one another's policies which come from incomplete or inaccurate understanding of those policies.''
After arriving in Peking aboard his Air Force plane, Mr. Weinberger was whisked into the city to receive military honors in front of a military museum. 
Chinese soldiers, sailors, and airmen in bright new uniforms stood at attention while the American and Chinese national anthems were played.
Then under a bright warm sun, Mr. Weinberger, who is in China for the first time, toured the Forbidden City built by the Ming emperors in the 15th century as a residence and seat of Government. 
Mr. Weinberger was heard to remark that the expansive palace was ''much more beautiful than the Pentagon.''

file: WEINBERGER HOPEFULE ON ARMS FOR CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a sign of warming Chinese-American relations, Secretary of Defense Caspar W. Weinberger ended talks with Chinese leaders today by announcing that President Reagan and Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang would exchange official visits next year. 
He said there had also been progress toward eventual sales of American arms to China.
But the Chinese balked at formal military cooperation involving American arms purchases or exchanges of training missions.
Secretary of Defense Caspar W Weinberger ends talks with Chinese leaders in Peking by announcing that Pres Reagan and Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang will exchange official visits next year; reports making some progress toward eventual sales of American arms to China, although Chinese are said to have balked at formal military cooperation involving American arms purchases or exchanges of training missions; photo (M)
Mr. Weinberger, who arrived Sunday for a five-day visit, told reporters that the progress made during his talks here could ''mature very quickly into actual transfers of weapons systems, if that is what the Chinese want.''
He said air-defense and antitank weapons had been among the items discussed but declined to give further details.
The Defense Secretary, who spoke at a news conference in the Great Hall of the People, announced that Prime Minister Zhao would visit the United States in January and that Mr. Reagan would come to China in April. 
The Secretary also said Defense Minister Zhang Aiping had accepted his invitation to visit the United States ''at a mutually convenient time.''
Â 
Curb on Technology Eased
Mr. Weinberger's announcement suggested that the Chinese leadership had been persuaded to go ahead with plans for the visits, which had been under discussion, after Mr. Weinberger gave assurances that the Reagan Administration was making sophisticated American technology more accessible to China.
Earlier this year, the Reagan Administration reclassified China as a ''friendly, nonallied country,'' making it eligible for some equipment intended for civilian use but with possible military applications. 
However, the items involved were not announced.
The agreement on an exchange of visits came after Mr. Weinberger apparently explained to the Chinese in some detail that, through the reclassification, the Reagan Administration was relaxing controls on exports to China of such sophisticated dual-use equipment as computers and semiconductors.
While there were signs of improved Chinese-American relations, Chinese leaders also made clear during the talks that American military sales to the Chinese Nationalist regime on Taiwan remained the major irritant between Peking and Washington. 
Mr. Weinberger met here with Deng Xiaoping, China's paramount leader, Prime Minister Zhao and Defense Minister Zhang.
Â 
Taiwan Issue Called 'Crux'
The New China News Agency reported that Mr. Deng had told Mr. Weinberger during their closed meeting that the Taiwan issue was at the ''crux'' of Chinese-American relations. 
On Tuesday Mr. Zhao called it ''the main obstacle'' in the relationship.

But he said he had emphasized President Reagan's commitment to the 1972 Shanghai joint communique, which recognizes that there is only one China with Peking as its capital.
The Chinese have accused Mr. Reagan of reneging on that pledge, first made by President Richard M. Nixon, and on a joint document of August 1982 that envisions a gradual reduction of American military sales to Taiwan. 
When a Chinese journalist asked about assurances that the United States would honor both communiques, Mr. Weinberger sharply replied, ''You have the assurances of the President of the United States.''
The Secretary of Defense described his meetings with Chinese military officials as ''very friendly and frank and productive.''
Mr. Weinberger flew this afternoon to the ancient capital, Xian, to tour an aircraft parts factory and a renowned archeological excavation there of terra-cotta soldiers.

file: WEINBERGER_S CHINA VISIT_ PLAYING THE SUPPLICANT.txt
text:
ï»¿
After a slow start, Secretary of Defense Caspar W. Weinberger ended a five-day visit to China here today having apparently achieved most of what he called the ''modest goals'' of this venture. 
He accomplished this, however, by taking the position of supplicant. 
Through Mr. Weinberger, the United States offered assistance and asked for Chinese cooperation. 
But the Chinese offered nothing and asked for nothing, dealing with Mr. Weinberger the same way they have treated with foreigners for centuries.
Mr. Weinberger was successful in obtaining Chinese consent to an exchange of visits between Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang, who was scheduled to go to the United States in January, and President Reagan, who plans to visit China next April.
Analysis of Defense Sec Caspar Weinberger's China trip suggests US, as 'supplicant,' offered China assistance and asked for cooperation, obtaining Chinese consent to exchange of visits between Prime Min Zhao Ziyang and Pres Reagan which may be politically advantageous to Reagan; notes Chinese 'condescension'; Weinberger illustrated
Preliminary negotiations for that exchange had gone through regular diplomatic channels, according to officials accompanying Mr. Weinberger. But an agreement and specific dates were unresolved and President Reagan gave the problem to the Defense Secretary to nail down.
Â 
Different Role for Weinberger
Asked why he had undertaken what is normally a diplomatic function of the State Department, Mr. Weinberger chuckled and said, ''One does what one is requested to do.''
A senior official in the airplane with Mr. Weinberger pointed out that the exchange of visits, plus another by the Chinese Minister of National Defense, Zhang Aiping, perhaps in the winter, was intended to improve relations between Washington and Peking.
What was left unmentioned was the political benefit President Reagan hoped to reap in a possible re-election campaign through a highly visible trip to the capital of China.
Mr. Weinberger also obtained, at least in principle, the agreement of the Chinese to exchange military missions beginning early in 1984. 
Those would be intended to give American officers a better idea of Chinese military needs and to enable Chinese officers to see how Americans train and operate.
Â 
Military Missions to China
There was some confusion, however, over just what would happen. 
Prime Minister Zhao, at a news conference in Peking, appeared to brush off the idea. 
But American officials said later that Mr. Zhao seemed to dismiss any thought that American soldiers would help train the Chinese Army.
A senior official in Mr. Weinberger's delegation said an array of possibilities for exchanging military missions had been put before the Chinese and that the Chinese would let them know later what they might want.
Perhaps the most difficult discussion was over the sale of United States weapons and military technology to China. 
Mr. Weinberger made it clear to the Chinese, according to a senior American official, that Washington would make available weapons such as antitank and antiaircraft missiles.
But those sales would be carefully limited by United States law, especially concerning the possible resale of the weapons and technology to a third nation. 
Discussions on that issue would continue, American officials said.
Â 
Chinese Stress Self-Reliance
Perhaps more important, the Chinese seemed to disparage the American offer, saying repeatedly in public that they would modernize their armed forces by relying primarily on their own efforts, not on foreign nations.
To underscore that, the Chinese Army issued a report on the first day of Mr. Weinberger's visit saying the army had accomplished 12,000 technical renovations solely through its own efforts.
Throughout his stay in China, Mr. Weinberger sought to enlist the Chinese in what he called ''strategic cooperation'' against the Soviet Union. 
While vaguely defined, that seemed to mean a convergence of actions but not a formal alliance.
The Chinese, however, would have none of that. 
Mr. Zhao and Defense Minister Zhang reiterated the Peking line that China would not attach itself to any power or bloc. 
In effect, the Chinese said they would go their own way even if they accepted help from the United States.
Â 
Maneuvers by Chinese
The evidence that the Chinese maneuvered Mr. Weinberger into the role of supplicant showed up in many ways, some great, others small.
In their first meeting, Defense Minister Zhang insisted that Mr. Weinberger speak first, thus getting the American side to show its cards. 
Even when Mr. Weinberger asked for comment, the Chinese persuaded him to continue exposing his hand.
Later Mr. Zhang suggested an air of condescension when he quoted to Mr. Weinberger, as reported by the official New China News Agency, an old Chinese saying, ''Coming from afar, you must have brought something to benefit our country.''
As the Chinese often do, they withheld many details of the schedule from the American delegation until the last minute. 
In one instance Mr. Weinberger's meeting with Mr. Zhao was postponed for an hour at the last minute.
Â 
'Barbarians Waiting at the Gate'
A knowledgeable Western resident of Peking explained this by saying, ''The Chinese like to keep the barbarians waiting at the gate.''
The way in which the Chinese dealt with Mr. Weinberger is almost as old as China. 
It is the mentality of the Middle Kingdom, in which the Chinese see themselves at the center of the world and all other countries as vassals or tributaries.
Diplomatically, the Chinese Government wants to keep its distance from the United States to retain its credentials in the third world. 
To take sides with the United States while Foreign Minister Wu Xueqian appealed to third world nations at the United Nations would have been contradictory.

file: WHAM IS A ROCK PREMIERE IN CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
For days Wham had been the talk of the town.
But when big-time rock music hit China today in the form of a concert by the British group, the reaction in the 12,000-seat Workers Stadium was characteristic of the perplexity that is common when Chinese encounter a new facet of Western culture first hand.
Western college students danced in the aisles as the British duo played some of the songs that have propelled them onto best-selling charts in the United States and Britain. 
But most Chinese remained stolidly in their seats, seemingly unsure what to make of the arcing strobe lights, the pulsing guitars and the rest of the paraphernalia that accompanies a Western rock band.
Article discusses rock music group Wham and their concert tour of China; reaction of Chinese audiences discussed; illustration (M)
The result was a concert that was curiously muted, at least by the frenetic standards for such performances in the West.
It was the first time that a major rock group had been allowed to perform here, and there was a recognition on both sides that it was something of a test. 
With minor exceptions, the only live performances of Western music that the Communist Party has allowed until now have been by symphony orchestras and smaller classical ensembles.
Â 
Landing in a Debate
When they flew to Peking last week with a 105-member entourage, George Michaels, 21 years old, the singer and songwriter, and Andrew Ridgeley, 22, who plays guitar, dropped into the middle of an ideological debate. 
Arrangements for the tour were made last year in the freewheeling atmosphere that pervaded many aspects of Chinese life before a shift in the political winds brought fresh questioning at high party levels about how far the country's ''open door'' policy should go.
At one level, the debate is about the extent to which the party should encourage foreign investment, private enterprise and other Western economic practices, but the debate has had a cultural dimension, too. 
A leftist faction associated with the party's chief of ideology, Deng Liqun, has voiced renewed concern about the ''spiritual pollution'' that can result if Western influences are admitted too freely.
Wham, which has sold more than 2 million copies of its current album, ''Make It Big,'' has paid all costs for the performance here today and for a second one in Canton on Friday. 
The band's managers estimate the costs at $750,000, which the group hopes to recoup through sale of a video that is being made of the tour.
Â 
Some Eroticism Is Cut
To obtain their invitation, the group tried to accommodate Chinese sensitivities. 
They submitted a videotape of a live performance, dropped at least one of their hit songs, ''Love Machine,'' from the concert and cut erotic sequences from a video that was played during intermission. 
This enabled the sponsoring organization, the All-China Youth Federation, to describe the group as healthy.
Since its arrival in China, the group, which appeared at the Beacon Theater in New York in February, had been careful to avoid political comments. 
But at the concert today Mr. Michael introduced a song called ''Freedom,'' which has been at the top of the charts in Britain. 
''We hope that one day it will be the No. 1 in China too, with your help,'' Mr. Michael said, punching his arm in the air.
There was no visible reaction from the Chinese audience, which did not have the advantage of translation. 
But there was little doubt that it registered with the senior officials who watched from a podium set to one side of the stage, with interpreters behind them. 
Among the officials was Gen. Xiao Hua, 70, who is a member of the party's Central Committee and an associate of the country's pre- eminent leader, Deng Xiaoping.
Â 
Some Scuffles Erupt
Something else that might disturb the officials was scuffles involving policemen. 
At the start of the concert an announcer asked the audience to ''remain seated and watch with patience.''
Batteries of policemen tried to enforce this, at least for the Chinese, but Western students intervened several times. 
As the concert ended, at least one Chinese was led away under arrest.
Opponents of the '' open door'' policy have been warning that giving freer rein to popular instincts could cause the authorities to lose control. 
Some of the gyrations of Mr. Michael and Mr. Ridgeley and Mr. Michael's decision to appear bare-chested beneath his white jacket seemed unlikely to win official friends.
Western diplomats who attended the concert said it was almost certain that a report would go to Deng Xiaoping. 
At times, when under pressure from the left, Mr. Deng has warned of what he called the pernicious influence of some aspects of Western culture. 
At other times, he has said that China has little to fear. 
In this mood, prevalent in recent years, he has permitted a latitude in cultural matters that was unthinkable in the days of Mao Zedong.
