text:
ï»¿
CHRISTOPHER S. WREN is the Times bureau chief in Peking.
Two hundred years ago an American merchant ship dropped anchor in the Pearl River at Canton, beginning the first contacts between China and the United States. 
Even in 1784, Canton, or Guangzhou as the Chinese call it, had been trading with the outside world for many centuries. 
Today, Canton, a scant 75 miles from Hong Kong, remains China's most accessible city. 
Last year, 350,000 Western tourists, nearly a third of them Americans, came to visit. 
They have not spoiled Canton, which looks more like a traditional Chinese city than many others here. 
Its 5.5 million inhabitants are kin to the largest group of Chinese who emigrated to the United States. 
They are gregarious, lively and refreshingly at ease with foreigners. 
A tourist can have greater freedom to explore Canton's sights and smells, its tree-lined back streets, grimy shop arcades and quaint old neighborhoods than would be possible for him in the Chinese interior.
Getting There
The usual gateway to Canton is Hong Kong, where a tourist visa for Canton can be obtained in a few days from the China International Travel Service or through most well-known travel agencies, if hotel and transportation are booked at the same time. 
Once in Canton, you can use the visa to travel on to other Chinese cities open to foreigners including Shanghai and Peking.
A flight from Hong Kong to Canton takes a bare half-hour and costs $36, but there are more interesting ways to go. 
The train from Hong Kong's Kowloon Terminal travels for three hours through the lush rice paddies and wooded hills of Guangdong province. 
A normal tourist ticket will cost about $12. 
It is also possible to ride a Hovercraft up the Pearl River to the port of Whampoa on Canton's outskirts. 
The three-and-a-half-hour trip costs about $17 and offers beguiling glimpses of the South China coast. 
Unless you thrive on chaos, you should ask to be met in Canton by a travel service guide and car, who will whisk you to your hotel.
Where to Stay
An influx of Hong Kong investment has improved the quality of Canton's once seedy accommodations. 
The elegant 18-story China Hotel opened this year across from the Canton Trade Fair grounds, with managers and chefs imported from Hong Kong and Europe to try to raise the service to luxury standards. 
It has 1,200 rooms, several good restaurants, a corner bar and a basement bowling alley. 
A double room costs $52. 
(The telephone is 66888.)
The 28-story White Swan Hotel opened last year on Shamian Island overlooking the Pearl River with 1,000 rooms. 
Designed by Chinese architects, it incorporates a garden and waterfall in its three-story lobby (telephone: 86968). 
A standard double room costs $35.
The 1,200-room Dongfang Hotel, the old hangout for Western businessmen and tourists, has been undergoing a face-lift now that it must compete with the China Hotel next door. 
A double room runs up to $30. 
Cheaper but more spartan hotels include the Baiyun Hotel on Huanshi Road (67700) and the Guangzhou and Overseas Chinese Hotels near downtown Haizhu Square. 
A double room at any of these establishments costs $22 or less.
Dim Sum
Starting at dawn, Cantonese spill out of their cramped homes and converge on the teahouses to sip tea and eat dim sum while they chat, play chess or read the newspaper. 
Canton is celebrated for its dim sum - bite- sized sweet or savory snacks that are generally pastries stuffed with such tasty fillings as shrimp, minced pork and bean paste.
The best dim sum, locally called yum cha, are found at the Banxi Restaurant at the eastern edge of Liwan Park. 
The Banxi attracts up to 10,000 customers a day and can seat 3,000 of them at a time. 
It usually does not seem crowded because the restaurant consists of more than 30 dining rooms arranged around a series of small gardens and a lake. 
The most popular date from the Qing dynasty, like the Greeting, the guest pavilion on the second floor with its 19th-century- style furniture and blue-and-white etched-glass windows. 
In good weather, customers also like to sit out in the patios near the lake.
A selection of a dozen varieties of pastries plus slender rice noodles and tea costs $4.30 a person. 
You can ask the staff to choose for you. 
The Banxi is open from 5:30 to 9:30 A.M. for breakfast, from 11 A.M. to 2 P.M. for lunch and from 5 to 9 P.M. for dinner. 
Reservations are necessary to get a good table (85655).
Dim sum are served in other restaurants in Canton, including the Village Restaurant of the China Hotel, where a dim sum lunch runs up to $8 a person. 
The pastries are pushed around on carts, and you pay only for the ones you take.
Sightseeing
Canton's most historically interesting area for Westerners is Shamian Island, a sandbank on the northern bank of the Pearl River that the British and French turned into a colonial enclave in the late 19th century. 
They built grand mansions, a couple of churches and promenades among the shady banyan trees on the island's 44 acres and closed its two bridges to shore at night to keep out the Chinese. 
Most of the Mediterranean-style buildings have now deteriorated, but the government plans to restore the island to something of its old architectural splendor.
In central Canton west of Renmin (People's) Road are a pair of ancient temples that recall China's Buddhist heritage. 
Guanxiao Temple, built in the fourth century, is one of the oldest in southern China and contains two small 10th-century iron pagodas. 
The Liurong (Six Banyans) Temple dates back to the fifth century. 
Near the main hall stands the nine-story Flower Pagoda, 180 feet high, which offers a good view of the city.
The Huaisheng Mosque, built in 627, is still in use by Chinese Moslems. 
It is south of Zhongshan Road. 
Canton's 19th-century Catholic Cathedral with its twin Gothic spires, on Yide Road, is now open for Sunday mass after being closed down by leftists during the Cultural Revolution.
The impact of China's new agricultural reforms is visible at the farmers market along Qingping Road. 
Here peasants from the countryside may sell their surplus produce privately. 
They squat and haggle with customers over live chickens, ducks, fish, snakes, frogs, herbs, vegetables and handicrafts. 
Spring flower markets also appear along Haoxian and Renmin Roads.
On the River
One of the pleasantest ways to view Canton is from a boat on the Pearl River, which winds through the city. 
The cruise boat with guide leaves from the No. 1 Pier near the old customs house on Yanjiang Road at 3 P.M. and spends two hours sailing back and forth across the river,dodging tugboats, barges and small sampans sculled by lone oarsmen. 
The trip costs 10 yuan, about $4 and includes soft drinks and snacks. 
A short voyage across the Pearl River on the local ferry, which leaves from a dock west of the White Swan Hotel, can be enjoyed for three fen - about a penny.
Restaurants
Other Chinese joke that the Cantonese will eat anything with four legs except a table, anything that flies except an airplane and anything that swims except a submarine. 
Canton has probably the best restaurants in China. 
The chefs work with a range of fresh ingredients that would intimidate lesser cooks, with an eye for color and a light touch with the spices. 
Foreigners are less likely to be segregated from Chinese diners in Canton than in other Chinese cities, so they can share in the conviviality that characterizes Canton's restaurants.
For those who do not speak Cantonese, it is best to agree upon a price per person, excluding drinks, when you make a reservation and have the restaurant arrange the menu, though you may want to specify a few favorite dishes.
The century-old Tao Tao Ju Restaurant (87306) on Xiaju Road seats 1,500 diners at a time. 
Its dishes include a whole chicken roasted with spices, $17.25, pan-fried frog with chives, $3.45, and roast pomfret (sea bream), $1.50. 
A meal will run up to $12.90 a person, without drinks. 
Look for the sign out front in the calligraphy of the Qing dynasty scholar Kang Youwei.
The Guangzhou restaurant ((87840) at the corner of Wenchang and Xiajiu roads is arranged round an indoor garden under a skylight. 
It is popular with residents because it is cheaper than most tourist restaurants and seats 2,000 customers. 
Specialities include pigeon cooked in tea, $5.60, and fried duck with crabmeat and eggwhites, $7.80. 
A full dinner will start at $6.50 a person. 
The Guangzhou also serves dim sum until midnight, which is shockingly late for China.
The Beiyuan or Northern Garden (33365) across from Yuexiu Park offers traditional-style pavilions with etched windows surrounding a garden. 
Dinner runs up to $12.90 a person. 
An American resident of Canton thinks that the Beiyuan serves the best suckling pig in town.
Although famous for its dim sum, the Banxi also offers a full dinner starting at $8.60, excluding drinks. 
Try the steamed melon soup, frog meat wrapped in ham and fried crab.
Visitors with bolder palates must try the Snake Restaurant (24679) on Jianglan Road. 
Do not be put off by the vipers slithering around the window display. 
Snake meat tastes like chicken, and is done best here in the meeting of the dragon, tiger and phoenix soup, as the brew of snake, cat and chicken meat is euphemistically called. 
An individual bowl costs $1.70. 
Or drink down a glass of snake bile ($8.60 to $12.90 depending on the number of snakes needed), which Cantonese say does wonders for your health.
Shopping
The usual tourist souvenirs, from cashmere sweaters to T-shirts printed with pandas, are stocked at the Friendship Store in the north wing of the China Hotel. 
If you want to browse away from the tourist route. walk along Xiajiu Road with its dozens of small shops. 
Bamboo wares are sold along Taikang Road. 
The Nanfang Department Store near the river carries everyday items for ordinary Chinese. 
You can find bargains like corduroy shoes for a couple of dollars. 
The store's underground annex used to be an air raid shelter.
Canton is not a good hunting ground for antiques, because the best pieces have already found their way to the antique shops of Hong Kong. 
The Guangzhou Antique Store (31241) on Wende Road sometimes gets a few pieces of the blue willow porcelain made for export during the later Qing dynasty (the 19th century). 
. Calligraphy scrolls and jewelry can also be good purchases. 
Make sure that anything you buy carries a red wax seal certifying it for export.
Night Life
Canton is slightly ahead of other Chinese cities in its nightlife, though it is still meager compared to that of the West. 
The China and White Swan Hotels both operate discoth eques for foreigners. 
Local Cantonese entertainment includes traditional Chinese Opera, called Yue Ju , at various theaters. 
A ticket costs from 21 to 52 cents, depending on who is performing. 
A children's acrobatic troupe, with artists as young as 9 years old, also puts on performances.
The best amusement can be found in good weather at the Cultural Park on Luersan Road near the Pearl River. 
Cantonese congregate here in the cool of the evening to stroll, roller skate, listen to music or watch open- air operas, dramas, puppet shows and films. 
Admission is only 4 cents but don't go unless you like crowds.
Country Trips
Canton lies at the edge of the Pearl River Delta, a lush rice bowl, crisscrossed with canals and streams, that is still ploughed by water buffalo. 
A half-day excursion may be arranged through the China International Travel Service (179 Huanshi Road) to the wealthy Dali Commune in Nanhai County. 
If you have a full day, you can go a few hours farther south to Shunde County, where you will also get a firsthand look at the prosperity brought about by the current agricultural reforms. 
It will cost about $17, including bus with guide and lunch, depending on the number of passengers.
When to Go
Canton enjoys a semitropical climate similar to Hong Kong's. 
The best seasons are spring and autumn, but the semiannual Canton Trade Fair, held in April and October, crowds hotels and restaurants. 
The winter is mild, with temperatures in the high 50's. 
The summer is hot and humid but still manageable if you stay at one of the air-conditioned hotels.

text:
ï»¿
Landing at Hong Kong's Kai Tak Airport is one of the world's more interesting flying experiences. 
The approach over the Kowloon Peninsula, where most Hong Kong residents live packed into tall apartment buildings sticking into the air like concrete teeth is such a close shave that you actually see people eating dinner. 
What's more, they probably see you.
Kai Tak, like most Asian airports, appears chaotic but is quite efficient. 
Some of its practices are typical of the Hong Kong ethos, however, which is based on the principle of the quick buck. 
One thing to beware of is the money changers, who offer at least 10 percent less for a dollar than local banks. 
Another thing to be careful about is the duty-free shops, which charge at least 10 percent more than the thousands of shops in this duty- free city. 
The reason is that the government imposes astronomical fees on shops at the airport.
Â 
Shopping
One of the main attractions of Hong Kong is shopping. 
Bargains are everywhere, but one special area is the so-called Golden Mile on Nathan Road in the Tsimshatsui District of Kowloon, where many hotels, restaurants and nightclubs are concentrated. 
If you are staying on Hong Kong Island, you can either take the Star Ferry for a delightful ride across the bay for 8 cents or the subway, called the M.T.R. 
(for Mass Transit Railway), for about 50 cents.
Ian Buruma What's Doing In article focuses on Hong Kong--shopping, where to stay, cultural events and sightseeing; photos; map (M)
Traditional Hong Kong bargains are cameras, pocket calculators, watches, radios, clothes and jewelry. 
Expensive brands are usually the best bargains. 
Hong Kong, not Paris, is the place to buy an Yves Saint Laurent outfit, for example. 
This is mainly because most luxury items are made in Hong Kong. 
But since the same artful hands that serve the boutiques of New York and Paris are equally good at producing fakes, be sure to read the label carefully before buying - Rallex is not Rolex and Selko is not Seiko. 
But even the correct label is not an absolute guarantee of authenticity.
Bargaining is expected, and you should compare prices in several shops before buying. 
However, prices are usually fixed in large department stores like Lane Crawford and such Japanese stores as Daimaru, Matsuzakaya and Mitsukoshi.
A Cartier watch for a woman costs about $400 at Lane Crawford (telephone 5-7909533), whose main store in Lane Crawford House in the central district on Hong Kong Island is open from 9 A.M. to 10 P.M. A Saint Laurent dress is about $350 and a man's Pierre Cardin suit $300.
Daimaru (5-767321) is on Paterson Street in Causeway Bay; Matsuzakaya (5-7906622) is at 6 Paterson Street, and Mitsukoshi (5-765222) is in Hennessey Center on Hong Kong Island. 
All three are open from 9:30 A.M. to 10:30 P.M.
A good place for inexpensive but high-quality merchandise from mainland China is China Products (5-7908321), whose main store is in Lok Sing Center on Hong Kong Island. 
The company sells everything from clothes (such as silk padded jackets) to foodstuffs and is open from 10 A.M. to 9 P.M. For carpets and other crafts, try Chinese Arts and Crafts (3-670061), whose main store at 233 Nathan Road is open from about 9 A.M. to 9 P.M. A 2-by-4-foot, hand-knotted woollen rug costs $20, a 9-by-12 $300.
Antiques
Although some would say that buying antiques in Hong Kong is a fool's game, there occasionally are bargains. 
Hollywood Road, with dozens of antiques shops a 10-minute uphill walk from the central district, is a good place to spend an afternoon browsing. 
Some shops offer little more than gaudy golden Buddhas, but one might find a Ming dynasty tea bowl for a few hundred dollars. 
One of the best antique dealers is said to be P. C. Lu and Sons with shops in the Peninsula Hotel (3-688436) in Kowloon and the Mandarin Hotel (5- 243395) on Hong Kong Island.
Â 
Bargain Hunting
For really good buys - jeans, chinaware, T-shirts, and the like - go to one of the many street markets. 
The one in the Stanley District on Hong Kong Island is a favorite with tourists, but for more Chinese ambiance the night market in the Mong Kok District on Kowloon is recommended. 
It is a bus ride (about 8 cents) away from the Golden Mile. 
The night markets open about 7:30 and close around 11:30 and are quite safe for Western visitors.
Â 
Tailoring
Hong Kong tailors are famous for speed and quality, but caution is needed, for shoddy craftsmanship abounds. 
It is best to avoid trying to have a suit made in 24 hours. 
The better bet, though not necessarily the cheapest, is to go to a tailor in one of the big hotels, such as George Chen in the Pensinsula (3-667248) or A-Man Hing Cheong in the Mandarin (5-247316). 
A man's suit will cost between $200 and $300. 
Also recommended is United Company at 28 Stanley Street (5-263952). 
A suit there can be made for $200. 
A word of advice: Give your tailor time for at least two fittings.
For shirts, try Ascot Chang (3-662398) in the Peninsula Hotel or Jimmy (5-259605) in the Landmark Building on Hong Kong Island. 
Prices for cotton shirts begin at $24, for silk at $40.
Â 
Where to Eat
Eating is a favorite recreation of most Chinese everywhere, and the Chinese food in Hong Kong is reason enough for a visit. 
Purists may say that Sichuan food is better in Taipei and Shanghai better in Shanghai, but Cantonese and Chao Zhou (from the northern part of Canton province) are unsurpassed in Hong Kong.
Every visitor should try at least one dim sum lunch or breakfast. 
The choice of restaurants for this feast of dumplings and other tidbits is endless, but the Luk Yu Teahouse (5-232973) at 24 Stanley Street is worth seeing for its old Hong Kong atmosphere (Art Deco Chinoiserie). 
The interior dates from the mid-1930's. 
In the 1970's the restaurant was rebuilt in its present location, and the marble-topped tables, the stained-glass windows, the wood paneling and most of the waiters were moved to the new place. 
Two can eat there for about $12.
For a more sumptuous dim sum experience at about the same price, try the Maxim Palace (5-766333) in the World Trade Center on Hong Kong Island.
For Chao Zhou food, the Carrianna Restaurant (5-8919776) on Tonnochy Road, is excellent. 
Specialties are goose in soya sauce ($3), minced pigeon wrapped in lettuce ($7) and spinach and minced chicken soup ($2.50).
For a Sichuan meal, try Sichuan Garden (5-214433) in the Landmark Building. 
Among its specialties: eggplant in hot garlic sauce ($6), prawn balls ($5.25) and duck smoked in camphor wood and tea leaves ($10 half, $17.50 whole).
A famous Western restaurant is Gaddi's (3-666251) in the Peninsula Hotel, where garoupa (Asian grouper), poached and served with oysters on top ($20), and crabmeat pancake ($12) are among the specialties. 
A less expensive Western restaurant is Landau's (5-7902901), 257 Gloucester Road. 
The gravlax ($4) there is good for starters. 
For the main course, Macau sole ($6) or New Zealand lamb ($7) are recommended.
First-class Indian food is served in the Ashoka Restaurant (5-249623), 57 Wyndham Street. 
Try the fish tikka ($3) and the rogan josh ($3.25). 
Indonesian food is especially good in the Indonesian Restaurant (5-779981), 27 Leighton Road. 
Specialties: calf's brains ($2) and beef rendang ($2.50).
Where to Stay
Hotels are often fully booked so reserve rooms well in advance, especially if you wish to stay at the best places, such as the Peninsula Hotel (3-666251). 
Rooms for two begin at $115 a night. 
The Mandarin (5-220111) is considered one of the best hotels in the world. 
Rooms for two there start at $136. 
The best of the new hotels built on a chunk of reclaimed land in Tsimshatsui East in Kowloon is the Regent (3-7211211), which charges $108 and up for a room for two. 
Slightly less plush but still very good is the Hong Kong Hilton (5-233111), which has rates ranging from $100 to $115 for two.
All major hotels offer free limousine service from the airport - usually a Mercedes-Benz. 
Normally a taxi ride to the hotel district costs $2.
Â 
Cultural Events
The main event of the current season is the Hong Kong International Film Festival from March 29 to April 13, featuring a retrospective of films by four deceased Asian directors: Sadao Yammanaka of Japan, Gerardo de Leon of the Philippines, Fei Mu of China and Ritwik Ghatak of India. 
Homage will also be paid to Douglas Sirk and Nicholas Ray, both of Hollywood.
The Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra, founded in 1975, plays in City Hall (5-7907521) from September to June. 
Ticket prices range from $2 to $4. 
In the same building near the Star Ferry on the Hong Kong side is the Hong Kong Museum of Art (5-224127). 
It is open without charge from 10 A.M. to 6 P.M. every day but Thursday. 
The permanent collection contains mainly 18th- and 19th-century works from the South China Coast.
Cantonese opera performances - noisier and more flamboyant than the Peking variety - are given at such theatres as the Lee, the Paladium and the Sunbeam. 
Tickets cost about $2.50.
Â 
Sightseeing
A walk around Victoria Peak offers some of the best panoramic views of Hong Kong, at least on clear days. 
The rest of the time the misty landscape reminds one of Scotland.
The other islands in the Crown Colony (there are 260 or so) are good for escaping the madding Hong Kong crowds. 
Lan Tau, the largest, is popular with mountain hikers. 
Lamma Island is more suited to walking. 
To reach it, take a boat to Yung Shue Wan from the Outlying Districts Services pier in Hong Kong, a few hundred yards west of the Star Ferry. 
A one-way ticket costs 10 cents.
Â 
Side Trips
Until the late 1970's, one of the thrills of visiting Hong Kong was peeking across the Chinese border. 
Now that China is no longer forbidden territory, the three-hour tour to the border, arranged by one's hotel for $8.50, may seem a little outdated. 
But the sight of a long barbed-wire fence cutting straight across duck ponds and rice fields is something to ponder.
Those who wish to go to China on a quick tour can book through the Hong Kong Tourist Association, Post Office Box 1597, General Post Office, Hong Kong (5-244191). 
One of their more interesting trips is a two-night excursion to Canton, costing $185 a person. 
Included in the package are Hovercraft transportation to get there, a train ride back, a visa, hotel accommodations and meals.
Information
Hong Kong Tourist Association, 548 Fifth Avenue (at 45th Street), New York, N.Y. 
10036 (212-869-5008).

file: WHAT_S DOING IN SAN FRANCISCO.txt
text:
ï»¿
You will enjoy this delightful place where life bubbles like champagne, the scenery is memorable, and laughter echoes in the night air. 
Be prepared to gain weight, to lose sleep, to arrive home tired and vaguely dissatisfied.
Bring something warm to wear at night. 
No matter how it is in Wilmington or Washington or Wichita in June, July and August, it is cold at night in San Francisco. 
Be not one of those blue-chilled tourists at Fisherman's Wharf hurrying along through the windy, foggy night in short sleeves and walking shorts.
Â 
Calendar
Until Sept. 
30 the Asian Art Museum, on Tea Garden Drive in Golden Gate Park (415-558-2993), will have a show called ''Treasures From the Shanghai Museum.''
The mid-10th to the early 20th centuries are represented in the 232 ceramics, bronzes, sculptures, paintings and jades. 
At the M. H. de Young Museum next door (415-558-2997), an exhibition of pre-Columbian American art will run through Aug. 
28. The summer exhibition of the California Palace of the Legion of Honor in Lincoln Park (415-558-2881) is of the works of the 19th-century French painter Henri Fantin-Latour.
You will enjoy this delightful place where life bubbles like champagne, the scenery is memorable, and laughter echoes in the night air.
The San Francisco Summer Opera at the Opera House (415-864-3300) performs ''La Boheme'' June 24 and 27; ''Carmen'' June 22, 26, 29 and July 2; ''Cosi Fan Tutte'' on June 23, 25, 28, July 1 and 3. 
At Davies Hall, the San Francisco Symphony's Beethoven Festival continues June 24, 25, 29, July 1 and 2.
There will be free Sunday concerts through Aug. 
21, plus July 4, at Stern Grove, 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard, featuring artists ranging from the San Francisco Symphony, San Francisco Ballet and Lola Montez Dancers to Turk Murphy, the jazz trombonist, and the Preservation Hall Jazz Band. 
Organ recitals will be given on June 26, July 10, July 24, and Aug. 
7, at 5 P.M. each day, at Grace Episcopal Cathedral, California and Taylor (415-776-6611). 
The Joffrey Ballet will be at the Opera House (415-864-3330) July 6-16.
''Master Harold and the Boys'' with James Earl Jones plays June 29-July 24 at the Curran Theater, 445 Geary Street (415-673-4400). 
''Zorba,'' with Anthony Quinn, plays July 20-Aug. 
20 at the Golden Gate Theater, Taylor and Market (415-775-8800). 
''Hello, Dolly!'' with Carol Channing will be at the Orpheum Theater, 1192 Market Street (415-474-3800), July 26-Aug. 
14.
San Francisco's 207th birthday will be celebrated June 26-29 with Spanish and Mexican music and dance in the Bandshell at Golden Gate Park, with mass at Mission Dolores and lunch at the Presidio Officers Club. 
Reservations: 415-282-8502.
''Crossroads of the Ancient World: Israel's Archaeological Heritage'' will continue through Sept. 
5 at the California Academy of Sciences, Golden Gate Park (415-221-8268).
Â 
Hotels
Even though new hotels seem to sprout every month and the variety is great, one is well advised to have a reservation. 
Of course, there usually is a vacant room a few miles north or south or east, even if locating it by telephone and then getting there cause a few gray hairs. 
But it isn't like being in the city.
The famous hotels deserve their imposing reputations. 
The Fairmont (415-772-5000), the Stanford Court (415-989-3500), the Four Seasons Clift (415-775-4700), the Hyatt Regency (415-788-1234), the Mark Hopkins (415-392-3434), the Huntington (415-474-5400) and others provide luxury that anyone could grow to love. 
Prices run about $65 for the least expensive single room to $190 for a room with twin beds.
A step down is still luxurious. 
Rooms at the San Franciscan (800-227-3050) are $95 top for two. 
The Westin Miyako (800-228-3000), with a Japanese flavor, has a $115 top. 
The Chancellor (415-362-2004) has a maximum rate of $55, and the El Cortez (800-223-5695) has kitchenettes at $50. 
There are even less expensive places. 
Bed and Breakfast International (415-525-4569) specializes in referrals.
Anyone planning to a visit cannot go wrong by writing the San Francisco Convention & Visitors Bureau, P.O. 
Box 6977, San Francisco 94010, and asking for the ''San Francisco Lodging Guide.''
Â 
Restaurants
First, let us understand the dark side of many San Francisco restaurants. 
Some close on Sunday. 
Outside of that I can think of nothing about them to criticize, except that a few will not take reservations.
Ernie's, 847 Montgomery Street (415-397-5969), is a truly splendid place where the captains and waiters come from central casting and the food comes from heaven. 
Others in this category are the Blue Fox, 659 Merchant Street (415-981-1177), La Bourgogne, 330 Mason Street (415-362-7352), L'Etoile, 1075 California Street (415-771-1529), or the Carnelian Room, atop the Bank of America World Headquarters at 555 California Street (415-433-7500). 
This is by no means the full list of top-drawer French and Continental restaurants where two people can scarcely feed themselves decently for under $75.
At Bardelli's, 243 O'Farrell Street (415-982-0243), and Alfred's, a steakhouse at 886 Broadway (415-781-7058), and similar places, two can dine well for $50 or $60. 
The Convention & Visitors Bureau will give you a copy of ''Restaurant and Night Life Guide.''
On those occasions when you have a group of eight or 10 - they will want to talk across and down the table during dinner - I always call on Jack's, a French restaurant, 615 Sacramento Street (415-986-9854), which has upstairs rooms of different sizes. 
You can order off the menu, and escape the fixed menu that you get saddled with even at Ernie's or the Blue Fox, both of which have basement rooms for large parties.
There are any number of Chinese restaurants, ranging in style from a half-dozen stools at a counter to places seating a hundred or so. 
The Chinese cuisine comes from all across Asia, a development of the last 20 years as Chinese from many nations have come into San Francisco. 
My favorite Cantonese restaurant is the Imperial Palace, Tommy Toy proprietor, at 919 Grant Avenue, (415-982-4440). 
The bill for four of us a month ago was $135. 
Hunan Village, 839 Kearny Street (415-956-7868), is less expensive. 
The Mandarin, at 900 North Point in Ghirardelli Square, offers excellent North China cuisine, and it takes reservations (415-673-8812), which Hunan Village does not.
There are several Japanese places, such as Yamato, 717 California Street (415-397-3456), and Nikko, 1450 Van Ness Avenue (415-474-7722).
There are Italian restaurants all around San Francisco, because the city has a big population descended from the fishermen and farmers who came from Italy a century ago. 
North Beach Restaurant, 1512 Stockton Street (415-392-1700), is northern Italian. 
Two people can eat for $40 to $50. 
Original Joe's, 144 Taylor Street (415-775-4877), is less expensive, and in the tomato sauce style.
Seafood is something special in San Francisco and generally I go to Fisherman's Wharf, straight to Castagnola's, 286 Jefferson Street (415-776-5015). 
Sometimes the sea lions will come into the Wharf, and if you have a window table you can watch them beg for scrap fish at the fish buyer's dock. 
There are other great places at the Wharf - Alioto's No. 8 Wharf (415-673-0183), and Scoma's on Pier 47 (415-771-4383), which is behind Castagnola's. 
Downtown, one of the best is Tadich Grill, 240 California (415-391-2373). 
Another is Sam's Grill, 374 Bush (415-421-0594).
Â 
Transportation
The cable cars are closed this year, to reopen in the summer of 1984 at the earliest. 
The system was about to fall apart from pure exhaustion.
However, San Francisco has an excellent system of buses, electric trolley coaches and streetcars called the San Francisco Municipal Railway. 
The fare is 60 cents, 25 cents for children under 17, five cents for the disabled or people over 65, who should be prepared to show a passport or drivers license or some other document, if the driver asks proof of age. 
The information telephone for the Muni, as the system is called, is 415-673-6864. 
It is attended 24 hours, seven days a week.
Even more good news is the weekend and holiday operation of 10 vintage streetcars on Market Street, beginning June 24 and running through Sept. 
26. The old cars have been gathered from Portugal, England, Melbourne, Milwaukee, Portland, Ore., and from the Muni's own back lot, which produced cars dating from 1912. 
During the week, the regular streetcars operate in a subway, but the old tracks and trolley wires have never been taken down from the surface and the San Francisco Chamber of Commerce helped the Muni put the streetcar package together as an answer to the loss of the cable cars.
Regional public transit is good, too. 
For Oakland, Berkeley, Richmond, San Leandro, Newark and Fremont, all across the Bay, you may use Bay Area Rapid Transit's trains (BART), or the AC Transit buses. 
BART schedules can be had by calling 415-788-2278, or AC Transit at 415-653-3535. 
Cities north of the Golden Gate Bridge in Marin and Sonoma county are served by the Golden Gate Bus system. 
The district also operates ferries to Sausalito and Larkspur. 
Information on all this can be obtained by calling 415-453-2100.
To go south down the San Francisco Peninsula to Burlingame, San Mateo, Palo Alto, or San Jose, call the Southern Pacific Railroad's commute schedule number, 415-495-4546, or the San Mateo County Transit District bus lines at 415-761-7000.
Â 
Tours
You can go on a tour to see or do almost anything around San Francisco, running typically around $20 a person. 
There are luncheon cruises (415-861-2165, China Basin Charter) and cocktail-dinner cruises (415-540-8352, San Francisco's Love Boat). 
There are helicopter tours (415-495-3333, China Basin tours) and you may trudge along in the steps of one of the great mystery writers by paying $4 to go on the Dashiell Hammett Tours (415-564-7021). 
Someone will even lead you through the War Memorial Opera House, the Louise M. Davies Symphony Hall and the Herbst Theatre on Monday from 10 A.M. to 2:30 P.M. or Wednesday at 1:30 and 2:30 P.M., all for $3.
There are horse-drawn buggies in Golden Gate Park (415-761-8272) or on Pier 39 (415-398-0857). 
There are city tours for an hour or so or all day. 
Gray Line (415-771-4000) and Dolphin Tours (415-441-6810) offer a broad range, with Gray Line ready to supply a Bay cruise and double decker bus, while Dolphin will take you to Muir Woods redwood grove and Sausalito. 
Lorrie's Travel & Tours (415-826-5950) offers Alcatraz Island, the long-vacant federal prison.
Upward of 20 percent of San Francisco's population is Oriental, which gives special meaning to the Chinatown and Japantown offerings of Dragon Tours (415-392-0244) and the Chinese Cultural Center (415-986-1822). 
Ding How Tours (415-981-8399) will take you through Chinatown and serve you dinner.
To the north, south and east of San Francisco Bay are the vineyards and wineries that produce the nation's premier vintages. 
There is an immense variety of wine tours, and the best way to pick the one you want is to get a copy of ''Visitors Guide to the Wine Country'' from the San Francisco Convention & Visitors Bureau (415-974-6900). 
The bureau maintains an office at Halliday Plaza, that sunken area where Powell Street runs into Market and where the Muni and BART trains stop.

text:

-------------------------------------------------------------------- HENRY KAMM is chief Asian diplomatic correspondent of The Times.
Â 
By HENRY KAMM
THE OTHER CHINA - Tourism in China need not be synonymous with fully pre-arranged and prepaid package travel, omnipresent official guides who avert their eyes and yours from what is ideologically out of fashion and shopping without bargaining. 
''Little China'' - the island of Taiwan, the hilly land that 16th-century Portuguese colonists named Formosa, the Beautiful - remains easily accessible and requires little more pre-arrangement than a weekend in the Catskills.
Tourist visas are quickly obtained from Nationalist Chinese consulates, which, since America's derecognition of Taiwan, go under the euphemism of Offices of the Coordination Council for North American Affairs. 
The New York office is at 801 Second Avenue, New York 10017 (697-1250-4); others are in Washington, D.C., Atlanta, Chicago, Houston, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle and Honolulu. 
A valid passport and three photographs are required for the visa, which is issued, without charge, the same day.
Trip to Taiwan is suggested as way to see "China" without going through red-tape and hassle
GETTING THERE - Northwest Orient Airlines, Singapore Airlines and China Air Lines each have several weekly direct flights between Taipei and such United States cities as Seattle, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Honolulu. 
Fares vary with type of service and advance booking; Singapore Airlines, for example, offers an advance purchase round-trip fare from Los Angeles, valid for a year, with no maximum or minimum stay requirement, for $960. 
All major Asian airlines fly at least once a day between their capitals and Taipei, so Hong Kong, Bangkok, Tokyo, Singapore , Manila or Seoul ar e also good starting places.
GETTING AROUND - Despite its shining modernity, Chiang Kai-shek Airport is antiquated in its customs procedures. 
It can take a good hour of being scuffed about by some of the noisiest and pushiest crowds in Asia and having one's most innocuous belongings, particularly printed matter, fussed over by rude customs agents before one is freed to be set upon by the hotel agents in the terminal lobby. 
It is best to take the hotel bus to town. 
The drive takes about a n hour, and the fare is about $5.50.
The language problem exists everywhere except places that are meant strictly for tourists. 
The only way to beat it is to decide upon each day's outing in advance, then ask a clerk at the hotel desk to write in Chinese, on separate slips of paper, all the places that you are likely to visit before returning to safe harbor. 
Your own job is to write the English equivalent on each slip, so that you will be sure you have given the taxi driver directions to take you to the museum rather than to the herbal medicine shop.
Public transportion is crowded and confusing, but taxis are cheap. 
All have meters, and tips are not expected, even from foreigners. 
Some meters still run on an earlier tariff, so the driver who asks you for more than is shown on the meter is not trying to cheat you. 
The roads are bumpy and potholed, the cabs have long ago exhausted their springs and shock absorbers and the drivers take no pains to avoid bad spots. 
Most drive at reckless speeds with lots of lastsecond jabs at the brakes.
MONEY - The currency is the New Taiwan dollar, locally known as the N.T., and 36 or 37 of them make one United States dollar. 
Traveler's checks are generally accepted, and hotels and bigger restaurants and shops take credit cards. 
One caution: After you have struck a hard bargain with a shopkeeper and pull out your credit card, the deal might collapse. 
You may then have to renegotiate whether you or he should pay the percentage that credit card companies charge shopkeepers, or pay cash.
THE CITY - It is not the physical beauty of Taipei that makes the trip worthwhile. 
Although the sprawling city has a lovely situation in a river valley surrounded by green mountains, it has made nothing of it. 
The old public buildings date to the period of Japanese rule, from 1895 to 1945, when Japan's idea of modern architecture was modeled on the squat and clumsy European government buildings of a century ago. 
Newer buildings, at their best, are of the featureless international style; at their worst, they are shapeless concrete tenements and factories or structures that look like them.
But Taipei is a marketplace of immense animation, with unceasing and unrestricted manufacturing, buying and selling. 
It makes New York look placid and approaches Hong Kong in cash-register cacophony. 
There is little respite, but if your spirits flag, make for the one authentic old-style (although the decor is tastefully modern) tearoom, Cha Yi Gwan, at 6 Alley 8, Lane 27, Ren Ai Road, Section 4. 
Strong tea ceremoniously brewed in tiny cups, taken in a setting of works of art, restores spirits and senses.
NATIONAL PALACE MUSEUM -What is perhaps the greatest single collection of Chinese art in the world is a short taxi ride from the heart of the city in the National Palace Museum. 
Its heart is the Imperial Collection, whose origins can be traced back to the Sung dynasty in the 10th century.
The collection's history is as vexed as it is long. 
The violent upheavals of Chinese history sometimes caused the collection to be scattered, or to be moved between the shifting capitals of the Middle Kingdom; it came to rest at the National Palace Museum in Peking in 1925, but not for long. 
In 1931, when the Japanese invaded China, the collection was sent to Shanghai, and then to Nanjing. 
It was further dispersed, in Sichuan and Guizhou, when the war spread over central China in 1937. 
At the end of World War II, the works of art were reassembled in Nanjing and Peking; they were taken to Taiwan shortly before the Communist triumph in the Civil War and were left crated and stored in mountain caves in the island's interior. 
Only in 1965, with the construction of the present museum, did they once more go on public display.
Only a fraction of the museum's riches - perhaps 6,000 to 8,000 pieces from a collection tentatively numbered at more than 600,000 - can be shown at one time. 
The scroll paintings, dating from the 10th to the 17th centuries, are the most striking exhibits, although the porcelain and ceramics, the jade and lacquerware, the bronzes and enamels are perhaps even more richly representative. 
Calligraphy and rare books and manuscripts complete the comprehensive view of Chinese culture, which is on view seven days a week at an admission price of about 50 cents.
There are frequent guided tours in English and, for special exhibitions, rental cassettes with a recorded English commentary. 
The museum also sells good reproductions of scroll paintings at a wide range of prices.
ADDED ATTRACTION - The National Palace Museum is surely the only major art gallery in the world that breaks with the standards of blandness that even museums adventurous in their art set for thei r nonspiritual foods. 
In a separate building ac ross a driveway, the museum offers splendidly unbland Sichuan cuis ine at rock-bottom prices. 
Some might say merely that this makes it possible to spend morning and afternoon at the museum without r eturning to town for lunch. 
Others, to whom the pleasures of the p alate are as important as the pleasures of the eye, might find that the museum restaurant, ahomely place with waitresses who have learned patience with nonspeakers of Chinese, is worth a trip by itself. 
A good meal can beput together for $2 or $3 a head, and a feast for not much more than that. 
The restaurant is crowded at noontime, so get there a few minutes earlier. 
Like the museum, it closes at 5 P.M.
RESTAURANTS - For many, the museum might by itself be reason enough to visit Taipei. 
For many more, the restaurants, even those without museums, are at least as important. 
All the cuisines of the Chinesespeaking world - the fare of Peking, Shanghai, Canton, Sichuan, Hunan, Shanxi and the hearty indigenous dishes of Taiwan itself - are amply available in this city of 2.2 million. 
Whatever you have learned to appreciate or would like to open your palate to, there are representative restaurants in all categories and price ranges. 
Except for what passes for western food and for the food served in the restaurants of major hotels, it is impossible to have a really bad meal - and the chances of finding a good one just by walking in off the street are higher here than anywhere else in the world.
The only problems are those of an embarrassment of riches - and, once again, language. 
Many menus are offered in Chinese only, but pointing at dishes on other tables is perfectly permissible, waiters sometimes have a bit of menu English and other diners tend to be helpful to those in linguistic distress. 
Here are a few good restaurants, but there are many others just as good. 
About $5 a person will fetch a good meal in any.
For Taiwanese food, strong in creatures of the sea, try Taiwan Shiau Diau, 71 Chuangshan North Road (561-0879). 
Specialties are roast fish with scallions and stir-fried oysters with fermented beans.
Shanghai specialties are featured at Fu Shin Yuan, 105 Chung Ching South Road (311-0751). 
Ask for shrimp with sticky-rice cakes, stirfried eel and smoked fish.
Hunanese food is the strong suit of Charming Garden Restaurant, 16 Nanking East Road, Section 1 (521-4131). 
The specialties are smoked ham, pigeon dumpling soup and a dessert, date dumplings.
Sichuanese food is good at Rong Shing, 45 Chulin Road (521-5341).Specialties include spicy bean curd, stewed carp with hot bean paste and pork with chopped garlic.
For a Cantonese meal, try An Lo Yuan, 232 Tunghwa Street (772-5929), and order pork ribs with tomato sauce, fried kale in oyster sauce and sweet and sour pork.
OTHER THINGS TO DO - A stroll through Snake Alley (ask the hotel clerk to instruct a taxi driver) any night will make the traveler from the West feel that he has really come a long way from home. 
A narrow and teeming street near the popular Lungshan, or Dragon Mountain, temple in the heart of the city's original center, Snake Alley has come by its name honestly. 
Many restaurants feature snake, to the eating of which people of southern China attach almost mystical properties. 
It is said to be good not only for what ails you but also for anything that might ail you much later in life. 
You may not wish to partake, but to watch the snake pitchmen in front of their shops display their charges and vaunt their qualities makes you aware that, despite leveling influences at work throughout the world, there remain great differences between its peoples. 
Other restaurants offer more conventional fare - do not worry about the monkeys in some of them. 
They are pets, not for eating.
Chinese opera flourishes in Taipei and has not suffered from the buffeting that the Cultural Revolution gave it on the mainland, when some of the greatest traditional practitioners were purged. 
The 600-year-old art form, whose conventions are highly stylized, is worth experiencing because it can hardly be explained. 
Costumes and makeup are extremely ornate, even exaggerated, to denote clearly the character who wears them. 
About 400 works are in the Taipei Opera's repertory; unless the visitor wants to make a serious study of the art form, he should perhaps not try to understand the plot but simply let the rich and exotic spectacle pour into his eyes and ears. 
Performances last for hours (and occasionally days); the audience wanders in and out at will, chatting and gossiping and eating box lunches. 
Again, hotel clerks can guide you to what is available. 
Tickets cost from about $1.50 to about $5.
The memorial to the late president Chiang Kai-shek, somewhat grandiose and bombastic in conception, is too big not to be a tourist site. 
A huge archway gives access to the memorial hall in classical Chinese style, size extra large.
SHOPPING - Taipei is a good place to buy coral and beads of semiprecious stones, Chinese knickknacks, bric-a-brac and bibelots. 
Antiques are rare, fakes plentiful. 
Textiles and shoes are inexpensive; suits can be quickly tailored for about $150 and u p. 
Electronic gadgets, such as games or lighters or ballpoint pens with built-in digital clocks, are plentiful and ch eap.
A nice and typical souvenir is a traditional name stamp, which took the place of a signature in days of illiteracy. 
These are made of soapstone or such more expensive materials as ivory or jade. 
For about $10, cr aftsmen in many shops will carve a Chinese approximationof your name into a carving of the Chinese zodiac sign of your birth.
ACCOMMODATIONS - Taipei has 22 hotels that meet the standards the official tourist organization has designated for ''international tourist hotels.''
Prices range from about $35 to $75 for a double room at any.
The Grand Hotel, on a hillock a little out of the center of town at 1 Chungshan North Road, is the ultimate in chinoiserie, a late Ming palace in a striking shade of red magnified to Disneyland dimensions, with an olympic-sized pool and other sports facilities. 
Its rooms are spacious, the housekeeping and service excellent. 
Avoid the restaurants except for the basement tearoom, which serves good noodles and dumplings. 
A double room costs between $36 and $65. 
Others in the same category are the Hilton, at 38 Chunghsiao West Road; Lai Lai Shangri-La, at 12 Chunghsiao East Road; President, at 9 Teh-hwei Street; and Miramar, at 3 Nanking East Road.
CLIMATE - Taiwan has a subtropical climate. 
Most of the year is summer, with daytime temperatures from May to September well above 90 degrees. 
May and June are rainy, but Taiwan is humid year-round. 
The cool season, when jackets or even topcoats come in handy, arrives in December and lasts through February.
EXCURSIONS - To get away from Taipei's humid heat and see some of the spectacular mountain scenery of central Taiwan, a number of plane, bus and rail tours are available. 
One of the most popular places within reach of two or three-day tours is Sun Moon Lake, which offers an exceptional view of 13,114-foot Mount Yushan and the Sea of Clouds that rings it. 
A drive through rugged mountains along the scenic East-West Cross-Island Highway, 120 miles long and ending at the eastern end in Taroko Gorge, is also rewarding. 
Three-day tours cost about $200, without meals.
Those who cannot resist the lure of tropical islands will be tempted by such romantically named offshore spots as the Pescadores or Orchid Island. 
The names are more attractive than the places, which offer nothing of sufficient interest to make up for the absence of good hotel and restaurant facilities.
INFORMATION - The Taiwan Visitors Association, 1 World Trade Center, Suite 86155, New York 10048 (466-0691) has free brochures, maps and guides as well as slides, cassettes and films that can be borrowed without charge.

text:
ï»¿
Fresh flowers and firecrackers will brighten February in Vancouver, British Columbia, when the city's Chinese community throws a party. 
The event is called Spring Festival, and its highlight is the celebration of the Chinese New Year, Feb. 
17, with a lion dance and costume parade through one of the largest Chinese communities in North America.
The Chinese first came to western Canada in 1858 in search of gold. 
Today there are more than 100,000 Chinese-Canadians living in or around the Pacific Coast city. 
In recent years the long-established Chinese community has been boosted by many new arrivals from Hong Kong, who are leaving in anticipation of the transfer of the British territory to China in 1997.
Spring Festival, which runs from Feb. 
6 to 28, will include a flower market and children's art show. 
The New Year celebration (call 604-687-0729 for details) marks the start of the Year of the Dragon, and the streets of Chinatown will explode with firecrackers to scare away evil spirits.
Antique light fixtures, widened sidewalks and pagoda-style telephone booths have helped in recent years to give Chinatown a special setting. 
The Chinese have done the rest. 
Vegetable stores spill out onto the sidewalk laden with bok choy (cabbage) and dung gwa (winter melon). 
Herb shops are crammed with jars of unidentifiable substances alleged to cure any ailment under the sun. 
And the vivid reds and yellows of store canopies alongside flashing neon signs make a kaleidoscope on the darkest winter day. 
But that bustling street scene is not the heart of the district. 
That label has now been placed, with great pride, on a garden of serene beauty that opened last year on the edge of Chinatown.
The Sun Yat-sen Garden, behind high white walls, is the first, full-size classical Chinese garden to be built outside China. 
Named for the revolutionary who led the overthrow of the imperial system in 1911 and who helped to establish the Chinese Republic, the garden was built with donations from individuals, corporations and governments. 
Construction was done by 52 workmen from Suzhou who used traditional methods and tools. 
Even in the rain, it's a lovely place. 
A waterfall splashes, wind rustles the bamboo, and its tranquility defies the traffic outside the walls. 
The garden unfolds like a landscape painting scroll of rockeries, evergreens, pebblestone paving and pools of jade green water teeming with goldfish.
The garden (578 Carrall Street; 604-689-7133) is open daily from 10 A.M. to 4:30 P.M. during the winter. 
Admission is $2.25, $1.50 for older people, students and children. 
And there's a gift shop where you can buy anything from a silk rug for $1,500 to a bar of sandalwood soap for 45 cents. 
(Prices throughout are given in United States dollars.) Also unique to Chinatown is what is claimed to be the narrowest commercial building in the world. 
Only six feet wide, the Sam Kee building, 8 West Pender Street, was recently fronted by a 100-foot-long lighted sidewalk of glass blocks; it has become a magnet for tourist cameras.
Â 
THE MOUNTAINS
The glory of the city of 1.2 million is its setting: the 4,000-foot peaks of the Coast Mountains drop steeply to a natural harbor. 
Ten sandy beaches are within easy reach - some by foot, others by bus or car - of the city center, and they are a playground for sailors and windsurfers almost year round.
The city's mild, wet winter has an average low temperature of around 35 degrees in January, but skiers should not abandon hope. 
The mountains that tower over the city, Grouse and Seymour, provide good skiing only a 20-minute drive from downtown. 
At Grouse (604-986-6262 for snow report) a daily lift ticket is about $17, at Seymour (604-986-3444 for snow report) about $12.
And 80 miles north is a two-mountain ski resort rapidly making an international name. 
Whistler and Blackcomb mountains (604-932-4191 for snow alongside an Alpine-style village, offer 10,000 vertical feet of skiing on 180 marked runs with 26 lifts. 
A day pass on either peak costs $24 and, with luck, skiing lasts well into spring. 
For accommodations, contact Central Reservations Service, Whistler, British Columbia V0N 1B0 (604-932-4222).
Blackcomb invested $25 million in new facilities this year, including three express lifts that whisk skiers to the mountaintop in 14 minutes rather than 45 on the old lifts. 
A transfer to the Seventh Heaven Express then takes a mere six minutes to reach powder country.
With 22 hotels and condominiums in the village and more under construction, the resort is turning into a year-round destination with a golf course, tennis courts, hiking trails, fishing and windsurfing.
Â 
CITY SIGHTS
In Vancouver the first-time visitor might head to Stanley Park, a five-minute cab ride a mile west of the downtown area. 
The park, a 1,000-acre-peninsula, combines near-wilderness forest, beaches, formal rose gardens, a waterlily lake and an excellent aquarium. 
The park is circled by an eight-mile seawall walk and one can rent a bike ($3.50 to $4.50 an hour) at the park entrance.
Granville Island, also a peninsula, is beside the inner city lagoon of False Creek. 
The island is a mixture of art and industry with a waterfront food market, theaters, restaurants and boats. 
For a good, inexpensive lunch one can buy a bagel with smoked salmon and cheese, and sit in the sun watching the jugglers and waving at the passing yachts.
Â 
NIGHT LIFE
At night, Vancouver's affluent young people converge at Pelican Bay, a waterfront club inside the Granville Island Hotel (604-683-7373). 
This is where California North - as Vancouver likes to think of itself -dances the night away (the night begins around 9:30; a cover charge of about $2 is charged weekends.) And long a night life favorite is Richard's on Richards (1036 Richards Street; 604-687-6794). 
There nearly always seems to be a well-turned-out lineup on the sidewalk waiting to get in to Richard's, where guests' cars are handed over to tuxedoed valets. 
(Cover charges vary under $5, depending on the night of the week.)
Â 
EVENTS
Five buildings stuffed with 341 cars from the world's leading manufacturers will make up the Pacific International Automobile Show Jan. 
15 to 24 at Exhibition Park in the east end of the city. 
For those who prefer floating to driving, there's the Vancouver International Boat Show from Feb. 
3 to 7 at the B. C. Place Stadium (604-669-2300). 
Everything from a rowboat to a 50-foot yacht will be on view.
The Vancouver Opera Association (604-682-2871) will present three operas in English at the Queen Elizabeth Theater (Hamilton and Georgia). 
Leos Janacek's ''Cunning Little Vixen'' will be performed Jan. 
30, Feb. 
2, 4 and 6; Benjamin Britten's ''Turn of the Screw'' March 12, 15, 17 and 19, and Johann Strauss's ''Fledermaus'' April 30, May 3, 5 and 7. 
Tickets range from $13 to $39.
The Vancouver Symphony (604-684-9100) will be conducted for the first time by a woman, French-born Catherine Comet, now music director of the Grand Rapids Symphony, March 13, 14 and 15 at the Orpheum (601 Smithe Street). 
On the program: Beethoven's Piano Concerto No. 1 in C Major, Debussy's ''Afternoon of a Faun'' and Hindemith's ''Mathis der Maler'' The Hungarian pianist Annie Fischer will be soloist. 
Tickets range from $6 to $19.
Â 
HOTELS
With Expo 86's millions of visitors now a memory, Vancouver's hotels have been suffering. 
But the tourist wins because competition is fierce, making for moderate prices and excellent service.
In the luxury class, the venerable Hotel Vancouver (900 West Georgia Street; 604-684-3131 or 800-268-9143) will always be a survivor. 
Its green copper roof is a city landmark and its central location is great. 
Recently an indoor pool was added to give the elegant, old hotel all the essentials of contemporary life. 
Doubles range from about $50 to $90.
More moderately priced but lacking in nothing is O'Doul's Hotel (1300 Robson Street; 604-684-8461 or 800-663-5491). 
Set on a street of boutiques and specialty stores, O'Doul's is only a short walk from Stanley Park. 
Rooms include writing desks and three telephones. 
Doubles are about $60 to $85.
There are studio suites with queen-size beds and kitchenettes in the Pagebrook Hotel (1234 Hornby Street; 604-688-1234 or 800-663-1234). 
Suite rates go up from about $60 a night; children under 16 are free.
A 12-minute ride across the harbor by SeaBus ferry is the Lonsdale Quay Hotel (123 Carrie Cates Court, North Vancouver; 604-986-6111). 
The small waterfront hotel has gorgeous views; double rooms are about $70 to $95.
Visitors on a budget will get good value at the Greenbrier Apartment Hotel (1393 Robson Street; 604-683-4558), which lacks decor but has a location as good as O'Doul's. 
Doubles start at $30.
For tourist information and more accommodation possibilities, including bed and breakfast's, contact the Travel InfoCenter (562 Burrard Street; 604-683-2000).
Â 
RESTAURANTS
A fine new restaurant called the Prow may now have the best view in the city. 
The restaurant is in the northern end of Canada Place, a striking building topped with white sails that juts into the harbor like a sailing ship. 
It was Canada's pavilion at Expo; now it houses a trade and convention center. 
At the Prow (604-684-1339) dinner for two with wine costs about $50. 
The menu is likely to include mussel cream soup with Pernod and grilled swordfish in pink peppercorn and orange sauce.
Not quite so pricey and very lively is Joe Fortes (777 Thurlow Street; 604-669-1940). 
Situated in a neighborhood of boutiques, Joe Fortes is named for a long-dead local character and is known for its oyster bar and live piano music. 
Dinner and wine for two costs about $45; among recent menu choices have been roast boneless duck with pear sauce and a cheesecake made with sour cream.
Well within budget range is the fine Japanese food at Kibune Restaurant (1508 Yew; 604-734-5216). 
The tiny place, which is decorated with lots of wood, has miso-shiru soup for 75 cents, and a house specialty called yosenabe that contains everything from seafood and tofu to chicken and bamboo shoots ($5.25).
The range of Chinese food is wide. 
Downtown there's the elegant black and white decor at the Beijing (865 Hornby Street; 604-688-7788), where a meal for two with wine costs $45 to $65; among the dishes might be a soup of bird's nest and crabmeat ($19) or spicy Szechuan chicken hot pot ($7).
For bargain hunters in the midst of Chinatown, there is Hon's Wun-Tun House (524 Main Street; 604-688-7018). 
An order of the quick-fried steamed dumplings, which come in a tangy sauce, costs only a bit more than $2. 
There's no liquor license but for $8 two people can eat their fill.

text:

China will no longer classify as secret the new national laws that local citizens and foreigners are obliged to obey, according to China's official newspapers.
New laws will henceforth be printed and publicly distributed, the newspapers reported Friday, emphasizing the advantages of such a system.
''The publication of regulations signed by China's Prime Minister will help the people to learn exactly what they are being asked to adjust themselves to,'' the official New China News Agency reported. 
In fact, almost all regulations already have been publicly released, but there have been some uncertainties even within the Chinese Government about whether some laws exist.
Last year, for example, China's Ministry of Public Health announced that it was a crime to engage in casual sex, while the Ministry of Justice said there was no such law.
Whatever the legal niceties, about a dozen foreigners were detained by the police last year after being found in what the police regarded as suspicious circumstances with Chinese nationals of the opposite sex in their hotel rooms. 
One West German was fined the equivalent of $2,700 and other foreigners were fined lesser amounts.
Â 
Glasnost a la Beijing
The announcement that laws would be publicly distributed apparently is part of China's current effort to increase toumingdu, the Chinese equivalent of the Russian glasnost, or increased openness. 
As part of toumingdu, often translated as transparency, China has increasingly been releasing timely information about natural disasters and cases of official corruption, as well as about its economic problems.
There remain well-defined limits to the new openness, however.
The State Council, the top-level Government body whose regulations are the subject of the latest decision, could not be reached to clarify the announcement that its regulations no longer would be confidential. 
The telephone numbers of the relevant departments in the State Council are unlisted.
While the Government has also begun to release snippets of biographical information about officials, much is still regarded as confidential - including birthdates. 
For example, the Communist Party General Secretary, Zhao Ziyang, is usually said to be 69 years old, but it is only known for certain that he was born in 1919. 
If his birthdate happens to be Dec. 
31, his age as reported is incorrect every day of the year but one.
The Government has also said that Mr. Zhao's wife is named Liang Boqi -it had not even been known if she was still alive - but almost nothing else is known about her.
Â 
Foreigners Welcome Decision
Foreigners engaged in business with China today welcomed the decision to circulate the State Council's regulations.
''If it means they're going to discontinue the practice of having internal regulations, and that all regulations and notices are going to be made public, then of course I would welcome it,'' said John Frisbie, director of China operations for the U.S.-China Business Council. 
''Anything that increases transparency in China's laws and regulations is bound to increase the confidence of foreigners and businessmen.''
The New China News Agency, in reporting the decision, said that the New China publishing house would regularly publish collections of Government regulations, ''including those that may not appear in newspapers and periodicals.''
The agency also said that previously all the regulations approved by the State Council were issued ''in documents with red characters designating them as restricted.''
Since in fact almost all were released, it is not clear in what way they were restricted.
Roderick W. Macneil, a lawyer based in Hong Kong who operates a consulting business on the China trade, noted that State Council regulations normally already were published in the official State Council gazette. 
The latest decision may simply have been an attempt to collect and publish the laws systematically, he said.

text:
