So officials in Yutian County were all ears when Mr. Liu sketched a deal under which the sets could be imported and resold for a profit of 30 million yuan, about $10.7 million.
As it turned out the whole thing was a fraud. 
After Mr. Liu had taken 12.6 million yuan in advance payments for the nonexistent sets, and placed two million yuan in his own bank account, he was arrested in a luxury hotel across the border from Hong Kong. 
With his fellow swindlers, he is awaiting trial on charges that carry a maximum sentence of death.
Article on 'epidemic' of official corruption that has developed in China in aftermath of market-oriented economic policy changes instituted by Deng Xiaoping; as people seek more consumer goods, some officials in charge of trade and pricing have sought to enrich themselves through scams; photo (M)
When the official New China News Agency carried an account of the fraud last month, it offered it as an example of the ''epidemic'' of official corruption that has developed in the aftermath of market-oriented economic policy changes. 
While the Government is trying to unshackle the country's productive forces from the bureaucracy's deadening hand, officials at every level have taken the new freedoms as an opportunity to enrich themselves.
Â 
Powers Widely Abused
The new leeway for importing foreign goods has been widely abused. 
So too have the freedoms Peking has given for the establishment of new companies, some of which have proved to be ''shell'' concerns created solely as a means of making profits as state- owned goods move along the economic chain. 
The power to raise prices has been widely exploited for private gain.
Officials have created jobs for relatives and friends, taken kickbacks in return for unearned wage increases and promotions, inflated expense accounts and taken bribes. 
The practices have spread to the army, once held up as a model of proletarian rectitude, which disclosed two weeks ago that officers in the Fuzhou Military Region, in the southeast, had turned a profit of more than $1.3 million with a variety of commercial scams.
For Deng Xiaoping, the country's 80- year-old leader, the corruption is of serious concern. 
If instead of inspiring the kind of entrepreneurship that creates wealth his policies serve only to fatten the lives of the official class, he will be handing a ready-made issue to opponents who see the policies as a betrayal of Marxist ideology.
The trouble is that it is the country's nine million cadres, or officials, who are in charge of putting the new system into effect. 
As centralized controls are relaxed a host of loopholes have been exploited, with results that are insistently denounced at high-level party meetings and in editorials in the party press.
Â 
'An Unhealthy Mood'
''At present, there is an unhealthy mood,'' the principal party paper, People's Daily, said in a commentator's article three weeks ago.
It added: ''Certain comrades turn a deaf ear to regulations such as the ban on the indiscriminate payment of bonuses and goods in kind and the prohibition on indiscriminate price increases, even though these have been reiterated again and again. 
They do just as they like.''
Mr. Deng's primary weapon so far has been a powerful party body called the Central Discipline Inspection Commission, aided by agents of the Ministry of Public Security, the Chinese equivalent of the K.G.B.
The Chinese leader has delegated one of his closest political confidants, 77-year-old Bo Yibo, to oversee the process of ''party rectification,'' which includes vetting political loyalties as well as seeking out embezzlers and profiteers.
At a gathering of party officials from across the country last month, Mr. Bo said that ''using one's position and powers to make a fortune from reform'' had become widespread, infecting not only factories, mines and other local institutions but officials all the way up to national ministries.
Since allowing such practices to go unchecked would threaten the basis for the economic changes, he said, it was essential ''they should not be tolerated.''
Â 
Cars Sold for Profit
One precaution ordered by Mr. Deng is a ban on party or government officials engaging in business. 
This is designed to stop the sort of abuse that developed among senior officials on Hainan Island, in the south, who were said by People's Daily to have imported dozens of duty-free cars, ostensibly for use in economic development, then sold them for a large profit to buyers on the mainland.
A circular put out by the inspection commission last month gave other examples of senior officials who had set up companies to trade in state-owned commodities in short supply, dividing the profits among themselves. 
The document cited the party committee in the steel city of Anshan, which was said to have set up an economic and technical cooperative company that bought 10,000 tons of low-priced steel from the city's huge steelworks, then resold it for a profit of $157,000.
In the central China city of Sanmenxia the culprits were officials of the city's ''propaganda and journalism departments,'' according to a People's Daily account.
The paper said that for more than two years, the officials had conspired with contacts from the Portuguese colony of Macao to smuggle cameras and other photographic equipment into the country for resale on the black market, making illegal profits of $150,000.
The army scandal in Fuzhou, also disclosed by People's Daily, involved 19 dummy trading companies that traded in army property and otherwise used the army's name to profiteer. 
The paper said that the party committee of the Fuzhou Military Region had cracked down last month, winding up the illegal companies, confiscating the $1.3 million in profit that had already been made and canceling 14 contracts worth $2.9 million more.
Many of the published accounts stopped short of detailing the punishments meted out to those responsible. 
But something of the scale of the trickery was suggested by a December report in the English-language newspaper China Daily, which said that 279 party officials in Tianjin, east of Peking, had been subjected to ''disciplinary measures'' and that 85 had been stripped of their party memberships in the preceding 13 months for ''crimes ranging from corruption to embezzlement.''

text:
ï»¿
When Thubten Samphel visited a Tibetan monastery near Clifton, N.J., he was surprised to find one of the monks waiting at the bus station in a car to drive him there.
''As the foreigners are fond of saying, the only wheel in Tibet is the prayer wheel,'' said Mr. Samphel, one of four native Tibetans studying in the United States under a new Congressional scholarship program.
Monks with driver's licenses and monasteries with hot and cold running water are the least of the cultural differences that Mr. Samphel, whose parents were servants 30 years ago of the Dalai Lama, the exiled leader of Tibet, has encountered in the last two months.
Recently, Mr. Samphel, who is studying at the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism, watched a game of touch football in Sakura Park in Morningside Heights and spoke of such differences.
'Getting Your Facts Straight'
''Tibetan culture and American society are so totally different,'' said Mr. Samphel, 32 years old, who followed the Dalai Lama to India after a Tibetan uprising against the Chinese was put down in 1959. 
In India, he attended Western-style schools and learned English.
''Tibetans are considered very spiritual,'' he said. 
''Here everything is material. 
Everyone seems to be working all the time.''
An experienced writer and editor in India - from 1980 until last August he edited the official English organ of the Dalai Lama's Government-in-exile in Dharmsala, India - he nonetheless is now getting his first formal training in journalism.
''The most important thing is getting your facts straight,'' said Mr. Samphel, who for class was recently assigned to cover the Larry Davis trial in the Bronx. 
''In India it's more laid back toward getting the story; you use the first word that comes to your mind. 
In China and Tibet, the Government is the newspaper. 
What the Government decides to inform the public becomes the daily news.''
Â 
Making Adjustments
One of Mr. Samphel's professors, Stephen D. Isaacs, said that Mr. Samphel had asked not to be treated differently from other students because of his language problems or cultural differences.
''You take anyone from out of town, much less out of this world, and send them to the Larry Davis trial - it's going to be difficult,'' Professor Isaacs said. 
Perhaps the most challenging assignment of all has been learning aggressive street reporting.
''We tend to be very polite,'' Mr. Samphel said. 
''Here you have to leave this pretense and get what you want.''
For now he hopes to work for an American newspaper after he graduates, but he can see himself ultimately returning to his old job in India. 
He even holds hope for an independent Tibet someday.
''We Tibetans have not too many choices,'' he said. 
''Emotionally we would like Tibet to be independent, free. 
But you run into these practical problems: How do you proceed to do that without an army, without anything, without the support of one single government?''
''Whether we like it or not, we have to adjust to the modern world,'' he said. 
''We must be absolutely realistic.''
Such feelings are common among young Tibetans, said Tenzin Chhodak, the director of the Office of Tibet, a New York branch of the Dalai Lama's government and a friend of Mr. Samphel for more than a decade. 
Mr. Chhodak, who administers the scholarship program for Congress, hopes to bring 11 more young Tibetans to the United States by next year.
Although Mr. Samphel received both his bachelor's and master's degrees in modern Chinese history, and his one visit to Tibet in almost 30 years was as part of a tour sponsored by the Chinese Government in 1985, like most Tibetans he retains deep hostility toward China.
''My next-door neighbor is from Beijing,'' Mr. Samphel said. 
''We have been very polite to each other.''

The departure of Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. surprised most of the American foreign policy establishment, dismaying those who saw him as a force for moderation in the Administration and pleasing those who regarded him as too moderate.
Some suggested that the resignation would be felt most keenly in Europe, where Mr. Haig had special ties dating from his days as commander of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization's military forces, and in China.
At the same time, specialists throughout the political spectrum praised Mr. Haig's successor, George P. Shultz, but raised questions about his business connections in the Middle East.
''I'm stunned,'' said Richard C. Holbrooke, former Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs in the Carter Administration, who expressed regret at the resignation, which he suggested would pose special problems for the nation's relations with China.
The departure of Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. surprised most of the American foreign policy establishment, dismaying those who saw him as a force for moderation in the Administration and pleasing those who regarded him as too moderate.'Appalling Piece of News'
''For the Europeans,'' said Fritz Stern, a professor of history at Columbia University and a member of the editorial advisory board of Foreign Affairs magazine, ''this will be an appalling piece of news.''
Mr. Haig, he said, ''was the person in the Administration the Europeans regarded as the most understanding, the most responsible and the one who understood them best.''
''At a time of considerable disarray in European-American relations,'' he said, ''this will be a considerable blow.''
''This is out of the blue,'' said Winston Lord, president of the Council on Foreign Relations, who described himself as ''very sad'' at the news.
''He was a very able man who was doing a good job - but I'm high on George Shultz,'' said Mr. Lord, who expressed surprise that Mr. Haig had resigned at a time he seemed to be at the point of ''prevailing'' over his chief political rival, Caspar W. Weinberger, Secretary of Defense.
Â 
Friction With Other Officials
Mr. Haig's troubled relations with a series of Administration figures were cited by Mr. Holbrooke, who praised Mr. Haig. ''All his life,'' he said, ''he had been the hardest-line man in Government, in bureacratic disputes. 
In this Administration, without changing his position he became a moderate in an Adminisration more hard-line than he had anticipated.''
Mr. Holbrooke, who is now with Lehman Brothers, the investment banking firm, said that the resignation would pose special problems for the nation's relations with China.
''China,'' he said, ''regarded him as the one person in the Administration who understood both the strategic and bilateral implications of Sino-American relations.''
Â 
'Fought the Heroic Fight'
''I believe,'' he added, ''that Al Haig fought the heroic fight to prevent the complete collapse of Sino-American relations,'' a reference to Mr. Haig's role in turning aside a drive within the Administation last year to strengthen American ties with the Nationalist Chinese Government on Taiwan.
''Absent Haig,'' he said, ''there would have been a major, frontpage crisis last year.''
Viewing the resignation from opposing perspectives, Bertram Gold, the president of the American Jewish Committee, called Mr. Haig ''a good Secretary of State,'' who had been ''supportive'' of Israel, while M..T. 
Mehdi, president of the Arab-American Relations Committee, called his resignation ''healthy.''
Mr. Haig, he said, was a ''militant militarist,'' who had been ''annoying and alienating.''
He said that partly because of his extensive business dealings with Arab nations, Mr. Shutlz promised to have a ''better understanding'' of the third world.
Â 
No Comment by Vance
There was no immediate comment from Cyrus R. Vance, who resigned as Secretary of State in a dispute over the decision to attempt to rescue American hostages from Iran during the Carter Administration, although he did not announce the move until the immediate crisis was over.
Henry A. Kissinger, who served as Secretary of State during the Nixon years, issued this statement: ''The nation owes an enormous debt to Alexander Haig for an extraordinary career of public service. 
He has served the nation well. 
George Shultz is one of the outstanding public men and finest human beings I have known. 
I know he will be a great Secretary of State in pursuit of President Reagan's goals of peace and justice.''
In Atlanta, where he is recovering from a hernia operation, Dean Rusk, who served as Secretary of State in the Administration of Lyndon B. Johnson, declined comment pending the ''unfolding'' of the full reasons behind the resignation,

file: _WHITE RAJAHS_ LINGER IN A MALAYSIAN TOWN.txt
text:
ï»¿
This is the town the White Rajahs built, and it revels in the distinction of having been the heart of one of the most eccentric ventures in the history of European colonialism.
From the polished brass cannon at the small fort on the hill to the stuffed animals in the museum near the Anglican Cathedral, there are reminders of the family that once ruled this territory on the northwest coast of Borneo with a mixture of pluck, paternalism and absolute authority.
Though Sarawak has been part of Malaysia for a quarter of a century, the people of Kuching are proud of their special geography and history. 
''It is hard to express to the rest of the world how we feel about Sarawak,'' Caroline Goh-Cheong, a publisher, said. 
''We have a special place.''
From 1841 to 1946, three men -James, Charles and Vyner Brooke -more or less owned Sarawak, a gift to James from a Brunei sultan grateful for help in quelling a local rebellion.
Â 
A Colonial Oddity
The Brookes were British, but England wanted nothing to do with this troublesome territory, populated by headhunters and perenially short of income. 
So the Brookes were free to rule as potentates, with the help of Malay aristocrats and tribal warriors.
Until 1946, when the territory was turned over to the Crown, there was no British colonial service here, only a few hardy freelance Europeans.
Resentful of Western intrusion, Chinese gold miners and traders from the interior attacked Kuching in 1857, burning the newly created symbols of authority and killing members of the first Rajah's entourage.
His nephew Charles (later the second Rajah) replied by unleashing his upcountry Iban tribesmen on the Chinese. 
The Ibans, headhunters, quickly sent the Chinese back to the hills.
Â 
Architectural Treasures
When James Brooke saw Kuching for the first time in 1839, the small village was the nearest permanent settlement to the muddy Sarawak River delta, where as early as the 11th century a ramshackle bartering center had been established. 
To the delta in their wooden boats came people from the interior and coastal settlements to trade their turtle eggs, feathers, camphor and hornbill ivory for manufactured goods from China and India - ceramics, textiles and metal objects.
Kuching grew rapidly under the Brookes. 
A classic, cloistered courthouse was built in 1874. 
A fort followed in 1879. 
In 1891 a museum opened. 
There were other homes and public buildings of distinction, among them several noteworthy Chinese temples.
Kuching has kept much of its character intact. 
Small wooden sampans are still ''taxis'' to the 300,000 residents, ferrying them along and across the river from dozens of landings. 
The fare is about 5 cents.
Â 
The 20th Century Encroaches
Lucas Chin, curator of the Sarawak Museum - housing one of Southeast Asia's most remarkable ethnic collections - told a visitor how committed Kuching was to saving and embellishing its architectural heritage.
''This whole part of Kuching has been preserved as a cultural center,'' he said, gesturing to take in the hill where his museum stands and the old downtown area, its open, grassy square leading to the waterfront markets.
But high-rise buildings are in evidence, primarily on the less-populated western bank of the river, and Kuching has begun to experience some of the problems common to urban life elsewhere.
Squatter settlements are mushrooming on the city's edges, the product of what the state's Chief Minister, Abdul Taib Mahmud, calls the ''one-way drift'' from Sarawak's interior with its mammoth rivers and uncharted jungles.
''We have been very secluded here,'' said Miss Goh-Cheong, the publisher. 
''We have not really been in touch with the world. 
TV came here only six years ago.''

file: _YOU START THE DAY FEELING GOOD_.txt
text:
ï»¿
THERE'S a little slice of China in Chester. 
Free public lessons in tai chi, the ancient Chinese system of exercises, are being offered by the National Theater of the Deaf, which is based in the Connecticut River Valley town.
Three mornings each week, 70 to 100 people assemble on the green by the 1793 Chester Meetinghouse to learn the traditional routines aimed at promoting harmony of mind and body.
The theater, made up of deaf and hearing actors, is known for its performances that combine sign language with the spoken word. 
Over the years, several members have practiced tai chi, according to David Hays, founder and artistic director of the company. 
But actors in the troupe became particularly interested in the exercises last year when they toured China with two plays.
One actor, wandering through the streets of Beijing, met an 80-year-old man who knew some English and taught tai chi. 
Soon the actor rounded up others from the theater to attend his new acquaintance's classes.
Mr. Hays had tried tai chi before and knew his level of ability. 
''I'm enormously unskillful at it,'' he said. 
Nonetheless, he joined the Beijing classes and attends those in Chester when his schedule permits.
Shanny Mow, a deaf actor with the troupe, attended the classes in Beijing and now leads those in Chester. 
He said he began practicing tai chi several years ago after receiving several bloody noses while learning karate.
''I decided there had to be something more gentle,'' Mr. Mow said through a sign language interpreter. 
Tai chi, he said, ''tones your nerves.''
''If you do it first thing every morning, you start the day feeling good,'' he added.
When members of the theater decided to make tai chi routines part of their summer schedule, they sought a spot large enough to accommodate actors, staff members, students from the National Theater of the Deaf's summer school for deaf theater personnel, and any friends, neighbors or others who might be interested. 
They settled on the tree-shaded green.
Tai chi on the green is not the same as tai chi in Beijing. 
For one thing, the Beijing exercises took place at 5 A.M., while the sessions on the green are conducted at the more acceptable 7:30 A.M. For another, many Chinese brought their pet birds in cages to the Beijing exercises, and although the theater has invited its tai chi students to bring birds, nobody has yet done so.
''But I'm still hopeful,'' said Germaine Schumacher, a copy editor and proofreader from Middletown who attends the classes and thinks birds would be a fine addition.
The lack of birds has apparently not discouraged attendance.Mrs. 
Schumacher and dozens of others have shown up faithfully for the lessons, undaunted even on a recent morning when rain had fallen most of the night, the skies were gray and the green was so wet that the class had to be conducted in the adjoining gravel parking lot.
That day, as usual, the participants carefully followed Mr. Mow, stretching their arms, raising their legs and bending their bodies in the slow, balanced, flowing movements of tai chi.
Only occasionally did Mr. Mow issue instructions through the interpreter.
''Please remember to keep your back straight; don't lean over,'' he reminded his followers at one point. 
Then he added, ''But don't worry if you don't get it right.''
The followers - encompassing teen-agers to the elderly - looked intent, but not worried. 
Some, like Rosemary Bleyer, a clinical psychologist from Middletown, were attending on their way to work.
A few, like Ruth Thayer, a retired newspaper photographer from Old Saybrook, were trying the routines for the first time. 
''They seem to exercise every muscle,'' Mrs. Thayer said.
Among those going through the paces set by Mr. Mow were five students from China who are attending the theater's summer school. 
These students were hardly more familiar with the tai chi routines than the other participants, noted Andrew Vasnick, director of the summer school.
In China, Mr. Vasnick explained, most of the practitioners of tai chi are older people. 
The theater invited foreign students to its summer school as part of its effort to encourage the formation of theaters of the deaf in other countries, he added.
Mr. Mow's students seemed to agree with him that tai chi was a good way to start the day. 
''I'm a terrible person in the morning,'' said Cathleen Riddley, a hearing actor with the theater. 
''I need a slow, pleasant way to get the body moving.''
''The exercises are so beautiful and graceful, and there's no strain on the body,'' said Mrs. Schumacher.
Robert Scheifer, a theater summer school student who lives in Chicago, said, ''I feel balanced; it helps my mind.''
Mr. Mow said that he had taught his students about a dozen moves. 
He uses a tai chi textbook in which photographs of the moves have titles like ''Moving Hands Softly Like Clouds'' and ''Stork Beginning to Spread Wings,'' but he said it was not important to memorize such romantic names.
What is important, he said, is to learn the movements well enough to ''concentrate on what you're doing, not on what you should be doing.''
''It's gratifying to see so many people want to learn,'' he added.
The classes will continue on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday mornings through July 11. 
Soon after that the actors are to begin rehearsals for their 1987-88 production, ''The Dybbuk'' by S. Ansky.
